How long, abusing his patience, shall we, like others, the greater part of the earth's inhabitants, which I dare to say is more than the people of Geneva, look at the judgments that are to come upon us? But if mortals, and even our own conscience, condemn us, what do we think his judgment will be like, he who sits on his high throne and is greater than our heart (1 John 3:20)? And whom we see now ready to publish his decree against us, how did he once pronounce against that barren fig tree (Luke 13:7), especially since he has urged us to repentance, with great patience, not for one or two years but for very many years, and has expected some fruit from us? When, I say, will we be ashamed of ourselves, and returning to a better mind, begin to have pity on ourselves? Finally, when shall we learn to worship sincerely him whose outstanding will and goodwill toward us has so many and such illustrious testimonies, and to venerate him before that Majesty before whom the very Angels cover their faces (Isa. 6)? May God Most Good and Great grant, brothers, that at the first opportunity we prepare ourselves for this, so that we, postponing it and giving no place to frequent admonitions, as we are wont to do, though we are sufficiently provoked also by frequent miracles wrought by God in our favour, do not at last, with the door shut, hear that answer which Matthew describes (Matt. 7:23): "I never knew you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity." But you, O Best God, according to your immense mercy, turn this evil away from us; rather grant that, led by a serious and sincere repentance, we may see and feel the bond of our sins, torn and blotted out and nailed to the cross of our Lord (Col. 2:14), and the forgiveness of our sins written and sealed by his blood, to the glory of your name and the consolation of all your people.

units.la: HOMILIA secunda.
units.tr: Second Homily

units.la: OMILIA superiore docuimus quomodo, & cur oportuerit Redemptorem nostrum fuisse & esse verum Deum & verum ho-mine, quod totius Noui Fœde-ris Euangelici subiectũ est, & nominatim hi-storiæ mortis & passionis illius: causas item quibus impulsus Dominus, hanc suis seruan-dis & glorificandis rationem elegit, excussi-mus. Tertium caput superest explicandum, quid pro nobis Christus perpessus sit, quod priusquàm attingo, necesse est hic nodum quendam expediam,quo sensu nimirum dica-mus Christum Iscum, verum Deum & homi-nem passum, quum videatur non modò sal-sum, sed etiam blasphemum & horrendum, dicere eum qui verus Deus est, æternus, incó-prehensibilis, inuisibilis, & infinitus, in vtero virginis fuisse conceptum, natum, mortuum, sepultum, à mortuis ante annos mille quin-gentos demum excitatum:Et tamen hoc prosi-temur in Symbolo: quod nisi verum esset ad-huc sub mortis imperio detineremur.Indigent
units.tr: In the previous homily we explained how and why our Redeemer had to be, and to remain, both true God and true man. This belongs to the whole of the New Gospel Covenant, and in particular to the history of his death and passion. We also examined the reasons that moved the Lord to choose this manner of saving and glorifying his own. The third head remains to be explained: what Christ suffered for us. Before I come to it, I must first untie a certain knot, namely in what sense we say that Christ, who is true God and man, suffered. It seems not only false but also blasphemous and dreadful to say that he who is true God, eternal, incomprehensible, invisible and infinite, was conceived in the womb of a virgin, was born, died, was buried, and was raised from the dead some fifteen hundred years ago. Yet we confess this in the Creed, and unless it were true we would still be held under the dominion of death. These matters therefore need a special explanation, so that, speaking with the Word of God, we may also receive the explanation from the same Word.

units.la: b. iij. igitur ista speciali quadam enodatione, vt cū verbo Dei loquentes etiam ab eodem explicationem accipiamus.
units.tr: b. iij. Therefore these matters need a special explanation, so that, speaking with the Word of God, we may also receive the explanation from the same Word.

units.la: Tenendum igitur est, Scripturam quoties Deo in Deitate sua considerato, siue Patri, siue Filio ante incarnationem, siue Sp. S. aliquid quod creaturarum est proprium tribuit, puta quum eum dicit iuisse aut venisse, vidisse, audiuisse, iratum fuisse, poenituisse, placatum esse, ascendisse aut descendisse, nō quidem Deū rebus creatis similem facere, vt somniarunt quidam haeretici: sed eum sic nobiscum balbutientem repraesentare, quo facilius ad eius notitiam nos perducat, sese ad captum nostrum sic accommodante, aut etiam visiones illas sensibiles aut intellectuales respiciente, quibus Deo visum est se alioquin invisibilem hominibus patefacere: quarum visionum plenae sunt sacrae literae.
units.tr: It must be held that whenever Scripture attributes to God, considered in his deity, whether to the Father, to the Son before the incarnation, or to the Holy Spirit, something that is proper to creatures, as when it says that he went or came, saw, heard, was angry, repented, was appeased, ascended or descended, it does not thereby make God like created things, as some heretics have dreamed. Rather, it presents him speaking to us in our own stammering way, so that he may lead us more easily to the knowledge of himself, accommodating himself to our capacity. Or it may refer to those visions, sensible or intellectual, by which God was pleased to reveal himself to men who otherwise could not see him. Sacred letters are full of such visions.

units.la: At quum de Dei Filio post eius incarnationem agitur, memoria semper repetendum est quod superius docuimus, in hac nimirum unitate personae, qua idem qui Filius Dei est, ac proinde verus Deus, etiam est Mariae Virginis Filius, ac proinde verus homo, duas naturas distinctas remanere, suaque retinere proprietates. Inde enim efficitur necessario non esse duos Christos, sed unicum, eodem existente Deo Homine qui homo Deus est: Deitate tamen minime in Humanitatem, nec vicissim Humanitate in Deitatem transeuntibus. Quibus positis & quidem verissimis, efficitur Humanimanitatis proprietates, putà conceptum esse de Spiritu S. natum de Maria Virgine, edisse, bibisse, dormiuisse, passum esse, mortuum, sepultum, à mortuis excitatum, & istiusmodi pleraque dici quidem de Deo (hac nimirum secunda Trinitatis persona) minimè tamen Deitatis eius respectu, sed quatenus Deus homo est: & vicissim, quæ Dei propria sunt, de hoc Homine dici posse, putà, Filium Dei esse, æternum, omnipotentem, vbique esse, non quidem Humanitatis ratione, sed quatenus hic homo est Homo Deus. Idcirco etiam, quü dicat Apostolus Deum gloriæ fuisse crucifixum 1. Cor. 2. 8. & D. Lucas cum qui conceptus erat in virginis vtero esse Altissimi Filiû, pie & orthodoxe Patres aduersus quartam hæresin de qua superiùs egimus decreuerunt, Virginem Mariam Dei matrem & Deiparam, posse nuncupari, nempe, quatenus Filius eius Homo Deus est, non autem Humanitatis eius seorsim extra diuinitatem consideratæ respectu. Nisi enim qui de Virgine Maria natus & conceptus est, verus Deus esset, quinam esset hominum Redemptor ac Seruator. Quòd si etiam illa respectu Deitatis eius seorsim consideratæ dicerentur qualis ista Deitas esset quæ suum esse à Virginis vtero duceret?
units.tr: But when we speak of the Son of God after his incarnation, we must always keep in mind what we taught above: that in this unity of person, by which the same one who is the Son of God, and therefore true God, is also the Son of the Virgin Mary, and therefore true man, the two natures remain distinct and retain their own properties. From this it follows necessarily that there are not two Christs but one, the same being God-man and man-God, yet with neither deity passing into humanity nor humanity into deity. Granted these premises, which are most true, it follows that the properties of the humanity, namely that he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, ate, drank, slept, suffered, died, was buried, was raised from the dead, and most such things, can indeed be said of God (that is, of this second person of the Trinity), but not with respect to his deity, only insofar as he is God-man. And conversely, what is proper to God can be said of this man, for example that he is the Son of God, eternal, almighty, present everywhere; not by reason of his humanity, but insofar as this man is man-God. Hence also, when the Apostle says that the Lord of glory was crucified (1 Cor. 2.8), and when St Luke says that he who was conceived in the Virgin's womb is the Son of the Most High, the pious and orthodox Fathers, against the fourth heresy of which we treated above, decreed that the Virgin Mary may be called the Mother of God and God-bearer. This holds insofar as her Son is man-God, not with respect to his humanity considered apart from the deity. For if he who was born and conceived of the Virgin Mary were not true God, who would be the Redeemer and Saviour of men? And if those things were said with respect to his deity considered separately, what sort of deity would that be which drew its being from the womb of a virgin?

units.la: Sic hodie falsi & erronei sunt doctores quot quot corpus & sanguinem Christi, id est, eius Humanitatem vbique esse docent, vel saltem tot locis quot panis consecratur. Verissimum enim esse fatemur & agnoscimus istum Ho- simum. minem, nempe Iesum Christũ esse Vbiq;, sed quatenus est Homo Deus: nam alioquin naturarum introduceretur confusio & mixtio. Sic vicissim quæcunque Filio Dei vnico passiones in Symbolo tribuuntur, ab eius conceptione ad Ascensum vsque, de ipso dicuntur quatenus Deus homo est, nó autē Deitatis respectu in se & seorsim consideratæ: quamobrē etiam non dicit Paulus nudè ac simpliciter Deum factum esse conspicuum, sed addit In carne sua. 1. Tim. 3. 16. Nec aliter D. Petrus de passionibus eius loquitur. 1. Pet. 4.1. Eratque istud ad salutem nostram necessarium, vt hic Homo, esset Homo Deus, vt nimirum passionibus eius diuina vis & efficacia nobis ad vitā æternā deducendis inęsset. Deniq;, Deū hominē passum esse & luctatū in sua humanitate, Hominem Deum victoriam reportasse vi suę Deitatis tenęamus, quod in hac historia pluribus sumus intelleċturi.
units.tr: So today those teachers are false and mistaken, all who teach that the body and blood of Christ, that is, his humanity, is everywhere, or at least in as many places as bread is consecrated. For we confess and acknowledge it to be most true that this man, namely Jesus Christ, is everywhere, but insofar as he is man-God. Otherwise a confusion and mixture of the natures would be introduced. Likewise, whatever sufferings are attributed in the Creed to the one Son of God, from his conception to his ascension, are said of him insofar as he is God-man, not with respect to his deity considered in itself and apart. For this reason Paul also does not say simply and absolutely that God was made manifest, but adds: In his flesh (1 Tim. 3.16). Nor does St Peter speak otherwise of his sufferings (1 Pet. 4.1). It was necessary for our salvation that this man should be man-God, so that the divine power and efficacy might be present in his sufferings, to lead us to eternal life. Finally, let us hold that God suffered and wrestled as man in his humanity, and that man as God obtained victory by the power of his deity. We shall understand this more fully in the course of this history.

units.la: Hæc porro licet mente nostra maneant infixa, vix tamen adhuc huic enodandę quęstioni sufficiant, & pacandis fulciendisque nostris conscientiis aduersus varios errores quos subinde vel ipse Satan excitat, vel intelleċtus noster sibi fingit, ad veritatem istam tenebris obscurandam, & fidei ac spei nostræ fundamēta radicitus conuellenda. Quæritur igitur an Dominus noster Iesus Christus semper iustus fuerit, & hodie sit, an vero aliquam peccati labem & maculam habuisse & iniustus fuisse dicendus sit. At si dixeris iniustum & aliqua peccati ma-
units.tr: These things, although they remain fixed in our minds, are still hardly sufficient to untie this question, and to settle and strengthen our consciences against the various errors which either Satan himself stirs up from time to time, or our own understanding invents for itself, to obscure this truth with darkness and to tear up the foundations of our faith and hope by the roots. The question is therefore asked whether our Lord Jesus Christ has always been just and is so today, or whether he is to be said to have had some stain of sin and to have been unjust. But if you say that he was unjust and defiled with some stain of sin, then, even granting that he is not God, since there is no fellowship of light with darkness (2 Cor. 6.14),

units.la: Christus in vtraque natura sua iustissimus semper fuit. macula fœdatum, age etiam negato verum esse aut fuisse Deum, quum nulla sit luci communio cum tenebris. 2. Cor. 6. 14. Præterea, nonne si iniustus est, alio etiam ipsemet indiguit Seruatore, & pro suis no pro nostris peccatis passus est? Et, quod longè maius est, quinam rei impuræ oblatio Dei purissimi & sanctissimi, omnemque impuritate detestantis irâ placari posset? Sed vice versa, quū natura toti simus corrupti & instar cadaueris in peccatis mortui Eph. 2. 1. quomodo ipsum verû hominem nasci potuisse dicas, quin labe aliqua contraxisse videatur, ex Virgine natus à Dauide oriunda, qui ab Abrahamo, idemque ab Adamo genus trahit, ad quem etiam Sp. S. hanc ob causam, ut ad primâ stirpe nos deducit, Luc. 3. 38? Nâ hoc nisi sit, sane primogenitus no esset inter multos fratres: Rom. 8. 29. nec nostrę carnis & sanguinis particeps esset factus. Hebr. 2. 14. Præterea quum Deus non minus eū detestetur qui innocente condemnat, quàm eum qui nocente absoluit. Prou. 17. 15. quomodo redemptioni nostræ coueniret cū Dei natura summè iusta, si ab homine Sanctissimo, imò etiam iustissimo pœnas exegerit tot peccatoribus debitas, Filiumque percusserit pro tot hominibus iniustis, immo pro singulis, quotquot fuerunt, sunt vel futuri sunt peccatorib. si modo ad huius redemptionis asylū refugerint? Indignum sane facinus & ne in tyranno quidè tolerandū.
units.tr: Christ was always most just in both his natures. Furthermore, if he were unjust, would he not also have needed another Saviour, and suffered for his own sins and not for ours? And, what is far greater, what sacrifice of an impure thing could appease the anger of the most pure and holy God, who abhors all impurity? But on the contrary, since we are all corrupt by nature and, like corpses, dead in sins (Eph. 2.1), how can you say that he could be born a true man, born of a virgin descended from David, who traces his lineage from Abraham and likewise from Adam, to whom the Holy Spirit for this very reason leads us back as to the first stock (Luke 3.38), without seeming to have contracted some stain? For unless he were so, he would not be the firstborn among many brothers (Rom. 8.29), nor would he have become a partaker of our flesh and blood (Heb. 2.14). Moreover, since God detests no less him who condemns the innocent than him who acquits the guilty (Prov. 17.15), how could it agree with our redemption, with the supremely just nature of God, if he exacted from a most holy, indeed most just man the penalties owed by so many sinners, and struck the Son for so many unjust men, indeed for each one of all who have been or will be sinners, provided only they flee to the refuge of this redemption? Surely an unworthy deed, not to be tolerated even in a tyrant.

units.la: Et quidè his artibus Satan, & ipsi homines sua stultitia sibi imponi patiuntur, & à Sp. S. per verbum Dei minimè edocti, fructu se huius veritatis priuant, & à salutis via procul aber-rant,salsissimas sibi fingentes conclusiones:eò magis fallaces quò magis callidè & versutè ex certis & indubitatis principiis inferuntur, vt versutus & veterator ille Spiritus in Angelum lucis se transformare consuevit.
units.tr: And indeed by these arts Satan, and men themselves through their folly, allow themselves to be deceived. Not being taught by the Holy Spirit through the Word of God, they deprive themselves of the fruit of this truth and wander far from the way of salvation, devising for themselves most absurd conclusions, all the more deceptive in that they are drawn more cleverly and craftily from certain and indubitable principles, as that crafty old deceiver the Spirit is accustomed to transform himself into an angel of light.

units.la: Hæc igitur contrà sunto nostræ fidei certissima, verissima, firmissimaque fundamenta iisdem rationibus quas antè attigimus subnixa, nimirum, Necesse fuisse Iesum Christum nasci,non solum verum hominem,sed etiam Iustissimum & Sanctissimum,inde à conceptionis suę momento:teste Angelo Gabriele.Luc. 1.35.Ioh.8.46.& 1.Pet.3.18. Et quicquid ex carne natum est carnem esse, ac proinde pollutum.Psalm.51.7.Ioh.3.6.Rom.5.14.Porro infinitam illam Dei Sapientiam & Potentiam hanc inuenisse rationem qua Redemptor noster Iustissimus sanctissimusque nasceretur, & tamen Adami filius, vt nimirum concipere-tur & nasceretur,non quidem ordine consuetonaturæ, peccator ex peccatore, sed virtute Spiritus S.non gignentis, sed ex Virginis substantia, prius sanctificata, formantis corpus humanum nostri Redemptoris,cui etiam eodem momento data fuit anima purissima & sanctissima,vnita & coniuncta indiuiduo nexu cum Filio Dei,trium illarum quam Trinitatem dicimus,secuda Persona. Quemadmodum enim primus Adam ab homine genitus non est, sed creatoris voluntate & potentia formatus. Genef. 1.27. & 2.22. totius humani generis stirps & origo futurus. ( vnde factum videmus vt non sibi solum Adamus sed toti suae posteritati integritatem & immortalitatem illam amiserit) Sic etiam Deo placuit nostrum Redemptorem secundum Adamum, carne sua hominem fieri, non quidem ab alio homine progenitum, & proinde peccatorem a peccatore, sed Sancti Spiritus virtute & efficacia, sicut dictum est, formatum iustissimum & sanctissimum, ex Adami tamen stirpe, in electa Virgine, vt in eo fide apprehenso, per eiusdem S.Sp. virtutem & efficaciam, omnes electi filij Dei per adoptionem spiritualiter facti, vitam illam aeternam gloriosissimam consequantur.
units.tr: These, then, are to be set against them as the most certain, true and firm foundations of our faith, resting on the same arguments we touched on before. Namely: it was necessary that Jesus Christ be born not only a true man but also most just and most holy from the moment of his conception, as the angel Gabriel bears witness (Luke 1:35; John 8:46; 1 Pet. 3:18). Whatever is born of flesh is flesh, and therefore polluted (Ps. 51:7; John 3:6; Rom. 5:14). Moreover, the infinite wisdom and power of God found a way by which our most just and most holy Redeemer might be born, and yet be a son of Adam, so that he might be conceived and born. This was not in the usual order of nature, sinner from sinner, but by the power of the Holy Spirit, who does not beget but forms the human body of our Redeemer out of the substance of the Virgin, which had first been sanctified. To this body was given at the same moment a most pure and holy soul, united and joined with the Son of God by an indivisible bond: the second Person of the three whom we call the Trinity. For just as the first Adam was not begotten by a man but formed by the will and power of the Creator (Gen. 1:27; 2:22), and became the stock and origin of the whole human race (whence we see that Adam lost his integrity and immortality not only for himself but for all his posterity), so God was pleased that our Redeemer, the second Adam, should become man in his own flesh. He was not begotten by another man, and so a sinner from a sinner, but was formed, as has been said, by the virtue and efficacy of the Holy Spirit, most just and most holy, yet from the stock of Adam, in the chosen Virgin. This was so that all the elect, who by faith apprehend him and through the same virtue and efficacy of the same Holy Spirit have been made sons of God spiritually by adoption, might attain that most glorious eternal life.

units.la: De altera vero quaestione, quomodo Dei Iustitiae conueniat, innocentem pro totreis percutere, & alieni sceleris ab eo poenas exigere: adeo vt, sicut per os Dauidis loquitur, Psal.69.5. reependerit quae non rapuerat, iustus pro inimicis afflictus. 1.Pet.3 18.Esa.53.5. sic habere, factum id, non quod esset ipse debitor, sed quod ex Dei Patris decreto, & sponte sua vadem & sponsore se noui Foederis constituerit. Heb. 7.22. & animam pro anima, corpus pro corpore fideiussit. Sed vnde nobis tantus Sponsor & fideiussor? Nimirum a Patre qui ita dilexit mundum, vt Filium suum vnigenitum dederit, vt quisquis credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Ioh.3.16. Ipse met etiam Filius seipsum dedit, tanta nos complexus charitate & benevolentia, vt animam suam posuerit pro amicis suis. Ioh.10.5. & 13. 15. Denique à Sp. S. per quem Patris decretum perfectum est. Luc. 3. 5. qui nos in omnem veritatem deducit. Ioh. 16. v. 13. qui nos adoptionis nostrę certiores facit. Rom. 8. 16. & per quem in omnibus angustiis, ad Deum clamamus Abba, id est, Pater, Rom. 8. 15. Galat. 4. 6. Sic igitur superioribus quæstionibus respon-sum esto, quarum enodatione plerique à suo ipsorum sensu petentes ab iltius veritatis semita procul aberrarunt.
units.tr: Concerning the other question, how it agrees with the justice of God to strike the innocent for the guilty and to exact punishment from him for another's crime, so that, as he speaks through the mouth of David, he restored what he had not taken, the just one afflicted for his enemies (Ps. 69:5; 1 Pet. 3:18; Isa. 53:5): this was done not because he himself was a debtor, but because by the decree of God the Father and of his own will he constituted himself the surety and sponsor of the New Covenant (Heb. 7:22), and stood surety, soul for soul and body for body. But whence did we get so great a Surety and Guarantor? Namely from the Father, who so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life (John 3:16). The Son himself also gave himself, embracing us with such charity and goodwill that he laid down his soul for his friends (John 10:5; 13:15). Finally, it comes from the Holy Spirit, through whom the Father's decree is brought to completion (Luke 3:5), who leads us into all truth (John 16:13), who makes us more certain of our adoption (Rom. 8:16), and through whom, in all our distresses, we cry out to God, Abba, that is, Father (Rom. 8:15; Gal. 4:6). Let the earlier questions be answered thus. In unfolding them, most people, seeking the answer from their own sense, have wandered far from the path of that truth.

units.la: Reliquus est adhuc quidam scrupulus: qui fiat vt quum sponsorem & Fideiussorem nostrum necesse fuerit omne nostrum debitum exoluere, mortis autem æternę rei simus, Redemptoris nostri morte, quę ab eius excellu ad resurrectionem usque fuit tantum sequidiei liberemur, & mortis æternę vinculis eripiamur. Aio igitur revera Dei Maiestate esse infinitam, ac proinde aduersus eam admissam offensam pœnam æternam mereri, vt pœna peccato aduersus infinitam Maiestatem admisso respondeat. Verum si huius pœnę infinitate qualis in se est considereres, creaturę non convenire facile dignosces: quum hoc respectu sola Deitas sit infinita, id est in sua essentia, creatura autem sit essentia sua, natura & qualitate finita. Quum dicimus igitur naturam corruptionem, & quod ab ea peccatum proficiscitur, mortem æternam mereri, pœnę perpetuitas illa vocatur infinita, id est sine fine, quod nunquam abrumpatur nec finiatur: quoniam autem creatura semel huic addicta pœnæ, nunquam nunquā potest eam exsoluere, idcirco in perpetuū illius maledictione premitur. At Vnicus ille noster Redemptor,nō solùm verus homo, sed etiā verus Deus, (ac proinde longè potentior exhauriedę pœnę quā peccatis nostris debitam in sua humanitate pertulit,quàm ipsius Humanitas illi sustinedę vt ab ea nō absorberetur par fuit,)ille,inquā, noster Redemptor, effecit vt nō solū eius Humanitas perpetuo plenè & perfectè Deo satisfecerit, mortíque nos exemerit æternę,sed etiā perfectā & absoluta obedientiā Legi præstādo, qua ius acquiritur ad vitā æternā,ex hac Legis formula.Qui hęc fecerit viuet in ipsis.Deut.27.26.nobis etiā ius illud ad vitā æternā acquisierit. Quemadmodū enim peccata nostra nō fuerunt in hoc Redemptore,sed super eū iniecta, & illi tanquā vadi & sposori nostro imputata vt nos liberaremur:sic perfecta eius & modis omnibus absoluta obedietia quatenus nobis imputatur & velut in codice accepta refertur, quasi in nobis esset inhærens,morti nos eximit æternæ,& vitā æterna acquirit huic sposę,quæ fide fit caro ex eius carne,& os ex eius ossibus. 2.Cor.5. 21.Eph.5 30.O ingēs & omnib.modis admirādū arcanū, carni & sanguini incognitū & inscrutabile,quo Deus iudicij sui immesam seue ritatē(quàin vadem nostrū summo iure exercuit) cū incóprehésa sua erga nos misericordia cóciliauit,quā inde ab omni euo nobispręparatā suo tādē exhibuit tépore. Tit.1.2. & 3.& cadē benevolētia nobis per S.suū Sp.applicat. O profundas diuitias,tum sapientiæ, tum cognitionis Dei! quàm inscrutabilia sunt eius iudicia,& eius viæ imperueftigabiles: quibus enim conuenientioribus verbis quàm Apostoli Rom.11.33.caput istud concluderemus?
units.tr: There remains still one further difficulty: how it comes about that, since our Surety and Guarantor had to pay our whole debt, and we are liable to eternal death, we are freed by the death of our Redeemer, which lasted only a day and a half, from the death of the cross to the resurrection, and are rescued from the chains of eternal death. I say, then, that in truth the majesty of God is infinite, and therefore the offence committed against it deserves eternal punishment, so that the punishment corresponds to the sin committed against an infinite Majesty. But if you consider the infinity of this punishment as it is in itself, you will easily see that it does not belong to a creature. In this respect only the Godhead is infinite, that is, in its essence, whereas a creature is finite in its essence, nature and quality. When we say, then, that our corrupt nature, and the sin that proceeds from it, deserve eternal death, that perpetuity of punishment is called infinite, that is, without end, never broken off nor finished. But since a creature once given over to this punishment can never pay it off, it is held under that curse forever. But that unique Redeemer of ours, who is not only true man but also true God (and therefore far more powerful to exhaust the punishment due to our sins than his humanity was able to endure without being absorbed by it), this Redeemer, I say, brought it about that his humanity not only satisfied God fully and perfectly for ever, and freed us from eternal death, but also rendered perfect and absolute obedience to the Law, by which a right to eternal life is acquired, according to this formula of the Law, "He who does these things shall live in them" (Deut. 27:26). So he acquired for us that right to eternal life. For just as our sins were not in this Redeemer but were laid upon him and imputed to him as our surety and sponsor, that we might be freed, so his perfect and in every way absolute obedience, insofar as it is imputed to us and is reckoned to us as if entered in a ledger, as though it were inherent in us, frees us from eternal death and acquires eternal life for this bride, who by faith becomes flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones (2 Cor. 5:21; Eph. 5:30). O great and in every way admirable mystery, unknown and unsearchable to flesh and blood, by which God reconciled the immense severity of his judgment (which he exercised against us as surety by the highest right) with his unfathomable mercy towards us, which he had prepared for us from all eternity and at last revealed in his own time (Tit. 1:2, 3), and applies the same goodwill to us through his Holy Spirit. O the deep riches both of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and his ways past finding out (Rom. 11:33)! With what more fitting words could we close this chapter than those of the Apostle?

units.la: Transeamus igitur ad reliqua , & quum sciamus,Quis sit sponsor ac fideiussor hic noster:Quibus causis adductus vices nostras subierit:Quóve respectu pro nobis passus sit,age quæ fuerint eius perpessiones attendamus. Ieiunè verò prorsus & minutè de Christi passionibus sentiunt , qui eas ad solos illos temporarios,quantumuis duros & sæuos corpori & animæ communes cruciatus referunt, omissis iis maximis animi angoribus, quos in ipsis penetralibus animæ iræ Dei sensu horribili sauciatæ pertulit, & quibus velut in profundam abyssum Dei iudiciorum immersus est. Hac enim re potissimū Christi perpessiones differunt ab iis cruciatibus quos tot beati Martyres propter Sanctum nomen eius pertulerunt. Ex ista verò non animaduersa perpessionum Christi Seruatoris distinctione, alius detestandus error prodiit eorum, qui in manifestam idololatriam lapsi, & tantundem merito mortis & Passionis Domini detrahentes, quantum addere se dignitati Martyrum existimauerunt,perpessiones Iesu Christi,permiscent cruciatibus quos Martyres pro eius nomine pertulerunt: qui denique tandem, quasi Martyribus adfuerit, quibus nō sibi solùm,sed etiam aliis tum viuis tum mortuis ad finem vsque mundi promeriti sint, quædam velut horrea istis meritis redundantia construxerunt, quorum claues Episcopo Romano committi sunt, vnde quibusuis quantum volet meritorum, quo libitum ipsi fuerit tempore, quàue mensura, numerato pretio admetiatur. Impium & abominandũ dogma, quantumuis specioso Religionis prætextu in Ecclesiam inuectum, quasi vero mors & passio Christi, qua vel ipsi Martyres, atq; adeo Christiani omnes redimuntur, sola non sufficiat: quasi etiam Iesus alios Iesus produxerit: quasi denique Christi & Martyrum perpessiones duobus his tantum differrent: Primùm quòd Christi passiones ex se mereantur. Martyrum verò merita ex Christi meritis vim suam trahant: Alterum, quòd Christi merita longè maiora sint & præstantiora, Martyrum verò inferiora: quæ tamen non sic extenuant, quin ea tum sibi ipsis tum reliquis hominibus Deo conciliandis sufficere putent. Vtinam verò saltem hic sibi in memoriam reuocarent quod quidam ex antiquioribus & purioribus Romanis Episcopis hac de re scripsit, sermone 2. in Passionem Domini, his verbis. Etsi multorum Sanctorum pretiosa mors coram facie Domini fuerit, nunquam tamen vllam cuiusquam innocentis mortem inuenias pro mundo factam propitiationem. Iusti enim acceperunt coronas & non largiti sunt: & ex forti fidelium constantia prodierunt exempla patientiæ, non dona iusticiæ. Priuata fuit enim vnaquæque mors eorum, quū nemo sua mor- te debitum alienum exoluerit : solus verò Ie- sus Christus Dominus noster in filiis homi- num existat, in quo omnes crucifiguntur, o- mnes moriuntur,omnesfepeliuntur,omnes à mortuis excitantur. Hæc sunt illius Episcopi verba, quæ ipsius fucceffloris sicut alia plera- que ne imitarentur, diligenter cauerunt,licet iam tum Antichristus myfteiij iniquitatis fun- damenta iaceret.
units.tr: Let us therefore pass on to the rest. Since we know who this our surety and guarantor is, what causes moved him to take up our place, and with what respect he suffered for us, let us now consider what his sufferings were. Those, however, who think of the sufferings of Christ in a crude and superficial way, and refer them only to those temporary torments, however hard and cruel, common to body and soul, omitting those greatest anguishes of mind which he endured in the innermost depths of his soul, wounded by the horrible sense of God's wrath, and into which he was plunged as into a deep abyss of God's judgments, are quite wrong. This above all is why the sufferings of Christ differ from those torments which so many blessed martyrs endured for his holy name. From this unnoticed distinction between the sufferings of Christ the Saviour arose another detestable error, of those who, having fallen into manifest idolatry, and detracting from the merit of the death and passion of the Lord as much as they thought they added to the dignity of the martyrs, mix the sufferings of Jesus Christ with the torments which the martyrs endured for his name. Finally, as if he had been present with the martyrs, they have built certain storehouses overflowing with merits, merits which they say were earned not only for themselves but for others, living and dead, until the end of the world. The keys of these storehouses have been committed to the Roman Bishop, so that he may dispense to anyone as much merit as he wishes, at whatever time and in whatever measure it pleases him, for a price paid. This is an impious and abominable dogma, brought into the Church under however specious a pretext of religion, as if the death and passion of Christ, by which even the martyrs themselves and indeed all Christians are redeemed, were not sufficient by itself; as if Jesus had brought forth other Jesuses; as if, finally, the sufferings of Christ and of the martyrs differed only in these two respects: first, that Christ's sufferings merit by themselves, while the merits of the martyrs draw their force from the merits of Christ; and second, that Christ's merits are far greater and more excellent, while those of the martyrs are inferior. Yet they do not so belittle the latter that they think them insufficient to reconcile both themselves and other men to God. Would that they at least called to mind what one of the older and purer Roman bishops wrote on this matter, in his second sermon on the Passion of the Lord, in these words: "Although the precious death of many saints has been before the face of the Lord, yet you will never find the death of any innocent man made a propitiation for the world. For the just received crowns and did not bestow them; from the strong constancy of the faithful came examples of patience, not gifts of righteousness. For each of their deaths was private, since no one paid another's debt by his own death. But Jesus Christ our Lord alone exists among the sons of men, in whom all are crucified, all die, all are buried, all are raised from the dead." These are the words of that bishop. His successors, however, carefully took care not to imitate them, as they did with many other things, although already at that time Antichrist was laying the foundations of the mystery of iniquity.

units.la: Vt tantum igitur tamque abominandum dogma vitemus,& vt propositæ quæstioni fa- tisfiat,paucis respondeo ex verbis ipsius Apo- ftoli.Gal.3. 13. Iesum Christum pro nobis esse factum execrationem,id est,pro nobis & ani- ma & corpore horrendum & immensum Dei furorem pertulilfe, quem in nos tum natiua corruptio,tum peccata nostra concitauerant, quæ ipsemet Christus sursum tulit in corpore suo super lignum crucis.1.Pet.2.24.sicut erat à Prophera prædictum.Esa.53 5.vt ibi chirohra- phum aduersus nosfcriptum deleret & affige- ret.Facilia dictu ista quidem,sed quis humana mente tanti furoris horrorem complectatur, quem ne ipse Christus quidem, nisi aliquid amplius quàm homofuiffet, quantumuis iu- ftum & fortem dicas,donis etiam acceptis abf que mensura. Ioh. 3. 34. imò nefi Angelus quidem inter Angelos præftantiflimus,atque adeò nisi Deus ipse fuisset Deo Patri coeeffen- tialis & coæternus, ab eo potius velut in pro- fundam abyflum immersus & in æternum obruendus, exhausisset? En cur damnatorum poenæ dicantur Ignis æternus, vermis arrodés, & qui non interit, fletus & stridor dentium sempiternus: quibus gaudium æternum, vita, felicitas, & regnum immortale, Iesu Christi cohæredibus præparatum, opponūtur. At neque harum nec similium vocum, imò ne totius quidem humanæ eloquentiæ tanta vis est vt salutis huius gloriam & dignitatem, in quam Seruator ille noiter profectus est, locum nobis paraturus Iohan.14. 2. eloquatur: aut contrà iudicij illius horrorem quod in eum effusum est, exprimat: cuius non portiunculam tantùm, sed plenum etiam calicem acerbissimæ potionis, non pro vnius hominis: sed pro omnium quotquot fuerunt, sunt vel futuri sunt ad finem seculorum, à Deo patre electorum peccatis exhausit. Nam fi vel minima illius amplius exhaurienda guttula superfuisset, ecquis eam absorbere niteretur quin perpetua morte demergeretur?
units.tr: So that we may avoid so great and abominable a dogma, and so that the question proposed may be answered, I reply briefly from the Apostle's own words. Galatians 3.13 says that Jesus Christ was made a curse for us, that is, that for us he endured, in both soul and body, the dreadful and immeasurable fury of God, which our native corruption and our sins had stirred up against us. Christ himself bore these up in his body on the wood of the cross (1 Peter 2.24), as the prophet had foretold (Isaiah 53.5), so that he might blot out and nail to the cross the bond written against us. These things are easy to say. But who can grasp in his human mind the horror of such a fury? Christ himself could not have endured it unless he had been something more than a man, however just and strong you may call him, and endowed with gifts received without measure (John 3.34). Indeed, unless he had been not merely the most excellent of the angels but God himself, co-essential and co-eternal with God the Father, he would have been plunged by the Father into a deep abyss and overwhelmed for ever, and would have been consumed. Here is why the punishments of the damned are called eternal fire, the worm that gnaws, the unquenchable fire, and the everlasting weeping and gnashing of teeth, set against which are eternal joy, life, happiness, and the immortal kingdom prepared for the co-heirs of Jesus Christ. But neither these nor similar words, nor indeed all the power of human eloquence, is great enough to express the glory and dignity of that salvation into which the Saviour went, to prepare a place for us (John 14.2), or, on the other hand, to express the horror of that judgment which was poured out upon him. Of this he drained not merely a small portion but the full cup of the most bitter draught, not for one man but for the sins of all the elect whom God the Father chose, whether they have lived, are living, or will live until the end of the ages. For if even the smallest drop had remained to be drained, who would try to swallow it without being plunged into everlasting death?

units.la: Immensa sunt sanè & plus quàm admiranda hæc mysteria: sed quorum cognitio & cóteplatio prorsus foret inutilis nili finis ad quem illa sunt referenda cognitus etiam effet, nimirum Dei gloriæ manifestatio & illuftratio, qui rerum omnium à Deo creatarum etiam præcipuus & vltimus finis est. Atque adeò nos ad hunc finem eò diligentius aspirare, decet, quò Redemptionis nostræ opus infinitis partibus Creatione excellentius & sublimius est, idque multis de causis. Nam in creatione Deus Crea-
units.tr: These mysteries are indeed immense and more than admirable. Yet their knowledge and contemplation would be wholly useless unless the end to which they are to be referred were also known, namely the manifestation and illustration of God's glory, which is the chief and final end of all things created by God. We ought therefore to aspire to this end all the more diligently, in proportion as the work of our redemption is excellent and sublime beyond creation in countless respects, and for many reasons. For in creation God the Crea-

units.la: c. j. tor,ex parte tantùm,vt ita dicam,se cognoscé- dum præbuit, quum infinitam sapientiam & potentiam, cum immensa bonitate coniun- ctam, & rebus omnibus à se creatis impref- sam patefecit. Verùm in hominis redemptio- ne multò cuidentius eius sapientia, potentia & bonitas emicuit. Quantò enim Iesus Chri- stus Deus homo,excellentior Adamo,licet ad imaginem & similitudinē Dei creato? quantò præstantior vita spiritualis,animali vita?coni- iugium illud æternum & purissimum Iesu Christi sponsi,& sponsæ ipsius charissimæ Ec- clesiæ ex eius latere eductæ, annon admirabi- lius & incredibilius creatione Euæ exipsius Adami costa conditæ? Et mortem,morte vin- cere,& superare,mortémque vita spirituali & cœlesti commutare,longè maius est quàm esse iubere , quod antea non existebat. Sed præter superiora illa omnia tá magna ráměue inef- sabilia arcana,vt eorum omnium fidem supe- rent quæ in sensus nostros,putà,visum, audi- tum, tactum, gustum , sensum , cogitationem denique nostram incurrunt, animaducrtendū etiá est,Deü in mundi creatione,nec iudiciorū suorum seueritatem , quod nihil nisi bonum creasset , ac proinde nihil esset iustitiæ ipsius obnoxium : nec misericordiæ suæ thesauros patefecisse , quum nulla dum miseria mũdum inuasisset , At in Redemptionis nostræ myste- rio , luculenter vtrumque demonstrauit : & quod maius est, viâ pro sua immensa sapiêtia qua vtrůq; conciliaret,inuenit, vt superiùs est à nobis demonstratū,vt non immeritò Paulus Apostolus huius mysterij latitudinē & longitudinem, profunditatem & sublimitatem omni cognitione maiorem commendet, cuius tantùm notitiam velut per speculum habemus tantisper dum hic peregrinamur: quum ipsos etiam Angelos in hæc desiderare introspicere dicat Petrus.1. Pet.1. 12. Denique summus & vltimus huius mysterij finis est gloria Dei, ad quem etiam solum omne huius secreti gloriam oportet referri. Verùm quum Domino etiam visum sit cum sua gloria salutem æternam eorum quos ad id ab æterno prædestinatos creauit Ephe.1.coniungere: vt sit ipse iustus & iustificans eum qui est ex fide Iesu Rom.3.26.idcirco vt veram & perfectam consolationem ex hac doctrina referamus, id est, pacem illam & tranquillitatem conscientiarum, qui alter est huius redemptionis medius finis,hoc etiam caput à nobis explicari locus iste postulat.
units.tr: tor showed himself to be known only in part, as it were, when he revealed his infinite wisdom and power, joined with immense goodness, and stamped upon all the things he had made. But in the redemption of man his wisdom, power and goodness shone out far more clearly. For how much more excellent is Jesus Christ, God and man, than Adam, though he was created in the image and likeness of God? How much more excellent is spiritual life than animal life? Is not that eternal and most pure marriage of Jesus Christ, the bridegroom, with his most beloved bride the Church, drawn from his side, more admirable and more incredible than the creation of Eve, formed from the rib of Adam? And to conquer and overcome death by death, and to exchange death for spiritual and heavenly life, is far greater than to command that something which did not exist should come into being. But besides all these higher things, so great and so ineffable in their mysteries, which surpass the faith in all the things that fall under our senses (sight, hearing, touch, taste) and finally under our thought, we must also notice that God, in creating the world, showed neither the severity of his judgments, since he had made nothing but good and so nothing liable to his justice, nor the treasures of his mercy, since no misery had yet invaded the world. In the mystery of our redemption, however, he has demonstrated both clearly. What is more, by his immense wisdom he found a way to reconcile the two, as has been shown above by us. Hence the Apostle Paul rightly commends the breadth and length, the depth and height of this mystery as surpassing all knowledge, of which we have only a knowledge as through a mirror while we sojourn here. Peter says that even the angels desire to look into these things (1 Peter 1.12). Finally, the highest and ultimate end of this mystery is the glory of God, to which the whole glory of this secret must alone be referred. But since it has also pleased the Lord to join the eternal salvation of those whom he created and predestined from eternity to this with his own glory (Ephesians 1), so that he may be just and the justifier of him who is of the faith of Jesus (Romans 3.26), this passage demands that we also explain this point, so that from this doctrine we may draw true and perfect consolation, namely that peace and tranquillity of conscience which is the other intermediate end of this redemption.

units.la: Sed antequam vlterius progressi bonitatis & beneuolentiæ Dei immensæ erga nos abyssum alteram ingrediamur, & profunditatem perscrutemur quam nos Deus duce Sp. S.vult etiam dum hac vita fruimur scrutari.1. Cor. 2. 10.error quidam ex quo plerique alij fluxerút detegendus est,in quem incautè & imprudenter lapsi sunt qui non satis attendentes Actiones vni Christo proprias & peculiares ab iis non distinxerunt, quas nobis imitandas proposuit.Exempli gratia:Christus Dominus noster quū se ad munus ad quod missus erat Mediatoris accingeret, quadraginta dies noctésque totidem ieiunauit:hoc itaque fundamento nonnulli Quadragesimam niti putant. Idē Dominus missis suis digitis in surdi cuiusdam aures, & Hebraicè illum compellás, Epphata, inquit, id est, Aperire, sic surdo vim audiendi reddidit. Matth. 7.34. Quum præterea cæcum natum sanauit, & spuens humi luto ex sputo facto illeuisset lutū oculis cæci,& ad piscinam Siloam lauandum remisisset, inde nate tā multę superstitiones inanes & ridiculę quibus Baptismus à Domino nostro Iesu Chri sto filio Dei institutus à sua simplicitate in ludicra & ridicula multa, ne dicam blasphemia degenerauit. Idem Dominus antequam sacrosanctam suam Cœnam institucret, pedes discipulorum lauit,eo facto declarans ex regionis illius & temporis instituto, lauandi pedes eorum quos amicè hospitio gratis hospites excipiebant,quod ex tota sacra vetere historia & nominatim ex Luc. cap. 7.44. perspicuum est,quæ sint cuiusque partes in exercendis mutuis inter se charitatis maiorum etiam erga minores officiis, vt loquitur Apostolus.1.Tim. 5.10.&hoc sensu iubens vt suo exéplo pedes alij aliorum lauemus. Sed hoc quod erat præceptum neglecto, ecce in Ecclesiam inuectus est, mos ille ridiculus duodecim pauperibus magno die Iouis quem vocant pedes abluendi. Apostoli nonnunquam ex Domini præcepto, vt est verisimile ad miraculosam ægrotorum rum fanationem oleum adhibuerunt: hinc e-tiam ortum est nouum extremæ vnctionis Sa-cramentum quod inutiliter & ridiculeiam à multis seculis ægrotis applicatur,quum Sana-tionis donum extraordinarium iampridem in Ecclesia desierit,quod erat illi à Domino con-cessum, tantisper dum Euangelij prædicatio aduersus incredulos sanciretur.Marc.16.17.& 20.1.Cor.14.22. Porrò (quod minus excusari potest) non ægrotis sanandis, sed desperata salute mox ad sepulchrum deducendis Sacra-mentum illud vnctionis adhiberi solet.Omit-to multarum istiusmodi traditionum, quæ nullo fundamento nituntur, infinitum nume-rum: quarum etiam aliæ ab Ethnicorum ritibus & superstitione, quam Christianos intus & foris abominantes procul oportuit elimi-nare, suam originem trahunt, aliæ à Phari-saismo quem toties Dominus coarguit: aliæ denique à Iudaicis ceremoniis ortum habet, quibus Christus omnibus sic finem attulit, vt Apostolus, illas omnes nomine Circumcisio-nis complexus,aperte &expresse dicat,Gal.5.2. Si circuncidantur Christu nihil prodesse. Itaque vt rem totam vno verbo absoluam,quem-cunque isti homines Religionis prætextum adferant, quamcunque antiquitatem prætexant, omnis ille ritualis cultus, quo verus & legitimus Dei cultus qui est in spiritu & veritate,in hiftrionicum & mimicum est transformatus,non modò vt vanus & inutilis est,reiiciendus, sed etiam abominandus & modis omnibus detestandus, quòd quum primùm in superstitionem degenerarit, tandem in horrendam etiam impietatem desierit.
units.tr: But before we go further and enter upon the other abyss of the immense goodness and benevolence of God towards us, and search the depth which God, with the Holy Spirit as our guide, wishes us to search even while we enjoy this life (1 Corinthians 2.10), an error must be exposed, from which many others have flowed. Into it those have fallen rashly and imprudently who, paying too little attention, did not distinguish from the actions proper and peculiar to Christ alone those which he set before us to imitate. For example: when Christ our Lord was preparing himself for the office of Mediator to which he had been sent, he fasted forty days and forty nights, and on this foundation some think that Lent rests. The same Lord, putting his fingers into the ears of a certain deaf man and addressing him in Hebrew, said Ephphatha, that is, "Be opened," and so restored the power of hearing to the deaf man (Matthew 7.34). Again, when he healed a man born blind, and having spat on the ground and made clay of the spittle, smeared the clay on the blind man's eyes and sent him to wash in the pool of Siloam, from this there arose so many vain and ridiculous superstitions that baptism, instituted by our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, has degenerated from its simplicity into many playful and ridiculous practices, not to say blasphemies. The same Lord, before he instituted his most holy Supper, washed the feet of his disciples. By this act he declared, according to the custom of that region and time, that guests freely received into the homes of those who welcomed them in friendship should have their feet washed. This is clear from the whole sacred ancient history and especially from Luke 7.44, and it shows what the parts of each are in performing mutual duties of charity, even of greater towards lesser, as the Apostle says (1 Timothy 5.10). In this sense he commanded that we wash one another's feet by his example. But this precept has been neglected, and behold, that ridiculous custom has been introduced into the Church: the washing of the feet of twelve poor men on the great day of Thursday, which they call the washing of feet. The apostles sometimes used oil, as is likely by the Lord's command, for the miraculous healing of the sick. Hence also arose the new sacrament of extreme unction, which for many centuries has been uselessly and ridiculously applied to the sick, although the extraordinary gift of healing, granted by the Lord for as long as the preaching of the gospel was to be confirmed against unbelievers, has long since ceased in the Church (Mark 16.17; 1 Corinthians 14.22). Moreover, and this can less be excused, that sacrament of anointing is customarily administered not to heal the sick, but to those whose salvation has been despaired of and who are soon to be taken to the grave. I omit the infinite number of traditions of this kind, which rest on no foundation. Some of them also draw their origin from the rites and superstition of the heathen, which Christians, abhorring them inwardly and outwardly, ought to have banished far away. Others come from Phariseeism, which the Lord so often refuted, and others finally have their origin in Jewish ceremonies, to all of which Christ put an end. So the Apostle, embracing all of these under the name of circumcision, plainly and expressly says: "If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing" (Galatians 5.2). Therefore, to finish the whole matter in one word: whatever pretext of religion these men bring forward, whatever antiquity they allege, all that ritual worship, by which the true and lawful worship of God, which is in spirit and truth, has been turned into a theatrical and mimic show, is to be rejected not only as vain and useless, but also to be abhorred and detested in every way. For once it has degenerated into superstition, it has at last ended in horrible impiety.

units.la: Sed vt illa tam superstitiosa támque blasphema missa faciam, an tamen possem silentio praeterire tam crassam, tá impiam, tá demque modis omnibus abominandam illam, in inferis fabricatam, & ab ipso Satana vomitam execrandi illius idoli quod S. Franciscum dicunt, cum magno illo & vnico Seruatore nostro Domino Iesu Christo verè Deohomine, & Homine Deo conformitatem, qua non ipsa sua Christo conceptio, non natiuitas, non vita, non mors, non resurrectio, non ascensio ad coelos, non denique ad dextram Dei sessio seruatur integra, quin cum suis stigmatibus infando & detestando illi idolo ea quae Christi maximè propria sunt applicentur, & quidem tanta cum impietate & flagitio, vt ei sacratissima verba haec tribuantur, Ego sum vitis, vos palmites: atque adeò imagines & statuae erigantur, dimidium Christum, & dimidium illum S. Franciscum praeferentes? O scelus lo impudentiam effrenem, quam vel ipse Satan forte fassis exhorreat. En tamen sanctum illum scilicet ordinem Franciscanorum idololatrarum eousque receptū & approbatum vt eū hodie ad Papalem dignitatem euectum conspiciamus. Sed has praetergressi spurcissimas cloacas age ad rem redeamus: quam quum pluribus explicare nos temporis angustiae prohibeant, in proximū sermonem differentes, age Deum optioptimum Patrem & Seruatorem nostrum precemur, vt quum nobis oculos aperuerit ad istiusmodi blasphemas abominationes agno-scendas & detcstādas,nos etiām magis ac magis ad veritatis notitiam conformet, vt vera viuáque & sincera fide prẹditi,salutis illius ę-ternæ tandem participes fiamus, & reliquum vitæ nostræ curriculum, per Sp. S. veri eiusi-mi᷑atores facti transfigamus.
units.tr: But, to pass over that mass which is so superstitious and so blasphemous, could I keep silent about that gross, impious and, in every way, abominable conformity between our one great Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, true God and true man, and the execrable idol they call St Francis, which was fabricated in hell and vomited up by Satan himself? In it, nothing of Christ is kept whole: not his conception, nor his birth, nor his life, nor his death, nor his resurrection, nor his ascension into heaven, nor finally his sitting at the right hand of God. Rather, with its stigmata, that accursed and detestable idol appropriates to itself the things that are most proper to Christ, and with such impiety and disgrace that the most sacred words, "I am the vine, you are the branches," are attributed to it. Indeed, images and statues are set up that present half Christ and half that St Francis. O crime! O unbridled shamelessness, which Satan himself might perhaps shudder at! Yet behold, that holy order of idolatrous Franciscans has been received and approved to such an extent that today we see it raised to papal dignity. But, having passed over these most filthy sewers, let us return to our subject. Since the shortness of time forbids us to explain it at length with many words, we defer it to the next sermon. Meanwhile, let us pray to God, the best and greatest Father and our Saviour, that, as he has opened our eyes to recognise and detest such blasphemous abominations, he may also conform us more and more to the knowledge of the truth, so that, endowed with a true, living and sincere faith, we may at last become partakers of that eternal salvation, and, made true worshippers of this kind through the Holy Spirit, may pass the remaining course of our lives.

units.la: HOMILIA tertia.
units.tr: Third Homily.

units.la: VELLEM, fratres, paucioribus à nobis initio proposita capita possent explicari, antequam ad huius historiæ contextum accedamus: sed difficultates occurrentes eæ sunt vt satis enodari non possint: tantáque ad nos inde redit vtilitas, vt de iis nunquam satis cogitari possit. Peruenimus autem ad quartum & vltimum caput, finem nimirum ad quem hæc omnia referenda sunt, vt fructum ex iis percipiamus. Hic verò commodè potest ad tria capita referri,quorum primum est, Patefactio gloriæ Dei longè maior & illustrior in Redemptionis quàm in Creationis opere: alterum perfecta nostra cum Deo reconciliatio : tertium denique conformitas nostra cum Christo per regenerationem. Horum priore pertractato , age ad secundum accedamus , in quo etiam præmonuimus diligenter cauendum , ne quæ sunt Christo Domino nostro Redemptori sic propria & peculiaria , vt insignis cuiusdam fuerit amen- tiæ velle illa imitari,cum iis confundamus,in quibus se exemplar imitandum nobis propo- suit.
units.tr: I would wish, brethren, that fewer of the chapters we proposed at the beginning could be explained before we come to the context of this history. But the difficulties that arise are such that they cannot be fully unfolded, and the usefulness that comes back to us from them is so great that one can never think about them enough. We have now reached the fourth and last chapter, namely the end to which all these things must be referred, so that we may gather fruit from them. Here they can conveniently be referred to three chapters. The first is the manifestation of God's glory, far greater and more illustrious in the work of Redemption than in the work of Creation. The second is our perfect reconciliation with God. The third is our conformity with Christ through regeneration. Having treated the first, let us now come to the second. In it we have also previously warned that we must take careful heed not to confuse with those things which are so proper and peculiar to Christ our Lord and Redeemer those things in which he has set himself before us as an example to be imitated. It would be a sign of remarkable folly to wish to imitate the former.

units.la: Primum igitur , quod Christi personæ proprium est & essentiale, illi soli proprium esto & permaneto , quòd nimirum Deus est & homo in vnitate Personæ: Deinde quæcunque Mediatoris inter Deum & homines officium spectant: tum quæcunque vt hoc munus impleret perfecit,, in quo ablit cogitemus habuisse ipsum, habere, vel in seculum habiturum esse vllum ex rebus omnibus creatis socium,etsi tamen ab eatum nonnullis præfiguratus sit & adumbratus. Atque adeò ita sunt hæc Christi personæ propria, vt licet tres Personæ Trinitatis simul sint & inseparabiliter nostram Redemptionem operatæ, tamen operatio Redemptoris nostri, qui est secunda persona Trinitatis, à Patris & Sp. S. operatione distincta sit. Solus igitur Iesus Christus propter nostram salutem in Mariæ virginis vtero conceptus est, natus Bethlehemi in stabulo: in Ægyptum delatus, in Iordane baptizatus. ptifatus:solus ipse tot miracula sua ipsius edi-dit vi ac poteltare: solus etiam ipse inter duos latrones pependit Hierosolymis: in cruce ex-pirauit, nullam in fcpulchro corruptionem sensit,sua vi tertio die resurrexit, & supra cœ-los omnes cuectus est, vbi Nomen supra nome omne consecutus: solus ipse vltimo illo die venturus est in Maiestate & gloria ad iudican-dum viuos & mortuos,qui iam omnem habet in cœlo & terra potestatem. Solus is est in quo & per quem Patris familia, nimirum Ecclesia proprie regitur & administratur: cuius vnius est conscientiis leges præfigere:in quo vno Pa ter conquiescit:in quo & per quem peccata o-mnia nostra nobis condonat,obsignante Sp.S. in cordibus nostris eam remissionem:solus il-le noster Sacerdos in æternum, qui per oblationem semel factam à semetipso, à morte suos redemptos,in vitam æternam asseruit:fo-lus ille est quo inter medio & intercelfore etiá hodie apud Patrem, preces nostræ gratæ sunt & acceptæ: quorum omnium gloria sic illi propria est, vt nulli rei creatę, nec cœlesti nec terrenæ,nec in totum nec ex parte communis esse possit.
units.tr: First, then, what is proper and essential to the person of Christ belongs to him alone and must remain so: namely, that he is God and man in the unity of one Person. Next, whatever pertains to the office of Mediator between God and men, and whatever he accomplished in order to fulfil this office, in which we cannot think that he had, has, or will ever have in the age to come any companion from among all created things, even though some of them were foreshadowed and prefigured. So truly are these things proper to the person of Christ that, although the three Persons of the Trinity are together and inseparably the authors of our Redemption, nevertheless the work of our Redeemer, who is the second Person of the Trinity, is distinct from the work of the Father and of the Holy Spirit. Therefore Jesus Christ alone, for our salvation, was conceived in the womb of the Virgin Mary, was born at Bethlehem in a stable, was carried into Egypt, and was baptized in the Jordan. He alone by his own power and might performed so many miracles. He alone also hung between two thieves at Jerusalem; he expired on the cross, felt no corruption in the tomb, rose again on the third day by his own power, and was carried up above all the heavens, where he obtained the Name above every name. He alone will come at that last day in majesty and glory to judge the living and the dead, he who now has all power in heaven and earth. He alone is the one in whom and through whom the household of the Father, namely the Church, is properly governed and administered. It is his alone to prescribe the laws to consciences; in him alone the Father rests; in him and through him he forgives us all our sins, the Holy Spirit sealing that remission in our hearts. He alone is our eternal Priest, who by the one offering made once for all, offering himself, has secured his redeemed from death into eternal life. He alone is the one through whom, as Mediator and Intercessor, even today before the Father, our prayers are pleasing and acceptable. The glory of all these things is so proper to him that it can belong to no created thing, heavenly or earthly, either wholly or in part.

units.la: Porrò quò melius Redemptionis nostræ partes per vnicum iltum Seruatorem intelli-gantur,age illas ad duo capita referamus:quo-rum primum eito,vt omnis ille reatus quo ad-ucrsum nos iram Dei prouocabamus,& quod æternæ morti obnoxios faciebat, penitus tol-latur & abolcatur: alterû vt quicquid nos Deo gratos & acceptos,eiúsque benedictione,quæ vita æterna est, dignos efficere potest, gratis consecquamur. Deum autem nobis infestum faciebant, primùm corruptio naturę nostræ, tum in anima,tum in corpore:deinde pessimę huius arboris fructus,omnis nempe generis peccata:quibus opponitur id quo apti & idonei reddimur ad vitam æternam adipiscen-dam ex ipsius promissionibus,plena nimirum & modis omnibus absoluta integritas, vnà cum eius fructibus,qui sunt perfectus amor Dei &proximi.In quę vero alium hoc vtrumque,cadit,nisi in vnicum illum Seruatorem & Redemptorem nostrum in quo primùm,vt in secundo nostro Adamo, tota natura nostra in longè præstantiorem,& infinitis partibus absolutiorem, constantioremque & firmiorem statum est redintegrata,quàm ab initio fuerat in Adamo creata: & qui per sui oblationem semel factam , quicquid tum natiuæ corruptioni nostrę, tum fructibus illius debebatur, persoluit,& cumulatissimè satisfecit? En qua ratione quicquid mortis reos efficiebat,penitus est obliteratum.
units.tr: Moreover, so that the parts of our Redemption may be better understood through that one unique Saviour, let us refer them to two chapters. The first is that all that guilt by which we provoked the wrath of God against us, and which made us liable to eternal death, is wholly removed and abolished. The second is that we obtain freely whatever can make us pleasing and acceptable to God, and worthy of his blessing, which is eternal life. Now what made God hostile to us was first the corruption of our nature, both in soul and in body, and then the evil fruits of this wicked tree, that is, sins of every kind. Opposed to these is that by which we are made fit and suitable to attain eternal life according to his promises: namely, a full and in every way complete integrity, together with its fruits, which are the perfect love of God and of neighbour. But where do these two things fall, unless in that one Saviour and Redeemer of ours? In him, as in our second Adam, first, our whole nature was restored to a state far more excellent, and infinitely more perfect, more constant and firmer than it was when created in Adam at the beginning. He also, by the one offering made once for all, paid whatever was owed both to our innate corruption and to its fruits, and satisfied it most abundantly. Here is the reason why whatever made us liable to death has been wholly blotted out.

units.la: Idem de secundo dicendum eandem, oblationem quum profecta sit ab amore perfectissimo,& obedietia quam Deus ab homine postulat, & ab incredibili & plus quàm perfecta dilectione qua suos inimicos amplexus est, nō solū esse satisfactione qua liberemur à morte, sed etiam perfectissimam impletionem eorū omnium quæ à sua creatura reposcebat Creator, in eo qui hoc vno eodemq; mysterio execratio factus est vt ab ea nos liberaret, Legique se subiecit, vt eius benedictionem in se no bis acquireret. Gal.3.13. & 14. vt iure optimo concludat Apostolus nullam superesse condemnationem iis qui sunt in Christo Iesu.Ro. 8.1.Immo potius esse benedictionem,quum in eo Lex stabiliatur.Rom.3.31.In quo igitur inesse & reperiri dicemus perfectissimam naturae nostrae puritatem, persolutionem pro peccatis, & perfectissimam iustitiam Legem? Nimirum in vno illo Seruatore Iesu Christo.
units.tr: The same must be said of the second chapter. Since that offering proceeded from most perfect love, and from the obedience that God demands from man, and from an incredible and more than perfect love by which he embraced his enemies, it is not only a satisfaction by which we are freed from death, but also the most perfect fulfilment of all those things which the Creator demanded from his creature. He became a curse for us in that one and the same mystery, so that he might free us from the curse, and subjected himself to the Law, so that he might obtain for us in himself its blessing (Gal. 3:13–14). Hence the Apostle rightly concludes that there is no condemnation left for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:1); rather, there is a blessing, since in him the Law is established (Rom. 3:31). In whom, then, shall we say that the most perfect purity of our nature, the payment for sins, and the most perfect righteousness of the Law are present and found? Certainly in that one Saviour, Jesus Christ.

units.la: At dicat aliquis, quomodo illa nostra sunt, quae in alterius haerent persona, quum homo non viuat alterius hominis anima: nec alterius iustitia iustus sit? Hic vero nos, hic inquā, si vsquam alibi, mirari decet admirandum Dei in nobis ieruandis consilium: qui quum nihil in nobis inueniret nisi quod eum aduersus nos provocabat, & nihil eorum quae requiruntur quo nobis conciliaretur: Filium suum iis omnibus ornatum quae supra recensuimus nobis dedit, cui soli, vt vadi & fideiussori nostro imputauit, tum corruptionem nostram, tum fructus ipsius, vt contrà nobis satisfactionem illius in codicem accepti referret, & gratuito nos à reatu mortis absoluerct, per integritatē illius & non simulatē sed reipsa obitam mortem: non aliter quàm si eius sanctitate sancti essemus, & ipsimet poenam peccatis nostris debitam subiiissemus. Idem esto iudicium de perfecta illa vtriusque tabulae Legis praestatio ne:cuius iustitia quum in vnica Iesu Christi persona reperiatur, & non in nobis, Pater eam nobis imputat eadem gratia, vt vitam aeternam nobis largiatur, nos in Filio suo dilecto non in nobis contemplans: sicuti contra, spon sore nostro percusso pro nobis, in illo nos intuitus quos a morte liberaret. Vt autem hanc imputationis doctrinam, quam vt ridiculam nonnulli exfibilant, certo niti fundamento conlter, istud fidei arcanum tenendum est, Iesu Christi persona licet a nostra persona semper distincta, sine vlla permixtione eius humanitatis essentialis cum nostra, quod sibi tamen plerique fingunt phanatici: tamen ex foederis formula, virtute Spiritus Sancti intrinseca & incomprehensibili ratione quadam spirituali, nulla tamen συσαφῆ substantiarum, nec locorum situ, ita vniri, atque adeo arcte coniungi cum omnibus cum vera fide tanquam manu quadam spirituali apprehendibus, vt ipse cum illis sit vnum corpus: id est aliquod totum spirituale & mysticum, non subitantiis corporum aut animarum coniunctum, quae sunt monstrosa commenta, & nihil habent cum hoc spirituali matrimonio commune: sed hac ratione vt quemadmodum vi & efficacia vnionis istius nos ipsi & quicquid habemus fimus ipsius, ita tamen vt nullam a nobis labem contrahat, ita vicissim per eandem imputationem, ipse cum omnibus suis thesauris fiat noster. Atque huius imputationis ararrham & sigillum verum & peculiare, Sacrosanctam Domini Cœnâ habemus, vt Deo reconciliemur & in Christo benedicamur, id est à morte liberemur, tanquam in ipso satisfe cerimus: & in illo digni vita æterna habeamur, propter sanctitatem naturæ nostræ quam assumpsit, & plenam Legis impletionem ab ipso factam: ad quæ tria capita, putà Satisfactionem, Naturæ nostræ integritatem seu sanctimoniam, & Legis impletionem, diximus gratuitam nostram iustificationem & imputationem referri.
units.tr: But someone may say: how can these things be ours which inhere in another's person, since a man does not live by another man's soul, nor is he righteous by another's righteousness? Here indeed we ought to wonder, here, I say, if anywhere else, at the admirable counsel of God in saving us. Since he found nothing in us but what provoked him against us, and nothing of those things which are required to reconcile him to us, he gave us his own Son, adorned with all those qualities which we have listed above, as our surety and guarantor. To him alone he imputed both our corruption and its fruits, and conversely reckoned his satisfaction to our account, and freely absolved us from the guilt of death, through his integrity and through death truly undergone, not feigned. It was as though we ourselves were holy by his holiness, and had ourselves undergone the punishment due to our sins. The same judgement holds concerning the perfect fulfilment of both tables of the Law: since its righteousness is found in the one person of Jesus Christ and not in us, the Father imputes it to us by the same grace, so that he may bestow eternal life upon us, regarding us not in ourselves but in his beloved Son. Likewise, conversely, when our surety was struck for us, he looked upon us in him, whom he would free from death. But so that this doctrine of imputation, which some mock as ridiculous, may be seen to rest on a sure foundation, this mystery of faith must be held: the person of Jesus Christ, although always distinct from our person and without any mingling of his essential humanity with ours, which nevertheless the fanatics fancy to be so, is yet united with all who apprehend him by true faith, as by a certain spiritual hand, by the form of the covenant, through the intrinsic power of the Holy Spirit and by a certain spiritual and incomprehensible manner. Yet this union is not by any confusion of substances, nor by any spatial position, so that he is one body with them, that is, a certain whole that is spiritual and mystical, joined not by the substances of bodies or souls, which are monstrous fictions and have nothing in common with this spiritual marriage. Rather, in such a way that, just as by the power and efficacy of this union we ourselves and whatever we have become his, yet in such a way that he contracts no stain from us, so in turn, by the same imputation, he himself with all his treasures becomes ours. And we have the pledge and the true and peculiar seal of this imputation in the most holy Supper of the Lord, so that we are reconciled to God and blessed in Christ, that is, freed from death, as we are seen to be satisfied in him, and in him we are counted worthy of eternal life, on account of the holiness of our nature which he assumed and the full fulfilment of the Law performed by him. To these three heads, namely satisfaction, the integrity or holiness of our nature, and the fulfilment of the Law, we said our free justification and imputation are to be referred.

units.la: Porrò quùnó in eum fine à peccatis absolvamur, vt iterū grauiore culpa Deū prouocemus, necabluamur, vt rursum coinquinemur: nec adDeum accedamus per Christū reconciliati, vt ab eo recilire pergamus, superioribus quartum nobis accedat oportet insigne Dei beneficium in eodem Domino nostro Iesu Christo, per veram fidem apprehenso ex conditione fœderi apposita.Ier.31.33.ne præcedentes gratiæ penitus irritæ fiat, sed plenum suum effectum finémque ad Dei gloriam & nostram salutem consequantur. Iltud est Regeneratio nostra, Christo nos ita sibi vnitos per sanctum suum Spiritum immutante, & nouas creaturas facientes: quod scriptura nouam creationem vocat. Gal.6.15.Ioh.3.6. non quòd aut corporum nostrorum aut animarum substantiæ, (vt somniant phanatici & male feriati quidam) sed tantùm qualitates immutentur, sine quibus gloriolæ immortalitatis participes fiēti nequeamus: moriente contrà paulatim in nobis naturali vitiositate, quam scriptura Veterem hominem dicit. Spiritualis autem hæc Regeneratio tribus potissimum de causis dicitur. Prima quòd Spir.S. hoc totum opus intrinsecum merito soli sibi vendicet: altera quòd illius ratio & modus auctori prorsus respondeat, spiritualis nimirum sit & nihil humani habeat nec naturale: tertia denique, quòd eius effectus etiam sit spiritualis, puta Renovatio animæ in omnibus ipsius qualitatibus & actionibus, tandemque vita spiritualis & æterna totius hominis sic regenerati. Habetis quartum beneficium ab eodem fonte quo tria superiora promanans, & ad eundem scopum collineans, à quibus tamen in hoc differt, quòd illa sunt extra nos, & in uno Christo: & tamen nostra fiunt imputatione: istud verò quartum beneficium intra nos est, & opus S. Sp. quod idcirco Regeneratio vocatur, quasi secundam creationem dicas, per Spir. Sanctum, carnali oppositam, ut pluribus cam Dominus. Ioh.3. & Apostoli in omnibus suis epistolis persequuntur. Sanctificatio etiam vocatur, eò quòd sanctos & puros efficiat, ad sanctitatis fructus ferendos, carnis operibus contrarios. Gal.5.19. Perperam autem cum imputata gratuita Iustificatione confunditur, quanuis adeò coniuncta sint hæc beneficia ut à se diuelli nulla ratione queant.
units.tr: Moreover, lest we be absolved from our sins only to provoke God again with a graver guilt, or be washed only to be defiled again, or come to God reconciled through Christ only to fall away from him once more, a fourth outstanding benefit of God must be added to those above. It is found in the same Lord Jesus Christ, grasped by true faith, and it comes from the condition of the covenant appended (Jer. 31:33), so that the preceding graces are not utterly made void but reach their full effect and end, to God's glory and our salvation. This is our regeneration, in which Christ, through his holy Spirit, so changes us, united to himself, and makes us new creatures. Scripture calls this a new creation (Gal. 6:15; John 3:6). This does not mean that the substance of our bodies or souls is changed, as some fanatics and half-mad people dream, but only the qualities, without which we cannot share in the glory of immortality. Meanwhile the natural viciousness that Scripture calls the Old Man gradually dies within us. This spiritual regeneration is called so chiefly for three reasons. First, the Holy Spirit rightly claims this whole inward work for himself alone. Second, its manner and mode correspond to its author: it is spiritual and has nothing human or natural in it. Third, its effect is also spiritual, namely the renewal of the soul in all its qualities and actions, and finally the spiritual and eternal life of the whole man so regenerated. You have the fourth benefit, flowing from the same source as the three above and aiming at the same goal. It differs from them in this: those are outside us and in Christ alone, yet they become ours by imputation; but this fourth benefit is within us, and is a work of the Holy Spirit. For this reason it is called regeneration, as if one were to say a second creation, wrought by the Holy Spirit and opposed to the carnal creation, as the Lord explains at length in John 3, and the Apostles pursue in all their epistles. It is also called sanctification, because it makes people holy and pure, able to bear the fruits of holiness, which are contrary to the works of the flesh (Gal. 5:19). It is wrongly confused with imputed free justification, although these benefits are so joined that they can in no way be separated from one another.

units.la: Ceterum ut quantum sit istud regenerationis beneficium, quatàque cum felicitate coniunctum melius adhuc intelligamus, quum ea vera sit electorum & iustificatorum, tandemq; glorificandorum nota: age singulas eius partes, Apostoli vestigiis inhaerentes, consideremus, prout illae nobis in Baptismi Sacramento repraesentantur. Rom. 6. 3. Ac primum quidem in prima nostra & carnali generatione occurrit natura nostra mortua in illa generali corruptione. Ephes. 2. 1. qua fit ut animus noster in tenebris mortis iaceat. Ephes. 4. 18. intellectus ineptus sit ad cogitandum ex sequae Dei sunt. 2. Cor. 3. 5. iudicium veritati divinae repugnans. Iacob. 4. 2. 1. Petr. 2. 11. & ad res spirituales penitus obtusum: voluntas vero captiua sit ad omnes prauas cupiditates. Rom. 7. 23. Deinde considerandi sunt huius corruptionis semper in deterius tuentis progressus: ac tandem etiam effectus, nimirum mors secunda, quae est aeterna condemnatio. Huic porro non tantum abolendo malo, sed etiam eius contrario stabiliendo, oppone eandem efficaciam Humanitatis Iesu Christi, qua factum est ut quo primum momento coepit oppugnare & vincere corruptionem non in se quidem haerentem, sed nostram quam in se aufumpserat, & Mortem, quam sponte subierat, quamque in ipsa sua penetralia, sepulchrum inquam perfecqui voluit, tandem expugnarit, sibique hac ratione via ad gloriosam suae carnis immortalitatem pararefecerit, quam nobis, in mundum venerat acquisiturus. Haec efficacia humanitatis Christi, a capite in reliqua membra sese effundens incipit ex quo primum illi fumus vera fide coniuncti Veterem hominem nostrum in nobis mortificare, & nouos fructus, primitias nouæ vitæ spiritualis, ab eius Morte procedentis, edere. Eadem in nobis perdetentim illam corruptionem sic abolet, vt, quemadmodum ipse in sepulchro & Mortis penetralibus cœptum opus perfecit, ita veteri nostro homine extincto, in nobis vim illam spiritualem augeat, tantifperdum, sicut ille per resurrectionem exutis omnibus caducæ huius vitæ infirmitatibus in gloriam Patris ingressus est, ita nos ad fe receptos vltimo die, gloriosæ illius suæ immortalitatis in anima & corpore faciat participes. Hinc illæ toties apud Apostolum repetitæ phrafes, nos in Christo mortuos esse, crucifixos, sepultos, & in eodem à mortuis excitatos: nos non amplius in nobis, sed illum in nobis viuere, viuificantem totum corpus Ecclesiæ, congruenter coagmentatum & compactum per omnes suppeditatas commissuras, ex vi intus agente pro mensura vniuscuiusque membri, ad totius corporis extructionem per charitatem Eph. 4.16. & vindicantem nos pedetentim à naturali seruitute peccati. Ioh. 8. 36. vt liberi fimus iustitiæ. Rom. 6. 16. illuminantem oculos nostri cordis, Ephef. 4. 18. & gradatim perficientem in nostri veteris hominis sepultura nostram sanctificationem 2. Corinth. 7. efficientem denique & velle & facere. Phil. 2. 13. En igitur fontem causas & effecta quarti illius beneficij neficij quod in Christo per Sp.S.suum in nobis agente, consequimur vt tandem hæredes Dei,coheredes autem eius efficiamur.Rom.8. 17.1.Pet.3.7.vsque adeò vt corpora etiam nostra nunc morti obnoxia, futura sint ipsius glorioso corpori conformia,Phil.2. 21. quum Deus erit omnia in omnibus. 1. Cor. 15. 28.sic Filio Patrem rogante & Patre Filium exaudiente, quum sit, Pater volo vt vbi ego sum, & illi sint mecum quos mihi dedisti. Ioh.17. 24. Huc porrò mecum mentem aduertite, ne Spiritus erroris insidiis, quas hic struit incautis,intercepti, non modò sint irriti nostri conatus dum bene agere tentamus,sed quod lógè maius est, Deo gratum opus facere cogitantes abominationi simus.
