units.tr: Furthermore, so that we may better understand how great this benefit of regeneration is, and how closely it is joined with happiness, since it is the true mark of the elect, the justified, and those to be finally glorified, let us take its parts one by one, following the Apostle's footsteps, as they are set before us in the Sacrament of Baptism (Rom. 6:3). First, in our first, carnal generation, our nature is found dead in that general corruption (Eph. 2:1), so that our mind lies in the darkness of death (Eph. 4:18). Our understanding is unfit to think those things that are of God (2 Cor. 3:5). Our judgment opposes divine truth (James 4:2; 1 Pet. 2:11) and is utterly dull toward spiritual things. Our will is captive to every depraved desire (Rom. 7:23). Next we must consider the progress of this corruption, always going from bad to worse, and finally its effect, namely the second death, which is eternal condemnation. Now, to abolish this evil, and to establish its contrary, set against it the same efficacy of the humanity of Jesus Christ. From the first moment he began to attack and conquer corruption (not clinging to himself, but to the nature he had assumed), and death, which he had undergone willingly and wished to pursue into its very innermost recesses, that is the tomb, he at last overcame it. In this way he prepared for himself a path to the glorious immortality of his flesh, which he had come into the world to acquire for us. This efficacy of Christ's humanity, pouring forth from the head into the other members, begins from the moment we are first joined to him by true faith: to mortify in us the Old Man, and to produce new fruits, the firstfruits of the new spiritual life proceeding from his Death. The same efficacy gradually abolishes that corruption in us, so that, just as he himself completed the work begun in the tomb and in the innermost parts of death, so, with our old man extinguished, it increases that spiritual power within us. Then, just as he rose again, having cast off all the infirmities of this fleeting life, and entered into the Father's glory, so he will receive us to himself on the last day and make us sharers of that glorious immortality of his, in soul and body. Hence those phrases so often repeated by the Apostle: that we have died in Christ, been crucified, buried, and raised from the dead in him; that we no longer live in ourselves, but he lives in us, quickening the whole body of the Church, fitly joined and knit together through every supplied joint, by an inward power working according to the measure of each member, for the building up of the whole body in love (Eph. 4:16); and that he gradually sets us free from the natural bondage of sin (John 8:36), so that we become free for righteousness (Rom. 6:16), enlightens the eyes of our heart (Eph. 1:18), gradually perfects our sanctification in the burial of our old man (2 Cor. 7:1), and finally both gives us the will and works in us the deed (Phil. 2:13). Here, then, is the source, the causes and the effects of that fourth benefit, which we obtain in Christ, through his Spirit working in us, so that at last we are made heirs of God and co-heirs with him (Rom. 8:17; 1 Pet. 3:7). So far does this go that even our bodies, now subject to death, will be made conformable to his glorious body (Phil. 3:21), when God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28). Thus the Son asks the Father, and the Father hears the Son: Father, I desire that where I am, there they also may be with me, whom you have given me (John 17:24). Moreover, mark this with me, lest, caught in the snares of the spirit of error, which he lays for the incautious, not only our endeavours, while we try to do good, be made void, but, far worse, we, thinking we are doing a work pleasing to God, become an abomination.

units.la: In has insidias primùm incurrunt, qui naturæ corruptio quanta sit ignorantes, fingūt in homine vim quandam naturalem inesse cuius ductu quæ de Deo scienda sunt cognoscat, cuius etiam voluntatem, præceptis eius præsertim edoctus,impleat.Quod sanè dogma non modò salsissimum est,& merito in Ecclesia damnatum, quandoquidem supernaturale gratiam euertit,ac proinde quæcunque nobis in Christo beneficia conferuntur: sed etiam non minùs ridiculum,quàm siquis dixerit cæcum natum cognitam habere viam quà sit iter ingressurus, tutiùs tamen ambulaturum si præmonstrata fuerit.
units.tr: Those first fall into these snares who, ignorant of how great the corruption of nature is, imagine that some natural power is present in man, by whose guidance he knows what must be known about God, and who, especially when taught by God's precepts, fulfils his will. This dogma is not only most unsound and rightly condemned in the Church, since it overturns supernatural grace and therefore all the benefits conferred on us in Christ. It is also no less ridiculous than if someone said that a man born blind already has a known way by which he will set out on his journey, and would walk more safely if it were pointed out to him beforehand.

units.la: Hinc à fidelibus Dei seruis depulsus Satan, alia fraude plerosque aggressus incautos. fallit, fefcellitque olim ,persuadens illis, mentem quidem nostram maximis tenebris circumfusam, longéque maiorem adhuc ἀπλξίαν in animæ partem sensitiuam peruasisse: superesse tamen aliquid Lucis in mente, & inclinationem aliquam ad verum bonúmque sequédum, quod Liberum arbitrium dicunt: quod à gratia supernaturali præuentum & concomitatum, veras de Dei cognitione conclusiones in mente producat, & voluntatis nostræ debilitatem ad bonum corroboret, vt velit & operetur quæ Deus à fidelibus postulat & requirit. Itaque siquis ipsorum opinionem locus est, necessariò statuendum est veram salutis nostræ notitiam & bona opera partim humanis viribus partim gratiæ deberi, sine qua natura nostra foret ad bonum inhabilis. Est quidem sanè magis fucatus & dissimulatus hic error, quàm ille superior, sed qui tamen ab illo parum aut nihil omnino differat, nisi quòd prior ille totum humanis viribus, hic verò alter partem gratiæ, partem humanis viribus attribuit.
units.tr: Satan, driven away from the faithful servants of God, has attacked many incautious people with another deceit. He has deceived them, and long ago deceived them, persuading them that our mind, indeed, is surrounded by the greatest darkness, and that a far greater insensibility [ἀναισθησίαν] has taken hold of the sensitive part of the soul. Yet some light remains in the mind, and some inclination to pursue the true and the good, which they call free will. This, prevented and accompanied by supernatural grace, produces true conclusions about the knowledge of God in the mind, and strengthens the weakness of our will for good, so that it wills and does what God demands and requires of the faithful. Thus, if one follows their opinion, it must necessarily be held that the true knowledge of our salvation and our good works are owed partly to human powers and partly to grace, without which our nature would be unfit for good. This error is indeed more disguised and concealed than the earlier one, but it differs little or not at all from it, except that the former attributes everything to human powers, while this latter attributes part to grace and part to human powers.

units.la: Vt autem abistiusmodi Satanæ salebris periculosissimis, & saluti viam præcludentibus nobis cauere discamus, duo sunt nobis cognitu necessaria. Horum primum est discrimé inter reliquias notitiæ illius de Deo, post peccatum in homine, & facultatem discernendi vitium à virtute: & cognitionem salutarem de Deo & eius voluntate, cui caro & sanguis resistit, tantùm abest vt à natura dispositionem
units.tr: But so that we may learn to beware of these most dangerous snares of Satan, which block the way to our salvation, two things must be known. The first is the difference between the remnants of that knowledge of God which remain in man after sin, and the faculty of distinguishing vice from virtue. The saving knowledge of God and of his will, which flesh and blood resists, is so far from being something we have by nature that we have no disposition

units.la: sivllam habeamus illa cognoscedi & sequendi. Rom.7.7.Alterum est,quo sensu dicamus hominis arbitrium non liberum, sed seruum, ac proinde in peccatis mortuum, donec à sola gratia, non quidem corroborante,sed vitium quod à natura nobis inhæret mortificante in libertatem asseramur: quæ age sigillatim expendamus.
units.tr: at all to know and follow it. (Rom. 7.7.) The second is the sense in which we say that the human will is not free but a slave, and so dead in sins, until it is set free by grace alone. That grace does not strengthen the vice which clings to us by nature, but mortifies it. Let us weigh these points one by one.

units.la: Quòd ad prius illud, fatcor in homine ge- neralem quandam Deitatis notitiam esse reli- quam, eámque ex rerum omnium creatarum superarunt, mediarum infimarúmque etiam contemplatione foueri atque conseruari. In sculpsit enim Deus in cœlo & terra veluti maioribus characteribus,&in minimis quibusque rebus creatis suam æternitate:est enim Creator re creata prior: suam Omnipotentiam, sine qua mundus nec creari olim potuisset nec adhuc hodie regeretur:Omnisapientiam,quæ in tot rerum creatarum varietate, dispositione & administratione resplendet: Immensam bonitatem, quòd quum nullius egeat,à nullo moueri potuerit ad hæc creanda nisi sola sua ipsius bonitate. Hoc à mundi sapientibus, quos Philosophos dicūt,visum est & animad-uersum,& multis egregiis sententiis celebratū sed illud imprimis Apostolus, præter tot psalmos & diuina cantica magnificis verbis imò diuinis docet primo cap:epist.ad Rom.& Act. Apost.cap.17.Sed parum illa naturalis cognitio mortales iuuat,quum videamus Sapientissimos quosquè inter Ethnicos bonis illis fundamentis delira & ridicula multa superstru-xisse. Quid enim de inuecta Deorum multitudine, de eorum coiugiis, de infinitorum Deorum gradibus aliud statuendum, quid denique de tot monstris quæ vix tradita & credita nobis persuaderi patiamur, nisi illud totius antiquitatis monumenta testarentur? Nec enim illa sunt in vulgus aut in ignaram plebem reiicienda, quum non aliam fuisse toto orbe terrarum religionem luce lit clarius: Excipe tamen populum illum Dei, melius edoctu, Patriarcharum nimirum documentis eruditum, & vestigiis ipsorum inhærentem. Adde quòd qui hæc coarguerunt figmenta, non melius tamen de Deitate senserunt, sed magnis erroribus in doctrina de Deitate sunt impliciti.
units.tr: As to the first, I admit that a general knowledge of the Deity remains in man, and that it is nourished and preserved by the contemplation of all created things, both the middling and the lowest. For God has engraved his eternity in heaven and earth as with larger letters, and in even the smallest created things; for the Creator is prior to what is created. He has engraved his omnipotence, without which the world could not once have been created nor is it still governed today; his omniscience, which shines forth in the great variety, arrangement and government of created things; and his immense goodness, in that, since he needs nothing, he could have been moved to create these things by nothing but his own goodness. The wise men of the world, whom they call philosophers, have seen and noticed this, and have praised it in many excellent sayings. But the Apostle teaches it above all, in magnificent, indeed divine, words, besides so many psalms and divine canticles (Rom. 1; Acts 17). Yet that natural knowledge helps mortals little, since we see that the wisest among the heathens built many absurd and ridiculous things upon those good foundations. For what else can be said of the imported multitude of gods, of their marriages, of the infinite grades of gods, or finally of so many monsters, which we could scarcely be persuaded to believe if they were handed down and believed among us, unless the monuments of all antiquity bore witness to them? Nor are these things to be dismissed as the talk of the common people or of an ignorant crowd, since it is clearer than light that the whole world had no other religion. Except that people of God, better taught, namely instructed by the teachings of the Patriarchs and clinging to their footsteps. Add that those who refuted these fictions did not think better of the Deity, but were entangled in great errors concerning the doctrine of the Deity.

units.la: Præterea tantùm abest vt illis salutaris hæc cognitio fuerit, vt contra quò maiorem diuinæ Maiestatis potentiam & puritatem agnouerunt, tantò maiorem ab ea recedendi occasionem habuerint, nisi Dei naturæ prorsus repugnantes cultus comminiscentes, illum rebus caducis & vanis oblationibus hominum ritu placare studuissent: quod vitium etiam Prophetæ passim populo Dei reliquarum prophanarum gentium ritu fascinato & erranti grauissimis increpationibus exprobrarunt.
units.tr: Moreover, that knowledge was so far from being saving for them that, the greater the power and purity of the divine Majesty they recognised, the greater occasion they had for turning away from it. They devised worship utterly repugnant to the nature of God, and tried to placate him with transitory and empty offerings, in the manner of men. The Prophets everywhere rebuked this fault in the people of God with the gravest reproaches, since that people had been bewitched and led astray by the customs of the other profane nations.

units.la: De posteriore verò, quod est de electione virtutis aut vitij, boni vel mali, nos quoque fatemur Deum, quum genus humanum vellet conseruare, ex quo suos electos sumeret, in hominum conscientia quædam vestigia, superiori-bus bus illis adhuc maio ra,rectitudinis illius quæ pars erat imaginis Dei reliquisse : adeo vt qui Deum in Lege sua loquentem nunquam audiuerũt,ipsi sibi Lex sint, cogitationibus corũ mutuo se accusantibus aut excusantibus : cuius rei testes sunto multorum insignium Philosophorum libri : tot etiam præclaræ leges quibus virtus laudatur,vitiis vero pœnæ constituuntur? Quid tum vero?Primum Sapientibus illis inter se non bene de plerisque conuenit : cuius rei argumento sunt tot iniquæ Leges etiā inter eas gentes quæ prudentissimæ putatæ sunt, latæ & in vsu habitæ. Deinde in hoc maximè defectus apparet,quod omnis illa cognitio,nisi ad eam aliquid aliud accedat, non meliores nos,sed contra peiores facit,donec Deus afflatu Sp.S.& gratia sua supernaturali,faciat in nobis Velle & Facere,vt superius dictum est. Nulla enim res magis accendit hominis ad malũ concupiscentiā, quàm prohibitio ne concupiscat, siue conscientia ipsa, siue alius quispiam id prohibeat:quod ipsum Apostolus de se etiam Legis diuinæ respectu tentatur Rom. 7.9. Inde natũ vetus illud tritissimum verissimúmque prouerbium, Nitimur in vetitum semper , cupimúsquè negata. Nam siqui in mundo præclaris dotibus & virtutibus præ aliis excelluerunt,(fuerunt autem,etsi pauci illi quidem , attamen non exigua laude dignissimi viri non pauci à quibus ex hodiernis Christianis hypocritæ multi coarguuntur) non tamen à regenerationis gra-
units.tr: As to the second point, namely the choice of virtue or vice, good or evil, we too confess that God, when he wished to preserve the human race, from which he would take his elect, left certain traces in the conscience of men of that uprightness which was part of the image of God, traces which were still greater than those of the earlier times. So much so that those who never heard God speaking in his Law are a law to themselves, their thoughts accusing or excusing one another. Let the books of many distinguished philosophers be witnesses to this, and so many excellent laws by which virtue is praised and punishments fixed for vices. What then? First, those wise men did not agree well among themselves on most matters; the proof of this is the many unjust laws, enacted and in use, even among those nations thought most prudent. Second, the greatest defect appears in this: that all such knowledge, unless something else is added to it, does not make us better but, on the contrary, worse, until God, by the breath of the Holy Spirit and his supernatural grace, makes in us the Will and the Deed, as was said above. For nothing so inflames a man's desire for evil as a prohibition, whether it comes from conscience itself or from someone else. The Apostle himself experienced this with respect to the divine Law (Rom. 7.9). Hence that old, very worn and very true proverb: "We strive for what is forbidden, and we desire what is denied." For if some in the world excelled others in outstanding gifts and virtues (there were such, though few, and men truly deserving of no small praise, not a few of whom expose many of today's Christians as hypocrites), still those virtues did not flow from the grace of regeneration, which is proper to the only sons of God, but because God was pleased to restrain in them the fruit of corrupt nature, and not to root it out entirely, for the preservation of orders and families on this earth, by the decree of his will. This is clear from the histories of every age. Therefore let us conclude this point with the Apostle, indeed with truth itself, confirmed by long experience (Rom. 1.20 and 32): those virtues are the ruins of the marks of the image of God, but they make us all the more inexcusable before the Lord; just as a mirror, the more brightly it shines, the better it reveals the stains which it nevertheless cannot wash away.

units.la: d. iij. tia, vnicorum filiorum Dei propria, virtutes illæ manarunt, sed quòd Deo fructus naturæ corruptæ in illis coercere, non autem radice penitus amputare placuerit ad ordinum familiarumque in his terris conseruationem ex suæ voluntatis placito: quod exsingulorum seculorum historiis perspicuum est. Quapropter hunc locum concludamus cum Apostolo, immo cum ipsa veritate longo usu comprobata. Rom. 1.20. & 32. virtutes illas imaginis Dei insignia esse rudera, sed quibus magis inexcusabiles coram Domino reddamur: quemadmodum speculum quo splendidius est co melius indicat maculas quas minime tamen eluit.
units.tr: I come to the second head, in what sense we say that man, enslaved to sin, is born and before regeneration has no free will for either good or evil, against the Semipelagians. They divide grace, assigning to man a part that is natural or animal (as the Apostle puts it, 1 Cor. 2.14), that is, such as man was born after the fall of Adam, and assigning to him another part of grace, which is conferred in Christ our true and only liberator (John 8.36). We do not say that through original sin man has lost the rational soul as to its essence, or as to its faculties of reasoning, or of drawing this or that conclusion from causes, since men still hold and teach the science of that faculty which they call Logic. Nor do we turn them into trunks or stumps

units.la: Ad alterum caput accedo, quo sensu dicamus hominem peccato mancipatum nasci nec habere liberam ad malum aut bonum voluntatem, ante regenerationem aduersus Semipelagianos, qui gratiam Dei diuidentes partem homini naturali siue animali, (ut loquitur Apostolus 1.Cor.2.14.)(id est qualis natus est Adami lapsum) partem vero gratiæ illi tribuunt quæ in Christo vero nostro soloque liberatore Ioh.8.36. confertur. Nos vero non dicimus hominem per peccatum originale animam rationalem quoad ipsius essentiam amisisse, aut quoad facultates ratiocinandi, aut ex causis hoc vel illud colligendi, quandoquidem homines huius facultatis scientiam tenent docentque, quam Logicam vocant. Nec illos etiam in truncos aut stipites trans-
units.tr: I come now to the second point: in what sense we say that man, enslaved to sin, is born without free will toward good or evil before regeneration. This is against the Semipelagians, who divide grace, granting to natural or animal man (as the Apostle calls him, 1 Cor. 2.14, that is, as he is born since the fall of Adam) one part, and attributing the other part of grace to him, the part conferred in Christ our true and only deliverer, John 8.36. We, however, do not say that through original sin man has lost the rational soul in its essence, or in its faculties of reasoning, or in its power to draw this or that conclusion from causes, since men still hold and teach the science of this faculty, which they call Logic. Nor do we turn them into trunks or stumps.

units.la: Quæ hominis ante regenerationem conditio, cum in intellige tia tum in voluntate. transmutamus, vt nulla ad hoc vel eligēdū vel fugiendum volūtate & προαιρέσει ferantur. Fanaticorum enim & amentium istud foret.Sed cum tota Scriptura & communi experientia docemus in rerum diuinarum quidem notitia mentem humanam magnis tenebris inuolutā & obscuratam, vt superius diximus: atque adeo scintillas illas lucis reliquas in hominum mente statim eum deserere, & quum maximè iuuare deberet deficere: At in eo quod præcipuum est, nempe tam in cognitione essentiæ Dei quantum eam vult Deus à nobis ad salutem cognosci, quàm in nostræ perditionis agnitione, veróque aduersus eandem remedio, tantùm abesse vt mens nostra viribus naturalibus ante regenerationem aliquid perspiciat vt contrà ad veritatis huius radios plane caecutiat. Quòd si mens, quam nostræ voluntatis atque adeò omnium affectuum moderatrice esse oportuit, eum non tantùm ignorat ad quem tanquam ad vnicum verum scopum illa omnia referenda sunt, vt bene velit quod vult, sed contrarium etiam sibi persuadet, quinam, obsecro, dicas in huius voluntatis motibus aliquid inesse puritatis? Non animā igitur homo, nec eius facultates amisit sine quibus amplius homo non esset: verùm lucem mentis eo quē diximus respectu perdidit, vnà cum voluntatis & affectionum integritate: quorum recuperandi potestatem non habet, nisi illi eadem diuina virtute Sp. S. cum Patre
units.tr: The condition of man before regeneration, both in understanding and in will, is not so changed that he is carried by no will either to choose or to shun this or that, and by no choice [προαίρεσις]. For that would be the view of fanatics and madmen. But since the whole of Scripture and common experience teach us that the human mind is wrapped in great darkness and obscured in the knowledge of divine things, as we said above, and that those remaining sparks of light in the human mind immediately fail it and give out just when they ought most to help, then in what is chief, namely in the knowledge of God's essence, so far as God wills that we know it for salvation, and in the recognition of our own perdition and of the remedy against it, our mind by its natural powers before regeneration perceives so little that, on the contrary, it is plainly blinded to the rays of this truth. But if the mind, which ought to be the moderator of our will and indeed of all the affections, not only does not know Him to whom all these things must be referred as the one true goal, so that it wills well what it wills, but even persuades itself of the contrary, then what purity, I beg you, can you say is present in the movements of this will? Man therefore has not lost his soul, nor those faculties without which he would no longer be man; but he has lost the light of the mind in the respect we have mentioned, together with the integrity of the will and the affections. He has no power to recover these unless they are restored to him by the same divine power of the Holy Spirit, together with the Father and the Son, who are co-eternal, and from whom in the beginning of creation he had received them, and with whom their soul had been adorned.

units.la: d. iiij. & Filio coæterni restituantur,à quo ab initio creationis eadé acceperât,& quibus eorū anima ornata fuerat.Exempli gratia,quandoquidem qui Filium non habet Patrem non habet, qui autem nec Patrem nec Filium nouit nullum Deum nouit,Ioh. 8.19. Ephef. 2. 11.quam dixerimus esse naturalis hominis de Deo notitiam? Quòd si cato & sanguis non reuelant nobis Christum Filium Dei viuentis,quomodo partim naturali notitiæ istud acceptum feremus,partim gratiæ?Matth.16.17.Huc nos etiam egregiæ illæ sententiæ deducunt, Deum nemo vidit vnquam,vnigenitus ille filius q ui est in sinu Patris, ille exposuit. Ioh. 1. 18. Quibus vero? nempe iis quos Filio Pater donat. Ioh.17.6.Nemo potest ad me venire,nisi Pater cum trahat. Ioh. 6.44. id est,nisi cui Deus cor aperuerit vt Dei sermonem intelligat. Act.16. 14.Homo animalis non capit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Sunt enim ei stultitia, nec potest ea cognoscere,quia Spiritualiter diiudicantur.1. Cor.2. 14. φρόνημα carnis (id est homo,vt alibi loquitur, animalis) est inimicitia aduersus Deum:Nec enim Dei Legi subiicitur,nec etiā potest. Rom.8.7. Non sumus idonei ex nobis ipsis ad cogitādum quicquam, velut ex nobis ipsis:sed quod idonei sumus ex Deo est.2.Cor. 3.5. Christus crucifixus est Iudæis scandalum, & Græcis stultitia.1. Cor.1. 18.quocirca Esaias vociferabatur, Cui reuelatum est brachium Domini? Denique vox hæc Regenerationis Spiritus, Generationi carnali opposita Ioh. 3. 6. facis dilucidè in hoc toto negotio ostendit, non minùs absurdum esse siquis doceat naturam nostram cum Dei gratia in hoc dono concurrere & cooperari, quo simus noua creatura, quàm siquis dixerit ante suam creationem autin ipso creationis actu hominem cum suo creatore cooperatum à se suum Esse, id est Ortus sui principium habere. Præterea quod sæpe Apostolus inculcat Spiritum Dei nos in peccatis nostris mortuos reperire, satis aperte demonstrat Spiritum Dei regenerare nos incipientem, nullam vitam in nobis reperire, nec motum vllum quem adiuuet aut comitetur, quod si quis contrà sentiat, non minùs sit absurdus & ridiculus, quàm siquis in cadauere facultates inesse respirandi, intelligendi, sentiendi & sese mouendi pertinaciter asseueraret. Fatemur quidem Mentem depulsa caligine illustratam Dei Spiritu & regenitam intelligere: veluti cæcus visu recuperato, videt: fatemur etiam ea nos credere, velle & facere, quæ credere, velle & facere iubemur, pro portione ac mensura Spiritus Dei habitantis in nobis: sed vt noui homines facti, per solam illam gratiam immutantem corda nostra lapidea in carnea per Sancti sui Spiritus gratiam supernaturalem. Ezechiel. 11. 19. & 36. 26. qui dat nobis vt credamus, Ephef. 2. 8. & etiam potestatem volendi & faciendi. Philip. 2. 13.
units.tr: restored to the Father and the Son, co-eternal, from whom at the beginning of creation they had received the same gifts, and with which their soul had been adorned. For example, since whoever does not have the Son does not have the Father, and whoever knows neither the Father nor the Son knows no God (John 8:19; Eph. 2:11), how can we say that there is any natural knowledge of God in man? But if flesh and blood do not reveal to us Christ the Son of the living God, how shall we attribute part of that knowledge to nature and part to grace? (Matt. 16:17). Those excellent sayings also lead us to the same conclusion: No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him (John 1:18). But to whom? Namely, to those whom the Father gives to the Son (John 17:6). No one can come to me unless the Father draw him (John 6:44), that is, unless God has opened the heart of the one to understand God's word (Acts 16:14). The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; they are foolishness to him, nor can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned (1 Cor. 2:14). The mind of the flesh [φρόνημα σαρκός] (that is, the man whom elsewhere he calls natural) is enmity against God; for it is not subject to God's law, nor indeed can it be (Rom. 8:7). We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God (2 Cor. 3:5). Christ crucified is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks (1 Cor. 1:18); wherefore Isaiah cried out: To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? Finally, this phrase, the Spirit of regeneration, set against carnal generation (John 3:6), shows clearly throughout this whole matter that it is no less absurd to teach that our nature concurs and cooperates with God's grace in this gift by which we become a new creation, than it would be to say that before his creation, or in the very act of creation, man cooperated with his Creator in producing his own being, that is, in having the origin of his existence. Moreover, what the Apostle so often impresses, that the Spirit of God finds us dead in our sins, demonstrates quite plainly that the Spirit of God, when he begins to regenerate us, finds in us no life and no motion which he might help or accompany; and if anyone thinks otherwise, he is no less absurd and ridiculous than someone who stubbornly asserted that a corpse has the faculties of breathing, understanding, feeling and moving itself. We do indeed grant that the mind, with the darkness driven away, is illuminated and regenerated by the Spirit of God and understands, just as a blind man whose sight has been recovered sees. We grant too that we believe, will and do those things which we are commanded to believe, will and do, in proportion and measure to the Spirit of God dwelling in us; but this is so as new men made by that grace alone which changes our stony hearts into fleshy ones, through the supernatural grace of his Holy Spirit (Ezek. 11:19; 36:26), who gives us to believe (Eph. 2:8) and also the power of willing and doing (Phil. 2:13).

units.la: Alterum illud periculum quod nobis summopere cauendum prælmonui, ne in bonorum operum doctrina circumuceniamur, in eo positum est ne nobis imponi sinamus, luci tenebras anteponentes. Facilè autem in hunc errorem abducimur pietatis & humilitatis quadam specie, quæ, vt inquit Apostolus, Col. 2. 23. rationem quidem habent sapientiæ in cultu voluntario, & summissione animi, & in eo quod corpori non parcant, nec eorum rationem habeant quibus farcitur caro, sed caput non retinent: quod videlicet istius dogmatis authores in ea se quæ non viderunt, ingerunt, & temerè vanis suis cogitationibus & commentis inflati, ea sibi arrogat, quæ soli nostrarum conscientiarum Legislatori & suæ Ecclesiæ capiti conueniunt & peculiaria sunt. Hinc sensim in Ecclesiam innumeri ritus inuecti sunt, quos falso traditionum Apostolicarum nomine venditant: quorum alij sunt Christianorum omnium: alij vero Religiosorum istorum scilicet conscientias peculiariter astringunt. Et quidem horum rituum, alij sunt mera delicia & ludicra, alij, vel ab origine sua, vel propter falsas quæ irrepserunt opiniones, tam ridiculæ superstitiones, quàm verus cultus exi-stimantur: alij denique fœda & abominanda idololatria, quæ quod Dei proprium est & Domini nostri Iesu Christi, falso prætextu Deum & Sanctos eius venerandi, ad infimas & vilissimas etiam res creatas transfertur. Quibus omnibus tam intolerandis erroribus, hęc oppo nunnuntur:Primùm quæcunque Deus olim variis vicibus per Prophetas Ecclesiæ suæ facienda & pro viribus tentanda præceperat ad salu- tem,eorum Dominum nostrum nihil omisisse nec quicquam reticuisse quin ea omnia primùm ore suo discipulis suis nota fecerit, Ioh. 15.15. deinde per Apostolos nobis eadé patefecerit, quos officio diligenter esse functos certū est, nihil eorum omittentes quæ ad illud præstandum requirebantur:nec etiam iis quicquá adiicientes quæ à Domino primùm audiue- rant,& quæ à Sp.S. non tanquam noua & inaudita dicebātur,sed eis in memoriā audita revocabantur. Matt.28.20. Ioh.16.13. 1.Cor.11.23. & 7.31. & 1.Pet.5.3. Deinde fideliter ipsos eadem monumentis scripta reliquisse, vt ex iis perfectus reddatur homo Dei, id est, qui Doctoris vices in Ecclesia debet obire. 2. Tim.3. 17. Denique quum Iesus Christus Filius unicus Dei paternæ domus curam omnem gerat, potestatemque habeat in cœlo & in terra. Iac. 4.12. non licet cuiquam,ac ne Angelis quidem ipsis quicquam ad filij doctrinam, & domus administrationem adiicere. Gal.1.8. quod qui aufert non immeritò fit Antichristus. Idcirco etiam sub vetere fœdere,licet imperfecto,non abs re per Esaiam Deus veterem populum obiurgabat,quòd colerent & timerent ipsum mandato & doctrinis hominum. Es. 29.13. & Esa.1.12. Quis, inquit, ista requisiuit ex manibus vestris?Idipsum Pharisæis Christus exprobrat.Matth.15 9.Quis vero tam demens est qui existimet Christum hoc tempore maiore de- disse potestatem iis qui longè deteriora in Dei Ecclesiam inuexerunt,& adhuc hodie suis rta ditionibus pessundare Dei mandata non desi- nunt, quàm fecerit olim Pharisæis? Denique quum obedientia præcepto nitatur, quinam hoc deficiente illam stabilias? Sed quid agas? Tales isti sunt humiles superbi, quos quum propria conscientia coarguat nullum esse in diuinis præceptis, ac ne minimum quidem quod vel sanctissimus quisque perfectè possit adimplere, non pudet tamen sperare, sibíque in animum inducere posse se plura quàm iu- beantur facientes vel ipsum cœlum perrum- pere. Quod quidem de iis qui specie quadam pietatis falluntur, non autem de impuris illis & perfristæ frontis hypocrstis dictum esto.
units.tr: The other danger, which I have warned you above all must be guarded against, is that we be deceived in the teaching of good works, by allowing ourselves to be imposed upon and by putting darkness before light. We are easily led into this error under a certain appearance of piety and humility, which, as the Apostle says, Col. 2:23, indeed have a show of wisdom in voluntary worship, in humility of mind, and in not sparing the body, nor in regarding the things with which the flesh is filled, yet they do not hold to the Head. Clearly the authors of this teaching thrust into things they have not seen, and, puffed up without reason by their own vain thoughts and inventions, claim for themselves those things which belong to the sole Lawgiver of our consciences and to his Church, his Head, and are peculiar to him. Hence countless rites have crept gradually into the Church, which they peddle under the false name of Apostolic traditions. Some of these belong to all Christians; others peculiarly bind the consciences of those religious men. Of these rites, some are sheer pleasures and trifles; some, either from their origin or because of false opinions which have crept in, are considered as ridiculous superstitions as they are a true worship; and finally some are foul and abominable idolatry, which, under the false pretext of venerating God and his saints, is transferred to the lowest and most worthless created things, though it is the proper due of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ. Against all these intolerable errors the following is set forth. First, whatever God in former times, in various ways through the Prophets, had commanded his Church to do and to attempt according to its powers for salvation, our Lord has omitted nothing of this nor kept anything back, but first made all of it known to his disciples by his own mouth (John 15:15); then through the Apostles he has revealed the same things to us, who certainly discharged their office diligently, omitting nothing of what was required for that task, nor adding anything to what they had first heard from the Lord; and those things which were not spoken by the Holy Spirit as new and unheard of, but were recalled to memory as things heard before (Matt. 28:20; John 16:13; 1 Cor. 11:23; 7:31; 1 Pet. 5:3). Then they faithfully left these things written in documents, so that through them the man of God may be made complete, that is, one who ought to discharge the office of teacher in the Church (2 Tim. 3:17). Finally, since Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, has all the care of his Father's house and power in heaven and on earth (James 4:12), it is not lawful for anyone, not even for the Angels themselves, to add anything to the doctrine of the Son and the administration of his house (Gal. 1:8); whoever takes away from it is not without reason made an Antichrist. For this reason also, under the Old Covenant, though imperfect, God rightly rebuked his ancient people through Isaiah, because they worshipped and feared him by the commandment and doctrines of men (Isa. 29:13; Isa. 1:12). Who, he says, has required these things at your hands? Christ reproached the Pharisees with the same thing (Matt. 15:9). But who is so foolish as to think that Christ at this time has given greater power to those who have brought far worse things into God's Church, and who still today do not cease to overthrow God's commandments by their own traditions, than he once gave to the Pharisees? Finally, since obedience rests on precept, who could establish it with that precept lacking? But what can you do? Such men are humble proud men, who, though their own conscience convicts them that there is nothing in the divine precepts, not even the smallest thing, which even the most holy man could perfectly fulfil, are not ashamed nonetheless to hope, and to persuade themselves, that they can by doing more than they are commanded even break through heaven itself. This, indeed, is said of those who are deceived by a certain appearance of piety, not of those impure and brazen-faced hypocrites.

units.la: Accedo iam ad tertium illud maximum & grauissimum periculum, quod est de bono- rum operum exLegis ipsius diuinæ præscri- pto & à Regeneratis duce S.Spiritus gratia sa- ctorum meritis & dignitate. Quantum enim falsi isti doctores bonis operibus tribuunt,tan tùm de vnici nostri Redemp. Christi puritate, satisfactione,obedientia detrahunt, docentes vitam æternam operibus nostris tanquâ mer- cedem condignam & congruam deberi. Sic Christi sanguis non erit Redemptionis no- stræ vnicum pretium, nec Iesus vnicus noster Iesus,id est Seruator, sed ita nos iustificauerit, vt precedentia fidem peccata quidem delue- rit,
units.tr: I now come to that third, greatest and most grievous danger, which concerns the worth and dignity of good works, which are done under the prescription of the divine Law itself and by the grace of the Holy Spirit leading the regenerate. For these false teachers attribute as much to good works as they take away from the purity, satisfaction and obedience of our one Redeemer Christ, teaching that eternal life is owed to our works as a fitting and suitable reward. Thus the blood of Christ will not be the sole price of our redemption, nor will Jesus be our sole Jesus, that is, Saviour, but he will have justified us in such a way that he has indeed wiped away the sins that preceded faith, and afterwards has made us fit to save ourselves, through works that follow faith.

units.la: Quæ sit bonorum operum dignitas. rit,deinceps vero nos idoneos nobis ipsis fer-uandis fecerit, per opera fidem subsequentia. Tandem vero ne prorsus Christum excludere videantur, addunt merita illa omnia ex Christi merito proficisci, nostra promouentis & gratiam illis conciliantis. Ita Christus erit, vt in Scholis loquuntur prima causa efficiens & supplementum nostrae salutis, quam alioqui noltris etiam viribus efficimus. Falsum dogma,impium,blasphemum, ex diametro repugnans Euangelicae doctrinae, quae docet nos in vno Iesu Christo, & per illum solum fide apprehensum iustificari: non ex Legis obedientia quam nos praestiterimus, sed quam Iesus plenissime pro nobis adimpleuit, sicut copiose iam supra docuimus. Miror autem qui fieri possit, vt quum Apostolus, tam sedulò, tam accuratè, tam viliter, tam denique diuinè istum errorem oppugnarit, inueniantur tamen quos (si modò cum iudicio vel a limine sacras literas salutarint)aduersus praecipuum caput officij Domini nostri Iesu Christi disputare non pudeat.
units.tr: What the worth of good works is. Finally, lest they seem to exclude Christ altogether, they add that all those merits proceed from the merit of Christ, who advances ours and wins grace for them. So Christ will be, as they speak in the Schools, the first efficient cause and the supplement of our salvation, which otherwise we bring about by our own strength as well. This is a false, impious and blasphemous doctrine, flatly opposed to the Gospel teaching, which teaches that we are justified in the one Jesus Christ and through him alone, apprehended by faith: not by obedience to the Law which we have performed, but which Jesus most fully fulfilled for us, as we have taught at length above. But I wonder how it can happen that, although the Apostle has assailed this error so diligently, so carefully, so earnestly, and finally so divinely, there are still found those who (if indeed they have greeted the sacred letters with judgment, at least from the threshold) are not ashamed to dispute against the chief point of the office of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Aio igitur voces illas Merendi & Meriti, quibus veteres Latini Patres vsi sunt longe alio sensu quàm Doctores Scholastici, nisi tribus his conditionibus in Ecclesia locum habere non possit. Prima, vt de suo aliquis largiatur. Nam qui de alieno largitur, & ex alterius voluntate, sic ei gratificatur cui dat, vt tamen laus omnis ad eum referenda sit a quo donum illud proficiscitur.
units.tr: I say, therefore, that those words "to merit" and "merit," which the ancient Latin Fathers used in a sense very different from that of the Scholastic Doctors, cannot have a place in the Church unless three conditions are met. The first is that someone bestows from what is his own. For one who gives from what belongs to another, and at another's will, shows favour to the one to whom he gives, yet all praise must still be referred to the one from whom the gift proceeds.

units.la: Altera, vt qui largitur, non teneatur id ex debito reddere, sed a pura puta gratia largiatur. Nam qui pretium quod debuit, persoluit, id demum ad quod obstringitur praestat. Tertia deniq; vt sit operis ac mercedis aequa proportio. Quicquid enim redundat, ex eius liberalitate proficiscitur, qui pauca multis compensat. At horum trium nullum nisi in humana quidem Christi natura distincte & seorsim a diuinitate considerata reperias. Quatenus enim humana Christi natura creatura est, & pro nobis apud Patrem fideiussit, quicquid persoluit ex debito persoluit. Deinde, quod haec natura suffecit exsoluendis nostris debitis, a gratia id habuit; quippe quae Spiritum acceperit sine mensura, & in Virginis utero vi Sp. S. concepta sit. Tertio, Deo quid dari potest quo fiat auctior? Etsi enim persona filij Dei, assumptam humanam naturam sibi vniuerit: & quicquid ab illa profectum est, immensae sit dignitatis: nulla tamen res creata gloriam illam aequi potest quam hac obedientia consequutus est. Quum igitur Christi Meritum proferimus, eius promissionis rationem habemus quam Deus ex mera gratia & liberalitate foederi Legali appositi, hominem nimirum, illius integra & perfecta praestatione gloriam aeternam consequuturum quam quum vnus Christus impleuerit, sequitur eam illi gloriam ex pacto deberi, atque eadem ipsum esse promeritum, non sibi, sed nobis, sicut etiam homo factus est, vt nos sibi vnitos & insitos Deo pro nostris peccatis satisfaciens ciens conciliaret. Idcirco Deus in Lege non quidem se persoluturum iis mercedem qui eum amore complexi & præceptis eius obse-quentes fuerint, sed benevolum & facilem fo-re promittit. Quod si ita est in Christo Iesu, in quo tamen fuit summa perfectio: quid homi-nibus fiet, qui ne ad cogitandum quidem ex seipsis idonei sunt, quæ Dei sunt, sed præterea peccatis infecti sunt, etiam ipsi maximè fideles & Regeniti?
units.tr: The second is that the giver is not bound to repay it as a debt, but gives out of pure grace. For one who pays the price he owed only does what he is obliged to do. The third is that there be a fair proportion between the work and the reward. For whatever overflows proceeds from the generosity of the one who repays few things with many. But you will find none of these three in Christ's human nature considered distinctly and apart from his divinity. For insofar as Christ's human nature is a creature, and has become surety for us before the Father, whatever it paid, it paid as a debt. Next, that this nature was sufficient to discharge our debts, it had from grace, since it received the Spirit without measure and was conceived in the Virgin's womb by the power of the Holy Spirit. Third, what can be given to God that makes him greater? For although the person of the Son of God united the assumed human nature to himself, and whatever proceeded from that nature is of immense dignity, yet no created thing can equal that glory which he obtained by this obedience. So when we put forward Christ's merit, we have in view the promise which God, out of pure grace and liberality, added to the Legal covenant: that man, by full and perfect performance of it, would obtain eternal glory. Since Christ alone fulfilled it, it follows that this glory is owed to him by compact, and that he merited it, not for himself but for us, just as he became man so that, making satisfaction for our sins, he might reconcile us to God, united and grafted into him. Therefore God, in the Law, promises not that he himself will pay wages to those who embrace him with love and obey his precepts, but that he will be kind and easy to please. If this is so in Jesus Christ, in whom there was yet the highest perfection, what will become of men, who are not even fit of themselves to think the things of God, but are moreover infected with sins, even the most faithful and regenerate?

units.la: Nec eos Paulinum illud iuuat, Non eos qui audiunt Legem iustos esse apud Deum, sed qui Legem præstant iustificari. Rom. 2.13. nec illa Legi adiecta. Hæc fac & viues: quum hæc ipsa verba conclusionem eorum destruant. Nam, ut docet Apostolus in hac toties ab ipso repetita disputatione, præsertim in ep. ad Ro-man. & Galatas, quis obsecro mortalium au-deat hoc de se prædicare, Legem à se ex ipsius præscripto ad amussim impletam, si unicum Iesum Christum iustum excipias, à quo solo impleta est, ut ab eius maledictione liberare-mur? Gal. 3.10. & alibi. Iubentur singuli Chri-stiani singulis horis Remissionem peccato-rum petere: & discipulus ille dilectus sese reli-quorum peccatorum gregi adiungens, licet maxime si quispiam aliu s regenitus exclamat, Si dixerimus nos peccatum non habere, nos ipsos fallimus, & veritas in nobis non est. 1. Ioh. 1.8. Quid verò Iacobus, annon aperte pro-fitetur, Quisquis totam Legem seruauerit, offenderit autem in vno, teneri omnibus, quatenus nimirum reus merito censetur violatæ Legis in genere, etiamsi cætera observarit? Iac.2.10.Ecquis igitur eò devenit impudentiæ, ut in iudicium intrare cum Deo cogitet?143.2. Dicamus igitur potius cum quodam ex Veteribus, Merita tua, Domine, sunt mea merita: totum meum perfugium est in tuis vulneribus. Et cum Esa.Pax nostra est ei imposita & liuore eius sanati sumus.
units.tr: Nor does that saying of Paul help them: "Not those who hear the Law are just before God, but those who do the Law will be justified" (Rom. 2.13), nor that addition to the Law: "Do this and you will live," since these very words destroy their conclusion. For, as the Apostle teaches in this disputation, which he repeats so often, especially in the epistles to the Romans and Galatians, who, I beg you, of mortals would dare to claim of himself that he has fulfilled the Law exactly according to its prescription, unless you except Jesus Christ alone, the only just one, by whom alone it was fulfilled, so that we might be freed from its curse? (Gal. 3.10, and elsewhere). Each Christian is commanded to seek the remission of sins every hour, and that beloved disciple, joining himself to the flock of the remaining sinners, though most of all regenerate, cries out: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 John 1.8). And what does James plainly profess? "Whoever keeps the whole Law but offends in one point is guilty of all" (Jas. 2.10), inasmuch as he is rightly judged guilty of violating the Law in general, even if he has kept the rest. Who, then, has come to such impudence as to think of entering into judgment with God? (Psal. 143.2). Let us rather say with a certain one of the ancients: "Your merits, Lord, are my merits; my whole refuge is in your wounds." And with Isaiah (Esa.): "The chastisement of our peace was laid upon him, and by his stripes we are healed."

units.la: Plurimum igitur Iustificatio nostra differt à Sanctificatione: & vehementer falluntur, qui alteram ab altera distinguere quum nesciant, vnā eandémque rē esse putant licet à se inuicè diuelli non posse minimè difficeamur. Illa enim in Christo, & non in nobis, nostra est: hæc vero in nobis est, & non in Christo, vtraque autem ex sola gratia & misericordia Dei in vnico & per vnicum Iesum Christum promanat. Sed quæ in Christo Iesu iustitia est, nō autem in nobis, nostra fit imputatione gratuita: quemadmodum vice versa peccata nostra facta sunt ipsius imputatione sola: altera vero in nobis inchoatur, vt paulatim illi fiamus conformes qui nos sibi sanctificauit & consecrauit. Illa numeris omnibus absolutissima, conscientias nostras tranquillat: hæc vero in hoc mundo tantum inchoatur, non perficitur, atque adeo à veteris hominis reliquiis tam vehementer oppugnatur, vt sæpe in hac pugna grauissimis vulneribus ad paralysin vsque & veternum grauissimum afficiatur. Absit igitur miseris nostris conscientiis in hac quietem
units.tr: Our justification therefore differs greatly from sanctification, and those who do not know how to distinguish the one from the other, and think them one and the same thing, are greatly mistaken, though we are by no means at a loss to see that they cannot be separated from each other. For the one is ours in Christ and not in ourselves, whereas the other is in us and not in Christ, yet both flow from the sole grace and mercy of God, in the one and through the one Jesus Christ. But the righteousness which is in Christ Jesus, and not in us, becomes ours by free imputation, just as, conversely, our sins were made his by imputation alone. The other is begun in us, so that we gradually become conformed to him who has sanctified and consecrated us to himself. The former, most perfect in every respect, calms our consciences; the latter is only begun in this world, not perfected, and is so vehemently assailed by the remnants of the old man that often, in this struggle, it is struck with the gravest wounds, even to paralysis and most grievous lethargy. Far be it, then, that our wretched consciences should seek quiet in this

units.la: Summa Differentia & Connexio in imputatione Iustificationem & Regenerationem & Sanctificationem in nobis inchoatam. tem & tranquillitatem quæramus: & tamen quatenus illa nostra Sanctificatio fructus est Spiritus adoptionis, testimonium etiam est nostræ gratuitæ electionis. 2. Pet. 1. 10. Siquidem illi filij Dei sunt qui Spiritu Dei in ipsis habitante ducuntur. Rom. 8. 11. & 14. & 15. atque adeò nos eadem etiam in lucta periculosissima & grauissimis certaminibus erigit ne deficiamus, aut manus hosti demus vincíque nos patiamur, ita tamen ut cum timore & tremore incedentes, & nostræ infirmitatis satis conscij, nouas semper vires nobis suffici & adaugeri postulemus, ne quum stare nobis videmur, repentino lapsu corruamus 1. Cor. 10. 12. Phil. 2. 12. vel si lapsi fuerimus, erigamur, hoc à Domino cũ Dauidè flagitates, Restitue mihi lætitiã salutis tuæ: & spiritu spontaneo confirma me. Psal. 51. 14.
units.tr: The greatest difference and connection between imputation and justification, and regeneration and sanctification begun in us, and tranquillity; and yet, insofar as our sanctification is the fruit of the Spirit of adoption, it is also a testimony of our free election (2 Pet. 1.10). For those are sons of God who are led by the Spirit of God dwelling in them (Rom. 8.14, 15). And so it raises us up even in the most dangerous struggle and the heaviest conflicts, so that we do not fail or give our hands to the enemy and allow ourselves to be conquered; yet, walking with fear and trembling, and well aware of our weakness, we always ask that fresh strength be supplied and increased for us, lest, when we seem to stand, we fall in a sudden slip (1 Cor. 10.12; Phil. 2.12), or, if we have fallen, that we be raised up, asking this of the Lord with David: "Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and confirm me with a willing spirit" (Psal. 51.14).

units.la: Interea non negamus bona opera sequi necessarió veram fidem, quandoquidem iustificatio imputata, & inchoata Sanctificatio indiuiduo nexu cohærent: vitæ etiam integritatem agnoscimus esse viam ad salutem: Domi-númque nouissimo die secundum opera cuiusque iudicaturũ, non differemur, eademque ipsum benedictionibus tum temporalibus tũ æternis cumulatissimè coronare: sed non ex merito aut vlla dignitate ne iustissimi quidem cuiusuis: quum contrà nullum sit opus vsque adeò integrum quod si summo iure Deus ad suæ Legis normam exigat non sit corruptum & vitio hominis fœdarum, ac proinde Deo ingratum. Coronat igitur illa quidem in suis fidelibus, sed ex mera gratia propter imputata Iesu Christi iustitiam, in quo nos elegit & iustificauit tandem glorificandos, qua fit vt illorum defectus & vitiositas eius conspectum fugiant: denique illa vt fidei nostrae testimonia qua Iesu Christo vnimur intuitus coronat non vt a nobis profecta, & vt nostra, sed vt ab eius Spiritu in nobis producta, & ipsius in nobis effecta, vt salutis nostrae initium, progressus & finis vnius Dei gratiae & misericordiae in ipsius Filio in solidum accepta referantur: Rom.3.26.& vita aeterna sit donum Dei in Christo Iesu Domino nostro.
units.tr: Meanwhile we do not deny that good works necessarily follow true faith, since imputed justification and begun sanctification cohere in an indissoluble bond. We also acknowledge that integrity of life is the way to salvation, and we do not disagree that the Lord will judge each one according to his works on the last day and will crown them most abundantly with blessings, both temporal and eternal. Yet this is not from merit or any dignity, not even of the most just man; for on the contrary, there is no work so complete that, if God were to demand it by the strictest right according to the rule of his Law, it would not be corrupted and befouled by human fault, and therefore displeasing to God. He crowns those works, then, in his faithful, but out of pure grace, on account of the imputed righteousness of Jesus Christ, in whom he chose us and justified us, to be glorified at last. The result is that their defects and faults flee from his sight. Finally, he crowns those works as testimonies of our faith, by which we are united to Jesus Christ, not as if they came from us and were our own, but as produced in us by his Spirit and effected in us by him, so that the beginning, progress and end of our salvation may be wholly attributed to the one grace and mercy of God in his Son (Rom. 3.26), and eternal life is the gift of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

units.la: Denique, vt reuerteatur oratio nostra ad tertium illud a nobis propositum caput, nempe Conformitatem cum Christo, & sanctis omnibus, quandoquidem ille ipse Spiritus qui Dominus noster accepit sine mensura secundum humanitatem tanquam caput vnicum omnia membra sua viuificans, congruenter coagmentata & compacta per omnes suppeditatas commissuras. Eph.4.16.is est qui in nobis bonos illos motus excitat a quibus sanctae cogitationes, dicta factaque bona proficiscuntur, sequitur Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum eum esse quem sequi & imitari pro viribus nos oportet, tanquam vnicum & absolutissimum exemplar ad quod effingi nos est necesse, vt in nobis Pater talem cum dilecto filio suo conformitatem agnoscens, ex mera gratia & misericordia gratos habeat & accipiat. Atque que vt hæc omnia paucis complectamur, vitam IesuChristi sciamus esse normam ad quam tum omnis vita nostra, tum cogitationes, affectiones, sermones, actiones denique secundum cuiusque vocationem componendæ sunt atque dirigendæ. Quòd si dum ita vitam componere studemus mundo fumus exosi, vt fuit ille prius, & pro iustitia patimur, ne propterea territi refugiamus, sed gaudio potius exultemus, eius insignibus decorati, vt totics ille in discipulorum persona nos præmonuit, quum præsertim Dei donum esse non minus quàm fidem pro Christo affligi dicat Apostolus. Phil. 1. 29. hoc considerantes, conformitatem illam capitis cum membris in eo odio quo mundus fideles persequitur, tandē etiā in conformitatem gloriæ ipsius & regni æterni commutandam esse. Rom. 8. 17. 2. Tim. 2. 12. Equidem non eo inficias quin veterum Patrum verè piorum & Christi imitatorum exempla nobis imitanda proponere debeamus, vt monet etiam Apostolus. 1. Corinth. 11. 1. & Heb. 6. 12. Sed hic est diligenter animadvertendum, ne quæ in Christo Domino nostro propositä nobis sunt ad imitandum exempla, cum sanctorum exemplis confundamus ac permisceamus. Primum enim in sanctissimorum etiam Patrum exemplis multæ sunt, fueruntque semper labes, quas ideo Scriptura silentio tegere noluit, vt sciamus maximum esse inter Patres discrimen, quod Prophetas sui seculi hominibus toties inculcare videmus: nec oportere nos vita & actiones nostras hoc vel illo modo inltituere, quod sic Pater hic vel ille fe geffe-rit:sed potius vt firmo fundamento nitamur, & non omnino ἀσυλλογίςως concludamus, ficratiocinandum elt,Vitam meam,sermones facta, cogitationes ad huius vel illius exemplar inftitua & componã, quod hunc vel illū Patre hæc cogitantem loquentem &facientem imitatoremChrifti fuisse compertum habeam.Sic Apoftolu videmus nō simpliciter iubere vt fui fimus imitatores, sed hac apposita coditione, sicut ego sum imitator Christi. Deinde istud est Domini nostri Iesu Christi sic proprium,vt nulli hominum ac ne Angelorum quidem conueniat, quod possunt quidem Angeli & Sancti homines exemplo esse omnium virtutum: sed Christus præterquàm quod solus est omnis sanctitatis & integritatis perfectissimu exemplar,feque nobis imitadum proponit, in nobis etiam perSancti fui Spiritus virtutem & efficaciam format & excitat eius imitandi desiderium: & præterea vim ac potestatem illud efficiendi largitur, pro spiritus mensura quam cuique vt visum est admetitur,quod rerum omnium creatarum vires exuperat.
units.tr: Finally, to bring our discourse back to the third head we proposed, namely conformity with Christ and with all the saints: since that same Spirit whom our Lord received without measure according to his humanity, as the one head quickening all his members, who are fitly joined and knit together through every supporting joint (Eph. 4.16), is the one who stirs up in us those good motions from which holy thoughts and good words and deeds proceed, it follows that Jesus Christ our Lord is the one whom we ought to follow and imitate as far as our strength allows, as the sole and most perfect pattern to which we must be shaped, so that the Father, recognising in us such conformity with his beloved Son, may favour and accept us out of pure grace and mercy. And to sum all this up briefly: let us know that the life of Jesus Christ is the rule by which our whole life, and our thoughts, affections, speech and actions, each according to his calling, are to be ordered and directed. But if, while we strive to order our life thus, we are hated by the world, as he once was, and suffer for righteousness, let us not be frightened and flee, but rather rejoice and exult, adorned with his marks, as he so often forewarned us in the persons of his disciples; especially since the Apostle says that it is a gift of God, no less than faith, to suffer for Christ (Phil. 1.29). Considering this, let us remember that the conformity of head and members in the hatred with which the world pursues the faithful is at last to be changed into conformity with his glory and eternal kingdom (Rom. 8.17; 2 Tim. 2.12). Indeed, I do not deny that we ought to set before us the examples of the ancient Fathers who were truly pious and imitators of Christ, as the Apostle also advises (1 Cor. 11.1; Heb. 6.12). But here we must take careful heed not to confuse and mix up the examples proposed to us for imitation in Christ our Lord with the examples of the saints. For first, even in the examples of the most holy Fathers there are many lapses, and there always have been, which Scripture did not wish to cover with silence, so that we may know there is the greatest difference between the Fathers, which we see the prophets of their own age inculcating again and again. Nor ought we to shape our life and actions in this or that way because this or that Father behaved so; rather, we should rest on a firm foundation, and not conclude unreasonably [ἀσυλλογίστως], as if we should reason: "I will set up and shape my life, words, deeds and thoughts after the pattern of this or that man, since I have found that he, thinking, speaking and doing these things, was an imitator of Christ." Thus we see the Apostle does not simply bid us be imitators of himself, but adds this condition: "as I am an imitator of Christ." Next, this is so peculiar to our Lord Jesus Christ that it belongs to no man, nor even to the angels. Angels and holy men can indeed be examples of all virtues; but Christ, besides being the sole and most perfect pattern of all holiness and integrity, and proposing himself for our imitation, also forms and stirs up in us, by the power and efficacy of his Holy Spirit, the desire to imitate him; and moreover he bestows the power and ability to effect it, in the measure of the Spirit which is apportioned to each as he pleases, a thing which surpasses the powers of all created things.

units.la: Habetis, fratres, quæ de præcipuis salutis capitibus præmittenda duxi, ad quæ susceptâ huius historiæ explicationem referre noueri-mus, prout feret locus, & mihi Deus id effi-ciendi gratiam largietur: Quam oro, mecum ab illo precibus ad nominis ipsius gloriam,& cuiusque nostrum salutem efflagitatē: Amen.
units.tr: You have, brethren, the main heads of salvation which I thought should be set forth beforehand, to which we shall know how to relate the explanation of this history we have undertaken, as the place allows; and may God grant me grace to accomplish this. I beg you to join me in asking him in prayer for the glory of his name and for the salvation of each of us. Amen.
