units.la: Xpositis hactenus Christianae religionis capitibus praecipuis: sine quorum intelligentia Euangelij vniuersa doctrina, & in primis haec Mortis & Passionis Domini nostri historia, nobis scandalum adferret, vt Iu-c. iij. daeis, & stultitia esset, vt prophanis gentibus, 1. Cor.1.23. aggredimur volētc Deo ad huius historię explicatione, ad cuius partes singulas re ferremus singula capita quæ attigimus, prout res postulare videbitur, & ab Euangelistis qua tuor conscripta est, aliis vel addentibus aliquid, vel fuisus exponentibus, quæ aliis vel omissa, vel breuius dicta fuerat. Vnde satis docemur, quàm diligenter cauere nos oporteat, nequid non satis diligenter animaduersum excidat.
units.tr: Having so far set out the chief heads of the Christian religion, without which the whole doctrine of the Gospel, and especially this history of the death and passion of our Lord, would be a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles (1 Cor. 1.23), we now, God willing, set about explaining this history, referring each of its parts to the heads we have touched on, as the matter shall require. The four Evangelists have written it, some adding something, others expounding more fully what the rest had omitted or stated more briefly. From this we are sufficiently taught how carefully we must take care that nothing is overlooked through lack of close attention.

units.la: Vno igitur ore memorant quatuor Euangelistæ, Christum vrbe sub vesperam egressum, addit vero Lucas, ex more Dominum idfecisse, quod pluribus Lucas persequitur cap. 21. 37. Sic igitur iis responsum esto, qui forte cogitaret Dominū hoc secellu voluisse suorum hostium insidias & manus effugere, vt antea sæpius illorum se insidiis subduxerat. Sed contra, si putaremus Dominum quum sciret tempus illud suum aduenisse fugam esse meditatū, næ sic fructus quæ ab eius morte expectamus, à fundamentis coauelleretur. Quina enim eius obedietia seruaremur, nisi mors ipsius voluntaria fuisset? Vrbe igitur egressus est non casu, nec temerè, sed omnia sibi euentura probè sciēs, vt sæpe antea prædixerat, & disertis verbis Ioānes scriptis suis mādauit. Ioh.18.4. Minime ergo fugā meditabatur, sed pro more & instituto, vel ipsis suis hostibus non incognito vrbem egressus est, nec in vrbe quæsitum nō inuenirent, sed in loco bene explorato & commodo modo deprehenderent, quasi Iudæ proditori locum dedisset, in quo cum satellitibus facillimè caperetur, vt disertis verbis id exprimit Ioan.Ioh.18.2.
units.tr: With one voice the four Evangelists relate that Christ went out of the city toward evening, and Luke adds that the Lord did this as was his custom, which Luke pursues more fully in chapter 21:37. Let this answer be given to those who perhaps think the Lord wished on this occasion to escape the snares and hands of his enemies, as he had often withdrawn from their snares before. But on the contrary, if we supposed that the Lord, knowing that his hour had come, had planned flight, then the fruits we expect from his death would be torn up from their foundations. For how would we be saved by his obedience, unless his death had been voluntary? So he went out of the city not by chance or rashly, but knowing well that all things would befall him, as he had often foretold and as John has plainly written (John 18.4). He was certainly not contemplating flight. Out of habit and custom he left the city, in a way not unknown even to his enemies. Nor would they have failed to find him if they sought him in the city; but they would seize him easily in a well-explored and convenient place, as if he had given Judas the traitor a place where he could most easily be taken with the guards, as John expressly states (John 18.2).

units.la: QuæUrat autem aliquis forsan, cur vrbem egredi sub vesperam Dominus hoc in vrbem vltimo ingressu, sit solitus: cui sic respondetur ut supra, præterquam quòd Dominus sæpe solitudinem quæsiuit, vt alibi docemur, Deum patrem solus precaturus, & quasi cum ipso & Angelis collocuturus, ita nos erudiens quomodo ad preces comparare nos oporteat, vt dicemus paulo post, magnam esse coniectu-ram, partim Dominum cogitasse faciliorem suis hostibus occasionem ipsum inuadendi præbere, quos verisimile est non ausuros illi violentas in vrbe manus iniicere, propter metum populi, ipsos propria conuincente conscientia: partim etiam discipulorum infirmitati consuluisse, quibus longè difficilius fuisset ex manibus hostium euadere siquid tale in vrbe vel interdiu vel noctu contigisset, cuius rei testimonium esto metus ille quo Petrus leuiore de causa perculsus est. Hinc igitur iterum agnoscamus, vnicum aduersus nostram cotumaciam ac rebellionem esse remedium, ac velut antiphar-macum Christi obedientia. Rom.5.19. omnibus suis partib absolutissima. Nam quòd ad priore illa Legis tabulam, videmus Filium ita se Patri obsequente in sua carne præbuisse in illo iudicio quod pro nobis immensum subiit, vt etiam quatenus potuit & debuit quilibet impedimenta
units.tr: One might ask why the Lord was accustomed to leave the city toward evening on his last entry into the city. To this the answer is given as above, besides the fact that the Lord often sought solitude, as we are taught elsewhere, to pray to God the Father alone, and as if to converse with him and the angels, thus teaching us how we ought to prepare ourselves for prayer, as we shall say shortly. There is a strong conjecture: partly that the Lord considered he would offer his enemies an easier opportunity of attacking him, since they were likely not to dare to lay violent hands on him in the city, for fear of the people and because their own consciences convicted them; partly also that he consulted the weakness of his disciples, for it would have been far more difficult for them to escape from the hands of enemies if anything of that kind had happened in the city, by day or by night. The fear by which Peter was struck on a slighter occasion is witness to this. Hence let us again recognize that there is one remedy against our stubbornness and rebellion, and, as it were, an antidote in Christ's obedience (Rom. 5.19), which is most complete in all its parts. For as to the first table of the Law, we see the Son so obeying the Father in his flesh, in that judgment which he undertook immeasurably for us, that he removed, as far as he could and ought, every hindrance by which delay might be brought to its execution. The second table he so fulfilled that, offering himself for the sake of his enemies, nothing more can be required of him.

units.la: c. iiij. quibus illius executioni mora poterat afferri sustulerit. Posteriorem vero sic impleuit, vt in hostium suorum gratiam seipsum offerens, nihil amplius ab eo requiri possit. Hinc igitur, fratres, hinc inquam cum & agnoscere & reuereri discamus, qui nos sibi tanto merito devinxit. Pudeat nos illius nomen dedecore afficere, cuius sunt erga nos immensę charitatis & beneuolentiæ tot tantáque testimonia.
units.tr: ...which could be used to delay its execution. He fulfilled the latter in such a way that, by offering himself for the sake of his enemies, nothing more can be required of him. Hence, brothers, hence, I say, let us learn both to acknowledge and to revere him who has bound us to himself by so great a merit. Let us be ashamed to dishonour the name of him to whom there are so many and so great proofs of immense love and goodwill towards us.

units.la: Hic autem quæstio non inutilis occurrit, An persecutionis tempore, à qua vix vnquam Ecclesia Dei respirat, ita fe faciles hostium fi-ue insidiis siue armis violentis præbere Christianos oporteat ex officio. Nam non longè post Apostolorum tempora fenfecunt non-nulli non licere Christiano sibi & saluti suæ, seu fuga seu alia qualibet ratione persecutionis tempore consulere, séque hostium manibus subducere. Dicam aliquid amplius penè incredibile, & tamen verissimum, in Africa, quam hodie Barbariam vocant, ita fuisse à Satana quoddam hominum melancholicorum genus quos Circumcelliones vocarunt, fascinatum & spiritu vertiginis dementatum, vt quum à quibus ad Martyrium raperentur non essent, ipsi se in omne tormentorum genus præcipites daret, vt martyrio vitam claudi videretur. Tanta est illius hostis nostri, vis & astutia in nobis dextra læuáque tentandis. A quibus nostro seculo non procul absunt ex Anabaptistis quidam. Facilis est autem ad propositam quæstionem responsio: si primo loco
units.tr: Here, however, a question not unprofitable arises: whether, in a time of persecution, from which the Church of God scarcely ever gets breath, Christians ought, as a matter of duty, to offer themselves so readily to the snares or violent weapons of their enemies. For not long after the times of the Apostles, some thought it was not lawful for a Christian to look after himself and his own safety, whether by flight or by any other means in a time of persecution, and to withdraw himself from the hands of his enemies. I shall say something more, almost incredible yet most true: in Africa, which today they call Barbary, a certain kind of melancholy men, whom they called Circumcelliones, were so bewitched by Satan and driven mad by a spirit of vertigo that, when they were not being seized and carried off to martyrdom by others, they would hurl themselves headlong into every kind of torment, so that their life might seem to be ended by martyrdom. So great is the power and cunning of that enemy of ours in testing us on the right hand and on the left. Not far from these in our own age are certain Anabaptists. The answer to the question proposed is, however, easy, if first of all

units.la: Quomodo & quatenus Christianus persecutionis tempore pericula potest fugere.
units.tr: How and how far a Christian may flee dangers in a time of persecution.

units.la: Circumcelliones.
units.tr: Circumcelliones.

units.la: Anabaptistæ. loco finem intueamur ad quem in omni vita nostra nobis est collimandum, Dei gloriam, non cõfuse quidem aut in genere tantum, sed ex cuiusque vocatione, siue publica illa siue priuata sit, vt hac certissima verissimáque nitamur conclusione, nimirum, Quæcunque ingruant pericula, aut quæcunque premant difficultates, primum cauendum ne illicitis mediis, à Deo nempe prohibitis, quàtumuis specisa videantur, abutamur, quum extra omne dubium sit, eum qui peccat, in odium Dei incurrere, ac proinde peccatori malum semper male cessisse. Deinde, minime prophanorum hac in re sequendum consilium, monentium de duobus malis minus eligendum: sed contra neutrum eligendum, immo summopere fugiendum, quum peccandi aut male agendi nulla sit vnquam opportunitas. Tertiò, pro illicitis habenda quæcunque vocationi nostræ repugnant. At si periclitantibus offeruntur media non modò licita, sed etiam vocationi non contraria, tum non tantum iis vti licere, sed etiam cum qui oblata pertinaciter respuat quin Deum tentet excusari non posse certum est. Id veterum Patrum exemplis comprobemus. Moses oraculo aut alia quauis ratione diuinitus edoctus se fore populi liberatorem, vt ait Steph. Act. 7. 25. quum munus illud suum cæso Ægyptio cœpisset aggredi, nec sibi tutum esse diutiùs in Ægypto morari videret, fuga sibi salutem apud Madianitas quæsiuit. Recténe verò fecerit si roges, aio non abs re Mo-
units.tr: Anabaptists. we look to the end at which in all our life we must aim, the glory of God: not vaguely or only in general, but from each person's calling, whether public or private, so that we may rest on this most certain and true conclusion, namely: whatever dangers threaten, or whatever difficulties press upon us, we must first take care not to abuse illicit means, namely those forbidden by God, however specious they may seem, since it is beyond all doubt that the one who sins incurs the hatred of God, and so for the sinner evil has always turned out badly. Next, the counsel of worldly men in this matter is not to be followed, those who advise that of two evils the lesser is to be chosen; rather, neither is to be chosen, and one must especially shun both, since there is never any opportunity for sinning or acting wickedly. Third, whatever is opposed to our calling is to be regarded as unlawful. But if means are offered to those in danger which are not only lawful but also not contrary to their calling, then it is certain that not only may they use them, but also that one who obstinately rejects what is offered cannot be excused from tempting God. Let us confirm this by the examples of the ancient Fathers. Moses, having been taught by an oracle or by some other means from God that he would be the deliverer of the people, as Stephen says in Acts 7.25, when he had begun to undertake that task by striking down the Egyptian, and saw that it was no longer safe for him to remain in Egypt, sought safety for himself among the Midianites by flight. If you ask whether he did right, I say that he was not without reason struck with fear, considering on the one hand his calling, which he had embraced with admirable faith, as the Apostle testifies in Heb. 11.24, and on the other the difficulty of carrying it out at that time, and, having received no special prompting from the Lord...

units.la: sen perculsum timore, hinc quidem vocationem suam considerantem, quam admiranda fide fuerat amplexus, vt testatur Apostolus ad Hebr. ii. 24. inde vero difficultatem illius eo tempore exequendæ, perpendentem, nulloque motu speciali à Domino admonitum, vt quadraginta post annis demum factum esset, non quidem de abiicienda vocatione cogitasse, sed opportunitatem illius implendæ maiorem expectasse: quam quum videret per tot annos differri, cogitare cœpisse, vt verisimile est, alium electum à Domino qui populi liberator esset: quod ex eo manifestum est, quòd quum vocanti illum è rubo Iehoua pluribus hoc munus à se reiicere conatus esset, in hæc verba tandem erupit, Obsecro, Iehoua, vt eum mittas quem missurus es. Hic vero duo sunt diligenter observanda: primum vt in tantis difficultatibus constituti ad Deum confugiamus, quo duce illas superemus, quum fortissimos quosque illis sic intricari conspiciamus: alterum, longè aliud esse ad tempus, sine vllius damno vel incommodo secedere, tantisper dum nubes calamitatum discutiantur, quàm vel metu vel perfidia stationem suam deserere. Ionas contrà, eòsque proiectus vt se Dei gloriæ & ministerij sui dignitati melius quàm Deum ipsum consulere cogitaret in grauissimum peccatum incidit, quod etiam Deus seuerissimè castigauit. Insignis est contrà tot alium rum Prophetarum constantia, quos nullæ difficultates, nulla quantumuis magna pericula popotuerunt vnquam à fui muneris executione deterrere, ac ne tantillum quidem remorari. Heb.11.36.& 37. Ieremias vero, quum eius vocatio non essèt Ierosolymorum mœnibus conclusa, vrbe paululum Chaldæorum obsidione liberata,non dubitat vrbe excedere,etsi Dominus illi viam præclusserit. Atque vt ex multis vnum nobis sufficiat, age D. Paulum intuemur: quid enim sanctissimus ille Dei seruus non pertulit vt munere suo fungeretur? Sed tamen quum se mox ab inimicis discerpendum animaduerteret, folertia quadam & prudenti, non vafro nec malo consilio viam inuenit qua furentium hostium vngues cuitaret: Act.23.6. & de insidiis admonitus sapienti illas consilio fugit. Act.23.17. tandemque ludicis animaduersa præuaricatione Romam prouocauit ad Cæsarem:qua in re tantum abest vt in vocationem peccarit, & ab eo quod erat protectatus. Act.21.13. alienum quidquam fecerit, vt contrà nisi mediis illis vteretur, Deum fuerit tentaturus, & Ecclesiæ magnam iniuriam illaturus. Quod vero memorat Lucas Act. 19. Apostolum in magna illa seditione Ephesi coorta à Demetrio, relicta Ephesina Ecclesia, Macedoniam petiuisse, maximè ad propositam quæstionem,hoc præsertim calamitosissimo Gallicarum Ecclesiarum statu facit. Domini nanque grauissimo testimonio Mercenarij dicuntur qui relictis ouibus aduentante lupo fuga sibi consulunt.Ergo-ne fratres nostros quos hospitio profugos, & ex tempestate saluos, suorum que hostium manibus clapsos excepimus, Mercenarios dicendos & suarum ouium desertores arbitrabimur? Absit. Aliud enim tum à Domino tum à suis quibus fidelitatis praeclarum testimonium habent. Hic igitur proderit Pauli exemplum, qui, vt narrat Lucas, Act.19.30, cupiebat quidem per medios illos seditiosos ad populum perrumpere: sed ab Ecclesia facere illud porhibitus est, non male iudicante quantam iacturam tum Ecclesia tum ipse pateretur, si in instituto pergeret: quod & Apostolus quanuis ardenti zelo flagrans agnouit, discipulorumque monitis morem gessit. Et sane cedens furibundae plebis furori, feris immanibus potius quàm hominibus similliraé, vt ipsemet loquitur. 1.Cor.15.32. tantùm abest vt Ecclesiam deseruerit, vt hoc pacto potius illi se conseruarit. Denique in tanta rerum perturbatione & angustis Ecclesiae temporibus, haec duo nobis de quibus egimus ponenda sunt fundamenta nempe esse primum omnia sine exceptione Deo, & vocationi nostrae poltponenda: deinde cum Deo & iis quorum maximè interest nostra communicanda consilia, vt quod è re magis esse videbitur, prout rerum, locorum, temporum, personarum ferent circunstantiae, Deo commendantes exitum, sequamur. Huius rei Christus Dominus noster nobis tum hic tum alibi seipsum exemplar perfectissimum proposuit, vt qui non semel hostium furori cesserit, quòd nondum eius hora venisset, ita tamen vt à sua vocatione ne latum quidem vnguem recesserit : contrà autem vbi hora illa ipsius aduenisset, sese Patri voluntati totum permiserit & obtulerit. Minimè verò hic expectanda nobis talis reuelatio, qualem habuit Christus, tum quâ Deus erat, tum quâ homo, rerum quæ nobis hac vel illa hora sunt eventuræ, cuiusmodi multas revelationes à Deo Prophetæ quondam acceperunt: sed tamen sperandum, fore vt positis iis quæ diximus fundamentis, rebus nempe omnibus priuatis Dei gloriæ nó-que vocationi postpositis, & Dei gratiæ commendatis, eius spiritu regamur & veluti manu ad ea quæ nostri erunt officij facienda deducamur, adeò vt vitæ nostræ terminum illius arbitrio permittetes, quid nobis futurum sit anxios esse nos non oporteat.
units.tr: Moses, struck with fear, on the one hand considered his calling, which he had embraced with an admirable faith, as the Apostle testifies (Heb. 11.24). On the other hand, weighing the difficulty of carrying it out at that time, and having been prompted by no special motion of the Lord, he did not, for forty years, indeed, think of giving up his calling, but looked for a better opportunity to fulfil it. When he saw it deferred through so many years, he began to think, as is likely, that the Lord had chosen another to be the deliverer of the people. This is evident from the fact that when Jehovah called him from the bush, he tried several times to refuse this office, and at last burst out with these words: "Please, Jehovah, send the one whom you are going to send" (Exod. 4.13). Two things here must be carefully noted. First, that when we are placed in great difficulties we should flee to God, and by his guidance overcome them, since we see even the bravest men so entangled in them. Second, that it is one thing to withdraw for a time, without any loss or inconvenience to anyone, until the clouds of calamity have passed, and quite another to abandon one's post through fear or treachery. Jonah, on the contrary, having been cast out, thought he could better consult the glory of God and the dignity of his ministry than God himself, and fell into a very grave sin, which God also punished most severely. Quite the opposite is the notable constancy of so many other prophets, whom no difficulties and no dangers, however great, could ever deter from the execution of their office, or delay even a little (Heb. 11.36–37). Jeremiah, since his calling was not confined within the walls of Jerusalem, did not hesitate to leave the city, once it had been freed for a little from the siege of the Chaldeans, even though the Lord had closed the way before him. And, to take one out of many for us, let us look at St. Paul. For what did that most holy servant of God not endure in order to discharge his office? Yet when he perceived that he was soon to be torn to pieces by his enemies, with a certain shrewdness and prudent, not crafty or evil, counsel, he found a way to escape the claws of the raging foes (Acts 23.6). Warned of the plots, he fled by wise counsel (Acts 23.17), and at last, when the judge's dereliction was noticed, he appealed to Caesar at Rome. In this he was so far from sinning against his calling, or departing from what he had professed (Acts 21.13), that, on the contrary, had he not used these means he would have tempted God and inflicted great injury on the Church. As for what Luke records (Acts 19), that the Apostle, when the great sedition was stirred up at Ephesus by Demetrius, left the Ephesian Church and made for Macedonia, this bears especially on the question proposed, and particularly in the present most calamitous state of the Gallic Churches. For by the most weighty testimony of the Lord, those are called hirelings who, when the wolf approaches, leave the sheep and look to their own safety (John 10.12). Shall we then, brethren, whom we have received as fugitives into our hospitality, who have been saved from the storm and escaped from the hands of their enemies, consider them hirelings and deserters of their own sheep? Far from it. For the Lord and their own people, to whom they bear a splendid testimony of faithfulness, judge otherwise. Here, therefore, the example of Paul will be useful, who, as Luke relates (Acts 19.30), indeed wished to break through to the people amid those seditious men, but was forbidden by the Church to do so, since it judged rightly how great a loss both the Church and he himself would suffer if he persisted in his purpose. This the Apostle, though burning with ardent zeal, recognised, and he yielded to the counsel of the disciples. And indeed, yielding to the fury of the raging crowd, more like wild beasts than men, as he himself says (1 Cor. 15.32), he was so far from deserting the Church that by this course he rather preserved himself for it. Finally, in such great upheaval and in the straitened times of the Church, these two things of which we have spoken must be laid down as foundations: first, that all things without exception must be placed after God and our calling; second, that counsels must be shared with God and with those whose interest is greatest, so that, as the circumstances of affairs, places, times and persons allow, we may follow what seems most fitting, committing the outcome to God. Christ our Lord has set himself before us as the most perfect example of this, both here and elsewhere: he who more than once yielded to the fury of his enemies because his hour had not yet come, yet never withdrew from his calling so much as a hair's breadth; but when that hour had come, he gave and offered himself wholly to the will of the Father. Yet we must by no means expect such a revelation as Christ had, both as God and as man, of the things that are to happen to us at this or that hour, such as the prophets of old were once given by God in many revelations. Rather we may hope that, once the foundations we have described are laid, namely that all private matters are placed after the glory of God and our calling, and are committed to the grace of God, we shall be ruled by his Spirit and led, as by his hand, to do the things that belong to our duty. So, leaving the end of our life to his judgement, we ought not to be anxious about what is to become of us.

units.la: Vt igitur ad contextum reuertamur, non simpliciter hic dicitur Christus vrbe exiuisse, sed prius excellentissimam illam diuinissimam doctrinam proposuisse, quam Ioannes pluribus à 14. capite ad 18. persequitur. Ita verò Seruator ille noster magis magisque suâ erga Ecclesiam charitatem immensam patefecit: non expectato crucis scandalo quin prius occurreret, & ante inflictum vulnus antipharmacum praeparaet, suósque aduersus grauissimum insultum confirmaret. Ecquid aliud, obsecro, quotidie erga nos facit? Annon sedulò praemonet, vt imminentia certamina cauteamus aduersus Satanam, mundum & nosipsos? Annon idem arma suppeditat, quibus, nifi per nos fiet, prius victoriam reportemus quàm cum hostibus manus conseramus? Quàm pauci verò, proh dolor! hæc meditantur, quàm pauci præbent aures attentas, & animis infigunt? Inde fit vt inopinantes multi deprehendantur, alij fluctuantes labascant, alij deniq; prorsus corruat. Absit igitur à nobis illis similes fiamus, sed ex animo Deū oremus, vt quæ nō semel tantū discipulis suis dicta, sed etiam in Ecclesiæ suæ perennem vsum in publicas tabulas referri voluit, quo singulari eius beneficio fit, vt eadem hodie nostris auribus hauriamus prælecta & explicata, eadem altissimas in nostris mentibus radices agant, quibus in aduersis rebus tanquam periti gladiatores ancipitibus gladiis vtamur.
units.tr: To return, then, to the context: it is not simply said here that Christ went out of the city, but that he first set forth that most excellent and most divine teaching which John pursues at length from chapter 14 to chapter 18. Thus our Saviour showed more and more his immense love toward the Church, not waiting for the scandal of the cross to come upon him, but going to meet it beforehand, preparing an antidote before the wound was inflicted, and strengthening his people against the gravest assault. What else, I beg you, does he do for us every day? Does he not diligently forewarn us to be on our guard against the struggles that threaten us, against Satan, the world and ourselves? Does he not also supply the arms by which, unless we do it through ourselves, we may win the victory before we join hands with the enemies? But alas, how few meditate on these things, how few give attentive ears and fix them in their minds! Hence it happens that many are caught unawares, others waver and totter, and others at last fall down altogether. Far be it from us, then, to be like them, but let us pray to God from the heart, that those words which he willed to be spoken not only once to his disciples, but to be recorded in public books for the perpetual use of his Church, so that by his singular kindness we may hear today with our ears these things read and explained, and that these same words may strike the deepest roots in our minds, by which in adverse circumstances we may use the two-edged swords like skilled gladiators.

units.la: Porro cadé Iesu Christi veri Pastoris de suorum salute cura & solicitudo declaratur in eo etiâ, quòd nô solus vrbe, sed vnà cū discipulis exiuit. Quid enim soli præstitissent, quos etiam præsente Christo tam infirmos fuisse cospicimus? Primus sanè parés ille noster magno exemplo est, quid nobis futurū sit vbi primū arbitrij nostri viribus permittimur. Si enim ille viribus adhuc integris Deo nō sustinente ipsum tā fœdo lapsu corruit, quinā obsecro staret, qui prius in illo lapsi ceciderūt, quotquot, inquâ, ab illo progeniti sunt mortales, hoc vnico excepto, in quo & per quē solū resurgimus? Multò verò minùs aut ex parte aut omnino suis viribus resurgerent, quos non modò truncatos aut mutilatos, illius instar cuius meminit Ioh. §.§. sed tanquam mortua cadauera in peccatis nasci docet Apostolus.Eph.2.1.
units.tr: Moreover, the care and concern of Jesus Christ, the true Shepherd, for the salvation of his own is shown also in this, that he went out of the city not alone, but together with his disciples. For what could they have achieved alone, whom we see to have been so weak even with Christ present? That first parent of ours is certainly a great example of what will become of us as soon as we are left to the powers of our own will. For if he, with his powers still whole, fell into so foul a lapse, when God did not sustain him, who, I ask, would stand, when those who fell in him before him, all the mortals, I say, who have been born of him, with the single exception of him in whom and through whom alone we rise again, have fallen? Much less, then, would they rise either in part or altogether by their own powers, those who, as the Apostle teaches, are born not merely maimed or mutilated, after the manner of him whom John mentions (Ioh. §.§.), but as dead corpses in their sins (Eph. 2.1).

units.la: Memoria tamen repetendū & obseruandū est Christi corpoream praesentiam, etsi fuerit Apostolis ad tempus nō parū vtilis tum ad eos de Prophetiarū impletionibus cōfirmandos, per realem Seruatoris exhibitionē, vt ipsemet Matth.13.16. propterea beatos illos praedicat: & Iohannes idem testatur Ioh.1.14. & 1. Ioh.1. 1. tum ad eos priuatim ipsius ore Doctoris erudiendos, tamē, (quòd infirmitate illa & carne visibili Iesu Christi tāquam velo tegeretur & obscuraretur eius Deitas, (cuius est infinitis partibus maior dignitas) immo etiam humilis ille & abiectus carnis Christi statu non pateretur eā vt Hominis Dei carnē cōsiderari, quod vel ex eo conspicuū est quòd eius discipuli resurrectione eius sibi persuaderi tā difficulter palli sunt: vnde etiā cōrigit, quēadmodū superius demonstratū est, vt tā multi haeretici quū hoc arcanū mente sua aflequi nequiuerint, ad illud impegerint, aliis Deitate eius negatibus, aliis verò Humanitatem infpectrum transfor mantibus) necesse fuit non tātum hanc carnis infirmitatem aboleri, salua tamen & integra manente Christo naturali sua existētia & perfectione, iis omnibus adimpletis quae ad salutē nostrā requirebatur: sed hac etiā humanitatem supra coelos omnes euehi, & in vltimū vsque die ab his terris & hominū cōspectu diuelli, vt praesētia Christi spirituali fruamur, tātō purio re & vita aeterna digniore & illi cōueniētiore quantò quod animo percipimus per auditum verbi diuini, & oculis fidei,nec caecis nec lippis intuemur, infinitis partibus est excellentius eo quod sensibus corporeis apprehendimus. Id ipsum diíerdis verbis Dominus ipse testatus est.Ioh.16. 7. & Apoft.2. Cor.5.16.docens modum omnem cognoscendi Christum secúdùm carnem deiuisse: licet spiritualis nostra cognitio nondum perfecta sit r. 13.12. Et Apostolos videmus, nósque etiam cum ipsis, eò fuisse ab Angelis ad nouissimum vsque diē remissos,Act.1.11.Quàm bene nouerat istud fidelis ille centurio,quum Christo diceret licere sibi eius liberalitate & vi spirituali frui licet sub tectum eius non intraret?Matth.8.8.
units.tr: Yet it must be remembered and observed that Christ's bodily presence, although for a time it was of no small use to the Apostles, both to confirm them in the fulfilment of the prophecies through the Saviour's actual manifestation (which is why he himself pronounces them blessed, Matt. 13.16), as John also testifies (John 1.14; 1 John 1.1), and to instruct them privately from the mouth of the Teacher, nevertheless had to be taken away. His deity was veiled and obscured, as it were, by that weakness and by the visible flesh of Jesus Christ, although his dignity surpasses it by infinite degrees. Indeed, that humble and abject state of Christ's flesh would not allow his flesh to be regarded as the flesh of God. This is evident from the fact that his disciples were so hard to persuade of his resurrection. Hence it also happened, as was shown above, that many heretics, unable to grasp this mystery with their minds, dashed against it: some denied his deity, others distorted his humanity. It was necessary not only that this infirmity of the flesh be abolished, while Christ's natural existence and perfection remained safe and whole, all the things required for our salvation having been accomplished; but also that this humanity be lifted above all the heavens and taken from this earth and from the sight of men until the last day, so that we might enjoy Christ's spiritual presence. This presence is purer, more worthy of eternal life, and more fitting to him, by as much as what we perceive in mind through the hearing of the divine word and behold with the eyes of faith, which are neither dim nor blear, is infinitely more excellent than what we grasp by bodily senses. The Lord himself testified to this in plain words (John 16.7), and Paul (2 Cor. 5.16) teaches that every mode of knowing Christ according to the flesh has been abolished, although our spiritual knowledge is not yet perfect (1 Cor. 13.12). We see that the Apostles, and we along with them, were sent back by the angels until the last day (Acts 1.11). How well that faithful centurion knew this when he said to Christ that it was enough for him to enjoy Christ's liberality and spiritual power, even though Christ did not enter under his roof (Matt. 8.8).

units.la: Quàm est igitur maximæ partis Christianorum ingens & admirandus stupor,vt non contenti Christum se ipsis & in verbo & in Sacramentis patefacientem cognoscere, videre, sibique vi spirituali & interna Spiritus efficacia applicare,etiam realem & essentialem corporis eius in terris præsentiam fingant & comminiscantur?Nos verò contrà quæramus eum vbi est,ad dextram Patris, quò secundùm carnem est euectus supra omnes cœlos, vnde nos expansis vlnis adse vocat, vbi nobis locum parat:qui sibi facta ducit quæcunque vel bona vel mala vni ex minimis ipsius seruis fiunt: quæramus inquam eum videre die illo facie ad faciem, spiritualis interim illius præsentiæ modo contenti,quo se nobiscum ad finem vsque seculi futurum promisit:suos tuentem cœlitus.
units.tr: How great, then, and how remarkable is the astonishment of the greater part of Christians, that they are not content to know, see, and apply to themselves, by the power of the Spirit and the inward efficacy of the Spirit, Christ who makes himself known in the word and in the sacraments, but they also imagine and invent a real and essential presence of his body on earth! We, on the contrary, should seek him where he is, at the right hand of the Father, whither he was carried according to the flesh above all the heavens, whence he calls us to himself with outstretched arms, and where he prepares a place for us. He counts as done to himself whatever good or evil is done to the least of his servants. We should seek him, I say, to see him face to face on that day, and in the meantime be content with the mode of his spiritual presence, in which he promised to be with us until the end of the age, watching over his own from heaven.

units.la: Miserefal luntur ef- sentiale Christi eor pus reipsa præsens in terris quæ rentes. litus, hostes vero suos sensim deprimentem illius potentiæ vi quam habet in cœlo & terra quáque tandem illos pedibus suis substratos conculcaturus est.
units.tr: Those who seek Christ's essential body really present on earth... (Christ has mercy on his own, and gradually brings down his enemies by the power he has in heaven and on earth, and will at last tread them under his feet, having subdued them.)

units.la: Sequitur apud Euangelistas locus ad quem se recepit, Gethsemane dictus, vt Matth. & Marc.vocant,in monte Olearum situs,ait Lucas.vbi hortus erat,vt Iohan.etiam specialiter designat: vt siquis exempli gratia, de aliquo dicat eum Geneuam venisse, in forum,in huius vel illius ædes. Quod ne quis temerè me putet obseruare:sed vt prophanorum quorundam occurram calumniis, qui hæc Euangelistarum verba detorquent quasi inter se non bene conuenientia. Quod autem locum Euangelistæ tam accurate descripserunt plurimum ad historiæ veritatem facit: nec diutius nobis in allegorico sensu harum vocum, putà Gethsemane,quæ vbertatis vel pinguedinis vallem:aut Cedron,quæ torrentem loci opaci & vmbrosi,aut montis Olearum,quod olea sit symbolum & signum pacis,immorandum est: licet quæ inde elicitur doctrina ad rem facere videri possit, vt nimirum doceamur quis ad nos fructus ex nostri Seruatoris carcere redeat à quo à mortis tenebris ad veritatis Lucem transferimur. Verum istiusmodi contemplationes allegoricæ,infirmo fundamento nituntur,& sæpissime sunt periculosissimæ, quod à vero scripturæ sensu nos ad inanes & vanas speculationes abducant.
units.tr: There follows in the Evangelists the place to which he withdrew, called Gethsemane, as Matthew and Mark call it, situated on the Mount of Olives, as Luke says, where there was a garden, as John also specifically indicates. This is like saying, for example, that someone has come to Geneva, to the market, or to this or that house. Let no one rashly think that I observe this without reason; I do so in order to meet the calumnies of certain profane men who twist these words of the Evangelists as if they did not agree well with one another. That the Evangelists described the place so carefully contributes greatly to the truth of the history. Nor need we dwell long on the allegorical sense of these words: Gethsemane, which means the valley of fertility or fatness; Kidron, which means the torrent of a dark and shady place; or the Mount of Olives, because the olive is a symbol and sign of peace. Although a doctrine drawn from these may seem to bear on the matter, namely that we may learn what fruit comes to us from the prison of our Saviour, through whom we are transferred from the darkness of death to the light of truth, yet such allegorical contemplations rest on a weak foundation, and are very often most dangerous, since they lead us away from the true sense of Scripture into empty and vain speculations.

units.la: Sed, vt ex Veteribus quidam obseruauit
units.tr: But, as one of the ancients observed:

units.la: f. j. non sine Dei singulari Prouidentia factum est vt quemadmodum ille prior Adamus in horto tentatus & victus, se & nos in eandem ruinam trahens pestumdedit: ita secundus alter ille noster Adamus in horto, sed ratione longe diuersa tentatus, victoriam sibi nobisque pepererit. Quae duo parallela, si cum ipsorum singulis circunstantiis inter se componantur, magnam profecto nobis consolationem allatura sunt: hinc quidem considerationibus quam foedus & horrendus fuerit illius rebellionis lapsus, in quo omnes lapsi sumus, inde vero quam magnifica, & quam triumphans illius obedientia, qui nos collapsos non tantum erexit, quasi aequis inter se ponderibus illius rebellio, & huius obedientia ferrentur, sed in longe sublimiorem quam fuerit vnquam prioris Adami aut nostra in illo dignitatem euexit.
units.tr: It was not without the singular providence of God that, just as that first Adam, tempted and conquered in a garden, drew himself and us into the same ruin and brought about our destruction, so that second Adam of ours, in a garden but tempted in a far different way, won victory for himself and for us. If these two parallels are set side by side, with each of their particular circumstances, they will surely bring us great consolation: on the one hand, by considering how foul and horrible was that fall of rebellion in which all of us fell; on the other, how magnificent and triumphant was the obedience of him who raised us up when we had fallen, not merely as if his obedience and that rebellion were weighed in equal scales, but he lifted us into a dignity far more sublime than that which the first Adam, or we in him, ever had.

units.la: Felicissimus igitur ille fuit status in quo parentes illi nostri primi carnales conditi fuere, in paradiso aspectu iucundissima & amoenissima, cuius fructibus liberè fruebantur, in quibus erat maxime insignis arbor illa vitae, quod eius fructu poller vita ipsorum animalis aliquin, id est, cibo & potu fouenda, in sempiternum conseruari & propagari: Arbor erat vnica ex omnibus quae illis interdictum est, quae gloriam & Maiestatem creatoris repraesentabat, qui vnus habet in res omnes creatas imperium, & à cuius arbitrio aequi rectique pendet regula, & solus quae facienda quaeque vitanda sunt nutu moderatur, idcóque boni & mali scien-tiæ arbor dicta: In hac arbore Maiestatem & Gloriam immensam sui Creatoris agnoscere ipsos & adorare par erat, ea dominatione con-tentos quam acceperant à Deo in res omnes creatas inferiores, nec altius ad ea quæ Dei propria sunt aspirare. Adde priori inhibitio-ni, pœnam additam mortem primam & secun-dam, vt saltem illius metu pœnæ in Dei timo-re & obedientia continerentur. Quid fuit igi-tur in tam felici statu quod eos ad creatorem tam benignum, tam liberalem & beneficum, agnoscendum, venerandum, & omni cultu prosequendum non commoueret, siue iuben-tem intuearis, siue mandata ipsa, siue eos qui iubebantur considerès, quorum erat singula-ris & plus quàm admiranda lux, intellectus, & voluntatis & affectuum integritas ac recti-tudo?
units.tr: That state was most happy in which our first carnal parents were created, in paradise, most delightful and pleasant to behold, whose fruits they enjoyed freely. Among them was especially notable the tree of life, because by its fruit their animal life, otherwise to be sustained by food and drink, was to be preserved and propagated forever. There was one tree among all those forbidden to them, which represented the glory and majesty of the Creator, who alone has dominion over all created things, and at whose will the rule of right and wrong depends, and who alone by his nod governs what is to be done and what avoided. For this reason it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. In this tree it was fitting that they should acknowledge and adore the majesty and immense glory of their Creator, content with the dominion they had received from God over all lower created things, and not aspire higher to those things which are God's own. Add to the prohibition the penalty appended, first and second death, so that at least by fear of that penalty they might be restrained in the fear and obedience of God. What, then, in so happy a state, could fail to move them to acknowledge, venerate, and pursue with every worship a Creator so kind, so generous, and so beneficent, whether you look at the one commanding, or at the commandments themselves, or at those who were commanded, in whom there was a singular and more than admirable light, integrity and uprightness of intellect, will, and affections?

units.la: At prima illa nostra parens, vbi serpenti ho-micidæ Ioh.8.44. placidam aurem acommo-dasset, & ambitionis venenum hausisset, quo repente lumen illud intelligentiæ penitus ex-tinctum est, & quidem eò vsque vt in animum suum aduersus Creatorem induceret, quæ na-turæ ipsius è diametro repugnant, aliud nimi-rum sensisse ipsum aliud prolocutum esse, & ea bona, commodaque quorum erat autor i-psis inuidisse, sibique contrarium eorum quæ minatus erat Deus euenturum persuasisset, nō modò quæ deteestari illam oportuit, appetiuit, sed reipsa Domini mandatum transgressa,
units.tr: But that first parent of ours, when she had lent a quiet ear to the murderous serpent (John 8.44) and had drunk the poison of ambition, by which that light of understanding was at once utterly extinguished, indeed to such a degree that she brought into her mind things flatly repugnant to the very nature of God, namely that she thought one thing and spoke another, and envied the good things and advantages of which God was the author, and persuaded herself that the opposite of what God had threatened would happen, she not only desired what she ought to have detested, but, actually transgressing the Lord's command,

units.la: f. ij. suam etiam operam Satanæ in marito in eán-dem ruinam & rebellionem,immo conspira-tionem aduersus Deum nefariam & modis o-mnibus abominandam pelliciendo commo-dauit.
units.tr: also lent her own effort to her husband, enticing him into the same ruin and rebellion, indeed into a nefarious conspiracy against God, to be abominated in every way.

units.la: Age vero contrà videamus quomodo se in horto gerat noster ille alter Adamus cælestis, sic dictus non tantum eo quòd frater noster est, eandem quam nos humanitatem à primo illo Adamo trahes excepto peccato, sed quòd quemadmodum Adamus in quo natura omnes eramus inclusi,in suæ posteritatis exitiu offensam suam propagauit, ita quoque nobis Adamus posterior natus est, in quo electi restituantur,in ipso facti Dei filij per adoptionē generatione spirituali. Rom. 5. 14. Fuit igitur ille quidem in se verè perfectus,& priore illo partibus infinitis superior,& longè maioribus dotibus ornatus,secundùm carnem: verùm aderat tanquam sponsor ac fideiussor noster, peccatis nostris coopertus, & in anima plus quàm horrendæ maledictionis Dei terroribus perculsus: ab omnibus derelictus, quasi rebus omnibus creatis miseram illam conditionem in quam per hominis lapsum deuenerunt Rom. 8. 20. in hoc nostro sponsore vindicantibus:hostium immanissimorum furoribus expositus: denique verme abiectior, vt ipse de se loquitur, Psal. 22. 7. & ad tempus quasi prorsus exinanitus.Phil.2.7.Stetit ille tamen hinc inde licet petitus, Satana contrà nihil in eo inueniente, confuso & profligato.
units.tr: Come now, let us look on the contrary at how that other, heavenly Adam, our Lord, conducted himself in the garden. He is so called not only because he is our brother, sharing the same humanity we derive from the first Adam, apart from sin, but because, just as Adam, in whom we were all included by nature, spread his offence to the ruin of his posterity, so also a second Adam was born for us, in whom the elect are restored and in whom, by spiritual regeneration, they are made sons of God by adoption. Rom. 5. 14. He was indeed, in himself and according to the flesh, truly perfect, and far superior to that first Adam in countless respects and adorned with far greater gifts. But he stood before us as our surety and guarantor, covered with our sins and, in his soul, struck with the terrors of God's most dreadful curse. He was abandoned by all, as though all created things, which in the fall of man had come into that wretched condition, were avenging themselves upon him as our surety. Rom. 8. 20. He was exposed to the furious assaults of most savage enemies, and finally, as he says of himself, he was more abject than a worm. Ps. 22. 7. For a time he was, as it were, utterly emptied. Phil. 2. 7. Yet he stood firm, though attacked on every side, while Satan found nothing in him and was confounded and routed.

units.la: Verus ille Iacob victoriam reportauit, & verus Israel fuit, cum ipso Iehoua luctatus, veritatem nobis exhibens eorum quae Genef. 32. 28. figurabantur. Sic peccatum viribus suis enervatum vnius hominis obedientia concidit, ac proinde mors ipsa lethali vulnere confi-citur.
units.tr: That true Jacob obtained the victory, and was a true Israel, when he wrestled with Jehovah himself, showing us the truth of what was prefigured in Gen. 32. 28. So sin, its strength broken, was overthrown by the obedience of one man, and therefore death itself is struck down by a deadly wound.

units.la: Quae vero mens humana tantam Dei sa-pientiam, cum tanta bonitate & potentia co-iunctam assequatur, quam ipsos etiam Ange-los suspicere merito considerimus? Tanta enim iustius obedientiae vis est, vt ante dixi, vt non modo peccatum illud per quod cum Adamo ce-cidimus, sed etiam aliorum infinitam multitu-dinem quae admissa sunt olim, admittuntur, aut in finem seculi sunt admittenda penitus ab-oleat. Nec vero mundi tantum vnius est iustud beneficium, sed etiam innumerabilium, si modo gratiam illam salutarem amplecterentur, quae mille mundis seruandis si tot extarent sufficit. Adde aliquid amplius, vitam nimirum spiritualem, pro vita illa quidem immortali, sed animali & mutabili quam Adamus sibi suisque perdiderat: pro hac terra & caelis transituris, nouam terram & caelos nouos nobis incomprehensibiles: pro statu illo à quo Adamus per lapsum excidit, alium longè excellentiorem, quo Angelis similes facti vita caelesti & spirituali perfruemur, Marc. 12. 25. ea quae oculus non vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec in mentem hominis venerunt, vitam illam nimirum aeternam & nulli mutationi obnoxiā, vnà cum gloria & præsentia illius qui sedet ad dextram patris, & nomen supra omne nomen adeptus est, illius facti cohæredes conspecturi 1.Cor. 2.9.1.Pet.3.7.Rom.8.17.Ioh.17.2. Quis inquam, humani viribus ingenij res istas tantas tamque obstupendas comprehendat? Adoremus igitur quæ captum nostrum superant: & à tam vasta, tamque profunda miseriarum voragine, ad tam immensam gloriam cuecti, ne benedictionem Esaui Iacobi benedictioni præferamus: sed paulatim ex his terris emergentes per Spiritum qui nobis datus est, magis ac magis sursum efferamur, ad illius paradisi non fallaces delicias, eo vocante nos & expectante qui in hoc horto terrestri & miseriarum pleno luctatus aduersus Satanam, peccatum & mortem, tandem ea debellauit & de illis feliciter triumphum reportauit.
units.tr: What human mind can grasp that great wisdom of God, joined with such goodness and power, which we rightly consider even the angels themselves must look up to with awe? For the power of his obedience is so great, as I said before, that it wipes out not only that sin by which we fell with Adam, but also the infinite multitude of other sins committed in past ages, or yet to be committed before the end of the world. Nor is his benefit confined to one world alone, but extends to countless worlds, if only they would embrace that saving grace, which would suffice to save a thousand worlds, even if so many existed. Add something more: a spiritual life in place of that immortal yet animal and changeable life which Adam had lost for himself and his descendants; in place of this earth and heavens, which will pass away, a new earth and new heavens beyond our comprehension; in place of that state from which Adam fell through his lapse, another far more excellent state, in which, made like the angels, we shall enjoy a heavenly and spiritual life. Mark 12. 25. Those things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, namely that eternal life, which is subject to no change, together with the glory and presence of him who sits at the right hand of the Father and has obtained a name above every name, we shall behold as his fellow heirs. 1 Cor. 2. 9; 1 Pet. 3. 7; Rom. 8. 17; John 17. 2. Who, I ask, can grasp by human powers of mind such great and astonishing things? Let us therefore adore what surpasses our understanding, and, raised from so vast and profound an abyss of miseries to so immense a glory, let us not prefer Esau's blessing to Jacob's blessing; but gradually rising from these earthly things, through the Spirit who has been given to us, let us be lifted up more and more on high, to the non-deceptive delights of that paradise, he calling us and waiting for us, who in this earthly garden, full of miseries, wrestled against Satan, sin and death, and at last overcame them and gained a happy triumph over them.

units.la: HOMILIA quinta.
units.tr: HOMILY five.

units.tr: 36. And he says to the disciples, Sit here, until I go over there and pray.

units.la: 37. Et assumpto Petro & duobus filiis Zebedæi, cœpit contristari, & grauissimè angi.
units.tr: 37. And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and to be very heavily distressed.

units.tr: 38. Then Jesus says to them, My soul is exceedingly sorrowful even unto death: remain here, and watch with me.

units.la: 39. Et progressus paululum, procidit in faciem suam, precans & dicens.
units.tr: 39. And going forward a little, he fell on his face, praying and saying.

units.tr: 32. Then he says to his disciples, Sit here until I have prayed.

units.tr: 33. And he takes Peter and James and John with him, and began to be greatly amazed and very heavily distressed.

units.tr: 34. And he said to them, My soul is exceedingly sorrowful even unto death: remain here and watch.

units.tr: 35. And going forward a little, he fell to the ground and prayed.

units.tr: 32. But when he had come to that place, he said to them, Pray that you do not enter into temptation.

units.la: 41. Tum ipse auulsus est ab eis quasi ad iactum lapidis, posuitque genibus precatus est dicens,
units.tr: 41. Then he was withdrawn from them about a stone's throw, and he knelt down and prayed, saying,

units.la: AVSAS superius audiuimus quibus impulsus Dominus discipulis suis comitatus vrbe sit egressus, supersunt quae ab illo cum suis discipulis dicta transactaque sunt, patefaciente ipsis quid in horto facturus ipse, & vicissim quae ipsorum extra hortum partes essent praescribente, tribus tantum ex illis quos secum duceret assumptis. Quod ad primum attinet, Christum Dominum ad orandum secedentem id discipulis aperuisse minime fuit nouum ac insolens, sic certis & indubitatis testimoniis non modo familiarita-
units.tr: We have heard above what moved the Lord to leave the city accompanied by his disciples. What remains is what he said and did with them: how he disclosed to them what he himself was going to do in the garden, and in turn set out what would happen to them outside it, taking with him only three of those he had with him.

units.la: f. iiij. tem summam ergo ipsos testatum suas etiam arcanas cogitationes illis patefaciendo, qua re vicissim in officio melius continerentur, nec ipsum sicut erat ab aliis facto deserer ent. Ioh. 6. 68. & Luc. 22. 28. sed etiam exemplo suo ad precum sedulitatem, quam saepe commendabat adhortantem.
units.tr: With regard to the first point, it was by no means new or unusual that Christ, withdrawing to pray, revealed this to his disciples. By this, with clear and undoubted testimonies, he showed not only his supreme familiarity with them, by disclosing to them even his secret thoughts (John 6:68; Luke 22:28), so that they would be better kept in their duty and would not desert him as he was deserted by others, but also, by his own example, he urged them on to diligence in prayer, which he often commended. f. iiij.

units.la: Hic autem non parui momenti quaestio se nobis offert. Nos enim miseros peccatores, non mirum est vrgeri necessitate precandi, quum etiam nobis quid utile sit aut quomodo petendum ignoremus, tantum abest ut nobis illud conferre valeamus. Rom. 8. 26. at Christum in vnitate personae θεάνθρωπον quid opus erat ea precibus impetrare, quae sibi ipse conferre poterat? Hinc factum ut quidam exstimarint Christum non necessitate, sed ut exemplo precum assiduo ad Deum fundendarum nobis praeiret esse precatum: sed logē vlterius nobis est progrediendum, quum in Evangelio passim doceamur Christum non tantum nostra causa sed sua ipsius Deum precibus sollicitasse: non quidem quod eas de atque nos precandi causas habuerit, ut dixi paulo ante, nec quod haec necessitas eius Deitatem vel tantillum attingat, aut eius humanitatem nisi spontanea & a libera voluntate profecta: sed quod quum aeternus Dei filius nostram naturam vnione personali assumpserit, quae iure creationis Creatori tenetur obsequium omne fidemque praestare, id officij reddere debuerit ei a quo in tanta dignitate vnione personali assumpserit. sumpta elt. Præterea quū naturam nostrá vnà cum omnibus infirmitati bus excepto peccato assumserit, sequitur volentè eum in carne sua necessitatè subiisse ab alio vires postuladi quibus oneri sibi imposito feredo par esset, tragrauí alioquin, vt nisi à Deitate humanitas sustinerctur,illi° oppressa mole fuerit occubitura.
units.tr: Here, however, a question of no small weight presents itself. It is no wonder that we wretched sinners are driven by the necessity of praying, since we do not even know what is useful for us or how we ought to ask, so far are we from being able to supply this ourselves (Romans 8:26). But in Christ, the God-man [θεάνθρωπον] in the unity of person, what need was there to obtain by prayers what he could bestow on himself? Hence some have judged that Christ prayed not out of necessity but to go before us as an example of pouring out prayers to God continually. But we must go further, since in the Gospel we are taught throughout that Christ sought God by prayers not only for our sake but for his own. Not indeed because he had reasons for praying of the kind we have, as I said a little earlier, nor because this necessity touches his Deity in the least, or his humanity otherwise than as something voluntary and proceeding from free will. Rather, since the eternal Son of God assumed our nature in personal union, a nature which by the right of creation owes its Creator all obedience and faith, he ought to render this duty to him from whom he had been assumed into such dignity by personal union. Moreover, since he assumed our nature together with all its infirmities, except sin, it follows that, willingly submitting in his flesh to the necessity of seeking from another the strength by which he might bear the burden laid upon him, otherwise his humanity, unless it were sustained by the Deity, would have sunk beneath the weight and perished.

units.la: Porrò si Hominem Deum, Fi ium Dei dilectū, in carne sua Sp.S.donis sine mefura cumu latū, nulla superueniete à peccato infirmitate labefactatum oportuit noctes diesq; ad Deum preces fundere(nec enim sine certamine vicifsetiat ni victor extitisset, quid nobis fieret miseris?)age,obsecro, quàta nostra est hac in parte væcordia? quid agimus, quid, nō minimam tèporis parte,molimur ac cogitamus? vnde fit vt singulis penè mometis inopinates nos hostis adoriatur,aut ipsi nos in eius laqueos coniiciamus, nisi à socordia nostra, aut, vt quod res est dicā,à malitia, qua duce aduersus nos ipsos militamus? Agedū igitur ista diligentius meditemur, vigilemus,singulis mometis Deū votis ardentibus sollicitemus,quandoquidem foris perpetuò excubantem holtem habemus, intus verò tot alios in nostram perniciem coiuratos sinu fouemus,serió,inquam,ista meditemur, quū ad primū illud caput cria accedat expressum Domini mandatū, discipulos suos difficillimo illo & periculosissimo,si aliàs vnquā, tépore ad preces incitatis:cui sanè tépora in quæ incidimus sunt simillima, quū tā multas immaniū omnis generis potentissimorum & infimæ plebis hominum nefarias conspirationes ad Christum iterum crucifigendum, immo in nihilum in membris suis redigendum, si quos ei Pater dedit perire posse nt tot iam seculis perpetiamur.
units.tr: Furthermore, the Lord took three most faithful witnesses of what would happen in that garden, so that these things might be written in records for our use in time to come. Although he was bound, from his resurrection, to teach his disciples most of what had happened, either by revelation of the Holy Spirit or in some other way, and to recall it to their memory, as he had promised them [John 16:13]. Clearly because at that time they were for the most part overcome by sleep, and Christ had uttered these prayers at a considerable distance from them, as Luke notes in chapter 22:41. For otherwise it could not have come about that the greater part of the Evangelists' writings should be set down so exactly, one by one, in records.

units.la: Cæterum Dominus tres sibi fidelissimos testes eorum quæ in horto illo contingerent futuros adsciuit, vt in no stru olim vsum ea monumentis scripta cederent: licet ipsum oportuerit à resurrectione sua maximam eorū partem, quę cōtigerant, vel Spiritus S. reuelatione vel alia ratione suos discipulos edocere, aliam autem in memoriam ipsis reuocare, vt erat ipsis pollicitus. Ioh.16.13. quòd nimirū eo tempore fuissent vt plurimum somno sopiti, & Christus satis ab ipsis procul has preces concepisset, vt notat Lucas cap.22. 41. Fieri enim aliter nó potuit vt tam accurate maxima pars Euangelicorum scriptorum monumentis sigillatim exprimeretur.
units.tr: Furthermore, the Lord took three most faithful witnesses of what would happen in that garden, so that these things might one day be written down in monuments for our use. Although after his resurrection he would have had to teach his disciples the greater part of what had happened, either by revelation of the Holy Spirit or in some other way, and to bring it back to their memory, as he had promised them (John 16:13). For at that time they were for the most part overcome by sleep, and Christ had prayed these prayers at a distance from them, as Luke notes in chapter 22:41. For otherwise it could not have come about that the greater part of the Gospel writers' records should set forth so accurately each detail.

units.la: Quòd verò tres istos speciatim aliis relictis assumpsit, minimè nouum fuit, vt ex transfigurationis historia perspicuum est, quà etiam iussit eos reticere donec à mortuis resurrexisset.Matth.17.9. Et fortasse non ignarus Christus quàm extraordinario terrore essent ipsius discipuli afficiendi, ex iis quæ in horto facientem & dicentem eum vidissent, aliis voluit parcere, his tribus delectis quos animo præsentiore & fortiore esse oportuit, memoria repetentes gloriæ illius cœlestis Maiestatem quam in monte suis oculis conspexerant, sermomonésque vltro citróque habitos à Christo, Mose & Elia, de iis qui Ierosolymis erant implenda. Luc. 9. 31.
units.tr: That he took these three in particular, leaving the others, was by no means new, as is plain from the history of the transfiguration, when he also ordered them to keep silent until he had risen from the dead (Matthew 17:9). And perhaps Christ, not unaware with what extraordinary terror his disciples would be struck by what they had seen him doing and saying in the garden, wished to spare the others and to take these three chosen ones, who ought to have had a more present and stronger spirit, so that they might recall by memory the majesty of that heavenly glory which they had seen with their own eyes on the mountain, and the conversations held back and forth by Christ, Moses and Elijah, about the things to be fulfilled at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31).

units.la: Verùm tunc temporis parùm ipsis ea profuerunt, vt in iis, quos tanta cura & sollicitudine à tanto Doctore scimus eruditos, quanta sit virium nostrarum imbecillitas intuemur: atque adeò Christianum fieri nec esse naturæ proprium nec vnius dei opus nouerimus. Ne pudeat igitur nos in nobis ea condemnare quæ nobis in discipulis hæc historia contemplanda proponit. Sed in illa tamen Apostolorum, quos Deus postea S. suo Spiritu replevit, infirmitate, discamus ambitionis vitium & liuoris in fratres, quos Dominus suis insignioribus exornatos dotibus nobis anteponit pro viribus fugere, quæ vitia magnis calamitatibus Ecclesiam iam inde à multis seculis afflixerunt. Etsi enim nonnunquam accidit vt quos Dominus erat inter discipulos speciali fauore prosequutus alij alios indignantes æmularentur. Marc. 10 41. non est tamen hoc loco & tempore, nec deinceps amplius id factù, ipsis contrà in vrbem in vnam domum coeuntibus & concordibus manentibus. Itaque detestandum ambitionis & liuoris vitium abominati, sciamus Deum cui & quantum vult largiri. 1. Cor. 12. 11. & quascunque dotes confert in aliquem eas ad totius corporis ædificationem conferri, ac proinde pro ambitione & liuore, non humanis sed verè Satanicis affectibus generis humani pestibus, Mosen illum fidelissimum Dei seruum imitari conemur, cuius haec vota legimus, Num. 11.29. Vtinam totus populus Iehouae essent Prophetae: & Iohannem Baptistam non modo non sibi arrogantem quas dotes acceperat, aut iis superbientem, sed contra de se haec praedicantem, Non sum dignus qui incuruatus soluam corrigiam solearum eius: & Apostolum epistolas suas exordientem a gratiarum actione propter dona quae in aliis Deus contulerat. Denique & istud attendamus eos qui in Dei domo grauiora sustinent onera, non sibi delicias facere, vt male qui ipsis inuident, arbitrantur.
units.tr: But at that time these things profited them little. Seeing how weak our powers are, we observe in those whom we know were taught with such care and diligence by so great a Teacher; and so we recognise that to become a Christian is neither natural to us nor the work of one man alone. Let us therefore not be ashamed to condemn in ourselves what this history sets before us to be contemplated in the disciples. Yet in that weakness of the Apostles, whom God afterwards filled with his Holy Spirit, let us learn to flee, as far as we can, the vice of ambition and the envy towards brothers whom the Lord has adorned with more distinguished gifts and set before us. These vices have afflicted the Church with great calamities for many centuries. For although it sometimes happened that those whom the Lord favoured with special kindness among the disciples were envied, and some were indignant at others (Mark 10:41), yet this is not so in this place and time, nor did it happen afterwards, since they came together in one house in the city, and remained in concord. Therefore, let us abhor and detest the vice of ambition and envy, knowing that God gives to whom and as much as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11), and whatever gifts he bestows on anyone, he bestows them for the building up of the whole body. Accordingly, let us strive to be free of ambition and envy, which are not human but truly Satanic affections, the plagues of mankind, and to imitate that most faithful servant of God, Moses, whose wish we read: "Would that all the people of Jehovah were prophets!" (Num. 11:29). Let us also imitate John the Baptist, who not only did not arrogate to himself the gifts he had received, nor take pride in them, but on the contrary declared of himself: "I am not worthy to stoop down and loose the thong of his sandals." And let us imitate the Apostle, who begins his epistles with thanksgiving for the gifts God had bestowed on others. Finally, let us also consider that those who bear heavier burdens in the house of God do not make delights for themselves, as those who envy them wrongly suppose.

units.la: Accedamus ad Christi precationem, rem sane modis omnibus admirandā & stupendam, si quid vnquam, nouum & admirandū cōtigit, immo quae prima fronte merito videatur quicquid de Christi Domini nostri excellentia & praestantia, tū Deitatis tū humanitatis respectu diximus, euertere, & nisi recte intelligatur salutis nostrae spem a fundamentis conuellere: vt contra ex hac bene intellecta precatione cognituri sumus quantū Christus pro nobis certamen inierit, quis sit ipse Dominus noster, & qualis: qui simus in nobis ipsis, quanta Deus ira peccata persequatur: quousque se magnus ille Seruator nostri causa demiserit: ac tandem quo nostra spes omnis aduersus mortem primam & secundam fundamento nitatur. Vt hanc igitur tam insignem doctrinam ordine pertractemus, primum dicemus quo respectu illa Christi persona tribuantur: deinde quae facrit fuerit illa tanta perturbatio, & illius vera causa: tum ad quem istæ preces dirigantur: quarto, quæ sit earum forma & summa: ac tandem postremo quid impetrarit Christus, & quis ad nos inde fructus perveniat.
units.tr: Let us come to Christ's prayer, a matter truly wonderful and astonishing in every way, if ever there was one. At first sight it seems to overturn everything we have said about the excellence and pre-eminence of our Lord Christ, both in respect of his deity and of his humanity, and unless it is rightly understood it would tear up by the roots the hope of our salvation. On the other hand, from this prayer, if it is rightly understood, we shall learn how great a struggle Christ undertook for us, who our Lord is and what kind of Lord he is, what we ourselves are, how greatly God pursues sins with his wrath, how far that great Saviour lowered himself for our sake, and finally on what foundation all our hope rests against the first and the second death. So that we may treat this so remarkable doctrine in order, we shall first say in what respect these things are attributed to the person of Christ; second, what that great disturbance was and what its true cause was; third, to whom these prayers are directed; fourth, what their form and substance are; and lastly, what Christ obtained and what fruit comes from it to us.

units.la: Quod enim quidam existimarunt Christum hic non in sua persona, sed Ecclesiæ tantum nomine loquutum, aut eorum respectu quæ populo Israëlitarum erant euentura, vt quidã ex Patribus scripserunt, tam est alienum ab huius historiæ scopo, vt omitti potius, quàm cogitari, dici, vel scribi oportuerit, quanquam neque aduersus fidem nostram, neque aduersus eam qua suos etiam hostes Christus est amplexus charitatem peccet.
units.tr: For some have thought that Christ here spoke not in his own person but only in the name of the Church, or with regard to what was to befall the people of Israel, as some of the Fathers have written. This is so foreign to the purpose of this history that it ought rather to be passed over than thought, said or written about, although it does not offend against our faith, nor against that love with which Christ embraced even his enemies.

units.la: Vt igitur de primo dicamus, quemadmodū superius docuimus, minimè cōfundendas aut miscendas, neque separandas Christi duas naturas, vt ex iis duæ personæ constituantur, aut ex duabus vna tertia natura cōfletur, sed tantùm distinguendas, ita sunt etiam prudenter earum essentiales proprietates sine vlla confusione aut separatione diuisionéve, ac proinde voluntates & operationes earum distinguendæ. Duæ sunt igitur in Christo voluntates considerandæ, Deitatis vna nimirum, Humanitatis autem altera: ac proinde tribuenda Deitati, quæ naturæ & voluntati diuinæ propria sunt: & viciflim humanæ naturæ & voluntati quæ illi conueniunt: qua ratione non magis à se duæ naturæ diuelluntur quàm corpus ab anima separatur, quum animam intelligere dicimus, aut hoc ex illo colligere, corpus vero vel edere vel bibere, quandoquidem nec corpus intelligit aut ratiocinatur, nec edit anima nec bibit: quemadmodum etiam oculum ab aure non separamus, quum oculum dicimus non item aures videre, & contra non oculum sed aurem sonos percipere. Et tamen hominem Totum considerantes dicimus intelligere, ratiocinari, bibere, edere, videre, viuere, mori: quae si singillatim excutiantur nullo modo homini conuenire dixeris omnium ipsius partium respectu, sed vnicuique parti singillatim sua esse tribuenda. Quibus positis, fatedum quidem est, quum Christus vna sit Persona Homo Deus, & Deus homo, Iesum Christum ad mortem vsque fuisse triste, anxium, obstupefactum, territum, minime id quidem Deitatis eius, nulli passioni obnoxie respectu, sed solius humanitatis: solius, inquam, non separatae sed distinctae, veluti quum illum dicimus, edisse, bibisse, dormiuisse, fleuisse, mortuum esse & a mortuis suscitatum. Et de primo hactenus.
units.tr: To speak first of the former point: just as we taught above, the two natures of Christ are not to be confused or mixed, nor separated so that two persons are made from them, or one third nature is compounded from two, but only distinguished. In the same way, their essential properties are likewise to be distinguished, without any confusion, separation or division, and therefore their wills and operations are to be distinguished too. There are therefore two wills to be considered in Christ: one of the deity, namely, and the other of the humanity. Accordingly, what belongs to the divine nature and will is to be attributed to the deity, and conversely what belongs to the human nature and will is to be attributed to the humanity. In this way the two natures are no more torn apart from each other than the body is separated from the soul, when we say that the soul understands, or infers something from something, and that the body eats or drinks, since neither the body understands or reasons, nor does the soul eat or drink. Likewise we do not separate the eye from the ear when we say that the eye sees but the ears do not, and conversely that the ear perceives sounds, not the eye. And yet, when we consider the whole man, we say that he understands, reasons, drinks, eats, sees, lives, dies. If these things are examined one by one, you will say that none of them belongs to the man with respect to all his parts together, but that each must be assigned singly to its own part. With these things laid down, it must indeed be granted that, since Christ is one Person, man and God, and God and man, Jesus Christ was sad, anxious, dismayed and terrified even to death. This was not in respect of his deity, which is subject to no suffering, but only of his humanity: only, I say, not separated but distinguished, just as we say that he ate, drank, slept, wept, died and was raised from the dead. So much for the first point.

units.la: De secundo: qui Christum exstimant tantum iniuriarum & cruciatuum imminentium metu perterritum, vehementer fallantur: minime quidem quod verus homo naturalis & anima & corpore ea omnia non horruerit, & vehementi sit affectus metu, vt loquitur Apostol. Heb. 4.15. & quae credere nos oportet, nisi maximam eorum partem quae pro nobis passus perpessus est tollere & exinanire volumus; Verum
units.tr: As to the second: those who think that Christ was terrified only by the fear of impending injuries and torments are greatly mistaken. Not that the true natural man did not shrink from all those things, body and soul alike, and was affected by a powerful fear, as the Apostle says (Heb. 4.15). And we must believe this, unless we wish to remove and empty out the greater part of those things which he suffered and endured for us. But

units.la: Non sim plex mor tis metus Christum ita percel suit sed apprehen sio incom- prehensi furoris di mini ad-
units.tr: Not the simple fear of death so troubled Christ; rather, it was the apprehension of the incomprehensible wrath of the Lord, ...

units.la: Vetùm quisvnquam cogitarit Christum à quo tanquam capite subiecta membra vitam & vires hauriunt, minùs animi habuisse quàm tot,omnis ætatis ac sexus homines,immo pue- rulos quorum tum ante tum post ipsius ad-uentum in adeundis summa alacritate, & sum ma constantia perferendis,non tantùm oppro briis,sed etiam immanissimis quibúsque à Sa-tana & eius satellitibus excogitatis tormentis & cruciatibus magnanimitatem & robur cóspicimus? Qui verò suos in mediis illis per-secutionibus exultare iubet. Matth.5.12. & in oppressionibus in Domino gloriari. Rom.5.3.& 8.17.quod ab omnibus sanctis propter iustitiam persecutionem passis factitatum videmus,Gal.6.14.Phil.1.29. an obsecro verus ipse Dux & antelignanus nosterad tanti certaminis intuitum coram militibus suis metu prostratus animum abiecisset? Quod si ita esset, quomodo verè suos hortatus animum illis addidisset,aiens,Confidite,ego vici mundum? Ioh.16.33. Quantum igitur illud certamen vnde tantus exortus est metus ab illo distat?Hoc ipsum Apostolus optimè nos docet, non tantùm dicens Seruatorem nostrum crucifixum, & cruci affixum mortuum, sed pro nobis factum execrationem. Gal.3.13. Quid igitur in Domini passionibus eum tantopere perterruit? Nimirum quod tam horrendum,stupendum est & terri ficum, vt illud nulla res creata mente aequatur, terribilis illius furor, ante cuius etiam non irati Maiestatem Angeli faciem suam operiunt, montes sudore liquefiunt, terra tremit tremebunda, mare fugit: coram quo denique tanquam iudice nulla res creata subsistit, quum nihil sit horribilius quàm in Dei viuentis manus incidere. Christum igitur, vt creaturam, & in diebus adhuc infirmitatis suae terruit, immensus ille Dei Patris furor, nō aduersus vnum hominem, aut vnum peccatum exardens, sed aduersus totam naturam hominum corruptionem, & omnia peccata omnium electorum, qui sunt, fuerunt, & ad fine vsque seculorum futuri sunt. Ecquis igitur eum amplius miretur tanto metu & horrore perculsum quantum nullæ humani ingenij vires imaginari possint.
units.tr: But could anyone think that Christ, from whom the subject members, as from their head, draw life and strength, had less courage than so many men and women of every age, and even small children, whom we see, both before and after his coming, showing great eagerness in enduring and great constancy in bearing not only reproaches but also the most savage torments and tortures devised by Satan and his henchmen, and thus showing magnanimity and strength? He who bids his people exult amid those very persecutions (Matt. 5.12), and glory in tribulations in the Lord (Rom. 5.3; 8.17), as we see all the saints who suffered persecution for righteousness have done (Gal. 6.14; Phil. 1.29). I ask you, would the true leader and forerunner of ours, overcome with fear at the sight of so great a struggle, have cast down his courage in the presence of his soldiers? And if that were so, how could he truly have encouraged them and added courage to them, saying, "Take heart, I have overcome the world" (John 16.33)? How far, then, is that struggle, from which such great fear arose, removed from him? The Apostle teaches us this very thing most clearly, saying not only that our Saviour was crucified and, fastened to the cross, died, but that he was made a curse for us (Gal. 3.13). What, then, so greatly terrified him in the Lord's sufferings? Surely it was that dreadful and astonishing and terrifying thing, which no created mind can equal: the terrible fury of him before whose majesty even the angels, though he is not angry, cover their faces; before whom the mountains melt in sweat, the trembling earth quakes, the sea flees; before whom finally no created thing stands as before a judge, since nothing is more dreadful than to fall into the hands of the living God. So it was the immense fury of God the Father, blazing not against one man or one sin, but against the whole corrupt nature of mankind and all the sins of all the elect, who are, who have been, and who will be until the end of the ages, that terrified Christ, as a creature, even in the days of his weakness. Who then could be astonished that he was struck with such fear and horror as no powers of human intellect can imagine?

units.la: Contrà vero, quid fideles Dei serui in mediis cruciatibus, quos asperrimos propter nomen sanctum ipsius perferunt, viderunt, videt aut olim visuri sunt? Coelos, inquam, apertos, vt teltatur D. Stephanus Act.7.56. Patrem in eo reconciliatum qui à dextris eius sedet, & constanter fidelibus suis ad exemplum D. Pauli certantibus iustitiæ coronam immarcescibilem porrigit. 2.Tim.4.8. Hinc gaudiū illorū & exultatio, non modò non formidantium mortem, sed ad Simeonis exemplum cum pace & animi maxima tranquillitate è viuis excedentium Luc.2.29. Hinc fit vt Apostolum imitati migrare desiderent & esse cum Christo Phil.1.23. reficiente illos & refocillante in mediis flammis Sancto Spiritu & in eorum cordibus has tâ eximias promissiones obsignante, fore vt qui hac de causa vitam amiserint eam inuenīat.Matt.10.38.& cum illo morientes,cum illo viuant in sempiternum.
units.tr: On the other hand, what did the faithful servants of God see, or what do they see, or what will they one day see, in the midst of the torments which they endure most bitterly for his holy name? The heavens opened, as St Stephen bears witness (Acts 7.56); the Father reconciled in him, who sits at his right hand, and who steadfastly offers the unfading crown of righteousness to his faithful ones who strive, after the example of St Paul (2 Tim. 4.8). Hence comes their joy and exultation: they not only do not fear death, but, after the example of Simeon, depart from this life in peace and the greatest tranquillity of mind (Luke 2.29). Hence it is that, imitating the Apostle, they desire to depart and to be with Christ (Phil. 1.23), while the Holy Spirit refreshes and revives them in the midst of the flames and seals in their hearts these so remarkable promises, that whoever for this reason loses his life will find it (Matt. 10.38), and dying with him will live with him for ever.

units.la: Verum vnde in dilectum filium, & iustissimum omnium iustorum hanc iram Patris deriuatam dicemus?
