Nempe, quod vt superiori-bus homiliis docui, & cuius satisfecisse meconfido,oportebat iustissimum aliquem & inomnibus obsequentem, vt esset Deo grata &accepta victima & expiatio pro nostris rebel-lionibus,Dei iudicio satisfacere,vt imprudensCaiaphas etiam praedixerat.Ioh.11.50.quod etiam praeter alios Prophetas, longe expressius Esaias significarat.c.53.4.Causa igitur in nobis erat,& in fideiussorem deriuata,in quo nos oportet quid sit peccatum velut in speculo contemplari, quo illud pro viribus auersati, refugiamus, quo tamen illecti, nimium indulgemus, vt sumus deinceps pluribus exposituri.
units.tr: But from whence shall we say this wrath of the Father was derived upon his beloved Son, the most righteous of all the righteous? Clearly, as I taught in the earlier homilies, and I trust I have satisfied this point, it was necessary that some most righteous one, obedient in all things, should be a victim pleasing and acceptable to God, and an expiation for our rebellions, to satisfy the judgement of God, as the unwitting Caiaphas had also foretold (John 11.50). Isaiah had also signified this much more clearly than the other prophets (Isa. 53.4). The cause, then, was in us, but it was derived upon the surety, in whom we must contemplate, as in a mirror, what sin is, so that we may turn away from it as far as we can and flee from it; yet we, enticed by it, indulge in it too much, as we shall be about to set out at more length afterwards.

units.la: Accipite porro quiddam omnino cognitu necessarium,nempe quemadmodum humanaIesu Christi natura, vere fuit naturalis, sed tamen sine vitio,ita etiam illius terrores sine vlla peccati labe fuisse,quum tamen naturae no-strae penitus in se corruptae affectus(tum etiam quum laude aliqua digni videntur, siquidem remanēt aliquod inter vitium & virtutem discrimen naturale)nihil aliud sint quam putidi fructus ex arbore putrida, ac proinde in duabus caulis deficientes,primum in arbore a qua produntur.Matth.7.18.& Luc.3.44.deinde fine,qui non potest esse veri Dei gloria, quan-
units.tr: Note next something altogether necessary to know: just as the human nature of Jesus Christ was truly natural yet without sin, so his terrors were free of any stain of sin. The affections of our nature, wholly corrupt in itself, are different. Even when they seem worthy of some praise (since a natural distinction between vice and virtue remains), they are nothing but rotten fruit from a rotten tree (Matt. 7.18; Luke 3.44). They fail in two respects: first in the tree from which they come, and then in their end, which cannot be the glory of the true God.

units.la: g. j. doquidem non idonei fumus ex nobis ipsis ad cogitandum quicquam eorum quae Dei sunt velut ex nobis ipsis.2.Cor.3.5. atque adeo intelligetia carnis est inimicitia adversus Deum. Rom. 8.7. Quod ad regenitos autem hic adhuc repentes attinet, quum ex parte tantum regeniti sint, nihil ab illis nasci potest vel intus vel foris, quod non aliquam a natiuae corruptionis reliquiis labem & maculam trahat. Denique ut rem in pauca conferam humanae omnes affectiones humanitatis Domini nostri Iesu Christi, quae in maxime regenitis semper aliqua rebellione, diffidentia aut desperatione mixtae sunt, in illo purae, naturales, ac proinde nulla macula foedatae fuerunt. Et quemadmodum horum omnium causa in nobis erat, & non in ipso, sed super ipsum tanquam vadem ac sponsorem nostrum: sic etiam poena in illo fuit, nec in nobis esset. O immensam bonitatem & plus quam incomprehensibilem Dei sapientiam, Dei filium eousque se exinaniuisse, ut in inferorum pro nobis gurgitem immersus fuerit, ut ipse victoria de hostibus reportata nos etiam supra coelos omnes euehéret.
units.tr: Since we are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves (2 Cor. 3.5), the mind of the flesh is enmity against God (Rom. 8.7). As for the regenerate who still crawl here, since they are regenerate only in part, nothing can come from them, inwardly or outwardly, that does not contract some stain or blemish from the remnants of native corruption. To put it briefly: all the human affections of the humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, which in even the most regenerate are always mixed with some rebellion, distrust or despair, were in him pure and natural, and so not defiled by any stain. Just as the cause of all these lay in us and not in him, but over him as our surety and sponsor, so the punishment fell on him, which would otherwise have fallen on us. O immense goodness and more than incomprehensible wisdom of God, that the Son of God emptied himself so far that he was plunged for us into the abyss of hell, so that, having won the victory over his enemies, he might lift us all above the heavens.

units.la: Quod ad tertium caput, hae preces ad patrem diriguntur, quod tamen mirum fortasse videatur. Nam quum Filius unus idemque sit cum Patre Deus, ac proinde non aliam a Patre essentiam, potentiam nec voluntatem habeat, inferendum videtur, (quod est absurdissimum) Christum seipsum precari, aut personam Patris a Filij persona separari, unde sequeretur dua s
units.tr: As to the third head, these prayers are addressed to the Father, which may perhaps seem strange. For since the Son is one and the same God with the Father, and so has no essence, power or will other than the Father's, it seems to follow (which is most absurd) that Christ prays to himself, or that the person of the Father is separated from the person of the Son, from which it would follow that there are two

units.la: Christus licet cum Patre sit in eadem essentia unus idemque Deus, non tamen semper duas esse Deitates & duos Deos: quod etiam de Sp. S. persona dici potest. Facilis responsio. Primum Filij personam & Patris personam duas esse personas: ac proinde dici non posse Filium precantem Patrem se ipsum esse precatum: quod saepe ab illo videmus factum ut nos hanc distinctionem non autem separationem docerer. Sic enim Filius a Patris persona distinctus est, ut esse proprium & particulare non habeat, quod in creaturis visu venit, quarum tot sunt essentiae numero diuisae, quot sunt res creatae, sed in eadem sola Essentia subsistit, in qua tres Personae subsistunt, quae hanc ob causam unus idemque sunt Deus, sed tamen non sunt una eademque persona, sed tres personae suis hypostaticis proprietatibus distinctae. Observa deinde nullum esse proprie in tribus illis personis gradum maiorem, aut minorem, sed summam aequalitatem: verum aliquem esse ordinem, quo fit ut persona Patris sit origo Filij, ac proinde prima persona, filius secunda, Spiritus Sanctus a Patre & Filio coniunctim procedens, tertia: quod Christus docere nos quum volucrit, Patrem semper in precibus nominauit, minime tamen silentio praeteriens, Patrem esse in se, & se in Patre eadem essentia & Deitate.
units.tr: Although Christ is one and the same God with the Father in the same essence, there are nonetheless not two Deities and two Gods; the same can be said of the person of the Holy Spirit. The answer is easy. First, the person of the Son and the person of the Father are two persons, so it cannot be said that the Son, praying to the Father, prayed to himself. We often see him do this, so that he might teach us this distinction, not separation. The Son is so distinct from the person of the Father that he does not have a proper and particular essence, as is seen in creatures, of which there are as many numerically divided essences as there are created things. Rather he subsists in the one and the same Essence, in which three Persons subsist. For this reason they are one and the same God, yet they are not one and the same person, but three persons distinguished by their hypostatic properties. Observe next that among those three persons there is properly no greater or lesser degree, but the highest equality; yet there is an order, so that the person of the Father is the origin of the Son, and so is the first person, the Son the second, and the Holy Spirit, proceeding jointly from Father and Son, the third. When Christ chose to teach us this, he always named the Father in his prayers, yet never passed over in silence that the Father is in himself and he in the Father, of the same essence and Deity.

units.la: Tertiò, notandum licet quum unica Dei sit essentia, potentia, & voluntas, etiam communes sint tribus personis omnes operationes quae sunt, ut loquuntur, ad extra, ut in primis duae illę excellentissimę, mundi creatio & hominis redemptio, nihilominus tamen quem-admodum tres illæ personæ in sua essentia distinctæ sunt, ita in earum operationibus eandem obseruari debere distinctionem. Pater igitur mundum condidit, sed per Sapientiam suam coæternam & coessentialem, qui filius est unigenitus, omnia disposuit & ordinauit. Genes. 1.3. Ioh. 1.3. & per Potentiam suam à Patre & Filio procedentem, quæ Sp. S. Persona est, eadem est executus, & hodie tanti operis molem fouet & conseruat. Genes. 1.2. Psal. 103. 29. & 30. Non absimili ratione in hominis redemptione tribus personis communi, Patris persona Filium misit, Filius nostram naturam sibi assumptam vniuit: Spiritus vero Sancti persona ea est cuius vi & operatione vnio illa Personalis in vtero Mariæ Virginis facta est, & per quam humana illa natura ad suum munus peragendum est sanctificata.
units.tr: Thirdly, it should be noted that although God's essence, power and will are one, and all the operations that are, as they say, ad extra are common to the three persons, as in the two most excellent, the creation of the world and the redemption of man, nevertheless, just as those three persons are distinct in their essence, the same distinction must be observed in their operations. The Father therefore created the world, but arranged and ordered all things through his Wisdom, coeternal and coessential, who is the only-begotten Son (Gen. 1.3; John 1.3); and he carried it out through his Power, proceeding from Father and Son, which is the person of the Holy Spirit, and today he cherishes and preserves the mass of so great a work (Gen. 1.2; Ps. 103.29–30). In a not dissimilar way, in the redemption of man, which is common to the three persons: the person of the Father sent the Son, the Son united our nature to himself by assuming it, and the person of the Holy Spirit is the one by whose power and operation that personal union was made in the womb of the Virgin Mary, and through whom that human nature was sanctified to perform its work.

units.la: Porro ad huius quæstionis enodationem, superioribus addendum quod est à quodam ex Patribus obseruatum non inepte, in hoc redemptionis nostræ mysterio, Personæ filij impositio, necesse fuisse naturam nostram in qua passurus erat, horrorem illius maledictionis Dei perspentiscere quam eramus meriti: nec aliud in Patris persona intueri ad tempus nisi horrendum & modis omnibus terrificum furorem illum iræ diuinæ, quam ipsum nostra causa subire & absorbere oportuit. Deitas autem ipsius personæ Filij respectu, quieuit ad tempus, nec vim suam exeruit, veluti Dei Patris
units.tr: Further, to unfold this question, something should be added to what was said above, which one of the Fathers observed not inappropriately. In this mystery of our redemption, the imposition of the person of the Son made it necessary that our nature, in which he was to suffer, should perceive the horror of that curse of God which we had deserved. Nor, for a time, did it see in the person of the Father anything but that horrible and in every way terrifying fury of divine wrath, which he had to undergo and absorb on our account. But the Deity of the person of the Son, as far as it was concerned, rested for a time and did not exert its power, as did God the Father.

units.la: Quomodo Iesus Christus licet Deus per terrimus fueris horrore furoris iusti Dei Patris, tris decreto conquiescens. Idem esto de Spiritus Sancti persona iudicium, qui in tanto discrimine naturam humanam eo usque tantum sustinuit, ne divino furore penitus absorbeatur. O immensam & incomprehensam Dei sapientiam, summo nobis beneficio revelatam, & palpabilem factam, quum tame in eam adhuc Angeli introspicere, scrutarique penitius illam exoptent. 1. Pet. 1. 2.
units.tr: How Jesus Christ, though God, was yet terrified by the horror of the just fury of God the Father, while resting by his decree. The same judgment holds for the person of the Holy Spirit, who in so great a danger sustained the human nature only so far, lest it be wholly swallowed up by divine fury. O immense and incomprehensible wisdom of God, revealed to us for the greatest benefit and made palpable, though the angels still long to look into it and search it more deeply (1. Pet. 1. 2.).

units.la: Quartum in hoc mysterio caput consideradu superest, vere maximu 1. Tim. 3. 16. & multis seculis abscondítum, Ephes. 3. 9. non minus quam reliqua stupendum. Primum enim Dominus noster Iesus Christus hic Patris potentiam cum Voluntate committere velle videtur. Deinde quum Patris decretum nosset, & ad illud implendum se comparasset, quod immutabile esse non ignorabat, quinam illum quae fieri nec potuerunt nec debuerunt suppliciter tamen deprecari patrem dicturi sumus? Praeterea quum nihil vnquam simulate, sed sincere omnia gesserit, quinam obsecro videbitur volens ea pertulisse quae nostri causa perpessus est, quum tam enixe poculum istud sit deprecatus? Quod si ita est, qui fieri potest ut eius obedientia nostra rebellio contegatur? Denique si velle quod Dei voluntati contrarium esse non ignoramus, est Deum offendere, qua tandem ratione Christum peccato liberabimus? Quid vero nobis fiet miseris, si qua in Christo inest peccati macula? Spinose sane admodum & immensae quaestiones, quas dum plerique ex Veteribus enodare studeant, plurimum ab huius historiae scopo recesserunt, sed eas iuuante Deo, facile dissoluemus, necessariamque ex illis consolationem hauriemus.
units.tr: The fourth head to be considered in this mystery remains. It is truly the greatest (1 Tim. 3.16), hidden for many ages (Eph. 3.9), and no less amazing than the rest. For first, our Lord Jesus Christ here seems to wish to set his power against the will of the Father. Then, since he knew the Father's decree and had prepared himself to fulfil it, which he knew could not be changed, whom shall we say he was begging, when he prayed humbly that things which could neither be done nor ought to be done might be averted? Moreover, since he never did anything feignedly but everything sincerely, who, I ask, will seem to have willingly endured what he suffered for our sake, when he prayed so earnestly that the cup might pass from him? If so, how can his obedience cover our rebellion? Finally, if to will what we know to be contrary to God's will is to offend God, by what reasoning shall we free Christ from sin? What then will become of us wretches, if any stain of sin is in Christ? These are indeed very thorny and immense questions. While many of the ancients strive to resolve them, they have strayed far from the aim of this history. But with God's help we shall readily dissolve them and draw from them the consolation we need.

units.la: Duobus igitur illis quae paulo ante exposuimus positis, nempe primum totum istud mysterium nominatim humanae Christi naturae tribuendum: deinde quum natura nostra corrupta sit, nullum in nobis affectum integrum supererse qui non pollutus sit, natura contra humanam Iesu Christi semper purissima fuisse et sanctissimam, licet se nostra causa maximis grauissimisque infirmitatibus subiecerit, ac proinde purissimas etiam et sanctissimas omnes eius affectiones fuisse: his, inquam positis statuendum est, prout hominis cogitatio mouetur operante obiecto sensuum in apprehensione, ita inde nascentes affectiones plus minus-ve viriu habere. Quum igitur obiectu moderate mouet apprehensionem, quae ad intellectum et rationem obiecta refert, tum etiam accidit affectiones temperatas et moderatas effici, ut velint quod velle, et ut velle oportet, contra nolint quae nolle oportet etiam sicut nolle oportet. At si sic ab obiecto moueatur apprehensio, ut ancipiti cogitatione modo huc modo illuc feratur, (quod Philosophi pugnam vocant inter rationem et hominum non regenerationum affectus, Scriptura vero S. in regeneratis, carnis luctam aduersus Spiritum nominat, qualem Apost. excellentissime depingit Rom.
units.tr: Therefore, with the two points we have just set out laid down (first, that this whole mystery is to be attributed expressly to the human nature of Christ; second, that since our nature is corrupt, no affection in us remains whole that is not polluted, whereas the human nature of Jesus Christ was always most pure and most holy, although for our sake he subjected himself to the greatest and heaviest infirmities, and so all his affections were most pure and most holy), it must be stated that, as the thought of man is moved by the object acting on the senses in apprehension, so the affections arising from it have more or less force. When the object moves the apprehension moderately, which refers the objects to the intellect and reason, then the affections also come to be temperate and moderate, so that they will what ought to be willed, and will it as they ought, and conversely are unwilling in what they ought to be unwilling, and as they ought to be. But if the apprehension is so moved by the object that it is carried in a wavering thought, now here, now there (which the philosophers call the struggle between reason and the affections of men who are not regenerate, while Holy Scripture calls it, in the regenerate, the struggle of the flesh against the Spirit, which the Apostle depicts most excellently in Rom. 7.15), then the affections, even in the unregenerate, remain for a time doubtful and wavering, until reason, as far as it can be in them, prevails by inclining them to embrace what they call the shadow of virtue and to shun vice; or, on the contrary, once reason is overcome,

units.la: Varii effectus apprehensionis in intellectu. Rom.7.15.) tum affectiones etiam in non regeneratis tantisper dubiae & ancipites remanent, dum ratio, qualis in ipsis esse poterit, inclinata vincat, ad amplectendam eam quam vocant virtutis umbram, & vitium fugiendum, aut contra superata ratione, in vitium feratur deliberatio non autem in virtutem. Sic in regeneratis saepe fit ut superior concupiscentia, format peccatum, Iac.1.15. contrà vero spiritu vires per Dei gratiam resumente, & in victorem cuadente fructus poenitentiae producantur. Multò magis igitur quum primo statim obtuitu obiectum ita movet phantasiam, ut ratiocinationi quae ad intellectum & rationem procedere debuerat via precludatur, tum sane nonnunquam ita voluntas quasi sublatis repagulis praeceps fertur ad ea appetenda quae erant fugienda, aut contrà reiicienda quae fuerant amplectenda: quae quidem perturbatio non potest non esse vitiosa, tum Dei respectu, ad cuius voluntatis amussim nostram exigere debemus, tum etiam hominum, quatenus ratio, quantulamcunque habent homines reliquam, affectus ipsorum regere & illis imperare debet. Nonnunquam etiam accidit ut voluntas non progrediatur usque ad absolutam conclusionem: sed ad tempus haereat anceps, nihil nisi cum conditione deliberans, donec tandem bona aliqua firmáque conclusione omnis illa fluctuatio terminetur: quae tamen omnia clariora fient exemplis. Iacobum eximia Rachelis forma
units.tr: Various effects of apprehension in the intellect. Rom. 7.15.) Then, in the unregenerate too, the affections remain for a while doubtful and wavering, while reason, such as it can be in them, prevails by inclining them to embrace what they call the shadow of virtue and to flee vice. Or, on the contrary, when reason is overcome, deliberation is carried into vice and not into virtue. So in the regenerate it often happens that the stronger concupiscence, once conceived, brings forth sin (James 1.15). But when the spirit, resuming its strength through the grace of God, prevails and the conqueror falls, the fruits of repentance are produced. Much more, therefore, when at the first glance the object so moves the imagination that the route of reasoning, which ought to lead to the intellect and reason, is blocked, then the will, as if the barriers were removed, is sometimes hurried headlong to desire those things which were to be fled, or on the contrary to reject those which were to be embraced. This disturbance cannot but be sinful, both with respect to God, to whose rule we ought to conform ours, and with respect to men, insofar as reason, however small a remnant men have, ought to govern their affections and command them. Sometimes it also happens that the will does not proceed to a complete conclusion, but remains for a time wavering, deliberating only conditionally, until at last by some good and firm conclusion all that fluctuation is ended. All these things will be made clearer by examples. Jacob, by the outstanding beauty of Rachel

units.la: g. iiij. mouit, vt eam appeterer, Gen.29.regitur tamē ille motus ratione cui Dei timor imperat, adeò vt eam non nisi caste & pudicè amet, etsi tantus est amor iste, tamque vehemens vt illum nec prius cum Lea coniugium, nec quatuor-decim annorum repetitum seruitium extinguere vel immutare potuerit. Etsi vero quiddam in hoc inest exemplo solis regeneratis peculiare, fatendum tamen est etiam in non regeneratis eosdem illos affectus, natura sua vitiosos, ita Deum quoties libet coercere vt ratione & intelligentia, quantulacunque restat hominibus, regantur, ne in actum erumpant, ad humani generis coseruationem aliquì mox periturì. Dauid contrà cospecta Bersabea, tanto impetu præceps fertur, vt nihil eum cohibeat, nec vlla primæ vel secundæ tabulæ præcepta, quibus in officio contineatur veniant illi in mentem, aut si veniunt, statim reiiciantur inaudita, ex quo perfidum illum, adulterum & homicidam factum videmus, donec sola sua gratia Deus à tanto veterno sopitum excitet, & ad facti veram pœnitentiam compellat.
units.tr: moved him to desire her (Gen. 29.). Yet that motion was governed by reason, over which the fear of God holds sway, so that he loved her only chastely and modestly. Although this love was so great and so vehement that neither the marriage with Leah nor the fourteen years of service renewed could extinguish or change it, it was still restrained. Although there is something in this example peculiar to the regenerate alone, it must be admitted that even in the unregenerate those same affections, vicious by nature, are restrained by God whenever he pleases, so that they are governed by reason and understanding, however small a remnant men have, lest they break out into act, to the preservation of the human race, some of whom would soon perish. David, on the other hand, having seen Bathsheba, is carried headlong with such impetus that nothing restrains him. No precepts of the first or second table, by which he would be kept in duty, come to his mind, or if they come, they are immediately rejected unheard. From this we see him made a treacherous adulterer and murderer, until God alone by his grace rouses him from so great a lethargy and compels him to true repentance for the deed.

units.la: Age vero aliud etiam alterius athletæ fortissimi, lapsi quidem sed non omnino prostrati exemplum discutiamus. Iobus miris & horrendis modis afflictus, stat tamen inuictus, donec ab amicis, etsi nihil minus cogitantibus irritatus, in cogitationes stupendas incidit, diem natalem execratus, integritate suam mirum in modum prædicans, atque adeo eo vsque deuceniens vt cū Deo querulus nimium expoltulet, cuius tandem excessus à Domino corripitur. Nihil tamen in tanta animi perturbatione aduersus Deum statuit, sed contrà, licet extra metas longiùs feratur, Dei fauore seipsum cohibet, & erigit etsi pendeat animi dubius, causas tantæ tamque repentinæ mutationis penitus non animaduertens. Age etiam Petri sociorúmque eius exemplum intueamur. Capto Iudæ proditione ipsorum Magistro sic terrentur, licet prænoniti, vt fugam capessant, minime tamen ab eo defeƈturi, aut ad Iudæos perfugarum instar transituri. Verùm metus & tam repentina & inopinata rerum facies, dubios facit & inopes consilij quàm viam sequantur: in quo tamen non omni vitio liberantur, nimio nimirum ad diffidentiam accedente metu. Petrus verò terrore perculsus longè vlteriùs progreditur, vt, si nō ex animo, saltem exteriusDominum suum abnegare, sibíque ipsi dicas imprecari non vereatur. Sed ne curiosius exempla istiusmodi perquiramus, quoties contingit vel ita, vel falsa voluptatis specie, vel periculi metu fortissimos quosque alios quidem momento alios sensim ac pedetentim vinci ac superari, tum harum passionum vi, tum negligentia Deum singulis horis sollicitandi precibus, ne in tentationem inducantur?
units.tr: Come now, let us examine the example of another most valiant athlete, fallen indeed but not wholly prostrated. Job, afflicted in wonderful and dreadful ways, nevertheless stands unconquered, until, provoked by his friends (though they were thinking nothing of the kind), he falls into astonishing thoughts. He curses his birthday, boasts of his integrity in a remarkable manner, and goes so far that, complaining against God, he expostulates too much, and for this excess he is at last rebuked by the Lord. Yet in so great a disturbance of mind he sets nothing against God. On the contrary, although carried further than the bounds, he restrains himself by God's favour and raises himself up, even though he hangs in doubt of mind, not fully perceiving the causes of so great and so sudden a change. Let us also look at the example of Peter and his companions. With Judas's betrayal of their Master taken, they are so terrified, although forewarned, that they take to flight, yet by no means about to desert him or to pass over to the Jews as deserters. But fear and so sudden and unexpected an aspect of things make them doubtful and without counsel as to which way to follow. In this they are not freed from all fault, since excessive fear adds distrust. Peter, however, struck down by terror, goes much further, so that, if not from the heart, at least outwardly, he does not hesitate to deny his Lord and even to invoke curses upon himself. But, not to search out examples of this kind more curiously, how often does it happen that the strongest men, now by one and now by another false appearance of pleasure, or by fear of danger, are overcome and defeated, some in a moment, others gradually and step by step? This happens both through the power of these passions and through neglect of pleasing God with prayers every hour, that they not be led into temptation.

units.la: Sed Christo Domino nostro quînam ista conuenire dixerimus quin cum in peccatorū & inordinatorum album referamus? Optimè sane, fi ex verbis eius etiam cogitationem metiamur,hoc posito quod ante docuimus, nullam fuisse in ipso luctam affectionum aduersus rationem, aut Spiritus cum carne, siquidem in ipso nulla caro fuit eiusmodi,id est vitiosa & corrupta. Duae sunt igitur huius partes: vna cum conditione, Si vis a me transferri hoc poculum: altera nuda & simplex, Id volo quod tu vis. In priore sane parte conditionali,apposita fubmiffione voluntatis Dei, nulla est inter Patris voluntatem, & Filij naturam humanam repugnantia. In altera vero tantum abest vt vlla sit voluntatum repugnantia, vt in ea contra perfectissimum habeamus exemplar ad quod duarum istarum voluntatum consensum exigamus. Rursum vero quaeritur,& no immerito quidem, quum Christus etiam secundum humanam naturam probe nosset decretum esse Patris immutabile vt poculum illud biberet, qui fieri posset vt in se motum illum sensserit,quamcunque conditionem apposuerit, quin aliqua mentem eius passio perstrinxerit Dei decreto minime consentiens, ac proinde non omni culpa vacet,quandoquidem cognita Dei voluntas nostram regere & sine vlla repugnantia mouere debet? Agnosco quidem in priore illa parte perturbationem aliquam, sed sine vitio tamen, sicut etiam Euangelistae ac Iohannes nominatim expresserunt,Christum fuisse perturbatum Ioh. 12. 27. adeo quidem vt in haec verba prorumperet, Nunc anima mea turbata est, &
units.tr: But to what extent can we say these things apply to Christ our Lord, unless we count him among the sinners and disordered? Certainly it is best, if we measure his thought also by his words, given what we taught before: that there was no struggle of the affections against reason in him, nor of Spirit against flesh, since in him there was no flesh of that kind, that is, vicious and corrupt. There are therefore two parts of this: one with a condition, "If it is possible, let this cup pass from me"; the other bare and simple, "I will what you will." In the former, conditional part, with the submission of the will to God's will added, there is no contrariety between the Father's will and the human nature of the Son. In the latter, there is so far from any contrariety of wills that we have in it the most perfect example to which we should require the agreement of these two wills. Again the question is asked, and not unreasonably: since Christ, even according to his human nature, knew well that the Father's decree to drink that cup was unchangeable, how could it be that he felt that motion in himself, whatever condition he added, without some passion touching his mind that did not agree with God's decree, and therefore was not free from all blame, since the known will of God ought to govern ours and move it without any contrariety? I acknowledge indeed in that former part some disturbance, but without sin, just as the Evangelists and John expressly state that Christ was troubled (John 12.27), so much so that he burst out into these words: "Now my soul is troubled, and"

units.la: & quid dicam? Pater, conserua me ab hac hora, sed propterea veni in horam hanc. Matthæus vero 26. 27. Græcum vocabulum vsurpat ἀδημονεῖν, quod præ mœrore concidere animo & inopem consilij esse significat: sicut etiam Marcus loquitur 14. 33. Primùm igitur obseruua non parùm differre vitium & naturalem infirmitatem à iusta causa proma-nantem, cuiusmodi fuisse iltam à sensu plus quàm humanæ vires apprehendant terrifico profectam videmus. Deinde perturbatio illa, quæ vix in quenquam mortalium sine aliquo rebellionis aut diffidentiæ sensu cadat, Christo non accidit ab illo interiore motu profecta, sed tantùm ab obiecto immensi furoris Dei aduersus eum vadem & sponsorem nostrum: cuius quidem aspectu sic eius perculsi sunt sensus vt ad tempus ratiocinatio subsisterit & velut abrupta fuerit: sed ita tamen vt neque eius vnquam intelligentia caligarit, aut ratio cæcutierit, nec etiá ex eius memoria decretum paternum effluxerit. Illa, inquam omnia quandiu fuit adeò terrificus pauor, interuenerunt: sed ita tamen temperata fuit perturbatio & composita, vt non longiùs abductus sit sed intra hos terminos se continuerit, vti transfiret hoc ab ipso poculum, si qua alia ratione patri placato liberer mundo reconciliari. Adde quòd ad breue tempus illa perturbatio sic cum perstrinxit, vt codem momento, licet tertiò redeunte perturbatione, toties etiam sit cohibitus, nō quidem vt vitio aliquo peccans, sed vt in omnibus fe Dei Patris voluntati prębens obsequentissimum. Minimè igitur Christus Dei Patris potentiam cum voluntate commisit: minimè Patris esse decretum irrevocabile dubitauit: minimè etiam contumacius id ad quod in mundum venerat exequi cogitauit, sed tantum ad tempus tanto diuini furoris terrifico intuitu perculsus est vt quæ sciens vol ens suscipiebat non attenderit. Agnosco tamen aliquam in his voluntatibus Patris & humanæ Christi naturæ diuersitatem, nullam autem repugnantiam aut contradictionem.
units.tr: and what shall I say? "Father, save me from this hour; but for this cause I came to this hour." But Matthew (26.37) uses the Greek word ἀδημονεῖν, which signifies to sink in spirit from grief and be without counsel, as Mark also speaks (14.33). First, then, observe that vice and natural weakness, arising from a just cause, differ not a little, such as we see that fear was, which came from a sense of terror beyond human powers. Then, that disturbance, which hardly falls upon any mortal without some sense of rebellion or distrust, did not befall Christ from an inward motion, but only from the object of the immense wrath of God against him, our surety and sponsor. By the sight of this his senses were so struck that for a time his reasoning stood still and was as it were broken off. Yet it was never so that his understanding was darkened, or his reason blinded, nor did the Father's decree slip from his memory. All these things, I say, happened for as long as the terrifying dread lasted. Yet the disturbance was so tempered and composed that he was not drawn further away, but kept himself within these limits, so that he would pass this cup from himself, if by some other means the Father could be appeased and he be freed and the world reconciled. Add that the disturbance seized him for only a short time, so that at the same moment, though it returned a third time, he was as often restrained. This was not as sinning by any fault, but as offering himself most obedient to the will of God the Father in all things. By no means, therefore, did Christ set the power of God the Father against his will; by no means did he doubt that the Father's decree was irrevocable; by no means did he even think of carrying out more stubbornly what he had come into the world for. He was only for a time so struck by the terrifying sight of divine wrath that he did not attend to what he was knowingly and willingly undertaking. Yet I acknowledge some difference between the wills of the Father and of Christ's human nature, but no opposition or contradiction.

units.la: Ardua hæc quidem, sed quæ tamen nisi huc vsque perscrutemur, nunquam satis comprehendamus nec quantum sit quamque detestandum peccatum: nec quantus sit quamque terrificus aduersus illud Dei furor: nec quàm immensa sit Patris charitas, filio suo propter nos non parcentis, nec quàm infinita filij dilectio tantam pro nobis sponte maledictionem subeuntis: tantum abest vt harum rerum curiosa, superflua aut inutilis sit meditatio. Atque hoc fuit quintum caput à nobis initio propositum, fructus nimirum quem ex tanta Seruatoris nostri exinanitione percipere nos oportet: vnicum fuisse explicandum quid ipsi Christo Domino nostro hæc precatio profuerit: quod Apostolus ad Hebr. 5.7. paucis & perspicuis verbis docet, eum dicens exauditum esse ex metu. Etsi enim in hoc exauditus non est ne poculum biberet, non tamen repulsam passus dici poterit, vt qui nihil nisi addita conditione petierit, à quae-tiam postea totus pependit. Sed in eo fuit exauditus, quòd mortis depositò pauore, victor, hostem prior aggreditur, vt in sequentibus fauente Deo sumus exposituri. Faxit verò Deus Opt. Max. vt haec tam ardua, tam magna, tam eximia, tam denique necessaria mysteria probè cognita, diligenter meditemur, & quandiu vita fruimur in vsum suum ad Nominis ipsius gloriam, & nostram salutem reuocemus,
units.tr: These matters are indeed difficult, yet unless we examine them thus far, we will never adequately grasp how great and how detestable sin is, nor how great and how terrifying God's wrath against it is, nor how immense the Father's love is, who did not spare his own Son for our sake, nor how infinite the Son's love is, who willingly underwent such a curse for us. So far is it from being the case that the careful meditation on these things is idle, superfluous, or useless. This was the fifth head that we proposed at the beginning: the fruit which we ought to receive from so great an emptying of our Saviour, namely, to explain what this prayer profited Christ our Lord himself. The Apostle teaches this in few and clear words at Heb. 5.7, saying that he was heard because of his fear. For although in this he was not heard, that the cup might not pass from him, yet it cannot be said that he suffered a refusal, since he had asked only on a condition, upon which he afterwards wholly depended. But he was heard in this: that, having laid aside the fear of death, he, as victor, goes forth first against the enemy, as we shall expound in what follows, God favouring us. May God, the best and greatest, grant that we diligently meditate on these difficult, great, excellent, and indeed necessary mysteries, once rightly understood, and that, as long as we enjoy life, we turn them to their proper use, for the glory of his name and our salvation.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA sexta.
units.tr: Homily 6.

units.la: MATTH. 26.
units.tr: MATTHEW 26.

units.la: 37. Et assumpto Petro & duobus filiis Zebedaei coepit contristari, & gravissime angi.
units.tr: 37. And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be saddened and to be sorely distressed.

units.la: 38. Tunc dicit eis Iesus, Vndiquaque tristis est anima mea vsque ad mortem: manete hic, & vigilate mecum.
units.tr: 38. Then Jesus said to them: My soul is sorrowful even unto death on every side; remain here and watch with me.

units.la: 39. Et progressus paululum, procidit in faciem suam, precans & dicens, Pater mi, si possibile est, abeat a me poculum istud: Verumtamen non ut ego volo, sed ut tu vis.
units.tr: 39. And going forward a little, he fell on his face, praying and saying: My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless not as I will, but as you will.

units.la: 42. Rursum secundo abiit, & precatus est dicens, Pater mi, si non potest hoc poculum abire quin bibam ipsum, fiat voluntas tua.
units.tr: 42. Again, for the second time, he went away and prayed, saying: My Father, if this cup cannot pass away unless I drink it, your will be done.

units.la: 44. Et relictis eis, rursus abiit & precatus est tertio, eundem sermonem locutus.
units.tr: 44. And leaving them, he went away again and prayed a third time, speaking the same words.

units.la: MARC. 14.
units.tr: MARK 14.

units.la: 34. Et dixit eis, Vndiquaque tristis est anima mea vsque ad mortem: manete hic & vigilate.
units.tr: 34. And he said to them: My soul is sorrowful even unto death on every side; remain here and watch.

units.la: 35. Progressusque paululum procidit in terram: & orabat ut si fieri posset, abiret ab ipso hora illa.
units.tr: 35. And going forward a little, he fell to the ground; and he prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him.

units.la: 36. Dixitque, Abba, Pater, omnia possibilia sunt tibi, Transfer a me istud poculum: verum non quid ego velim, sed quid tu.
units.tr: 36. And he said: Abba, Father, all things are possible to you; take this cup from me; yet not what I will, but what you will.

units.la: 39. Et quum rursus abiisset, precatus est, eundem sermonem locutus.
units.tr: 39. And when he had gone away again, he prayed, speaking the same words.

units.la: LVC. 22.
units.tr: Luke 22.

units.la: 40. Quum vero peruenisset ad eum locum, dixit eis, Precamini ne intretis in tentationem.
units.tr: 40. When he had come to that place, he said to them, "Pray that you do not enter into temptation."

units.la: 41. Tum ipse auulsus est ab eis quasi ad iactum lapidis, positisque genibus precatus est.
units.tr: 41. Then he himself was withdrawn from them about a stone's throw, and, kneeling down, he prayed.

units.la: 42. Dicens, Pater, si vis, transfer poculum a me: verumtamen non mea voluntas sed tua fiat.
units.tr: 42. Saying, "Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done."

units.la: 43. Visus est autem ei Angelus, e coelo corroborans eum.
units.tr: 43. And an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.

units.la: 44. Et ipse constitutus in angore, intentius orabat. Erat autem sudor eius quasi grumi sanguinis descendentes in terram.
units.tr: 44. And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly. And his sweat became like drops of blood falling down upon the ground.

units.la: Nodatis hactenus difficultatibus in hanc Domini precationem incurrentibus, & illius summa propositia, superest ut eius singulas partes explicemus, ab hisChristi verbis facientes initium, Vndiquaque tristis est anima mea vsque ad mortem. ex quibus exim ia plurima documenta nobis colligenda sunt. Ac primum quidem filium Dei veram & integram humanam naturam, vera anima humana veróque corpore constantem in solidum non ex parte tantum assumpsisse, sibique vniuiisse, quo nimirum, tum corpora nostra, tum animas nostras, facta pro vtriusque tum corpore tum anima satisfactione redimeret a morte: quod aduersus eorum haeresin obseruandum est, qui Deitate fuisse humano Christi corpori loco animae, errore vt salsissimo itapericulo finxerunt.
units.tr: Having so far dealt with the difficulties that arise in this prayer of the Lord, and having set out its general sense, it remains that we explain its individual parts, beginning with these words of Christ, "My soul is sorrowful on every side, even unto death." From these many teachings are to be gathered for us. And first, the Son of God assumed, and united to himself, a true and complete human nature, consisting of a true human soul and a true body, entirely and not merely in part, so that by making satisfaction on behalf of both body and soul he might redeem from death both our bodies and our souls. This must be observed against the heresy of those who, in a most foolish and dangerous error, imagined that the Deity took the place of the soul in the human body of Christ.

units.la: Deinde docemur his verbis, Christum non tantum naturam humanam cum essentialibus proprietatibus, sine quibus non esset vera natura humana, sed mane quid & imaginarium, verum etiam omnes illius passiones & affectus absque vlla tamen vllius vitij labecula, ne minima quidem assumpsisse. Sunt autem illi naturales affectus trifariam considerandi: primum respectu naturae humanae qualis fuit ante lapsum in Adamo: deinde prout post lapsum in Adamo, plum eftin eodem immutata: ac postremo vt in Christo postquam nostram infirmitatem exuit, spectatur. Iesus Christus igitur sibi naturam nostram personaliter assumens, etsi longe purior & perfectior in illo fuerit quam ante lapsum in Adamo, assumpsit tamen eam statu & conditione longe inferiore. Nec enim Adamus ante lapsum nondum a Deo alienatus, vel timori vel tristitiae erat obnoxius: quum res omnes creatae quas eius imperio Deus subiecerat ab eius nutu penderent: & nihil esset in tota orbis machina inordinatum ac perturbatum, sed omnia singulari perfectione temperata. Praeterea donatus erat immortalitate, quandoquidem per peccatum mors in mundum peruasit. Christus autem homo factus homini instaurando peccatis nostris debitas poenas luendo, humanam naturam sua, sponte tamen, & absque vllo vitio, let hiferis omnibus doloribus, & tristibus omnibus perturbationibus & affectibus, quibus vita haec calamitosa carere non poterat: atque adeo, quod in priprimis confideradum est morti illi tam crude-li & ignominiosæ cum hortibili & terrifica Dei maledictione coniunctę subiecit. Tandem verò munere illo suo perfunctus infirmitatis suæ tempore, ea deposita vitam nunc viuit, non animalem & iis quibus illa superior obnoxia: sed spiritualem, æternam, gloriosissimam, in summo dignitatis gradu constitutam, ad quā etiam singula membra sua pro cuiusque men-sura, felici illo die vltimo enecturus est, vt Apostolus 1. Corint. 15. luculentissimè demon-strat.
units.tr: Next, we are taught by these words that Christ assumed not only human nature with its essential properties, without which it would not be a true human nature, but also, I might add, its imaginary qualities; indeed, he assumed all its sufferings and affections, yet without any stain of sin, not even the smallest. Now these natural affections are to be considered in three ways: first, with respect to human nature as it was before the fall in Adam; second, as it was after the fall, when it was changed in Adam; and finally, as it is seen in Christ, after he put off our weakness. Jesus Christ, therefore, personally assuming our nature, though it was far purer and more perfect in him than before the fall in Adam, nevertheless assumed it in a condition and state far lower. For Adam before the fall, not yet estranged from God, was subject neither to fear nor to sadness, since all created things that God had placed under his rule depended on his nod; nothing in the whole machine of the world was disordered or troubled, but all things were governed with singular perfection. Moreover, he was endowed with immortality, since death entered the world through sin. But Christ, made man to restore man, by paying the penalties owed to our sins, of his own accord yet without any fault, submitted his human nature to all the bitter pains and sad disturbances and affections from which this calamitous life could not be free. And so, what must be considered above all, he submitted himself to that death, so cruel and shameful, joined with the dreadful and terrifying curse of God. Finally, having discharged that office of his in the time of his weakness, he laid that weakness aside and now lives a life not animal, subject to those things by which that life is burdened, but spiritual, eternal, most glorious, placed at the highest degree of dignity, to which he will bring his individual members, each in proportion to his measure, on that final happy day, as the Apostle 1 Cor. 15 most clearly demonstrates.

units.la: Animaduerte porrò multis modis hanc Christi tristitiam & horrendum dolorem, à naturalibus nostris affectibus & doloribus moeroribusque differre. Non parum enim peccant homines in moerorum & angorum suorum causis, vt qui saepe dolore exiis afficiantur, ex quibus laetitiam sperare debuerant: & contrà laetitiam percipiant, ex quibus moerore ipsos affici decuerat. Deinde, liqua subest iulta doloris causa, tum modum teruare nescientes, grauissimè peccant, quòd vel tristitiam æquo citius abiiciant, vel immoderatius illi indulgeant, adeò vt alij ex impatientia Deo ipsi obloquantur, alij distorta & obliqua consilia capiant quibus vel ex malis emergant, vel in desperationem præcipites ferantur. Denique si eorum attendas consilia, qui eiusmodi se ærumnis exoluere conantur, sola illos ægritudine malorum ac suæ fortis tangi, & suæ quietis ac tranquillitatis amore ferri coperies. At Iesu
units.tr: Furthermore, observe that this sadness and dreadful pain of Christ differ from our natural affections, sorrows, and griefs in many ways. For men sin greatly in the causes of their sorrows and distresses, since they are often afflicted by pain from things from which they ought to hope for joy, and conversely they receive joy from things by which they ought to be grieved. Then, when there is some just cause of sorrow, those who do not know how to keep measure sin most gravely, either by laying sadness aside too quickly or by indulging in it too immoderately; so that some, from impatience, even speak against God himself, while others adopt crooked and devious counsels by which they hope either to escape their evils or are carried headlong into despair. Finally, if you consider the plans of those who try to free themselves from such troubles, you will find that they are moved only by the sickness of their misfortunes and their own situation, and carried along by love of their own peace and tranquillity. But the grief and sadness of Jesus Christ our Lord,

units.la: h. j. Christi Domini nostri dolor & tristitia, cuius origo, non in ipso incrat, sed in nobis, & super ipsum tantum, iustissima fuit & inevitabilis, sensus nimirum horrendi furoris Creatoris adversus peccata quae in se susceperat. Etsi vero fuit ille sensus irae Dei tam immensus, ut nulla posset eum humana mens aequi, fuit tamen omni vitiosa perturbatione vacuus: itaque tam bene compositorum affectuum, idem etiam finis fuit, gloria Dei Patris cum omnium electorum salute coniuncta, quod ubique testatus est, sed in primis toto.17.Ioh.capite.
units.tr: whose origin lay not in himself but in us, and which bore upon him alone, was most just and unavoidable: namely, the sense of the dreadful wrath of the Creator against the sins that he had taken upon himself. And although that sense of the wrath of God was so immense that no human mind could grasp it, it was nevertheless free from every sinful disturbance; and so, of these affections so well ordered, the end was also the same: the glory of God the Father joined with the salvation of all the elect, which he attested everywhere, but especially in the whole of John 17.

units.la: Tristitia igitur illa qua Christus devorata victor extitit, quam nos nunquam emersuri perferre debebamus, vere nostrum est gaudiu & consolatio, ut eius exinanitio & humiliatio, nostra est exaltatio & glorificatio, ac tandem mors eius & resurrectio, vita nostra est salúsque sempiterna. Ac ni ita esset, quomodo fieret Evangelium laetus pacis nuntius in umbra mortis sedentibus: Esa.9.1. Medicina corde contritis, captivis libertas, & annus Domini placabilis omnibus lugentibus? Esa.61.1. & gaudium illud ingens ab Angelorum multitudine pastoribus annuntiatum. Luc.2.10. & 14. Non igitur immerito Paulus adhuc hodie fideles in Philippensium persona compellat, aiens, Gaudete in Domino semper, & iterum dico, Gaudete, & Psalmes dicit, psal.118 5. Voce exultationis, triumphi & liberationis in tabernaculis iustorum audiri.
units.tr: That sadness, therefore, through which Christ emerged victorious, having swallowed it up, which we ourselves were bound to endure and never to escape, is truly our joy and consolation; his emptying and humiliation are our exaltation and glorification; and finally, his death and resurrection are our life and everlasting salvation. And if this were not so, how would the Gospel be a joyful message of peace to those who sit in the shadow of death? Isa. 9:1. The remedy for the brokenhearted, freedom for the captives, and the acceptable year of the Lord for all who mourn? Isa. 61:1. And how would that great joy be announced to the shepherds by a multitude of angels? Luke 2:10 and 14. It is not without reason, then, that Paul even today addresses the faithful in the person of the Philippians, saying, "Rejoice in the Lord always, and again I say, rejoice," and the Psalm says that the voice of exultation, triumph, and deliverance is heard in the tents of the righteous. Ps. 118:15.

units.la: Verumenimuero dicat aliquis, Christus felicilicitatem & gaudium iis qui lugent pollicetur Matth. 5. 4. & sapiens Ecclesiastes ait, Sapientum cor in domo luctus versari, sed cor stultorum in domo laetitiae. Cur etiam tantopere cor contritum & abiectum requiritur, nisi vt coram Domino fleamus & lugeamus?
units.tr: But someone may say: Christ promises blessedness and joy to those who mourn, Matt. 5:4, and the wise Ecclesiastes says that the heart of the wise dwells in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools in the house of joy. Why, then, is a broken and humbled heart so greatly required, unless that we may weep and mourn before the Lord?

units.la: Denique idem vsuuenisse videmus olim & adhuc hodie vsuuenire fidelibus Dei seruis quod de se Iacobus apud Pharaonem profitebatur, Genef.47 9. pauços & malos fuisse dies annorum vitae suae, nisi quod eam plerique fidelium longam quidem sed luctuosissimam & diuturnis acerbissimis erumnis iactatam ducunt, nec enim sunt filij Dei passionum naturalium animeve corporis, immunes aut prorsus ἀπαθεῖς, licet iidem fidelissimi sint constantissimique Agnosco lubens illa omnia; sed aio maximum esse discrimen inter eos qui huius Euangelicae laetitiae viam nondum ingressi sunt: eos qui illud stadium ingressi decurrunt, & cos tandem qui feliciter ad metam peruenerunt. Priores illos vero mirum non est tanti beneficij non esse participes, quod alij nunquam degustarunt, alij vero semel degustatum illico vomuerunt, in quos illud vere quadrat, quod Iob 14. 1. legitur. Quod ad eos aute qui adhuc stadium istud ingressi decurrunt, iis quae a tergo sunt relictis, ad ea quae sunt a fronte contendentes, Philip. 3. 13. aio discrimen esse maximum constituendum inter carnis reliquias, fructus amarissimos adhuc proferentis, & dulces illos Spiritus fructus ita temperantes carnis fructuum acerbitatem,vt tandem etiam illis in medicinam cedant. Huiusmodi fuerunt Petri lachrymæ post abnegatum à fe Dominum, Matth. 26. 55. & Dauidis fletus à sensu peccati promanantes, Pfalm. 38. 4. & 51. & alibi passim. Vt igitur de morbis ferendum est iudicium, non ex ipsorum initio, progressu aut aliis symptomatibus sed ex eorum exitu, sic aio iudicandum de tristitia quæ non simpliciter à veneno peccati procedit, & ad inferos sine vlla spe exitus deducit, sed ea quam Apostolus vocat secundum Deum tristitiam 2. Cor. 7. 10. quæ dicitur etiam cor contritum, sauciatum & abiectum, quo peccatores quidem verè pœnitentes ad inferos vsque deducuntur sed tandem educedi 1.Sam. 2.6. cuius initium est sensus amarissimus peccati, coniunctus cum ægritudine qua propter læsam Dei bonitatem afficimur, quos statim excipiunt illi gemitus inenarrabiles à Dei Spiritu procedetes Rom.8 26. & acerbitatem illa sic temperantes, illius vi & efficacia qui lucem e tenebris elicit, vt tandem exclamet cum Dauide verè pœnitens, Quàm mihi bonum & salutare fuit, quòd humilis & demissus factus sum. Psal. 119. 71. & 51. 10. tantum abest vt hac tristitia gaudium illud extinguatur, aut pax eripiatur, quam mundus nec dare nec tollere potest Ioh. 14. 27. & Rom. 5. 1. cuius rei testes sunt o locupletes quibus datu est coram Deo, quem graviter offenderant, sese veniam expectantes deiicere & humiliare. Addo præterea, alias esse moeroris & angustiarum maximarum species,quibus tantum abest vt huic ineffabili tranquillitati quicquam detrahatur, vt contrà,quum ab amore Dei & odio mali proficiscantur eximiæ consolationis plenissimę sint, tanquam certissima nostræ salutis & adoptionis testimonia. Talis est Apostoli gemitus conquerentis se bonum quod vellet, non facere,& malum facere quod nollet: quod quidem non aliunde quàm à Spiritus aduersus carnem lucta Dei filiorum propria proficiscitur,sperantium Dei Spiritum fore victorem, quandoquidem non amplius eis dominatur, sed gratia. Rom. 6.14. Huc illud etiam Apostoli spectat, 2.Cor. 11. 29. Quis affligitur? quin ego affligar? quis offenditur, quin vrar? Quod vnde quæio manat aliunde quàm à zelo ardeti gloriæ Dei,ac proinde quàm pulchrè illi cum pace illa & tranquillitate qua in Domino fruuntur conuenit?
units.tr: Finally, we see that what Jacob professed before Pharaoh about himself, that the days of his life were few and evil, Gen. 47:9, happened in the past and still happens today to the faithful servants of God; for most of the faithful consider their life long indeed, but most sorrowful and tossed about by lasting and very bitter troubles. For the children of God are not free from natural passions, or from the passions of soul and body, nor are they altogether [ἀπαθεῖς] impassible, even though they are most faithful and most steadfast. I willingly grant all this; but I say that there is a very great difference between those who have not yet entered the way of this evangelical joy, those who have entered that race and are running it, and those who have at last reached the goal happily. It is no wonder that the former are not partakers of so great a benefit, since some never tasted it, and others, having tasted it once, immediately vomited it up; and what is read in Job 14:1 fits them exactly. As for those who have entered that race and are still running, forgetting what lies behind and straining toward what lies ahead, Phil. 3:13, I say that a very great distinction must be drawn between the remnants of the flesh, which still bear most bitter fruits, and those sweet fruits of the Spirit which temper the bitterness of the fruits of the flesh, so that at last they turn even to medicine for them. Such were Peter's tears after he had denied the Lord, Matt. 26:55, and David's weeping arising from a sense of sin, Ps. 38:4, and Ps. 51, and everywhere else. Therefore, just as the judgment about diseases must be made not from their beginning, their progress, or other symptoms, but from their outcome, so I say that we must judge concerning that sadness which does not proceed simply from the poison of sin and lead down to hell without any hope of escape, but concerning that which the Apostle calls godly sorrow, 2 Cor. 7:10, which is also called a broken, wounded, and humbled heart. By this sorrow penitent sinners indeed are led down even to hell, but are at last brought up again, 1 Sam. 2:6. Its beginning is the most bitter sense of sin, joined with the grief by which we are affected because the goodness of God has been wounded; and immediately upon this follow those unutterable groans proceeding from the Spirit of God, Rom. 8:26, and the Spirit tempers the bitterness in such a way, by his power and efficacy who draws light out of darkness, that the truly penitent man at last cries out with David, "How good and how profitable it was for me that I was humbled and brought low." Ps. 119:71; and Ps. 51:10. So far is this sadness from extinguishing that joy, or taking away that peace which the world can neither give nor take away, John 14:27 and Rom. 5:1, that the witnesses to this are those rich men to whom it has been granted, before God whom they had grievously offended, to cast themselves down and humble themselves while awaiting pardon. I add further that there are other kinds of grief and the greatest anguish, by which so far from anything being taken away from this ineffable tranquillity, on the contrary, since they proceed from love of God and hatred of evil, they are full of the most excellent consolation, as the most certain testimonies of our salvation and adoption. Such is the groan of the Apostle lamenting that he does not do the good he wishes, and does the evil he does not wish; which indeed arises from nothing other than the struggle of the Spirit against the flesh, the proper struggle of the children of God, who hope that the Spirit of God will be victor, since sin no longer has dominion over them, but grace. Rom. 6:14. To this also the Apostle's words apply, 2 Cor. 11:29: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" And whence does this come, I ask, if not from a zeal burning for the glory of God? And how beautifully does it agree with that peace and tranquillity which they enjoy in the Lord!

units.la: Denique tantum abest vt crux, oppressio, angustia,persecutio,fames, nuditas, periculu, gladius,Rom.8.34.pacem eorum interturbet, & gaudium solidum,in eorum pro Dei gloria & iustitia perpessionibus interrumpant, vt contrà, Domini pollicitationibus & exhortatione freti Matth.5.11.12. & 13. probe tenentes, minimè paria esse quæ præsenti tempore perpetiuntur futurę gloriæ in electis retegendæ,Rom.8.18. regno illi nimirum cœlorum æterno ante mundi constitutionem ipsis præparato, Matth.25.34. atque adeò certo persuasi passionum istas esse singulare Dei donum, Phil. 1. 29. & speciale membrorum cum capite conformationem, Rom. 8.29. in oppressionibus etiam exultent Rom. 5.2. & in Domino glorientur, Gal. 6.14. adeò ut ipsorum lachrymae, siquae sunt, non à tristitia sed ab inenarrabili pace & gaudio promanent.
units.tr: In short, cross, oppression, distress, persecution, hunger, nakedness, danger and the sword are so far from disturbing their peace, or interrupting the lasting joy they feel in suffering for the glory and righteousness of God, that, on the contrary, trusting in the Lord's promises and exhortation (Matt. 5.11-13), they firmly hold that the sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed in the elect (Rom. 8.18), namely the eternal kingdom of heaven prepared for them before the foundation of the world (Matt. 25.34). Persuaded of this, they regard these sufferings as a singular gift of God (Phil. 1.29) and a special conforming of the members to the Head (Rom. 8.29). They even exult in their afflictions (Rom. 5.2) and glory in the Lord (Gal. 6.14), so that their tears, if they shed any, flow not from sadness but from an inexpressible peace and joy.

units.la: Quū sit autē haec lucta vel ipsis athletis fortissimis grauissima, durissimaque, hoc ipsum Christo Domino nostro, quatenus homo erat & nostrer sponsor ac fideiussor, & ipsius Apostolis, satis testatibus, bene cōscios infirmitatis nostrae esse nos oportet, ne virium nostrarum inani confidentia freti nostrae ruinae fiamus instrumenta: aut contrà nimium infirmitate nostra territi despondentes animum hosti faciliorem victoriam faciamus. Vnicum adversus illa omnia remedium nos Dominus hic suo exemplo praesentissimum ac certissimum docet, preces, quae, ad quem, & sicut oportet dirigantur, ut facere videmus hoc loco Christum, quod quàm paucissimis à me fieri poterit expediam.
units.tr: This struggle is most grievous and most severe even to the bravest athletes. We ought to be well aware of this, as our Lord Christ himself, in so far as he was man and our surety and guarantor, and his Apostles, bear witness to it, lest, trusting in an empty confidence in our own strength, we become the instruments of our own ruin; or, on the other hand, lest, too terrified by our weakness and losing heart, we make the enemy's victory easier. The Lord, by his own example here, teaches us that there is one remedy against all these things, most ready and most certain: prayer, addressed to the right person and in the right way, as we see Christ doing in this place. I will explain briefly, as far as I can, what he does.

units.la: Ad quem igitur preces nostras dirigendae? nimirum ad quem ab ipso nostro Mediatore deducimur, Patrem nostrum coelestem, & quē ipse nos docet Spiritus Sanctus, adeò ut in sanctis & legitimis precibus, semper concurrant Pater, Filius & Sp. S. irrito alioquin & inani futuro precum fundamento. .Porrò, preces duabus hisce veluti columnis niti par est firmissimis, Dei Omnipotentia & summa erga nos Beneuolentia. Quae si diuella-mus à se inuicem, vt an possit quod velle ipsum optamus in dubium reuocemus, contumeliosi in Deum sinmus, cum esse negantes Deum qui Deus sit, & ludibrio ipsum habentes maximo: aut ea vicissim postulantes quae velle non possit, quod faciunt qui Deum sua rum passionum & cupiditatum, vel animi impotentis administrum & executorem vellent, nae hoc sit lucem in tenebras transformare, & ipsi Deo in faciem exspuere.
units.tr: To whom, then, should our prayers be directed? Surely to him to whom our Mediator himself leads us, our heavenly Father, and whom the Holy Spirit himself teaches us to address. So in holy and lawful prayers the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit always concur; otherwise the foundation of prayer would be vain and empty. Moreover, prayer ought to rest on two most firm pillars: the omnipotence of God and his supreme goodwill toward us. If we tear these apart from one another, so that we call into doubt whether he is able to do what we wish, we insult God, denying that he is God, and making him a laughingstock. Or, conversely, we ask for things he cannot will, as those do who wish God to be the servant and executor of their passions and desires, or of an unbridled mind. That would be to turn light into darkness and to spit in God's face.

units.la: De Dei Omnipotentia, vel ipse communis sensus dictat minime dubitandum: verum quia non quicquid potest semper efficit, sed ea demum quae fieri vult ac decernit, in hoc omnis sita est difficultas, an velit Deus quod sumus postulaturi. Atque hac in parte plerique omnes offendunt & omnibus seculis halluci-nati sunt, sibi persuadentes Deum concessurū, quaecunque vel ipsi sibi confinxerint, vel ab aliis conficta crediderint, qua in re multis modis grauiter peccatur. Mirum enim ni hoc modo saepissime falsum pro vero multi amplectantur: deinde licet in se bona sint & Dei voluntati vniuersali non repugnantia quę petuntur, non tamen sequitur illa simpliciter & absolutè postulanda vel speranda, quum non quicquid in se bonum est, etiam omnibus persona, locis & temporibus expediat. Rursum tamen Iacobus & tota passim Scriptura cla-mat, frustra eum precari qui dubitanter & in incertum precatur.Iac.1.6.
units.tr: Concerning God's omnipotence, common sense itself tells us there is no room for doubt. But since God does not always accomplish everything he is able to do, but only what he wills and decrees, the whole difficulty lies here: whether God wills what we are about to ask. In this respect nearly all men go astray, and in every age they have erred, persuading themselves that God will grant whatever they have invented for themselves or believed invented by others. In this matter there are many ways of sinning gravely. Indeed, it would be surprising if many did not in this way often embrace falsehood as truth. Again, although the things we ask for may be good in themselves and not opposed to God's universal will, it does not follow that they are to be asked or hoped for absolutely and without qualification, since not everything that is good in itself is expedient for every person, place and time. Yet James and Scripture everywhere cry out that the one who prays doubtfully, and at random, prays in vain (James 1.6).

units.la: En igitur aduersus illa praesens remedium, vt quum in animo nostro solam Dei gloriam & proximi charitatem in solidum nobis pro-posuerimus,preces noftrę nitantur promissio-nibus quas nobis Deus in verbo suo offert, & intra metas illas nos continentes, nec vlterius progrediamur,nec regrediamur etiam,sed vera fide, & assensu firmissimo illas amplectamur. Exempli gratia, Vniuersalis illa est promissio, Inuoca me in die tribulationis, & te exaudiam, nulla tamen apposita conditione, qua in te,quo modo,quo tempore,quibus rationibus, cuiusmodi promissiones passim in sacris occurrunt. Fidelis igitur quilibet quaecunque tandem ingruat calamitas humanarum rerum statum respiciens, Deum inuocabit, & eius beneuolentiae hac conditione sua omnia permittet,seu moderari & lenire,seu etiā afflictionū altum vehementius excitare & intendere,seu prorsus etiam sedare voluerit,interea tamen sine conditione peccatorum remissionem, necessariam patientiam,fidei incrementū,Sp. S. ope & auxilium efflagitaturus:haec enim & similia poenitentibus, & Deum inuocantibus absolute promittuntur:ideoque licet non statim suae precationis fructum percipiat, nunquam cessaturus, sed placidè bonam Dei voluntatem quando & quomodo placuerit promissionem impleturi praestolaturus. Qua in te
units.tr: Here, then, is the present remedy against these things: when we have set before our minds the glory of God and the love of our neighbour as our sole and entire aim, let our prayers rest on the promises which God offers us in his Word. Keeping ourselves within those limits, let us neither go further nor fall back, but embrace them with true faith and the firmest assent. For example, there is that universal promise: "Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will hear you" (Ps. 50.15), with no condition attached as to what, in what manner, at what time, or by what means. Promises of this kind occur everywhere in Scripture. Therefore every believer, whatever calamity at last comes upon him, looking to the state of human affairs, will call upon God, and will leave all things to his goodwill, on this condition, to moderate and soften them, or to stir up and intensify the affliction more severely, or indeed to put it wholly to rest, as he wills. Meanwhile, without condition, he will ask for the forgiveness of sins, the necessary patience, the increase of faith, and the help and aid of the Holy Spirit. For these and similar things are absolutely promised to penitents and to those who call upon God. Therefore, although he does not at once perceive the fruit of his prayer, he will never cease, but will calmly wait for God's good will, to fulfil the promise when and how it pleases him.

units.la: Promissio nu formu lam fidei noftrę amussim esse opor tet. re nunquam harum promissionum effectu, Petite in meo nomine, & dabitur vobis, pul-sate & aperietur, est excisurus.
units.tr: The promise must be the exact rule of our faith, and it will never fail to bring about the effect of these promises: "Ask in my name, and it shall be given you; knock, and it shall be opened" (Matt. 7.7; John 16.24).

units.la: Sed quandiu peculiares fuerunt reuelatio- nes, san�em patres vlterius progredi potuerunt debuerunt speciali promissione freti. Sic potuit debuitque Abrahamus sobolem pro- missam postulare, patienter tamen illius esse- ctum expectare dum praescriptum promissio-ni tempus aduenirer quain re grauiter Abra-hamus & Sara lapsi sunt, non diffidentia quidem sed impatientia, nato Ismaele ex ancilla cui hæreditas non debebatur. Sic debuerunt Israelitæ lapsis annis quadringentis liberationem sperare & postulare. Sic Dauid accepta promissione de regno & vnctione per Samuelem, passim in Psalmis Dominum confidenter interpellat, sed quum præfixum illi tempus certum non esset, pedetetim progressus est interrogato in omnibus cōsiliis semper ore Domini, prout tunc temporis Dominus per os Prophetarum suorum loquebatur. 2. Sam. 2. 1. Sic Daniel fide precatus est, quum à Ieremia captiuitatis prædictum tempus impleri videret. Apostolus quoque diu Romam eundi sibi fieri potestatem optauit, sed hac conditione, si ex Dei voluntate ipsi concederetur, qua in re non est primo quoque tempore exauditus. Rom. 1. 10. & 13. at accepta speciali reuelatione, Act. 23 11. futurum vt Romæ coram Cæsare sisteretur, tum illud audacter esflagitauit, & exauditus est. Act. 27. 25.
units.tr: But as long as revelations were special, the Fathers could and ought to go further, relying on a special promise. Thus Abraham could and should ask for the promised offspring, yet patiently wait for its fulfilment until the time fixed by the promise arrived. How gravely Abraham and Sarah fell, not through distrust but through impatience, when Ishmael was born of the maidservant, who had no right to the inheritance (Gen. 16). Thus the Israelites, after four hundred years had passed, ought to hope for and ask for deliverance. Thus David, having received the promise of the kingdom and of anointing through Samuel, appeals to the Lord confidently in the Psalms throughout; yet, since the time fixed for him was not certain, he advanced step by step, always inquiring of the mouth of the Lord in all his counsels, as the Lord then spoke through the mouth of his prophets (2 Sam. 2.1). Thus Daniel prayed in faith when he saw the time of captivity foretold by Jeremiah being fulfilled. The Apostle also long desired the opportunity to go to Rome, but on this condition, that it should be granted to him by the will of God; in this matter he was not heard at the first opportunity (Rom. 1.10, 13). But when he received a special revelation that he would stand before Caesar at Rome (Acts 23.11), then he boldly asked for it, and was heard (Acts 27.25).

units.la: Caucendum est autem summopere nequis hic sibi divinam revelationem fingat sua sponte omnia, sicuti hodie quidam fanatici homines, Libertini & Anabaptistae facitant. At siquid Deus nobis patefaciat, quod ad ipsius gloriam spectet, & e re sit proximorum, sive publica sive privata, id sane licet a Deo precibus postulare, sed tamen addita semper conditione, & cum Domino precationem claudentes, voluntatem nostram Dei voluntati submittere, cui uni acquiescimus, & nos nostraque permittimus.
units.tr: We must take the greatest care here that no one invents for himself a divine revelation of everything on his own initiative, as some fanatical men today, Libertines and Anabaptists, do. But if God reveals anything to us that pertains to his glory and is useful to our neighbours, whether public or private, then it is certainly lawful to ask this of God in prayer, yet always with the condition added, and, closing our prayer with the Lord, to submit our will to the will of God, to which alone we consent, and to which we commit ourselves and all we have.

units.la: En quibus armis muniri nos oporteat, non quod proprie precibus nitamur, (esset enim illud sibi ipsi confidere, Maledictus autem qui alibi quam in Domino confidit) aut preces nostrae sint meritorie, ut quidam imaginantur, sed quod sint instrumentum quo suas in nobis promissiones Deus vult ratas facere, licet ipsius sint revera priores hac in re partes, ut qui se faciat ab iis inveniri qui ipsum non quaerebant. Esa. 65. 1. & in cor & in os immittat preces quibus illum invocemus. Rom. 8. 26.
units.tr: These are the weapons with which we ought to be armed. Not that we rely properly on our prayers (for that would be to trust in ourselves, and "cursed is he who trusts in anything other than the Lord" (Jer. 17.5)), nor that our prayers are meritorious, as some imagine; but they are the instrument by which God wills to make his promises in us effective, although in this matter the initiative is truly his, as he lets himself be found by those who were not seeking him (Isa. 65.1), and puts into our hearts and mouths the prayers by which we call upon him (Rom. 8.26).

units.la: Quando vero, fratres, quando inquam ad hoc remedium confugiemus nisi hoc Ecclesiae calamitosissimo tempore, undique nos obsidentibus coniuratis hostibus, & Satana spiritu erroris tanta efficacia grassante, & furibundis hostibus Ecclesiae tam immaniter eam ferro flammaque vastantibus? Porro, quid obstat quominus Deus optimus ille noster parens, & Dominus noster Iesus Christus superiora illa quæ ab hinc anno vidimus miracula, nouis quotidie cumulet? Næ eadem est eius Omnipotentia & erga nos licet miseros peccatores beneuolentia: sed præterquàm quòd infinita apud nos scelera grassantur impunè, quibus nos indignos præbemus erga quos suam potentem ac beneficam manum exerat, ita refrixit precandi studium, vt, hinc malorum noua seges, singulis ex arbitrio viuentibus, nobis metuenda sit. Omitto nimium multas manus innoxio sanguine fœdatas, Deo & hominibus pœnas aliquando luituras. Vtinam verò dies ille nobis statim beatissimus illucescat, quo Deus nobis meliorem mentem largitus faciat vt his admonitionibus, hortationibus & obtestationibus locum demus, & ad meliorem frugem redeamus. Id ni fiat, edico, non sine ingenti animi mœrore, aut Gencua mentem mutabis, aut Deus ipse te mutabit, immò prorsus abiiciet. Interea, siqui inter nos hæc scelera detestati rebus melioribus student, agite fratres, ad sacram hanc anchoram confugiamus, memores eorum quæ Dominus olim Abrahamo promittebat, Non euertam eam, inquit, de Sodoma loquens, si vel decem in ea iusti reperiantur: & conquerentis Domini aduersus Icrusalem, sed nec vnum quidem in ea inueniße. Esa.63.5. Itaque, fratres, votis ardentibus opus esse quum videamus, sedulò & continuò Deum nostris precibus sollicitemus, eas persuasi non esse verborum inanem tinnitum, sed inuicta Dei potentia armatas, & Dei immutabili veritate & beneuolentia fretas maximum apud illum pondus sicut olim semper habituras. Precibus aquæ in sanguinem versæ sunt: precibus impetratæ ranæ & culices Pharaonis superbiam debellarunt: Precibus Ægyptus cœlitus est fulminibus conquassata, primogeniti cæsi, mare scissum: e rupibus aquæ eductæ: Solis ac Lunæ, cursus cohibitus: cœli clausi & aperti, mortui excitati: denique precibus ipse furor Domini repressus. Exod. 32. 10. Hoc igitur esto nobis perfugium, hoc esto præsidium, hoc asylum & auxilium certissimum. Faxit id Deus Opt. Max.
units.tr: When, brothers, when, I ask, shall we take refuge in this remedy, if not in this most calamitous time for the Church, when enemies conspire on every side against us, when Satan with the spirit of error rages with such power, and when furious enemies lay waste the Church so savagely with sword and fire? Moreover, what hinders that God, our best Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, from heaping new miracles daily upon those greater ones which we saw a year ago? For his omnipotence and his goodwill toward us, miserable sinners though we are, are the same. But apart from the fact that countless crimes run rampant among us unpunished, by which we make ourselves unworthy of having his powerful and beneficent hand stretched out over us, zeal for prayer has so cooled that, from this, a new crop of evils is to be feared, since each man lives at his own pleasure. I pass over the many hands stained with innocent blood, which will one day pay the penalty to God and to men. Would that that most blessed day might dawn for us at once, on which God would grant us a better mind, so that we give place to these admonitions, exhortations and entreaties, and return to better fruits. If this does not happen, I declare, not without great grief of mind, that you will either change your mind, or God himself will change you, and indeed will cast you off altogether. Meanwhile, if any among us who detest these crimes strive for better things, come, brothers, let us take refuge in this sacred anchor, mindful of what the Lord once promised Abraham, speaking of Sodom: "I will not overthrow it, if ten righteous men are found in it," and of the Lord's complaint against Jerusalem, that he found not even one in it (Isa. 63.5). Therefore, brothers, since we see that burning prayers are needed, let us continually and diligently importune God with our prayers, persuaded that they are not the empty noise of words but are armed with the invincible power of God, and, relying on God's unchanging truth and goodwill, will always have great weight with him, as they did of old. By prayer waters were turned into blood; by prayer frogs and gnats, sent in answer, overcame the pride of Pharaoh. By prayer Egypt was shaken by thunderbolts from heaven, the firstborn were struck down, the sea was divided, waters were drawn from rocks, the course of sun and moon was halted, heaven was shut and opened, the dead were raised; and finally, by prayer, the fury of the Lord was restrained (Exod. 32.10). Let this, then, be our refuge, this our defence, this our sanctuary and most certain help. May God, the best and greatest, grant it.

units.la: Istud autem insuper adiiciamus, non solum Dei filium esse precatum, sed esse ter precatum, & quidem tanto ardore ut grumi sanguinis ex ipsius facie profluerent. Quod si fuit ei necesse qui nullum in se peccatum habebat, sed nostra in se receperat, quanto studio, quo ardore, quanta sedulitate & assiduitate Deus est nobis precibus sollicitandus? Euge vero Dauid quo Gentium abscessisti qui tuum lachrymis cubile rigabas? Psalm. 6. 7. qui media nocte surgebas ad Deum celebrandum, licet eum septies de die precatus? Psalm. 119. 62. & 164. Euge, euge quàm metuo ne similium tui iam pridem interierit proles. Orandus vero Dominus ut iterum illam exsuscitet, quod utinam atque o utinam nobis largiatur.
units.tr: Let us add this besides: the Son of God not only prayed, but prayed three times, and with such ardour that drops of blood flowed from his face. If this was necessary for him who had no sin in himself but had taken our sins upon himself, with how much zeal, what ardour, what diligence and constancy must God be entreated by us in prayer? Where, then, O David, have you withdrawn from the nations, you who watered your couch with your tears? (Psalm 6.7). You who rose at midnight to praise God, and prayed to him seven times a day? (Psalm 119.62, 164). Alas, alas, how I fear that the offspring of men like you have long since perished. The Lord must be prayed to raise that offspring up again; O that he would grant it to us!

units.la: Sed quousque tandem abutemur Dei nostri patienpatientia, nouis eum subinde lacessentes sce-leribus? Nunquam ne serio quid sit ira Dei discemus omnium iustorum Iustissimum humi proltratum, & grumos sanguinis horrore furoris diuini sudantem intuentes? Quis vero illum nisi peccatorum nostrorum pondus & scelerum onus prostrauit? Nos vero erecta ceruice superbe incedemus? in coelum ipsum exspuemus? voluptatibus & deliciis inebriati volutabimur?
