Sanguinem Christus pro nobis prae horrore sudauit: nos vero sanguinem innoxium fratrum nostrorum fundemus hauriemusque caedibus, auaritia, oppressionibus, dolis, conspirationibus seu monopoliis, omnique tandem fraudum genere? Tantumne vero nos esse dementes, vt haec non visurum Dominum, aut obliuioni traditurum speremus? Absit. Pudeat igitur nos nostri, & innatam superbiam nimiolque illos spiritus deponentes, & cor illud ferreum conterentes, cum Daniele vere & ex animo coram Domino sic nos abiicia-mus, Domine Deus peccauimus, iniquitatem fecimus, impie egimus & desciuimus a te. Tibi quidem Domine iustitia, nobis autem confusio faciei, regibus nostris, principibus nostris, & patribus nostris qui peccauerunt, iuuenibus & senibus, paruis & magnis, maribus & foeminis. Sed tu Domine secundum omnes promissiones tuas clemens esto, ira tua a ciuitate tua Ierusalem super quam innocatum est nomen tuum auertatur,fer o pem,nec differas propter te, Daniel. 9. Et cum Dauide dicamus, Agite, incurui prosternamur, procumbamus, genua submittamus ante conspectum Domini qui nos fecit. Nam ipse est Deus noster,nos vero populus pascuorum eius, & oues manus eius.
units.tr: But how long shall we abuse the patience of our God, provoking him with fresh wickednesses again and again? Will we never learn in earnest what the wrath of God is, when we look upon the Most Just of all the just, cast down on the ground, sweating drops of blood from the horror of divine fury? Who but the weight of our sins and the burden of our crimes laid him low? And shall we walk on proudly with necks erect? Shall we spit into heaven itself? Shall we wallow, drunk with pleasures and delights? Christ sweated blood for us from horror; and we shall shed the innocent blood of our brothers, and drink it up in slaughters, greed, oppressions, frauds, conspiracies, monopolies, and at last every kind of deceit? Are we so mad as to hope that the Lord will not see these things, or will forget them? Far from it. Let us then be ashamed of ourselves; let us lay aside our innate pride and those overweening spirits, and break that heart of iron; and with Daniel, truly and from the heart, let us cast ourselves before the Lord thus: "Lord God, we have sinned, we have done iniquity, we have acted wickedly and have revolted from you. To you, Lord, belongs righteousness; to us, shame of face; to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, who have sinned; to young and old, small and great, men and women. But you, Lord, be merciful according to all your promises; let your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem, over which your name is invoked, and do not delay for your own sake" (Daniel 9). And with David let us say: "Come, let us bow down and prostrate ourselves, let us kneel before the presence of the Lord who made us. For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand" (Psalm 95).

units.la: Cæterum Filius quidem Dei in faciem suam procidit, horrore iudicij Dei quod propter peccata nostra sustinebat perculsus: sed hoc Dei filij beneficium exeo præterea consequuntur, quòd audent cum omni fiducia & reuerentia caput attollere: vbi obseruandum est iustissimo Dei decreto factum, vt hic Adamus posterior sic humi prosterneretur, vt prioris Adami culpam Deo creatori se æquare cupientis istius humilitate repararet.
units.tr: Moreover, the Son of God indeed fell on his face, struck down by the horror of the judgement of God which he bore for our sins. But from this benefit of the Son of God we also gain this: that we dare to lift up our heads with all confidence and reverence. Here it must be noted that by the most just decree of God it came about that this second Adam should thus be cast down on the ground, so that by his humiliation he might repair the fault of the first Adam, who wished to make himself equal to God the Creator.

units.la: Adde superioribus, Dominum qui corpus hominum non minus quàm animam condidit, ab vtroque debitum sibi honorem repescere. Quapropter non solum ad mutuam ædificationem, sed ad cultum Deo præstandum, qui & intus & foris illi debetur à nobis, ne putemus ἀδιάφορον esse, sed necessarium, quantum fieri potest, vt ad preces etiam gestus & habitus accedat qui sine hypocrisi internam humilitatem ante Maiestatis illius tribunal, coram quo dicuntur Angeli vultum operire, Esa. 6. verf. 2. signis aliquibus externis testificetur. Hic vero cogor in quorundam impietatem inuehi, quos quum nulla premat necessitas, vel ætatis
units.tr: Add to what has been said that the Lord, who created the body of man no less than his soul, reclaims the honour owed to him from both. Therefore, not only for mutual edification but for the worship that is owed to God from us, both inwardly and outwardly, we should not think that posture is [ἀδιάφορον] indifferent, but rather that it is necessary, as far as possible, that prayer be accompanied by gestures and bearing which, without hypocrisy, bear witness by some outward signs to the inward humility before the tribunal of that Majesty, before whom the angels are said to cover their faces (Isaiah 6.2). Here I am compelled to inveigh against the impiety of certain persons, who, though no necessity of age or of adverse health presses them,

units.la: vel aduersæ valetudinis, in medio nostrum conspicimus, operto capite dum Psalmi canûtur, aut admini strantur Sacramenta, summum Dei contemptum præ se ferre, quos sane, si apud nos omnia composita forent eo ordine quo par est, digito indicatos nostris cœtibus eliminaremus, quo tandem, sane nobis si, nisi resipiscant, deueniendum erit. Mel iorem vero Deus illis mentem i niiciat. Porrò quòd huiusmodi ceremoniarum abusus conisque excreuit, vt non runt omnes, vt Dei cultus exterior in mimicas gesticula tiones & scurriles iocos sit transformatus, quibus hypocritarum istiusmodi superstitiosorum fuc us detegitur, Propheticæ admonitionis memores esse nos oportet. Corda, iubentis, franger enon vestimenta. Ioel. 2. 13. Est igitur adhibe ndus modus in ritibus, pro locorum & tem porum circunstantia, & summopere vitanda ἀκοσμία. Turpe foret enim hodie, exempli gratia, in Templo saltantes exemplo se Dauidis tueri, qui Spiritus instinctu speciali & pio motu coram Arca Domini exiliebat, quod adeo fuit acceptum Domino vt scuer iter in eam à quo fuerat ludibrio habitus animaducrterit 2. Sam. 6. 16. & 21. Sæpe etiam legimus stantem populum pansas ad cœlum manus expandisse: sæpe genibus flexibus & iunctis manibus orasse: sæpe etiam prostratum fuisse qui fuit adorantium gestus. Denique quæcunque ad ædificationem fa ciunt, hic sunt obseruanda, quum plerunque istud eueniat vt qui ritibus illis externis diligentiús incumbunt, interiús à Domino sint magis alieni. Sed in primis illud memoriæ infigendum, cordis & corporis humilitatem ac reuerentiam Deo deberi: qui vtinam efficiat vt tam multa præclara & eximia documenta quæ hactenus audiuimus mentibus altiús hæreant infixa, & in vsum à nobis reuocentur, tantisper dum magni illius nostri Seruatoris Maiestatem coram inspiciamus, quum nos per exinanitionem suâ pro nobis in gloriam illam cœlestem in quam receptus est euexerit, vt cum vnà cum beatissimorum Angelorum choro perpetuis & meritis laudibus in æternum celebremus, Amen.
units.tr: are seen in the midst of us with their heads covered while the Psalms are sung or the sacraments administered, displaying great contempt for God. Such persons, indeed, if all things among us were arranged in the proper order, would be pointed out with a finger and expelled from our assemblies; to which, indeed, we shall have to come, if they do not repent. May God, however, put a better mind into them. Moreover, since the abuse of such ceremonies has grown to such a degree that the external worship of God has been transformed into mimicry, gestures and buffoonish jokes, by which the pretence of such superstitious hypocrites is revealed, we ought to remember the prophetic admonition: "Rend your hearts, and not your garments" (Joel 2.13). Therefore moderation must be observed in rites, according to the circumstances of places and times, and [ἀκοσμία] indecorum must be avoided above all. For it would be shameful today, for example, to defend dancing in the Temple by the example of David, who, moved by a special impulse of the Spirit and a pious emotion, leapt before the Ark of the Lord; which was so well received by the Lord that he afterwards took notice of her who had mocked him (2 Samuel 6.16, 21). We also often read that the standing people stretched out their hands spread towards heaven; often they prayed with bended knees and joined hands; often too those who worshipped were prostrate, which was the posture of adorers. Finally, whatever serves to edification must be observed here, since it usually happens that those who devote themselves more diligently to those outward rites are for the most part more estranged from the Lord inwardly. But above all this must be fixed in memory: humility and reverence of heart and body are owed to God. May he grant that the many excellent and remarkable lessons we have heard hitherto cling more deeply in our minds and are recalled by us into use, while we behold the majesty of that great Saviour of ours, until, through his emptying of himself for us, he raises us up into that heavenly glory into which he has been received; so that together with the choir of the most blessed angels we may celebrate him for ever with perpetual and deserved praises. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA septima.
units.tr: HOMILY seven.

units.la: MATTH. 26.
units.tr: MATTHEW 26.

units.la: 40. Tunc venit ad discipulos, & reperit eos dormientes: & dicit Petro, utáne non potuistis unam horam vigilare mecum?
units.tr: 40. Then he came to the disciples and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, "Could you not watch one hour with me?"

units.la: 41. Vigilate, & orate, ne introeatis in tentationem: spiritus quidem promptus: sed caro infirma est.
units.tr: 41. Watch and pray, that you do not enter into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.

units.la: 43. Et quum venisset reperit eos rursum dormientes.
units.tr: 43. And when he came back, he found them sleeping again.

units.la: 45. Tunc venit ad discipulos suos, & dicit eis, Dormite quod superest, & requiescite: ecce, appropinquavit hora, & Filius hominis traditur in manus peccatorum.
units.tr: 45. Then he came to his disciples and said to them, "Sleep on now and take your rest. Behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of man is betrayed into the hands of sinners."

units.la: 46. Surgite, eamus: ecce, appropinquavit qui me prodit.
units.tr: 46. Rise, let us go. Behold, the one who betrays me is at hand.

units.la: MARC. 14.
units.tr: MARK 14.

units.la: 37. Tunc venit & invenit eos dormientes: dicitque Petro, Simon dormis? non potuisti unam horam vigilare?
units.tr: 37. Then he came and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, "Simon, are you sleeping? Could you not watch one hour?"

units.la: 38. Vigilate & precamini ne introeatis in tentationem: Spiritus quidem promptus est, sed caro infirma.
units.tr: 38. Watch and pray, that you do not enter into temptation: the spirit is indeed willing, but the flesh is weak.

units.la: 40. Et reversus invenit eos rursum dormientes, (erant enim oculi eorum granati) neque sciebant quid ei responderent.
units.tr: 40. And when he returned, he found them sleeping again (for their eyes were heavy), and they did not know what to answer him.

units.la: 41. Et venit tertio, dicitque eis, Dormite quod superest, & requiescite: sufficit, venit hora: ecce traditur Filius hominis in manus peccatorum.
units.tr: 41. And he came the third time and said to them, "Sleep on now and take your rest. It is enough; the hour has come. Behold, the Son of man is betrayed into the hands of sinners."

units.la: 42. Surgite, eamus: ecce, qui prodit me appropinquavit.
units.tr: 42. Rise, let us go. Behold, the one who betrays me is at hand.

units.la: LVC. 22.
units.tr: LUKE 22.

units.la: 45. Et quum surrexisset à precatione, venisset que ad discipulos suos, invenit eos dormientes prae tristitia.
units.tr: 45. And when he had risen from prayer and come to his disciples, he found them sleeping for sorrow.

units.la: 46. Et dixit eis, Quid dormitis? surgite & precamini ne intretis in tentationem.
units.tr: 46. And he said to them, "Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray, that you do not enter into temptation."

units.la: IOH. 18.
units.tr: JOHN 18.

units.la: 4. Iesus autem sciens omnia quae eventura erant in se, prodiens dixit eis, Quem quaeritis?
units.tr: 4. Jesus, therefore, knowing all that was to come upon him, went forward and said to them, "Whom do you seek?"

units.la: 5. Responderunt ei Iesum Nazarenum. Dicit eis Iesus, Ego is sum: Stabat autem cum eis etiam Iudas qui prodebat eum.
units.tr: 5. They answered him, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus said to them, "I am he." Judas also, who betrayed him, was standing with them.

units.la: 6. Ut ergo dixit eis, Ego is sum, abierunt retrorsum, & ceciderunt humi.
units.tr: 6. So when he said to them, "I am he," they drew back and fell to the ground.

units.la: 7. Iterum ergo rogavit eos, Quem quaeritis? Illi autem dixerunt, Iesum Nazarenum.
units.tr: 7. Again, therefore, he asked them, "Whom do you seek?" And they said, "Jesus of Nazareth."

units.la: 8. Respondit Iesus, Dixi vobis me eum esse, ergo si me quaeritis, sinite hos abire.
units.tr: 8. Jesus answered, "I told you that I am he. So if you seek me, let these go their way."

units.la: 9. Ut impleretur sermo quem dixerat, Ex iis quos dedisti mihi non perdidi quenquam.
units.tr: 9. That the word he had spoken might be fulfilled: "Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one."

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters]VPERIORE sermone vidimus quid Dominus sui respectu in tam graui lucta fecerit, quam non sua sed nostra causa lubes nobis redimedis subiit: hic vero docemur quo-
units.tr: In the earlier sermon we saw how the Lord conducted himself in so grave a struggle, which he undertook not for his own sake but for ours, to redeem us. Here, however, we are taught how

units.la: quomodo fe erga tres illos discipulos gefle- rit,quos,praeterquam quod sponte sua & coru memorcs quę vltima Coena fuerant illis à Do- mino dicta,etiam gestus & verba Magistri fui fatis officij admonere debuerant,voluit tamen ipse Dominus tum exemplo suo tum praece- ptis quid opus eslet facto tam periculoso tem- pore cómonere, ex quo maiore etiam eorum deinceps culpam fuisse docturi sumus. Prius quàm vero vltra progrediamur, hic proposi- tum exemplum Christianis omnibus est imi- tandum, in procuranda alij aliorum salute, & Pastoribus in primis, quos ex Christo discere oportet salutem ouium sibi commissarum re- bus omnibus priuatis chariorem esse oportere,& iis omnibus anteponendam.En igitur in maximas angustias redactum Dominum no-strum Iesum Christum, quarum minima non est cum maximis rerum creatarum cruciatibus æquanda: & tamen vix absoluta prima precatione,de suis discipulis solicitus ad eos accurrit,non ignarus quas illis Satan insidias struer-et,& quanta ipsorum infirmitas,reipsa comprobans quàm verè dixisset Ioh.13.1.se dilexisse ipsos vsque ad fine. Hoc igitur omnes omniú ordinum homines speculum intuentor,Patres liberorum institutioni rerum mundanarum curam postponere discunto : Magistratus hac curam gerunto vt à subditis Deus honore debito colatur : scandalis obuiam eunto, si quæ euenerunt emendanto, priuata negotia Dei gloriæ & quieti tranquillitatiqve publicæ posthabento. Pastores, vero discamus à Domino dies ac noctes Domini gregibus inuigilare, & docendi, arguendi, corrigendi, exhortandi, tempestiue & intempestiue instandi, obiurgandi, exhortandi cum omni lenitate & doctrina. 2. Tim. 3. 16. & 4. 2. publicè & per singulas domos, Act. 20. 20. finem nullum facere.
units.tr: he behaved towards those three disciples. Apart from the fact that, of their own accord, they should have remembered what the Lord had said to them at the last supper, the gestures and words of their Master ought to have been enough to remind them of their duty. Yet the Lord himself wished, both by his own example and by his precepts, to admonish them what was needed at so dangerous a time. From this we shall later learn that their fault was all the greater. Before we go further, we must note that this example set before us is to be imitated by all Christians in caring for one another's salvation, and especially by ministers. From Christ they must learn that the salvation of the sheep committed to them ought to be dearer to them than all their private concerns, and ought to be placed above all of them. Behold, then, our Lord Jesus Christ reduced to the greatest distress, a distress whose smallest part cannot be compared with the greatest torments of created things. Yet scarcely has he finished his first prayer when, anxious about his disciples, he runs to them, not unaware of the snares Satan was laying for them and of how weak they were. In fact he proved how truly he had said (John 13:1) that he loved them to the end. Therefore let all people of every rank look upon this mirror: fathers should learn to put the care of worldly affairs behind the upbringing of their children; magistrates should take this care, that God is given the honour due to him by their subjects; they should go to meet scandals and correct whatever has happened, placing private business behind the glory of God and the peace and tranquillity of the public. As for ministers, let us learn from the Lord to watch over the flocks day and night, and to teach, rebuke, correct, exhort, press on in season and out of season, reprove and exhort with all gentleness and sound teaching (2 Tim. 3:16; 4:2), publicly and from house to house, making no end (Acts 20:20).

units.la: Denique hic omnibus Christianum nomen profitentibus speculum eximium proponitur, ex quo suum alij erga alios officium in iis tum sermone tum exemplis aedificandis discat: quum tamen proh dolor! Dei gloriam & proximorum salutem hodie videamus rebus omnibus posthaberi, unde necessario fatendum est maximam scandalorum & confusionum partem, quibus hodie terrarum orbis concutitur, proficisci, coniunctam cum horrendis iudiciis Domini quibus euerti familias, & urbes, regna, regiones, longe lateque vastari, nemo tam caecus est qui non videat. Nam quum eos Deus honoret a quibus colitur, eos contra decorat qui debito illum honore non afficiunt, ac proinde multo magis a quibus decoratur.
units.tr: Finally, here is an outstanding mirror set before all who profess the Christian name, from which each may learn to build up others, by word and by example, in the duty owed to one another. And yet, alas, we see today that the glory of God and the salvation of our neighbours are placed behind everything else. Hence it must necessarily be confessed that the greatest part of the scandals and disorders by which the world is now shaken comes from this, joined with the dreadful judgements of the Lord, by which households and cities, kingdoms and regions are overthrown and laid waste far and wide. No one is so blind as not to see this. For since God honours those by whom he is honoured, he likewise brings contempt upon those who do not give him the honour due, and so much more upon those by whom he is dishonoured.

units.la: Quum vero Dei regnum quaerentibus reliqua omnia adiiciantur Luc. 12. 31. requitur contra ingratis, parum illud curantibus (cuiusmodi nos maxima ex parte sumus) & vel vilissimę rei posthabentibus, illa etiam omnia tollenda. Et ne longius in exquirendis exemplis abeam, adeste qui apud nos Christianissimum diebus tantum Dominicis, aut forte Iouis profitemini, parum memores dicti illius Domini nostri, Qui amat patrem aut matré supra me non est me dignus. Matth. 10. 37. vt eos omittam omni excusatione indignos, quibus nunquam vacat aut coetibus Christianorum interesse aut etiam de Deo cogitare, quin sua prius negotia vel viliffima confecerint. Quo vero loco censeri vos posse dicā, abominandos sacrilegas, ventres detestādos, qui Pastorū Ecclesię sanctū venerandúmque nomen miscrè prophanatis, de olla & vetre tantū solliciti, reliqua omni abiecta Pastorum cura, lupi rapaces, non oues? Sed his omissis hominum inquinamentis quos ad Dei tribunal ablego, sensuris olim quod Mich. 3 2. in istiusmodi hominum monstra prædixit, nos ipsos attendamus, Deúmque tum priuatim tum publicè precemur vti nos ita regat in posterum, ne dū in alios inuchimur, ipsi aduersum nos sententiam protulisse videamur.
units.tr: Yet, while all other things are added to those who seek the kingdom of God (Luke 12:31), the contrary holds for the ungrateful, who care little for it (which is what most of us are) and set it below even the most worthless things: all these things will be taken away from them. And, not to go on too long in seeking examples, here are you who among us profess yourselves Christians only on the Lord's days, or perhaps on Thursdays, little mindful of that saying of our Lord, "He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me" (Matt. 10:37). I say nothing of those who are beyond all excuse and to whom it never falls free either to attend the assemblies of Christians or even to think of God, before they have first dispatched their own affairs, however trivial. But in what rank shall I say you may be counted, you abominable sacrilegious men, you bellies to be detested, who wretchedly profane the holy and venerable name of ministers of the Church, anxious only about the pot and the belly, with all care of the flock cast aside: ravening wolves, not sheep? But setting aside these pollutions of men whom I send away to God's tribunal, let us consider ourselves in the words which he once foretold of such monsters of men (Mich. 3:2), and let us pray to God, both in private and in public, that he may so rule us in future that, while we inveigh against others, we may not seem ourselves to have pronounced sentence against us.

units.la: Christus igitur precibus abruptis ad discipulos venit quos dormientes inuenit. Ne putemus igitur Christum à suis in maximis suis cruciatibus vllam percepisse consolationem: Oportebat enim contra in secundo Adamo sarciri prioris illius Adami lapsum (qui aduersus Dominum Creatorem suum conspirans hoc erat promeritus, vt omnes illum res creatæ deserrent quarum dominatione exciderat, indignus tanto Creatoris beneficio, licet Dominus in illum summo iure non animaduerterit) nullam inuenientc consolationem aut auxilium à quoquam mortalium, vt multis ante seculis in Dauidis persona prædictum erat Psal.69.21.
units.tr: Christ, therefore, broke off his prayers and came to the disciples, whom he found sleeping. Let us not suppose, then, that Christ received any consolation from his own people in his greatest torments. For it was necessary that, in the second Adam, the fall of that former Adam should be made good. He, conspiring against the Lord his Creator, had merited that all the creatures over whom he had lost dominion should desert him, unworthy of so great a benefit from his Creator, although the Lord did not punish him as he might rightly have done. So the Lord found no consolation or help from any mortal, as had been foretold many ages before in the person of David (Ps. 69:21).

units.la: Cæterum quis hic merito discipulorum ignauiam, hac circunstantia temporum, locorum & personarum excusret? Nam illa, quæso, quo tempore acciderunt? Quum ceruicibus iplorum immineret gladius, ante tamen totics prænomoniti, Quo loco? In horto, ex quo vix nisi magno discrimine poterant effugere. Quibus? Inter duodecim illos præcipuis, Dominum suum in statu si alias vnquam afflictissimo conspicientibus. Quis igitur non eos grauiter incusct? Verum in nos ista potius contorquea-mus, & hoc exemplo aliisque non paucis dis-scamus, nullam esse tantam inertiam, stupiditatem, infidelitatem ac perfidiam in qua non etiam robustissimi quique incidant, si vel tantillum ab adiuuantis Dei gratia deserantur, & suis viribus permittantur. Horum sane fide faciunt tot variis & fœdis modis lapsorum hominum myriades, ab hinc annis triginta, & adhuc hodie non paucos istiusmodi summo nostro dolore conspicimus.
units.tr: Moreover, who could justly excuse the sloth of the disciples on account of these circumstances of time, place and persons? For, I ask, at what time did these things happen? When the sword hung over their necks; yet they had been warned so often before. In what place? In the garden, from which they could hardly escape except with great peril. To whom? To the twelve chief men, who saw their Lord in a state more afflicted than ever before. Who, then, would not censure them severely? But let us rather turn these things upon ourselves, and from this example and many others learn that there is no inertia, stupidity, unfaithfulness or treachery so great that even the most robust do not fall into it, if they are but a little forsaken by the grace of God who helps them and are left to their own strength. Indeed, the countless myriads of men who have fallen in so many various and foul ways during the last thirty years bear witness to this, and even today, to our great sorrow, we see not a few of this kind.

units.la: Quid ad hæc Dominus? Næ summo iure vt perfidos abiiceret: sed misericors & benignus tolerat, non tamen omnino iudulget quin corripiat: qua in re docet, nos a proximis lxsos non oportere vindictæ esse cupidos: sed potius in quantum se periculum iniiciant & quam fibiipsis iniuriam faciant conspicientes illorum potius miscreri, quàm nostra farcire incomoda. Præterea Christus hic optimus est nobis mediocritatis magister, inter infirmitatem quæ leuius arguenda est, & prauitatem quæ durius corripienda prout facti ratio postulat discrimen constituens.
units.tr: What, then, does the Lord say to this? Certainly he could justly have cast off the faithless, but being merciful and kind he endures them, though he does not altogether allow them to go unrebuked. In this he teaches us that we ought not to be eager for revenge against those who have wronged us, but rather, seeing how far they expose themselves to danger and how much harm they do to themselves, to pity them rather than to make up for our own losses. Moreover, Christ is here the best teacher of moderation for us, distinguishing between weakness, which is to be rebuked more gently, and wickedness, which must be corrected more sharply, as the nature of the fault requires.

units.la: Et ideo Matthæus addit oculos eorum somno grauatos fuisse: & Lucas tristitia facti illud annotat: quod quidem illos non omni culpa liberat, sed tantum eam eleuat. Qua in re iterum animaduertimus ea quibus inuari nos oportuerat sæpe nobis in detrimentum cedere, adeo est hominis natura corrupta & depravata. Quod enim discipuli præceptoris sui casum tantopere mœrent, à bonis sane profectum est initiis: sed in eo peccatum est ab ipsis quod tristitia sic consternantur vt somno magis violento quam voluntario consopiantur, quos oportuerat potius excitari, & verbis saltem Domino condolere, qui licet paululum ab eis abscesserat, tamen, vt Lucas diserte exprimit 22.44. in angore constitutus, orabat intentius, & quidem ait Apoll. Heb.5.7. cum clamore valido, adeo vt vox eius exaudiri posset: vel etiam tristitiam piis sermonibus leuare: suasque preces cum illius precibus coniungere. Quare illorum exemplo nobis horis singulis ac momentis caueamus, & quum vel tristitia, vel gaudio affici nos contigerit, iusta sit licet harum affectionum causa & finis legitimus, Deum precemur illas moderetur, & sancto suo Spiritu regat, vt quod bene coeptum erit melius adhuc perficiatur.
units.tr: So Matthew adds that their eyes were heavy with sleep, and Luke notes it was from sorrow. This does not free them from all blame, but only lessens it. Here again we notice that things by which we ought to have been helped often turn to our harm, so corrupt and depraved is human nature. That the disciples were so grieved at their master's fall certainly came from good beginnings, but their fault lay in this, that sorrow so overwhelmed them that they fell asleep in a heavy stupor rather than by choice. They ought rather to have been roused and at least to have sympathised with the Lord in words, for although he had withdrawn a little from them, yet, as Luke clearly says (22:44), he was in anguish and prayed more earnestly, and indeed, as the Apostle says (Heb. 5:7), with a loud cry, so that his voice could be heard. They should have eased his sorrow with pious words and joined their prayers to his. Therefore, following their example, let us take care every hour and moment, and whenever we happen to be affected by sorrow or joy, though the cause of these feelings may be just and their end lawful, let us pray that God will moderate them and rule them by his Holy Spirit, so that what has been well begun may be brought to even better completion.

units.la: Accedamus ad Domini verba, primùm discipulos increpantis, deinde remedium adhi-bentis, rationémque eo bene vtendi docentis: in quo exemplar quod in omnibus istiusmodi casibus imitemur nobis est propositum.
units.tr: Let us come to the words of the Lord, first rebuking the disciples, then applying a remedy, and teaching the right use of it. In this we have set before us a pattern to imitate in all such cases.

units.la: Primùm igitur Petrum nominatim compellat, vt qui soleret, vt erat natura promptus & feruens, prior inter socios loqui, quasi diceret, Tene Petrum dormire? socios enim tuos haud miror, sed tuus ille tantus amor, quem haud dudum testabaris iactabundus, te etsi moriendum tibi foret, nunquam me defertu-rum, quò tandem euanuit? Hic discamus primùm non sufficere quum necessitas postulat hoc vel illud reprehendere in genere, sed res & personas suo nomine appellandas, quum ferè semper soleant homines moniti in alios censuram reiicere. Quod non temerè faciendum sed cum ædificatione, vt hac in re nobis Apostolus optimus est magister, tum in pleriisque suis epistolis, tum etiam exemplo suo in hoc ipso Petro coram omnibus arguen do.Gal.2.14.
units.tr: First, then, he addresses Peter by name, since Peter, being by nature quick and fervent, was accustomed to speak first among his fellows, as if he were saying: "Peter, are you sleeping? I am not surprised at your companions, but where has that great love of yours gone, which you lately boasted of, that even if you had to die, you would never desert me?" Here let us learn first that when necessity requires us to rebuke something, it is not enough to do so in general terms; things and persons must be named, since people who are admonished almost always tend to pass the blame on to others. This is not to be done rashly, but with edification. In this matter the Apostle is our best teacher, both in many of his epistles and by his own example, in rebuking Peter himself publicly before everyone (Gal. 2:14).

units.la: Nec leuiter sunt hæc verba prætereunda, Mecum, in quibus non modò grauis inest exprobratio, sed etiam tacita quædam officij commonefactio, non debuisse illos tantùm maiore quadam diligentia suum erga Præceptorem affectum testari, sed diligentiùs cum illo sua communicare consilia, & ab illo quem satis norant consilium & opem exspectare.
units.tr: Nor should these words, "with me", be passed over lightly. They contain not only a heavy reproach but also a silent reminder of duty: they ought not merely to have shown their love for their Teacher with greater diligence, but also to have shared their plans with him more diligently, and to have looked for counsel and help from one whom they knew so well.

units.la: In Præceptorem igitur suum & in seipsos iniuri
units.tr: Therefore, in their injury against their Teacher and against themselves, they sinned, and it is right to rebuke the sinning

units.la: ficit pec-cante in-crepare, sed adhi-bendū ta-le reme-dium quo posset vti. Non sem per iuuat in genere facta re-prehensio-nes. iniuriij fuerunt, vt reuera nunquam proximus lædituř quin peccetur in seipsum is qui lædit. Sic igitur aperte vitia alij aliorum reprehen- dere nos oportet,non dissimulanter,sed vt res ipsa postulabit.
units.tr: but a remedy must be applied that can actually be used. Rebuke in general terms does not always help. The injuries were such that truly no neighbour is harmed without the one who does the harm also sinning against himself. So we ought to rebuke one another's faults openly, not covertly, but as the matter itself requires.

units.la: Superest videamus quomodo præparati sint discipuli quò aduersus tantum discrimen commodo remedio velut medicina vtcrentur, his verbis, Vigilate, &c, Precamini ne intretis in tentationem:ac deinceps,quàm omnibus nobis hæc aduersus eosdem morbos medicina sit necessaria. Vigilandi vox opponitur somno cuius eos reprehendit: sed quæ additur Precandi vox satis ostendit Spiritus vigilatiam, vt longè præstantiorem à Domino præcipi: ac proinde per Vigilandi verbum, præparationem ad preces necessariam intelligemus, quæ in eo sita est vt Spiritus acer sit & vigil,vt postulat periculi magnitudo, quum tamen mœrore nimio consopitos fuisse conspiciamus.
units.tr: It remains to see how the disciples were prepared, so that against so great a danger they might use a suitable remedy, as if it were medicine, in these words: "Watch, etc., Pray that you do not enter into temptation", and then how necessary this medicine is for all of us against the same diseases. The word "watch" is set against the sleep for which he rebukes them, but the word "pray" that is added shows clearly that the Lord commands a spiritual watchfulness, far more excellent. So by the word "watch" we understand the preparation necessary for prayer, which consists in this, that the spirit be keen and wakeful, as the greatness of the danger demands, whereas we see them overcome with excessive sorrow.

units.la: Quoniam autem plenus vetersomnum naturalem adfert,idcirco ieiunium vt plurimum tanquam vigilantiæ causa in sacris cum publicis precibus extraordinariis coniungi solebat: qui mos Ecclesiæ Christianæ fuit diebus festis solennibus,& etiam adhuc inter Catholicos Romanos obtinet, etsi in abusus intolerandos euasit. Atque sub Lege etiam alterum è sacrificiis ordinariis mane fiebat, Esaia Propheta graui exprobratione de iis conquerente, qui mane surgebant non vt sacrificiis participarent,sed vt ebrietati indulgerent,
units.tr: Since a full stomach brings on natural sleep, fasting was therefore commonly joined, as an aid to watchfulness, with extraordinary public prayers in the sacred assemblies. This custom was kept by the Christian Church on solemn festival days, and it still prevails among the Roman Catholics, although it has grown into intolerable abuses. Under the Law also, one of the ordinary sacrifices was offered in the morning, the prophet Isaiah complaining with severe reproach of those who rose early not to take part in the sacrifices but to indulge in drunkenness.

units.la: Vespertinum etiam sacrificium legale ante cibum peragebatur: vt ex Act. 3. 1. colligitur. Idcirco etiam factum est, vt licet Dominus propter figuram agni Paschalis institutionem sacrosanctae Coenae, post Coenam reiecisset, vt apud veteres solebat in Agapis illis Christianorum Coena celebrari, vt ex Actis Apost. & nominatim cap.20.7. perspicuum est, tamen hic mos sic mutatus, & sacrosanctus ille cibus à communi seiunctus, autore ipso Paulo Apostolo 1.Corint.11.22.vt coeperit Ecclesia communi consensu Coenam mane ieiuna celebrare. Agnosco quidem hic non agi de solenni & extraordinaria vigilia, summumque maximum esse Dei beneficium, non vtile modo sed etiam necessarium: Verum hic admonemur in discipulorum persona, non tantum sobrietatem à Christianis perpetuò colendam, sed etiam somnum naturalem, quoties praesertim irae Domini non dubia signa apparent, sic cohibendum, ne sopiti corpore vel animo deprehendamur: & praeterea noctis illud tempus, quo per interualla quaedam quiescens animus vigilat, optimè posse precibus ac piis meditationibus dari, vt docet exemplo suo Dauid, Psal.6.7. & 21.3. & 42.9. & 77.7. & 119.55. & 62. quum longe lit Christiano indignus ac foedius sopitum inueniri, quum de Deo dies noctesque cogitandum est, quam vel patrifamiliàs de furis sub noctem aduentu praemonito, Matth. 24.43. vel mercatori de nundinis cogitanti, vel militi excubias agenti.Pfal.130.6.
units.tr: The evening sacrifice of the Law was also offered before food, as is gathered from Acts 3:1. For this reason also it happened that, although the Lord, because of the figure of the Paschal lamb, instituted the sacred Supper after supper, as the Christians of old were accustomed to celebrate the Lord's Supper in those love-feasts (as is clear from the Acts of the Apostles, and especially Acts 20:7), yet this custom was so changed, and that holy food was separated from the common meal, by the authority of the Apostle Paul himself (1 Cor. 11:22), that the Church by common consent began to celebrate the Supper in the morning, fasting. I acknowledge that this is not a question of a solemn and extraordinary vigil, and that the greatest gift of God is not only useful but also necessary. Yet here we are admonished, in the person of the disciples, that Christians must not only always cultivate sobriety, but also so restrain natural sleep, especially when the signs of the Lord's anger are not doubtful, that we are not found drowsy in body or mind. Moreover, that time of night, when the mind rests and yet keeps watch at certain intervals, can very well be given to prayers and pious meditations, as David teaches by his own example (Ps. 6:7; 21:3; 42:9; 77:7; 119:55, 62). It is far more unworthy and shameful for a Christian to be found asleep, when he ought to be thinking of God day and night, than for a householder who has been forewarned of a thief's coming at night (Matt. 24:43), or a merchant thinking about the fair, or a soldier keeping watch (Ps. 130:6).

units.la: Hanc etiam ob causam quidam ex puriori- bus illis veteribus Patribus adducti sunt ut collegiatim in loca quædam ab hominum commercio remotiora secederent, & certis legibus victum & somnum, absque voto tamen aut vlla superstitione regerent, & absque omni Meriti opinione, qualis est paulò post à phanaticis nonnullis in monasteria paulatim inuecta, quæ non longo tempore omnis spurcitiei tum corporis tum animi cloacæ fœtidissimæ putidissimæque facta sunt, quibus etiamnum hodie Ecclesiam Dei adhuc infici summo nostro dolore conspicimus, non definentibus istis miseros mortales nouis inuentionibus & victus rationibus, dementare, quarum nullum extat fundamentum, nec in sacris, nec in exemplis quæ nobis in iis imitanda proponuntur. Nam quid eos Prophericorum cœtuum siqui persecutionum temporibus in Israele fuerunt, exempla iuuant, quum tantum illi differant ab istorum Mendicantium, aut istiusmodi monachorum conuentibus, eodem nixis fundamento quo Pharisæi volantes olim non solùm viduarum, sed etiam Regum & Principum domos longarum precum pro viuis & mortuis prætextu, quantum distat lux à tenebris: quod ipsa satis docet experientia quorcunque superstitionis fascina & iusto Dei iudicio minimè sunt excæcati. Ac sanè fatendum est statim ab initio cœtus istiusmodi & collegia monachorum, vana
units.tr: For this reason also some of those purer ancient Fathers were led to withdraw together into places somewhat remote from human dealings, and to govern their food and sleep by fixed rules, yet without any vow or superstition, and without any notion of merit. Such a notion was soon afterwards gradually introduced into monasteries by certain fanatics, and in a short time these became the foulest sewers of every filth, both of body and of mind. To our great sorrow we still see the Church of God infected by them today, since these people never cease to drive wretched mortals mad with new inventions and rules of life, of which there is no foundation either in the sacred writings or in the examples proposed to us for imitation. For what help are the examples of those prophetic assemblies which existed in Israel in times of persecution, since they differ as much from the gatherings of these Mendicants, or of monks of this kind, as the light differs from darkness? Both rest on the same foundation as the Pharisees, who once flew about the houses not only of widows but also of kings and princes, under the pretext of long prayers for the living and the dead. Experience itself teaches this well enough to all who have not been blinded by the spells of superstition or by God's just judgement. Indeed, it must be confessed that from the very beginning such assemblies and colleges of monks were founded more on empty opinion than on sound reason, as if seeking hiding places, far from the crowds of men and withdrawing from the general assemblies of the Church, supposing that greater holiness of life was contained in this, although people who thus flee all society of men for ever would not be entangled in any other error...

units.la: potius opinione quàm recta ratione fuisse instituta, quasi latebras quaerere, procul ab hominum frequentia, & à generalibus Ecclesiae coetibus secedere vitae sanctimoniam maiorem in se contineret, quum tamen hominum in perpetuum hoc modo societatem fugere, etsi nullo alio errore implicaretur hoc vitae genus, ex diametro pugnet cum legitimo Dei donorum usu, quae singula membra oportet ad totius corporis aedificationem conferre, ita tamen ut quisque se intra vocationis fines contineat, ut diserte monet Apost. 1. Cor. 12. & Prophetae & Apostoli usu ipso comparunt.
units.tr: Such assemblies and colleges of monks were founded more on vain opinion than on sound reason. People supposed that seeking hiding places far from the crowd of men, and withdrawing from the general assemblies of the Church, contained a greater holiness of life. Yet to flee human society in this way for ever, even if this manner of life were not entangled in some other error, runs directly against the lawful use of God's gifts. Each of these gifts ought to contribute to the building up of the whole body, but each person must keep himself within the limits of his calling, as the Apostle clearly warns (1 Cor. 12), and as the Prophets and Apostles show by their very practice.

units.la: Frustra etiam se Ioannis Baptistae & exemplo & authoritate tuentur. Nam praeterquam quod tantum est discrimen inter doctrinam & mores viri huius sancti, quantum inter aërum & album, veritatem & mendacium, etiam est luce clarius vocationem eius specialem & peculiarem fuisse ad Domino vias praeparandas, cui nihil commune fuerit nec cum Esseniis, nec cum Pharisaeis, quibus cum agnosco iubens huius saeculi Monachis pulchre conuenire. Sed aio praeterea locum in quo Iohannes commorabatur non fuisse desertum inhabitabile incultumque, quum in eo Zacharias habitaret, & quidem in urbe, ut Luc. loquitur Luc. 1. 39. sed Desertum dictam illam regionem, quod montoia esset & minus urbibus celebris ac frequentata. Nec ibi IohanIohannes perpetuò solitariam egisse vitam dicitur, sed vsque dum munus suum inchoaret. Luc. 1. 80. Verùm enim verò qua fronte autsint illi qui se à mundo separatos iactitant, quem sinu suo fouent & circumferunt quocunque tandem excurrant, vel Iohannis desertum praetexere, vel veterum Prophetarum quorum fit mentio 2. Reg. 4. quum iam ante multa secula paulatim suis fraudibus in maximas vrbes sibi viam patefecerint, & Principum amplas & superbas domos inuaserint, & nundinationem animarum exercuerint.
units.tr: Nor do they defend themselves in vain by the example and authority of John the Baptist. For apart from the fact that there is as great a difference between the teaching and the manners of this holy man as between black and white, truth and falsehood, it is clearer than light that his calling was special and peculiar: to prepare the ways for the Lord. It had nothing in common either with the Essenes or with the Pharisees, with whom, I admit, the monks of this age agree well. I also say that the place where John stayed was not an uninhabitable and uncultivated desert, since Zacharias lived there, and indeed in a city, as Luke says (Luke 1:39). That region was called a desert because it was mountainous and less frequented and famous for its cities. Nor is it said that John lived a solitary life there continually, but only until he began his office (Luke 1:80). But with what face can those who boast that they are separated from the world, whom they cherish in their bosom and carry about wherever they run, plead either the desert of John or the old Prophets mentioned in 2 Kings 4? For many centuries ago they had gradually, by their frauds, opened a way for themselves into the greatest cities, invaded the ample and proud houses of princes, and carried on a trade in souls.

units.la: Denique si de vitae perfectione ferendum est ex aultera vita iudicium, (quàm verò seueram & austeram ducant testes iunto plerorumque facies & ventres) quaero quis fuerit perfectior, & ad cuius exemplar vitam componere nos magis oporteat, Ioannes Baptista neque panem edens, neque vinum bibens, an verò Christus reliquorum hominum instar edens ac bibens? Apostolus ipse Christianos passim ad sobrietatem & ieiunium cohortetur licet, quoties necessitas postulat, iubet tamen eosdem iis omnibus vesci quae in foro vaeneunt, nihil inquirentes propter conscientiam, & praeterea perfectionem quam isti tantopere iactant in exercitatione corporali, paululum utilitatis habere dicit. 1. Tim. 4. 8. Adde quod dissimulari nulla ratione potest, ex iis quàm plurimos qui vitae istud austerum genus ac institutum secuti sunt, etiam ante abusus subortos, istud effecisse vt inordinatis istiusmodi iciuniis debiliores facti Deo & Ecclesiae facti sint inutiles,contra quàm tum ipsi docuerunt,tum monumentis scriptum reliquerunt.
units.tr: Finally, if judgment about the perfection of a life is to be made from its outward appearance (how severe and austere the faces and bellies of most of these men show themselves to be), I ask who was the more perfect, and to whose example we ought rather to shape our lives: John the Baptist, who neither ate bread nor drank wine, or Christ, who ate and drank like other men? The Apostle himself urges Christians everywhere to sobriety and fasting whenever necessity requires it. Yet he bids the same people to eat all those things that are sold in the market, asking nothing for conscience' sake. Moreover, he says that the perfection these men boast of so greatly, which lies in bodily exercise, is of little use (1 Tim. 4:8). Add to this that it cannot be denied in any way that of those very many who followed this austere kind of life and institution, even before abuses arose, a great number were made weaker by such disordered fastings and so became useless to God and to the Church. This was contrary to what they themselves taught and left written in their records.

units.la: Accedamus ad remedium quod vere possumus amuletum aduersus quosuis corporis & animi morbos dicere, preces nimirum vt parest compositas: quarum tamen tanta vis est nō suo quidem relpectu, sed quod hanc nobis Deus rationem dederit, tum ipsius omnipotentia tum promissionibus firmissimis sufficultam, qua quod pollicitus est impetramus, quę tamen sufius in praesentia non persequor, etsi dignissima quidem, sed quod superius iam sint pertractata.
units.tr: Let us come to the remedy which we may truly call an amulet against any diseases of body and mind: namely, prayers composed as they should be. Their force is great, not indeed in respect of themselves, but because God gave us this method, supported both by his omnipotence and by his most firm promises, through which we obtain what he has promised. However, I do not pursue this further at present, although it is most worthy of attention, because it has already been treated above.

units.la: At hic quaeritur, & non immerito quidem, quū sanctæ illius precationis exemplar, quod Deus ipse per Iesum Christum nobis praescripsit, ad quod omnes nostras preces oportet exigi, sex petitiones contineat, quomodo Christus vltimae tantum petitionis hic meminerit, qua postulamus ne nos in tentationem inducat. Duplex responsio. Prima Christum hic potissimum ratione eius habuisse periculi quod suorum discipulorum ceruicibus imminebat. Altera, nisi ista petitio nobis in primis concedatur, idest, si superior sit tentatio, aut nos nunquam Deum precaturos; aut si precari coepimus, non persuaueraturos, aut etiam preces irritas fore.
units.tr: But here it is asked, and not without reason, why Christ mentions only the last petition here, in which we ask that he not lead us into temptation, when that model of holy prayer which God himself prescribed to us through Jesus Christ, and to which all our prayers ought to be directed, contains six petitions. There is a twofold answer. First, Christ had especially in view here the danger that hung over the necks of his disciples. Second, unless this petition is first granted to us, that is, if the temptation is too strong for us, then either we shall never pray to God, or if we have begun to pray, we shall not prevail, or even our prayers will be in vain.

units.la: Prius quàm verò progrediamur vlterius, quid Tentationis vox sibi velit diligenter est excuexcutiendum. quid item Intrare in tentatio- nem. Tentare idem est aliquando ac Periculum facere,quo sensu Dominus sæpe suos tentare dicitur.Gen.22.1.Exod.16.4. Deut.13.3.nó quòd nó norit qui scimus, quod melius quàm nos ipsi cognouit. Pfalm.139.2.& 2. sed vt ipse nos nobis ipsis & aliis patefaciat : qua ratione etiam tribulationes dicuntur in sacris Probationes & Explorationes. Rom.5.3.Iac.1.3.& 1. Pet.1.6. quo sensu iubet Apostolus 2.Cor.13.5. fideles seipsos probare an sint in fide:quę tentationes sanctæ sunt & laudabiles : illæ verò impiæ, infideles, detestandæ quibus homines Deum tentant,periculum nimirum de eius potētia aut veritate facientes quod Deus expref-fis comminationibus olim prohibuit, & in veteri populo seueris iudiciis vltus est. Alias verò Tentare accipitur pro ad malum inducere & impellere, quod Deo nisi cum blasphemia tribui nó potest. Iac.1.13. Proprium enim illud Satanæ,qui propterea Tentator.Matt.4.3. quod suo nostróque periculo primi illi parentes plus satis experti sunt. Deinde eorum omnium quorum ad id abutitur opera,in quibus primum locum obtinemus, aducrsus nos prauis nostris concupiscentiis coniurantibus, quibus tanquam esca Satan delinitos in flammas præcipitat: cuius alioqui nullæ in nos essent vires sine nobis ipsis:futuris externis tentationibus aut penitus irritis, aut non magni momenti, si aures, oculos, aliósve sensus nostros diligenter obturatos ab iis obiectis auerteremus quæ in eos incurrunt, & imaginatio- nibus quæ in mente formantur, & memoriam sollicitant resisteremus.
units.tr: Before we go further, we must carefully examine what the word temptation means, and likewise what it means to enter into temptation. To tempt is sometimes the same as to make a trial, in which sense the Lord is often said to tempt his people (Gen. 22:1; Exod. 16:4; Deut. 13:3). This is not because he does not know what he has known, for he knows us better than we know ourselves (Ps. 139:2), but so that he may reveal us to ourselves and to others. In this way also tribulations are called, in Scripture, proofs and trials (Rom. 5:3; Jas. 1:3; 1 Pet. 1:6). In this sense the Apostle bids the faithful to prove themselves, whether they are in the faith (2 Cor. 13:5). Such temptations are holy and praiseworthy. But those by which men tempt God, making trial of his power or truth, are impious, faithless, and detestable. God long ago forbade these by express threats, and avenged them with severe judgments on his ancient people. At other times, to tempt is taken to mean to lead into evil and to impel towards it, which cannot be ascribed to God without blasphemy (Jas. 1:13). That is the proper work of Satan, who for this reason is called the Tempter (Matt. 4:3). Our first parents have had more than enough experience of it, to their own peril and ours. Then, of all those whose services he abuses to this end, we ourselves hold the first place. Our evil lusts conspire against us, and with them, as with bait, Satan, having enticed us, hurls us into the flames. Otherwise he would have no power against us apart from ourselves. External temptations in the future would be either entirely vain or of no great moment, if we diligently stopped our ears, eyes and other senses, turned them away from the objects that strike them, and resisted the imaginations that form in the mind and stir up the memory.

units.la: Præsens igitur aduersus illa omnia remedium, hic in discipulorum persona docemur, ad Deum confugere, bene instructi vniuersa Christiani militis armatura, quàm pulchrè describit Apost.Ephes.6.13.& 1.Thess.5. 8.vt si exterius Tentatio nos sollicitat, in eam non ingrediamur, sed viriliter à nobis repellamus, Deum deprecati, ne ingrato animo nostro merito prouocatus, nos Satanæ, in cor nostrum intrare cupientis, Ioh.13.27.& 2.Tim.2.26. aut noxtris cupiditatibus Rom.1.24. permittat. Sic enim sunt hæc voces intelligendæ, Ne nos inducas in tentationem, non vero quòd malum oriatur à Domino.
units.tr: The present remedy against all these things is taught here in the person of the disciples: to flee to God, well instructed in the whole armour of the Christian soldier, which the Apostle describes so beautifully (Eph. 6:13; 1 Thess. 5:8). Thus, if temptation from outside solicits us, we do not enter into it, but manfully repel it, praying to God that he not permit us, justly provoked by our ungrateful heart, to be given over to Satan, who desires to enter into our heart (John 13:27; 2 Tim. 2:26), or to our own desires (Rom. 1:24). For these words must be understood in this way: "Lead us not into temptation" does not mean that evil arises from the Lord.

units.la: Vtilis sane immo necessaria prorsus horis omnib. & metis hæc doctrina nobis quibusque res est cum hoste dolosissimo, indefinetep nobis insidiante, & qua nos in perniciem adducat ecam in nobis reperiente. Ecquid igitur fratres, hoc tempore calamitosissimo belli nobis agendum putamus, quod revera probationis tempus est, quo sæpe contingere videmus, vt Angeli in Diabolos transformentur, id est fortissimi quique & virtute præditi, in multa vitia præcipites ferantur, quorum nullum tam immane quod armorum licentia non suadeat? Annon in hoc vnum incumbendum, vt omnes cuiusuis ordinis, dignitatis aut sexus, Deum votis ardentibus & assiduis gemitibns sollicitent, tět, vt propter immensam suâ benignitate nos in bellicis istis perturbationib. regat & inspi- ret, ne iusta ac necessaria defensio polluatur iis sceleribus quæ nimium frequenter in hu- iusmodi schola discuntur: in qua Dauidem ip- sum videmus, licet non immerito de se prædi- cantem manus suas ad prælium edoctas, & digitos ad bellum à Domino Psalm.144. 1. ta- men hoc adeptum, vt indignus haberetur à Domino templum ipsius ædificandi, quòd, in- quit ipse Iehoua nominatim, multum sangui- nem fudisset, & magna bella confecisset. 1. Chronic. 22. 8. & 28. 3. Erat, inquam in istud si alias vnquam sedulo incumbendum, sed con- tra proh dolor! quæ non modò petulantia, & generis omnis lasciuia grassatur, sed quàm horrenda, & detestanda facinora passim apud nos iam impunita vigent: vt merito, & quidem summo nostro cum dolore, Geneua in qua vix quatuor lustrorum spatio, duæ cædes, aulim affirmare patratæ sunt, quarum altera meritis poenis expiata est, Geneua inquam dici possis spelunca latronum & ciuitas sanguinū. Quo- modo igitur ad Deum manus nostras sangui- ne plenas attollemus illum precaturi? Horret animus bonorum omnium. Vos verò nomi- natim appello, Iudices, quos Deus gladio ar- mauit ad bonos tutandos, malos verò coër- cendos, qui leges politicas & militares condi- tas & sancitas habetis, qui vobis commissorum populorum olim rationem eltis reddituri, ve- strum inquam, est cogitare quis ille sit qui vos ex alto speculatur, & quàm diligenter hac in parte sitis officio veltro defuncti, quod nunquam à vobis satis maturè fiet.
units.tr: This doctrine is useful, indeed altogether necessary, at all hours and in every measure for us all, since we have to do with a most crafty enemy, who lies in wait for us without end and finds in us the very things that lead us to destruction. What, then, brothers, do we think must be done in this most calamitous time of war, which is truly a time of trial? We often see that Angels are transformed into Devils, that is, the bravest and most virtuous men are hurled headlong into many vices, none so monstrous that the licence of arms does not urge it. Should we not devote ourselves to this one thing: that people of every order, dignity and sex solicit God with ardent vows and constant groans, so that in his immense goodness he may rule and inspire us in these warlike disturbances, lest just and necessary defence be polluted by those crimes which are learned all too often in such a school? In this school we see David himself. Although he rightly declared of himself that his hands had been taught for battle and his fingers for war by the Lord (Ps. 144:1), he nonetheless obtained this: he was deemed unworthy by the Lord to build his temple, because, as Jehovah himself says by name, he had shed much blood and waged great wars (1 Chron. 22:8; 28:3). There was, I say, always need to devote oneself diligently to this. But on the contrary, alas! not only does wantonness and every kind of lasciviousness run riot, but also horrible and detestable crimes flourish everywhere among us, now unpunished. Hence, deservedly, and indeed to our greatest grief, Geneva, where within the space of scarcely four lustra two murders, I dare say, have been committed, of which one has been expiated by deserved punishment, Geneva, I say, may be called a den of robbers and a city of blood. How then shall we lift our hands, full of blood, to God, about to pray to him? The mind of all good men shudders. But I name you particularly, judges, whom God has armed with the sword to protect the good and restrain the wicked, who have political and military laws established and sanctioned, and who will one day have to render account for the peoples committed to you. It is for you, I say, to consider who it is that watches you from on high, and how diligently you have discharged your duty in this matter, which will never be done quickly enough by you.

units.la: Superest rationem expendamus quam Dominus annectit, vt in discipulorum persona discamus, quàm sit eadem nobis necessaria, nisi perire volumus. Spiritus, inquit, promptus est, caro vero infirma. Primùm verò, vt fructum ex his aliquem percipiamus, notandum est Carnis nomine, Spiritui ex more Scripturæ oppositæ, non tantùm corpus aut sensitiuam hominis partem intelligi, nec carnis illum aculeum quo impelluntur homines ad res venereas, sed hominem totum qualis est sua natura corruptus, cuius proinde mens est densissimis cracissimisque tenebris obscurata & voluntas, ac potiùs libido, immoderata, cupiditatisque effrænata.
units.tr: It remains for us to weigh the reason the Lord adds, so that in the person of the disciples we may learn how necessary it is for us too, unless we wish to perish. "The spirit," he says, "is willing, but the flesh is weak." First, however, so that we may gain some fruit from this, it must be noted that by "flesh," which Scripture usually sets against "spirit," is meant not only the body or the sensitive part of man, nor merely that sting of the flesh which drives men to sexual desire, but the whole man as he is corrupted by his nature. His mind is therefore darkened by the thickest and blackest shadows, and his will, or rather his lust, is immoderate and unbridled in its desires.

units.la: Contrà Spiritus nomine non intelligendam Animam, nec ipsum Sanctum Spiritum, sed alteram hominis partem, quatenus eius intellectus veri Dei cognitione cœpit illustrari: & voluntas regi ad bonum probandum optandumque, malum autem detestandum ac fugiendum, Deíque voluntati subiici: affectiones autem rectæ rationi & intellectui illustrato parere. Proprium est igitur illud regeneratorum. Alij enim quorum intellectus veri Dei cognitione privatus est, & voluntas cogitationesque aut vanæ ac inanes, aut iniquæ, & quos reliquiæ rationis & conscientiæ tantùm magis inexcusabiles faciunt Ephes. 2. 3. & 12. Rom. 1. 20. fru-
units.tr: By "spirit," on the other hand, we must not understand the soul, nor the Holy Spirit himself, but the other part of man, insofar as his understanding has begun to be enlightened by the knowledge of the true God, and his will is ruled so as to approve and desire the good, to detest and flee evil, and to submit to the will of God, while his affections obey right reason and the enlightened understanding. This is therefore the mark of the regenerate. Others, whose understanding is deprived of the knowledge of the true God, and whose will and thoughts are either vain and empty or wicked, and whom the remnants of reason and conscience only make the more inexcusable (Eph. 2:3, 12; Rom. 1:20), fru-

units.la: Quid his vocibus Infirmæ Carnis & Spiritus promptu sit intelligendum. frustrà sollicitarentur ad cum inuocandum, quem nec caro nec sanguis docent. Matth. 16. 17.& nemo possit Iesum Dominum dicere nisi per Spiritum Sanctum 1.Cor.12.3.Huius igitur loci sensus hic esto. Quum Dominus discipulos suos corripere & simul animos dare cogitaret, nec durius exceptu rus nec etiam assentaturus, aliquam quidem eorum alacritatem & promptitudinem ad officium faciendum, quam ex ipsius gratia acceperant, agnoscit, sed tamen etiam contrà non tantùm eos atque par esset profecisse docet, immo maximam adhuc ignauiam ac infirmitatem naturæ suæ reliquias ostendit in ipsis superesse, ac proinde necesse esse vt in hoc discrimine quod eminus adhuc conspiciebant, ad eum confugerent, qui vires ingenij suppeditando & adaugendo, simul coërcet & emendat quicquid ad officium ignauos facit. Nam quo maiores homo regeneratus vires capit, eò promptior est & alacrior: contrà quò magis quod in nobis regenitum non est, quo ad bonum vel dicendum vel cogitandum inhabiles reddimur domatur & debilitatur, eò vires eius minores sunt. Ne putemus igitur sic locum hunc intelligendum quasi Caro in se infirma diceretur, cuius eximia sæpe vis est ac violentia aduersus Spiritu: sed quòd illa nos ad præstandam Spiritui obedientiam debitam ignauos efficiat. Dicendum enim alioqui fuisset, Vigilate & orate, Spiritus enim infirmus est, caro autem prompta est ac valida.
units.tr: What is to be understood by these words, "weak flesh" and "ready spirit"? They would labour in vain to call upon him whom neither flesh nor blood teaches (Matt. 16:17), and no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:3). The sense of this place, then, is this. When the Lord was about to rebuke his disciples and at the same time to encourage them, he neither wished to receive them more harshly nor to flatter them. He acknowledges indeed some eagerness and readiness in them to perform their duty, which they had received from his grace; but on the other hand he teaches that they had not advanced as far as they ought, and shows that the greatest sloth and weakness, remnants of their own nature, still remained in them. It was therefore necessary that in this crisis, which they still saw only from afar, they should flee to him who, by supplying and increasing the strength of their minds, at the same time restrains and corrects whatever makes them slothful in their duty. For the more strength a regenerate man receives, the readier and more eager he is; on the contrary, the more what in us is not yet regenerate is tamed and weakened, by which we become unfit to say or think what is good, the less strength it has. Let us not think, then, that this place is to be understood as if the flesh were called weak in itself, although its force and violence against the spirit is often remarkable, but because it makes us sluggish in rendering the obedience owed to the Spirit. For otherwise he should have said: "Watch and pray, for the spirit is weak, but the flesh is ready and strong."

units.la: k. ij.
units.tr: k. ij.

units.la: Tempus autem est ad reliqua pergamus, & quomodo sic praeparati discipuli sese cum Domino ad hanc luctam incundam accinxerint, intelligamus. En igitur Dominum reipsa tenstantem non frustra se dixisse principem mundi venisse, sed in se non habuisse quicquam. Ioh.14.30.& foras eiectum iri.Ioh. 12. 31. Tertium illum igitur tam stupendum & perturbationem immensam eluctatus, ut docet Ap. Heb.5.7. hinc quidem suos militespraeparat, inde seipsum ad certamen accingit, & holte non expectato,prior ipse occurrit,primas sibi partes vendicans tanquam strenuus & impertterritus Imperator,non pari tamen animo sequentibus cum discipulis. Venit igitur ad discipulos, quos tertio inventos somno sopitos excitat,& paulo acrius quam prius fecerat,increpat, quasi sic eos compellans, Quousque tandem istertetis?annon pugnandi tempus est? Agite,expergiscimini, hostis adest,eamus,obviam ipsi procedamus. Est enim hic sermo Domini totus ironicus, sed sancta ironia, ad peccati agnitionem & ruborem incitantur, cuius ipsi deinde memores in sui muneris functione facti sunt alacriores & alios etiam excitarunt: & adhuc hodie nobis tum exemplo tum sanctis suis exhortationibus praelucere debent. At (dicat aliquis ignarus discriminis quod maximum est inter luctam spiritualem, & eam quae armis carnalibus conficitur) fortis-ne censes factum Imperatoris se in manus hostium sponte concedere?& quod longe ma-ius
units.tr: It is time now to go on to the rest, and to understand how the disciples, thus prepared, girded themselves to join the Lord in this struggle. Behold, then, the Lord himself truly tempted, who said that he had not come in vain as the prince of the world, but had found nothing in himself (John 14:30), and that the prince would be cast out (John 12:31). Having thus wrestled through that third and so astonishing trial and immense perturbation, as the Apostle teaches (Heb. 5:7), he on the one hand prepares his soldiers, and on the other girds himself for the contest. Without waiting for the enemy, he himself goes forth first, claiming the first place for himself as a vigorous and undaunted commander, though his companions did not follow with the same spirit. He comes, therefore, to the disciples, whom he finds asleep for the third time and rouses, and rebukes them a little more sharply than before, as if addressing them thus: "How long will you sleep on? Is it not time to fight? Come, wake up, the enemy is here; let us go, let us meet him." For the whole of the Lord's speech here is ironic, but it is a holy irony, meant to stir them to acknowledge their sin and to blush; and mindful of this afterwards, they became more eager in the performance of their office and roused others too. Even today they ought to shine before us both by their example and by their holy exhortations. But (someone unaware of the great difference between spiritual warfare and that which is waged with carnal arms may say), do you think it was the act of a brave commander to surrender himself voluntarily into the hands of his enemies? And, what is far more to the point, to forbid his own men to check the wrong by force of arms?

units.la: Exemplum sanctissimae perfectissimaeque fortitudinis in Domino nostro Iesu Christo a precibus. ius est, suos ne prohibeant armis iniuriam cohibere? Talis sane est carnis, nihil nisi quod in sensus incurrit videntis ratiocinatio. Oculis igitur fidei soliS videtur invisibilis, hi soli discrimen inter audacem & timidum, victorem & victum patefaciunt. Obsecro vero, cuius maiorem vim dixeris, aut eius qui gladium gladio confoderit, aut qui cataphractum militem solo bacillo visus humi fusum prostraverit? Sic David ingentem illum Goliathum aggressus funda praecipitem dedit, & proprio ipsius gladio caput eius amputavit. Idem praestat hic verus ille noster David, vere suam divinam virtutem exercens, dum solo verbo suos inimicos territos profligat, ut dicturi sumus paulo post, & eosdem captos vincit ut Satanae duci ipsorum iisdem vinculis catenatos tradat, quibus ipse vinciri voluit mundum condemnans ipse condemnatus: mortem denique sua morte confodiens: atque adeo virtutem eandem etiam imbecillimis communicans ut in eorum infirmitate triumphet. 2. Cor. 12. 9. quibus armis freti & ducis sui vestigia sequentes nihil arduum aut impossibile putant esse in eo a quo sustinentur, quod de se non immerito praedicat Apostolus, magnus ille bellator, Philip. 4. 13. & 2. Cor. 10. 5.
units.tr: An example of the most holy and perfect fortitude in our Lord Jesus Christ, from his prayers. Such, indeed, is the reasoning of the flesh, which sees only what falls under the senses. Therefore the invisible is seen by the eyes of faith alone; only these reveal the difference between the bold and the timid, the victor and the vanquished. I ask you, whose force would you call greater: that of the man who ran his sword through a sword, or of the man who laid low an armoured soldier with a mere staff, as it seemed, and threw him flat on the ground? So David, attacking that huge Goliath, struck him down headlong with a sling, and cut off his head with his own sword (1 Sam. 17). The same thing is done by this true David of ours, truly exercising his divine power, while he routs his enemies, now terrified, by a word alone, as we shall say a little later; and he binds them when captured, so that he might hand them over, bound with the same chains, to Satan their leader, by which chains he himself wished to be bound, condemning the world while he himself was condemned; and finally, by his own death he pierces death. And so he also communicates the same power to the weakest, so that he triumphs in their weakness (2 Cor. 12:9). Trusting in these arms and following the footsteps of their leader, they think nothing arduous or impossible in him by whom they are sustained, which the Apostle, that great warrior, rightly says of himself (Phil. 4:13; 2 Cor. 10:5).

units.la: Nequis igitur nobis Imperatoris nostri vincula, ne quis capturam exprobret, qui captores suos coepit. Contra vero, quum eidem nos hodie verbis hortetur, Eamus, in membris suis triumphare gestiens, ut in seipse triumphauit, agite fratres intrepidi premamus eiusvestigia, Crucem nostram cum illo singuli portantes. Quisquis enim aliam semitam instituerit, nec procul aberrans in aliud ab illo alienius hospitium perveniet. Illum igitur imitati, armis quae ipse largitur dextra laevaque vtamur, nullo modo dubitantes quin si cum illo patiamur, etiam cum illo triumphantes simus regnaturi, qui non amplius in illa visibili infirmitate iacet, qua olim, sed supra caelos evectus, & potestatem omnem adeptus in caelo & terra, suis deesse nec vult nec potest. Porro quam de hostibus loquor, non ago tantum de iis, quibus hodie cingimur militibus, aduersus quorum minas crudelitatis plenas praesens Dei sensimus auxilium, sed de Satana & eius Angelis, de vanitate nostra, de auaritiae spiritu, de diffidentia, de incredulitate, de scortatione, de helluationibus, & proh dolor! de caedibus ac blasphemiis, quae nos undique non tantum cingunt, sed in medium nostrorum penetrarunt, & plerosque tanquam miserta mancipia ad suam voluntatem praestandam captant. 2.Tim. 2.26. quae daemonia dixit Dominus nonnisi precibus ac ieiuniis expelli. Matth. 17. ver. 21. ad quae nos Apostolus tam sollicite suo etiam exemplo cohortatur. Act. 20.19. & Philipp. 2. ver. 12. & tristitia illa secundum Deum quae salutarem poenitentiam gignit. 2.Corint. 7. ver. 10. At quum istis contraria faciamus, quid superest aliud, oro attendite quod coram Deo & Angelis vobisque omnibus testor, quàm tristitia secun-dum mundum, quæ mortem gignit? Tunc futurum est ut lugeamus, sed non in tempore, quandoquidem nec lætis & prosperis rebus, sanctè exhilarari: nec aduersis ut par erat, flere voluimus. Matth. 11. verf. 17. itaque occluso ostio, aperte dicetur, Non noui vos, Discedite à me qui facitis iniquitatem. Matth. 7. ver. 23.
units.tr: Let no one, then, reproach us with the chains of our Commander, nor with his capture, since he captured his own captors. On the contrary, since he today urges us with words to the same course, "Let us go," eager to triumph in his members as he triumphed in himself, "Come, brothers, fearless, let us tread in his footsteps, each bearing our cross with him." For whoever shall take up another path, though he strays but a little, will come to a lodging far alien from him. Let us therefore imitate him, and use the arms which he himself bestows, right hand and left, in no way doubting that if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him in triumph, he who no longer lies in that visible weakness in which he once lay, but, raised above the heavens and having obtained all power in heaven and earth, neither wishes nor is able to forsake his own. Moreover, when I speak of enemies, I do not mean only those soldiers by whom we are today surrounded, against whose threats full of cruelty we have felt God's present help; but I mean Satan and his angels, our own vanity, the spirit of avarice, distrust, unbelief, fornication, drunken revelries, and, alas, murders and blasphemies, which surround us on every side, and have penetrated into the midst of us, and capture many as wretched slaves to perform their will (2 Tim. 2:26). These demons, the Lord said, can be expelled only by prayers and fasting (Matt. 17:21), to which the Apostle exhorts us so earnestly, even by his own example (Acts 20:19; Phil. 2:12), and to that godly sorrow which produces a salutary repentance (2 Cor. 7:10). But since we do the opposite of these things, what else remains, I beg you, mark what I testify before God and the angels and all of you: only a worldly sorrow, which produces death? Then it will come about that we shall mourn, but not at the right time, since we have wished neither to be holily cheered in happy and prosperous circumstances, nor, as was fitting, to weep in adversity (Matt. 11:17). Therefore, the door being shut, it will be openly said: "I do not know you; depart from me, you who work iniquity" (Matt. 7:23).

units.la: Narrat historia deinceps Christum eorum omnium quæ venturæ erant præscium, qua in re voluntariam & spontaneam suam in omnibus obedientiam testatus est, sine qua ctiam captura eius & vincula non fierent nobis liberatio, progressum hostibus suis obuiam interrogasse, Quem quærerent, adeo ut proditore ipsis ad eum indicandum opus non fuerit: & se eum esse quem quærerent palam professum, quo dicto abiisse illos retrorsum & humi cecidisse. Qua in re duo sunt præter ea quæ diximus excellentissima & cognitione digna doctrinæ capita.
units.tr: The history next tells us that Christ, knowing beforehand all the things that were about to happen, showed in this his voluntary and spontaneous obedience in everything. Without this, his capture and bonds would not have brought us deliverance. He went out to meet his enemies and asked whom they were seeking, so that they had no need of a traitor to point him out to them. When he openly declared that he was the one they sought, they drew back and fell to the ground. Besides what we have said, there are two most outstanding heads of doctrine in this matter, worthy of our attention.

units.la: Prius, hominem illum visibilem, & eousque abiectum & exinanitum verè Deum æternum esse & Omnipotentem, de cuius Maiestate & gloria carnis humilitas & abiectio nihil detraxerit. Qualis igitur est quantaque blasphemia perditorum quorundam & furiosorum hominum, quos quum ad tantam Dei bonitatem obstupescere, & immortales gratias agere oporteret, quòd qui Patri æqualis est eiusdemque naturæ, & unus Deus cum ipso, eò vsque se forma serui assumpta exinanierit, cum tamen sua Deitate spectoliare non sunt veriti, ac proinde à fundamentis effi-caciam salutarem omnium ipsius passionum, fidei, spei, & salutis nostræ conuellere? Quis enim solo verbo potuit armatos milites prosternere, nisi ille cuius ad nutum montes ipsi sudant, & mundi fundamenta concutiuntur, quemadmodum eodem verbo condita sunt & stabilita?
units.tr: The first is that this man, visible and so humbled and emptied, is truly the eternal and almighty God. The lowliness and abasement of his flesh took nothing away from his majesty and glory. What a great blasphemy, then, is it of certain lost and frenzied men, who ought rather to be struck dumb at such great goodness of God and to give immortal thanks that he who is equal to the Father, of the same nature, and one God with him, emptied himself to such a degree by taking the form of a servant. Yet they have not been afraid to strip him of his Deity, and so to tear up from the foundations the saving efficacy of all his sufferings, our faith, our hope and our salvation. For who could strike down armed soldiers by a word alone, except him at whose nod the mountains sweat and the foundations of the world are shaken, just as they were founded and established by the same word?

units.la: Alterum ad prius illud accedat oportet, verbum nimirum loquentis, vt sciamus vim quidem & potentiam diuinam in ipsius esse Deitate, atque adeo Deitatem ipsam, sed tamen medium quoddam esse cuius interuentu hæc potentia suum effectum producit, siue condat siue destruat, seu deiiciat, seu erigat: seu viuifi-cet, seu interficiat: seu benedicat seu maledicat: verbum eius nimirum Sacrosanctum, per quod iam ab initio seculorum voluntate suam patefecit, primum ex parte & multis vicibus patribus per Prophetas loquutus, & tandem per vnicum Filium suum Heb.1.1. fratrem nostrum factum. Hebr.2.12.Ioh.15 15. vt hanc Dei erga homines egregiam voluntatem plene pa tefaceret. Is vero quum à nobis carne sua recederet, fidos elegit seruos quibus eam promulgandam & monumentis ad nos transmittendam commisit, Matth. 28.ver.20. qui fideliter commissum sibi munus exequuti sunt. Act.20. 27. & adhuc quotidie spiritum suum largitur iis quos Pastores mittit & doctores ad templi sui spiritualis ædificationem Ephes.4. verf.11. superstructi super fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum Ephes. 2. verf. 20. & 1.Cor.3.verf.10. vsque ad consummationem seculorum.
units.tr: The second point must be added to the first, namely the word of the one who speaks. We should know that the power and might of God lie in his Deity, and indeed that the Deity itself is the power; yet there is a certain means through which this power produces its effect, whether it creates or destroys, casts down or raises up, gives life or kills, blesses or curses. This means is his most holy Word, by which from the beginning of ages he has made known his will. He spoke at first in part and in many ways to the fathers through the prophets, and at last through his only Son, made our brother (Heb. 1:1; Heb. 2:12; John 15:15), so that he might fully reveal this remarkable will of God towards men. When he withdrew from us in his flesh, he chose faithful servants to whom he entrusted the task of publishing it and transmitting it to us in writings (Matt. 28:20), and they faithfully carried out the office committed to them (Acts 20:27). Even now he daily bestows his Spirit on those whom he sends as ministers and teachers for the building of his spiritual temple (Eph. 4:11), built upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles (Eph. 2:20; 1 Cor. 3:10), until the end of the ages.
