So too, although he knew, and indeed had foretold, that unavoidable destruction of the city of Jerusalem, he nevertheless wept over it, lamenting with that most mournful complaint: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often have I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings! O if you had known, at least on this your day, the things that belong to your peace!" (Matth. 23.37; Luke 19.42).

units.la: Immo ne tam procul haec exempla petamus, qualem sese nobis praebet Dominus adversum quos deberet optimo iure caelitus denonare, quos suo fulmine ad ima Tartara detrudere, in quos ferream illam virgam exercere potuit? Annon contra summa nobis clementia adhuc agit? Quod si nobis plagam inflixit, xit, annon miscricordia omnem ipsius seueri-tatem superauit? Ita est omnino. Quin etiam nunc licet paulo altius tonare, atque adeo ver-berare nos coepit, nobis illum profecto vel inuitum ad hoc opus adigentibus, quod suum opus esse negat Esa. 28.21. nonne tamen tristi-bus potius querelis & plancibus quam ira illa sua tam formidabili in nos vtitur? Quid ergo? quum Dominus exitium illud deploret quod ipsi peccando nobis accersimus, annon tandem nos pudebit nobis peccando placere, & eum contumelia afficere? & quum ille nihil de suo in nos amore remittat, nunquam ne ab eo dedecorando, vel tantillum saltem tempo-ris intermittemus? Quum denique nos ille ad deplorandam miseriam nostram, & ad seriam poenitentiam inuitet, queforis etiam sese prodat, semperne tristitia afficiemus Spiritum il-lum Sanctum Dei? Ephes. 4.30. Nostrane culpa semper pretiosum illud Dei nomen ex quo cognominamur contumeliis afficietur inter impios? Rom. 2.24. Quando tandem, inquam, suspiria illa inenarrabilia eximo pectore ad Deum vsque ducemus? Rom. 8.25. Quando tristitia illa tacti ingemiscemus, quae est secundum Deum ad salutem. 2. Cor. 7.10. Quando cor illud contritum & afflictum Deo offeremus ab ipso nunquam neglectum? Psal. 51.17. Nunquam profecto nisi nos ille totos a capite ad calcem immutet. Immuta nos igitur Domine & pater clementissime: & illud tuum sanctum opus in nobis, propter sacrosanctum tuum nomen perage. Alioqui periimus. At tu certè Domine perditione tuorum non oblectaris.
units.tr: Indeed, not to seek examples from far away, what manner of man does the Lord show himself toward us, against whom he might by the best right thunder from heaven, whom he could cast down with his thunderbolt into the depths of Tartarus, and upon whom he could wield that iron rod? Does he not still act toward us with the highest clemency? If he has inflicted a blow upon us, has not his mercy surpassed all his severity? So it is entirely. Even now, though he has begun to thunder a little more loudly and to beat us, while we, even against his will, compel him to this work, which he denies is his own (Esa. 28.21), does he not use sad complaints and tears rather than that terrible anger of his against us? What then? When the Lord laments the ruin which we bring upon ourselves by sinning, will we not at last be ashamed to take pleasure in sinning and to put him to shame? And since he remits nothing of his love toward us, shall we never cease, even for a short time, from dishonouring him? Finally, since he invites us to lament our misery and to serious repentance, and reveals this even outwardly, shall we always grieve the Holy Spirit of God (Ephes. 4.30)? Shall that precious name of God, by which we are called, always be dishonoured among the impious through our fault (Rom. 2.24)? When at last, I say, shall we draw those inexpressible sighs from our inmost breast up to God (Rom. 8.25)? When shall we groan, touched by that sorrow which is according to God unto salvation (2. Cor. 7.10)? When shall we offer to God a heart broken and afflicted, which he will never despise (Psal. 51.17)? Surely never, unless he changes us wholly, from head to heel. Change us, therefore, Lord and most merciful Father, and carry out your holy work in us for the sake of your most holy name. Otherwise we perish. But you, Lord, certainly do not delight in the destruction of your own.

units.la: ACTENVS intelleximus quomodo seipso superior factus Dominus victor tandem euaserit ex tam horrifica illa trepidatione, tantaque animi consternatione, quanta creaturae posiit incumbere, & qua vel ipsi Angeli, qui sic lapsi sunt vt nulla spes illis vnquam pristini status recuperandi sit reliqua, ceu fulmine sunt ad ima tartara depressi. Haec nobis parta victoria, remedium vnicum est nostris pacandis conscientiis & tranquillandis aduersus sensum & horrorem quę ex veneno lethifero peccati sentimus, cuius nos rei sumus: Christus autem eum expertus est, vt poenam illi culpae debitam quam in se receperat, quae quidem in nobis tota haerebat, non autem in illo. Qua vero constantia & animi magnitudine suis hostibus obuiam sese vltro tulerit audiuimus, quam etiam in quibusuis perturbationibus & hostium insultibus ab eodem in suos dimanare & ab eo vnico efflagitandam esse, certum est.
units.tr: So far we have seen how the Lord, master of himself, at last came through that dreadful trembling and that great consternation of soul, the greatest that a creature could fall into, and which the very angels felt, who fell in such a way that no hope of recovering their former state remains for them, and were cast down to the depths of hell as if struck by lightning. This victory, won for us, is the only remedy for calming our consciences and quieting the terror and horror we feel from the deadly poison of sin, of which we are guilty. Christ, however, experienced that terror so that the punishment due to that guilt, which he had taken upon himself, might not cling to us, as it wholly did, but not to him. We have also heard with what constancy and greatness of spirit he went out of his own accord to meet his enemies, and it is certain that this same courage flows from him into his own people in every disturbance and every assault of the enemy, and must be sought from him alone.

units.la: Iam discendum nobis est quomodo Satan, qui nunquã minus ad nos decipiendos promptus est quàm quum secure de victoria cogitamus, eodem impetu & iisdem dolis quibus nuper Magistrum aggressus fuerat, etiam discipulos adoriri tentarit: vniuersúmque adeò Dei consilium, fi hoc in eius potestate fuisset, subuertere conatus sit. At is contra quem nec fraus, nec dolus, nec vis maior quicquam potest, non modò conatus istos omnes fregit, sed etiam iis vsus est ad eos confirmandos & stabiliendos quos Satan deturbare se posse sperarat, vt tanto illustriorem suam virtutem in summa ipsorum infirmitate redderet: & hostes suos ipsos tum nostrae salutis tum suae propriae perditionis instrumenta faceret: ac tanto certiorem fidem iis adferret quae de toto mysterio nostrae salutis olim Propheta praedixerat. Psalm. 118. 23. nempe admirandum hic Dei opus, in haec verba, A Iehoua factum est istud quod mirabile est in oculis nostris: haec est dies quam fecit Iehoua.
units.tr: We must now learn how Satan, who is never less ready to deceive us than when we are confidently thinking of victory, tried to attack the disciples with the same assault and the same tricks with which he had lately assailed the Master, and indeed tried to overturn God's whole plan, if this had been in his power. But he against whom neither fraud, nor trickery, nor greater force can prevail not only broke all these attempts, but also used them to confirm and establish those whom Satan had hoped to overthrow, so that he might render his own virtue all the more illustrious in their great weakness, and make his enemies themselves the instruments both of our salvation and of their own destruction. He also gave greater certainty to what the Prophet had long before foretold concerning the whole mystery of our salvation (Ps. 118:23): this is the wonderful work of God, in these words: It has been done by the LORD; it is marvellous in our eyes. This is the day which the LORD has made.

units.la: En igitur excitatos à somno discipulos, in vnum coactos, & tum verbis, tum exemplo sui magistri, praesenti animo hostibus obuiam euntes, ardentes & erectos, maximè verò, reens illud immensae ipsius potestatis testimonium quo solo verbo suos hostes prostrauerat, habentes adhuc ob oculos & in recenti memoria. Ad quae omnia quum accederet Iudaeorum facinoris indignitas & atrocitas, tantam in ipsorum Magistro iniuriam inferentis, non dubiun
units.tr: Here, then, the disciples are roused from sleep and gathered together, and by the words and example of their master they go out to meet the enemy with presence of mind, ardent and upright. Above all, they keep before their eyes and in fresh memory that proof of his immense power by which he had laid his enemies low with a single word. To all this was added the unworthiness and atrocity of the Jews' crime, which inflicted such a great injury on their Master. There is no doubt

units.la: b'um est quin vno consensu in hanc sententiam iuerint, (acpræfertim Petrus illius dicti memor quo fe magistrum ad mortem vsquè fequuturum sanctissimè receperat,non perinde memor eorum quæ ipsi Christus responderat) quicquid tandem accidisset non inultum tantum facinus relinquendum, sed vim vi repellendam esse. Hic vero siquid de Magistratus authoritate cogitarunt, verisimile est illos tum non censuisse pro Magistratibus habendos, qui tam nefariè sua authoritate abuterentur.En quæ mentem ipsorum in hac perturbatione subierit cogitatio, quam ipse Satan pro viribus auxit & promouit, vt nouit ille cupiditates nostras accendere, rationibus ac modis planè nobis incognitis & incomprehensibilibus, licet certissimis, quum non frustra dicatur Diabolus in cor Iudæ ingressus, vt eum ad prodendum magistrum impelleret.Iohan.13 2.At Dominus, qui non sinit vt quicunque tentantur in tentationem intrent, & supra id quod possunt tententur 1. Corint. 10.13.mature huic malo occurrit.Et sanè ni factum id esset, quasi superior Satan exultasset: quum Apostolorum vim vi repellentium factum videretur certum esse aduersus Christum præiudicium, immo certissimum indicium ac testimonium, cum licet viri boni speciem præ se ferret,tamen seditiosum ac factiosum hominem, discipulis eiusdem farinæ hominibus stipatum, quibus ad pacem & otium publicum perturbandum vteretur
units.tr: that by common consent they went over to this opinion (and especially Peter, mindful of that promise by which he had most solemnly undertaken to follow the Master even to death, but not equally mindful of what Christ had answered him): that whatever happened, so great a crime must not be left unavenged, and force must be repelled by force. But if they thought anything about the authority of the magistrate, it is likely they then did not judge those to be magistrates who so wickedly abused their authority. Behold the thought that came into their minds in this disturbance, which Satan himself increased and promoted as far as he could, for he knows how to kindle our desires by means wholly unknown and incomprehensible to us, though most certain; for it is not without reason said that the Devil entered into the heart of Judas to impel him to betray his master (John 13:2). But the Lord, who does not allow those who are tempted to enter into temptation, and who does not let them be tempted beyond what they can bear (1 Cor. 10:13), promptly met this evil. And indeed, had this not happened, Satan would have exulted as if he were the superior, for it would have seemed certain that the Apostles, repelling force with force, were a sure prejudgment and most certain sign and testimony against Christ, since, although he showed the appearance of a good man, he was a seditious and factious man, surrounded by disciples of the same sort, whom he would use to disturb public peace and quiet.

units.la: Discipuli vero eiusmodi consilio & facto longe etiam magis inextricabiles laqueos sibi inducebant, exitium illis duplici via parante Satana. Alterutrum enim horum oportebat contingere, nisi tempestiue Christus occurrisset, & aduersus Diabolum ipsum fraudes ipsius retorsisset, nempe vt aut discipuli cohortem istam victores superarent, aut ipsi contra casi omnes, aut pars ipsorum caderent, aut saltem in vincula cum Magistro coiicerentur, ac proinde vt probatum & certissimis testimoniis eiusdem Christo impositum seditionis & coniurationis crimen haberetur, quod à Magistratibus missae cohorti vim attulissent, & sacrosanctam iustitiam violassent: unde foeda totius Euangelicae doctrinae proculcatio, aduersus Christum & discipulos cunctis insurgentibus consequeretur.
units.tr: By such counsel and deed the disciples were binding themselves in even more inextricable snares, Satan preparing ruin for them by a double route. For one of two outcomes had to follow, unless Christ had come in time and turned Satan's own frauds back upon him: either the disciples would overcome that cohort as victors, or they would all fall, or some of them would, or at least they would be cast into prison together with their Master. Then the crime of sedition and conspiracy would be held as proven and laid upon Christ by the most certain evidence, because they had used force against the cohort sent by the magistrates and had violated sacred justice. From this would follow a foul trampling down of the whole Evangelical doctrine, with everyone rising up against Christ and the disciples.

units.la: Hinc vero discamus quàm veteratorie & dolose Satan nobiscum agat, laeua nos dextraque adoriens, nunquam magis metuendus quàm quum in Angelum lucis se transformat: & quàm nobis ipsis diffidere & suspectos nobis ipsis esse nos oporteat, & quàm diligenter omnia nostra consilia & deliberationes, ne nimium praecipiti iudicio ferantur, decet expendere, ne dum nobis sapere videmur, retamen ipsa stulti comperiamur. Rursum igitur hic quomodo fuerint Apostoli tum à Satana tum à seipsis decepti videamus. En igitur quibus fundamentis tanquam argumentis firmissimis fucum sibi fecerint: No dubitandum quin duce tali Magistro cuius erat tata promptitudo, tantumque robur vt vel vnico verbo suos hostes profligarent, facile d'suis hostibus victoriam reportarent: summam esse causę suæ æquitatem: vel vitæ suæ periculo notam ingratitudinis & ignauiæ in tam bono Magistro ciam innocente tutando & aduersus vim hostium protegendo, redimendam. Egregia sanè speciosa quæ argumenta, sed tamen huic causæ minimè congruentia, & male applicata. Sequebatur quidem ex prima illa ratione posse Christum armis suos hostes superare & plane prosternere: velle autem minimè sequebatur: quum contrà longè aliis armis quàm ferreis mundum superandum illos tum dictis tum exemplo, nimirum inuocatione, fide, & patientia, docuisset, sequè à discipulis, crucem suam baiulantibus, non autem vel eam detrectantibus, vel in alios reiicientibus sequendum. Præterea, quoties eos, tum verò maximè post vltimam illam cœnam, de iis quæ ex Dei Patris decreto & consilio immutabili sibi nocte illa erant eventura sedulo præmonuerat? Et quum animaduerterent solo verbo Christum sic hostes perterruisse vt prosternerétur, cur ei rem totam non permittunt? Sed insuper, quum eodem momento prostratos hostes viderent se erexisse, annon eos oportuit Magistri sui voluntatem ex eo dignoscere? Ad alteram verò rationem quòd attinet quis dubitat insignem iniuriam ipsorum Magistro factam esse, ac proinde iustitiæ æquitate potiores esse suis hostibus? An vero quorumuis est ius administrare, & illatam iniuriam armis vindicare? An eorum erant immemores quae Deus in Lege dixerat? Mihi, inquit Dominus, vindicta & retributio. Deut. 32. 35. Ammon etiam Dominus quum Pharisaeorum adulterinam expositionem in haec verba, oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente refelleret, diserte praescripserat, Ne malo resisteret, sed, ai: quisquis te caedet in dextram tuam maxillam obverte ei & alteram. Matth. 5. 29. En igitur & hac in parte sophisticam conclusionem. De tertia, verum illud quidem est amicum in re incerta deferre, & proximo debitum officium non praestare, summum esse ingrati animi crimen, & probro ducendum merito iudicari: at quicquid proximo praestatur recti & honesti omnibus est metiendum, quod & ipsi prophani de verae amicitiae legibus differentes, perspicue satis indicarunt. Quapropter etiam cum qui amet patrem aut matrem, filium aut filiam supra se, dignum se esse negabat Dominus. Matth. 10. 37. Iterum igitur inculco, fratres, ne nobis ipsis sapiamus, sed ipsi nobis suspecti, rationes, etiam speciosissimas, cohibeamus & comprimamus: & satis non esse norimus de certo loco adeundo cogitantibus eo tendere, sed etiam esse viam quae ad eum ducit ingrediendam: quo non obseruato sed neglecto consilio fit ut multi in maxima praecipites ferantur incommoda, quorum sera nimis poenitentia ducantur: est enim verissimum illud tritum proucrbium, Nullos magis insanire quàm qui satis sibi ipsis sapere videantur.
units.tr: Here let us learn how craftily and deceitfully Satan deals with us, attacking us on left and right, never more to be feared than when he transforms himself into an angel of light; and how we ought to distrust ourselves and be suspicious of ourselves, and how carefully it is fitting to weigh all our plans and deliberations, so that they are not carried away by too hasty a judgment, lest while we seem wise to ourselves, we are found to be fools. Again, then, let us see how the Apostles were deceived both by Satan and by themselves. Here are the grounds on which, as on most firm arguments, they deceived themselves: that there is no doubt that with such a leader, whose readiness was so great and whose strength so great that with a single word he could strike down his enemies, they could easily win the victory over their enemies; that the justice of their cause was supreme; or that the stain of ingratitude and cowardice toward so good a Master, in defending the innocent and protecting him against the violence of enemies, must be redeemed at the risk of their life. These are certainly fine-looking arguments, but not at all suited to this cause, and badly applied. It did indeed follow from the first reasoning that Christ could overcome his enemies by arms and utterly overthrow them, but it by no means followed that he wished to. On the contrary, he had taught them that the world must be conquered with quite different weapons than iron, namely by word and example, by invocation, faith and patience, and that they must follow him bearing his cross, not refusing it or throwing it onto others. Besides, how often had he carefully forewarned them of what, by the decree and unchangeable counsel of God the Father, was to happen to him that night, especially after the last supper? And when they noticed that Christ had so terrified his enemies that they were laid low by his word alone, why did they not leave the whole matter to him? Moreover, when they saw the enemies, prostrate at that same moment, rise again, ought they not to have recognised their Master's will from this? As for the second reason, who doubts that a notable injury was done to their Master, and that therefore they were superior to their enemies in the equity of justice? But is it for anyone at all to administer justice and avenge an injury with arms? Were they forgetful of what the Lord had said in the Law: "Vengeance is mine, and recompense" (Deut. 32:35)? Likewise, when the Lord refuted the Pharisees' corrupt exposition, "an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth," he expressly prescribed: "Do not resist the evil one, but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also" (Matt. 5:39). Here, then, is the sophistical conclusion on this point too. As to the third: it is indeed true that to abandon a friend in an uncertain matter, and not to render the duty owed to a neighbour, is the greatest mark of an ungrateful mind and rightly judged a disgrace; but whatever is rendered to a neighbour must be measured by what is right and honourable for all, as even profane men, discussing the laws of true friendship, have sufficiently shown. Therefore the Lord also declared that one who loves father or mother, son or daughter, more than himself is not worthy of him (Matt. 10:37). Again, then, brothers, I urge: let us not be wise in our own eyes, but be suspicious of ourselves, and restrain and check our reasons, even the most specious. Let us know that it is not enough for those thinking about going to a certain place to aim at it; the way that leads there must also be entered. When this counsel is not observed but neglected, many are carried headlong into the greatest calamities, and repent of them too late. For that familiar proverb is most true: no one is more mad than those who seem wise enough to themselves.

units.la: Hæc porrò incommoda, non solùm, nec proprie nos humana prudentia, longo viu acquisita, fugere docet, non pretiosissima quæ in schollis discitur verum à falso diiudicandi scientia, (quæ duo tamen eximia Dei dona sunt quòd ad res humanas attinet,) sed integritas conscientiæ, conscientiæ, inquam verbo Dei edoctæ, ad cuius vnius nutum omnes nostras actiones, verba & cogitationes tanquam ad amussim certissimam exigendæ sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, human prudence, acquired through long experience, does not teach us to flee these misfortunes, and not even properly. Nor does the most precious knowledge learned in the schools, the ability to distinguish true from false (though these two are excellent gifts of God as far as human affairs are concerned). What teaches us is integrity of conscience: conscience, I say, taught by the Word of God, by whose sole nod all our actions, words and thoughts must be measured, as by a most certain rule.

units.la: Ab hoc igitur omnes nostræ deliberationes inchoandæ, sic in iis progrediendum & perseuerandum, vt verè cum Dauide testari possimus, Psal.119. 105. Lucerna pedibus meis est verbum tuum, & lumen semitæ meæ.
units.tr: Therefore all our deliberations must begin from this, and we must proceed and persevere in them, so that we can truly say with David, Psal. 119. 105: "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path."

units.la: Et hoc ipsum Scriptura vocat Interrogare os Domini, non quòd tamen id fieri debere dicamus ea ratione qua apud veteres illos apud quos reuelationum dona vigebant. Quum enim nobis longè illustrior & certior diuinæ erga nos voluntatis declaratio iam illuxerit, & Lex ipsa quid fugiendum sit doceat, & quid sequendum: & cuique vocationi sui fines præscripti sint vltra quos nihil tentandum, neque sufficiunt illa, si modo vacui simus omni animi perturbatione, tum deliberando, tu etiam invocato Dei nomine recte cogitata perficiendo, rerum omnium euentu Deo committere, & ab eius prouidentia in solidum pendere docti.
units.tr: Scripture itself calls this "to inquire at the mouth of the Lord." Yet we do not say that this must be done in the way of those ancients among whom the gifts of revelation flourished. For since a much clearer and more certain declaration of the divine will has now dawned upon us, and the Law itself teaches what is to be avoided and what is to be followed, and the limits of each calling have been prescribed, beyond which nothing is to be attempted, those things are not enough, if we are only free of all agitation of mind. Then, both in deliberating and, with the name of God invoked, in carrying out what has been rightly thought, we are taught to commit the outcome of all things to God, and to depend wholly on his providence.

units.la: En igitur quid ex officio cuiusque sit. Sed alij in
units.tr: Here, then, is what belongs to each person's duty. But others

units.la: ipso limine impingunt, alij in medio hærent, alij denique in ipso fine vehementer hallucinantur. In principio aberrant à recto qui post habita Dei voluntatis & suæ vocationis ratione præiudiciis suis sibi fucum faciunt, & sua consilia recta esse sibi persuadentes de eorum executione tantum sollicité sunt, non veriti Deum invocare, & eius etiam opem & auxilium expectare, in rebus tamen quæ si accuratè expendantur, temerè susceptæ comperiuntur, aut quod Dei voluntati non consentiant, aut quòd ab ipsorum vocatione sint alienæ. In progressu verò hallucinantur, qui certò persuasi nihil se nisi bonum & voluntati Dei, suæque vocationi consentaneum suscipere, quibus mediis tamen illud exequantur parùm sunt solliciti, Unde plerunque fit ut quæ benè cœpta fuerant suum exitum minimè sortiri possint nec etiam debeant: tumque illos in hunc vel illum culpam reiicere, vel etiam ipsi Deo quodammodo contingat obloqui. Denique peccant in fine, qui Dei gloriam suis deliberationibus postponentes, Dei loco habent sua somnia, atque adeò suas cupiditates & libidines, earum libenter socium & administrum sempiternum numen facturi. Aberrant etiam procul à scopo quorum principiis felicibus quum Deus etiam annuere visus sit, sui quasi immemores extra viam excurrunt, quamtamen decurrere ipsos inoffenso pede ad finem vsque oportucrat. Horum autem errorum exempla tum sacræ tum prophanæ historiæ nobis affatim suppeditant praeter ea quę quotidiana nos experientia tum in aliis, tum in nobis ipsis docet.
units.tr: stumble at the very threshold, others stick in the middle, and others finally go badly astray at the very end. They go wrong at the beginning who, having set aside consideration of God's will and of their own calling, deceive themselves by their prejudices. Persuaded that their plans are right, they are anxious only about carrying them out, not scrupling to call upon God and to expect his help; yet these are matters which, if weighed carefully, turn out to have been rashly undertaken, either because they do not agree with God's will or because they are foreign to their own calling. They go astray in the course of the work who, firmly convinced that they undertake nothing but what is good and consistent with God's will and their own calling, are little concerned about the means by which they carry it out. Hence it often happens that what was well begun cannot, and indeed should not, have a good outcome; then they lay the blame on this or that person, or even somehow find fault with God himself. Finally, they sin at the end who, putting God's glory after their own designs, make their own dreams into a god, and so willingly make their own desires and lusts an eternal deity, its partner and minister. They also wander far from the goal: those whose beginnings God seemed to favour, who, as if forgetful of themselves, run out of the way, whereas they ought to have run the course to the end with unstumbling foot. Examples of these errors sacred and profane history supply us in abundance, besides those which daily experience teaches us, both in others and in ourselves.

units.la: Omitto curiosos qui stellas duces & autho-res in omnibus consiliis sequuntur: omitto detestandos illos Prognosticos,Genethliacos, Calendariorum & Praedictionum inuentores, & caeteros id genus Altrologiae quam vocant, iudiciariae doctores,qui suae artis quam profitentur cancellos, intra quos se continere debuerant,causas puta naturales, & quidem admodum illas incertas, propter varium causarum secundarum quae ab illis reguntur subiectorum concursum,praetergressi,audent etiam de statu mundi loqui quasi arcanis Dei consiliis interfuisse: & quod eorum sacrilegam audaciam magis arguit, quid cuique priuato sit eventurum denuntiant: audax facinus,tam disertis verbis à Domino saepe prohibitum: tam generi humano perniciosum, legibus etiam Imperialibus prohibitum: tam denique falsum & severissime vindicatum omni seculo ut mirum sit apud eos qui Christianismum profitentur huiusmodi praedictiones, immo impostoras, scelera, flagitia & impietates tolerare fuisse & adhuc hodie tolerari.Sed talibus Prophetis mundus est dignissimus. Sed ut unde digressa est nostra recurrat oratio,nimirum hac in re praeceps fuit Apostolorum conclusio,ut docuimus,in eo tamen laude digni, quod praeceptorem interrogant an sint percussuri, si modo responsum expectassent; iis non absimiles qui alios consulunt, non vt quæ facienda vel omittenda sint cognoscant, sed vt explorent, num quæ iam sibi constituta sunt, & quorum certa sententia, reperiant qui approbent: quorum alij quidem patientem accommodant aurem iis quæ dicuntur, sed non propterea sententiam mutant : alij verò non expectato responso morę impatientes vlterius progrediuntur, & sibi suisque plurimum negotij facessunt.
units.tr: I pass over the curious who follow the stars as guides and authorities in all their counsels. I pass over those detestable prognosticators, genethliacs and inventors of calendars and predictions, and the other sort of so-called astrology, the teachers of judicial astrology. These men, having overstepped the bounds within which they should have kept themselves in their art, namely natural causes, and indeed very uncertain ones because of the varied concourse of the secondary causes which they claim to govern, dare also to speak of the state of the world as if they had been present at God's secret counsels. What shows their sacrilegious audacity even more, they announce what will happen to each private person. It is a bold deed, so often forbidden by the Lord in such plain words, so pernicious to the human race, forbidden also by imperial laws, so false and so severely punished in every age, that it is strange that among those who profess Christianity such predictions, or rather impostures, crimes, wickednesses and impieties have been tolerated in the past and are still tolerated today. But the world is most worthy of such prophets. But to return our discourse to where it digressed: certainly in this matter the Apostles' conclusion was rash, as we have shown. Yet they deserve praise in this, that they asked their Teacher whether they should strike, if only they had waited for an answer. They are not unlike those who consult others, not so as to learn what should be done or left undone, but to test whether they can find approval for what has already been decided. Of these, some indeed lend a patient ear to what is said but do not on that account change their opinion; others, impatient of delay and not waiting for the answer, press on further and make much trouble for themselves and for others.

units.la: Idipsum hoc loco discipulis,& nominatim Petro,aliorum duci,primas nimirum & in deliberando &in exequendo partes agente contigisse videmus,cuius imprudentia factum est, vt quum coeusque progressus esset vt quendam militem gregarium sed Summi Sacerdotis tamen seruum vulneraret,nostræ salutis quodam modo mysterium exinaniretur &in nihilum redigeretur; & se suosque socios immo totam Ecclesiam hoc vno ictu simul ac semel pessundederit. Ecquis verò dubitat quin Deo permittente Satan manum Petri ad hoc vnius infligendum direxerit, licet antea dictum illi fuisset, Tu es Petrus?
units.tr: We see the same thing happening to the disciples in this place, and by name to Peter, who took the leading role both in deliberating and in acting. Through his imprudence it came about that, when he had gone so far as to wound a common soldier, yet the servant of the High Priest, the mystery of our salvation was in a certain way emptied out and reduced to nothing. With a single blow he at once destroyed himself, his fellows, and indeed the whole Church. Yet who doubts that, with God permitting, Satan directed Peter's hand to inflict this blow, although it had been said to him before, "You are Peter"?

units.la: Et hoc saltem eos oportuerat animaduertere, quos immani quodam furore non pudet Spiritum S. non quidem Petro etsi iuste sron multò post à Paulo Antiochiæ correpto: sed iis alligare qui se salsissimè & impudentissimè petri Successores iactitant: nisi forte suo iure id faciunt, in eo Petrum imitati, qui vt animi nimium præcipiti ferebatur æstu, sacinus omnium mnium periculosissimū,nisi Dominus auertis- set, aggrediebatur, sic isti iam à multis seculis flagitiosi homines omnium bellorū & turba- rum,quæ in toto Christiano orbe sunt excita- tæ, semina sparserunt, & etiamnum hodie sæ- uorum incendiorum faces in vniuersum ter- rarum orbem inferunt.
units.tr: At least those ought to have noticed this who, with a certain monstrous fury, are not ashamed to bind the Holy Spirit to those who boast most saltily and shamelessly that they are the successors of Peter, not indeed rightly rebuked soon afterwards by Paul at Antioch. Unless perhaps they do so by right, imitating Peter in this: carried away by an excessively headlong heat of mind, he would have undertaken the most dangerous deed of all, had the Lord not turned him aside. So these men, for many centuries now shameless and wicked, have sown the seeds of all the wars and disturbances that have been stirred up throughout the Christian world, and even today they cast the torches of savage fires over the whole orb of the earth.

units.la: Hic vero vicissim nos Dei sapientiam ex i- ipsis tenebris Lucem educentis contemplari decet: poterat enim ille quidem arcana illa sua virtute, aut verbo solo Petrum & socios e- ius sic cohibere ne facinus tantum attentaret, sed illustriorem triumphum de hoste suo re- portaturus,quæ moliebatur cum perficere vo- luit, tanto maiorem illi ignominiam influ- rus. Nam quum speraret Satan opportunam se nactum occasionem ex ista voluntaria Domi- ni nostri Iesu Christi exinanitione,omnem il- lius apud homines authoritatem imminuen- di, & totam eius discipulorum Apostolatus dignitatem conuellendi, en contrà Dominus miraculum edit tam procul ab humanæ natu- ræ viribus remotum,vt nulli potentiæ nisi so- li Deitati essentiali tribui merito possit:quum nulla ratione vel arte humana ,sed sola Dei potentia nulli rei creatæ communicabili, hu- manum membrum à corpore resectum & marcidum denuò corpori possit adiungi & in integrum restituì:quemadmodum in cæci nati miraculo Ioh.9.contigit,cuius oculos nemo sanare potuit præter eum à quo primùm crea- ti fuerant.Hoc igitur Satan vnum agebas,hoc
units.tr: Here, in turn, it is fitting for us to contemplate the wisdom of God, who brings light out of darkness itself. For he could indeed, by his hidden power or by a word alone, have restrained Peter and his companions so that they would not even attempt such a crime. But about to win a more illustrious triumph over his enemy, he wished to carry through what the enemy was devising, and so to inflict on him all the greater disgrace. For while Satan hoped that he had found an opportune occasion in this voluntary self-emptying of our Lord Jesus Christ, to diminish all his authority among men and to overthrow the whole dignity of his disciples' apostleship, on the contrary the Lord performed a miracle so remote from the powers of human nature that it can rightly be attributed to no power but the essential Deity alone. For by no human reason or art, but only by the power of God, which cannot be communicated to any created thing, can a human member cut off from the body and withered be joined to the body again and restored to wholeness. So it happened in the miracle of the man born blind, John 9, whose eyes no one could heal except him by whom they had first been created. This, then, Satan, was the one thing you were doing, this you were striving to bring about: to persuade men that Christ is scarcely to be counted among ordinary little men, and has no power to defend himself against enemies, much less the power to bring death upon others.

units.la: n. j. moliebaris,vt hominibus persuaderes (Christū vix inter gregarios homunciones habendum, & fe tutandi aduersus hostes vim non habere, nedū vt alios morte affercndi potestatē habe-ret. Age verò,quid tibi Petri temeritas, qua ni-tebaris abuti,profuit?Cōtrà enim tu hanc ratio-ne Christo, vt ita dicā amplā materiā suppedi-tasti qua se sensibiliter & palpabiliter patefa-ceret, non tantùm hominem diuinum, (id est, virtute aliqua insignem qua reliquos longè superaret)sed verum hominem & verum Deū viuentem, sine quo nihil eorum quæ sunt factum est. Tu seditiosum illum & tanquam immanem aliquam cladem populo pręparan-tem calumniari studebas:sed ille contra tuum aduersus te consilium retorquet, & facinus ad quod discipulum impulisti in hunc vsum coūertit, vt vel ipsis ęcęutientibus patefaciat, ve-nisse malum bono compensaturum, & suis hostibus bonum malo repensurum, restituta nimirum illi auricula cui tu illam abscideras. Tu hac ratione te sperabas Apostolatum & Apostolos posse subuertere: sed hac ratione melius quàm antea qualem magistrum habe-rent agnouerunt, & quæ essent erga ipsum officij sui partes meliùs intellexerunt. Nihilo-minus tamen etiā Dei filius ex tenebris Lucem educit, tenebrę semper manent tenebrę, nec vnquam malè agendum est spe alicuius inde boni prouenturi. Cæterùm quod Dominus tantum Satanæ & suis discipulis permiserit, plurimùm nobis confert ad omnes illos no-stros stros impotentes animi affectus cohibendos, ne quoties animaduertimus Deum suis hostibus laxas, vt ita dicam, habenas permittere, omniaque in peius ruentia, sas deque ferri, cum impiis illis Epicureis & Atheis inferamus, Nô videre nec cognoscere Deum Iacobi. Ps. 94. 7. Quoties igitur talia cóspicimus, qualia multa si alias vnquâ nostra repestate cótingunt, tum norimus à Domino nouum aliquod & extraordinarium opus expectandum, vt seculorum omnium experientia satis id testatur, & propediem bene fauente nobis Deo magis ac magis testatum facier.
units.tr: Come now, what good did Peter's rashness, on which you tried to rely, do you? For by this means you supplied Christ, so to speak, with ample material by which he might reveal himself sensibly and palpably, not merely as a divine man (that is, one distinguished by some virtue which far surpasses the rest), but as a true man and the true living God, without whom nothing that has been made was made. You were eager to slander him as a seditious man, one who was preparing, as it were, some monstrous disaster for the people. But he turns your plan against you, and converts the deed to which you drove the disciple to this use: so that even to the blind he might make plain that he came to repay evil with good, and to repay good to his enemies for evil, namely by restoring the ear which you had cut off. By this means you hoped to subvert the apostleship and the Apostles; but by this means they recognised better than before what kind of Master they had, and understood better what their office required of them. Nevertheless the Son of God brings light out of darkness; darkness always remains darkness, and one must never act wickedly in hope of any good that may come from it. Moreover, that the Lord permitted this only to Satan and his disciples contributes greatly to restraining all those impotent passions of the mind. Whenever we notice God, as it were, giving his enemies loose reins, and everything rushing to worse and being carried headlong, we must not join with those impious Epicureans and Atheists in saying, "The Lord does not see, nor does the God of Jacob perceive" (Ps. 94. 7). Whenever we see such things, of which many happen in our own times, as the experience of all ages sufficiently attests, let us know that some new and extraordinary work is to be expected from the Lord, which, with God favouring us, will before long be shown more and more clearly.

units.la: Iam ad Christi reprehensionem & eius fundamentum accedamus. Petrum igitur gladium iubet in vagina recondere, nec ferro tantū & armis rē agere prohibet, sed etiam ob incœptum facinus, & temeritatem in gladio ad fundendum humanum sanguinem sumendo grauiús incusat. Et hoc diligenter animaduertite aduersus quosdam perfrictæ frõtis homines, quos non potuit dicere gladium à Christo non fuisse Petro sublatum, sed tantùm iussum eum in vaginam recondere tantisper dum illo tempus esset vtendi. Sed vbi tandem tempus istud gladij stringendi reperient, quum discrte Dominus temporalem iurisdictionem à spirituali distinxerit? Matth. 20. 25. Non tantum ambitionem damnat, sed etiam quantum inter se duæ, istæ iurisdictiones discrepét ostendit, nisi forte si quando extra ordinem aliquos ad vtrumque munus obeundum excitauerit. Hanc etiam ob causam scipsum considerans, non quidé quatenus Deus est æternus, & ipsis Regibus balthea sua præcingit, & in cœlo & terra summum imperium obtinet, sed quatenus est Ecclesiæ suæ caput, diliti nácte dicit suum regnum non esse ex hoc mundo. Ioh. 18. 36. nec hæreditatem inter fratres dividere voluit. Luc. 12.13. nec de adulterafornse iudicium ferre: adeo ut quam tibi temporalem potestatem nonnulli Ecclesiastici quocunque tandem prætextu vendicant, minime sit ferenda, Dei nimirum ordinationi repugnans ex diametro, quam à Regibus & Principibus iltos postulare, multò vero minus inuadere fas non fuit: nec vicissim ipsis eam largiri Reges ac principes oportuit. Relictus est igitur hic quidem gladius Petro, & hodie Christianis omnibus permittitur, minime sane humano fundendo sanguini, nec ciuili vlli vsurpandæ auctoritati sed in alios vsus, quibus sunt hæc instrumenta destinata.
units.tr: Now let us come to Christ's rebuke and its foundation. He bids Peter put the sword back into its sheath. He forbids him not only to act with the sword and arms, but also blames him more severely for the crime he had begun and for his rashness in taking up the sword to shed human blood. Mark this carefully against certain brazen-faced men, who cannot say that Christ did not take the sword from Peter, but only ordered him to return it to the sheath for the time being, until the time for using it should come. But where will they ever find that time for drawing the sword, since the Lord has clearly distinguished temporal jurisdiction from spiritual? Matt. 20. 25. He not only condemns ambition but also shows how far apart these two jurisdictions are, unless perhaps he has at some time, beyond the ordinary course, called certain people to discharge both offices. For this reason too, considering himself not as he is eternal God, who girds kings with their swords and holds supreme power in heaven and earth, but as he is the head of his Church, he plainly says that his kingdom is not of this world. John 18. 36. Nor did he wish to divide an inheritance between brothers. Luke 12. 13. Nor did he pass judgement on the adulteress. So the temporal power that some churchmen claim under whatever pretext is by no means to be tolerated, since it is directly opposed to God's ordinance. They ought not to demand it from kings and princes, much less to seize it, and kings and princes ought not to bestow it on them. So the sword is indeed left to Peter, and today it is permitted to all Christians. Certainly it is not for shedding human blood, nor for any civil assumption of authority, but for the other uses for which these instruments are destined.

units.la: Prima istius reprehensionis ratio generalis est, & omnibus priuatis, id est, nec magistratu nec functionem vllam publicam administrantibus communis. Nam, inquit, qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit. Hic vero nobis in primis à furiosorum Anabaptistarum errore cauendum est, Magistratus ipsos gladio priuantibus: quod salsissimum est dogma, nullamque præ se ferens rationis speciem. Quorsum enim Dominus capitis supplicia Legibus iis præfixisset, quas Magistratibus tradidit, nisi voluisset earum allertores esse ac vindices? Na-
units.tr: The first and general ground of this rebuke applies to all private persons, that is, to those who hold neither magistracy nor any public office. For, he says, whoever takes the sword will perish by the sword. Here, however, we must above all beware of the error of the frenzied Anabaptists, who deprive magistrates of the sword. This is a most foolish dogma, bearing no appearance of reason. For why would the Lord have prescribed capital punishments in the laws he handed to the magistrates, unless he had wished them to be the upholders and avengers of those laws? Na-

units.la: Naturalis æquitas & inuiolabilis etiam aperte morte dignum homicidam clamat, Gen. 9. 6. & quidem in cœde voluntaria spem impunitatis omnem tollit Num. 35. 31. sicut etiam Apostolus perspicue docuit Rom. 13. 4. vt mirum sit adeo stupidos aliquos existere, id in dubium qui revocent. Porrò quum de magistratus gladio loquimur, non tantum hunc vel illum capitale supplicium promeritum, ex bonarum legum instituto plectendi potestatem intelligimus, sed autoritate suos etiam subditos armadi quò se suamq; libertate aduersus quosli-bet hostes protegant ac tueantur, quod historia sacra tota testatur, & naturalis æquitas postulat. Etsi fateor sane tantam armorum esse tamque effusam & indomitam licentiam, tantamque malorum omnium segetem proferre (quod, proh dolor! quotidie iam ex quo sumus ad hanc necessitatem impulsi nimium experimur) vt nunquam satis illius Ethnici licet poetæ sententiam considerare & in visu habere possimus, Sapientem omnia consilio priùs quàm armis experiri decere.
units.tr: Natural equity and the inviolable law also openly declare that a murderer deserves death. Gen. 9. 6. Indeed, in deliberate murder it removes all hope of impunity. Num. 35. 31. As the Apostle also plainly taught. Rom. 13. 4. So it is strange that there should be such dullards as to call this in doubt. Moreover, when we speak of the magistrate's sword, we understand not merely the power, under the institution of good laws, to punish this or that man who deserves capital punishment, but also the authority to arm their subjects, so that they may protect and defend themselves and their liberty against any enemies. All sacred history attests this, and natural equity demands it. Yet I freely admit that the licence of arms is so great, so widespread and unbridled, and produces such a harvest of all evils (as, alas! we experience daily now that we have been driven into this necessity), that we can never sufficiently consider and keep before our eyes the saying of that heathen poet, that a wise man ought to try everything by counsel before arms.

units.la: Alter eorum error est, qui animadvertentes conscientias nulla vi humana cogi posse, & non aliis armis à Domino quàm gladio spiritual fuisse Apostolos Pastores ac doctores instructos, vt regnum eius est spirituale, docent non licere Magistratibus in causa religionis & conscientiæ mera puta: gladium vel in privatum quempiam, vel in hostem publicum stringere. Agè verò si ita est, impunitas homi-
units.tr: Another of their errors is that of those who, noticing that consciences cannot be compelled by any human force, and that the Apostles, pastors and teachers were equipped by the Lord with no weapons but the spiritual sword, since his kingdom is spiritual, teach that magistrates may not draw the sword against any private person or public enemy in a matter of religion and conscience alone. But if this is so, impunity is offered to murderers and other criminals

units.la: Magistratus etiam oportere veræ religionis cultum armis tueri. cidis & aliis facinorosis hominibus propona- tur , quorum ingenia Magistratus nom magis quantumuis atrocibus suppliciis immutauc- rint,quàm conscientiam hominumvbi de fide & religione agitur coègerint. Ar fi sup plicio- rum,putà rotę aut ignium atrocitate multi de- terrentur & coërcentur , & fi pœnarum etiam leuium publicè editarum supplicio multi ad meliorem frugem castigati redeunt,quid cau- sæ est cur non idem etiam de iustis pœnis sen- tiamus quibus Ecclesiæ pacis ac tranquillita- tis perturbatores corripiantur?Iustas dico pœ- nas, quæ vera iustitia & æquitate niduntur, quibus opponitur iniustitia ac latrocinium potius religionis obductum inuoluctio , sicut videmus olim Prophetas persecutionem à Re- gibus & pseudoprophetis passos,ipsúmque e- tiam Dei filium , & fratrum nostrorum pene immensam multitudinem , hoc etiam iniusti- tiæ nomine sub se zelum qui sine scientia est complectente. At vbique iuris æquitate vim suam retinente , primùm quòd ad impietatem attinet , qualem in atheis plerisque cernimus adeò profligatæ impudentiæ, vt libris eam e- ditis testari non erubescant,quis ausit insicia- ri,licet de Religione quæratur,quin sit Magi- stratus officium tam flagitiosos homines ca- pitali supplicio si nullis admonitionibus aut pœnis leuioribus locum dederint , aut ad me- liorem mentem reuocari noluerint de medio tollere?Quòd ad hærefin vero,quum non quili- bet error hæresis sit:nec quiuis hæreticus ne- cessario cessatio sit pacis & tranquillitatis publicę Religionis perturbator habendus: & in hæresin possit quispiam incidere, qua vel aliquis articulus fidei Christianæ fundamentalis conuelletur, qui tamen sibi se rectam viam insistere persuadeat, si hoc casu, quibus commissus est spiritualis gladius, quo solo pestiferæ radices iniusmodi resecantur, quod ex officio fuerit, habita rei de qua agitur & personæ ratione frustrà tentarint, quid impedit quominus Magistratus, quem in primis sollicitum esse oportet, ut Deus à subditis cognoscatur & colatur, etiam gladio utatur, si necessitas itapostulet, ut sacta tecta Religio maneat? & quidé eò diligentius quò sunt animarum prædones magis infesti & metuendi quàm illi corporum homicidę vel sicarij? & statuum omnium basis ac firmamentum sit unicus Dei cultus? Hîc quidam obiiciunt zizaniorum parabolam quæ discipuli prohibentur eradicare Matth. 13. 29. Sed quid ad rem? Nam vel ipso Christo teste & parabolę interprete, quotquot vel in moribus vel in doctrina sunt aliis offendiculo, fructúmque Euangelij remorantur nomine zizaniorum intelliguntur. Quare si huic expositioni locus daretur, non magis essent de medio tollendi qui flagitiosè viuunt, quàm qui falsam doctrinam profitentur.
units.tr: Magistrates too ought to defend the true worship of religion with arms. Impunity is offered to murderers and other criminals, whose natures magistrates have not changed by however atrocious punishments, if they have not compelled the consciences of men where faith and religion are at issue. For if by punishments, such as the wheel or the atrocity of fires, many are deterred and restrained, and if by the public execution even of light penalties many are chastened and return to a better way of life, what reason is there why we should not think the same of just punishments by which the disturbers of the Church's peace and tranquillity are corrected? I say just punishments, which rest on true justice and equity, as opposed to injustice and robbery, which is rather cloaked under the guise of religion. As we see, the prophets of old suffered persecution from kings and false prophets, and the Son of God himself, and an almost immeasurable multitude of our brothers, who under this name of injustice embraced a zeal that is without knowledge. But everywhere the force of legal equity remains. First, as regards impiety, which we see in most atheists, of such flagrant shamelessness that they do not blush to attest it in published books: who would dare to deny, even if the question concerns religion, that it is the magistrate's duty to remove from the midst by capital punishment such shameless men, if they have given no room to admonitions or lighter penalties, or have refused to be recalled to a better mind? As for heresy, not every error is heresy, nor is every heretic necessarily to be held a disturber of the peace and tranquillity of public religion. Someone may fall into a heresy by which some fundamental article of the Christian faith is overthrown, and yet persuade himself that he is walking the right path. If in this case those to whom the spiritual sword has been committed, the only means by which such pestilent roots are cut out, have, as is their duty and having weighed the matter in question and the person, tried in vain, what hinders the magistrate, who above all ought to be anxious that God be known and worshipped by his subjects, from also using the sword, if necessity so requires, so that the true religion may remain safe and whole? And all the more diligently, since the plunderers of souls are more hostile and to be feared than those murderers of bodies or assassins, and the sole worship of God is the base and foundation of all states? Here some object the parable of the tares, where the disciples are forbidden to root them up. Matt. 13. 29. But what does this have to do with the matter? For by Christ's own testimony and the interpreter of the parable, all who are a stumbling-block to others, whether in morals or in doctrine, and who hinder the fruit of the gospel, are understood by the name of tares. Therefore, if this interpretation were allowed, those who live scandalously should be no more removed from the midst than those who profess false doctrine.

units.la: Quinetiam ex similitudinis conclusione satis est conspicuum, Dominum illic non agere de cura quam vel Pastores vel Magistratus in area Domini repurganda ex suæ vocationis
units.tr: Moreover, from the conclusion of the similitude it is quite clear that the Lord is not there speaking about the care which ministers or magistrates ought to take, according to the prescription of their calling, in cleansing the Lord's field. Rather, he forewarns the Church that until the end of the ages it will remain mixed with hypocrites.

units.la: n. iii. præscripto gerere debent: verùm præmonere Ecclesiam ad finem vsque seculorum pperpe-tuò permixtam hypocritis fore. Alij obiiiciunt Christum gladio noluisse defendi, sed hoc e-tiam est alienum à proposito. Quod enim in nostræ redemptionis negotio fuit obferuan-dum, minimè Legem Magistratibus in re pror sus diuersa præscribit: alioqui peccasset Paulus quum ad Cæsarem protocauit, atque adeò præfectum de sibi itructis insidiis certiorem fecit: quando quidem ipse Dominus noster Iesus Christus, vt erat ab Esaia propheta prædictum, ne os quidem ad sui defensionem aperuit Es.53.7. At si Magistratus officium postulat vt in calibus superius expositis gladij potestatem exerat, an manus vinctas habituram arbitrabimur, Religionis perturbatoribus turmatim & cateruatim inter subditos grassantibus? Age verò, infidelli Magistratu fidelem aggredienti, quem vna cum ditione veritatis thesauro spoliare conetur (vt hac nostra tempestate & iam olim Turca in Christianos saeuiet: nec stat per Apostolicæ sedis incendiarios quin eiusmodi plurimæ coniurationes summa crudelitate exerceantur) non quæro licet ne Magistratui fideli vim vi repellere, & suos subditos aduersus coniuratum hostem irmare, sed an vlla ( e possit excusatione coram Deo vel hominibus purgare, si neglectis quæ Deus offerebat iustæ defensionis mediis, sibi suisque defuerit. Addo aliquid amplius, & iio i Magistratus qui iusto sanctoque fœdere societatem tem inter se sanxerunt ad communem & iu- ftam patriæ suæ defensionem, vbi tantùm de rebus ad hanc vitam pertinentibus agitur, sibi ex fœderis pacti conditionibus mutuam operam & auxilium præstare tenentur, nisi gravissimo periurio se coram Deo & hominibus obstringere velint, potiori iure vbi Religiomis etiam ad superiora vinculum accedit, summæ ac detestandæ ignauiæ perfidiæque notam illos sibiipsis inurere nisi ex pacti fœderis conditionibus mutuas operas & auxilia communicarint. Sed hanc controuersiam ipse Dei Spiritus in Deboræ cantico præclarè diiudicat. Iud. 5. v. 16. 17. & 23. Et hoc amplius etiam adiicio, Ecclesiam Dei Catholicâ quocunque tandem loco terrarum sit, quum vnicum efficiat corpus in vnum fidei & mutuæ charitatis vinculum deuinctum, compactum, & coagmentatum, singula corporis istius, si vera essent, membra, sic fore inter se affecta, vt ne vel minimum quidem in iis quæ hoc vinculum spirituale concernunt offendi possit, aut vim aliquam maiorem qua diuellatur à corpore pati, quin eius doloris sensu cætera omnia tangerentur, ac reipsa fratrum quoque suorum afflictiones ad se pertinere testarentur, quum sint præsertim nobis à Domino tum humanæ tum spirituales, ad eius gloriam promouedam, hostium suorum noftrorumq; conatus infringendos, Duce tamen nobis in omnibus eius Sp. Sancto præeunte, concessæ facultates. Nequis verò calumnietur istud esse
units.tr: Others object that Christ did not wish to be defended with the sword, but this too is beside the point. What had to be observed in the business of our redemption does not prescribe the law for magistrates in a wholly different matter. Otherwise Paul would have sinned when he appealed to Caesar and so informed the prefect of the snares laid for him. For our Lord Jesus Christ himself, as the prophet Isaiah had foretold, did not even open his mouth in his own defence. Isa. 53. 7. But if the duty of the magistrate requires him to exercise the power of the sword in the cases set out above, shall we suppose he will have his hands bound while disturbers of religion rage in troops and bands among the subjects? Come now, if an unfaithful magistrate attacks a faithful one, seeking to rob him, along with his dominion, of the treasure of the truth (as the Turk in our own time, and already long ago, rages against Christians, and the incendiaries of the apostolic see do not refrain from carrying out many such conspiracies with the utmost cruelty), I do not ask whether it is lawful for a faithful magistrate to repel force with force and to arm his subjects against the conspiring enemy. I ask whether he can clear himself before God or men of any excuse if, neglecting the means of just defence that God offered, he failed himself and his own. I add something more. Magistrates who have sworn by a just and holy covenant to form a fellowship for the common and just defence of their country, where only matters pertaining to this life are concerned, are bound to render mutual service and aid to one another under the terms of that covenant, unless they wish to bind themselves by grievous perjury before God and men. With all the more reason, where the bond of religion also reaches to higher things, those who have not shared mutual service and aid under the terms of the covenant brand themselves with the mark of the utmost and detestable cowardice and treachery. But the Spirit of God himself judges this controversy clearly in the song of Deborah. Judg. 5. 16, 17, 23. And I add this further: the Catholic Church of God, wherever on earth it may be, since it makes up one body bound, joined and fitted together by the one bond of faith and mutual charity, would, if its individual members really were members of that body, be so disposed toward one another that not even the least offence could be given in those things which concern this spiritual bond, nor could any greater force be suffered by which a member might be torn from the body, without all the other parts being touched by a sense of that pain. They would in fact testify that the afflictions of their brothers pertain to themselves as well, since, especially, both human and spiritual means have been granted to us by the Lord, to advance his glory and to break the attempts of our enemies and theirs, yet with his Holy Spirit going before us as our guide in all things. But lest anyone slander this as meaning

units.la: homines vi & gladiorum ictibus ad Christia-nismu adigere, aut vltro vi armata sanctaa terra velle conquirere, aut religionem armis ffetreis fulcire:quum sit potius se suaq; omnia Deo ad eius gloriam magis magisque promouendam, & iustam conscientiae libertatem,aducrsus iniustos aggressores, Dei perinde atque hominum hostes allerendam dedere ac consecrare. Porro deficientibus humanis istis facultatibus vtrorumque respectu,(quod vidimus ipsi saepe & adhuc in nobis experimur) nihilo nos tamen debiliores factos existimemus. Na quum Dei gloria noftraq; salus nec carnis brachio, nec vllo mortalium robore nitatur, adsint, desint, humanae vires,nihilominus victore esse Deum & veritatem oportet emergere. Contra igitur in has angustias redacti,sciamus(quod vt inam Deus nostris mentibus magis ac magis infigat) Ecclesiam fide & patientia felicissime semper depugnando victoria potitam triumphasse, seculorum praeteritorum omnium experientia teste : nec magis vnquam virtutem supernam quam humanis viribus deficientibus esse conspicuam.Interea tamen,iustus patitur. Verum: sed patiendo victor est, Heb.11.33. & hanc nobis viam summus ille Dux nolter nobis cum cruce triumphans praeiens Coloss.2.14.& Eph. 4.8.dedicauit.Heb.10.20.
units.tr: men by force and the blows of the sword to Christianity, or to seize the Holy Land by armed violence, or to prop up religion with iron weapons. Rather, we should dedicate and consecrate ourselves and all that we have to God, to promote his glory more and more, and to defend the just liberty of conscience against unjust aggressors, who are enemies of God just as they are of men. Moreover, if those human resources fail on either side (as we have often seen ourselves and still experience in ourselves), let us not think ourselves any the weaker for it. For since the glory of God and our salvation rest neither on the arm of flesh nor on any strength of mortals, then whether human powers are present or absent, God and the truth must nonetheless emerge victorious. Therefore, reduced to these straits, let us know (and may God fix this more and more in our minds) that the Church, always most happily victorious by fighting with faith and patience, triumphs, as the experience of all past ages bears witness; and never is supernatural virtue more conspicuous than when human strength fails. Meanwhile, "the just suffers." True, but by suffering he is victor (Heb. 11.33). That is the way our supreme Leader, triumphing over the cross, went before us (Col. 2.14; Eph. 4.8) and dedicated it (Heb. 10.20).

units.la: Dominus igitur gladio vti prohibe sad vitam hominibus eripiendam,eius vtu minime limpliciter interdixit, vt vafani illi iuxta atque improbi Anabaptistae perperam contra Dei man-
units.tr: The Lord therefore did not simply forbid the use of the sword for taking away men's lives; he by no means absolutely prohibited its use, as those crafty and wicked Anabaptists teach, wrongly and contrary to God's command and to all equity.

units.la: Exempla quibus fit periora co prmatur. mandatū & omne æquitatem docent: Nec Ecclesiam suam omni Magistratuum defensione, ferro ac armis suscepta, vbi res ita postulat, siue aduersus priuatos, siue aduersus maiorem vim priuare voluit, vt ex toto Deut.13. cap.liquet.& 17.2.quod ipsum etiam Moses factitauit. Exod.32 27. Hac de re legimus sancta piorum Regum edicta, quos simulationis nō ferēdę damnaremus, si chartis illa tantū inscribi necad susum reuocari voluisse putaremus. 2.Chro.15. 13.& huc plurimū cōducunt Regum exempla, puta Iehu,2.Reg.10.22.Iosiæ.2.Reg.25 20.Ioiadæ.2.Reg.12.15.& Eliæ,cōcessa nimirū ipsi deficiente Magistratu extraordinaria potentia.1. Reg.18.40. vt ea præterceam quæ Deus etiam à prophanis Regibus extorsit iudicia. Dan.3. Esd.6.12. & 7.15. Nec vero sunt hic audiedi qui tempus Legis ante aduentū, & Gratiæ tempus sub Euangelio inuicem opponunt, quū in genere dicat Apost.Rom.13.4.Magistratū gladio armatū,vt terrori sit male facientibus,nec Ecclesię perturbatores in negotio Religionis exceperit, nisi fortè volumus eos ex improborum eximere numero:quū contrà diserte monuerit Reges & alios Magistratus non tantum à Deo cōstitutos vt honestæ vitę inter homines tranquillitatē sartam tectā coseruent, sed etiam vt pietatem confirmēt. Paulus vero prouocans ad Imperatorem Neronem omnium qui vixerunt sceleratissimum, vt se aduersus accusatorum violentiam tutaretur in Religionis negotio,annon quæ fidelis Magistratus hac in re partes essent satis superque demonstrauit?
units.tr: Examples by which the foregoing is confirmed. Nor did God wish to deprive his Church of all the defence of the magistrates, who take up the sword and arms when the situation demands it, whether against private persons or against a greater force. This is clear from the whole of Deut. 13 and 17.2, and Moses himself did the same (Exod. 32.27). On this matter we read the holy edicts of pious kings, whom we would condemn as hypocrites if we thought those edicts were written on paper only and not meant to be carried out (2 Chron. 15.13). The examples of kings are very much to the point here: for instance Jehu (2 Kings 10.22), Josiah (2 Kings 23.20), Jehoiada (2 Kings 11.15), and Elijah, who, when the magistrate was failing, had extraordinary power granted to him by God (1 Kings 18.40). I pass over the judgments that God extorted even from profane kings (Dan. 3; Ezra 6.12; 7.15). Nor indeed are those to be listened to who set the time of the Law before the coming of Christ and the time of Grace under the Gospel in opposition to each other. For the Apostle says in general that the magistrate is armed with the sword to be a terror to evildoers (Rom. 13.4), and he did not exempt the disturbers of the Church in matters of religion, unless perhaps we wish to count them outside the number of the wicked. On the contrary, he plainly admonished that kings and other magistrates are appointed by God not only to preserve the tranquillity of an honest life among men, but also to confirm piety. Paul, appealing to the Emperor Nero, the most wicked of all who ever lived, so that he might defend himself in a matter of religion against the violence of his accusers: has he not sufficiently and more than sufficiently shown what part a faithful magistrate ought to play in this matter?

units.la: In his igitur Iesu Christi verbis quæ necessario sunt ad Petri lapsum referenda, hoc loquendi genus, Gladium accipere, non significat cædendi alicuius causa gladium exercere: sed eos qui gladij potestatem acceperūt à Domino, vt in sceleratos vitæ ac necis potestatem habeant, cuiusmodi sunt diuersorum ordinum Magistratus, à priuatis distinguit, qui sibi hanc potestatem, priuata tantum auctoritate, contra Dei mandatum illud expressum, Non occides, arrogant. Quemadmodum enim solus Deus hominem ad imaginem suam condidit, sic eius vnius est eundem ex arbitrio suo tollere: quod exequitur, non tantùm quum ipse manum vltricem admirandis suis iudiciis extraordinariis vt vult admouet: sed quum eorum vtitur ministerio quos in eum finem gladio armauit. Gen. 9. 6. Rom. 13. 4. Sed hic duo sunt maximi momenti capita ad hoc argumentum melius intelligendum & ad vsum reuocandum obseruatione dignissima: Primum est eos qui permissa sibi gladij potestate abutuntur, in eorum censeri numero, non qui à Domino illum acceperunt, sed qui sibi ipsis vendicarunt. Hic tamen priuati teneant sibi nō licere nec posse bona conscientia superioribus potestatibus armata manu resistere: sed in hoc casu sibi intra suæ vocationis fines, subditorum nimirum subsistendum, & ad veram Christianorum armaturam, preces & patientiam, quæ sanctorum est victoria consu-giendum : maximè verò quum ad profiganda
units.tr: In these words of Jesus Christ, which must necessarily be referred to Peter's fall, the phrase "to take the sword" does not mean to wield the sword for the sake of striking anyone. Rather, it distinguishes those who have received from the Lord the power of the sword, so that they hold power of life and death over wicked people (such as the magistrates of the various orders), from private persons, who arrogate this power to themselves on their own private authority, against the express command of God: "Thou shalt not kill." For just as God alone made man in his own image, so it is his alone to take him away at his own will. He does this not only when he himself applies the avenging hand, at his wonderful and extraordinary judgments, as he pleases, but also when he uses the ministry of those whom he has armed with the sword for that end (Gen. 9.6; Rom. 13.4). But there are two main points of the greatest importance here, which deserve careful notice if this argument is to be better understood and put to use. (1) First, those who abuse the power of the sword granted to them are to be counted among those who have claimed it for themselves, not among those who received it from the Lord. Yet private persons should hold that it is neither lawful nor possible, in good conscience, to resist the superior powers armed by force. In this case they must remain within the limits of their own calling, that is, as subjects, and take refuge in the true Christian armour of prayers and patience, which is the victory of the saints. This is especially so since God opens to us no ways of overthrowing tyranny by the laws and institutions of kingdoms or such principalities.

units.la: Longe inter se differunt Gladium accipere, exercere, & Gladium acceptum exerere. dam tyrannidem, nullas Deus nobis ex legibus & institutis regnorum aut eiusmodi principatuum vias aperit. Alias enim si quae fuerit eiusmodi ratio, ea pollumus ac debemus uti, saluo tamen honore & respectu qui superioribus debetur. Alterum est, quoties legibus armantur priuati, toties etiam veluti Dei manu gladium ipsos accipere, quo se aducrsus maiorem vim protegant. Quapropter minime vocatio noua est aduersus praedonem peregrinanti, ad sui iustam defensionem, vel gestandi gladium vel cum euaginandi, exspectanda: immo etiam in eiusmodi necessitate libera est conscientia ferentium Magistratui suppetias. Aio praeterea licere vim iniuste nos aggredientis vi repellere, qua de re luculentum extat testimonium, Exod.21. v.13. si commoda loci illius adhibeatur explicatio. Verum in istiusmodi casibus necesse est Deo nos commendemus, quod vix ac ne vix quidem in talibus motibus animi affectus cohiberi possint, & tamen omnis vindictae cupiditas a Deo prohibeatur, quo spectat illud Matth.5.ver.39.qua in re se nobis Christus ipse praebuit exemplar quod imitemur, & eius exemplum imitati veri omnes Christiani, eodem Spiritu quo ipse ducti.
units.tr: Taking up the sword and exercising it are far different from exercising a sword already taken up. (2) Otherwise, if there is any such method, we may and ought to use it, saving nevertheless the honour and respect owed to superiors. The second point is that whenever private persons are armed by law, then they too receive the sword from God's hand, as it were, so that they may protect themselves against a greater force. Therefore a traveller who is attacked by a robber need not wait for a new calling before he carries a sword or draws it in his just self-defence. Indeed, even in such necessity, the conscience of those who bring aid to the magistrate is free. I maintain, moreover, that it is lawful to repel force with force against one who unjustly attacks us, and there is clear testimony to this in Exod. 21.13, if the context of that passage is rightly explained. But in cases of this kind we must commend ourselves to God, since in such movements of the mind the passions can scarcely be restrained at all, and yet every desire for vengeance is forbidden by God. To this refers Matt. 5.39. In this matter Christ himself has shown himself to us as an example to imitate, and all true Christians, led by the same Spirit as he was, imitate his example.

units.la: Et illa quidem superiora de ordinariis vocationibus dicta sunto, quibus tamen non ita Dominus astringitur, quin sua iudicia quotiescunque & quibuscunque instrumentis ipsi libuerit exequatur, quod est in historia Phinees conspicuum, Num.25.8. & plerisque iudicum exemplis,& nominatim in Ehud Iud.3. & similiter in Ichu, 2.Reg.9. immo & rem ipsam si attendas in Petro & Diuo Paulo, Act.5.5. & 10.& in Apostolo Act.13.11. Et huiusmodi sanè magnarum rerum extraordinarie gestarum exempla Deus quotidie statuere potest: sed cauendum diligenter ne nobis vocationes eiusmodi extraordinarias rarissimas & valde suspectas temere fingamus: quas videmus ab eorum maxima parte quibus committebantur non sine magna sollicitudine suscepras, maximis licet & insignibus a Deo visionibus confirmarentur: non frustra monete Christo suos discipulos, temere in exemplum factum illud Eliae trahentes, uti diligenter viderent quo Spiritu ducerentur. Luc.9.55. quum tandem prodat exitus haec consilia non a Deo promanasse, sed aut a zelo sine scientia ac proinde maxime perniciosso, & crudelitatis ac saeuitiae auctore & suasore. Ioh.16.2. Act.3.17. & 23.12. aut a temerario & praecipiti spiritu, aut veriginoso, aut ambitioso, aut vindictae cupido, aut alia quauis animi perturbatione qua se illi homines & alios in ruinam & exitium praecipites ferunt.
units.tr: These things said above concerning ordinary callings must stand as said. Yet the Lord is not so bound by them that he may not carry out his judgments whenever and by whatever instruments it pleases him. This is conspicuous in the history of Phinehas (Num. 25.8), in many examples of judges, especially Ehud (Judg. 3), and likewise in Jehu (2 Kings 9). Indeed, if you consider the matter itself, it is seen in Peter and the divine Paul (Acts 5.5; 10), and in the Apostle (Acts 13.11). God can certainly establish such examples of great things done extraordinarily every day. But we must take care diligently not to rashly invent for ourselves extraordinary callings of this kind, which are very rare and highly suspect. We see that most of those to whom they were committed undertook them not without great anxiety, even though they were confirmed by very great and remarkable visions from God. Christ rightly warned his disciples, who were rashly drawing that deed of Elijah into an example, to see carefully by what Spirit they were being led (Luke 9.55). Finally, the outcome shows that such counsels did not come from God, but either from zeal without knowledge, and therefore most pernicious, with cruelty and savagery as its author and promoter (John 16.2; Acts 3.17; 23.12); or from a rash and headlong spirit, or a fiery one, or an ambitious one, or one desiring vengeance, or any other disturbance of the mind, by which those men carry themselves and others headlong into ruin and destruction.

units.la: Plena sunt exemplis huiusmodi temporum omnium historiarum monumenta: sed ne procul abeam, quales oblecro fuerunt in Angla conspirationes,& coitiones quorundam coiuratorum de Reginae caede inferenda, Dei tamen singulari & admiranda prouidentia patefactae, proditae ac fractae dissipataeque
units.tr: The records of all the histories of every age are full of examples of this kind. But not to go far afield: what, I beg you, were the conspiracies in England, and the plots of certain conspirators to inflict murder on the Queen? These were brought to light by God's singular and admirable providence, and were betrayed, broken, and scattered.

units.la: Quid vero bella ciuilia commemorem, quæ aduersus Ecclesiam Dei, aduersus regio sanguine procreatos Principes & regni Gallici proceres, iam ab annis triginta & amplius excitata, gens infausti nominis aluit & fouit, quę quum ante a Regum ipsorum consiliis deceptorum authoritate frustra tegerent & fucū facere conarentur, tandem abominandam illam ac detestandam armorum societatem quam Ligam vocant suscitauit, quam tanto furore exercet, vt præter alia generis omnis immania flagitia ac facinora, nō reuerita nativi sui germani Regis ac Principis Maiestatę, proprio ipsius sanguine suas dextras summo scelere contaminarit, ad quod patrandū flagitiū vsa monacho ex Dominicanorū lustris eruto, satis, proh dolor! quo ducatur spiritu cośpicuum fecit? Nihilominus tamen tantus est authorum ac fautorum tantorum istorum facinorū summa cum impudentia furor coniunctus, & tam cæca mens eorum qui illos ab ipsis fascinati sequuntur, vt si verbis non factis fides adhibeatur, dicas illos zelo ardentissimo Christianæ Catholicæ Religionis flagrare, adeo vt Martyrij sacrosanctum nomē ementitos, eo suum abominandū illud & maximè, si quid aliàs vnquam, non in Gallia tantū sed vbiuis terrarū detestandū admissum est, regere & decorare nō pudeat. Tua vero laus est Deus Opt. Max. & summè admirande, quod tantum sceleris longè maiora spirans non passus sis suum exitium sortiri, sed illud, etiam ferò, tamen omnium oculis tandem exhibueris, & tam admirandis modis hostium consilia & conatus frangere coeperis: opus illud quum tibi visum erit perfecturus, eo Rege in tuam fidem & clientelam suscepto, quem tua sceleratorum vere ultrix & vindex dextra & innocentium assertrix tantorum scelerum ultorem & Dei iudiciorum executorem, ad Nominis sui gloriam, & totius Christianissimi tranquillitatem suscitauit. Et haec quidem in hunc locum caeteris in aliud tempus reiectis dicta sunto.
units.tr: But why should I recall the civil wars which that people of ill-omened name has nursed and fostered against the Church of God, against princes born of royal blood and against the nobles of the kingdom of France, stirred up now for thirty years and more? At first they tried in vain to cover and disguise these wars under the authority of the kings themselves, whom they had deceived. At last they raised up that abominable and detestable association of arms which they call the League. They pursue it with such fury that, besides other monstrous crimes and outrages of every kind, not reverencing the majesty of their own native brother, the king and prince, they have defiled their right hands with his very blood in the greatest wickedness. For carrying out that crime they used a monk dragged from the dens of the Dominicans, and alas! they have made conspicuous enough by what spirit they are led. Nevertheless, the fury of the authors and supporters of such great deeds is joined with the utmost impudence, and the blindness of mind of those who follow them, bewitched by them, is so great that, if faith is given to deeds rather than words, you would say they burn with the most ardent zeal for the Christian Catholic Religion. So much so that they are not ashamed to rule and adorn with the sacred name of martyrdom that abominable deed of theirs, which is most detestable, if anything ever was, and which has been committed not only in France but everywhere on earth. But the praise is yours, O God, Best and Greatest, and most admirable: although such a crime, breathing far greater things, you have not suffered to achieve its own destruction, yet at last, though late, you have displayed it before the eyes of all, and have begun in such wonderful ways to break the counsels and attempts of the enemies. You will complete this work when it seems good to you, the King having been taken into your faith and protection, whom your right hand, truly the avenger of the wicked and the defender of the innocent, has raised up as the avenger of such great crimes and the executor of God's judgments, for the glory of your name and the tranquillity of the whole Most Christian kingdom. These things are said for this place; others are reserved for another time.

units.la: HOMILIA decima.
units.tr: Tenth Homily.

units.la: MATTH. 26.
units.tr: MATT. 26.

units.la: 52. Quicunque acceperint gladium, gladio peribunt.
units.tr: 52. Whoever takes the sword shall perish by the sword.

units.la: 53. An putas me non posse nunc precari Patrem meum, qui hic sistat mihi plures quam duodecim legiones Angelorum?
units.tr: 53. Do you think I cannot now pray to my Father, who would at once send me more than twelve legions of angels?

units.la: 54. Quomodo ergo implerentur Scripturae, quae dicunt sic oportere fieri?
units.tr: 54. How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, which say that it must happen this way?

units.la: 55. In illa hora dixit Iesus turbae, ut adversus latronem exiistis cum gladiis & fustibus, ut ompreprehenderetis me? quotidie apud vos sedebam docens in templo, nec prehendistis me.
units.tr: 55. In that hour Jesus said to the crowd: "Have you come out against a robber with swords and clubs to seize me? Every day I sat among you teaching in the temple, and you did not seize me.

units.la: Hoc autem totum factum est vt implerentur Scripturæ Prophetarum.
units.tr: But all this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.

units.la: MARC. 14.
units.tr: MARK 14.

units.la: Et respondens Iesus dixit eis, vt aduersus latronem exististis cum gladiis & fustibus ad comprehendendum me?
units.tr: And Jesus answered and said to them: "Have you come out against a robber with swords and clubs to seize me?"
