units.la: Quotidie eram apud vos in templo docens, nec cepistis me, sed oportet vt impleantur Scripturæ.
units.tr: Every day I was among you in the temple teaching, and you did not take me; but the Scriptures must be fulfilled.

units.la: LVC. 22.
units.tr: LUKE 22.

units.la: Dixit autem Iesus iis qui ad ipsum venerant, nempe primariis Sacerdotibus, & præfectis templo & senioribus, vt aduersus latronem existis cum gladiis & fustibus?
units.tr: Then Jesus said to those who had come to him, namely the chief priests, the prefects of the temple and the elders: "Have you come out against a robber with swords and clubs?"

units.la: Quum quotidie vobiscum fuerim in templo, non extendistis manum in me: sed hæc est hora illa vestra & potestas tenebrarum.
units.tr: Since I was with you daily in the temple, you did not lay hands on me; but this is your hour, and the power of darkness.

units.la: ROXIMO sermone substitutus in graui illa comminatione adducrsus eos qui sibi gladij potestatem in exitium proximi vendicant, perituros nimirum & ipsos gladio: quæ pulchrè congruunt cum verbis Legis Gen. 9. 6. Eius qui sanguinem hominis in homine fuderit, sanguinem quoque effusurum iri. Quod disertissimis verbis in Lege repetitum est, Exod. 21. Levit. 24. Num. 35. Deut. 19. Et hac quidem sane Lege nihil æquius ac iustius est, quam etiam omnium politiarum iura tàquam ipso Dei digito in omniù quamlibet corruptissimorum & depravatissimorum hominum mentibus insculptam ecoprobarunt.
units.tr: Having just finished his discourse, Christ sets a grave warning against those who claim for themselves the power of the sword for the destruction of their neighbour: that they will certainly perish by the sword themselves. These fit well with the words of the Law, Gen. 9. 6: "Whoever sheds the blood of a man, by man shall his blood be shed." This is repeated in the most explicit words in the Law: Exod. 21, Lev. 24, Num. 35, Deut. 19. Indeed nothing in the Law is more equitable and just than this, which all commonwealths have approved as if written by the very finger of God in the minds of even the most corrupt and depraved men.

units.la: Sed quoniam a Magistratibus fere omnibus non est tanti facta Lex ista ut eam in recto usu haberent, ad Dei tribunal vsque cominscendum est, qui non finit inultos nec ipsos homicidas, nec ludices, qui poenas illis condonarunt, nec Regum inclementem clementiam, aut aliorum summorum Magistratuum, qui contra ius omne diuinum & humanum sceleratis impunitatem concedunt, quod fieri tamen Dominus severe prohibuit. Num.35. 31.&33.
units.tr: But since almost all magistrates have held this Law in so little regard that they do not keep it in right use, we must come to the tribunal of God, who suffers neither the murderers themselves nor the judges who have remitted their punishments to go unavenged, nor the cruel clemency of kings or of other supreme magistrates, who grant impunity to criminals against all divine and human law, which the Lord strictly forbade. Num. 35. 31 & 33.

units.la: Atque adeo tam seueriter, ut etiam ex altaris sui cornibus auelli iubeat homicidam, nulla cuiuspiam habita ratione, ut in loabo factum est. 1.Reg.2.29. & ab ipsa refugij ciuitate Deut.19.12. tantum abest ut Dominus Ecclesiasticorum illorum, clementissimorum hominum scilicet factum approbet, qui quum non animaduerterent nunquam aliquid fuisse in eum finem institutum vel concessum ut facinorosi legibus eriperentur, sed ut iudicia rite exercerentur, ut scriptum est, Num.35.12. templa tamen sua & monasteria sacrarum, & consecrationis lege tuta esse confugientibus ad ea, quia anuis perditissimis & quos terra ferat indignissimis, sacrofanto pietatis & clementiae nomine abusi, voluerunt. Sic Dauid, licet accepta peccati venia, quum Rex esset, & nullus in hominibus esset a quo iudicaretur, non tamen impune prorsus tulit suum facinus, quin per prophetam suum minaretur ei Dominus poenam, fore nimirum ut quod Vriam Hethaeum gladio peremisset, ex eius domo gladius nunquam recederet. 2. Sam. 12. 10. & proditio qua fidum servum perdiderat, in ipso filiorum propriorum conspiratione vindicaretur: quod Abfalomi coniuratione 2. Sam. 15. & alterius ex liberis ipsius Adoniae 1. Reg. 1. 5. completum est: & adulterium etiam cum Amnonis incesto. 2. Sam. 13. 14. tum maxime Absalomi concubinas patris foeda libidine constuprantis 2. Sam. 16. 21. est flagitio punitum. Et ne procul istiusmodi exempla repetam, quibus ipsae etiam historiae profanae plenae sunt, quid summis duobus principibus accidit nostra memoria, quum ob privatas simultates ab iis defecissent quibus cum eos esse coniunctissimos oportuerat? quam vero mercedem is retulit qui ipsos sollicitaverat? Quid vero factum est immanibus illis fratrum nostrorum mactatoribus? quam eorum multi manum ac vindictam diu inam effugerunt? Qua vero tandem illi manu qui tam misere superioris auctoritate fuerant ad suos nefarios illos conatus perficiendos abusi ceciderunt? Non igitur Dei manum effugiunt, quibus homines indulserint, nec liber est a metu poenae, qui laqueum iugulo circumfert. Nam quum Dei vindictae tempus advenit, Madianitarum carnifices ipsi sunt Madianitae.
units.tr: So severely does he command that a murderer be torn even from the horns of his altar, without regard to anyone's status, as was done to Joab: 1 Reg. 2. 29; and from the very city of refuge, Deut. 19. 12. So far is the Lord from approving the deed of those ecclesiastics, most merciful men as they were, who, not noticing that the cities of refuge were never established or permitted for the purpose of snatching criminals from the laws, but so that judgments might be duly carried out (as is written, Num. 35. 12), nevertheless abused the sacred name of piety and clemency to make their temples and monasteries, safe by the law of consecration, a refuge for the most abandoned and unworthy men the earth bears. So David, although his sin was pardoned, and although as king there was no man among men to judge him, did not wholly escape punishment for his crime; the Lord threatened through his prophet that he would be punished by this: because he had struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword, the sword would never depart from his house (2 Sam. 12. 10); and the treachery by which he had destroyed a faithful servant would be avenged in the conspiracy of his own sons. This was fulfilled in the conspiracy of Absalom (2 Sam. 15) and in that of another of his sons, Adonijah (1 Reg. 1. 5). Adultery too, together with Amnon's incest (2 Sam. 13. 14), and especially Absalom's foul lust in defiling his father's concubines (2 Sam. 16. 21), was punished as a crime. And, not to seek such examples from afar, of which even profane histories are full: what happened to the two highest princes in our own memory, when they revolted from those with whom they ought most closely to have been joined, out of private quarrels? What reward did he receive who had incited them? What became of those savage butchers of our brothers? How many of them escaped the hand and the long vengeance? And by what hand at last did those fall who had been so wretchedly misused, under superior authority, to carry out those wicked attempts? Therefore those whom men have indulged do not escape the hand of God, nor is he free from the fear of punishment who carries a noose about his throat. For when the time of God's vengeance comes, the executioners of the Midianites themselves become Midianites.

units.la: Nec vero nos in alios hanc sarcinam reii-o. ij. cere decet,quin ipsi magnam in nos huius re-prehensionis partem recipiamus. Quid enim dicam,quàm quod nimiùm,proh dolor! experientia verum esse docet? Nam vt pleniorem huius mandati, Non occides,explicationem omittam,quam ipse nos iudex ac Legislator noster Christus ore suo sacro docuit.Matth.5.21. oro & obsecro,ex quo maximè nos iniusta vicini modisque omnibus intoleranda violentia compulit ad iustam & necessariam defensionem, quot cædes immanes & nefariæ factæ sunt hostili nomine tectæ,quod multi ex suorum affectuum perturbatione metiuntur, & totam hanc regionem polluerunt, vt Dominus loquitur?Num.35.33. Quæ verò tandem istis licariis irrogata pœna est unquam? Et quod longè maius est,& nunquam à vobis expectassem, annon impunitum gratia concessa dimisistis eum,qui vltrò,nulla iniuria lacessitus innocentem obtruncauerat? cuius etiam immane flagitium multæ circunstantiæ magis ac magis augere videbantur?Verumamur igitur iam in urbe languinis, vindictam à Domino postulantis, certò & inevitabiliter imminentem noltris ceruicibus:sed quę tamen vtinam Deo sic nostris annuente precibus, clementia & longanimitate mitigetur: vt qui tatorum sib scelerum minimè conscij lugent,illorum suppliciis non inuoluantur: sed vt nostri misericordes preces potius nostras, quas eadem cum Dauide fundimus. Psal.26.9. exaudiat. Necvos, qui tantum facinus admisistis quidquan iuuat uat supremam illam quam accepistis à Domino potestatem praetexere. Neque enim vos Deus in suo folio collocauit, ut pro animi vestri libidine leges quas Deus perpetuas & inuiolatas esse voluit impunitate concessa refigatis. Agite igitur, ferio lugete & ingemescite, meliorémque mentem induite, si quod adhuc poenitentiae tempus superest, ne forte manus ad Dominum attollentes eius auxilium imploraturi, quae maxima nobis, si alias vnquam incumbit necessitas, repulsam patiamur, & manus cruore foedatas procul à se reiiciat, ut olim per Prophetam minatus est. Esa.1.15. Euge vero Domine, largire nobis ipse quod à nobis postulas, alioqui periimus. Nam sepe Deus ob paria leuioràque etiam peccata graui sua vindicta plerosque longe vobis potentiores, & in longe sublimiori dignitate quàm sitis vnquam futuri constitutos depressit ac penitus attriuit. Denique conseruatio, vel etiam diuini fauoris amplificatio non promittitur abutentibus ad Dei contumeliam, sed demum acceptis à Domino talentis recte vtentibus. Matth.25.21.&23.
units.tr: Nor indeed ought we to shift this burden onto others; rather we ourselves should accept a large share of this rebuke. For what shall I say, but what experience, alas, too much shows to be true? For, to pass over a fuller explanation of this command, Thou shalt not kill, which our judge and lawgiver Christ himself taught with his holy mouth (Matt. 5. 21), I beg and beseech you: since the unjust and in every way intolerable violence of our neighbours has driven us to a just and necessary defence, how many monstrous and nefarious murders have been committed under the name of hostility, which many measure by the disturbance of their passions, and have polluted this whole region, as the Lord says (Num. 35. 33)? And what punishment has ever been inflicted on those cutthroats? And, what is far worse, and what I would never have expected from you, did you not dismiss with pardon the man who, without any provocation and unprompted by any injury, had cut down an innocent? A crime whose monstrous nature many circumstances seemed to make greater and greater. But let us now consider the city of blood, which demands vengeance from the Lord, hanging certainly and inevitably over our necks. Would that by God's granting of our prayers it might be softened by clemency and long-suffering, so that those who mourn, innocent of such crimes, may not be caught up in their punishments; and that our merciful God may hear our prayers, which we pour out with David (Ps. 26. 9). And you who have committed so great a crime, do not try to excuse yourselves by the supreme power you received from the Lord. For God did not place you on his throne so that you might, at the pleasure of your mind, break with impunity the laws which God willed to be perpetual and inviolable. Come then, strike your breasts, mourn and groan, and put on a better mind, if any time for repentance still remains; lest perhaps, lifting our hands to the Lord to implore his help, which we need most of all if ever necessity lay upon us, we suffer rejection, and he cast away from himself our hands stained with blood, as he once threatened through the prophet (Isa. 1. 15). Well then, Lord, grant us yourself what you ask of us, otherwise we perish. For often God, for equal or even lighter sins, has with his heavy vengeance brought down and utterly crushed many who were far more powerful than you, and placed in a far higher dignity than you will ever attain. Finally, preservation, or even an increase of divine favour, is not promised to those who abuse it to God's dishonour, but to those who at last use the talents received from the Lord rightly (Matt. 25. 21 & 23).

units.la: Caeterum ad suam reprehensionem Dominus duas alias maximi ponderis rationes adiecit, sed quae ipsum proprie respiciunt, quarum prior haec est, sibi nimirum si vim vi repellere voluisset, longe alias quàm Petri aut aliorum hominum quorumcunque vires adesse: quum potuerit, si voluisset a Patre myriadas Angelorum in sui defensionem impetrare. Hinc e-
units.tr: Besides this rebuke, the Lord added two other reasons of the greatest weight, which concern himself in particular. The first is this: that if he had wished to repel force with force, he had strength far different from that of Peter or of any other men whatever, since he could, had he wished, have obtained from his Father myriads of angels for his defence. Hence arises a futile question: could Christ indeed have uttered such a prayer?

units.la: o. iij. mergit futilis quæstio, potuerit ne Christus equidem iusmodi preces concipere. Nam certum quidem est, ut memorat Lucas cap.22.43. in durissimo illo agone cœlitus Angelu corroborando illi missum fuisse: unde rursum animadvertimus quoque quemadmodum se demiserit, ut Psal.85.6. & Heb.2.9. docetur, quum nihil ab Angelis, nec secundum quidem suam humanam naturam discere potuerit, ut qui ei servire prius didicisset. Matth.4.11. at nec ipse Angelum illum poltulasse, nec Angelus vicissim aduersus Iudæorum impetum illum defensurus, venisse dicitur, quod facere nec potuit nec debuit: Missus autem est Angelus cum in tanto certaminis isthuc agone subleuaturus. Preces autem illas non ait se Christus aut potuisse aut voluisse ad Deum patrem fundere (quod fieri nec potuit, nec debuit, non simpliciter quidem & absolute, sed decreti paterni respectu) sed addita conditione loquitur, eius quem alloquebatur mentem & consilium attendens, quasi verbis cum istiusmodi coargueret, Quid cogitas Petre nimium præceps & temerarie? Nam etsi liceret quam tentas armis defensio, annon animadvertis non posse tantam hostium cateruam tam exiguis viribus profligari? An ego quis sim ignoras, & quis Pater meus? Quum vero me tuo gladio sperasti percuntem alioqui liberare posse, quo tandem miser amentiæ deuenisti. Hic vero lapis est ad quem fere omnes homines, atque adeo sapientissimi quique quotidie impingunt, nisi sibi diligenter cauerint. diligenter caueant:Nam subinde,si quæ vehementior ingruat necessitas, Deum causis secundis alligamus,& quidem tantùm prout eas vel mentis ratiocinatione prospicimus, vel quatenus easdé corporeis sensibus deprehendimus. Inde sæpe transuersi rapimur, & consilia non obliqua modò,sed perniciosa & Dei voluntati maximè repugnantia sequimur.
units.tr: For it is certain, as Luke relates (Luke 22. 43), that an angel was sent from heaven to strengthen him in that most severe agony; whence we also notice how he humbled himself, as Psal. 85. 6 and Heb. 2. 9 teach, since he could learn nothing from angels, not even according to his human nature, having previously learned to serve them (Matt. 4. 11). Yet it is not said that he asked that angel, nor that the angel came in turn to defend him against the assault of the Jews, which he could neither do nor ought to do; rather an angel was sent to sustain him in the midst of that struggle. Yet Christ does not say that he could or wished to pour out those prayers to God the Father (which could not and ought not to be done, not simply and absolutely, but with respect to the Father's decree). Instead he speaks conditionally, attending to the mind and counsel of the one he addressed, as if rebuking Peter with such words: "What are you thinking, Peter, so rash and reckless? For even if the defence you attempt with arms were allowed, do you not see that so great a band of enemies cannot be overthrown with such small forces? Or do you not know who I am, and who my Father is? When you hoped that I could be freed from perishing by your sword, to what wretched madness have you come!" Here is the stone against which almost all men, and indeed the wisest of them every day, stumble, unless they take careful heed. For sometimes, if some more violent necessity presses, we bind God to secondary causes, and indeed only so far as we foresee them by the reasoning of the mind, or insofar as we perceive them by the bodily senses. Thence we are often swept off course, and follow plans not merely crooked but pernicious and most opposed to the will of God.

units.la: Sed vt istis incómodis occurratur,rectam in rebus omnibus nostris viam ingressi,aduersus quæliibet tentationum genera, certissima hæc & indubitata axiomata opponamus, Deum Omnipotentem & Optimum esse iis qui rectam viam insistant.Psalm.73 1.Non decet illi rationes multas quibus suos ex periculis eripiat,, Amentem esse qui sperat saluti suæ, fortunis, honoribus & reliquis huius vitæ commodis cum Dei offensione,& mandatorum eius a conscientiæ violatione se consulturum.
units.tr: But so that we may meet these inconveniences, let us enter the straight path in all our affairs and set against every kind of temptation these most certain and indubitable axioms: that God is Almighty and the Best to those who keep to the right path (Psalm 73:1). It is not fitting that he lacks many means by which to rescue his own from dangers. He is mad who hopes to secure his safety, fortunes, honours and the other advantages of this life by offending God and, against conscience, violating his commandments.

units.la: An vero quum tam densa nubium caligine circumfundimur, vt mutuus nobis eripiatur aspectus, Solem in cœlo nullum esse putabimus, cuius radiis tam densæ nubes loco & tempore dissipentur? An vero Lux non est quod eam cæci,vel qui sponte cæcutiunt non percipiant? Sic Petrus hic errore duplici peccabat: primùm quòd Dominum in has redactum putaret angustias virium aliquarum inopia, parum eorum memor quę de ipso prædicauerat, Filium eum viuentis Dei dum confiteretur. Deinde quòd huic malo nullum aliud super-
units.tr: When we are surrounded by so thick a darkness of clouds that we are robbed of sight of one another, shall we think there is no sun in the heavens, whose rays disperse such dense clouds in their time and place? Or is there no light because the blind, or those who wilfully blind themselves, do not perceive it? So Peter erred here in two ways. First, he thought the Lord had been reduced to these straits by a lack of some power, being little mindful of what he had declared about him when he confessed him the Son of the living God. Second, he thought there was no other remedy for this evil than that he himself should use his own strength in defence of his Master. See what counsel the prudence of the flesh supplies, scarcely seeing what lies at its feet.

units.la: o. iiij. esse putat remedium quàm si ipse viribus ad Magistri sui defensione vteretur. En quæ carnis prudentia, vix quæ ante pedes sunt conspiciens, consilia suppeditet. Talis erat Prophetæ seruus de quo 2.Reg.6.15.agitur, donec precibus Prophetæ perspicacioribus oculis donatus præsens Angelorum auxilium aspectaret. Sic nos in omnibus tentationibus, tum aduersus carnem & sanguinem, tum aduersus inuisibiles inimicos, Deum oportet noctes diesque precari, vt fidei nos oculis donet, quibus inuisibilem conspiciamus Moßs exemplo Hæb. 11. 27. & Dauidis Psalm. 37. & Psal. 16.8. & 27.1. & alibi locis pene infinitis, iuxta illud quod tam sæpe de sanctis patribus inculcatur, nempe ante Domini faciem ambulauisse. Porro quærendus Dominus vbi se fidei, non autem oculis carnis, conspiciendum præbet, in sanctis eius nimirum promissionibus, quarum visibilia signa sunt nobis data Sacramenta: & supe ratis alacriter omnibus difficultatibus hac vnica spe freti præsens Dei auxilii & ope eo demum repore & modo quo visum ipsi fuerit exspectemus.
units.tr: Such was the servant of the prophet of whom 2 Kings 6:15 speaks, until, granted eyes more far-seeing through the prophet's prayers, he saw the present help of the angels. So in all temptations, whether against flesh and blood or against invisible enemies, we ought to pray God night and day that he may grant us the eyes of faith, by which we may see the invisible, following the example of Moses (Hebrews 11:27), of David (Psalm 37; Psalm 16:8; Psalm 27:1), and of almost endless other passages, according to what is so often impressed upon us concerning the holy fathers, namely that they walked before the face of the Lord. Moreover, the Lord is to be sought where he shows himself to be seen by faith and not by the eyes of the flesh, namely in his holy promises, of which the sacraments are given to us as visible signs. Overcoming all difficulties readily, and relying on this one hope, let us await the present help and aid of God at last, at the time and in the manner that shall seem good to him.

units.la: De Angelorum autem præsidio, tota Scriptura testatur eorum opera Dominum vti ad iusta sua in hostes suos exercenda iudicia, sicut eosdem etiam in suis hiuc corripiendis hiuc cófolandis & confirmandis administros adhibet, adeo etiam vt mali spiritus vel inuiti cogantur eius exequi mandata, siquidem ei dicto esse obedientes nō studeant: & ita Dominus eos suæ domus quam disturbare & demoliri modis omnibus cupiut, velu-
units.tr: Concerning the protection of angels, the whole of Scripture testifies that the Lord uses their work to carry out his just judgments against his enemies, and likewise employs them as ministers in chastising, comforting and confirming his own. So much so that evil spirits, even unwillingly, are compelled to carry out his commands, since they do not strive to obey him willingly; and thus the Lord compels them, as masons and architects, to build the house which they desire by every means to disturb and demolish.

units.la: velutri cæmentarios & architectos esse cogat: cuiuss rei nobis luculetum exemplum hæc historia suppeditat, in qua verè Satan nostra cau sa liceret præter mentem ac consilium, lògè plus pręstitisse, quàm aut Apostoli, aut quiuis alius dici possit: tanta est Dei nostri támque admirandia tum sapientia tum potentia.
units.tr: This story gives us a splendid example of this matter, in which Satan, though against his own mind and purpose, has in truth accomplished far more for our cause than the Apostles or anyone else could be said to have done. So great, and so admirable, are both the wisdom and the power of our God.

units.la: Att hic cauendum, ne ita seu bonis seu malis Dei administris inhærearnus, vt honor illis aut timor soli Domino debitus vllatenus attribuatur. Ac primùm sciamus, Deum nulla necessitate, sed ex mera sua voluntate rebus creatis vti, cuius tanta vis est, vt quascunq; ad vllum opus obeundum adhibuerit, ranas putà vel muscas, quod ex Pharaonis historiaconspicuum est, & Ioel Propheta meminit 2.11. per eas quidlibet exequatur. Vnde apparet illi soli cuiuscunque recti operis laudem & gloriam merito attribuendam. Prior enim loquatur, & eiusdem mandatum præeat oportet: ac proinde nullo modo sunt Angeli invocandi: sed invocandus quidem Deus vt eos mittat. Quapropter vnus Deus religiosa adoratione, id est spirituali, quæ sit supra ciuilem & communem hominum sortem colendus est. Neque verò nos hic quicquam movere debet futilis illa & ridicula Sophistarum distinctio, perperam adorationis religiosæ gradus plures constituentium: adeòque etiam quòd ad conscientiam attinet, & in eo maximè quod à Deo petere debemus, non solùm Angelos adorantium, cótiá quàm difcrtis verbis Apostolus monuit Coloss.2.18. & contra id quod Ioanni maiestatis Angelicæ fulgore percusso dictum est Apocal. 19.10. & 22.9. sed etiam mortuos homines inuocantium, quos inter suos diuos retulerunt, & cœlo, si Deo placet, indigitarut, immo etiam eorum sepulchra & ofla colcrium. Quidni enim id faciant, qui Chrisma illud suum adorant, cantillantes, Aue sanctum chrisma. Numquid amplius? Immo & Papas suos, Suæ Sanctitatis nomine copellantes eos Numinis instar obseruant, licet omnium plerumque qui in terris viuunt perditissimos: vel iis testibus queᵱ de vita plerorumque Pontificum literarum monimentis etiam à suis historicis prodita sunt. Et quidem aiunt, in honorem D. Petri sic eos coli, quos tamen certè cœlitus detrestetur & abominetur, iisdem eos verbis etiamnum hodie quibus olim Cornelium compellans Act. 10.26. sicut etiam Paulus Act.14.15. quem diuo Petro socium quoties libuit adiungunt.
units.tr: Here we must take care not to cling so closely to the good or evil ministers of God that the honour or fear due to the Lord alone is in any way transferred to them. First, let us know that God makes use of created things not from any necessity but from his sheer will, and his power is so great that whatever he has employed for any work, even frogs or flies, as the history of Pharaoh makes plain and the prophet Joel mentions (Joel 2:11), he carries out anything through them. Whence it is clear that praise and glory for any right work ought rightly to be ascribed to him alone. For he must speak first, and his command must go before; therefore angels must in no way be invoked, but God must be invoked to send them. Hence the one God is to be worshipped with religious adoration, that is, spiritual adoration, which rises above the civil and common lot of men. Nor should that futile and ridiculous distinction of the Sophists move us, who set up several degrees of religious adoration. Thus, as far as conscience is concerned, and especially in what we ought to ask of God, they not only adore angels (although the Apostle warned against this in plain words, Colossians 2:18, and contrary to what was said to John, struck down by the brilliance of angelic majesty, Revelation 19:10 and 22:9), but they also invoke dead men, whom they have enrolled among their gods and assigned to heaven, if it pleases God, and they even venerate their tombs and bones. Why would they not do so, who adore their chrism, chanting "Hail, holy chrism"? Anything more? Indeed, they also address their popes with the title of His Holiness and observe them as if they were deities, though these are for the most part the most depraved of all who live on earth, as the testimonies of the lives of most popes, handed down in the written records of their own historians, bear witness. And indeed they say that these men are honoured in this way in honour of St Peter, whom, however, heaven surely detests and abhors. They address them with the same words even today with which Peter addressed Cornelius (Acts 10:26), as Paul also was (Acts 14:15), whom they add as a companion to the divine Peter whenever they please.

units.la: Quod autem à me dictum est nullum religiosum honorem aut cultum Angelis in quocunque gradu collocati sint deberi, quoniam cum sibi Deus tanquam vni proprium vendicat, ad eum etiam terrorem pertinet quo nos potenti manui Dei submittere iubemur. Pet. 5.6. Vbi videmus Satanâ ipsiúsque malos Angelos, propterea quòd quandoque Deus illos effusis habenis & libero cursu ferri, & longè latéque homines raptare permittit, hoc tandem à prophanis gentibus obtinuisse, vt non miminùss religiosè colerent quos sibi noxios crederent genios, quàm quos sibi propitios & fauentes futuros putarent: Quinetiam num hodie im egregia illa pseudoecclesia Romana, quàm multa, quaeso, Diuorum & Diuarum nomina in eorum letaniis, & eorundem altaribus disposita simulachra religiosè coluntur, non commodi quidem vllius ipe aliqua, sed quasi captandae illorum beneuolentiae causa, ne infestis eorum telis peratur, quae in ipsorum potestate ad hos vel illos pro libidine puniendos esse putant? Haec erat nimirum Manichaeorum haeresis blasphema duos deos statuentium, bonum vnum, à quo lux & quicquid bonum esset oriretur: alterum malum à quo Tenebrę & mala omnia promanarent. Praeterea nónne quotiescunque cum Diabolo transigitur, aut alicuius spe commodi, vt Dominum ipsum sollicitare Satanam nó puduit, Matth. 4. 9. aut mali alicuius vitandi causa, vt solent miseri illi & infelices venefici: & quoties hominum adductimetu sponte homines in Deum peccant, toties Saran ipse & homines supra Deum ipsum euehuntur? Quid vero de Magis dicam & aliis Daemonum cultoribus? Istis vero omnibus haec veritas opponatur, quae docet solum Deum viuentem religiosa obseruantia & pio timore colendum, & tum mente tum corpore venerandum, improbis illum quidé terribilem & formidolosum, cuius furori cedant oportet singula: & contrà misericordię & immensę gratiæ plenum erga pios, cuius fauore freti nobis à nulla re quidquam fit metuen-dum Psalm.27.1.2.&3. & Rom.8.30. vt è con-trario tuta etiam omnia sunt iis metuenda qui-vlla ex parte maleuolum & inimicum ipsum experiuntur.
units.tr: As for what I have said, that no religious honour or worship is owed to angels, of whatever rank they may be, since God claims it as his own alone, this also belongs to the fear by which we are commanded to submit ourselves to the mighty hand of God (1 Peter 5:6). Here we see that Satan and his evil angels, because God sometimes permits them to be carried along with loosened reins on a free course and to snatch men far and wide, have at last obtained this from the profane nations: that they worshipped no less religiously those genii whom they believed to be harmful to them than those whom they thought would be propitious and favourable. Indeed, even today in that notable pseudo-church of Rome, how many names of gods and goddesses, I ask, are religiously honoured in their litanies, and their images set upon their altars? Not for any benefit, certainly, but as if to win their goodwill, lest they be struck by their hostile darts, which they believe lie in their power to punish these or those at will. This was surely the blasphemous heresy of the Manichaeans, who set up two gods: one good, from whom light and whatever is good arose, and another evil, from whom darkness and all evils flowed. Besides, is it not the case that whenever men bargain with the Devil, either in hope of some advantage, as Satan himself was not ashamed to solicit the Lord (Matthew 4:9), or to avoid some evil, as those wretched and unhappy poisoners are accustomed to do; and whenever men, led on by fear, sin willingly against God, Satan himself and men are then raised above God himself? What shall I say of the Magi and other worshippers of demons? To all of these this truth must be set against them, which teaches that the living God alone is to be worshipped with religious observance and pious fear, and to be revered in both mind and body: terrible and dreadful indeed to the wicked, before whose fury all things must yield, but full of mercy and immense grace towards the pious, by whose favour we, being sustained, have nothing at all to fear (Psalm 27:1-3; Romans 8:30). Conversely, all things are to be feared by those who in any way experience him as hostile and an enemy.

units.la: Postremum quod obiecit Petro Christus hoc est, oportere nimirum Scripturas impleri. Quae pretiosa sane commonefactio plurimum debet valere nobis in omnibus afflictionibus consolandis, & opportunis consiliis in maximis rerum angustiis erigendis, necnon etiam in immoderatis animi nostri perturbationibus fraenandis & cohibendis. Petro vero fuit eiusque sociis peculiariter accommodata, ex qua nimirum discerent, non modo ridicu-lum & futile fuisse suum consilium, sed quod gratius est Deo maxime ingratum, quod ipsos etiam oportuerat praeuidisse, memores eorum quae prae-mature & tam saepe ipsis eorum magister inculcarat. Et quidem hac in parte maior fuit Petri quam alterius cuiusquam lapsus, quem oportuerat altius infixisse memoriae quae in Magistri transfiguratione didicerat, in qua Moses & Eliam cum Christo colloquentes audierat de ipsius exitu, quo futurum erat ut defungeretur in Hierusalem. Luc.9.31. Idem vero nobis rheu quam saepe vsuenit, non satis attenden-tibus ad ea quae verbo Dei docemur, ad cuius tamen ormaomnes nostras cogitationes, verba & actiones dirigere & expendere debemus: quod denique vt cum Dauide loquamur, lucerna pedibus nostris esse debet, Psal.119.105.
units.tr: The last thing Christ objected to Peter is this: that the Scriptures had to be fulfilled. This precious admonition ought to avail us greatly in consoling all afflictions, in raising up apt counsels in the greatest straits of affairs, and also in restraining and curbing the immoderate disturbances of our minds. It was particularly suited to Peter and his fellows, that they might learn that their counsel was not only ridiculous and futile but, what is more displeasing to God, most ungrateful to him, since they ought to have foreseen it, mindful of what their Master had taught them early on and so often. And indeed in this respect Peter's fall was greater than that of any other, since he ought to have fixed more deeply in his memory what he had learned at the Master's transfiguration, where he heard Moses and Elijah speaking with Christ about his departure, by which he was to die in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). But alas, how often this happens to us too, when we do not sufficiently attend to those things we are taught by the Word of God, to which, however, we ought to direct and weigh all our thoughts, words and actions. In short, to speak with David, it ought to be a lamp to our feet (Psalm 119:105).

units.la: Hanc
units.tr: This

units.la: Certitudo effectuum Decreti dimini, certissimum sutissimumque est in omnibus difficultatibus asylu & perfugium.
units.tr: The certainty of the effects of God's decree is most sure and steadfast, a refuge and shelter in all difficulties.

units.la: Hanc tamen doctrinam metiendam fateor ex mentisura reuelationis diuinę voluntatis nobis patefactę, adeo vt hic non omnes eâdem cũ Petro culpa teneamur, quatenus peculiari rationae singularia quædã arcano Dei consilio decretæa non tam liquidò nobis côstant quàm Prophetis per quos olim loquebatur, aut Apostolis quos tã familiariter erudierat.Hinc sæpe fit vt ea facere cogitemus quæ Deus tamē impleri nminimè vult,quamquis per se licita,&nostræ vocationi consentanea, adeo vt, hac in parte,comni in Deum contumaciæ crimine vacui simus. Sic,exempli gratia, Paulus Apostolus,vt ingenuè profitetur Rom.1.13.sæpe optauit, decreuit, & apud se constituit Romā proficisci, cuius ei tamen itineris obeūdi copiam diuinaa voluntas minimè faciebat, quum ipsi subinde noua obiiceret impedimenta.Contrà verò idem Apostolus Hierosolymam, volente Deo contendebat: omnes autem Ecclesiæ per quas iter facit,& quidē in primis Agabus Propheta, quum Deo quoque iltud reuelante sciret,Apostolū Ierosolymis in vincula coniectū iri, alb incœpto itinere quantū in se est illū revocare conatur.Act.20.23.&21.12.&14. Idcirco vero dixerimus aut Apostolum,aut eos qui iter illud dissuaderent, Dei voluntati reluctatos? Absit. Nam sane audito Paulo pariter omnes vltrò Dei decreto cesserunt.
units.tr: I admit, however, that this doctrine must be measured by the rule of the revelation of the divine will made known to us, so that here not all of us are bound by the same fault as Peter. Some singular matters, decreed by God's hidden counsel, are not as clearly known to us as they were to the Prophets through whom he spoke of old, or to the Apostles whom he had taught so intimately. Hence it often happens that we intend to do things which God nevertheless does not at all wish to be accomplished, even though in themselves they are lawful and agree with our calling. In this respect, then, we are free of any guilt of obstinacy against God. Thus, for example, the Apostle Paul, as he frankly confesses (Rom. 1.13), often wished, resolved and determined in himself to set out for Rome. Yet the divine will did not grant him the opportunity to make that journey, since it kept throwing new obstacles in his way. On the other hand, the same Apostle pressed on to Jerusalem at God's will. Yet all the churches through which he travelled, and in particular the Prophet Agabus, who knew by God's revelation that the Apostle would be cast into chains at Jerusalem, tried as far as they could to turn him back from his undertaking (Acts 20.23; 21.12, 14). Should we therefore say that the Apostle, or those who advised against that journey, resisted the will of God? Far from it. For indeed, once Paul had been heard, all of them yielded willingly to the decree of God.

units.la: Sic igitur nos in huiusmodi rebus nunc geramus oportet, vt in primis singulis horis, imò singulis momētis, siue quid dicedū,siue cogitandum
units.tr: So in such matters we ought to conduct ourselves in this way: especially every hour, indeed every moment, whether something is to be said or thought,

units.la: Standum est iis quae de voluntate sua in sacris Scripturis Deus nobis revelavit.
units.tr: We must abide by what God has revealed to us about his will in the holy Scriptures.

units.la: Huius doctrinae usus in omnibus nostris negotiis. dum,siue sit agendum,os Dei cófulamus: minime id quidem quasi sit ipse descendurus è cœlo, nos in aurem alloquuturus, sicut vertiginosi nonnulli somniant,sed vt diligenter omni semota mentis perturbatione expendamus,num per se licita sint an illicita quæ mente versamus & nobiscum deliberamus „ quod Dominus Lege sua,& propriæ cuiusquæ conscientiæ testimonio bene in iis quæ Deo probantur vel improbantur ex ipsius mandatis eruditæ planum & apertum facit. Deinde,quoniam quicquid per se licitum est non tamen à quovis promiscuè, distinctis à Deo nimirum vniuscuiusque muneribus & officiis, suscipi debet:idcirco priori illi posterior hæc quoque cautio est adhibenda,vt placido & sedato animo, & ab omni præsertim leuitate, & ambitione, quæ zeli plerumque speciem præse ferunt libero,sedulo nobiscum reputemus,num quæ à nobis suscipiuntur cum nostra vocatione congruant. Certa enim illa est quam vitæ bene degendæ normam tradit Apostolus; nempe vt in qua quisque vocatione vocatus est in ea maneat.1.Cor.7.20. in quo duplex est nobis præcipitium diligenter cauendum, ne videlicet per ignauiam aut diffidentiam restitemus, aliáve aliqua segnescamus animi perturbatione, vel audaculi potius & temerarij quàm fortes & intrepidi merito videamur.Denique, quòd propter varias locorum, temporum & personarum circūstantias, quicquid etiam licet & nostræ vocationi congruum est, nō semper tamen expediat, consulendus iterum est Dominus, & attente consideranda quo animo rem illam aggrediamur, Diuinæ nos in illius executione quam mentibus nostris inspirarit prouidentiæ permittentes. Vt igitur hac Domini præclara feliciter vtamur admonitione, hoc est in omnibus difficultatibus diligenter à nobis obseruandum, vt primùm animo nostro Dei promissiones teneamus, quas terricu-lamentis quibusuis semel opponamus, quibus vel tantillum ab ea perseuerantia in qua con-stanter ad finem vsque perseuerandum est, abducì possemus: deinde & illud adiiciendum vt veneratibus eius minis ac iudiciis moueamur, nequibus criminibus nostras conscientias ir-retiamus, aut aliqua peccandi licentia extra metas, excurramus. Sic inquam nos præstantis-simam hanc sententiam minarum & promis-sionum Dei veritate & constantia nixam ad vsum reuocare decet. Quòd si nobis hanc ratio-nem secuti, aliter omnino Deus quàm pro-miserit nobiscum agere, vel saltem promissio-num suarum implectionem longius quàm par sit differre videatur, cauendum ne in diffi-dentiæ aut desperationis barathrum incida-mus, sed contra, sanctorum exemplo, aduer-sus impatientiam luctandum, explòratum ha-bentes euentuum momenta in Dei manu reposita, quæ singula tam prudenter administret, vt quicquid futurum est suo & loco & tempore sit euenturum. Quid autem iustius est quàm vt omnis nostra voluntas ab eius arbitrio pendeat? Est hæc autem doctrina, in priuatis nostris rationibus cum primis necessaria, in quibus licet quidem nobis, & ipsa fides dictat, non solùm in genere diuinù auxilium implorare, sed distinctè quoque hoc vel illud à Domino postulare, sed tamen hac addita semper conditione, si gloriæ Dei interfit: si visum ei sic fuerit: secus verò minimè: quòd in singularibus huiusmodi rebus nullam reuelationé peculiarem habeamus. Cæterùm in Scripturis reperiùtur quidè nonnullorù exempla, quibus peculiari quoque reuelatione commonefactis, & Deum ducem ac authorem sequutis, res tamen prorsus ex animi sententia non successit. Exempli gratia, Si quod vnquam atrocissimum facinus extitit, pro culdubiò illud est à Beniamitis patratum, de quo Iud. 19. & 20. Hic verò decem tribus, æquissima seruata moderatione, eáque semel atque iterum tentata, diuino responso fretæ, manus conseruerunt, in quibus conflictibus cæsis ex suis quadraginta millibus, bis sunt superati. Quid hic ergo sentiamus? Deúmne aliud esse locutum, aliud effecisse? Minimè gentium. Tribus enim aliæ Dei responsa in vtraque illa expeditione latiùs quàm par esset, extenderunt, quum primò consultus Deus tantùm respondisset vti Iuda bello præesset: secundò verò duntaxat vt sese contra Beniamitas in viam darent, de quibus etiam tandem Dominus poenas sumpsit. Ex hoc igitur exemplo discamus non esse nobis in rebus nostris suscipiendis aut gerendis dis fingendas ex animi voluntate Dei promis-siones, sed intra verbi eius septa manentibus, & bonam conscientiam seruantibus rerum omnium cuentum eius esse manui permittendum.
units.tr: The use of this doctrine applies to all our affairs. Whenever something has to be done, we consult the mouth of God, not of course as though he were about to come down from heaven and speak into our ear, as some giddy people dream, but so that we may carefully weigh, with every disturbance of mind set aside, whether the things we turn over in our minds and deliberate upon with ourselves are lawful in themselves or not. The Lord makes this plain and clear by his Law and by the testimony of each person's own conscience, which is taught from his commands what pleases or displeases God. Next, since whatever is lawful in itself must not be undertaken by just anyone indiscriminately, God having assigned to each person his own duties and offices, this further caution must be applied after the first: with a calm and settled mind, and especially free from all levity and ambition (which often wear the appearance of a zeal), we should diligently ask ourselves whether the things we take up agree with our calling. For the rule the Apostle gives for living well is certain: that each should remain in the calling in which he was called (1 Cor. 7.20). Here there are two precipices which we must carefully avoid: lest through sloth or distrust we hold back, or lest through some disturbance of mind we grow slack, or rather seem, and rightly so, to be bold and rash rather than brave and fearless. Finally, since because of the various circumstances of places, times and persons, something that is lawful and agrees with our calling is not always expedient, we must consult the Lord once more, and carefully consider with what spirit we are approaching the matter, entrusting ourselves in its execution to the providence of God, which he has breathed into our minds. So, to make good use of this excellent admonition of the Lord, we must carefully observe this in all difficulties: first, we must hold God's promises in our minds, and set them against every kind of terror, lest we be drawn away, even a little, from that perseverance in which we must steadfastly persevere to the end. Then we must add this too: that we are moved by the reverence due to his threats and judgments, lest we entangle our consciences in any crimes, or run out beyond the bounds into any license of sinning. In this way, I say, it is fitting for us to bring into use this most excellent saying of threats and promises, resting on the truth and constancy of God. But if, following this reasoning, God seems to deal with us in a way quite other than he has promised, or at least seems to defer the fulfilment of his promises longer than is right, we must take care not to fall into the abyss of distrust or despair. On the contrary, following the example of the saints, we must struggle against impatience, holding it as certain that the moments of events are in God's hand, and that he administers each of them so wisely that whatever is to come will happen in its own place and time. And what is more just than that our whole will should depend on his judgment? This doctrine is especially necessary in our private affairs, in which, as faith itself dictates, we are free not only to implore divine help in general, but also to ask the Lord for this or that in particular. Yet this is always to be added as a condition: if it is for the glory of God, if it seems good to him, and otherwise not at all; because in such singular matters we have no special revelation. Moreover, the Scriptures do indeed record some examples of men who, though admonished by a special revelation and following God as their leader and author, nevertheless did not succeed in the matter at all according to their own inclination. For example, if there was ever a most atrocious crime, it was certainly that committed by the Benjamites, of which we read in Judges 19 and 20. Here the ten tribes, observing the most fair moderation, and having made the attempt once and again, relying on the divine answer, joined battle; and in these encounters, after forty thousand of their own men had been slain, they were twice defeated. What then should we think here? That God said one thing and brought about another? By no means. For the other tribes extended the responses of God in both those campaigns more widely than was right, since when God was first consulted he had only answered that Judah should lead the war, and secondly only that they should set out against the Benjamites, on whom at last the Lord also took vengeance. From this example, then, let us learn that in undertaking or carrying out our affairs we must not invent promises of God according to our own wishes. Rather, remaining within the bounds of his word and keeping a good conscience, we must leave the outcome of all things in his hand.

units.la: Discamus etiam saepe Dominū aut prorsus nostras preces nobis denegantem, aut in tempus aliquod differentem, etiamsi nec illae sint illicitae, nec vocationi nostrae repugnent, saepe eo ipso quod nostras petitiones repudiat nostri miserericordiam, vt qui solus vere quid ex vsu nostro sit intelligat.
units.tr: Let us also learn that the Lord sometimes either refuses our prayers altogether or defers them to some later time, even when they are neither unlawful nor opposed to our calling. Often, by the very fact that he rejects our petitions, he shows us his mercy, since he alone truly understands what is good for us.

units.la: Teneamus praeterea Deo constare consilij sui rationes occultas, quae solo exitu patefiant: quas penitius inuestigare nobis non liceat, quum potius in eius sancta prouidentia conquiescere sine exceptione teneamur.
units.tr: Let us further hold that the reasons of his hidden counsel are known to God and are revealed only in the outcome. We may not search them out more deeply, but are bound rather to rest without exception in his holy providence.

units.la: Praeterea saepenumero contingit vt dignio-res simus poenis & suppliciis quàm ij aduer-sus quos Dominū bona licet conscientia pre-camur: vnde fit vt ipse duo simul exequatur, vt ex Beniamitarum historia satis liquet, in qua satis est conspicuum reliquas tribus nimium conscias fuisse & participes generalis illius confusionis, quae populum à morte losuae perualerat.
units.tr: Moreover, it often happens that we are more worthy of punishments and torments than those against whom we pray to the Lord, even with a good conscience. Hence it comes about that he carries out both together, as is quite clear from the history of the Benjamites, in which it is plain enough that the remaining tribes were too much aware of, and partakers in, that general confusion which had overwhelmed the people since the death of Joshua.

units.la: Est autem istud, fratres, nobis quàm attente perpendendum, qui in hoc bellum incidi-mus aduersus Principem vicinum, bellum, in-quam, non modo quantum equidem scire & iudicare possum, iustissimum, sed etiam necessarium, ad iustam, nimirum nostram defenfionem suscEptum, ad conscientiarum libertatem, totiusque Reipublicæ salutem. At tamen si quæ sit, & iam olim fuerit vitæ nostræ ratio paulò diligentius excusserimus, næ merito dici poterunt à nobis iustificati prophani, vt Prophetæ clamant à Iuda fuisse iustificatum Israelem, Ezechiel.16. 51. maximè verò si nobiscum reputauerimus quot & quantis vitiis polluta sit, ex quo bellum istud coeptum est immensis flagitiis foedatum & coinquinatum, an mirabimur aliquot nobis inflictas plagas, quos potius virga illa ferrea contritos oportuit? Sed hoc longè grauius est, quòd nullum adhuc tantæ calamitatis finem nec modum cernimus, à qua tamen Deus nos huc vsque inuisitata quadam & plus quàm admiranda ratione fartos rectos aleruit, sacrosancti quidem sui nominis gratia, nullo autem nostro merito. Vos igitur, oro & obtestor, mentibus hæc infigite, & quidem omnes ita penitentes, vt dum tempus est, cuiuscunque ordinis homines de seria pœnitentia cogitemus, veniam præteritorum à Deo supplices efflagitantes, nec eius in posterum fauore quæ admirandum modis omnibus hactenus experti sumus nos indignos præbeamus: sed precemur vt propter Nominis sui gloriam omnibus nostris deletis iniquitatibus, & sui fœderis memor, ratum nobis faciat quod veteri suo populo pollicitus est. Ezech.16.60.
units.tr: Now, brethren, we must weigh this very carefully. We have been drawn into this war against a neighbouring prince, a war which, as far as I can know and judge, is not only most just, but also necessary, undertaken for our just defence, for the freedom of our consciences and for the safety of the whole commonwealth. Yet if we examine a little more carefully what our manner of life has been, and has been for some time, we may rightly be called unrighteous profane people, just as the Prophets cry out that Israel was made righteous in comparison with Judah (Ezek. 16.51). And above all, if we consider with ourselves how many and how great are the vices by which we have been polluted, and how, from the time this war began, it has been defiled and stained with immense crimes, shall we wonder that some blows have been inflicted on us, when we ought rather to have been crushed by that iron rod? But what is far more serious is that we still see no end or limit to so great a calamity, from which nevertheless God has up to now preserved and kept us safe in some unseen and more than wonderful way, for the sake of his most holy name, but not on account of any merit of ours. I therefore beg and entreat you all to fix these things in your minds, and indeed that all of us, of whatever rank, should repent in earnest while there is time, humbly begging God for pardon for past sins, and not render ourselves unworthy of his favour in the future for the things we have so far experienced in all sorts of wonderful ways. Rather let us pray that for the glory of his name, with all our iniquities blotted out, and mindful of his covenant, he may make good to us what he promised to his old people (Ezek. 16.60).

units.la: Denique hic & alibi videmus Christum suos discipulos, ad dignoscendam Dei voluntatem,
units.tr: Finally, here and elsewhere we see Christ sending his disciples back to the Scriptures to learn God's will, and in them he sets aside every human tradition and embraces the books of Moses and the Prophets.

units.la: Sacrarum Scriptutatem, adscripturas remittere, quibus, repudiata qualibet hominum traditione, libros Mosis & Prophetarum complectitur: Quanto magis igitur hodie reipsa praestita & adimpleta hac sacrosancta voluntate, Filij adventu, qui de cruce clamauit, Impleta omnia: eademque insuper planissimè & maximè conspicuè ab Euangelistis & Apostolis scriptis mandata & in eius Ecclesia quam nostris temporibus rediuiuam esse voluit, clarè personante, quo tandem alio quàm ad easdem Scripturas à seipsis earundem expositione & interpretatione petita confugiemus? Quos verò potius pro pseudopastoribus & Antichristis habuerimus quàm qui imperitæ plebeculæ earum lectionem interdicunt? qui eam adulterant, id ubi tantum ex ea reliqui facientes quo ad sua confirmanda mendacia possint abuti? qui denique non nisi ex misellarum animarum perditione viuunt? Contrà igitur sanctum hoc & pretiosum vitæ verbum attendamus, meditemur, animo nocte dieque, versemus, concipiamus ac digeramus oportet, illius in nobis effecta, modis omnibus proferentes, quandoquidem diuina patientia nobis tantum beneficium adhuc conceditur. Sin minus, meminerimus seruum eum esse dignum qui plagis grauioribus cædatur, cui quum esset nota domini sui voluntas, illam parui faciens secus se gesserit Luc.12.47.
units.tr: How much more, then, now that this most holy will has been carried out and fulfilled in fact by the coming of the Son, who cried from the cross, All is fulfilled, and now that the same will has been set forth most plainly and conspicuously by the Evangelists and Apostles in writing, and sounds clearly in the Church which he willed to be revived in our own times, to what other source shall we finally turn than to those same Scriptures, sought from their own exposition and interpretation? Those who forbid the reading of Scripture to the unlearned common folk, who corrupt it, who keep back only so much of it as they can use to bolster their lies, who in the end live only by the ruin of poor souls, should we not rather hold them to be false shepherds and Antichrists? Let us therefore set our attention on this holy and precious word of life, and it is right that we meditate on it, turn it over in our minds night and day, take it in and digest it, and bring it forth in every way in our lives, since God's patience still grants us so great a blessing. If not, let us remember that the servant who knew his master's will and disregarded it, acting otherwise, deserves to be beaten with heavier blows (Luke 12:47).

units.la: Subiiciunt deinceps Euangelistæ grauissimam Christi reprehensionem aduersus eam cohorte quæ manus in ipsum iniectura venerat. Hic vero primum obiectua non hoc à Christo factum quò in suam eos gratiam flecteret, & eorum manus effugeret: sed partim vt eorum conscientiam grauiter vulneraret, siquam tamen ex ipsis aliqui non prorsus stupidam aut putrefactam habuerunt: partim vero & præcipuè quidem vt ita palam faceret, hoc se modò captum quòd capi voluisset, non autem quasi non potuisset, præsertim noctu, in tenebris & in horto suburbano, facilius ex eorum manibus elabi, quàm plena Luce & in templo in quo docuerat, & quod erat in hostium suorum potestate.
units.tr: The Evangelists next record Christ's most severe rebuke of the band of soldiers who had come to lay hands on him. First, it should be noted that Christ did this not to bend them to his favour and so escape their hands, but partly to wound their conscience sharply, if any of them had a conscience that was not utterly dull or rotten, and partly, and above all, to make it plain that he was now taken because he had willed to be taken, and not as if he could not have been taken otherwise. For he could have escaped their hands more easily at night, in darkness and in a garden outside the city, than in broad daylight and in the temple where he had taught, and yet he was in the power of his enemies.

units.la: Ex his igitur verbis, & superiora illa omnia quæ diximus, & suum stuporem satis agnoscere potuerunt: sed nulla tanta est meris cæcitas, nulla tanta vecordia quæ cum iis comparanda sit qui iam improbitatis aut etiam affectatæ ignorantiæ callum obduxerunt. Nos vero contrà ex eo in quo miseri isti homines non profecerunt, fructum aliquem eliciamus, ac primùm discamus minimè nouum esse vt filij Dei, quibus indignus est mundus. Heb. 11. 38. non tantùm perinde accipiantur atque perditissimi quique & omnium sceleratissimi & quidem religionis & iustitiæ specie: sed etiam impurissimis & profligatissimis hominum monstris, posthabeantur, vt in hac historia maiorem Barrabbæ quàm Domini inter duos latrones crucifixi rationem habitam fuisse videbimus.
units.tr: From these words, and from all the things we have said above, they could well have recognised their own stupidity. But no blindness is so great, no madness so extreme, as to be compared with those who have already hardened themselves into obstinate wickedness or even deliberate ignorance. Let us rather, on the contrary, draw some fruit from that in which these wretched men did not profit. And first let us learn that it is no new thing for the sons of God, of whom the world is not worthy (Heb. 11:38), to be treated as the most abandoned and most wicked of men, and indeed under the appearance of religion and righteousness, and to be set below the most impure and debauched monsters of humankind; just as in this history we shall see that Barabbas was given more regard than the Lord, crucified between two thieves.

units.la: Deinde, vt Christus captiuus licet, libere loquatur, & his verbis suos hostes iudicet attendamus. Sic quoque fideles Dei servi, vbi sic ei libuit, in vincula quidem coniiciuntur, catenisque vinciuntur, & constringuntur, sed Dei nihilominus verbum minime vincitur.2.Timot.2.9. Quinam enim vincula, quibus os aperuit Dominus, iis obstrue- rent, quum adhuc etiam mortui loquantur, & ad consummationem vsque seculi loquuturi sint? Neque enim absre illud est quod doctrinam Apostolicam in missione Sancti Spiritus cum magna vi venti & linguis igneis Apostolis traditam legimus Act.2.2. & 3. quo quidem illud nobis significatur quod hoc nostro seculo plus satis euincitur, si alias vnquam, nō esse nimirum magis in Diaboli & mundi potestate situm, quicquid agant ac moliantur, Euangelicæ prædicationis cursum remorari, quàm spirantis venti flatum coercere, & igni suum splendorem aut calorem eripere.
units.tr: Next, let us observe that Christ, although a captive, speaks freely, and judges his enemies by these words. So too the faithful servants of God, when it has so pleased him, are indeed cast into chains, bound with fetters and constrained, but the word of God is by no means bound (2 Tim. 2:9). For what chains could stop the mouth which the Lord has opened, since the dead still speak and will go on speaking until the end of the age? Nor is it out of place that we read how the Apostolic teaching was delivered to the Apostles at the sending of the Holy Spirit with a great rush of wind and tongues of fire (Acts 2:2-3). This signifies to us what our own age has proved more than enough, if ever any age has: that it is no more in the power of the devil and the world, whatever they do or plan, to hold back the course of the Gospel preaching, than to check the blowing of a wind that is blowing, or to snatch away the brightness or heat of fire.

units.la: Fateor quidem non eodem modo semper ventum istum spirare, nec pari vi & effectu, quam etiam ob causam à quodam ex Veteribus non inepte Lunæ comparatur Ecclesia, quatenus non eodem semper aspectu Solis irradiatur. At istis contingentibus nihilominus tamen veritati nihil in se decedere sciendum est, sed eam integram & illibatam permanere, atque adeò tum promerentibus istud nostris peccatis, tum Domino suos sic explorante, tenebrarum etiam aliquod esse tempus, vt quum mundus indignus sit cui Sol affulgeat, & nostra fides subinde probatione indigeat, necesse fit Spiritum mendacij quandoque erroris efficaciam habere, & spiritualis huius cibi penuriam, eorum qui vesci solent appetitum excitare: Domino tamé Ecclesiam suam nunquam deferente, quę nunquam melius nec illustrius quàm sub cruce triumphat. Huius rei testis est tum tota Sacra Scriptura, tum perpetua seculorum omnium experientia, quum præsertim Ecclesiæ Domini dignitas non in multitudine consistat, sed in credentium fide, quos semper exiguo numero fuisse, esse & fore ad finem vsque mundi, testatur ipse Dominus Iesus Christus, de iis suos diserte monens. Luc. 18.8.
units.tr: I admit that this wind does not always blow in the same way, nor with equal force and effect, and for this reason one of the ancients not unaptly compares the Church to the moon, inasmuch as it is not always lit by the sun from the same aspect. Yet it must be understood that truth loses nothing of itself through these changing circumstances, but remains whole and unimpaired. Indeed, both because we deserve it by our sins and because the Lord thus tests his own, there is at times a season of darkness too, so that, since the world is unworthy to have the sun shine upon it, and our faith from time to time needs to be tested, it is necessary that the spirit of lies should sometimes have the power of error, and that the lack of this spiritual food should stir the appetite of those who are wont to feed upon it. Yet the Lord never abandons his Church, which never triumphs more splendidly or more brightly than under the cross. The witness to this is both the whole of Holy Scripture and the constant experience of all ages, especially since the dignity of the Church of the Lord does not consist in multitude but in the faith of believers, who, as the Lord Jesus Christ himself testifies, warning his own plainly about this, have always been few in number, are so now, and will be so until the end of the world (Luke 18:8).

units.la: Exempli gratia, iam conspicimus quid Dominus ipse præstiterit, ex quo placuit ipsi iam ab hinc annis septuaginta, veritatis suæ radiis orbem illustrare, dissipatis tot seculorum tantis támque densis tenebris vt vix millesimo cuique Christiano Veteris & Noui Testamenti liber vel superficie tenus cognitus effet, vel discrimen sciret Legis & Euangelij, vel certa fidei definitionem, tam crassa támque supina in singulis ignorantia vigente, & passim Sophistice, id est, bruta & garrula subtilitate in scholis regnante, cum linguarum & bonarum scientiarum ignorantia: & superstitione maximam hominum partem occæcante, paucis tantum exceptis, & iis Deo potius quàm hominibus notis. Rursum vero quum eandem homi-
units.tr: For example, we now see what the Lord himself has accomplished, since it has pleased him, some seventy years ago, to light up the world with the rays of his truth, when such great and such dense darkness of so many ages had been scattered that scarcely one Christian in a thousand had known even superficially the books of the Old and New Testament, or knew the difference between Law and Gospel, or a sure definition of faith; such gross and dull ignorance prevailed in every quarter, and everywhere Sophistry, that is, a brutish and garrulous subtlety, reigned in the schools, together with ignorance of languages and of the good sciences, and superstition blinded the greater part of mankind, with only a few exceptions, and those known to God rather than to men. Yet again, when the same people [...]

units.la: homines veritatem tam male exceperint, & contra sint eam tam pertinaci studio fere omnes persequuti, & quasi cruci affixerint in tot fidelibus Dei seruis, videmus uti iam densiores quàm antea tenebrae rursum exoriantur, cuomente & reponente nobis abyllo putei abominandas quasque haereses renouatas à Libertinis, Anabaptistis, Arrianis, Sabellianis, Nestorianis, Eutychianis, Pelagianis, & aliis eiusdem farinae hominibus, quibus nec auditores, nec fautores desunt: & praeterea producta Monachorum illorum proluuie, qui nobis Iesu nomen eripere conantur, quibus seu fulcris abominandae illius sedis Apostaticae Babylonis, authoritas fulciatur: & tandem excitatis, tu Epicureis & Atheis, tum philosophicę Christianitatis inuentoribus, (rem sane visu & auditu deplorandam) adeo ut tempus illud implectionis Gentium de quo vaticinatus est Apostolus Rom. 11. 25. non dubiis aut indubitatis signis appropinquare conspiciamus. Etsi autem singulari Dei misericordia factum est ut hactenus haec Ecclesia fuerit ab istiusmodi pestibus libera, quanuis non defuerint qui sanam hic doctrinam suis figmentis consspurcare conati sint, tamen, nisi prorsus caecutimus, annon animaduertimus Solem illum iam ad occasum vergere, immo pene occidere nobis, quibus in iudicium potius quàm in salutem exortus illuxerit, nisi alios poenitentiae dignos fructus adferamus? Vbi enim, obsecro, studiu illud audiendi verbi quo ante annos quadraginta flagrasse ferè omnes testis ipse ego sum oculatus? vbi feruor ille scandalis occursandi? & de improbis seuerum supplicium sumendi, quo vel nobis infensissimos hostes pudore suf- susos vidimus,quum etiam huius loci fama ad longissimè remotas regiones peruagaretur? vbi illa in cultu simplicitas & modestia, vbi decor ille vestium ad collum vsque honestè clausarum, qui maximè in aduenis elucebat? Cessit ille primum profligatus à scutulatis illis vestibus quas Vertugadas vocant, quibus tandem successerunt immensa illa collaria,& instar ventilari pistrini alata: suffarcinati illi in acutum desinentes virorum thoraces seu ventres: mulierum pudendæ illæ tomento à tergo infartæ tympanorum instar, & aliæ item variegatæ, segmetatæ, arte phrygionica laboratæ vestes, cum reliquis istiusmodi mundi muliebris ornamentis tantis tamque variis vt filiarum Sionis luxum infinitis partibus superent. Vos igitur hic mulieres Geneuenses nominatim appello,& ad Esaiç caput 3.amando, ex quo quid sit vobis iamiam imminens expspectandum intelligatis. Annon enim, obsecro,Deum ipsum oportet hunc verbi sui contemptum vlcisci propria manu,& eorum ignauiam castigare qui sua tam impunè patiuntur edicta sacrosanata violari? Vos item appello, iuuenes,& idem denuntio iudicium vel etiam longè grauius, quos non pudet collariis istis maioribus comptos& ornatos incedere, cedere, crispatos & cincinnatos alios mu-liebrem in morem, alios vero hirtos crines instar aprorum setas prae se ferentes, quos de-nique pari luxu & lasciuia diffluentes idem exspectat iudicium. Idem vobis etiam di-ctum esto parum prudentibus maritis, vestras vxores in tenellas & delicatulas puppas transformantibus. Vobis etiam parentibus, quos olim poenitebit tam parum fuisse solicitos de liberis vestris in Christiana modestia educandis & fouendis. Ausim affirmare annorum plus quam triginta spatio vix vllum gladio sicaue fuisse ad sanguinem vsque vulneratum, exceptis duobus homicidiis, quorum alterum ad vrbis portas admissum, satis est negligenter a Magistratu requisitum, etsi qui tunc caesus est non foret in minima culpa: alterum in ipsa vrbe admissum, & ea qua par erat poena multatum. At iam, Deus bone! quo deuenimus? Annon siquis est iniuriosius appellatus, sibi probro ducit nisi aut ipse alterum ad duellum prouocet, aut prouocatus suscipiat? Quod si forte non etiam ad necem progressi multi sunt, per quos stetit quominus id fieret? At, proh dolor! si quotquot nefaria caede sublati sunt hodie loqui possent & conqueri: si quotquot caesi, aut omni contumeliarum genere sunt affecti libere possent apud aequos iudices expostulare, & ius exspectare, etiam mulierculae, quot quaeso inter nos eminent quibus esset quam gratissimae latebrae, nequid grauius in eos dicam. Totam vidi vrbem commoueri, ficui Geneuæ blasphema vox excidisset, non quieturam nisi agnita & castigata blasphemia: adeò vt peregrinis etiam impunè deierare nō liceret, statim cum corripientibus qui audiuerant, immo etiam terram exosculari iubentibus. Quid verò nunc? annon aër totus & intra vrbem & extra est plenus lögè latéque horrendis deierationibus, & execrandis in ipsam Dei Maiestatem blasphemiis vt etiam in morè abeant, & mirù fit quomodo nō tellus ima nobis absorbendis dehiscat? Summa est vini caritas, & tamen ebriosis refertæ sunt cauponæ. Ecquos verò potiùs incusem quàm ditiores quibus abundè suppetit vini copia, quam cauponibus malunt quocũque pretio addicere, quàm plebeculam minutatim ac particulatim illud diuidendo subleuare? Panis pretium & aliarum quarumlibet mercium mirum in modū excreuit, vt mirum fit Geneuam adhuc aliquam esse: ferro & igni nostris oculis omnium segetes, vites, domus cum habitatoribus absumi conspeximus: bellum ad portas atrocißimù omnia minatur extrema, hic verò non quæro quis ad saccum & cinerem ad quæ nos Deus inuitat procurterit: sed quis nostrum quæve tandem hæc animaduertat, quis feriò cogitet, quis vel vultu, vel gestu, vel denique tota vitæ suæ ratione iudiciis se Dei commoueri testetur? quid igitur nobis sperandum putamus? Næ si meis illud verbis expressero, haud estis arbitror creditauri: Ergo age vos ipse alloquatur Elaias, Esaias, quem si vos adhuc hodie compellantem audire neglexeritis, quid vobis futurum sit vel ex eorum saltem exemplo discite quos ipse coram alloquutus est, eius Nomine, qui viuit etiam idem hodie, & sui semper similis, nec mutatus, nec in seculum mutandus perdurat. Haec igitur Prophetæ verba diligenter auscultate, Esa.22.12. In die illa vocauit Dominus Deus exercituum ad fletum, & ad planctum, ad caluitium & ad cingulum sacci: & ecce gaudium & lætitia, occidere vitulos, & iugulare arietes, comedere carnes & bibere vinum. Comedamus & bibamus: cras enim moriemur. Et reuelata est in auribus meis vox Domini exercituum. Si dimittetur iniquitas hæc vobis donec moriamini. Porrò longius a textu digressum me aliquis forte dixerit: sed nego. Meminit enim horæ potestatis tenebrarum, quarum miserandū statum vobis repræsentare studui, vt maturè singuli cogitemus, ne nobis idem contingat quod prædicit expressè Dominus Luc. 11.26. nempe ne per Dei gratiam a nobis eiecto malo spiritu, septem alij peiores illo intra nos ingressi multum promouisse comperiantur. Dominus Deus pro illa sua immensa erga nos misericordia, cæteris in Ægyptiacis tenebris relictis eodem erga nos se modo gessit atque olim erga populum suum in terra Gosen, conuertendo nos a tenebris ad lucem, & a potestate Satanæ ad Deum, vt remissionem peccatorum & fortem inter sanctificatos acciperemus per fidem quæ est in Christo. Act.26. 18. & qui dixit ut è tenebris lux splendesceret, is est qui splenduit in cordibus nostris ad præbendum lumen cognitionis in facie Iesu Christi.2.Cor. 4.6.nónc igitur ad vomitum rursus instar canum reuertemur? 2.Pet.2.v.21.immo etiam in cœno malitiæ & tenebrarum magis quàm priùs volutabimur?Heu,proh dolor!nimium iam diu reuerti cœpimus ad nostras tenebras. Faxit verò Deus Opt. Max. vt hoc peccatum agnoscentes seria ducamur pœnitentia, & hanc gratiam largiatur vt tanquam filij Lucis ambulemus, antequàm in densiores tenebras incurramus: tandémque nos sancta sua misericordia ad veram illam & æternam lucem quam suis præparauit ante mundi creationem felicissimè deducat.
units.tr: Since men have received the truth so badly, and have nearly all pursued it with such stubborn zeal, and as good as nailed it to the cross in so many faithful servants of God, we see darker shadows than before rising again. From the abyss of the well, as it were, there come up and are set before us the abominable heresies revived by the Libertines, Anabaptists, Arians, Sabellians, Nestorians, Eutychians, Pelagians, and other men of the same stamp, who lack neither hearers nor supporters. Besides this, the brood of those Monks has been brought forth, who try to snatch the name of Jesus from us, and whose support lends authority to that abominable apostate Babylon. Finally, Epicureans and Atheists have been roused, and so have the inventors of a philosophical Christianity (a thing truly to be deplored in sight and hearing), so that we see the time of the fullness of the Gentiles, of which the Apostle prophesied (Rom. 11:25), drawing near by signs that are not doubtful but beyond doubt. Although by the singular mercy of God this Church has so far been free from such plagues, and although there have not been lacking those who have tried to defile sound doctrine with their inventions, yet, unless we are utterly blind, do we not notice that the Sun is already sinking towards its setting, or rather almost going down for us, to whom it has risen for judgment rather than for salvation, unless we bring forth fruits worthy of repentance? For where, I beg you, is that zeal for hearing the Word which, as I myself have seen with my own eyes, almost everyone burned with forty years ago? Where is that fervour for opposing scandals and for exacting severe punishment from the wicked, by which we saw even our most hostile enemies put to shame, when the fame of this place was spread abroad even to the most distant regions? Where is that simplicity and modesty in dress, where is that decency of garments modestly closed up to the neck, which shone most of all in strangers? That decency first gave way to the slashed garments which they call Vertugadas, and these in turn to those immense ruffs, winged like the fan of a mill; to those men's doublets stuffed and ending in a point, the bellies of men; to the women's shameful padding stuffed behind like drums; and to other variegated, slashed garments made in the Phrygian manner, together with the other such worldly adornments of women, so many and so various that they surpass the luxury of the daughters of Zion in countless respects. Therefore I address you here, the women of Geneva, by name, and I bid you attend to Isaiah chapter 3, so that you may understand what is already imminent for you. For must not God himself avenge this contempt of his Word with his own hand, and punish the indolence of those who suffer his sacred edicts to be violated with such impunity? I address you too, young men, and I announce the same judgment, or even a far heavier one, to those who are not ashamed to walk about adorned with those larger ruffs, to strut and swagger with curled and ringleted hair in the manner of women, or others who carry stiff hair like the bristles of wild boars. Finally, the same judgment awaits those who wallow in equal luxury and wantonness. Let this also be said to you, imprudent husbands, who turn your wives into tender and pampered dolls. And to you parents too, who will one day regret having been so little careful to bring up and cherish your children in Christian modesty. I dare to affirm that in the space of more than thirty years hardly anyone has been wounded with a sword or dagger to the point of bloodshed, except in two homicides. Of these, one was committed at the city gates, and the magistrate made a rather careless inquiry into it, although the man who was killed was not in the least to blame; the other was committed within the city itself, and the offender was punished as was fitting. But now, good God, to what have we come? If someone is insulted in a more injurious way, does he not count it a disgrace unless he either challenges the other to a duel or accepts the challenge? And if many have not gone so far as killing, is it not for lack of will on their part? But, alas! If all who have been slain by unspeakable bloodshed could speak and complain today, and if all who have been struck down or treated with every kind of insult could freely demand justice before fair judges and expect redress, even the little women, how many, I ask, among us would stand out in whom there would be the most welcome hiding-places (not to say anything more grievous against them)? I have seen the whole city stirred up when a blasphemous word had slipped from anyone in Geneva, and it would not be quiet until the blasphemy was acknowledged and rebuked; so much so that it was not even permitted for strangers to swear with impunity, and at once those who had heard would rebuke them, even ordering them to kiss the ground. But what now? Is not the air, both within the city and outside it, full far and wide of dreadful oaths and of execrable blasphemies against the very Majesty of God, so that they have become a custom? And it is a wonder that the lowest earth does not gape open to swallow us up. Wine is very dear, and yet the taverns are full of drunkards. But whom should I rather blame than the richer people, who have an abundant supply of wine and prefer to sell it to the taverners at any price, rather than relieve the common folk by dividing it out to them bit by bit? The price of bread and of all other goods has grown in a wonderful way, so that it is a wonder that Geneva still exists. We have seen before our very eyes the crops, vines and houses, with their inhabitants, consumed by fire and sword; a most savage war threatens all things to the utmost at our gates. Yet here I do not ask who has run to sackcloth and ashes, to which God invites us, but who among us, or what kind of person, takes note of these things, who thinks seriously about them, who bears witness by his face, his gesture, or finally by the whole course of his life that he is moved by the judgments of God? What then do we think we have to hope for? Indeed, if I express this in my own words, I think you will not believe me. Therefore let Isaiah, Isaiah himself, address you. If you neglect to hear him speaking to you even today, learn at least from the example of those to whom he spoke in person what will befall you. He speaks in the name of him who lives, who is the same today, always like himself, neither changed nor to be changed for ever. Listen carefully, then, to the words of the Prophet (Isa. 22:12): "In that day did the Lord God of hosts call to weeping and to mourning, to baldness and to girding with sackcloth; and behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen and killing sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. And it was revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts: Surely this iniquity shall not be purged from you till you die." Yet perhaps someone will say that I have wandered rather far from the text. But I deny it. For I have been mindful of the hour of the power of darkness, whose pitiable state I have striven to set before you, so that each of us may think carefully and in good time, lest what the Lord plainly foretold (Luke 11:26) should happen to us: that, after the evil spirit has been cast out of us by the grace of God, seven others worse than it should enter in and be found to have made much progress within us. The Lord God, in his immense mercy towards us, has left the rest in Egyptian darkness and has dealt with us in the same way that he once dealt with his people in the land of Goshen, turning us from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, so that we might receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among the sanctified through faith which is in Christ (Acts 26:18). And he who said, "Let light shine out of darkness," is the one who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor. 4:6). Shall we now, then, return to our vomit like dogs (2 Pet. 2:21), or wallow even more than before in the mire of wickedness and darkness? Alas, alas! We have begun to return to our darkness far too long already. May God, the best and greatest, grant that, acknowledging this sin, we may be moved to a serious repentance, and bestow this grace that we may walk as children of the Light before we fall into still thicker darkness; and at last may his holy mercy most happily lead us to that true and eternal light which he prepared for his own before the creation of the world.

units.tr: Amen.

units.tr: HOMILY eleven.

units.tr: MATT. 26.

units.la: 56. Tunc discipuli omnes, relicto eo, fugerunt.
units.tr: 56. Then all the disciples forsook him and fled.

units.la: 57. Illi vero prehensum Iesum abduxerunt ad Caiaphan Pontificem Maximum, vbi Scribæ & Seniores coacti erant. MARC. 14. 50. Tunc relicto eo omnes fugerunt. 51.
