Quidam autem iuuenis sequebatur eum, amictus sindone super nudum corpus: & prehenderunt eum iuuenes. 52. Ipse vero derelicta sindone, nudus effugit ab illis. 53. Tunc abduxerunt Iesum ad Pontificem Maximum, cum quo conuenerunt omnes primarij Sacerdotes, & Seniores, & Scribæ. LVC. 22. 54. Comprehensum autem eum duxerunt, & introduxerunt domum Pontificis Maximi. IOH. 18. 12. Cohors igitur & Tribunus & ministri Iudæorum comprehenderunt Iesum, & vinxerunt eum. 13. Et abduxerunt primum ad Annâ: erat enim socer Caiaphæ, qui erat Pontifex Maximus anni illius: is vero misit eum vinctum ad Caiaphan Pontificem Maximum.
units.tr: 57. But those who had seized Jesus led him away to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered. MARK 14. 50. Then they all forsook him and fled. 51. A certain young man followed him, wrapped in a linen cloth over his naked body, and the young men laid hold of him. 52. But he left the linen cloth and fled from them naked. 53. Then they led Jesus away to the high priest, with whom all the chief priests, the elders and the scribes came together. LUKE 22. 54. They took him and led him into the house of the high priest. JOHN 18. 12. So the band, the captain and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him. 13. And they led him first to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. He sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.

units.la: 14. Erat autem Caiaphas is qui consilium dederat Iudaeis expedire ut unus homo moreretur pro populo.
units.tr: 14. Now Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jews that it was expedient that one man should die for the people.

units.la: 19. Pontifex Maximus ergo interrogauit Iesum de discipulis & doctrina ipsius.
units.tr: 19. The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching.

units.la: 20. Respondit ei Iesus, Ego palam loquutus sum mundo: ego semper docui in synagoga & in templo, quo undique Iudaei conueniunt, & in occulto loquutus sum nihil.
units.tr: 20. Jesus answered him, I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews come together, and I have said nothing in secret.

units.la: 21. Quid me interrogas? Interroga eos qui audierunt quid sim ipsis loquutus: ecce hi sciunt quae dixerim ego.
units.tr: 21. Why do you question me? Ask those who heard what I said to them; behold, they know what I have said.

units.la: 24. Miserat igitur eum Annas vinctum ad Caiaphan Pontificem Maximum.
units.tr: 24. Annas therefore sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.

units.la: Vò longius in hac historia progredimur, eò magis ac magis quò vsque se Dei filius pro nobis abiecerit: ac proinde quàm sit horrendum aduersus peccata Dei iudicium perspicere nos oportet, vt primum caueamus ne illorum blanditiis inescati decipiamur, deinde vt in omni vita nostra diligenter meditemur immensam bonitatem gratiam & misericordiam, tum Patris coelestis Filio suo vnigenito non parcetis, ad eos seruandos ex inimicis suis quos ab aeterno filio selectos dederat: tum Filij seipsum pro nobis ad mortem, mortem, inquam, crucis exinanientis. Hactenus igitur se Christus ad certamen accinaccinxit, quod iam reipsa strenuè aggredi-tur.
units.tr: The further we advance in this history, the more and more we see how far the Son of God humbled himself for us. Hence we must look closely at how dreadful God's judgment against sins is, so that first we may take care not to be lured and deceived by their flatteries, and then so that throughout our whole life we may diligently meditate on the immense goodness, grace and mercy of the heavenly Father, who did not spare his only-begotten Son but gave him up to save from his enemies those whom the eternal Son had chosen from eternity; and on the Son, who gave himself for us to death, yes, to the death of the cross, by which he emptied himself. Thus Christ has now girded himself for the contest, which he now in fact undertakes with vigour.

units.la: Atque hic primùm occurrit res admodum noua & inaudita, putà Dei Filium, hominem etiam integerrimum, & ipsis longè Angelis perfectiorem, à flagitiosissimis & impurissimis hominibus, captum vinctúmque, & à suis etiam dilectis discipulis fuga sibi consulentibus derelictum trahi. Quod ad prius illud, sanè ab impiis & scelestis hominibus & non ab aliis Christum oportuit capi. Cuius enim viri boni mentem vel ista subiisset cogitatio?
units.tr: And here there first meets us a thing quite new and unheard of: the Son of God, a man most blameless and far more perfect than the angels themselves, is seized and bound by the most wicked and impure men, and is dragged away, deserted even by his beloved disciples, who fled to save themselves. As for the former, it was surely necessary that Christ be seized by impious and wicked men and by no others. For what good man would even have entertained such a thought?

units.la: Verum hic altius nobis est suspiciendum. Primum enim oportuit veritatem figuris congruere: quemadmodum igitur capiebantur pecudes ad sacrificium destinatæ, vinctæque laqueo ad Sacerdotem ducebantur, sic verus ille Agnus qui mundi peccata tollit captus, vinctus, deductus est. At in iis magnum discrimen. Pecudes enim aliæ insciæ ad laniena, reluctantes etiam aliæ vi trahebantur: at sciuit hic Agnus quo iret, & cur, sponte etiam manibus in vincula porrectis, quod nimirum capi, vincirique vellet. Quem quicunque sequi vt par est, cupiunt, imitari debet, pari cum Magistro ratione suorum hostium violentiam & crudelitatem superantes, eâdem cœlitus ipsis concessa patientia, cum eodem etiam in triumphi partem venturi.
units.tr: But here we must look higher. For first it was necessary that the truth agree with the figures. Just as the animals destined for sacrifice were seized, bound with a cord and led to the priest, so that true Lamb who takes away the sins of the world was seized, bound and led away. But there is a great difference between them. For some of the animals were led to the slaughter without knowing it, and others were dragged along by force, struggling. But this Lamb knew where he was going and why, and of his own accord he stretched out his hands to be bound, since he wished, of course, to be seized and bound. Whoever desires to follow him as is fitting ought to imitate him: with the same reasoning as their Master, overcoming the violence and cruelty of their enemies by the same patience granted to them from heaven, and with him they will also come to share in the triumph.

units.la: Deinde licet isti non minus quàm Herodes & Pilatus & similes ipsis hic nihil fecerint nisi quæcunque manus & consilium Dei prius definierat facienda, vt diserte dicitur Act.4. 26.hoc tamen impio rum malitia non excula-tur. Nam quibuscunque Deus vtatur instru-mentis,tanquam in res suas creatas imperium habens, bene semper agit: maximum autem & praestantissimum omnium operum diuino-rum nostra est redemptio. Contrà vero mala instrumenta, nimirum impuri spiritus, & ij quorum abututur opera,quanquam nihil nisi quod Deus bene decreuerit efficere possunt, nunquam tamen bene agunt, neque vt Deo pareant, quum arbor mala fructum bonum producere nequeat.
units.tr: Next, although those men, no less than Herod and Pilate and others like them, did here nothing except what the hand and counsel of God had previously determined should be done, as is expressly said in Acts 4. 26., this does not excuse the malice of the wicked. For whatever instruments God uses, as one who has dominion over his own creatures, he always acts well; and our redemption is the greatest and most excellent of all the divine works. On the other hand, evil instruments, namely unclean spirits and those whose work they use, although they can accomplish nothing except what God has decreed well, never act well, nor do they act to obey God, since a bad tree cannot bring forth good fruit.

units.la: Tertio loco hic maxima Dei gloria, lucem e tenebris educentis refulget,malis illis instrumentis suis semper consiliis excidentibus, vt infelix eorum exitus tandem ostendit ipsis in caucam quam foederunt praecipiti casu ruentibus. Ps.l.7.16. & Proverb.26.27. cuius rei hoc loco, & in hac historia tota luculentissimum exemplum nobis exhibetur. Annon enim Christus ipse dum se vinciendum praebet, se vincientes irretiuit, & quidem indissolubili iusti sui furoris vinculo? Quid aliud etiam Satan hoc loco quàm se magis ac magis illaqueauit & constrinxit?Quis vero nos vinculis peccati & mortis eripuit quàm haec ipsa Christi vincula? Ne nos igitur huius captiui pudeat. Eius enim captiuitas nostra libertas est, eius ignominia, nostra gloria, infirmitas voluntaria, potentia Dei est ad nostram salutem.
units.tr: Thirdly, here shines forth the greatest glory of God, who brings light out of darkness, since those evil instruments of his always fail in their counsels, as their unhappy outcome at last shows, as they fall headlong into the pit they dug. Psalm 7. 16. and Proverbs 26. 27. The clearest example of this is set before us here and throughout this whole history. For did not Christ himself, while he offered himself to be bound, ensnare those who bound him, and indeed with the indissoluble bond of his just wrath? What else does Satan do here than entangle and constrict himself more and more? And who has rescued us from the chains of sin and death, if not these very chains of Christ? Let us therefore not be ashamed of this captive. For his captivity is our liberty, his disgrace our glory, his voluntary weakness the power of God for our salvation.

units.la: Absit autem idololatras imitemur, adorantes vel ipsa vincula, vel crucem, clauos, lanceam, aliáue crudelitatis hostium instrumenta, licet eadem ipsa elle constaret, quæ tamen nihil nisi merę sunt imposturæ:sed potius veneremur vinctum, crucifixum,clauis affixum, transfixum pro nobis, imo, vt quod est dicamus,à nobis ipsis,quòd in nobis passionum eius vera causa reperiatur inhærens; Et de istis hactenus.
units.tr: But let us by no means imitate the idolaters, who worship the chains themselves, or the cross, the nails, the spear, or other instruments of the enemies' cruelty, even if it were certain that these were the very objects, which yet are nothing but mere impostures. Rather let us venerate him bound, crucified, fixed with nails, pierced through for us; and indeed, to say what is true, let us venerate him as bound, crucified, nailed and pierced on account of ourselves, because the true cause of his sufferings is found clinging to us. Let this be enough on these points.

units.la: Quòd ad discipulos, in primis est animad-uertenda summa in illos præceptoris benignitas & clementia, non modò tolerantis eorum infirmitatem, sed ex tanto illo discrimine in quod erant Petri temeritate coniecti, sua illos potentia liberantis, quod etiam Ioan.discertis verbis expressit, Ioh.18.8.& 9. In quo cius quod nos Apostolus tum verbis docet Rom. 14.1. & 1.Thes.5.14.tum exemplo suo 1. Cor.9.22.nobis vsus demonstratur: quæ Christianis omnibus necessaria doctrina est, vt sese mutuò ædificent: sed in primis pastoribus, quibus in horas postulandus est à Deo discretionis Spiritus, tam in tanta tum morborum, tum ægrorum varietate: quàm vt agnoscant quantum intersit inter personarum acceptionem toties tamque expresse prohibitam & circumspectionem accuratamque considerationem personarum, temporum, locorum, minimè illam quidem quam carnis prudentia, iuste ab Apostolo damnata, 2. Tim. 4 2. dictat, sed ex zelo charitate, & charitate zelo temperata q. j. proficiscentem,ex quibus rectam illam & sanctam mensuram discemus.
units.tr: As for the disciples, first we must notice the great kindness and clemency of their Teacher, who not only bore with their weakness, but also, delivering them from that great danger into which Peter's rashness had thrown them, by his own power, which John also expressed in plain words, John 18. 8. and 9. In this we are shown by his own example what the Apostle teaches us in words, Romans 14. 1. and 1 Thessalonians 5. 14., and also by his example, 1 Corinthians 9. 22. This is a doctrine necessary for all Christians, so that they may build one another up; but especially for ministers, who must every hour ask God for the spirit of discernment, both in such great variety of diseases and of the sick, and so that they may recognise how great is the difference between the acceptance of persons, so often and so expressly forbidden, and the careful consideration of persons, times and places. This is not indeed the wisdom of the flesh, which the Apostle rightly condemns, 2 Timothy 4. 2., but a consideration that proceeds from zeal tempered by charity and from charity tempered by zeal. From these we learn that right and holy measure.

units.la: Caeterum hic iterum videmus Dominum in nostrae redemptionis opere socium habuisse nullum, sed eius unius hanc laudem omnem & gloriam esse propriam, ideoque diligenter cavendum ne Martyrum quantumuis excellentium, sanguis cum Christi sanguine permiceatur. Porro, quemadmodum primus ille nostèr Parens turpissima illa sua in Deum rebellione meritus erat ut omnes ab eo creaturae deficerent, imo ut in eum omnes insurgerent, quam tamen Deus poenam ut ipsi libuit moderatus est: sic oportuit eum qui pro nobis spopondit ac fideiussit a quodam ex suis prodituum a reliquis omnibus deseri: ut eius obedientia qui pro peccatis nostris passus est, exsoluto omni nostro debito, in gratiam recipiamur, concives sanctorum ac domestici Dei, Ephes. 2. 19. ut nato Christo clare & sonore Angeli cecinerunt. Luc. 2. 14.
units.tr: Moreover, here again we see that the Lord had no partner in the work of our redemption, but that all this praise and glory belongs to him alone; therefore we must take diligent care that the blood of the most excellent martyrs be not mingled with the blood of Christ. Further, just as our first parent, by his most shameful rebellion against God, deserved that all creatures should revolt from him, and indeed rise up against him, a punishment which God moderated as he pleased, so it was necessary that he who undertook and became surety for us should be deserted by all the rest, by one of his own who would betray him: so that through the obedience of him who suffered for our sins, all our debt being paid, we might be received into favour, as fellow citizens of the saints and members of God's household, Ephesians 2. 19., just as the angels sang clearly and resonantly at the birth of Christ. Luke 2. 14.

units.la: Praeterea certum est discipulos non tantum naturali timore perculsos imminentis periculi (qui cadere in quoslibet quum possit per se vitio caret, nisi quatenus affectiones nostrae peccant in excessu temper a medio recedentes) sed etiam illis adhaesisse diffidentiam in eo sane maiore dignis reprehensione, quod toties & tam longo ante tempore, fuisset de futuro certaminis iustius exitu laetissimo praemoniti, nec se orphanos derelictum iri: & praesertim longo illo sermone qui in ultima coena habitus
units.tr: Moreover, it is certain that the disciples were not only struck with the natural fear of the impending danger (which, since it can fall upon anyone, is in itself without fault, except insofar as our affections sin by excess, always departing from the mean), but also that distrust clung to them, which deserves all the greater reproach because they had been forewarned so often and so long before about the most joyful outcome of the coming conflict, and that they would not be left as orphans; and especially by that long discourse which was delivered at the last supper

units.la: Quae discipulorum Magistri sumum deferentium culpa fuerit: & quae ad nos inde redeat utilitas. tus à Iohan. à cap.14. vsque ad17. narratur. Sed ecce quid nobis fiat, etiam fortissimis. Nec tamen ideo qui cadit reiiciendus est: quin potius statuendum hodie infirmum, crastino die confirmatum Dei gratia fortiorem fore: quod Apostolis ipsis contigisse videmus, alios postea confirmante cuius inter ipsos lapsus fuerat grauissimus. Luc.22.32. Et revera, licet discipuli dispersi sint, duobus exceptis, de quibus paulo post dicturi sumus, se crucem tamen fugere non crucifixum satis superque testati sunt, quum non in suas aedes se receperint, aut in alium locum profugerint, sed in vrbem reuersi, vna etiam permanserint. Ex quibus satis conspicitur ipsos interius à Domino in sua illa infirmitate maxima sustentatos corroboratosque fuisse, & ita promissioni illi fidem fieri qua nos in omnibus tentationibus oportet erigi, Dominum nimirum, etsi alij aut sua ipsorum culpa, aut quòd expediat, incidant, in maiorem tentationem quàm alij, nunquam tamen permittere suos supra vires tentari. 1. Cor.13. & 2. Cor.4.8.
units.tr: What was the fault of the disciples who forsook their Master, and what benefit comes to us from it, is related in John from chapter 14 to 17. But see what happens to us, even the bravest. Yet he who falls is not therefore to be cast off. Rather, we should hold that one weak today will, by the grace of God, be strengthened tomorrow and become stronger. We see this happened to the Apostles themselves, who were later confirmed, though Peter's fall was the gravest among them (Luke 22:32). And indeed, although the disciples were scattered, with two exceptions of whom we shall speak shortly, they amply showed by not fleeing the cross once Christ was crucified: they did not retire to their own homes or flee to another place, but returned to the city and stayed together. From this it is sufficiently clear that they were sustained and strengthened inwardly by the Lord in that great weakness of theirs, and so the promise is fulfilled in which we ought to be lifted up in all temptations: that the Lord, although others fall through their own fault or as is expedient, never allows his own to be tempted beyond their strength (1 Cor. 13; 2 Cor. 4:8).

units.la: Sequitur apud Marcum iuuenem quendam (cuius nomen non exprimitur & de quo etiam magnopere laborandum non est, vt nec fit verisimile fuisse dilectu discipulu, tum eo quod in horto esset, qui Christus caperetur, tu propter ea quae deinceps dicuntur) his occurrisse, & quum essent eum prehensuri, nudum ex eorum manibus aufugisse, relicta sindone qua vna tegebatur. Additum hoc videtur ad horum indicandam petulantiam, quae saepe, grassante nimirum armorum licentia, longe lateque fertur. Quinetiam probabile est iltos in fugientes discipulos impetum fecisse: sed ex eorum manibus ereptos a Domino fuisse, quemadmodum & hunc iuuenem, qui ex lecto, ut verisimile est, audito nocturno tumultu excitatus, in vicum procurrerat. Nouum igitur hodie nobis videri non debet, si zeli & iustitiae praetextu, in persequendis calamitolis Dei filiis, lasciuia & petulantia passim grassantur.
units.tr: Next, in Mark, a certain young man (whose name is not given, and about whom we need not labour greatly, since it is not likely he was the beloved disciple, nor one who was in the garden when Christ was seized, for the reasons that follow) met them, and when they were about to seize him, slipped out of their hands naked, leaving behind the linen cloth in which he alone was wrapped. This seems to have been added to show the wantonness of these men, which, with the license of arms running rife, is commonly spread far and wide. Indeed, it is probable that they made an assault on the fleeing disciples, but that these were snatched from their hands by the Lord, just as this young man was, who, as is likely, had been roused from his bed by the nocturnal tumult and had run out into the street. It ought not, therefore, to seem strange to us today if, under the pretext of zeal and justice, wantonness and insolence run rife everywhere in persecuting the afflicted children of God.

units.la: Discamus vero vicissim, Dominum nihilominus ex eorum vnguibus quoscunque velit eripere: cuius rei frequentissima sunt exempla fugientibus aliis cum sarcinis & amictu: aliis cum sarcinarum parte, aliis denique nudis viram saltem incolumem retinentibus, quod huic iuueni contigisse videmus. Sed tamen quaecunque sors ferat, quisquis Iesum Christum induitus, reliqua permittit hostium libidini, nam ille veris diuitiis dives est, & hac tectus veste, longe Regum omnium principum ve, qualiber purpura felicior & insignior. Caducorum vero bonorum iacturam qua ratione se compensaturum Dominus promittat Marc.10.30. memores esse nos oportet: & contra, nihil cum elle lucratum, qui animae dispendio totum mundum lucratus fuerit. Matth.16.26. In primis vero quum res nobis sit cum hoste capitalissimo, Satana, Deum precemur ut nos eius faucibus eripiat, ut si nos vel toga, vel pallio, vel interiore tunica, paupertatis metu deterritos, aut bonorum & dignitatum iactura perculsos venetur, libenter ei praedam istam omnem concedentes,ad Dominum nudi confugiamus,in cuius domo potius eligamus, perennibus ipsius deliciis potari censeri inter minimos Pfalm. 84. 10. quàm in hoc mundo maximos honores adipisci.
units.tr: But let us learn in turn that the Lord nonetheless snatches from their claws whomever he wills. There are very many examples of this: some flee with their baggage and clothing, others with part of their baggage, and others at last naked, keeping only their life safe, as we see happened to this young man. Yet whatever fortune brings, whoever is clothed with Jesus Christ and leaves the rest to the lust of enemies is rich with true riches, and, covered by this garment, is more fortunate and more distinguished than the purple of any kings or princes. We ought to remember what recompense the Lord promises for the loss of perishable goods (Mark 10:30); and conversely, that he has gained nothing who has gained the whole world at the cost of his soul (Matt. 16:26). Above all, since we have to do with the most deadly enemy, Satan, let us pray God to snatch us from his jaws, so that if he hunts us down, frightened by fear of poverty or struck by the loss of goods and dignities, and seizes upon our cloak, our outer garment, or our inner tunic, we may willingly yield him all that booty and flee naked to the Lord. In his house let us rather choose to be made drink of his everlasting delights and to be counted among the least (Ps. 84:10), than to obtain the greatest honours in this world.

units.la: Pergamus ad iudicij formam, exiis quae à Iohanne memorantur,explicandam,duo quae-dam ab aliis Euangelistis omissa capita , dili-genter obseruante , quo nimirum Christus vinctus primùm deductus fit, quif-ve primus fuerit huius iudicij actus coram Summo Sa-cerdote. Ac primum quidem ad Annam de-ductus fuisse dicitur, quod eflet Socer Caia-phae: ex quo patet ordine nihil hic gestum. (Reum enim ad Caiapham primò deducî o-portuit & ibi de eius causa agi) sed in Annae gratiam Christum tam miserando habitu illi oblatum , cui non minus esset quàm eius ge-ner infensus:vtroque socero generóque,icele-ratis & flagitiosis hominibus, vt Iosephus Iu-daeus historicus, non suspectae fidei plurimis locis testatur. Ad quae aliam adde rationem, quae ex Marc.14.15. colligi potest,nimirum fa-ctum id tantisper dum apud Caiapham consi-lium cogeretur,quum pars sacerdotum & se-niorum etiam ipsi praesentes adfuissent Chri-ftum vincientibus, vt memoratur Luc. 22. 52. Hinc iterum apparet Iesum Christum quum vices nostras subierit, omne genus contume-liarum quas ipsi meriti eflemus,sponte pertu-
units.tr: Let us go on to explain the form of the judgment from what John records, observing carefully two points omitted by the other Evangelists: namely, where Christ was first led away bound, and who was the first to act in this trial before the High Priest. First, he is said to have been taken to Annas, because he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas. From this it is plain that nothing was done here in proper order, for the accused had to be taken first to Caiaphas and the case dealt with there. But Christ was presented to Annas, as a favour to him, in so pitiable a state, since Annas was no less hostile to him than his son-in-law was. Both father-in-law and son-in-law were wicked and shameful men, as the Jewish historian Josephus, whose credibility is not in doubt, attests in many places. To these add another reason, which can be gathered from Mark 14:15: this was done while the council was being assembled at Caiaphas' house, when some of the priests and elders were present in person, binding Christ, as is recorded in Luke 22:52. Hence again it appears that Jesus Christ, when he took upon himself our place, voluntarily underwent every kind of contumely which we ourselves had deserved.

units.la: q. iij. lisse, tanto quidem ad id à patre, tanquam vadem & sponsorem nostrum damnatum, quãto ipse clementius illud subiit iudicium, & à Iudæis indignius & detestabilius est exceptus. Ac sane talem etiamnum hodie mundum ergo se filij Dei experiuntur, vt ita membris cum suo capite pulchrè conueniat.
units.tr: So much the more readily did he undergo that judgment from the Father, as our surety and sponsor, condemned, as he endured it more mercifully and was received by the Jews more shamefully and detestably. Indeed, even today the children of God experience such a world for his sake, so that they agree fittingly with their head as members.

units.la: Porro leuiter prætereundum hoc loco non est quanto ardore iudices causam hanc egerint, vix expectato diluculo: quod quidem tã magna laude dignum esset, causa iusta si fuisset, quàm est furoris ipsorum aduersus innocentissimum & iustissimum omnium mortalium horrendum testimonium: qua in re nimium multos, proh dolor! imitatores habent, de quibus olim etiam est Propheta conquestus his verbis, Pedes eorum ad malum currunt, & ad humanum fundendum sanguinem festinant, cogitationes eorum, cogitationes iniquæ. Esa. 59. 7. At tamen ab iniquis iustis iudicibus tã in suo scelere diligentibus coarguuntur, qui scientes prudentes, seu malitia seu negligentia lites in diem extrahunt, seu in iudices, seu in litigantes, procuratores & aduocatos, seu denique tabulas istius mali culpa reiiciatur: iusto Dei iudicio sic mundum castigante vt maxima pars aliorum fouendis litibus & controuersiis viuat: & bonæ leges ad lites præueniendas, vel si exortæ fuerint mature compescendas latæ, quorundam quidem malitia, aliorum autem nefariis dolis ac praua conscientia, causis etiam liquidissimis obscuran-
units.tr: Nor should we pass lightly over how eagerly the judges pursued this cause, scarcely waiting for daybreak. Indeed, this would deserve as much praise as a just cause would, if it had been just; but it is a dreadful witness to their rage against the most innocent and most righteous of all mortals. In this matter, alas, they have far too many imitators, of whom the Prophet long ago complained in these words: "Their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed innocent blood; their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity" (Isa. 59:7). Yet even so, those who, knowingly and deliberately, prolong lawsuits into the day, whether through malice or negligence, whether the fault lies with judges, litigants, procurators or advocates, or finally with the records themselves, are convicted by just judges who themselves delight in their own wickedness. Thus God in his just judgment chastises the world so that the greater part of men live by stirring up lawsuits and controversies. Good laws were enacted to forestall lawsuits, or, if they had arisen, to curb them early; but through the malice of some and the wicked tricks and crooked consciences of others, even the clearest causes are obscured, judges' sentences are entangled, unjust trials are conducted under the pretext of equity, and litigants are finally drained of their money.

units.la: ludices in causis di iudicem dis nun-quam sa-tis magna adhibere diligentia possint. randis, iudicum sententiis implicandis, æquitatis prætextu iudiciis iniquis regendis, litigantibus denique sumptibus exhauriendis inseruiant. Vtinam verò atque vtinam Dei verbum in nostras conscientias tantùm posset, vt qui hæc saltem in causarum decisionibus animaduertunt, & in rabulas istiusmodi & iuris corruptores potestatem habent, serió tandem de his rebus cogitarent, vt de nobis conquerendi merito nullus locus relinqueretur. Nec tamen ex istis efficitur, quaslibet lites, aut crimina posse diei vel noctis vnius spatio, sicut ab istis factum est, componi ac decidi: Verissimum enim illud prouerbium, Stulti iudicis, breue iudicium. Nihilominus danda est opera vt lites quæ si fieri posset vel in exortu essent suffocandæ, sine mora componantur ac penitus amputentur.
units.tr: Would that, and would that the Word of God could prevail in our consciences so far, that those who at least notice these things in deciding cases, and who have power over such pettifoggers and corrupters of the law, would at last think seriously about these matters, so that no proper ground for complaint against us would remain! Yet it does not follow from these things that any lawsuits or crimes can be composed and settled within the space of one day or night, as was done by these men. For the proverb is very true: "The judgment of a fool is brief." Nevertheless, effort must be made that lawsuits, which would be stifled at their birth if that were possible, be settled without delay and entirely cut out.

units.la: Cæterum inter Iudices primum hic fit mentio Maximi Pontificis, vt spiritualis iurisdictionis principis: immo & temporalis quantum quidem eis per Romanos licebat, non quòd ita Dominus Lege sua constituisset, qua iudiciorum hæ species distinguuntur & ab ipso Domino diuersis personis assignantur. Docet enim historia Exod. 18. 23. & 21. Moses ciuili regendæ politiæ præpositum: quod in eo qui Sabbathum violarat puniendo nominatim est conspicuum. Num. 15. 33. & in blasphematore, quatenus eratvtrumq; istud crimen Lege tum ciuili tum spirituali capitale, Leuit. 24. 11. Aaronem verò cum reliquis sacerdotibus de rebus mundis aut immundis, & aliis rebus spiritualibus & ad Dei cultum pertinentibus iudicabit. Verum tamen quod Leges ciuiles libris Moisis continerentur, quarum erant interpretes Leuitae ac Sacerdotes, in casibus dubiis agnosco fuisse consulendos Sacerdotes & Leuitas, qui in rebus occultis & controuersis verum Legis sensum & vsum aperiebant. Deut. 17.8. Denique distinctas fuisse iurisdictiones illas & iudices olim, ex eo ordine quem Iosaphatus restituit, maxime conspicuum est. 2. Chron.19.18.
units.tr: Furthermore, among judges the first mention here is of the chief Pontiff, as prince of spiritual jurisdiction; indeed of temporal jurisdiction too, as far as the Romans allowed them. This was not because the Lord had so established it by his law, in which the kinds of judgments are distinguished and assigned by the Lord himself to different persons. For history teaches (Exod. 18:23 and 21) that Moses was set over the civil governance. This is most clearly seen in the punishment of the man who violated the Sabbath (Num. 15:33), and of the blasphemer, inasmuch as both crimes were capital under both civil and spiritual law (Lev. 24:11). But Aaron, with the other priests, would judge concerning clean and unclean things and other spiritual matters pertaining to the worship of God. Yet, that the civil laws were contained in the books of Moses, whose interpreters were the Levites and priests, I grant: in doubtful cases the priests and Levites were to be consulted, and they, in obscure and disputed matters, unfolded the true sense and use of the Law (Deut. 17:8). Finally, that those jurisdictions and judges were distinct in former times is most evident from the order Jehoshaphat restored (2 Chron. 19:8).

units.la: At ex quo Macchabaei, quos vocat, vtramq; iurisdictione tibi arrogarunt, & ab Herodis magni morte, filiisque eius Archelai, redacta a Romanis in prouinciam Iudaeam, qui fuit eius status Pilati quibus haec cōrigerunt temporibus, Iudaeis Romani permiserant tum iudicandi de rebus in ipsorum religione controuersis, tum etiam ordinaria iustitiae potestate, puta in vincula coiiciendi, quod olim Paulo dum adhuc in Ecclesia fuerat munus delegatum, Act.9.2. & quidem cum moderata coercitione, vt verberu, ad triginta nouem vsque plagas ex Legis praescripto. Deut. 25.3.2. Cor.11 24. sed non capite plectendi, vt suo loco videbimus. Ex illorum igitur temporum vsu, praesertim vero quod de doctrina quaereretur, nihil ab iis peccatu est, Christu falsae doctrinae & blasphemiae, atque adeo impietatis accusatum, adducetibus ad Pontificem Maximum, cou ocatis aliis Sacerdotibus ac Scribis, id est Legis doctoribus, & aliis populi gubernā bernatorib* quos Scniores dicebat, ex quibus septuaginta virorū confiliū maius cōstabat,vt scriptū est Num.ii.16.& Deut.i.15 Et hæc quidem de istorum iudicum potestate hactenus, de quibus aliquid etiā deinc epsdicturi sumus.
units.tr: But from the time when the Maccabees, as they are called, claimed both jurisdictions for themselves, and after the death of Herod the Great and his son Archelaus, when Judaea was reduced by the Romans to a province (which was the state of affairs in Pilate's time), the Romans permitted the Jews both to judge matters disputed within their own religion and to exercise ordinary judicial power, that is, to cast people into prison. This was once a commission given to Paul while he was still in the Church (Acts 9:2). The punishment was moderate, such as beating, up to thirty-nine blows according to the prescription of the Law (Deut. 25:3; 2 Cor. 11:24), but not capital punishment, as we shall see in its place. From the practice of those times, especially since the inquiry concerned doctrine, nothing was done by them amiss. Christ was accused of false doctrine and blasphemy, and so of impiety, and was brought before the High Priest, with the other priests and scribes (that is, teachers of the Law) and the other rulers of the people, whom he called elders, of whom the council of seventy men was made up (as it is written, Num. 11:16; Deut. 1:15). So far concerning the power of these judges, of which we shall say something further later.

units.la: At minime leuiter prætereundum quod notat Iohannes,Caiaphām fuisse Pontificem Maximum illius anni: sic enim notatur abusus intolerandus, qui paulatim in hunc populum irrepserat. Nam Lege Dei sacerdotium vita non anno finiebatur: at in ipsos Sacerdotes tum auaritia tum ambitio tanta vi grassabantur, vt tam pretiosum & sacrosanctum munus, quo verum, vnicum & æternum Ecclesiæ caput adumbrabatur, passim esset vænale, vt ipse Josephus temporum illorum historicus testatur.
units.tr: Nor should it be passed over lightly that John notes that Caiaphas was High Priest of that year. For thus is marked the intolerable abuse which had gradually crept into this people. By the Law of God the priesthood was not limited to a year. But avarice and ambition raged among the priests themselves with such force that so precious and sacred an office, by which the true, only and eternal Head of the Church was foreshadowed, was everywhere for sale, as Josephus himself, the historian of those times, testifies.

units.la: En igitur imaginem illius horrendæ confusionis, quæ in Ecclesiam Christianam inuesta pedetentim, tam altas radem egit radices, Romanorum Episcoporum,& eorum quos in orbe Christiano fautores habent partim auaritia,partim ambitione, vt nonnili solius Dei potentis manu posse conuelli videatur. Primum enim sibi præter omne ius humanum ac diuinum secularis gladij potestatem, etiam in omnes Reges & Dominatores arrogarunt: deinde, spirituale ius passim vænale est, etiam editis & diuulgatis pretiorum libellis: tertiò denique, postquam imitati Caiaphæ & suorum exemplum, omnem mouerunt lapidem, sed irrito conatu, vt partim vi aperta, partim etiam dolis & per cuniculos, Euangelicæ veritatis cursum remorarentur, tandem ad illa sua Concilia tanquam ad sacram anchoram recurrunt, in quibus actorum & iudicum partes sustineant, quod nostro seculo nimium experti sumus. Sed longe adhuc ab iis peccatur grauius quàm sit à Caiapha peccatum. Erat enim tum Pontificis Maximi, tum aliorum Sacerdotû, Seniorúmq; populi, tum septuaginta virorû munus ac dignitas instituta ab ipso Domino, adeò vt ipsis non res ipsa, sed abusus vitio verti deberet. At vbi quæso vel in sacris, vel in tota vetere Ecclesia verè Apostolica istum Papatus Romani, Cardinalium, Primatum, Archiepiscoporum, imò & Episcoporum gradum reperias? Nam in tribus illis, vltimum Episcopi nomen in Ecclesia Apostolica, cum Paltoris nomine commune erat, diceba-turque sui gregis, non autem collegarum ac συμπρεσβυτέρων respectu. Archiepiscoporum verò & qui deinde nati sunt Primatum nomina, non dignitatis aut superioris potestatis fuerunt, quasi alij aliis præesse nt, sed tantum ordinis causa sunt inuecta ad confusionem in coetibus Ecclesiasticis euitandam.
units.tr: Here, then, is an image of that horrible confusion which, once introduced into the Christian Church, took root so deeply, through the avarice and ambition of the Roman bishops and of those whom they have as supporters in the Christian world, that it seems it can be uprooted only by the mighty hand of God alone. For first, they have claimed for themselves, beyond all human and divine right, the power of the secular sword, even over all kings and rulers. Second, spiritual jurisdiction is everywhere for sale, even with price lists published and circulated. Third and finally, after imitating Caiaphas and his men, they have moved every stone, though with futile effort, to delay the course of evangelical truth, partly by open force and partly by tricks and underground mines. At last they run back to their councils as to a sacred anchor, in which they play both the parts of actors and of judges, as we have experienced too much in our own century. Yet a far graver sin is committed by them than was committed by Caiaphas. For the office and dignity of the High Priest, of the other priests, of the elders of the people and of the seventy men were instituted by the Lord himself, so that the fault should lie not in the thing itself but in its abuse. But where, I ask, in the sacred writings or in the whole ancient and truly Apostolic Church, will you find that Papal rank of the Roman See, the Cardinals, the Primates, the Archbishops, and even the rank of bishops? Among these, the last name, that of Bishop, was in the Apostolic Church common with the name of minister (pastor), and was used of a man's own flock, not with regard to his fellow-presbyters [συμπρεσβυτέρων]. But the names of Archbishop and Primate, which came later, were not names of dignity or superior power, as if some were to preside over others. They were introduced merely for the sake of order, to avoid confusion in Church assemblies.

units.la: Verùm his omissis ad eam iudicij formam accedamus quàm in Christo Domino nostro iudicando secuti sunt. Vbi sumus iterum visuri quàm pulchrè inter se conformes sint ij de quibus aliquid attigimus. Primùm igitur interrogatur Christus: deinde audiuntur testes: tertiò denique quum neque Christi respon-sum,
units.tr: But let these matters be set aside, and let us come to that form of judgment which they followed in judging Christ our Lord. Here we shall again see how beautifully the things we have touched upon agree with one another. First, Christ is questioned; then witnesses are heard; thirdly, when neither Christ's answer nor the testimony of the witnesses is sufficient to decide the cause, Christ is compelled to deny or affirm categorically what he is asked.

units.la: Iudicii for mam Caiapha ad uersus Christum, hodie in-stificant Papa sum, neque testium fidem ad causam diiudi- candam sufficerent, cogitur Christus catego-ricè quod rogatur negare vel affirmare. Quid in hac iudicij forma requiras? Nihil sanè, nisi priùs quàm in eum manus iniicerent diligen-tiorem inquisitionem. At quò maior extrinse-cus apparet iuris æquitas, tantò iniquior isto-rum animus & voluntas: quanquam hocipso facto quantumuis iniqui iudices nostri tem-poris Caiaphas coarguunt, furorum Gallico-rum & lanienæ illius horrendæ auctores ac promotores, qui diu præmeditata bella ciui-lia tandem non sine maximo passim horrore pepererunt, & quidem sanctæ Religionis Ca-tholicæ prætextu, quàm Romanæ titulo con-uenienter adornant. Nec enim esse Christiana potest quæ publicam fidem violare docet, quę sanguinem innoxium sine discrimine & causę cognitione, quo vel ipsi fluuij tingantur, fun-dere: quæ denique proprium Regem nefario scelere trucidare, quæ passim istius flagitij pi-cturas venditare, quæ grassatores indigetare summæ sibi laudi ducit.
units.tr: What would you look for in this form of judgment? Nothing indeed, except that before they laid hands on him they should have made a more careful inquiry. But the greater the appearance of legal fairness on the outside, the more unjust the mind and will of these men. Yet by this very deed, however unjust our judges of today may be, they convict Caiaphas: they are the authors and promoters of the French fury and that horrible slaughter, which, after long premeditated civil wars, has brought forth, not without the greatest horror everywhere, and indeed under the pretext of the holy Catholic Religion, which they suitably adorn with the Roman title. For that cannot be Christian which teaches the violation of public faith, which teaches the shedding of innocent blood without distinction and without examination of the cause, so that even the rivers are stained with it; which finally teaches the wicked slaughter of one's own King; which everywhere offers for sale pictures of this crime; and which considers it the highest praise to call on assassins.

units.la: Caiaphas igitur Dominum superipsius doc-trina, & discipulis, non tantùm tanquam sal-sæ doctrinæ reum, sed etiam seditionis auto-rem & partium in Ecclesia principem inter-rogat. Verùm annon illi inter se dissidebant in religionis etiam præcipuis capitibus? annon etiam singulæ sectæ suos fouebant discipulos? Nam Sadducæi mortuorum resurrectionem negabant, immo nec Angelos vllos nec Spiritus agnoscebat. At fatebantur utrumque Pharisaei. Act.23.8. Sed tamen illi praeter suas traditiones & falsas expositiones quibus Dei mandata faciebant irrita. Matth.15.3. & Marc.7.v. 3.& 4.gratuitae iustificationis articulum & verum cultus ceremonialis vsum adulterabant. Rom. 10.3. Quid alia ex parte Effeni, nonne suos ritus & suum caelibatum religionis ac fidei suae fundamentum subsisternebat? Ad horum autem exemplar Monachos efformatos fuisse certissimum est. Herodianos autem, Nazarenos & istius farinae multos alios omitto: quae sectae tamen tolerabantur, quod omnes circumcisionem & cultum in templo Domini praeferrent. Talis eorum est hodie, qui se Ecclesiae Christianae columnas vocant, concordia, consentientibus nimirum inter se in Papa, Missa & auriculari confessione veneran-dis. Quos tamen siquis iubeat sigillatim, fidem suam & eiusdem fundamentum ore vel scripto profiteri, (licet eorum tamen maxima pars vix unquam de vllo fidei articulo serio cogitarit,) quot ex iis, quos clamosissimos experimur aduersarios, hic haerere, magis mutos quam piscs reperias? Quam vero multis repugnantibus opinionibus implicita fides quam iactant inuoluta conspiceretur? Doctores ipsos quod attinet, (in quibus nisi mentiri velis, caue recenseas vel Episcopos vel Sacrificulorum maximam partem) aquam potius igni quam inter se Scholasticos doctores concilia-veris. In vno tamen capite, persequenda nimirum
units.tr: Caiaphas therefore questions the Lord about his own teaching and his disciples, asking him not only as one guilty of false doctrine, but also as the author of sedition and the leader of factions in the Church. But were they not themselves at odds with one another even on the chief heads of religion? Did not each sect also foster its own disciples? For the Sadducees denied the resurrection of the dead, and acknowledged neither angels nor spirits, whereas the Pharisees confessed both (Acts 23:8). Yet the Pharisees, besides their own traditions and false expositions by which they made God's commandments void (Matt. 15:3; Mark 7:3–4), corrupted the article of free justification and the true use of ceremonial worship (Rom. 10:3). And what of the Essenes? Did they not uphold their rites and their celibacy as the foundation of their religion and faith? It is quite certain that monks were modelled on their pattern. I pass over the Herodians, the Nazarenes and many others of that kind; yet these sects were tolerated, because all of them upheld circumcision and worship in the Temple of the Lord. Such is today the harmony of those who call themselves the pillars of the Christian Church, agreeing among themselves in venerating the Pope, the Mass and auricular confession. Yet if anyone ordered them one by one to profess their faith and its foundation, orally or in writing (although the greater part of them has hardly ever seriously thought about any article of faith), how many of those whom we experience as the most clamorous adversaries would you find sticking here, more mute than fish? How many conflicting opinions would be seen in the implicit faith which they boast of, once it was unwrapped? As for the teachers themselves (among whom, unless you wish to lie, beware of counting either the bishops or the greater part of the sacrificing priests), you would sooner reconcile water with fire than reconcile the Scholastic doctors with one another. On one point, however, namely the persecuting of the truth and the crucifying of Christ daily in his wretched members, I confess that they agree splendidly with one another,

units.la: rum rũ veritate, & Christo quotidie in miseris suis membris crucifigendo fateor illos inter se pulchrè cósentire, tantisper dum Dominus, qui vete ris populi discordias vi & efficacia Euangelij compescuit, idem in orbe Christiano pro sin- gulari suo fauore & gratia tandem efficiat.
units.tr: for as long as the Lord, who by the power and efficacy of the Gospel restrained the discords of the old people, does not likewise bring this about in the Christian world, by his singular favour and grace.

units.la: Christi verò responsum haud satis appositum hic videatur, sed imitatus potius vitiligatores, qui nec rem de qua agitur attingant, ambages quaerunt, fucúmque multis inciden- tibus faciunt: rem sanè peßimam, tátum abest vt de Christo dici possit ex quo nos candorem & simplicitatem oportet ediscere. Cur ego, dicat aliquis, non copiosè & perspicuè de sua doctrina respondit? Primùm, quòd noßet minimè istud Caiapham discédi animo percontari, sed tantùm vt haberet vndè suis calumniis & falsis criminationibus fucum faceret, tandémque morti addiceret, vt tandem factum eßt, Christo de se clarè quod erat profitente.
units.tr: Christ's answer, however, may seem not quite to the point here. But this is because he imitated, not those who quarrel, who neither touch the matter in question, but seek circumlocutions and make a smokescreen of many incidental points. That is a truly very bad thing, and so far is it from being said of Christ, from whom we ought to learn candour and simplicity. Why, someone may say, did he not answer fully and clearly about his teaching? First, because he knew that Caiaphas did not ask with a mind to learn, but only so that he would have material to make a show of his calumnies and false accusations, and finally hand him over to death, as indeed came to pass, Christ clearly professing about himself what he was.

units.la: Hic verò diligenter observandum, oportere quidem nos semper esse paratos ad respondendum cuilibet petenti rationem eius spei quae in nobis est, cum lenitate & reuerentia, 1.Pet.3.15. sed vt hoc casu Dei gloriam & proximi salutem cordi nostro & linguae, praeire oportet cum sancta confidentia, sic etiam quando nobis cum canibus & porcis, quales illi fuerunt, res est, non esse illis res sacras, temerè proiiciendas: nec dandam dilaniandi nos occasionem: sed adhibendam, praeeuntibus iis quae attigimus, sanctâ prudetiam, qua noßram simplicitate iubet Dominus tem̃perari. Matt. 10.16. & 17. cuius exemplum in Apostolo memorabile nobis exhibetur. Act.23.6.
units.tr: Here, however, we must carefully observe that we ought always to be ready to give an account of the hope that is in us to anyone who asks, with gentleness and reverence (1 Pet. 3:15). But in this case, where the glory of God and our neighbour's salvation must come before our heart and tongue with holy confidence, we must also recognise that when we have to deal with dogs and swine, such as they were, holy things must not be cast rashly before them, nor should we give them an occasion to tear us apart. Instead, following the points we have touched on, we must apply that holy prudence with which the Lord bids us temper our simplicity (Matt. 10.16. & 17.), whose memorable example is set before us in the Apostle (Act. 23.6.).

units.la: Deinde quum se hic stitisset Dominus, non absoluendum, vt merebatur, sed tanquam sponsorem & vadem nostrum condemnandum, nec sanctam illam seueritatem adhibere voluit, qua prius missos à Pontificibus & Pharisaeis qui ipsum comprehenderent obstupefactos coercuerat. Ioh.7.46. & auditorum suorum corda inflammauit.Luc.24 32.nec vim illam diuinam qua ipsos satellites humi verbo solo deiecerat. Ioh.18.6. sed alias penitus conticuit, alias etiam loquutus est, sed parce & sobrie, ob eam quam supra diximus causam.
units.tr: Then, when the Lord had stood before them, he did not seek acquittal, as he deserved, but was condemned as our surety and bail. Nor did he use that holy severity by which he had earlier struck down, and left astonished, the men sent by the chief priests and Pharisees to seize him (John 7:46), and which had inflamed the hearts of his hearers (Luke 24:32). Nor did he use that divine power by which he had cast the guards to the ground with a word alone (John 18:6). Rather, in some respects he kept entirely silent, and in others he did speak, but sparingly and soberly, for the reason we mentioned above.

units.la: Nec se tamen etiam vllo suffugio tutatus est, à suorum auditorum testimonia totus pendes. Alterû vero caput illud de discipulis, quo tanquam factionis princeps & quidè clandestinus accusabatur, aperte & expresse pernegauit, afferuerans contrà se palàm docuisse, quolibet, qui vellet audiente: quin etiam se Synagogis interfuisse & in ipso templo, adeò vt manifesta calumnia premeretur.
units.tr: Yet he did not shelter himself by any refuge at all, but relied wholly on the testimony of his hearers. As for the other charge, that concerning his disciples, by which he was accused as the leader of a faction and indeed a secret one, he flatly and expressly denied it. He affirmed that on the contrary he had taught openly, before anyone who wished to listen, and that he had been present in the synagogues and in the temple itself, so that he was pressed by a manifest calumny.

units.la: Quod sane non tam sui tuendi, quàm doctrinæ & discipulorum à crimine afferendorum causa protulit. At, dicat aliquis, quinam quod dicit Christus, se nihil secreto docuisse cum eo conuenient, quòd ipse in aurem illis se loquutum esse testatus est Matth.10.27.& cum parabolarum explicatione familiari & domestica, ftica, Matth.13.11? Optimè. Nec enim hoc di-ctum voluit, se nusquam nisi publicè docuis-se,aut in templo & synagogis:tot enim priua-tim conciones,atque in primis excellentes illi sermones extrema cœna ad discipulos habiti refragantur:sed se doctrinarū duo genera, priuatum discipulorum,aliud verò publicum habuisse negauit.
units.tr: He brought this forward indeed not so much for his own defence as for the sake of clearing his teaching and his disciples of the charge. But someone will say: how do the words of Christ agree with his claim that he had taught nothing in secret, when he testified that he spoke in their ear (Matt. 10:27), and gave a familiar and domestic explanation of the parables (Matt. 13:11)? Very well. He did not mean that he had taught nowhere except publicly, in the temple and the synagogues. For the many private discourses, and especially those excellent sermons delivered to the disciples at the last supper, refute that. What he denied was that he had two kinds of teaching, one private for his disciples and another public.

units.la: Quo refellitur iterum eorum falsa & diabolica traditio, qui vulgus imperitū à lectione sacrorum,lingua vernacula præsertim, arcent: libenter persuasuri veram theologiam (quæ cognitio est eorum quæ à nobis fieri vel credi debent,) solis suis scholis deberi, in quibus tamè impudetius & impurius quàm vsquâ sacra adulterantur. Quasi verò Moses aliiqué omnes Prophetæ non loquuti sint & scriptis oracula sua mandarint, lingua Dei populo vulgari:quasi denique nõ essent libri Mosis ac Prophetarum in singulis synagogis frequenti vitorum ac mulierum sexus omnis concione præleƈti, addita etiam per singula sabbata familiari interpretatione: quasi denique Christus ipse, sicut hic aperte testatur, non palàm omnibus indistinctè patris sui voluntatem,pa tefcifset: quasi denique frustrà vel temerè suis-set illud elogium cruci tribus linguis, tum in orbe toto præcipuis affixum, Hebræa, Græca, Latina: quasi denique non essent hoc exemplum Apostoli sequuti, in suis Ecclesiis tum loquendo tum scribendo, Græcè Græcis, Latinè Latinis, sicut Hebræis Hebraicè, & sic deinceps? effuso etiam in Apostolos primùm lin-guarum dono, deinde in alios plerosque, vt in coetibus illis vterentur, sed non nisi adhibito interprete, sicut expresse declarat Apostolus, &multis inuictis rationibus euincit. 1.Cor.14. tantùm abest vt tunc Ecclesiastici coetus Deo cantilenis & quidem peregrina lingua decantatis satisfactum putarent, vix illis ipsis cogni-ta qui totum Dei cultum in istiusmodi rithmos commutarunt, quorum alij ex centonibus Scripturarum miserè laceratorum constant, alij autem, paucissimis exceptis, non tantùm ineptiarum & barbarici, sed quòd longè peius est, impietatis & blasphemiarum pleni sunt.
units.tr: By this, their false and diabolical tradition is refuted again. They keep the unlearned common people from reading the sacred books, especially in the vernacular, and willingly persuade them that true theology (which is the knowledge of what we must do or believe) is owed only to their own schools, where nevertheless they corrupt sacred things more shamelessly and impurely than anywhere else. As if Moses and all the prophets had not spoken, and committed their oracles to writing, in the language of God's people, the common tongue. As if the books of Moses and the Prophets were not read in every synagogue, in the frequent assembly of men and women of every sex, with a familiar interpretation added on every Sabbath. As if Christ himself, as he openly testifies here, had not openly and without distinction made his Father's will known to all. As if that inscription fixed to the cross in three languages, Hebrew, Greek and Latin, the chief languages of the whole world, had been set up in vain or rashly. As if the Apostle had not followed this example, speaking and writing in his churches, in Greek to Greeks, in Latin to Latins, in Hebrew to Hebrews, and so on. Even though the gift of tongues was poured out first on the Apostles and then on many others, so that they might use it in those assemblies, yet they used it only with an interpreter present, as the Apostle expressly declares and proves by many unanswerable arguments (1 Cor. 14). So far were the ecclesiastical assemblies then from thinking that God was satisfied with songs, sung in a foreign tongue scarcely known even to those who turned the whole worship of God into such rhymes. Some of these consist of cento-patchworks of Scripture miserably torn apart; others, with very few exceptions, are full not only of silliness and barbarism but, what is far worse, of impiety and blasphemy.

units.la: Atque hic nosiisdem quibus superiùs adueꝛsariis respondere, locus monet, criminan-tibus quòd prædicemus in occulto sub caminis, vt aiunt, & hunc aduersum nos locum, sed parùm appositè torquentibus, quum Christū non minùs priuatim quàm publicè docuisse, sit extra omnem controuersiam. Cur igitur, inquiunt aduersarij, templa nostra & scholas non acceditis? Non minùs impudenter sanè, quàm si latrones de viatoribus quererentur, quòd ad sibi paratas insidias vitandas alio de-flexissent, & in ius illos idcirco traheret. Nam, obsecro, quis vnquam latro tam crudeliter in vitam & facultates viatorum grassatus est, quàm in eos isti sæuierunt, quos inauditos & indemnatos pro terrerrimis habent hæreticis? Pseudoprophetarum igitur agnosco lubens esse proprium clam spargere falsam doctrinā, & latebras lucis inimicas seducendis hominibus apertissimas quaerere, qui sane pro merito caltigandi sunt & coercendi, tum censuris Ecclesiasticis, tum, si erit opus, poenis & suppliciis convenientibus, ut ipse Dominus in Lege sua diligenter cavit. Deut. 13. Sed in primis legitimum examen doctrinae praecat ex sacris Scripturis, ut siqua subest in doctoribus ignorantia, ex ipsis sacris docentur: si vero malitia & pertinacia peccaverint, ab Ecclesia separentur, ut monet Apostolus. 1. Tim. 1. 20. Galat. 5. 12. Tit. 3. 10. Tale igitur quidpiam in nobis probent adversarij, aut cuiusipsorum calumnia patefiat. Quid enim contra magis efflagitamus quam ut liberè nobis convenicndi docendique palam potestas fieret? Quid vero magis & quidem ex professo prohibuerunt, & pro viribus impedierunt? Nihil enim revera magis quam lucem odit mendacium. Caeterum, non ubique locorum Ecclesiae Christianae ab arcanis coetibus initium fecerunt. Annon enim obsecro, quos Deus in Germania & Helvetia nostro tempore suscitavit, ut erroribus & impostoris, quae pedetentim in Ecclesiam Christianam irrepserant, sese viriliter opponerent, publicis disputationibus & scriptis aediis coram Imperatoribus, Principibus & Statibus Ecclesiae causam egerunt? Quid? an defuerunt qui in media Sorbona, & aliis Academiis, vel locis Galliarum celeberrimis veritatem intrepide promulgarent? Idem etiam
units.tr: Here too the place bids us reply to the same adversaries as above. They accuse us of preaching in secret, under the hearth, as they say, and they twist this passage against us, though too little to the point, since it is beyond all controversy that Christ taught privately no less than publicly. "Why then," the adversaries say, "do you not come to our temples and schools?" This is no less shameless than if robbers should complain about travellers because the travellers had turned aside to avoid the ambushes laid for them, and on that account dragged them to court. For, I ask you, what robber ever raged so cruelly against the lives and property of travellers as these men have raged against those whom they hold, unheard and uncondemned, to be the most terrible heretics? I therefore gladly acknowledge that it is the mark of false prophets to spread false doctrine in secret and to seek hiding places hostile to the light, so as to deceive men. Such men indeed deserve to be punished and restrained, both by ecclesiastical censures and, if need be, by fitting penalties and punishments, as the Lord himself carefully provided for in his Law (Deut. 13). But first, the lawful test of doctrine is to be made from the sacred Scriptures, so that if there is ignorance in the teachers, they may be taught from the sacred texts themselves. If they have sinned through malice and obstinacy, they are to be separated from the Church, as the Apostle warns (1 Tim. 1:20; Gal. 5:12; Titus 3:10). Let the adversaries, then, prove something of this kind in us, or let some calumny of theirs be exposed. For what do we demand more urgently than the freedom to meet and teach openly? What have they, on the other hand, forbidden more expressly, and hindered with all their might? Indeed, lies hate nothing so much as light. Moreover, the Christian churches did not everywhere begin from secret assemblies. Did not those whom God raised up in our own time in Germany and Switzerland, to oppose manfully the errors and impostures that had crept little by little into the Christian Church, plead their cause publicly, by disputations and by writings published before the Emperors, Princes and Estates? What of those who, in the very Sorbonne and in other academies, or in the most famous places of France, fearlessly proclaimed the truth? The same may be said of other nations as well.

units.la: j. de aliis Gentibus dictum esto. At si legitimus aliquando metus horrendæ crudelitatis & omnis generis iniustitiæ (cuius rei pseudoconsilium illud Constantiense contra ius omne diuinum humanumque, violata fide publica & manifesto periurio, luculentum præbet testimonium) Dei fideles seruos adegit, non vt vocationem abiicerent, sed vt suum cuiusque saluti consulerent, quis illos merito reprehendat, aut etiā culpauerit de eo quod Christus ipse docuit Matth.10.v.16.&17. & ipsemet suo exemplo confirmauit? Matt.4.11.& tota Hierosolymorum Ecclesia? Act.12.12.atque adeo vetus ipsa sub regibus Israëlis Ecclesia, puta sub Achabo & aliis persecutoribus: & Ecclesia Christiana ante Constantini magni tempora, testibus ipsis antris & speluncis in quas conuenientes Christianos etiam feri isti leones & imminanes tigres venabantur. Quid verò dicam de tot viris insignibus, qui veritatem non modò prædicarunt, sed suo sanguine obsignarunt, minimè quidem in ligneis aut lapideis pulpitis, sed in pyris & rogis in quibus pro veritate cum flammis ad vltimum vsque spiritum prædicantes dimicarunt & victoriam fortiter occumbendo reportarunt? Quæ verò natio, immo quæ ciuitas hodie talibus præconibus non gloriatur? Sed frustrà surdis canitur. Agite verò iam, fratres, serió meditemur, vt ab initio diximus, in hoc exemplo quoque Redemptorem nostrum peccata nostra deduxerint, ea vt oderimus & detestemur: quoquousque fe magnus ille noster Redemptor nostri causa demiserit iutucamur, vt eum ex animo diligamus ac veneremur. Quanta fit improborum nequitia, & quàm late serpat contemplemur, in quibus sæpius accidere videmus, vt siue ex Magistratibus, siue Ecclesiasticis ij sint omniù pessimi & detestabiles, quos mederi confusis rebus oportuerat. Denique Deum ardentibus votis oremus, vt quam à suis constantiam ac magnanimitatem requirit eandem ipse nobis largiatur: vt res omnes sine exceptione, atque adeò vitam nostram, eius sacrosanđti nominis honori atque glorię postponamus. Amen.
units.tr: But if at any time a lawful fear of dreadful cruelty and every kind of injustice (of which the pseudo-council of Constance, against all divine and human law, with public faith violated and manifest perjury, offers a clear proof) has driven the faithful servants of God, not to abandon their calling, but to look to the safety of each one, who could rightly blame them, or find fault with them, for doing what Christ himself taught (Matt. 10.v.16.&17.) and confirmed by his own example (Matt. 4.11.), and what the whole Church of Jerusalem did (Act. 12.12.)? Indeed, the ancient Church under the kings of Israel, namely under Ahab and other persecutors, did the same, and so did the Christian Church before the times of Constantine the Great, with the very caves and dens as witnesses, into which the gathering Christians were hunted even by those fierce lions and menacing tigers. But what shall I say of so many famous men who not only preached the truth but sealed it with their blood? They did this not in wooden or stone pulpits, but in fires and on pyres, where, preaching for the truth, they fought with the flames to their last breath and won the victory by dying bravely. What nation, indeed what city, does not today glory in such heralds? But it is sung in vain to the deaf. Come now, brothers, let us seriously meditate, as we said at the beginning, on how in this example also our Redeemer has set our sins before us, so that we may hate and detest them; and on how far that great Redeemer has humbled himself for our sake, so that we may love and revere him from the heart. Let us consider how great the wickedness of the wicked is and how widely it creeps, since we often see that those who are the worst and most detestable, whether among the magistrates or the ecclesiastics, are the very men who ought to have remedied disordered affairs. Finally, let us pray to God with ardent vows that he will bestow on us the same constancy and magnanimity that he requires from his own, so that we may set all things without exception, and so our very lives, after the honour and glory of his most holy name. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA duodecima.
units.tr: Homily twelve.

units.la: MATTH. 26.
units.tr: MATT. 26.

units.la: 59. Principes autem Sacerdotum & Seniores & totus consessus quærebant falsum testimonium contra Iesum, vt eum morte multarent.
units.tr: 59. Now the chief priests and the elders and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus, that they might put him to death.

units.la: 60. Et non invenerunt: etiam quum multi falsi testes accessissent, non invenerunt. Postremo verò adnenientes duo falsi testes,
units.tr: 60. And they found none, though many false witnesses came in. At last, however, two false witnesses came forward,

units.la: 61. Dixerunt, Iste dixit, Possum dissoluere tem-
units.tr: 61. And said, This man said, I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to build it in three days.

units.la: r. ij. plum Dei, & triduo ipsum ædificare.
units.tr: r. ij. ...the temple of God, and in three days to build it up.

units.la: 62. Et surgens Pontifex maximus dixit ei, Nihil respondes? Quid illud est quod isti aduersum te testificantur?
units.tr: 62. And the high priest stood up and said to him, Do you answer nothing? What is it that these men testify against you?

units.la: 63. Iesus autem silebat.
units.tr: 63. But Jesus held his peace.

units.la: MARC. 14.
units.tr: MARK 14.

units.la: 55. Principes autem Sacerdotum & totus concilium quærebant testimonium, aduersus Iesum, ut eum morte multarent, nec inueniebant.
units.tr: 55. Now the chief priests and the whole council sought testimony against Jesus to put him to death, and found none.

units.la: 56. Nam multi falsum testimonium dicebant aduersus eum: sed non erant pares ipsorum testimonia.
units.tr: 56. For many bore false witness against him, but their testimonies did not agree.

units.la: 57. Tunc quidam surrexerunt, & falsa testati sunt aduersus eum, dicentes,
units.tr: 57. Then some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying,

units.la: 58. Nos audiuimus eum dicentem, Ego destruam templum hoc, quod est manu factum, & triduo aliud absque manibus factum ædificabo.
units.tr: 58. We heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and within three days I will build another made without hands.

units.la: 59. Sed nec sic quidem par erat eorum testimonium.
units.tr: 59. But even so their testimony did not agree.

units.la: IOH. 18.
units.tr: JOHN 18.

units.la: 22. Hæc autem quum ipse dixisset, unus ex ministris qui astabat baculo cecidit Iesum, dicens, Itane respondes Pontifici Maximo?
units.tr: 22. When he had said these things, one of the officers who stood by struck Jesus with a rod, saying, Do you answer the high priest like that?

units.la: 23. Respondit ei Iesus, Si male locutus sum, testare de malo, sin bene, cur me cædis?
units.tr: 23. Jesus answered him, If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike me?

units.la: PRIMUM actum istius aduersus Christum Dominum nostrum iudicij coram Pontifice maximo nuper audiuimus, cuius si forma externam tantum cōsideres, suis absolutam numeris esse dixeris. At quæ nobis exponenda supersunt & à Iohanne su- perioribus adiiciuntur singulari Dei proui- dentia contigerunt, vt omnium oculis pateat insignis istorum improborum iudicum hy- pocrisis, atque adeò contrà consolandis omni- bus credentibus innocentia Seruatoris nostri priusquàm damnaretur Sole clarius innote- sceret. Nam quæ maior esse contumelia potest quàm in ipsa iuris dicundi sede, reum coràm Iudice percuti? Et quidem à lictore cuius e- rat partes iussa tantùm Magistratuum exequi? Ecquod igitur facinus vnquam magis indi- gnum, impudens ac minus tolerandum ad- missum est, siue factum in se, siue percussi per- sonam, siue locum, siue tempus ipsum, siue eos in quorum præsentia perpetratum est consi- deres? At hic ad Dei summam & admirandam sapientiam & prouidentiam oculos attolla- mus, hac flagitiosorum impudentia nimirum abutentis, tum ad huius rei innocentiam ma- gis magisque patefaciendam : tum ad totum hunc conseruum indelebili macula notandu: cuius essent illi ipsi auctores, quandoquidem suo furore excaecati non agnouerunt hac in- iuria suam auctoritatem magis quàm illius rei personam violari. Et tamen quàm ille li- ctor perfrictæ frontis est, vt iniuriam non tan- tùm excuser, sed etiam speciosa ratione lauda- re & approbare conetur? Nam, inquit, itáne respondes Pontifici maximo? Sed quid tam impium est quod isti non aggrediantur? tam nefarium, quod non exequantur? quid deni-
units.tr: We have only recently heard of the first proceeding against Christ our Lord before the high priest. If you consider only its outward form, you would say it was complete in every detail. But what remains for us to set out, and what John adds to the account above, came about by a singular providence of God, so that the remarkable hypocrisy of these wicked judges is plain to everyone, and so that the innocence of our Saviour, before he was condemned, became more clearly known than the sun. For what greater insult could there be than to be struck as a prisoner before the judge, in the very seat of judgment? And it was done by a lictor, whose job was only to carry out the orders of the magistrates. Has any crime ever been committed that was more unworthy, more shameless and less tolerable, whether you consider the deed itself, the person struck, the place, the time, or those in whose presence it was done? Yet here let us lift our eyes to the great and wonderful wisdom and providence of God, which made use of this shamelessness of wicked men, both to make the innocence of this matter more and more evident, and to brand with an indelible stain the whole company of those who were its authors. Blinded by their fury, they did not see that by this injury it was their own authority, rather than the person of that man, that was violated. And yet how brazen-faced that lictor is, to try not only to excuse the injury but even to praise and approve it with a specious argument! "So," he says, "do you answer the high priest like that?" But what is so impious that these men do not attempt it, so wicked that they do not carry it out? What is so shameless that they do not dress it up with some pretence?

units.la: r. iij. que tam impudens,cui fucum non inducant?
units.tr: r. iij. ...and what is so shameless that they do not dress it up with some pretence?

units.la: Sic ab omni seculo persequentibus Eccle-fiam Ægyptiis, Philistæis, Assyriis, Chaldæis, Persis, Syris & Romanis non defuerunt spe-ciosæ rationes quas prætexerent, vel retum re-petendarum, vel potissimum Religionis & cultus Numinis, licet Christiani Doctores sanctis suis Apologiis sese suósque greges ad-uersus istiusmodi calumnias satis defenderent. Et quidem ex quo meretrix illa quæ vrbi septem collium insidet Apo.17.9. Reges omnésque adeo incolas terræ fascinauit eadem omnino iudicij forma seruata est aduersus fideles quæ aduersus Christum, habita prius inquisitione, deinde in vincula coniectis, interrogatis, & tanquam criminis conuictis, iudicatis, tandémque miseris illis, quos hæreticos nominabant, secularibus iudicibus traditis, exis- psorum sententia & voluntate ad vltimum supplicium rapiendis. Sed quodnam obsecrò genus sæuitiæ & crudelitatis in ipsorum conspectu Iudicum non exercuerunt lictores dum miseros in vincula,& cryptas trudunt? Annon vero tandem magna impunitate plebi permissum est in eos initar crudelissimorum carnifi-cum sæuire? Annon est cuiuis flagitioso facta potestas, cædendi, mactandi, trahendi, sub-mergendi, præcipites dandi ante Solis aspectum, quoscunque libido iubebat sine sexus, dignitatis aut ætatis ratione, sine inquisitione, sine causæ cognitione, sine forma denique vlla iudicij? Et hæc quidem probantibus, sua-dentidentibus, laudantibus, prædicantibus incen-diariis iltis concionatoribus,ore & scriptis omnis generis,adeò vt etiam pergulæ Romanę talibus picturis exornentur? Ecquis verò non nouit quæ veneficia,quas coniurationes,quas cædes cœlorum promissa redemptione meditati sint?Et harum quidem aliæ aduersus Serenissimam Angliæ Reginam, irritæ singulari Dei gratia,aliæ verò sic permittente Deo tanto furore patratæ, vt ne regi quidem naturali & longè magis quàm ipsi Catholico peperce-rint. Et qui cumulus est ipsorum impudentiæ, posteris sanè futurus incredibilis, quid amplius istos potuisse dixeris, quos non puduit, monstra illa nimirum tantorum scelerum administros in suorum indigetum album referre? Quid amplius igitur Caiaphū incusamus, quid veteres omnes tyrannos,quos viros, vt ita dicam, fuisse bonos dixeris si cum nostri temporis hominibus, immo monstris, contuleris? Quòd si merito Pilatus execrandus est quòd Iesum Christum vi & metu licet adactus morti adiudicarit, quid iis futurum putamus qui tam horrendas & inauditas cædes probant & laudibus in cœlum efferunt? Et ne longius in requirendis exemplis abeamus, annon milites eius hostis à quo cingimur obsidione, quisque Sanctæ istius Vnionis vnus est ex Ducibus præcipuis, nudius tertius in proprios Principis subditos miseros rusticos, operi vacantes, & nihil minus exspectantes, nulla virorum habita ratione,non mulierum, non denique infantium Turcis ipsis & maximè barbaris inauditæ crudelitatis omne genus exercuerunt? At vidit ista Deus, vidit inquam, & viuit, viuitque in æternum, qui sanctos suos affligentes seuerissimis vltus est pœnis: non leuioribus eos vlturus qui superiorum omnium seculorum monstra crudelitate longè superat, vt præ his illi iusti fuisse videantur. Nó ne vero contrà, fratres, tam molles ac timidos fore vt cædi, colaphis incuti, mactari, trucidari, cremari, submergi, modis omnibus indignissimis haberi nos pigeat pro eo qui longè grauiora nostra causa perpessus est? Et hoc tanè non omnibus posse datur, sed dilectis tantùm: cuius rei etiam in Michea Propheta, in Achabi con spectu colaphis cæso 1. Reg. 22. 24. & 27. & Apostolo cæso in os in medio consessu iudicum, iussu Ananiæ Caiaphæ successoris, & illo longè adhuc impudentioris, Act. 23. 2. exemplum habemus.
units.tr: So from the earliest ages, the Egyptians, Philistines, Assyrians, Chaldeans, Persians, Syrians and Romans, who persecuted the Church, never lacked specious reasons to put forward, whether about the recovery of property or, above all, about religion and the worship of the divinity, although the Christian teachers defended themselves and their flocks well enough against such calumnies in their holy apologies. And indeed, since that harlot who sits on the city of seven hills (Rev. 17.9) enchanted the kings and all the inhabitants of the earth, exactly the same form of judgment has been observed against the faithful as against Christ: first an inquiry is held, then they are thrown into chains, questioned, and judged as if convicted of crime, and at last those whom they called heretics are handed over to the secular judges, to be dragged to the final punishment by the decision and will of the judges themselves. But what kind of cruelty and savagery did the lictors not practise, in the sight of those judges, while they thrust the wretched men into chains and dungeons? Indeed, was not the common people at last allowed, with great impunity, to rage against them in the manner of the most cruel executioners? Has not every criminal been given the power to beat, slaughter, drag, drown and hurl down before the light of the sun whomever his lust commanded, without regard to sex, rank or age, without inquiry, without hearing the cause, and in short without any form of judgment at all? And these things have been approved, urged, praised and proclaimed by those fiery preachers, by speech and writing of every kind, so much so that even the Roman shop-fronts are decorated with such pictures. And who does not know what poisonings, what conspiracies, what murders they have plotted with the promise of heavenly redemption? Some of these were aimed against the most serene Queen of England, and by the singular grace of God they came to nothing; others were carried out, by God's permission, with such fury that they did not spare even their natural king, much less their own Catholic one. And the height of their shamelessness, which will surely seem incredible to posterity, is this: what more could one say of those men, who were not ashamed to enter among their own saints those monsters, the ministers of such great crimes? Why then do we blame Caiaphas any more? Why call all the ancient tyrants good men, if you compare them with the men of our own time, or rather with monsters? If Pilate deserves to be cursed because, although he was forced by violence and fear, he condemned Jesus Christ to death, what do we think will become of those who approve such dreadful and unheard-of murders and raise them to heaven with praise? And, not to go further in seeking examples, did not the soldiers of that enemy by whom we are now besieged, the very man who is one of the chief leaders of this Holy Union, only the other day inflict on the poor countrymen of their own prince, who were working in the fields and expected nothing less, every kind of unheard-of cruelty, sparing neither men, nor women, nor even infants, in a way that surpassed the Turks themselves and the most barbarous peoples? But God saw this, I say he saw it, and he lives and lives for ever, and he who takes vengeance on those who afflict his saints will punish them with the most severe penalties, not lightly, since they surpass in cruelty all the monsters of all the earlier ages, so that by comparison those others seem righteous. Shall we not rather, brothers, be ashamed to be so soft and timid that we should be unwilling to be beaten, struck with blows, slaughtered, butchered, burned, drowned and treated in every most unworthy way, for the sake of him who suffered far heavier things for our cause? And this is given not to all, but only to the beloved. We have an example of this in the prophet Micaiah, who was struck on the cheek in the sight of Ahab (1 Kings 22.24, 27), and in the Apostle, who was struck on the mouth in the midst of the assembly of judges, at the command of Ananias, the successor of Caiaphas, a man even more shameless than he (Acts 23.2).

units.la: Sed ad contextum reuersi, causam quam egregius ille lictor præterexuit examinemus, quæ honore Pontifici maximo debito tota nititur. Sed quid dixerat Dominus quo Pontificis honos violaretur, quum diceret se quòd ad doctrinam suam auditorum stare vel cadere testimonio: de discipulis autem & seditione se prorsus esse innocentem? Contrà verò quinam eò deucnire impudentiæ potuit lictor ille, contra ius omne & æquum, sine summo Pontificis Maximi & Senatorum ludibrio? Sed quid agas:verum probatur prouerbium,Qualis Do minus,talis famulus.
units.tr: But let us return to the context and examine the case which that outstanding lictor pretended to plead, a case which rests entirely on the honour owed to the high priest. But what had the Lord said by which the honour of the high priest was violated, when he said that he stood or fell by the testimony of his hearers concerning his teaching, and that concerning the disciples and sedition he was entirely innocent? On the contrary, to what depth of shamelessness could that lictor descend, against all law and right, to the mockery of the high priest and the senators? But what can you do? The proverb is proved true: "Like the master, like the servant."
