units.la: Fateor quidem si dignitatem Pontificis Maximi consideres, cum insigni illo quod thiara praeferebat elogio, ex ipsius Domini praescripto, his verbis, Sanctitas Iehovae, Exod.24.36. & quatenus erat summi & aeterni Pontificis patribus promissi figura,nullam in toto terrarum orbe fuisse illi comparandam. Praeterea Caiapham etsi malis artibus ad hoc fastigium peruenisset, & sceleratus esset, teste ipsius improbo consilio,Ioh.11.49.& hac forma iudicij quae hic memoratur, tamen agnosco fuisse ex dignitate venerandum. Atque adeo, vt eo loco notat Euangelista, flexerat Dominus eius linguam,non autem cor, vt nostrae salutis causam, praeter mentem tamen praedixeret Ioh.11.51.
units.tr: I admit that if you consider the dignity of the High Priest, with that distinguished title which he bore on the mitre, from the Lord's own prescription, in these words, Holiness to Jehovah, Exod. 24.36, and inasmuch as he was the figure of the eternal High Priest promised to the fathers, there was nothing in the whole world comparable to him. Moreover, although Caiaphas reached this height by wicked arts and was wicked, as his own evil counsel shows (John 11.49), and although this form of judgment recorded here was wicked, I acknowledge that he was to be revered for his office. Indeed, as the Evangelist notes in that place, the Lord had guided his tongue, though not his heart, so that he foretold, beyond his own intention, the cause of our salvation (John 11.51).

units.la: At nusquam Pontifices maximos adoratione religiosa cultos,aut ab ipsis crepidam cum adoratione deosculandam praebitam, aut Regibus ac Imperatoribus ad officia seruilia abusos legimus. Contra Sacerdotes Regibus debitum honorem exhibuisse, minime tamen illis in iis quae ex officio suo erant parcentes, quod ex Azariae aduersus Oziam Regem facto certissimo testimonio comprobatur 2.Chron.26.18.&20.& male cum Ioas actu est quod Zachariam sacerdotem cotempsisset, At quo iure meretrix illa Babylonica cum suis scortatoribus& lenonibus vel minima eius honoris cuius hic agitur particulam sibi vendicarent? Nam quibus titulis suam dignitatem tuebuntur, vbi trium coronarum ius, vbi trabeæ Imperialis, vbi priuilegium nullius mortalis iudicio subiectum esse? vbi potestas merita sanctorum, id est fumos, vendendi? vbi denique auctoritas de iure diuino & humano dispensandi, immo etiam quidlibet in sacrosancto & immutabili Dei verbo mutandi, addendi & resecandi? Quo vero iure D. Petro nituntur, quem ab iltis rebus alienissimum fuisse, sicut & reliquos eius collegas, & memorem eorum fuisse quæ didicerat ex Magistro tum verbis Matth. 23. 8. tum reipsa, licet ipsi omnis honos & gloria deberetur, Ioh. 13. 8. vel ex eo liquidò constat quòd Petrus extraordinariam salutationem ferre non potuit, Act. 10. 25. & 26. & tam diligenter cauit ne suorum gregum conscientiis, pastores dominarentur? 1. Petr. 5. 3. Quòd si Sancti isti Patres omisso Petro, quod quum libet faciunt, ad Diui Pauli suffugiant exemplum, annon idem ipsis erit responsurus quod scriptis suis mandauit, Omnis anima, sine exceptione potestatibus esto subiecta Rom. 13. 1. & exemplo suo comprobauit coram Imperatoris præsidé, Act. 24. 1. & 25. 6. tandemque se Imperatoris ipsius iudicio stetit, Imperatoris, inquam, quo nullum magis vnquam horrendum monitrum in orbe terrarum fuit? Sin de persona quæritur, ecquis igno rat saltem à multis seculis, nullum in hanc tedem cæctum fuisse qui nō re ipsa coram Deo & hominibus, prouerbium istud inter eos vulgati. gratissimum, Bonus Papa, malus homo, comprobarit? Sin etiam quibus modis & gradibus eo conscendant attendatur, electionibus ipsorum, omnibus notissimis, quid faedius, quidve tetrius fieri posse dicemus?
units.tr: Yet we never read that the High Priests were worshipped with religious adoration, or that a slipper was offered them to be kissed with adoration, or that they were used for servile duties by kings and emperors. On the contrary, priests did render the honour due to kings, yet they were not at all subservient to them in those matters that belonged to their own office. This is proved by the most certain testimony of Azariah's act against King Uzziah (2 Chron. 26.18, 20), and it went badly for Joash when he despised the priest Zechariah. But by what right do that Babylonian harlot and her fornicators and pimps claim even the smallest part of that honour of which we are speaking? For by what titles do they defend their dignity? Where is their right to the three crowns, where the imperial robe, where the privilege of being subject to no mortal's judgment? Where is the power of selling the merits of the saints, that is, smoke? Where, finally, is the authority to dispense by divine and human law, or even to alter, add to and cut away anything from the holy and unchangeable Word of God? And by what right do they rest on St Peter, who was far removed from such things, as were his fellow colleagues, and who remembered what he had learned from the Master, both in words (Matt. 23.8) and in deed, though all honour and glory were owed to him (John 13.8)? This is clear above all from the fact that Peter could not bear an extraordinary salutation (Acts 10.25, 26), and was so careful that ministers should not lord it over the consciences of their flocks (1 Pet. 5.3). But if these holy Fathers, passing over Peter, as they like to do, take refuge in the example of St Paul, will not the same Paul answer them with what he wrote, "Let every soul be subject, without exception, to the powers" (Rom. 13.1)? And by his own example he proved this before the governor of the Emperor (Acts 24.1; 25.6), and at last he stood before the Emperor's own judgment, the Emperor, I say, than whom there was never a more dreadful monster on the earth. But if we ask about the person, who does not know that for many centuries no one has been put into this seat who has not, in fact, before God and men, proved that proverb commonly current among them, most agreeable to them: "Good Pope, bad man"? And if we consider the means and steps by which they climb to it, namely their elections, which are all too well known, what can we say could be more foul or more hideous?

units.la: Sed de his plus satis. Ad Caiapham & concilium istud reuertamur, in quo rem omnibus seculis inauditam & stupendam primum animaduertamus. Tunc enim erat vnica toto terrarum orbe visibilis Ecclesia tantum inter Iudaeos: hic confessus, quod ad politiam Dei nitebatur auctoritate ad iurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam exercendam: Scribae Moses & Prophetas in synagogis interpretabantur: Sacerdotes accedebant ad altare: Pontifex Maximus visibilis erat figura promissi Patribus redemptoris: & haec quidem elogia non tantum insignia fuerunt, sed etiam sancta venerandaque. Ac sane quum oporteret Iesum Christum tanquam vadem ac sponsorem nostrum ignominiam & condemnationem quam eramus meriti sustinere, necesse fuit eum coram tali tribunali tanquam ore Dei condemnari. Personas vero si respexeris, quis unquam talia monstra fuisse dicat, pseudoprophetas, populi seductores, caecos, caecorum duces, qui Domum Altissimi in speluncam latronum converterant, Iudae proditionis redemptores, falsarios, testium adornatores, denique contra propriam conscientiam auctoris vitae parricidas? Age vero quis oro, quis inquam, coram istis vinctus, irrisus, damnatus, omnibus contumeliis affectus, colaphis caesus, sputo exceptus comparet? Annon ille coëssentialis aeternus Dei filius, homo natus ex Virgine, Sancto Spiritu conceptus sine labe & macula, spes vnica patrum, lumen Gentibus promissum, veri Israelis decus ac gloria, veritas & substantia figurarum, in quo solo promissiones omnes ratae factae sunt, denique mundi Iudex? Hic igitur veritas & figurae concurrunt. Sed quàta cū repugnātia? Sedent iudices, improbi & flagitiosi homines: stat ante ipsos verus mundi Iudex ipse iudicandus: mendacium aduersus veritatem fert sententiam; mendacio creditur, veritati locus nullus relinquitur. Ne miremur igitur propterea terram motu concussam, Solem obscuratum, fissas denique petras, scelceratis istis haec exprobrantes, qui soli tamen ad mutarum & inanimatarum rerum creatarum tam illustre testimonium nec obstupuerunt nec commoti sunt. Verum absit a nobis fratres, ut in hunc numerum adscribamur: sed tantam confusionem a nostris iniquorum peccatis innectam attente considerantes: ferio territi pertimescamus: Deumque sedulo precemur ut nostras discutiat tenebras, precemur ut cordis infringat duritiem: vera fide complectamur & veneremur cum qui se ea vsque nostra causa demisit: quo fiet ut quemadmodum flagitiosi isti & detestandi homines tandem experti sunt horrenda Dei vindicta, Iudicem esse suum quem prius ipsi iudicarant: nos contra in ipsius vincu-lis nostram liberationem, in ignominia, gloriam, in condemnatione, absolutionem, tandemque in morte, vitam inuenia-mus.
units.tr: But enough of these matters. Let us return to Caiaphas and that council, in which we first notice a thing unheard of and astonishing in every age. For at that time the only visible Church in the whole world was among the Jews alone. Here the state, which rested on the authority of God's polity, professed to exercise ecclesiastical jurisdiction; the scribes interpreted Moses and the Prophets in the synagogues; the priests approached the altar; the High Priest was the visible figure of the Redeemer promised to the fathers. These distinctions were not only remarkable but also holy and venerable. And indeed, since it was fitting that Jesus Christ, as our surety and sponsor, should bear the shame and condemnation that we had deserved, it was necessary that he be condemned before such a tribunal as though by the mouth of God. But if you look at the persons, who could say that such monsters ever existed: false prophets, seducers of the people, blind men, leaders of the blind, who had turned the house of the Most High into a den of robbers, redeemers of Judas's betrayal, forgers, suborners of witnesses, and finally murderers of the author of life against their own conscience? Come now, who, I ask, who appears before these men bound, mocked, condemned, loaded with every insult, struck with blows, and spat upon? Is it not that eternal Son of God, of one essence with the Father, the man born of the Virgin, conceived by the Holy Spirit without stain or blemish, the one hope of the fathers, the light promised to the Gentiles, the honour and glory of the true Israel, the truth and substance of the figures, in whom alone all the promises were ratified and fulfilled, and finally the Judge of the world? Here, then, truth and figures meet. But what a contradiction! The judges sit, wicked and shameless men; before them stands the true Judge of the world, himself to be judged; a lie pronounces sentence against the truth; the lie is believed, and no place is left for the truth. We should not wonder, therefore, that the earth was shaken by an earthquake, the sun was darkened, and the rocks were split, reproaching these wicked men with these things, who, however, were neither astonished nor moved by so illustrious a testimony from mute and inanimate created things. But God forbid, brethren, that we should be counted in that number. Rather, considering attentively how great a confusion is brought upon us by the sins of the wicked, let us tremble, seriously terrified; and let us earnestly pray to God that he will dispel our darkness and break the hardness of our hearts, and that we embrace and revere with true faith him who for our sake humbled himself so far. In this way, just as those wicked and detestable men at last experienced the dreadful vengeance of God, when the one whom they had judged proved to be their judge, so we, on the contrary, will find in his bonds our liberation, in his disgrace glory, in his condemnation absolution, and at last in his death life.

units.la: Accedamus ad exceptionem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qua se tamen absolui potuisse minime sperauit. (Sciebat enim suorum iudicum mentem & animum, & futura probe cognoscebat, in quorum etiam se praeparauerat euentum) sed voluit tamen simpliciter, etsi grauiter de illata sibi iniuria conquerendo, suae exinanitionis scandalo mederi: iudicum suorum conscientiam, si quam habuissent, stimulare: denique in ipsa sua exinanitione nihilominus palam testari se domus Patris sui reformationi commissum esse, quod suo tandem illi magno sunt experti detrimento.
units.tr: Let us come to the answer of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which he hardly hoped that he could be acquitted. (For he knew the mind and intention of his judges, and he clearly foresaw the future, for which he had prepared himself.) Yet he wished, simply, though with grave complaint about the injury done to him, to remedy the scandal of his humiliation; to goad the conscience of his judges, if they had any; and finally, in his very humiliation, to testify openly nonetheless that he had been entrusted with the reform of his Father's house. This they at last experienced to their great loss.

units.la: Exiterunt vero iam olim quidam contemptores, & in primis Imperator ille detestandus Iulianus dictus Apostata, qui Christo obiicerent, transgressorem illum & violatorem primum eius Legis fuisse quam tulerat Matth. 5. 39. qua iubet eum qui in dextra maxilla fuerit laesus, alteram obuertere. Sed canes isti Dei Filio allatrantes non alio digni sunt responso nisi ut ille fulmine suo tactos eos tandem coerceat, quod ipse sane Apostata reipsa expertus est.
units.tr: Now indeed certain scorners arose long ago, and above all that detestable emperor called Julian the Apostate, who objected to Christ that he was the transgressor and first violator of that law which he had given (Matt. 5.39), in which he bids the one who has been struck on the right cheek to turn the other as well. But those dogs barking at the Son of God deserve no other answer than that he should at last restrain them by a thunderbolt, which the Apostate himself in fact experienced.

units.la: Sed tamen facilis & aperta responsio. Nam illa loquendi forma Dominus nihil voluit minus quàm iubere affectos iniuria nouam occasionem alterius ad priorem adiiciendae con-tumeliosis & iniuriis offerre. Nec queri etiam laesos prohibuit, & ius suum aduersus contumeliosos persequi, quantum tamē id & quatenus charitas permittit: sed omnem suis interdixit impatientiam, & vindictae cupiditatem, iniuriarum patientes eos esse docens, ut primam iniuriam potius secunda,& iacturam minorem maior excipiat, quàm vel re vel cogitatione malum malo compensare studeant.
units.tr: Yet the answer is easy and plain. For in that manner of speaking the Lord wished nothing less than to command those who suffer injury to offer a new occasion to another for adding to the earlier insult and wrong. Nor did he forbid the injured to complain, or to pursue their right against the insolent, so far as charity permits, and in the way it permits. But he forbade his people all impatience and every desire for vengeance, teaching them to be patient under injuries, so that a second wrong would rather receive the first, and a greater loss the smaller one, than that they should try to repay evil with evil, either in deed or in thought.

units.la: Sic igitur illa est intelligenda exceptio, ex qua discimus licere, immo & aliquando necesse esse testimonium de malo perhibere coram iis qui mederi possunt & ex officio debent: modò tamē nec ambitionis spiritu, quo iustitia quadam aliis excellere & eminere cupiamus, nec curiositate, nec levitate, nec aliqua denique siniistra mentis & affectuum perturbatione ducamur: sed contrà zelo bene composito nos impellente, spiritum illum discretionis à Domino flagitemus, quum non quaeuis peccata vulgari,nec quaeuis dissimulari,tegive, nec cuiuis sine discretione revelari necesse sit: qua in re nobis charitatis spiritus & cognitionis rectitudo, futuri sunt Duces optimi.
units.tr: That exception, therefore, is to be understood in this way: from it we learn that it is lawful, and indeed sometimes necessary, to bear witness to wrongdoing before those who can remedy it and are bound to do so by their office. Provided, however, that we are not driven by a spirit of ambition, by which we desire to excel and stand out above others by a certain show of righteousness, nor by curiosity, nor by levity, nor finally by any perverse state of mind or disturbance of the passions. On the contrary, impelled by a well-ordered zeal, let us ask the Lord for that spirit of discretion, since it is not necessary to make known every sin indiscriminately, nor to conceal or overlook every sin, nor to reveal it to everyone without discretion. In this matter the spirit of charity and the rectitude of knowledge will be our best guides.

units.la: Alterum ex hoc loco nobis obseruandum, in vocationis nostrae terminis diligenter considerandis positum est. Nam si de publica coercitione quaeritur, nimirum illa Magistratus est propria, vt superius in illa Domini ad Petrū admonitione vidimus. Sin de domestica ftica, parentū esse aut eorū qui vices parentum gerunt in liberos & præceptorū in discipulos animaduersionem propriam extra omnem est controuersiam. Ita tamen vt moderata casti- gatio sit, ad eorum qui lapsi sunt emendatio- nem, & prout factum postulare videbitur. Haud equidem dixerim permissam in vxores maritis coërcionem, licet maritus caput sit, & apud quosdam populos illa in vsu fuerit. Nec enim in sacris vel Legem vel exemplum legere memini, quo hæc auctoritas nitatur, etsi satis experientia doceat nonnunquam aliquid maritorū impatientiæ cōdonandū, quos despera- ta & inemendabilis vxorum malitia nimium impoteter agit. Inemendabilem dico, quum maritus quæcunqu e ferri possunt toleratis, & frustrà tentatis omnibus Christianis admoni- tionibus nihil promouet. Quo quidem casu nequaquam senserim cum plerisque aliis in- ter Christianos libellum diuortij locum ob- tinere posse, (falsa enim est hæc doctrina, teste ipso Iesu Christo. Matth. 19. 9.) dico tamen Magistratum vt obuiam eatur pluribus quæ inde nasci possunt scandalis, & quieti publicæ consulatur, posse debereque necessarias adhi- bere correctiones. Sed tantò magis in cusandi mariti, quos quum sibi suisque vxoribus o- portcat sapere, quid præ se Mariti nomen fe- rat immemores, tam crudeliter in miseras vxo- res sæuiunt, & tam male familias regunt, vt in suis ipsorum domibus inferos sibi faciant: tam indignè sacrosanctum matrimonij vinculum polluentes, quod tantopere Deus cohonestauit vt eo ad magnum illud mysterium coniunctionis Christi & Ecclesiæ significandum & adumbrandum vtatur: & eos quidem ad ipsum Dominum, ex ore cuius reprehensiones audiat ablego. Malach. 2. 14. & 15. Denique pudendum est talia in Ecclesia conspici scandala, in qua præsertim locum habere & vigere suauissimam & sanctissimam exhortationem Apostoli decebat, his verbis maritos compellantis, Viri diligite vxores vestras, sicut & Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, & semet expo-suit pro ea. Item: Sicut Ecclesia subiecta est: ita & vxores suis viris in omnibus. Ephes. 5. verf. 24. & 25.
units.tr: Another point to observe from this passage concerns carefully weighing the limits of our calling. If the question is public coercion, that belongs properly to the magistrate, as we saw above in the Lord's admonition to Peter. If the question is domestic correction, the right to discipline children belongs to parents, or to those who stand in their place, and the right to discipline pupils belongs to their teachers; there is no dispute about this. Such correction, however, must be moderate, aimed at the amendment of those who have fallen, and proportioned to what the deed seems to require. I would not, indeed, say that husbands are permitted to coerce their wives, although the husband is the head, and among some peoples this has been the custom. For I do not recall reading in Holy Scripture either a law or an example on which such authority could rest. Yet experience teaches well enough that the impatience of husbands sometimes deserves some allowance, when the desperate and incorrigible malice of wives drives them beyond measure. I say incorrigible when a husband has endured whatever can be endured, and, after all Christian admonitions have been tried in vain, achieves nothing. In such a case I would by no means agree with most other Christians that a bill of divorce can have a place here (for that doctrine is false, as Jesus Christ himself testifies, Matth. 19. 9.). Still, I say that the magistrate can and should apply the necessary corrections, so that the many scandals that may arise from this are prevented and public peace is safeguarded. But all the more should those husbands be blamed who, when they ought to be wise for themselves and their wives, forgetful of what the name of husband implies, rage so cruelly against their unhappy wives and govern their households so badly that they make a hell for themselves in their own homes. They defile so unworthily the sacred bond of marriage, which God has so greatly honored that he uses it to signify and foreshadow that great mystery of the union of Christ and the Church. I send such men to the Lord himself, from whose mouth they will hear reproof. Malach. 2. 14. & 15. Finally, it is shameful that such scandals are seen in the Church, in which above all the most sweet and holy exhortation of the Apostle ought to hold sway, addressing husbands in these words: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself up for her. And again: As the Church is subject, so also wives to their husbands in all things. Ephes. 5. vers. 24. & 25.

units.la: Nec posswm etiam dicere dominis famulos famulasve cædere licere, eo quòd olim in seruos domini vitæ necisque potestatem haberent. Nam qui hodie famulantur liberi sunt, & tantum mercede conducti: quibus sæpe mercedem retineri aut etiam ictibus persolai, non sine maxima iniquitate conspicimus. Quod ita tamen dictum esto, vt ætatis eorum habita ratione qui mercede conducuntur nihil impediat quominus heri vel heræ moderatis, paternis ac maternis castigationibus in eos animadvertant, quos velut in familiæ numerum exceperunt. Faxit vero Deus vt in genere omnes cuiusuis dignitatis sexus aut ætatis ita quæ nostri sunt officij, seu iubendo seu obsequendo partes intelligamus, & sic alij erga alios affecti, & inuicem vniti compactique sumus, vnius eiusdemque Spiritus intus agentis vi, tanquam vnius eiusdemque corporis mem-bra, vt eò nunquam sit dolendum : sed alij alios perpetuò potius mutuis officiis ædifice-mus.
units.tr: Nor can I say that masters may beat their male or female servants, on the grounds that in former times masters had the power of life and death over their slaves. For those who serve today are free, hired only for wages; and we see, not without the greatest injustice, that their wages are often withheld or paid out with blows. Yet let this be said with the proviso that, with regard to the age of those who are hired, nothing prevents the master or mistress from administering moderate, fatherly and motherly corrections to those whom they have taken into the number of their household. May God grant that all of us, of whatever rank, sex or age, understand in general the parts of our duty, whether in commanding or in obeying, and so be disposed toward one another and joined together by the power of the one and the same Spirit working within us, as members of one and the same body, that there may never be cause for grief, but that we rather build one another up continually by mutual services.

units.la: Alij duo Euangelistæ, Matthæus & Marcus deinceps secundum iudicij actum aduersus Seruatorem nostrum describunt, in quo magis quàm in priore malitia sua Iudices isti sunt excæcati, aut ipsi potius detecti, quò magis accusati patefierent innocentia, ac proinde ipsi quidem omni excusationis specie carere viderentur, innocente homine condemnato, non ignorantia quidem, quod eorum plerisq; contigisse qui vociferati sunt, Tolle, tolle, crucifige eum, vel ipse Christus in cruce testatus est Luc. 23. 34. & Petrus præceptorem sequutus Act. 3. 17. sed contra propriam conscientiam quæsita & affectata improbitate : decretum vero diuinum esse vt Iesus Christus non pro suis, quæ nulla habuit, peccatis : sed tanquam noster sponsor nostris in se receptis condemnaretur. Narrant igitur Euangelistæ illos oblatum sibi aduersus Christum maximum argumentum existimantes, quòd essent ad eorum abegati testimonium qui doctrinam eius audiissent, testes quæsiuisse, non quidem de veritate rei inquisituros vt dubios & incertos, sed sic adornaturos vt ex ipsorum falso testimonio quod erat Caiaphæ consilio decretum alia specie iuris exequerentur. At primùm quàm pudendum ipsis est prius in eum manus in eciffe quàm inquisiuisse? Quanquam haud
units.tr: The other two Evangelists, Matthew and Mark, next describe the course of the trial against our Saviour. In it these judges were blinded in their malice even more than in the earlier part, or rather they were themselves exposed, so that the innocence of the accused would be made plainer, and so that they themselves would seem to lack every appearance of excuse, since an innocent man was condemned. It was not through ignorance, for that was the case with most of those who shouted, Away, away with him, crucify him, as Christ himself testified on the cross (Luke 23. 34.), and Peter, following his Master, testified (Acts 3. 17.). Rather, it was a deliberately sought and assumed wickedness, against their own conscience. Yet it was the divine decree that Jesus Christ should be condemned not for his own sins, for he had none, but as our surety, with our sins taken upon himself. The Evangelists therefore relate that these men, thinking they had gained a great argument against Christ because they had been given witnesses against the one who had taught his doctrine, sought witnesses not to inquire into the truth of the matter as men in doubt and uncertainty, but to arrange things so that by their false testimony, which Caiaphas had already resolved upon, they might carry out the sentence under some other appearance of law. But first, how shameful it is for them to have laid hands on him before inquiring!

units.la: {f} j. equidem inficior sæpe tales casus incidere, præsertim quum in ipso facinore quis deprehenditur, vt à vinculis potius quàm ab inquisitione faciendum sit initium: qua in re non pauci peccât iudices, mercenarij potius quàm iuris dicendi studiosi, de mercede prius agentes quam sibi certam esse volunt, quàm aut inquirant, aut facinorosos in vincula coniiciant nisi sit actor qui reum persequatur: sed contrario prorsus lapsu peccarunt de quibus hic agimus. Et hic quidem primus esto lapsus maximus, quo inexcusabilis cædis rei peraguntur. Sed præterea consideremus quantopere Deus illos in suis consiliis excæcarit. Nam quis impediret quominus haberent tot testes falsos & falsa testimonia quot sibi opus esse duxissent? Næ in signe hic illius opus apparet, adversus quem nec viribus nec dolis est vllus locus.
units.tr: Yet I do not deny that such cases often happen, especially when someone is caught in the very act of crime, so that the proceedings begin with chains rather than with inquiry. In this matter many judges err, being hirelings rather than zealous administrators of justice, who discuss their fee before they are willing to inquire, or to cast malefactors into chains, unless there is a plaintiff to pursue the accused. But those of whom we are speaking here sinned by the exact opposite error. And this should be regarded as the first and greatest fault, by which the guilty commit an inexcusable murder. Consider, moreover, how greatly God blinded them in their counsels. For what would have prevented them from having as many false witnesses and false testimonies as they thought necessary? Indeed, here appears the work of God, against whom there is no place for force or for trickery.

units.la: Quæ res etiam huius capitis membra debet in omnibus quas pro Dei nomine patiuntur afflictionibus magnopere consolari. Quàm multa vero possent ciusmodi nostri temporis exempla proferri, & in illa potissimum insignium illorum & fidelium Dei seruorum laniena quæ nostro seculo contigit, aduersus quos admissam crudelitatem quicunque iudicij specie regere tentarunt, nulla ratione melius illorum innocentiæ consulere, suam vero malitiam & peruersum spiritum patefacere potuissent: ipso cælitus etiam Domino quotidie prolatis sententiis, & horrendis suæ vindictæ ćtæ testimoniis illud ipsum confirmante.Quicunque casus enim ingruant, Deo tandem suam constare iustitiam fatendum est.
units.tr: This matter should also greatly console the members of this Head in all the afflictions they suffer for the name of God. How many examples of this kind could be brought forward from our own times, and especially from that massacre of the distinguished and faithful servants of God which happened in our century! Against them those who tried to rule by some appearance of judgment, having committed cruelty, could by no means have better served their innocence, nor have revealed their own malice and perverse spirit. Meanwhile the Lord himself pronounces sentences from heaven every day, and his dreadful testimonies of vengeance confirm this very point. Whatever calamities may fall upon us, it must in the end be confessed that God's justice stands.

units.la: Sed quemadmodum Deus falsorum istorū iudicum hypocrisin manifestè per seipsos hac ipsorum procedendi ratione,detexit:sic vicifim accusati notissimam fecit innocentiam,in se nimirum perfectissimam & absolutissimā. Quemadmodum enim ab humanæ naturæ corruptione, nemo sine vitio viuit, ita vix cuiusquam vita tam priuata & incognita fuerit, aut tam iusta & integra præ reliquis, quin si fuerit in eam diligenter inquisitum aliquod saltem defectus testimonium reperiatur. Præterea, quum nulla tanta sit tamque atrox calumnia qua non etiam vitæ quispiam integerrimæ possit verisimiliter premi, vel iniquis iudicibus, vel falsis testibus, quis non videt quàm integræ vitæ & immaculatæ Christus fuerit, quam nulla potuit nec iudicum peruersitas, nec testium falsitas obscurare? Et sanè quoties cum hostes viuum calumniati fuerant, toties eis etiam os occlusum fuerat vt penitus obmutescerent, adeò vt non sine legitima causa pridem ex iis quæsiuisset, quis inter illos eum peccati redargueret. Ioh. 8. 46.Solus ille est igitur quæcunque tandem aduersus eum lata sit sententia, in quo Patri complacuit, imaginem illam in ipso reperiente Deo, ad quam ab initio creauerat hominem, immo etiam longè tum qualitate tum mensura perfectiorem, solus, inquā, ille vere iustus pro iniustis mortuus est, pro quibus rependere voluit quæ rapuerant, vt de se per Dauidem prædixerat. Psal.69.5. & Esa. 53.4. & 5. Quod est in hac historia tota diligenter obseruandum, vt aduersus omnes hæreses articulus ille nostræ fidei confirmetur quo credimus conceptum non humana generatione, sed sola Spiritus Sancti virtute in beata Virgine: siquidem ex corrupto nihil nisi corruptum nasci potest Iob. 14. 4. & Ioh.3 6.
units.tr: But just as God has openly revealed the hypocrisy of those false judges by this very manner of proceeding of theirs, so in turn he has made the innocence of the accused most well known, a innocence in him most perfect and absolute. For just as no one lives without fault, because of the corruption of human nature, so hardly anyone's life is so private and unknown, or so just and upright beyond others, that, if an inquiry is diligently made into it, at least some testimony of defect will not be found. Moreover, since there is no calumny so great or so atrocious that it cannot plausibly press even the most blameless life, whether by unjust judges or false witnesses, who does not see how blameless and spotless the life of Christ was, which neither the perversity of judges nor the falsehood of witnesses could obscure? And indeed, as often as his enemies had slandered him while he was alive, so often had their mouths been shut, so that they were utterly struck dumb; so much so that, not without good reason, he had long before asked them which of them could convict him of sin (John 8. 46.). He alone, therefore, whatever sentence was at last passed against him, is the one in whom the Father was well pleased, God finding in him that image to which he had created man at the beginning, and even one far more perfect both in quality and in measure. He alone, I say, the truly just one, died for the unjust, for whom he was willing to repay what they had seized, as David had foretold concerning him (Psal. 69. 5.; Isa. 53. 4. & 5.). This must be carefully observed throughout this whole history, so that against all heresies this article of our faith may be confirmed, by which we believe that he was conceived in the blessed Virgin not by human generation but by the sole power of the Holy Spirit; for from what is corrupt nothing but what is corrupt can be born (Job 14. 4.; John 3. 6.).

units.la: Ex istis porrò tenebris age lucem aliquam eruamus, quum præsertim de Iudicibus istis dicatur(tanta etiam in scelcratissimis cóscien-tiæ vis est Deo volente) non aulos adornatis à sctestibus abuti, quòd inter se non conuenirent: est enim verissimum vetustum illud proverbium, tam facile esse veritatem profiteri, quàm difficile eandem alterare. Hic verò monentur Iudices, à Deo quum de testimoniis agitur iudicium & bonam conscientiam potulare, ne leuiter inquisitiones prætereant, sed singulas sine animi perturbatione diligenter examinent, non obiter nec superficie tenus, sed minutatim omnibus circustantiis appensis & examinatis: quod quum secus fiat plerunque improbos dimitti, iustos verò condemnari, videmus.
units.tr: From these darknesses, let us now bring out some light, especially since it is said of these judges (so great is the power of conscience even in the most wicked, by God's will) that they were not suborned by the false witnesses, because the witnesses did not agree with one another. For that old proverb is most true: it is as easy to profess the truth as it is difficult to alter it. Here judges are admonished, when testimony is weighed, to invoke God's judgment and a good conscience, so that they do not pass over inquiries lightly, but examine each one diligently, without disturbance of mind, not cursorily or superficially, but minutely, with all the circumstances weighed and examined. We see that when this is not done, the wicked are commonly let go and the just condemned.

units.la: Nihilominus in falsis illis testibus duo tandem inter se consentientes reperti sunt, & ab istis falsis iudicibus accepti quidem, sed non vsque adeò plurimi facti, non repetitis aut compositis cū reo: senserat nimirum hoc leue fore,si admitteretur a Christo, vanitatis potius argumentum, quàm scelerisaducrsus Templum, quod se momento restituturum & redin tegraturum pollliceretur. Quoniam autem odiosus ipsis admodum erat destructionis Templi, quacunque ratione id fieret, sermo, ideò testimonium istud vrgere noluerunt. At nobis aliquid de templo isto materiali dicendum superest, de quo tamen non erat Christus loquutus, sed de sui corporis templo, quod differtis verbis monet Ioan.cap.2.21. Tenendum igitur locum in quo prius à Salomone fuerat aedificatum, deinde à Nehemia post reditum à captiuitate redintegratum, & ab Herode magno tandem exornatum, ab hominibus nec delectu fuisse nec decreto: sed expresso oraculo diuino Dauidi per Gadum Prophetam praefactum. 2.Sam.24.18. non quidé vt illi loco sanctitas inesset peculiaris, siue materia, siue solum, aedificium-ve consideres: nec vt Deus aede tanquam domo concluderetur: etsi Dei domus dictum sit: sed ad vsum sacrosanctum, cultum nimirum ordinarium ceremoniarum exercendum, ex Domini praescripto, Deut.12.24.quam etiam ob causam Hierosolyma Dei ciuitas est nuncupata, & eadem Regni Metropolis. Idcirco etiam factum est, vt quemadmodum vnum fuit prius tabernaculum, sic vnicum fuerit toti populo templum destinatum, vt omnes tribus in vnam fide ac religione coirent. Quibus adde figuram fuisse templum illud corporis Iesu Christi, humanae ni-
units.tr: Nevertheless, among those false witnesses two were at last found agreeing with each other. They had been taken on by those false judges, but not so many as to be made up, and their testimony was not repeated or coached with the accused. They had judged, no doubt, that this would be a light matter if it were brought against Christ: an argument of vanity rather than of crime, that he would destroy the temple and restore it in a moment, as he promised. Since, however, the destruction of the temple, by whatever means it came about, was very hateful to them, they did not want to press that testimony. But we still have something to say about that material temple. Christ did not speak of it, but of the temple of his body, which he advises in riddling words (John 2:21). We must hold that the place where it was first built by Solomon, then restored by Nehemiah after the return from captivity, and at last adorned by Herod the Great, was chosen neither by men nor by decree, but was designated by the express divine oracle given to David through the prophet Gad (2 Sam. 24:18). This was not because any peculiar holiness dwelt in that place, whether you consider the material, the soil, or the building; nor because God was enclosed in the temple as in a house, although it is called the house of God; but for the holy use of carrying out the ordinary worship of the ceremonies, by the Lord's prescription (Deut. 12:24). For this reason too Jerusalem was called the city of God and the metropolis of the kingdom. Hence also, just as there was formerly one tabernacle, so one temple was appointed for the whole people, so that all the tribes might come together in one faith and religion. To these add that the temple was a figure of the humanity of Jesus Christ, of his human

units.la: f. iij. mirum cius naturæ, in qua Deitatis plenitudo inhabitat. Coloss. 2. 9. non in figura, sed corporaliter, nec in umbra, sed substantialiter: non cooperante Spiritu vt solet in sanctis: sed in unitate personæ.
units.tr: signature mark f. iij. nature, in which the fullness of the Deity dwells (Col. 2:9): not in a figure but bodily, not in a shadow but substantially; not with the Spirit cooperating, as is usual in the saints, but in the unity of the person.

units.la: En vsus excellentissimos huius templi, in totidem maximos abusus conuersos, ipsis Doctoribus populum in istis erroribus auaritiæ suæ explendæ causa fouentibus. Nam quod ad primum vsum, licet à Solomone mature admoniti. 1. Reg. 8. 27. idem illis postea D. Stephano exprobrante. Act. 7, 48. & 49. sic tamen huius templi visibilis præsentiæ inhæserunt, & ceremoniis externis, vt Deum templo stante sibi quodammodo deuinctum retinerent, licet illud in speluncam latronum, Christo id ipsum illis exprobrante. Matth. 21. 13. vt multis ante seculis fecerat Ieremias cap. 7 11. convertiflent. En cur tam effrænatis & immodicis cla moribus, aducrsus Prophetas, templi destructionem prædicentes inuehcrentur, his vocibus, Templum, templum, templum æterni: atque adeo vt Ieremias ipse de vita sit propterea periclitatus. Ierem. 26. 11. & Diuus Stephanus sit lapidibus obruatus. Act. 6. 14.
units.tr: Behold the most excellent uses of this temple, turned into as many greatest abuses, the teachers themselves fostering the people in these errors for the sake of satisfying their greed. As for the first use, although Solomon had warned them early (1 Kings 8:27), and St Stephen later reproached them with the same (Acts 7:48-49), they nonetheless clung to the visible presence of this temple and to its external ceremonies, so that, while the temple stood, they kept God bound to them in some way. Yet Christ reproached them for turning it into a den of robbers (Matt. 21:13), as Jeremiah had done many centuries before (Jer. 7:11). Here is why they railed against the prophets who foretold the destruction of the temple with such unbridled and immoderate clamour, crying out, "The temple, the temple, the temple of the Eternal!" So much so that Jeremiah himself was put in danger of his life for this (Jer. 26:11), and St Stephen was stoned to death (Acts 6:14).

units.la: Quid vero de superstitionibus in Ecclesiam Christianâ inuectis, & adhuc hodie tanta pertinacia traditionum nomine seruatis, quas audet etiam nonnunquâ Apostolicas appellare, dicturi sumus? Nam si meritas pœnas Iudæi & seuerissimas luerunt, templo & ceremoniis ab ipso Deo præscriptis ea tribuentes quæ sic Dei pro-
units.tr: But what shall we say about the superstitions introduced into the Christian Church, and still kept today with such stubbornness under the name of traditions, which men even sometimes dare to call apostolic? For if the Jews paid deserved and most severe penalties, because they ascribed to the temple and to the ceremonies prescribed by God himself those things which belong so properly to God

units.la: Maximi abusus à Iudæis introducti cum circa templum etiam cultum exteriore plusquam fas sit tribuere do. propria sunt vt alteri communicari non possint, vim nimirum & potestatem diuinam, cuius illa tantum erat signa visibilia: quid fiet iis qui idem attribuunt, aut saltem suae salutis partem ascribunt suo chrismati, aquae lustrali, crucibus, reliquiis, imaginibus, omnibus denique suis somniis quae bonarum Intentionum nomine tegunt? Qui vero non istud facerét quos no pudet imaginaria sua merita cum Iesu Christi merito confundere? Sed vt istorum figmenta missa faciamus, quum aquae Baptismi tribuunt alium vsum aut virtutem quàm fidei nostrae significandi & repraesentandi Iesu Christi sanguinem: & ita confirmata fide, magis ac magis in nobis obsignandi peccatorum remissionem & nostram regenerationem: & quum proinde nec signum à re significata distinguunt, nec Baptismum externum, administratum ab eo cui hoc in Ecclesia munus est impositum, ab interno, promanante à sola Dei virtute, annon in idem peccatum in quod Iudaei prius incidunt, & diuini cultus specie, Baptismi Sacramentum manifesta & intoleranda idololatria polluunt?
units.tr: alone. The greatest abuses introduced by the Jews, when they gave even outward worship around the temple more than is lawful, belong so properly to God that they cannot be shared with another: namely, divine power and authority, of which those things were only visible signs. What will happen to those who ascribe the same to their chrism, lustral water, crosses, relics, images, and finally all their dreams, which they cover with the name of good intentions, or who at least ascribe a part of their salvation to these things? And why speak of those who would not do this, who are not ashamed to confuse their imaginary merits with the merit of Jesus Christ? But to set aside their fictions: when they assign to the water of Baptism another use or power than that of signifying and representing to our faith the blood of Jesus Christ, and so, with faith confirmed, of sealing in us more and more the remission of sins and our regeneration; and when accordingly they distinguish neither the sign from the thing signified, nor the external baptism administered by the one to whom this office has been committed in the Church from the internal, which flows from God's power alone, do they not fall into the same sin into which the Jews fell before, and under the appearance of divine worship pollute the sacrament of Baptism with manifest and intolerable idolatry?

units.la: Magis vero stupendum & intolerandum, in altero Sacrosancto Coenae Domini Sacramento errorem admittunt. Nam vt omittam infinitas alias Coenae pollutiones, quum Sacramentum mysticae nostrae cum Iesu Christo coniunctionis, & εὐχαριστία sacrificium, in realem & expiatoriam pro viuis & mortuis oblationem commutarunt: nec contenti, quod in aqua Baptismi fecerant, vim aliquam diuinam inhaerentem pani & vino sacrosanctę Coenae ascribere, panem & vinum in Iesu Christi carnem & sanguinem transformarunt, illa vocantes verum suum Deum & Seruatorem, quem manu capi & ore comedi, realiter & essentialiter tam ab infidelibus quàm fidelibus afferunt: quod si ipsis concedatur vt docent & credi volunt, & quidem tanquam vnum ex praecipuis articulis fidei, quìnam, nisi summa & inexcusabili cum impudetia, negare audeant, quin ipsis dentibus vel ore saltem, humanas carnes dum vorant Carnivori dicendi sint, immo & Deivori? Sed ad Capernaitas, licet ignorantia crassa peccantes, ipsos populi Christiani impostores ipsorum suffragio condemnandos ablegemus.
units.tr: Even more amazing and intolerable is the error they admit in the other most holy sacrament, the Lord's Supper. To omit the countless other pollutions of the Supper: they have turned the sacrament of our mystical union with Jesus Christ, and the sacrifice of the eucharist [εὐχαριστία], into a real and expiatory offering for the living and the dead. And not content with what they did in the water of Baptism, ascribing some divine power inhering in the bread and wine of the holy Supper, they have transformed bread and wine into the flesh and blood of Jesus Christ, calling them their true God and Saviour, whom they assert is taken in the hand and eaten by the mouth, really and essentially, by unbelievers as well as believers. If this were granted them, as they teach and wish to be believed (and indeed as one of the chief articles of faith), who, unless with the greatest and inexcusable impudence, would dare to deny that they should be called flesh-eaters, indeed God-eaters, since with their teeth, or at least with their mouths, they devour human flesh? But let us leave the Capernaites, who sin through gross ignorance, and send the very impostors of the Christian people to be condemned by their own vote.

units.la: Alter Iudaeorum error, minus suis Sacramentis quàm par est tribuentium, ac se proinde praecipuo ipsorum fructu priuantium minus est adhuc quàm ille superior excusandus, quo in idololatriam labebantur, plus quàm par est illis tribuentes, vt superius diximus. Tantum enim abest vt agnouerint templum illud visibile, in quo Dominus Sacramentaliter habitabat, id est signis illis visibilibus se quodammodo videndum offerebat, esse figuram humanae naturae Messiae, in qua vera & essentialis Deitas corporaliter habitaret in vnitate personae, vt contrà quum visibilem hominem tantùm intuerentur, accusarint eum & tanquam blasphemum condemnarint, quòd Deum Patrem suum appellaret. Ioh.19.7. etsi verus esse Messias ac Redemptor nó potuerit, nisi in vnitate personæ verus Deus vt verus homo fuisset. Sunt igitur hac in re, sicut in aliis omnibus rebus extrema duo fugienda.
units.tr: The other error of the Jews, of those who attribute less to their sacraments than is fitting and so deprive themselves of their chief fruit, is still less excusable than that higher error, by which they slid into idolatry through attributing more to those things than is fitting, as we said above. For they were so far from recognising that visible temple, in which the Lord dwelt sacramentally (that is, by those visible signs he offered himself in some way to be seen), as a figure of the human nature of the Messiah, in which true and essential Deity dwelt bodily in the unity of the person, that on the contrary, when they looked only at the visible man, they accused him and condemned him as a blasphemer because he called God his Father (John 19:7). Yet he could not have been a true Messiah and Redeemer unless, being true man, he were also true God in the unity of the person. In this matter, therefore, as in all other things, the two extremes are to be avoided.

units.la: Nec ab simili est Anabaptistarum & illis similium doctrina, Sacramentū Baptismi, tantum esse testeram qua Christiani ab aliis populis distinguuntur alterutrum, vt diffidentes interse nationes ex suis testeris dignoscuntur. De Coena vero nihil aliud statuunt, nisi quòd dicunt testimonium esse mystici illius corporis, quod est Ecclesia, ex pluribus membris collectis, & charitate inter se compactis, sicut panis ex pluribus frumenti granis, vinum ex multis acinis conficitur. Ac sane fatemur hunc etiam mysterium huius Sacramenti nobis ab Apostolo 1. Cor.10.17. demonstrari, quam ob causam veterum Christianorum communia cœniuia dicebantur Agapæ, quasi Charitates dicas, quorum maxima pars erat Cœna Dominica. Sed in eo magnus eorum error est, quòd hic subsistentes, præcipuam Sacramenti partem omittunt, corporis huius caput, Christum, cuius communicatio, mutuam coniunctionem charitatis inuicem præcedit, vt causa suum effectum. Nam in illo & per illum, & non per alium vnum fumus, primùm cum ipso, deinde ipsi inter nos (hoc ipsum nimirum à patre potulante Christo Ioh.17.21.) viuificati in vitam æternam ex vi Sancti Spiritus intus agente in singula huius corporis membra. Ephes. 4. 15.& 16.
units.tr: The teaching of the Anabaptists and those like them is not similar, who hold that the sacrament of Baptism is merely a mark by which Christians are distinguished from other peoples, just as nations that distrust one another are known by their marks. As for the Supper, they state nothing else except that it is a testimony of that mystical body which is the Church, gathered from many members and joined together by love, just as bread is made from many grains of wheat and wine from many grapes. Indeed we admit that the mystery of this sacrament is shown to us by the Apostle (1 Cor. 10:17); for this reason the common feasts of the ancient Christians were called agapae, that is, feasts of love, most of which were the Lord's Supper. But their great error is that, by stopping here, they omit the chief part of the sacrament, Christ, the head of this body, whose communion precedes mutual union in love among us as a cause precedes its effect. For in him and through him, and not through another, we are one: first with him, then with one another (which Christ prayed for from the Father, John 17:21), quickened into eternal life by the power of the Holy Spirit working inwardly in each single member of this body (Eph. 4:15-16).

units.la: Porro praeter illa superiora omnia, singularem hic Dei providentiam admirari nos convenit. Nec enim Christus dixerat, Destruam, vt apud Marcum falsi testes loquuntur, nec, Possum destruere, vt apud Matth. nec etiam Dei templum, nec, hoc templum manufactum, nec, possum illud redintegrare, nec, aliud manufactum redintegrabo, vt apud Marcu dicunt, in quo etiam inter haec duo testimonia repugnantia eadem quae in aliis inter se non consentientibus conspicitur: ac simpliciter & perspicue de sui corporis teplo loquutus, dixerat, Destruite templum hoc, & triduo illud reaedificabo, de sua nimirum resurrectione vi sua a se ipso futura illud intelligens, certissimo & irrefragabili testimonio suae Deitatis, cuius auctoritate ex templo Dei patris illud profanantes flagello eiecerat: Deus vero tam mirabiliter omnia disposuit & administrauit, vt non modo quod ore suo protulerat, ex eius sensu ratum haberetur, sed etiam quod fingebant reipsa tandem praeter ipsorum tamen & eorum a quibus erant subornati mentem impleta sint. Dixerat igitur de suo corpore Christus, Destruite hoc templum, non hoc ipsos iubens, sed quid essent facturi praedicens: vt sane separantes animam ab eius corpore, quantum in ipsis fuit, humanitatem eius destruxerunt. At ipsemet sua vi templi sui partes seruauit. Anima enim immortalem occidere non potuerunt, quae separata nequaquam in inferis aut limbis quibus dam
units.tr: Moreover, beyond all those things mentioned above, we should here admire God's singular providence. Christ had not said "I will destroy," as the false witnesses report in Mark, nor "I am able to destroy," as in Matthew, nor "God's temple," nor "this temple made with hands," nor "I am able to rebuild it," nor "I will rebuild another made without hands," as they say in Mark. In these two conflicting testimonies, too, we see the same disagreement among witnesses that appears elsewhere. Rather, he spoke simply and plainly about the temple of his own body: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." By this he meant his own resurrection, which he would bring about by his own power, a most certain and irrefutable testimony to his Deity. By his authority he had driven out, with a whip, those who profaned the temple of God the Father. God, however, so wonderfully ordered and administered all things that what Christ had uttered with his mouth was not only held valid in its meaning, but what the witnesses were inventing was in fact fulfilled, though beyond the intention of themselves and of those who had suborned them. Christ had said concerning his body, "Destroy this temple," not commanding them to do so but foretelling what they would do. Indeed, by separating the soul from his body, as far as they could, they destroyed his humanity. But he himself preserved the parts of his temple by his own power. For they could not kill his immortal soul, which, once separated, was in no way in hell or in some limbo, as many have long imagined, but was in paradise itself, in that blessed rest which he had already granted to the soul of the converted thief, as is expressly said in Luke 23:43. The soul was separated from the body only until the third day, when he himself restored the body to remain forever.

units.la: [Marginal notes, left: Admiranda Dei providentia in Christi verbis; eorundem verborum falsa interpretatio; ex falsis testibus falsatione.] dam vt pridem finxerunt multi, sed in ipso paradiso fuit, & in ea beata quiete qua iam tum animę latronis illius conuersi dedit, vt expressè dicitur Luc.23.43. tantisper dum corpus repeteret, ab anima tantum vsque ad diem tertium separatum, quo ipsemet illud in æternum permansurum restituit. Falsorum vero testium dictum quod attinet, ipsi reuera templum, de quo loquutus erat Christus destruentes quantum in ipsis erat, templum illud materiale, ad quod falsò Iesu Christi verba detorquebant, & Christus etiam ipse, sed plane contrario sensu destruxerunt. Peruicax enim eorum improbitas Dominum vt ita dicam ad ea quæ tot Prophetarum vaticiniis, & ore suo tandem erat ipsis comminatus Luc.13.35. implenda coegit, vt defecti nimirum sine ciuitate, sine religione & politia vagarentur, quod nostro seculo cuiuis conspicuum est, sic Deo suam exerente iustitiam. At vicissim, & pro sua in Ecclesiam misericordia, sic terrestrem Ierosolymam aboleuit, vt pro figuris veritatem exhibuerit, & umbras in veram Lucem commutarit: sic Caiaphæ, nihil minus cogitantis, ad verbum, præter eius tamen intentionem, impleta Prophetia. Verè enim Christi morte populus saluus fuit, verus ille nimirum Dei populus de quo ille non loquebatur: illo contra de quo loquebatur, destructo & pessundato. Quapropter minimè cum Deo verbóque eius iocandum est.
units.tr: [Marginal notes, left: The wondrous providence of God in Christ's words; the false interpretation of the same words; falsification by false witnesses.] As for the saying of the false witnesses, they truly destroyed the temple of which Christ spoke, as far as lay in them, that material temple, to which they falsely twisted the words of Jesus Christ, and Christ himself too, but in a plainly contrary sense. For their stubborn wickedness, so to speak, forced the Lord to fulfil what he had threatened them with by his own mouth (Luke 13:35) and what many prophets had foretold: that they would wander, deprived of city, religion and polity. This is plain to anyone in our own age, as God exercises his justice. But in turn, and in accordance with his mercy toward the Church, he abolished earthly Jerusalem so that he displayed the truth in place of figures and changed shadows into the true Light. Thus the prophecy was fulfilled, word for word, in Caiaphas, who was thinking of nothing of the kind, yet beyond his intention. For by Christ's death the people were truly saved, that true people of God of whom he was not speaking, while the other, of which he was speaking, was destroyed and ruined. Therefore we must by no means trifle with God or with his word.

units.la: Denique Dominus interrogatus an aducer- sus testimonium illud aliquid exciperet, con-ticuisse dicitur, non tantum reipsa perfectę illius patientię quæ in ipso erat, de qua loquutus erat Isaias cap.53.7. (specimen editurus, aut testaturus se in omnibus Dei patris iudicio, quod tanquam sponsor nolter sustinebat, acquiescere: sed etiā testium testimoniique illorum fidem eluaturus, illos resposo dedignatus. Et hoc satis animaduertit Pontifex, pluribus illud testimonium non persequutus: & deinceps Christum tacetem coram Pilato visuri sumus, minime tamen quum Deo Patri sua laus tribuenda, vel sua doctrinę suę veritas asserenda sit etiam. Nimirum ab ipso & eius S. Spiritu discendum loquendi vel tacendi tempus opportunum. Et linguę, licet exigui membri, regendę scientia, cuius abusus non minus perniciosus & exitialis, quàm verus illius visus maximus & summa cum utilitate coniunctus. Iacob. 3.5. Quod in omni linguę usu diligenter obseruandum, sed maximè quum diuinę Veritati testimonium coram Deoferendum est: & a verbis nostris proximi damnum aut commodum, immo vitā necemue pendere conspicimus, ex diuinę Legis præscripto, in ore duorum aut trium testium ratū fore omne verbū. Deut.19.15.
units.tr: Finally, when the Lord was asked whether he would take any exception to that testimony, he is said to have kept silent. He did this not only to display in fact the perfect patience that was in him, of which Isaiah spoke (Isa. 53:7), intending to give a specimen or to attest that, as our surety, he acquiesced in all the judgment of God the Father which he bore. He also did it to refute the faith of those witnesses and their testimony, deigning not to answer them. Pilate noticed this well enough, and did not pursue that testimony at length. Hereafter we shall see Christ silent before Pilate, yet by no means when God the Father's praise is to be given or the truth of his doctrine is to be asserted. We must learn from himself and his Holy Spirit the opportune time for speaking or for keeping silent. We must also learn the skill of governing the tongue, though it is a small member, whose abuse is no less pernicious and deadly than its proper use is great and joined with the greatest benefit (James 3:5). This must be carefully observed in every use of the tongue, but especially when testimony to divine truth is to be borne before God. We see that the damage or advantage, indeed the life or death, of our neighbour depends on our words, and by the prescription of divine law every word shall stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses (Deut. 19:15).

units.la: Ex hoc præterea loco discamus, non modo falsum eum habendum teitem qui nouum aliquid fingit, sed quiveritate quibusdam additis, mutatis aut detractis adulterat: vt in tribus istis capitib. falsi testes de quibus agimus pecca-rum. runt. Animaduertendū præterea in vocatis ad ferendum veritati testimonium, falsitatis esse speciem id quod scias, vel parte eius reticere, præsertim eius nomine qui veritatis Deus est adactis iurciurando verum profiteri. Quo sanè crimine nullum est humanæ societati magis perniciosum, Deóque & ipsis hominibus inuisum, quod à nobis Deus auertat: & contrà nostris mentibus documenta quæ nobis copiose locus hic suppeditauit magis ac magis infigat.
units.tr: From this passage, moreover, let us learn that not only is he to be considered a false witness who invents something new, but also he who corrupts the truth by adding, changing or removing certain things, as the false witnesses of whom we speak did in these three chapters. It must further be noted that among those called to bear witness to the truth, the appearance of falsehood lies in knowingly concealing what one knows, or part of it, especially when one swears to tell the truth in the name of him who is the God of truth. Surely no crime is more pernicious to human society, or more hateful both to God and to men themselves (may God avert it from us). On the contrary, may the lessons which this passage has so richly supplied to us fix themselves ever more deeply in our minds.

units.la: HOMILIA decimatertia.
units.tr: HOMILY THIRTEEN.

units.la: MATTH. 26.
units.tr: MATTHEW 26.

units.la: 62. Et surgens Pontifex Maximus dixit ei, Nihil respondes? Quid illud est quod isti aduersum te testificantur?
units.tr: 62. Then the high priest stood up and said to him, "Do you make no answer? What is it that these men testify against you?"

units.la: 63. Iesus autem silebat.
units.tr: 63. But Jesus remained silent.

units.la: MARC. 14.
units.tr: MARK 14.

units.la: 60. Tum Pontifex Maximus quum assurrexisset in medium, interrogauit Iesum dicens, Non respondes quicquam? quid illud est quod isti aduersum te testificantur?
units.tr: 60. Then the high priest stood up in the midst and questioned Jesus, saying, "Do you make no answer at all? What is it that these men testify against you?"

units.la: 61. Ipse verò silebat, & nihil respondit.
units.tr: 61. But he kept silent and answered nothing.

units.la: LVC. 22.
units.tr: LUKE 22.

units.la: 61. Et vt ortus est dies, coactum fuit presbyterium populi, & primarij Sacerdotes & Scribæ, & adduxerunt eum in suum consessum,
units.tr: 61. And when day came, the council of the people assembled, both the chief priests and the scribes, and they led him into their council,

units.la: 67. Dicentes, Num tu es ille Christus? Dic nobis.
units.tr: 67. Saying, "Are you the Christ? Tell us."

units.la: HActenus secundum actum iudicij coràm Caiapha aduersus Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum audiuimus, in quo singulari Dei prouidentia potentiaque magis ac magis ipsius perfecta tum innocentia, tum integritas illuxerunt, vt probè teneremus non ob aliquem quo reus esset lapsum, sed pro nostris tantum peccatis fuisse, tam iustè quidem à Domino, quatenus sponsor noster erat, quàm perfidè & malitiosè ab hominibus condemnatum, sic ipsis abutente Deo vt improbitatis ipsorum non sit particeps, quàm deinceps iustè & seuerè vindicauit. At, vt purissimè semper operatur, quibuscunque tandem instrumentis vtatur, sic maximum omnium suorum operum, & in omnibus admirandum, omnium nimirum quibus electi rei erant peccatorum punitionem, & eorundem redemptione per omnium quos orbis haberet nequissimos & sceleratissimos perfecit, plus quàm admirandâ nostræ salutis Lucè ex tenebris educens. Nâ obsecro, quibus aliis instrumetis Dominus ad iusti condemnatione quàm Diabolo & omnium hominum sceleratissimis vteretur? Tertius & vltimus in hoc consessu
units.tr: Thus far we have heard of the first act of the trial before Caiaphas against our Lord Jesus Christ. In it, by the singular providence and power of God, his perfect innocence and integrity shone out more and more, so that we may firmly hold that he was condemned not for any fault by which he was guilty, but only for our sins. He was condemned by the Lord, insofar as he was our surety, most justly, and by men most treacherously and maliciously; yet God so used them that he himself took no part in their wickedness, and he then avenged it justly and severely. But God always works most purely, whatever instruments he uses. So he accomplished his greatest work of all, and one to be admired above all others, namely the punishment of the sins of the elect and their redemption, through the most wicked and criminal men the world could have, bringing us out of darkness into the light of our salvation, more than admirable. For I ask you, what other instruments could the Lord use to condemn the just One than the Devil and the most wicked of all men? The third and last act of this session

units.la: Quicquid Deus facit, bene facit, quibuscunque instrumentis ad illud vtatur. sessu aduersus nostrum Seruatorem actus explicandus superest, in quo idem quod superius visuri sumus, Dominū opus suū absoluentem, & impios suā malitiam paulatim cumulantes.
units.tr: Whatever God does, he does well, with whatever instruments he uses. There remains to be explained the act against our Saviour in this session, in which we shall see the same thing as above: the Lord finishing his work, and the wicked gradually piling up their malice.

units.la: Sed prius quàm istud aggredimur, egregius iste locus est, ex quo discamus ab eo qui prius tacuit, deinde tamen est loquutus, quando & quousque tacendū loquendúmve: vt cōtrà in falsis testibus & Caiapha videamus quale vitium admittant loquentes quum tacendū est: aut cōtra silentes quū loquendū est. Nō vtilem modò sane doctrinā, sed omnino necessariam, quum lingua quidem exiguum sit in humano corpore membrū, sed (sicut copiosè docet Iacobus epistolæ suæ Catholicæ cap.4.) vt vsus excellentissimi, sic abusus cōtrà maximè perniciosi. Atq; vtinā hoc loco, in quo iam pridem verū eius vsum ex Dei verbo didicisse debueramus, non essent linguarū leuium & temerè volubiliū nimium multa præ reliquis testimonio nis: quod nō sine magno animi mœrore dico.
units.tr: But before we take up that, this is an outstanding passage from which we may learn, from the one who first kept silent and then spoke, when and how far one ought to be silent or to speak. Conversely, in the false witnesses and in Caiaphas we may see what fault those commit who speak when they should be silent, or those who are silent when they should speak. This is not only a useful teaching but a wholly necessary one, since the tongue, though a small member of the human body, is (as James teaches at length in ch. 4 of his Catholic epistle) of the most excellent use when used well, and of the most destructive abuse when abused. Would that in this place, where we should long since have learned its true use from the Word of God, there were not so many tongues, light and rashly voluble, beyond all others in bearing witness. I say this not without great grief of mind.

units.la: Vt autē in summā quæ huius doctrinæ pria sunt conferam, aio Dei Legē, nostrarum cogitationum, dictorum, factorūmque normā esse oportere. Quid verò Lex requirit? Nimirum zelum & amorem ardentem Dei nostri, & charitatem erga proximos, id est quosuis homines, quorum honori & commodis studere nos decet, dum gloria Dei non lædatur.
units.tr: To sum up the main points of this teaching: I say that the Law of God must be the rule of our thoughts, words and deeds. And what does the Law require? Namely zeal and ardent love for our God, and charity toward our neighbours, that is, toward whatever men we ought to care for in their honour and welfare, so long as the glory of God is not harmed.

units.la: Primum igitur quum lingua sit nostrę mentis interpres, maximus ab iis error admittitur qui non præmeditati loquuntur: aut si meditantur & loquuntur: quum plerunque dicenda in mentem tardius veniant. Atque id natura, quantumuis corrupta, docere videtur, quum linguam labiis tanquam septis duobus vallauit, & iterum dentibus vt muro ad eius volubilitatem cohibendam cinxit, vt cogitandi spatium daret tantisper dum aperirentur labia, dentésque reserarentur. Nec cogitasse sufficit, nisi prius quàm loquaris bene cogites: porrò cogitationes vt bonæ sint regi oportet Legis diuinæ summa quam superius attigimus, & mente nostra Dauidis illa precatio semper meditanda Psal. 51. 15. Domine labia mea aperi, & os meum annuntiabit laudem tuam. Idcirco etiam psal. 40. v. 4. Cantica sibi à Domino in os indi profitetur. Et Apostolus ipse, licet tanta vi eloquentiæ prædītus, à Domino postulat oris adapertionem Ephes. 6. 19. Sed ista magis adhuc distinctè consideranda. Tenendum igitur in primis, inanes omnes sermones, quibus nec Dei gloria nec proximi commodum promouentur, putà mille facetiarum aut scurrilitatis genera graues offensas esse aduersus Deum, quarum etiam rationem reddituri simus. Matth. 12. 36. Et tamen sermones nostri isti sunt vt plurimum: & quod longè grauius est, infelix hoc seculum libris istiusmodi facetiarum plenis repletum est: quæ ludicra vocantur à multis, sed quæ magno tandem tum qui delectantur ipsi, tum alios qui illis parcunt redempturi sunt.
units.tr: First, then, since the tongue is the interpreter of our mind, the greatest error is made by those who speak without forethought, or who think and speak but whose words come to mind rather slowly. Nature itself, however corrupted, seems to teach this, when it has walled in the tongue with the two fences of the lips and again girded it with the teeth as with a wall, to restrain its volubility, so as to give time for thinking while the lips are opened and the teeth unlocked. Nor is it enough to have thought, unless before you speak you think well. Moreover, for our thoughts to be good they must be governed by the sum of the divine Law which we touched on above; and David's prayer should always be meditated in our mind: "Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praise" (Ps. 51:15). Hence also in Ps. 40:4 he professes that the Lord put a new song into his mouth. And the Apostle himself, though endowed with such power of eloquence, asks the Lord to open his mouth (Eph. 6:19). But these matters must be considered more distinctly. We must hold first of all that all empty talk, by which neither the glory of God nor the good of our neighbour is advanced, for example a thousand kinds of witticisms or buffoonery, are grave offences against God, for which we shall also have to give an account (Matt. 12:36). And yet our speech is for the most part of this kind; and, what is much more serious, this unhappy age is filled with books of this sort of witticisms, which many call playful, but for which, in the end, both those who delight in them and those who spare them will have to pay dearly.

units.la: Quid igitur iis linguis futurum putas, quæ sacrosanctum Dei Nomen, quod nunquam nec in mente nec in buccâ sine debita Numi-nis veneratione venire debet, quotidie tamen immo singulis momētis temerè effutiunt, quū tamē Angeli coră eius Maiestatę faciem obue-lent?Ef.6.2. Atque vtinā salte de horrenda illa comminatione ad tertium præceptum addita cogitarent, putà Deum non habiturum eum innocentem, id est, inultum relicturum, qui nomen eius in vanum acceperit.
units.tr: What then do you think will become of those tongues which rashly and daily, indeed every moment, pour out the most holy Name of God, which should never come into mind or mouth without due reverence for the Divinity, while the angels veil their faces before his majesty (Isa. 6:2)? Would that they at least considered that dreadful threat added to the third commandment: that God will not hold guiltless the one who takes his name in vain.

units.la: Porrò, si Deum tantùm nominare, tam est coram eius facie detestandum, quid fiet iis qui Iurantes eum nominant, id est iudicem ac te-stem inuocant in rebus leuibus, quod supra iam ante docuimus crimen esse detestandum?
units.tr: Furthermore, if merely to name God is so detestable in his sight, what will become of those who swear by naming him, that is, who call upon the Judge and Witness in trivial matters, which we have already taught above is a crime to be detested?

units.la: Quid verò miseris iis qui mentientes etiam ac fallentes scienter prudenter iurant, quod perinde est (res horrenda dictu) ac si Satanam mendacij Spiritum, in ipso Dei solio collocarent?
units.tr: And what of those wretches who, lying and deceiving, swear knowingly and deliberately, which is (a horrible thing to say) no different from setting the Satan, the spirit of lies, on the very throne of God?

units.la: Sed multò magis rei estis quos iam nominatim appello, vos, inquam, daemonibus haud absimiles, infandi ac detestandi blasphemi, deieratores, Numinis contemptores, ac profcifiores quantum in vobis est æterni Dei viuentis, quem ipsi Diaboli etiam horrent. Deū enim vnū esse credūt &tremūt, inquit Iac.2.19. Et horum quidem non est exiguus, sed ingens numerus, atque adeò eorum qui ad aliquam dignitatem euecti sunt, ista qui parui faciant, vel potius irrideant &subsannent. Euge vero, Domine, Deus, nósne in hæc incidisse tempo-
units.tr: But much more guilty are you whom I now name individually: you, I say, hardly unlike demons, unspeakable and detestable blasphemers, perjurers, despisers of the Divinity, and, as far as in you lies, betrayers of the eternal living God, whom even the devils themselves abhor. "The devils also believe, and tremble" (James 2:19). And the number of such men is not small but great, and indeed includes those who have been raised to some dignity, who make light of these things, or rather mock and scoff at them. Good heavens, Lord God, have we fallen into these times

units.la: {&} j. ra quibus hæc videamus & auribus percipia-mus? Quàm verò bonus es & patiens? Tellus quomodo non talibus monstris absorbendis ima dehiscis! Sed de hoc crimine pluribus deinceps acturi sumus.
units.tr: {&} j. in which we see and hear these things! How good and patient you are! How is it that the earth does not open its depths to swallow such monsters! But we shall deal with this crime at greater length later.

units.la: Quid verò dicam de putidis illis & olidis nonnullorum linguis seu cloacis, spurcos & infectos sermones subinde vomentibus: quid de tot scriptis vitiorum omnium illecebris & cupiditatum lenociniis, in primis verò turpiu istorum & lupanarium admissariorum, tum veterum tum recentiorum poëtarum, Græco-rum, Latinorum, Gallicorum omnium Gen-tium sacram poësin prophanantium, quibus hodie totus orbis plus quàm alias vnquam inficitur? Ecquis verò miretur talibus spurcitiis ab vn-guiculis imbuta esse multorum ingenia, quum Gymnasiorum & Academiarum maxima pars totidem lupanaria sint, immo totidem Sodo-mæ ac Gomorrhæ, in quibus tam spurcorum, & detestandorum scriptorum etiam auditur inter-pretatio? Verùmenimuerò, dicite, quid iuuat nos è Scholis nostris istiusmodi lenones pro-fligasse, Dei beneficio, si Lugduno accersun-tur, passim à mulieribus ac virginibus in œdi-bus & officinis legendi? Videt ista Deus, Deus, inquam, ista videt, rationémque tandem ali-quando postulabit: & à vobis potissimum, quibus impediendi data quidem potestas, sed qua segniùs vtimini.
units.tr: And what shall I say of those foul and stinking tongues, or sewers, of some men, which now and then spew forth filthy and corrupt talk; what of so many writings that offer every allurement of vice and the enticements of lust, especially those of the shameless and pimping poets, ancient and modern, Greek, Latin and French, who profane sacred poetry, by whom the whole world is today infected more than ever before? And who could be surprised that the minds of many have been steeped in such filth from their earliest years, since the greater part of gymnasiums and academies are so many brothels, indeed so many Sodoms and Gomorrahs, in which the interpretation of such filthy and detestable writers is heard? But tell me, what good does it do that we have, by God's blessing, driven such pimps out of our schools, if they are fetched back from Lyons and read everywhere by women and virgins in their homes and workshops? God sees these things, God, I say, sees them, and will at some time demand an account, and especially from you, who have been given the power to prevent them, but use that power more sluggishly.

units.la: Quid denique de linguis iniuriosis, male-dicis, detractionum, litium, querelarumque pl cplenis futurū putamus?quas ad Pf. 10. ablego, & alios Scripturæ locos non paucos quibus omnibus satis arguuntur.
units.tr: Finally, what do we suppose will be said about abusive, slanderous tongues, and those full of detraction, lawsuits and complaints? I refer these to Ps. 10 and to many other passages of Scripture by which all of them are sufficiently condemned.

units.la: Denique si lingua nostra Deo (veritatis Patri, vt Satan est autor mendacij) consecranda est, mendacem efficitur esse coram Deo maxime detestandam. Quod vitium si in priuatis negotiis tantopere condemnandum, quid futurum est quum ante ora Iudicum & pro eorum tribunali, in ipsius Æterni Dei atque ipsius Angelorum conspectu, aut litigantes partes, aut procuratores & Aduocati, aut denique falsum quiddā scientes prudetes afferunt, aut quoquomodo veritate alterant, vt fucum faciant & æquum iniquum, & contrà dicant? Hæc animaducrtite Litigatcs: Vos enim Deus videt, vos audit & notat, quem tandem suo tempore veritatis vindicem & assertorem eltis experturi, & quidem in loco in quo non hominibus decipiendis erit, sed gemitibus & dentium stridori locus.
units.tr: Finally, if our tongue is to be consecrated to God, the Father of truth (since Satan is the author of lies), then a liar is most detestable before God. If this vice is so strongly condemned in private affairs, what will become of those who, before the faces of judges and in their tribunal, in the sight of the eternal God himself and of his angels, either as litigants, or as proxies and advocates, or indeed knowingly put forward something false, or alter the truth in any way, to make a fraud and make the just unjust, and speak the opposite? Litigants, take this to heart. God sees you, God hears you and takes note of you, and in his own time you will learn that he is the avenger and vindicator of the truth. And this will happen in a place where there is no one to deceive, but only groaning and gnashing of teeth.

units.la: Dicam aliquid amplius, & aperte dicam ac dilucidè aduersus eos qui tuentur neminem teneri partis aduersæ ius adiuuare: non peccare qui se coram Iudice professus sit ignorare quod tamen optimè notum habcat: & ita litigantem aduersarium grauare vt causa cadat, quum fortassis Ignorantes isti sæpe iuris suorum aduersariorum tabulas habeant in potestate, nec velint profiteri quod sciunt: hos, inquam, omnes aio in mendacium numero reponendos, quos propria conscientia coar-
units.tr: I will say something more, and say it openly and clearly, against those who hold that no one is bound to help the opposing party in their right, and that a person does not sin if he declares before a judge that he does not know what he nevertheless knows very well, and so burdens his opposing litigant that the case is lost, when perhaps these ignorant men often hold the records of their opponents' rights in their power and do not wish to state what they know. All of these, I say, must be counted among the liars, whom their own conscience convicts,

units.la: ij. guat, & iniquarum sententiarum reos, quę nō sint iudicibus, quos ex allegatis & probatis sententiam ferre par est, imputandæ, sed speciosæ illorum ignorantiæ & simulationi: tandémque pœnas acerbissimas ipsi Domino luituros, apud quem nihil eos Iudicum sententiæ, literæ vel sigilla sint iuuatura, quum provocationes miserorum sæpe non diu relinquat inultas. Quid si verò contingat Iudices Caiaphæ similes & eius esse cófessui? Nimirum scelerus ille cumulus est, paribus etiam pœnis tandem vindicandi.
units.tr: and who are guilty of unjust sentences, which are to be imputed not to the judges, who must pronounce judgment on what has been alleged and proved, but to their own feigned ignorance and pretence. In the end they will pay the most bitter penalties to the Lord himself, before whom the sentences of judges, their letters or their seals will not help them at all, since he often does not leave the appeals of the wretched unavenged for long. What if it happens that the judges are like Caiaphas and belong to his council? Surely that is the heaped-up measure of wickedness, which will at last be punished with equal penalties.

units.la: Hactenus autem iis auditis in quibus sermone plurimum peccatur, facile perspicitur si rerum earum cogitatio quæ nisi male loquendo non possunt exprimi prohibetur, multo magis præcipi vt quæ male cogitata sunt, coprimantur: licut in vtroque tam à Caiapha quàm à falsis testibus peccatum est. Christus verò solus is est ex quo discere nos oportet quando silendum, & quando & quomodo silentium abrumpendum, & loquendum.
