units.tr: Having thus heard the matters in which people most sin by speech, it is easily seen that if the thought of those things which cannot be expressed except by speaking evil is forbidden, it is much more commanded that what has been evilly thought should be covered over. In both respects sin was committed by Caiaphas as well as by the false witnesses. Christ alone is the one from whom we must learn when to keep silent, and when and how to break the silence and speak.

units.la: Discemus igitur ex Christi silentio, licet loquendi materia non deficiat, (vt Christo suppetebat abundè, quippe qui suppeditat etiam aliis ipse Sancto suo Spiritu quantum satis est) non semper tamen eloquendum quod liceat: aut quod res nobis sit cum porcis aut canibus Matth.7.6.cuiusmodi Caiaphas & ceteri tus ille confessus fuerunt: aut quod Dei gloriæ proximive commodo non expediat, cuius exemplum habemus. Act.23.6. Sic igitur Christus stus tum coram his Iudicibus, tum deinceps coram Pilato, quòd sciret se condemnandum stare, & ex hac condemnatione mundi salute pendere, falsorum Iudicum istorum quam poterat malitiam arguere noluit: aut etiam quòd tacendo saepe plus efficitur, quàm loquendo, ac proinde quum vellet tum hic tum coram Pilato quàm absurda sibi crimina obiicerentur demonstrare, respondo illa dedignatus clarissimè coarguit. Et has quidem circumstantias Spiritus Sanctus loco suo & tempore bona conscientia praeditos docet, & quidem lögè melius quàm humana prudentia docet tacendum loquendum-ne sit & quousque sit in sermone progrediendum.
units.tr: We shall learn therefore from Christ's silence that, although the matter of speaking does not fail (as Christ had abundant material, since he himself supplies to others through his Holy Spirit as much as is sufficient), yet we should not always say whatever is permitted, either because we are dealing with swine or dogs (Matt. 7.6), such as Caiaphas and the others of that council were, or because it does not serve the glory of God or the good of our neighbour; of this we have an example in Acts 23.6. So Christ, both here before these judges and afterwards before Pilate, knowing that he stood as one to be condemned and that the salvation of the world hung upon this condemnation, was unwilling to rebuke the wickedness of those false judges as he could have done. Also, because by keeping silent he often achieves more than by speaking, when he wished, here and before Pilate, to show how absurd were the crimes laid against him, he most clearly refuted them by disdaining to answer. The Holy Spirit teaches these circumstances to those endowed with a good conscience in their proper place and time, and indeed far better than human prudence teaches whether one should be silent or speak, and how far one should proceed in speech.

units.la: Obseruandum praeterea non paruum errorem saepe committi in veritate proferenda, puta, quum malo animo profertur, aut quando, vbi, & apud eum effertur, quem nec ad Dei gloriam, nec ad vtilitatem proximi expediat: aut quum efferri veritas à nobis non potest, quin improborum malitiae patrocinemur. Quâ ob causam multis nostro seculo Martyribus cōtigisse videmus vt quosuis cruciatus perferre quàm hostiū rabie ac furore in suos fratres armare maluerint, sic tamen vt mendacio abstinerent: valde enim inter se, Non omnia quae scias dicere, & Mentiri, differunt. At quum silentium cum diuini nominis abnegatione coniunctum est, aut proximi detrimento: tum abrumpendum & ore aperto nihil dissimulandoloquendum est, etiamsi de vita, si centum
units.tr: Furthermore, it must be observed that a not small error is often committed in declaring the truth: for example, when it is declared with an evil intent, or when, where, and to whom it is uttered, when this is not conducive either to the glory of God or to the benefit of our neighbour; or when the truth cannot be expressed by us without becoming a defender of the wickedness of the wicked. For this reason we see that many martyrs in our age preferred to bear any torments rather than arm the rage and fury of their enemies against their brothers, yet so that they abstained from lying; for "not to say everything you know" and "to lie" differ greatly. But when silence is joined with the denial of the divine name, or with harm to a neighbour, then silence must be broken, and one must speak openly, dissembling nothing, even though we were to be imperilled in life, even if we had a hundred lives, as we have an express command (Matt. 10.32). And Christ himself has gone before us, both in his whole life (which was a continual profession of the truth for which he came), and in this history of his passion, in front of Caiaphas and Pilate, by his example. The faithful servants of God in the Church have done the same. And so far concerning this chapter of doctrine, which may God engrave ever more deeply on our minds.

units.la: { } iij. haberemus, periclitaremur, vt mandatum expressum habemus. Matth. 10. 32. & nobis ipse Christus tum reliqua tota vita (quae perpetua fuit veritatis ad quam venerat professio) tu in hac passionum eius historia coram Caiapho & Pilato suo praeiuit exemplo. Idem fidi Dei in Ecclesia serui praestiterunt. Et haec hactenus de huius doctrinae capite, quam vtinam Deus nostris mentibus magis ac magis insculpat.
units.tr: Let us therefore pass on to that third act of Caiaphas against the Lord, in which again everything, as far as the outward appearance of judgment is concerned, is praiseworthy, but worthy of no reproach. For what was more worthy of the care and concern of the High Priest than to know whether the true Messiah had come? Who ought rather than he himself to inquire? And who could answer more certainly than he who asks? But there is no vice more detestable than that which clothes itself in the covering of virtue. Christ wished to strip this mask from those hypocrites even before he answered them, as the blessed Luke expressly records (Luke 22.67–68), saying that they would not believe him, even though they professed to ask, and that far from acquitting him on the basis of his answer, they would seek from it an occasion for condemnation. And here a broad field of manifold doctrine is opened to us, provided we sincerely do what we see they did deceitfully and with an evil mind.

units.la: Transeamus igitur ad tertium istum Caiaphi actum aduersus Dominum, in quo rursus omnia, speciem externa iudicij quod attinet, laudabilia, nulla vero reprehensione digna. Na quid erat magis cura & sollicitudine Pontificis Maximi dignum, quam scire an verus Messias aduenisset? quis potius quam ipse debuit inquirere? Quis vero certius respondere poterat quam is ipse qui interrogat? At nullum magis detestandum vitium quam quod se virtutis induit inuolucro. Et hanc etiam prius quam responderet istis hypocritis laruam Christus detrahere voluit, vt expresse Diuus Lucas illud etiam expressit 22.67. & 68. non credituros sibi dicens, licet profiteretur, tantumque abesse vt ex responso ipsum absoluerent, vt ex eo contra condemnationis occasionem quaererent. Et hic multiplicis doctrinae campus nobis aperitur, modo sincere faciamus, quae dolose iltos & malo animo fecisse conspicimus.
units.tr: Let us therefore pass on to Caiaphas's third action against the Lord. In it, as far as the outward appearance of judgment goes, everything was again commendable and nothing worthy of blame. For what was more worthy of the care and concern of the High Priest than to learn whether the true Messiah had come? Who ought rather than he to make that inquiry? And who could answer more surely than he who was asking? Yet no vice is more detestable than the one that dresses itself in the cloak of virtue. Christ wished to strip this mask from these hypocrites even before he answered them, as the blessed Luke expressly recorded (22:67-68), saying that they would not believe him, even though he professed it. They were so far from acquitting him on the basis of his answer that they sought from it an occasion for condemnation. Here a field of many-sided teaching opens before us, provided we set out sincerely what we see they did deceitfully and with an evil mind.

units.la: Primum igitur teneamus Pastorum esse potissimum quos Deus ad suorum coagmentationem, & ad aedificationem corporis Christi,
units.tr: First, then, let us hold that it is above all the task of ministers, whom God has appointed for the joining together of his people and the building up of the body of Christ, to search night and day into the secrets of God, of which they are the stewards.

units.la: Eph.4.11. constituit, nocte dieque Dei arcana scrutari, quorum sunt dispensatores. 1. Cor. 4.1. Quomodo enim quod ignorat ipsi alios docere? Porro sic proprium illud esse Pastorum intelligendum est ad oues docendas, ut sit illis etiam cum omnibus commune, ad fermentum Pharisaeorum praecavendum, Mar.8.15. & spiritus, quos audire, ab iis quos fugere oportet discernendos, 1. Thes.5.21. vocem quam audire debet, Ioh.10.4.&5. ab erroris spiritu. 1. Tim.4.1 se in Angelum Lucis transformate. 2. Cor.11.13.&14. Tale Aaronem & veros eius successores fuisse certum est, quibus tot Pseudoprophetae averis saepe reprehensi, nominatimque Caiaphas & totus iste consessus opponuntur.
units.tr: (Eph. 4:11; 1 Cor. 4:1.) For how can a man teach others what he does not know himself? Moreover, that task which belongs to ministers must be understood as the teaching of the sheep, yet it is also common to all men: they must guard against the leaven of the Pharisees (Mark 8:15), and must distinguish spirits, which to hear and which to flee (1 Thess. 5:21), and the voice which they ought to hear (John 10:4-5), from the spirit of error (1 Tim. 4:1), and from those who transform themselves into angels of light (2 Cor. 11:13-14). It is certain that Aaron and his true successors were of this kind, against whom so many false prophets have often been rebuked, and against whom Caiaphas by name and that whole assembly are set.

units.la: Inde necessario sequitur, quod quemadmodum quum lapis angularis iste Iesus Christus, ab ipsis architectis ut erat praedictum, Ps. 118.22. reiiceretur, apparuit veram Ecclesiae Israeliticae notam non simpliciter a personali successione, sed a continuatione doctrinae Propheticae, Mosis aliorumque Prophetarum libris comprehensae, quibus nihil addatur, nihil detrahatur, pendere, Deut.4.2. Sic hodie fatendum exterior & genuinam veram Ecclesiae notam, cuius esse membrum ad salutem oportet, non esse Successionem Romanorum Episcoporum, aut aliorum quorumlibet locorum, sed Apostolicae doctrinae continuatione, scriptis Novi foederis comprehensae, quibus itidem nihil adiiciatur, nihil detrahatur. Nam alioquin Apostolorum scripta longe scriptis Prophetarum essent imperfectiora,
units.tr: It follows necessarily from this that, just as when that cornerstone, Jesus Christ, was rejected by the very builders, as had been foretold (Ps. 118:22), it became clear that the true mark of the Israelite Church depended not simply on personal succession but on the continuance of the prophetic doctrine, contained in the books of Moses and the other prophets, to which nothing is to be added and from which nothing is to be taken away (Deut. 4:2). So today we must acknowledge that the external and genuine mark of the true Church, of which one must be a member for salvation, is not the succession of the Roman bishops or of any other places whatever, but the continuance of apostolic doctrine, contained in the writings of the New Covenant, to which likewise nothing is to be added and from which nothing is to be taken away. For otherwise the writings of the Apostles would be far less perfect than the writings of the Prophets,

units.la: t. iiij. id est, Lucis splendor figuris & vmbris pede-tentim dissipatis obscurior. Heb.1.1. quum nō plures Ecclesiæ, sed vnica sit, Propheratum & Apostolorum innixa fundamento. Ephes. 2. verf.20.
units.tr: Vol. iv., that is, the splendour of light grows dimmer as the figures and shadows are gradually dispelled. Heb. 1.1. Since there is not a plurality of churches but only one, resting on the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles. Eph. 2.20.

units.la: Sed adhuc inter istos de quibus agimus, & aduersarios nostros magna est discrepantia. Nam etsi Caiaphas & totus ille confessus nihil minus essent quàm vera Ecclesia, siquidem nō modò nō agnouerūt, sed condēnauerūt cru-cique adiudicarūt verum Ecclesiæ caput, sed-bant tamen in Moisis cathedra, quam ipsi pol-luebant: & Ierusalem ipsa vocatur à Domino, ciuitas Dei. At vbi tandem iste Papa Oecume-nicus à Deo constitutus reperiatur? vbi Cardi-nales? vbi Romana sedes ordinata vt esset vni-uersalis Ecclesiæ sedes? Annon contrà ciuitas illa est septem colles habens, super quos insi-det illa meretrix, vt veteres ipsi sunt interpre-tati, licet etiam ipsi nonnunquam illius ine-briati poculo fuerint? Apoc.17.9. Laudes verò quas Apostolus tribuit, non vrbi quidem, sed Ecclesiæ quæ tunc erat Romæ, easdem sanè de Thessalonicensibus etiam expressius prædicat. 1.Thess.1.8. De neutra tamen tam multa quàm de Ierosolyma dicuntur, quæ tamen Prophe-tarum necis rea facta est, tandemque ipsius auctoris vitæ crucifixi. Deinde quantum abest ut illud cum triplici corona idolum, & Epi-scopi reliqui suis illis lituis & mitris insignes cum Caiapha & hoc toto Hierosolymorum consessu comparari possint? Nam illi saltem cum Scribis & Pharisæis à Deo præscriptum in templo suo cultu retinebant: hi vero nihil nec in toto Dei cultu nec in Sacramentis, quç rituali illi cultui successerunt, integrum reliquerunt. Illi per singula Sabbatha Mosen & Prophetas legebant: hi à lectione Scripturarum lingua vulgari plebem imperitam arcent: nec legunt ipsi, sed in particulas concisam lingua barbara, sæpe ipsis etiam lectoribus incognitam modulantur & cantillant: vt omittam maximam eorum partem, qui maiores præsertim dignitates occupant, sibique nomen Ecclesiæ Repræsentatiuæ tribuunt, nunquam de solo in illis versu vel legendo vel intelligendo cogitasse: solis ex hac tota turba reliquis qui ex Scripturarum adulteratione viuunt, quos fateor à Caiapha & eius consiliariis hic ad viuum siue sigillatim ipsi, siue vniuersa ipsorum consilia considerentur expressos.
units.tr: Yet between those of whom we are speaking and our opponents there is still a great disagreement. For although Caiaphas and that whole council were by no means the true Church, since they not only failed to acknowledge but condemned the true Head of the Church and handed him over to the cross, nevertheless they sat in Moses' seat, though they polluted it; and Jerusalem itself is called by the Lord the city of God. But where, then, is that Pope, the Oecumenical, appointed by God? Where are the cardinals? Where is the Roman see ordained to be the seat of the universal Church? Is that city not rather the one that has seven hills, upon which that harlot sits, as the ancients themselves interpreted, although they too were sometimes made drunk with her cup? Rev. 17.9. The praises which the Apostle gave, not to the city but to the Church which was then at Rome, he proclaims even more expressly of the Thessalonians. 1 Thess. 1.8. Yet about neither are so many things said as about Jerusalem, which nonetheless became guilty of the murder of the Prophets and at last of the author of life himself, crucified. Next, how far is it from possible to compare that idol with the triple crown, and the remaining bishops, notable for their litui and mitres, with Caiaphas and this whole council of Jerusalem! For the Jews at least, together with the scribes and Pharisees, retained in the temple the worship prescribed by God; these men, however, have left nothing intact, neither in the whole worship of God nor in the sacraments which succeeded that ritual worship. Those read Moses and the Prophets every Sabbath; these keep the ignorant common people from reading Scripture in the vernacular tongue. Nor do they read it themselves, but chop it into fragments and chant and warble it in a barbarous language, often unknown even to the readers themselves. I say nothing of the greater part of them, especially those who hold higher dignities and claim for themselves the name of the representative Church, who never once thought of reading or understanding a single verse of it. From this whole crowd only those are left who live by the adulteration of the Scriptures, and I confess that these are here portrayed to the life by Caiaphas and his counsellors, whether their persons are considered individually or their councils as a whole.

units.la: Porrò & illud hic addiscendum, Caiapham si serio & ex animo Christum interrogasset, eorum hodie iudicem futurum, qui pene innumeras quæstiones quas vocant Scholasticas mouent, alias quidem vanas & inanes, alias ridiculas, alias denique plenas impietatis, quibus Doctorum Scholasticorum libri referti sunt, & adhuc hodie scholæ theologales personant: quù nostro hoc seculo cöspiciamus homi ingenia rebus inanibus maximè si alias vi quam pasci ac delectari, frustrà tot locis Apostolo monente & hortâte vt à curiosis quæstionibus abstineatur, & nominatim, Col.2.8, 18. & 23. quos oportebat contrà sobrie & reuerenter de rebus ad salutem pertinentibus, & verbo Dei nobis revelatis incumbere: quarum summa est cognitio tum Personae Christi tum eiusdem officij in quo summus completi, Coloss. 2. 10. quandoquidem in ipso sunt omnes thesauri sapientiae ac cognitionis abscondite. Coloss.2.3. & in quo rata sunt omnes promissiones. 2. Cor. 1.20.
units.tr: Furthermore, let this also be learned here: if Caiaphas had seriously and sincerely questioned Christ, he would be the judge of those who today raise almost countless questions, which they call Scholastic. Some of these are vain and empty, others ridiculous, and others finally full of impiety; the books of the Scholastic doctors are stuffed with them, and the theological schools still resound with them today. In our own age we see men's minds busied with empty things, most of all when they are exercised in them rather than fed and delighted by them, although the Apostle warns and exhorts us in so many places to abstain from curious questions. He names them specifically at Col. 2.8, 18 and 23, and says instead that we should apply ourselves soberly and reverently to matters pertaining to salvation and revealed to us in the Word of God. The sum of these is the knowledge both of the Person of Christ and of the office in which he is the Highest, complete; for you are complete in him, Col. 2.10, since in him are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden. Col. 2.3. And in him all the promises are yea and amen. 2 Cor. 1.20.

units.la: Discamus insuper ab hoc hypocrita, non tamen vt ipse, à quo huius Filij Dei, in quo solo nostra salus posita est, cognitio sit haurienda, nimirum ab eodem. Quis enim hanc sapientiam nos doctu-rus est, nisi qui vera Patris est sapientia? 1. Cor. 1 24. is per quem loquutus est Spiritus Prophetarum. 1. Pet. 1.11. ex cuius plenitudine nos omnes oportet haurire. Ioh. 1. 16. qui mittit Paracletum in hanc veritatē nos deducturum. Ioh. 16. 13. qui denique nobis ex sinu Patris eum annuntiat quem nemo nisi in illo & per illum vidit? Ioh. 1. 18.
units.tr: Let us learn further from this hypocrite, not indeed to imitate him, that the knowledge of this Son of God, in whom alone our salvation is placed, is to be drawn from the very same source, namely from him. For who will teach us this wisdom, except he who is the true wisdom of the Father? 1 Cor. 1.24. He is the one through whom the Spirit of the Prophets spoke. 1 Pet. 1.11. From his fullness we must all draw. John 1.16. He sends the Paraclete to lead us into this truth. John 16.13. And finally, who declares to us from the bosom of the Father him whom no one has seen except in him and through him? John 1.18.

units.la: Quid ergo miramur, eos qui Dei cognitione in humana sapientia immo potius stultitia, (qui tamen à seipsis nec cogitare quidè possunt quae Dei sunt 2. Cor. 3. 5.) & iustitiam qua coram Deo consistant in seipsis quaerunt, operâ ludere? Tales sunt qui religione in Platone aut Aristotele quaerunt, in quo duplicitèr hallucinantur. Namque illi atque eorum similes, licet insignes viri fuerint, & eximiis virtutibus ornati nihil unquam de Deo didicerunt, nec etiam
units.tr: Why then do we wonder that those who seek the knowledge of God in human wisdom, or rather foolishness (who yet cannot of themselves even think anything that is of God, 2 Cor. 3.5), and who seek in themselves the righteousness by which they stand before God, labour in vain? Such are those who seek religion in Plato or Aristotle, and in this they go astray in two ways. For they and those like them, although they were distinguished men adorned with outstanding virtues, never learned anything about God, nor

units.la: docere possunt, nisi quantum naturæ humanæ lumen illis suppeditat: quæ omnis cognitio tantum nobis inexcusabilibus reddendis est idonea. Rom.1. 20. nisi quòd longè peius quiddā subest, vt eodem loco testatur Apostolus. Magni enim illi Philosophi vani facti sunt in suis cogitationibus. Exempli gratia: si Aristoteli fidem adhibemus, mūdus hic aspectabilis nunquam creatus fuerit: & Dei prouidentia nō fertur in res singulares. Si Platoni credimus pecudum iisdē argumentis nō minus immortales quàm hominū futuras animas, easdemque ex vno corpore in aliud transituras, nobis persuadebimus. Quinâ verò de rebus istis verum quicquam docerent, qui nec de creatione, nec de hominis corruptione, & multò minus de eius remedio nihil vnquā cognouerunt, quū in rebus etiā puris naturalibus ita cæcutiāt vt alij aliis cōtradicant? Agnosco quidē in veteribus nōnullis supernaturalis illius sapientiæ vestigia, tanquā reliquias doctrinæ quā Patriarchæ professi sunt. At vicissim quicquid in ea purū videtur, quàm multis erroribus velut cœno quodam deturpatur? Non est igitur ab istis inquirenda scientia, nisi ad Atheos & Epicureos ex seipsis coarguendos. Sed haurienda veritas ab illa vera scaturigine, quæ semper in Dei pulo saliit perennis, quā non hominū voluntate, sed à sanctis Dei hominibus, quos agebat Spiritus S. allatam docet Petrus. 2. Pet. 1. 20.
units.tr: can they teach anything, except as much as the light of human nature supplies them; and all such knowledge is only fit to render us inexcusable. Rom. 1.20. But something far worse lies beneath it, as the Apostle testifies in the same place: those great philosophers became vain in their thoughts. For example, if we give faith to Aristotle, this visible world was never created, and God's providence does not extend to particular things. If we believe Plato, he will persuade us that the souls of beasts will be no less immortal than those of men, and that they too will pass from one body into another, by the same arguments. And how could those who knew nothing of creation, nor of the corruption of man, and much less of its remedy, teach anything true about these matters, since even in purely natural things they are so blind that they contradict one another? I do indeed recognize in some of the ancients traces of that supernatural wisdom, as remnants of the doctrine which the patriarchs professed. But conversely, how many errors defile whatever seems pure in them, as if with some mire! Therefore knowledge is not to be sought from these men, except to convict atheists and Epicureans by their own standards. Rather, truth is to be drawn from that true spring which always leaped up perennially among the people of God, and which Peter teaches was brought not by the will of men but by holy men of God, moved by the Holy Spirit. 2 Pet. 1.20.

units.la: Longè verò magis adhuc falluntur qui verā religionem in multitudine, in consuetudine, in aliquo temporum interuallo quærunt, quasi vero non inde ab omni ævo plures ituli fuerint quàm sapientes: quasi vero vel consuetudo vel tempus aurum ex plumbo faciat, aut mendacium in veritatem conuertat. Cauendæ porrò nobis hîc sunt diligenter insidiæ Satanæ, & illa veri Christi nostri cómonefactio est in memoriâ reuocanda, qua suos apud Matt. 24. 23. præmonebat surrecturos pseudochristos & pseudoprophetas cum erroris efficacia maxima. Et hoc ipsum Apostolorum temporibus impleri coepisse conspicimus. 2. Thess. 2. 11. 1. Tim. 4. 1.
units.tr: Much more, however, do those err who seek true religion in multitude, in custom, or in some lapse of time, as if from every age there have not been more fools than wise men; as if custom or time makes gold out of lead, or turns a lie into truth. Moreover we must carefully beware here of the snares of Satan, and that warning of our true Christ must be recalled to memory, by which he forewarned that false christs and false prophets would arise with the greatest power of deception. Matt. 24.23. And we see that this very thing began to be fulfilled in the times of the Apostles. 2 Thess. 2.11; 1 Tim. 4.1.

units.la: Igitur ne hac in parte incautiores decipiamur, primùm tempora distinguamus. Patriarcharum enim temporibus ad Mosen usque, salutis doctrinam ipse Deus per visiones & umbras docuit, quæ à patribus perpetua successione filiis erat tradita, quod ex Abrahami potissimum historia conspicuum est, cum quo Deus fœdus suum renouauit, quam ob causam etiam, Credentium pater nuncupatus est. Facile verò fuit veritatem doctrinæ tueri Patriarchis longiorem vitam agentibus, quum Adamus primus homo, primi seculi testis oculatus, Lamechum à se octavum hominem docuerit. Et Sem Noachi filius diluvij testis oculatus ipsi etiam Abrahamo superuixerit.
units.tr: Therefore, that we may not be deceived in this matter through too little caution, let us first distinguish the times. For from the times of the patriarchs until Moses, God himself taught the doctrine of salvation through visions and shadows, and this was handed down from fathers to sons by unbroken succession. This is most evident especially from the history of Abraham, with whom God renewed his covenant, and for which reason he was also called the father of believers. Indeed it was easy to preserve the truth of doctrine among the patriarchs, who lived longer lives, since Adam, the first man and eyewitness of the first age, taught Lamech, the eighth man from himself. And Shem, the son of Noah, an eyewitness of the flood, even outlived Abraham himself.

units.la: At hominum ætate decrescente, & Patriarcharum doctrina paulatim evanescente, fidelem suum servum Moses suscitavit Dominus, cum mandatis expressis non tantùm populû, vt reuelabat ei Dominus suo nomine docen-di : sed etiam monumentis totam veterem & sacram historiam inde ab ipsa m undi origine repetitam cum hac supernaturalis veritatis doctrina tradendi, cui nihil adderet,immuta-ret, aut denique detraheret, Deut. 12. ver.32. &i 5.32.
units.tr: But as the age of men declined and the teaching of the Patriarchs gradually faded, the Lord raised up his faithful servant Moses. He gave him express commands not only to teach the people what the Lord revealed to him in his own name, but also to hand down, in written records, the whole ancient and sacred history from the very beginning of the world, together with this doctrine of supernatural truth. Nothing was to be added to it, changed, or taken away, Deut. 12.32 and 5.32.

units.la: Huius verò doctrinæ, ac cultus legitimi si-mul etiam ordinarios interpretes ac ministros Sacerdotes & Leuitas constituit Leuit. 19. 10. & Deut.30. 9. Deinde quum præsciret non omnes Sacerdotes Aaroni vel Phinéazo similes fore, & quod salutis doctrina traderetur adhuc cum mensura, extraordinariè Prophetas suscitabat, vt olim promiserat, Deut. 18. 15. quorum ministerio, Christus Dominus nolter antequam ipse in mundum carne assumpta veniret, ipsis variis modis apparens, quando & vt res postulabat, ad populum suum commonefaciendum vsus est : & quidem in duos fines,quorum prior erat, tum vt paulatim vmbris dissipatis, tandem apparens veritas perfectius & magis conspicuè agnoscerctur,tum etiam vt sacræ historiæ, singulorum temporū series continuaretur, & cessantibus ordinariis Scripturarum interpretibus, Prophetæ pseudoprophetis oppositi, ad cuiusuis ætatis ac conditionis homines monendos, arguē-dos increpandos substituerentur ac surrogarentur. Alter erat finis magis specialis & particularis, eousque se Domino ad populi sui captum & infirmitatem accommodante (ne vi-delicet ad diuinos, magos ac incantatores confugeret, vt fit huius rei mentio. Deut. 18.9. & Leuit. 19. 26. & 31.) vt suis Prophetis multa singularia patefaceret, de quibus interrogabantur, quod maximè ex I. Sam.9.6. & tota prophetarum Eliæ & Elizæi historia conspicuum est.
units.tr: For this doctrine and lawful worship he also appointed, as ordinary interpreters and ministers, the priests and Levites, Lev. 19.10 and Deut. 30.9. Then, since he foresaw that not all priests would be like Aaron or Phinehas, and that the doctrine of salvation would still be given only in measure, he raised up prophets extraordinarily, as he had long before promised, Deut. 18.15. Through their ministry our Lord Christ, before he came into the world in assumed flesh, appeared to them in various ways and used them to remind his people, when and as circumstances required. He did this for two ends. The first was that, as the shadows were gradually dispelled, the truth might at last appear and be recognised more perfectly and more plainly. The second was that the series of sacred history for each period might be continued. With the ordinary interpreters of the Scriptures ceasing, prophets were set over against false prophets and put in place to admonish, refute and rebuke men of every age and condition. The second end was more special and particular: the Lord so accommodated himself to the capacity and weakness of his people (lest they flee to diviners, magicians and enchanters, as is mentioned Deut. 18.9, Lev. 19.26 and 31) that he revealed to his prophets many singular things about which they were asked. This is most clearly seen from 1 Sam. 9.6 and the whole history of the prophets Elijah and Elisha.

units.la: Porrò Dominus admiranda prorsus ratione scripta illa, Iudæorum lingua conscripta in mediis illis tot tantisque tempestatibus, quibus agitati sunt & vehementer conquassati conseruauit, & ad seculorum finem est conseruaturus, quòd iis doctrina veritatis generalis & omni tempore ad salutem Ecclesiæ necessaria contineatur. 2.Pet. 1.19. Rom. 15.4. tum vt facta collatione prædictionum Prophetarum cum earundem in Euangelio impletione & animaduersa conformitate, imò potius identitate Prophetarum & Christi ipsius doctrinæ hæc ab illa confirmetur, & vicissim, vt ipse Christus admonet Iohan. 5. 39. & passim etiam ipsemet fecit, licet testimonium eius per se satis firmum esset & omni exceptione maius: & vt Iudæi Beroeenses fecerunt. Act. 17. 11. Temporibus igitur quibus vixit populus Iudaicus, ad verum Christum Dei Filium cognoscendum, doctrinæ salutis scopum vnicum, ad Legem & testimonium fuit recurrendum & ibi subsistendum. Esa. 8. 20. idest Mosen & Prophetas, vt Abrahamus, diuitem illum epulopulonem allocutus explicat, Luc. 16.29. & 31. absque vllo traditionum humanarum fermen to,Esa.29.13.
units.tr: Moreover, the Lord, in a wonderfully remarkable way, preserved those writings, written in the Jewish language, amid all those so many and great storms by which they were tossed and violently shaken, and he will preserve them until the end of the ages. This is because in them the doctrine of the truth, general and necessary for the salvation of the Church at all times, is contained, 2 Pet. 1.19; Rom. 15.4. This also happens so that, when the predictions of the prophets are compared with their fulfilment in the Gospel, and their agreement, or rather the identity of the prophets' doctrine with that of Christ himself, is observed, the one is confirmed by the other, and vice versa. Christ himself urges this, John 5.39, and often did it himself, though his own testimony was firm enough in itself and greater than any objection. So did the Jews of Berea, Acts 17.11. Therefore, in the times in which the Jewish people lived, to recognise the true Christ, the Son of God, the one aim of the doctrine of salvation was to be sought in the Law and the testimony, and to remain there, Isa. 8.20. That is, Moses and the Prophets, as Abraham explains when he addressed the rich man in the feast, Luke 16.29 and 31, without any leaven of human traditions, Isa. 29.13.

units.la: At postquam venit plenum tempus. Gal.4. 4. ipse Filius in mundum venit. Heb. 1.2. cum Legalibus umbris finem allaturus. Ioh. 19.30. tum doctrinam veritatis & salutis perfecte no- bis annuntiaturus & perfecturus. Ioh. 15. verf. 15. Quandiu igitur vixit in terris, vnicus ille fuit ex quo salutis mysterium fuit discendum & quaerendum Matth.3.verf.17. Act.3. verf.22. cuicunque tanquam oui in eius caulam recipi cupienti Ioh. 10.3. Solus ille verúsque fuit fons quo sitis expleretur Ioh. 6.35.&7.37. Idcirco dixi Caiapham vere ex ipso quaesiui-se, quod illum oportuit inquirere. At non vt futurus discipulus ad Christum accedebat, sed contra vitae doctrinam in venenum mortiferum commutaturus, non tantum ex natiua illa corruptione qua excaecantur omnes mortales, ne velint aut possint, veram Lucem intueri: sed etiam destinata quadam, in qua pridem occaluerat, improbitate, id ipsum quod inuitus probe tenebat etiam suffocante, quod eis obiecit Christus Iohan. 7. verf. 28. Sanctóque Spiritui resistente, vt ipsi remitti peccatum illud minime potuerit. Matth. 12. verf.31.
units.tr: But when the fullness of time had come, Gal. 4.4, the Son himself came into the world, Heb. 1.2, to bring an end to the Legal shadows, John 19.30, and to announce to us and perfect the doctrine of truth and salvation, John 15.15. As long as he lived on earth, he alone was the one from whom the mystery of salvation was to be learned and sought, Matt. 3.17; Acts 3.22, by anyone who wished to be received as a sheep into his fold, John 10.3. He alone, and truly, was the fountain by which thirst might be satisfied, John 6.35 and 7.37. Hence I have said that Caiaphas truly asked of him what he ought to have sought. But he did not approach Christ as a future disciple; rather, he was about to turn the doctrine of life into deadly poison. This was not only from that natural corruption by which all mortals are blinded, so that they neither wish nor are able to behold the true Light, but also from a settled wickedness in which he had long since grown hot, and which he suppressed even while knowingly holding the truth against his will. Christ charged them with this, John 7.28. And, resisting the Holy Spirit, he could by no means have that sin forgiven him, Matt. 12.31.

units.la: Tertium in quod incidimus tempus superest, ab Ascensione Domini in coelos inchoatum, & ad mundi consummationem perduraturu, qua etiam ob causam, Vltimum
units.tr: There remains the third time into which we have come, begun from the Ascension of the Lord into heaven, and to last until the consummation of the world. For this reason also it is called the last

units.la: tempus nuncupatur, quo Christus secundum carnem in coelis receptus est permansurus, & inde sancto suo Spiritu non autem reali sui corporis praesentia suam Ecclesiam ad seculorum vsque consummationem gubernaturus. Matth.28.20. Act.3.21. Quam crassus igitur est eorum error, qui praesentem in terris quaerunt? Et sane qui tam amentes sum, ut eum sibi persuadeant se oculis intueri, manibus palpare, atque adeo realiter & essentialiter in os iniicere, dicere non possunt cum esse Iesum Christum cuius ore docendi sumus, ac proinde verum esse Christum. Nam quem sibi Christum fingunt, neque os ad loquendum, neque aures ad audiendum, nec pedes ad ingrediendum non magis quam ligneus aut lapideus crucifixus habet. Quare panis ille quem adorant, in horrendum idolum ab ipsis transmutatur.
units.tr: time, in which Christ, according to the flesh, has been received into heaven to remain, and from there will govern his Church, by his holy Spirit and not by the real presence of his body, until the end of the ages, Matt. 28.20; Acts 3.21. How gross, then, is the error of those who seek him present on earth! Indeed, those so mad as to persuade themselves that they see him with their eyes, touch him with their hands, and even put him into their mouths really and essentially, cannot say that this is Jesus Christ, from whose mouth we are taught, and therefore that it is the true Christ. For the Christ they imagine has neither a mouth for speaking, nor ears for hearing, nor feet for walking, any more than a wooden or stone crucifix has. Therefore that bread which they adore is changed by them into a horrible idol.

units.la: Porro sic supra coelos omnes euchi, ut plerique Doctores Contemplatiui, & in primis sanctus ille patronus ipsorum Franciscus somniarunt, delirium est, & immanis furor. Nam in his terris non in coelis suos electos per Euangelij praedicationem Christus colligit semel in coelis recipiendos. Prophetas vero: D. Paulum, dilectum discipulum, & D. Petrum in ecstasin raptos fuisse certis testimoniis credimus, sed extraordinariu illud fuisse & peculiare ipsis, nec temere imitandum aut in consequentiam trahendum: quum praesertim istis ecstasibus obseruandum sit noui alicuius articuli fidei non allatam cognitionem, sed speciales earum rum causas & occasiones fuisse. Sin excipiat aliquis idem etiam egregiis Patribus istis extraordinarie contigisse, næ falsitatis apertæ certissima sunt argumenta, quod quæ boni illi Patres in ecclesiis fe didicisse profitentur, nō magis conueniant cum iis quæ sancti illi viri quos ad tempus Deus velut ex mŭdo sustulit, fui temporis hominibus retulerunt, & tā verbis quàm scriptis docuerunt, quàm Luci conuenit cum tenebris: Sunt enim vt plurimùm istorum Contemplatiuorum patrum somnia, aut res plane ridiculæ & mera ægri somnia, aut aperta vel historiæ sacræ, vel puritatis doctrinę,& puri cultus diuini falfimonia,aut denique manifestissimæ fraudes ac impoftur̄e. Adde quòd harum fabularum contemplatiuarū maxima pars non paucioribus mēdaciis scateat quàm falsa illa & vana miracula quibus eorum legendæ plenæ sunt.Quid igitur opus est facto,& quoniam, inquiet aliquis, abeundum est ad veri Iesu Chriiti percipiendam cognitionem?
units.tr: Moreover, to pray thus above the heavens, as most contemplative Doctors, and first of all their holy patron Francis, have dreamed, is delirium and monstrous madness. For Christ gathers his elect not in heaven but in these lands, through the preaching of the Gospel, to be received once in heaven. We believe on certain testimonies that the prophets Paul, the beloved disciple, and Peter were caught up into ecstasy. But that was extraordinary and peculiar to them, and not to be rashly imitated or drawn into a consequence. This is especially so since in such ecstasies one must observe that they brought not the knowledge of some new article of faith, but their own special causes and occasions. But if someone objects that the same thing happened extraordinarily to those eminent Fathers, there are most certain arguments of plain falsehood. What those good Fathers profess to have learned in the Church agrees no more with what those holy men, whom God for a time took up as if out of the world, reported to the men of their own time and taught both in word and in writing, than light agrees with darkness. For for the most part the dreams of these contemplative fathers are either utterly ridiculous and the mere dreams of a sick man, or manifest falsifications of sacred history, or of the doctrine of purity and of pure divine worship, or finally most obvious frauds and impostures. Add that the greater part of these contemplative fables abound with no fewer lies than the false and vain miracles with which their legends are full. What, then, is to be done? And whither, someone will say, must we go to acquire knowledge of the true Jesus Christ?

units.la: An ad eum Spiritum quem sibi Libertini, Anabaptistæ,Enthufiaftæ in aurem omnia reuelare mentiuntur? Apagefis. Sed ad eos omnino recurrendum quibus dictum est,Mitto vos vt à Patre missus sum,Ioh.20.21.quíque sibi commisso munere fideliter,nihil addentes, detrahentes aut immutantes functi sunt:quicquid à Magistro didicerant,& à Sancto Spiritu reuocatum erat in memoriam, omne Dei de nostra salute consilium annuntiantes.Act.
units.tr: To that Spirit which the Libertines, Anabaptists and Enthusiasts falsely claim reveals everything into their ear? Away with that! Rather, we must certainly have recourse to those to whom it was said, "As the Father sent me, so I send you," John 20.21, and who, faithfully discharging the commission entrusted to them, added nothing, took nothing away and changed nothing. Whatever they had learned from the Master, and what the Holy Spirit had brought back to their memory, they announced: the whole counsel of God concerning our salvation, Acts 20.27; Gal. 1.8 and 12.

units.la: V. j. 20. 27. & Gal. 1. 8. & 12. At è viuis excesserunt inquiet aliquis: & à mortuis peti consilium Deus vetat.Deut.18. 11. Fateor: ac proinde qui sanctorum monumenta vel reliquias adorant, quarum pleraque sallsæ sunt, prorsus sunt inexcusabiles. At de quibus agimus adhuc in scriptis suis à Sancto Spiritu dictatis, viuunt & homines erudiunt, in hunc etiam vsum ipsis à Domino mirabiliter conseruatis.
units.tr: But they have departed this life, someone will say, and God forbids seeking counsel from the dead, Deut. 18.11. I grant it. Therefore those who adore the relics or remains of the saints, most of which are false, are utterly inexcusable. But those of whom we are speaking, who still live in their writings dictated by the Holy Spirit and instruct men, have been wonderfully preserved by the Lord for this very use.

units.la: Nam illud est Ecclesiæ fundamentum de quo mentio fit Ephes. 2. 20. & Apoc. 21. 14. cui quod aliud superinduciatur, annon videbitur Deus melius Ecclesiæ veteri sub Lege, quàm Christianæ confultum voluisse si Apostolorum aut Euangelistarum scripta ad hominem perfectum reddendum, minus idonea sunt quàm Mosis ac Prophetarum?2 Tim.3.16. In iis igitur, & nusquam alibi salutis quaerenda cognitio. Admittimus nihilominus omnia decenter & ordine in domo Domini fieri oportere.1.Corint.14.40.ac proinde qui domui illi præest, ut Ierusalem illa cœlesti fundaret, (Ecclesiam puta ab Oriente in Occidentem collectam, & ideo Catholicam idest vniuersalem nuncupatam) primum misit Apostolos, Prophetas, Euangelistas, Pastores & Doctores, quorum scripta nobis tradita sunt, quibus fidei noltræ doctrina perfecte continetur, immo quod maius est, quicquid est essentiale in ordine totius administrationis sacri ministerij spiritualis, nempe munera & cuiusque muneris officium: ad quæ quicquam adiicere detrahere ue
units.tr: For that is the foundation of the Church, mentioned in Eph. 2. 20 and Rev. 21. 14. If some other foundation were laid on top of it, will it not seem that God took better care of the old Church under the Law than of the Christian Church, if the writings of the Apostles and Evangelists are less fit to make a man perfect than those of Moses and the Prophets? 2 Tim. 3. 16. The knowledge of salvation is to be sought in those writings, and nowhere else. We grant nonetheless that all things must be done decently and in order in the house of the Lord. 1 Cor. 14. 40. Accordingly, he who presides over that house, in order to found that heavenly Jerusalem (the Church, that is, gathered from East to West and therefore called Catholic, or universal), first sent Apostles, Prophets, Evangelists, Pastors and Teachers, whose writings have been handed down to us, and in which the doctrine of our faith is perfectly contained. What is more, whatever is essential in the order of the whole administration of the sacred spiritual ministry is there too: namely, the offices and the duty of each office. It is no more lawful to add to these, or to take from them, or to change them, than it is to alter the articles of faith themselves.

units.la: Doctrina perfecte ab Apostolis monumentis tradita in psa per se est textus & glosa seu interpretatio. here-ue aut etiam immutare non magis quam articulis ipsis fidei licuit.
units.tr: The doctrine that the Apostles delivered perfectly in their writings is in itself both the text and the gloss or interpretation. It is no more lawful to add to it, take from it, or alter it, than it is to do so with the articles of faith themselves.

units.la: Sed quoniam homines non contenti hac sacrosanćta politia Ecclesiastica, quam ipse Spiritus Sanctus per os & scripta suorum Apostolorum loquutus instituerat, hierarchiam illam ad Imperij Romani exemplar erexerunt, ex mortalium ingenio ac prudetia, plus quam Deus ipse sapere cupientes, quae statim in abominandam tyrannidem defecit: inde prima Satan fundamenta iecit Ecclesiae in miserum illum statum in quem est redacta transformandae. Vt igitur ad sermonem unde sumus digressi reuertamur, ad eius Ecclesiastici aedificij, ab Apostolis fundati constructionem & conservationem, Deus voluit & vult, Ecclesiam a Pastoribus & Doctoribus ad finem usque seculorum doceri: vel legitime vocatis ab hominibus quandiu viget ordo a Filio Dei in Ecclesia institutus, vel ab eodem immediate & extraordinarie, quum postulat necessitas suscitatis: vt supra docuimus in veteri populo, Prophetas ab eodem excitatos extraordinarie, quos Sacerdotibus & Leuitis, quum necesse esset, surrogaret aut adiungeret.
units.tr: But since men, not content with this most holy ecclesiastical polity, which the Holy Spirit himself instituted, speaking through the mouth and writings of his Apostles, have erected that hierarchy after the pattern of the Roman Empire, desiring to be wiser than God himself by the cleverness and prudence of mortals, and since this quickly fell away into an abominable tyranny, Satan laid there the first foundations for transforming the Church into that wretched state to which it has been reduced. So, to return to the subject from which we have digressed: God willed, and still wills, that the Church be taught by Pastors and Teachers until the end of the ages, for the construction and preservation of that ecclesiastical building founded by the Apostles. These are either men lawfully called by other men, for as long as the order instituted in the Church by the Son of God remains in force, or men raised up immediately and extraordinarily by the same Son when necessity requires it, as we taught above concerning the ancient people, where God raised up Prophets extraordinarily, whom he set in place of, or added to, the Priests and Levites, when this was necessary.

units.la: Et hoc quidē nominatim esse dico Pastorum ac Doctorum munus. Nam quod ad fundatores, sic proprie dictos, Apostolos puta, Prophetas & Euangelistas, vocationis ipsorum adimpleta causa (fundatione nimirum Ecclesiae Christianae tum voce tum scriptis) vocatio cessavit Apostolica. At Pastores ac Doctores vj. ij. À Domino sunt instituti, non ad iacienda fundamenta, sed ad singulos super fundamento positio iam ab ipsis Apostolis ac Prophetis aedificandos. At non omnes probi sunt architecti. Alij enim aurum, argentum, lapides pretio fos aedificant: suos nimirum greges fouent fana doctrina, & ordine seruato fundamento illi electi pretiosisque lapides conuenienti. Esa. 28.16. Apoc.21.18.
units.tr: I say that this is indeed by name the office of Pastors and Teachers. As for the so-called founders, namely the Apostles, Prophets and Evangelists, their calling ceased with the fulfilment of its purpose, which was the founding of the Christian Church, by word and by writings, so the Apostolic calling came to an end. But Pastors and Teachers were instituted by the Lord, not to lay foundations, but to build on the foundation already laid by the Apostles and Prophets, each in his own place. Not all architects are good. Some build with gold, silver and precious stones, that is, they nourish their flocks with sound doctrine, and, keeping the foundation intact, they build with those chosen and precious stones that fit it. Isa. 28. 16; Rev. 21. 18.

units.la: Alij ligna, fœnum, stipulam aedificant, 1. Cor.13.12. res puta vanas & inanes, cuiusmodi sunt infinitae illæ ceremoniae, aut potius mimicæ illegesticulationes quae in Ecclesiam aedificatorum culpa pedetentim irrepserunt: quae tamen ad veritatis Dei splendorem subito dis- pantur.
units.tr: Others build with wood, hay and stubble, 1 Cor. 3. 12, that is, with empty and vain things, such as those countless ceremonies, or rather mimicking gesticulations, which crept into the Church little by little through the fault of its builders. Yet these are suddenly scattered by the splendour of God's truth.

units.la: At longè peiores istis alij sunt aedificatores, cuiusmodi olim Pharisaei suam iustitiam itabilientes: & Sadducaei, negantes esse animas, & mortuorum resurrectionem: quae tamen huic fundamento superstrui nullo modo possunt. Tales fuerunt, sunt & ad seculorum finem erunt falsi omnes pastores, quorum doctrina cum fidei Christianæ articulis nequit consistere. Atque ita dicimus & audacter asseueramus, nullum esse caput eorum quae ad Christi officium spectant, quo Iesus dicitur, (id est Seruator) & Christus, idemt vnctus à Patre & consecratus vt solus esset æternus & summus Rex, Spiritualis Doctor, ac Propheta, & Sacerdos Ecclesiae suae) quod non ab ipsis fundamentis conuellat illius Ecclesiae doctrina quae se Catholitholicam hodie mentitur.
units.tr: But there are builders far worse than these, such as once the Pharisees, who boasted of their own righteousness, and the Sadducees, who denied that there are souls and a resurrection of the dead. Yet such men can in no way be built upon this foundation. Such have been, are, and until the end of the ages will be, all false pastors, whose doctrine cannot stand with the articles of the Christian faith. Thus we say, and boldly assert, that there is no head of those things which pertain to the office of Christ, by which Jesus is called (that is, Saviour) and Christ (that is, anointed by the Father and consecrated, so that he alone might be the eternal and supreme King, Spiritual Teacher, Prophet and Priest of his Church), which does not overturn from its very foundations the doctrine of that Church which today falsely claims to be Catholic.

units.la: Quaerat autem aliquis, quomodo veri Pa- ftores, quos audire, a falsis, quos contra fugere oportet, discernantur? Dignoscetis eos, inquit Christus a fructibus eorum. Pastoris vero fructus proprius & peculiaris est doctrina. Qui nos igitur in hoc argumento ad personalem Successionem ablegant, salsissimo fundamento niituntur, falsos nimirum Pastores veris succedere non posse: quod per se absurdissimum est, & sacra historia tota salsissimum esse clamat: & hoc saltem exemplo tum Caiaphae, quem Scribae imitantur, tum omnium Sacerdotum magni huius consilij ante Domini adventu satis comprobatur. Id vero posse accidere, immo reipsa eventurum Ecclesiae Christianae none diserte toties tu Christus ipse tum Apostoli praedixerunt, ut nominatim etiam in teplo Christi quae eius est Ecclesia felsurum Antichristum praemonuerint? Denique toties illud accidit, & ad finem usque seculorum eventurum est, ut si quis dubitet, etiam an Lux sit ambigere videatur.
units.tr: But someone may ask how true pastors, whom we ought to hear, are to be distinguished from false ones, whom we ought to flee. "You shall know them," says Christ, "by their fruits." Matt. 7. 16. The proper and distinctive fruit of a pastor is doctrine. Those, then, who in this matter send us back to personal succession rest on a most unsound foundation, namely that false pastors cannot succeed true ones. This is in itself most absurd, and the whole of sacred history cries out that it is most false. This is sufficiently proved by that one example of Caiaphas, whom the Scribes imitate, and by all the priests of that great council before the coming of the Lord. Moreover, that this could happen, and indeed would happen in the Christian Church, Christ himself and the Apostles foretold so often and plainly, even warning that Antichrist would sit in the temple of Christ, which is his Church. Finally, it has happened so often, and will happen until the end of the ages, that if anyone doubts it, he may seem to doubt whether light is light.

units.la: Itaque quum ne maxime quidem contumacces hac in parte, Scripturas Propheticas & Apostolicas audiunt negare, verbum esse Dei, ac proinde verbum veritatis, quem alium electuri sumus iudicem quam Deum veritatis, quo mendaces a veracibus discernantur? Quinam vero id fieri posset, nisi haec eadem Scriptura sit vera certaque regula istius discrimi-
units.tr: Therefore, since even the most stubborn in this matter do not dare to deny that the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures are the Word of God, and therefore the word of truth, whom shall we choose as judge, if not the God of truth, by whom liars may be distinguished from truthful men? And how could this be done, unless this same Scripture is the true and certain rule of that distinction?

units.la: nis?Quibus concessis,quę negari non possunt, necessario sequitur, excipientibus aduersariis agi inter nos de Scripturarum interpretatione, quarum illi quum veram se retinere,nos etiam idem contrà profitearmur,dicendum esse, aut Deo tursus è cœlis apparendum, non sufficiente eius doctrina,ad veritatem à falso discernendam, quòd omnia non expresserit, aut obscurius loquutus sit(quod cogitari non potest quin dicatur Deus non satis abundè per Scripturas Ecclesiam suam docuisse, aut hominibus illusisse,)aut illis admittendum Scripturas si sufficiunt veracibus à mendacibus discernendis, ac proinde veritati à mendacio, etiam esse sufficientissimas ad veram ipsarum interpretationem à falsa distinguendam.Vt igitur veram esse loci alicuius Scripturæ interpretationem,& doctrinam illa nitentem probes,nò te multitudo, non deniq; vetustas eorum qui sic intellexerunt & docuerunt iuuat. Falli enim omnes illi &à multis seculis potuerunt, quod satis est conspicuum ex corruptelis omnium eorum capitum Religionis quæ hactenus in mundo grassatæ sunt,quum seducentium ac seductorum non exiguus semper numerus fuerit. Tum verò de Interpretationis cuiuslibet veritate certò constabit, quum bene illi conueniet cum nostræ fidei articulis & fundamentis fideliter ex tota Scriptura in nostrum Symbolum collectis , quæque vt summa doctrinæ Christianæ capita vtrinque admitadmittuntur. Contrà verò non conueniens istis interpretatio, manifestæ falsitatis arguitor. Non pendet igitur huius litis ac controuersiæ decisio, nec à Pastorum successione, nec à multitudine, nec ab antiquitate, nec à consuetudine: (licet ista non sint temerè aut leuiter contemnenda) at sedeat ipse Dominus in solio suo iudex, non de nouo sententiam dicturus, aut è cœlis euocatus iterum loquuturus, sed exiis quæ iam olim primùm per Prophetas, deinde tandem postremis temporibus per Filium vnigenitum, tam ore proprio quàm per Euangelistas & Apostolos pronuntiauit, controuersiam dirempturus.
units.tr: These things being granted, which cannot be denied, it necessarily follows, since our opponents also claim to hold the true interpretation of the Scriptures while we profess the same, that one of two things must be said. Either God must appear again from heaven, because his teaching is not sufficient to distinguish truth from falsehood, since he did not express everything or spoke too obscurely (and it cannot be thought otherwise than that God has not taught his Church abundantly enough through the Scriptures, or has mocked men). Or else we must admit that the Scriptures, if they are sufficient to distinguish truthful men from liars, are therefore also most sufficient to distinguish the true interpretation of them from a false one, and truth from falsehood. Therefore, to prove that the interpretation of some passage of Scripture, and the doctrine resting upon it, is true, neither the multitude of those who have so understood and taught it helps you, nor finally its antiquity. For all of them could have been, and for many centuries have been, deceived, as is plain from the corruptions of all those articles of religion which have prevailed in the world up to now, since the number of deceivers and deceived has never been small. Then, indeed, the truth of any interpretation will be certainly established when it agrees well with the articles and foundations of our faith, faithfully gathered from the whole of Scripture into our Creed, which both sides admit as the chief heads of Christian doctrine. On the other hand, an interpretation that does not agree with these is convicted of manifest falsehood. The decision of this dispute and controversy therefore depends neither on the succession of Pastors, nor on multitude, nor on antiquity, nor on custom (although these are not to be lightly or rashly despised). Rather, let the Lord himself sit on his throne as judge, not about to pronounce a new sentence, nor summoned again from heaven to speak once more, but to settle the controversy by those things which he has already pronounced: first through the Prophets, and at last in these final times through his only-begotten Son, both by his own mouth and through the Evangelists and Apostles.

units.la: Duplex porrò Dei verbum pro Christianæ Religionis norma qui in medium adferunt, scriptum vnum, alterum ἀγραφον, quum sine ratione pertinaciter id vrgeant, responsione ἀγραφος indigni sunt. Quod si tamen illis, licet nec verum nec etiam verisimile concederetur, nihil tamen promouerint, donec probauerint impias illas suas superstitiones non scriptas (quas revera nunquam fideles Dei serui nec ore nec scripto docuerunt) cum Scripto verbo consentire. Næ verò id præstiterint, quum vnum & idem esse Christum & Belialem, Lucem ac Tenebras ostenderint.
units.tr: Moreover, those who bring forward a double Word of God as the rule of the Christian religion, one written and the other unwritten [ἄγραφον], and who urge this stubbornly without reason, are unworthy of an answer. But even if it were granted to them, though it is neither true nor even probable, they would gain nothing, unless they proved that those impious superstitions of theirs, which are unwritten (and which the faithful servants of God never taught either by mouth or in writing), agree with the written Word. Indeed, in attempting that, they would show that Christ and Belial are one and the same, and that light and darkness are one.

units.la: Ecquis igitur miretur Christianum populum iam à multis seculis, vt olim populus Iudaicus, miserum instar ouium erraticarum, sine pastore passim errare,
units.tr: Who then would wonder that the Christian people, for many centuries now, like the Jewish people of old, wretched as sheep without a shepherd, wander about everywhere?

units.la: de quibus Esa.56.11.Ier.10.11. & 22.22.& 23.1.& 50.6.& Ezech.6.8.& Zach.10.2. Matth.9.36.& alibi plerisq; locis agitur? Sed in primis an est tantopere mirandum si qui maxime inter alios omnes, qui Scripturas hodie tractant, vt olim Caiaphas, Pharisæi & Sadducæi, non maiorem earum habent cognitionem quàm Caiaphas & totus Ierosolymitanus ille confessus? quū ipsis vsuenerit quod iam ante tot secula Deus istiusmodi hominibus erat interminatus, Esa.29.14. qui sibi cognitionis clauem arrogant, ipli tamen non introeuntes, & alios introire prohibentes.Luc.11.52.Et illa quidem de veris clauibus dicuntur, quas sibi comissas pessimi domusDei administratores gestabant, at non de ementitis illis Romanis clauibus, quas minime dicam Petro vel aliis Apostolis ereptas fuisse, (nam illæ permanent in Ecclesia Dei & in seculum permansuræ sunt) sed tamen ausim affirmare ad earū exemplar adulteratum, modis omnibus falsitatis, additione puta, detractione & immutatione, egregios istos ædificatores non tantum nouas claues, sed nouas etiam seras, nouas portas, nouos cœlos, limbos, purgatoria & inferos finxisse, quos ipsis claudendos aperiendos iis qui talibus delectantur libenter relinquimus.
units.tr: Of these people Isaiah 56:11, Jeremiah 10:21 and 22:22 and 23:1 and 50:6, Ezekiel 6:8, Zechariah 10:2 and Matthew 9:36, and many other passages, speak. But above all, is it so very surprising that those who most of all, among all who handle the Scriptures today, have no greater knowledge of them than Caiaphas, the Pharisees and Sadducees had, and than all that Jerusalem council? It has happened to them just as God threatened such men long ago (Isaiah 29:14): they claim for themselves the key of knowledge, yet they do not enter in themselves, and they forbid others to enter (Luke 11:52). Those words are indeed spoken of the true keys, which the wicked stewards of God's house held entrusted to them, but not of those false Roman keys, which I will not say were taken away from Peter or the other Apostles (for those remain in the Church of God and will remain for ever). Yet I dare to affirm that, using those true keys as a corrupted model, by every kind of falsehood, namely addition, omission and alteration, these outstanding builders have devised not only new keys but also new locks, new gates, new heavens, limbo, purgatory and hells, which we gladly leave for them to lock and unlock, for those who take delight in such things.

units.la: Denique fratres, vt dicendi finem faciam, etsi non in Caiaphæ schola tanta hæc tamque ardua mysteria discenda sint ad salutem necessaria; tamen quum ex contrario vno discatur altealterū, visum est mihi non alienū à proposito si aliquid paulò fusius de grauibus istis & præ-cipuis fidei nostræ capitibus dicerem, in qui-bus maximam orbis partem errare conspici-mus. Agamus igitur Domino gratias immor-tales quòd nos in viam cognitionis Domini nostri Iesu Christi, in qua vita æterna posita est,Ioh.17.3.introduxerit:de qua dicebat Apo-stolus se nihil nisi Iesum Christum,& eum cru-cifixum scire sibi proposuisse. Agamus, in-quam, illi gratias quandiu vita fruimur de tanto nobis concesso thesauro, quòd inueniri se fecerit à quibus non quærebatur. Esa.65.1. Quoniam verò quandiu in terris degimus, ex parte tantum cognoscimus, agite in dies in-crementum faciamus: & quam nacti sumus cognitionem ad vsum suum referentes, in o-culis eum præsentem semper habeamus, & Spiritum ipsius in nobis ipsis, donec tandem cum ipso propiùs coniuncti, Regno illo æter-no ante mundi constitutionem nobis præpa-rato feliciter perfruamur. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, brothers, to bring my speech to an end: although these great and difficult mysteries are not, for salvation, to be learned in the school of Caiaphas, nevertheless, since one learns each thing from its opposite, it seemed to me not out of place to my purpose to say something somewhat more fully about these weighty and chief heads of our faith, in which we see the greater part of the world erring. Let us therefore give immortal thanks to the Lord, that he has led us into the way of the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which eternal life consists (John 17:3), of which the Apostle said he had resolved to know nothing but Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). Let us, I say, give him thanks, as long as we enjoy life, for so great a treasure granted to us, that he has let himself be found by those who did not seek him (Isaiah 65:1). Since, however, while we dwell on earth we know only in part, let us make progress day by day: referring the knowledge we have obtained to its proper use, let us always have him present before our eyes, and his Spirit within ourselves, until at last, more closely joined with him, we happily enjoy that eternal kingdom prepared for us before the foundation of the world. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA decimaquarta.
units.tr: Homily fourteen.

units.la: MATTH. 26.
units.tr: MATT. 26.

units.la: 63. Et respondens Pontifex Maximus dixit ei, Adiuro te per Deum viventem ut dicas nobis an tu sis Christus ille Filius Dei.
units.tr: 63. And the high priest answered and said to him, I adjure you by the living God, that you tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.

units.la: 64. Dicit ei Iesus, Tu dixisti: quin etiam dico vobis, Ab hoc tempore videbitis Filium hominis sedentem ad dextram potentiae Dei, & venientem in nubibus coeli.
units.tr: 64. Jesus said to him, You have said it. Moreover I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of the power of God, and coming in the clouds of heaven.

units.la: 65. Tunc Pontifex Maximus dirupit vestimenta sua, dicens, Blasphemauit: quid amplius egemus testibus? Ecce, nunc audistis blasphemiam eius. Quid vobis videtur?
units.tr: 65. Then the high priest tore his clothes, saying, He has blasphemed. What further need have we of witnesses? Behold, now you have heard his blasphemy. What does it seem to you?

units.la: 66. Ipsi vero respondentes dixerunt, Teneur mortis poena.
units.tr: 66. But they answered and said, He is worthy of death.

units.la: MARC. 14.
units.tr: MARK 14.

units.la: 61. Rursum Pontifex Maximus eum interrogauit, & dixit ei, Tu-ne es ille Christus Filiusil-lius Benedicti?
units.tr: 61. Again the high priest questioned him and said to him, Are you that Christ, the Son of the Blessed?

units.la: 62. Iesus autem dixit, Ego sum, & videbitis Filium hominis sedentem ad dextram potentiae Dei, & venientem cum nubibus coeli.
units.tr: 62. But Jesus said, I am; and you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of the power of God, and coming with the clouds of heaven.

units.la: 63. Pontifex Maximus vero diruptis vestibus suis suis dixit, Quid adhuc nobis opus est testibus?
units.tr: 63. The high priest, however, tearing his garments said, What further need do we have of witnesses?

units.la: 64. Audistis blasphemiam, quid vobis videtur? Illi vero omnes contra eum iudicarunt, ipsum teneri mortis poena.
units.tr: 64. You have heard the blasphemy; what does it seem to you? And they all condemned him, that he was worthy of death.

units.la: 65. Et coeperunt quidam insputare in eum, et obtegere faciem eius, et colaphos ei infligere: et dicere ei, Vaticinare: ministri vero baculorum ictibus eum caedebant.
units.tr: 65. And some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to strike him with their fists, and to say to him, Prophesy! And the attendants struck him with rods.

units.la: LVC. 22.
units.tr: LUKE 22.

units.la: 66. Et ut ortus est dies, coactum fuit presbyterium populi, et primarii Sacerdotes et Scribae, et adduxerunt eum in suum concilium.
units.tr: 66. And when day came, the council of the elders of the people gathered, both the chief priests and the scribes, and they led him into their council.

units.la: 67. Dicentes, Num tu es ille Christus? dic nobis. Dixit autem eis, Si vobis dixero, nequaquam credetis.
units.tr: 67. Saying, Are you the Christ? Tell us. But he said to them, If I tell you, you will by no means believe.

units.la: 68. Quod si etiam interrogavero, nequaquam respondebitis mihi, neque (me) absoluetis.
units.tr: 68. And if I also ask you, you will by no means answer me, nor let me go.

units.la: 69. Ab hoc tempore erit Filius hominis sedens ad dextram potentiae Dei.
units.tr: 69. From now on the Son of man will be sitting at the right hand of the power of God.

units.la: 70. Dixerunt autem omnes, Tu ergo es Filius ille Dei? Ipse vero dixit eis, Vos dicitis: nam ego sum.
units.tr: 70. Then they all said, Are you then the Son of God? And he said to them, You say it, for I am.

units.la: 71. At illi dixerunt, Quid amplius egemus testimonio? Ipsi enim audivimus ex ore ipsius.
units.tr: 71. And they said, What further need do we have of testimony? For we ourselves have heard it from his own mouth.

units.la: VVM homilia superiore quaedam generaliora capita ad nostra aetate dificatione ex hoc loco deduximus, quae no erant tamen huius historiae propria, age sensum illius proprium et peculiarem inuestigemus. Caiaphas igitur quum animaduerteret nullis testimoniis innocentiam Christi laedi: & aequi bonique iudicis partes implere se simularet, ore proprio Christum voluit respondere: hoc enim ordo iustitiae postulat vt reus ipse de facto suo respondeat. Qua quidem in re, si formam consideres, Caiaphas cum toto presbyterio culpari nequeunt: at interius malum occultatur: horrendae siquidem indurationis exemplum hic nobis ob oculos ponitur. Nam qui potuerunt in propósito perseuerare, quum ipsa experirentur nullis testimoniis etiam a se subornatorum testium innocentiam huius rei laedi posse. Quinam adeo frontem perfricuerunt vt capitale iudicium instruant, nulla facta prius inquisitione, nullis argumentis verisimilibus praeparatis, id est sine fundamentis aedificent? Quomodo vero tam repente exciderat illis memoria, quoties sermones illius aucupates, nihil nisi pudorem retulissent? Sed quid agas? Eo tandem deueniant oportet qui contra conscientiam, ad Pharaonis, Saulis, Iudae & similium illorum exemplum in propositio facinore pergunt. Vt nimirum vulnera quibus conscientias afficiunt, paulatim in gangraenam commutentur, in veternum incidentibus conscientiis, & ipsis tandem veluti nouaculam in Domini manu iniicientibus horrendorum ipsius iudiciorum, quibus non singulares tantum homines, sed vrbes, nationes, integrae monarchiae, tandem pessundantur & radicitus e terra viuentium exstirpatur. Eheu, non tantùm tota vetus historia , sed totius Christiani orbis quam oculis aspicimus ruina, testis est horum iudiciorum,sublatis& extinctis candelabris non tantùm septem Ecclesiarum Asiæ,quarum fit in Apocalypsi metio , sed totius Orientis vsque ad Hungariæ fines: totiúsque Meridiei à Mahumeto, & totius Occidentis à scorto septem montibus insidente, paucissimis exceptis quos Deus variis locis seruauit,& quibus annis ab hinc septuaginta cœpit purissimæ ni tidiffimæque Lucis diuinæ splendor illucescere. Sed heu ! heu inquam ! maximè metuendum est ne fit vltimus ille fulgor citissimè transiturus de quo Dominus loquitur apud Matth.24. 27. & Luc.17. 24. Ne igitur, fratres , veterno quodam sopiti desideamus, sed potiùs ad sapientum illarum virginum exemplum accensas lampades in manibus habeamus , sponso obuiam ituri. Matth.25.4 ne Sanctum Spiritu m afficere trifiitia pergamus. Ephef. 4.verf.30.sed potiùs in paracleto magis magísque gaudeamus,potiùs quàm retrogreffi, vno à Domino extra nos eiecto maligno Spiritu , septem peioribus domum adornemus.Matth.12. 45. Quandiu Lux illius ingentis gratiæ Dei nobis illucet progressum in ea faciamus , ne in densiores quàm alias vnquam tenebras incidamus. Ioh. 12. verf.35.
units.tr: In the previous homily we have drawn from this passage some more general headings, applicable to our own age, which were not, however, peculiar to this history. Let us now investigate its proper and particular sense. Caiaphas, then, when he noticed that the innocence of Christ was not harmed by any testimony, and pretended to play the part of a fair and good judge, wanted to hear the answer from Christ's own mouth; for the order of justice requires that the accused himself answer for his deed. In this matter, if you consider the outward form, Caiaphas and the whole council cannot be blamed; but the evil is hidden within. For here is set before our eyes an example of dreadful hardening. For how could they persist in their purpose, when they themselves experienced that the innocence of this matter could not be harmed even by witnesses suborned by themselves? Who had so hardened their brow as to prepare a capital trial, with no prior inquiry made, with no plausible arguments prepared, that is, to build without foundations? And how had memory so suddenly failed them, that every time they had lain in wait for his words, they had brought back nothing but shame? But what can one do? Those must come to that end who, against conscience, persist in a planned crime after the example of Pharaoh, Saul, Judas and such like. So that, of course, the wounds with which they afflict their consciences gradually turn into gangrene; consciences fall into lethargy, and at last they themselves lay the razor in the hand of the Lord, to his terrible judgments, by which not only single men but cities, nations and whole monarchies are at last destroyed and rooted out from the land of the living. Alas, not only the whole ancient history but the ruin of the whole Christian world, which we see with our eyes, is a witness to these judgments: the lampstands of not only the seven churches of Asia, which are mentioned in the Apocalypse, but of the whole East as far as the borders of Hungary, and of the whole South by Mahomet, and of the whole West by the harlot sitting on seven hills, have been taken away and extinguished, with very few exceptions whom God has preserved in various places, and in whom, about seventy years ago, the splendour of the purest and most brilliant divine Light began to shine. But alas, alas, I say! It is greatly to be feared lest that last flash, of which the Lord speaks in Matt. 24.27 and Luke 17.24, should pass very quickly. Therefore, brothers, let us not be lulled to sleep in some lethargy, but rather, after the example of those wise virgins, let us have lamps lit in our hands, ready to go out to meet the bridegroom (Matt. 25.4). Let us not continue to grieve the Holy Spirit (Eph. 4.30), but rather rejoice more and more in the Comforter; let us not turn back, lest, once the evil spirit has been cast out of us by the Lord, we adorn the house for seven worse ones (Matt. 12.45). While the light of that immense grace of God shines on us, let us make progress in it, lest we fall into darker shadows than ever before (John 12.35).

units.la: Caiaphas igitur iustissimo Dei iudicio sic induratus à seipso, non agnit o splendore qui lucebat ipsi, in Filij Dei ante oculos suos persona, (licet tenebris illius quam volens subiers rat exinanitionis tecta) Dominum etiam adiuratum interrogat. Horrendum sane & inaudi- tum spectaculum, eum adiurari cuius in nomine quæuis adiuratio legitima fieri debet: & reum adiuratum, Deum æternum esse cum Patre viuentem. At, qui rapinam minime ducit Deum esse, se eovsque pro nobis miseris peccatoribus volens abiecit, accepta serui forma, sed ita tamen vt sic adiuratus diem etiam falso isti Iudici & assessoribus dixerit, qua se coram eius tribunali præsentes sistant qui de adiurato, damnato, crucifixo, mortuo & sepulto, non ita multo post factus est eorum sine prouocatione iudex: eadem etiam omnium ipsis similium futura tandem conditione. Cæterum Adiurandi vox non hoc loco significat Iuramentum deferre, sed potius interposito Dei nomine & auctoritate, non simpliciter vt teste, sed maximè vindice cordis ac conscientiæ futuro iubere & quodammodo adigere.
units.tr: Caiaphas, therefore, hardened by himself through the most just judgment of God, did not recognise the splendour that shone upon him in the person of the Son of God before his eyes (although it was veiled by the obscurity of the humiliation which he had willingly undertaken), and he adjures the Lord and asks him. A truly horrible and unheard-of spectacle: that he should be adjured in whose name every lawful oath ought to be made, and that the accused, being adjured, should be the eternal God living with the Father. Yet he who did not consider it robbery to be God, but for us miserable sinners willingly humbled himself so far, taking the form of a servant, nevertheless, while so adjured, declared to that false judge and his assessors the day on which they would stand before his tribunal, when he would become, not long after, the judge of them without appeal, though he himself had been condemned, crucified, dead and buried, and they would at last meet the same fate as all those like them. Moreover, the word "to adjure" does not here mean to administer an oath, but rather, with the name and authority of God interposed, to command and in some way compel the heart and conscience, not simply as a witness, but above all as the future avenger.

units.la: Res enim creatas omnes etiam sensus experiles testes possumus quidem, Moses ad exemplum & aliorum, vocare. Deut. 32. 1. Esa. 1. 1. Mich. 6. 2. 1. Tim. 5. 21. quum tamen abominanda sit idolatria per alium quàm per viuentis Dei nomen iurare, qui solus nouit & iudicat hominum corda, & qui, vt ita dicam, in suæ iustitiæ folio peculiari collocatur, quum ea qua decet veritate & reuerentia iuratur: tantum abest vt per se ac simpliciter omne iuramentum sit prohibihibitum, quod falso docent Anabaptistæ, quū sæpe Deus ipse per Nomen suum iurarit, & Prophetæ sæpe: & Iuramentum in Dei viuentis nomine præstitum in veræ religionis testimonium, Esa. 19. 18. & 65. 16. & alibi passim adferatur.
units.tr: For we can indeed call on all created things, even those perceptible to the senses, as witnesses, as Moses did, and others too (Deut. 32.1; Isa. 1.1; Mic. 6.2; 1 Tim. 5.21). Yet although it is abominable idolatry to swear by any name other than that of the living God, who alone knows and judges the hearts of men, and who, so to speak, is set on the particular throne of his justice, when an oath is taken with the truth and reverence that are fitting. So far is it from being the case that every oath is in itself and simply forbidden, as the Anabaptists falsely teach, since God himself has often sworn by his own name, and the prophets often did; and an oath taken in the name of the living God, as a testimony to the true religion, is mentioned in Isa. 19.18 and 65.16, and elsewhere everywhere.

units.la: Faxit vero Deus vt Christiani omnes siue Magistratus, siue priuati, de Dei nomine sacrosancto nunquam vel cogitent vel loquantur, nisi cum sancta veneratione Maiestatis illius & gloriæ, cuius ne Angeli quidem splendorem ferre possunt: cuius sunt cœli thronus, terra vero pedum eius scabellum: qui mensus est pugillo suo aquas, & cœlos spithama expendit, & complexus est trientali puluerem terræ: & ponderauit statera montes, & colles lancibus: Hæc meditantes discemus cum in rebus inanibus nunquam nominare, multò vero minus in falsis: nec etiam in veris, omni loco, aut omni tempore, sed cum diuinæ gloriæ, & charitatis proximi quo docet respectu, cum recta semper coram illo conscientia, siue cum priuatis sit negotium, siue coram Magistratibus, qui Dei sunt facies aspectabilis. Quinimo nos tantopere sacrosanctum Nomen eius decet reuereri, vt si forte peieraturū suspicemur, cui delatum iuramentum fuerit, Dei gloriam & proximi salutem rebus omnibus terrenis etiam pretiosissimis & charissimis anteponamus. Hic me vero cogit locus dicere quosdam Magistratus plerisque locis magnū peccatū, reis capitalibus, iuramentū deferentes admittere. Nimirum enim istud est ipsa comprobatum experientia quosuis homines, & in primis profligatæ vitæ quidlibet vitæ fuę conseruandæ causa dicturos esse facturósque. Adde quòd deficientibus demum aliis omnibus argumentis, iuriiurando, controuersiasquibus adhibetur semel dirempturo, locus esse debet.
units.tr: May God grant that all Christians, whether magistrates or private persons, never either think or speak of the most holy name of God except with holy reverence for that Majesty and glory, whose splendour not even the angels can bear: whose throne is the heavens, and the earth his footstool; who has measured the waters in his fist, and weighed the heavens with a span, and gathered the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance. Meditating on these things, we shall learn never to name it in empty things, much less in false ones; nor even in true ones, at every place or every time, but with respect to the divine glory and to the love of our neighbour, which he teaches, always with a right conscience before him, whether the matter concerns private persons or magistrates, who are the visible face of God.
