units.tr: 56. But a certain maidservant, seeing him sitting by the fire, looked intently at him and said, "This man too was with him."

units.la: 57. Ipse vero abnegauit eum, dicens, Mulier, non noui eum.
units.tr: 57. But he denied it, saying, "Woman, I do not know him."

units.la: 58. Et paulo post alius videns eum, dixit, Et tu, ex ipsis es. Petrus vero ait, Heus tu, non sum.
units.tr: 58. A little later another, seeing him, said, "You too are one of them." But Peter said, "Man, I am not."

units.la: 59. Et interposita quasi hora una, alius quidam id affirmabat, dicens, Vere & iste cum illo erat: etenim Galilaeus est.
units.tr: 59. After about an hour had passed, another man insisted, saying, "Surely this man too was with him, for he is a Galilean."

units.la: 60. At autem Petrus, Heus tu, nescio quid dicas. Et illico adhuc ipso loquente, vocem emisit gallus.
units.tr: 60. But Peter said, "Man, I do not know what you are talking about." And immediately, while he was still speaking, the cock crowed.

units.la: IOH. 18.
units.tr: IOH. 18.

units.la: 15. Sequebatur autem Iesum Simon Petrus, & alius discipulus. Discipulus vero ille notus erat Pontifici Maximo, & simul introiit cum Iesu in aulam Pontificis Maximi.
units.tr: 15. Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. That disciple was known to the high priest, and he went into the courtyard of the high priest together with Jesus.

units.la: 16. Petrus autem stabat extra ad ostium. Exiit ergo discipulus ille alter qui notus erat Pontifici Maximo, & loquutus est ostiariae, & introduxit Petrum.
units.tr: 16. But Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out, spoke to the doorkeeper and brought Peter in.

units.la: 17. Dixit ergo Petro ancilla ostiaria, Num & tu ex discipulis es hominis istius? Dicit ille, Non sum.
units.tr: 17. The maid who kept the door therefore said to Peter, "Are you too one of this man's disciples?" He said, "I am not."

units.la: 18. Adstabant autem servi & ministri qui prunas congesserant, quia frigus erat, & sese calefaciebant, erat vero cum eis etiam Petrus adstans, & sese calefaciens.
units.tr: 18. Now the servants and officers, who had made a charcoal fire because it was cold, stood there warming themselves; and Peter was standing with them, warming himself.

units.la: 25. Stabat autem Simon Petrus, & (sese)calefaciebat: dixerunt igitur ei, Num & tu ex discipulis eius es? Negavit ille, & dixit, Non sum.
units.tr: 25. Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, "Are you too one of his disciples?" He denied it and said, "I am not."

units.la: 26. Dicit ei quidam ex servis Pontificis Maximi, cognatus eius cuius absciderat Petrus auriculam, Nonne ego te vidi in horto cum eo?
units.tr: 26. One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said to him, "Did I not see you in the garden with him?"

units.la: 27. Rursus ergo negavit Petrus, & statim gallus vocem emisit.
units.tr: 27. Peter denied it again, and at once the cock crowed.

units.la: {a}VT fuerit ab hostibus suis manifestis Christus Iesus Dominus noster tractatus audiuimus, nimirū Caiapha totaque illa Ierosolymitana Ecclesia, ad cuius effigiem quæ hodie nos Ecclesia persequitur est efformata, vt sit quemadmodū inter Christum & eius membra, sic inter Satanam & ministros eius conformitas. Superest dispiciamus quinam se famuli dominorum ad exemplum aduersus eum gesserint, in quibus vetus illud tritumque prouerbium confirmaretur, Vt dominus, sic seruus: quum nullum iniuriæ, nullū contumeliæ, nullum ignominiæ genus præterierint, quo non affecerint eum quem licet merito capitali iudicio damnatum putarent, nulnullam tamen adhuc à iudice sententiam acceperat, qui non Caiaphas erat, sed Pilatus, vt tunc illius Prouinciæ res ferebant. At, quod longè maiùs est, quum non modò capitis sententiam reus accepit, sed in carnificis etiam manus est traditus, annon est summum flagitium, aliquid ad sententiam adiicere, nedū reo manus inferre, nisi quibus executionis cura demandata est? Verùm Magistratibus aliis exemplum iniustitiæ præbentibus, & passim impunitate regnante quid mirum est torrentis instar stagnantis & refusi passim grassari violentiam?
units.tr: {a}We have heard how Christ Jesus our Lord was treated by his open enemies, namely by Caiaphas and the whole Church of Jerusalem, which the Church that is persecuted today has been shaped to resemble; so that there is a likeness between Christ and his members, and in the same way between Satan and his ministers. It remains for us to see how the servants of these masters behaved toward him, following that example, and so confirmed the old and well-worn proverb, "As the master, so the servant." They left no kind of injury, no kind of insult, no kind of disgrace, by which they did not treat him, even though they thought he deserved condemnation to death; yet he had not yet received sentence from a judge, and that judge was not Caiaphas but Pilate, as the affairs of that province then stood. But what is far worse: when the accused has received not only a sentence of death but has also been handed over into the hands of the executioner, is it not the greatest outrage to add anything to the sentence, let alone to lay hands on the accused, unless one has been charged with carrying out the execution? Yet when other magistrates offer an example of injustice, and impunity reigns everywhere, what wonder is it that violence, like a torrent that has stagnated and spilled over, rages everywhere?

units.la: Præsertim verò Satana viam inueniente qua eorum ministerio qui sine scientia zelum habent abutatur. Sic passim annis ab hinc sexaginta, miseræ plebeculæ ab incendiariis istis excitatæ magna licentia sæuiunt, non tantum miseris reis è manibus carnificum ereptis, sed sine inquisitione vlla aut iudicij forma hinc inde cum immani ac inaudito omnis sæuitiæ & crudelitatis genere grassantibus & furentibus populis dementatis: quarum tragœdiarum luctuosissimarum hodie, misera Gallia, si alias vnquam, horrendum est spectaculum.
units.tr: Above all, Satan finds a way to abuse, through the service of those who have zeal without knowledge. So everywhere, some sixty years ago, the wretched common people, stirred up by these firebrands, raged with great license. The unhappy prisoners were snatched from the hands of the executioners, and without any inquiry or form of trial, the peoples, driven out of their minds, ran hither and thither, raging with every kind of cruelty and savagery, unheard of and monstrous. Of such most mournful tragedies, wretched France, today, if ever, presents a dreadful spectacle.

units.la: Interea verò quo maioribus Seruator noster iniuriis affectus est, eò certiores sumus de peccatis nostris ad vltimum obolum exsoluendis: vt tanto melius in tam horrendo spectaculo hinc quidem quantus & quàm immensus sit iræ Dei in nostra peccata furor perspiciamus, quò tanto magis & illa nobis examino displiceant: inde vero quàm immensa sit, quàm infinita cœlestis Patris illius nostri clementia ac misericordia, vnico filio suo non parcentis vt nobis reconciliaretur: sicut contemplemur ac summam nobisque incomprehensam magni illius & vnici Filij Dei charitatem, cò vsque se pro suis hostibus exinanientis meditemur. Hæc igitur omnis Filij se fratrem nostrum facientis obedientia, qua nos cœlestis illius hæreditatis suo sanguine partæ facit participes: sputa illa omnia quibus veneranda ipsius facies tam improbè conspurcata fuit: colaphi illi quibus cæsus est, exiguo tempore in gloriam inenarrabilem transmutati sunt, in istorum conspu-torum & verberonum ora tota tandem ignominia recidente. Et horum quidem, in filiis Dei persequendis imitatores idem etiam excepit & exceptur us est exitus. Testis esto Hierosolymorum & totius gentis cuersio, qua perfidi isti nebulones longè maiorem ignominiam & colaphos alios à Domino passi sunt: testes sunto nostra recenti memoria quæ Deus in suos hostes exercuit iudicia, tot perfidos & abominandos fratrum nostrorum carnifices pari vindicta grauiter vltus.
units.tr: Meanwhile, the more our Savior was afflicted with injuries, the more certain we are that our sins are being paid off to the last penny. So that in so dreadful a spectacle we may see, on the one hand, how great and how immense is the fury of God's wrath against our sins, and so much the more displeasing to us ought they be; and on the other hand, how immense and how infinite is the clemency and mercy of that heavenly Father of ours, who spared not his only Son, that we might be reconciled to him. Let us contemplate and meditate on the supreme and incomprehensible love of that great and only Son of God, who emptied himself to such a degree on behalf of his enemies. This whole obedience of the Son, who made himself our brother, makes us partakers of that heavenly inheritance obtained by his blood. All those spittings by which his venerable face was so shamefully defiled, and those blows with which he was struck, were in a short time changed into unspeakable glory, while all the shame falls back at last upon the mouths of those spitters and strikers. And the same end has met, and will meet, those who imitate them in persecuting the sons of God. Let the overthrow of Jerusalem and of the whole nation be a witness, in which those faithless scoundrels suffered far greater shame, and other blows, from the Lord. Let our recent memory be witness to the judgments that God has executed on his enemies, having heavily avenged with equal retribution so many faithless and abominable executioners of our brethren.

units.la: Sed, oro, annon istis nisi prorsus profani fuissent à tam pretiosa Prophetandi voce in illa sua petulantia oportuit abstinere? Sic hodie videas magnos illos suarum superstitionum pessimo fundamento nixarum defensores, sacerdotes etiam incogitates, maximè in Dei nomen
units.tr: But, I ask you, ought they not, if they were not utterly profane, to have refrained from this precious voice of prophesying in their own wantonness? So today you may see those great defenders of their superstitions, which rest on a most wretched foundation, and even the thoughtless priests, most abusive and blasphemous against the name of God,

units.la: Pretiosam esse oportet Prophetandi vocem. men & suorum Diuorum cife contumeliosos ac blasphemos, vt nullus fit ipsis nec apud Deum, nec apud homines, necapud seipsos excufatioui locus.
units.tr: The voice of prophesying ought to be precious. and against the saints and their divine ones, so that neither before God, nor before men, nor before themselves, can they have any ground for excuse.

units.la: Iesus Christus igitur, in sua quum venerit,à suis tamen receptus non est. Iohan. 1. verf. 11. At de quibus hactenus egimus aperte fuerunt iurati hostes ipsius ? sed de quibus iam acturi fumus, etiam dilecti domestici fuerunt, & tanta quidem hactenus in eum amoris fui signa dederant, vt etiam ipsum fequuturi cuncta relinquerent. Matth. 19. verf. 27. in quibus tamen vnus etiam ipsius œconomus perfidus proditor cum argenteis triginta prodidit : alter vero, inter duodecim, eius amantissimus & animofiffimus, ter tamen eum abnegauit; alij vero, vnico excepto, qui tamen obmutuit, fuga turpi sibi consuluerunt : magna illa sane & prorsus stupenda, sed Dei, summa sapientia & prouidentia sic in suorum electorum vtilitatem & nostram maximam erudition em disposita. Primum igitur ista sic euenifle tenendum est, vt foli Christo nostræ redemptionis beneficium acceptum feratur, vt qui solus istud perficere mysterium potuerit, Apostolis ipsis non redemptoribus, sed ex eius gratia & misericordia redemptis. Quod fi ita est, vt est sane verifimum, vnius Domini nostri Iesu Christi morte & passione redeptos efle omnes, fine exceptione electos, qua re tandem nitentur Sanctorum quæ vocant merita, tanta dignitate & numero, vt iis à quibus præstantur non modò sufficiant, sed aliis etiam innumeris supersint, & ad finem seculorum superfutura sint, quæ hic auro & argento redempta, Deo tandem in satisfactionem offerantur? Qua in re, inquain, tam falsa doctrina niti potest, quin hæc longè absurdissima consequantur, ab Apostolis & aliis satisfactum pro iis quorum erat iam æs alienum exolutum? Apostolis igitur potius credamus, minimè docentibus à le pro nobis esse satisfactum, sed contrà tum verbis, tum scriptis, tum denique tota vita nos miseros peccatores ad vnicam Iesu Christi satisfactionem deduce ntibus.
units.tr: Jesus Christ, therefore, "came to his own, and his own did not receive him" (John 1:11). But those of whom we have spoken so far were open enemies who swore against him; those of whom we are now to speak were beloved household members, and up to this point had given such signs of their love for him that they left everything to follow him (Matt. 19:27). Yet among them, one of his treasurers, a faithless traitor, betrayed him for thirty pieces of silver; another, among the twelve, most loving and most courageous of him, denied him three times; and the others, with one exception who nevertheless kept silent, saved themselves by shameful flight. These are indeed great and utterly astonishing things, but they were so arranged by God's highest wisdom and providence for the benefit of his chosen ones and for our greatest instruction. First, then, we must hold that these things happened in such a way that the benefit of our redemption is credited to Christ alone, since he alone could accomplish this mystery, and the Apostles themselves were redeemed not as redeemers, but by his grace and mercy. If this is so, as is certainly most true, that all are redeemed by the death and passion of our one Lord Jesus Christ alone, all being chosen without exception, then on what grounds do they rely, those so-called merits of the saints, of such dignity and number that they not only suffice for those by whom they are performed, but also overflow to countless others, and will remain to the end of the ages, and are at last offered to God in satisfaction, being bought with gold and silver as it were? In this matter, I say, how can so false a doctrine stand, without the most absurd consequences following, namely that the Apostles and others made satisfaction for those whose debt had already been paid? Let us therefore rather believe the Apostles, who did not teach that satisfaction had been made for us by themselves, but on the contrary, by their words, their writings, and finally their whole life, led us wretched sinners to the one satisfaction of Jesus Christ.

units.la: Obseruanda deinde hoc loco Ecclesiæ quàdiu in his terris peregrinatur conditio, nimirum, suis illam viribus minimè gentium subiectere, sicut nec à seipsa suum ortum habet: sed sola Dei potentia seruari incolumem in petra illa, super quam fundata est inhabitatem, quæ minimè Petrus est, sed is quem ipse Petrus vocat, cuius Ecclesiæ nomine confessus est. Matth. 16. verf. 16. Et id ipsum, de seipso, Petrus in re longè minoris momenti quàm ipsa sit Ecclesiæ firmitas palàm profitetur, à se nimirum miracula non edi, sed à solo Dei filio, credentibus illa fide percipientibus. Act. 3. 12. 1. Pet. 1. Nec Paulus ipse fundamentum est, sed ex fundatoribus vnus 1. Cor. 3. 10. Quamobrem vt à sola Dei bonitate & clementia, vt causa primaria suum ortum habet Ecclesia: sic etiam eadem causa conseruatur in hoc mundo dum plenè glorificetur: sic eorum opera qui plantant & rigant vtente Domino vt ipse laboribus eorum benedicens det incrementum. 1. Cor. 3. 7.
units.tr: Next, we must observe the condition of the Church while it journeys on this earth: it is by no means subject to the nations by its own strength, just as it does not have its origin from itself. Rather, by the power of God alone it is kept safe on that rock upon which it has been founded, which is not Peter but him whom Peter himself names, in whose name he confessed the Church. Matt. 16:16. Peter himself openly declares this about himself, in a matter of far less importance than the firmness of the Church: miracles are not performed by himself but by the Son of God alone, received by those who believe with faith. Acts 3:12; 1 Pet. 1. Nor is Paul himself the foundation, but one of the founders. 1 Cor. 3:10. Therefore, just as the Church has its origin as a primary cause from the goodness and clemency of God alone, so the same cause preserves it in this world until it is fully glorified. Likewise, the labours of those who plant and water are such that the Lord, using them and blessing their labours, gives the increase. 1 Cor. 3:7.

units.la: Tertio loco, quod Christus de huius Ecclesiae visibili in his terris conditione tot parabolis docuit Matth. 13. ad vivum hic nobis ob oculos ponitur, nimirum non esse Christianum quicunque se venditat, ac proinde semper Ecclesiam permixtam fore non tantum infirmis & fortibus, sed etiam electis & reprobis, & Angelis, vt ita dicam, & Diabolis ad seculorum visque finem: & quidem praestantissimas quasque Ecclesias huic obnoxias esse malo futuras, vt Samosatenus extitit in celeberrima illa Antiochena, in qua de Christi nomine primum fideles dicti sunt, Act. 11. 26. Arium produxit famosissima illa Alexandrina Ecclesia: Nestorium autem, Eutychetem & Macedonium & alios non paucos noua Roma Constantinopolis progenuit: & tandem in florentissima illa Ecclesia Romana, mysterium illud iniquitatis, quod Apostolorum temporibus peragebatur Imperij Romani casu. 2. Thess. 2. 7. pedetentim absolutum est, ac proinde meretrix illa super septem montes sedens thronum suum pedetentim erexit, in quo huc visque adhuc hodie tanta cum erroris efficacia regnat, vt erat a Domino praedictu. Matt. 13. 22. adeoq; tecto & inuoluto errore, vt multi alioquin excellentes Dei serui, eminus illum licet conspicati, tamen suis studiis multum promo-
units.tr: Third, that Christ taught in so many parables about the visible condition of this Church on earth (Matt. 13) is here set before our eyes to the life. Not everyone who boasts himself a Christian is one; so the Church will always be mixed, not only with the weak and the strong, but also with the elect and the reprobate, and with angels, so to speak, and devils, until the end of the ages. Indeed, the most distinguished churches will be liable to this evil. Samosatenus arose in that famous Antiochene church in which the faithful were first called by the name of Christ (Acts 11:26). Arius was produced by the most notorious Alexandrian church. New Rome, Constantinople, brought forth Nestorius, Eutyches, Macedonius and not a few others. At last, in that most flourishing Roman church, the mystery of iniquity which was already at work in the times of the Apostles (2 Thess. 2:7) was gradually completed with the fall of the Roman Empire. So that harlot sitting on seven hills gradually raised her throne, in which up to the present day she reigns with such efficacy of error, as the Lord foretold (Matt. 13:22). The error is so hidden and wrapped up that many otherwise excellent servants of God, although they caught sight of it from afar, nevertheless promoted it greatly by their studies.

units.la: z. }. uerint. Habet tamen in hac tanta confusion visibilis Ecclesia quo se his verbis Domini co-soletur, Ne time, parue grex, Luc. 12. 32. licet nonnunquam eo redigatur vt a solo Deo dignoscatur, eam in petris & saxis conseruante, quod Eliae temporibus factum consipicimus. 1. Reg. 18.13. & 19.18. Heb. 11.37. & 38. & ante vltimum aduentum Domini euenturum, Dominus praedixerat. Luc. 18.8.
units.tr: Yet in this great confusion the visible Church has a way to console itself with these words of the Lord: "Fear not, little flock" (Luke 12:32). Although at times it is reduced to such a state that it is known only by God, who preserves it among rocks and crags, as we see happened in the times of Elijah (1 Kings 18:13; 19:18; Heb. 11:37-38). The Lord had foretold that this would happen before his last coming (Luke 18:8).

units.la: Quarto, in hac ipsa materia discimus quanta sit etiam firmissimorum infirmitas: sibi ipsi suisque fidere viribus, quantum sit: quanta sit nostri Seruatoris benignitas: unde vera poenitentia proficiscatur, & quae sit, cui ex aduerso horrendorum Dei in eos iudiciorum exemplum proponitur, quos quum suam infirmitatem lugere potius oportuerat, pedetetim tamen in stuporem & indurationem immedicabilem praecipites feruntur: quae singula doctrinae nobis admodum vtilis ac necessariae sunt capita.
units.tr: Fourth, in this very matter we learn how great is the weakness even of the firmest, how much trust in oneself and one's own strength is worth, how great is the kindness of our Saviour, whence true repentance proceeds and what it is. On the other side, the example of God's dreadful judgments is set before us, against those who, when they ought rather to have mourned their weakness, are nevertheless gradually carried headlong into stupor and incurable hardening. These single points are most useful and necessary heads of doctrine for us.

units.la: De triplici iam Petri lapsu nobis dicendum foret: sed priusquam illud aggrediamur, non alienum erit primum considerare Domini hac in re consilium, qui quum in hac tentatione Petrum, vt cateros, ne caderet sustinere potuerit, non tamen fecit, vt exemplum humanae infirmitatis in tanto viro & inter Christi Dei Filij domesticos praecipuo, sit tanto magis conspicuum, & vigilando cauere sibi discant, etiam fortissimi quique ne ipsos ex improuiso aggrediente hoste decipiantur.
units.tr: We would now have to speak of Peter's threefold fall. But before we take that up, it will not be out of place first to consider the Lord's counsel in this matter. Though he could have sustained Peter in this temptation, as he did the others, so that he would not fall, he did not do so. This was so that the example of human weakness might be all the more conspicuous in so great a man, and one pre-eminent among the domestic servants of Christ the Son of God; and so that they might learn by watchfulness to beware, and that even the very strongest might not be deceived when the enemy attacks them unexpectedly.

units.la: Sed praeterea minimè in dubium reuoco qnin Dominus quum praeuiderct vlcimis istis temporibus homines erroris spiritu deceptos Petrum eius discipulum in idolum transformaturos, quod viuo ipsi bis cōtigisse cōspicimus,nisi vehementer esset reluctatus, Act.3.12. & 10.25.& 26.& D. Paulo Barnabeque Act.14. 14.& 15.& quod maius est,eò vsque dementādos,vt in vnius Dei filij æterni & omnipotentis Ecclesiæ capitis solium eos eucherent qui Petri successorum nomen sibi salsissimè & impudentissimè arrogarent, expressè Petrum inter omnes suos discipulos elegisse, in quo quantulæ sint hominum vires patefaceret: vt quicunque excellentem illum Apostolum essent visuri vel auditurí, seruum esse scirent in Domini locum minimè reponendum: & ipse vicissim Dei donis non abuteretur. Et hoc etiam ipse diligenter in posterum cauit,nullum in suos condiscipulos dominatum sibi arrogans, sed paratus potiùs ipsis sui muneris rationem reddere Act.11.2. & 4.coràm omnibus etiam se argui passus,Gal.2.14.se cum ipsis eodem appellans nomine, & dominatum in clerum Domini diligenter prohibens.1. Pet. 5. 1.& 3.ad exemplum Pauli, Iacobi & Ioannis, Gal.2 9.& 1. Cor. 1. 13. & 7.35.Nec hoc tantùm loco Dominus abusum istum præuenire studuit: nam in illis duodecim nullum animaduertas durius vnquam exceptum à Domino, Satanam etiam eum vocante,& à se his verbis seucrioribus repellente, Non sapis quæ sunt Dei, sed quæ sunt hominum, Matth. 16. 23. & quidem eodem pene momento quo egregiam illam suorum condiscipulorum & suo nomine confessionem ediderat, ad id eum impellente naturali quadam animi promptitudine, quæ præcipitem eum sæpe dedisset nisi Deus illam temeritatem esset moderatus, tandemque in eximiam fidem & excellentissimū zelum commutasset. Esto igitur Petrus Dei gratia factus præ sociis suis excellens Apostolus, adeò ut tam graviter lapsus, aliis tamen confirmandis deinceps inseruierit, & sæpe coetibus ipsorum præierit, non ambitione, sed pio zelo sinceróque animo, & ordine legitimo. An vero propterea gradum in alios cum aliquem obtinuisse censebimus? Aut à Christo vicarium in terris relictum, qui contraria decerneret iis quæ ipse in cœlo constitueret: quum ipse Iesus Christus nō simpliciter hanc dignitatem Capitis Ecclesiæ, quatenus homo perfectissimus sustineat, sed in primis quatenus verus Deus, cui soli datum est, & non ipsis Angelis, naturam utramque coniunctam in se habere. Sceleratos vero illos, hominum etiam nomine, iam à tam multis seculis, indignissimos, sibi Capitis Ecclesiæ, & quidem vniuersalis nomen arrogare? Et tamen si ipsis creditur, Petrus, qui non ita multò post à confessione Satan est nominatus, is est super quem Ecclesia fundata est: detestandus nimirum error. Nam quæcunque tribuatur huic Apostolo præeminentia, non tamen ipse fundamentum, tum, sed ex fundatoribus tantum praecipuus erit: quod iterum esse falsum comperietur ex qualitate quae instituitur Petri cum aliis columnis Gal. 2. 9. & eo quod Apostolus abomni tamen primatu procul remotus, de sui laboris efficacia testatur. 1. Cor. 11. 10. minime tamen contemptis collegis. Phil. 4. 3. Quamobrem etiam in illa ciuitate Dei quae describitur Apoc. 21. 17. minime Petro prae aliis fundamentum aliquod aut συλῶνες tribuuntur: quod Christo nunquam in mentem venit, adeo quidem ut quemadmodum Christus respiciens Petri promptitudinem, quam eius condiscipuli etiam admittebant, & in primis rectam confessionem quam ediderat, Petri quidem nomine, quod idem ac Rupes est, ipsum exornarit, sed etiam aperte distinxerit a rupe fundamentali, scilicet nimirum, qualem Petrus fuisse erat quo vnico, & alio nullo, teste Apostolo 1. Cor. 3. 11. quum Ecclesia nitatur, & hoc etiam Petrum ipsum fundamento niti par est: tantum abest vt ipse sit fundamentum, aut solus fundator.
units.tr: Moreover, I do not in the least doubt that the Lord, when he foresaw that in these last times men deceived by the spirit of error would transform Peter, his disciple, into an idol (which we see happened twice even while he lived, unless he had strongly resisted: Acts 3:12; 10:25-26; and to Paul and Barnabas, Acts 14:14-15), and, what is greater, would go so far mad as to set upon the throne of the Church, which belongs to the one eternal and almighty Son of God, the head of the Church, those who most wickedly and impudently arrogate to themselves the name of successors of Peter, clearly chose Peter from among all his disciples in order to show how small human strength is. So whoever was going to see or hear that excellent Apostle would know that a servant is not to be put in the place of the Lord, and that he himself, in turn, would not abuse God's gifts. And he himself also took diligent care for the future, claiming no lordship over his fellow disciples, but being ready rather to render an account of his office (Acts 11:2 and 4). He allowed himself to be openly rebuked before all (Gal. 2:14), calling himself by the same name as them, and diligently forbidding lordship over the clergy of the Lord (1 Pet. 5:1, 3), after the example of Paul, James and John (Gal. 2:9; 1 Cor. 1:13; 7:35). Nor did the Lord seek to forestall this abuse only in this place. Among those twelve you will notice no one ever rebuked more harshly by the Lord, when he even called Satan and repelled him with these severer words: "You do not savour the things of God, but the things of men" (Matt. 16:23). This was almost at the same moment in which he had put forth that excellent confession in the name of his fellow disciples and in his own name, when a certain natural readiness of spirit impelled him to it. That readiness would often have hurled him headlong had God not moderated that rashness and at last changed it into remarkable faith and most excellent zeal. So let Peter be granted, made by the grace of God an excellent apostle beyond his fellows, so that, though he fell so gravely, he afterwards served to strengthen others, and often went before their assemblies, not from ambition but from pious zeal, a sincere mind and a lawful order. But shall we therefore judge that he obtained a rank above the others? Or that he was left on earth by Christ as his vicar, to decree things contrary to those which he himself establishes in heaven? Jesus Christ himself sustains this dignity of Head of the Church not simply as most perfect man, but chiefly as true God, to whom alone it was given, and not to the angels themselves, to have both natures joined in himself. Shall those wicked men, now for so many centuries most unworthy even of the name of men, arrogate to themselves the name of Head of the Church, and indeed of the universal Church? And yet, if they are believed, Peter, who not long after was called Satan, is the one on whom the Church is founded. This is a detestable error, to be sure. For whatever pre-eminence be attributed to this Apostle, he will not himself be the foundation, but only a chief among the founders. This will again be found false from the relation instituted between Peter and the other pillars (Gal. 2:9), and from the fact that the Apostle, far removed from all primacy, testifies to the efficacy of his own labour (1 Cor. 11:10), yet without despising his colleagues (Phil. 4:3). Therefore also, in that city of God which is described in Rev. 21:17, no foundation or pillar [στύλους] is assigned to Peter above others. This never came into Christ's mind. Indeed, Christ, regarding Peter's readiness, which his fellow disciples also admitted, and above all the right confession which he had made, adorned him with the name Peter, which is the same as Rock. But he also clearly distinguished him from the foundation rock, namely, such as Peter was not: the one and only, and no other, as the Apostle testifies (1 Cor. 3:11). Since the Church rests on this, it is fitting that Peter himself also rests on the foundation. So far is he from being the foundation, or the sole founder.

units.la: At demus iis, qualem nobis Diuum Petrum fingunt, quo tandem iure Successorum eius sibi nomen tribuunt? Ecquis vero iussit Roma & eius Episcopum, esse caput vniuersalis Ecclesiae, vt olim vrbs illa & Imperator eius erunt Imperij Romani caput? Ecquis vero dixerit vnquam Ecclesiam vniuersalem, vnius Imperij Romani finibus contineri? Denique an ausint negare saepe falsum Pastorem in locum veri Pastoris succedere? Quorsum igitur successio personalis vniuersalis Ecclesiæ nota dicetur, quum vt boni Pastores sequendi ita sint falsi Pastores fugiendi?
units.tr: But grant them the Peter they imagine. By what right, then, do his successors claim his name for themselves? Who ever ordered that Rome and its Bishop should be the head of the universal Church, just as that city and its emperor were once the head of the Roman Empire? Who has ever said that the universal Church is confined within the bounds of the Roman Empire? And can they deny that a false minister often succeeds in the place of a true one? Why, then, should personal succession be called a mark of the universal Church, when good ministers are to be followed and false ministers to be avoided?

units.la: Dicam aliquid amplius, excepta Noui fœderis Veteri Successione (quorum differentia nec in Legislatore, nec in Substantia, nec in fine fœderis posita est, sed tantum in varia dispensatione nostræ salutis) nullam esse in Ecclesia Christiana doctrinæ Successionem, at perpetuam esse oportere continuationem verorum Pastorum aliorum aliis succedentium: quam in Ecclesia Romana Successionem minus quàm in vlla alia repertum iri dico, si doctrina ipsorum, ad verum lapidem Lydium, Sacras puta Scripturas, quarum summam fidei nostræ articuli continent, examinetur: vt reliquas istius sedis horrendas pollutiones in præsentia silentio tegam quibus iampridem Vniuersus orbis polluitur, vel istis tritis in omnium ore prouerbiis testibus, Bonus Papa, malus homo, &c., Nunquam bonus equus aut homo Romam eundo melior factus est.
units.tr: I will say something further. Apart from the succession of the Old and New Covenants (whose difference lies neither in the Lawgiver, nor in the substance, nor in the end of the covenant, but only in the varied dispensation of our salvation), there is no succession of doctrine in the Christian Church. There ought to be a continuous succession of true ministers following one another. I say that this succession will be found less in the Roman Church than in any other, if their doctrine is examined by the true touchstone, that is, the Holy Scriptures, whose summary of articles contains our faith. I will pass over in silence the other horrible pollutions of that see, by which the whole world has long been defiled. Let these commonplace proverbs on everyone's lips bear witness: "A good pope, a bad man," and so on: "A good horse or a good man never became better by going to Rome."

units.la: Denique cuius nullu est principiu qua eius Successionem esse dixeris. Vbi vero tandem in Sacris Scripturis Oecumenicus ille fiue Vniuersalis Papatus, huius, quam vocant totius Hierarchiæ caput? Et hoc truncato capite, quid nisi fœtidum cadauer reliqua membra futura sunt? Et quod maius est, annon idololatria est, immo intoleranda impietas homines (quales vero, quæso, iam ab annis quingetis homines? ac non potius horrenda & toti mundo detes-tanda monstra) in foliû Vniuersalis Ecclesiæ capitis euchere? Annon tandem eo deuentum est, quod expressè præcauerat Apostolus, vt nimirum Scortum istud efferretur aduersus quicquid dicitur Deus aut numen? An non enim, obsecro, supra Deum se effert qui reipsa sibi Scripto verbo Iehouæ Prophetico & Apostolico addédi, detrahendi, immutandi potestatem arrogat? Annon hic is est qui sibi in suis Canonibus auctoritate ex nihilo aliquid faciédi tribuit? Qui Paradisi potestate absoluta occludendi recludédíq; sibi vindicat? & à pœna & culpa absoluendi, licet Dominus noster Iesus Christus (vt istius Scorti dicunt patroni) culpam tātùm aboleuerit, pœnâ verò retinuerit in Purgatorio sustinendâ, quâ tamen bonus iste Vicarius vno momento possit tollere? Annò iste seruus seruorū est, qui (licet verus ille & vnicus Ecclesiæ caput, Christus cū Petro diserte persoluerit Imperatori Romano tributum: & voluntaria obedientia coră Pilato demóstrarit Regnũ suū non esse ex hoc mūdo) super omnes Reges & Monarchas eminet: & humeris etiam instar idoli portatur: & audet sibi arrogare & in moneta cudere (vel illo tcite mo nstro horrendo & detestádo Iulio tertio noltro seculo) quod ne Christo quidem ipsi conuenirer, niū homo Deus esset, nimirum illud apud Esa.60. 12. Gens & regnū quæ non seruierint tibi peribunt, & hæ gentes penitus desolabuntur. Denique, qui cumulus est omnis impietatis, an-
units.tr: Finally, of whom there is no beginning, you would call his succession. Where at last in the Holy Scriptures is that so-called Oecumenical or Universal Papacy, the head of the whole so-called Hierarchy? And with this head cut off, what will the remaining members be but a stinking corpse? And what is worse, is it not idolatry, indeed intolerable impiety, to set men on the throne of the head of the Universal Church (what sort of men, I ask, for fifteen hundred years? Rather horrible monsters, to be detested by the whole world)? Has it not finally come to what the Apostle expressly foresaw, namely that this harlot would be lifted up against everything called God or divine? For does he not, I beg you, exalt himself above God, who claims for himself the power to add to, subtract from and alter the written word of Jehovah, prophetic and apostolic? Is this not the one who attributes to himself, in his canons, the authority to make something out of nothing? Who claims for himself the absolute power to shut and open Paradise, and to absolve from punishment and guilt? Although our Lord Jesus Christ (as this harlot's patrons say) has abolished only the guilt, but retained the punishment to be undergone in Purgatory, which this good Vicar could yet remove in a moment. Is not this the servant of servants, who (although the true and only head of the Church, Christ, expressly paid tribute to the Roman emperor with Peter, and by voluntary obedience before Pilate showed that his kingdom is not of this world) rises above all kings and monarchs, is even carried on shoulders like an idol, and dares to claim for himself, and to stamp on coin (with that horrible and detestable Julius III in our age as witness), what would not even suit Christ himself, unless he were God and man? Namely that passage in Isaiah 60:12: "The nation and kingdom that will not serve you shall perish, and those nations shall be utterly laid waste." Finally, to crown all impiety, is not that man utterly lost who, in the Decretals (that is, his Koran), declares of himself in the most express words that no one may judge him, and that, dragging souls by cartloads into hell, he cannot be asked, "What are you doing?"

units.la: z. iiij. non ille perditus est, qui in Decretalibus (idest Alcorano suo) verbis expressissimis de se praedicat, se à nemine iudicandum: & trahentem plenis plaustris animas in inferos, neminem interrogare posse, Quid agat?
units.tr: z. iiij. Finally, of whom there is no beginning, you would call his succession. Where at last in the Holy Scriptures is that so-called Oecumenical or Universal Papacy, the head of the whole so-called Hierarchy? And with this head cut off, what will the remaining members be but a stinking corpse?

units.la: Agite, igitur, fratres, Dominum mecum ipsi dignis laudibus extollite, quòd nostro seculo dignatus sit turpis illius scorti foetorem retegere, & oris sui Spiritu conficere coeperit: supplicibus votis ab eo postulemus ne noxtris peccatis, nostra ignavia & ingratitudine merito provocatus eius consolidari vulnera patiatur, sed ut potius propter sanctum suum Nomen, magnum illud suum opus perficiat. In primis vero Papatu sic exuamus, ut verum Christianismum, cum eius gloriae vero zelo, & vera in proximum charitate coniunctum induamus. Hicque etiam nobis non tantum à manifestis capitalibus hostibus caveamus, sed à Mediatoribus quibusdam, qui dubitant ipsi, & alios dubitare docent, an Ecclesia cuius Scortum illud caput est, & à qua Dei beneficio secessionem fecimus, vera sit ecclesia, nec-ne: atque adeo libenter aliquam nos ad vomitum reducendi rationem inirent, & Ecclesiam ex sui cerebri fantasiis fingerent: quorum utinam Deus perniciosa consilia & conatus, ut perniciosissimorum Ecclesiae hostium infringat.
units.tr: Come, therefore, brothers, let us extol the Lord with me in worthy praises, that in our age he has deigned to uncover the stench of that vile harlot and has begun to consume it with the Spirit of his mouth. With suppliant prayers let us ask him that, provoked justly by our sins, our sloth and ingratitude, he not allow his wounds to be healed, but rather accomplish his great work for the sake of his holy Name. First of all, let us so strip off Papacy that we may put on true Christianity, joined with true zeal for his glory and true love toward our neighbour. And here we must beware not only of the manifest, chief enemies, but of certain Mediators, who themselves doubt, and teach others to doubt, whether the Church, of which that harlot is the head and from which by God's benefit we have seceded, is a true church or not; and so they would gladly undertake some plan to lead us back to the vomit, and fashion a Church out of the fantasies of their own brain. May God frustrate their pernicious counsels and attempts, as those of the most pernicious enemies of the Church.

units.la: Denique hic quatuor Euangelistarum obseruandus candor, codiscipuli sui lapsum ore uno fuse describentium, cuius etiam poenitentiam, & ingenuitatem minime reticuerunt, qui tantum etiam abfuit vt gloriæ suæ studem- ret,vt contrà non modò non quæsierit culpam suam silentio tegi,sed etiam,si verum est quod veteres quidam monumentis traditum reli- querunt, Euangelium secundum Marcum à Petro dictatum, ille ipse testis esse ad vsque mundi consummationē voluerit,ad Dei sum-mam gloriam, ad exemplū Mosis & Aaronis, Num.20.12.& 27.14.&Dauidis ipsius,cuius est Psalmus quinquagesimus primus,pœnitentiæ luculentum testimonium. Vtinam verò Dominus,hanc mentem tum Pastoribus tum Magistratibus donet, ne sint ποιμένες:& nobis omnibus Christianismum profitentibus, talem ac tam sinceram peccatorum nostrorum detestationem, coram Deo & hominibus,quum ita res feret,largiatur.
units.tr: Finally, here we must note the candour of the four Evangelists, who with one voice describe in detail the fall of their fellow disciple, and did not at all pass over his repentance and frankness. He was so far from seeking his own glory that, on the contrary, he not only did not wish his fault to be hidden in silence, but, if it is true, as certain ancient writers have handed down, that the Gospel according to Mark was dictated by Peter, he himself wished to be a witness of it until the end of the world, for the highest glory of God, after the example of Moses and Aaron (Num. 20.12 and 27.14), and of David himself, whose Psalm is the fifty-first, a clear testimony of repentance. Would that the Lord grant this disposition both to the ministers and to the magistrates, that they may not be shepherds [ποιμένες]; and grant to all of us who profess Christianity such a sincere detestation of our sins, before God and men, as the case may require.

units.la: Iam ad Petri lapsum accedamus:ac primùm obseruemus qua via tam grauiter lapsus sit: deinde qualis sit eius lapsus, ne minorem eum maioremque quàm par sit faciamus:ac tan- dem quale fuerit remedium & vnde prose- ctum inspiciamus.In quo multa sunt quæ nos alieno periculo discamus. Ac primū animad-uertite quanta sit etiam sapientissimorum sæ-citas,nisi sibi diligenter caueat, & alios quàm seipsos Duces sequantur,quum etiam pulchrè aliquid facere, & quidem optimo nixi funda-mento, sed malè aptato, cogitantes, in maxi-ma errata præcipites ferantur: atque adeò la-psi, quod longè deterius est,ex Scylla in Cha-rybdin ruant, nisi alia quàm sua sapientia regantur. Ecquid enim, obsecro, laudabilius quàm amicum in re incerta non deserere, cui præsertim plurimum debeas? Quem si iuuare non possis, saltem oculis sequaris, & tua præsentia memoria non excidisse eius beneficia referis? Etquidem talis fuit Petri zelus, qui quum reipsa & verbis agnouisset Domino displicuisse, quod in eius gratiam fecerat, quid minus præstare potuit, quàm promisi sui memoriam eum non omnino cum reliquis deserere? Quinetiam eminus tătum eum secutus magis ad offensam cauendam, quàm ex timiditate videtur. Iter enim cœptum persequens, nondum timore se superatum fuisse testatur.
units.tr: Now let us come to Peter's fall. First, let us observe by what way he fell so grievously; then, what sort of fall it was, so that we do not make it smaller or greater than it is; and finally, what the remedy was and whence it came, let us examine. In this there are many things from which we may learn from another's danger. And first, notice how great is the blindness even of the wisest, unless they take careful heed to themselves and follow leaders other than themselves, since, while thinking to do something fine, and indeed relying on an excellent foundation but fitting it badly, they are carried headlong into the greatest errors; and so, fallen, they rush (which is far worse) from Scylla into Charybdis, unless they are guided by something other than their own wisdom. For what, I ask, is more praiseworthy than not to desert a friend in an uncertain matter, especially one to whom you owe very much? If you cannot help him, at least do you not follow him with your eyes, and show by your presence that his kindnesses have not slipped from your memory? Such indeed was Peter's zeal: when he had recognised by both deed and word that what he had done for their sake had displeased the Lord, what could he do less than, as he had promised, not wholly desert with the rest those whose memory he held? Moreover, in following him only from a distance, he seems to do so more to avoid giving offence than out of timidity. For in pursuing the journey he had begun, he testifies that he had not yet been overcome by fear.

units.la: Verumenimuero, nullus hic excusationi locus est: Dominus enim cuius Petrum verbis itare par fuit, quis esset futurus euentus si se in periculum istud iniiceret satis præmonuerat. Deinde quos erat Dominus loquutus sermones, manus in eum hostibus iniicientibus, Si me quæritis, istos dimittite: & tam miraculose repressus furiosorum istorum furor, annon satis cum quid facto esset opus admonebant? Hinc igitur discamus, quod iam ante fusius explicauì, & hic iterum repeto, in omnibus consiliis, prius interrogandum os Domini, quàm manus ad opus admouendas.
units.tr: Yet there is no room here for excuse. For the Lord, whose words Peter ought to have heeded, had already warned sufficiently what the outcome would be if he exposed himself to that danger. Then, what words the Lord had spoken when the enemies laid hands on him, "If you seek me, let these go" (John 18.8), and how the raging fury of those men was so miraculously restrained, did not these things sufficiently warn what needed to be done? Let us therefore learn from this what I have already explained more fully before, and repeat here again: in all counsels, the mouth of the Lord must be asked before the hands are set to the work. Above all we must consider whether what we undertake or leave undone agrees with the will of God or not. For if the Lord has forbidden it, there is no room left for deliberation, but we must abstain from it altogether.

units.la: Videndum igitur ante omnia an quæ suscipimus aggredienda vel relinquenda Dei voluntati congruant, necne. Nam si Dominus interdixit, nullus superest deliberationi locus, sed prorsus ab iis est abstinendum.
units.tr: First of all, then, we must see whether the things we undertake or leave undone agree with the will of God or not. For if the Lord has forbidden them, there is no room left for deliberation, and we must altogether abstain from them.

units.la: Nec propterea tamen, rem alioqui per se concessam, statim aggredi fas est. Variae sunt enim ac distinctae singulorum vocationes. Quamobrem istud adiiciendum ad superiora, sedulo nimirum inquirendum, & sine perturbatione, ex vocatione sit, necne quod aggredimur: nam in recenti memoria semper est habenda Paulina illa sententia, Ut vnumquemque vocauit Dominus, ita incedat. 1.Cor.7.17. non quod Dominus extraordinariis motibus agere non possit, sed quod illi valde suspecti sint & periculosi: vel ipso teste Domino, suos discipulos temere factum Eliae imitantes, acriter corripiente.Luc.9.55.
units.tr: Yet even a thing otherwise permitted in itself must not be undertaken at once. For the callings of individuals are various and distinct. Therefore this must be added to what has been said: we must carefully inquire, and without agitation, whether what we are undertaking comes from our calling or not. For we must always keep in mind that saying of Paul: "As the Lord has called each one, so let him walk" (1 Cor. 7:17). This is not because the Lord cannot act through extraordinary impulses, but because such impulses are very suspect and dangerous, as the Lord himself bears witness when he sharply rebuked his disciples for rashly imitating Elijah (Luke 9:55).

units.la: Sed aliquid adhuc superioribus adiiciendum. Non enim quicquid licet, & vocationi conuenit, etiam semper expedit: quamobrem tertium quiddam superiorum omnium difficillimum accedat oportet. Primum enim illud satis ex Lege Dei perspicuum est: alterum vero non ita difficile, intra suae vocationis terminos se continere, modo absit ambitio, vel immoderatus periculorum metus, vel quaeuis alia denique mentis perturbatio. Tertium difficilius, non cuiuis ore suo Domino peculiariter, quid agendum fugiendumve sit reuelante, quod saepius tamen Patribus contigisse legimus in sacris historiis, & speciatim admonitum a Domino Petrum videmus. Optimum vero aduersus haec incommoda remedium, feriae preces: minime quidem quibus noua nobis in aure oracula dari postulemus, sed serio conscientiam excutiamus, an ab omni vitioso fit asse-ctu, fiue in aggrediendo, fiue in fugiendo ne-gotio quopiam aliena, licet per fe licito, vocationíque nostræ non repugnanti. Denique co-fulendi qui nos consiliis suis iuuare possunt. Infigne in Apostolo nobis proponitur huius rei exemplum, qui pro excellenti zelo, quem acceperat à Domino, prodituru in medium fcditioforum Ephefinorum, à fratribus ne fa-ceret rogatus, abstinuit: idem in illa vltima Hierosolymam profectione facturus, nisi monitis contrariis Sancti Spiritus ductus fuisset, vt testatur Act.20.22.& 21.13. Hac igitur ratione medio fempe ribimus tutissimi, nihil temere suscipientes, nihil etiam ignaue refugientes, quum maledicat Dominus ageti fuu opus fraude Ier.48.10. & vicissim dicente sapiente, Quærentem periculum in illud incidere:quod ipsum etiam Dominus in parabola turrim ædificantis non supputatis prius sumptibus, docet. Quibus ita politis, facile colligitur Petrü quòd ad prius illud attinet in genere consideratum à culpa fuisse prorsus immunem, iubente Domino, vt proximo feratur auxilium, & discipulus magistrum adiuuet, dum parentes coli iubet. Ac proinde nec in altero peccasse, vt prius gladio temere abusus fecerat. At in tertio grauiter impegit, duplici ratione: prima, quòd melius sibi notas suas vires quàm Domino existimauit: altera, quòd moneti Domino non est obfequutus, & quidem non simpliciter vlterius progredi prohibeti, sed etiam propropter iam factum graviter eum increpanti. En quibus tanquam gradibus tam graviter lapsus Apostolus, exemplo nobis esse debet, ut cautius incedere discamus.
units.tr: But something must still be added to what has gone before. For not everything that is permitted and fits one's calling is always also expedient; therefore a third consideration, the most difficult of all those above, must be added. The first is clear enough from the Law of God. The second is not so difficult: to keep oneself within the bounds of one's calling, provided there is no ambition, no excessive fear of dangers, and no other disturbance of mind whatever. The third is more difficult: that the Lord, with his own mouth, reveals to someone in particular what is to be done or avoided. Yet we read that this happened to the Fathers fairly often in the sacred histories, and we see the Lord specifically admonishing Peter. The best remedy against these inconveniences is daily prayer: not that we should demand new oracles be given to us, but that we should seriously examine our conscience, whether it is free from every vicious affection, whether in undertaking or in avoiding some business foreign to us, though lawful in itself and not opposed to our calling. Finally, we should seek the counsel of those who can help us. A notable example of this is set before us in the Apostle, who, though he had received from the Lord a great zeal to appear in the midst of the Ephesian sedition, abstained when the brethren asked him not to do so. He would have done the same on his last journey to Jerusalem, had he not been led by contrary warnings of the Holy Spirit, as Acts 20:22 and 21:13 testify. By this method, then, we shall always walk the safest middle way, undertaking nothing rashly and refusing nothing sluggishly. The Lord curses the one who does his work deceitfully (Jer. 48:10), and conversely the wise man says that he who seeks danger falls into it, which the Lord himself also teaches in the parable of the man building a tower who did not first count the cost. With these things settled, it is easily gathered that Peter, as far as the first point is concerned, considered in general, was wholly free from fault, since the Lord commands that aid be brought to a neighbour, that a disciple should help his master, and that parents be honoured. Therefore he did not sin in the second point either, when he had rashly abused the sword as before. But in the third he fell grievously, for two reasons: first, because he thought more highly of his own powers than of the Lord's; second, because he did not obey the Lord's warning, and indeed was not merely forbidden to go further, but was also sharply rebuked by the Lord for what he had already done. These are the steps by which the Apostle fell so gravely; he ought to be an example to us, so that we learn to walk more cautiously.

units.la: Cæterum si culpam Petri, vel ex eius qui offensus est qualitate metiaris, Filij nimirum æterni Dei, quem ipse Petrus probè cognitum profes-sus erat, vel ex eius qui offendit persona (qui unus ex dilectissimorum discipulorum est numero) sane non poterit non esse maxima: quam quidem licet minorem, mortalem tamen & inferis dignam fuisse fatendum est, quum ea peccatorum omnium, etiam leuissimorum natura sit. Rom. 6. vers. 23.
units.tr: But if we measure Peter's fault by the quality of the one offended, namely the eternal Son of God, whom Peter himself had openly acknowledged, or by the person who offended, one of the most beloved of the disciples, it certainly cannot fail to be very great. Although it was the lesser kind, it must be confessed that it was still mortal and worthy of hell, since such is the nature of all sins, even the slightest (Rom. 6:23).

units.la: At quum minime propterea sint æqualia peccata, & illud si cum gravioribus comparetur, dicturi sumus (licet non ignoranter à Petro admissum, ut contrà Paulus Christum persequens ignorabat) non tamen à praua conscientia profectum, qualis fuit Caiaphæ Iudæque cóscientia, nec de industria aduersus Magistrum peccasse Petrum: cuius etiam penitus extinctam fuisse fidem absit dicamus. Sustinuit enim eum ipse ut erat pollicitus Dominus, Luc. 22. vers. 32. & longè aliud est mentiendo negare sibi cognitam Christi personam, eiúsque se discipulum abnegare, quàm falsi doctrinam eius condemnare. Aio etiam amplius aliquid, Petri erga Christum amorem in corde ipsius immutatum, permansisse, nulloque modo imminutum, sed tamen infirmitate & metu mortis intus cohibitum ac repressum, aliud nimirum reuera Petro Dominum ore quidem abnegante, sed aliud corde sentiente. At multa factum istud mirum in modum grauant: puta in primis stulta & confidens nimium de suis viribus opinio, qua memoria illi tam expressa Domini admonitio penitus est excussa, & ratio consiliumque depravatum, quum cum oportuerit clausis sibi Maximi Pontificis foribus diuina factum agnoscere prouidentia, aditum denegante, monenteque ne se in periculum daret.
units.tr: But since sins are by no means equal, and if this one is compared with graver ones, we shall say (though it was committed by Peter not in ignorance, as Paul ignorantly persecuted Christ) that it did not proceed from an evil conscience, as the conscience of Caiaphas and the Jews did, nor that Peter sinned deliberately against his Master. God forbid that we should say his faith was utterly extinguished, for the Lord sustained him, as he had promised (Luke 22:32). It is far different to deny by lying that one knows Christ's person and to disown oneself as his disciple, than to condemn his doctrine as false. I say something more: Peter's love for Christ, though it was changed in his heart, remained and was in no way diminished, but was nevertheless restrained and suppressed inwardly by weakness and fear of death. Thus Peter, denying the Lord with his mouth, really felt something else in his heart. Yet many things make this deed grievous in a remarkable way: above all, a foolish and overconfident opinion of his own powers, by which the clear warning of the Lord was entirely driven from his memory, and his reasoning and counsel were corrupted. For when he ought to have recognised divine providence in the doors of the High Priest's house being closed to him, refusing him entrance and warning him not to put himself in danger...

units.la: Deinde, quantæ fuit, obsecro, arrogantiæ, iam satis animaduersa infirmitate, vt qui ad vocem vnius ancillulæ territus fuisset, pergere nihilominus, & ad primum galli cantum aures obturare, imò etiam peierare? Et quidem quum inter secundam & tertiam abnegationem horæ spatiū, vt ait Lucas, lapsum esset, quid causæ fuit cur tantum illi de se spatium cogitandi dante Domino, nihilominus sese magis magisque præcipitem dederit, adeo vt contra conscientiæ testimonium sese diris deuoueret? Quàm multa igitur sese inuicem hic peccata mutuo nexu consequuntur. Et quis dubitat quin nisi iterato Galli cantu fuisset à Domino excitatus, & quidem nisi Dominus eius misertus iniectis in eum oculis esset in eius corde operatus, miser sese præcipitem in exitium daret? In hoc igitur viro quisque se contemplator omnis de se suisque viribus opinio abesto: dies noctésque, immo singulis momentis ne in tentationis barathrum immergatur preces funfundito : denique ne pedem moueamus, quin sciamus, quantum sciri potest ac debet, Dominum à dextris nostris esse: & fortissimos etiam quosque ad folij susurrum trepidare ac deiici Domino minimè fretos, experientia docti teneamus. Præterea & istud attendamus, semel extra recti itineris carceres pedem mouentes, iam nimium deuios aberrasse: nullúmque tam abominandum esse peccatum, in quod in peius ruentes, non præcipitesferamur. In maximis autem nostris infirmitatibus precibus à Domino contendamus, vt saltem sacrosanctū cius Nomen magno sit semper apud nos in pretio, ne ad offensam proximi, sacrosancti diuini Nominis etiam accedat pollutio, veluti Petrum hic videmus ad Magistri sui abnegationem etiam iuramentum & diras addidisse: quod nimium sæpe, proh dolor! in violentis illis quibus agimur perturbationibus solet contingere.
units.tr: Then, I ask, what great arrogance it was, when he had already been sufficiently warned of his weakness, that he who had been terrified by the voice of one little maidservant nevertheless went on, and, at the first crowing of the cock, stopped his ears, or even swore! And indeed, since, as Luke says, an interval of an hour had passed between the second and third denial, what reason was there that, although the Lord gave him so much time to think about himself, he nevertheless hurled himself more and more headlong, so that he cursed himself against the testimony of his conscience? How many sins, then, follow one another here in a mutual chain! And who doubts that, unless he had been roused by the cock crowing a second time, and unless the Lord, having pity on him, had worked in his heart by casting his eyes upon him, the wretched man would have thrown himself headlong to destruction? In this man, therefore, let every observer put away every opinion about himself and his own powers. Day and night, indeed at every moment, let us pour out prayers that we not be plunged into the abyss of temptation. Finally, let us not move a foot without knowing, as far as it can and should be known, that the Lord is at our right hand. Let us hold, taught by experience, that even the bravest tremble and are cast down at the rustle of a leaf when they do not rely on the Lord. Moreover, let us consider this: once we have moved a foot out of the starting-gates of the right path, we have already wandered far astray, and there is no sin so abominable that we, rushing into worse, are not carried headlong into it. In our greatest weaknesses, however, let us entreat the Lord that at least his most holy Name may always be held in great value among us, lest the offence against our neighbour be joined also with the pollution of the most holy divine Name. Here we see Peter adding even an oath and curses to his denial of his Master, which, alas, very often happens in those violent disturbances by which we are driven.

units.la: Sed antequam ad Petri pœnitentiam accedamus, non leuiter prætercundum quod à D. Iohanne animaduersum est, nimirum Petrum in ædes Caiaphæ nō admissum prius ab ostiaria, tandem gratia discipuli cuiusdam in ædibus Caiaphæ noti, cuius tamen hic nomen reticetur, introductū : siue is esset dilectus discipulus, cuius deinceps meminit historia, siue alius aliquis discipulus extra numerum duodecim, nec magnopere laborandum, nec quis esset iste discipulus, nec vnde illa apud Caiaphum notitia. Minimè, inquam, istud leuiter prætereundum. Præterquàm quod enim oc- clusum ostium Pertum admonere debuit quò præceps incautus ferretur: hoc exemplo nobis insignis Satanæ fraus & astutia detegitur, sæpe nobis ipsis abutentis nostráque temeritate, vt dum iuuare studemus amicos, perditionis ipsorum instrumenta fiamus. Ac si dilectum esse discipulum Sanctum Iohannem arbitra- mur, quum fieri non posse videatur, quin Pe- trum à Domino præmonitum audiuerit, vix à culpa liberabimus cum quin graui potius re- prehensione dignum dicamus, quòd discipu- lum à cœpto dimouere potius quum debuis- set, autor illi tamen fuisse videatur. Denique quum vera amicitia, sine qua mundum consi- stere non posse, prophani ipsi iudicarunt, quàmque tantopere suis Dominus commen- dat, vehementissimus sit affectus, petendum est à Domino precibus assiduis, vt ea bene vtendi rationes suppeditet. Qua in re duo potissimum occurrunt obseruatione digna capita, quibus neglectis maximi sequatur errores necesse est. Primù vt ad Dei dilectione, tanquà ad amui- sim, hominù amicitia examinetur, sic vt nùquà amicos vel iuuemus ipsi, vel eorum auxilium ad malum imploremus. Nec enim istud esset amicitiæ sacrosancto nomine, sed coniuratio- nis potius nuncupandum. Deinde, si Deum amare simul & alteri placere non possumus, amorem Dei præire necesse est sine exceptio- ne, vel ipso Domino disertis illud verbis sic at- testante, Matth. 10. 37. & Luc. 14. 26. & exemplo præpræeunte. Matt.12.48. & Luc.2.49. etiamsi adversus cognatos ipsos & amicos esset ad Leuitarum exemplum progrediendum. Exod.32. 28. & 29. quam etiam ob causam summis laudibus exornantur & compensationem accipiunt. Deut.33.9. & 10. Alterum est, ut in promouendis aut commendandis amicis sanctam à Domino prudentiam & iudicium, quo nostri regantur affectus exposcamus: quum sæpe nimium vsuueniat hunc affectum præsertim inter cognatos & necessarios tantam mentibus caliginem offundere, ut nulla dignitatis ipsorum, aut industriæ ad quæsitum illis officium implendum ratio habeatur: quod summo cum Reipublicæ detrimento coniunctum esse tum eorum qui sic promoti sunt pernicie frequenti nimium exemplorum experientia compertum est. Et in his quidem non vltimum locum Petrus obtinuisset, nisi Dominus esset eius, pro sua singulari clementia, misertus.
units.tr: But before we come to Peter's repentance, what John has observed must not be passed over lightly. Peter, not admitted into the High Priest's house at first by the doorkeeper, was at last brought in through the favour of another disciple known in Caiaphas' house, whose name is here passed over in silence. Whether he was the beloved disciple whom the history mentions later, or some other disciple beyond the number of the twelve, we need not labour greatly over, nor over who this disciple was or how he came to be known to Caiaphas. Certainly, I say, this must not be passed over lightly. Besides, the closed door ought to have warned Peter where he was being carried, heedless and headlong; and by this example the notable fraud and cunning of Satan is revealed, who often abuses us ourselves, so that, by our rashness, while we are eager to help friends, we become instruments of their ruin. If we think John was the beloved disciple, since it seems impossible that he did not hear Peter forewarned by the Lord, we shall scarcely free him from fault. Indeed we must say he deserves a grave reprehension, because, when he ought rather to have turned the disciple away from his undertaking, he nevertheless seems to have been its author for him. Finally, since true friendship, without which the world cannot stand, has been so judged even by profane men, and since the Lord commends it so greatly, its very vehement affection must be sought from the Lord by constant prayer, that he may supply the reasons for using it well. Two chief points present themselves in this matter, worthy of observation, and neglect of them must necessarily lead to very great errors. First, the friendship of men must be tested by the love of God, as by a touchstone, so that we never either help friends ourselves or implore their aid for evil. For that would not be friendship, to be called by the sacred name, but should rather be named a conspiracy. Next, if we cannot love God and at the same time please another, the love of God must take precedence without exception. The Lord himself attests this in plain words (Matt. 10:37; Luke 14:26), and sets the example (Matt. 12:48; Luke 2:49), even if one has to proceed against kinsfolk and friends after the example of the Levites (Exod. 32:28-29), for which reason they are also adorned with the highest praises and receive a reward (Deut. 33:9-10). The other point is that in advancing or recommending friends we seek from the Lord holy prudence and judgement, by which our affections may be governed. For it very often happens that this affection, especially among kinsfolk and relatives, casts such darkness over minds that no account is taken of their dignity or of their diligence in fulfilling the office sought for them. Frequent experience of examples has shown that this is joined with the greatest harm to the commonwealth and with the ruin of those so promoted. And in these matters Peter would not have held the last place, had not the Lord, in his singular clemency, been merciful to him.

units.la: Supersunt quæ de iterato, ut nominatim Marcus expressit, Galli cantu dicuntur exponenda: quod ut altius repetamus, aio duplicem hic nobis bonarum rerum à Deo in hominis gratiam conditarum visum proponi considerandum: quorum prior & nobis proximus ut iis ad hanc vitam tolerandam vtamur, verbo Dei nobis cum gratiarum actione sanctificatis 1.Tim.4.3. alter est & quidem priore longe excellentior, vt totidem nobis sint immensæ Dei gloriæ præcones Psalm.19.1. & 145.10. to-
units.tr: What remains to be explained is what is said about the second crowing, which Mark expressly calls the crowing of the cock. To go back a little further: I say that two kinds of good things, created by God for the benefit of man, are set before us here for consideration. The first and nearer kind is to be used to sustain this life, having been sanctified to us by the word of God and by thanksgiving (1 Tim. 4.3). The second is far more excellent than the first, since they are for us so many heralds of the immense glory of God (Ps. 19.1; 145.10).

units.la: A. j.
units.tr: A. j.

units.la: tidémque specula in quibus infinitam fapien-tiam,potentiam,& bonitatem Creatoris con-templemur. Rom.1.20. Act. 17.27.& duobus quidem iltud modis, primùm puta in generali illa & vniuersali rerum omnium creatarum consideratione:deinde speciali quodam refpe-ctu, quo Dominus iis ad verbum suum obfi-gnandum abutitur : seu respiciat illud morta-les omnes vt voluit Dominus Iridem, quæres est naturalis, clfe signum illius promissionis mundum vniuersum cataclysmo nunquam perituram,Genef.9.12.quo pertinent etiam om-nes figuræ,& Sacramenta omnia,tum vete-ris fœderis, quod implctum deliit, tum Noui, quod durat & duraturum est in finem seculo-rum : seu priuatos respexerit, vt plena est Scri-ptura signorum quibus Deus sanctorum visio-nes confirmauit. Sic Galli cantus huic vsui fuit destinatus,Petri nimirum,sopitæ quasi ve-terno quodam, longe periculosiore quàm ille fuit somnus cuius est à Domino in horto re-prehensus,excitandæ conscientiæ. Qua etiam in re nota est inter signum & rem significatam analogia, quum hæc auis fit dici prænuntia. Quin Petrus igitur mature fit præmonitus, & quidem quacunque fieri ratione potuit, per Dominum non ltetit, vt tantò fit grauius & & minus excusandum Petri peccatum. At vt merito Petrum hac in re condemnamus, ita velim vt nos in hoc speculo contemplemur, qui fanc futuri fumus,præsertim hoc seculo in quod incidimus, Petro longè magis adhuc nocennocentiores.Nunquid enim ab hinc annis citer septuaginta, non aues quid suus notet cantus ignarae, non etiam ferrei aeneive Galli, quales in campanilibus ac templorum summitatibus conspiciuntur miserorum illorum superstitiosorum,quorum diutur nus est futuras somnus, si suorum Gallorum cantum expectent,sed insignes viri sunt excitati? At quales viri obsecro, quales, inquam, quantique Dei servi, qui nullum docendi, monendi, arguendi,exhortandi,vociferandi. tum ore,tum pretiosissimis scriptis, ad expergefaciendos etiam maxime consopitos, finem fecerunt? At quàm multi eos audiuerunt & serio sunt ad eorum vocem experrecti? Quàm multi etiam eorum qui semel experrecti fuerant, iterum obdormierunt? Sed retrolapsa relinquamus, age, quot hodie serio lucem iltam sic amplectantur, ut à mundi tenebris non consopiantur? Quandiu vero tandem lethargus ille durraturus est? Quando tandem nos lucis filios, non autem noctis nec tenebrarum esse testabimur? Quando tandem sobrii erimus, induti thorace fidei & charitatis, & pro galea, (spe salutis: ut monet Apostolus. 1. Thess. 5 4. An expectamus dum nox incautos deprehendat? Ioh. 9. 4. aut sit hostium occlusum? Matth. 7.22. & 25.10. At si suavis illa verbi Dei & pacis ac tranquillitatis harmonia, pro laetitia & sanctis vigiliis quibus totos nos incumbere par erat, somnum potius ac veternum maxima nostra culpa, induxit, annon clangore tubarum peritrepente,
units.tr: And mirrors in which we may contemplate the infinite wisdom, power and goodness of the Creator (Rom. 1.20; Acts 17.27). This may be done in two ways: first, in that general and universal consideration of all created things; and then in a more particular respect, in which the Lord makes use of them to seal his word. Whether He looks upon them as they concern all mortals, as He willed with the rainbow, which is by nature a sign of his promise that the whole world will never again perish by a flood (Gen. 9.12), a promise to which all figures and sacraments pertain, both of the old covenant, which has been abolished, and of the new, which endures and will endure to the end of the ages; or whether He regards them as they concern private persons, as Scripture is full of signs by which God confirmed the visions of his saints. So the crowing of the cock was appointed for this purpose, for Peter, as if lulled by a certain lethargy, far more dangerous than that sleep for which he was rebuked by the Lord in the garden, to rouse his conscience. In this matter too there is a notable analogy between the sign and the thing signified, since this bird is said to be a forerunner of the day. Peter, then, was warned in good time, and the Lord, by whatever means possible, did not cease to warn him, so that Peter's sin might be all the graver and less excusable. But just as we rightly condemn Peter in this matter, so I would have us look at ourselves in this mirror, for we are much more guilty than Peter, especially in this age into which we have fallen. For has it not been about seventy years since not birds, ignorant of what their song signifies, nor iron or bronze cocks such as are seen on bell towers and the tops of churches, but distinguished men were roused, whose long sleep would be prolonged if they awaited the crowing of their own cocks? But what men, I beg you, what men, I say, and how great servants of God, who have ceased to teach, admonish, rebuke, exhort and cry out, both by voice and by their most precious writings, even to rouse those who are most deeply lulled? But how many have heard them and have been seriously roused by their voice? How many of those who were once roused have fallen asleep again? But let us leave aside what has slipped back. Come, how many today seriously embrace that light in such a way as not to be lulled to sleep by the darkness of the world? How long, moreover, will that lethargy last? When at last shall we bear witness that we are sons of the light, and not of the night or of darkness? When at last shall we be sober, clad in the breastplate of faith and love, and with the hope of salvation for a helmet, as the Apostle warns (1 Thess. 5.4)? Are we waiting until the night overtakes us unaware (John 9.4), or until the door is shut against us (Matt. 7.22; 25.10)? But if that sweet harmony of God's Word, of peace and tranquillity, which ought to have kept us wholly intent upon joy and holy watchfulness, has instead, through our very great fault, brought on sleep and lethargy, will we not at last be roused and awake, when the clangour of trumpets strikes our ears, and, as it were, the thunder of drums, God having impelled us to this by our sins, and will we not then imitate Peter, whom, alas, we have followed too much in his lethargy, now that he has been roused? But you, O God, grant us this grace. For it is time, brethren, if ever, to think seriously about these things. Amen.

units.la: A. ij. & tympanorum vt ita dicam tonitru, nostras aures feriente, Deo nostris peccatis ad id impulso, excitati tandem euigilabimus, Petrum quem in ipsius veterno, nimium proh dolor! sequuti sumus, excitatum deinceps imitaturi? Tu vero Deus nobis hanc gratiam largire: tempus enim est, fratres, de istis, si alias vnquam serio cogitandi. Amen.
units.tr: and the thunder of drums, as it were, striking our ears, God having driven us to this by our sins, shall we at last awake, and imitate Peter, whom, alas, we have too far followed in his slumber, now that he has been roused? But you, O God, grant us this grace. For it is time, brethren, if ever it was, to think seriously about these things. Amen.

units.tr: 75. And Peter remembered the words of Jesus, who had said to him, Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times. And he went out and wept bitterly.

units.tr: 72. Then the cock crowed a second time, and Peter remembered the word that Jesus had said to him, Before the cock crows twice, you will deny me three times. And when he had rushed out, he wept.

units.tr: 61. Then the Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said to him just now, Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.

units.tr: 62. And Peter went out and wept bitterly.

units.la: VERA & proprie dicta Resipiscentia, gratuitaque peccatorum Remissio indiuiduo lesce inuice nexu, reste ipso Domino, Luc. 24.47. & alibi, quum consequatur, etiam illas probe nosse & ad vsum reuocare, mortem effugituros, & contra vitam aeternam fruituros par est. Non mirum igitur si Satan vtramque pro viribus adulterare conatus est. Aio vero conatum Satanam pro viribus, quod duo quaedam natura sic hominibus inhaerent, vt nunquam penitus eradicentur, ne iniis quidem qui sibi libenter persuaserint, nullum paradisum, nullosque inferos, quos tamen velint nolint perpetuo secum circumferunt.
units.tr: True and properly so-called repentance [resipiscentia] and the free forgiveness of sins are joined together by an indissoluble bond, as the Lord himself says (Luke 24:47) and elsewhere. Since the one follows the other, those who know both well and put them to use ought to escape death and enjoy eternal life. It is no wonder, then, that Satan has tried with all his strength to corrupt both. I say that Satan has tried with all his strength, because two things cling so naturally to human beings that they are never wholly uprooted, not even in those who have happily persuaded themselves that there is no paradise and no hell; yet whether they like it or not, they carry these two things with them always.

units.la: Omnis igitur religio nititur hoc fundamento, quod peccatum sequitur sensus quidam & apprehensio diuinitatis, cuius sit gratia concilicanda, cum proposito non in delicto persequerandi: Inhaesit, inquam, & inhaerebit istud in prophanissimorum hominum mentibus, quae tamen mali conscientia grauissimum omnibus vulnus infert, cuius anando remedium quaerere coguntur. At Dei vnius proprium est sancto suo Spiritu, in verbo suo nos illud edocere, non immerito Dei Ecclesia sibi hanc cognitionem vt proprium thesaurum vindicantt, verbis istis suauissimis innitente Seruatoris vnici nostri. Matth.11.29. Venite ad me omnes qui fatigati estis & onerati, & animabus vestris requiem inuenietis. Hæc doctrina nobis hic in duobus insignibus præ aliis omnibus exemplis consideranda proponitur, ex quorum altero veram ad salutem Resipiscen-tiam discamus: in altero vero falsam Pœni-tentiam quæ ad mortem via est intueamur. Hæc vero pro virili nostra conabimur di-lucide explicare, vt ab iis quas in Ecclesiam inuexit Satan corruptelis, miserarum animarum dispendio, veritatem discerna-mus.
units.tr: All religion therefore rests on this foundation: that sin is followed by a certain sense and apprehension of the divine, whose favour must be won, with the purpose of not persisting in the offence. This, I say, has stuck and will stick in the minds of the most profane men, and the evil conscience inflicts the gravest wound on everyone, for which they are compelled to seek a remedy. But it is the proper work of the one God, by his Holy Spirit, to teach us this in his Word. The Church of God rightly claims this knowledge as its own peculiar treasure, relying on the most sweet words of our only Saviour: "Come to me, all you who are weary and heavy laden, and you will find rest for your souls" (Matt. 11:29). This doctrine is set before us here to be considered in two outstanding examples above all others. From the one we learn true repentance unto salvation; in the other we look at false penitence, which is the way to death. We shall try, as far as we can, to explain these things clearly, so that we may distinguish the truth from the corruptions which Satan has introduced into the Church, to the loss of wretched souls.

units.la: Primum igitur ne verborum homony-mia decipiamur, distinguenda illa sunt: occurrunt autem ista Pœnitentia & Resipiscen-tia, quorum, etsi videtur, non vna tamen ea-demque est significatio. Ac Pœnitentiæ qui-dem duplex acceptio. Vulgo enim Pœniten-tia dicitur pœna quam sibi aliquis irrogat, vel eidem ab alio imponitur ob aliquod deli-ctum, vnde illa Pœnitentiam faciendi phrasis, & illæ quibus veteres vsi sunt Theologi vo-ces, Pœnitentis, Pœnitentiarij, Pœnitentiæ. Alias Pœnitentia generaliter sumitur pro vo-luntatis mutatione, qua quod factum est, siue bonum, siue malum, esse infectum cupimus: ac proinde generale nimium est ad id distin-ctè intelligendum quod tantopere nobis commendatur, & via est ad Remissionem pec-catorum ac proinde salutem obtinenda m, & ea Resipiscentia nominatur, longéque vlte-rius progreditur, & idem est atque ex imprudente redire ad meliorem mentem,& ab errore in rectam viam regredi: vt pœnam hic affectus non tantùm respiciat, sed malum ipsum oderit & damnet,eò quòd malum est, ac proinde totam hominis in melius immutatione adferat.Pœnitentiam igitur Iudæ suique similibus relinquamus:in Petro veram Refipiscen tiam consideraturi,Euangeliltarum etiam hac in re vestigia sequuti,qui duabus diuersis Græcis vocibus μεταμέλειας & μετάνοιας vsi sunt.
units.tr: First, then, so that we are not deceived by the ambiguity of words, these things must be distinguished. The terms penitence [pœnitentia] and repentance [resipiscentia] occur, and although they seem to be the same, they do not have one and the same meaning. Penitence has a twofold sense. Commonly, penitence means the punishment that someone inflicts on himself, or that is imposed on him by another, for some offence; hence the phrase "to do penance," and the words the old theologians used: penitent, penitentiary, penance. Otherwise, penitence is taken generally for a change of will, by which we wish that what has been done, whether good or evil, be undone. This general notion is therefore too broad for us to understand distinctly that which is so strongly commended to us, which is the way to obtain forgiveness of sins and so salvation.
