Sic vitulum aureum Dominus non modò conteri & cremari, sed puluerem etiam eius in aquas abiici, Exod.32.20. Cananæorúmque lucos & altaria passim vastari penitúsque aboleri voluit. Nec vero inficior in bonos vsus conuerti posse quę olim malis inseruierunt: sed magnam tamen eorum habendam rationem aio, modísque omnibus quibus Deus maledixit detestanda.
units.tr: The Evangelist adds that Judas threw the silver into the temple, though the priests would not receive it. From this we must learn (though our mind ought to be other than Judas's) how far evil is to be detested: namely, that one should not only abstain from evil, or only have sorrow of mind follow the evil committed, but that ill-gotten things should be cast away so that they are not even lightly touched, even if they are ill-gotten gains. Iud. 23. Under the Law of old, whatever had been touched by the polluted was itself polluted. And the Lord himself commanded not only that the harlot be kept far from his temple, but abhorred even the harlot's wages, Hag. 2. 14; Deut. 23. 18. Hence let us hear David too protesting that he holds it a religious offence even to utter the names of false gods, Ps. 16. 4. So the Lord willed the golden calf not only to be crushed and burned, but its dust to be cast into the waters, Exod. 32. 20, and the groves and altars of the Canaanites to be laid waste everywhere and utterly abolished. Nor do I deny that things which once served evil can be turned to good uses; but I say that their value must be carefully considered, and that they must be detested in every way in which God has cursed them.

units.la: Euge vero, quàm ampla mihi pluribus hac doctrinam vrgendi præbetur, quòd sine ingeti dolore non possum, occasio: quum passim tum viros tum mulieres etiam extra vrbis portas obuiam prædatoribus euntes videas,à quibus prædam male partam quæstui inhiantes vili pretio redimant, rem, dico, scelcratissimam, quam suo tandem periculo lucrosa-ne fit sanè iunt experturi. Hoc quoque plerisque rem suam ex dococtorum ac nepotum profusione quos venantur facientibus:& vobis etiam furtorum receptoribus receptricibúsq; qui nulla conscientia scientes prudentes, vel ablata furto, vel pessima conscientia vænum exposita, redimitis, dictum esto: vos, vos,in-quam,omnes his artibus quaestuum facientes ad profligatum istum Iudam, vestrum olim, si perres exeritis futurum tempore & loco iudicem ablego.
units.tr: Well then, how wide an opening this occasion gives me to press this teaching at greater length, which I cannot do without great grief! For everywhere you may see men and women, even outside the city gates, going out to meet the plunderers, from whom, gaping for gain, they buy ill-gotten booty at a cheap price. This is a most wicked thing, I say, and they will at last learn to their peril that it is not profitable. Many also do this from the prodigality of the young men and nephews they hunt down. And to you too, receivers of stolen goods, men and women, who knowingly and wittingly, with no conscience, buy back either goods taken by theft or goods put up for sale with a wicked conscience, let it be said: you, I say, you, all who make gain by these arts, I dismiss to that abandoned Judas, your former judge, if you persist, at a time and place to come.

units.la: Narratur deinceps non tantum abiisse,sed ab hominibus secessum petiisse. Hæc enim vocabuli quo vtitur Euangelista vis est: nec caret suo pondere: quum ea sit mali Spiritus fraus, vt quos agit maxime conspectum hominum refugiant, nequis eorum conatus vel auertat, vel remoretur.
units.tr: It is further told that he not only departed but sought withdrawal from men. For this is the force of the word the Evangelist uses, and it is not without weight, since it is a trick of the evil spirit that those whom he drives most flee the sight of men, lest anyone turn them aside or hinder their attempt.

units.la: Et reuera non sine causa Dominus ipse pronuntiauit, Non esse bonum homini esse soli Genef.3.18. infinitis de causis: minime quidem quòd non sit satius solum esse quàm praua consortia sectari, multaque occurrant quæ seccessum etiam requirant. Ecquis enim nescius est olim Prophetas & deinceps saltu persecutionū sub Romanis Imperatoribus passim flagrante coactos sanctos viros errare in desertis,seque montibus ac speluncis ac terræ cauernis abdere?Hebr.11.38.Sed ne procul abeamus annon miseros fratres nostros in locis Cabriores & Merindol & aliis non paucis etiam nostro seculo, sunt ili carnifices in ipsis eorum latibulis & speluncis inaudito furore persecuti, Saulis ad exemplum Dauidem ex rupe in rupem insequentis? Agnosco non inuitus mul tos pietatis insignis & studiorum amantes viros vt studia sua promouerent sanctisque exercitiis commodius vacarent, secessum & o-tia tia pro variis temporum, locorum & personarum circunstantiis quæsiuisse. At etiam assiduo & verè allevero, vitam solitariam ex professo degentes, & quidem voto & religione, non modò stultæ deuotionis accusandos, sed tanquam in charitatem proximi peccantes arguendos: tantum abest vt Eremitam aut Monachum esse, vitam Christianam, aut, vt mentiuntur quidam impudenter, Apostolicam respiciat. Nam contrà secessus ille fugaque socictatis humanæ in perpetuum ex diametro Christianæ cuilibet vocationi, priuatæ publicæ-ue: ciuili vel Ecclesiasticæ repugnat. Et reuera licet inter tot myriadas istiusmodi fanaticorum hominum, immo verè potius onagrorum, doctrina & pietate insignes extiterint nonnulli, ad functiones etiam Ecclesiasticas vocati, tamen purioribus iplis temporibus quum pleraque monasteria, vel totidem bonarum artium, & in primis piratis essent Scholæ, vel confessus aliquot simpliciū hominū magnum labore victū sibi quæ rentiū & precibus certis horis vacatium, Monachorum ambitio & superstitio probis viris iam tum multum exhibebat negotij: monumentis eorū istiusmodi querelarum plenis, & Conciliorū historiis, etsi tunc temporis Monachi tantum in Laicorum non autem in Cleri numero censerentur. At postquam vrbes quoque penetrarunt, & in ordines Ecclesiasticos admissi sunt, (sine vlla tamen Ecclesiastica functione, quod longe est absurdissimum & plane ridiculum)& ab Episcopis exemptiones consecuti, Patres Confc-fores facti sunt, & hoc praetextu, Principatus, Comitatus & Ducatus inuaserunt (digna nimirum illa seculo renuntiaffe fc profitetibus) &in primis ex quo medici illi sibi Curialium, Pastorum & Doctorum titulum arrogarunt, & locustarum illa pestis alieno labore, messe acfementc ventrem explens, quis ignorat nullam esse in toto terrarum orbe minus tolerandam, & non tantum inutilem, sed magis pestiferam & exitialem viuendi rationem? Sic pedetentim ex istis collegiis simplicium que hominum coetibus nec sibi nec aliis multum noxiis aut vtilibus, emerserunt multi simiae, multis artibus & gefticulationibus instructi, mimorum more, quorum alij tandem in praepingues & obtlos porcos, alij in latrantes canes, alij denique in lupos, ac tigres ferásque immanilfimas euaserunt, à quibus vtinam tutus fit aliquando mundus & immunis.
units.tr: Indeed, not without cause did the Lord himself declare that it is not good for man to be alone, Gen. 3. 18, for countless reasons. Not that it is not better to be alone than to follow wicked company, and many situations arise that call for withdrawal. For who does not know that the prophets of old, and afterwards holy men, driven by the persecutions that raged everywhere under the Roman emperors, wandered in deserts and hid themselves in mountains, caves and clefts of the earth, Heb. 11. 38? But not to go far afield: did not the cruel executioners, in our own century too, pursue our wretched brethren in the places of Cabrières and Mérindol and many others, in their hiding places and caves with unheard-of fury, like Saul pursuing David from rock to rock? I acknowledge that many men distinguished for piety and devoted to study have sought withdrawal and leisure, so that they might advance their studies and devote themselves more conveniently to holy exercises, according to the varying circumstances of times, places and persons. But those who live a solitary life as a matter of profession, and indeed by vow and religious obligation, must be accused not only of foolish devotion but must be charged with sinning against the love of their neighbour. So far is it from the Christian life, or, as some shamelessly lie, from the apostolic life, to be a hermit or a monk. For that withdrawal and flight from human society, lasting for ever, is diametrically opposed to every Christian vocation, whether private or public, civil or ecclesiastical. And indeed, although among so many myriads of such fanatical men, or rather wild asses, some have been distinguished by learning and piety and even called to ecclesiastical functions, yet in the purer times, when most monasteries were also schools of the liberal arts, and especially of sacred studies, or when a few men of simple life supported themselves by hard labour and devoted themselves to set prayers at fixed hours, the ambition and superstition of the monks already gave good men much trouble. Records of such complaints abound, and so do the histories of the councils, although at that time monks were counted only among the laity and not among the clergy. But after they had also entered the cities and were admitted into ecclesiastical orders (though without any ecclesiastical function, which is by far the most absurd and plainly ridiculous), and had obtained exemptions from the bishops, they became "Fathers" and confessors, and under this pretext seized principalities, counties and duchies (things worthy of a profession that renounced the world!). Above all, since those physicians of souls arrogated to themselves the titles of courtiers, pastors and teachers, and that plague of locusts, feeding its belly on the labour and harvest of others, who does not know that there is no way of life in the whole world less to be tolerated, one not only useless but more pestilent and deadly? Thus gradually out of those colleges and assemblies of simple men, which were of little harm or use to themselves or others, there emerged many apes, equipped with many arts and gestures, after the manner of mimes. Some of them at last became exceedingly fat and sluggish pigs, others barking dogs, others finally wolves, tigers and the most savage beasts, from which may the world one day be safe and free.

units.la: Mundum igitur praecipuum aduersus quem nobis pugnandum est, ipsi circumferimus, cui non locorum sed animorum & voluntatum mutatione resistitur, quod opus est Sancti Spiritus etsi fugienda sunt interea praua consortia, & tempus est quaerendae solitudinis, tempus vero societatis ineundae: quae nos Spiritus charitatis est doctus, & vocatio ad quam à Domino ad mutuas operas inuicem praestandas vocati fumus. Obiter tamen istud admonebo, melancholicis natura ingeniis, praesertim in maximis grauissimisque tentationibus, periculosam esse nimio studio quaesitam solitudinem, quo tempore potius ne Charybdi vitata in Scyllam incidant, maximè requirendum est eorum consortium à quibus tum consolatoriis sermonibus, tum mutuis precibus adiuuentur & consolationem accipiant.
units.tr: The chief world we must fight against is the one we carry about ourselves. It is overcome not by a change of place but by a change of minds and wills, and that is the work of the Holy Spirit. Meanwhile bad companionships must be avoided, and there is a time to seek solitude, but there is also a time to enter into fellowship. The Spirit of charity teaches us this, and the Lord calls us to render mutual services to one another. I will add this in passing: for melancholic natures, especially in the greatest and heaviest temptations, it is dangerous to seek solitude too eagerly. At such times, lest they avoid Charybdis only to fall into Scylla, they most need the company of those by whom they may be helped with comforting words and mutual prayers, and so receive consolation.

units.la: Tandem igitur ad horrendum iltius mali exitum accedamus, nimirum perditum iltum, de quo dixerat Christus bonum fuisse si nunquam natus fuisset, laqueo sibi ipsi gulam frangere. Adde quod nominatim obseruat D. Petrus Act. 1. 18. praecipitem factum medium crepuisse, omniaque eius viscera effusa, quod omnibus habitantibus Hierosolymae innotuerit, seu Praecipitandi voce intelligamus eum sic mortem maturasse, ad eorum morem qui suspendio vitam finiunt, & paulo post ventrem eius crepuisse effusaque intestina, seu praecipitem se dante illo strangulanteque, tum arbor ipsa, tum ab ea pendulus in praecipitium ruerint, & sic infaustum illud cadauer ad eorum instar quos 2. Chronic. 25. 12. praecipites factos legimus, crepuerit: horrendum, sane mortis genus, quo monemur quantum eminet exitium fesc impuro illi Spiritui permittentibus vt loquitur Apostolus 2. Timot. 2. 26. non tantum bonam mentem, sed totam eam hominibus eripientes. Praeterquam quod enim natura sensus mortis horrendus est, annon perditus ille sibi persuadens Dei se iudicia morte effugiturum, amens est? Nam quum in genere Dei manus effugiat nemo, mors praeterea compensa diofius ad illud iudicium iter est, imo ipsa est in seuerissimis acerbissimisque Dei iudiciis primum, vt Iudas fuerit in flammam se ad fugiendum ignem coniicienti simillimus. En quò morsus immedicabilis illius canis furentis, & rugientis leonis corpora & animas nostras sitientis ferat eos qui aduersus verum & vnicum remedium, veram putà resipiscentiam &ad Deum conuersionem, occalluerunt: quorum quidem vt in hoc conspicuum est exemplo & multis aliis, accurataque dignum est obseruatione, non tantum est infelix exitus: sed, quum ita Deo visum est, scelerati sibiipsi sunt carnifices, vt idem sit cum carnifice reus. Nec vero silentio hic aliquid prætereundum, quò melius appareat quanta multis iam seculis in hominum tyrannidem Satan exerceat, sidem omnē superaturum nisi id veteres omnes prophanorum historiæ testarentur, nimirum eti natura cunctis sit mors formidabilis, tamē sibi sponte violentas manus inferre, mortemque conscire, non modò toleratum, sed magni fortisque animi suisse indicium habitu, sic agente Satana miseros, vt alios metu ignominiæ, quod Sauli contigit, alios tædio vitæ sic ad sponta-neam mortem impelleret. Exemplis Romanorum, Græcorum, Barbarorumque plenæ sunt historiæ, licet inter prophanos hanc opinionem multi certis & indubitatis rationibus oppugnarint, in quibus hanc pulcherrimam non possum non recensere, putà nos hic velut in custodiis ab Imperatore nostro collocatos, cuius iniussu non sit ex hominum vita mi-grandum. Ac sanè si manus alteri violentas inferre Legibus inhibetur, nè multò magis sibi mortem consciscere : quod sapientissimi quíque Legislatores tanquam nefarium homicidium etiam Legibus condemnarunt.
units.tr: Let us now come at last to the dreadful end of that evil man, the lost one of whom Christ said it would have been good for him if he had never been born, who broke his neck with a noose. Add that St Peter notes specifically (Act. 1.18) that he fell headlong, burst in the middle, and all his bowels gushed out, which became known to all who dwelt in Jerusalem. Whether we take "falling headlong" to mean that he hastened his death in the manner of those who end their lives by hanging, so that his belly burst a little later and his entrails spilled out; or whether, as he was strangling himself and falling, both the tree and the man hanging from it plunged down the drop, so that the unhappy corpse burst open like those whom we read in 2 Chron. 25.12 were thrown headlong. It is a dreadful kind of death, and by it we are warned how great the ruin is when we let that unclean spirit, as the Apostle says (2 Tim. 2.26), snatch from people not merely a good mind but the whole of it. Besides, the very sensation of death is dreadful in its nature. Is not that lost man mad, who persuaded himself he would escape God's judgments by death? For although no one escapes the hand of God in general, death is moreover a shorter road to that judgment; indeed it is itself the first of God's most severe and bitter judgments, so that Judas was very like a man who throws himself into the fire to flee the fire. See where the incurable bite of that raging dog, and of the roaring lion who thirsts for our bodies and souls, carries those who have grown callous against the true and only remedy, namely true repentance and conversion to God. Of these, as is evident in this example and in many others, and as deserves careful notice, not only is the end unhappy; but since God so willed, the wicked became their own executioners, so that the guilty man is the same as the executioner. Nor should I pass over here something in silence, so that it may better appear how much Satan has for many centuries exercised his tyranny over men. It would be hard to believe unless all the histories of the profane bore witness: although death is by nature dreadful to all, to inflict violent hands on oneself and bring about one's own death was not only tolerated but was held a sign of a great and brave spirit. Satan so drove wretched men that some he impelled to voluntary death through fear of disgrace, as happened to Saul, and others through weariness of life. The histories of Romans, Greeks and barbarians are full of examples. Although many among the profane have attacked this opinion with sure and certain arguments, I cannot fail to mention the most beautiful of them: that we are placed here as if in prisons by our Emperor, at whose command we must not depart from human life. And indeed, if laws forbid one man to inflict violent hands on another, how much more on oneself; the wisest lawgivers condemned this even by law as a wicked homicide.

units.la: Quid igitur fiet multis immo penè infinitis suiipsorum homicidis huius sceleris nimium cosciis? Nā, obsecro, quotquot in peccatis suis, aducrsus tam crebras cohortationes obdurecscunt, annon ipsi sibi mortis causa sunt, Dominum ad vitam ipsis abrumpendam, quos ferre amplius non possit, simúlque ad mortem æternam addicendos cogentes? Sed ne paulò seuerior multis hac ratione videar, age istud in nonnullis, coram hominibus ipsis prorsus inexcusabilibus inuestigemus. Ecquis igitur, audeat inficiari, quin gulosi & ebriosi illi veneri tantùm dediti homines sibi ipsis aperte mortem consciscant? Quid verò impuri illi scortatores, quos viuos mortuos paulatim cócidere passim conspicias, annon ipsi sibi mortis causa sunt? Quid verò dicam de infaustis illis & detestandis auaris, quos dum argenti fames ceterorum sanguinem sitire cogit, ipsi suum sitiunt, & à male partis diuitiis veluti laqueis strangulantur? Quam igitur multi coram hominibus probitatem simulant, coram Deo ramen homicidæ, hoc vnico à luda differentes, quòd hic scse temerè in ipsos inferos præcipitem dedit, illi verò tantùm longo circuitu tandem istud iter consiciunt? Quo verò loco di-
units.tr: What then will become of the many, indeed almost countless, self-murderers who are too much bound to this crime? For, I ask, all who harden themselves in their sins against so many frequent exhortations: are they not the cause of their own death, compelling the Lord to cut off the life of those whom he can no longer bear, and at the same time to consign them to eternal death? But lest I seem to many too severe by this reasoning, come, let us examine this in some people who are wholly inexcusable before men. Who would dare to deny that gluttonous and drunken men, given over only to pleasure, openly bring death on themselves? And what of those impure fornicators, whom you may see everywhere gradually falling, dead while still alive: are they not the cause of their own death? And what shall I say of those unhappy and detestable misers, whom the hunger for money, while it makes them thirst for the blood of others, also makes them thirst for their own, so that they are strangled as with nooses by riches wrongly gotten? How many, then, feign uprightness before men, yet before God are murderers, differing from Judas only in this: that he rashly threw himself headlong into hell itself, while they reach the same end only by a long detour? In what place do we think those are who provoke one another to slaughter, and think it a disgrace unless they bring death on themselves or their neighbours willingly? For such are the times now, alas! and such are the morals of men. Since these things are so, dreadful indeed and proved too plainly by sight itself, let us pray to God Best and Greatest every moment that, since by his immense generosity he has given us this life to use and enjoy, he would also grant that we consecrate and dedicate it to the Giver, exercising each one his calling as those who will render account of it at every moment. Yet in this matter two extremes must be carefully avoided. We must not value life more than is fitting, as most do, redeeming it at the cost of God's own dishonour or the harm of our neighbours; nor value it less, as those do who sell it so cheaply. Above all let us humbly pray God that, amid so many great storms and tempests of this age and most dangerous temptations, he so governs us that he does not hand us over into Satan's power, the avenger of his just wrath against us, as we see was done to this unhappy man and others like him.

units.la: {*} Multæ sunt species auaritiæ. (Marginal note, right: "Multæ sunt species avarorum" with Greek φρόνων.) gnos putamus eos, qui sese mutuò ad cædem prouocant? sibíque dedecori verti existimant, nisi vel ipsi sibi, vel proximis sponte mortem inferant? Hæc sunt enim hodie, proh dolor! tempora, & hi mores hominum. Quæ quum ita sint, horrenda sane nimiúmque visu ipso comprobata, Deum Opt. Maxim. singulis momentis precemur, ut quum hanc nobis vitam vtendam fruendam pro immensa sua liberalitate dederit, hoc etiam largiatur ut eam datori consecremus ac dedicemus, ita suam vno quoque vocationem exercente, ut in momen ta singula rationem eius reddituro. Qua in re tamen duo sunt extrema nobis caute fugienda: ne videlicet aut pluris eam quàm par sit æstimemus, quod plerique faciunt illam vel Dei ipsius contumelia vel proximorum detrimento redimentes: aut minoris etiam eam faciamus, ut solent eam qui tam parvo vendunt. In primis verò supplices Deum oremus, ut nos in tot tantisque huius seculi procellis ac tempestatibus, & periculosissimis tentationibus ita regat ne in Satanæ potestatem, iusti sui aduersus nos furoris vindicem, tradat, quod factum in hoc infelici & eius similibus aspicimus.
units.tr: {*} There are many kinds of avarice. (Marginal note, right: "There are many kinds of the avaricious" [φρόνων].) Whom do we think those are who challenge one another to murder, and count it a disgrace to themselves unless they bring death on themselves or on their neighbours willingly? For such are the times now, alas! and such are the morals of men. Since these things are so, dreadful indeed and proved too plainly by sight itself, let us pray to God Best and Greatest every moment that, since by his immense generosity he has given us this life to use and enjoy, he would also grant that we consecrate and dedicate it to the Giver, exercising each one his calling as those who will render account of it at every moment. Yet in this matter two extremes must be carefully avoided: namely, that we value life either more than is fitting, as most do, redeeming it at the cost of God's dishonour or our neighbours' harm; or that we value it even less, as those do who sell it so cheaply. Above all let us pray God humbly that, in so many great storms and tempests of this age and most dangerous temptations, he so govern us that he does not hand us over into Satan's power, the avenger of his just anger against us, as we see was done to this unhappy man and others like him.

units.la: Reliquum est ut aliud horrendum in Sacerdotes & Seniores, non minus in emendo scelera-tos, quàm ille facinorosus in vendendo, Dei iudicium expedamus, eòdem utroque iudicio recidente, licet non eadem via Dei vindicta procedente. Iudas enim etsi veram non est adeptus resipiscentiam, peccatum suum agnognouit & confessus est: isti verò longè magis, tum animis obdurati, tum vana sua supersti- tione & hypocrisi, cæcutierunt. Etsi autem qualis eorum fuerit, vt Iudæ cõstat exitus, non legimus, facile tamen & sine mendacio conii- citur eòdem eos quo Iudam, eiusdem putà cri- minis reos deuenille, nisi Deus ex ipsis quos- dam à capite ad calcem pro immensa sua mi- sericordia immutarit. Et sanè quæ horrenda modis omnibus paulò pòst tum toti natio- ni, tum maximè Hierøsolymæ ac templo ipsi vt prædixerat Dominus contigerunt, eorum non fuisse meliorem conditionem satis te- stantur.
units.tr: It remains that we set forth God's judgment on another dreadful matter, concerning the priests and elders, who were no less wicked in buying than that criminal was in selling. Both judgments come to the same end, though God's vengeance proceeds by a different way. For Judas, though he did not attain true repentance, acknowledged his sin and confessed it; but these men, much more, were blinded both by hardened minds and by their vain superstition and hypocrisy. And although we do not read what their end was, as we do for Judas, it is easily and without falsehood conjectured that they came to the same end as Judas, guilty of the same crime, unless God, in his immense mercy, changed some of them from top to bottom. And indeed the horrors that afterwards befell, as the Lord had foretold, both the whole nation and especially Jerusalem and the temple itself, sufficiently testify that their condition was no better.

units.la: Primùm igitur hoc ad eos misso præcone, manu pecuniam ferente, & facti veritatem pa- lam profitente, quantus iste fuit stupor, sese mutuò respicientes saltem pudore non suf- fundi, sed eiusdem criminis conscium irride- re, suíque tandem muneris immemores etiam dicere, Quid ad nos? Tu prouideris. Nam cur sibi Pastoris nomen vindicaret, qui curam o- uium non gerit, & audet idipsum tum re tum verbis profiteri? An istud est Ezechielis do- ctrinam Ezech.33. 6. in vsum reuocare, aut de iis quæ tam copiosè toto 34. capite intonuit cogitare? Atque vtinam ne idem in Ecclesiam Christianam aut longè peius adhuc irrepsis- set, nullo dum tam deplorandæ desolationis exitu nobis apparente. Fratres, hæc qui mecum auditis, & quibus idem est in Ecclesia docen- di munus impositum, absit à nobis, vt talis vnquam nostras mentes subeat cogitatio aut ore nostro verbum elabatur, Quid ad nos? quam vt à nobis cogitationem, is cui animarum rationem semel reddituti fumus auertat, votis ardentibus eum deprecemur. Ecquid enim est de quo magis esse nos oporteat, quàm de minimo minimæ nobis commissæ ouiculæ peccato sollicitos?In memoriam nobis potius bonum illum pastorem, nunquam nisi recepta oue aberrante conquiescentem, Matt. 18.vers.12.& insignes illas fidelis Apostoli sententias, reuocemus, Quis offenditur quin ego vrar?2.Cor.11.29. &, Omnia sum factus omnibus. 1.Cor.9.22. Deus autem Opt.Max. nostris nobis cœdonatis infirmitatibus istam gratiam oro largiatur.
units.tr: First, then, when the herald was sent to them, carrying the money in his hand and openly professing the truth of the deed, what great stupor there was! Looking at one another, they were not even brought to blush with shame; instead they laughed at their accomplice in the crime, and, forgetting their office at last, even said: "What is that to us? You will see to it." For why should he claim the name of Shepherd who does not care for the sheep and dares to profess this both in deed and in word? Or is that to recall to use the teaching of Ezekiel (Ezek. 33.6), or to think about those things which he thundered so fully throughout chapter 34? And would that the same had not crept into the Christian Church, or something far worse, with no end of so deplorable a desolation yet appearing to us. Brothers, you who hear me, and to whom the same office of teaching in the Church has been imposed, far be it from us that any such thought should ever enter our minds, or any such word slip from our mouths: "What is that to us?" Rather let us beseech God with burning prayers to turn that thought away from us, he to whom we shall one day have to render account of souls. For what ought we to be more anxious about than the sin of the least sheep committed to us? Let us rather call to mind that good shepherd, who never rests except when the straying sheep is recovered (Matt. 18.12), and those famous sayings of the faithful Apostle: "Who is offended, and I do not burn?" (2 Cor. 11.29), and "I have become all things to all men" (1 Cor. 9.22). And may God Best and Greatest grant us this grace, pardoning our infirmities.

units.la: Porrò quum singulorum Christianorum proprium sit ut alij aliorum salutem promoueant, hac etiam ratione sciamus nos, ut ita dicam, omnes Pastores aliis alios constitutos inuigilare oportere ut ex irae Dei flamma mutuo nos eripiamus. Iud. 23. Siquis igitur afflictus occurrat, cuiusmodi multi nobis ob oculos obuersantur, absit dicamus, cogitemus-ue, Quid ad nos, viderint alij, aut, Abite cum pace, calescite & saturamini, Iac.2.16. sed potius tum verbo tum reipsa miserum egenum subleuemus. Siquis dicto factoue peccet, absit etiam dicamus, Quid moror, viderit ille, aut quos hæc cura tangit. Contrà sanctis admonitionibus & reprehensionibus proximorum morum salutem nobis esse curæ testemur, tanquam eiusdem corporis membris, atque adeo quoscunque iuuare possumus, licet ignotos proximos esse à nobis vt nos ipsos diligendos iciamus.
units.tr: Since it is the proper task of each Christian to promote the salvation of others, we should also remember, so to speak, that all of us who are pastors have been appointed to watch over one another, so that we may snatch each other from the flame of God's wrath. Jude 23. If therefore any afflicted person meets us, of the kind that many throw in our way, let us never say or think, "What is that to us? Let others see to it," or, "Go in peace, be warmed and filled," James 2:16, but rather relieve the wretched and needy both by word and by deed. If anyone sins by word or deed, let us not say, "Why should I trouble myself? Let him see to it, or let those whom this concern touches see to it." On the contrary, we should show that we care for the salvation of our neighbours by holy admonitions and rebukes, as members of the same body, and so we should love, as ourselves, all whom we can help, even if our neighbours are unknown to us.

units.la: Admonitus porrò abest monentem incusfet, Quid tua refert, res tuas age, eos de quibus agimus, Ægyptiumque illum sic Mosi respondantem imitatus, Exod.2.vers.14. contrà vero monentem nos Dominum quocunque tandem vtatur instrumento, gratiámque suam offerentem ne repudiemus, sapientis insignem istam sententiam memoriæ altius infigentes, Melius esse audire sapientis increpationem, quàm stolidi cantilenam, Eccles.7. vers.5. Et sanè laudari periculosius est quàm reprehendi. Porrò improborum istorum Sacerdotum, sic ex conscientiæ obduratione excæcatorum, vt sui muneris & proximorum obliuiscerentur, non minor fuit in superstitione cæcitas, Nam religioni non ducunt pecuniam ad innocentem prodendum ex sacro depromere, licet intus & foris polluti ac detestabiles, sed in thesaurum reponere scrupulo stimulantur ac retinentur, quòd sit nimirum pretium sanguinis. At si propterea polluta est pecunia, quid iis fiet qui cum Iuda contraxerunt? Nam si ex sacro depromere licuit, cur vitium fuerit reponere? aut si nefas fuit reponere, quinam tandem depromere fas fuerit? Præterea si iure Christus morti addictus est, qua tandé ratione pollutam quæ capiendo illi inseruierit pecuniam dicas?Sic sane dum improbi isti latebras quærunt, magis ac magis seipsos produnt, cū Iuda venditore agnoscentes Iesu Christi mortem esse hominis innocentis cædem, non autem, de reo supplicium. Ecquis igitur hac in parte magis quàm ipsi Iudices noxius?Sed quid agas?ij sunt hypocritarum Deóque illudentiū mores, quales apud Prophetas passim occurrunt reprehensiones. Atque ipse Dominus tam sæpe támque expresse de istis hos ipsos hypocritas arguerat, & nominatim Matth. 23. Sed hac omissa misera natione, totus ille cultus ceremonialis pedetentim in Ecclesiam Christianam inuectus, ab aqua lustrali vsque ad sanctum suum oleum, torquē Deum tu viuis tum mortuis conciliandi ritus, qualis tandem erit, ad rectam trutinam appensus, nisi mera Dei illusio & contemptus omnium Iudæorū ac Ethnicorum ipsorum inanibus gesticulationibus & ceremoniis longè magis exitiosus? Hoc verò factum quòd attinet, maximam inter istos quantumuis induratos hypocritas & superstitiosos, & nostri seculi quibuscum nobis est negotium Sacrificulos agnosco differentiam. Nam illis fuit religio pecuniam illā in thesaurum reponere, istis verò non est religio totius orbis facultates, si offerrentur, in suos vsus corradere. Quos si suos codices & tabulas proferre iubeteris, quibus etiam in Dominatus maximos inuaserunt, næ maximā istorum partem ex hoc fonte promanare comperies peries, quòd boni isti nimirum Patres Confessores in prædæ partem venerunt eorum qui ex bellis reduces sic peccata sua redimebant, etiam frustratis legitimis hæredibus,quod istis olim hypocritis ipse Christus exprobrarat, Matth.15.4.& 23.14.En verò vt mundus falli & fallere delectatur, Domino interea iustas ab hominibus pœnas repetentc, salutem ipsius gratis in sacrosancti verbi ipsius oblatum prę-dicatione respuentibus Ioh. 7. 37. (etsi tanto pretio homines, non auro nec argento, sed proprio sanguine Christi redempti sint.1. Pet. 1.18. )vt devotionibus suis, non tantum inanibus, sed etiam superstitiosis & impietatis plenis, vel corporum, facultatum & animarum suarum periculo inhæreant.
units.tr: Moreover, the one who is admonished should not shrink from the one admonishing him, with the words, "What business is it of yours? Mind your own affairs," imitating that Egyptian who answered Moses in this way, Exod. 2:14. On the contrary, whatever instrument the Lord uses to admonish us, and whenever he offers his grace, we should not reject it, but fix deeply in our memory this notable saying of the wise: It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise than the song of fools, Eccles. 7:5. Indeed, to be praised is more dangerous than to be rebuked. But the blindness of those wicked priests, who were so blinded by the hardening of their conscience that they forgot both their office and their neighbours, was no less in superstition. For they did not scruple to take money out of the sacred treasury for the betrayal of an innocent man, though they were polluted and detestable within and without; but they were pricked with scruple to put it back into the treasury and keep it there, because, of course, it was the price of blood. But if the money was therefore polluted, what will become of those who have made a bargain with Judas? For if it was lawful to take it out of the sacred treasury, how could it be a sin to put it back? Or if it was wrong to put it back, who then could have had a right to take it out? Moreover, if Christ was rightly delivered to death, on what ground can you call the money polluted that served to take him? So indeed, while these wicked men seek hiding places, they betray themselves more and more, acknowledging with Judas the seller that the death of Jesus Christ was the slaughter of an innocent man, and not the punishment of a guilty one. Who then is more guilty in this respect than the judges themselves? But what can you do? Such are the manners of hypocrites who mock God, and such are the rebukes that occur everywhere in the Prophets. And the Lord himself had so often and so expressly accused these very hypocrites of this, and by name in Matt. 23. But, leaving aside that wretched nation, that whole ceremonial worship, gradually carried into the Christian Church, from the lustral water to its holy oil, the rites for propitiating God both for the living and the dead, what will it be, weighed in the true balance, unless it is pure mockery of God and contempt, and far more destructive than the empty gestures and ceremonies of all the Jews and even the Gentiles? As for this deed, I recognize a great difference between those hypocrites and superstitious men, however hardened, and the little sacrificers of our own age with whom we have to deal. For to those men it was a matter of religion to put that money into the treasury; but to these it is no religion to gather together for their own uses the wealth of the whole world, if it were offered to them. If you ordered them to produce their own codes and tables, by which they have even invaded the greatest dominions, you would find, I say, that the greater part of their power flows from this source: that those good fathers and confessors came into the share of the booty of those who, returning from the wars, thus redeemed their sins, even though the lawful heirs were cheated, which Christ himself once reproached in those hypocrites, Matt. 15:4 and 23:14. And see, the world delights to be deceived and to deceive, while the Lord demands just punishments from men, and they reject his salvation freely offered in the preaching of his holy Word, John 7:37 (though men have been redeemed at such a price, not with gold or silver, but with the precious blood of Christ, 1 Pet. 1:18), so that they cling to their devotions, which are not only empty but also superstitious and full of impiety, at the peril of their bodies, goods and souls.

units.la: Sed quæ huic superstruantur fundamento, dispiciamus.Consilium capiunt,An cognituri rectène an secus fecerint?an iste iudiciorum Dei præco,Iudas verum dixerit,necne? Minimè gentium. Nam præterquàm quòd Ordinis habenda ratio est,vt eius dignitati consulatur, quis audeat vel per somnium cogitare Pontificem maximum totúmque adeò Hierosolymitanum magnum consilium, non tantum labi posse, sed etiam tanti sceleris reum esse? Apage igitur rem istam. Quid hac igitur pecunia futurum est? Nam & de hac olim futuri sunt hominum sermones. Quibus obuiam vt eatur, & de nobis bene sentiatur, agerad peregrinorum devotionis ergo templum nostrum visitantium sepulturam emendus est.
units.tr: But let us examine the foundation on which these things are built. They take counsel: would they know whether they had acted rightly or not? Or whether that herald of God's judgments, Judas, spoke the truth or not? By no means. For, apart from the fact that regard must be had for the office, so that its dignity is preserved, who would dare even in a dream to think that the high priest, and indeed the whole great council of Jerusalem, could not only err but could also be guilty of so great a crime? Away with such a thing! What then will become of this money? For there will be talk of it among men in time to come as well. To avoid this, and to have a good opinion of us, the burial place should be bought for strangers who visit our temple for devotion's sake.

units.la: Ecquid porrò toto isto consilio aliud agitatur, nisi quod iam à multis seculis boni nostri Romani Catholici factitarę confuecuerunt? Nam obsecro, an ex quo visum est Deo mundum discussis tenebris excitare, in tot habitis Romæ coetibus Consistorialibus, tot consiliis Ecclesiasticis, quæ vocant, vnquam est de illius Caiaphæ qui in Christianam Ecclesiam irrepsit, potestate & auctoritate dubitatum? Quot annis tandem Tridentinum illud constructum est Conciliabulum, non ad corrigendos Romanæ tyrannidis abusus, sed contrà summa impudentia felluris iisdem reis & iudicibus, ad totius Christianismi cū ruina & confusione maiorem auctoritatem illi conciliandam?
units.tr: Moreover, what else is being done in this whole counsel, except what good Roman Catholics have been accustomed to do for many centuries now? For I ask you, since it pleased God to raise the world out of the shadows, in so many consistorial assemblies held at Rome, in so many so-called ecclesiastical councils, has the power and authority of that Caiaphas, who crept into the Christian Church, ever been called into doubt? How many years has that Tridentine conciliabulum now been in building, not to correct the abuses of the Roman tyranny, but, on the contrary, with the greatest impudence, to secure greater authority for the same guilty men and judges, to the ruin and confusion of all Christendom?

units.la: Ac si in coetibus nonnullis coepit aliquid agitari, an non iltud fuit ad mundi ludibrium? Testem adiuoco datum Paulo III. Papæconsiliuų à septė, quos ipsemet elegerat, Cardinalibus, typis excusum & publicatum, quo praeter reliqua monetur ipse vt penitus Mendicantium Monachorum ordines aboleat, cum plurimis aliis istiusmodi reformationibus. At quorsum haec omnia, nisi vt fumos venderent fucumque facerent, & spe vana omnes lactarent, quos sibi tum conciliare necesse fuit?
units.tr: And if some matter began to be discussed in some of these assemblies, was it not for the mockery of the world? I call as witness the counsel of seven cardinals chosen by Pope Paul III himself, printed and published, in which, among other things, he is advised to abolish utterly the orders of the mendicant monks, together with very many other reforms of this kind. But to what end were all these things, except to sell smoke and make a show, and to cheer everyone with vain hope, whom it was then necessary to win over?

units.la: Tantùm enim abest vt istis locus aliquis reformationibus fuerit, vt contrà non ita multò post vnus ex septem illis Cardinalibus Papa factus & Iulius tertius dictus, sederit, videntibus ac scientibus omnibus, eorum omnium qui vnquam in illa sede fuerunt, monstrum detemaxime detestandum. Tota vero illa qualiscunque prouisio, non de doctrinæ pietate, sed de horrenda simonia quam in diripiendis pauperum bonis profligati isti homines exercent, cuius aliqua fit mentio in quadam huius Concilij totiens interpolati sessione, ad quid profuit nisi ad bullarum clausulas rogatorias amplificandas? Quibus omnibus tegendis sordidibus sufficit persuasum habere Papam à nemine posse iudicari, ne si quidem animas plenis plaustris in inferos detruserit, sunt enim hæc ipsissima ab ipsis in suis Canonibus verba monimentis conscripta traditaque : deinde certos quosdam lituaros & mithratos homines vniuersam esse Ecclesiam repræsentatiua: denique nullam maiorem hæresin quàm siquis eorum Ecclesiam errare potuisse vel posse dixerit. Quorsum vero hæc omnia? Nempe vt imperita plebecula sibi hac vnica esse religionem ac devotionem persuadeat: nullámque sine bonis istis Prælatis, totóque hoc tam elegánti splendidóque Dei cultu fore amplius in toto terrarum orbe salutem ac Ecclesiam.
units.tr: For so far was there any place for reforms among these men, that on the contrary, not long after, one of those seven cardinals became pope and was called Julius III, and sat in that see, while all who had ever been in that seat saw and knew him to be a most detestable monster. And that whole so-called provision, not concerned with the piety of doctrine but with the horrible simony which these profligate men practise in plundering the goods of the poor, of which some mention is made in one session of this council, so often patched up, what did it serve, except to enlarge the clauses of requests in their bulls? To cover all these filthy practices, it is enough to hold it as settled that the Pope can be judged by no one, even if he should thrust souls into hell by cartloads; for these are the very words written and handed down in their monuments by themselves in their Canons. Then, that certain mitred and crosier-bearing men represent the whole Church; and finally, that there is no greater heresy than if anyone should say that their Church could err or could be able to err. But to what end are all these things? Namely, that the unlearned common people may be persuaded that religion and devotion are to be found in them alone, and that without these good prelates, and without this whole so elegant and splendid worship of God, there will be no salvation or Church any more in the whole world.

units.la: Quid igitur? Nimirum is aduersus quem nec dolus, nec vlla vis hominum quicquam poterit, Sacerdotibus istis & Scnioribus ad propriam infamiam detegendam vsus est instrumentis: ita arcana sua prouidentia toto hoc administrato negotio, vt quod erat tot retro lapsis seculis de Sacerdotum istorum vltimo excidio & Sacerdotij Leuitici fine prædictum ab istis fuerit maximo suo dedecore tandem
units.tr: What then? Surely he against whom neither the craft nor any force of men can prevail has used those priests and elders as instruments to reveal their own infamy: so, by his secret providence, he has so ordered this whole affair that what had been foretold by the Prophets many ages ago, concerning the final ruin of those priests and the end of the Levitical priesthood, was at last fulfilled by them, to their great shame, [the field of the potter having been bought with that money], which in their language (as Peter expresses the circumstance, Acts 1:19) was called Akeldama, that is, the field of blood, which could not be called anything else but that the buyers and judges were openly called murderers, for a time, until they fell...

units.la: D. j. adimpletum, ab ipsis nimirum agro figuli pecunia redempto, qui eorum lingua (quam Petrus circunstantiam exprimit, Act. 1.19.) Acceldama, hoc est, ager sanguinis diceretur, quod tamen dici non potuit quin emptores ac iudices aperte vocarentur homicidæ: tantisper dum lapsis circiter annis triginta septem hortendum Domini iudicium ad mortem prima & secundam non solum in emptores istos & falsos iudices ferretur, sed etiam (Domino suâ Ecclesiam Hierosolymis miranda quadam ratione prius eductam conseruantè) in eos qui vociferati fuerant, Tolle, tolle, crucifige eum, immo & in eorum liberos, ut ad mortem properans Dominus, eos præmonuerat. Luc. 23.28.
units.tr: ...was fulfilled, namely when the field of the potter had been bought with that money by the very men themselves. In their language (as Peter expresses it, Acts 1.19) it was called Akeldama, that is, the field of blood, a name that could not be given to it without the buyers and judges being openly called murderers. Then, about thirty-seven years later, the dreadful judgement of the Lord fell in death, first and second, not only on those buyers and false judges but also on those who had shouted, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him." The Lord, who preserved his Church in a wondrous way by leading it out of Jerusalem beforehand, sent this judgement, and even on their children, as the Lord had forewarned them while hastening to his death. Luke 23.28.

units.la: Ecquis vero tam cæcus non animaduertit iam à multis seculis, scortum illud septem montibus insidens nulla re magis quàm suis sordibus infamatum, quas ipsius etiam amatores ferre amplius non potuerint? & quidem tantisper dum euenant quæ præparata sunt ab eo in cuius potestate sunt momenta & tempora Apoc. 14. 17. & 18. Hac in re vero Dei summâ & admirandam prouidentiam admirari nos oportet. Nec enim emptores illi, nec figulus aliud quàm de huius agri venditione & emptione cogitarunt: at Dominus longius prospiciebat, ea nimirum perficiens quæ tot retro lapsis seculis, puta quingentis circiter sexaginta duobus annis, per Zachariam Prophetam de tam pudenda populi aduersus suum Pastorem ingratitudine, futura que inde desolatiolatione prædixerat: Zachariam, inquam, nam in hunc locum Ieremiæ nomen errore librariorum irrepsit, qui tamen Euangelistæ tribui non potest. Ita Dominum videmus impleturũ quæ per Micheam prophetam ante annos octingentos de Domini nostri Iesu Christi Seruatoris in Bethlehem natiuitate prædixerat, Edicto Imperatoris Augusti nihil minus cogitantis abusum. Digna sane doctrina quam mentibus nostris altius infigamus, ut in Dei promissa spe firma recumbamus, quamcunque tandem remoram rebus iniici conspiciamus, nec vlla impletionis illorum ratio nobis affulgeat, immo ferri in contrarium omnia videantur. Cæterum in hac Prophetia Dominus noster Iesus Christus, verus semper & vnicus populi sui Pastor, in visione, modo in propria modo in Prophetæ persona, loquutus, defensu se illorum rebellionibus profitetur, baculum suum cui nomen Iucunditas abrumpit, mercedemque suis laboribus dignam eos in posterum abiecturus reposcit: quæ triginta nummis argenteis æstimatur & appenditur, qua se tantopere contemptum videns Prophetam sic alloquitur, Hanccine vero tot meis laboribus mercedem? Accipe eos argenteos, & proiice in figulum: quod feci, inquit Propheta, & accipiens triginta argenteos proieci in domum Iehouæ, in figulum. Illud igitur hoc loco noster Euangelista docet in Christo reipla impletum, à populo suo tantopere contempto, ut non sit ab eo maioris æstimatus quàm ferebat illa visio Prophetica, mox sequuturo populi Pastore destituti ultimo exitio, manente tamen interea figuli illius agro, coram Deo & hominibus illos graviter incusante & sceleris arguente.
units.tr: Who indeed is so blind as not to notice that for many centuries now that harlot sitting on seven hills has been defamed by nothing more than her own filth, filth which even her lovers can no longer endure? And this will happen, indeed, while the things prepared by him in whose power are the moments and times come to pass, Rev. 14.17 and 18. In this matter we must marvel at the great and admirable providence of God. For neither those buyers nor the potter were thinking of anything but the sale and purchase of this field. But the Lord was looking further ahead, bringing about what he had foretold through the prophet Zechariah some five hundred and sixty-two years earlier, concerning the people's shameful ingratitude toward their Shepherd and the desolation that would follow from it. I say Zechariah, for the name of Jeremiah crept into this place through an error of the copyists, though it cannot be attributed to the Evangelist. So we see the Lord fulfilling what he had foretold through the prophet Micah about eight hundred years before, the birth of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ in Bethlehem, even though the Emperor Augustus, in his edict, was thinking of nothing of the kind. This is indeed a teaching worth fixing deeply in our minds, so that we may rest firmly on God's promises, however great the obstacle we see thrown in the way of their fulfilment, and though no reason for their fulfilment shines upon us, and everything seems to move in the opposite direction. Moreover, in this prophecy our Lord Jesus Christ, always and alone the true Shepherd of his people, speaks in a vision, sometimes in his own person and sometimes in the prophet's, and declares that he is defended against their rebellions. He breaks his staff named Favour, and demands the wages due to his labours, which he is about to cast off from them in the future. These wages are valued and weighed at thirty silver coins. Seeing himself so despised, the prophet addresses them thus: "Is this the wage for my labours? Take those silver coins and throw them to the potter." "I did so," says the prophet, "and taking the thirty silver coins I threw them into the house of the LORD, to the potter." This, then, our Evangelist here teaches was fulfilled in Christ in reality, by a people who so greatly despised him that he was valued at no more than that prophetic vision recorded, soon to be followed by the final destruction of the people, now left without their Shepherd. Yet meanwhile the field of that potter remains, gravely accusing them and convicting them of their crime before God and men.

units.la: At cur figuli potius quàm alterius? Nempe ita Dei prouidentia decretum erat, vt quum hæc contingerent figulus agrum haberet venalem. Nec alienum est à proposito si dicamus, ita Dominum ipsis in memoriam pristinum illum statum ex quo maiores eorum eduxerat, fictilia nimirum Ægypti, Psal. 81. v. 7. revocare voluisse: Sed quæcunque tandem ratio fuerit, quis merito populum illum hac in parte non reprehendat?
units.tr: But why the potter rather than someone else? Surely because it was decreed by God's providence that when these things happened the potter should have a field for sale. Nor is it foreign to our purpose to say that the Lord wished to recall to them that earlier condition from which their forefathers had been led out, namely the pottery of Egypt, Ps. 81.7. But whatever the reason was, who could rightly fail to rebuke that people in this respect?

units.la: At quot, obsecro, in nobis, qui tamen Ecclesiæ reformatæ nomen profitemur, longè adhuc istis deteriores? Nam quis audeat infici quoties huius seculi negotiis sic occupamur, vt quæ nostræ salutis sunt illis longè postponamus, toties à nobis Christum & eius Euangelium æstimari, & in alteram partem bilancem inclinari, etiamsi non de triginta argenteis, sed longè re minore, immo nullius momenti agatur? Testes sunto mihi locupletes, qui obolum lucrifacturi, aut etiam deambulationis tantum causa, tres, quatuor, immo plures conciones facillime negligunt, ignari tamen num amplius Dominum loquentem sint audituri. Tanti autem mali causam eandem quæ istis vltimum exitium peperit, thesauri illius Euangelici nimium crassam & supinam asseaffectatam ignorantiam esse puta. Quaerimus enim quae magni facimus, eademque summo studio conseruamus. Alij igitur haerent dubij, sit-ne post hanc vitam alia expectanda, verane sint an falsa quae de paradiso & inferis praedicantur: alij vero probe quidem tenent, sed parum afficiuntur, huius mundi negotiis sementem quae in spinas decidit suffocantibus. Matth. 13. 22. alij etsi abundant, ex diffidentia tamen quae habent non possident, & in mediis opibus egent, vento se huius mundi pascentes donec tandem crepent. Quando igitur tandem vere Christiani thesauros in coelis reconde-mus? quando tandem didicerimus hoc unicum aduersus huius mundi miserias & inopiam esse remedium, Quaerite primum regnum coelorum, & haec omnia vobis adiicientur, Matth. 6. 33. Quando denique ex ipsis auiculis huius vitae solicitudines in Dei prouidentiam abiicere didicerimus? Luc. 12. 27. At cogitandi si alias vnquam tempus est, ne sero nimis non cogitasse nos poeniteat.
units.tr: But how many of us, I ask, who nonetheless profess the name of the Reformed Church, are still far worse than they? For who would dare deny that whenever we are so occupied with the affairs of this age that we put those of our salvation far behind them, Christ and his Gospel are valued by us so often and the scales are tipped to the other side, even when the matter at stake is not thirty silver coins but something far smaller, indeed of no account at all? Let those who would gain a halfpenny, or who go out merely for a walk, be my abundant witnesses: they very easily neglect three, four, or even more sermons, though they do not know whether they will ever hear the Lord speaking again. As for the cause of such great evil, the same that brought those people to their final destruction, consider it to be the excessively gross and lazy ignorance, even affected, of that treasure of the Gospel. For we seek the things we value, and we keep them with the greatest care. Some therefore hang in doubt whether anything is to be expected after this life, and whether what is preached about paradise and hell is true or false. Others indeed hold it well enough but are little moved, and like seed that falls among thorns, are choked by the cares of this world (Matt. 13.22). Others, though they abound, do not possess what they have through distrust, and they are in want amid their resources, feeding on the wind of this world until at last they burst (Hos. 12.1). When, then, shall we at last store up treasures in heaven as true Christians? When shall we at last learn that this is the one remedy against the miseries and poverty of this world: "Seek first the kingdom of heaven, and all these things will be added to you" (Matt. 6.33)? When at last shall we learn from the very birds of this life to cast our anxieties upon God's providence (Luke 12.27)? But if there has ever been a time for thinking, it is now, lest we regret too late that we did not think.

units.la: De sepultura vero qua de hic agitur, sciendum Peregrinos hic multos intelligi qui etsi non essent Iudaei naturales, ex variis tamen religionibus in magnam illam vrbem Hierosoly-mam conueniebant, alij mercimoniae causa, alij Hierosolymis adoraturi, quod superioribus temporibus non semel contigisse, sacra testatur historia in Danielis & Nehemiae monumentis, cogente Domino saepius ipsos Ethnicos Hebraeorum Deum adorare, eiusque opem implorare: praeterea propiùs accedente Gentium vocatione, Lux illa mundo paulatim illucescebat, quod ex Actorum Apostolicorum cap. 2. & historiis ipsis prophanis satis est conspicuum. Boni tamen isti Sacerdotes dona quidem à quibuslibet viuentibus & largitiones accipiebant: at quum se aliis longè sanctiores arbitrarentur, etsi spurij Abrahami filij, quales eos Dominus depingit, Matth. 12. 41. religioni ducebant eos eadem qua natiuos Iudæos humo sepulturæ mandare. Ac sanè licet omnis terra sit Domini, & Euangelij praedicatione parietis intergerini septum dirutum sit,Ephes.2.14.si tamen accidat vt in eadem urbe mixti sint Iudæi ac Turcæ Christianis, ipse ordo aliquam locorum distinctionem ad vtrorumque sepulturam postulare videtur:modò tamen adhibeatur modus, & absit omnis superstitio: qua in re tamen Romanos nostros Catholicos aduersum nos grauiores experimur,superstitionem foucntibus ac augentibus ipsorum sacrificulis, ad quos etiam non parvus ex terræ suæ sanctæ, quam vocant, vendicione quæstus redundat, ita sibi viuis ac mortuis factis vectigalibus & tributariis.
units.tr: Concerning the burial of which we are speaking here, it should be understood that many strangers are meant, who, though not natives of Judea, gathered from various religions into that great city of Jerusalem: some for the sake of trade, others to worship at Jerusalem. That this had happened more than once in earlier times the sacred history bears witness, in the records of Daniel and Nehemiah, where the Lord repeatedly compelled the very Gentiles to worship the God of the Hebrews and to implore his help. Moreover, as the calling of the Gentiles drew nearer, that light was gradually dawning on the world, as is sufficiently clear from Acts chapter 2 and from the profane histories themselves. Yet these good priests received gifts and offerings from whomsoever was alive, and yet, since they considered themselves far holier than others, though they were spurious sons of Abraham, as the Lord describes them (Matt. 12.41), they thought it a matter of religion to commit to the earth the same burial that they gave to native Jews. Indeed, although the whole earth is the Lord's, and the dividing wall of partition has been broken down by the preaching of the Gospel (Eph. 2.14), if it should happen that Jews and Turks are mingled with Christians in the same city, the very order of things seems to call for some distinction of places for the burial of each. Provided, however, that a method is observed and all superstition is absent. In this matter, however, we experience our Roman Catholics as more grievous opponents than ourselves, since their little priests foster and increase superstition, and from the sale of what they call the Holy Land a considerable profit flows to them too, thus making themselves tax-collectors and tributaries of both the living and the dead.

units.la: Cæterum, vt magno in pretio apud nos sepulturam esse oportet, non tantum docente nos natura magnum inter hominis mortui corpus & bestiæ cadauer interesse discrimen: sed maximè propter spem resurrectionis: hoc ipsum testante voce Κοιμητήριον inter Christianos iampridem vsitatissima: fatendum etiam est
units.tr: Moreover, just as burial ought to be held in high esteem among us, not only because nature teaches us that there is a great difference between the body of a dead man and the carcass of a beast, but chiefly because of the hope of resurrection, which the word κοιμητήριον [cemetery], long in common use among Christians, itself testifies, it must also be admitted

units.la: Verus usus & contra abusus sepulturarum. est magnos in eam abusus irrepsisse, alios humanis quidem affectibus, erga parentes & defunctos amicos, sed omnem modum excedentibus: alios, eorum ambitione qui apud posteros sui nominis propagandi nimium cupidi fuerunt: alios denique vana superstitione & stultis devotionibus. Quibus facile obviam ibitur, modestia & simplicitate, & quaecunque ad aedificationem faciunt observatis, pompa omni vanaque ambitione valere iussa, nostros ob oculos semper versante morte, quae satis unica quantula sint hominum corpuscula testatur: denique sincera coram Deo & hominibus humilitate & simplicitate sic humo commendatis mortuorum corporibus, hanc esse viduarum & orphanorum aliorumque tunc indigentium consolationem sciamus, quod unum ex praecipuis capitibus in Christianorum sepulturis & parentalibus observandum est. Faxit Deus ut de istis serio cogitemus.
units.tr: The true use and the abuses of burials. It is true that great abuses have crept into them: some arising indeed from human feelings toward parents and dead friends, but exceeding every measure; others from the ambition of those who were too eager to propagate their name among posterity; and finally others from vain superstition and foolish devotions. These may easily be met, if we observe modesty and simplicity, and whatever contributes to edification; if we bid farewell to all pomp and vain ambition, keeping death always before our eyes, which sufficiently testifies how small and frail human bodies are. Finally, if the bodies of the dead are committed to the earth in this way, with sincere humility and simplicity before God and men, we should know that this is a consolation for widows and orphans and others in need at that time, which is one of the chief points to be observed in Christian burials and funeral feasts. May God grant that we consider these things seriously.

units.la: HOMILIA decimaoctaua.
units.tr: Homily 18.

units.la: MATTH. 27.
units.tr: MATT. 27.

units.la: 1. Mane autem quum esset, consilium ceperunt omnes primarij Sacerdotes & Seniores populi aduersus Iesum, vt eum morte multarent.
units.tr: 1. Now when it was morning, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus, to put him to death.

units.la: 2. Et vinctum eum abduxerunt ac tradiderunt Pontio Pilato praesidi.
units.tr: 2. And when they had bound him, they led him away and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor.

units.la: MARC. 15.
units.tr: MARK 15.

units.la: 1. Statim autem mane consilio inito primarij Sacerdotes cum Senioribus & Scribis, totúsque consessus vinctum Iesum abduxerunt, tradiderúntque Pilato.
units.tr: 1. And straightway in the morning the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council, and bound Jesus, and led him away, and delivered him to Pilate.

units.la: LVC. 23.
units.tr: LUKE 23.

units.la: 1. Tunc surgens vniuersa multitudo eorum, duxit eum ad Pilatum.
units.tr: 1. And the whole multitude of them arose, and led him unto Pilate.

units.la: 2. Coeperunt autem eum accusare, dicentes, Comperimus istum peruertere Gentem, & vetare tributa dare Caesari, dicendo se Christum (id est) Regem esse.
units.tr: 2. And they began to accuse him, saying: We found this fellow perverting the nation, and forbidding to give tribute to Caesar, saying that he himself is Christ, a King.

units.la: IOH. 18.
units.tr: JOHN 18.

units.la: 28. Ducunt ergo Iesum à Caiapha in Praetorium: erat autem mane, & ipsi non introierunt in Praetorium ne polluerentur, sed vt ederent Pascha.
units.tr: 28. Then led they Jesus from Caiaphas unto the hall of judgment: and it was early; and they themselves went not into the judgment hall, lest they should be defiled, but that they might eat the passover.

units.la: Exiuit
units.tr: He went out

units.la: 29. Exiit ergo Pilatus ad eos, & dixit, Quam accusationem adfertis aduersus hominem istum?
units.tr: 29. Pilate then went out unto them, and said: What accusation bring ye against this man?

units.la: 30. Responderunt & dixerunt ei, Nisi iste esset facinorosus, non tradidissemus eum tibi.
units.tr: 30. They answered and said unto him: If he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up unto thee.

units.la: 31. Dicit ergo eis Pilatus, accipite eum vos, & secundum Legem vestram condemnate eum. Itaque Iudæi dixerunt ei, Nobis non licet occidere quenquam.
units.tr: 31. Then said Pilate unto them: Take ye him, and judge him according to your law. The Jews therefore said unto him: It is not lawful for us to put any man to death.

units.la: 32. Vt sermo Iesu impleretur quem dixerat, significans qua morte futurum erat vt moreretur.
units.tr: 32. That the saying of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spake, signifying what death he should die.

units.la: ISI Caiaphas cum suis assessoribus, omnis quantumlibet effrenis peruersitatis fines transiliisset, indignissimeque illæ modis omnibus contumeliæ quibus affectus fuerat Christus, & immanis illa proteruus aduersus rerum quemlibet agendi ratio, satis superque libidinem istorum explere debuisset. Sed non ita facile Satanæ qui semel se manciparunt renuntiant, eiusque se laqueis eripiunt. Nam illis contra sic imperat, vt eos ad suum libitum tanquam vilissima mancipia cogat. 2. Tim. 2. 26. Quòd si ad impios tam pertinaces ad malum efficiendos tanta Satanæ vis est, annon longè maiorem esse oportet Spiritus S. in nobis ad bonum constanter persequendum efformandis? Et ex hac certè potissimum nota veros Dei filios à spuriis dignoscimus, quòd in fide semper augescentes, benefaciendo nunquam segnescunt. Heb. 6. 12. Sed hic, vt in hac historia tota, nobis est altius, ad Dei nimirum in salutis suorum dispensatione prouidentiam assurgendum. Etsi enim Deus cum horum instrumentorum prauitate nihil habet commune, nihil tamen hic factum fuit, quod non iam inde ab omni aeuo decretum fuerit vt fieret, Act. 4. 28. quatenus videlicet hoc toto negotio quod hic geritur, salutis & redemptionis nostrae mysterium continetur. Quum igitur coram iusto Dei tribunali pro peccatis nostris plena satisfactio requiratur, quicquid adhuc a Caiapha & ipsius adeclis Christus perpessus erat, nondum ad nos plene Deo reconciliandos satisfaciebat. Erat enim morte Deus placandus, ac proinde necesse fuit a Caiapha ad Pilatum abduci Christum, vt plene pro nobis Deo satisfieret. Hinc factum vt istorum magis magisque malitia crescente, nec tamen ipsis desiderium suum explere valentibus, quod illis per Romanos non liceret capitalia iudicia exercere, Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum ad Pilatum Tyberij Caesaris tum Romanum Imperium obtinentis in Iudaea procuratorem vinctum adduxerint, idque summo mane, vt diserte scribitur, quum totam noctem insomnem, & quod est temporis a summo diluculo ad ipsum mane, Christo falsis testimoniis & calumniis obruendo traduxissent, vt nominatim commemoratur. Luc. 22. 66.
units.tr: Caiaphas, with his assessors, had already overstepped the bounds of whatever unbridled wickedness one might imagine; and the most unworthy insults by which Christ had been treated in every way, together with that savage and insolent manner of conducting affairs, ought to have been more than enough to satisfy their lust. But those who have once surrendered themselves to Satan do not easily renounce him or escape his snares. For he commands them in such a way as to drive them at his pleasure like the most worthless slaves (2 Tim. 2:26). If Satan has such power over impious men so obstinate in doing evil, ought not the Holy Spirit to have far greater power in us, to form us to pursue what is good constantly? And certainly from this mark above all we distinguish the true sons of God from the spurious: that, always growing in faith, they never grow slack in doing good (Heb. 6:12). But here, as throughout this whole history, we must rise higher, namely to the providence of God in the dispensation of the salvation of his people. For although God has nothing in common with the wickedness of these instruments, nothing was done here which had not been decreed from all eternity to be done (Acts 4:28), inasmuch as the mystery of our salvation and redemption is contained in this whole business that is going on here. Since, therefore, full satisfaction for our sins is required before the just tribunal of God, whatever Christ had so far suffered from Caiaphas and his adherents did not yet satisfy fully for reconciling us to God. For God had to be appeased by death, and therefore it was necessary for Christ to be led from Caiaphas to Pilate, so that full satisfaction might be made to God for us. Hence it came about that, as their malice grew more and more, and yet they could not achieve their desire, since the Romans did not allow them to exercise capital judgments, they brought our Lord Jesus Christ, bound, to Pilate, procurator in Judea under Tiberius Caesar, who then held the Roman empire; and this at the very early morning, as is plainly written, when they had spent the whole night sleepless, and the time from the first dawn to the morning itself in overwhelming Christ with false testimonies and calumnies, as is named expressly (Luke 22:66).

units.la: Haec autem circumstantia minime leuiter praetercunda, quū vel hac re maxime sese Magistragiftratus commendent, fi nó solùm suum cui-que ius reddant,sed etiam ea qua par est vtan-tur diligentia,quum sæpissimè fit in mora pe-riculum, cúmque multis longè melius agatur, fi causa statim excidant, quàm eandem fi ferò nimis iudicio vincant. Hanc porro fedulita-tem in veris Iudicibus Dei timor cum æquita-tis amore coniunctus efficiat oportet,quam in impiis excitauit animi impotentia: sceleratis istis iudicibus alioquin aduersus eos furrectu-ris,qui tamen iusti iudices haberi volùt. Chri-ftus igitur à Caiapha ad Pilatum abducitur, quod etiam hodie in prouerbium abiit, vbi quis,siue Iudices in iure dicundo fgniores na-ctus, siue id actoris malitia contingat, ab ali-qua fede ad aliam remittitur, donec tandem ex iniquo iudice in iniquiorem, tanquam ex Charybdi in Scyllam incidat.
units.tr: This circumstance must not be passed over lightly, since magistrates especially commend themselves by this very thing, if they not only render to each his right but also use the diligence that is fitting, since very often danger lies in delay, and it goes far better when cases are settled at once than when they are won by a judgment delayed too long. The fear of God, joined with love of equity, ought to produce this diligence in true judges, which in the wicked was stirred up by the unruliness of their minds, since those wicked judges would otherwise rise against those who nevertheless wish to be regarded as just judges. Christ, then, is led from Caiaphas to Pilate, a thing which has even today passed into a proverb: when someone, whether because the judges in giving judgment proved ignorant or negligent, or because of the malice of the plaintiff, is sent back from one seat to another, until at last he falls from an unjust judge into a more unjust one, as from Charybdis into Scylla.

units.la: Hic porro nobis est rursus ad diuinam illam prouidentiam aflurgendum, sic iniquorum i-ftorum Iudicum vtentem peruersitate, vt per illos nihil minus cogitantes maximum nostræ salutis mysterium peregerit. Vt enim Christus Ecclesiam, id est cœtum electorum ad salutem mortis suæ beneficio adduceret, non tantùm ex vetere populo, sed etiam ex cæteris orbis terrarum gentibus collectam,secundum promissionem Abrahamo factam, Genef. 12. 3. & Rom. 4. v. 13. & hi omnes arguerentur totum istud à mera Dei gratia & misericordia prosi-cisci, Christum tum à Iudæis tum à Gentibus repudiari damnarìque oportuit: Pilato videlicet Maximum tunc orbis terrarum Imperatorem repraesentante : sic Domino cunctos sub peccato concludete, vt nemo nisi per misericordiam seruaretur, quod argumentu Paulus Rom.ii.copiose persequitur. Tantum abest igitur vt abiectus hic Christi Itatus & opprobrium quod volens subiit, & de quo saepe suos discipulos praemonuerat, deterrere nos ab illo debeat, vt contrà ex eo quòd eousque se demisit, vt apud iudicis & quidem prophani tribunal damnari capitis poena sustinuerit, sancta illa confidentia promanet, qua fit vt eius vinculis à captiuitate peccati & mortis liberati, & eius opprobrio summo decore cohonestati, eius denique condemnatione ab omni reatu absoluti, ad thronum illum patris nostri coelestis accedamus intrepidi.
units.tr: Here again we must rise to that divine providence which so used the perversity of these unjust judges that, through men thinking of nothing less, it carried out the greatest mystery of our salvation. For in order that Christ might bring the Church, that is, the assembly of the elect, to salvation by the benefit of his death, gathered not only from the old people but also from the other nations of the world, according to the promise made to Abraham (Gen. 12:3; Rom. 4:13), and that all these might be taught that this whole matter proceeds from pure grace and mercy of God, it was necessary that Christ be rejected and condemned both by the Jews and by the Gentiles, Pilate, of course, representing the then greatest emperor of the world. Thus the Lord shut all under sin, so that no one would be saved except through mercy, which argument Paul pursues at length in Romans 11. So far, then, is this humiliation of Christ, and the reproach which he willingly undertook, and about which he often forewarned his disciples, from being a reason to frighten us away from him, that on the contrary, from the fact that he so lowered himself as to suffer the punishment of capital condemnation before the tribunal of a judge, and indeed a profane one, there springs that holy confidence by which, freed by his bonds from the captivity of sin and death, adorned with the highest honour by his reproach, and finally absolved from all guilt by his condemnation, we may approach that throne of our heavenly Father fearlessly.

units.la: Age vero nunc quam isti iudicij formam sequuti sint, & quomodo hanc egerint, dispiciamus. Ac primùm attendite bonos istos Iudices, quibus quum paulò ante nulla fuerit religio, vitam innocentis à proditore numerata pecunia redimere, testes adornare, tam iniquè cum eo quem integrum esse, vitae sceleriique purum, ipsi sibi nullius non sceleris conscij, cognoscebant, agere non puduerat, nunc scilicet religione teneri, quominus Pilati tectū, quod Praetorium dicebatur à Praetore, qui hic improprie pro prouinciae procuratore sumitur, subeant, ne, vt inquit Iohannes, polluti, domum nimirum incircumcisi ingressi, à sacro Pascharis epulo, ex Lege pollutorum, Num.9.10.arcerentur.
units.tr: Come now, let us examine what form of judgment they followed, and how they conducted it. And first observe those good judges, who, although a little before they had no scruple about buying the life of an innocent man from a traitor with counted money, and about hiring witnesses, and were not ashamed to act so unjustly toward him whom they knew to be upright, pure in life and innocent of crime, while they themselves were conscious of every kind of crime, now, of course, are held by religion, so that they will not enter the house of Pilate, which was called the Praetorium, after the praetor, a name here used improperly for the procurator of the province. For fear, as John says, of being defiled, namely by entering an uncircumcised house, they would be kept from the sacred feast of the Passover, according to the law concerning the defiled (Num. 9:10).

units.la: Sed quædam hic,quòd ad historiam attinet, suboritur difficultas. Tres enim,vno ore,Euangelistæ Christum cum suis discipulis pridie eius dici quàm caperetur sub vesperam, proximo videlicet azymorum ineunte die Pascha celebrasse commemorant, Matth.26.17.Marc.14.12.Luc.22.7.&15.de quo tamen celebrando ilti postridie laborabant. Sciendum itaque est fuisse hanc vnam ex traditionibus maiorum, qua Iudæi quotiescunque primus dies Azymorum qui festus erat, à vespera quinti diei hebdomadis, quem nos Iouis diem vocamus, incipiebat, & in vesperam sequentis diei, qui Veneris dicitur, desinebat, cum agni Paschæ in posterum sabbatum reiiciebant, vt duarum sese proximè subsequentium feriarum concurrum vitarent, quarum erat obseruatio difficilis, eò quòd diebus istis cibum etiam coquere vetarentur, Exod.16.23.&35.3. Feriarum autem legem longius etiam trahebant isti,adeò superstitiosè vt Christum etiam ipsum tanquam Sabbati violatorem sint calumniati, quòd ægrotum sabbato sanasset : immo etiam quòd ipsius discipuli sabbato spicas auulsas manibus confricantes comedissent, Matth.12.2.quòd denique morbo confectum quendam, pristinæ sanitati redditum iussisset in humeros lectulum attollere.Iohan.5.10.&16. Sic igitur Iudæi suis traditionibus Legem Domini transgredi consueuerant,quas quum Christus, non minus quàm Pharisaicas lotiones, Marc.7.1. nollet imitari, Pascha rite ex Dei patris instituto, quo die & tempore Lex ferebat, celebrauit.
units.tr: But here a difficulty arises as far as the history is concerned. For the three Evangelists, with one voice, record that Christ celebrated the Passover with his disciples on the evening before the day on which he was taken, that is, at the beginning of the day of unleavened bread which was next, and yet they were labouring on the following day to celebrate it (Matt. 26:17; Mark 14:12; Luke 22:7, 15). It must therefore be known that there was one of the traditions of the fathers by which the Jews, whenever the first day of unleavened bread, which was a festival, began at evening on the fifth day of the week, which we call Thursday, and ended at evening of the following day, called Friday, they postponed the paschal lambs to the following Sabbath, so that they might avoid the coincidence of two consecutive festival days, the observance of which was difficult, because on those days they were forbidden even to cook food (Exod. 16:23; 35:3). The Jews, however, extended the law of rest even further, so superstitiously that they accused Christ himself as a violator of the Sabbath, because he had healed a sick man on the Sabbath; indeed also because his disciples, rubbing ears of corn in their hands on the Sabbath, had eaten them (Matt. 12:2); and finally because he had ordered a certain man, worn down by disease and restored to his former health, to take up his bed on his shoulders (John 5:10, 16). Thus the Jews had been accustomed to transgress the law of the Lord by their own traditions, which Christ, no less than the Pharisaic washings, was unwilling to imitate (Mark 7:1); and so he celebrated the Passover rightly, according to the institution of God the Father, on the day and at the time the law prescribed.

units.la: Ac certè quum Dominus in vetere fœdere tam expresse præscripsisset, non tantum quidnam, sed etiam quibus mensibus, diebus & horis agendum esset, illud de quo hic agitur præcise & ex præscripto peragi oportuit, ab eo præsertim qui iustitiam omnem impleturus aduenerat. Matth.3.15. Quum verò totius istius ceremonialis cultus seruitus sit Christi aduentu abrogata, vt qui fuerit eius veritas & substantia, Act.15.10. & Colos.2.16. necessario fatendum est quæstionem istam de tempore Paschatis celebrandi ab Ecclesia Christiana, (quam quum olim in Ecclesiam nonnulli iniecissent, factum est illorum incogitantia, vt nisi serpenti malo Irenæi Lugdunensis Episcopi doctissimi prudentia aduersus Victoris decimi tertij Episcopi Romani imprudentiam mature fuisset allatum remedium, iam tum oriens totus ab occidente discerperetur) rem esse mirum in modum pudendam: quæque plus satis tectetur quàm non absre Paulus 2. Thessal. 2. verf. 7. iam tum peragi mysterium iniquitatis Ecclesiam præmonuerit: quum tamen vix ducentesimus nonagesimus annus à Christi natiuitate tunc agetur.
