units.tr: Certainly, since the Lord had prescribed in the Old Covenant so expressly not only what was to be done but also in which months, on which days and at which hours, this matter that we are discussing had to be carried out exactly and according to that prescription, especially by him who had come to fulfil all righteousness. Matt. 3.15. But since the whole ceremonial worship has been abolished by the coming of Christ, who is its truth and substance, Acts 15.10 and Col. 2.16, it must be admitted that the question of when the Christian Church should celebrate Easter is a most shameful matter. (When some people, through their carelessness, first introduced this question into the Church, unless the wise foresight of Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons, had promptly applied a remedy against the imprudence of Victor the Thirteenth, Bishop of Rome, the whole East would already have been torn apart from the West, like a serpent.) The matter is more concealed than it should be, though Paul, 2 Thess. 2.7, had warned the Church that the mystery of iniquity was already at work, even though it was scarcely the 190th year after Christ's birth at that time.

units.la: Sed hoc minus adhuc excusandum, quidquid à sapientibus tentatum ad istam controuersiam penitus abolendam fuerat effi-ccere
units.tr: But this is even less excusable: whatever the wise had attempted to abolish this controversy altogether, they failed to achieve.

units.la: Concilium Nicenum tanti macere non potuisse quominus ad Nicenum vsque Concilium primum ea serperet, in quo centum quadraginta circiter post annis tota hæc decisa fuit controuersia, nitentibus hoc maximè fundamento patribus, quòd in Christianismum minimè Iudaismus esset introducendus, licet Asiaticæ Ecclesiæ auctoritatem Apostolorum obtenderent.
units.tr: The Council of Nicaea could not, despite its great authority, prevent the question from creeping on until the First Council of Nicaea, where this whole controversy was settled about one hundred and forty years later. The Fathers relied chiefly on this foundation: that Judaism must in no way be introduced into Christianity, although the churches of Asia appealed to the authority of the Apostles.

units.la: Sed ita tamen decisa quæstio fuit(absit autem vt vel tantillum de auctoritate sanæ doctrinæ aduersus Arrianos in eo Concilio celeberrimo stabilitæ quod dicturus sum detra-hat)vt istius mali radix, superstitiosa videlicet quædam festi quod Paschatis vocant celebrandi necessitas minimè fuerit abolita. Quis enim eorum qui quibus in rebus sit verus positus Christianismus,ex iis quæ disertè scribit Apostolus Coloss. 3. 16. intelligunt,verum esse, ac ne verisimile quidem sibi persuaderi patiatur, à Christianis fuisse, præsertim Apostolorum temporibus,memoriam resurrectionis Domini non minùs quàm eius Natiuitatis & Ascen-sionis,Sanctisque Spiritus missionis, sic obser-uatam, vt aliquam temporum & dierum di-stinctionem in Ecclesiam Christianâ reuehe-rent, & Lunæ cursum obseruari vellent, sicut olim Pascha Iudæis erat constitutum? Aio igitur liberè quod sentio, nempe sicut Dominus Paschatis diem illum ipsum solennem esse voluit Iudæis quo sunt ex Ægypto educti, nulla habita ratione in quemcunque septimanæ diem incidisset, ita quum Christianorum Pascha non alium in finem institutum fuerit quàm ad memoriam Domini celebrandam, longè futurum fuisse & fore adhuc consultius & ab omni superstitione remotius, si ab illo ipso die recurrente quo resurrexit non recederetur, siue in Dominicum siue in alium diem incidat, siue Plenilunium siue Nouilunium sit, quod in Natalis Domini die festo factum adhuc fuisse videmus, non observatis diebus, nec Lunæ habita ratione: aut saltem ad multarum feriarum effugiendum concursum, quæ & superstitionis plenæ sunt, & publicis commodis incommodæ, eiusmodi festi dies in proximum quemque diem Dominicum reiiciantur, ut hac ratione nec Lunatica festa, nec Lunaticum Christianismum haberemus: quod de reliquis etiam omnibus annuis diebus festis, quibus celebris alicuius facti Christi Domini nostri memoria retinetur, dictum velim, habita nihilominus locorum, temporum & personarum, quantam ad ædificationem adhiberi par est, ratione.
units.tr: But the question was settled in such a way (let it be far from me to detract even slightly from the authority of the sound doctrine established against the Arians at that most celebrated Council, which I am about to discuss) that the root of this evil, namely the superstitious necessity of celebrating the feast they call Easter, was by no means abolished. For who among those who understand, from what the Apostle writes plainly in Col. 3.16, in which things true Christianity consists, would allow himself to be persuaded, or even to think it likely, that Christians, especially in the time of the Apostles, observed the memory of the Lord's resurrection, no less than that of his nativity, ascension and the sending of the Holy Spirit, in such a way as to bring into the Christian Church some distinction of times and days, and wished the course of the moon to be observed, as Easter was once fixed for the Jews? I therefore say freely what I think: just as the Lord willed that the Passover be a solemn day for the Jews, on which they were led out of Egypt, with no regard to which day of the week it fell on, so, since the Christian Passover was instituted for no other purpose than to celebrate the memory of the Lord, it would have been and would still be far more advisable, and far more removed from all superstition, if we did not depart from that very day on which he rose again, whether it falls on the Lord's day or another day, whether it is a full moon or a new moon. We see that this was already done on the feast day of the Lord's Nativity, the days not being observed nor regard being had to the moon. Or at least, to avoid the crowding of many holidays, which are full of superstition and harmful to public convenience, such festival days should be moved to the nearest Lord's day, so that by this means we would have neither moon-dependent feasts nor a moon-dependent Christianity. I would wish the same said of all the other yearly festival days on which the memory of some deed of our Lord Jesus Christ is kept, nevertheless with due regard, as far as edification requires, to places, times and persons.

units.la: Quod vtinam Episcopi & pastores, pro tam sollicita & superstitiosa dierum festorum distinctione, qui in immensum excreuerunt, & verum patrum instituto penitus repugnant, vti iam pridem agitantur, sedulam nauassent operam in plebe fideliter erudienda, & ad Christi Domini nostri beneficiorum vsum revocanda. Sed quid agas? En abolito fine cuius causa talis illarum maximarum rerum commoratio fiebat, habemus Astrologicam & sollicitam licitam festorum, cùm mobilium, tum fixo- rum, quæ vocant, supputationem.
units.tr: Would that the bishops and ministers, instead of such anxious and superstitious distinction of festival days, which have grown beyond measure and are wholly contrary to the institution of the Fathers, as has long been urged, had devoted careful effort to instructing the people faithfully and recalling them to the use of the benefits of our Lord Jesus Christ. But what can one do? Now that the end for which such a dwelling upon those greatest matters was undertaken has been abolished, we have an astrological and anxious reckoning of feasts, both movable and so-called fixed.

units.la: Atque adeò nostro seculo bonus ille Papa Gregorius decimus tertius Kalendarij Chri-stianorum emendandi non ex eo sumpsit occasionem, quod maximè factum oportuit, vt motus orbium cœlestium ad multas humanæ vitæ res necessarij, propter neglectas aliquas intercalationes computentur, sed vt Paschatis festum ad illud ipsum tempus quod fuit quum habita est Synodus illa Nicena revocetur: quasi vero in talibus obseruatiunculis summa Christianæ religionis vertatur: quasiquespe- ciosò prætextu omnia in Dei Ecclesia κατὰ τάξιν gerendi 1. Cor. 4.10. nouus quidam Iudais- mus sit Christianis obtrudendus, noua distin- ctio dierum sastorum & nesastorum revocan- da: quasi denique nos ab illis cæremoniis Iu- daicis idcirco Christus asseruerit, vt nouis a- liis longè onerosioribus & maiore numero substitutis opprimeremur: qua de re quidam ex melioris notæ patribus iam olim ante ali- quot secula, sed frustra conquestus est.
units.tr: And so in our own age the good Pope Gregory XIII undertook to correct the Christian calendar, and he took his occasion not from what most needed doing, namely that the movements of the heavenly bodies, which are necessary for many matters of human life, be reckoned correctly despite some neglected intercalations, but so that the feast of Easter might be restored to the very time when that Nicene Synod was held. As if the sum of the Christian religion turned on such petty observances! As if, under the specious pretext of doing everything in the Church "in good order" [κατὰ τάξιν] (1 Cor. 4.10), a new Judaism were to be foisted on Christians and a new distinction of festive and non-festive days revived! As if, finally, Christ had freed us from those Jewish ceremonies only so that we might be burdened with other new ones, far more onerous and far more numerous in their place. Some of the more reputable Fathers complained of this long ago, some centuries back, but in vain.

units.la: Vt autem ad historiam nostram reuertamur, quòd ad Iudæos attinet veritos incircumcisi domum subire, fatendum est sanè populum illum Israëliticum à reliquis Gentibus fuisse diuinitus separatum, ac proinde quum reliquæ Gentes nullam dierum nec ciborum distinctionem à Lege Mosis præscriptam obser- uarent, Iudæos si Gentium consuetudine fa- miliarius ad mutuum vsque conuictum vs E. j.
units.tr: But to return to our history: as for the Jews, who feared to enter the house of the uncircumcised, it must certainly be admitted that that Israelite people was divinely set apart from the other nations. Therefore, since the other nations observed no distinction of days or foods prescribed by the Law of Moses, had the Jews been too familiar with them, living together as the Gentiles did, they could easily have fallen into many legal pollutions (to which also belongs that complaint of certain people against Peter, Acts 11.3). The Jews therefore had to take the greatest care in this matter, lest they be polluted by such fellowship. But what they feared was pure superstition, as if the air itself, or the walls of Pilate's house, were polluted. So it must be said that they had a special reason connected with the Feast; otherwise they would never have entered their governor's house, and I do not think it likely that they observed this rule.

units.la: Superstitione festi Paschatis Gregorius 13. fouet.
units.tr: Gregory XIII fosters superstition about the feast of Passover.

units.la: Dei præcepta in superstitiones à Iudeis transformata. fuissent, facilè in Legales multas pollutiones incidere potuisse (quo etiam referri querelam illam nonnullorum aduersus Petrum. Act. 11. 3.oportet) ideòque Iudæis hac in re summam sollicitudinem adhibendam fuisse, ne illorum conuictu polluerentur. Sed quod isti metue-runt, mera fuit superstitio, quasi aut aër ipse scilicet, aut Pilati parietes essent polluti. Rationem itaque peculiarem Festi habuisse illos dicendum est: alioqui nunquam fuissent illis sui Gubernatoris ædes adeundæ, quod ab ipsis obseruatum fuisse mihi quidem verisimile non videtur.
units.tr: Once God's precepts had been turned by the Jews into superstitions, it was easy for them to fall into many legal defilements (to which that complaint of certain people against Peter also belongs, Acts 11:3). Therefore the Jews had to take the greatest care in this matter, lest they be defiled by contact with others. But what they feared was pure superstition, as though the air itself, or the walls of Pilate's house, were polluted. So we must say that they had a peculiar regard for the feast; otherwise they would never have avoided entering their governor's house, and I do not think it likely that they observed this for any other reason.

units.la: Quid autem præ istis de monachalibus illis superstitionibus istorum sentias, qui se Religiosorum nomine commendant, quasi cæteris summa quadam pietatis perfectione præstent, cuiusmodi sunt eximij illi Franciscani, Magistri sui Diui Francisci non absimiles discipuli, quibus quidem summa religio est auream monetam argenteam-ue summis digitis attingere, quos tamen non pudet totum orbem alienis sumptibus verbum Dei cauponando peruagari, voto quo se ad desidiam adstringere, quum tamen quidam ex veteribus illis celeberrimus famosissimúsque iam olim dixerit, & scripto sit testatus Monachum manibus nō laborantem pro prædone habendum. Sed quid dicas de sanctis illis catamitis Carthusianis, qui se tantopere fœminas abhorrere profitentur, adeò vt (rem gestam dico) quum nostra memoria Regina quædam curiosior ipsorum cœnocœnobium inuisisset, stramine adulto vestigia ipsius lustrarint?
units.tr: Now, what do you think of the monastic superstitions of those who commend themselves under the name of Religious, as if they excelled everyone else in a certain supreme perfection of piety? Such are those outstanding Franciscans, disciples not unlike their master, St Francis. For them the height of religion is to touch gold or silver coin with the tips of their fingers, yet they are not ashamed to roam the whole world at other people's expense, peddling the Word of God like hucksters, while binding themselves by a vow to idleness. Yet one of the ancients, very famous and notorious, once said and testified in writing that a monk who does not labour with his hands should be regarded as a robber. But what shall we say of those holy catamites, the Carthusians, who profess such horror of women that (I speak of a real event) when a rather inquisitive queen of our own time visited their monastery, they swept away her footprints with straw?

units.la: Sed de sordibus istis hactenus dictum esto. Denique docemur hoc exemplo, quantum geminæ istæ pestes, quasi sorores, superstitio & hypocrisis in hominum cerebro conceptæ ad illos excerebrandos valeant. Ecquis enim sceleratis istis magis vesanus, qui nulla tot tamque atrocium scelerum cura tacti, sibi tamen persuaserunt sanctè se nihilominus posse Pascha, quo fœdus illud cum populo suo initum Deus sanciebat, celebrare, si ab incircuncisi illius ædium ingressu, quem tamen nefariæ suæ libidinis ministrum esse cogebat, abstinerent? Quòd si forsan hæc illorum mens non fuit, sed sanctitatis quadam specie populo se commendare studuerunt, quid aliud cit apertum esse Dei contemptorem, si hoc non est?
units.tr: But let enough be said of these filthy things. Finally, we are taught by this example how greatly these two twin plagues, like sisters, superstition and hypocrisy, conceived in the brains of men, can serve to addle them. For who is more mad than these wretches, who, untouched by any care for so many and so atrocious crimes, nevertheless persuaded themselves that they could celebrate with a clean conscience the Passover by which God sanctioned the covenant made with his people, if they abstained from entering the house of that uncircumcised man, whom they nevertheless compelled to be the minister of their wicked lust? But if perhaps this was not their intention, and they strove to commend themselves to the people under some appearance of holiness, what else is this, if not a plain contempt of God?

units.la: Hinc autem semper recidant necesse est, quicunque sibi ipsis suēque conscientiæ quicquid iuris libuit præscribunt: cuius rei testes sunt falsæ maiorum superstitiones, Deos etiā quos adorabant palàm irridentium: testes denique sunt qui nobis hodie suas Traditiones tanto-pere venditant: quum contrà qui ex solo Dei verbo tum sese nosse, tum de rebus statuere, tū etiam vitam instituere didicerunt, simul etiam & superstitionem à vera Religione, & veram Christianismi professionem à falsa & fucata, fidem denique vero suo nixam fundamento, à fanaticis aliis omnibus opnionibus facilè discernant.
units.tr: Those who prescribe for themselves and their own consciences whatever right they please must always fall back into this. Witnesses to it are the false superstitions of our forebears, who openly mocked the gods they worshipped; and finally there are those who today so eagerly peddle their own traditions to us. Whereas those who have learned from God's Word alone both to know themselves, to decide about things, and also to order their lives, easily distinguish superstition from true religion, and the true profession of Christianity from a false and painted one, and, finally, faith resting on its true foundation from all other fanatical opinions.

units.la: Porrò sicut extremum istud, Superstitio vi- delicet, quæ tandem in apertam idololatriam definit, magnopere vitandum est, sic est diligenter cauendum, ne in aliud extremum incurratur, in quod plerunque incidunt, qui parum attente quibuscum versentur, consideràt, tandemque se ipsos sibi malum & exitium arcessiuisse, sed sero nimis experiuntur. Ad hæc autem vitanda pericula extant à sapientibus huius seculi non pauca præclarè dicta, è quibus etiam vnum Apostolus dignum existimauit quod suis scriptis insereret, 1.Cor.15.33. Bonos nempe mores mala commercia corrumpere: quod quàm verum sit vel ipsa nos huius loci incolas multorum tristissimorum exemplorum experientia docet. Atque vtinam illud iter ingressi maturè pedem referant. Quum vero satis superque sint hæc in re, ideoque in deligendis quibuscum versentur prouidi qui sunt ad rem faciendam attentiores, & non contemnenda consilia capiant, quum de captando lucro quæritur, in ilt iusmodi rebus abhit vt diutius hæreant, sed ea quæ conscientiam spectant, & nostri sunt muneris explicabo. Enimvero ii vt vno verbo dicam, huius seculi sapientes rebus suis cauere tam sollicitè norunt, quanto maior eorum est habenda ratio quæ conscientiam lædunt, & vitam æternam vel adferunt vel auferunt?
units.tr: Moreover, just as that extreme, namely superstition, which at last ends in open idolatry, must be greatly avoided, so one must take care not to fall into the other extreme, into which those fall who pay too little careful attention to the company they keep, and who find out too late that they have brought evil and ruin upon themselves. To avoid these dangers there are not a few well-said sayings of the wise of this age, and the Apostle thought one of them worth inserting in his writings: 1 Cor. 15.33, that bad company corrupts good morals. How true this is, the experience of many very sad examples teaches even us who live in this place. And would that those who have entered that path would turn back in time. But since these things have been said sufficiently and more than sufficiently, and since those who are prudent in choosing their companions, attentive to their business, and ready to take sound advice when seeking gain should not linger longer on such matters, I will explain what concerns conscience and belongs to our office. Indeed, to put it in one word, the wise of this age know how anxiously to guard their possessions; how much greater care should be taken over those things which injure conscience and either bring eternal life or take it away?

units.la: Ad hunc autem fine à Deo conditi quum cuncti simus, vt illi tum corpore tum animo seruiamus, quam tandem excusationem apud Deum præteprætexeant, quibus summa sapientia est quouis loco, & cum quibuslibet sine vllo discrimine versari? Et tamen horum alij tantam sibi prudentiam arrogant, vt cum corruptissimis quibusque cohabitare se posse iactitent, nunquam nec in moribus, nec in religione corrumpendis, haud secus quàm siquis secum carbonariis vicitare posse fuligine nunquam inficiendum profiteretur: alij vero cum aperto quoque Dei contemptu non verentur sese Christi cum publicanis conuersantis exemplo tegere, & Pauli Athenis inter idola & idololatras positi, atque adeo eiusdem dicto abuti profitentis sese omnibus omnia factum, vt omnes lucrifaceret. Quòd autem ad primos illos attinet, testes ipsorum insipientis sapientiæ sunto quæ mox ipsis eueniunt, nempe vt mox iis similes quibuscum versantur, aut etiam iis deteriores euadant, illius nimirum obliti aut etiam penitus ignari quod scribit Ioh. cp. 2. 10. Siquis venit ad vos, & hanc doctrinam non adfert, ne recipite eum domum, nec Aue ei dicite. Qui enim dicit illi Aue, communicat eius operibus malis: tantum abest vt arctior vlla societas iniri cum illis possit, veluti matrimonij & cæterorum istiusmodi: Etenim, vt inquit hisce de rebus Apostolus, Quæ communicatio Lucis cum tenebris? 2. Cor. 6. 14. Excipe tamen mutua necessaria huius vitæ commercia, quatenus quidem illa citra offendiculi occasione possunt ex Apostoli regula 1. Cor. 5. 10. exerceri. Illis vero quos apertos numinis irrisores dixi-
units.tr: Since we have all been created by God for this very end, that we should serve him in body and in soul, what excuse could they put forward before God, those for whom the highest wisdom is to live in any place and with anyone at all without distinction? And yet some of them claim such great prudence for themselves that they boast they can live with the most corrupt of men without ever being corrupted in morals or religion, just as if someone professed he could live among charcoal-burners and never be blackened by their soot. Others, with open contempt for God, do not shrink from covering themselves with the example of Christ, who associated with tax collectors, and of Paul, who stood among idols and idolaters at Athens, and who professed that he had become all things to all men that he might gain all. As for the first kind, let the things that soon befall them be witnesses to their foolish wisdom: namely, that they soon become like those with whom they associate, or even worse, forgetting, or indeed utterly ignorant of, what John writes, Ioh. cp. 2. 10: If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house, nor say Hail to him. For whoever says Hail to him shares in his evil works. So far is any closer fellowship to be entered into with such people, such as marriage and others of that kind. For, as the Apostle says on these matters, "What fellowship has light with darkness?" 2 Cor. 6.14. Yet exclude the mutual dealings necessary for this life, insofar as these can be carried on without occasion of offence, according to the Apostle's rule, 1 Cor. 5.10.

units.la: E. iij.
units.tr: E. iij.

units.la: mus, equidem meliorem mentem precari ma-lo, quàm cum huiuscemodi prophanis lon-giorem disputationem instituere: Hoc tamen vnum velim ex me intelligant, túcipsos Chri-fti & Apoltolorum exempla quibus vtuntur verè imitaturos, quando peritorum medicorū instar, morbis vitiorum laborantes inuestiga-bunt, remedium illis, non autem fomenta morborum allaturi, vel saltem cam cautione qua opus est ne illorum contagione infi-ciantur.
units.tr: ...mus. I would rather pray for a better mind for those I have called open mockers of God than enter into a lengthy dispute with such profane men. Yet this one thing I would have them understand from me: that they will truly imitate the examples of Christ and the Apostles, which they use, when, like skilled physicians, they investigate those who labour under the diseases of vice, bringing a remedy to them and not fomentations for the diseases, or at least with the caution that is needed, lest they be infected by their contagion.

units.la: Deinceps historia narrat, Pilatum quum a-nimaduerteret egregios istos homines ab æ-dium suarum ingressu abhorrere, vltrò ad i-pfos egressum, sciscitatúmque eccuius crimi-nis reum illum accusarent. Est autem in tantæ auctoritatis viro obseruanda summa ista mo-deratio: cui etsi erat ignominiosum quòd i-pfius æ… dium ingressum eflent isti dedignati, nihilominus tamen eò vsque fe demisit, vt ad illos ipse vltrò accederet, fiue nequid in tanto tumultu peius contingeret metuens, fiue na-tura sic æquus & benignus, summo tum hac in re, tum in hoc toto reliquo negotio Iudæorū dedecore, qui sese Dei populum esse iactabat.
units.tr: Next the history tells that Pilate, perceiving that these distinguished men shrank from entering his house, went out of his own accord to them and asked what crime they accused the man of. In a man of such authority this great moderation is to be observed. Although it was disgraceful to him that they disdained to enter his house, nevertheless he humbled himself so far as to approach them himself, either fearing something worse in so great a tumult, or being by nature so fair and kind. This was to the great dishonour of the Jews, both in this matter and in the whole rest of the business, who boasted that they were God's people.

units.la: Verùm ex iis quæ de Pilati moribus fcripferût historici longè verifimilius est illum metu Iu-dæorum sese vsque adeò demisisse: quod omni-bus Magistratibus sua nescientibus vti auctò-ritate contingat oportet, nempe vt eos me-tuant à quibus metui oportuerat. Nihilomi-nus tamen principem virum comitas facili-tásque tásque cum grauitate coniuncta maximè decet. Sic enim Magistratus quidè decet munus suum honoratum reddere, vt tamen seueritatem à superbia plurimum abesse sciant.
units.tr: But from what the historians have written about Pilate's character, it is far more likely that he humbled himself so far out of fear of the Jews. This generally happens to all magistrates who, without knowing it, use their authority so that they fear those whom they ought to have made fear them. Nevertheless gentleness and affability joined with dignity especially befit a leading man. For thus it befits magistrates to render their office honourable, while yet knowing that severity is far removed from arrogance.

units.la: Porrò Iudæorum resposum summam ipsorum impudentiam magis ac magis patefacit.Primùm enim actorem oportet paratum adperagendum reum accedere. At isti perfri&tæfrontis homines iam tum Pilatum voluissentipsorum conscientiis acquiescentem, & præ-supponentem nunquam fuisse Iudæos reumaliquem nisi insignis alicuius facinoris conui-ctum ad ipsius tribunal adducturos, sententiam aduersus Christum, absque ampliore vlla inquisitione, ad ipsorum libidinē, ferre, ad quod tandem etiam ipsum coegerunt.Sed ista sic omnino contingere diuina voluit proui-dentia, vt totidem haberemus certissima illius integerrimæ Christi innocentiæ testimonia, non pro suis, quæ nulla fuerūt,sed pro nostris peccatis morientis. Summa igitur illorum & prorsus intoleranda tum hic, tum in hoc toto reliquo negotio fuit impudentia.
units.tr: Moreover the Jews' answer reveals more and more their great impudence. For first the accuser ought to come prepared to prosecute the accused. But these men, brazen-faced, were already then wishing Pilate to acquiesce in their consciences and to presuppose that the Jews would never bring anyone before his tribunal unless he were convicted of some notable crime, and to pass sentence against Christ at their pleasure, without any further inquiry; and to this they at last forced him. But divine providence willed that these things should happen in exactly this way, so that we might have so many most certain testimonies to the most upright innocence of Christ, who was dying not for his own sins, of which there were none, but for ours. Therefore the impudence of these men was great and utterly intolerable, both here and in the whole rest of the business.

units.la: Sed agedum altius etiam paulò causam i-stius ipsorum facti peruestigemus.Impotenternempe ferebant isti Romanorum iugum, exquo tandem ipsis vltimum exitium creatumest, quoniam inter alia sic erat ipsis quidemsua relicta sarta tecta religio & αὐτονομία, vt ta-men illis esset aliquatenus adempta ciuilis ad-ministratio, Romanis sibi capitalium causarum cognitionem seruantibus, quod in reli-
units.tr: But come, let us trace a little more deeply the cause of this deed of theirs. The Jews bore the yoke of the Romans impatiently, and from it their final destruction was at last brought about. For among other things, although their religion and [autonomia] were left to them intact and whole, nevertheless civil administration was in some measure taken from them, the Romans reserving to themselves the hearing of capital cases, as they were accustomed to do in the other provinces.

units.la: E. iiij. quis Prouinciis factitare consueuerant. Enigitur cur istam causae disquisitionem refugientes a Pilato postulent vt fecundum ea quae apud Caiaphan ex magni fynedrij sententia gesta fuerant, statim Christum ad poenam raperet, in quo tamen aduersus Christum capitis ferre sententiam ausi non fuerant, sed blasphemiae duntaxat crimine ex Lege sua tenen-ti, ac proinde morte dignum esse pronuntiarant, quem capitis poena damnaret Pilatus, cuius praeiudicij causam instituta rursus accusatione reddi a se oportere molestissime ferebant: quod tandem etsi inuiti facere coacti sunt. Ioh.19.7.
units.tr: E. iiij. Why, then, fleeing this examination of the case, do they demand of Pilate that, according to what had been done before Caiaphas by decision of the great Sanhedrin, he should at once hand Christ over to punishment? Yet they had not dared to pronounce capital sentence against Christ; holding him guilty only of blasphemy under their Law, they had declared him worthy of death, and it was Pilate whom they wanted to condemn him to capital punishment. They bore it most grievously that the prejudging of the cause had to be renewed by a fresh accusation brought before him; which at last they did, though unwillingly and compelled. John 19.7.

units.la: Eccui vero istam historiam legenti non videatur ista Sacerdotum iniqua & impudens postulatio? Annon autem, obsecro, eadem fuit iam pridem & est adhuc hodie agendi ratio iis in locis in quibus aliqua Ecclesiastici iudicij species obseruatur in iudiciis aduersum nos, quos haereticos vocant, coram nostri seculi Caiaphis aut eorum Officialibus instruendis? Nec enim apud illos de iure, sed de facto tantum quaeri solet, vt statim sine alia disquisitione reus haereseos & igne cremandus iudicetur quisquis vel Papam, vel Missae sacrificium, vel Sanctorum mortuorum inuocationem, vel Purgatorium, vel preces pro mortuis, & istiusmodi ipsorum fidei articulos non comprobarit: & hoc vnum superfit vt Pilatus minus adhuc quam iste Pilatus religiosis sic conuicti rei, capite plectendi tradantur. Quinetiā
units.tr: And to anyone reading this history, does not this demand of the priests appear unjust and shameless? Is it not, I ask, the same method of proceeding that has long been, and is still today, in those places where some form of ecclesiastical judgment is observed, in trials against us whom they call heretics, before the Caiaphases of our age or their officials? For there the question is usually not one of right but only of fact, so that at once, without any other inquiry, whoever has not approved the Pope, the sacrifice of the Mass, the invocation of the dead saints, Purgatory, prayers for the dead, and such articles of their faith, is judged a heretic and to be burned with fire. And this alone remains: that persons so convicted in religious matters should be handed over to be put to death, even less than Pilate did with Christ. Moreover

units.la: {a} Collatio huius formae iudicij aduersus Christum, & eius deinceps memoria. eò tandem deuentum (nisi de quorundam degradatione quam vocant agatur) vt ad vitandos iltos circuitus, Iudices seculares omnem hæreticos cognitionem adse perrtrahant: excipe loca in quibus Domina Sancta Inquisitio, gladium vtrumque sibi vindicauit, quam potestatem tanta tamque horrenda & ab omni cum diuino tum humano iure alicna tyrannide, vt incredibilis plerisque videatur.Cæterùm aduersus ista,cæteráq; huiusmodi vnicum certissimum remedium sanctis superest,patientia videlicet, præceptoris sui hac in parte exemplar imitantibus, & eadem quæ passus est perpeti non ægrè ferentibus, tantisper dum ille suo tempore & loco vindicem manum suam exerat, quam tandem Caiaphas & Pilatus, totáque denique misera gens illa non effugit.
units.tr: {a} The comparison of this form of trial against Christ, and its later memory. It has come to this (unless we are speaking of the degradation of certain men, as they call it) that, to avoid these detours, secular judges take over the whole cognizance of heretics. The exception is places where the Lady Holy Inquisition has claimed both swords for herself, a power so vast, so horrible, and so alien from every divine and human law, a tyranny, that it seems incredible to most people. But against these things, and others like them, the saints have one sure remedy: patience, namely, imitating the example of their teacher in this respect and bearing without bitterness what he suffered, until he, in his own time and place, stretches out his avenging hand. Caiaphas and Pilate did not escape that hand, nor did that whole wretched nation.

units.la: Initio verò Pilatum recitat Iohannes accusatoribus istis respondisse,quandoquidem inquisitione habita, Christum eius criminis cuius cognitio & iudicium penes ipsos esset (alioquin enim seditionis & violatæ Cæsareæ potestatis scipsos accusassent) conuictum teneri pronuntiarant, minimè opus fuisse vt illum ad se perducerent: sicut igitur cœperant, ita secundum ipsorum Legem in eum agere pergerent. Vt autem istud Pilati responsum & Iudæorum exceptionem melius intelligamus, quæ paucis superius attigi de Iudæorum illis temporibus statu & conditione sunt nobis repetenda. Diximus ergo Romanos, Iudæa in
units.tr: At the start, John records that Pilate answered those accusers thus: since an inquiry had been held and they had declared Christ held guilty of a crime whose cognizance and judgment lay with them (otherwise they would have accused themselves of sedition and of violating Caesar's power), there was no need for him to be brought before Pilate. Therefore, they should continue to proceed against him according to their own law, just as they had begun. To understand this response of Pilate and the Jews' objection better, what I touched on briefly above about the state and condition of the Jews in those times must be repeated. We said, then, that the Romans, having reduced Judea into

units.la: Ita Pilatus respondet vt nihil amplius Iudæis permittat quā quod erat ipsis ab Imperatore concessum. prouinciam redacta, Iudæis suæ religionis αὐ-τομίαν, & causarum quæ inde directè pendebant cognitionem cöceffiffe, eò vsque vt prehenfionis ac etiam coërcitionis moderatæ ius haberent, (puta virgarum, vt Lex ipsa huic pœnæ modum præscribit, Deut.25.3. cuius etiam exemplum extat Act.5.40. & 2.Corinth.11.24.) quod ex hac historia Christi tota liquet. Minimè fuit igitur Pilato propositum iurisdictionem illis à Romanis concessam amplificare (quod in ipsius potestate positum nö erat) nec etiam, vt opinor, ironicè cum illis egit: sed quum nullam adhuc aduersus Iesum accusationè audiret, operæpretium se facturum existimauit, tum suæ liberandæ conscientiæ, tum vt sese ab istis expediret, quos furiosè Christum persequi perspiciebat, si ipsum ad illos reiiceret, quantum tamen ipsis concesserant Romani iudicia ex Iudaicis legibus exercere. Et hæc causa fuit cur Iudæi, quibus erat in animo Christū vt blasphemū ad mortē vsque rapere ex Legis diuinæ præscripto, quod sibi per Romanos non licebat, in hoc Pilati responso acquiescere se non posse magnis clamoribus sint testati. Reum enim Christum esse capitis, sicut ipsi cognita causa statuissent: ac proinde hoc vnum superesse vt Pilatus eorum cognitioni subscribens in Christum damnatum animaduerteret.
units.tr: a province, had granted the Jews self-government [αὐτομίαν] in their religion, and cognizance of the causes that directly depended on it, to such an extent that they had the right of arrest and also of moderate coercion (namely of rods, since the Law itself prescribes a measure for this punishment, Deut. 25:3; there are examples of it at Acts 5:40 and 2 Cor. 11:24), as the whole of this history of Christ makes clear. Thus Pilate answers so as to grant the Jews nothing more than what the Emperor had conceded to them. It was not Pilate's purpose to enlarge the jurisdiction granted to them by the Romans, which was not in his power, nor, I think, did he speak to them ironically. But since he heard no accusation yet against Jesus, he judged it worthwhile, both to free his own conscience and to rid himself of those whom he saw furiously pursuing Christ, to hand Christ back to them, so far as the Romans had allowed them to exercise judgments under their own laws. And this was the reason why the Jews, who intended to drag Christ to death as a blasphemer under the prescription of the divine Law, which the Romans did not allow them to do, declared with loud cries that they could not acquiesce in this response of Pilate. For Christ was guilty of a capital crime, as they themselves had determined after examining the case; and therefore only this remained: that Pilate, subscribing to their verdict, should punish Christ as condemned.

units.la: Horrendum hic igitur in primis fuit ab iis quibus erat præcipue Christus promissus, & a quibus pene solis illum agnosci & coli oportuit. tuit, ad mortem tamen, nulla neque diuini neque humani iuris habita ratione exposci. Pilatum autem prophanum hominem, veri Dei cognitionis expertem, nec ab historicis alioquin ab vlla probitate commendatum, innocentiæ Christi aduersus Iudæorum rabiem patrocinari. Hoc autem diuinitus accidisse dicimus, tum vt Iesu Christi innocentiam idem ille iudex referretur à quo postea fuit damnatus: tum vt discamus eos tadem omnium euadere pestimos qui plurimis à Deo acceptis beneficiis vtuntur: neque id sane iniuria. In iis enim qui nunquam illo puro Dei verbo sunt edocti, sola naturalis illa toti humano generi communis labes inest, quæ nö statim omnem conscientiæ & æquitatis sensum abolet, vt in isto Pilato animaduertimus, nisi qui penitus improbitati sunt dediti. In quibus vero labes illa per veri Dei cognitionem per ipsius verbum certum videlicet illius mali medicamentum clui coeperat, si ad ingenium redeant, &c, donec ἀναίδεια iusto Dei iudicio prorsus euadant, peccata peccatis cumulent, quis non videt fieri non posse quin cæteros omnes omni scelerum genere longè superent, quum inter cæcorum superstitionem, & prauam eorum maliciam qui Dei lucem in suis cordibus suffocant, plurimum interfit?
units.tr: It was a horrible thing, first of all, that Christ should be demanded for death by those to whom he had been especially promised, and by whom he should almost alone have been acknowledged and worshipped, with no regard had to either divine or human law. Pilate, a profane man ignorant of the knowledge of the true God, and otherwise not commended for any uprightness by the historians, defended Christ's innocence against the rage of the Jews. We say this happened by divine providence: first, so that the same judge by whom Christ was afterwards condemned should bear witness to his innocence; and second, so that we may learn that those who enjoy many benefits received from God end up the most wicked of all, and not without reason. For in those who have never been taught by that pure Word of God, there is only that natural stain common to the whole human race, which does not at once abolish every sense of conscience and equity, as we see in that Pilate, unless they have been utterly given over to wickedness. But in those in whom that stain had begun to be washed away through the knowledge of the true God, through his Word, which is the certain remedy for that evil, if they return to their former disposition and finally, by the just judgment of God, pass over into shamelessness [ἀναίδεια], heaping sin upon sin, who does not see that they cannot fail to surpass all others in every kind of wickedness? There is a great difference between the superstition of the blind and the depraved malice of those who stifle God's light in their own hearts.

units.la: Huius autem horrendi iudicij diuini, quot, obsecro, nobis ante oculos exempla obuer- santur? Nam quòd ad Iudæos attinet, ne nunc quidem satiata est ipsorum rabies, nullo superstite Christiano vsquam futuro, si prauæ ipsorum voluntati vires respondercnt. Deinde si Turcarum cum catholicis nostris Romanis comparationem institiuas, & quorum erga nos minus iniqua sit voluntas disspicias, næ Mahumetanos erga Christianos ditionem i- psorum incolentes, aut mercaturam apud eos exercentes,in Christianæ religionis visu libero illis relinquendo multò quàm nostros Catho- licos,nihil nisi cædes & ferinam immanitatem spirantes,humaniores comperias.Quòd si in- ter hos ipsos discrimen statuamus,tantum cæ- teros qui nos persequuntur à nostris Apostatis differre cognoueris, quantum à tigribus lupi distant.Quod quò hac manifestius,annon,ob- secro,Iudæi Romæ & aliis Papæ subiectis lo- cis, licet horrendis eorum aduersus Christum blasphemiis totus æther persoēt, tamen tolerantur: in nos vero nullum adhuc satis atrox supplicium reperitur?nulla denique nobis cru- ciandis quantumuis immanis crudelitas suffi- cit?Vtinam vero Deus nos vtrorumque manibus eripiat.Quum tamen Dominus noster Iesus Christus nobis hic præcat,agedum quoties ita Domino visum fuerit, illorum furori cer- uices nostras subiicere nos quoque non dubitemus.
units.tr: Of this horrible divine judgment, how many examples, I beg you, present themselves before our eyes? As for the Jews, even now their rage is not sated, and no Christian would be left anywhere if their wicked will had the strength to match it. Next, if you compare the Turks with our Roman Catholics, and consider whose will towards us is less unjust, you will find that the Mahometans living under their rule among Christians, or carrying on trade with them, are far more humane towards Christians, allowing them free exercise of the Christian religion, than our Catholics, who breathe nothing but slaughter and savage brutality. But if we make a distinction among these very people, you will find that the others who persecute us differ from our apostates as much as wolves differ from tigers. How much more manifest this is: are not the Jews, I beg you, tolerated at Rome and in other places subject to the Pope, although the whole sky resounds with their horrible blasphemies against Christ? Yet against us no punishment atrocious enough is found. In short, no cruelty, however monstrous, is enough for tormenting us. Would that God would snatch us from the hands of both! Yet since our Lord Jesus Christ here bids us, whenever it has seemed good to the Lord, to subject our necks to their fury, let us not hesitate to do so.

units.la: At istorum cæcitatem alia circunstantia ma- gis adhuc patefacit. Nam si non licebat ipsis in quenquam supplicio capitis animaduerte- re, multò minùs in innocentem licebat: de quo tamen eos sua conscientia satis arguebat, quum
units.tr: But another circumstance reveals their blindness even more. For if they were not permitted to inflict capital punishment on anyone, much less were they permitted to do so against an innocent man. Their own conscience convicted them of this sufficiently,

units.la: quium Caiaphas ipse perniciosum illud consilium de tollendo Christo Iudæis suggerens Ioh.11. 50. nullum aduersus Christum crimen, sed imaginarium tantum Gentis periculu prætexuisset. Deinde, quantu quæso interest, si per te an per alium quemlibet facinus quodpiam perpetres? Immo, nonne minus peccatu fuisset si Christum ipsum et sustulissent, Pilatumque miseramque plebe innocentis hominis morte secu reos non fecissent? Immo Iudice ad ferendam sententiam reluctate conscientia cogere quantum est? En quo ferat semel laxas habenas nacta libido! en quomodo Satan vnius hominis opera ad multos perdendos abutatur.
units.tr: since Caiaphas himself, in suggesting to the Jews that pernicious plan of removing Christ (John 11:50), pretended no crime against Christ, but only an imaginary danger to the nation. Next, how much, I ask, does it matter whether you commit some crime through yourself or through some other person? Indeed, would it not have been less sinful if they had killed Christ themselves, and had not made Pilate and the wretched common people guilty through the death of an innocent man? Indeed, how great a thing it is for a judge's conscience to be forced to pronounce sentence against its will! See where unbridled lust carries a man once it has got loose reins! See how Satan uses the work of one man to destroy many.

units.la: Cæterum Ecclesiastici Romani locum i-stum adducentes vt se capitalibus iudiciis eximant, aperte nimis suam tum ignorantiam tum impudentiam produnt. Ignorantiam, inquam, quòd Iudæi non tanquam per se illici tum dicant sibi istud non licere, sed à Romanis illis adempta potestate. Impudentiam vero prorsus effrænem, quòd hac in parte Iudæorum vestigiis insistant. Nam quid hic scelerati isti faciunt? Iesum Christum morte dignum, tanquam læsæ maiestatis reum iudicant: quùmque per Romanos in cum ipsis animaduertere non liceret, Pilatum nefariæ suæ cupiditatis ministrum fecerunt. Quid vero noltri seculi Caiaphæ, etiam obseruata aliqua erga nos iudicij forma? Tanquam hæreticos iudicatos, seculari brachio tradunt. Ac ne forte quidam
units.tr: But Roman ecclesiastics, citing this passage in order to exempt themselves from capital judgments, betray both their ignorance and their impudence all too plainly. Their ignorance, I say, because the Jews did not claim that it was not permitted to them in itself, but that the power had been taken away by the Romans. Their impudence is utterly unbridled, because in this respect they tread in the footsteps of the Jews. For what do these wicked men do here? They judge Jesus Christ worthy of death as one guilty of treason, and since it was not permitted them to put him to death themselves, they made Pilate the minister of their wicked lust. And what do the Caiaphases of our own age do, even when some form of judicial procedure is observed? They hand over men judged as heretics to the secular arm. And lest perhaps some

units.la: Iudices ex sola criminatione aut ex aliena con-scientia quempiam hæreseos condemnare in-iecto conscientiæ scrupulo refugiant, ideo no-ui isti Pharifæi & Sacerdotes, veterum illorû Pharifæorum & Sacerdotum exemplar imita-ti,læsæ Maiestatis regiæ sedulò nos apud Iu-dices criminantur, impetratisque Regiis edi-ctis & diplomatibus suorum affectuum mini-ftros Iudices esse cogunt. At tamen inquiunt boni isti Religiosi, nunquam Ecclesia manus humano sanguine polluit,ac ne fontium qui-dem,quorum vnicam salutem expetit.O infi-gnes hypocritas! Annon enim eiis perfecu-tionum incendiarij? annon gladios & ignes spiratis? qui subinde Magistratuum auribus cruentorum vestrorum executionem decre-torum ingeniis? ipsi denique deficientibus carnificibus vices eorum impleturi? Annon denique ij estis qui Caiaphæ & assessorum ipsius malitiam & sæuitiam longè superantes, non contenti Iudicum & magistratuum con-scientias vestræ crudelitati addixisse,lanienam illam horrendam suggessistis,atque adeò ma-gna pars carnificum fuistis, vestrásque manus miserorum sanguine, sine causæ cognitione nullo discrimine conditionis,ætatis, sexus de-nique fœdastis? Imò qui tandem vestrum Re-gem sacrosanctum, cuius miseri tamdiu con-scientiæ illuseratis, coniuratione facta tam perfidè, tam nefariè, tam proditorie necastis, sicariúmque ipsum indigetare non erubuistis? Nouum sane,horrendum, detestandum, abo-minanminandum, fine vllo ab omni vsque memoria exemplo, facinus. Et sunt ipsi tamen, si fides incendiariis & proditoribus sicariis adhibeatur, Ecclesia, quae cunctis suos lapsus benignè ignoscit: omnia qui capitalia iudicia refugiùt: quum tamen Religiosorum scilicet istorum auctoritate & auspiciis Romæ & in omnibus Papalis ditionis locis causæ capitales agantur. Annon etiam idem ab aliis factitatur in suis ditionibus vsurpata dominatione temporali, Regibus & principibus ad id sua simplicitate conniuentibus, quam tamen nec Reges largiri, nec iltos oblatam accipere decuit? Sed hactenus de iis de quibus paulò post erit etiam dicendi locus.
units.tr: judges, from mere accusation or from another's conscience, shrink from condemning anyone for heresy, because a scruple has been cast into their conscience, therefore these new Pharisees and priests, imitating the example of those old Pharisees and priests, accuse us diligently before the judges of wounding royal majesty, and, having obtained royal edicts and decrees, compel the judges to be ministers of their feelings. Yet, they say, these good religious men: the Church has never polluted her hands with human blood, nor even with the springs of blood, whose sole salvation she seeks. O notable hypocrites! Are you not the incendiaries of persecutions? Do you not breathe out swords and fires? Do you not, again and again, dictate to the ears of magistrates the execution of your bloody decrees? Will you yourselves, finally, when the executioners fail, fulfil their office? Are you not, finally, those who, far surpassing the malice and cruelty of Caiaphas and his assessors, were not content to have bound the consciences of judges and magistrates to your cruelty, but suggested that horrible butchery, and so were for the most part the executioners, and defiled your hands with the blood of the wretched, without any examination of the cause and without distinction of condition, age, or sex? Indeed, which of you finally killed your most holy King, whose wretched consciences you had long mocked, by a conspiracy so treacherous, so wicked, so traitorous, and did not blush to call him a sicarius? A new, horrible, detestable, abominable deed, without any example in all memory. And yet they are, if credence is given to incendiaries, traitors and assassins, the Church, which kindly pardons all their lapses; they all shun capital judgments, although under the authority and auspices of these religious men capital cases are conducted at Rome and in all places under papal rule. Does not the same thing also happen in other realms, where temporal domination has been usurped, with kings and princes conniving at it through their simplicity, which the kings ought not to grant nor those men to accept? But so far concerning these matters, about which there will also be an occasion to speak a little later.

units.la: Sic igitur haec omnia gesta narrat historia, vt nec Pilatus hoc se iudicio potuerit expedire, nec Iudæis Pilati responso satisfactum sit, vt impleretur quod Christus de morte sua prædixerat. Dixerat porrò non semel se à Iudæis Gentibus tradendum, damnandum ac tandem crucifigendum, quod si Pilati sententiæ locus esset datus non eueniset.Nam etsi Iudæi Christum ex Legis præscripto damnandi & ad supplicium rapiendi potestatem habuissent, minimè sanè Crucci illum affixissent, sed ex Lege Moris Leuit. 24. 13. lapidibus obruissent, quòd apud Iudæos Crucis inusitatum esset supplicium. Abiit tamen Christi prædictionem vel causam huius tam iniquo iudicio dediisse, vel commune cum illo quicquam habere cogitemus. Nam, vt est à quodam ex Veteribus distum præclarè, licet prædictæ res à Prophetis & ab ipso Christo, quos mendaces non fuisse certum est, aut iam euenerunt, aut suo tempore euenturæ sunt, vt ante prædictæ sunt, non ideò tamen quòd prædictæ sunt euenerunt, sed quòd euenturæ essent prædictæ sunt. Quòd si altius, quò tandem est deueniendum, oculos attollamus, sanè cum vera sanctáq̃ue Hierosolymitana Ecclesia dicemus. Act. 4.27. Herodes & Pilatum cum Gentibus & populis conspirasse, vt facerent quæcunque manus Dei & consilium eius priùs definierat vt fierent. Hoc nisi fatemur, quomodo redempti essemus secundùm ipsius propositum & nobis datam eius gratiam (idest prædestinatam quæ nobis detur) ante omnium sæculorum tempora? Hic porrò accuratè distinguendum opus Dei, quæ nostra redemptio est, ab opere Iudæ, quæ Proditio est: Caiaphæ totiúsque Synedrij, quæ Improbitas est, crudelitas & detestanda cædes: & Pilati, plus homines quàm Deum ad innocentem condemnandum reluctante conscientia metuentis, quorum tamen omnium Deus autor, nec mediatè nec immediatè, dicendus est, sed ipsorum propria malitia. Deo tamen sic tum Satanæ tum pessimis istis instrumentis abutente, iustissimè quidem, vade ac sponsore nostro percusso: clementissimè autem, dato vnico Filio ad mortem ad suorum electorum redemptionem: Satana & sceleratis illis quòd ad proprium & spontaneum motum attinet nihil minus quàm Dei gloriam quærentibus, ac proinde meritas poenas ab illis Deo repo-scente, vt ab Assyriis olim, Chaldaeis & aliis quibus tamen Dominus ad suum populum castigandum vsus fuerat.
units.tr: Thus the history relates all these events in such a way that Pilate could not free himself from this judgment, and the Jews were not satisfied by Pilate's answer, so that what Christ had foretold about his death might be fulfilled. He had said more than once that he would be handed over by the Jews to the Gentiles, condemned and at last crucified; and if the sentence of Pilate had not been given, this would not have happened. For even if the Jews had had the power, under the prescription of the Law, to condemn Christ and hand him over to execution, they would certainly not have fixed him to a cross, but would have stoned him according to the Law of Moses (Lev. 24:13), since crucifixion was an unusual punishment among the Jews. Yet we should not think that they brought about this most unjust judgment in order to fulfil Christ's prediction, or that they had anything in common with it. For, as one of the Ancients has rightly said, things predicted by the Prophets and by Christ himself, who are certainly not liars, either have already happened or will happen at their appointed time; they are not fulfilled because they were predicted, but were predicted because they were going to happen. But if we lift our eyes higher, to where at last we must come, we shall certainly say with the true and holy Church of Jerusalem that Herod and Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples, conspired to do whatever the hand and counsel of God had determined beforehand to be done (Acts 4:27–28). Unless we confess this, how were we redeemed according to his purpose and the grace given to us (that is, predestined to be given to us) before the beginning of time? Here the work of God, which is our redemption, must be carefully distinguished from the work of Judas, which is betrayal; from the wickedness, cruelty and detestable murder of Caiaphas and the whole Sanhedrin; and from the work of Pilate, who, fearing men more than God and with his conscience struggling against it, condemned the innocent man. God is not to be called the author of all these, neither mediately nor immediately, but their own malice is. Yet God, justly indeed, used Satan and these wicked instruments, so that our surety and guarantor was struck; but most mercifully, in giving his only Son to death for the redemption of his elect. As for Satan and those wicked men, who by their own spontaneous motion sought nothing less than the glory of God, God demanded from them their deserved punishment, as he once did from the Assyrians, the Chaldeans and others whom the Lord nevertheless used to chastise his people.

units.la: Hinc vero nobis doctrina consolandis Dei filiis aptissima colligenda est, nempe quæcun-que Satan, & quos impellit homines molian-tur, & decernant aduersum nos, nihil tamen eorum omnium, siue consilia ipsa, siue tempo-rum circumstantias aut mediorum species, præter Dei decretum euenturum, quum ne passer quidem in terram sine Dei decreto vo-luntateque decidat, ac proinde multo minus capillus vel minimi inter Dei filios, quos omnes numeratos esse dicit Dominus. Matth. 10. 30. & 31. Nihil autem velle Deum suos aduersi perpeti quod non ad ipsius gloriam & suorum salutem redundet, testatur Apostolus. Rom. 8. 28. & perpetua seculorum omnium experientia docet.
units.tr: From this we must draw a doctrine most fitting for consoling the sons of God: whatever Satan and the men he drives on plan and decree against us, nothing of all that will come about except by the decree of God, whether the counsels themselves, the circumstances of the times, or the kinds of means; since not even a sparrow falls to the ground without the decree and will of God, and therefore much less a hair of the least of the sons of God, all of whom the Lord says are numbered (Matt. 10:30–31). And that God does not will his own to suffer adversity which does not turn out to the glory of himself and the salvation of his people, the Apostle testifies (Rom. 8:28), and the constant experience of all ages teaches.

units.la: Deinceps historia secundum Lucam narrat (sic enim est narratio primi actus quaestionis coram Pilato de Christo agitatae connectenda) Iudaeos tandem, Iudicem, licet idololatram, tamen aequi & recti amantiores nactos, accusationemque capitalem aduersus Iesum Christum exhibere coactos, laesae ipsum Caesareae Maiestatis accusasse, quod praecipuum fuit huius criminis caput, vocantes in inuidiam eum apud Pilatum, quod populum quantum in ipso erat a pendendis Caesari tributis auerteret, ac proinde ab Imperio Romano defectionis cau-
units.tr: Next, the history according to Luke relates (for the narrative of the first stage of the question about Christ, debated before Pilate, must be joined to it in this way) that the Jews, having at last found a judge who, though an idolater, nevertheless loved what was fair and right, and being compelled to bring a capital charge against Jesus Christ, accused him of injuring the majesty of Caesar, which was the chief point of this accusation. They tried to stir up hatred against him before Pilate, saying that, as far as he was able, he turned the people away from paying tribute to Caesar, and so sought a cause of revolt from the Roman Empire.

units.la: F. j. fas quaereret. Quærat autem hic aliquis non immerito, cur non blasphemiæ ac læsæ Maiestatis diuinæ potius crimen obiecerint. Nimirum hæc ratio est, si quis tamen in ipsis rationis sensus erat, Iudæos non ignorantes quàm ipsorum Religio tum apud Romanos tum apud alias idololatricas nationes esset abominanda, metuisse ne Pilatus parui criminatione illam faceret, vt Gallion ille Achaiæ proconsul, cuius meminit Lucas Act. 18. 14.
units.tr: Someone may not unreasonably ask here why they did not bring the charge of blasphemy and of wounding the divine majesty instead. The reason, surely, if there was any sense in their reasoning, was this: the Jews knew well how abominable their own religion was to the Romans and to the other idolatrous nations, and they feared that Pilate would make light of a charge of that kind, as that Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, whom Luke mentions (Acts 18:14), did.

units.la: Sed an, obsecro, priore criminatione excitatum dentibus noua fuit confingenda? Nec enim solum Christi doctrina, totaque eius ante acta vita contrarium testabantur, vt qui etiam cognito plebis de se correpto Rege faciendo consilio solus in montem secessisset, Ioh. 5. 15. qui tributum, etiam ipso iure immunis, pro se & Petro discipulo Matth. 17. 27. persoluisset, qui iudicium oblatum hercisцundæ familiæ recusasset. Luc. 12. 14. qui denique mulierem adulteram condemnare noluisset. Ioh. 8. 11. Sed, quod maius est, etiam insidiantibus inimicis, & quærentibus licere Cæsari tributum soluere, nec ne, disertis expressisque verbis, Deo reddenda quæ Dei sunt, Cæsari vero quæ Cæsaris Matth. 22. 17. respondisset. Et sane criminationem quidem istorum audimus, sed sine testibus ac documentis, tanta fuit tamque insignis nostri Redemptoris integritas. Sed quid agas? Satanæ manciparos ipsius artes versare non est absonum, qui propterea Diabolus etiam, id est, calumniator nuncupatur, quem vt mendamendacem insignem, minime puduit ipsum æternum Iehouam apud primos illos noltros parentes, tum malignitatis tum falsitatis,insi-mulare.Genef.3.4.&5.
units.tr: But, I ask you, after the first accusation had stirred them up, was a new one to be invented? For not only the doctrine of Christ and his whole life before this testified to the contrary, since he withdrew alone to the mountain when the people wanted to make him king (John 6:15), and since he paid the tribute, although by right he was exempt, for himself and for his disciple Peter (Matt. 17:27), and since he refused to judge the inheritance dispute offered to him (Luke 12:14), and finally since he would not condemn the adulterous woman (John 8:11). More than this, when his enemies laid snares and asked whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not, he answered in plain and express words that what is God's must be rendered to God, and what is Caesar's to Caesar (Matt. 22:17–21). And indeed we hear their accusation, but without witnesses or proofs; so great and so remarkable was the integrity of our Redeemer. But what can you do? It is not out of character for the servants of Satan to practise his arts, which is why he is called the Devil, that is, the calumniator; and as a notorious liar he was not ashamed to accuse the eternal Jehovah himself, with both malice and falsehood, before our first parents (Gen. 3:4–5).

units.la: Porro si falsitas quæuis & calumnia tum humano tum diuino iure prohibetur, næ tum maximè detestanda, omnibúsque suppliciis, quum de iure quæritur, est coercenda. Nam, obsecro, quale Iudicum tribunal? Annon ipsius Dei, qui se ibi præsidere velle tanquâ Iudicem iudicum & Regem Regum per Prophetas profitetur? Psal.82.1.&Dan.2.47. Age igitur,coram Magistratu mentiri & calumnias struere, quid aliud est quâ Deo ipsi oppedere, & Magistratus ipsos instrumenta Satanæ facere, quò veritas à mendacio illorum autoritate suffulto facilius opprimatur? Vos itaque nominatim Iudices, vos litigiosos, vos pragmaticos & aduocatos, hoc loco admonitus, copello. Atque vtinam qui sinceram huc conscientiam timorémque suprémi Iudices adferunt, à Domino maioribus in dies donis augeantur, tanquam ipsius os & instrumenta, quibus mutua inter homines pax foueatur. Sed oro, quos alios hodie maiorem litibus diiudicandis moram adferre dixeris, quàm quorum adeò scelerata est conscientia, vt parui faciant causas suas variis pigmentis & mendaciis adornare? nouos iubinde casus fingere? quæcunque denique, quo iure, quàue iniuria cudere potuerint in medium adferre? aliis quidem ex aliorum solis litibus quæstum quærientibus: aliis vero siue agant siue defendant, tantum iudicio causam quo iure quaue iniuria vincere cupientibus? Sed quid aliud potius quam iltiufmodi iuris corruptela Regna ipsa & Monarchias pessundedit: Hæc vero iamdiu cum hic, tum aliis passim locis, videmus, monemus, vociferamur, querimur: quis vero commouetur? quis operi manum admouet? An non contrà sus deque omnia ferri, & singulis horis in peius ruere conspicimus? Vidit tamen ista Deus, & videt: ipse vindicem manum, ne dubitate, tum hic tum alibi tandem cunctantibus hominibus exerturus: & quidem his sceptrum aliis tradendum erepturus. An vero, quasso vos, tam est aliquis stupidus, tamque plumbeus, qui iam maximæ terrarum partis regna concuti & nutare non sentiat? Vtinam vero atque vtinam Deus Opt. Max. pro immensa sua clementia statum istum noltrum iam pene nutantem propitius, ac benevolus stabiliat, vobisque Domini, mentem hanc iniiciat, vt tanti mali, quod pene iam immedicabile factum est magnitudinem sedulo pensitetis: & quandoquidem Dei sacrosanctum verbum coercendis istis hominibus tam exiguum pondus habet, etiam atque etiam quales viros iuri dicundo præficiatis, sedulo prospiciatis: ac deinceps Status eos qui bonis Legibus reguntur imitati, & ab Imperatoribus veteres illas sanctasque Leges positas sequuti, ne putate pulchre vos officio defunctos si eos a quibus stat iniuria iudicio damnaueritis: at in eos etiam ingentibus ac seueris multis animaduer-tite, quos praua conscientia, tam malis artibus sacrosanctū iustitiæ tribunal polluere cognoueritis: sed nominatim temerè & malitiosè à Prætoris sententia prouocantes compescite. Hoc si factum à vobis erit, spero vos intra paucos dies, Deo sic annuente, constitutum optimum ordine conspecturos: sin autè erit à vobis neglectū aut segnius curatum, vehementer metuo ne vestris ceruicibus imminente ruina, nisi vestri misereatur Dominus, acceleretis.
units.tr: Moreover, if every falsehood and calumny is forbidden by both human and divine law, then surely it is most to be detested in a court of law, and must be restrained with every punishment whenever justice is sought. For, I ask you, what kind of judgment-seat is this? Is it not that of God himself, who through the Prophets declares that he wishes to preside there as the Judge of judges and the King of kings (Ps. 82:1; Dan. 2:47)? Come then: to lie before a magistrate and to devise calumnies is nothing other than to resist God himself, and to make the magistrates instruments of Satan, so that the truth may more easily be crushed by the falsehood propped up by their authority. And so I now admonish and reprove you, judges by name, litigious men, pleaders and advocates. Would that those who bring to this office a sincere conscience and fear of the supreme Judge may be increased by the Lord with greater gifts every day, as his mouth and his instruments by which mutual peace among men is nourished. But I ask: whom today could you name who cause greater delay in deciding lawsuits than those whose consciences are so wicked that they think little of adorning their cases with various pigments and lies, constantly inventing new circumstances, and bringing forward whatever they can devise, by whatever right or wrong? Some seek profit from the quarrels of others alone; others, whether they prosecute or defend, desire only to win their cause in court, by right or wrong. But what else than this corruption of justice has overthrown kingdoms and monarchies? We see these things for a long time now, here as well as in other places everywhere; we warn, we cry out, we complain. But who is moved? Who lays a hand to the work? Do we not see everything carried along topsy-turvy and rushing to worse every hour? Yet God has seen these things and sees them: he will surely, do not doubt it, stretch out his avenging hand here and elsewhere, when men at last hesitate, and indeed he will snatch the sceptre from some to hand it to others. But are you, I ask, so stupid and so leaden that you do not perceive that the kingdoms of the greater part of the earth are already shaken and tottering? Would that, would that God Almighty, in his immense mercy, would kindly and graciously stabilise this state of ours, now almost tottering, and would put into your minds, sirs, the thought of carefully weighing the magnitude of so great an evil, which has now almost become incurable. And since the most holy Word of God has so little weight in restraining these men, take even more care to set over the administration of justice men of what character you can, and then, imitating those states which are governed by good laws and following the ancient and holy laws laid down by the emperors, do not think you have discharged your duty well if you condemn in judgment those from whom injustice comes; but punish with great and severe penalties also those whom you know to have polluted the most sacred tribunal of justice with such wicked arts through a depraved conscience; and restrain especially those who rashly and maliciously appeal from the sentence of the praetor. If this is done by you, I hope that within a few days, with God so granting, you will see the best order established; but if it is neglected by you or cared for too sluggishly, I greatly fear that, with ruin hanging over your necks, you will hasten it, unless the Lord has mercy on you.

units.la: Et hactenus quidem de caulis ciuilibus. Quum autem hominum bonam famam vitamque facultatibus quibusuis longè pretiosiorem esse nemo nesciat, tanto sincerior & æquior in capitalium caularum decisione conscientia requiritur. Quò magis inexcusabiles aduersarij nostri redduntur, qui metuentes ne solam hæresin criminati, Deóque per verbum suum sedente admiłóque iudice, causa lua facillime cadant, eò effrænis impudentiæ deuenerunt vt Magistratibus persuaserint, nos eam doctrinam profiteri, qua Reges, Principes ac Magistratus de foliis suis deturbare moliamur, mundóque rerum omnium confusionem inuchere, quum tamen eos minimè fugiat tantùm abesse vt in Prouinciis quæ nostras Ecclesias exceperunt, Magistratibus suus honor non reddatur, vt contra in iis Libertini, Anabaptistæ, & illis non absimiles homines eiusmodi confusiones inuchentes capitalibus pœnis etiam coërceantur.
units.tr: So much for civil causes. But since no one doubts that a person's good name and life are far more precious than any possessions, a more sincere and fair conscience is required in deciding capital causes. This makes our adversaries all the less excusable. Fearing that their case would collapse easily if only heresy were charged, with God sitting in judgment through his Word, they have fallen into such shameless impudence that they have persuaded the magistrates that we profess a doctrine by which we are plotting to tear kings, princes and magistrates from their thrones and bring confusion upon all things. Yet they surely know that in those provinces which have received our churches, the magistrates are far from being denied their honour; on the contrary, Libertines, Anabaptists and men not unlike them, who bring in such confusion, are punished even with capital penalties.

units.la: Denique si de doctrina nostra quæritur, an nó confessiones nostræ, commentarij, tot denique hominum millia doctrinam nostram ex ore nostro quotidie audientia, falsi convincendis impudentibus istis calumniatoribus sufficiunt? Regerunt, fateor, excitatum in Germania bellum, & in Gallia bella ciuilia. Sed quod ad Germaniam, sane Germani Principes suam iustitiam plus satis cunctis patefecerunt, & Dominus ipse castigato suo populo, litem illam dirimens, summo cum aduersariorum detrimento, satis est à cuius partibus staret æquitas testatus, nequid amplius de re ista dicam. Atque utinam Deus voluisset excitatum in Gallia incendium istud intestinum tam citò quàm in Germania sopitum, quo tamē adhuc tota flagrans Gallia suis ipsa viribus ruit.
units.tr: Finally, if the question is about our doctrine, do not our confessions, our commentaries, and the many thousands of people who daily hear our doctrine from our own mouths, suffice to convict these shameless calumniators of falsehood? They reply, I admit, that war was stirred up in Germany and civil wars in France. But as for Germany, the German princes have certainly made their cause plain enough to everyone, and the Lord himself, chastising his people and settling that quarrel to the great loss of our adversaries, has shown clearly enough on whose side justice lay, so I will say no more about that matter. Would that God had allowed that internal fire in France to be quenched as quickly as it was in Germany, yet France, still wholly ablaze, is collapsing by its own strength.

units.la: Sed quibus inceirdiariis, oro, toties excitatum, &accensum? An non iis qui violatores edictorum, legitimè iureiurando firmatorum, Regum nostrorum Gallorum credulitate & iuuentute sunt abusi? Quod si tum boni Principes, non peregrini nec noui, sed ipsa vetere regia Gallica stirpe oriundi, cognoscentes tyrannos illos nomen Religionis prauis suis tegendis consiliis & conatibus prætexere, & Regibus iuuenibus quos incendiarij illi habebat in potestate instrumentis ad Francicam Monarchiam ad peregrinos transferendam abuti, vim vi repellere conati sunt, & tot miseroum hominum tam scelerate modis omnibus oppressorum causam susceperunt, se denique suásque facultates, vitam & animas tutati sunt, quis vt contumaces audeat interpellare vel criminari? Sed ea fuit Domini voluntas, cuius sacrosan�below rium ipsum in Diuorum suorum & Indigetum album retulerint? Vbinam vero gentium tam nefaria, tam horrenda, tam detestanda facinora nata, cusa, fabricata, & tandem excusa sunt? Anapud eos quos per inuidiam Haereticos vocant, ac nó potius in penitioribus conclauibus Christianismi totius zelatoribus? in secretioribus spuriorum FrancoHispanorum coniurationibus? in venerādorum scilicet Iesuitarum Patrum, iuratorum Hispanorum tyranni mangonum seminariis? denique in sacrosancta Dimi Dominici schola? Sed esto, superiora omnia omittamus: quaenam tandem ista est impudentia, vt ij quorum caput sua in omnes Reges & Principes potestate passim gloriatur, qui suis artibus tantum effecerunt, vt ne Regibus quidem liceat aduersus quemlibet vel ostiarium Monachum ferre sententiam, crimen seditionis & laesae Regiae Maiestatis impingere non erubescant, iis qui praeterquam quod puritatem doctrinae sectantur, qua minime politiae humanae cuertuntur, sed potius firmantur stabiliuntúrque, nihil magis quàm iurisdictionis Ecclesiasticae à ciuili distinctionem vrgent? Sed Caiapharum & veterum Sacerdotum soboles nequaquam cum illis periit, nec seruis nouum peregrinúmque debet videri, si quam passus est Dominus conditionem, & ipsi ferre coguntur. Sed Reges & caeteros Magistratus diligenter cauere necesse est, ne Pilati exemplo metum sibi à suis iniici, multóque minus se decipi patiantur, ne sic scesceleratorum & nefariorum hominum malitiæ & crudelitatis instrumenta fiant.
units.tr: But, I ask, by whose incendiaries was it so often kindled and fanned? Was it not by those who abused the credulity and youth of our kings of France to violate edicts confirmed by lawful oath? If good princes, not foreign or new but sprung from the ancient royal stock of France, recognised that those tyrants were using the name of religion as a cover for their wicked plans and attempts, and were abusing the young kings, whom those incendiaries held in their power, as instruments for transferring the French monarchy to foreigners, and so tried to repel force with force, and took up the cause of so many wretched men oppressed in every way so wickedly, and at last protected themselves, their property, their lives and their souls, who would dare to challenge or accuse them as rebels? But such was the Lord's will... Where, then, were such nefarious, horrible, detestable crimes born, devised, fabricated and at last published? Was it not among those whom out of envy they call heretics, rather than in the innermost chambers of the zealots of all Christianity? In the secret conspiracies of the spurious Franco-Spaniards? In the seminaries of those venerable Jesuit fathers, the sworn tyrants' hired men of Spain? Finally, in the holy school of St Dominic? But granted, let us pass over all that has gone before. What impudence is this, that those whose head everywhere boasts of its power over all kings and princes, who by their arts have so far achieved that not even kings may pronounce sentence against any doorkeeping monk without being charged with sedition and treason against the royal majesty, are not ashamed to press that distinction between ecclesiastical and civil jurisdiction against those who pursue the purity of doctrine, which by no means subverts human polity but rather strengthens and stabilises it? But the offspring of Caiaphas and the old priests did not perish with them, and it ought not to seem new or strange to the servants if they are compelled to bear the same condition the Lord himself suffered. Yet kings and the other magistrates must take care not to let themselves be frightened by fear of their subjects, following the example of Pilate, and still less allow themselves to be deceived, lest they become the instruments of the malice and cruelty of wicked and nefarious men.

units.la: HOMILIA decimanona.
units.tr: Homily nineteen.

units.la: IOH. 18.
units.tr: John 18.

units.la: 33. Introiuit ergo rursus in Prætorium Pilatus, & vocauit Iesum, dixitque ei, Tu ne es Rex Iudæorum?
units.tr: 33. Then Pilate entered into the judgment hall again, and called Jesus, and said unto him, Art thou the King of the Jews?

units.la: 34. Respondit ei Iesus, A te ipso tu hoc dicis, an alij dixerunt tibi de me?
units.tr: 34. Jesus answered him, Sayest thou this of thyself, or did others tell it thee of me?

units.la: 35. Respondit Pilatus, Num ego Iudæus sum? Gens tua & principes Sacerdotum tradiderunt te mihi, quid fecisti?
units.tr: 35. Pilate answered, Am I a Jew? Thine own nation and the chief priests have delivered thee unto me. What hast thou done?

units.la: 36. Respondit Iesus, Regnum meum non est ex hoc mundo: si ex hoc mundo esset regnum meum, ministri mei certarent ne traderer Iudæis: nunc autem regnum meum non est hinc.
units.tr: 36. Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews; but now is my kingdom not from hence.

units.la: Progredientibus nobis in huius historiæ meditatione, illius innocentia qui in se peccata nostra recepit magis ac magis elucet, quo certiores fiamus esse Deo pro nobis ab illo plene satisfactum. In ea etiam magis magisque facinus illud horren-dum de quo superius egimus conspicitur,Eth-nicus nimirum amantissimus æqui boniqúe, iis contrà præter omne ius & æquum sæuien-tibus, suamque peruersitatem testantibus, qui tunc ex toto terrarum orbe foli visibilis & conspicuæ Ecclesiæ notas iure sibi vendica-bant: quod vel ipsum sufficiat ori occludendo Religiosis illis,qui nostro seculo longè minùs specioso prætextu, Ecclesiæ nimirum Catho-licæ Romanæ (id est vniuersalis particularis) abutentes,à suis galeris,lituis & mitris ita pen-dere Sp.S.volunt, vt in nullis vnquam doctri-næ articulis errare possint, quum sit tamen ab Apostolo multis ante seculis diserte prædi-ctum,fore vt ad Caiaphæ exemplum, summus Antichristus in medio templi Dei, quod est Christianorum coetus sedeat, id est præsideat 2. Thessal. 2. verf.4. quod esse paulatim ac pe-detentim adimpletum vel ipsis oculis nostris intueri cogimur.
units.tr: As we advance in meditating on this history, the innocence of him who took our sins upon himself shines forth more and more, so that we may be more certain that God was fully satisfied on our behalf. In it the dreadful crime of which we spoke above is also seen more and more clearly. A Gentile, most loving of what is fair and good, is set against men who raged against all right and equity and bore witness to their own perversity, men who then claimed for themselves, from the whole world, the marks of the visible and conspicuous Church, and claimed them rightly. This alone should be enough to silence those religious men of our own age who, with a far less specious pretext, abuse the Catholic Roman Church (that is, the universal particular Church). They want the Holy Spirit to hang upon their caps, crooks and mitres, so that they can never err in any article of doctrine. Yet the Apostle clearly foretold many centuries ago that the chief Antichrist would sit in the middle of God's temple, which is the assembly of Christians, and preside there, as Caiaphas did (2 Thess. 2:4). We are compelled to see this being fulfilled little by little, even with our own eyes.

units.la: Pilatus igitur non sine magna contentione, tandem accepto crimine cuius Iudæi Chri-stum Dominum nostrum accusabant, cœpit eum ex tempore de crimine interrogare, sic iure ipso postulante, vt quum de re ex aperta & minime fulpecta rei ipsius confessione con-stat, aliis testimoniis & coniecturis abstinea-tur.
