Sed quòd ad tanti criminis accusationem, quod si fuisset, vel aliquam veri speciem ha-buisset,maturum remedium postulabat, Pila-tus non admodum commouetur, ipsum satis ofteнostendit crimen illud Christo impositum nec pro vero nec pro verisimili habuisse, quum eos certo sciret non tam studiosos defensores Romanorum potestatis esse, quorū excutiendi iugi, quod tandem exitus comprobauit, omnes occasiones venari conspiceret, etsi quò Iudæis omnem de se conquerendi præcidat occasionem, in Christum inquirere non desinit.
units.tr: Pilate therefore, not without great contention, having at last received the charge on which the Jews accused Christ our Lord, began to question him about the crime on the spot, as the law itself required, so that once the matter was established by an open and in no way doubtful confession of the accused, recourse would not be had to other testimonies and conjectures. But as for the accusation of so great a crime, which, if it had been true, would have demanded a prompt remedy and would have had some appearance of truth, Pilate is not much moved. He shows well enough that he regarded the charge laid on Christ as neither true nor plausible, since he knew that the Jews were not such zealous defenders of Roman power. He saw them constantly seeking every occasion to shake off that yoke, as the outcome later proved. Although Pilate cut off from the Jews every occasion to complain about him, he did not cease to inquire into Christ.

units.la: Et istud ipsum effecit ne primò Christus ipsi palàm ad quæsita responderit, quòd sic eius vellet paulatim sopitam suscitare conscien-tiam, non quòd hac se ratione paratam sibi & ineuitabilem condemnationem, quam etiam volens ac sponte subibat effugere posse spera-ret : sed quòd quandiu vixit in his terris, nul-lam vnquam, ne in maxima quidem & difficil-lima lucta, peccatores ad pœnitetiam vocan-di, quod & tota hæc historia testatur, occasio-nem elabi siuit. Perinde fuit igitur ac si con-scientiam eius interrogasset, ecquid ipsi vide-retur, antalem de ipso antea opinionem ex e-ius vllo dicto factoque concepisset: sic satis admonens quid à Pilato factum oportuerit, nempe si dubitaret de facto, cogeret accusato-res testimoniis illud conuincere.
units.tr: This very thing meant that at first Christ did not answer the questions openly. He wished in this way to rouse a conscience that had gradually been lulled to sleep, not because he hoped by this means to escape the condemnation prepared for him, which he undertook willingly and of his own accord and could not avoid. Rather, as long as he lived on this earth, he never let slip the opportunity to call sinners to repentance, not even in the greatest and most difficult struggle. This whole history attests to it. It was therefore just as if he had asked Pilate's conscience whether it thought anything of him, or had formed any opinion of him from any word or deed of his. In this way he sufficiently reminded Pilate what he ought to have done: if he doubted the deed, he should have compelled the accusers to prove it by witnesses.

units.la: Ad hoc ita respondet Pilatus, etsi non sine quadam indignatione, vt quid sibi videatur non occultè significet, & interim quàm auer-setur totam nationem minimè dissimulet : in quo tamen sua etiam laude dignus est, quòd à Iudæis lacessitus, non erumpit in iram quæ dictum vllum factúmve inordinatum illi extor-quëat: in eo quoque commendatione non indignus, quòd tam opportunam Iudæos sibi conciliandi rationem nactus, & quòd Christus, quem respondere tanquam reum oportuerat, illum ipsum interrogaret, nihil tamen ad illorum gratiam contra cõscientiam fecit: qua in re lõgè se fortius ac melius quàm Festus ille gessit, de quo in Actis cap.25.9. multíque Magistratibus longè illo inferioribus quomodo se in iudiciis gerere debeant, exèplo præit.
units.tr: Pilate replies to this, though not without some indignation, so that he does not openly hide what he thinks, and meanwhile he does not conceal how much he abhors the whole nation. In this he is nonetheless worthy of praise: though provoked by the Jews, he does not break out into anger that might wring from him any unseemly word or deed. He is also not unworthy of commendation in that, although he had found such a convenient way of winning over the Jews, and although Christ, whom he ought to have answered as an accused man, asked him this very question, he did nothing against his conscience to gain their favour. In this respect he went far more bravely and better than that Festus of whom we read in Acts 25:9. He sets an example to many magistrates, far inferior to him, of how they ought to conduct themselves in judgments.

units.la: Et hæc quidem tum Iudæorum tum Pilati mens fuit. Sed Christi responsum longè altius longiúsque mentes nostras erigit, quum immensa Dei bonitas & clementia fecerit, vt ex quæstione, & ad illam responso, quatuor maximi momenti salutis nostræ capita ac fontes nobis aperiantur. Primum, est certum teltimo nium cum cui soli innitimur, verè Regem esse: alterum, Qualis Rex sit: tertium quæ sit huius regni administratio, & in quo consistat: quartum denique, qui, qualesve sint veri regni huius subditi: quæ singula prout hic proponuntur capita sunt ordine nobis explicanda.
units.tr: These were indeed the minds of the Jews and of Pilate. But Christ's answer lifts our minds far higher and further, since God's immense goodness and mercy have brought it about that from the question, and from his answer to it, four chief points of the greatest importance for our salvation are opened to us. First, the sure testimony on which alone we lean, that he is truly King. Second, what sort of King he is. Third, what the administration of this kingdom is and in what it consists. Fourth and finally, who and what sort of subjects this true kingdom has. Each of these points, as they are set out here, we must explain in order.

units.la: Regem igitur hic se in primis Iesus Christus agnoscit, excellentem illam professus confessionem, quam tanto pere commendat Apostolus 1.Tim.6.13.& nō sine causa. Quinam enim alioquin miseri Dei filij Satanæ, peccati, & mortis vinculis eriperentur, quomodo etiam ereptis, in tantis certaminibus quibus quotidie sunt obnoxij, vires sufficerent, nisi eas mi-
units.tr: Here, then, Jesus Christ first acknowledges himself to be King, making that excellent confession which the Apostle commends so highly, and not without cause (1 Tim. 6:13). For otherwise, who would rescue the wretched sons of God from the chains of Satan, sin and death? And once they were rescued, how would they have the strength for such struggles, to which they are exposed every day, unless these strengths were supplied

units.la: nistrate ipsis Rege, omnium Regum maximo & inuicti ssimo? Ac sane nomine illo Hebraeo, Messias,& Græco,Christus,quod vnctū signi- ficat,propter vnctionem illam videlicet Regū apud Iudæos vsitatā, illud ipsum continetur. Verumenimuerò sciendū est Patribus abinitio nomen istud non omnino perspicuè patefactū. Adamum enim & Patriarchas fuisse nomine Seminis mulieris contentos oportuit:& Iacobus ipsum demū Scilo, id est filium suum nuncupauit. Sed Dauidi demū Regi Filius iste cum Regis elogio promissus est, & quidē cuius regnum esset in perpetuum duraturū, sub vmbra & typo Regis Salomonis. 2. Sam.7.13. 1.Chr.22.10. cæterisque deinceps tèporibus in singulas ætates,tū Rex ipse tū regnū ipsius, magnificentissimis elogiis fuit & in Psalmis passim & ab omnibus Prophetis decantatū, & ita graphicè repræsentatū,vt ne cogitari quidem illa potuisse videatur:quod etiam Angelus Mariæ Virgini commemorauit. Luc 1.32.nec ipsis sapientibus Orietalibus fuit incognitū. Matt. 2.2. Adde quod & ipsi historici prophani testantur, passim apud Getes exteras vulgatum fuisse Iudæis Magnum aliquem & potentē Regē nascituru: quo factū est vt Herodes in magnā suspicionē inciderit, maxima tamē huius populi culpa,qui de mūdano terreno q; dicta putabat quæcunq; olim Prophetæ de cœlesti spiritualiq́ue Regis huius futuro regno prædixerant, talé ipsum in Synagogis docētibus Rabbinis,vnde etiā accidit vt ad huc scopulū ipsi Apoltoli sæpius impegerint. Matth. 20. 22. & Mar. 9. 34. licet ab ipso filio doctore sæpius tum verbis tum exemplis contrarium edocti fuissent, ac suum errorem in victima illa Iesu Christi Hierosolymam profectione facile ex eorum quæ oculis intuebantur, cum ii;s quæ à Zachar. 9. v. 9. de Regis huius in urbem Hierusalem ingressu fuerant prædicta collatione cognoscere potuissent. Et quod peius est, etiam ab ipsius resurrectione hic iterum hære re videntur, ex quæstione illa Domino proposita, Act. 1. 6. tantum est difficultatis in carnalibus cogitationibus & inueteratis opinionibus ex hominum qui carnei sunt cerebro euellendis, tum vero maxime quum ad antiquitatem etiam hominum multitudo & respectus accesserit.
units.tr: by the King himself, the greatest and most unconquerable of all kings? Indeed, the very thing is contained in the name Messiah in Hebrew and Christ in Greek, which means anointed, on account of that anointing of kings customary among the Jews. But it must be recognised that this name was not altogether clearly revealed to the Fathers from the beginning. Adam and the patriarchs had to be content with the name "seed of the woman", and Jacob finally called him Shiloh, that is, his son. But this Son was promised to King David with the title of king, and indeed one whose kingdom would last for ever, under the shadow and type of King Solomon (2 Sam. 7:13; 1 Chr. 22:10). In the following ages, both the King himself and his kingdom were celebrated in the Psalms everywhere and by all the Prophets with the most magnificent titles, and portrayed so vividly that it seems they could not even have been imagined otherwise. The angel also recalled this to the Virgin Mary (Luke 1:32). Nor was it unknown even to the wise men from the East (Matt. 2:2). Add that the secular historians themselves bear witness that it was commonly reported among foreign peoples that a great and powerful king would be born among the Jews. From this it came about that Herod fell into great suspicion. Yet the greatest fault lay with this people, who thought that whatever the prophets had once foretold about the heavenly and spiritual kingdom of this King had been said of a worldly and earthly one. The rabbis taught this in the synagogues, and so it also happened that the Apostles themselves often stumbled against this stone (Matt. 20:22; Mark 9:34), although the Son himself had often taught them the opposite, both in words and by examples. They could easily have recognised their error from the things they saw with their own eyes, namely Jesus Christ's journey to Jerusalem as a sacrifice, by comparing them with what was foretold in Zech. 9:9 about this King's entry into the city of Jerusalem. What is worse, even after his resurrection they seem to cling to this error again, as the question put to the Lord shows (Acts 1:6). So much difficulty is there in uprooting carnal thoughts and inveterate opinions from the brains of men who are of flesh, and especially when the multitude of men and respect for antiquity are added to them.

units.la: Scfe igitur Iudæi sua ipsorum ingenti culpatam firma solidàque filiorumque Dei propria consolatione priuarunt: quare diligens adhibenda nobis est cautio ne Iudæos imitati cœlum cum terra, sicut mox dicturi fumus, commutemus. Agite igitur fratres, forti animo præfentíque fimus. Non fine Rege fumus, eóque nec terreno, nec olim interituro, sed cœlesti & in omne seculum permansuro, etsi tanquam oues mactationi destinatæ æstimemur. Pfal. 44. 22. & mundi purgamenta facti fimus. 1. Cor. 4 13, Si quæ forte nobis igitur minæ intentantur, vel etiam fi lædimur, eia feruorum illorum & seruarum exemplum, quorum meminit Psalmus. 123. 2. imitemur. Verum enimenimuerò,num ille nobis tuendis & protegè-dis par elt? Apage tanto Rege indignam quæ-stionem, quem ipse pater eius Dauid Dominū suum appellat,Psal.110.1.quem ipse Deus æ-ternus filium suum agnoscit.Psal 2.2.& 6.&7. quem ab Angelis adorari iubet. Psal. 97.7. quem denique sceptro ferreo metuedum ho-stibus armat, quos, instar figuli vasa sua con-fringentis, comminuat, Psal. 2.9. An verò i-psum hostes ipsius & nostri metuunt? Immò vero, atque adeo quidem vt & ipsi Diaboli in porcos sine ipsius permissu intrare non potue-rint.Matth.8.31.vt morbus etiam absentis mā-data statim intelligat & recedat. Matth. 8.8.& 13.vt mors ad illius iussum etiam abactam prę-dam relinquat. Ioh. 11.43. cui Angeli ipsi in-seruiunt. Matth.4.11. qui mari, qui ventis im-perat, Luc. 8. 25. Ecto vero tanta potestas, sed an eius illi responder voluntas? Quînam verò non responderet, quum prior ille nos eligat. 2. Thesl. 2. 13. quum is sit qui facit inueniri se ipsum non quærentibus.Esa.65.1.quum bonus ille sit pastor qui aberrantem ouem quærit? Matth.18.12.quum sit custos Israël qui nunquâ dormitat? Psal. 121. 4. quum ille sit etiam qui seipsum seruandis suis ouibus deuouet.Ioh.10. 15. qui sibi factum putat quod vni ex minimis suis factum est. Matth. 25. 4. 5. qui denique se persecutionem ab illis pati profitetur qui suos persequuntur.Act.9.4.Vnde fit igitur,dicet a-liquis, vt tam sæpe suos hostium ipsorum ob-iiciat & exponat libidini?Matth.17.12.& sæpe nullum fit tantum sæuitiæ genus quod non experiantur? Heb. 11.37. Aio tantùm abesse vt tunc eorum curam abiecerit, vt contrà maximè præsens sit,& eos tunc maximè suo dignos ordine recipiat, tantò futura gloria ipsorum insigniore, quantò lucta fuerit,acrior & difficilior: de qua etiam tàtùm abest vt pugnantes conquerantur, vt contrà maximè tunc exultent. Matth. 5 12 Gal. 6.14. & 17.2. Tim. 4.7. & 8. Interea vero pari iustum, excipiet aliquis. Adde verò & patiendo vincere: adde quoque minimè esse patria quæ præsenti tempore perpetimur, futuræ gloriæ in nobis retegendæ. Rom. 8. 18. Tunc enim verè vitam adipiscuntur quum illius facere iacturam eos mundus arbitratur. Matth. 10.38. & 16.25. Quinam verò excipiet iterum aliquis mysteriorum nostræ salutis imperitus, scilicet suorum hostium non eripuit manibus? En igitur causam certissimam. Qui potuit discipulos suos captus ipse tutos à capientibus se dimittere, qui armatos illos satellites ad se comprehendendum paratos solo verbo prostrauit. Ioh. 18.6. & 8. qui latroni vitam æternam in ipso mortis articulo largitus est. Luc. 23 43. qui Solem ipsum postquam animam estlallet tenebris industis Luce priuauit, terram ipsam concussit, monumenta reclußit, annon poterat captorum manus effugere? Captum igitur accipite, vinctum, colaphis impetitum, irrisum, virgis cæsum, crucifixum, lancea perfossum, quòd sic voluit: voluisse autem quòd nostram vicem subierit, pecpeccata nostra in corpore suo super lignum perferens. 1.Pet. 2.24. Porro si quis istius certaminis fuerit exitus attentius perpendamus, næ comperiemus vinctum Christum se vincientes, nobis in libertatem asserтis, vinxisse: suisq; vinculis, Diaboli, peccati, mortis vincula quibus detinebamur, soluisse, & contra vinculis æternis constrictos à quibus prius tenebatur alligasse: per opprobria & contumelias suas in Patris sui gloriam ingressum, & in cœlum nobis ab eodem aditum fuisse patefactum, hostibus suis nostrisque in sempiternam ignominiam & dedecus immersis: vulneribus ipsius nos sanatos, hostibus suis in æternum prostratis: in crucem elatum reuera fuisse modis omnibus cuectum, nósquc ad se supra mundum attraxisse, morientem, in vitam ingressum & nos in vitam intromisisse, mortem in sepulchrum vsque ipsius nempe mortis penetralia persequutum, ipsi lethale vulnus inflixisse, quo vice versa mors ipsa nobis ad vitam & incorruptionem fiat introitus. En igitur, Regis nostri triumphum, ante se captiuos hostes agentis. Psal. 69. 19. in hunc finem missi. Esa. 61.1. iam plenam quòd ad se attinet victoriam adepti. Heb. 2. 9. sed adhuc in membris suis decertantis, donec vltimo tandem hoste deuicto membrorum cum suo capite sempiternus sit triumphus. 1.Cor.15. 23. Denique fratres, quùm Regem habeamus etiam Hominem Deum, verum nostrum Immanuelem, ad Patris dextram sedentem, omnē potestatem in cœlo & in
units.tr: Thus the Jews, by their own great fault, deprived themselves of the firm and solid consolation of the sons of God. So we must take careful heed not to imitate the Jews and exchange heaven for earth, as we shall soon say. Come then, brothers, let us be brave and steadfast in spirit. We have a King, and he is not earthly, nor one who will one day perish, but heavenly, and he will endure for ever, even if we are reckoned as sheep destined for slaughter (Ps. 44. 22) and have become the offscouring of the world (1 Cor. 4. 13). If therefore any threats are aimed at us, or even if we are harmed, let us imitate the example of those male and female servants of whom Psalm 123. 2 speaks. But is that King not equal to protecting and defending us? Away with such an unworthy question about a King whom his own father David calls his Lord (Ps. 110. 1), whom the eternal God himself acknowledges as his Son (Ps. 2. 2, 6, 7), whom he commands to be worshipped by the angels (Ps. 97. 7), and whom he finally arms with an iron sceptre to dash his enemies to pieces, as a potter breaks his vessels (Ps. 2. 9). Do his enemies, then, and ours, fear him? Indeed they do; so much so that even the devils could not enter the swine without his permission (Matt. 8. 31). Disease, at his command, understands at once even when he is absent, and departs (Matt. 8. 8, 13). Death, at his bidding, gives up its prey, even when it has been driven off (John 11. 43). Angels themselves serve him (Matt. 4. 11). He commands the sea and the winds (Luke 8. 25). But granted that such power is his, is his will the same as the power? Why would it not respond, since he is the one who first chooses us (2 Thess. 2. 13), since he is the one who is found by those who do not seek him (Isa. 65. 1), since he is the good shepherd who seeks the straying sheep (Matt. 18. 12), since he is the keeper of Israel who never sleeps (Ps. 121. 4), since he is the one who devotes himself to save his own sheep (John 10. 15), who counts as done to himself what is done to one of his least (Matt. 25. 40), and who finally professes that he suffers the persecution of those who persecute his people (Acts 9. 4)? How then, someone will say, does it come about that he so often exposes his own people to the lust of their enemies (Matt. 17. 12), and often they undergo every kind of cruelty (Heb. 11. 37)? I say that he has so far from abandoned their care in that time that, on the contrary, he is most present and then most of all receives them into the rank that is their due, the more glorious their future glory will be, the fiercer and harder the struggle has been. Far from complaining as they fight, they then exult the more (Matt. 5. 12; Gal. 6. 14; 2 Tim. 4. 7, 8). Meanwhile, someone will object that this is just a matter of equal justice. Add, moreover, that by suffering they conquer; add also that what we endure in the present time is not worthy to be compared with the glory to be revealed in us (Rom. 8. 18). For they truly attain life when the world thinks they have lost it (Matt. 10. 38; 16. 25). But someone, ignorant of the mysteries of our salvation, will again ask: did he not snatch his followers from the hands of their enemies? Here, then, is the most certain reason. He who, though taken himself, could release his disciples unharmed from those who seized him, and who by a word alone threw down the armed soldiers ready to arrest him (John 18. 6, 8), who granted eternal life to the thief at the very moment of death (Luke 23. 43), and who, after he had yielded up his spirit, deprived the sun of its light by a dark shadow, shook the earth itself and broke open the tombs, could he not have escaped the hands of his captors? Hear, then, that he was taken, bound, struck with blows, mocked, scourged, crucified and pierced with a spear, because he so willed it. And he willed it because he undertook our place, bearing our sins in his own body upon the tree (1 Pet. 2. 24). Moreover, if we consider closely the outcome of this conflict, we shall find that Christ, though bound, by binding those who bound him, set us free; by his own chains he loosed the bonds of the devil, of sin and of death by which we were held, and by binding in everlasting chains those by whom he had previously been held, he entered into his Father's glory through his reproaches and insults, and opened to us from the same Father a way into heaven, while his enemies and ours were plunged into everlasting shame and disgrace. By his wounds we are healed, and his enemies are cast down for ever. Lifted up on the cross, he was truly drawn in every way, and he drew us up above the world to himself. Dying, he entered into life, and brought us into life; he pursued death even into the sepulchre, into the very innermost parts of death itself, and inflicted a deadly wound upon it, so that, conversely, death itself becomes for us an entrance to life and incorruption. Behold, then, the triumph of our King, leading his captive enemies before him (Ps. 68. 19), sent for this end (Isa. 61. 1). He has already gained, as far as he is concerned, the full victory (Heb. 2. 9), but he still contends in his members, until at last, when the final enemy is conquered, his triumph with his members and their head is everlasting (1 Cor. 15. 23). Finally, brothers, since we have a King who is also God made man, our true Immanuel, seated at the right hand of the Father, having all power in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28. 18), almighty, best, most truthful, who loves us with a singular and unchanging love, who loses none of those whom the Father has given him (John 17. 2, 12; 18. 9), who casts none out (John 6. 37), and from whose love neither height nor depth, nor any created thing, shall be able to separate us (Rom. 8. 39), what, I beg you, can there be that would strike us with fear? We are few. But, he says, "Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom" (Luke 12. 32). Do not more legions of angels surround us than have ever existed, or ever will exist, among all the mortals of the world, or myriads? (Ps. 34. 8). The prince of this world still breathes threats, and he is indeed to be greatly feared, but already conquered in battle he keeps himself within his own stronghold (John 12. 31; 14. 30). The world itself mixes all things with clamours and tumults, but "Take heart," says the King, "I have overcome the world" (John 16. 33). The gospel is a mockery to the world, but let us not therefore be ashamed of it, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes (Rom. 1. 16). That stone, I say, crushes all those on whom it falls (Matt. 21. 44), and bears up all those built upon it against all opposition (1 Pet. 2. 5). But we must ask our King for those eyes which he granted to our father Moses to see the invisible (Heb. 11. 27), and which he gave to the prophet's servant to behold those fiery chariots by which we are surrounded (2 Kings 6. 17). May God grant that this may be more and more effected in us.

units.la: G. j. terra habentem, Matt. 21. 18. omnipotente, optimum, veracissimum, singulari & immutabili nos amore prosequentem, neminem eorum quos Pater ipsi dedit amittentem, Ioh. 17. 2. & 12. & 18. 9. neminem foras pellentem, Ioh. 6. 37. a cuius charitate neque sublimitas neque profunditas, neque ulla res creata separare nos poterit. Rom. 8. 39. ecquid erit, obsecro, quod metum nobis inferat? Pauci sumus. At, inquit ille, ne time parue grex, Nam visum est patri vestro dare vobis regnum. Luc. 12. 32. An non etiam plures Angelorum nos circumstant Legiones, quàm vnquam in toto terrarum orbe mortalium extiterunt, vel extiturae sunt myriades? Psal. 34. 8. Princeps huius mundi minas quidem adhuc valde metuendus spirat, sed iam acie victus propugnaculo se suo continet Ioh. 12. 31. & 14. 30. Mundus ipse clamoribus & tumultibus omnia miscet, sed agite, inquit Rex, forti estote animo, ego vici mundum. Ioh. 16. 32. Euangelium mundi ludibrium est, sed ne propterea illud erubescamus: Est enim potentia Dei ad salutem cuiuis credenti. Rom. 1. 16. Lapis, inquam, ille est eos omnes super quos ceciderit conquassans. Matth. 21. 44. & contra omnes illi superaedificatos sustinens. 1. Pet. 2. 5. Sed a Rege nostro poltulandi sunt oculi, quos Patri nostro Mosi, ad invisibilem cernendum concessit, Heb. 11. 27. & quos Prophetae seruo ad igneos illos currus quibus circundamur intuendos. 2. Reg. 6. 17. Quod vtinam Deus in nobis magis ac magis efficiat. ciat.
units.tr: ...holding all power in heaven and on earth, almighty, best, most truthful, loving us with a singular and unchanging love, losing none of those whom the Father has given him, casting none out, from whose love neither height nor depth, nor any created thing, will be able to separate us. Rom. 8. 39. What, I beg you, could there be that would bring fear upon us? We are few. But, he says, fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom. Luc. 12. 32. Do not even more legions of angels surround us than have ever existed, or ever will exist, in the whole world of mortals, myriads upon myriads? Psal. 34. 8. The prince of this world still breathes threats, and is indeed very much to be feared, but already beaten in battle he keeps himself within his own stronghold. Ioh. 12. 31. & 14. 30. The world itself throws everything into confusion with its clamours and tumults, but take courage, says the King, I have overcome the world. Ioh. 16. 32. The gospel is a laughingstock to the world, but let us not therefore be ashamed of it: for it is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes. Rom. 1. 16. That stone, I say, is the one which will crush all those on whom it falls, and will bear up against all those built upon it. 1. Pet. 2. 5. But from our King we must ask for eyes, such as he granted to our father Moses to see the invisible, Heb. 11. 27. and such as he granted to the prophet's servant to behold those fiery chariots with which we are surrounded. 2. Reg. 6. 17. May God grant this in us more and more.

units.la: Sed ne spes inanes pascamus, & melius ad- huc teneamus, quid nobis à nostro Rege & ab ipsius regno sit expectandum,age quæ de se & suo regno paucis commemorat attente per- pendamus:Meum regnum, inquit,non est de hoc mundo. Obseruate vero in primis hoc loco Mundi nomine non simpliciter cœlum & ter- ram, quæque illis continentur significari, nec genus humanum absolute, multoque minus reproborum & impiorum cœtum vniuersum, cui filij Dei opponuntur, qui de mundo illo non sunt:sed status & politias quæ vitam præ- sentem spectant, & quæcunque ad illam per- tinent intelligi. Obserua deinde non hic de regni istius finibus, sed de regno ipso, putà modo & ratione illius administrandi agi:qua-si diceret Christus ita se Regem ac verè Re-gem esse, vt nec Imperatoris Romani nec a-liorum istius orbis terrarum Regum quicquā interfit, vel de illorum tantillum decedat au-ctoritate: tantùm abest vt homines à Cæsaris auertat obedientia, quum ipsius regni longè alia sit quàm terrenorum administratio,& ni-hil minus quàm politiarum & Magistratuum quibus humanum genus ad seculi consumma-tionem vsque fouetur:euersionem cogitet. Ex quibus facile quilibet animaduertat detestan-dæ calumniæ reos esse quicunque Christianos vt turbulentos & seditiosos accusant: & con-trà Anabaptistas, Libertinos, & similis farinæ homines,iure tum diuino tum humano meritis poenis afficiendos. Notandum praeterea Christum hic minime de suprema illa diuina potentia soli Deo Patri, Filio & Sp. S. propria quam in omnes res creatas sine distinctione, vel exceptione obtinet loqui: sed agere speciatim & expresse de illo regimine spirituali, Filio tanquam primogenito inter multos fratres attributo. Rom.8 28. cuius etiam respectu quum fratrem se noltrum fecisset, & adimpleto in his terris quod in se suscepepat munere in coelum ascendisset, in carne nostra in illius Imperij possessionem venturus, Caput Ecclesiae suae dicitur & Mediator noster, ad dextram patris sedens, tanquam is in cuius persona Pater, etiam ante iacta mundi fundamenta, electos sui bene placiti colligere, sibi conciliare, & tandem ad gloriam suam adducere decreverat: Et hoc est a Filio secundum temporum dispensationem in his terris fideliter adimpletum, ipso iam e solio illo suo Ecclesiam suam adversus omnes hostes tuente: haec lucta tam diu duratura dum penitus subactis, & sub pedibus suis in aeternum prostratis hostibus, Dei regnum in suo tranquillum & pacatum in aeternam felicitatem duret. 1.Cor.15 28. Quamobrem attente considerate non dixisse Christum, Regnum suum non esse in hoc mundo: sed non esse ex hoc mundo, puta mundanum, terrenumque ac reliquorum instar terrenorum mutationi & vanitati obnoxium. Nam quod ad ipsius Regni fines attinet, in illis coelum & terra, imo quicquid est supra coelos in qui-
units.tr: But, lest we feed empty hopes and hold on to what is better, let us attentively weigh what we are to expect from our King and from his kingdom, as he briefly recounts concerning himself and his kingdom: "My kingdom," he says, "is not of this world." Joh. 18. 36. Observe first of all that by the name "world" here is meant not simply heaven and earth and the things contained in them, nor the human race absolutely, and much less the whole assembly of the reprobate and impious, to whom the sons of God are opposed, who are not of that world; but the states and polities which concern the present life, and whatever pertains to it. Observe next that here he is speaking not of the limits of that kingdom but of the kingdom itself, that is, of the manner and mode of its administration: as if Christ were saying that he is King, and truly King, in such a way that it makes no difference to the Roman Emperor or to the other kings of this earthly orb, nor does it take away the least part of their authority. So far is he from turning men away from the obedience due to Caesar, since the administration of his kingdom is quite different from that of earthly kingdoms, and he has in mind nothing less than the overthrow of the polities and magistracies by which the human race is sustained until the consummation of the age. From these things anyone may easily see that those who accuse Christians of being turbulent and seditious are guilty of a detestable calumny; and, on the contrary, that Anabaptists, Libertines, and men of that stamp deserve to be punished with merited penalties under both divine and human law. It must further be noted that Christ here by no means speaks of that supreme divine power which belongs to God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit alone, and which they hold over all created things without distinction or exception; but speaks specifically and expressly of that spiritual rule which is attributed to the Son as firstborn among many brothers. Rom. 8. 29. In respect of this rule, when he had made himself our brother, and had accomplished on this earth the office he had undertaken, and had ascended into heaven, about to come in our flesh into possession of that dominion, he is called the Head of his Church and our Mediator, sitting at the right hand of the Father, as the one in whose person the Father, even before the foundation of the world, had decreed to gather his elect according to his good pleasure, to join them to himself, and at last to bring them to his glory. And this is faithfully carried out by the Son on this earth, in accordance with the dispensation of the times, he himself now from that throne defending his Church against all enemies; this struggle is to last as long as the enemies, being wholly subdued and laid prostrate under his feet for ever, leave God's kingdom tranquil and at peace in eternal happiness. 1. Cor. 15. 28. Wherefore, consider carefully that Christ did not say his kingdom is not in this world, but that it is not of this world, that is, not worldly and earthly, nor subject to change and vanity like earthly things. For as far as the limits of his kingdom are concerned, in them are contained heaven and earth, indeed whatever is above the heavens, in which the throne of his dominion is properly located; add whatever is in the very abysses, since he has received a name which is above every name. Phil. 2. 9. & 10. and Isa. 45. 23. And indeed expressly insofar as he is the Son of man. Joh. 5. 27.

units.la: quibus Imperij ipsius thronus est proprie cötinetur, adde quicquid est in ipsis abyssis, quü nomen acceperit quod est supra omne nomē Phil. 2. 9. & 10. & Esa. 45. 23. & quidem diserte quatenus Filius hominis est. Ioh. 5. 27. In hoc enim potissimum sita nostra est consolatio: quòd nisi nobis etiam secundum carnem nostram coniunctus esset, vt membra corporis ipsius, caro ex carne, ossa ex ossibus sieremus, Ephes. 5. 30. & Heb. 2. 11. gloria illa & vita spiritualis minimè possint in nos defluere. Caue autem putes vel Angelos vel Sanctos Christū hominem ea adoratione quæ Deo soli debetur venerantes esse idololatras: est enim Homo Deus in vnitate Persönæ: ac proinde quòd ad naturarum distinctionem (quę semper integra mansit & mansura est, quòd gloria illa cœlestis in quam Christus secundum carnem euectus est minimè isti carni essentiam aut essentiales proprietates ademerit, sed suis demum spoliarit infirmitatibus) hinc, quatenus nempe Deus est, seipso maior est, & supra seipsum humanitatis suæ respectu, inde verò quatenus homo est, seipso minor, & infra seipsum & Deum Patrem est, Diuinitatis nempe suæ respectu, nec propterea tamen vnitas persönæ diuellitur. Denique vt hunc locum absoluam, Regni huius scopus est non vita præsens, non hanc vitam spectantes commoditates, sed vitam æternam, & ad illam adipiscendam quæcunque faciunt, vt mox sumus intellectuari. Etsi vero Rex iste & Caput proprium est Ecclesiæ, nihilominus tamen reliqua pars hominum quæ mundus appellatur, & à quo Ecclesia dicitur est, quæque Tyranno mundi huius mancipata est, nostro etiam Regi subiecta est, cuius tantam esse docemur potestatem vt in hostium medio regnet, virgámque ferream armatus ad suos hostes confringendos & comminuendos. Psalm. 2.9. & 110.2. vnà cum ipsorum quantumlibet reluctante tyrano, gestet. Luc. 11.28. Ecquis enim alioquin obsecro Rex iste foret, nisi in suos & nostros inimicos imperium obtineret? Et hoc etiam respectu regnum illud, etsi non terrenum sed cœlestè sit (quo sensu toties Ecclesiam regni cœlorum nomine designari videmus, quasi iam in superna loca peruenisset. Colos. 3. 1.) tamen in his terris regit & administrat, is qui in mundo est & ad seculi consummationem vsque futurus est. Matth. 28.20. Ne vero præterea putemus ab hoc spirituali regno quæ corpora nostra & præsentem vitam spectant excludenda, quatenus mediis illis ad nos in superna dedicedos Deus vtitur. Quinimo certo nobis persuadeamus hoc respectu etiam Regem nostrum cœlestem & spiritualem peculiari cura de nostris corporibus in hac vita tutandis & illis necessariis ad victu rebus suppeditandis tangi, & quidem tanto studio foucendis, vt vel capillorum nostrorum non sit immemor. Matth. 10. verf. 30. Verùm in primis hoc est obseruandum, cuncta illa terrena beneficia tantùm instar appendicis habenda, quibus bus ad maiorum bonorum eorúmque præci-puorum fruitionem deducamur. Deinde & illud sciendum illius vnius esse Regis nostri, cui melius quàm nobis ipsis noti sumus, nobis quæ ad hanc vitam traducendam necessaria sunt ex bonæ voluntatis beneplacito dispensare, non autem ex cupiditatum nostrarum, libidine, quibus si vel tantillum concederet vt solent imperiti medici male patientibus ægrotis, inox de nobis actum foret. Quod ita se habere satis nos quotidiana docet experientia. Annon enim licet adeò misera sit & caduca vita nostra, & mille periculis obnoxia, ægre tamen ex illa, adeò nobis caro & sanguis dominantur, excedimus? Quid ergo fore putamus, si tam secundis rebus vteremur quàm cuperemus? Annon subinde Deo suum in cœlis paradisum relinquentes hic nos relinqui nostræ felicitati postula□emus? Annon iusculo, Esauum imitati, benedictionem Isaaci commutaremus? Habet igitur, fateor, pietas promissiones vitæ præsentis ac futuræ. 1. Timoth. 4. 8. sed perpetuò sunt etiam illa nobis Christi verba, Regnum ipsius, nempe, non esse ex hoc mundo, memoria repetenda.
units.tr: over which the throne of his rule is properly located. Add whatever is in the abysses themselves, to him who has received the name that is above every name (Phil. 2:9-10; Isa. 45:23), and indeed expressly as he is the Son of Man (John 5:27). For our consolation rests chiefly on this: unless he were joined to us also according to our flesh, so that we become members of his body, flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones (Eph. 5:30; Heb. 2:11), that glory and spiritual life could not flow down into us. Yet take care not to think that by worshipping Christ the man, with that adoration which is due to God alone, the Angels or the Saints are idolaters. For the Man is God in the unity of the Person. Therefore, as regards the distinction of natures, which has always remained whole and always will, that heavenly glory into which Christ was carried according to the flesh has not taken away from that flesh its essence or its essential properties, but has rather stripped it of its weaknesses. Thus, insofar as he is God, he is greater than himself, and above himself with respect to his humanity; but insofar as he is man, he is less than himself, and below himself and the Father of God, namely with respect to his divinity; yet the unity of the Person is not thereby torn apart. Finally, to finish this point: the aim of this Kingdom is not the present life, nor the advantages that regard this life, but eternal life, and whatever they do to attain it, as we shall soon be made to understand. Although this King is indeed the proper Head of the Church, nevertheless the rest of mankind, which is called the world, and from which the Church is said to be called out, and which is handed over to the tyrant of this world, is also subject to our King. We are taught that his power is so great that he reigns in the midst of his enemies, and bears, armed, a rod of iron to break and crush his enemies (Ps. 2:9; 110:2), together with the tyrant, however much he resists. (Luke 11:28.) For, I ask you, what kind of king would he be otherwise, unless he held rule over his enemies and ours? And in this respect too, that kingdom, although it is not earthly but heavenly (in which sense we see the Church so often designated by the name of the kingdom of heaven, as if it had already reached the higher places; Col. 3:1), nevertheless rules and governs in these lands him who is in the world and will be until the consummation of the age (Matt. 28:20). Nor, moreover, should we think that those things which concern our bodies and the present life are excluded from this spiritual kingdom, insofar as God uses those means to lead us up to heavenly things. Indeed, let us firmly persuade ourselves that in this respect too our heavenly and spiritual King is touched with particular care for protecting our bodies in this life and for supplying the things necessary for our sustenance, and indeed with such zeal for cherishing them that he is not unmindful even of the hairs of our head (Matt. 10:30). But first of all this must be observed: all those earthly benefits must be held merely as an appendix, by which we are led on to the enjoyment of greater goods and of those chief goods. Next, it must also be known that it belongs to that one King of ours, who knows us better than we know ourselves, to dispense to us, by the good pleasure of his will, what is necessary for passing through this life, and not according to the lust of our desires. If he were to yield to us even a little in these, as unskilled physicians are wont to do with sick people who are ill-tolerant, we would soon be undone. Daily experience teaches us enough that this is so. For does not our life, however wretched and frail, and exposed to a thousand dangers, still with difficulty get us out of it, so much do flesh and blood dominate us? What then do we think would happen if we enjoyed prosperity as much as we wished? Would we not from time to time demand that God leave his paradise in the heavens and leave us here to our own happiness? Would we not, imitating Esau for a little broth, exchange the blessing of Isaac? I admit, then, that godliness has promises for the present life and for the future (1 Tim. 4:8). But those words of Christ must always be kept in mind: that his kingdom is not of this world.

units.la: Quapropter diligenter est in hoc incumbendum vt Dauidis admonitionem sequuti. Psal. 16 5. & 11. & 17. 14. & 15. & veterum imitati Patrum exempla, minimè in terris, sed superius in cœlis thesauros congeramus. Matth. 6. 19. Mercatorem illum æmulemur, cunctas suas facultates vel vni margaritæ postponentem.
units.tr: Therefore we must diligently apply ourselves to this, following the admonition of David (Ps. 16:5; 11; 17:14, 15), and imitating the examples of the ancient Fathers: let us gather treasures not on earth but higher up in heaven (Matt. 6:19). Let us imitate that merchant who set aside all his possessions for the sake of a single pearl.

units.la: Huius do ctrinæ applicatio.
units.tr: The application of this teaching.

units.la: Matth. 13. 46. Rebus terrenis & caducis posthabitis coelestia & spiritualia perquiramus. Colos. 3. 2. Ne mundi istius praetereuntis speciem attentius inhaerentes contemplemur. 1. Cor. 7. 31. sed mundus contra nobis crucifixus esto, & nos mundo. Gal. 6. 14. Et quandoquidem Iesus Christus, Veteribus propter promissionum obscuritatem paulo crassius habitis, diserte monet conformia fieri oportere membra capiti in perpessionibus, si conformia fieri volunt illi in gloria. Rom. 8. 17. 2. Tim. 2. 11. & 12. non esse ipso dignum qui non tollit crucem suam & sequitur eum a tergo. Matt. 10. 38. non esse discipulum supra magistrum. Matt. 10. 24. ne putemus Deum quae coniunxit, crucem videlicet ab Euangelij recta professione, aut ab Euangelij vera professione nostram salutem seperaturum esse. Mundus amat quae sua sunt, & quae illius mundi sunt, peritura sunt. Ecquod maius igitur nobis contingat beneficium, quam si nos mundus & odit & persequitur, quum ex odio mundi certissimo argumento colligere possimus nos ex hoc mundo non esse? Ioh. 15. 19. En cur Rex iste qui sibi nos vindicavit, quique mundum a se devictum esse profitetur, Ioh. 16. 33. preces ad Deum Patrem pro iis qui adhuc sunt in mundo fudit, quem exauditum quum nemo dubitet, ecquid erit quod metum nobis iniiciat? Ioh. 17. 11. Quid igitur est reliquum? Nempe ratum fixu illud est, oppressionem in mundo nos perpessuros. Ioh. 16. 33. Itaque si quis contrarium sibi persuaserit opiopinione deceptum iri.Sed eum qui tentatio-nem immittit, & qui in nostra infirmitate triumphare vult fidelem esse nouimus. 2.Cor. 12.9. quíque nō finit nos supra vires quas ipse-met largitus est tentari.1.Cor.10.13.sic operante ipso in nobis vt in omnibus pressi, non tamen coarctemur, hæsitantes, non prorsus hæreamus,persecutionem patientes, in ea nō deferamur,deiecti,non tamen perceamus. 2.Cor. 4.8.& 9.Et hæc sunt verè Christianorum insignia & notæ,quam etiam ob causam afflictiones illæ quas pro Iesu Christo tolerant fideles Probationes appellantur. Heu! verò,heu inquam , quàm est istorum exiguus numerus: quàm verè fi vnquam alias , hodie dicere possumus raram admodum esse terram illam quæ sementi excipiendæ & fructui ferendo fit accommoda ! Quando verò lux illa illucebit qua visuri fumus ambitiosos,auaros, fæneratores, ganeones , confpiratores & monopoliorum nouarúmque artium quibus annonæ caritas crescat inuentores , ex animo credere Christo profitenti regnum suum non esse ex hoc mundo ? Vtinam verò atque vtinam illa nobis hodie lux affulgeret: vtinam voti mei compos gaudio exultare possem. Sed magnopere vereor ne fi centum annorum spatio fieri id postularim, adhuc periculiter ne nō fiat, quum tot scelera nostris oculis intueri quotidie cogamur. At scitote Deum fore vindicem , cuius manum illo mundum & vos iudicante nunquam fugis cuafuri : itaque vobis aut omnino pereundum est aut in melius mores commu-tandi.Hoc verò vtinam Deus Opt.Maxim.vo-bis largiatur ab illo verò vos sartos tectos tueatur.
units.tr: Having set aside earthly and perishable things, let us seek out heavenly and spiritual ones (Matt. 13:46). Let us not look too closely at and contemplate the appearance of this passing world (Col. 3:2; 1 Cor. 7:31), but rather let the world be crucified to us and we to the world (Gal. 6:14). And since Jesus Christ, who for the sake of the obscurity of the promises was taken by the ancients somewhat too crudely, clearly warns that the members must be conformed to the head in sufferings if they wish to be conformed to him in glory (Rom. 8:17; 2 Tim. 2:11, 12), that he is not worthy of him who does not take up his cross and follow him from behind (Matt. 10:38), and that the disciple is not above the teacher (Matt. 10:24), let us not think that God will separate what he has joined together: namely, the cross from the right profession of the Gospel, or our salvation from the true profession of the Gospel. The world loves what is its own, and what belongs to that world is perishing (1 John 2:15). What greater benefit could befall us than that the world both hates and persecutes us, since from the hatred of the world we can gather a most certain proof that we are not of this world (John 15:19)? See why this King, who has claimed us for himself, and who professes that he has overcome the world (John 16:33), poured out prayers to God the Father for those who are still in the world (John 17:11). Since no one doubts that these were heard, what could there be that would strike fear into us? What then remains? Surely it is settled that we shall suffer oppression in the world (John 16:33). Therefore, if anyone has persuaded himself of the contrary, he will be deceived by his opinion. But we know that he who sends temptation, and who wishes to triumph in our weakness, is faithful (2 Cor. 12:9), and who does not allow us to be tempted beyond the strength that he himself has given (1 Cor. 10:13), so that, with him working in us, we are pressed on all sides but not crushed, perplexed but not utterly at a loss, persecuted but not forsaken, cast down but not destroyed (2 Cor. 4:8, 9). These are truly the marks and signs of Christians, and for this reason also those afflictions which the faithful endure for Jesus Christ are called proofs. Alas, alas, I say, how small is the number of such people! How truly, if ever at any other time, can we say today that that land is very rare which is suited to receive the seed and to bear fruit! And when will that light shine by which we shall see the ambitious, the greedy, the usurers, the gluttons, the conspirators, and the inventors of monopolies and of new arts by which the price of food rises, believing from the heart in Christ, who professes that his kingdom is not of this world? Would that, would that that light might shine on us today; would that I might rejoice, having had my wish fulfilled. But I greatly fear that even if I were to ask for this over the space of a hundred years, it would still be doubtful whether it would happen, since we are daily forced to see so many crimes with our own eyes. But know that God will be the avenger, whose hand you will never escape when he judges both the world and you. Therefore either you must perish altogether, or change to better ways. May God the best and greatest grant this to you, and may he keep you safe and sound, protected by himself.

units.la: Cæterùm Dominus amouens à se sibi ab inimicis impositum crimen non est illos imi-tatus, qui nullis testimoniis suam criminatio-nem confirmarant,sed ratione cuiuis manife-sta suum responsum fulcit,nempe se si vera fo-ret accusatorum criminatio,& sic populum,i-pse regnum affectans,docuisset,stipatoribus& armatis satellitibus armatum, Iudæis inimicis suis fuisse restituturū: quorum verborum ea-dem vis est ac si Pilatum iuberet attentius per-pendere quàm absurdum &ridiculum crimen accusatores illi imponerent,cuius ab omni re-gni affectatione vita fuisset aliena, & satis o-mnibus perspecta:cuius item satis cogniti fa-miliares & quotidiani stipatores. Vide igitur, obsecro , quàm grauiter Petrus gladio euagi-nato,contra Præceptoris sui defensione, impe-gerit , quantam istis delatoribus occasionem calumniandi præbuerit, nisi Dominus singu-lari sua prouidentia maturè tanto malo reme-dium,vt iam superius attigimus, attulisset.
units.tr: Moreover, when the Lord shook off the false charge laid on him by his enemies, he did not imitate those who had confirmed their accusation with no evidence at all. Instead he met it with an answer that was plain to anyone who thought about it. If the accusers' charge were true, he said, he would have taught the people to aspire to the kingdom himself, and he would have restored an armed kingdom to the Jews, his enemies, with bodyguards and armed attendants. The force of these words is the same as if he were bidding Pilate to weigh carefully how absurd and ridiculous a charge those accusers had brought, since his life had been far removed from any ambition for a kingdom, and was well known to everyone. Likewise his close companions and daily attendants were well known. Consider, I beg you, how gravely Peter, drawing his sword in defence of his Master, gave those informers an opportunity to slander him, had the Lord not, by his singular providence, as we touched on above, applied a timely remedy to so great an evil.

units.la: Age verò,quæstionem non parui momenti quæ laboritur hoc loco perpendamus: quæri-tur autem an legitima vi armata propulsatio, tantopere cum regno Iesu Christi Domini no stri spirituali pugnet , vt simul illa consistere non possint. Nam sanè quum in conscientia vera religio sita sit,quam nec ferro,nec alia vi-la vi la vi cogere quisquam,sed sola spontanea per-suafione potest inducere, nullus vel gladio vel vlli violentiæ locus hic esse non immerito videretur. Verùmenimuero contrarium docemur,Deo ipso disertis & expressis verbis capitis sententiam, sine delicti gratia aduersus apostatas ad falsos Deos deficientes, & aduersus Pseudoprophetas,ferente. Exod.22.20 & 5.pr. vers.Deut.13.ad vers.17. vsque. & 17.2 3.4. & 5. quod àMose, Exod.32.27. ab Aza. 2.Chron.15. 13.à Iofia 2.Reg.23.5. & 16.factitatum fuisse legimus. Nec alió extraordinaria illa Eliæ 1. Reg.18 40. & Pauli Elymam Magum cæcitate propter religionem ferientis Act.13.11. exempla referenda,longiúsve trahenda sunt.En habes etiam edicta Nebucadnezaris Dan. 3.16. Darij.Ezd.6.11. Artaxerxis, quibus in eos qui veram religionem profanarint graues & capitales etiam pœnæ statuuntur, quæ sacra historia in Regum illorum summam commendationem suis monumentis inseruit. Quum autem Religio vera sit Dominiorum & Imperiorum omnium vnicum firmum fundamentum, & Apostolo teste, 1.Tim.2.2. Regibus & quibusuis in eminentia constitutis Deus hanc potestatem dederit vt eorum subditi tranquillam & quietam vitam,non solùm cum omni honestate, sed etiam cum omni pietate degant, efficitur in hanc illos potissimum curam oportere incumbere,vti verus Dei cultus stabiliatur & sartus rectus sit, ad quod præstandum & implendum ea quam à Domino gladij potestatem acceperunt, quum ita casus feret, vti ipsos, tum aduersos domesticos turbatores, tum aduersus extraneos oppreslores oporteat.Sed hic quædam sunt diligenter obseruanda, ac in primis quidem diligenter cauendum ne decipiamur falsum pro vero capientes: quod facile cauebitur si hominum opiniones cum Dei verbo, quod in fidei nostræ articulis perspicuis & indubitatis comprehensum est, conferantur. Et hic est vnicus gladius ille spiritualis quo hæreses rescindun-tur, & morbidis conscientiis medicina præbetur: quòd authoritas & iudicium Magistra-tuum non proprie ad conscientias vi adigen-das (extra hominũ enim est istud potestatem) adhibeatur: sed maximè ad malitiam & per-tinaciam alioquin immedicabilem Ecclesiæ perturbatorum cohibendam, ita tamen vt ad-uersus eos æquis & iustis agatur conditio-nibus. Deinde quis nescit plurimum isthæc inter se differre, subditos populos in vera i-sorum Religione tutari aduersus eorum violentiam qui inuitos ad nouam cogerent: & alios in quos alioquin nullum ius & potesta-tem habeas ad mutandam religionem inuita-re, quod nec fas quidem aduersus falsæ religio-nis professores foret?
units.tr: Come now, let us weigh a question of no small importance that is debated at this point. The question is whether the lawful use of armed force to repel attackers is so opposed to the spiritual kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ that the two cannot stand together. For since true religion lies in the conscience, which no one can compel by iron or any other violence, but can induce only by free persuasion, it might not unreasonably seem that there is no place here for the sword or for any violence at all. But on the contrary we are taught, since God himself, in plain and express words, pronounces the sentence of death, without any mercy for the offence, against apostates who fall away to false gods, and against false prophets (Exod. 22.20; Deut. 13.6–17; 17.2–5). We read that this was done by Moses (Exod. 32.27), by Asa (2 Chron. 15.13), and by Josiah (2 Kings 23.5, 16). Nor need we cite or lengthen the list with the extraordinary examples of Elijah (1 Kings 18.40) and of Paul striking Elymas the magician with blindness on account of religion (Acts 13.11). Here too are the edicts of Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 3.29), of Darius (Ezra 6.11), and of Artaxerxes, by which grave and even capital punishments are laid down for those who profane the true religion. Sacred history has inserted these into its records as high praise of those kings. Since true religion is the one firm foundation of all dominions and empires, and, as the Apostle witnesses (1 Tim. 2.2), God has given this power to kings and to all who are set in high office, so that their subjects may live a quiet and peaceful life, not only with all honesty but also with all piety, it follows that kings above all must take this care, that the true worship of God be established and kept whole and upright. To perform and fulfil this, they must use the power of the sword which they have received from the Lord, as the case may demand, against domestic disturbers and against foreign oppressors alike. But there are some things here that must be carefully observed. Above all we must take care not to be deceived by taking the false for the true. This will be easily guarded against if men's opinions are compared with the Word of God, which is contained in the clear and indubitable articles of our faith. This is that one spiritual sword by which heresies are cut away and remedy is given to sick consciences. The authority and judgement of magistrates are to be applied not properly to forcing consciences (for that power lies outside man), but chiefly to restraining the malice and obstinacy of those who otherwise incurably disturb the Church, and even then they must proceed on fair and just terms. Furthermore, who does not know that these two things differ greatly: protecting subject peoples in the true religion against the violence of those who would force them into a new one against their will, and, on the other hand, trying to induce to a change of religion people over whom one has no right or power at all, which would not even be lawful against professors of a false religion?

units.la: Quapropter etsi Principes Christianos inter se tanquam vnius eiusdemque corporis membra consentire & conspirare posse ac debere certum est vt sociis armis sese aduer-sus
units.tr: Therefore, although it is certain that Christian princes, as members of one and the same body, can and ought to agree and join together, so that with allied arms they may protect and defend

units.la: sus communes hostes infidelis protegant ac tutentur, cuiusmodi fuerunt patrum nostro- rum temporibus Sarraceni: & iam à multis seculis Turcæ Mahumetani Prouincias Christianas opprimunt: non tamen hoc prætextu tutandæ religionis, de qua præcipuè non agebatur, quum Turcæ populorum quos imperio suo subegerant conscientiis vim nullam adferent, licuit illis, nec hodie licet infidelis bello ad Christianismum conuertendos adoriri, quod sæpe nimis Papæ per suos illos bullarum præcones persuaserunt, belli aduersus infideles nomine ad suas indulgentias amplificandas abutentes, & humano sanguine terrarum orbem vniuersum replentes ad opes turbatis temporibus hauriendas & accumulandas, quod strenuè ab illis præstitum, & multorum seculorum experientia docet, & opes illæ immensæ quas maxima ex parte ex amplissimarum Christiani orbis familiarum ruina, promouendæ fidei Christianæ prætextu corraserunt, satisque perque teltantur. Et hic est ingens ille zelus eiusdem Romanæ sedis, non Apostolicæ sed Apostaticæ, de qua loquuti sunt non obscuris verbis D. Petrus. 2. Petr. 2. verf. 10. & 15. & D. Paulus quorum se successores insigniter mentiuntur. 2. Thessal. 2. 3. & 4. & adhuc apertius Iohannes in suæ Apocalypseos maxima parte, sub nomine Babylonis & Meretricis septe collibus insidetis, ipsis testibus Græcis &
units.tr: themselves against common enemies of the faith, such as the Saracens were in the times of our fathers, and as the Mahometan Turks have for many centuries oppressed Christian provinces, yet this does not give a pretext for defending religion, which was not chiefly at issue, since the Turks have not used any violence against the consciences of the peoples whom they subdued to their rule. It was not lawful for them, and it is not lawful today, to attack the unbelievers in war in order to convert them to Christianity. The Popes have too often persuaded people of this through their bull-criers, abusing the name of war against the infidels to enlarge their indulgences, and filling the whole world with human blood, so as to seize and hoard wealth in troubled times. That this was vigorously carried out by them is taught by the experience of many centuries, and those immense riches, which they have amassed for the most part from the ruin of the most powerful families of the Christian world, under the pretext of advancing the Christian faith, bear witness to it sufficiently and more than sufficiently. And this is that huge zeal of the same Roman see, which is not apostolic but apostate, of which Peter spoke in unmistakable words (2 Pet. 2.10, 15), and which Paul likewise (2 Thess. 2.3–4), and still more plainly John in the greater part of his Apocalypse, under the name of Babylon and the harlot seated on seven hills (as the Greek and the old Latin translators testify, though we see that they were themselves in part infected with the poisons of that harlot). This zeal, I say, is today the zeal of that impure Antichrist, with which he and his satellites burn against heretics, whom, merely changing the names, they now call Lutherans and Huguenots, just as they once called the Saracens and Mahometans.

units.la: {x} Mahumetani Prouincias
units.tr: {x} the Mahometan provinces

units.la: Latinis veteribus interpretibus,quos tamen ipsos ex parte meretricis istius veneficiis infectos fuisse videmus, hic, inquam, hodie zelus est impuri illius Antichristi,quo ipse cum suis satellitibus aduersus hæreticos flagrat, quos mutatis tantùm nominibus pro Sarracenis & Mahumetanis,Lutheranos & Huguenotos ab hinc paucis annis,vocant.Sed quid agas? Sanè quemadmodum hactenus feliciter Dei Opt. Max. ope & auxilio freti, ab illis excitatos ignes,chartis & atramento dimicantes extinximus,& illorum secures nostris calamis retudimus,& fidei quam nobis Deus est largitus clypeum,nulli potuerunt tormentorum bellicorum ictus penetrare, sic nos in hoc spirituali prælio fortiter ad extremum dimicaturos speramus,certo persuasi tempore àDomino prænscripto Impium illum Spiritu oris nostri Regis conficiendum , & illustri ipsius aduentu abolendû.2.Thess.2.8.atque adeo fore vt quum Regi nostro promissiones suis factas adimplere visum fuerit , Reges ipsi & Principes, quibus scorti illius fraudes agnoscere datum fuerit,Apoc.17.16.Socia arma sua temporalia veræ Ecclesiæ spiritualibus armis, ad huius abominandæ sedis ruinam & excidium iungant: cuiusmodi non paucos nostris temporibus excitatos variis locis aspicimus,quos vtinam atque vtinam Magnus ille Rex Regum magis magisque Sancto suo Spiritu regat,zelúmque in primis gloriæ suæ qui secundum scientiam est in illis adaugeat,& ab omnibus tum ad læ-uam uam tum ad dextram tentationibus protegat, ac tandem illis omnibus dona necessaria ad beatam felicemque consolationem tot modis afflictæ Ecclesiæ suæ,& eiusdem liberationem, quàm cumulatissimè largiatur. Et hæc quidem hac de re hactenus dicta sunto.
units.tr: But what can one do? Truly, as hitherto, relying on the help and aid of God Almighty, we have happily quenched the fires kindled by them, fighting with paper and ink, and have blunted their axes with our pens, and since the shield of faith which God has granted us has not been pierced by the blows of their war engines, so we hope that we shall fight bravely to the end in this spiritual battle. We are firmly persuaded that at the time prescribed by the Lord that impious one will be consumed by the Spirit of our King's mouth and abolished by the brightness of his coming (2 Thess. 2.8). And so it will be that when it has seemed good to fulfil the promises made to our King, the kings and princes themselves, to whom it has been given to recognise the deceits of that harlot (Rev. 17.16), will join their temporal arms to the spiritual arms of the true Church for the ruin and destruction of this abominable see. We see not a few such men raised up in various places in our times. Would that, and would that again, the great King of kings would rule them more and more by his Holy Spirit, increase in them the zeal for his glory which is according to knowledge, protect them from every temptation on the left and on the right, and at last bestow upon them and upon his Church, so grievously afflicted in so many ways, all the necessary gifts for its blessed and happy consolation and for its deliverance, in the fullest measure. And these are the things that have been said so far on this matter.

units.la: Verùmenimuerò licet ex iis quæ hactenus diximus, & iis quas expositimus conditionibus, Regnum Christi temporale non absolutè diuellatur à spirituali,sed tamen expresse semper distinguatur, vt tum ex iis quæ Christus ipse hoc loco declarauit, tum quæ toto vitæ suæ curriculo fecit satis est perspicuum, quippe qui tributum ipse persoluerit.Matth.17.27. qui iudicium hercisicundæ familiæ recusarit. Luc. 12.14. qui adulteram condemnare detrectarit. Ioh. 8.11. qui toties discipulos suos discrimen inter ministerium spirituale, & regnũ temporarium docuerit.Luc.22 25.& Paulus ipse generalem & certissimam regulam utriusque regiminis præscripserit. 2. Tim. 4. & 2. Cor. 10. 4. quid tandem, quæso,de perditi illius deperata impudentia dicturi sumus, qua ipsam vrbem Romam, tórque alios Principatus & Dominationes inuasit, quas tam perfrida fronte Petri patrimonium vocat? Anà Deo,vel ab eo,cuius se nimis impudenter Vicarium vniuersalem mentitur, triplicem illum coronam, ornatum Imperatorium, & aureas crepidas accepisse dixerimus? Et quinam, obsecro, Filio hominis, quem vnicum nostrum caput agnoscimus, quíque quandiu in terris vixit,vbi caput reclinaret non habuit.Matth.8.20.cum infando illo scorto,suis satellitib. stipato, Regibus ad ipsius obsequiū submissis,& ipsorum colla pedibus proculcate conuenient? Idem etiam dictum esto de reliquo toto illo comitatu, Primatum, Archiepiscoporum, Episcoporum, Priorum, Curatorum, Abbatum denique & caeterorum omnium quotquot se ex illo Satanico clericatu, temporarios & spirituales dominos profitentur, At quibus titulis? quo iure? qua fide? qua conscientia? quo exemplo? An ipsius Iesu Christi, cuius contrariam fuisse prorsus rationem cuius est perspicuum? an Apostolorum? an denique verorum omnium Episcoporum & Pastorum Ecclesiae primitiuae, priusquam auaritia & ambitio tam horrendam confusionem inuexisset? Sed ipsi fe fortasse Melchisedeci Regis Salem, & Sacerdotis altissimi, & Domini nostri Iesu Christi figura, sunt exemplo futuri. Sed quorsum illum in exemplum trahcrent, quum Deus postea in ordinem cogens quae antea non potuerant, tam accurate Sacerdotium Aaronicum,a munere Mosis distinxerit, & ab vtriusque posteris diligenter obseruandum curarit? tandemque manum extremam edificio templi sui spiritualis admouens, per os filij sui proprij & Apostolorum, tam sollicite tamque aperte & dilucide distinxerit, imo separarit, quod ad eorum personam attinet quibus haec munera committuntur, quaecunque regnum coelorum spectant, ab iis quae ad terrenarum istarum rerum statum & gubernationem referuntur? Quàm bene verò Machabæis posterioribus quos vocant, istud cessit, quum vtramque sibi potestatẽ vindicarunt? Vltimum suum asylum, donationes & fundationes Imperatorum & Regum, quanta impudentia proferunt, ac illam in primis tam impudenter & tam aperte ementitam donationem Constantini: quam falsitatem historiarum omnium ordo ac series tam clarè mendacij coarguit, vt hoc ipsorum crimen, si lustriæ locus esset, sedi illi detetiandæ in perpetuũ cum infamia exauthorandæ sufficiat. Quòd ad illas verò largitiones & infeudationes minimè dubias attinet, age obsecro, an Regibus & Principibus Christianis quæ Dei Filius tam expresse discreuerat fas fuit aliquando confundere? Atq; adeò, vt ex ipso mortalium iure agam, an sic Magistratibus licuit discerpere & abalienare temporalem quam à Deo acceperant potestatem? Istis verò qui fraudulentis illis suis adulationibus facilibus nimium Magistratibus imposuerunt, sasne fuit ab hominibus accipere quod tam expresse Christus illis interdixerat? Hæc igitur ita se habent: qua in re siquibus fortasse videbor esse paulò seuerior, legant obsecro, quæ de hac re olim scripsit Bernardus, satis cognituri vix me centesimam eorum partem attigisse. Denique si Christi firmum est argumentum, regnum suum verè & merè spirituale esse ex eo probantis, quòd Regum & Magistratuum rebus terrenis se non immisceret, an non vice versa firmam conclu-sionem efficiemus, Papalem gubernationem, vt nunc est, nec spiritualem esse, nec à Iesu Christo, quum revera mere sit temporalis ac terrena, & quicquid in ea spirituale praetexi-tur, nihil nisi spectrum atque larua sit? En igi-tur, inquam, habetis in conspicuo veritatem. Quousque tandem vero vos Imperatores, Re-ges, Principes, caeterique Magistratus seculares dormitabitis? quando tandem excitati res istas in pristinum statum reducetis? quando tandem quae vobis tam caute sunt erepta postliminio repetita vendicabitis, vt tandem aliquando desolata nunc Dei Ecclesia, cuius vos nutritios esse decet, fidos & sui muneris peritos nacta doctores, magni illius Regis auspiciis tuta re-focilletur? Quod tandem aliquando Deo mundum miserante futurum est.
units.tr: But although, from what we have said so far and from the conditions we have set out, the temporal kingdom of Christ is not absolutely separated from the spiritual, it must always be expressly distinguished from it. This is clear enough from what Christ himself declared in this passage, and from what he did throughout the course of his life. He paid the tax (Matth. 17.27), refused to judge a dispute over an inheritance (Luke 12.14), and refused to condemn the adulteress (John 8.11). He so often taught his disciples the difference between the spiritual ministry and the temporal kingdom (Luke 22.25), and Paul himself laid down the general and most certain rule for both governments (2 Tim. 4; 2 Cor. 10.4). What, then, I ask, shall we say of the desperate impudence of that lost man, who has seized the city of Rome itself, and the other principalities and dominions, which with such a brazen face he calls the patrimony of Peter? Shall we say that he received from God, or from the one whose universal Vicar he impudently pretends to be, that triple crown, the imperial insignia and the golden sandals? And who, I ask, would gather with that infamous harlot, surrounded by her attendants, and with kings submitted to her service and placing their necks under her feet, when we acknowledge the Son of Man as our only Head, who, as long as he lived on earth, had nowhere to lay his head (Matt. 8.20)? The same must be said of the whole retinue that follows him: the primates, archbishops, bishops, priors, curates, and finally the abbots and all the rest, as many as profess themselves temporal and spiritual lords by that Satanic clericate. But by what titles? By what right? In what faith? With what conscience? After what example? Of Jesus Christ himself, whose manner was plainly the opposite of this? Or of the apostles? Or, finally, of all the true bishops and ministers of the primitive Church, before avarice and ambition introduced such a horrible confusion? But perhaps they will be offered as examples by saying that they are a figure of Melchizedek, king of Salem, the most high priest and figure of our Lord Jesus Christ. But why would they drag him in as an example, when God afterwards, bringing into order what previously could not be ordered, distinguished so carefully the Aaronic priesthood from the office of Moses, and took care that it be diligently observed by the descendants of both? And finally, putting the last hand to the building of his spiritual temple, he distinguished, nay separated, through the mouth of his own Son and of the apostles, so carefully, so openly and so clearly, with respect to the persons to whom these offices are committed, those things which concern the kingdom of heaven from those which pertain to the state and government of these earthly things. How well did that turn out for the so-called later Maccabees, when they claimed both powers for themselves? Their last refuge, the donations and foundations of emperors and kings, they bring forward with such impudence, and above all that donation of Constantine, so impudently and so openly fabricated, whose falsity the order and sequence of all the histories so clearly convicts of lying that, if there were a place for repentance, their crime alone would be enough to brand that seat for ever with infamy and to strip it of all authority. As for those grants and enfeoffments which are not at all doubtful, come now, I ask, was it ever lawful for Christian kings and princes to confuse what the Son of God had so expressly distinguished? And, to argue from the very law of mortals, was it lawful for magistrates to tear apart and alienate the temporal power which they had received from God? And for those who, with their fraudulent flatteries, imposed upon magistrates who were too easily won over, was it right to receive from men what Christ had so expressly forbidden them? These things are so. If some perhaps think I am being somewhat severe in this matter, let them, I beg, read what Bernard once wrote on this subject, and they will realise that I have scarcely touched a hundredth part of what he said. Finally, if the argument of Christ is firm, when he proves that his kingdom is truly and purely spiritual from the fact that he did not mix himself in the affairs of kings and magistrates, shall we not, conversely, draw the firm conclusion that the papal government, as it now is, is neither spiritual nor from Jesus Christ, since in reality it is purely temporal and earthly, and whatever is pretended in it to be spiritual is nothing but a phantom and a mask? Here, then, I say, you have the truth set before your eyes. How long, then, will you, emperors, kings, princes, and the other secular magistrates, go on sleeping? When at last, roused, will you restore these matters to their former state? When at last will you claim back by right of return those things which were so craftily snatched from you, so that the Church of God, now desolate, of which you ought to be the nursing fathers, having found faithful teachers skilled in their office, may at last be restored and made safe under the auspices of that great King? This will at last happen, God willing to have mercy on the world.

units.la: HOMILIA vicesima.
units.tr: Homily 20

units.la: IOH. 18.
units.tr: John 18.

units.la: 37 Dixit ergo ei Pilatus. Num igitur rex es tu? Respondit Iesus, Tu dicis me regem esse. Ego ad hoc natus sum, & ad hoc veni in mundum, vt dem dem testimonium veritati. Quisquis est ex veritate audit vocem meam.
units.tr: Then Pilate said to him, Are you a king then? Jesus answered, You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.

units.la: 38. Dicit ei Pilatus, Quid est veritas? Et quum hoc dixisset rursum venit ad Iudaeos, & dicit eis, Ego nullum invenio crimen in eo.
units.tr: Pilate says to him, What is truth? And when he had said this, he came again to the Jews and says to them, I find no crime in him.

units.la: DIScIM v s ex huius historię serie Pilatum rectè ex Christi respon-so collegisse, Regium nomen ab ipso admissi, sed quum addi-tam distinctionem audiret, & Iudaicam Religionem superstitionis & fanatici erroris haberet loco, parui criminationem illam fecisse: qua tamen in re minime sua laude priuandus est, quòd hactenus in Iudæorum gratiam conscientiam non læserit. Iesum Christum etiam alia ex parte videmus iterum nomen illud & titulum Regis, sed omni cum modestia, vt erat sane quoquo modo regiam potestatem intelligas, verè & proprie rex, agnouisse, & aliquid amplius addidisse. Quorsum verò illud, inquies, quum nimirum quicum sibi negotium esset satis perspectum haberet, & Pilatum salutis nostræ mysteria docere, nihil aliud esset nisi oleum & operam perdere? Aio itaque primùm, Lucem salutis non tantùm electis docendis proponi, sed etiam reprobis inexcusabilibus reddendis, Ioh. 15. 24. Deinde Christum tam excellentem illam confessionem vti de illa Paulus loquitur, 1. Tim. 6. 13. non Pilati respectu, sed Ecclesiæ suæ totius ad seculi consummationem vsque edidisse : & ita nos ab ipso in quo vera huius Regni administratio consistat, in vera nimi- rum omnis Veritatis veritate, cuius solus ipse sit verus præco & nuntius edoctos fuisse.
units.tr: From the sequence of this history we can see that Pilate rightly gathered from Christ's answer that he had admitted the royal name. But when he heard the added distinction, and regarded the Jewish religion as superstition and fanatical error, he made little of that accusation. Yet he must not be deprived of his due praise in this matter, in that up to this point he had not offended his conscience for the sake of the Jews. On the other side we see Jesus Christ again accepting the name and title of King, yet with all modesty, so that, however you understand his royal power, he truly and properly was a king, and he added something further. But why, you will say, since he knew well enough with whom he had to deal, would teaching Pilate the mysteries of our salvation be nothing but wasted oil and labour? I answer, first, that the light of salvation is set forth not only to teach the elect but also to render the reprobate inexcusable, John 15.24. Then, that Christ made that most excellent confession, of which Paul speaks, 1 Tim. 6.13, not with regard to Pilate but for his whole Church until the consummation of the age. And so we were taught by him, in whom the true administration of this kingdom consists, namely in the true truth of all Truth, of which he alone is the true herald and messenger.

units.la: Istud igitur nobis in primis est tenendum, Christum quum antea dixisset regnum suum ex hoc mundo non esse, minimè hic tanquam Physicum de veritate, quæ in causis & effectis naturalibus quæritur, nec tanquam Iuriscon- sultum de veritate facti alicuius, aut de iure quæstionis alicuius ciuilis agere: sed de cognitione veritatis illius loquutum quam intelligentiæ & conscientiæ ex veri Dei salutari cognitione normam esse oportet, qua extra mundum hûc altiùs euchimur, quæ cognitio profusus cœlestis & diuina, sola tam excellenti & pretioso isto Veritatis nomine digna est.
units.tr: Therefore this above all must be held: that Christ, having said earlier that his kingdom is not of this world, did not here speak as a natural philosopher about the truth that is sought in natural causes and effects, nor as a jurist about the truth of some fact or the law of some civil question. He spoke of the knowledge of that truth which ought to be the rule of understanding and conscience, drawn from the saving knowledge of the true God, by which we are lifted higher, beyond this world. This knowledge is heavenly and divine, and alone worthy of this excellent and precious name of Truth.

units.la: Duplex porrò cognoscédi Dei via est, naturæ prior, supernaturalis altera ex spirituali reuelatione. Ac naturalis illa quidé imaginis illius qua Deus initio primi parétis animâ exor- narat reliquiæ sunt, & velut scintilla residua lucis illius quâ in hominis intelligétiam infuderat, quæ quicquid de Deo creatore ad eum honorandum & colendum sciri debet cognosce- ret, omnibus suis affectibus ad illius obsequiū compositis, sola homini post peccatū ea reli- -cta cognitione qua reddatur inexcusabilis, vt pluribus Apostolus istud argumentum primo capite epist.ad Rom. persequitur: Supernatu- ralis illa verò, quam nec caro nec sanguis re- uegit. Matth.16. 17. à Deo ipso nobis in verbo suo reuelatur,per quam quod erat veri reliquū in nobis ex illa naturali notitia,magis magis-que confirmatur, atque adeo ad longè altiore essentiæ Dei cognitionem deducimur,Deíque præterea nobis consilium omne de nostra sa-lute, Act. 20.17. & de rebus iis quas nobis est gratificatus, 1. Cor. 2. verf. 12. & ingenti-bus mysteriis regni cœlorum, patefit. 1. Cor. 4.verf.1.
units.tr: There are two ways of knowing God: the first natural, the other supernatural, from spiritual revelation. That natural knowledge is indeed the remnant of that image with which God adorned the soul of the first parent at the beginning, and like a residual spark of that light which he had poured into man's understanding. It would know whatever ought to be known about God the Creator in order to honour and worship him, with all its affections turned to his service. But after sin only that knowledge was left to man by which he is made inexcusable, as the Apostle pursues this argument at length in the first chapter of Romans. That supernatural knowledge, however, which flesh and blood has not revealed, Matt. 16.17, is revealed to us by God himself in his word. Through it what was true and left in us from that natural notion is more and more confirmed, and so we are led to a far higher knowledge of God's essence. Moreover, the whole counsel of God about our salvation is opened to us, Acts 20.17, and the things he has graciously given us, 1 Cor. 2.12, and the great mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, 1 Cor. 4.1.
