units.la: En vero scopulum ad quem inde ab omni seculo maxima mundi pars fraudibus Satanæ impulsa allisit, & adhuc hodie allidunt per-multi, nunquam Satanæ deficientibus fanati-cis ingeniis, quibus ad prædicandos & per-suadendos errores crassissimos in sua Theo-logia, & vana somnia fidelibus vtatur instru-mentis: cuius rei tot magorum species testes sunto, tot homines à malis spiritibus demen-tati, per quos oracula sua reddere confuerat:tot pseudophilosophi theorici, quos Cō-templatiuos dicunt, seipsos & alios manibus suis ratiocinationibus excæcantes, testibus i-psorum monumentis,quibus hodie videas ad-huc plerosque miserè fascinatos,licet Apostolus tam solicitè tot ante lapsis seculis Eccle-siam præmonuerit ne se per Philosophiam & inanem deceptionem secundùm traditionem hominum, & scientiam falsò sic nominatam seduci pateretur,Coloss.2.8,1.Tim.6.20.Porrò quum de vera & salutari Theologia quæritur, quam Zacharias Ioannis Baptistæ pater,Scie-tiam salutis dicit.Luc.1.77.cognitionem videlicet vnius veri Dei & eius quem misit Iesu Christi, sunt omnibus illis inanibus ratiocinationibus opponenda: primum quod dicit Apostolus, hominem animalem a spirituali discretum, eorum quae sunt spiritus Dei non esse capacem. Efle enim illi stultitiam. 1. Cor. 2. 14. Deinde quod Iohannes 1. 15. scribit, Deum a nemine vnquam visum, sed vnigenitum illum qui est in sinu patris hominibus illum exposuisse, cui loco concinunt quæ tum hic, tum permultis aliis locis dixit, se ad hoc natum & in mundum venisse, ut veritati testimonium ferat: ac proinde sicuti Moses ille fuit vnus a cuius ore tanquam fidelis seruus, populum Legem excipere oportuit, & ita quidem ut ei nihil adiiceret, aut detraheret, ita Filius is est, a quo, tanquam in domo patris domino. Heb. 3. 5. & 6. Pater, id quod Veritatem hoc loco dicit, in mundum afferri, & in eo praedicari voluit. Iohan. 1. 17. sicut erat a Patre prius praedictum & promissum. Deut. 18. 18. Act. 3. 22. & ipse Pater expresse de coelo vocem edens, Audiri illum, praecepit. Matth. 3 17.
units.tr: Here indeed is the rock against which the greatest part of the world, driven by the frauds of Satan, has dashed itself since every age, and very many still dash themselves today, Satan never lacking fanatical minds through which he uses instruments to preach and persuade the grossest errors in his theology, and vain dreams to the faithful. Of this the many kinds of magicians are witnesses; so many men driven mad by evil spirits, through whom he was accustomed to give his oracles; so many theoretical pseudo-philosophers, whom they call contemplatives, blinding themselves and others with their own reasonings. Their own writings bear witness, in which you may see many still miserably bewitched today, although the Apostle so earnestly warned the Church many ages ago not to allow itself to be seduced through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men and the knowledge falsely so called, Col. 2.8; 1 Tim. 6.20. Moreover, when we inquire about true and saving theology, which Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, calls the knowledge of salvation, Luke 1.77, namely the knowledge of the one true God and of him whom he sent, Jesus Christ, all those empty reasonings must be set against it. First, because the Apostle says that the natural man, distinct from the spiritual, is not capable of the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, 1 Cor. 2.14. Next, because John, 1.18, writes that no one has ever seen God, but the only-begotten who is in the bosom of the Father has made him known to men. To this place agree what he said here and in very many other places, that he was born and came into the world so that he might bear witness to the truth. Therefore, just as Moses was the one from whose mouth, as a faithful servant, the people had to receive the Law, and in such a way that nothing was to be added to it or taken from it, so this Son is the one by whom, as lord in the Father's house, Heb. 3.5 & 6, the Father willed that this truth, which he speaks of here, should be brought into the world and preached in it, John 1.17, as had been foretold and promised by the Father beforehand, Deut. 18.18; Acts 3.22. And the Father himself, uttering a voice expressly from heaven, commanded that he be heard, Matt. 3.17.

units.la: Sed quoniam hoc loco Christus Nascendi & in mundum Veniendi vocibus vsus est, primum illud obseruandum est hic ipsum de se Humanitatis suę respectu loqui, non quidem a diuinitate separatae, sed tamen distinctae, qua ob rem etiam a Patre Seruus suus, Esa. 53. 11. & ab Apostolo Ministerr circumcisionis dicitur. Rom. 15. 8. Nam etsi Mediatoris officium inter Patrem & nos in naturarum vnione insepara-bili
units.tr: But since Christ here used the words of being born and of coming into the world, first this must be observed: he speaks here of himself with respect to his humanity, not indeed separated from his divinity but nonetheless distinguished from it. For this reason he is also called by the Father his Servant, Isa. 53.11, and by the Apostle the minister of the circumcision, Rom. 15.8. For although the office of Mediator between the Father and us is considered in the inseparable union of the natures,

units.la: Ioh. 1. 18. bili consideratur:in huius tamen muneris exe-cutione,tribuenda sunt opera diuina,Diuini-tati eius,humana vero, in quibus est iustius veritatis,quod Euangelium est,praeconium, humanitati ipsius & formæ serui,sicut eum vocat Apostolus. Philip.2.7. Deinde,ne forte nobis in mentem veniat haec cogitatio, veritatem hanc ab aduentu Christi demum in has terras in mundo praedicari coepisse (quo posito necesse foret aut nullam ante Christi in carnem aduentum in terris Ecclesiam fuisse, aut ante ipsius aduentum alios iustius praecones veritatis) sciendum est hanc personam Filij Æterni Dei, eius verbum coaeternum & coessentiale, praeordinatum vt in temporum plenitudine frater nolter fieret, electis suis locutus esse inde ab Adamo, illos ex mundo colligentem,patribus se per varias visiones & supernaturales revelationes, quarum historia sacra plena est, conspicuam praebentem, 1.Petr.1.11.&2.1.21. quo etiam respectu is ipse est qui Angelus Domini,viam Israelitis per desertum monstrans, dicitur,1.Corinth.10.9. donec tandem assumpta carne venit ipsemet ad oues perditas Israelis. Matth.15.24. & Rom.15.8 quibus omnem iustam sine exceptione veritatem patefecit.Ioh. 15.15. Etsi igitur ante assumptam suam humanitatem non est in ea ipsa mundum allocutus, is tamen vnus est & nō alius per quem est haec veritas, tum per os Prophetarum ipsius afflatorum Spiritu, tum per veteres illas figuras & vmbras, quarum ipse corpus est & substantia,
units.tr: John 1.18. ...is considered. Yet in the execution of this office, divine works are to be attributed to his divinity, but human works, in which the proclamation of truth, which is the Gospel, is more properly located, to his humanity and the form of a servant, as the Apostle calls it, Phil. 2.7. Next, lest perhaps this thought come to us, that this truth began to be preached in the world only from the coming of Christ into these lands (given which it would be necessary either that there was no Church on earth before Christ's coming in the flesh, or that before his coming there were other heralds of the truth), it must be known that this Person, the Eternal Son of God, his Word coeternal and coessential, foreordained to become our brother in the fullness of time, has spoken to his elect from Adam onwards, gathering them out of the world, showing himself visibly to the fathers through various visions and supernatural revelations, of which sacred history is full, 1 Pet. 1.11; 2.1, 21. In this respect too he is the very Angel of the Lord who shows the way to the Israelites through the desert, as it is said, 1 Cor. 10.9, until at last, having assumed flesh, he came himself to the lost sheep of Israel, Matt. 15.24; Rom. 15.8, to whom he laid open all just truth without exception, John 15.15. Therefore, although before assuming his humanity he did not address the world in that very humanity, yet he is the one and no other through whom this truth is made known, both through the mouths of the prophets inspired by his Spirit and through those old figures and shadows, of which he himself is the body and substance,

units.la: H. iiij. patefacta, Coloss.2.17. & Heb.10.ver.1. per quas umbras etiam Abrahamus & caeteri Patriarchae Domini diem eminus conspexerunt. Ioh. 8.56.
units.tr: Revealed (Col. 2:17; Heb. 10:1), and through these shadows Abraham and the other patriarchs also saw the Lord's day from afar (John 8:56).

units.la: Et hodie quoque, postquam suam humanitatem longe supra omnes coelos extulit, Ephe. 4.10. Heb.4.14. quibus ad secundum vsque suum aduentum, quae mundi futura erit consummatio, continebatur. Act.3.21. solus ipse suos Apostolos, quosque illis adiunxit Euangelistas extraordinaria Sancti Spiritus mensura cumulauit, quos ab Oriente in Occidentem huius veritatis perfecte annuntiandae praeconesmisit, & suarum Ecclesiarum fundatores, tum doctrinae, tum Ecclesiastici ipsius regiminis firmis & immotis positis fundamentis.
units.tr: And today too, after he had raised his humanity far above all the heavens (Eph. 4:10; Heb. 4:14), he still holds those things until his second coming, which will be the consummation of the world (Acts 3:21). He alone endowed his apostles, and the evangelists whom he joined to them, with an extraordinary measure of the Holy Spirit. He sent them from East to West as heralds to proclaim this truth perfectly, and he made them the founders of his churches, both of its doctrine and of its ecclesiastical government, having laid firm and immovable foundations.

units.la: Tandem vero primi illi fundatores, sic iactis fundamentis eius aedificij quod Dei Ciuitas nominatur, qualis Apocal.25. describitur, vt erat prius etiam praedictum Psal.87. Pastores in ea Doctoresque constituerunt etiam dictos Episcopos, id est propriorum suorum gregum inspectores. Act.20.28. & 1.Pet.5.2. & Tit.1.5. sed minore tamen Spiritus mensura, minime nimirum aliquid additurosdetractu-ros, immutaturos, istis ante positis, tum Doctrinae tum Ecclesiasticae gubernationis fundamentis: sed potius sanctis admonitionibus, exhortationibus & reprehensionibus Ecclesiam superstructuros, quae auro, argento, & lapidibus pretiosis comparantur: vt contra quaelibet humanae inventiones, licet fundamentum minime... minimè conuellentes, fœno, paleæ ac stipulæ conferuntur. 1. Corinth.3.2. En igitur vt hæc Veritas in cuius administratione positum est regnum istud cœleste per vnicum hunc Regem,& sub eodem vnico,ad finem vsque fecu-lorum est continuanda perpetuandáque.Eph. 4.11.&1.Cor.15.28.
units.tr: Then, indeed, those first founders, having laid the foundations of that building which is called the City of God, as it is described in Revelation 21 and was foretold earlier in Psalm 87, appointed in it ministers and teachers, also called bishops, that is, overseers of their own flocks (Acts 20:28; 1 Pet. 5:2; Titus 1:5). They did so with a smaller measure of the Spirit, and certainly without any intention of adding to, subtracting from, or changing the foundations of doctrine and of ecclesiastical government that had been laid before. Rather, they built up the Church by holy admonitions, exhortations and rebukes, which are compared to gold, silver and precious stones, whereas any human inventions, even if they do not overturn the foundation, are compared to hay, straw and stubble (1 Cor. 3:12). Thus this truth, in whose administration the heavenly kingdom is set through this one King, is to be continued and perpetuated under the same sole King until the end of the ages (Eph. 4:11; 1 Cor. 15:28).

units.la: O vtinam vero fuissent posteri hac in re magis religiosi, debitámque reuerentiam feruaf-fent Filio, qui solus caput & Legislator in domo Patris est, etiam cum potestate coercendi: Matth.21.12.Ioh.2.14.Hebr.3.6.Iac.4.12.in quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ ac cognitionis absconditi. Coloff.2.3. quíque omnia perfectissimè, Ioh.19.30. fiuc ipse in propria persona, fiue deinceps per Apostolos consumma-uit, quum tamen iam ante multa secula, vix dum morte sublatis Apostolis,(sicut ante præuiderat Apostolus 1. Cor.3.10. & prædixerat 2. Thef.2.7.)religionis prætextu(hic enim omitto falsos illos doctores scienter prudenter malitiosos) & quidem vt Christianorum cultus commendatior redderetur,&Sacramenta magis efficerentur veneranda, fœnum & stipula super hoc Apostolico fundamento cœpta sint ædificari, id est infinitæ ceremoniæ, quarum pars Iudaismum sapit, pars vero ex Ethnicorum superstitionibus est depromta, omni tandem illo cultu in intolerandas superstitiones & ridiculas imitationes conuerso, ita quidem vt totus exterior Ecclesiæ cultus in cantiunculas & gefticulationes abierit. Sed quod magis dolendum est, tantum Spiritus erroris & mendacij pedetentim promouit, vt fundamentorum ante iactorum tum doctrinę Christianæ, tum Ecclesialticæ disciplinæ, partem tanto astu subruerit, vt ipsos pene oculos hominum effugerit.
units.tr: Would to God that later generations had been more devout in this matter, and had kept due reverence for the Son, who alone is the head and the lawgiver in the house of the Father, with power also to restrain (Matt. 21:12; John 2:14; Heb. 3:6; James 4:12), and in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. 2:3), and who has brought everything to the most perfect completion (John 19:30), whether himself in his own person or afterwards through the apostles. Yet many centuries ago, when the apostles had scarcely been taken away by death, (as the apostle had foreseen, 1 Cor. 3:10, and had foretold, 2 Thess. 2:7), under the pretext of religion (for I here pass over those false teachers who were knowingly, cunningly and maliciously at work), and indeed so that the worship of Christians might be made more commendable and the sacraments might be made more venerable, hay and stubble began to be built upon this apostolic foundation. That is, countless ceremonies were added, some of which smack of Judaism, while others were borrowed from the superstitions of the Gentiles. In the end the whole of that worship was turned into intolerable superstitions and ridiculous imitations, so that the entire outward worship of the Church dwindled into little songs and gestures. But what is more to be lamented is that the spirit of error and lies advanced little by little, and with such cunning undermined part of the foundations laid earlier, both of Christian doctrine and of ecclesiastical discipline, that it almost escaped people's very eyes.

units.la: Porrò quemadmodum horrenda illa calamitas Dei domum afflixit, quòd non ad amussim huius Regis & solius Legislatoris in domo Patris sui præcepta sunt in omnib.diligenter obseruata, sed in iis multa immutata, sublata multa vel adiecta: ita nullum aliud remedium superesset, nisi repositis quę sublata, redintegratis quæ immutata, penitúsque reiectis quæ fuerant adiecta, vt in omnibus huius Dei Filij & Regis solis mandatis pareatur. Ecquis enim mortalium, oro, sceruum domi sibi impe rantem ferat, quis illi concedat quæ sibi isti in magni illius Filij Dei domo concedi volunt? Quinam verò quod in veteré fœdere, alioqui tamen imperfecto, non licuit, sed expresse fuit inhibitum & punitum, sub nouo, suis partibus omnibus ab soluto, licuerit?
units.tr: Furthermore, just as that dreadful calamity afflicted the house of God, because the precepts of this King and sole Lawgiver in the house of his Father were not carefully observed in all things, but in them many things were changed, many removed or added, so no other remedy would remain except to restore what had been removed, to renew what had been changed, and utterly to reject what had been added, so that obedience is rendered to all the commands of this Son of God and sole King. For who among mortals, I ask, would tolerate a slave commanding him in his own house? Who would grant to them what they wish to be granted to them in the house of that great Son of God? And what is it that was not permitted under the old covenant, which was nonetheless imperfect, but was expressly forbidden and punished, that would be permitted under the new covenant, which is wholly perfect in all its parts?

units.la: Hactenus igitur de tribus illis capitibus, quæ diximus ex Domini nostri Iesu Christi confessione colligenda, dictum esto, quartum superesset, quos nempe Rex iste veros subditos sui Regni dicat & agnoscat, nimirum vocem sui Regis audientes. Quo loco primùm nobis excutiendum, quænam vox illa sit, cuius illa, quiue sint illius auditores veri iudicandi.
units.tr: So much, then, concerning those three heads which we said should be gathered from the confession of our Lord Jesus Christ. The fourth remains: whom this King calls and acknowledges as true subjects of his kingdom, namely those who hear the voice of their King. Here we must first examine what that voice is, and who are rightly to be judged its true hearers.

units.la: Vocem istam dicimus Euangelium, id est, felix illud nuntium doctrinæ illius in qua sa- lus nostra consistit, oblatum vt iam ante dixi, & iterum repeto, & propositum hominibus à sanctis Patriarchis, deinde à Mose in tabulas relatum, & figuris Legalibus adumbratum: tum plenius à Prophetis Sancto Christi Spiri- tu affiatis & impulsis edoctum. 1. Petr. 1. vers. 11. quod tandem vbi temporum à Domino prædinitorum aduenit plenitudo Christus ipse veniens in carne realiter exhibuit ratúmque in propria persona fecit. Iohan. 1. vers. 17. Rom. 1. vers. 2. 3. & 4. Hebr. 1. vers. 1. & 2. Inde facile cuius illa vox sit, Filij nempe Dei & vnius nostri Regis Iesu Christi, patet, à quo sem per est inde ab Adami lapsu mundo reuelata, per os Prophetarum ante suum in carne aduetum, deinde in propria persona Heb. 13. 1. randémq; post ipsius supra cœlos omnes ascensione per Apostolos & Euangelistas loquuto: cuius denique nùc interpretatione & applicatione fidis doctorib. & pastorib. ad seculi consummationé vsque cómissam scire nos operæpretiu est.
units.tr: We call that voice the Gospel, that is, the joyful message of that doctrine in which our salvation consists, which, as I have said before and repeat now, was offered and proposed to men by the holy patriarchs, then committed to tablets by Moses and foreshadowed by legal figures, and then more fully taught by the prophets, inspired and moved by the Holy Spirit of Christ (1 Pet. 1:11). When at last the fullness of the times appointed by the Lord arrived, Christ himself, coming in the flesh, displayed it in reality and confirmed it in his own person (John 1:17; Rom. 1:2–4; Heb. 1:1–2). From this it is easy to see what that voice is: it is the voice of the Son of God and our one King Jesus Christ. From the fall of Adam onwards it has always been revealed to the world, through the mouth of the prophets before his coming in the flesh, then in his own person, and finally after his ascension above all the heavens, through the apostles and evangelists speaking. It is worth our knowing how this voice has now been entrusted, until the consummation of the age, to faithful teachers and ministers for its interpretation and application (Heb. 13:7).

units.la: Hæc si diligeter vt par est perpenderimus, optima verù Euangeliù à falso, veros pastores & doctores, de quibus dixit Dominus, Qui reci- pit vos, me recipit, à falsis & hypocritis, à quorum fermeto diligerer esse cauendũ idé præmonuit, ac proinde veram Ecclesiam, extra quam non est salus, à spuria & mēdace, schola nimi- rum perditionis, discernendi viam docebi- mur. Verù igitur, cui soli nobis est inhærendũ, Euangelium, est illa Filij vox, alienę voci penitus repugnans Ioh. 10.5. omni doctrinæ nimirum, aut recens in hominum excusæ cerebro, aut vel tantillum immutanti, detrahenti vel adiicienti verbo illi quod nobis Dei filius annuntiauit & interpretatus est: quibus, vti diximus, positis non magnopere laborandum erit in veris Pastoribus, à mendacibus quibus ex diametro repugnant, in Ecclesia vera, falsa illi opposita dignoscenda. Nam hoc Rege vocem suam dicente, omnibus aliis vt spuriis abdicatis, solam suam totam, integram & non fucatam intelligit.
units.tr: If we weigh these things carefully, as is fitting, we shall be taught how to distinguish the true Gospel from a false one, true ministers and teachers from false and hypocritical ones (of whom the Lord said, "He who receives you receives me," and whose deceit he also warned us to beware of diligently), and thus how to distinguish the true Church, outside of which there is no salvation, from a spurious and lying one, a school of perdition. Therefore the Gospel, to which alone we must cling, is that voice of the Son, which wholly rejects every other voice (John 10:5), that is, every doctrine either newly hatched in the brain of man, or any word which changes, takes away from or adds to that word which the Son of God has announced and interpreted to us. Once these things are established, we shall not have to labour much in distinguishing true ministers from the liars whom they directly oppose, or the true Church from the false opposed to it. For when this King speaks his voice, having rejected all others as spurious, we understand that it alone is whole, entire and unadulterated.

units.la: Age vero quid hic obiiciant aduersarij paucis expendamus. Primum aiunt, non quæcunque vel Christus vel Apostoli docuerunt scriptorum esse monumentis tradita, ac proinde verbum Euangelicum esse duplex, scriptum vnum, ἀγράφον alterum. Deinde Scripturæ interpretationem & applicationem non cuiusuis priuati, sed Ecclesiæ propriam esse. Tertio, Christum adhuc Ecclesiam suam hodie alloqui, & ad seculorum finem per Apostolorum successores, doctores & Pastores Ecclesiæ allocuturū: quę tria capita quū agnoscamus quidę, sed probe intellecta, nō aute vt sunt ab aduersariis cotorta ia ordine singula discutiam*.
units.tr: Come now, let us briefly weigh what our opponents object here. First, they say that not everything that Christ or the apostles taught was handed down in written records, and therefore the Gospel word is twofold: one written, the other unwritten [ἄγραφον]. Second, they say that the interpretation and application of Scripture belong not to any private person but to the Church alone. Third, they say that Christ still speaks to his Church today, and until the end of the ages will speak through the successors of the apostles, the teachers and ministers of the Church. Although we acknowledge some of these points, when they are rightly understood, I will not discuss each one in order as our opponents have twisted them.

units.la: Primum vero scriptis quæcunque Christus vel dixit vel fecit testē Ioh. 21.25. minime mandata fuisse libenter agnoscimus. Nec etiam inficiamur, quōd ad doctrinam quam promulgauit attinet, præcepta non fuisse ad verbum folifolicitè descripta.Quòd si factum foret,nç tum ipsius Christi tum A postolorum conciones ę- quò breuiores & compendiosiores fuisse vide- rentur.Sed Euangelistas dicimus, quibus in i- psorum præceptoris ac Magistri historia con- scribenda tanquam scribis vsus est Dominus, & Apostolos insuis e piftolis,quemadmodum à Dei Spiritu veritatem omnem sine exceptio ne fuerant edocti, & in memoriam illis loco & tempore quæ prius auribus perceperant re- uocata, ita summa fide ac diligentia totam hanc doctrinam collegisse,&scriptis ad poste- ros transmisisse,non habita tantùm eorum ra- tione quos coràm docere non poterant, sed totius in seculi consummationem vsque Ec- clesiæ futuræ, quò fides eius scriptis Apostoli- cis niteretur: Ioh. 20. 31. atque adeò quemad- modum suo munere fideliter functi minimè fuissent,nisi quæcunque in mandatis accepe- rant docuissent, omne videlicet sine exceptio- ne Dei consilium annuntiantes,Act.20. 27.ita fuisse, nisi omnem hanc doctrinam bona fide descriptam Ecclesiæ tradidissent officio de- futuros,multisque hæreticis,velut Valentino, Marcioni,Montanistis, Manichæis, & similibus quotidie pullulatibus hæreticis, peculiares suas reuelationes obtrudentibus, portam aperturos. Addimus etiam Apostolorum ipsorum ætate totam hanc doctrinam bona fide in capita quædam & articulos fidei perspicuos & dilucidos,quos symbolum,propterea dictum Apostolicum, complectitur, fuisse collectam.
units.tr: First, we gladly acknowledge that not everything Christ said or did was committed to writing, as John 21:25 bears witness. Nor do we deny that the precepts of the doctrine he proclaimed were not all carefully written down word for word. If that had been done, the sermons both of Christ himself and of the apostles would seem much shorter and more concise. But we say that the evangelists, whom the Lord used as scribes to write the history of their teacher and master, and the apostles in their epistles, having been taught all truth without exception by the Spirit of God, and having had brought back to their memory at the proper place and time what they had earlier heard with their ears, gathered all this doctrine with the greatest faith and diligence and transmitted it in writings to posterity. They did this not only with regard to those whom they could not teach in person, but for the whole Church that would exist until the end of the age, so that its faith might rest upon the apostolic writings (John 20:31). Indeed, just as they would not have faithfully discharged their office unless they had taught everything they had received in their commission, proclaiming the whole counsel of God without exception (Acts 20:27), so they would have failed in their duty unless they had handed down all this doctrine, faithfully written, to the Church. Otherwise they would have opened the door to many heretics, such as Valentinus, Marcion, the Montanists, the Manichaeans and similar heretics who sprang up daily and forced their own peculiar revelations upon people. We add that, even in the lifetime of the apostles themselves, this whole doctrine was gathered in good faith into certain chief points and clear and plain articles of faith, which are contained in the creed, and for that reason called the Apostles' Creed.

units.la: Et sane ni ita esset, longè meliorem veteris illius populi fuisse olim quàm nunc Ecclesiæ Christianæ conditionem dicendum esset, cui tam accurate tum doctrinæ tum cultus illius licet imperfecti tabulæ conscriptæ datæ sunt, quibus ne tantillū quidé adiicere detrahereve licuerit. Deut. 4.2. & 12.32. in quibus nihil vnquā, nisi forte ex Prophetarum reuelationibus diuinitus immissis innouatū fuit, 2. Chron. 29. 25. quicquid cæci Rabini de Cabala sua garriant: cuius rei toties per Prophetas repetitæ comminationes testes sunt, ac potissimū hæc verba Prophetæ, Quis hæc requisiuit ex manibus vestris? Esa. 1.12. testes denique locupletissimi, scilicet illæ Christi aduersus traditiones Pharisaicas cõciones. Abiit autem cogitemus aut verisimile esse dicamus Dominum minus fuisse de Ecclesia sua quàm de vetere illo populo sollicitū, vt nō caueret illi nō modo ne in incerti ex successione tradita doctrina fluctuaret, ac nō potiùs vt authenticis & validis fundemore nixa tabulis ab ipso S. Spiritu dictatis & obsignatis in æternum maneret. Sed aliquid amplius obiicimus aduersus omnes fidei articulos quos Romani nostri Catholici, ad verbum scriptū adiiciunt, nēpe Spiritu S. sibi nunquam contrariū, nunquā potuisse velle, nec etiā voluisse per verbum ἀγράφον verbo scripto ex diametro repugnatia docere: quà repugnantia in iis omnibus doctrinæ articulis in quibus à nostris Catholicis dissentimus, certissimis argumentis probare parati semper fuimus & erimus.
units.tr: And indeed, if this were not so, it would have to be said that the condition of that ancient people was far better long ago than that of the Christian Church today. To them the tables of both doctrine and worship, though imperfect, were written out so precisely that nothing could be added or taken away (Deut. 4.2; 12.32). Nothing was ever changed in them, except perhaps by revelations sent from God through the Prophets (2 Chron. 29.25), whatever the blind Rabbis chatter about their Cabala. The repeated threats of the Prophets against this are witnesses, above all these words of the Prophet: "Who required these things at your hands?" (Isa. 1.12). Finally, the most abundant witnesses are Christ's own sermons against the Pharisaic traditions. But let us consider, or say it is likely, that the Lord cared less for his Church than for that ancient people, so that he took no care that the doctrine should waver in an uncertain tradition handed down by succession, but rather that it should remain forever, founded on authentic and valid tablets dictated and sealed by the Holy Spirit himself. But we raise something further against all the articles of faith which our Roman Catholics add to the written word: the Holy Spirit could never be contrary to himself, could never wish, nor even did wish, to teach through an unwritten word [ἄγραφον] what is diametrically opposed to the written word. We have always been, and shall be, ready to prove this opposition by the most certain arguments in all those articles of doctrine on which we dissent from our Catholics.

units.la: Quid igitur, inquiunt, si tantum ea vobis pro- bantur quae disertis & expressis verbis in sacris Biblicis libris scripta sunt, quid nominib. Trinitatis, personarū, coessentialis fiet, quibusve testimoniis expressis Paedobaptismū probaue- ritis? In propriu est aduersum hac calumnia re- spondeo. Scriptū nepe dicimus verbū nō tantum quod totidem syllabis scriptis expressum est, sed etiam quicquid ex iis quae scripta sunt necessaria consecutione sequitur & elicitur, cuiusmodi superiora illa esse & similia multa agnoscimus, cuiusmodi sunt multorum veterū expositiones in suis symbolis collectis fideliter ex sacris Scripturis aduersus pullulates haereses, quibus Apostolico symbolo maiore lucem adferrent.
units.tr: "What then," they say, "if only those things are approved by you which are written in plain and express words in the sacred books? What will become of the names Trinity, persons, consubstantial? Or by what express testimonies would you have proved infant baptism?" I answer this calumny as follows. We call the written word not only what is expressed in written syllables, but also whatever follows and is drawn out by necessary consequence from those things which are written. Of this kind we acknowledge the foregoing and many similar things to be, such as the explanations of many of the ancients, faithfully gathered from the holy Scriptures into their creeds against the sprouting heresies, by which they brought greater light to the Apostles' Creed.

units.la: Quaerūt praeterea nū arbitremur omnes ritus quibus Apostolorū temporibus Christiani tū in ordinario cultu tū in Sacramentorū administratione Deū venerati sunt, scriptis & monumentis traditos esse: quod si non est, an oēs qui in Ecclesia obseruatur tanquam spurios repudiemus. Minimē vero, inquā: verū alienā à proposito quaestione hanc dicimus. Agimus enim de fide & doctrina, quā semper vnā eandemque esse oportet, quàm de essentiali & immutabili forma gubernationis spiritualis & Ecclesiasticæ: quae duo capita sunt distinguenda à ritib. ordine & aedificatione Ecclesiae spectatib. quos prout tulerunt temporū, locorū, personarū circūstantiæ subinde variis subiectos fuisse mutationib. nullus audeat inficiari. Saepe enim commingit vt quæ huic tempori, huic loco conueniunt & vtilia sunt, alteri loco & tempori sint noci-tura. Exempli gratia: Primis illis Apostolorum temporibus Christiani vnà edentes bibentésque epulabantur, sanguine & suffocato in Iudæorum gratiam abstinebant, multóque aliós istiusmodi ritus obseruabant, quos deinceps optimis rationibus paulatim obfoleuif-fe videmus, & ab ipso Apostolo fuisse ordinatos 1.Cor.11.34. Coloff.2.16. Eiusdem Apostoli temporibus, apertum caput, auctoritatis, opercum vero, fubmiffionis signum fuisse conspicimus: hodie vero vice versa contrarium vsus obtinuit. Denique, vt vno verbo rem totam complectar, quæ doctrinam & conscientiam proprie spectant, ab exterioribus ritibus ordinis & ædificationis causa tantum institutis distinguenda sunt. Nec vero diximus vnquam cenfuimuf-ve ritus & ceremonias inde ab Apostolorum, aut etiam posterioribus temporibus vsitatas esse repudiandas, sed hoc diximus, quod vtinam nimis esse verum experientia non probaret, diligeter esse in illos omnes ritus inquirendum & animaduertendū, quòd in eos mille errores irrepserint, quibus repurgandis, necessario superflua & ridicula sint re-secanda, multóque magis amputanda superstitiosa & idololatrica, quæ tanto scelere paulatim Ecclesiam, partim negligentia quorundam, partim etiam ignorantia, imo plerúque malitia pastorum iampridem inuaserunt: quæ vero vtilia & ædificationi commoda fuerint, necessariis adhibitis cautionibus ac prouifio-nibus nibus retinenda.
units.tr: They ask further whether we think that all the rites by which Christians in the times of the Apostles worshipped God, both in ordinary worship and in the administration of the sacraments, were handed down in writings and records; and if not, whether we reject as spurious all those observed in the Church. Not at all, I say; but we consider this question foreign to the matter. For we are dealing with faith and doctrine, which must always be one and the same, and with the essential and unchangeable form of spiritual and ecclesiastical government. These two heads must be distinguished from the rites, order and building up of the Church, which, as the circumstances of times, places and persons have brought them, have at various times been subject to changes, as no one dares deny. For it often happens that what suits and is useful for one time and place may be harmful at another time and place. For example, in the first times of the Apostles, Christians ate and drank together at the common meal, abstained from blood and from what was strangled for the sake of the Jews, and observed many other rites of this kind. We see these were gradually made obsolete for excellent reasons, though they had been ordained by the Apostle himself (1 Cor. 11.34; Col. 2.16). In the same Apostle's times we see an uncovered head was a sign of authority and a covered head a sign of submission; today the contrary custom prevails. Finally, to sum up the whole matter in one word: what properly concerns doctrine and conscience must be distinguished from the external rites instituted only for the sake of order and edification. Nor have we ever said or judged that the rites and ceremonies used from the time of the Apostles, or even from later times, are to be repudiated. What we have said, and would that experience did not prove it too true, is this: those rites must be diligently examined and observed, because a thousand errors have crept into them. To purge these, superfluous and ridiculous things must necessarily be cut away, and much more the superstitious and idolatrous, which with such wickedness have gradually invaded the Church, partly through the negligence of some, partly through the ignorance, and indeed often the malice, of ministers. What was useful and suitable for edification is to be retained, with the necessary cautions and provisions.

units.la: Altera obiectio est, Scripturæ interpreta- tionem & applicationem vnius Ecclesiæ, non etiam priuatorum, esse propriam. Esto sane. Fatemur enim in Ecclesia Domini rite & ordine cuncta fieri & administrari oportere, necnon omnes Christianos ad docendum in Ecclesia sed tantum eos qui legitimè sunt electi vocatos agnoscimus. Verum quum nemo possit inficias ire, quin nimis verum sit quod tum Scriptura locis infinitis, tum experientia tot-orum omnium testatum facit, & in primis quod ipsi Christo & Apostolis ipsius accidit, nempe sæpissime confusionem sub ordinis specie ac forma vigere, falsos pastores pro veris quorum locum occupant (e venditare, falsas & commentitas coitiones sub veræ Dei & non fucatæ Ecclesiæ nomine delitescere, efficitur ipsos nequaquam auctoritate illa Sacras Scripturas interpretandi & applicandi quam Ecclesiæ datam asseuerant adiuuari, nisi prius se eam Ecclesiam, cuius hæc sit auctoritas, esse demonstrarint. Istud vero nunquam probaturos eos dicimus, nisi prius cum mendacio veritatem, & tenebras cum luce permutarint. Quum igitur negent quod affirmamus, & affirment quod negamus, prius quam de ipsorum interpretationibus & applicationibus quicquam statuatur, nodus hic expediendus est, sint-ne ipsi vera Ecclesia nec-ne.
units.tr: The second objection is that the interpretation and application of Scripture belongs to the Church alone, not also to private persons. Granted, certainly. For we confess that in the Church of the Lord all things must be done and administered properly and in order, and that not all Christians, but only those who have been lawfully chosen and called, are to teach in the Church. Yet since no one can deny that it is only too true, as Scripture attests in countless places and as the experience of everyone confirms, and especially as happened to Christ himself and his Apostles, that very often confusion reigns under the appearance and form of order; that false ministers put themselves forward in place of true ones; and that false and feigned assemblies lurk under the name of the true and unfeigned Church of God, it follows that they are by no means helped by that authority to interpret and apply the Holy Scriptures which they claim was given to the Church, unless they first prove that they are that Church to which this authority belongs. Yet we say they will never prove this unless they have first exchanged truth for lies and light for darkness. Since therefore they deny what we affirm, and affirm what we deny, before anything is decided about their interpretations and applications this knot must be untied: whether they are the true Church or not.

units.la: Esse vero ipsos nihil minus quam veram Ecclesiam quo facilius constet, omissa longiore I. j. & accuratiore rei istius inuestigatione, dici-mus & asseueramus veram notam qua veræ Domini nostri oues dignoscuntur, idest Ecclesia non spuria nec fucata, hanc vnam esse exipsius Christi verbis. Ioh.10. 3. Oues meæ vocem meam audiunt: ac proinde veram Ecclesiam eam esse non posse, quæ & loqui & iubere Sponsi loco, imo verba illius corrigere non erubescit. Hic vero solus abusus intolerandus quum in nostrorum aduersariorum cœtu cō-spiciatur, qui se Ecclesiam Catholicam Apostolicam falsò profitetur, Leges conscientiis præsigens satis idoneum est argumētu ad illos arguendos & falsitatis conuincendos, spōsam videlicet castam illam Sponsi non esse, sed potius verum illud Scortum Babylonicum. Iniuriam autem à nobis sibi fieri si forte clamitent, sane iudicio stare non renuimus, non quidem coram iis quos & iudicis & actoris partes sustinere non æquū est, sed coram libero Concilio, in quo verbum illud præeat quo Dominus olim ille Rex noster mundum est iudicaturus.
units.tr: That they are in fact nothing less than the true Church may be established more easily, if we pass over a longer and more exact investigation of the matter. We say and assert that the true mark by which the true sheep of our Lord are recognised, that is, a Church that is neither spurious nor feigned, is one only, and it is taken from Christ's own words: "My sheep hear my voice" (John 10.3). Therefore that cannot be the true Church which not only speaks and commands in the place of the Bridegroom, but is not ashamed even to correct his words. This abuse alone is intolerable. It is seen in the assembly of our adversaries, who falsely profess themselves the Catholic and Apostolic Church while prescribing laws to consciences; this is a sufficiently suitable argument to refute them and convict them of falsehood. They are not that chaste bride of the Bridegroom, but rather that true Babylonian harlot. If they cry out that we do them wrong, we indeed do not refuse to submit to judgment: not before those whom it is not fitting to have as both judge and party, but before a free Council, in which that word goes before by which our King of old will judge the world.

units.la: Præterea quum minimè putem cos inficiaturos iam olim Scripturam pallam esse falsas & interpretationes & applicationes, quod eorum plerunque partim ignorantia partim malitia factum est qui Ecclesiæ præfuerunt, tertius accedat iudex necesse est tantas lites com-ponituros. Ecquis vero tandem ille nisi solus Dominus futurus est? quomodo vero Dominus nisi perverbum suum scriptum? Nisi forte iterū cœlo Dominū deducere paramus. At, inquiunt quiūr,quīnā Scripturæ lites istas cōponet,quū deillius ipsius interpretatione maximè inter nos queratur?Aio vero quū de Religione que- ritur nō leuē culpa admitti si alio quàm ad Sa- cras Scripturas quas à Spiritu Sancto prolatas & dictatas esse constat confugiatur.Quid enim aliud est quam de solio suo Dominum deturbare? Nec leuius peccat siquis existimet Sp.S. dilucidius & apertius per mortalium quemlibet loqui voluisse, quàm per fidos illos & omni exceptione maiores seruos suos , quibus tanquam amanuensibus ad veritatem omne ad salutē necessariam scriptis consignandamvsus est.Tertiò, vt omittam egregia multa veterum cùm Græcorum tum Latinorum præcepta quibus eorum quæ in Scripturis occurrunt difficiliorum & obscuriorum locorum explicandorum rationem docent,Diuus Paulus certissimam nobis regulam discernendi falsas interpretationes à veris præscripsit Rom.12 6. vti videlicet omnia ad articulos fidei probatos & receptos referantur;quum vel inuitos etiam omnes fateri sit necesse S.Sp.sibi ipsi minimè repugnare, atque adeò contradicentem illi omnem Spiritum falsum & mendacem esse quum veritatis magister solus Sp. S. dicendus sit. Itaque nullus hic exceptioni locus est,etsi iam ab initio seculi, vt ita dicam, recepta, & mille conciliis approbata foret,istiusmodi Scripturarum interpretatio. Deniqueque Scripturas sacras & textum & glossam esse oportere constanter asserimus, & limites citra quos nequit consistere rectum.Sic Esaias pseudoprophetas sui temporis ad Legem & testimonium revocat.Esa.8.v.20. Eodem nos etiam & non alio Dauid Psal.19.8. & 119. toto remittit, etsi vetus foedus longe sit Euangelica luce inferius,& cum ea minime comparadum. Non aliter Apostoli,praeceptoris sui noltrique vestigia legentes. Ioh.5.39. doctrinam suam Propheticis scriptis confirmarunt. Nec alio pater Abrahamus erudiri cupientes amanda- uit.Luc.16.29.& 31.Denique sic veteres in veris Conciliis aduersus haereticos sui temporis Scriptis propheticis & Apostolicis pugnantes eosdem expugnarunt:a quo certamine tantum abest vt nos talibus armis induti subducamus, vt contra nihil tantopere expetamus & modis omnibus vrgeamus, nullam etiam interpretationem,nec veterum Patrum nec scriptorum neotericorum repudiantes, modo tamen ad hunc Lydium lapidem examinentur, & ad hanc trutinam appendantur,quod veteres omnes pios doctores de suis scriptis fieri voluisse quis tandem ignorat?
units.tr: Moreover, since I do not think they will deny that long ago Scripture was made to appear false, both in interpretations and in applications, which for the most part happened partly through the ignorance and partly through the malice of those who presided over the Church, a third judge is necessary to settle such disputes. Who indeed will he be, unless the Lord alone? And how could the Lord judge except through his written word? Unless perhaps we intend to bring the Lord down from heaven again. "But," they say, "who will settle those disputes of Scripture, since its very interpretation is what is chiefly contested among us?" I answer that when religion is in question, it is no slight fault to flee to anything other than the Holy Scriptures, which are known to have been uttered and dictated by the Holy Spirit. For what else is this than to cast the Lord down from his throne? Nor does he sin less who thinks that the Holy Spirit wished to speak more clearly and openly through any mortal whatever than through his faithful servants, who are above all exception, and whom he used as amanuenses to commit to writing everything necessary to salvation. Thirdly, to omit the many excellent precepts of the ancients, both Greek and Latin, which teach how difficult and obscure passages of Scripture are to be explained, the divine Paul prescribed to us a most certain rule for distinguishing false interpretations from true ones (Rom. 12.6): namely, that everything be referred to the articles of faith that have been proved and received. For even all unwilling men must admit that the Holy Spirit does not contradict himself, and so any spirit contradicting him is false and a liar, since the Holy Spirit alone is to be called the teacher of truth. Therefore there is no room here for exception, even if such an interpretation of Scripture had been received from the beginning of the age, as one might say, and approved by a thousand councils. Finally, we constantly assert that the holy Scriptures must be both text and gloss, and that they are the limits within which right judgment must remain. Thus Isaiah calls the false prophets of his time back to the Law and the testimony (Isa. 8.20). David likewise sends us, throughout Ps. 19.8 and 119, to the same and to no other, although the Old Covenant lies far beneath the light of the Gospel and is in no way to be compared with it. The Apostles, following the footsteps of their teacher and ours, confirmed their doctrine by the prophetic writings in no other way (John 5.39). Nor did Abraham send those who wished to be taught elsewhere (Luke 16.29, 31). Finally, in this way the ancients in true Councils fought against the heretics of their own time, contending with the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures, and overcame them. From this contest we are so far from withdrawing, armed with such weapons, that on the contrary we seek and urge nothing so earnestly, and in every way: we reject no interpretation, neither of the ancient Fathers nor of the recent writers, provided only that it is tested at this touchstone [Lydium lapidem] and weighed on this scale. Who indeed does not know that all the pious ancient teachers wished this to be done with their own writings?

units.la: Accedo iam ad tertiam obiectionem, Iesum Christum videlicet Ecclesiam suam adhuc hodie per Ecclesiae Pastores & Doctores alloqui,& ad finem vsque seculi allocuturum. Quod nos & ipsi libenter agnoscimus.Quum enim fides ex auditu sit,auditus autem per verbum.Rom.10.17.deficiente verbo,fidem etiam ac proinde Ecclesiam deficere necesse fuisset. Sed in hoc ab aduersariis vehementissime dissentisentimus,quod quum exiftimene Iesum Chri- ftum & Apostolos multa posteris iniis quęfi- dem & religionem Christianam spectant di- cenda reliquisse, nos contra dicimus & asse- ueramus intolerando illos in errore versari in Dei Ecclesia, quum Iesum Christum certum fit quæcunque ad salutem nostram require-bantur diligenter implcuisse, & fideliter A-postolis tradidisse, de quorum fide merito nullus dubitarit. Ioh.15.15. & 17.4. Matth. 28. 20. Act.20.27. Et hanc vnicam notam agnosci-mus, qua veri pastores & doctores à falsis di-scernantur, si nempe nihil in doctrina Prophe-tica & Apostolica de suo adiecerint, nihil im-mutarint, aut de eadem detraxerint, qua vnica suis veluti fundamentis nixam stare veram Dei domum docet Apostolus, Ephef. 2. 10. & Apoc. 21. 14. cui Pharifaicum fermentum ex diametro repugnat, Matth.16.6.& cauponatio illa sermonis Dei cuius Apostolus.2.Cor.2.17. meminit, de quibus omnibus à nobis superius pluribus actum est.
units.tr: I come now to the third objection: that Jesus Christ, namely, still today addresses his Church through the ministers and teachers of the Church, and will continue to do so until the end of the age. This we ourselves gladly acknowledge. For since faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word (Rom. 10.17), the word failing, faith and therefore the Church would necessarily have failed as well. But we dissent most vehemently from our adversaries on this point: they think that Jesus Christ and the Apostles left to posterity many things still to be said that concern the faith and the Christian religion, whereas we say and affirm that they err intolerably in the Church of God, since it is certain that Jesus Christ diligently fulfilled everything that was required for our salvation and faithfully handed it on to the Apostles, whose faithfulness no one may rightly doubt (John 15.15; 17.4; Matt. 28.20; Acts 20.27). And we acknowledge this as the one mark by which true ministers and teachers are distinguished from false ones: namely, if they have added nothing of their own to the prophetic and apostolic doctrine, changed nothing in it, and taken nothing away from it. By this one mark, the true house of God, resting as on its foundations, is shown to stand, as the Apostle teaches (Eph. 2.20; Rev. 21.14), and to this the Pharisaic leaven is wholly opposed (Matt. 16.6), as is that huckstering of the word of God of which the Apostle speaks (2 Cor. 2.17). All these matters we have treated at greater length above.

units.la: En paucis quænam illa vox sit, quâ vnicam audiri necesse est: verùm ex sementem facien- tis parabola. Matth. 13. & pluribus aliis locis, non vnam auditorum esse speciem discimus. Nec verò quicunque Scholam frequentant in ea progressus faciunt, quòd alij arguendi po- tius quàm discendi, Matt.22.15. alij cauillandi studium adferant: alij vescentibus quidem sed non concoquentibus sint similes, qui siquid antea didicerint, parvo momento tradant I. iij. obliuioni. Iac. i.23. De iis igitur hic Christus loquitur, qui sermonem eius audiunt, & auditum obseruant, ex ea regula quam ipsemet praescripsit. Luc.11.28. & in eo sanctae Virginis exemplum imitantur. Luc. 2.19. & Apostoli praescriptum sequuntur.Coloss.3.16.
units.tr: Briefly, what that voice is which must alone be heard, we learn from the parable of the sower (Matt. 13) and from many other places: there is not one kind of hearer. Nor do all who attend the school make progress in it; some bring to it a zeal for arguing rather than for learning (Matt. 22.15), others a zeal for cavilling; others are like those who eat but do not digest, who, whatever they have learned before, soon hand over to oblivion (James 1.23). Christ therefore speaks here of those who hear his word and keep what they have heard, according to the rule he himself prescribed (Luke 11.28), and in this they imitate the example of the holy Virgin (Luke 2.19) and follow the precept of the Apostle (Col. 3.16).

units.la: Hic vero sitis mirari, imo lugere, non posse sum miseram & deploratam hominum conditionem, qui quum haec veritas tam excellens & pretiosa sit, cum ea coiuncta felicitate, quae mortalium ingeniorum capacitate imo etiam Angelorum superat, tanto tamen illam afficiunt dedecore: atque odio iam pridem, tam pertinaciter aduersus seipsos tam misere coniurantes persequuntur. Unde vero istud, obsecro, quum alioquin homines natura ferantur ad earum rerum quas sibi utiles esse iudicant indagationem? Nam tanti mali scaturiginem in primis a naturae nostrae corruptione, mentem nostra ne lucem caelestem illa aspiciat primum excaecante, deinde iudicium nostrum ad approbandas tenebras peruertente, tandemque affectiones nostras in contrarium rapiente manare fatendum est: deinde vero quo magis prouchuntur homines in istis tenebris tanto magis in iis confirmari, & ex ignorantibus, malitiosos, ex malitiosis peruersos fieri, tandemque in contemptores & induratos hostes deuenire, praesertim eos quos non tantum conscientia nondum putris, sed etiam verbu Dei redarguit. Est enim natiua nostra corruptio ferae immani non absimilis, quo magis lacessitur eo magis etiam furit,
units.tr: Here you may well be astonished, or rather grieved, that I cannot express the wretched and hopeless condition of mankind. Although this truth is so excellent and precious, and joined with a happiness that surpasses the capacity of human minds and even of the angels, people treat it with such dishonour, and for a long time now have pursued it with hatred, so stubbornly and wretchedly conspiring against themselves. But whence does this come, I beg you, since by nature people are otherwise inclined to investigate those things which they judge useful to themselves? We must confess that the source of so great an evil flows chiefly from the corruption of our nature, which first blinds our mind so that it cannot look upon the heavenly light, then perverts our judgement so that it approves darkness, and finally drags our affections in the opposite direction. Moreover, the more people are driven forward in these shadows, the more they are confirmed in them, and from being ignorant they become malicious, and from malicious they become perverse, and at last they arrive at being scorners and hardened enemies, especially those whom not only a conscience not yet rotten, but also the Word of God, rebukes. For our natural corruption is not unlike a savage beast: the more it is provoked, the more it rages, and it reveals its brutish nature. [Rom. 7.9.]

units.la: Vera cau sa contem ptus Enä gelii. furit, suamque ferinam naturā patefacit. Rom. 7.9. Sibi ipsis igitur istiusmodi homines, & alteri nulli, suæ rebellionis & perditionis causam imputent, & in seipsis quærant: contrà vero veritatis amatores, & Regis nostri vocem audientes, vt hic Iesus Christus Dominus noster loquitur, non sibi ipsis id attribuant, sed eius gratiæ acceptum ferant, qui mutato in melius eorū ingenio ad se illos trahit, Ioh. 6. 45. & 65.
units.tr: (The true cause of contempt for the Gospel.) Let such people, therefore, impute the cause of their rebellion and destruction to themselves and to no one else, and seek it within themselves. But let those who love the truth, and who hear the voice of our King, as our Lord Jesus Christ speaks here, not attribute this to themselves, but credit it to that grace of his which, by changing their disposition for the better, draws them to himself. [John 6.45, 65.]

units.la: Porrò nullus hic est rebellibus & contumacibus, quòd non vnà cum aliis trahantur, quorelæ locus. Nec enim ipsorum ab hoc fonte perditio, manat, sed à natiua malitia & vitiositate, quam si Deo in ipsis corrigere non est vitium, non est tamen quòd coquerantur, quum nemini sit debitor Deus. Quis verò miretur quòd Deus hanc gratiam in singulos minimè conferat, quum illud sit potius admiratione dignissimum, immò immensam & admirandam Dei bonitatem commendet, quòd vel vnius hominis misereri dignetur, quem à primo parente tracta labes detestandum omnino & indignissimum Dei misericordia mortalem facit? Oro vos igitur & obtestor, fratres, vt Opt. Dei nostri clementiam infinitam sedulò pensitemus, quòd nostros oculos aperire & aures perforare dignatus sit, vt lucem illam intueri & vocem eius audire possemus, nos, inquam, quos tum hic, tum alibi ex variis orbis regionibus coactos sacrosancto suo verbo fovet, quod etiamnum apud nos hodie sartum tectum mira longanimitate conseruat, tot tamen regnis, regionibus, populis & familiis in superstitionibus & idolomaniis suis derelictis: illud, inquam, serio nocte dieque versantes animo, tantum ipsius fauorem, tantamque benignitatem ad eius honorem & gloriam referamus, & ad mutuam nostram aedificationem per eam charitatem quam indiuiduam commitem fides aseifcitne Pilatum imitemur, qui de eo quidem de quo oportuit quid esset haec veritas, sed per ludibrium quaesiuit, at responsum ab eodem non expectauit. At Deus bone! quanto maioribus donis a Domino sumus affecti, in quibus non modo desiderium inquirendae veritatis efformauit, sed quorum multis subinde redditis responsis, aures ad excipienda illa perforauit, tanta etiam cum efficacia (laus illi in perpetuum soli reddatur) vt extra suam patriam singuli bonum illum pastorem sequuti simus, quid iam fiet nobis miseris, si quum ex mera ipsius gratia a Spiritu inchoauerimus in carnem tadem desinamus? Si quum nos Dominus no in Aegyptum quandam relegarit, sed in aedes suas tam benigne, tam comiter receperit, fratribus nostris a quibus in sua tecta recepti sumus hanc gratiam referimus, vt nostri obliti scandalum illis inferamus, pars quidem vanitatem praeferentes, pars vero malis artibus operam dantes: quid denique fiet nobis si Euangelium, quod omnibus, etiam iis qui foris sunt, commendare vitae sanctitate nos oportuit, & sanctum illud nomen quod super nos est inuocatum, omnium mnium ludibriis & sannis exponimus, annon conditio nostra posterior, priore deterior est futura?Matth.12.41. annon durius quàm cæteri omnes vapulabimus? Luc.12.47. annon denique peiore conditione quàm Sodoma Gomorrhæ fumus futuri. Matth. 11.23. An verò speramus eum, qui ramis naturalibus, vel ipsa teste Hierosolyma in vastitatem redacta, & iam in singulas orbis oras iactato, Deique furoris testimonium vbique prædicante vetere illo populo, nobis infititiis ramis. Rom.11.21. imò palmitibus inutilibus, Ioh. 15.6. parcitu-rum?Heu verò,fratres,ista ferio cogitate,quorum quidem est semper cogitandorum tempus,sed illa iam sunt tempora,quibus, aut nunc quàm,sedulò sunt hæc pensitanda,quum præ-fertim seculo nostro securim ad arborum radicem non tàtùm appositam, sed,dolor! multas etiam eximias fyluas penitus decussas,multas ex parte succisas conspiciamus, immo ante omnium ora nostris ipsis mœnibus armatos hostes Dei ipsius furente gladio fucceffiffe conspiciamus. Faxit verò Deus ille Opt. Max.cuius adhuc vocem illam fan-ctam nostris auribus haurire conceditur,ne ferò nimis pœnitere didcerimus.
units.tr: Moreover, there is no ground for complaint for the rebellious and stubborn, that they are not drawn along with others. For their destruction does not flow from this source, but from their natural malice and wickedness. And if God chooses to correct this in them, it is no fault; yet they have no reason to complain, since God owes nothing to anyone. Yet who would be surprised that God does not bestow this grace on each individual? It is rather most worthy of admiration, and it displays God's immense and wonderful goodness, that he deigns to show mercy even to a single man, whom the taint inherited from our first parent makes mortal, utterly detestable and most unworthy of God's mercy. I therefore beg and entreat you, brothers, that we diligently consider the infinite clemency of our best God, because he has deigned to open our eyes and pierce our ears, so that we might behold that light and hear his voice. I mean us, whom he gathers from various regions of the world, here and elsewhere, and cherishes with his holy word; whom he still preserves among us today, intact and sheltered, with wonderful patience, while so many kingdoms, regions, peoples and families remain abandoned in their superstitions and idolatries. Let us, I say, keep this seriously in mind night and day, and refer such great favour and such great kindness of his to his honour and glory, and to our mutual edification, through that charity which faith brings in as its inseparable companion. Let us not imitate Pilate, who indeed asked what this truth was concerning him, of whom it was fitting to ask, but asked it in mockery, and did not expect an answer from him. But good God! With how much greater gifts have we been endowed by the Lord! In us he has not only formed a desire to seek the truth, but, after many answers have been given to us, he has also pierced our ears to receive them, and with such effectiveness (may praise be given to him alone for ever) that each of us, following that good shepherd, has come out of our own country. What then will become of us wretches, if, having begun in the Spirit by his pure grace, we at last end in the flesh? [Gal. 3.3.] When the Lord has not banished us to some Egypt, but has received us so kindly and graciously into his own house, do we repay this grace to our brothers, from whom we have been received into their homes, by forgetting ourselves and bringing scandal upon them? Some display vanity, and others busy themselves with evil arts. What, finally, will become of us if we expose the Gospel, which we ought to commend to all, even to those who are outside, by the holiness of our lives, and that holy name which has been invoked over us, to the mockery and scorn of all? Will not our latter condition be worse than our former? [Matt. 12.41.] Will we not be beaten more severely than all the others? [Luke 12.47.] And finally, will we not be in a worse condition than Sodom and Gomorrah? [Matt. 11.23.] But do we really hope that he will spare us, the grafted branches, when he did not spare the natural branches? Jerusalem itself bears witness, reduced to desolation, and that ancient people, now scattered to every shore of the world, proclaims everywhere the testimony of God's wrath. [Rom. 11.21.] Indeed, we would be useless branches. [John 15.6.] Alas, brothers, consider these things seriously. There is always a time for such thoughts, but these are times in which these matters must be weighed diligently now, or never. Especially in our age we see the axe laid not only to the root of the trees, but, alas, we see many splendid forests utterly felled and many partly cut down. Indeed, before the eyes of all, we see the enemies of God armed, having advanced right up to our own walls, with his own raging sword. May God, the best and greatest, whose holy voice we are still permitted to drink in with our ears, grant that we do not learn to repent too late.

units.la: 11. Iesus autem stetit coram Praeside, & interrogauit eum praeses, dicens, Tu-ne es Rex illle Iudaeorum? Dixit autem ei Iesus, Tu dicis.
units.tr: 11. Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor asked him, saying, Are you the King of the Jews? Jesus said to him, You say so.

units.la: 12. Et quum ipse accusaretur a principibus Sacerdotum & Senioribus, nihil respondit.
units.tr: 12. And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing.

units.la: 13. Tunc dicit ei Pilatus, Non audis quam multa aduersum te testificentur?
units.tr: 13. Then Pilate said to him, Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?

units.la: 14. Et non respondit ei ad ullum verbum: ita vt miraretur praeses valde.
units.tr: 14. And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor wondered greatly.

units.la: MARC. 15.
units.tr: MARK 15.

units.la: 2. Tunc interrogauit eum Pilatus, Tu-ne es ille Rex Iudaeorum? Ipse vero respondens dixit ei, Tu dicis.
units.tr: 2. Then Pilate asked him, Are you the King of the Jews? But he answered and said to him, You say so.

units.la: 3. Et multum accusabant eum principes sacerdotum.
units.tr: 3. And the chief priests accused him much.

units.la: 4. Pilatus autem rursus interrogauit eum, dicens, Non respondes quicquam? ecce quam multa aduersum te testificantur.
units.tr: 4. Pilate asked him again, saying, Do you answer nothing? See how many things they testify against you.

units.la: 5. Iesus autem nihil amplius respondit, adeo vt miraretur Pilatus.
units.tr: 5. But Jesus answered nothing more, so that Pilate wondered.

units.la: 3. Pilatus autem interrogauit eum, dicens, Tu ne es Rex Iudæorum? Ipse verò respondens ei dixit, Tu dicis.
units.tr: 3. Pilate then asked him, saying, "Are you the King of the Jews?" And he answered him, "You say so."

units.la: 4. Ait verò Pilatus ad principes Sacerdotum & turbam, Nullam inuenio noxam in hoc homine.
units.tr: 4. Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowd, "I find no guilt in this man."

units.la: 5. At illi inualescebant, dicentes, Concitat populum, docens per uniuersam Iudæam, exorsus à Galilæa huc usque.
units.tr: 5. But they grew more insistent, saying, "He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee even to this place."

units.la: 6. Pilatus verò audita Galilæa, interrogauit num Galilæus esset.
units.tr: 6. When Pilate heard the word "Galilee," he asked whether the man was a Galilean.

units.la: 7. Et quum cognouisset eum ad Herodis potestatem pertinere, remisit eum ad Herodem, qui & ipse Hierosolymis erat per eos dies.
units.tr: 7. And when he learned that Jesus belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him to Herod, who was himself also in Jerusalem in those days.

units.la: ACTENVS initium primi actus illius examinis intra praetorium à Pilato de Christo habiti, quod solus Iohannes ab aliis omissum expressit, explicauimus. Hic enim qui sequitur actus secundus à priore illo pendet, vt patet tum ex iis quae diserte Iohannes exprimit cap. 18. 28. Iesum à Pilato in Praetorium introductum fuisse, & v. 33. ibi primum de Christo quaestionem habuisse, postquam recusantibus Iudæis in Praetorium ingredi, ad eos egressus, & auditis accusationis summis capitibus, in illud effet regressus: praeterquâ quòd in primo examine dicitur Christus aperte & plenè respondisse, absentibus Iudæis ipsius accusatoribus, quâ tamē
units.tr: So far we have explained the beginning of the first act of that examination of Christ held by Pilate inside the praetorium, which John alone, of the others, sets out. The second act that follows depends on that first, as is clear both from what John expressly states in chapter 18: that Jesus was brought by Pilate into the praetorium (v. 28), and that there, at v. 33, Pilate first questioned him about Christ, after the Jews had refused to enter the praetorium and he had come out to them, heard the main heads of the accusation, and gone back in. Besides, in the first examination Christ is said to have answered openly and fully, though his accusers were absent, whereas in this second examination he deigned not to answer.

units.la: in hoc fecundo examine respondere fit dedi-gnatus. Pilatum igitur constat,quum perfun-ctorie, & per ludibrium de Christo quæfiuif-set,ecquid eflet Veritas,extra Prętorium etiam illum secum eduxisse,& tunc coram Iudęis fe-cundum istius examinis actum institutum,quā circunftantiam differte Lucas exprimit, Luc. 23. 14. Et sane ni res ita eflet, vt exiens extra Prætorium Pilatus Christum vnafecum edu-xiffet, res inter illos ex composito gesta fuisse iudiciumque clam testibus informatum vide-rerur: quæ quidem ad historiæ nostræ feriem melius dignofcedam dicta funto. Vt vero rem ipsam aggrediamur, fi horrendū visu & indi-gnum modis omnibus spectaculum fuit: Dei Filium tanquam reum capitali supplicio di-gnum vinctū ante Caiaphæ Summi Sacerdo-tis tribunal adstare, à quo tamen ante omnes mortales agnosci ipsum oportuit, à quo reli-quos ad illius religiosum cultum adduci de-cuit, cuius ipse in mundo figura erat, annon quæso,multo magis stupendum fuit,magnum illum populi fui Liberatorem, à suis ipsis po-pularibus in manus hominis Ethnici & ido-lolatræ capitali supplicio damnandum esse traditum. Sacerdotij enim in ipso considerati magna fuit auctoritas & dignitas: sed quid miferoilli ethnico cum Chriito cuius ne vo-cem quidem vnquam audire dignus erat? En tamen illam iudicem eius qui modis omni-bus Angelos ipsos dignitate superat. Absit vero, absit, inquam, vt propterea nos ab illo vel tantillum offensi resiliamus. Luc.7.23. quū contrà pacandis nostris conscientiis certissi- mam hinc consolationem eruere nos oportet. Quemadmodum enim eius vinculis qui vices nostras subiit soluti sumus, sic eius ludi- briis coram Deo reddimur honorifici, eius condemnatione, absoluimur, morte denique vitæ reddimur. Quum igitur primorum paren tum nostrorum cum Satana conspiratio reos læsæ Maiestatis nos effecerit, Gen.3.22. pecca- tum istud necesse fuit coram spirituali iudice, qui fuit summus Sacerdos, condemnari, tam iustè quidem nostri ratione, quorum vices sponsor ille noster subierat, quàm iniustè & magno scelere, si Caiaphi conscientiam, & condemnati personam inspicias. Quòd verò primus ille noster parens peccato suo Deum creatorem suum de solio & imperio quod in mortales obtinet deiicere molitus est, imperiū affectans cuius administrationem tantùm be- nigna Dei manu acceperat, huius etiam cri- minis reum peragi sponsorem nostrum opor- tuit, coram eo qui personam Maximi tunc in orbe Imperatoris sustinebat. Sed age, dic qui- bus tandem ministris Filius Dei prehensus, & in Pilati manus traditus est? Iudæis nempe, quos hac in parte merito nostro calculo no- tamus, & quos etiam Dominus sicut Pilatum seuerißimis pœnis vltus est.
units.tr: It is clear that Pilate, after questioning Christ casually and mockingly, "What is truth?", also led him out with him beyond the praetorium, and that it was then, before the Jews, that the second act of this examination was conducted. Luke sets out this circumstance expressly (Luke 23:14). Indeed, if things were not so, and Pilate had led Christ out alone with him, the matter between them would appear to have been transacted by prior arrangement, and the judgment would seem to have been framed in secret, with no witnesses. These points are worth noting to better grasp the sequence of our history. But let us come to the matter itself. It was a horrible sight to see, and in every way an unworthy spectacle: the Son of God, bound as one deserving capital punishment, standing before the tribunal of Caiaphas the high priest, by whom he ought above all mortals to have been acknowledged, and to whom the rest ought to have been led for his religious worship, of whom the high priest himself was a figure in the world. Is it not, I ask, far more astonishing that the great Liberator of his own people was handed over by his own countrymen into the hands of a heathen and idolater, to be condemned to capital punishment? For the priesthood, considered in itself, had great authority and dignity; but what had that wretched heathen to do with Christ, whose voice he was not even worthy to hear? Yet there he stands as judge of him who surpasses even the angels in every kind of dignity. Far be it, I say, far be it, that we should therefore shrink back, offended in the least from him (cf. Luke 7:23). Rather, we ought to draw from this the most certain consolation for quieting our consciences. For just as we are loosed from the chains of him who took our place, so by his mockeries we are made honourable before God, by his condemnation we are absolved, and by his death we are restored to life. Since the conspiracy of our first parents with Satan made us guilty of treason against majesty (Gen. 3:22), that sin had necessarily to be condemned before a spiritual judge, who was the high priest. This was just on our account, whose place that surety of ours had taken, but unjust and a great wickedness if you look at the conscience of Caiaphas and the person of the one condemned. Moreover, since our first parent, by his sin, sought to cast God his creator from the throne and rule he holds over mortals, grasping at a dominion whose administration he had received only by God's kindly hand, our surety also had to answer for this crime, before the one who then bore the person of the greatest emperor in the world. But come, tell me: by what ministers was the Son of God at last seized and handed over into Pilate's hands? By the Jews, namely, whom in this matter we rightly count in our reckoning, and whom the Lord also punished, as he did Pilate, with the most severe penalties.

units.la: Verumenimuerò si penitius ista scrutemur, causam horum omnium nostra peccata com- periemus. Age igitur in nos ipsos conuerta-
units.tr: But if we examine these things more deeply, we will find the cause of all of them in our own sins. Come then, let us turn to ourselves.

units.la: Vsus huius doctrinæ. mur,nos ipsos incusemus, aduersum nos indi-gnemur potius quàm aduersus eos in quos iã lata sententia elt, peccatû, quod tanto pretio Dei filius expiauit,ex animo detestemur: infi-nitam illam Dei Patris bonitatem adoremus, qui ex horrendis illis nostris lapsibus occasio-nem infinitæ exhibendæ clementiæ ccpit: Fi-lium hunc sponte colamus, amemus, venerę-mur, quem sese tam humile facere vt nos tam sublimes eucheret non potuit: sed in primis hanc consolationem velut in penum recóda-mus,ex quo tandé in extremo illo certamine, quum Deus coram suo tribunali nos ipsos fi-stit, siue per morbum, siue alia ratione vocet, depromamus quæ nobis confirmandis suffi-ciant.Leuiter enim ista,dum præterit ætas,co-gitamus, sed vbi se nobis ingens illud & for-midabile Dei tribunal offert,& magnus ille iu-dex illi insidens, iustissimus, inquam, ille, cui nihil occultum est nostris mentibus occurrit, Deus bone, quàta mortales formidine percuti necesse sum est! Tunc igitur, quicquid hòmines vana sibi fingentes somnia garriant, sola hæc consolatio terrorem excutit,qua cum Dauide sic animam nostram affari discimus,Psalm.42. Quid consternata es anima mea,& cur tumul-tuaris intra me? Expecta eum qui te suis vin-culis solutam redemit, qui tuam rebellionem obedientia sua texit, qui mortalis tribunal non refugit vt in eo condemnatus tibi apud Patris cœlestis solium gratiam & iudicij ab-solutionem conciliaret
units.tr: Use of this doctrine. let us accuse ourselves, and be angry with ourselves rather than with those against whom sentence has already been pronounced. Let us detest from the heart the sin that the Son of God expiated at such a price. Let us adore the infinite goodness of God the Father, who from those dreadful falls of ours took occasion for showing infinite mercy. Let us willingly cherish, love and honour this Son, who could not make himself so lowly in order to raise us so high. And above all, let us store up this consolation as in a pantry, so that at last, in that final struggle, when God sets us before his own tribunal, whether he calls us by sickness or by some other means, we may draw from it what suffices to strengthen us. For we think of these things lightly while our life passes, but when that vast and formidable tribunal of God presents itself to us, and that great judge sitting upon it, most just, I say, who knows nothing hidden from our minds, then, good God, with what terror must mortals be struck! Then, whatever vain dreams men may babble, this consolation alone drives out fear, and with David we learn to address our soul thus, Psalm 42: "Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me? Wait for him who has redeemed you from your bonds, who covered your rebellion with his obedience, who did not shun a mortal tribunal, so that, condemned in it, he might win for you favour and absolution of judgment before the throne of the heavenly Father."

units.la: Deinceps vero narrat historia, accusatores in accusando perrexisse, Pilato in examine, ad quod tamen Christus respondere sit dedignatus. Plurimae vero quaestiones non leviter pretereundae se nobis hic obserunt. Ac primum quidem silentium istud, Christi etiam a Iudice interrogati non respondentis, rebellionis aut contemptus accusari posse videtur, & ab adversariis obiectum Christo crime confirmare. Absit vero cogitemus tale quid in mente illi venisse, qui licet Rex Regum esset, sese tamen hactenus ita gessit ut debita Magistratib. obedientia praestiterit, & nobis suis discipulis eandem, per suos Apostolos, doctrina tam sedulo proposuerit. Quamobrem etiam nec ipsius accusatores nec ipse Pilatus ex contemptu vel superbia silentium illud profecto esse suspicati sunt, tanta nimirum erat tamque aperta ipsius innocentia & facilitas, ut non difficile fuerit cuilibet dignoscere silentium eius esse instar omnis responsi, tam erant absurda & a veri specie aliena de quibus adversarii falso illum criminabantur.
units.tr: Next the story relates that the accusers persisted in their accusation, while Pilate conducted the examination, to which, however, Christ deigned to make no reply. Here several questions present themselves that should not be lightly passed over. First, that silence of Christ, when questioned by the judge and not answering, may seem to be accusable as rebellion or contempt, and to confirm the crime charged against Christ by his adversaries. But far be it from us to think any such thing came into the mind of him who, though he was King of kings, nevertheless so conducted himself up to this point that he rendered the obedience owed to magistrates, and through his apostles proposed the same teaching to us his disciples with such care. Therefore neither his accusers nor Pilate himself suspected that this silence was truly due to contempt or pride. Such was his innocence and openness, so plain, that it was not difficult for anyone to recognize that his silence was equivalent to any answer, so absurd and alien to the appearance of truth were the things of which his adversaries falsely accused him.

units.la: Deinde, quum hic ageretur de Iesu Christi capite, an voluit ilusmodi tam alto silentio docere (quod sibi phanatici quidam persuadent, ad intellectum suum detorquentes illa Christi verba, Petenti tunicam, etiam veltem dimittito) non licere coram Magistratibus ius tuum, sive agendo sive excipiendo tueri, & iis mediis quae Deus ipse instituit ius suum persequi? Minime gentium. Sunt enim Magistratus & bonae Leges in maximis Dei donis numerandæ, fine quibus humana societas stare nequeat: Et sanè tota sacra Scriptura, & factum illud in primis Apostoli in sua captiuitate fatis superque testantur ab Euangelio ciuiles politias minimè destrui,sed ab eodé potius stabiliri & ordinari.Verba verò illa Christus non ideo protulit. Matt.5.40.quasi deiuftitiæ ciuilis exercitio quicquam detrahére cogitaret, sed vindictæ cupiditatem refrænans Christianam patientiam commendauit.Apostoli verò ad Corinthios scribentis mens non fuit prohibere quominus ius suum apud Iudices repeterent, sed vt contentionum & litium amantes compesceret, docereτque debere ipsos quauis iactura, fi opus foret, bonorum terrenorum, sacrosanctum illud Christiani nomen,quod alios alij vocantes in iudicium sannis iudicum infidelium cæterorúmque exponebant, redimere. Nihil tale nos igitur suo silentio Christus Dominus docuit.
units.tr: Next, since here the question concerns the head of Jesus Christ, did he wish by such a deep silence to teach something of this kind? Some fanatics persuade themselves of this, twisting Christ's words, "To one who asks for your tunic, give also your cloak," to mean that it is not lawful before magistrates to defend your right, whether in bringing suit or in answering one, and to pursue your right by those means which God himself has instituted. By no means. For magistrates and good laws are to be counted among the greatest gifts of God, without which human society cannot stand. And indeed the whole of Holy Scripture, and especially that deed of the apostle during his captivity, bear ample witness that civil polities are not destroyed by the Gospel, but rather are established and ordered by it. Christ did not utter those words as if he intended to take anything away from the exercise of civil justice, but in restraining the desire for vengeance he commended Christian patience. Nor was it the intention of the apostle writing to the Corinthians to forbid people to seek their right before judges, but to restrain those who love strife and lawsuits, and to teach that Christians ought to redeem that sacred name of Christian, which others, summoning one another into court, exposed to the mockery of unbelieving judges and others, even at the cost of some loss of earthly goods, if need be. Christ the Lord, therefore, taught us nothing of this kind by his silence.

units.la: Quare verò tandem, inquies, sic altum egit silentium, vt ne motire quidé voluerit? Népé, inquam docturus quoddam loquendi, quoddam verò silendi tempus esse,quod vtrumque reipsa præstitit, modò silens qui tamen de se apud Caiapham ipsum tam magnificè loquutus erat,Matth.26.64.& coram Pilato. Ioh. 18. 22. Idcirco verò antea loquutus est, ne nimis alto suo silentio, tum doctrinæ suæ, tum officio præiudicium afferret, cui sic prouidit vt expedire iudicauit. En cur tandem, etiam adiuratus, apud Caiaphum, tam magnificè verum rum fe Dei filium & mundi iudicem ellc professus fit.
