En etiam cur intra prætorium de regno suo tam honorificè, non habita quidem Pilati ipsius, sed Ecclesiæ suæ totius ratione loquutus fit. Iam vero quid ipsum attinebat loqui? Iudæos enim quatuor iam annos fine intermissione docebat & hortabatur, & fatis erat illi notus ipsorum animus, vnde factum est vt silere maluerit quàm os suum aperire, ne aut peccandi præberet ipsis occasionem, aut causæ suæ æquitatem tuendo, condemnationem quam sibi præstitutam sciebat effugere velle videretur. Nec ipsum latebat hoc vnum Pilatum moliri, vt illum absoluerer, cuius illi tamen rei esse nolebat auctor.
units.tr: Why then, you will ask, did he keep such a deep silence that he did not even wish to stir? Indeed, I answer, because he was going to teach that there is a time for speaking and a time for keeping silent, and he showed both in practice. He kept silent now, although before Caiaphas he had spoken so grandly of himself (Matt. 26.64), and before Pilate too (John 18.22). He spoke earlier so that his deep silence would not prejudice either his teaching or his office, and he provided for this as he judged fitting. Here is why, even when put on oath before Caiaphas, he professed so magnificently that he was the Son of God and the judge of the world. Here too is why, within the praetorium, he spoke so honourably of his kingdom, with regard not to Pilate himself but to the whole of his Church. But what purpose would speaking have served for him? He had been teaching and exhorting the Jews without interruption for four years, and their disposition was well known to him. So it came about that he preferred to be silent rather than open his mouth, lest he either give them an occasion for sinning, or seem, by defending the justice of his cause, to wish to escape the condemnation he knew had been decreed for him. Nor was he unaware that Pilate was striving to acquit him by this one means, though he himself did not want to be the author of that outcome.

units.la: Habes tanti huius silentij causas peculiares. Quum verò tantum fit, vt præclarè monet Iacobus, vel in silentio vel in sermone momenti Iac. 3. 2. nostræ sunt partes Deum ferìò vtíque ardentibus interpellare, vt nos linguam moderari nostram, & illi modum imponere doceat, Spiritum nobis discretionis quo carnis etiam prudentiam superemus benignè largiendo. Quum verò propter infinitam rerum in hoc orbe varietatem certas speciales & peculiares regulas præscribere fit admodum difficile, fi tamen vt par est, veri rectíque amantes fuerimus, fi zelo Dei gloriæ, & proximi salutis incensi fuerimus, fi nostris affectionibus priuatis imperauerimus, fi denique Deum supplices vt nobis os vel claudat vel aperiat oraueri-mus, tunc sanè futurum est vt quo tempore fi-
units.tr: You have here the particular causes of this silence. Since it is so true, as James wisely warns, that we offend in many things, both in silence and in speech (James 3.2), it is our part to pray earnestly to God that he may teach us to govern our tongue and set a limit to it, graciously granting us a spirit of discernment, by which we may even surpass the prudence of the flesh. Since, however, because of the infinite variety of things in this world, it is very difficult to prescribe fixed and particular rules, still, if we are, as we should be, lovers of what is true and right, if we are inflamed with zeal for the glory of God and the salvation of our neighbour, if we have brought our private affections under control, and finally if we pray as suppliants to God that he either shut or open our mouths, then certainly it will come about that we shall not be ignorant of when to be silent and when to speak.

units.la: K. j. lendum, quo loquendum, non ignoremus.
units.tr: When to be silent and when to speak we may not be ignorant.

units.la: Sed vt ad generalem illam de Christi silen- tio doctrinam aliquid addamus, obsecro, si quum Iesu Christo tam insignis illata iniuria tam multas apud Iudicem ius suum tutandi iustissimas causas ei praebuit, tamen consilium illud Patris & finem in quem in hunc mundū missus erat considerans, ne aperire quidem os voluit, vt quod de ipso praedictum erat ab Esaia cap.53.7. impleretur, quam tandem excusationem allaturi sunt, quos quū propria conscientia facinoris cuiuslibet reos faciat, aut admonitionibus proximorum redarguantur, aut eorum censura, quorum auctoritati subiecti sunt, admoneantur, respondendi tamen finem nullum faciunt, siue negantes quod verissimū esse non possunt inficiari, siue lapsus suos excusantes, vel longe minores facientes, exemplum in eo sequuti, primi parentis nostri Adami Genes. 3. 12. & Saulis.1.Sam.13.11.& 15.15? Ecquis vero, inquies, istud facit? Nempe vt plurimum qui maxime sunt in culpa, licet suam probitatem plenis buccis praedicent, quam vt tucantur mendacium secus opinantibus obiectant, ad duellum alij alios provocant, & quid non etiam peius designant? Quod si homines suo calculo improbant, quid iis futurum existimamus, quos Caini coram Domino sermonem non pudet imitari? Genes. 4.9. Horrenda sunt ista, fratres, & modis omnibus metuenda: quum contra peccatorum ingenua confessio coram Deo & fratribus tantopere nobis comcommendetur, & tot habeat consequendae misericordiae promissiones. Cauete igitur,fratres,cogitetis peccatis peccata deleri, non secus quàm sordes sordibus elui.Contrà verò si-quid aduersus Dominum deliquimus,vt multa solemus,pudore suffusi responsationis loco capita demittamus, & manum ori apponamus,Iob. 39. 37. Dauidem imitati peccata sincere confitentem 2.Sam. 12.13. & Psal. 32. 5.Siquid vero aduersus fratrem peccauimus, ne super peccatum Sol occidat, Ephes. 4. 26. Siquid contrà peccatum est aduersum nos ipsos, fratres nostros à quibus etiam laesi sumus Domino lucremur ne in perditionem & exitium ruant. Apage igitur tot apud Praetorem lites, quarum vix centesima quaeque, licet iusta, vel micam in se charitatis continet. Quod si Deo videtur priuatas nostras offensas retegere,gloriam illi debitam absque vlla responsatione tribuamus, quum hanc ipse nobis vnicam viā peccata nostra coram Deo & hominibus tegendi in sempiternum commonstrarit.Psal.5r. Matth.3.6.Act.19.18.
units.tr: But to add something to that general doctrine about Christ's silence, I ask: when such a remarkable wrong was done to Jesus Christ, and so many most just grounds were given him to defend his right before the judge, yet, mindful of the Father's counsel and of the end for which he had been sent into this world, he did not wish even to open his mouth, so that what had been foretold of him by Isaiah (Isa. 53.7) might be fulfilled, what excuse will they bring forward, those who, though their own conscience makes them guilty of some crime, are either rebuked by the admonitions of their neighbours or warned by the censure of those to whose authority they are subject, yet make no end of answering? Some deny what cannot be denied because it is most true; others excuse their lapses or make them much smaller, following in this the example of our first parent Adam (Gen. 3.12) and of Saul (1 Sam. 13.11; 15.15). Who, you will say, does this? Indeed, for the most part, those who are most in fault, though they proclaim their own uprightness with full cheeks, object to others who think otherwise, in order to cover their lie, and challenge one another to duels, and what do they not even devise that is worse? But if men condemn such conduct by their own reckoning, what do we suppose will become of those who are not ashamed to imitate the words of Cain before the Lord (Gen. 4.9)? These things are dreadful, brethren, and to be feared in every way, whereas a frank confession of sins before God and the brethren is so strongly commended to us, and carries with it so many promises of obtaining mercy. Take care, therefore, brethren, to think that sins are blotted out by sins no less than filth is washed away by filth. On the contrary, if we have sinned against the Lord, as we often do, let us, overcome with shame, bow our heads instead of answering, and lay a hand upon our mouth (Job 39.37), imitating David, who sincerely confessed his sins (2 Sam. 12.13; Ps. 32.5). If we have sinned against a brother, let not the sun go down upon our anger (Eph. 4.26). If we have sinned against ourselves, and even against our brethren by whom we too have been wronged, let us gain them for the Lord, lest they fall into perdition and ruin. Away, then, with so many lawsuits before the praetor, of which scarcely one in a hundred, even if just, contains a grain of charity. But if it seems good to God to uncover our private offences, let us give him the glory due to him without any answer, since he himself has shown us in perpetuity the one way of covering our sins before God and men (Ps. 51; Matt. 3.6; Acts 19.18).

units.la: Praeterea quum maxime tunc nobis loquendi datam occasionem persuadeamus, quum facto aliquo dictóve laesi sumus, vnde tot rixas ac dissensiones suboriri conspicimus,hic abi-pso Dei Filio,quid hac in re facto sit opus discamus. Ecquis enim eo deuenit amentiae, vt quantumuis multis dotibus excellat, sese Dei Filio faciat aequalem?Ecquam vero tantam ab hominibus pati possumus iniuriam,quę Chri-
units.tr: Moreover, we should be persuaded that we are then especially given an occasion for speaking when we have been wronged by some deed or word, and we see from this that many quarrels and dissensions arise. Here let us learn from the Son of God himself what must be done in this matter. For who has come to such madness that, however much he excels in many gifts, he makes himself equal to the Son of God? And what wrong can we suffer from men that could answer to the wrongs and insults offered to Christ, or even come close to them at the least? He kept silent, and shall we speak? Shall we quarrel? Shall we strike? And shall we think ourselves nicely covered if we plead that we were not the authors of the quarrels?

units.la: K. ij. sto illatæ iniuriæ & contumeliis respondeat, aut ad eas vel minimum accedat?Siluit tamen, nos vero loquemur? rixabimur? cædemus? & pulchrè nos tectos existimabimus si rixarum auctores nonfuisse nos causabimur? At Christus, inquiet, aliquis, non semper in hac causa siluit, quod iam in hac ipsa vidimus historia.Ioh.18.23. nec Paulus in suo negotio prorusus obmutuit. Act.23.3. Nec vero hoc ago vt nemo lacessitus iniuriam à se repellat,sed Christianè id faciat effiagito, quum ira malù malo compensandum dictet, Christiana verò doctrina malum bono compensare nos iubeat, Rom.15.19. illius exemplum imitatos qui Solem suum super bonos & malos lucere facit. Matth. 5. 45. qui etiam patrem pro se crucifigentibus interpellauit. Luc.23.34. vnde illis tandem parta salus est. Act.2.17. quemadmodum etiam eiusmodi precibus Stephani, pro se lapidantibus precantis, deberi Paulum non malè quidam ex veteribus obseruauit,Act.7. 60. Obsecro verò si qua iniuria lacessiti nostra patientia proximum aberrantem in viam salutis reducimus, & se præcipitem in Leonis gulam ferentem faucibus illius eripimus,sicut à Christo docemur,Matth.5.22.annon magis abundè nobis satisfactum esse oportuit, quàm si millies iniuriam nostram cum nostra & illius perditione vlti essemus? Nec repugno quin apud Iudicem suum ius quilibet repetat, & iure se tucatur,Perinde enim est ac si ad Deum ipsum confugeret, modò tamè primùm id res postulet, let, prius omnibus tentatis viis lenioribus, quū maioris sit Magistratuum authoritas facienda quàm vt subinde talibus negotiis implicetur: deinde abest omnis vindictæ cupiditas. Nam qui secus faxit, is sane iustitiæ solium misere fœdauerit, Iudicibus ipsis ad suam explendam libidinem abusus: qua in re quæso, quàm graviter quotidie labimur: qui tamē haberi Christiani volumus? Ecquid verò amplius? Discimus insuper exemplo Domini nostri Iesu Christi, sæpissimè etiam quum maximis afficimur iniuriis, longè melius agi nobiscum si prorsus conticuerimus, quàm casdem si repellere conati fuerimus.
units.tr: But, someone will say, Christ did not always keep silent in this matter, as we have already seen in this very history (John 18.23), nor did Paul altogether hold his peace in his own case (Acts 23.3). Nor am I arguing that no one who is provoked should repel the wrong done to him, but that he should do so in a Christian way, which I urge. For anger bids us repay evil with evil, whereas Christian teaching bids us repay evil with good (Rom. 12.19 [printed as 15.19]), imitating the example of him who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil (Matt. 5.45), who also prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23.34), whence salvation was at last procured for them (Acts 2.17). Likewise, some of the ancients rightly observed that Paul owed his conversion to the prayers of Stephen, who prayed for those stoning him (Acts 7.60). But I ask: if, when we are provoked by a wrong, we through our patience lead back a neighbour who has strayed from the way of salvation, and snatch him from the jaws of the lion, as we are taught by Christ (Matt. 5.22), ought we not to think ourselves far more fully satisfied than if we had avenged our wrong a thousand times, to the ruin of both ourselves and him? Nor do I object that anyone should seek his right before his judge and defend himself by law, for this is the same as if he fled to God himself, provided, however, that the matter first requires it, and that all gentler ways have been tried beforehand, since the authority of magistrates ought to be preserved, and they should not be constantly entangled in such affairs. Then too, all desire for revenge must be absent. For whoever acts otherwise surely befouls the throne of justice miserably, abusing the judges to satisfy his own lust. In this matter, I ask, how gravely do we daily fall, we who nonetheless wish to be counted Christians? And what more? We learn besides, from the example of our Lord Jesus Christ, that even when we are most heavily wronged, it is far better for us to keep silent altogether than to try to repel the same wrongs.

units.la: Sed omisisis cæteris, en quam nobis eximiam suo filetio Christus Dominus consolationem adferat. Cur enim potissimum sibi silentiū indixit? Nempe quòd quum fideiussorem & vadem se noltrum constituerit, eorum omnium quæ sunt illi impositta crimina, & quorum eramus conuicti, culpam in se admisit pro nobis satisfacturus. Felix itaque, felix, inquam, & pretiosum silentium, quo nobis os aperitur, non solum vt Deum alloquamur, sed vt magna cum fiducia clamemus, Abba, Pater, Rom. 8. 18. & Gal. 4. 6. tantùm abest vt illo nos oporteat offendi.
units.tr: But, setting aside the rest, see what a remarkable consolation the Lord Christ brings us by his silence. Why did he impose silence on himself especially? Clearly because, having made himself our surety and bondsman, he took upon himself the guilt of all the crimes laid upon him, and of those for which we had been convicted, to make satisfaction for us. Happy, then, happy I say, and precious is that silence, by which our mouths are opened not only to address God, but to cry out with great confidence, "Abba, Father" (Rom. 8.15; Gal. 4.6). So far is it from being fitting for us to be offended by it.

units.la: Deinceps narrat historia Pilatum in innocentia Iesu Christi tuenda perseuerantem palam professum, se nullum in eo crimen reperire, cuius conuictus teneri possit: parte verò ex alia Iudæos in malitia non modò perrexisse fuisse. fc,sed magis ac magis obduruisse,nulla tamen testium productorum facta mentione, aut in tali casu requisitæ disquisitionis, Qua in re primùm istud obseruandum occurrit, sic admirandam illam Dei prouidentiam, ad tempus filium suum hostium suorum libidini in electorum salutem permisisse,vt tamen voluerit istud omnibus innotescere tum ex Iudicis ipsius ore sæpe repetito & extorto testimonio, tu ex aduersariorum plus quam effræni impudentia,Dominum nostrū Iesum Christum iustum & insontem pro iniustis & fontibus pati, vt tanto maius sit Diuinę bonitatis testimonium quanto maius est crucis scandalum.Rom. 5. 8. & pro scandalo magis ac magis nos console-tur, & in salutis spe confirmet: quum tamen accidisse videamus, vt non pauci res istas tam nouas,tam inauditas,tam humano iudicio peregrinas considerantes,inde Christianæ Religionis habendæ ludibrio ceperint occasione, & tanquam absurdæ immo ridiculæ abiicien-dæ: alij verò per speciem tantum, non autem reipsa res istas gestas fuisse sint arbitrati. Nos verò ridiculis illis omissis hic potiùs agnoscamus, hinc quidem terribilem aduersus pecca-tum Dei furorem, quod non nili tam atrociбus & horrendis suppliciis à nostro sponsore & fideiussore potuerint expiari, ac proinde quid iis futurum sit in quorum caput tantus furor est deriuandus seriò pensitemus:inde verò tantæ istius abyssum clementiæ & misericordiæ Diuinæ Patris quidem filio proprio non parcentis ad nos miseros peccatores sibi reconciliandos, filij vero ad mortem vsque, mortem, inquam crucis vltro sese demittentis, ad eos ex suis inimicis quos illi Pater dedit redimendos, suspiciamur.
units.tr: Next the history relates that Pilate, persevering in defending the innocence of Jesus Christ, openly declared that he found no crime in him for which he could be held guilty. On the other side, the Jews not only persisted in their malice but grew more and more hardened, though no witnesses were produced and no inquiry of the kind required in such a case was made. In this matter, first, this must be noted: God's wonderful providence allowed his Son, for a time, to the lust of his enemies for the salvation of the elect. Yet he willed this to become known to all, both from the judge's own mouth, which repeatedly extracted the testimony, and from the more than unbridled impudence of the adversaries, that our Lord Jesus Christ, just and innocent, suffers for the unjust and the guilty, so that the testimony of divine goodness is all the greater as the scandal of the cross is greater (Rom. 5. 8). We are consoled more and more by the scandal and confirmed in the hope of salvation. Yet we see that it has happened that not a few, considering these things so new, so unheard of, and so foreign to human judgment, have taken from them an occasion to mock the Christian religion and cast it aside as absurd, even ridiculous. Others thought that these things were done only in appearance and not in fact. But, setting aside those ridiculous notions, let us here rather acknowledge, on the one hand, God's terrible wrath against sin, which could not be expiated except by such atrocious and horrible sufferings from our surety and guarantor, and so seriously consider what will become of those upon whom so great a wrath is to be drawn. On the other hand, let us gaze upon the abyss of this great clemency and mercy of the divine Father, who did not spare his own Son to reconcile us miserable sinners to himself, and of the Son, who of his own accord submitted even to death, death, I say, of the cross, to redeem those from among his enemies whom the Father gave him.

units.la: Praeterea quanta sit natiua nostra corruptio ex hoc misero populo, & potissimum ex eius ducibus & Gubernatoribus discamus agnoscere, & quidem in iis maxime quos maioribus donis Dominus cumulauit, si semel Satanae, & propriis concupiscentiis ipsos permittit, vt diligenter exempla istiusmodi sicuti par est meditantes assiduis precibus Deum intercpellemus, optimum patrem nostrum, ne nos in tentationem inducat, & nos nobis ipsis permittat, quum nullus sit nobis capitalior hostis, quam nos ipsi, nostrae libidini laxas habenas remittentes: Denique quum tanta sit filiorum huius seculi in malo pertinacia, quantam futuram exprobrationem putamus a Domino si minus attente ista considerantes tam segnes & negligentes ad bonum esse perrexerimus?
units.tr: Besides, let us learn to recognize how great our natural corruption is, from this wretched people and especially from its leaders and governors, and indeed most of all in those whom the Lord has heaped with the greatest gifts, if once he permits them to Satan and to their own lusts. So, diligently meditating on examples of this kind, as is fitting, let us with constant prayers entreat God, our best Father, not to lead us into temptation and not to leave us to ourselves, since no enemy is more deadly to us than we ourselves, loosening the reins for our own lust. Finally, since there is such obstinacy in the sons of this age in evil, what reproach do we think we will receive from the Lord if, considering these things less attentively, we proceed to be so sluggish and negligent in good?

units.la: Pilatus contra, non sine magna huius tam miserandi populi ignominia, in ea quam a natura didicerat aequitate, & recti amore, perseuerat, sed tamen, vt sequens historia docebit, non ea qua par erat alacritate & constantia. Itaque perseuerantia illa Pilati longo distat interuallo ab ea quae a Dei gratia & fauore speciali manat. Quoniam vero praesertim istis temporibus est nobis haec doctrina perutilis, pluribus eam hoc loco persequi minime graua-bor. Aio igitur coronam gloriæ nobis reposi-tam, minimè se intra carceres continentibus, aut stadij mediam tantùm partem decurrenti-bus, sed solis metam contingentibus deberi, ac proinde hoc constantiæ & perseuerantiæ esse inter omnes Christianas virtutes proprium & peculiare, vt præmium apprehendat. Verùm quo magis excellit & est necessaria hæc virtus, eo sunt nobis hic Satanæ fraudes diligentius vitandæ, imò nos, nobis ipsis, quatenus homines sumus carnei, suspectos esse oportet, ne virtutem illam ambientes in contrarium vitium incidamus, quod sæpe tamen alienam formam induit, tanta quidem specie vt nisi caute prospiciatur incautos fallat, pertinacia nimirum, constantiæ & perseuerantiæ nomen assumat, non sine magno detrimento, quòd quemadmodum facit perseuerantia vt optatum finem assequamur, sic contrà pertinacia nos auocatos à recta via, non tantùm sperata felicitate priuat, sed inanes & irritos ad eam assequendam labores reddat, quod experientia satis superque demonstrat, & Paulus in Galatarum persona, Gal.5.7. monet. Extant in sacris historiis infinita pene, tum huius virtutis, tum contrarij vitij exempla, in quibus nobis ij proponuntur, tum qui ab hac virtute, alij citius alij tardius defecerunt, quíque quum bene cœpissent, pessimè tandem perierunt: tum qui feliciter cœptum curriculum decurrerunt, & speratam felicitatem assecuti sunt,
units.tr: Pilate, on the contrary, not without great shame to this so pitiable people, perseveres in that fairness and love of right which he had learned from nature. Yet, as the following history will teach, not with the readiness and constancy that was fitting. Therefore that perseverance of Pilate is far removed from that which flows from God's grace and special favour. Since this doctrine is especially useful to us in these times, I will not hesitate to pursue it at some length here. I say, then, that the crown of glory laid up for us is owed not to those who remain within the prison walls, nor to those who run only the middle part of the course, but to those who reach the goal of the race. Therefore this is the proper and peculiar mark of constancy and perseverance among all Christian virtues: that one lays hold of the prize. But the more this virtue excels and is necessary, the more diligently must we avoid here the frauds of Satan. Indeed we ought to be suspicious of ourselves, insofar as we are fleshly men, lest, while aiming at that virtue, we fall into the contrary vice. This vice often takes on another's form, in such a guise that, unless one takes care, it deceives the unwary: obstinacy, namely, assumes the name of constancy and perseverance, to great harm. For just as perseverance makes us attain the desired end, so obstinacy, once it has drawn us away from the right way, not only deprives us of the hoped-for happiness but renders our labours to attain it empty and vain. Experience demonstrates this sufficiently and more than sufficiently, and Paul warns of it in the person of the Galatians (Gal. 5. 7). There exist in the sacred histories almost countless examples both of this virtue and of the contrary vice. Some are set before us who fell away from this virtue, some sooner, some later, and who, when they had begun well, at last perished miserably. Others ran the course they had begun happily and attained the hoped-for happiness,

units.la: hic ficalios Dei iuuante gratia, vt inoffenso pede superatis & exantlatis quibusuis difficultatibus, in quorum numero sunt præcipui Prophetæ & Apostoli, perrexerint: alios verò semel à recta via deuios eadem Dei gratia revocarit in viam, & in eadem stabilierit.
units.tr: some of whom, by God's helping grace, proceeded with unstumbling foot, having overcome and endured every difficulty (among them are the chief prophets and apostles). Others, whom the same grace of God had once drawn aside from the right way, it recalled into the way and established in it.

units.la: Nec verò mirari quenquam oportet, quòd etiam fortium virorum nonnunquam labascit, & veluti frangitur constantia. Nam præterquàm quòd infirmitas quam à natura circumferimus, plena est infinitis passionibus quibus in varias partes rapimur, nihil Satan odit magis quàm quum vocationem quisque priuatam vel publicam sequitur: quod oro vos fratres, vt memoriæ penitius infigatis. Scit enim ille noster hostis, ita Deum tanquam ad truti-nam hominum vocationes appendisse, vt manentibus singulis intra suæ vocationis terminos, nulla sit vnquam confusio mundum turbatura. Iterum igitur dico, fratres, non sine magna causa moneri singulos ab Apostolo tam sedulò, vt in qua quisque vocatione fuit vocatus maneat. 1.Cor. 7. 20. quum nulla re magis quàm istiusmodi constantia Satan offendatur, quam modis omnibus labefactare conatur.
units.tr: Nor ought anyone to wonder that even the constancy of brave men sometimes wavers and, as it were, is broken. For besides the fact that the weakness we carry about from nature is full of endless passions by which we are dragged in various directions, Satan hates nothing more than when anyone follows his private or public calling. This I beg you, brothers, to fix more deeply in your memory. For that enemy of ours knows that God has so weighed the callings of men in a balance that, while each remains within the bounds of his own calling, there will never be any confusion to disturb the world. I say again, then, brothers, that it is not without great cause that the Apostle admonishes each so earnestly that each should remain in the calling in which he was called (1 Cor. 7. 20), since Satan is offended by nothing so much as by such constancy, and he tries in every way to weaken it.

units.la: Exemplo sit Abrahami sancta familia. Sara non desperat quidem de futura Abrahamo prole, prout erat ipsis ore ipso Domini promissa, sed morae impatiens, & sterilitatis suae memor, diffidere incipit, & ab hac diffidentia consilium petens, Dei promissionem secus decepit. quàm deberet interpretata, marito Agarem ancillam substituit, quod & si Deo consilium initio,acceptum esse videtur nato Ismaele, tamen non diu mansit inulta diffidentia, ancillæ filio mox,etiam iubente Deo, foras eiecto,Sara & eius marito quantum in ipsis erat salutare fœdus quod Dominus cum illa familia percusserat,penitus irritum facientibus.
units.tr: Let the holy family of Abraham be an example. Sarah does not indeed despair of the future offspring of Abraham, as had been promised to them by the very mouth of the Lord. But, impatient of delay and mindful of her own barrenness, she begins to distrust. Seeking counsel from this distrust, she interpreted God's promise otherwise than she ought, and gave her husband the maidservant Hagar in her place. Although this seemed at first to be pleasing to God when Ishmael was born, the distrust did not remain unpunished for long. When the maidservant's son was soon cast out, even by God's command, Sarah and her husband, as far as lay in them, rendered utterly void the saving covenant which the Lord had struck with that family.

units.la: Israelitæ Dei populus quum per exploratores cognouissent quantæ vires essent Canaanæorum,de repetenda Ægypto itinere remenso cogitant, hoc ipsum etiam facere parati quum in monte Moses longiorem moram trahere videretur. Annon ipse Moses tot laboribus obrutus animum penè desponder? Num. 11.15. Quid verò factum iis omnibus sine Dei speciali gratia foret? Saulem prudentiæ suæ confisum, Samuele,vt erat iustus, intra septimum diem non expectato, nonne cum regno etiam perdidit impatientia? 1.Sam. 11. Salomon quum bene coepisset, pessimè tandem desiit, vt & illum sequutus Aza. 2.Chro.16.12. Ioas denique etiam peius.2.Chro.24.17. Contrà verò Dauid Psalm. 40. 1. Exspectando, inquit,exspectaui Iehouam:& inclinauit scse ad me, & audiuit clamorem meum:quem tamen ambitio sic adorta est, vt dinumerato populo contra Dei mandatum,sine ingenti Dei misericordia,præcipitem eum datura fuerit.2.Sam. 24.1.& 10.
units.tr: The Israelites, God's people, when they learned through spies how great the strength of the Canaanites was, thought of retracing their journey back to Egypt, and were ready to do this very thing when Moses seemed to be delaying longer on the mountain. Was not Moses himself, overwhelmed by so many labours, almost despairing in spirit? (Num. 11. 15). But what would have become of all of them without God's special grace? Saul, trusting in his own prudence, did not wait for Samuel, who was just, beyond the seventh day. Did impatience not destroy him, together with his kingdom? (1 Sam. 13). Solomon, when he had begun well, at last ended very badly, and Asa followed him (2 Chron. 16. 12). Joash, finally, did worse still (2 Chron. 24. 17). On the contrary, David: "I waited patiently," he says, "for Jehovah, and he inclined himself to me and heard my cry" (Ps. 40. 1). Yet ambition rose up in him so strongly that, by numbering the people against God's command, it would have dashed him headlong without the great mercy of God (2 Sam. 24. 1, 10).

units.la: Scriptura denique similibus exemplis est referta. Vt autem huic tanto malo remedium adhibeat adferatur, hoc primum agedum,vt de sua cui- que vocatione, siue publica, siue priuata, siue temporaria,siue spirituali certò constet.Dein- de prius quàm quicquam agas suscipiasve his tribus in primis rectam conscientiam verbo Dei illustratam regi oportet: Primum est, vt quod in deliberationem cadit iustum sit:alte-rum,vt iustis mediis illud persequaris:tertium denique ne vocationis limites transilias, quibus vt firmo fundamento substratis,tunc prudentiæ naturali demum locus esto, prouidendis iis quæ requirentur,quū non semper quicquid licet expediat. Pro licet media quibus propositum persequamur,siue sub initium,siue medio iam cursu, defuerint, cauendum tamen est summopere ne tantillum à vocatione deflectamus, aut quidquam aduersus Deum proximúmve peccemus, aut mala consilia incamus, denique nequa nos difficultas aut ἀ-δυναμία dimoueat ab officio, sed in vnicam Dei prouidentiam incumbendum est, cui nec voluntas deest,nec potestas, quíque sequentibus vocationem præsens ipse dux adest, ipsorum consilia fortunaturus, teste passim tota Scriptura,sed in primis Iudicum historia.
units.tr: Scripture is finally full of similar examples. But so that a remedy may be applied to this great evil, let this first be done: that one be certain of one's own calling, whether public or private, temporary or spiritual. Then, before you do or undertake anything, your conscience must be ruled, above all in these three respects, and enlightened by the word of God: first, that what falls into deliberation be just; second, that you pursue it by just means; third, that you do not overstep the limits of your calling. With these laid as a firm foundation, let natural prudence then have its place, in providing for those things which will be required, since whatever is permitted is not always expedient. As for the means by which we pursue our purpose, whether they are lacking at the beginning or in the middle of the course, we must nevertheless take great care that we do not deviate the least bit from our calling, sin in any way against God or our neighbour, or form evil counsels. Finally, lest difficulty or inability [ἀδυναμία] move us from our duty, we must lean upon God's providence alone, to which neither will nor power is lacking, and who is himself present as a guide to those who follow their calling, to make their counsels fortunate. The whole of Scripture attests this throughout, but especially the history of the Judges.

units.la: Vt verò tam necessariam hanc doctrinam ad vsum nostrum referamus, age tempus illud in quod incidimus,exempli gratia,diligentius consideremus, quum potissimû iam decimum sextum mensem crudelissimum bellum ab im- manissimo & potentissimo holte perpetia- mur, necdum eius finiendi nobis vlla spes affulgeat, vnde minimè miror accidere vt non pauci, iíque non omnium ineptissimi, multa voluant animo suo peregrina consilia. Verùm ne rebus iis territi quæ in oculos ingruentia, tam perniciosa & exitiosa consilia suggereret quàm bona & salutaria putaremus, semel est obstinandus animus, firmisque & salutaribus fundamentis fulcienda conscientia, nimirum iisquæ superius attigimus. Dixi igitur, & iterum dico, cum qui bene & iuste rem aliquam aggressus est ex suæ vocationis officio, quo erga Deum & proximos tenetur, si recesserit ab instituto per ignauiam & animi deiectionem non potest nō vehementer peccare, yno hoc tamen excepto, nisi nimirum certis & indubitatis signis Deus testatus sibi quod hactenus factum est satisfecisse, vlterius cum pergere prohibeat: quod age ex Dei verbo in hoc ipso nostro negotio, examinemus. Vix verò mihi persuaserim quenquam ignorare quàm legitimis tabulis & iustis monumentis freti, aduersus iniquissimas postulationes hostis, auitas inimicitias persequentis decertemus. De belli illius autem iustitia quis dubitet, nisi qui approbator & fautor esse velit flagitiosæ illius factionis, & detestandæ conspirationis, excitatæ, vt iam tandem oculis omnium patet, non proprie nec solùm vt à subditis aduersus suum Regem, aut à vicino peregrino Principe aduersus suum nostrumque vicinum, sed ad hoc vt tum veram Religionem, tum singulos Principes illam amplexos, populos & nationes v-na inna internecione coniurati deleant? Excipiet aliquis, non tamen necesse esse quicquid licet, nec etiam expedire.
units.tr: But so that we may apply this necessary doctrine to our own use, let us look more carefully at the time we have fallen into, for example. For now more than sixteen months we have been suffering a most cruel war from a most huge and powerful enemy, and no hope of ending it yet shines upon us. So I am not surprised that not a few people, and not the least foolish among them, turn over in their minds many strange plans. But so that we are not frightened by those things which press upon our eyes and suggest plans that seem good and wholesome but are in fact most destructive and deadly, our minds must once and for all be made firm, and our consciences propped up on sound and wholesome foundations, namely those which I have touched on above. I have said, and I say again, that whoever has undertaken some matter well and justly, in keeping with the duty of his calling, by which he is bound towards God and his neighbours, cannot but sin grievously if through laziness and discouragement he withdraws from what he has begun. There is only one exception to this: when God clearly and unmistakably signals that what has been done so far is enough, and forbids him to proceed further. Let us now examine this from God's Word, in regard to this very matter of ours. I can hardly persuade myself that anyone is unaware on what legitimate records and just documents we rely as we contend against the most unjust demands of an enemy who pursues ancient enmities. Yet who could doubt the justice of that war, unless he wished to be an approver and supporter of that scandalous faction and detestable conspiracy, which has now at last become plain to everyone's eyes? It was raised not properly, nor only, by subjects against their king, or by a foreign prince neighbouring another, but so that, with a single slaughter, they might destroy both the true religion and the individual princes who have embraced it, along with their peoples and nations, in a conspiracy. Someone will object: "Yet it is not necessary that whatever is lawful is also expedient."

units.la: Persuaderi vero mihi facile patior neminem fore qui, modo sana mente & non perterrita, ea quæ nostris muris præparata iam ante multos annos imminebant attentius consideret, quæque vt humanitus loquamur à nostris cæruicibus repellere non erat in nostra potestate, nisi Deus misericors aliunde vocatis auxiliis, totum illum apparatum magna vi subuertisset, non iudicet minimè temerè & præcipiti, sed maturo & necessario consilio susceptam à nobis iustam hac aduersus communé hostem esse defensionem. Defensionē, inquam. Nam, vt omittam, tot, tam diu, tamque patienter iam à multis annis toleratas iniurias, tot proditiones, mira quadam & protus diuina ratione patefactas & fractas, quo tandem quasi nomine, admotum nostris mœnibus ad secundum lapidem exercitum, aggressionem illam vi aperta factam ad Lacum: Valdesium regionem tentatam, & pene, nisi Deus opportune fraudes detectas comprensisset, occupatam vocabimus, nisi manifestissima & perditissimam inuasionem dixerimus? Si vero quæritur quid expediat, obsecro, quæ maior, quæ speciosior occasio se nobis offerre poterat ea quam ipse Dominus sua manu nobis offerebat? Quæ si non penitus speratum fructum protulit, non ideo tamen vana aut inanis illa fuisse spes dicenda est, aut malo nixa fundamento. At si nó quidquid fieri potuit factum est, tamen quod factum est cum eo statu collatu in quem praecipites incidebamus tantum est, ut sane magnam occasionem nobis Deo summas agendi gratias oblatam esse vel inuitos fateri necesse sit. Quod si est huiusmodi fundamentum, quo pudore, quave conscientia nunc ab illo recedere cogitauerimus? Nempe, inquiet aliquis, quod Deus sublata nobis pergendi in incepto facultate non indubie testetur nolle se ut vltra progrediamur: quod in quaestionem quum veniat, de eo nobis est differendum & certum aliquid statuendum. Esto igitur, (quod tamen Dei beneficio longe secus est) omnia nos humana deficiant auxilia, an cessandum concludemus, nisi forte fidis Dei seruis quotquot omnibus humanis auxiliis, imo etiam omni spe subsidij destituti fortiter tamen & feliciter in coepto perseuerarunt nostro calculo condemnatis. Populum Israeliticum Aegypto egressum testem aduoco, cuius nobis ante oculos exemplum toties Dauid caeterique Prophetae passim in Psalmis proponunt. Ezechiam voco a Sennacheribo polt auxiliarium ab Aegypto copiarum internecionem obsessum: Iosaphatum, quem tot coeuntes nationes inopinantem aggressae fuerant: Gedeonem, cum trecentis illis suis, totidem ampullis armatis militibus: Saulem ipsum quantumuis licet impium cum sexcentis illis inermibus. Age vero nos in eiusmodi angustias coarctatos, cur non eadem spes non sustinebit, quum caufa nostræ defensionis àduersus hostem illis nō meliorem fit nobis cum illis communis?Sanè, vt ex hominum ipsorum sensu loquar, ratio ipsa communis dictat, vitam pro patria & iusta libertate pulchrum esse profundere. Sed ne longius abeam, quoties, vos Geneuenfes appello, patres vestri aduersus hos ipsos hostes, in extremas angustias redacti, constantissimè, pro tuenda, quam vobis reliquerunt libertate, dimicarunt? Eandem verò à patribus acceptam spero & confidere audeo, vos iuuante Domino, iustiore adhuc quàm patres vestros causa nixos, ad extremum conseruaturos. Nam vt omittam iugum miserrimæ seruitutis quod nostris ceruicibus imponere moliuntur, nunc de Dei gloria & veritate, de nostris animabus, de conscientiis, de salute æterna bello decernitur, quocunque colore suas hostes nostri fraudes fucare nitantur. Egregias verò illas vobis ab hostibus factas pollicitationes accipietis, quorum vobis eit tot experimentis vtrōque summo periculo cognita perfidia? Nos verò peregrini quos ex variis regionibus eiectos tempestate locus hic, non tanquam Ægyptus inhospita, sed cum omni lenitate & mansuetudine suscepit, patiemur-ne quenquam ex nostro numero tam perfidè támque ingrate tectum quo profugus est receptus deferere, ac non potius reipfa & ad extremum etiam vitæ habitum testabimur, solo nos gloriæ Dei zelo, & studio verbi illius depascendi, puréque colen di ductos, abiectis mundi commodis omnibus tam pretiosam margaritam quæ nos hic tanto fulgore irradiat, quæsiuisse? Abest credam hoc posse contingere: nec etiam ob hanc propriè causam suam ista loquutus, verùm ad scrupulum iis omnem exi-mendum hoc sermone qui fortassis hærent dubij, & ad alios, si qui forte sunt perterriti, confirmandos.
units.tr: Indeed, I readily allow that no one will be found who, if he is of sound mind and not terrified, and considers attentively what was prepared long ago and hanging over our walls, and what, humanly speaking, was not in our power to repel from our necks, unless merciful God, by auxiliaries summoned from elsewhere, had overthrown that whole apparatus with great force, will judge that the defence undertaken by us against our common enemy was unjust, or taken up rashly and hastily, rather than by a mature and necessary decision. A defence, I say. For, to pass over the injuries endured for so many years, so long and so patiently, and the many betrayals, brought to light and broken by a wonderful and almost divine providence, what name shall we finally give to that army brought up to within a second milestone of our walls, to that open assault made at the Lake, to the attempt on the Vaud region, and to the near occupation of it, had not God in time caught the frauds as they were revealed? Shall we call it anything other than a most manifest and most ruinous invasion? And if you ask what was expedient, I beg you, what greater and more promising opportunity could present itself to us than the one the Lord himself offered with his own hand? If this has not brought the fruit we fully hoped for, that hope cannot for that reason be called vain or empty, or resting on a bad foundation. But even if not everything that could be done has been done, what has been done, compared with the state into which we were headlong falling, is so great that even against our will we must admit that God has offered us a great opportunity, for which we owe him the highest thanks. If this is the kind of foundation we have, with what shame, or with what conscience, could we now think of withdrawing from it? "Surely," someone will say, "because God, by taking away from us the power of going on with what we have begun, does not clearly show that he is unwilling for us to advance further." This question, when it comes up, we must postpone, and settle with something certain. Grant, then (though by God's goodness it is far otherwise), that all human aids fail us. Shall we conclude that we must stop, unless perhaps, by our reckoning, we condemn all the faithful servants of God who, destitute of all human aid, and even of all hope of help, nevertheless persevered bravely and successfully in what they had begun? I call as witness the people of Israel, having come out of Egypt, whose example David and the other prophets set before our eyes so often throughout the Psalms. I call Hezekiah, besieged by Sennacherib after the destruction of the Egyptian auxiliary forces. I call Jehoshaphat, whom so many nations gathering together attacked while he was unaware. I call Gideon with his three hundred men, and as many pitchers and armed soldiers. I call Saul himself, however impious, with his six hundred unarmed men. Now, when we are pressed into such straits, why should the same hope not sustain us, since the cause of our defence against the enemy is no worse for us than it was for them? Indeed, to speak in terms of human feeling, common reason itself dictates that it is a noble thing to pour out one's life for one's country and for just liberty. But not to wander too far: how often, I appeal to you, the people of Geneva, did your fathers, reduced to the utmost straits, fight most steadfastly against these very enemies, to defend the liberty they had left to you? I hope, and dare to trust, that you, with the Lord's help, will preserve it to the end, relying on a cause even more just than that of your fathers. For, to pass over the yoke of most miserable slavery which they are plotting to lay upon our necks, now the war is being decided concerning God's glory and truth, concerning our souls, our consciences, and our eternal salvation, whatever colour our enemies strive to disguise their frauds with. But will you receive those splendid promises made to you by the enemies, whose treachery you have so often learned by experience, to your great peril on either side? And we, foreigners whom the storm has driven out of various regions, whom this place has received, not as an inhospitable Egypt, but with all gentleness and kindness, shall we allow anyone from our number to desert so faithlessly and ungratefully the roof under which he took refuge as a fugitive? Shall we not rather show, by deeds and even at the last hour of life, that we sought, moved by zeal for the glory of God alone and by the desire to feed on that Word and to worship in purity, and having cast aside all the advantages of the world, that precious pearl which shines upon us here with such brilliance? I trust that this cannot happen. Nor have I spoken these things for this reason alone, but to remove every scruple from those who perhaps hesitate in doubt, and to strengthen others, if there are any who are frightened.

units.la: Nec enim, inquit Apostolus, fraudes inimici nostri nescimus, quantæque sit infirmitas nostræ carnis, etiam in viris sanctissimis, ut est à nobis paulò ante pluribus explicatum. Age verò, num tantæ sint difficultates atque finguntur, discutiamus. Cibaria defecisse nemo sine ingenti mendacio dixerit: qua in re nisi Dei magnam & extraordinariam liberalitatem agnoscamus, toties iam ab hinc aliquot annis expertam, ruinam nobis non modò bello, sed etiam fame iam iam prope proculque minantibus, annon ingratus ille animus merito quod metuimus, & adhuc longè peiora nobis à Domino arcessiuerit? Ecquis vestrum est, obsecro, huc qui conuenistis, qui si bellum istud vel trimestre tantùm fore cogitasset, qualem illud mensem decimum septimum toleramus, fore in foro quidquam venale Geneuæ sibi persuaderi palius sit? Id tamen effecit contra omnium expectationem Deus, messe licet cum vindemia deperdita, imo & tota regione tot incendiis longè lateque vastata. Ecquid erit igitur quod nos ad diffidentiam nisi sola præteritorum obliuio sollicitet? Quid verò amplius? Annon miseri illi Parisienses cum cæteris aduersus sus suum Regem & seipsos coniurati, eò devenerunt insanię vt prius quàm à perdita conspiratione recedant, equorum asinorúmue suorum carnibus non abstineant, nósne vero tam abiecti esse animi, vt tā cito, nihil adhuc simile passi à tam iusta defensione, qua nos no strásque aras & focos aduersus infensissimum tutamur hostem, territi recedamus? Pecunia, belli neruus deficit, aut penitus defecit. Esto: num putatis meliore loco nostrum hostem esse? Agite igitur quicunq; casus ingruat, eo qui nobis hactenus necessaria prouidit minimè mortuo, nec vnquâ morituro speremus nihil vnquam nobis defuturum. Discedentibus vero mercede tantum seruientibus militibus, cuius rei nos iacturam passos esse nisi hominum instabilium, quibus minimè fidendum erat, dixerimus? Annó vel vnius ciuis fide erga Deum, zelo ipsius gloriæ, & charitate erga patriam armati mille militibus erit virtus præstantior? Ducum maxima pars vel morbo vel plagis afflicti iacent. Esto, Deus sanè suo tempore misertus eos quum erit è re nostra pristinæ restituet valetudini. Sed quoties experti sumus, non sine Ducum ipsorum maximo stupore, Dei exercituum robur, nec à prudentia, vel peritia Ducum, nec à militum fortitudine sic pendere, quin vel ipse solus quoties sic illi visum est opus suū perficiat? Quando vero dicas illi visum est? Nempe quum timentium ipsum & ipsi fidentium requirit necessitas. At, inquiunt, qui iuuandi nos & studio maiore
units.tr: For, says the Apostle, we are not ignorant of the devices of our enemy, nor of how great is the weakness of our flesh, even in the most holy men, as has been explained by us a little earlier at some length. Come now, let us examine whether the difficulties are as great as they are made out to be. No one could say without great lying that the food supplies have failed. In this matter, unless we acknowledge God's great and extraordinary generosity, which we have experienced so many times during these past years, when ruin threatened us not only from war but also from famine, now near and now farther off, would not that ungrateful mind have brought upon itself, and rightly so, what we fear, and far worse things from the Lord? Which of you, I ask, who have gathered here, if he had thought that this war would last even three months, would have believed it plausible that anything would be for sale in the market at Geneva, when we endured that seventeenth month as we have? Yet God, contrary to everyone's expectation, has brought it about, even though the harvest and the vintage were lost, and the whole region was laid waste far and wide by so many fires. What then will trouble us into distrust, if not the mere forgetting of past things? What more is there to say? Did not those wretched Parisians, conspiring with the rest against their king and against themselves, come to such madness that, before abandoning their lost conspiracy, they did not abstain from the flesh of their horses and asses? Shall we, then, be so base of spirit that, having suffered nothing like this yet, we are frightened away so quickly from a defence so just, by which we protect our walls, our altars and our hearths against a most hostile enemy? Money, the sinews of war, is failing, or has entirely failed. Granted. But do you think our enemy is in a better position? Come then, whatever misfortune befalls us, let us hope that he who has hitherto provided what we need, and who is by no means dead, and never will die, will never let us lack anything. As for the soldiers who serve only for pay, and who are leaving, what loss of this kind could we say we have suffered, except that of unstable men, in whom we should never have put our trust? Will the virtue of one citizen, armed with faith towards God, zeal for his glory, and love for his country, not be more excellent than a thousand soldiers? Most of the commanders lie stricken, some by sickness and some by wounds. Granted, God in his own time, having pity on them, will restore them to their former health when it is to our advantage. But how often have we found, to the great astonishment of the commanders themselves, that the strength of God's armies depends neither on the prudence or skill of the commanders, nor on the courage of the soldiers, and that he himself alone accomplishes his work whenever it seems good to him? And when, you may ask, does it seem good to him? Surely when the need of those who fear him and trust in him demands it. "But," they say, "he who is able to help us, and who is more eager to help, is hindered by his own business, and has more resources." I grant it. But unless we acknowledge that God, helping us with wonderful favour, advances these things, we are surely too blind or too ill-disposed. Yet grant that all those hopes are empty: with what plan, I ask, should we rather...

units.la: L. j. fertur,&copiis plus potest,ipse suis impeditur negotiis.Fateor. At ni agnoscamus Deum admirando fauore resipsius adiuuantem promouere,quod nobis bonam spem in posterum omni fugata diffidentia faciat,næ nimium cæci vel maligni sumus. Sed sint illæ spes omnes inanes:quo tandem consilio,quæso,potiùs nos eius libidini submittemus, vel si mauis in fidé & potestatem illius permittemus,quem nostrę Religionis iuratum hostem,& libertatis quam à patribus accepimus hostem capitalissimum nouimus,quàm egregiam & sinceram promissionem sequemur Christianissimi re & nomine Regis, longè etiam per Dei gratiam, pos-sum alscuerare, potentioris & melioribus nixum fundamentis statum possidentis, quum sua illi pax annuente Deo reddita fuerit & de nobis optime meriti quàm quidquid de Indis Orientalibus & Occidentalibus fingitur? Paucis diebus binas plagas accepimus, de quibus tamen non admodum triumphant hostes.Nec enim id eorum animus nec fortitudo fecit,sed nostra in consiliis capiendis temeritas,& in exequendis confusio malum nobis peperit: & vt ad ipsum fontem recurramus, peccata nostra tam insignia, tot menses iam aliis alia cumulata, Deum sic, lenissimè tamen, castigare voluisse fatendum est, summo nostro bono, si modò nobis pro ingenti sua clementia, Deus meliorem mentem concesserit. Decem illæ tribus aduersus Beniamitas iustissimum & necessarium bellum gerentes quadraginta mille homihomines duobus praeliis caesos desiderarunt, nec propterea tamen coepto destiterunt, sed quod iustissimo freti fundamento coeperant ad felicem exitum perduxerunt. An vero duarum velitationum, quarum infaustus, nostra culpa fuit exitus, maior erit vis in nobis terrendis, & ab officio ad sinistra consilia pertrahendis, quàm sex & amplius longè duriorum praeliorum aduersus maiores hostis nostri copias in nobis excitandis & animandis, Deo ipso tum duce tum comite? Sin vero Dominus ad nominis sui gloriam animas nostras in sacrificium poscit, quid oro vos felicius, quid optatius nobis contigerit quàm pro Dei gloria, & pro patriae libertate vitam profundendo, mortem cum vita aeterna commutare?
units.tr: ...I admit it. But unless we acknowledge that God, by his wonderful favour, helps and advances us, which would give us good hope for the future and drive out all distrust, we are far too blind or ill-willed. But let all those hopes be empty. Then by what plan, I ask you, would we rather submit ourselves to his lust, or, if you prefer, entrust ourselves to the good faith and power of him whom we know to be the sworn enemy of our religion and the most deadly enemy of the liberty we received from our fathers? What splendid and sincere promise would we follow from the most Christian King, in deed and in name, who (by God's grace I can confidently affirm) holds a state of greater power, resting on firmer foundations, once his peace has been restored with God's consent, and who has deserved better of us than anything that is invented about the East and West Indies? A few days ago we received two blows, over which the enemy does not greatly triumph. For that was not the work of their spirit or their courage, but our rashness in taking decisions and our confusion in carrying them out brought this evil upon us. And to return to the very source: we must confess that God wished to chastise our sins, so conspicuous and piled up month after month, in this way, though most gently, for our greatest good, if only God, in his great mercy, grants us a better mind. Those ten tribes, waging a most just and necessary war against the Benjamites, lost forty thousand men in two battles, yet they did not on that account abandon their undertaking, but brought to a happy end what they had begun on a most just foundation. Or will the force of two skirmishes, whose unhappy outcome was our own fault, have more power to terrify us and draw us from our duty into harmful counsels, than six and more far harder battles against the greater forces of our enemy would have to arouse and encourage us, with God himself as both leader and companion? But if the Lord demands our souls as a sacrifice for the glory of his name, what, I ask you, could happen to us that is happier or more desirable than to pour out our life for the glory of God and the liberty of our country, and to exchange death for eternal life?

units.la: Siqui vero sunt quos vera de qua loquimur constantia destitutos ignauia cogat ad primarium vexillum nostrum, quod Iesu nomen prae se fert deserendum, quònam obsecro fugientes manibus Imperatoris nostri sese subduxerint? Absit vero fratres, vt tanquam buccinator ad bellum animos incitem, aut classicum canam, quod vtinam Deus Opt. Max. ille noster pater felici tandem consopire dignetur exitu, ter misero, qui pacem primum apud Deum, deinde apud homines quauis ratione non persequitur. Sed vt illam assequamur, ne diffidentiam in consilium aduocemus, neque nimiam negotiorum ingruentium difficultatem, sed in memoriam revocantes initia a quibus ortisumus, ad eum qui miserorum asylum & ambitiosorum superborūmque contrà sc-uerus est vindex confugiamus: lapsus nostros quibus factum est vt quod bene coeptum erat & sanctè non eodem pede promotum est a-gnoscentes, ad bonam frugem redeamus: noua ab ipso subinde zeli gloriæ ipsius fideique pe-tamus incrementa, ne mediis istis obruti flu-ctibus submergamur, sed ad felicem portum per medias procellas & tempestates nauè no-stram appellamus: neue brachium ipsius à bra-chio carnis suspendamus: sed in eius vnicam prouidentiam incumbentes liberationis no-strę modum & tempus illi permittamus: illi primùm qui fortium est fortissimus vniamur, tum etiam mutua inter nos charitate deuin-ciamur, vt cum Dauide tandem exultantes di-camus, Psal. 40. Expectando expectaui Ieho-uam: & inclinauit sese ad me. Id si præstiteri-mus, ecquis erit nobis mortalium metuendus, quum Deus ipse ster à nostris partibus, & mors ipsa sit nobis ad vitam aditus? Sin minus, erit proculdubio reuocandum in vsum quod ab Israëlitis ad bellum proficiscentibus factitari Dei mādato cōsueuerat, vt in castris hæc pro-mulgarentur. Deut. 20. 8. Quis est ille vir, qui timidus & mollis corde est? abiens reuertitor domum suam, vt non liquescat cor fratrum e-ius, sicut cor eius. Sed de vobis meliora o-mnia, ac Iehouam Deum exercituum mira-culis suis nos esse magis ac magis cumulatu-rum spero. Amen.
units.tr: But if there are any whom the lack of that true constancy of which we speak, and cowardice, drive to desert our chief standard, which bears the name of Jesus: where, I ask, will those fugitives hide themselves from the hands of our Emperor? Far be it from me, brethren, to incite your minds to war like a trumpeter, or to sound the call to arms; may God, our best and greatest Father, at last deign to lull that to rest with a happy outcome, for the wretched man who does not first pursue peace with God, and then with men, by any means. But so that we may attain it, let us not summon distrust as our counsellor, nor the excessive difficulty of the business that presses upon us. Rather, recalling the beginnings from which we sprang, let us take refuge with him who is the refuge of the wretched and the avenger, severe against the ambitious and the proud. Acknowledging our lapses, by which it has come about that what was well begun and holily undertaken has not been advanced with the same steps, let us return to good conduct. Let us ask from him, continually, new increases of zeal for his glory and of faith, lest, overwhelmed by these waves, we be drowned, but let us bring our ship through the midst of storms and tempests to a happy harbour. And let us not hang his arm upon the arm of flesh; but, resting upon his sole providence, let us leave to him the manner and time of our deliverance. Let us first cling to him who is the strongest of the strong, and then let us be bound to one another by mutual charity, so that at last, exulting with David, we may say (Ps. 40): "I waited patiently for Jehovah, and he inclined himself unto me." If we shall have done this, who among mortals will be to us to be feared, since God himself stands on our side, and death itself is for us the entrance to life? But if not, then assuredly must be revived the practice that was customary among the Israelites when they set out to war by God's command, that these words should be proclaimed in the camp (Deut. 20:8): "Who is the man that is fearful and faint-hearted? Let him go and return to his house, lest the heart of his brethren melt like his heart." But I hope for all better things from you, and I trust that Jehovah, the God of hosts, will by his wonders increase us more and more. Amen.

units.la: HOMIL.
units.tr: HOMILY

units.la: HOMILIA VICESIMASECUNDA.
units.tr: HOMILY TWENTY-SECOND.

units.la: LVC. 23.
units.tr: LUKE 23.

units.la: 6. Pilatus vero audita Galilaea, interrogauit num homo iste Galilaeus esset.
units.tr: 6. When Pilate heard of Galilee, he asked whether this man was a Galilean.

units.la: 7. Et quum cognouisset eum ad Herodis potestatem pertinere, remisit eum ad Herodem, qui & ipse Hierosolymis erat per eos dies.
units.tr: 7. And when he learned that Jesus belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem in those days.

units.la: PILATVM cum Iudaeis conferentibus maxima inter illos magis ac magis apparebit differentia, Pilato hactenus rectam conscientiam, duce sola naturali Luce seruante. Mansit enim in homine sic volente Deo principium illud, Innocentem minime condemnandum, magnumque esse inter vitium quod vituperandum, & virtutem quae in pretio habenda est discrimen. Verum, vt monet Apostolus. Rom. 1. 21. & 2. 15. Lux illa quantacunque est statim in tenebras in intelligentia mutatur: variaeque animi perturbationes saepius eorum effectum remorantur quae tamen aequum esse vt fierent conscientia
units.tr: When Pilate is compared with the Jews, the great difference between them becomes more and more evident. So far Pilate kept a upright conscience, guided by natural light alone. For God so willed it that the principle remained in the man that the innocent must by no means be condemned, and that there is a great difference between vice, which deserves blame, and virtue, which is to be prized. But, as the Apostle warns (Rom. 1.21 and 2.15), that light, however great it is, is at once turned into darkness in the understanding, and the various disturbances of the mind often hinder the outcome of what the conscience judges ought to be done, so that the good principles do not match the end.

units.la: L. iij. iudicat, vt principiis bonis minimè finis respondeat. Imò, quod longè peius est, in eo sibi delicias faciunt homines, quasi aliquid magnū præstitisse nt, non statim ab initio deficientes. Et reuera maxima inter Caiapham (quem improbè & malitiosè à vero aberrantem, omnis æqui & recti principia suffocante vidimus) & Pilatum strenuè tanto sceleri reluctantem videtur esse differentia. At singulis diligenter expensis, eodem tandem istæc recidunt, Pilatum nihil iuuantibus tot testimoniis quæ de Christi innocentia ediderat, immò magis accusantibus. Sciens enim prudens aduersus eum sententiam capitis dixit quem prius ipse pronuntiauerat innocentem, quum tamen eorum non pauci à quibus ad Christum damnandum erat impulsus tantum errore quodam à Sacerdotibus nimirum persuasi peccauerint. Nec tamen habent hi vel ille quam vel coram Deo, vel coram sani iudicij hominibus excusationem prætexant. En igitur eximium speculum in quod intuentes agnoscamus quàm vana sit reliqua in homine Lux & Intelligentia naturalis, ad eum inexcusabilem reddendum tantùm vtilis: virtutésque illas Morales de quibus Mundi Sapientes tantopere inter se disputarunt, ad eos præ cæteris quorum non tanta fuit de rebus istis cognitio coarguendos tantùm sufficere.
units.tr: Indeed, what is far worse, men take pleasure in this, as if they had accomplished something great, because they did not fail from the very beginning. And truly, the difference between Caiaphas, whom we have seen wickedly and maliciously straying from the truth and suffocating every principle of justice and right, and Pilate, who struggled vigorously against so great a crime, seems very great. But if each is weighed carefully, these things come down in the end to the same thing: Pilate, though he had published so many testimonies to Christ's innocence, did not help him at all, but rather accused him. For knowingly and deliberately he pronounced a sentence of death against the man whom he himself had earlier declared innocent. Yet not a few of those by whom he was driven to condemn Christ sinned only through a kind of error, persuaded by the priests. Nor do these or that man have any excuse to offer, either before God or before men of sound judgment. Here, then, is a remarkable mirror, in which, looking, we may recognize how empty the rest of the natural light and understanding in man is, useful only to make him inexcusable; and those moral virtues over which the wise men of the world disputed so much are sufficient only to convict those who, compared with others, had less knowledge of these matters.

units.la: Sola igitur Dei gratia nos ad imaginem suam per Sanctum suum Spiritum reformans, mentis tenebris dissipatis in nobis velle & facere cere creat, secundum eam mensuram virium quam sufficit, vt aduersus infirmitatem nostra pugnemus,tantisper dum in altera illa vita ple ne reformemur:& ita quidem, vt licet tantum sit inter hominem Ψυχικὸν & hominem regeneratum discrimen quantum inter eum qui in tenebris & eum qui Meridie ambulat,non habeat tamen vterque de quo in sese glorietur.
units.tr: Therefore only the grace of God, reforming us to his own image through his Holy Spirit, and dispelling the darkness of the mind, creates in us both the will and the deed, according to that measure of strength which suffices for us to fight against our weakness, for as long as we are not fully reformed in that other life. And so, although the difference between the natural [ψυχικὸν] man and the regenerate man is as great as between one who walks in darkness and one who walks at noon, yet neither has anything in which to glory in himself.

units.la: Porrò vt ex his exemplis ad nos aliquis fructus redeat,non tantum scire nos oportet quinam eorum exciderint quibus in bono perse- uerādum erat,sed etiam quomodo ceciderint, vt eorum exemplo sapiamus. En igitur primū lapidem ad quem Pilatus offendit, non serua- to,vt cœperat,recto tramite:Quod nimirū cognitam Iesu Christi innocentiam quū authoritate sua tueri ad finem vsque ipsum oportere,medium quoddā ἀμεταβλήτως quæsiuit, in alium istius negotij reiecta cognitione.Et hæc ipsius ratiocinatio.Pro virili hactenus innocentiam hominis istius tuitus,nihil tamen promoui.Et huc vsque mansit illæsa conscientia.
units.tr: Moreover, I see that this people's temper is such that this business can hardly be carried through without a remedy, and without tumult. What, then, is needed here? Clearly, both alternatives must be avoided if possible: that I should, if I must come to that, condemn him, or that I should not enter into the judgment at all, since he was condemned by another; and that the Jews should have no occasion to rise against me or to make an uproar. But an opportunity presents itself spontaneously, to send him to his own judge, with whom the Jews may deal as they see fit, while my conscience remains unharmed. Here is Pilate's reasoning, to which this might also be added: that this would also be the way of making a reconciliation between himself and Herod, so that one faggot would whiten two walls, as the wise men of this age are wont to say.

units.la: Porrò tantum istius populi animum esse conspicio, vt vix ni remedium adferatur sine tumultu res ista possit transfigi,Quid hic igitur opus est facto?Nimirum vtrque casus fugiendus, si fieri poterit, vt hoc, si co deueniendum erit, ab alio condemnato, in partem iudicij non veniam: & aduersum me insurgendi tumultuandiue Iudæi nullam occasionem habeant. Occurrit autem sponte opportunitas, illæsa mea conscientia, ad suum iudicem illum ablegandi, quicum agant Iudæi vt videbitur. En Pilati ratiocinationem, ad quam etiam hoc accedere potuit, hanc etiam fore inter fe & Herodem reconciliationis ineundæ rationem, vt vna fidelia duos ita dealbaret parietes, vt huius seculi sapientes loqui solent.
units.tr: You have, I say, as the matter itself speaks, Pilate's reasoning, in which he departed not a little from what is fair and right. For thinking he had nobly discharged his duty, he is gravely mistaken. For did he not, as he later boasted (John 19:10), have the power to release him, and not merely to protest his innocence? Therefore he had not yet fulfilled all the parts of his authority. But if he had thought about the parts of his duty rather than about his power, he would never have slipped so shamefully, since both the laws and his own conscience argued more than enough that a man who wishes to discharge his office must absolve an innocent one.

units.la: Habes, inquam, vt res ipsa loquitur, Pilati ratiocinationem, in qua non parum ab æquo rectóque recessit. Nam officio fe pulchrè defunctum existimans, vehementer fallitur. Annon enim, vt deinceps gloriatus est ipse Ioh. 19.10. potestatem habebat ipsum absoluendi, &non tantum de eius innocentia protestandi? Nondum igitur omnes suæ auctoritatis partes impleuerat. Quòd fi de officij fui partibus potius quàm de sua potestate cogitaffet, nequaquam tam fœdè lapsus effet, quum & Leges, & ipsa illum conscientia plus fatis arguerent innocentem absoluendum ab co qui cupiat officio defungi.
units.tr: You have, I say, as the matter itself speaks, Pilate's reasoning, in which he departed no little from what is fair and right. For thinking he had discharged his duty well, he is greatly mistaken. Did he not have, as he afterwards boasted (John 19.10), the power to release him, and not merely to bear witness to his innocence? So he had not yet fulfilled all the parts of his authority. But if he had considered the parts of his office rather than his power, he would by no means have fallen so shamefully, since both the laws and his own conscience argued more than enough that the innocent man must be acquitted by one who desires to discharge his office.

units.la: Deinde, non palàm de Christi innocentia testimonium tulerat, sed effugium quærens, vt qui femiore aperto loquuntur, dixerat, Nullum fe in eo crimen inuenire, Luc.23.ver.4.& Iohan.18 38. En igitur falsam omnino perfuasionem, quatamen suam conscientiam fulcire nitebatur.
units.tr: Then, he had not openly borne witness to Christ's innocence, but, seeking an escape, like those who speak with a half-open mouth, he said that he found no crime in him (Luke 23.4 and John 18.38). Here, then, is an altogether false persuasion, which yet he struggled to uphold for his own conscience.

units.la: Accedamus ad aliam istius consilij, de vitando in hoc populo tumultu partem, qui metus tandem cum à recto deflectere coëgit: & salsissimo principio nititur, quod humana prudentia dentia filiorum huius seculi dictat, e duobus malis minus eligendum. Quod quidem haud inuitus admittam, si Mali nomine damnum aut incommodum quod exitium exterius minetur intelligas, vt Deus Dauidi extribus poenis optionem alicuius permisit. 2. Sam. 24. 13. At si Malum intelligas quod cum Dei aut proximi offensione leuissima coniunctum est, ratum fixum hoc esto, nunquam male faciendum, licet officio nobis fungentibus caelum terrae misceri videatur. Apage igitur istam in officina Satanae excusam opinionem, carnis stulta & insana prudentia nos fascinatem. Annon enim obsecro furor est, malum ferentem, bonum demetere si posse sperare: & laesa conscientia quidquam boni exspectare? En tamen egregiam Caiaphae, aliorumque Sacerdotum conclusionem, Ioh. 11. 47. Et ne procul abeamus, certum est, & maxime deplorandum, quotidie hac in parte mille modis peccari, etsi inter Ethicos Philosophos sapientissimi sola Luce naturali duce, firmissimis rationibus probarint vtile ab honesto separari nunquam posse.
units.tr: Let us come to another part of this policy, that of avoiding a tumult among this people, which fear at last forced him to turn aside from what is right; and it rests on a most salty principle, which human prudence, the prudence of the sons of this age, dictates: that of two evils the lesser is to be chosen. This I would indeed admit, not unwillingly, if by evil you understand a loss or inconvenience, or an outward destruction that threatens, as God gave David the choice of certain punishments (2 Sam. 24.13). But if you understand by evil what is joined with the offence of God or of a neighbour, even the slightest, let this be settled and fixed: that we must never do evil, even though the heavens seem to be mixed with the earth while we discharge our duty. Away, then, with that opinion, forged in the workshop of Satan, which the foolish and insane prudence of the flesh has bewitched us with. For, I ask you, is it not madness to hope that one can gather good while bearing evil, and to expect anything good from a wounded conscience? Yet here is the remarkable conclusion of Caiaphas and the other priests (John 11.47). And not to go far away: it is certain, and most lamentable, that daily in this matter sin is committed in a thousand ways, although among the ethical philosophers, the wisest men, guided by natural light alone, have proved by most firm arguments that the useful can never be separated from the honourable.

units.la: Danda igitur nobis, in primis opera, fratres (quos Deo visum est longe illustriore caelesti Luce docere) in omnibus negotiis ne nos incautos fallax illa mentis imaginatio decipiat: contrà vero, quum ex Apostoli doctrina, quod per se licet etiam peccatum sit aliquando, Rom. 14. 21. fidei mysterium cum pura conscientia teneamus, 1. Tim. 3. 9. & contingentibus istiusmodi modi casibus à Deo & eius sacrosancto verbo consilium petamus, quem ducem, tanquam praelucentem facem, sequuti, cogitationibus, verbis & factis nostris legem imponamus, futura etiam eadem Lucc olim factorumque dictorumque nostrorum Iudice, non autem nostris opinionibus: quòd si male agentes cor ipsum nos redarguit, quicquid praetexamus, quid eo qui corde nostro longè maior est futurum arbitramur? 1. Ioh. 3.20.
units.tr: Therefore, brethren (whom it has pleased God to teach by a far brighter heavenly light), our first task must be that in all affairs that deceitful imagination of the mind not deceive us, being unwary. On the contrary, since from the Apostle's teaching, that even what is in itself lawful may sometimes be sin (Rom. 14.21), we hold the mystery of the faith with a pure conscience (1 Tim. 3.9), and in such chance cases we seek counsel from God and his most holy Word, following that Guide as a torch shining before us, let us impose a law on our thoughts, words and deeds, with that Light as judge of our deeds and words, both now and in the future, and not with our own opinions. But if our own heart, when we act badly, rebukes us, whatever we pretend, what do we think will be the case with him who is greater than our heart? (1 John 3.20).

units.la: Eâdem porrò carnis prudentia, Pilatus praeterea quadam alia ratione deceptus est, dum sibi persuaderi pallus est, satis esse ad pacandam conscientiam si ipse non peccaueris: qua in re duplex error est. Docet enim ipsa natura corrupta, non tantum abstinendum à malo, sed bonum etiam faciedum, vt diserte Psalmo 34. 15. dicitur. Ecquis enim boni ciuis eum loco habeat, qui patriam quidem minimè prodiderit, boni tamen ciuis officio minimè defunctus sit? Patrem qui filios quidem ad malum non impulerit, sed non tamen bene educauerit? Annon verò venit in partem peccati, quisquis vel leuissimam eius occasionem sciens praebuit, vel ipsis testibus Legibus de conscis facinorum? En in quę praecipitia ruant praecipites qui tantillum à recto veróque, modò metu, modò spe inani delinati, recedunt.
units.tr: Again, by the same prudence of the flesh, Pilate was deceived in another way too, while he persuaded himself that it was enough to pacify his conscience if he himself had not sinned. In this there is a double error. For corrupt nature itself teaches not only that we must abstain from evil, but also that good must be done, as is plainly said in Psalm 34.15. For who would regard as a good citizen a man who has indeed not betrayed his country, but has not discharged the duty of a good citizen? Or a father who has indeed not driven his sons into evil, but has not brought them up well? Does not whoever knowingly offered even the slightest occasion of wrong fall into a share of the sin, or, by the very testimony of the laws, become an accomplice in crimes? See into what precipices they fall headlong who, led astray now by fear and now by vain hope, depart even a little from what is right and true.

units.la: Quibus omnibus veteris cuiusdam egregium dictum est opponédum, Deum metuentem, non habere quod metuat, contrà Deúnō metuenti,omnia magna & parua formidanda: doctrinam sane omni seculo omnibus necef- sariam,sed in primis munus publicum, Ciuile vel Ecclesiasticum sustinentibus, quo magna- nimitate illa præditi sint, quam Icthro Mosis socer, in iis recensendis virtutibus quæ publi- co munere fungentem decent minimè præter- misit, Exod 17. v.21. Vos ne igitur, Magistratus, pulchrè defunctos officio putabitis, fi huius vel illius inimicitias effugientes, aut alicui gra tificari studentes, quum primas sedes occupa- re vos oportuerit, subterfugia quæsieritis ne causæ alicuius decisioni interfitis? Næ fi sic iu- dicatis, longè fallimini. Nam etsi metus ali- quis subesset iniustitiæ in iudicio aliquo futu- ræ, quæ nulla prohiberi posse ratione videre- tur, tantùm abest vt illi se iudicio quenquam subducere liceat, vt contrà, maximè interesse, & pro iure forti animo stare, conscientiam saltem liberaturum oporteat: quum sæpe v- nius hominis constantia multorum impro- borum consilia fregerit.
units.tr: All of these objections can be met with a fine saying of an old writer: one who fears God has nothing else to fear, while one who does not fear God has everything great and small to fear. This is certainly a teaching necessary at all times for everyone, but above all for those who bear a public office, civil or ecclesiastical. Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, did not omit to list, among the virtues that befit a man holding public office, that greatness of spirit (Exod. 17.21). So, magistrates, do not think you have discharged your office well if, in order to escape this or that man's enmity, or to win someone's favour, you look for ways to avoid taking part in the decision of some case when you ought to occupy the first seats. No, if you judge like that you are gravely mistaken. Even if some fear were hanging over you of injustice in a certain trial, one that seemed impossible to prevent by any means, it is by no means permitted to withdraw from the judgment, as if to escape it. On the contrary, you ought to take a particular interest in it, stand firm for what is right with a brave spirit, and at least free your conscience, since the steadfastness of one man has often broken the plans of many wicked men.

units.la: Denique, non tantùm malo non est assen- tiendum,sed viriliter resistendū: in quo quum plerosque cessare videamus, minimè mirum est horrendas & immedicabiles multas con- fusiones in Status incidere,hac ratione iugum subeuntibus sua auctoritate spoliatis quos ef- se terrori improbis oportuerat: & contrà do- minantibus terrorémque incutientibus, quos parere & metuere par erat. Eadem est, imò longè deterior Pastorum conditio, metuentium homines potius quàm eum cui semel a-liquando rationem sunt reddituri, & ita in canes mutos, aut abominandos adulatores degenerátium, lupis in gregem impetum facientibus, miserámque & deplorandam calamitatem inferentibus. Vtinam Deus meliora, vtrúmque istud à nobis malum auertens, pro sua beneuolentia zelum gloriæ suæ in singulis nostrum accendat, rectámque in omnibus conscientiam largiatur.
units.tr: In short, we must not only refuse to assent to evil, but resist it manfully. Since we see most people failing to do so, it is no wonder that dreadful and incurable confusions often fall upon states.
