In this way, those who should have been a terror to the wicked are stripped of their authority and placed under the yoke, while those who rule and strike terror into others are the very ones they ought to obey and fear. The condition of ministers is the same, or rather far worse: they fear men rather than him to whom they will one day have to render an account. So they degenerate into dumb dogs or despicable flatterers, and like wolves they fall upon the flock and bring on it a wretched and deplorable disaster. May God grant better things, turning away both of these evils from us, and in his goodness kindle zeal for his glory in each of us, and bestow a upright conscience on us all.

units.la: Narrat deinceps historia, Pilatum quum audiuisset Christum esse Galilæum & id credidisset, ambabus, vt aiunt, vlnis hanc occasionem ipsum ad Herodem Tetrarcham Galilææ remittendi amplexatum esse. Hic vero primum crassam Iudæorum ignorantiam animaduerte, communem errorem foucentium, Iesum Christum Nazaretha vrbe Galilææ esse oriundum, adeò vt inde Nazarenus sit denominatus, immo sit ab impuro illo Iuliano Apostata per contemptum Galilæus quòd ita male Galilæorum gens audiret, appellatus Ioh. 1.46. & 7.52. Non carebat autem hic error speciosò prætextu, quum Mariæ & Iosephi, cuius habebatur filius, domicilium esset Nazarethæ. Luc. 1. 26. vbi fuerat etiam ab Ægypti reditu educatus, Matt. 2.23. Paucis enim erat eius ortus Bethleemæ cognitus: quo errore Satan callidius abusus est, vt videmus ab eo etiam Christum vocari Nazarenum Marc. 1.24. & Luc. 4. 34. quòd oraculis Prophetarum Messias ē tribu Iuda promissus esset, ad quam minimè Galilæa lilæa pertinebat : præsertim verò Scribæ & Legis doctores Bethleemæ nasciturum sci-rent, Matth.2.verf.5.ex quo facilè cognoscitur quàm crassa essèt Philippi ignorantia, quem postea Dominus in duodecim Apostolorum numerum asciuit, Iesum Christum Messiam simul & Iosephi Nazarethæ nati filium existimantis, Iohan.1.ver.45. Quicquid autem isti prætexatur ignorantiæ, sanè, si Iudæorum doctores, non absrecæci ductores cæcorum dicti, Matth.15. verf.14. Danielis septimanas attentè considerassent, etiam ab Herode & Orientis sapientibus excitati, Matth.2.v.3.& pastoribus credidissent, Luc.2. 17. quódque Zacharias Iohannis Baptistæ pater palàm prædicauerat expendissent Luc.1.68.& deinceps Simeonem & Annam in ipso templo illum agnoscentes auscultassent, Luc.2.30.& 38.si denique ex officio suo Regnum cœlorū aperire studuissent, minimè tam facilè in vulgus hic error inualuissèt. Oro verò vos atque obsecro, quot istiusmodi errores & salsissimæ fabulæ, tam de præteritis quàm futuris recensseri possent inter Christianos illapsæ veritatique maximè repugnantes, quæ tamen tam altas in mentibus multorū tū maioris dignitatis tum plebeiæ conditionis hominū radices egerunt, vt nullis exhortationibus, nullis documentis euelli possint, immo qui eas reiiciat in Deum esse contumeliosus videatur? At nostrum officium est, Apostoli exhortationi locum dantes, istiusmodi fabulis, veteribus aut nouis non attendere.Ephef.4.4.& Tit.1.14.
units.tr: The history goes on to relate that Pilate, having heard that Christ was a Galilean and believing it, seized upon this opportunity, as they say, with both hands, to send him back to Herod, the tetrarch of Galilee. Herod, however, first noticed the gross ignorance of the Jews, who fostered the common error that Jesus Christ was born in the city of Nazareth in Galilee, so that he was called "the Nazarene" from there. Indeed, the impious Julian the Apostate, in contempt, called him "the Galilean," because the Galileans had such a bad reputation (John 1.46; 7.52). This error did not lack a plausible pretext, since the home of Mary and Joseph, whom he was thought to be the son of, was in Nazareth (Luke 1.26), where he had also been brought up after the return from Egypt (Matt. 2.23). For few knew of his birth at Bethlehem. Satan abused this error more cunningly, as we see from the fact that he called Christ "the Nazarene" (Mark 1.24; Luke 4.34). The Messiah had been promised by the prophets' oracles as coming from the tribe of Judah, to which Galilee by no means belonged. Especially since the scribes and teachers of the Law knew that he would be born at Bethlehem (Matt. 2.5), it is easy to see how gross Philip's ignorance was, who was later admitted by the Lord into the number of the twelve Apostles, yet who thought that Jesus Christ was both the Messiah and the son of Joseph, who was born in Nazareth (John 1.45). Whatever excuse of ignorance they may plead, surely, if the Jewish teachers, who are called blind guides of the blind (Matt. 15.14), had carefully considered Daniel's weeks, having been roused by Herod and the wise men from the East (Matt. 2.3), and had believed the shepherds (Luke 2.17), and had weighed what Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, had openly proclaimed (Luke 1.68), and had then listened to Simeon and Anna, who recognised him in the temple itself (Luke 2.30, 38); and if, finally, they had striven to open the kingdom of heaven as was their office, this error would by no means have taken such easy hold among the common people. But I beg and entreat you: how many such errors and most absurd fables, both about past and future things, could be listed, which have crept in among Christians and are most opposed to the truth? Yet they have struck such deep roots in the minds of many, both of higher rank and of humble condition, that they cannot be torn out by any exhortations or any teaching, and whoever rejects them seems to be insulting God. But it is our duty, giving heed to the Apostle's exhortation, not to pay attention to fables of this kind, whether old or new (Eph. 4.4; Titus 1.14).

units.la: Interea tamen ecce Iesus Christus per Hierosolymitanos vicos raptatur, & contumeliose habitus à Praetorio ad Herodem, vt prius à Caiapha ad Pilatum, deducitur, vt in repetitis istis cotumeliis, nō semel, sed toto vitae nostrae curriculo meditemur quàtus sit peccatorum nostrorū horror, quae nō potuerint nisi istiusmodi satisfactione deleri, quae ad ipsum Dei tribunal ascendit, Filio suo vnico non parcentis, sed tam grauiter in eum tanquam nostrum sponsorem ac fideiussorem corporum & animarum animaduertentis: quanta item & quàm immensa sit bonitas, tum Patris istiusmodi nobis satisfactionem decernetis, tum Filij eandem vltrò subeuntis, non tantùm ab aeternae mortis ignominia nos liberaturi, sed etiam ius ad aeternae & inenarrabilis eius gloriae consequendam possessionem acquisituri.
units.tr: Meanwhile, behold, Jesus Christ is dragged through the streets of Jerusalem and, treated with contempt, is led from the praetorium to Herod, just as before he had been led from Caiaphas to Pilate. Let us meditate on these repeated insults, not once but throughout the whole course of our life, on how great the horror of our sins is, which could not be blotted out except by such a satisfaction. This satisfaction ascends to the very tribunal of God, who did not spare his only Son but punished him so severely as our surety and guarantor for our bodies and souls. Consider also how great and how immeasurable is the goodness both of the Father, who decreed such a satisfaction for us, and of the Son, who undertook it of his own accord, so that he might free us not only from the disgrace of eternal death but also acquire for us the right to obtain the possession of his eternal and inexpressible glory.

units.la: Obseruandum praeterea Dominum vt Ecclesiam suam ex multis hominum generibus elegit, ita voluisse nostrum Redemptorem in varij generis facinorosos incidere, quò nostrae salutis fons & origo solius illius gratiae accepta feratur. En igitur hinc quidem Iudaeos, nomen Populi Dei praeferentes, & tamē apertos hostes, & deploratos illius persequutores, in quo salus & vera vita consistit. Inde verò Romanos, miseros infideles, Dei expertes in mundo, & à pactis promissionis extraneos: Ephef. 2. 12. Ac tandem Herodem cum suis velut inter illos medium locum tenentes, & hinc inde claudicantes, duarúmque fcllarū homines, Romanorum Iudæorúmque simul beneuolentiam sibi conciliare studentes, ad illius exemplum Herodis magni, cuius hic erat filius cognomine Antipas, hæres Tetrarchiæ Galileæ,Luc. 3.1.quibus nulli sunt magis prophani magisqueperniciosi.Et quidem hodie mundi tribus istis hominum generibus pleni talis est conditio. Romanus enim ille, quem vocant, clerus, qui falso Iudaismo successit minore prætextu, maiore vero corruptione, siue doctrinam, siue disciplinam externam Ecclesiæ spectes,is est hodie à quo aduersus Christi membra veritatem amplexa persecutiones commouentur & inflammantur. Quemadmodum autem tunc temporis, tres erant Iudæorum species, aliis quidem vt Caiapha & primariis Sacerdotibus in Christum immedicabili improbitate & furore sæquientibus:aliis leuitate & ignorantia magnum quid præstare se putantibus si cum Sacerdotibus Crucifigendum vociferarentur:qui tamen Christi precibus.Luc. 23.34. veniam erroris adepti sunt:Act.3.17. aliis vero Christum, cuius erat ipsis ignota doctrina, boni viri loco habentibus,& iniustitiam quidem istam ægrè ferentibus,sed tamen omnino silentibus:Sic hodie tres istas hominum species, apud Catholicos, vt vocantur, hodie miseri Dei filij experiuntur. Inde vero Turcæ & alij infideles passim, Romanis qui tum temporis vixerunt simillimi,longè sunt æquiores & mitiores Christiftianis in ditione sua degentibus, illæsam religionem & conscientiam permittentes, vt olim Romani priusquàm Nero Christianos, importunis Iudæorum & improborum quorundam aliorum calumniis persequi cœpisset. Ecce vero tandem certos quosdam Mediatores, Herodianis illis non absimiles, quorum alij vana fui opinione & ambitione turgent: alij de Religione non aliter quàm de humanis politiis sentiunt: alij quietis suæ tranquillitatisque tantùm, & conscientiæ quodammodo sopiendæ, studiosi, quod olim Iudæi iam à Syrorum & Ægyptiorum Regum temporibus factitabant, sibi & aliis persuadere nituntur, non tantam esse doctrinæ discrepantiam quam multi sunt imaginati: tantumque esse reformandam Ecclesiam, non autem transformandam: & ita Missam cum Euangelio componunt, vt olim Herodiani cum Iudaismo Paganismum. Porrò sunt isti postremi, quòd omnibus Pacis & Tranquillitatis nomè dulce fit, hostes Ecclesiæ maximè omniù metuendi: à quibus Deum oro vt pro immensa misericordia nos tueatur: Ea tunc igitur Christi conditio fuit: eadem hodie nostra: sed animum præstemus. Victor enim Dei filius in propria persona, olim aducrfus istiusmodi homines, fuit etiam hactenus, & ad seculorum vsque consummationem in membris suis futurus est.
units.tr: We should further observe that, as the Lord chose his Church from many kinds of men, so our Redeemer willed to fall among criminals of various kinds, so that the fountain and origin of our salvation might be credited to that grace alone. Here, then, are the Jews, who bore the name of the people of God, and yet were open enemies and deadly persecutors of him in whom salvation and true life consist. There are the Romans, wretched unbelievers, without God in the world and strangers to the covenants of promise (Eph. 2.12). And finally there is Herod with his followers, who held a middle place between these, wavering on both sides, men with two stools, seeking to win the goodwill both of the Romans and of the Jews at once. He was the son of Herod the Great, surnamed Antipas, heir to the tetrarchy of Galilee (Luke 3.1), and of all men these are the most profane and the most pernicious. And indeed today the condition of the world is full of these three kinds of men. For that so-called Roman clergy, which succeeded the Jews under a false pretext, though with a greater corruption, whether you look at its doctrine or its external discipline, is today the very party from which persecutions are stirred up and inflamed against the members of Christ who have embraced the truth. Just as at that time there were three kinds of Jews: some, like Caiaphas and the chief priests, raged against Christ with incurable wickedness and fury; others, through levity and ignorance, thought they were doing something great when they shouted with the priests, "Crucify him"; yet these obtained pardon for their error through the prayers of Christ (Luke 23.34; Acts 3.17); and others regarded Christ, whose teaching was unknown to them, as a good man, and bore this injustice with difficulty, but kept entirely silent. So today the wretched children of God experience these three kinds of men among the so-called Catholics. Meanwhile the Turks and other unbelievers everywhere, though very like the Romans who lived at that time, are far more fair and gentle towards the Christians who live under their rule, allowing them their religion and conscience unharmed, just as the Romans once did before Nero began to persecute the Christians at the importunate instigation of the Jews and certain other wicked men. But see, at last, certain mediators, not unlike those Herodians, some of whom swell with vain self-opinion and ambition, others think about religion no differently than about human policies, and others, eager only for their own peace and tranquillity and for somehow lulling their conscience to sleep, strive to persuade themselves and others that the difference in doctrine is not as great as many imagine, and that the Church needs only to be reformed, not transformed. And so they combine the Mass with the Gospel, just as the Herodians once combined paganism with Judaism. Moreover, these last are the most dangerous enemies of the Church of all, since the name of peace and tranquillity is sweet to everyone. I pray God to protect us from them in his immense mercy. Such, then, was the condition of Christ at that time, and our own today is the same, but let us show courage. For the victorious Son of God, in his own person, fought against such men long ago, has fought them until now, and will continue to do so in his members until the consummation of the ages.

units.la: Vt igitur ad historiam reuertamur, dicitur Herodes viso Iesu Christo magnopere gaudisus. sus. Et sanè magna lætandi illi oblata erat occasio, si probè eum qui ante se stabat cognouisset: & oculis quibus eius quem hoc miserò & abiecto statu sibi oblatum videbat, virtutem & gloriam contemplatus esset: At improbum illum hæc cura non tangebat: sed prophana tantùm curiositas, vt deinceps narrat Euangelista: nam quùm Christum histrionis tantum haberet loco, sperabat aliquid ab ea ludicrum de cuius miraculis aliquid fama perceperat: vnde quàm esset in peius mutatus ex quo magni illius serui Dei sanguine manus fœdarat, satis animaduertimus. Prius enim dicitur licet incestuosus, & vt paucis dicam, improbus, tamen metuisse Dei seruum, eumque obseruasse, & libenter etiam audiuisse, Marc. 6.20. imò de Christo quùm aliquid audiuisset initio, existimasse Iohannem illum esse Baptistam ab inferis excitatum. Marc. 6.16. At semel auribus conscientiæ suæ obturatis, in profanum & apertum contemptorem euasit. Verùm in ipsum & eius scortum, teste Iosepho historico, tandem ille contemptus recidit. En verò quomodo pedetentim homines ex minoribus peccatis incidant in maiora flagitia, & tandem in deploratos contemptores & irrisores euadant, Psal. 1. 1. rem sanè deplorandam, & tamen nimium frequentem & ordinariam. Vtinam verò nè vnquam in medio nostrum tam tristia exempla conspexissemus, nec esset vlla occasio nobis in posterum illa metuendi.
units.tr: Now to return to the history: Herod, on seeing Jesus Christ, is said to have rejoiced greatly. Indeed, he had a great occasion for rejoicing, if he had known the one who stood before him and had looked with the eyes of faith on the power and glory of the one he saw in such a wretched and humble state. But that wicked man was not moved by this concern, only by profane curiosity, as the Evangelist relates afterward. Since he regarded Christ as nothing more than a performer, he hoped for some entertainment from him, having heard some report of his miracles. How far he had changed for the worse since he stained his hands with the blood of that great servant of God is plain enough. Earlier, although he was incestuous and, to put it briefly, wicked, he feared the servant of God, observed him, and even listened to him gladly (Mark 6:20). Indeed, when he first heard something about Christ, he thought John the Baptist had been raised from the dead (Mark 6:16). But once he had stopped the ears of his conscience, he became an open and profane despiser. Yet, as the historian Josephus testifies, he finally fell back into contempt, both for himself and for his mistress. See how men gradually fall from lesser sins into greater crimes, and at last turn into hardened scorners and mockers (Ps. 1:1). This is indeed a deplorable thing, yet all too common and ordinary. I wish we had never seen such sad examples among us, and that there were no occasion for us in future to fear them.

units.la: In primis verò discamus quibus intueri nos M. j. Iesum Christum oculis oporteat, ad fructum vitae ex eius intuitu, non autem iudicium reportandum. Tres sunt igitur inde a mundi initio Christi apparitiones, quartam autem & ultimam perfectissimam exspectamus.
units.tr: Above all, let us learn with what eyes we ought to look upon Jesus Christ, so that we may gain the fruit of life from looking on him, and not judgment. There are therefore three appearances of Christ since the beginning of the world, and we await a fourth and final one, most perfect.

units.la: Prima fuit duplex, primum nimirum invisionibus omnis generis Patriarchis primum exhibitis, deinde Prophetis. Ille enim est quem Abrahamus vidit & adoravit. Ioh. 18.17. ille, qui populum Israeliticum per defectum deduxit. 1.Cor.10.4.& 9. ille cuius Esaias gloriam conspexit. Ioh.12.41. ille denique semper apud Patrem Ecclesiae Mediator: cuius futurae tandem in carne manifestationis erant visiones illae certissima praeludia. Deinde sub Mose sunt Legis umbrae & ceremoniae certo ordine dispositae, quarum erat venturus Christus substantia & corpus Col.2.17.
units.tr: The first appearance was twofold: first, to the Patriarchs, who were shown him in visions of every kind, and then to the Prophets. This is the one whom Abraham saw and worshipped (John 8:56); the one who led the people of Israel through the wilderness (1 Cor. 10:4, and 9); the one whose glory Isaiah beheld (John 12:41); and finally the one who is always the Mediator of the Church before the Father, whose visions were the most certain foretastes of his future manifestation in the flesh. Then, under Moses, came the shadows and ceremonies of the Law, arranged in a fixed order, of which Christ was to be the substance and body (Col. 2:17).

units.la: Altera in propria persona in carne manifestatio facta est, assumpta a vero unico Dei Filio Deo Patri coessentiali & coaeterno integra natura nostra, reali, visibili & palpabili, in unitatem personae, quae hac ratione θεάνθρωπος & ἀνθρωπόθεος est. Fuit autem haec in terris apparitio, inde ab eius ex Virgine in Bethlehem nativitate usque in eius supra caelos omnes Ascensum. Ephes. 4.10. quibus illum oportet contineri usque ad tempora consummationis & restitutionis rerum omnium. Act. 3.verf.21. ex quibus illum exspectamus 1.Thes.1.10.
units.tr: The second was the manifestation in his own person, in the flesh. The true and only Son of God, co-essential and co-eternal with God the Father, took our whole nature, real, visible and tangible, into the unity of his person, and so is God-man [θεάνθρωπος] and man-God [ἀνθρωπόθεος]. This appearance on earth lasted from his birth of the Virgin in Bethlehem to his Ascension above all the heavens (Eph. 4:10), where he must remain until the times of the consummation and restoration of all things (Acts 3:21), and from which we await him (1 Thess. 1:10).

units.la: Tertia ea est quae ab Apostolica praedicatione cum Sacramentorum administratione in orbe terrarum vniuerso coepit cum mundo demum finienda, quarta & vltima tandem illam exceptura, in qua, secundum mensuram noltram, sumus eum qualis elt in gloria sua, ad æternam salutem noltram conspecturi. 1. Ioh. 3. verf. 2.
units.tr: The third is the one that began with the apostolic preaching and the administration of the sacraments throughout the whole world, and is to end only with the world itself. The fourth and last will receive it, in which, according to our measure, we shall see him as he is in his glory, for our eternal salvation (1 John 3:2).

units.la: Priores autem illæ duæ manifestationes illud habuerunt commune, quòd oculi visibile obiectum intuiti sunt, sed tamen diuersa dispensatione. Nam nec visiones ipsæ in se, nec Legales umbræ fuerunt ipsemet Iesus Christus, nec Deitatis respectu, nimirum invisibilis & incomprehensibilis: nec etiam Humanitatis, vt pote nondum conceptæ, sicut in secunda manifestatione fuit. Quamobrem etiam dicuntur eum Patres eminus conspicati, Heb. 11. 13. fidei nimirum oculis, ea intellectu docentis quæ his visionibus repræsentabantur.
units.tr: Now those two earlier manifestations had this in common: that the eyes beheld a visible object, but under a different dispensation. For neither the visions in themselves nor the legal shadows were Jesus Christ himself, nor were they so in respect of his Deity, which is invisible and incomprehensible, nor in respect of his humanity, which had not yet been conceived, as it was in the second manifestation. Therefore the Fathers are said to have seen him from afar (Heb. 11:13), with the eyes of faith, understanding by the intellect what was represented by these visions.

units.la: Quo si est plurimum adiuta veterum fides, multo magis præsentia reali & corporea Iesu Christi cum ipsius Verbo & factis coniuncta commoti sunt & recreati credentes, teste Simeone & Anna prophetissa, & eo ipso quod discipulis dicebat. Matth. 13. 17. Sed quemadmodum qui solas figuras carnis oculis intuebantur, fide nequaquam intuentes quod per eas illorum intellectui repræsentabatur: ita qui non aliter quàm Herodes Iesum Christum conspexerunt, nimirum in corporea illa natura solis eum carneis oculis contemplantes & manibus contingentes, & solum verborum ipsius sonum auribus haurientes, aduersus ipsos testimonium tantum retulerunt, vt pote Iesum Christum Hominem Deum & Seruatorem non agnoscentes.
units.tr: If the faith of the ancients was greatly helped by this, believers were moved and renewed much more by the real and bodily presence of Jesus Christ, joined with his Word and deeds, as Simeon and the prophetess Anna bear witness, and by what he himself said to the disciples (Matt. 13:17). But just as those who looked only on the figures with fleshly eyes, not seeing with faith what was represented to their minds through them, so those who saw Jesus Christ no differently than Herod did, that is, who contemplated him in that bodily nature only with carnal eyes, touched him with their hands, and took in only the sound of his words with their ears, bore witness against themselves, since they did not acknowledge Jesus Christ as God-man and Saviour.

units.la: Accessit, hominum etiam eorum qui sapere visi sunt, infirmitate ad superiora quidā error in hac manifestatione, quòd Iesus Christus hominum oculis, sese tam vili & contempto habitu offerens, licet tum verbum tum miracula satisque superque Maiestatem ipsius patefacerent, & capitalissimos inimicos satis de virtute eius diuina & extraordinaria commonefaceret, discipulosque eius & bonos auditores supra humana omnia attollerent, caro tamen eius instar veli prospectum eius quod erat in illo summum ac praecipuum Deitatis, putà essentialis, corporaliter in ipso habitatis, impediebat. Coloss. 2.9. Hinc factum vt alij doctrinam eius audientes & opera conspicientes haereret dubij & attoniti Luc. 8. 25. & Ioh. 7. 46. alij offensi blasphemum cum nuncuparet. Ioh. 5. 18. Multi vero Filium Dei vocarunt, quid loquerentur ignorantes. Matth. 27. 54. Et quod longè maius erat, etsi videntur eum agnouisse discipuli, Petri confessionem admittentes, Matth. 16. non tamen penitus quid loquerentur intellexerunt, aut statim illud obliuioni tradiderunt, vix ac ne vix quidem resurrectionem eius nuntiantibus adhibita fide Ioh. 20. 9. & Luc. 24. 11. donec aperte tandem cum Thomas agnoscerat Deumque suum palam confiteretur. Ioh. 20. 28. Quid amplius? etsi tot modis, rotque effectis testatam à Prophetis & Apostolis Filij Dei coæterni & coëssentialis Deitatem, tamé Samosatenianí & Arriani hodie adhuc negant: & Marcionitæ cum similibus hæreticis, magnum istud mysterium suis sensibus non percipientes 1.Tim.3.16. pertinaciter docuerunt Dei Filium tantu specie tenus hominem fuisse, & in humanitate omnia specie tenus fecisse: quod pluribus sub istius historiæ principium persequuti sumus. En cur discipulis suis Christus diceret expedire ipsis vt abiret ex hoc mundo, ne corporeus eius aspectus & carnalis eos diutius in terris retineret. Ioh.16. 7. Idcirco igitur eŭ relictis terris quod ad humanitatem in cœlos ascédere oportuit, vt disceremus cum non amplius secundum carnem nosse, inquit Apostolus 2.Corint.5.16. id est in his terris, tanquam in humanitate sua præsentem, qua sese inuicem homines norunt, quum à nobis quòd ad humanitatem absens, fidei sit oculis contemplandus, in cœlis gloria sua illa venerandus.
units.tr: Moreover, a certain error arose in this manifestation from the weakness even of those who seemed to be wise. Jesus Christ presented himself to human eyes in such a mean and despised form that, although his word and miracles revealed his majesty more than enough, and although he warned his most bitter enemies sufficiently about his divine and extraordinary power, and lifted his disciples and good hearers above all human things, nevertheless his flesh, like a veil, blocked the view of that supreme and chief thing in him, namely the Deity dwelling bodily in him, essentially (Col. 2:9). Hence it came about that some who heard his teaching and saw his works were left doubting and astonished (Luke 8:25; John 7:46), while others, offended, called him a blasphemer (John 5:18). Many indeed called him the Son of God, not knowing what they were saying (Matt. 27:54). And what was far worse: although the disciples seem to have recognised him, admitting Peter's confession (Matt. 16), they did not fully understand what they were saying, nor did they at once forget it. When the women announced his resurrection, they scarcely, or hardly at all, gave it credit (John 20:9; Luke 24:11), until at last Thomas openly acknowledged him and confessed him publicly as his God (John 20:28). What more? Although the Deity of the Son of God, co-eternal and co-essential, has been attested by the Prophets and Apostles in so many ways and by so many effects, the Samosatenes and the Arians still deny it today; and the Marcionites, with similar heretics, not perceiving this great mystery with their senses (1 Tim. 3:16), have stubbornly taught that the Son of God was a man only in appearance, and that in his humanity he did everything only in appearance. We have pursued this at greater length at the beginning of this history. Here is why Christ told his disciples that it was expedient for them that he should go away from this world, so that his bodily and carnal presence would not keep them longer on earth (John 16:7). Therefore he had to leave the earth and ascend into heaven, as far as his humanity was concerned, so that we might learn not to know him any longer according to the flesh (2 Cor. 5:16), as the Apostle says. That is, he is no longer to be known in these earthly things, as present in the humanity by which men know one another, but since he is absent from us as regards his humanity, he is to be contemplated with the eyes of faith and revered in heaven in his glory.

units.la: Quis igitur quantúsque stupor est illú adhuc hodie in terris secundum humanitatem quærere, quem à nobis oportuit recedere, vt eum in superioribus quærere disceremus? Lögè sanè dissimilis fuit illius Centurionis tantopere laudata fides, Christo licet adhuc in carne terris præsente, Matth.8.v.10. Nam contrà palàm professus est, nò opus esse vt ad exerendam virtutem domum ipsius contenderet, sed verbo tantùm loquutum id efficere posse.
units.tr: What great stupidity, then, is it that even today people seek him on earth according to his humanity, when we ought to have departed from him so that we might learn to seek him above? The faith of the Centurion, so greatly praised, was certainly very different, even though Christ was still present on earth in the flesh (Matt. 8:10). For he openly professed that it was not necessary for Christ to go to his house to exercise his power, but that he could accomplish it by a word alone.

units.la: M. iij. Zachæus etiam cuius meminit Lucas 19.2. etsi minimè neglexit visum eius corporeum, quæ summopere quæsiuit, vt tunc potuit, satis tamè palàm fecit iam à se illum fidei oculis perceptum, qua in cognitione conquiescere. En tamen fundamentum, en summam, en denique numeris omnibus absolutum aduersariorum Christianismum, vt credant in Missa Iesu Christi corpus realiter & substantialiter videri, tangi & à Sacrificulo deuorari, & ab ipsis etiam in sua communione maducari, sub speciebus, quas vocant, id est, iisdem ipsis expositoribus, sub colore & sapore panis & vini, tam crassum ac longum quàm est in humana sua natura & semel in cruce pependit. Hinc fit vt malè docti in verborum Sacramentalium interpretatione, à Missa sua reuersi, dicat sibique persuadeant, se Deum vidisse, & Deum accepisse, cùm tamen secundum Deitatem sit invisibilis, & secundum humanitatem, extra hunc mundum collocatam. Quòd si quæras ex doctoribus quomodo corpus essentiale Iesu Christi præsens sit ipsorum oculis, manibus & oribus, modo nimirum invisibili, impalpabili & insensibili responsuri sunt: quod si ita est, annon obsecro tres præcipuos & indubitatos Christianæ fidei nostræ articulos falsi arguì necesse est?
units.tr: Zacchaeus too, whom Luke mentions (19:2), although he by no means neglected his bodily sight, which he sought above all as far as he then could, nevertheless made it sufficiently plain that he had already perceived Christ with the eyes of faith and rested in that knowledge. Here, however, is the foundation, here the sum, here finally the Christianity of our opponents, complete in every particular: they believe that in the Mass the body of Jesus Christ is really and substantially seen, touched, and devoured by the sacrificing priest, and is also eaten by them in their communion, under what they call the species, that is, under the very colour and taste of bread and wine, as large and as long as it is in his human nature, and as it once hung on the cross. Hence it happens that badly taught men, when interpreting the sacramental words, return from their Mass and say and persuade themselves that they have seen God and received God, although according to his deity he is invisible, and according to his humanity he is placed outside this world. But if you ask the teachers how the essential body of Jesus Christ is present to their eyes, hands and mouths, they will answer: in an invisible, impalpable and insensible mode. But if this is so, must not, I beg you, the three principal and indubitable articles of our Christian faith be declared false?

units.la: Primus est articulus Filij Dei incarnationis, assumpta in vnitatem personæ vera nostra natura, anima nimirum verè humana, & humano corpore, vero corpore: vtroque in se finito, ani-
units.tr: The first is the article of the incarnation of the Son of God: our true nature being taken up into the unity of his person, namely a truly human soul and a human body, a true body, each finite in itself, the soul

units.la: Eorum exempla refutatio qui quærunt adhuc Christi humanitate in his terris. anima videlicet proprietate sua spirituali, nulli subiecta dimensioni & inuisibili: corpore vero tribus suis dimensionibus praedito, altitudine, longitudine & crassitie, ac proinde visibili & palpabili: locoque aliquo secundum suam quantitatem comprehenso. Tale igitur fuit Iesu Christi corpus, vt tota historia Euangelica nobis id testatur à conceptione in vtero Virgineo vsque ad eius Ascensionem & in posterum. Ex quo e duobus alterum sequatur necesse est, aut tale adhuc hodie existere, aut immutatum, ac inuisibile & impalpabile factum. Nec enim vtrumque simul in se ipso esse potest, quum hae qualitates e diametro sint inter se repugnantes. Praeterea, si corpus istud essentialiter praesens est, non tot locis quot sunt ciboria, quotque à Sacrificulis Catholicis Romanis Missae celebrantur, sed duobus tantum diuersis eodem tempore locis, necessario statuendum est corpus istud ex finito factum infinitum, ac proinde corpus amplius non esse, sed ex nefaria damnataque Eutychetis opinione, Humanitatem factam Deitatem, quod sola sit infinita Deitas: quod ne Angelicae quidem spirituali naturae, aut humanae animae tribui potest. Manifeste autem manifestumque in aeternum verum corpus ex eo apparet, quod ab eius Ascensu visus est in coelis à D. Stephano Act. 7. 56. & ab Apostolo in tertium coelum rapto. 1. Cor. 12. 2. & 15. 8.
units.tr: Refutation of those who still seek the humanity of Christ on these earth: the soul, namely, with its spiritual property, subject to no dimension and invisible; the body, however, endowed with its three dimensions, height, length and thickness, and therefore visible and palpable, and contained in some place according to its quantity. Such, then, was the body of Jesus Christ, as the whole Gospel history testifies to us, from his conception in the Virgin's womb to his Ascension and beyond. From this one of two things must necessarily follow: either it still exists today in such a form, or it has been changed and made invisible and impalpable. For both cannot be in him at the same time, since these qualities are directly opposed to one another. Moreover, if that body is essentially present not in as many places as there are ciboria, and as many as the Roman Catholic sacrificing priests celebrate Mass in, but in two different places at the same time, it must necessarily be held that this body has gone from finite to infinite, and therefore is no longer a body, but, from the damnable and condemned opinion of Eutyches, that the humanity has been made deity, since only the deity is infinite; and this cannot be attributed even to the spiritual nature of the angels or to the human soul. Moreover, that the true body is eternal and manifest appears plainly from the fact that after his Ascension it was seen in heaven by Stephen (Acts 7:56) and by the apostle who was caught up into the third heaven (1 Cor. 12:2; 15:8).

units.la: Reliquae enim illae apparitiones in terris Apostolo exhibitae, Act. 9. 9. & 10. & 22. 17. &
units.tr: For those other appearances shown to the apostle on earth (Acts 9:9, 10; 22:17) and

units.la: M. iiij. 23. II. visiones tantùm fuerunt intellectuales. Deinde considerationem idem est ex eo quod differte Scriptura testatur fore in illo secùdo suo aduentu quem exspectamus conspicuum, & visum iri. Act. i. ii. Matth. 24. 30. & 26. 64. Ioh. 19. 37. Denique si aliter foret, non amplius in cœlo fratrem haberemus: falsaque eius esset resurrectio & cmentita, corpore videlicet ab ipsa non glorificato sed abolito: ac proinde eo quod tam excellenter Apostolus disputat 1. Corinth. 15. de incorruptione & gloria corporum nostrorum suscitatorum vt Iesu Christo capiti nostro fiant conformia, prorsus vano & irrito futuro:electis per resurrectionem hac ratione non adducendis ad gloriam cœlestem, secundum mensuram eorum, sed capitis instar ἀνθρώπου euasuris. Et, vt rem illam in pauca conferam, hæc fuit omnium seculorum Ecclesiæ Christianæ communi consensu recepta doctrina, gloriam quidem cœlestem humanitatem Christi vitæ huius animalis infirmitatibus, & qualitatibus quas ad implendam nostram redemptionem suscepera exuisse: sed naturæ substantiam, putà proprietates essentiales, quibus corpus verè corpus est, non ademisse.
units.tr: M. iiij. 23. II. were merely intellectual visions. Next, the same follows from the consideration that Scripture testifies that at his second coming, which we await, he will be seen and visible (Acts 1:11; Matt. 24:30; 26:64; John 19:37). Finally, if it were otherwise, we would no longer have a brother in heaven; his resurrection would be false and feigned, since the body would then not be glorified but abolished. Consequently, what the apostle argues so excellently in 1 Corinthians 15 concerning the incorruption and glory of our raised bodies, that they should be made conformable to Jesus Christ our head, would be entirely vain and void, and the elect would not, by such a resurrection, be brought to heavenly glory according to their measure, but would escape as a man in the manner of the head. And, to sum up the matter briefly, this was the doctrine received by the common consent of the Church of Christ in all ages: that the humanity of Christ, in heavenly glory, has put off the infirmities and qualities of this animal life which he took up to accomplish our redemption, but has not removed the substance of his nature, that is, the essential properties by which a body is truly a body.

units.la: Alter articulus errorem de quo agimus condemnans, Ascensio realis est Domini visibilis & veritissima, qua Iesus Christus, verè quòd ad humanitatem, relictis terris, supra cœlos omnes cuectus est, quibus velut in folio continetur & ad ultimum usque suum aduentum regnet. Nam alioqui dicendum esset, nullam Ascensione factam esse loci mutationem: ac proinde illusoriam fuisse Ascensionem, qua ex visibili, invisibilis, ex palpabili, non palpabilis, euaserit.
units.tr: The second article, condemning the error we are discussing, is the real and most true visible Ascension of the Lord, by which Jesus Christ, truly as to his humanity, having left the earth, was carried above all the heavens, in which he is contained as if in a fixed place, and there reigns until his final coming. For otherwise it would have to be said that the Ascension involved no change of place, and so the Ascension would have been illusory, by which he passed from visible to invisible, and from palpable to non-palpable.

units.la: Tertius est, quo credimus venturum e coelis, vivos & mortuos iudicaturum. Nam si iam in his terris realiter & substantialiter praesens est, necessario concludendum est iam ipsum advenisse, aut terris nunquam excessisse, diéque illo ultimo Aduentum eius fore, non vt ex loco in alium veniat, sed tantum vt ex invisibili fiat iterum visibilis, & ex impalpabili palpabilis.
units.tr: The third article is that by which we believe he will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead. For if he is already really and substantially present on this earth, it must necessarily be concluded either that he has already come, or that he never left the earth, and that on that last day his coming will not be a coming from one place to another, but only that he will become visible again from invisible, and palpable from impalpable.

units.la: En quibus nos contradictionibus & mendaciis eorum imaginationes inuoluant, qui deuotionis praetextu, quodque fides sensibus humanis sit longe superior, ex Sacramentali praesentia, quae Intellectum respicit non autem sensus corporeos: quaeque nos ab inferioribus istis euehit ad superna, fidem nostram euerterunt, & verum Sacramentorum vsum sustulerunt, terrę coelum miscentes, & in istis inferioribus nos detinentes, quum Deus ad se nos, tum Sacrosancto verbo, tum vsu Sacramentorum legitimo, sursum vocet. Frustra vero excipiant, Physice nos non autem Theologice de Christi corpore disputare. Contra enim vera e sacris Scripturis hausta Theologia docet nos ita de Christo, vestigia etiam ipsius legentes, loqui, hoc eodem argumento sui corporis veritatem asserente, Luc.24.39, Frustrà item nos Dei Omnipotentiam abnegare: Nec enim ipsa cum eius veritate pugnat, qu1 duo contradictoria simul velle non potest, quòd mentiri non possit, ex duabus autem contradictoriis alteram esse falsam, tum natura tum Theologia docet. Cæterum tantùm abest vt absentia corporis Iesu Christi(supra cœlos omnes existentis & non alibi) ab Ecclesia in terris versanti & non alibi separationem inuehat membrorum à capite, vt contrà nostris sensibus appareat longè magis admiranda & incomprehensibilis in illa spirituali, innarrabili, & virtutis ac efficaciæ plena coniunctione & vnione capitis cum membris, tanto licet interiecto locorum interuallo, quàm in præsentia illa essentiali in cœlo & terra tótque diuersis locis simul. Quid enim Dei omnipotentia iuuat, ad duo simul vnienda, si vtrumque realiter & essentialiter coniungitur, hoc etiam concedo ex duobus alterum inuisibiliter adesse, nempe Christi corpus, alterum verò visibiliter, nostras putà personas præsentes esse? Ex superioribus igitur istud tandem conclu-dendum, copoream Filij Dei manifestationem à sua in terris natiuitate exordium habuisse, & eius Ascensione finitam esse, ad Ecclesiæ suæ summam vtilitatem & ædificationem.
units.tr: See with what contradictions and lies those who, under the pretext of devotion, and because faith is far superior to human senses, have overturned our faith by means of a sacramental presence which regards the understanding and not the bodily senses, and which, they say, lifts us from these lower things to the higher, have wrapped up our imaginations! They have destroyed the true use of the sacraments, mixing heaven with earth and holding us in these lower things, when God calls us upward, both by his most holy Word and by the lawful use of the sacraments. Nor do they succeed when they object that we dispute about the body of Christ physically and not theologically. For a theology drawn from the true sacred Scriptures teaches us to speak of Christ in this way, following even his footsteps, since he asserts the truth of his body by this very argument (Luke 24:39). Equally vain is their charge that we deny the omnipotence of God. For this does not clash with his truth, since he cannot will two contradictories at the same time, because he cannot lie; and nature and theology both teach that of two contradictories one must be false. Moreover, the absence of the body of Jesus Christ (who exists above all the heavens and nowhere else) does not so much introduce a separation of the members from the head among the Church that lives on earth and nowhere else, as it makes plain to our senses that the union of the head with the members, in that spiritual, unspeakable, and vigorous union, is far more admirable and incomprehensible, even with so great an interval of place between them, than it would be in that essential presence in heaven and on earth and in so many different places at once. For what use is God's omnipotence in uniting two things at once, if both are joined really and essentially? I grant this as well: one of two things is present invisibly, namely the body of Christ, and the other visibly, namely our persons. From the foregoing, therefore, this must finally be concluded: the bodily manifestation of the Son of God began with his birth on earth and was ended by his Ascension, for the greatest use and edification of his Church.

units.la: Iam igitur propiùs ad tertiæ manifestationis ipsius considerationem accedamus, cuius respectu secundum Humanitatem discedens à nobis, se nobiscum esse & fore dixit ad mundi vsque consummationem, Matth. 28. v. 20. in sacro-
units.tr: Let us now therefore draw nearer to the consideration of his third manifestation, in respect of which, departing from us according to his humanity, he said that he would be with us until the end of the world (Matt. 28:20), in the sacred

units.la: Ampla consideratio tertiæ manifestationis Iesu Christi. sacrosancto nimirū Verbo, & duobus Sacramentis Baptismo & sancta Cœna, qua quidem manifestatione minimè capitis oculis exhibetur conspiciendus, quibus eum multi quidem, sed frustrà sunt intuiti, sed fidei, ipsum in sacrosancto Verbo & Sacramentis intuenti & complectenti, ratione quadam & virtute spirituali, nunquam eos qui nec ad lœuam nec ad dextram aberrant decipiente.Hæc verò manifestatio priore illa secundáque longè est excellentior quarum vtraque corporea fuit, non sine causa dicente Iesu Christo, Thomæ incredulitatem arguente, isti corporeæ & sensuali præsentiæ nimium inhærentis, beatos fore qui crederent in ipsum etiamsi non viderent.Nam quòd ad primam attinet, multum abest quin veteris fœderis Verbum & Sacramenta, ac ne Prophetiæ quidem ipsæ, salutis nostræ mysterium aperuerint, cœlósque patefecerint, tanta perfectione & luce quanta Verbū Euangelij & Sacramēta Christianis exhibēt. Quòd ad corpoream autem manifestatione attinet quā secunda diximus, aio perinde esse atque, vt quæ sunt in hominis penetralibus scrutanti non sufficit oculis eum intueri, sed loqui eum & intelligi necesse est, immo etiam non semper ore ipso vox educta requiritur, sed sufficit scripto testatam esse voluntatem: ita de Scriptis Apostolorum & Euangelistarum prorsus eadem ratione iudicandum esse, quibus (admiranda cum certitudine & Maiestate diuini per eos loquentis scribentisque Spiritus) quicquid de Patris ad salutem nostram voluntate sciendum erat plenissime continetur. Absit autem ista tabulam mutam cogitemus, sed viuam potius picturam, in qua Seruator illenoster plenissime perfectissimeque nobis depingitur, vt loquitur Apostolus, Galat.3. verf.1. in qua fidem oportet Christum contemplari, & completi per virtutem Spiritus Dei, vt in nobis copiose per verbum istud in aeternum inhabitet. Colos.3.16. Sic igitur ad viuum depictus, & nihil minus quam mutus, dissimillimus est Crucifixorum illorum, aliarumque manu hominum factarum imaginum,in quibus ab hominibus effictae res mortuae tantum conspiciuntur, nec possunt aliud mortalibus conferre, quàm alicuius historiae memoriam refricare. Sed quorsum tandem, si nullus alius superest fructus. Nam quid obsecro iuuit carnifices profanolque alios omnes Christi crucifixi conspectus? Multo vero magis quid mortis & passionis Dominicae memoria iuuat mortales conspecto Crucifixo nisi simul quis ex hac morte fructus sit colligendus doceamur? Quis autem hoc a Crucifixo sperct, multo, a quo minime Christianos homines, sed facile quidem de Christianis idololatras fieri posse certum est? Et istud, proh dolor, iam multorum seculorum experientia docuit & adhuc docet, non frustra toties tamque disertis verbis Domino se in vllis imaginibus coli prohibente.
units.tr: A full consideration of the third manifestation of Jesus Christ: namely, in the most holy Word and in the two sacraments, Baptism and the holy Supper. This manifestation is not presented to the eyes of the head, so that he can be seen; many have gazed upon him with bodily eyes in vain. Rather, it is presented to faith, which beholds and embraces him in the most holy Word and the sacraments, by a certain spiritual reason and power, a power that never deceives those who do not wander either to the left or to the right. This manifestation is far more excellent than the first and second, both of which were bodily. Not without cause did Jesus Christ, rebuking Thomas's unbelief, say that those are blessed who believe in him even though they do not see him, since Thomas clung too much to a bodily and sensible presence. As for the first manifestation, it is far from true that the Word and the sacraments of the old covenant, or even the prophecies themselves, opened the mystery of our salvation and laid open the heavens with such perfection and light as the Word of the Gospel and the sacraments present to Christians. As for the bodily manifestation, which we called the second, I say that it is much the same: just as one who searches the secrets of a man's heart cannot be satisfied by looking at him with his eyes, but must hear him speak and understand him, and indeed the voice need not always be drawn out of the living mouth, but it is enough that his will is attested in writing, so the Scriptures of the Apostles and Evangelists must be judged in exactly the same way. In them (with the wonderful certainty and majesty of the divine Spirit speaking and writing through them) whatever had to be known about the Father's will for our salvation is most fully contained. But let us not think of this as a dumb tablet; rather, it is a living picture, in which that Saviour of ours is most fully and perfectly portrayed to us, as the Apostle says, Gal. 3. v. 1, in which we ought to contemplate Christ by faith, and be filled through the power of the Spirit of God, so that he may dwell richly in us through this word forever, Col. 3. v. 16. Thus depicted to the life, and by no means mute, he is wholly unlike those crucifixes and other images made by human hands, in which the dead things fashioned by men are only looked at, and can offer mortals nothing more than a reminder of some history. But to what end, if no other fruit remains? For what, I beg you, does the sight of Christ crucified profit executioners and all other profane men? Much more, what does the memory of Christ's death and passion profit mortals who look upon the crucifix, unless we are taught what fruit is to be gathered from this death? And who could hope for this from a crucifix, since it is certain that it can make idolaters of Christians, though it can by no means make Christians of men? And this, alas, the experience of many centuries has taught and still teaches, and not in vain, since the Lord has so often and so plainly forbidden himself to be worshipped in any images.

units.la: En igitur apparitionem qua se Dominus suis electis patefecit, & ad finem seculorum est patefacturus: vt hanc tandem suo tempore quarta illa vltima & perfectissima manifestatio excipiat, in qua, tum oculis mentis illustratæ, tum corporeis oculis incorruptione indutis, nos, nos inquam integri, non amplius vitam animalem sed spiritualem viuentes, & hodie nobis incomprehensibilem, fumus illum qualis est conspecturi, in gloria & Maiestate sua, quum Deus erit omnia in omnibus: vt pluribus hæc Apostolus persequitur. 1. Corinth. 15. ad cuius felicitatis fruitionem Deum Optim. Maxim. qui nos ad eam vocauit supplicibus votis oremus, vt nos etiam breui pro sua immensa misericordia deducat.
units.tr: Here, then, is the appearance by which the Lord has revealed himself to his elect, and which he is to reveal again at the end of the ages; so that at its proper time this fourth, last and most perfect manifestation may follow, in which, with the eyes of the mind illumined and with bodily eyes clothed in incorruption, we, we, I say, whole, no longer living an animal but a spiritual life, shall behold him as he is, who is for us today incomprehensible, in his glory and majesty, when God will be all in all; as the Apostle pursues these things at length, 1 Cor. 15. Let us pray with earnest vows to God, the best and greatest, who has called us to the enjoyment of that blessedness, that by his immense mercy he may soon lead us to it as well.

units.la: HOMILIA VICESIMATERTIA. LVC. 23.
units.tr: HOMILY TWENTY-FOURTH. LUKE 23.

units.la: 8. Herodes autem viso Iesu, gauisus est valde: nam à multo tempore cupiebat eum videre, eo quòd audiuisset multa de eo: & sperabat se signum aliquod visurum ab eo fieri.
units.tr: 8. Now when Herod saw Jesus, he was exceedingly glad: for he had desired to see him of a long time, because he had heard many things of him: and he hoped to have seen some miracle done by him.

units.la: 9. Interrogauit autem eum multo sermone: sed ipse nihil ei respondit.
units.tr: 9. Then he questioned him in many words; but he answered him nothing.

units.la: 10. Adstabant autem primarij Sacerdotes & Scribae, magna contentione eum accusantes.
units.tr: 10. And the chief priests and scribes stood and vehemently accused him.

units.la: 11. Herodes autem cum militibus suis, quum eum pro nihilo habuisset, & illusisset ei, amictum veste splendida remisit ad Pilatum.
units.tr: 11. And Herod with his men of war set him at nought, and mocked him, and arrayed him in a gorgeous robe, and sent him again to Pilate.

units.la: 12. Et factifunt amici inter se Pilatus & Herodes eo ipso die: nam antea inimici erant inter se.
units.tr: 12. And the same day Pilate and Herod were made friends together: for before they were at enmity between themselves.

units.la: HISTORIA quam explicandam aggredimur, continet omne genus contumeliarum quibus Iesus Christus Dominus noster exceptus est ab Herode, Diuina Prouidentia summa & admiranda sic omnia dispensante, ut de nostrae redemptionis perfectione certiores fieremus, sicut superiore sermone copiose docuimus. Dicitur igitur Herodes viso Iesu valde gauisus: licet eum revera minime conspiceret, nec intus (quod erat praecipuum, in quo perditus iste prorsus caecutiebat) nec foris etiam, nisi admodum deformem & abiectum: exteriore forma nequaquam cum excellentia & dignitate illi propria congruente: qualem etiam nobis Esaias depingit, Esa. 53. 2. & 3. non tantum assumpta serui forma sed etiam in illa sese ipsum exinanientem Phil. 2.7. Nec vero dubium quin hic Christi habitus, praeterquam quod Herodes minime quaerebat, quod erat tamen in Christo quaerendum, etiam de opinione quam fama perlatis ad eius aures miraculis à Christo editis de ipso conceperat, multum detraxerit. Et tamen habitus ille satis cum admonebat spontaneam istam abiectionem esse, & ad causæ illius inuestigationem impellebat. At eum hæc cura non tangebat, nec Herodem Magnum illum Tyrannum patrem eius, puerorum Bethleemiticorū σαρκοφόντων. Non mirum igitur minimè vidisse illum quod videbat vt erat videndum, & contempsisse quod satis laudari æstimarique non poterat. Hanc sibi ipsis iniuriam intulerunt, qui splendorem illum cœlestem in Christi doctrina tot insignibus miraculis confirmata micantem cum stupore admirati, vltrò sibi ipsis offendiculum acceperant illum vt fabrū fabri lignarij filium considerantes. Matth. 13. 55. & Marc. 6. 3. Itidem qui in patria ex qua putabant oriundum hærebant. Ioh. 1. 46. & 7. 41. Et denique qui Apostolis solam literarum imperitiam, & è plebe conditionem exprobrabant.
units.tr: The history we now take up in explanation contains every kind of insult with which Jesus Christ our Lord was received by Herod, the highest and most admirable Divine Providence so arranging all things that we might be more certain of the perfection of our redemption, as we taught at length in the previous sermon. It is said, then, that Herod was exceedingly glad when he saw Jesus: although in truth he did not see him at all, neither inwardly (which was the main thing, and in which this utterly lost man was completely blind), nor even outwardly, except as very misshapen and abject, his outward form in no way agreeing with the excellence and dignity proper to him, such as Isaiah also portrays for us (Isa. 53:2–3), not only the form of a servant having been taken, but also he emptying himself in it (Phil. 2:7). Nor is there any doubt that this appearance of Christ, apart from the fact that Herod did not seek what nevertheless was to be sought in Christ, also greatly detracted from the opinion which, from the miracles wrought by Christ brought to his ears by report, he had formed of him. And yet that appearance was enough to warn that this self-chosen abjection was something else, and to urge him to investigate its cause. But this care did not touch him, nor did it touch his father, the great tyrant Herod, murderer [σαρκοφόντων] of the children of Bethlehem. It is no wonder, then, that he did not see what was to be seen as it was, and despised what could not be sufficiently praised and esteemed. Those who, marvelling with astonishment at that heavenly splendour shining in Christ's doctrine confirmed by so many remarkable miracles, had of their own accord taken offence, considering him as the son of a carpenter, the craftsman's son (Matt. 13:55; Mark 6:3), did the same. So too did those who clung to the idea that he was from the homeland they supposed (John 1:46; 7:41). And finally, those who reproached the Apostles for mere lack of learning and for their common condition.

units.la: Et ne procul istiusmodi exempla vestigemus, qua re hodie tot magni viri Philosopho-rum, & Græcorum oratorum Latinorumque omni sapientia & eloquentia huius seculi exornatis scriptis affuceti, magis à salutis cognitione, quàm simplicitate sermonis Prophetarum & Apostolorum deterrentur? Quamobrem etiam sæpe videas homines istiusmodi parùm de Religionis controuersiis solicitos, ad alios hanc curam reiicere, de rebus istis, aut tanquam Academicos aut etiam plane α᾽θεὼς ἐπι-χείρ. Hodie vero quot Romani Cleri multitudinem, & externum ornatum, & cultum tam multis ritibus insignem, templaque auro, argento & margaritis fulgentia, mirantes, & ea cum exiguo nostro numero, & simplicitate comparantes, Iesum Christum Bethleemæ in stabulo natum obliuiscuntur? & Hierosolymis crucifixum? in mundo versantem non habuisse vbi caput inclinaret? Luc.9.58. D.Petrum & D.Iohannem eleemosynam pauperi facturos, nec aurum nec argentum habuisse? Act.3.6. D. Paulum manibus suis vt plurimum sibi victum quæsiuisse? Act.20.34. Apostolos fuisse piscatores? maioris notę hominibus ad nuptias venire recusantibus, claudos & mancos in viis & plateis inopia domicilij manētes in aulam conuiuij introduci, Luc.14.21. Dominum ipsum gratias agere Deo Patri, quod mysteria sua detexisset infantibus quę sapientibus & intelligentibus abscondissët? Matt.11.25. Dominum elegisse mundi infirma, imò quæ nō sunt vt aboleret ea quæ sunt? Nequis autem excipiat humilem illam Ecclesiæ conditionem fuisse tantùm Ecclesiæ primordiis propriam, audiat contrà dicentem Dominum Regnum Dei non venturum μὴ ... Luc.17.20. An verò merito nobis hæc insignia per Dei gratiam aptemus (quanquam per fe nec diuitiæ, nec paupertas veri falsi-ue Christianismi notæ sint, sed doctrinæ veritas aut falsitas) iudicio verbi diuini semper stetimus: & audemus, mus, Deo laus huius rei testes aduocare tot è media plebe abiectorum virorum in mediis ignibus excellentes confessiones: quibus non irritum esse quod suis Dominus promisit aduersus magnos Rabinos & Doctores satis abundè testatum fecit.
units.tr: And, not to seek such examples far off, why today do so many great men, trained in the polished writings of the philosophers, of the Greek orators and of the Latin orators, with all the wisdom and eloquence of this age, get turned away more by the knowledge of salvation than by the plain speech of the Prophets and Apostles? Hence you will often see men of this kind, little concerned about the controversies of religion, leave this care to others, treating these matters either as Academics or even plainly as atheists [ἀθεὼς ἐπιχείρ.]. Today, indeed, how many, marvelling at the multitude of the Roman clergy, their external ornament, and a worship so notable for so many rites, and at temples gleaming with gold, silver and pearls, and comparing these with our small number and simplicity, forget Jesus Christ born in a stable at Bethlehem, and crucified at Jerusalem, who while living in the world had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58)? Forget that Peter and John, when they were to give alms to a poor man, had neither gold nor silver (Acts 3:6)? That Paul, for the most part, sought his own food with his own hands (Acts 20:34)? That the Apostles were fishermen? That when men of higher rank refused to come to the wedding, the lame and maimed, remaining in the streets and lanes for lack of a dwelling, were brought into the hall of the feast (Luke 14:21)? That the Lord himself gave thanks to God the Father because he had revealed his mysteries to infants, which he had hidden from the wise and understanding (Matt. 11:25)? That the Lord chose the weak things of the world, indeed the things that are not, that he might bring to nothing the things that are (1 Cor. 1:27–28)? But lest anyone take that humble condition of the Church to have been proper only to the Church's beginnings, let him hear the Lord saying on the contrary that the kingdom of God does not come [μὴ ...] (Luke 17:20). But whether we rightly apply these marks to ourselves through the grace of God (although in themselves neither wealth nor poverty are marks of true or false Christianity, but the truth or falsity of the doctrine is), we have always stood by the judgment of the divine Word; and we dare, to God's praise, to call as witnesses of this matter so many excellent confessions, made in the midst of the fires by men of the common people and cast down, which have sufficiently and abundantly shown that what the Lord promised against the great Rabbis and Teachers was not in vain.

units.la: Nihilominus, vt ad historiam reuertamur, Herodes abiectum illum Iesum Christum statum intuitus, & memor eorum quæ fide dignis testibus de illo acceperat, aliquid incisse in eo putauit, & curiosus simul ac profanus miraculum ab eodem expetiuit: cuiusmodi plurosque videas hodie miracula flagitantes: alios, multis de isto, vt vocant, Euangelio fama ad se perlatis, aliquam concionem audire cóscientes, velut histrionicum quid essent audituri: sed frustrà tamen, nisi quòd hac ratione Deus ad se quosdam allicit, curiositate illa in studium veritatis immutata. Quoniam igitur miracula, sunt noua quædam & inusitata metem intuentium superantia, ad stuporem vsque, non mirum est Herodem curiosum simul ac prophanum, tam multis ad se fama perlatis, aliquod expetiisse miraculum: nullis præsertim à Iohanne Baptista, licet tam insigni viro, miraculis editis, Ioh.10. 41. At quum fieri non posset quin vt de miraculis ita de doctrina Iesu Christi aliquid audiuisset, qui sit vt hac neglecta sit tantum illius appendicis studiosus? Nempe erat illi molesta doctrina ad quam Iohannes homines ablegabat, ex miraculis autem voluptatem quandam expectabat.
units.tr: Nevertheless, to return to the history: Herod, looking upon that abject Jesus Christ, and mindful of what he had received about him from trustworthy witnesses, thought that something was to be gained from him, and, curious at once and profane, sought a miracle from him. Such people you may see today demanding miracles in the same way: others, having heard in many reports about this so-called Gospel, go to hear some sermon, expecting to hear something theatrical; but in vain, except that in this way God draws some to himself, turning that curiosity into a zeal for truth. Since, then, miracles are certain new and unusual things which surpass the minds of onlookers, even to astonishment, it is no wonder that Herod, curious and profane at once, when so many reports had come to him, sought some miracle: especially since no miracles had been done by John the Baptist, although he was so remarkable a man (John 10:41). But since it could not be that he had not heard something of the doctrine of Jesus Christ as well as of his miracles, how is it that, neglecting this, he was eager only for that appendage? Surely the doctrine to which John sent men was disagreeable to him, while from the miracles he expected some pleasure.

units.la: N. j.
units.tr: N. j.

units.la: Praeterea, si tam erat miraculorum cupidus, cur in hoc tempus distulit, quum Christus vt plurimum fit in Galilaea commoratus? Nimirum metuebat ne, vt a Iohanne prius, sic a Christo coargueretur, quem propterea capitali odio persequebatur: Luc.13.31.adde dedignatam eius Altitudinem,vt loquuntur hodie fabrum quaerere, & eius doctrinam audire.Eti vt plerumque summae dignitatis viri, summa Dei sibi oblata domi beneficia, atque adeo propriam salutem,respuant.
units.tr: Moreover, if he was so eager for miracles, why did he put it off until this time, when Christ had for the most part stayed in Galilee? Doubtless he feared that he would be rebuked by Christ as he had been before by John, whom for that reason he persecuted with deadly hatred (Luke 13:31). Add that he disdained his lowliness, as men today say when they seek a carpenter and hear his teaching. And, as men of the highest rank commonly do, he rejected the great benefits of God offered to him at home, and indeed his own salvation.

units.la: Porro quum maximi momenti sint in miraculis abusus,quibus si aliis vllis Satan ad dementandos homines abutitur,non alienum erit quid de hac re sentiendum sit,semel explicare. Etsi igitur vox ista miraculi possit aliquando de iis omnibus quae in admirationem rapiunt accipi: proprie tamen intelligenda est de eo quod non tantum inusitato & penitus peregrino modo fit,sed virtute quae longe potentiam & vim naturalem omnem superat,vt exempli gratia, Sol iussus subsistere Iof. 10.13. umbra eiusdem retrograda 2.Reg.20.11.& innumerabilia multa tota passim Scriptura, praesertim vero in Iesu Christi & Apostolorum historia, conspicua.
units.tr: Furthermore, since the abuses of miracles are of the greatest moment, with which Satan abuses them to deceive men more than with any other means, it will not be out of place to set out once what ought to be thought about this matter. Although, therefore, the word "miracle" can sometimes be taken of all those things which carry us away into wonder, it is properly to be understood of that which happens not merely in an unusual and wholly strange manner, but by a power that far surpasses all natural power and force: for example, the sun commanded to stand still (Josh. 10:13), the shadow turned back (2 Kings 20:11), and countless other things conspicuous throughout Scripture, but especially in the history of Jesus Christ and the Apostles.

units.la: Hinc sequitur vnius esse Dei propriam miraculorum editionem, in cuius vnius potestate sit, vt semel causas omnes naturales creauit,eadem etiam immutare, immo penitus abolere. Quam potestatem sic habet proprium vt eam nulli rei creatae communicet, relioalioquin creata in Deum euasura.Pfal.72.18.& 136.4. Quoties igitur ad alicuius editione mi- raculi causis vti naturalibus ei visum est, vt ve- to Occidentali ad locustas rollendas,Exod.10. 19.& ad maris fundum exsiccandum.Exod.14. 21. non aliqua causa naturali ordinaria ventus ille suscitatus spirauit : sed Dei decreto extra- ordinarie causam naturalem commouentis Ita singulis diebus Man in aere creatum est. Eadem illa diuina virtus, ranas in Ægyptum, muscas & grandinem immiíit, extraordinarie causas naturales,seu immediate vi sua,seu per bonos suos aut malos spiritus mouens. At quum aquas in sanguinem, Mosis virgam in serpentem commutauit, aut quum in genere tot sunt à Christo verbo solo edita miracula, illa non tantum extraordinaria virtute, sed e- tiam ἀντιξυσικῇ contigerunt: qualis etiam eius fuit sola Virtute Altissimi in Virginis vtero conceptio. Sic quum vel Angelorum vel hominum in similibus operibus ἀντιξυσικοῖς exequendis vsus est ministerio, minime quidem illis suam potentiam communicauit,teite Petro,Act. 13. 12. & 16. sed tantum illis administris vsus est suæ voluntatis & ordinationis,cuifc causæ omnes fecundæ subiiciunt, Dominum in iis quorum vtitur opera cognoscentes. Non igitur virga Mosis, non ipse Moses in Ægypto miracula ediderunt,sed illius sola virtus à quo virgam acceperat, vt ipsi tandem Magi fateri coguntur, Exod.8.19. Non etiam vmbra Petri fanati sunt ægroti, quum ne Petrus ipse quidem ediderit miracula. Idcirco fideles Dei servi precibus ad Deum in rebus istis confugerunt. Qui si iubere visi sunt (vt contigisse videmus Iof.10.12.2.Reg.1.10.& 12.) minime potestatem illam sibi nec mediate nec immediate tribuentes, sed tanquam Dei nuntij, imo tanquam os ipsius iusserunt. Immo licet Θεάνθρωπος sit Christus, ac proinde Creator & res creata simul in vnitate personae, & nunquam duae illae naturae separandae sint, distinguendae tamen sunt in suis operationibus in eodem miraculo simul concurrentibus. Humanitas igitur Christi Lazarum ex sepulchro foras exire iussit: at Deitas eius animam corpori Lazari reiunxit. Manus quidem Christi Petri socrum attigit, & caeci oculos: sed eius Deitas febrim expulit, & novos oculos creavit. Non vestis Cananeae fluxum sanguinis compescuit, sed virtus Deitatis Iesu Christi manas ab eo: quod de reliquis omnibus editis a Iesu Christo miraculis & de ipsius resurrectione nominatim est intelligendum.
units.tr: From this it follows that the working of miracles belongs to God alone, in whose power it lies, having once created all natural causes, to change them as well, or indeed to abolish them altogether. This power is so proper to him that he imparts it to no created thing, otherwise the creature would become God (Ps. 72:18; 136:4). Whenever, therefore, it has seemed good to him to use natural causes in the working of some miracle, as when he raised the west wind to roll away the locusts (Exod. 10:19) and to dry up the bed of the sea (Exod. 14:21), that wind did not blow from some ordinary natural cause, but by God's decree moving the natural cause extraordinarily. So too the manna was created daily in the air. That same divine power sent frogs into Egypt, flies and hail, moving natural causes extraordinarily, whether by its own power immediately, or through its good or evil spirits. But when he changed the waters into blood, or Moses' rod into a serpent, or when in general so many miracles were wrought by Christ by his word alone, those things happened not only by extraordinary power but also [ἀντιφυσικῇ] against nature: such was also the conception in the Virgin's womb by the power of the Most High alone. So when he has used the ministry of angels or of men in carrying out similar works [ἀντιφυσικοῖς], he has by no means communicated his power to them (as with Peter: Acts 13:12; 16:...), but has used them only as instruments of his will and ordinance, to which all secondary causes are subject, while those who know the Lord in those whose work he uses. Therefore the rod of Moses, and Moses himself, did not work miracles in Egypt, but the power alone of him from whom he had received the rod did so, as the Magicians themselves are at last compelled to confess (Exod. 8:19). Nor were the sick healed by Peter's shadow, although Peter himself did not work miracles. For this reason the faithful servants of God had recourse to prayer to God in these matters. Those who seemed to command (as we see it happened: Josh. 10:12; 2 Kings 1:10, 12), in no way ascribing that power to themselves either mediately or immediately, but as messengers of God, indeed as his very mouth, commanded. Moreover, although Christ is the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], and so Creator and created thing together in the unity of person, and those two natures are never to be separated, yet they are to be distinguished in their operations which concur together in the same miracle. Thus the humanity of Christ bade Lazarus come forth from the sepulchre; but his Deity joined the soul again to the body of Lazarus. Christ's hand indeed touched Peter's mother-in-law and the eyes of the blind man; but his Deity drove out the fever and created new eyes. The garment of the Canaanite woman did not stop the flow of blood, but the power of the Deity of Jesus Christ went out from him. What must be understood of all the other miracles wrought by Jesus Christ, and of his resurrection in particular.

units.la: En igitur quae vera sint miracula falsis opposita, quae nimirum impostores venditant, & maligni spiritus imitantur.
units.tr: Here, then, are the true miracles, set against the false ones which impostors peddle and evil spirits imitate.

units.la: Impostorum autem tria genera. Nam alij manifeste falsi sunt, vt olim idolorum sacrificuli pecunia & largitionibus corrupti, ac eorum nutum & voluntatem a quibus consulebantur, oracula fingebant, artemque suam venditabant: quae tamen non sunt praeteriti tantum temporis praestigiae, quum nostro seculo culo non pauci sacrificuli similia miracula confinxerint, ad miseram plebeculam parrochialium idolorum autoritate & potentia decipiendam, detecta tandem ab accuratius intuentibus, & meritis poenis affecta deceptorum istorum fraude.
units.tr: There are three kinds of impostors. Some are plainly false, like the priests of the idols in former times, who were corrupted by money and gifts. They made up oracles according to the nod and will of those who consulted them, and sold their trade. Yet these are not tricks of past times only. In our own age not a few priests of this kind have devised similar miracles to deceive the wretched common folk by the authority and power of their parish idols. These deceptions were at last detected by those who looked more carefully, and the frauds of these deceivers were punished as they deserved.

units.la: Alij plebeculæ ignaræ dexteritate quadam & industria imponunt, vt solent histriones & ludiones illi quos Serlatanos dicũt, qui existimatur à vulgo edere miracula, licet mereʒ sint impostureʒ, aut sola corporis agilitas, aut naturales tantum rationes: quos tã impunè passim alieno viuere pestima conscientia nimium tolerant summo suo dedecore quibus potestas in illos animadvertendi data est.
units.tr: Others impose on ignorant common people by a certain dexterity and cleverness, as do those stage performers and jugglers whom they call charlatans. The crowd thinks they work miracles, though these are mere tricks, produced either by sheer bodily agility or by natural causes alone. People tolerate such men living at others' expense everywhere, and with great shame to themselves, though they have the power to punish them.

units.la: Tertium denique genus superiorum omnium pestimum est eorum quos vocant Magos & veneficos, quibus cum malignis spiritibus intercedit familiaritas, ac proinde digni qui tanquam Dei & humani generis hostes abominandi profligentur. Hic vero siquis roget quænam igitur à malignis illis spiritibus fiant miracula: paucis aio quum vera de quibus egimus miracula nonnihil ab vnius Dei virtute, ipsis Angelis & Sanctis Dei seruis incomunicabili proficiscantur, necessario etiam sequi malignis illis spiritibus iustiusmodi proprie dicta miracula potestatem edendi tribuentes, eos velut in Dei solium collocare: ad quem scopum collimarunt olim & adhuc collimant impuri spiritus, & consequuntur, in iis quos hodie vt olim etiam excæcarunt.
units.tr: Finally, the third kind, the worst of all, is that of those whom they call magicians and poisoners, with whom familiarity exists between them and evil spirits. Therefore they deserve to be abhorred and destroyed as enemies of God and of the human race. But if anyone asks what miracles are then worked by those evil spirits, I answer briefly. Since the true miracles we have discussed proceed partly from the power of the one God, which is incommunicable even to the angels and the saints, the evil spirits, it follows necessarily, would be granted the power of working such miracles properly so called, and so would be set, as it were, on the throne of God. This aim the impure spirits both aimed at in former times and still aim at now, and they attain it in those whom, as formerly, they have blinded today.

units.la: Semper igitur in istiusmodi malignorum spirituum miraculis falsitas inest, at non eiusdem generis. Illusiones enim tantum aliae sunt in hominum nonnunquam inhaerentes phantasia, quod saepe phreneticis visuuenire conspicimus, oculis videre se & auribus audire putantibus quod non est nisi sola imaginatione: cuiusmodi multa esse verisimile est quae falso sibi Magi & venefici vera esse persuadent, non minus tamen propterea detestandi quod cum malignis spiritibus communicent atque consentiant.
units.tr: Therefore falsehood is always present in the miracles of such evil spirits, but not of one kind. For some illusions cling to the imagination of men, as we often see happen to the mad, who think they see with their eyes and hear with their ears what exists only in imagination. It is likely that many such things are what magicians and poisoners falsely persuade themselves are true. They are no less to be detested on that account, because they have fellowship and agreement with evil spirits.

units.la: Quorundam vero maligni Spiritus ipsos exteriores sensus tantum fallunt, ut videre & audire sibi videantur, quod tamen in rerum natura non est, (specie tro illorum oculos tantum feriente, aut aliqua specie externa, ut ita delusus se in lupum commutatum arbitretur, & talis etiam forma conspicientibus exhibeatur: sunt enim in istis operibus admodum subtiles immundi illi Spiritus, modoque nobis incoprehensi, Deo laxante ipsis habenas, operantur. Et sane vehementer falluntur qui falsum esse & confictum sibi persuadent quicquid de istiusmodi visionibus nationum omnium & temporum historiae profanae monumentis perscripta reliquerunt: quum falsarum visionum pseudoprophetis vigilantibus aut dormientibus exhibitarum Sacrae Scripturae mentionem expressam faciant: & maxima ex parte invocationes mortuorum, & reliquiarum & imaginum adorationes, no ab alio fonte quam ab istis illusionibus manarint, fi fides iis ipsis adhibetur, qui talium illusionum historias auctoritatem ipsis conciliaturi, conscripserunt.
units.tr: But the evil spirits sometimes deceive only the outward senses, so that men seem to see and hear what is not in nature. They do this by striking the eyes with an image, or some external appearance, so that a man thus deluded thinks he has been changed into a wolf, and the same form is shown to onlookers. For those unclean spirits are very subtle in such works and work in ways beyond our grasp, God giving them free rein. And they are greatly mistaken who persuade themselves that whatever the monuments of profane history, in all nations and times, have written about such visions is false and made up. For Holy Scripture expressly mentions false visions shown by false prophets, whether awake or asleep. And for the most part, the invocations of the dead and the adorations of relics and images have arisen from no other source than these illusions, if credit is given to those who wrote histories of such illusions in order to win them authority.

units.la: In omnibus autem exemplis, quibus hæc confirmantur, insigne est & minime dubium exemplum apparitionis illius pseudoSamuelis à Pythonissa euocati Saulem alloquentis, & mortem illi prædicentis. 1.Sam.28.11. Quicquid enim nonnulli senserint, & scriptis mandarint, minime verum est, nec etiam verisimile Diabolum, (cuius nimirum intelligentia Pythonysa spectrum illud euocauit) tantum potuisse vt veri Samuelis quietem corporis aut animi perturbaret. Quod aperte satis historiæ tota series ostendit. Si enim verus Samuel euocatus esset, nec non tantum Pythonissæ, sed etiam ipsi Sauli, cui vocabatur, factus fuisset conspicuus.
units.tr: Among all the examples by which these points are confirmed, the notable and least doubtful one is that apparition of the pseudo-Samuel, summoned by the witch of Endor, who spoke to Saul and foretold his death (1 Sam. 28:11). For whatever some have thought and committed to writing, it is by no means true, nor even likely, that the devil (whose intelligence the witch summoned that phantom) could have disturbed the rest of body or mind of the true Samuel. The whole course of the story shows this plainly enough. For if the true Samuel had been summoned, he would have become visible not only to the witch but also to Saul himself, whom he was called to.

units.la: Addam aliquid amplius, prout iusto suo iudicio Deus laxas habenas Spiritui erroris permittit, non esse difficile malignis spiritibus cadauere abuti, & in eo ad aliquem eludendum loqui: non aliter ac lingua viuentium Dæmoniacorum vtitur. In quo tamen etiam inest illusio, re nimirum mortua, nec in se viua, nec loquente, viuentis hominis instar, sed maligno spiritu cadauere induto.
units.tr: I will add something more. Since God, by his just judgment, grants the spirit of error free rein, it is not difficult for evil spirits to misuse a corpse and speak through it to deceive someone, just as they use the tongue of living demoniacs.
