Yet even here there is illusion, since the thing is dead, not alive in itself, and does not speak as a living man does, but an evil spirit has clothed itself in a corpse.

units.la: Et hactenus quidem de malignorum spirituum illusionibus, quibus opponuntur visiones in quibus Deus bonorum sanctorumque Spirituum visus est ministerio sine fraude aut
units.tr: So far concerning the illusions of evil spirits, which are set against visions in which God, by the ministry of good and holy spirits, appeared without deceit or falsehood.

units.la: Cadauere possunt abuti diabolo ad loquendum.
units.tr: Devils can misuse a corpse to make it speak.

units.la: falsitate: quarum aliae quidem ecclaticae fuerunt, de quibus agit Apostolus, Act. 22. 17. & 2. Corin. 12. 3. aliae per somnium aut rationem aliam in imaginatione formatae, sed sine fraude tamen aut deliratione, quarum in Sacris exempla non pauca sunt. Alias autem reales visiones quod attinet, Angeli nunquam ludendis humanis sensibus in spectris apparuerunt. Deo contra virtute sua divina & ἀντιτυπικῇ vera ipsis adaptante corpora, & in iis veram articulatam vocem effingente: & ad visionis actum non autem ad nutriencia corpora edendi bibendique facultatem largiente. Quinetiam ipse Dei Filius, ante hypostaticam incarnationem cum duobus Angelis apparuit Abrahamo, & cum eo in vero corpore comedit ac bibit: non quidem in unitatem personae sibi adjuncto, sed ad illud tantum effectum adjuncto. Gen. 18. 13. Et Moses deinde in ardente rubo, Exod. 3. 2. & 4. ubi Angelus dicitur, non quidem in creatis spiritibus accessus: sed quod semper fuerit Patris verbum apud Ecclesiam, idcirco Admirabilis consiliarius nuncupatus. Esa. 9. 5. istis nimirum apparitionibus futurae suo tempore in unitatem personae in aeternum incarnationis minime dubiis testimoniisatque praeludiis.
units.tr: Of these falsehoods, some were ecstatic, the kind the Apostle speaks of at Acts 22. 17 and 2 Corin. 12. 3. Others were formed in the imagination through a dream or some other mental process, yet without deceit or delusion, and Scripture offers no small number of examples of these. As for real visions, angels never appeared in phantoms to mock human senses. Rather, God, by his divine power, fitted true bodies to them, which were antitypical [ἀντιτυπικῇ], gave them a true articulated voice, and granted them the ability to see, not to feed and drink with bodies that need nourishment. Indeed, the Son of God himself, before his hypostatic incarnation, appeared to Abraham with two angels and ate and drank with him in a true body. He was not joined to that body in a unity of person but only for that particular purpose. Gen. 18. 13. Likewise Moses, in the burning bush, Exod. 3. 2 and 4., where he is called an angel. This was not an approach through created spirits, but because he was always the Word of the Father among the Church, and for this reason he is named "Wonderful Counsellor," Isa. 9. 5. Those appearances were assuredly testimonies and preludes, in their time, to the incarnation that would in eternity take place in a unity of person.

units.la: Transeamus ad malignorum spirituum non illusoria, ut superiora illa facta. Sunt enim realia quaedam & reipsa qualia in sensus nostros incurrunt, non proprie tamen dicenda miracula. Nec enim illa virtute vita ὑπερφυσικῇ aut
units.tr: Let us pass to the non-illusory works of evil spirits, unlike those earlier deeds. For there are certain real things, which really fall under our senses, yet are not properly to be called miracles. For these things do not come about by supernatural [ὑπερφυσικῇ] or preternatural power.

units.la: Maligni Spiritus Deo illis potestate concedere multa fa aut ἀντιφυσικὴ contingunt (solius enim illa Dei propria) sed solis naturalibus causis, extraordinarie tamen, & ita mentis humanæ captum excedentibus, vt esse ὑπερφυσικὰ facillimè sibi decepti homines persuaderi patiantur, aut ἀντιφυσικὰ quæ tamen non sunt. Duo sunt igitur in primis verissima capita præsupponeda. Primum motus & mixtiones naturales & ordinarias causarum secundarum ad effecta sua producenda, admirandis arcanis moueri & impelli. Arcana, voco, quæ nunquam hominibus in mentem venerunt, probè tamen malignis istis cognita spiritibus, & aëris principibus (vt vocat eos Apostolus Ephes. 2. 2.) tum vi naturæ suæ spiritualis, tum certa rerum experientia quam ex quo de statu suo deturbati sunt visu longo sibi comparunt.
units.tr: Evil spirits, with God granting them power, do many things. These are not supernatural [ὑπερφυσικὰ] or contrary to nature [ἀντιφυσικὰ], which belong to God alone, but come about only from natural causes, though extraordinarily, and so far beyond the grasp of the human mind that deceived men allow themselves to be persuaded that they are supernatural or contrary to nature, though they are not. Two most true principles must therefore be presupposed. First, the natural motions and mixtures of the secondary causes, by which their effects are produced, are moved and driven by wonderful secrets. I call them secrets which have never come into the mind of man, yet are well known to those evil spirits and to the princes of the air (as the Apostle calls them, Eph. 2:2), both by the power of their spiritual nature and by the sure experience of things which they have gathered over a long time since they were thrown down from their state.

units.la: Deinde præter motus illos & ordinarias commixtiones, quibus hic orbis regitur, tenen dum est multos esse extraordinarios motus & mixtiones, minimè quidem illas ὑπερφυσικὰς aut ἀντιφυσικὰς, sed Dei permissione contingentes, ad peculiares effectus, eas pro voluntate & arbitrio Domino dispensante: in quibus tamen cœlestes influentias, quatenus certo ordine & mensura reguntur, minimè comprehendo. In iis autem efficiendis Dominus pro arbitrij voluntate, vel bonis suis rebus creatis ad suorum salutem, vtitur: aut malignis & improbis ad suos probandos, aut scelleratos puniendos: spiritui erroris efficacia cócessa. Eph. 4.14. 2. Thes. 2.11.1. Reg. 12.12. Exempli gratia, Cœlitus in Iobi greges immissus ignis: ventus excitatus ad domum in quam filij Iobi convenerant obruendam, ulcera quibus Iobum afflixit, minimè illusoria fuerunt, sed verissima certissimáque, nec ea quidem miraculosa, sed naturaliter Deo permittente producta, extraordinarie tamen, quatenus nimirum ea non aëris naturali & ordinaria dispositione, contigerunt, sed momento & extraordinarie causis naturalibus excitatis à Satana permittrete Deo ad serui sui explorationem.
units.tr: Next, besides those motions and ordinary combinations by which this world is governed, it must be held that there are many extraordinary motions and mixtures. These are by no means supernatural or contrary to nature, but happen by God's permission, the Lord dispensing them for particular effects according to his will and pleasure. Yet in these I do not include the heavenly influences, insofar as they are governed by a fixed order and measure. In bringing these things about the Lord uses his good created things for the salvation of his people, or evil and wicked ones to prove his own, or to punish the wicked, the efficacy being granted to the spirit of error (Eph. 4:14; 2 Thess. 2:11; 1 Kings 12:12). For example, fire sent down from heaven upon Job's flocks, the wind raised to overthrow the house in which Job's sons had gathered, and the ulcers with which he afflicted Job, were by no means illusory, but most true and certain. Nor indeed were they miraculous, but were produced naturally, God permitting, yet extraordinarily, insofar as they came about not by the natural and ordinary disposition of the air, but in a moment, and by natural causes stirred up extraordinarily by Satan, God permitting, to test his servant.

units.la: Sic in prophanis historiis sæpius occurrit, bruta animantia imo & idola fuisse loquuta: quod minimè quidem tanquam falsum reiiciendum est. Asinam etiam Balaami loquutam legimus. Num. 22.28. Quid ad hæc igitur dicturi sumus? Nempe asinam Balaami loquutam ex miraculo, sola nimirum divina vi ἀντιφωνικῶς, Deo linguam illi, vt expresse dicitur, folucnte. At loquutas bestias aut idola quæ referunt historiæ prophanæ, non ex miraculo factum est, nec loquutæ fuisse credendæ sunt bestiæ aut idola illa, sed malus spiritus, Deo permittente, non ignarus quibus mediis naturalibus humana vox formetur, quorum longè maiorem habet quàm homines peritiam, sibi in illis vocem formauit: non magis miraculosè quàm quum in serpente loquebatur Euam seducturus: aut sibi vocem in dæmoniacis, instrumentis tantùm σαλπιγκοῖς effingit: qua ratione potest in cadaueribus loqui, mortuorum ita resurrectionem apud Necromanticos, cos,simulans:& in Ethnicorum idolis, Esa.19. 3.ac deinceps in imaginibus quas decepti Chri ftiani, contra Dei mandatum, in templis suis adorarunt.
units.tr: Thus in profane histories it often occurs that brute animals, and even idols, are said to have spoken, and this is not to be rejected as false in itself. We also read that Balaam's ass spoke (Num. 22.28). What, then, shall we say to this? Namely, that Balaam's ass spoke by a miracle, by divine power alone, [ἀντιφωνικῶς], God loosing her tongue, as is expressly stated. But the talking beasts or idols that profane histories report did not speak by a miracle, and those beasts or idols are not to be believed to have spoken. Rather, the evil spirit, God permitting, who is not ignorant of the natural means by which human voice is formed, and who has far greater skill in these than men, formed a voice for himself in them. This was no more miraculous than when he spoke through the serpent in order to seduce Eve. Or he fashions a voice for himself in demoniacs, using only [σαλπιγκοῖς] instruments. By the same method he can speak in corpses, and so he counterfeits the resurrection of the dead among the necromancers; he does so in the idols of the Gentiles (Isa. 19.3), and afterwards in the images which Christians, deceived and contrary to God's command, worshipped in their churches.

units.la: Denique nullum est miraculofum Dei opus quodmali isti spiritus hoc modo non sint imitati, & adhuc hodie, Domino ipsis causas fecundas & naturales extraordinarie mouere permittente, non possint imitari. Ita Satanæ facile fuit, non quidem facere, sed Magorum opera subtiliter & industrie, edita in Ægypto miracula,simulare:vero serpente realiter sub- ftituto, fascinatis intuentium oculis, pro veris draconibus, eadem subtilitate Magorum vir- gis ex intuentium afpeetu subtractis: similiter etiam facile naturalis sanguinis copiam inuenit quam Ægyptiacis aquis misceret: quum Deus contra potentia sua non solum ὑπερφυ- σικὴ sed ἀντιφυσικὴ Mosis Virgam in draconem commutaffet, & aquas Ægypti in sanguinem verè conuertisset: non tamen data illis reliqua in Ægypto edita miracula imitandi facultate, quæ potuissent etiam eadem ratione nisi Deus eorum malitiam compescuisset. At fortissimis durissimisque duabus habenis à Domino fræ-nantur, nihil amplius illis permittente quàm causæ naturales extraordinarie motæ ferant: deinde ne istud quidem illorum arbitrio & pessimæ voluntati permittente, sed suo ipsius arbitrio certos illis fines præscribente, Ioh.&. 12.& 2.6. Sic apud Dei populum ipsum Satan suos emisit pseudoprophetas, & inter Ethnicos prophanos vates futura prædicentes. Mirum autem illud & nouum merito videatur, quum Deo nihil magis proprium sit quàm Diuinare. Esa. 41.2. Facilis respōsio. Non enim quicunque futurum aliquid prædicit, ideo diuinat: testibus ipsis Astronomis quibus difficile non est ex astrorum motibus horam & minuta futurarum oppositionum, aspectuum & eclipsium, ad annorum myriadas si tandiu mundus esset duraturus prædicere. At hoc non est Diuinare. Causæ enim necessariæ cognitio, docet etiam futurum necessarium effectum. Sic sæpe Agricolas tempestatem futuram certius quàm ipsos Astrologos prædicentes videas, longa nimirum causarum obseruatione peritos.
units.tr: Finally, there is no miraculous work of God that these evil spirits have not imitated in this way, and even today they can imitate such works, since the Lord permits them to move secondary and natural causes in an extraordinary manner. Thus it was easy for Satan not indeed to perform, but to counterfeit subtly and skilfully, the miracles wrought in Egypt by the works of the Magi: a real serpent was substituted, and the eyes of the onlookers were bewitched so that they took it for true dragons; by the same subtlety of the Magi, the rods were withdrawn from the sight of the onlookers. Likewise he easily found a quantity of natural blood with which to mix the waters of Egypt. For God, by his power, had not only done things above nature but contrary to nature, when he changed Moses' rod into a dragon and truly converted the waters of Egypt into blood. Yet he did not give the Magi the power to imitate the other miracles wrought in Egypt, which they could have done by the same method had God not restrained their malice. But they are held in by two very strong and harsh reins from the Lord: he permits them nothing more than that natural causes, moved in an extraordinary way, may bear fruit. Then not even this is left to their own will and wicked intention, but he, by his own will, prescribes certain limits for them (Ioh.&. 12.& 2.6.). Thus among God's people Satan himself sent forth his pseudo-prophets, and among the profane Gentiles he sent soothsayers who foretold the future. This may rightly seem strange and new, since nothing is more proper to God than to divine (Isa. 41.23). The answer is easy. Not everyone who foretells something future therefore divines. The astronomers themselves bear witness to this, for from the motions of the stars it is not difficult for them to predict the hour and minutes of future conjunctions, aspects and eclipses, even for myriads of years, if the world were to last that long. Yet this is not divining. For knowledge of a necessary cause also teaches the necessary future effect. Thus you often see farmers foretelling an approaching storm more certainly than the astrologers themselves, being skilled through long observation of causes.

units.la: Quanto magis igitur illi nunquam senescentes senes spiritus, tantam causarum naturalium & vt plurimum ex iis nascentium effectorum experientiam assequuti, multa eiusmodi possunt etiam longo ante quàm accidant tempore prædicere? Oraculorum autem quæ variis ediderunt temporibus incertitudo sæpe testata est quàm ambigue de effectibus non pendentibus à causis naturalibus & necessariis loquerentur. Præterea quàm multa putas ex verorum Prophetarum didicisse prædictionibus? & hucsane recor equidem e Sibyllarum libris multa de nostra salute mysteria referenda. Addece etiam Dominum ipsis quoisquesque & quomodo ipsi visum est ad exequenda sua iudicia plurimum vti. Quid igitur mirum, fi quæ didicerunt, etiam pf ædicunt? Quo referendum arbitror quod malus ille spiritus per Samuelis spectrum Sauli breui futurum prædixit. Interrogatos verò malos illos spiritus de præteritis rebus hominibus incognitis, non mirum de iis vt sunt gestæ respondere, quas inter homines conuersantes non difficulter norunt, quum sæpe improborum ac sceleratorum consiliis interfuerint, vt facilè à quo quid dictum patratumue sit flagitij renuntient, quod sanè, si proprie loquimur, minimè diuinatio est.
units.tr: How much more, then, can those spirits, who never grow old, and who have attained such great experience of natural causes and of the effects arising for the most part from them, predict many such things long before they happen? The uncertainty of the oracles which they gave at various times has often shown how ambiguously they spoke about effects that do not depend on natural and necessary causes. Moreover, how many things do you think were learned from the predictions of the true prophets? I should indeed refer to this the many mysteries of our salvation that are found in the books of the Sibyls. Add that the Lord makes great use of them, whoever they are and however it seems good to him, for carrying out his judgments. Why, then, is it a wonder if they also foretell what they have learned? To this, I think, should be referred what that evil spirit foretold to Saul, shortly, through the spectre of Samuel. But when those evil spirits are questioned about past events unknown to men, it is not surprising that they answer about them as they were done. Living among men, they do not find these things hard to know, since they have often been present at the counsels of the wicked and the criminal, so they can easily report who spoke or committed any crime. Surely, if we speak properly, this is by no means divination.

units.la: Denique, vt rem in pauca conferam, aio Deum proprie solum edere miracula: Quoniam autem Deus omnia opera, tum ex ordine naturæ tum miraculo, rudioribus & magis incredulis inter homines ad cognitionem suæ Diuinitatis & reuerentiæ quæ sibi debetur adducendis facit, ideo maligni spiritus, homines Deo surrepturi, eius folium cum Magis quorum opera vtuntur inuadere cupientes. Act.8.verf.10. inde ab omni ævo Dei miracula pro viribus effingere conati sunt. Nec sanè frustrà tentarunt, cuius rei tot superstitiones & ἐθελοθρησκεία hac ratione inter homines natæ & ratæ habitæ, restes sunt omni exceptione maiores. Quid igitur est opus facto ? Discernendæ nimirum quantum fieri potest impostura & illusiones à rebus quæ verè fiunt ac realiter: deinde ex Domini mandato, ex arborum natura de fructu iudicandum: quod non vsque adeo difficile futurum est, fi non ad tam noua & peregrina facta nimis attoniti, quæ merito in admirationem rapiunt, patienter quem ad finem illa deducant, intueamur.Generale enim est axioma,quum prę fertim de religione & conscientia agitur, noua illa & inuiitata nunquam eflc nec à Domino miraculosè nec à malis Spiritibus extraordinarie facta, vt in illis simpliciter hæreamus: sed vt ex iis tot tantarumque rerum auctorem & opificem agnoscamus, admiremur, ac veneremur.Marc. 16. 20. Heb. 2. v.4. Facile igitur vera à Deo edita miracula, quibus ad veri Dei cognitionem cultumque illi debitum ducimur, discernentur à factis extraordinariis malignorum spirituum, quibus à vero Deo cultúque illi debito abducimur. Talis erat Simon ille Magus Act.8.10.& Bariefu. Act.13.6. Et hic alius occurrit nobis diligenter cauendus Satanæ dolus, de quo hactenus loquuti non fumus. Satanam nempe ad Homines inducendos in errorem aut confirmandos in superstitionibus & idololatria, verborum quodam ac rerum & rituum inuolucro tegere, quæ ipse per naturalia quædam arcana extraordinaria & hominibus incognita persidit.
units.tr: Finally, to sum up the matter briefly, I say that God alone properly performs miracles. But since God makes all his works, both by the order of nature and by miracle, in order to bring the ruder and more unbelieving among men to knowledge of his divinity and to the reverence due to him, therefore evil spirits, wishing to steal God's place among men, desire to invade with the magicians whose works they use (Acts 8.10). From every age they have tried to counterfeit God's miracles as far as they could. Nor have they tried in vain; so many superstitions and [ἐθελοθρησκεία] born in this way among men and held valid are proof beyond all exception. What, then, is to be done? Namely, we must distinguish, as far as possible, imposture and illusions from things that truly and really happen. Then, by the Lord's command, we must judge from the fruit, by the nature of the tree. This will not be very difficult, provided we do not gaze too astonished at such new and strange deeds, which rightly carry us into admiration, but patiently look to where they lead. For it is a general axiom, especially when religion and conscience are at stake, that those new and unheard-of things were never done either miraculously by the Lord or extraordinarily by evil spirits, so that we should simply stick fast in them. Rather, through them we should acknowledge, admire and venerate the author and maker of such great and numerous things (Mark 16.20; Heb. 2.4). Therefore the true miracles wrought by God, by which we are led to the knowledge of the true God and to the worship due to him, will easily be distinguished from the extraordinary deeds of evil spirits, by which we are drawn away from the true God and from the worship due to him. Such was that Simon Magus (Acts 8.10), and Bar-Jesus (Acts 13.6). And here another deceit of Satan meets us, which must be carefully guarded against and which we have not discussed so far. Namely, to lead men into error, or to confirm them in superstitions and idolatry, Satan covers with a certain wrapping of words, things and rites what he accomplishes through certain hidden natural powers, extraordinary and unknown to men.

units.la: Sic incantatores voces peregrinas & non intellectas, fimplicioribus in stuporem adducendis: vel è sacris etiam depromptas edere foleit, summa & horrenda prophanatione,vt ita deceantur homines vim foli Deo propriâ verborum ipsorum sono tribuere, quæ ne Angelis lis quidem sine impietate dari poterit. His artibus verum signi Crucis vsum, Satan euertit, lustralem aquam inuexit, & similia multa quibus Magi & Incantatores ad fascinationes ventuntur, ita tegente Satana suum opus & scopum, apud eos quibus unde quod quaerunt remedium proficiscatur cordi non est. Hoc ipsum per Mosen diserte docet Dominus, Deut.13.1. de dono Prophetiae loquutus: quod etiam ad alias omnes artes quibus maligni Spiritus imitari solent opera Dei referendum est.
units.tr: Thus enchanters are wont to utter foreign and unintelligible words, to strike simpler people with amazement, or even to draw them from the sacred writings with the greatest and most horrible profanation. In this way men are deceived into attributing to the sound of the words themselves a power proper to God alone, which cannot be given even to angels without impiety. By these arts Satan overturns the true use of the sign of the cross, introduces lustral water, and many similar things by which magicians and enchanters resort to bewitchings. Satan thus conceals his work and aim, so that those who seek a remedy do not care whence it comes. The Lord teaches this very thing expressly through Moses, speaking of the gift of prophecy (Deut. 13.1). This is also to be referred to all the other arts by which evil spirits are wont to imitate the works of God.

units.la: Quid igitur de tot miraculis quibus aureae illae quas vocant Legendae plenae sunt, dicturi sumus? Nempe totidem mendacia libere alleuerabimus quot fidelibus Dei seruis attribuuntur in illis miracula, non minus impudenter ab illis effecta, quam ab his stolide credita. Nā reuera sunt in iis quaedam Poetarum fabulis magis etiam ludicra: alia crassissimam auctorum suorum ignorantiam produnt: & in uniuersum praeterquam quod Legendarum istarum auctores ignoti sunt, vix in egregiis istis narrationibus vllum doctrinae caput vel leuiter attingitur. Ex quibus efficitur quum miracula sint doctrinae signa & appendices, egregias istas (scilicet narrationes, licet veras concederemus, inutiles tamen esse futuras, non minus quam quotcunque voles signa nullis publicis instrumentis appensa: En cur Sacrosancta Scriptura miracula semper & insepa-rabiliter cum doctrina coniungat, penes quam est ipsa veritas, licet de veritate miracula ferat testimonium. At longe pcius adhuc in istis miraculis malum subest, quibus quum homines dementati in idololatriam & superstitionem ruerint, dicendum sane, vel istis peßime abusos homines in eo quod tam expresse D. Petrus reprehendit. Act. 3. 12. aut, quod vero propius est, a falsis doctoribus ista partim effecta, partim a malis Spiritibus exorta. Idem etiam esto dictum de iis quibus hodie tantopere aduersarij gloriantur, quorum omnium ide scopus ac finis est superstitionü & idololatriæ confirmatio, ex eadé proinde prodeuntiu officina, etsi nec maliciosè per impostu-ram, nec illusorie edita istiusmodi miracula concedremus. Quid ni enim maligni spiritus aquæ lustrali cederent, aut Signo crucis, aut ad Sanctorum inuocationem & alios istiusmodi ritus fugarentur, quibus animarum multæ myriades in aquæ lustralis, crucis & aliorum abusuum ex diametro nostræ salutis & veri Dei cultus fundamento repugnantium magis inagisque confirmantur? Quod autem à nobis noua miracula postulant: quum extra dubium sit miraculorum donü fuisse ad tempus tantum concessum, idem illis respondemus quod fui temporis Scribis & Pharisæis Christus respondit, Matth. 12. 39. & 16. 4. quanquam illi speciosiorem illa petendi videantur occasionem habuisse quàm nostri seculi homines, quo iam pridem accepimus Euangelium infinitis miraculis satis superque confirmatum. Dicimus igitur à nobis hodie miracula flagitantes, quæ semel facta sunt & Scripturarum monumentis ad nos perlata vel negare vel in dubium vocare: vt hodie non de miraculis controver- tatur, sed de doctrina quam profitemur, eáne Christi sit & Apostolorum nec-ne. Et hactenus quidem de miraculorum recto vsu & abusu.
units.tr: What, then, shall we say of the many miracles with which those golden legends, as they call them, are full? Namely, we shall freely assert as many lies as there are miracles attributed in them to the faithful servants of God, effected by them no less shamelessly than they were stupidly believed by those who read them. For in truth some of them are even more playful than the fables of the poets; others betray the very great ignorance of their authors. In general, apart from the fact that the authors of these Legends are unknown, scarcely any head of doctrine is even lightly touched in those outstanding narratives. From this it follows that, since miracles are signs and appendages of doctrine, those outstanding narratives, even if we granted that they were true, would nevertheless be useless, no less than however many signs you like hung on no public instruments. This is why Sacred Scripture always and inseparably joins miracles with doctrine, since the truth itself lies in doctrine, although doctrine bears witness to the truth of the miracles. But far worse still is the evil lurking in those miracles by which men, driven mad, have rushed into idolatry and superstition. It must surely be said that men were very badly abused in that which St Peter so expressly rebukes (Acts 3.12); or, what is nearer the truth, that these were partly done by false teachers and partly arose from evil spirits. The same is to be said of those things in which our adversaries glory so much today, whose whole aim and end is the confirmation of superstition and idolatry. They proceed, therefore, from the same workshop, although we would not concede that such miracles were performed either maliciously by imposture or illusorily. For why should evil spirits not yield to lustral water, or be put to flight by the sign of the cross, or by the invocation of the saints, and other such rites, by which many myriads of souls are ever more firmly confirmed in the abuses of lustral water, the cross and the others, which are diametrically opposed to the foundation of our salvation and the true worship of God? As for what they demand of us, namely new miracles: since it is beyond doubt that the gift of miracles was granted only for a time, we give the same answer that Christ gave to the Scribes and Pharisees of his time (Matt. 12.39; 16.4). Yet those men seem to have had a more plausible occasion for asking than the people of our age, to whom the Gospel has long since been delivered, sufficiently and more than sufficiently confirmed by countless miracles. We say, therefore, that those who demand miracles from us today either deny or call into doubt those things which were done once and have been handed down to us in the monuments of Scripture. Thus today the controversy is not about miracles, but about the doctrine we profess: whether it is the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles or not. And so far, indeed, concerning the right use and abuse of miracles.

units.la: Vt igitur historiam nostram repetamus, dicitur Herodes multis termonibus Christum interrogasse, quos tamen Euangelista non expressit: nec abs re quidem. Nam quid obscuro, potuit ab ore tam prophano dignum Ecclesia Dei manare? Merito igitur Christus eum ore suo sacro, ne ad arguendum quidem, est dignatus, quem satis suorum scelerum conscientia coargueret: quorum etiam alibi iudicium illi imminebat, ac primum quidem Romæ, vbi non longo post tempore, damnatus est, & ad cœleste Dei tribunal euocatus. Nec vero docere ipsum etiam voluit, quem non tantum sciebat altitam esse vulpem, vt vocat eum, Luc. 13. 32. sed vere canem & porcum, quibus margaritas proiicere, Matth. 7. verf. 6. prohibemur.
units.tr: To return to our story: Herod is said to have questioned Christ at length, though the Evangelist does not record what he asked, and rightly so. For what could come from the mouth of so profane a man that was worthy of the Church of God? Christ therefore did not deign to answer him with his holy mouth, not even to rebuke him, since Herod's own conscience of his many crimes was rebuke enough. A judgment already hung over him elsewhere: he was condemned at Rome not long afterwards, and summoned to the heavenly tribunal of God. Nor did Christ wish to teach him, since he knew him to be not merely "that crafty fox," as Christ calls him (Luke 13:32), but a dog and a pig, before whom we are forbidden to cast pearls (Matt. 7:6).

units.la: Hinc igitur discamus vere Iesum Christum eum fuisse quem praesentem in carne oportuit interrogari, ex cuius ore salutis doctrina disceretur, quem adhuc hodie Pastorem per Prophetas & Apostolos locuntem, in ore fidelium pastorum & doctorum agnoscunt ipsius oues, cuius vnius vocem audiunt,Ioh. 10.3. & 5. A quo responsum accepturos oportet,pro impuris& prophanis, sanctitatis & puritatis cupidos esse: & pro curiosis in eorum abiectorum & humilium album accenseri, quibus Deus arcana sua revelat,quæ magnis & superbis abscondit.Psal.19. 8.Matth.11.25.
units.tr: Let us therefore learn from this that Jesus Christ is the one who, while present in the flesh, ought to have been questioned, and from whose mouth the doctrine of salvation was to be learned. He still speaks today as the Shepherd through the Prophets and Apostles, and his sheep recognise him in the mouths of faithful ministers and teachers, and hear his voice alone (John 10:3, 5). Those who wish to receive an answer from him must be eager for holiness and purity, not for the impure and profane; and they must count themselves among the lowly and humble, to whom God reveals his hidden things, which he conceals from the great and proud (Ps. 19:8; Matt. 11:25).

units.la: In his omnibus Herodes turpiter lapsus est, eiúsque vestigiis omnes inhærentes labuntur, quorum hodie maximus est numerus, in suum accersentes caput quod ex Esaiæ Prophetæ prædictione veteri populo contigit,Esa.29.14. vt nimirum quum nulli cæciores essent in pulo conductoribus ipsorum, oues errantes sine Pastore facti sint,Matth. 9. 36. En cur hodie Dei veritas,nullos capitaliores hostes,nullos sæuiores persecutores patiatur, quàmqui quotidie Scripturas versant,Dominum interrogantes, sed,si non tam curiosos ac prophanos quàm fuit Herodes, in re tamen maiore grauiùs peccantes. Vt enim Herodes Christum non interrogat vt discipulus aliquid discendi gratia,sed tanquam iudex,re iam præiudicata: ita fit etiam hodie in Scholasticorum scholis, eorúmque Conciliis, immo & priuatis cuiusque studiis.Hæret enim in eorum animis istud penitus infixu axioma, Ecclesiâ (quâ ex personali Successione metiuntur,& lituis,mitris,gaferis,& in primis ex triplici illa corona cui S. Spiritu alligant) nunquâ errare potuisse. Quo pacto fundamento tàquam certissima regula, hoc vnum agunt vt Scripturas accommodent, vel potius detorqueat ad prius facta à fe conclusionem.Quid mirum igitur si perinde agitur cum ipsis atque cum fabro lapidario, non ad lineam aut perpendiculum suum ædificium dirigenti, & expendenti, sed normam ad tortuosum ædificium accommodanti: quod etsi grauius nihil patiatur, non est diuturnū futurum? Qui cupit igitur à Domino doceri, idest verus esse Christianus, tanquam discipulus, cum humilitate & discendi studio ad Christū accedat, & præiudicium adferat, non quale diximus: sed quod certum & indubitatum est Symbolum Apostolicum, veram fidei Christianæ summam complectens, veram nostram Catechefin, ad quod quæ in Sacris Scripturis lecturi sumus si applicuerimus, aut quæ à docentibus audituri, facile fuerit eum animum quem diximus adferentibus tum falsos ac proinde fugiendos doctores, à veris & audiendis pastoribus discernere: tum falsam doctrinam veterem aut nouam à qua nobis cauendum est, Matth. 16. v. 6. & 11. à vera in qua nobis ad finem vsque, nec ad læuā nec ad dextram declinatibus, perstandum est. Sic verè fideles Christiani Christum alloquuntur: sic vicissim ille responder.
units.tr: In all these things Herod fell shamefully, and all who cling to his footsteps stumble after him. Their number today is very great, and they bring upon their own heads what came upon the ancient people through the prophecy of Isaiah (Isa. 29:14): namely, that although their leaders were the most blind, the sheep went astray and were left without a shepherd (Matt. 9:36). Hence it is that the truth of God today suffers no more deadly enemies and no more savage persecutors than those who handle the Scriptures every day and question the Lord, yet are not as inquisitive and profane as Herod was, though they sin more gravely in a greater matter. For just as Herod did not question Christ like a disciple seeking to learn something, but like a judge with the case already decided, so it is done today in the schools of the Schoolmen, in their councils, and indeed in the private studies of each one. For that axiom has fixed itself deep in their minds, that the Church (which they measure by personal succession, and by staves, mitres and cloaks, and above all by that triple crown to which they tie the Holy Spirit) could never err. On this foundation, as on the most certain rule, they labour only to adapt the Scriptures, or rather to twist them, to conclusions already made by themselves. Is it any wonder, then, that they act toward the Scriptures just as a stonemason does who does not direct and measure his building by line and plumb, but fits the rule to a crooked building? Even if such a building suffers nothing serious for now, it will not last long. Whoever therefore wishes to be taught by the Lord, that is, to be a true Christian, must come to Christ as a disciple, with humility and eagerness to learn, and bring with him not the kind of prejudgment we have described, but what is certain and beyond doubt: the Apostles' Creed, which embraces the true sum of the Christian faith, our true catechism. If we apply to this whatever we are about to read in the Holy Scriptures, or hear from teachers, it will be easy for those who bring such a mind to distinguish false teachers, who must therefore be shunned, from true ministers, who must be heard; and to distinguish false doctrine, old or new, against which we must be on guard (Matt. 16:6, 11), from the true doctrine, in which we must persevere to the end, turning neither to the left nor to the right. In this way truly faithful Christians address Christ, and in turn he answers them.

units.la: Quod sequitur Christum ab accusatoribus suis accusatum,& primariis licet Sacerdotibus & Scribis vehementiore quàm antea vsis contentione, tamen ab Herode non condemnatum, nec in Galilæam relegatum, magis ac magis patefacit tam accusatorum ipsius efsræ.
units.tr: What follows, that Christ was accused by his accusers, and that although the chief priests and scribes pressed their charges more vehemently than before, he was not condemned by Herod, nor sent back to Galilee, more and more reveals the wickedness of his accusers.

units.la: O. ij. nem improbitatem, nec loquentem Christum ferentiam, nec silentem, quàm immesam Iesu Christi patientiam, cui nihil erat aliud propositum quàm se Deo Patri in omnibus obedientem praestare, próque inimicis mortem oppetere, à quo proposito nunquam se ad dextram aut laevam in tantis tàmque immanibus contumeliis ab vlla mentis perturbatione passus est dimoveri.
units.tr: Christ's patience, as he neither spoke nor kept silent, was greater than their wickedness. His only purpose was to show himself obedient to God the Father in all things, and to face death for his enemies. From this purpose he never allowed himself to be turned aside, to the right or to the left, by any disturbance of mind, amid such great and savage insults.

units.la: Idem hodie nobis cum nostris aduersariis veris istorum successoribus faciendum, suas aduersum nos calumnias vomentibus, & tum voce tum scriptis omni calumniarum genere nos gravatibus, & hac ratione lituos & mitras venantibus, siue ipsis respondeamus, siue silentium altum premamus: sic saltem sperate Satana, nos à melioribus nostris laboribus ordinariis, qui in ouium nostrarum edificatione toti sunt, auocatos, refutandis illorum millies repetitis & refutatis scriptitationibus occupatum iri. Nos vero contra non obliti, quid, quo loco, & tempore sit ipsorum falsitati respondendum, impositū nostris humeris onus excquamur, omni cum diligentia, Dei nostri providentiae nos nostraque omnia Christi Domini nostri exemplum sequuti committamus, futuro nimirum Deo semper tempore & loco nobis tutore & conseruatore.
units.tr: Today we must do the same with our adversaries, who are the true successors of those men. They spew their calumnies against us, burden us with every kind of slander both in speech and in writing, and in this way hunt for staves and mitres. Whether we answer them or keep a deep silence, Satan hopes thus at least to draw us away from our better and ordinary labours, which are wholly devoted to building up our sheep, and to keep us busy refuting their scribblings, repeated and refuted a thousand times. Yet we, not forgetful of what must be answered to their falsehoods, and in what place and at what time, will bear the burden laid on our shoulders with all diligence. Following the example of Christ our Lord, we will commit ourselves and all that is ours to the providence of our God, who will always be, at the proper time and place, our guardian and keeper.

units.la: Sed praeter superiora omnia, nouû hic innocentiae Domini nostri Iesu Christi testimonium expendamus. Nam quum ante Iudicis tam male affecti tribunal reus staret, tot tàmque infestis vrgentibus aduersariis,& quidem tan-tæ auctoritatis, ipso non depellente crimina-tionem, quid Herodis malitiam compescuit, nisi ipsamet Iesu Christi innocentia,tanto cō-spectior & insignior, quantò maioribus & inanioribus testimoniis premebatur?
units.tr: But beyond all that has been said, let us weigh here another testimony to the innocence of our Lord Jesus Christ. For while the accused stood before the tribunal of a judge so ill-disposed, with so many and such hostile adversaries pressing him, and men of such great authority at that, he did not refute the accusations. What restrained Herod's malice, if not the innocence of Jesus Christ itself, all the more conspicuous and remarkable because it was weighed down by greater and more empty accusations?

units.la: Nec quidem inficias ausim ire, quin huma-nitus accidere potuerit,vt Herodes aliqua Pi-lati immo ipsius Imperatoris Romani tange-retur reuerentia, sententiâ, capitis præsertim, ferre veritus in alieno solo ac ditione putà Ma-iestatis Imperialis, ad se licet misso captiuo: quibus etiam addesi placet hanc occasionem redeundi apud Pilatum in gratiam quæsitam: Maximè tamen animaducrte diuinam prouidentiam hic nobis satis aperte demonstrare in sua manu esse posita hostium nostrorū corda, linguam & manus,sic Deo hæc omnia dispensante,vt nihil fieret nisi quod erat & sicut erat diuinitus constitutum.
units.tr: Nor would I dare to deny that it could have happened humanly that Herod was moved by some respect for Pilate, or rather for the Roman Emperor himself. He feared to pronounce sentence, especially a capital one, on foreign soil and within the dominion, as one might say, of the Imperial Majesty, even though he had sent the prisoner back to him. To these reasons one may also add that Herod sought this occasion to regain Pilate's favour. Yet above all we should note that divine providence shows us here quite plainly that the hearts, tongues and hands of our enemies are placed in God's hand, and that God so disposed all these things that nothing happened except what was and as it was divinely ordained.

units.la: Iesus igitur Christus ad Pilatum remitti-tur, Herode in partem iniquitatis istius,con-tra omnem iudicij formam venire. Nam ob-secro,quo iure hæc illusio nitebatur,quum ni-hil Christus respondisset, & nulli testes dicā-tur aduersus eum examinati? At si Herodes ex Iesu Christi silentio confessione obiectorum criminum collegit,non modò dignus erat qui sic palam illuderetur, sed qui tanquam læsæ Maiestatis humanæ ac diuinæ conuictus capite plecteretur. Videtur igitur Herodes Iesum Christū pro stolido & sanatico habuisse quem
units.tr: Jesus Christ was therefore sent back to Pilate, with Herod coming in on the side of that injustice, against every form of judgment. For I ask you, on what right did this mockery rest, since Christ had answered nothing and no witnesses were examined against him? But if Herod gathered from Christ's silence a confession of the crimes objected to him, he was not only worthy to be mocked openly in this way, but should have been convicted of treason against both human and divine majesty and put to death. Herod therefore seems to have regarded Jesus Christ as a fool and a madman, whom

units.la: O. iij. metu Iudæorum, alba veste indutum ad Pilatum remiserit, ad Romanorum fortasse morem alludens cuius non erat ignarus, candidatos nimitum & munera ambientes, quorum erat penes populum electio, candidis vestibus induí solitos : vt Pilato significaret Iesum Christum Regnum Iudæorum ex sola ltultitia ambiuisse : vt solent miseri illi qui se Monarchas somniant.Nec sane primum Herodis de Christo fuit hoc iudicium : sed ex cognatis ipsius & propinquis nonnulli iam inde ab initio prædicationis illius sic sensérant,cum prehendere conati,quod apud se non esse putarent,Mar.3.21. & Iudæi dæmonium ei & insaniam exprobrarant.Ioh.10.20.
units.tr: for fear of the Jews he sent back to Pilate, clothed in a white robe. Perhaps he was alluding to a Roman custom, of which he was not ignorant: candidates, that is, who sought offices and gifts, and on whom the people's choice depended, were accustomed to wear white garments. By this he would signal to Pilate that Jesus Christ had sought the kingship of the Jews out of sheer foolishness, as those wretched men do who dream themselves to be monarchs. Nor was this judgment of Herod's about Christ the first. Some of his relatives and kinsmen had thought the same from the very beginning of his preaching, when they tried to seize him, supposing he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), and the Jews charged him with a demon and madness (John 10:20).

units.la: Nec melior Pauli apud Festum conditio fuit. Act. 26.24. Gentibus Euangelij prædicatione stultitiam habentibus.1.Cor.1.13.& 2.14. Et nostro seculo, qui nos odio capitali no persequuntur, pro miseris tamè stultis ac fanaticis habent. Quid igitur? A filiis suis iustificata est Sapientia,Matth.11.19. ad Deum prouocantibus apud quem mundi sapientia mera stultitia est.1.Cor.3.19. & quam mundus vocat stultitiam vera sapientia est inter perfectos. 2. Cor.2.6.
units.tr: Paul's situation before Festus was no better (Acts 26:24). The preaching of the gospel seems foolishness to the Gentiles (1 Cor. 1:13; 2:14). And in our own age, those who do not persecute us with deadly hatred still regard us as wretched and foolish fanatics. What then? Wisdom is justified by her children (Matt. 11:19), who appeal to God, before whom the wisdom of the world is sheer folly (1 Cor. 3:19), and what the world calls folly is true wisdom among the perfect (1 Cor. 2:6).

units.la: Verum præter illa superiora, quàm diuina prouidentia,præter Herodis mentem, illatam Christo contumeliam inuerterit, animaduertendum.Nam vt Sacra Scriptura docet,candida veste & nitens puritatis & maiestatis signum est.Candida igitur illa vestis qua induitum tum Christum ad Pilatum Herodes remisit, diuina prouidentia sic disponente, fuit veluti visibile testimonium coelitus per Herodis ministerium demissum, quo longe alius esse Christus cognosceretur, quàm ab accusatoribus diceretur, purus nimirum & innocens, breuiqué in regni sui coelestis splendorem & possessionem venturus, sicut prius illud ipsum in eius transfiguratione vestis candida designarat, Matth.17.2. & saepe multae Angelorum apparitiones. En igitur vt Dominus improborum consilia, illorum ipsorum opera vsus quando ipsi videtur ad suum honorem & gloriam, suorumque filiorum consolationem, inuertat.
units.tr: Yet beyond the points already made, we should notice how divine providence turned to Christ's advantage the insult offered him, apart from Herod's intention. As Sacred Scripture teaches, white clothing is a sign of purity and majesty. That white robe in which Herod sent Christ back to Pilate, with divine providence so ordaining, was like a visible testimony sent from heaven through Herod's agency, by which Christ might be recognised as far different from what his accusers said: pure, that is, and innocent, and soon to come into the splendour and possession of his heavenly kingdom. The same white garment had earlier signified this at his transfiguration (Matt. 17.2), and so did the frequent appearances of angels. See, then, how the Lord turns the plans of the wicked to his own honour and glory, and to the comfort of his children, by means of the very deeds of those men.

units.la: Denique dicuntur Herodes & Pilatus, inter quos tam bene prius quàm inter canes os vnum arrodentibus conueniebat, hoc facto conciliati, inimicitiarum istarum causas Euangelista reticente, quas etiá anxius inquirere nihil iuuat, quum tamen verisimile sit causam illis praebuisse Galilaeorum caedem illam, quorum sanguinem Pilatus miscuerat cum ipsorum sacrificiis. Luc.13.1. quam Herodes illatam suis subditis iniuriam aegrè quum ferret, Pilatus misso ad illum misso lesu Christo factum emendare conatus sit. At occasionem quaecunque fuit missam facientes, Christum illusum & ad vtrorumque ludibrium male habitum intrucamur: cuius ignominiae non pauca nostrum seculum peperit exempla: quod membris nouum esse non debet quum iam pridem ita sit caput ipsum exceptum.
units.tr: Finally, Herod and Pilate, who before this had been no more friendly than dogs gnawing the same bone, are said to have been reconciled by this act. The evangelist is silent about the causes of their enmity, and it does no good to inquire anxiously into them. Yet it is likely that the slaughter of the Galileans, whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices (Luke 13.1), gave them cause. When Herod took badly the wrong done to his subjects, Pilate tried to make amends by sending Jesus Christ to him. But whatever the occasion was, by sending him back we make Christ the mockery of both and treat him shamefully. Our own age has produced no few examples of this disgrace; this should not seem new to the members, since the Head himself was treated in the same way long ago.

units.la: O. iiij.
units.tr: O. iiij.

units.la: Praeterea hic obseruandum non paruum discrimen inter mundi amicitiam & veram eam charitatem quae in vere Christianorum cordibus a Sp.Sancto formatur, adeo vt etiam inimicos suos amore nunquam finiendo prosequantur, vel ipso teste Christo pro inimicis suis media morte orando.Luc.23.34. & D.Stephano. Act. 7. 60. & Apostolo. Rom. 9. 3. & Mose. Exod. 32. 32. At huius mundi amicitia multis occasionibus scinditur & abrumpitur: cessante etiam omnis consanguinitatis proximitatisque respectu.Esa.49.15.
units.tr: Moreover, we must observe here no small difference between the friendship of the world and that true charity which the Holy Spirit forms in the hearts of true Christians, so that they pursue even their enemies with an unending love, as Christ himself witnessed when he prayed for his enemies at his death (Luke 23.34), and as Stephen did (Acts 7.60), and the Apostle (Rom. 9.3), and Moses (Exod. 32.32). But the friendship of this world is torn and broken by many occasions, and every respect for kinship and nearness ceases (Isa. 49.15).

units.la: Plurimum autem Satan in transformandis hominibus & a natura inditis affectibus spoliandis abutitur falso zelo sine scientia, sicuti praemonuit ipse Dominus.Matth.10.v.36.&ipsemet expertus est.Ioh.1.11. fecuIorum que omnium experientia nimium est testata,nostroque adhuc seculo restatur.
units.tr: Satan, moreover, abuses most of all false zeal without knowledge to transform men and strip them of the affections implanted by nature, as the Lord himself forewarned (Matt. 10.36), and as he himself experienced (John 1.11). The experience of all ages has testified this too much, and our own age still bears witness to it.

units.la: Abiit igitur vt in re tam leui confidamus, contra vero charitatem illam a Domino qua nos ipse dilexit, efflagitemus, sic apud Esaiam loquutus cap. 49.15. An obliuisci poterit mulier foetus sui, vt non misereatur filij uteri sui? Etiam haec obliuisci possint, tamen ego non obliuiscar tui. Et hanc nos indui charitatem est necesse,si in Christi fratribus censeri volumus,sic loquente Christo,Iohan.15.12.Hoc est praeceptum meum vt diligatis alij alios sicut dilexi vos. At si quae forte rixa suborta sit,praeclaram illam Apostoli sententiam in memoriam reuocemus. Ephes.4.25. Irascimini,& nc pecca-
units.tr: Let us therefore not trust in such a light thing, but rather seek from the Lord that charity by which he himself loved us, speaking thus through Isaiah (49.15): "Can a woman forget her infant, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yet even these may forget, but I will not forget you." And we must put on this charity if we wish to be counted among Christ's brothers, Christ himself saying (John 15.12): "This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you." But if perhaps some quarrel has arisen, let us call to mind the excellent saying of the Apostle (Eph. 4.25): "Be angry, and do not sin:

units.la: peccate: sol ne occidat super iracundiam ve-ftram. Neque date locum Diabolo. Sic à fan-ctis Dei feruis factitatum est. Quid amplius? En infideles Herodem & Pilatum tam facile in gratiam redeuntes, quàm facile rixati exer-cuerant: Quid igitur vobis fiet, tum viris tum mulieribus, implacabilibus & inexorabilibus, fi coram Deo & hominibus ipsi vos Ethnici condemnant: Quę fi fuit alias vnquam doctri-na necessaria maxime est hoc tempore, quo Satanæ conspicimus tantam esse vim & autoritatem in ligandis & vt ita dicam, congluti-nandis perditis ac improbis hominibus, ad-uersum Dei filios coniuratis & conspiranti-bus: Quid nos igitur? quousque tandem in ar-rodendis alij aliis, lancinandis, dilaniandis perrecturi fumus? Auertat Deus istam à nobis mentem, largiatúrque potiùs vt inuicem con-gruenter coagmentati & compacti, sancto il-lo corporis vnius vinculo, cuius meminit A-poftolus Ephef.4.16. mutuò nos foueamus, ne forte in sacrosanctum conuiuium introducti, & fine nuptiali veste reperti, foras eiiciamur in tenebras exteriores, vbi nihil nisi fletus & stridor dentium Matt.22.13.vt vera contrà cha-ritate præditi vltimo die faustam illam ac fe-licem vocem audituri fumus, Venite benedi-cti Patris mei, regnum vobis à mundi iactis fundamentis paratum possidete.
units.tr: do not let the sun go down on your wrath. Neither give place to the devil." Thus it has been done by the holy servants of God. What more? See how readily the unbelievers Herod and Pilate returned to favour, as easily as they had quarrelled. What then will happen to you, both men and women, implacable and unyielding, if the Gentiles themselves condemn you before God and men? If there was ever any teaching most necessary, it is necessary especially at this time, when we see Satan has so great a power and authority in binding together, and, as I may say, cementing the lost and wicked men conspiring and plotting against the sons of God. What then shall we do? How far at last shall we proceed in gnawing, tearing and rending one another? May God turn that mind away from us, and rather grant that, being fitly joined and knit together by that holy bond of the one body, of which the Apostle speaks (Eph. 4.16), we cherish one another, lest perhaps, introduced into the sacred feast and found without the wedding garment, we be cast out into the outer darkness, where there is nothing but weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 22.13); so that, endowed with true charity, we may on the last day hear that joyful and happy voice: "Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world."

units.la: HOMILIA VICE-simaquarta.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXIV.

units.la: MATTH. 27.
units.tr: MATTHEW 27.

units.la: 15. Præses autem singulis festis consueuerat turbæ dimittere vnum vinctum, quem voluissent.
units.tr: 15. Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release to the crowd one prisoner, whomever they wished.

units.la: 16. Habebant verò tunc vinctum insignem, qui dicebatur, Barabbam.
units.tr: 16. And at that time they had a notorious prisoner, who was called Barabbas.

units.la: 17. Ipsis igitur congregatis dixit eis Pilatus, vtrum vultis dimittam vobis, Barabbam, an Iesum qui dicitur Christus?
units.tr: 17. So when they had gathered together, Pilate said to them, Whom do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?

units.la: 18. Sciebat enim quòd per invidiam tradidissent eum.
units.tr: 18. For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy.

units.la: 19. Sedente autem eo in tribunali, misit ad eum vxor eius, dicens, Nihil tibi rei sit cum iusto illo: multa enim passa sum hodie in somnio propter eum.
units.tr: 19. While he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent to him, saying, Have nothing to do with that just man; for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him.

units.la: 20. Primarij verò Sacerdotes & Seniores persuaserunt turbæ vt peterent Barabbam, Iesum verò perderet.
units.tr: 20. But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas, and to destroy Jesus.

units.la: 21. Respondens autem præses dixit eis, Vtrum è duobus illis vultis vt vobis dimittam? Ipsi verò dixerunt, Barabbam.
units.tr: 21. The governor answered and said to them, Which of the two do you want me to release to you? And they said, Barabbas.

units.la: 22. Dixit eis Pilatus, Quid igitur faciam Iesu qui dicitur Christus? Dicunt ei omnes crucifigatur.
units.tr: 22. Pilate said to them, What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ? They all said to him, Let him be crucified.

units.la: 23. Præses autem ait, Enimuerò quid mali fecit? At illi amplius clamabant, dicentes, crucifigatur.
units.tr: 23. The governor said, Why, what evil has he done? But they cried out all the more, saying, Let him be crucified.

units.la: MARC. 15.
units.tr: Mark 15.

units.la: 6. Cæterùm singulis festis dimittebat eis vnum ex vinctis quemcunque postulassent.
units.tr: 6. Now at each feast he used to release to them one of the prisoners, whomever they asked for.

units.la: 7. Erat verò quidam qui dicebatur Barabbas, vinctus cum seditionis sociis, qui cædem per seditionem fecerant.
units.tr: 7. There was a man called Barabbas, bound with the rebels who had committed murder in the uprising.

units.la: 8. Et vociferans turba cœpit petere vt faceret prout semper ipsis fecerat.
units.tr: 8. And the crowd, shouting, began to ask him to do as he had always done for them.

units.la: 9. Pilatus autem respondit eis, dicens, Vultis dimittam vobis regem illum Iudæorum?
units.tr: 9. But Pilate answered them, saying, "Do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?"

units.la: 10. (Noverat enim eum per invidiam traditum fuisse à primariis Sacerdotibus.)
units.tr: 10. (For he knew that the chief priests had handed him over out of envy.)

units.la: 11. Primarij verò Sacerdotes concitarunt turbam vt potiùs Barabbam ipsis dimitteret.
units.tr: 11. But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have Barabbas released to them instead.

units.la: 12. Tum Pilatus respondens, rursum dixit eis, Quid ergo vultis faciam isto quem dicitis regem Iudæorum.
units.tr: 12. Then Pilate, answering, said to them again, "What then do you want me to do with him whom you call the King of the Jews?"

units.la: 13. Ipsi verò rursum clamauerunt, Crucifige eum.
units.tr: 13. But they shouted again, "Crucify him."

units.la: 14. Pilatus autem dicebat eis, Enimuerò quid mali fecit? Illi autem amplius clamauerunt, Crucifige eum.
units.tr: 14. Pilate said to them, "Why, what evil has he done?" But they shouted all the more, "Crucify him."

units.la: LVC. 23.
units.tr: LUKE 23.

units.la: 13. Pilatus verò conuocatis primariis Sacerdotibus & Magistratibus ac populo,
units.tr: 13. Then Pilate, calling together the chief priests, the magistrates and the people,

units.la: 14. Dixit eis, Obtulistis mihi hunc hominem, vt qui auertat populum: & ecce, ego in vestri conspectu quæstione habita, nullam noxam inueni in homine isto, ex iis de quibus accusatis eum.
units.tr: 14. said to them, You brought this man before me as one who turns the people away. And behold, I have examined him in your presence and found no fault in this man concerning those things of which you accuse him.

units.la: 15. Sed neque Herodes quidem: nam remisi vos ad illum, & ecce, nihil dignum morte factum est ab eo.
units.tr: 15. Nor indeed did Herod either, for I sent you back to him, and behold, nothing worthy of death has been done by him.

units.la: 16. Castigatum ergo eum dimittam.
units.tr: 16. I will therefore chastise him and release him.

units.la: 17. Necesse autem habebat dimittere eis singulis festis vnum(quempiam.)
units.tr: 17. For he was obliged to release one prisoner to them at each feast.

units.la: 18. Exclamauit autem simul vniuersa turba, dicens, Tolle hunc, dimitte vero nobis Barabbam.
units.tr: 18. But the whole crowd cried out together, saying, Away with this man, but release Barabbas to us.

units.la: 19. Qui erat propter seditionem quandam & caedem factam in vrbe, coniectus in carcerem.
units.tr: 19. Barabbas had been thrown into prison for a certain sedition and a murder committed in the city.

units.la: 20. Rursus ergo Pilatus alloquutus est (eos) volens dimittere Iesum.
units.tr: 20. Pilate therefore spoke to them again, wishing to release Jesus.

units.la: 21. Ipsi vero reclamabant, dicentes, Crucifige, crucifige eum.
units.tr: 21. But they protested, saying, Crucify, crucify him.

units.la: 22. Ille autem tertio dixit eis, Quid enim iste malifecit? nullam noxam capitalem inueni in eo: castigatum ergo eum dimittam.
units.tr: 22. And he said to them a third time, Why, what evil has this man done? I have found no capital offence in him. I will therefore chastise him and release him.

units.la: IOH. 18.
units.tr: JOHN 18.

units.la: 38. Pilatus rursum egressus est ad Iudaeos, & dicit eis, Ego nullum inuenio crimen in eo.
units.tr: 38. Pilate went out again to the Jews and said to them, I find no crime in him.

units.la: 39. Est autem vobis consuetudo vt vnum dimittam vobis in Pascha: vultisne ergo dimittam vobis regem illum Iudaeorum?
units.tr: 39. But you have a custom that I release one prisoner to you at the Passover. Do you want me, then, to release to you the king of the Jews?

units.la: 40. Clamauerunt autem rursum omnes dicentes, Ne istum, sed Barabbam. Erat vero iste Barabbas latro.
units.tr: 40. Then they all cried out again, saying, Not this man, but Barabbas. Now this Barabbas was a robber.

units.la: Vod esset incredibile Iudaeos, quibus proprie Messias erat promissus, & qui soli verum Dei verbum versabant, Iesum Christum non agnitum ad mortem vsque tam pertinaciter fuisse persequuturos, si verum illum esse promissum Messiam, immo virum rum bonum existimassent, ideò Euangelistæ tam diligenter & minutatim singula ipsius in- nocentiæ testimonia conscripserunt, alia aliis cumulantes, vt hactenus audiuimus, & adhuc audituti sumus. Quas Christi passiones quæ hic describuntur si cum iis quæ à prophetis e- rant prædicta conferamus, præsertim ex locis ab Euangelistis & à Iohanne nominatim alla- tis, totidem habebimus argumenta certissima quibus eum esse & non alium qui promissus erat, & omnia nostra debita exsoluisse certo persuadeamur. Quibus item quantus sit pec- catorum nostrorum horror doceamur in eo contemplari & agnoscere, qui tam horrendas pœnas, innocens tamen ipse, nostris illis peccatis debitas, vt sponsor noster ac fideiussor exsoluerit: & parte ex alia tanto melius immen- sam Dei bonitatem perpendamus, vnico Filio suo pro inimicis suis non parcentis: quibus denique tam distinctè & sollicitè descriptis certiores fiamus plenè esse pro nobis satisfa- ctum, vt quandiu vita nobis superest illa sigil- latim & inotio distinctè meditemur & expen- damus. Fauit hoc Deus Opt.Max.siquidem in eo posita nostra salus est.
units.tr: It would be incredible that the Jews, to whom the Messiah had been specifically promised, and who alone held to the true word of God, would have persecuted Jesus Christ, whom they did not recognise, so stubbornly even to death, if they had thought him to be the true promised Messiah, or even a truly good man. For this reason the evangelists wrote down each testimony of his innocence so carefully and in such detail, piling one upon another, as we have heard so far and shall hear still. If we compare these sufferings of Christ, which are described here, with those foretold by the prophets, especially with the passages the evangelists and John cite by name, we will have as many most certain arguments by which we may be persuaded that he is the one and no other who was promised, and that he has paid all our debts. By these we are also taught to contemplate and acknowledge in him how great is the horror of our sins, since he, though innocent himself, endured such horrible penalties owed for those sins, as our surety and guarantor. On the other side, we may weigh all the more the immense goodness of God, who did not spare his only Son for the sake of his enemies. Finally, having been informed of these things in such distinct and careful detail, we may be assured that satisfaction has been fully made for us, so that as long as life remains to us we may meditate on and weigh each of these things separately and distinctly. May God, the Best and Greatest, grant this, for our salvation lies in it.

units.la: En igitur Iesum Christum quartò iam per mediam Icrosolymam misero & abiecto statu rapratum. At quæ vrbs Ierulalem? Dei Ciuitas, Dei Sanctuarium, Dei quies: Domini nempe respectu: sed quantum in hominibus erat, Pro- phetarum trucidatrix, atque ipsius tandem Fi- lij Dei. Matth. 21. 39. profligatissimorum latronum cauerna. Luc.19.v.46.denique desperatæ rebellionis ac contumaciæ rea præ aliis omnibus. Quid ad hæc igitur dicturi sunt qui inseparabili nexu Sanctum Spiritum D.Petri Romano templo alligant,quòd(inquiunt,præter alia, cum summa impudentia) D. Petri & D. Pauli sanguis Romæ fusus est? Egregium sane sanctitatis τεκμήριον. Annon verò potius evidens & palpabile testimonium consonantiæ & congruentiæ inter duas istas urbes, sceleratas trucidatrices, illam quidem Prophetarum & ipsius Iesu Christi, hanc verò duorum insignium Christi Apostolorum: & deinde iam a multis seculis miserorum Dei filiorum incbriatam sanguine quem nondum adhuc satiata sitit? Teneamus igitur adveniente iudicij tempore Babylonem scorti illius septem collibus insidentis sedem, non meliore loco & conditione futuram quàm rebellis illa & sanguine Prophetarum Christíque ipsius infamis Hierusalem.
units.tr: Here, then, we see Jesus Christ led for the fourth time through the middle of Jerusalem in a miserable and abject state. But what city is Jerusalem? God's city, God's sanctuary, God's resting place, indeed, with respect to the Lord. But as far as men were concerned, it was the slayer of the prophets and at last of God's own Son (Matt. 21:39), a den of most abandoned robbers (Luke 19:46), and, above all others, guilty of desperate rebellion and obstinacy. What, then, will those say in response who bind the Holy Spirit inseparably to the Roman temple, arguing (among other things, and with the greatest impudence) that the blood of St Peter and St Paul was shed at Rome? A splendid proof of holiness, indeed! Is it not rather a clear and palpable testimony of the agreement and likeness between these two cities, both guilty slayers, the one of the prophets and of Jesus Christ himself, the other of two outstanding apostles of Christ? Moreover, for many centuries now the one has been drunk with the blood of God's miserable children and still thirsts, not yet satiated. Let us hold, then, that at the time of judgment Babylon, the seat of that harlot who sits on seven hills, will be in no better place or condition than that rebellious Jerusalem, infamous for the blood of the prophets and of Christ himself.

units.la: Vt igitur historiam nostram persequamur, tertius hic actus iudicij coram Pilato aduersus Christum inchoandus nobis ab eo est quod Luc. 23.13. & sequentibus versiculis narratur: in quo Pilatum adhuc in illa æquitate perstitaretur confspicimus, Iesu Christi tuentem innocentiam, eo maxime argumento quòd Herodes neglectis accusatorum criminationibus indemnatum cum ad se remisisset: qua in re sua laude dignus est. Verùm hæc æquitas cummanifesta fuit iniustitia coniuncta: qua in re iterum
units.tr: So that we may follow our history, the third act of the trial of Christ before Pilate is to be begun by us here, as it is narrated in Luke 23:13 and the following verses. In it we see Pilate still persisting in that fairness, defending the innocence of Jesus Christ, chiefly on the ground that Herod, having disregarded the accusers' charges, had sent Jesus back to him unconvicted; in this he deserves praise. But this fairness was joined with manifest injustice. In this matter, again,

units.la: Pilatus sola natu rali æqui tate do- ctus pau- latim de- clinat. Sed Christi in- nocentia magis ac magis pa tefit. rum obseruandum est quàm longo interuallo inter fe dissideant,conscientia Spiritu Dei regenita,& quæ sola reliqua naturali Luce regitur, qua tantùm magis reddimur inexcusabiles. Nam,obsecro, quid in Christo dignum ne lenissima quidè coercitione Pilatus animaduerterat? Nam contrà probè norat, (vt Matthæus diserte id exprimit Matth.27.18.)Iudeorum illum inuidia deplorata fuisse traditum. Quid ergo?Pilatus etsi erat reipsa expertus nihil se promouisse obliquam viam vt se hoc negotio expediret sequutum, dictarétque illi conscientia rationem vnicam, innocentem planè absoluendi, redit tamen ad ingenium, & in idem peccatum incidit, quod illum experientia ipsa cum conscientiæ iactura plus satis edocuisse debuerat.
units.tr: Pilate, taught by natural fairness alone, gradually declines, but the innocence of Christ becomes ever more evident. We must observe how far apart those two things are: the conscience reborn by the Spirit of God, and that which is guided only by the remaining natural light, by which we are made all the more inexcusable. For, I ask you, what was there in Christ, even worthy of the mildest correction, that Pilate had found? For he well knew (as Matthew expressly states, Matt. 27:18) that Jesus had been handed over out of the envy of the Jews. What then? Pilate, though he had in fact found that he gained nothing by following a crooked path to extricate himself from this business, and though conscience dictated to him the one course, to acquit the innocent man outright, nevertheless returned to his own disposition and fell into the same sin, which experience itself should have taught him well enough, at the cost of his conscience.

units.la: Sed priusquàm hoc aggredior, age ex hoc loco discamus,quid sit Liuor & Inuidia, quàque sit vitium illud coram Domino, imò coram omnibus sanæ mentis hominibus detestandum. Aio igitur etsi vitia quibus tota humana natura infecta est,ab eadem fœda scatu-rigine prosiliant,peccato putà primi nostri parentis, & à consecuta indè corruptione in nobis nascantur,verè tamen posse ac debere dici in reliquis omnibus vitiis inuidiam primum corruptionis locum occupare. Natura enim licet corrupta,tamen quod esse bonum existimat, probat & expetit: contrà quod malum iudicat,damnat & refugit.Hinc videas natura licet Hagitiosos homines,nisi prorsus fascinati, ti, mirari tamen apud fe quam in aliis vident virtutem, vt natura pauper diuitem aspiciens, laudat diuitias, & diuitem fe optat. Inuidus vero sic alterius afficitur mœrérque bonis, vt plerunque non tantum illi cuius ista bona sunt male velit, & ea eripere cupiat: sed eo vs- que progrediatur vt boni pollelforem & bonum ipsum etiam odio vehementi prosequatur. Quod naturæ simpliciter corruptæ penitus repugnat. Nullum autem huius rei certius & magis detestandum exemplum habemus, eo à quo tam detestandum istud vitium ad homines dimanauit, Satana. Nam quid eum in qua fuerat primus homo conditus integritas offendebat? Annon illa Dei imago speciosa de se ipsa insignem amorem concitabat? At perditus ille Satan non modò itatu huncin homi ne ferre no potuit: sed vt totus est in malo immersus, sic offensus est, tum homine, tu ea qua præditus erat integritate, vt quantum in ipso fuit no nisi vtroque profligato coquicuerit: vt etiam num hodie maledicti illi Spiritus suum Creatorem oderunt, cuius gloriam pro viribus abolere niturtur, de solio si possent detur- baturi. Hac contagione ij de quibus agimus Christi inimici infecti fuerunt, suntque etiam hodie omnes illorum similes. Nam quæ causa fuit cur odio plus quàm Variniano iustissimorum iustissimum vnum persequerentur? eum inquam, qui malum bono compensare nó desinebat, nisi quòd nequissimi homines non modò iustum eos arguentem ferre non potc- iant, rant, sed etiam eius memoriam si fieri possit extinctam cupiebant: canem ad praescpe nimirum imitari, nec hordeo vescentem, & eodem equum vesci vetantem? Et hac re inuidus & aemulus inter se differunt. Aemulus enim alteri bonum inuidet quo solus ipse frui cupiat: invidus autem etiam in odium usque provehitur alterius & ipsius boni: ut non immerito istiusmodi inuidi corporei carneique daemones dicendi sint.
units.tr: But before I take this up, let us learn from this passage what envy and jealousy are, and how detestable that vice is before the Lord, indeed before all sane people. I say, therefore, that although the vices with which all human nature is infected spring from the same foul source, arising in us from the sin of our first parent and the corruption that followed from it, nevertheless envy may truly be said, and ought to be said, to hold the first place of corruption among all the other vices. For nature, though corrupt, nonetheless approves and seeks what it judges good, and condemns and shuns what it judges evil. Hence you may see that nature, unless utterly bewitched, even admires in itself the virtue it sees in others, as the poor man looking at the rich praises riches and wishes to be rich himself. But the envious man is so affected and grieved by another's goods that he usually not only wishes ill to the one whose goods they are and desires to snatch them away, but proceeds so far as to pursue with violent hatred both the possessor of the good and the good itself. This is wholly repugnant to simply corrupt nature. We have no more certain or more detestable example of this than Satan, from whom this detestable vice flowed to men. For what offended him in the integrity in which the first man was created? Did not that beautiful image of God arouse in itself a remarkable love? But that lost Satan not only could not bear this integrity in man; as he is wholly immersed in evil, so he was offended both by the man and by the integrity with which he was endowed, and as far as he could, he rested only when both were destroyed. Even today those cursed spirits hate their Creator, whose glory they strive by all their power to abolish, and they would overthrow him from his throne if they could. Those of whom we speak, Christ's enemies, were infected with this contagion, and all their like are infected today. For what was the cause why they persecuted the one most just of the just with a hatred greater than that of Varinius? I mean the one who did not cease to repay evil with good, except that the most wicked men could not bear not only that he rebuked them as unjust, but also desired that his memory be extinguished if possible, imitating, of course, the dog in the manger, which neither eats the barley nor allows the horse to eat it. In this respect the envious and the emulous differ. For the emulous man begrudges another a good that he himself wishes to enjoy alone; but the envious man is carried even to hatred of the other and of the good itself, so that such envious persons may not unjustly be called corporeal and fleshly demons.

units.la: Porro si quod vitium ex diametro repugnat officio Christiano, istud est, primum quòd ad Legis primam tabulam, Dei gloriam penitus abolens, tanto illustriorem quo eius benedictiones sunt magis inter homines conspicuae. En cur, quum esset Mosi nuntiatum Eldadum Medadumque in castris prophetisare, tantum abest ut ipsis inuiderit, ut contra non solos sceptuaginta illos cum quibus deinceps populum erat gubernaturus, sed vniuersum etiam populum Sp. S. agi & prophetare in votis habuerit. Num. 11. 26. Simili ratione Iohannes Baptista non aegre tulit, imo maximè laetatus est Lucem Domini pedetentim augescentem famuli quodammodo Lucem obscurare Ioh. 3. 30. Et Apostolus in omnibus suis Epistolis non minores Deo de acceptis multis ab ipso beneficiis, quàm de iis quae erat in alios collata gratias agit. Idem esto de charitate in proximum iudicium, quae secundae tabulae summa est. Nam obsecro, quinam proximorum miseriis afficeretur, aut eius commodis laetaretur, & studeP. j. ret, qui eius rebus fecundis mœret & illis ipsum ipoliare nititur? quînam inuidus inimicos diligeret, quum non tantùm amicos odërit, sed quos nunquam vidit aut cognouit?
units.tr: Moreover, if any vice is directly opposed to the Christian duty, it is this: first, that it utterly abolishes, against the first tablet of the Law, the glory of God, which is all the more illustrious the more conspicuous his blessings are among men. Hence, when it was reported to Moses that Eldad and Medad were prophesying in the camp, he was so far from envying them that, on the contrary, he wished that not only those seventy with whom he was to govern the people from then on, but the whole people, might be moved by the Holy Spirit and prophesy. (Num. 11.26.) In a similar way John the Baptist was not grieved but greatly rejoiced that the light of the Lord, gradually increasing, was in a sense obscuring the servant's light. (John 3.30.) And the Apostle in all his Epistles gives thanks to God for the many benefits he has received from him no less than for those conferred on others. The same judgment holds for love of neighbour, which is the sum of the second tablet. For I ask you, who would be affected by the miseries of neighbours or rejoice in their advantages, and who would strive for that? Or who would want to strip of their prosperity the very person whose prosperity grieves him? What envious person would love his enemies, when he hates not only his friends but also those whom he has never seen or known?

units.la: Addam aliquid ad superiora, nempe quum singula Dei dona spiritualia vel temporalia Christianorum sint ita propria, vt communem eorum vsum esse oporteat, vt egregia illa similitudine membrorum humani corporis docet Apostolus. 1. Cor. 12. necessario inde sequi nullum inuidere proximo, quin in suum ipsius damnum conspiret: vnde alio inuidos esse inter vitiosos omnes tetterrimas peltes, tam ab omni Christiana Religione alienos & tá inimicos, vt sint inimici perditissimi Dei, proximorum & suiipsorum.
units.tr: I will add something to what has been said above. Since the individual spiritual and temporal gifts of God belong to Christians in such a way that they ought to be shared in common, as the Apostle teaches by that outstanding likeness of the members of the human body (1 Cor. 12.), it necessarily follows that no one who envies his neighbour fails to conspire to his own harm. Hence envy, among all the vices, is the most foul pest, so alien and hostile to every Christian religion that its practitioners become the most destructive enemies of God, of their neighbours and of themselves.

units.la: Quid igitur iuuat pluribus disputare? Nam si simplex alterius boni concupiscentia cum nomine Christiano pugnat, quid fiet detestanda illa inuidia quę longe vlterius progreditur, totque in orbem Christianum calamitates & confusiones inuchit? Nullum igitur hic medium. Vos hæc igitur, oro & obtestor, attendite, & vestris membris altius infigite, & melius quàm hactenus in vsum reuocate: si minus sciitote, Deum Æternum Iehouam iobis iltam tandem esse detracturum quam oltentamus reformatæ religionis larvam, interea tamen corde & externis operibus naturam Diabolicam fouentes: réque ipsi tandem patefacturum nobis Euangelium in ruinam & exitium vt olim Hierosolymis, non ad salusalutem, praedicatum.
units.tr: Why then does it help to argue at greater length? For if a simple desire for another's good conflicts with the Christian name, what will become of that detestable envy which goes much further and brings so many calamities and disorders upon the Christian world? There is therefore no middle ground here. I beg and implore you, then, to attend to these things, to fix them more deeply in your hearts and to put them into practice better than you have hitherto. If you do not, know that the eternal God, Jehovah, will at last strip away from us that mask of the reformed religion which we display, while in our hearts and external works we nurture a diabolical nature; and that he will at last reveal to us the Gospel, which is preached for our ruin and destruction, as once at Jerusalem, and not for our salvation.

units.la: Ad Pilatum reuertitur oratio, qui conscie- cientia excitatus ne Iesu Christi innocentiam laederet, & cognita accusatorum inuidia, qua impellente Christum detulerant, & tandem ab vxore, tanquam oraculo, ne Christum offen deret admonitus, se quidem hoc negotio explicare conatus est, sed frustra, quaesitis videlicet ambagibus, quum rectam viam insistere ipsum oporteret, & ita magis ac magis in istud barathrum immersus est. Idem accidat oportet necessario omnibus vel tantillum a recto & aequo recedentibus, & ad dextram aut laevam suas cogitationes flectentibus. Idipsum prophanos etiam agnouisse, ex Lucis mensura quae in hominibus est reliqua videmus, magnis eos laudibus efferentes, qui virtutis & recti studiosi rebus omnibus immo vitae suae illud anteponebant, quo minus est Pilatus coram Deo & hominibus excusandus.
units.tr: The discourse returns to Pilate, who, stirred by conscience lest he harm the innocence of Jesus Christ, and recognising the envy by which the accusers were moved when they denounced Christ, and at last warned by his wife as if by an oracle not to offend Christ, did indeed try to extricate himself from the matter, but in vain. He sought devious circuits when he ought to have kept to the straight path, and so he was more and more immersed in that abyss. The same must necessarily happen to all who depart even a little from what is right and fair and turn their thoughts to right or left.
