We see from the measure of light still left in men that even profane people have recognised this, greatly praising those who put virtue and righteousness before all things, indeed before their very lives. By this standard Pilate is all the less excusable before God and men.

units.la: De vxoris autem Pilati admonitione cauenda est vt in reliquis nimium curiosa inquisitio, ne pro veritate somnia nostra obtrudamus. Sufficiat nosse Deum sua prouidentia voluisse foeminam quoque istam de Iesu Christi innocentia testem adhibere, quo minus haberet Iudex a quo damnatus est excusationis: seu Deus hoc somnium mulieri illi immiserit, vt aliis saepe non magis ad Ecclesiam pertinentibus Pharaoni puta & Nebucadnezari & similibus: seu, quod vero propius videtur, non ignara fuerit tumultus passim tota vrbe excitati, & Christum ad maritum mane summo adductum fuisse, multa animo apprehenderit quibus istud omnium in phantasia formatum sit: quum etiam non alienum à vero sit ad eius aures aliquid de Christo, eiusque sermonibus & factis tota illa septimana fuisse perlatum, vt non immerito luctum cum nuncuparit. Haec, inquam, non curiosis sufficiunto.
units.tr: As for the warning of Pilate's wife, we must take care, as in other matters, not to pursue too curious an inquiry, lest we foist our own dreams upon the truth. It is enough to know that God, by his providence, willed this woman too to bear witness to the innocence of Jesus Christ, so that the judge who condemned him would have less excuse. Whether God sent this dream to that woman, as he often did to others not much belonging to the Church (Pharaoh, for instance, and Nebuchadnezzar and such like), or whether, which seems nearer the truth, she, not unaware of the tumult stirred up throughout the whole city, and that Christ had been brought to her husband early in the morning, had taken in many things in her mind from which this whole image was formed in her fancy (since it is not foreign to the truth that something about Christ, his words and deeds, had been reported to her ears throughout that whole week, so that she not unjustly called it a time of mourning). These things, I say, are enough for those who are not curious.

units.la: Quid igitur? Pilatus quem oportuerat recti tenacem conscientiam illesam retinere, quum haec via missio ad Herodem Christo non succeßisset, aliam aggreditur, longe peiorem superiore illa, quo in effugio triplex error est. Primus quod si Christum venia data dimissset, noxium cum suo calculo & morte dignum iudicasset, de cuius antea innocentia tam illustre testimonium ediderat: alter in eo quod Christum cum nefario & profligato Barabba componens, maximo illum dedecore & infamia notabat. Tertius, quod animaduertere Pilatum oportuerat, quum D.Matth.27.15.& D. Marc.15.1. expresse dicant penes populum eius quem vellent liberari nominationem fuisse Iudaeos Barabbae facinora considerantes potuisse respondere neutrum eorum se velle liberari, tertiumque alium eligere. Sed eò tandem deuenient oportet quibus leue est conscientiam ledere, speciose praetexta sibi fucum facientibus, quod satis experientia, sed sero nimis, summo cum eorum dispendio restatur.
units.tr: What then? Pilate, who ought to have kept his conscience upright and unharmed, when this way of sending Christ to Herod had not succeeded, took up another, far worse than the former, and this escape involves a threefold error. The first: if he had dismissed Christ with pardon, he would have judged him guilty and deserving of death by his own reckoning, whose innocence he had previously attested so clearly. The second: by setting Christ alongside the wicked and abandoned Barabbas, he branded him with the greatest disgrace and infamy. The third: since Matth. 27.15. and Mark 15.1. expressly say that the choice of whom to release lay with the people, Pilate ought to have noticed that the Jews, considering Barabbas's crimes, could have answered that neither of them was to be released, and chosen another. But those who find it a light matter to injure their conscience must come to this, pretending to cover themselves with specious pretexts; which experience proves, though too late and at great cost to themselves.

units.la: In omnibus igitur negotiis discamus primum mùm Dei verbo niti, bonúm-ne sit an malum quod in deliberationem venit, idest Dei verbo mandatum an prohibitum explorantes: deinde an vocationi nostræ respondeat, nécne:nostro nimirum erga Deum & proximum officio: quibus positis nulla vnquam difficultas, nullum incommodum, nullum periculum ab hominibus imminés nos ab officio ne passum quidé vnů dimouebút. Certú enim est & extra omne dubium, nullos vnquam turiús agere quàm qui ex animo præstitutam sibi à Domino viá fortiter insistunt, Deúmque ducentem sequuntur: contrà neminem magis, quàm Deo resistentem, periclitari.
units.tr: In all affairs, then, let us learn first to rest on the Word of God, examining whether what comes into deliberation is good or evil, that is, whether it is commanded or forbidden by God's word; and then whether it answers to our calling, that is, to our duty towards God and neighbour. Once these are settled, no difficulty, no inconvenience, no danger threatening from men will ever move us a single step from duty. For it is certain and beyond all doubt that no one ever acts more safely than those who, from the heart, resolutely keep to the way marked out for them by the Lord and follow God as he leads; conversely, no one is in greater peril than one who resists God.

units.la: Hic autem nobis expendenda occasio illa huius effugij quærendi, consuetudo nimirum dimittendi Iudæis captiuum aliquem singulis festis solennibus, quam quidem initium à prouinciarum Præsidibus cœpisse verisimile est, redaćta Iudæa in prouinciam, sic Romanis sibi nouos tributarios conciliare volentibus, ac proinde si Josepho Iudæo historico fidem habemus, non fuisse hanc consuetudinem annorum plus quàm viginti duorum. At longè minore temporis spatio praua consuetudo inuehitur & inualescit, vt experimur quotidie, tam difficulter eradicanda, quàm facilè inualuerat.
units.tr: Here we must weigh that occasion for seeking this escape: the custom, namely, of releasing to the Jews some prisoner at each solemn feast. It is likely that this custom began with the governors of the provinces, after Judea was reduced to a province, thus winning new tributaries for the Romans. Therefore, if we trust the Jewish historian Josephus, this custom had not existed for more than twenty-two years. Yet in a much shorter span of time a bad custom is introduced and gains strength, and, as we experience every day, it is as hard to root out as it was easy to establish.

units.la: Quid igitur? Nempe quod ab omnibus admittitur fatendum est aduersus Deum non sese præscriptionem: vnde sequitur nullam vnquam temporis diuturnitatem efficere vt dici possit aut debeat bonum, quod Deus improbat & malum dicit: quum bonæ aut malæ alicuius rei qualitas in se ipsa sit, non a temporis qualitate pendeat. Vt igitur homo nequam, non melior quo senior, sed eo peior habetur qui demum esse malus incipit: sic inveterata mala consuetudo, eo magis est condemnanda & corrigenda, quo magis speciosa venerandæ antiquitatis nomine tecta, decipiendis hominibus est accommoda.
units.tr: What then? It must be admitted that prescription does not hold against God, and so no length of time can make into something good what God disapproves and calls evil, nor make it deserve to be called good; for the quality of a thing as good or bad in itself does not depend on the quality of time. Just as a wicked man is not considered better the older he grows, but is all the worse if he only begins to be wicked at last, so an ingrained bad custom is all the more to be condemned and corrected, the more it is covered with the specious name of venerable antiquity and is suited to deceiving men.

units.la: Romanis igitur Catholicis nobis in hodiernis controversiis suarum traditionum & rituum antiquitatem, quam millenariu numerum excedere, obiectantibus (cuiusmodi sane illos etiam longe veteriores ritus habere non dissitemur, ut qui ad annorum tria millia referantur, puta quos vel ex Ethnicismo hauserunt, vel ex Iudaismo retinuerunt) respondemus non ideo meliores nec commendatiores fieri: & ut quidam ex veteribus loquitur, Veterem consuetudinem, veterem errorem esse, eo magis abolendum. Præterea, si ad vetustatem recurrendum est, bonum ac verum dicimus malo & falso fore semper prius. Contra vero morem aliquem aut ritum Dei voluntati consentaneum, & ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem spectantem licet recens exortum, tamen bonis conditionibus laudandum & admittendum.
units.tr: So when the Roman Catholics, in today's controversies, object to us the antiquity of their traditions and rites, which exceeds a thousand years (and indeed we do not deny that they have even much older rites, dating back some three thousand years, which they either drew from heathenism or retained from Judaism), we reply that they do not thereby become better or more commendable. As one of the ancients says, an old custom is an old error, and so all the more to be abolished. Moreover, if we must appeal to antiquity, we say that the good and the true will always come before the evil and the false. On the contrary, a custom or rite that accords with God's will and serves the building up of the Church, even if it has only recently arisen, is to be praised and admitted, provided the conditions are good.

units.la: Vt autem propius ad rem de qua agitur accedamus, accipite quibus nominibus mos iste recis Veniam dandi commendetur, pretiosa nimirum Clementiæ & Misericordiæ, quibus ut sibi propriis Reges, Principes, & summi Magistragiftratus, maximè gaudent, tanquam ea re ad magni illius Regum Regis, à quo sceptra sua acceperunt, imaginem bonitatis & mifericor- diæ propiùs accedentes. At nulla magis me- tuenda vitia iis quæ virtutis pallio teguntur. Aio igitur, non quicquid Clementiam imitatur Clementiæ nomine dignum esse:non secus ac lupum manibus tenens eúmque dimittens, nomine Clementiæ & bonitatis indignus est, qui mille ouibus causa mortis sit. Verè igitur laudanda & commendanda Clementia crudelitati immò etiam Summo iuris rigori opposita. At in ea duo potissimum requiro : primùm vt bono fundamento nitatur:alterum vt Temperata sit.Id verò fit,quum Summus Magistratus Clementia sua nec contrà Dei mandatum peccat : nec in suorum subditorum commodum & publicam quietem, cuius illum acceptæ à Domino custodem ac conservatorem esse oportet.
units.tr: But to come closer to the matter in question, consider the names by which this custom of kings granting pardon is commended: namely the precious names of clemency and mercy. Kings, princes and the highest magistrates take great delight in these, as though by them they came nearer to the image of the goodness and mercy of that great King of kings, from whom they have received their sceptres. Yet no vices are more to be feared than those that are covered with the cloak of virtue. I say, therefore, that not everything that imitates clemency deserves the name of clemency. Just as a man who holds a wolf in his hands and lets it go is unworthy of the name of clemency and goodness, so is one who causes the death of a thousand sheep. Clemency is rightly praised and commended when it is opposed to cruelty, and even to the strict rigour of the highest law. Yet in clemency I require two things above all: first, that it rest on a good foundation; second, that it be tempered. This happens when the highest magistrate in his clemency does not sin either against God's command, or to the advantage of his subjects and the public peace, whose guardian and preserver he ought to be, as one who has received this charge from the Lord.

units.la: Hic igitur summi Reges ac Monarchæ dicunto, magnum illum Iehouam qui solus miseretur cuius vult, cuius voluntas est æqui rectique omnis sola regula, nunquam hominibus vitæ necísque potestatem absolutam dedilse, aut daturum esse,quam soli sibi reservat,vt qui in omnes à se res creatas imperium, quo nunquam abutitur,solus obtineat.Exempli gratia. Si de facinorosis nunquam ad meliorem frugem redeuntibus agitur, maxima est differentia inter magnam Dei patientiam, qua tolerat ipsos ad tempus, vt eò magis sint
units.tr: Let the highest kings and monarchs therefore hear this: the great Jehovah, who alone has mercy on whom he wills, whose will is the sole rule of all equity and righteousness, has never given, and will never give, to men an absolute power over life and death. This power he reserves for himself alone, so that he alone may hold dominion over all created things, a dominion he never abuses. For example: when we are dealing with wicked men who never return to better conduct, there is a great difference between God's great patience, by which he tolerates them for a time so that they may be all the more [inexcusable (ἀναπολόγητοι)],

units.la: P. iiij. ἀναπολόγητοι, & impunitatem, quam vt plurimum ne in hac quidem vita effugiunt: à qua si qui in hac vita sunt immunes, centuplo tamen eam in alia vita, in omnem æternitatem compesant. Quorum vero tum hic tum in alio seculo miseretur, nunquam impune miseretur, quorum peccatis debitam pœnam Iesus Christus totam exhausit, ac plenè Deo satisfecit.
units.tr: (page 4) and impunity, which for the most part they do not escape even in this life. If some are free from this in this life, they will nonetheless pay for it a hundredfold in another life, throughout all eternity. But those whom God has mercy on, both here and in the next age, he never pardons without penalty, since Jesus Christ has exhausted the due punishment for their sins and has fully satisfied God.

units.la: Quibus positis certissimis & invictissimis fundamentis, aio & alioquin in criminibus quæ Deus capitalia iudicat, per reliquam in homine illam Legem naturalem, quæ certissima & immutabilis Dei vox est, nullu esse locu Veniç, qua vita redimatur, vt hoc qui audeat, quod vnius Dei proprium est sibi arroget. At priusquam capitale dicatur crimen, diligenti singulari circumstantiarum opus est inspectione, quod ex ipsius Domini præscripto, in homicidij casu examinando satis est apertum: cum quo Iuris etiam ciuile pulchre conuenit. Addo, multas incidere circumstantias quibus crimen, merito capitale iudicatum, tamen possit in pœnam non minus capitalem, sed tamen leniorem de seueriore commutari: semper tamen stante hoc quod ait ipse Dominus, Oculus tuus non parcet homicidæ. Quod de omnibus ciusdem naturæ criminibus dictu volo: multòque magis de grauioribus, si quæ sunt.
units.tr: On these most certain and unconquered foundations I affirm also that, in crimes which God judges capital, there is no place for a pardon by which a life is redeemed, by the natural law that remains in man, which is the most certain and unchanging voice of God. Anyone who dares to grant such a pardon arrogates to himself what belongs to God alone. But before a crime is called capital, a careful and particular examination of the circumstances is needed. This is sufficiently clear from the Lord's own prescription for examining a case of homicide, and civil law agrees well with it. I add that many circumstances may arise under which a crime rightly judged capital may nonetheless be changed, as a punishment, from the more severe to one not less capital but milder; yet the saying of the Lord himself always stands: "Your eye shall not spare the murderer." I wish this to be said of all crimes of the same nature, and much more of the graver ones, if there are any.

units.la: Nec iuuat exceptio, Iudæorum nos Legibus non obligari. Quod certissimum est in iis quæ huic genti propria fuerunt, at non in iis quæ naturali & vniuersali æquitate nituntur. Nec maioris momenti sunt Dauidis exem-pla, Ioabo homicidæ parcentis, Ammoni fo-roris suæ incerto raptori, Absalomo fratricidæ, & siquæ sunt illis similia. Nam vt veteri trito Veróque proverbio dicitur, Legibus non exemplis iudicandum est: quibus adde Dauidem ipsum tandem de Ioabo culpam agnouisse & emendasse: quum sæpe Magistratus contingat non posse quæ alioqui vellent exequi: de reliquis autem eius lapsibus non diu dilatam pœnam, quam seueram expertus est.
units.tr: Nor does the objection help, that we are not bound by the laws of the Jews. This is most certainly true of those things that were proper to that people, but not of those that rest on natural and universal equity. Nor are the examples of David of greater weight: his sparing Joab the murderer, Ammon the ravisher of his sister, and Absalom the fratricide, and any others like them. For, as the old, worn and true proverb says, judgment must be made by laws, not by examples. To these add that David himself at last acknowledged and corrected his fault concerning Joab, since it often happens to a magistrate that he cannot carry out what he would otherwise wish. As for his other lapses, the punishment was not long delayed, and he found it severe.

units.la: Eiusdem ponderis est quorūdam argumentum istud, Si priuatus alteri condonans offensam pulchrè facit, potiore ratione Principem posse admissum contra se crimen remittere. Hoc enim posito sequeretur, Principi nunquā in facinorosos animaduertendū, quum priuatos Deus iubeat proximis, immo & inimicis ipsis omnes offensas remittere. Obseruandum igitur longo hæc inter se interuallo distare de suo iure cedere, & de Dei, puniri aliquid mandantis, iure remittere. Deinde, eiusmodi de quibus agimus crimina nec admitti, nec in iudicio considerari tanquam in priuatum patrata, cui possit ciuiliter satisfieri, sed vt in tranquillitatem & commodum publicum peccantia, cuius Principe sic esse custodé oportet vt de iure nihil remittat, quum contra tum à Deo, tum à populo potestate hac acceperit, vt meritis suppliciis scelleratos afficiat. Tertiò aio veniā quā proximo debemus proprie conscientia respicere, odioq; & vindictę cupiditati opponi, sic tamen vt qui iniuriam passus est, ius suum, si opus est & ita videbitur, etiam apud iudicem persequi non prohibeatur, absit modo odium aut alia animi perturbatio charitati contraria.
units.tr: Of the same weight is the argument of certain people: if a private person does well in pardoning an offence done to him, then by stronger reasoning a prince may remit a crime committed against himself. For if this were granted, it would follow that a prince should never punish wrongdoers, since God commands private persons to remit all offences to their neighbours, and even to their enemies. We must observe, therefore, that there is a long interval between giving up one's own right and remitting, by right, something that God has commanded to be punished. Next, crimes of the kind we are discussing are neither to be admitted, nor to be considered in judgment as if they had been committed against a private person, to whom satisfaction could be made in civil terms; rather they are offences against the tranquillity and public good, and the prince ought to be the guardian of these in such a way that he gives up nothing of his right. For he has received this power from God and from the people, so that he may punish the wicked with deserved penalties. Thirdly, I say that the pardon we owe to our neighbour must be considered in conscience, and must be set against hatred and the desire for revenge, yet in such a way that the one who has suffered the wrong is not prevented from pursuing his right before a judge, if necessity requires and it seems fit, provided only that hatred or some other disturbance of mind contrary to charity is absent.

units.la: At si quum eximendi rei supplicio capitali quaedam subesse videtur iuris species, tamen illicitum est Veniam dare, quid de iis iudicandum putamus qui Venias eiusmodi vel amicorum gratia & fauore, vel corruptis iudicibus, vel leuitate, vel prauo Magistratuum aut Principum consilio, vel peiore adhuc alia qualibet ratione redimunt? Nempe illos aio quod Dei proprium est sibi arrogare: bonas leges & statuta euertere, sine quibus humana societas stare nequeat: aio etiā eiusmodi Venia aut Gratias totidem esse periuria, in praestitu Deo & subditis iuramentū, qui se tutelae ipsorum aduersus improbos & tranquillitatis publicae perturbatores tradiderunt. Aio denique totidem esse maledictiones tandem in ipsorum capita, & saepe etiā posteritatis recidentes, quum verum sit tritum illud proverbium, Ereptum patibulo flagitiosum quempiam, in illud suum redemptorem immittere.
units.tr: But if, although some appearance of right seems to attend the removal of a capital punishment, it is nonetheless unlawful to grant a pardon, what are we to judge of those who redeem such pardons for the sake of friends and favour, or by corrupt judges, or out of levity, or by the perverse counsel of magistrates or princes, or by any other still worse reason? I say that they arrogate to themselves what belongs to God: they overthrow good laws and statutes, without which human society cannot stand. I say also that such pardons or favours are as many perjuries, since an oath has been sworn to God and to subjects by those who have handed themselves over to the protection of their subjects against the wicked and the disturbers of public peace. Finally I say that they are as many curses, which at last fall back upon their own heads, and often upon their posterity as well, since that old proverb is true: "a wicked man snatched from the gallows will turn upon his rescuer."

units.la: De facinoribus vero minime natura sua capitalibus, sed tantum quarundam legum priuatis de causis institutarum respectu: aio vt haec leges ab iis quibus istiusmodi politias instituendi potestas est, specialibus de causis latae sunt, eadem etiam auctoritate posse ipsas non tantum mitigari, sed etiam abrogari. Multo magis igitur pœna potest leuior statui aut etiā omnino aduersus eas peccantibus ex gratia remitti: modò tamen id bonis rationibus, iustis, & maturo consilio deliberatis, sine dolo, sine fraude,aut praua alia qualibet animi perturbatione fiat: sine vllo publicæ tranquillitatis incommodo. Legum enim violationem Statibus omnibus exitiosam esse, pedetentim autem ipsas istiusmodi veniis tāquam per cuniculos tentari violarique, aliis primò quidem contortis, aliis omnino tandem abrogatis?certum est.
units.tr: As for crimes that are by their nature not capital at all, but only in respect of certain laws established for private reasons, I say that just as such laws were passed by those who have the power to establish such polities, for special reasons, so by the same authority they can not only be mitigated but even abrogated. Much more, then, may a lighter penalty be set, or even a complete remission be granted as a favour to those who offend against them, provided this is done for good reasons, just and deliberately considered, without deceit, without fraud, or any other perverse disturbance of mind, and without any detriment to public tranquillity. For it is certain that the violation of laws is destructive to all states, and that, when laws are gradually attacked and violated by such pardons, as if through mines, first some are twisted and at last all are entirely abrogated.

units.la: Habetis,fratres,quod hactenus de hac materia,tum ex diuini verbi fontibus,tum ab ipsa naturali ratione didici: quod quum tanti sit momenti si iampridem esset animaduersum & obseruatum,non esset hac in parte tam graviter peccatum: quod vtinam iis Dominus à quibus peccatum est condonet,& immunes in posterum ab eiusmodi lapsu tueatur. Quid si merito tales Gratiæ notantur, quid futurum iis est, qui Gratia indignos si crimen fassi deprecarentur, tamen absolutos dimittunt? Næ multi cristas attollunt, quos in altum cleuari, vt Pharaonis pistorem oportuerat. Gen. 40.19.&22.
units.tr: You have heard, brethren, what I have learned thus far on this subject, both from the fountains of the divine Word and from natural reason itself. Since the matter is of such great importance, had it long since been noticed and observed, we would not have sinned so grievously in this respect. May the Lord pardon those by whom the sin has been committed, and keep them in future free from such a fall. But if such favours are rightly branded, what will become of those who, though unworthy of favour, have been acquitted and dismissed after confessing their crime? Indeed many raise their crests, who ought to have been lifted up on high like Pharaoh's baker. [Gen. 40.19 & 22.]

units.la: Nullo igitur legitimo fundamento,consuetudo illa de qua hic agimus nitebatur. At non mirum est Imperatores Romanos sibi vitæ necísque subditorū potestatem attribuisse, quos non puduit se Deos nominare, sibíque aras, pontifices, sacrificia viuentibus adhuc in terris dicare. Et notum est quod Esaias Regibus Babylonis exprobrat, Esai. 14. 13. ex cuius loci falsa interpretatione factum est, ut Lucifer dictus sit Satan. At dolendum est inter Christianos, sive adulatorum culpa id accidit, à quibus iam olim Reges & Principes fascinantur: sive ij quos Deus in altum Dignitatis quempiam gradum evexit, facile sibi tantum arrogant, non tantum Imperatores & Reges, sed multos Principes & Dominos subalternos, & Magistratus liberarum Rerumpublicarum, eò deveniste ut penes se esse potestatem veniam, quibuscunque volent, concedendi sibi persuaserint: ut qui neget, datam illis hanc potestatem laesae Maiestatis reus teneatur. Dixi tamen quod res est.
units.tr: No lawful foundation, therefore, supported that custom of which we are speaking. Yet it is no wonder that the Roman emperors claimed for themselves the power of life and death over their subjects, they who were not ashamed to call themselves gods and to dedicate to themselves, while still living on earth, altars, priests and sacrifices. And it is well known that Isaiah reproaches the kings of Babylon, [Isa. 14.13], from whose false interpretation of that passage it came about that Lucifer was called Satan. But it is to be lamented that among Christians this happens, either through the fault of flatterers, by whom kings and princes have long been bewitched, or through those whom God has raised to some high degree of dignity, who easily arrogate so much to themselves: not only emperors and kings, but many subordinate princes and lords and magistrates of free commonwealths. They have come to such a point that they persuade themselves that the power of granting pardon to whomever they will lies in their hands, so that whoever denies that this power was given to them is held guilty of treason against majesty. I have said it nonetheless, as the matter stands.

units.la: En vero iterum admirandum hac in re abusum Episcoporum, alioquin etiam insignium virorum, culpa: quibus oculos specios illa Lenitatis & Clementiae nomina perstrinxerunt. Nempe Deo se rem gratam & ad eius gloriam promouendam accommodam facturos arbitrati sunt, si etiam criminum capitalium reis carceres, festis illis solennibus, aperirent, quod ex multis Imperialibus constitutionibus est conspicuum. Fateor quidem excipi ab ipsis maiora crimina, homicidium puta, veneficium, adulterium, laesae Maiestatis crimen, raptum, adulterationem monetae. Sed quorsum istas exceptiones? Annon furor est impunitatem eorum qui supplicio digni sunt, putare partem esse cultus illius, qui diserte pronuntiat non miminus sibi abominandum eum esse qui absoluit improbum, quàm qui iustum condemnat?Proverb.17.15.
units.tr: Here again we see an abuse, worthy of wonder, in this matter, and the fault lies with bishops, otherwise distinguished men, whom the specious names of Mildness and Clemency have dazzled. They thought they would be doing God a pleasing service, and one suited to advancing his glory, if at those solemn festivals they opened the prisons even to those accused of capital crimes, as is evident from many imperial constitutions. I grant that they exclude greater crimes: murder, poisoning, adultery, treason, rape, and debasing the coinage. But why these exceptions? Is it not madness to think that impunity for those who deserve punishment is part of that worship which plainly declares that he who acquits the wicked is no less abominable to God than he who condemns the just? (Prov. 17.15.)

units.la: Ac sanè tantum abest vt his exceptionibus modus sit abusui aliquis adhibitus, vt contrà momento exceptiones illæ euanuerint: sibique quotidie summi Magistratus quibuslibet criminibus Veniam largiendi potestatem arrogent, hac addita clausa, Sit pro ratione voluntas:quod tamen Deo Opt.Max.cuius semper æquissima rectissimaque voluntas, soli debetur.
units.tr: Indeed, these exceptions have so far from being any limit on the abuse that they have quickly vanished. Each day the highest magistrates claim for themselves the power to grant pardon for any crimes whatever, adding this clause: "Let it be as he wills." Yet this belongs to God alone, the best and greatest, whose will is always most just and right.

units.la: At longè peius istis quiddam adhuc committit. Nam penè incredibili abusu quidam olim Episcopi adeò malè docti fuerunt & impudentes, vt à Regibus impetrarint verè Satanicam potestatem, vt die sui ingressus minimè sanè Episcopalis, sed Dominis potius aut Regibus proprij, & ex diametro Christi illi ingressui repugnantis, quicunque ad hanc impunitatem accurrerint cuiuscunq; criminis rei, nulla distinctione criminum aut personarum absoluatur. Atque adeò testor me hisce oculis conspexisse, plusquàm quingentos criminum capitalium reos, ab Aureliamensi quodam Episcopo numerata pecunia pro æstimatione & numero cædium aliorum ve criminum absolutos:& quidem in Dei honorem & gloriam. Siccine vero Dei, quem etiam ab altaris sui cornibus homicidam ad supplicium rapi voluisse legimus?
units.tr: But they commit something far worse still. By an almost incredible abuse, some bishops of old were so ill-taught and shameless that they obtained from kings a truly satanic power. On the day of their entry, which was by no means episcopal but rather that of their own lords or kings, and diametrically opposed to Christ's entry, whoever ran to this impunity, guilty of any crime, was absolved with no distinction of crimes or persons. So I testify that I have seen with my own eyes more than five hundred guilty of capital crimes absolved by a certain bishop of Orléans for money counted out, according to the valuation and number of murders or other crimes, and indeed for the honour and glory of God. Is this really the way of God, who, we read, wanted a murderer dragged from the horns of his altar to punishment?

units.la: En etiam aliquid non minus stupendum, ex quo appareat quantum Satan in fascinandis hominibus religionis ac devotionis speciē potuerit. Iampridem enim in Gallia mos innualuit, vt si quis facinorosus adeo sceleratus est, vt omnibus viis gratię consequendæ, veniam impetrare non potuerit, in magnum diem Veneris, quem vocant refernetur, & eo die per Confessorem suum Rex ita solli citatur, vt tandem in honorem Dominicæ passionis, ad eam quam millies recusauerat iniustitiam adigatur. Quid aliud autem istud, quam quod à Iudæis factum est, Pilatum Barabbam dimittere cogentibus? Et quo melius adhuc Gratiosorum istorum cum hac historia cognoscatur conuenientia: sæpius eodē tempore contigit Barabbas istos impunæ dimitti, Christúmque in miseris membris suis ad flammas trahi: vt res sit inaudita, veniam iltis aut rogatam aut concessam. Nec vero sunt rei coram hominibus vt ab eis Veniam efflagitent: immò à quibus persequutionem patiuntur singulari gratia & remissione peccatorum opus habent.
units.tr: Here is something no less astonishing, from which it appears how much Satan could enchant men with the appearance of religion and devotion. For long ago in France a custom took hold that if someone was so wicked that he could obtain pardon by no means, he was reserved for the great Friday, as they call it. On that day the King is so pressed through his Confessor that at last, in honour of the Lord's passion, he is driven to that injustice which he had refused a thousand times. What else is this than what the Jews did, forcing Pilate to release Barabbas? And to see even better the resemblance of these Gracious men to that history: it often happens at the same time that such Barabbases are released with impunity, while Christ is dragged to the flames in his wretched members. So it is an unheard-of thing for pardon to be either asked or granted to them. Nor indeed are these men guilty before people, so that they should beg pardon from them; rather, they need the singular grace and forgiveness of sins from those whom they persecute.

units.la: Eccui porro nouus iste abusus videbitur Episcoporum, seu hanc potestatem impetrarūt, seu sibi vindicarūt, quum certissimum sit nullum tam horrendum crimen esse tamque detestandum, ne parricidio quidem excepto, cuius impunitatis curia Romana pretium non æstimarit, & illud quidem vile satis, hac ratione pœna capitali commutata in Pœnitentiam numerata pecunia redemtam, dummodo ad illius Crepidæ osculum, & Pœnitetiarij istius, id est Pœnitentiopolæ conspectum veniatur? Idem aio de asylorum quacunque specie quibus ad gratiam consequendam gradibus peruenitur, pro quibus Ecclesiastici tamdiu contenderút. At, quæso vos, quinam Deo gratum & acceptum, quinam Ecclesiæ decorum, tem- pla & κοιμητηεια latronum ac perditorum hominum speluncas & latibula fieri, quum Deus ipse diserte iubeat ab altaris fui cornibus homicidam ad supplicium rapi? Quod in magno Duce illo Ioabo ob crimina multos ante annos patrata factum, Dauidis etiam ipsius iustissimo decreto conspicimus. 1.Reg.2. 6. & 31. minime propterea altari nec loco Sancto iterum consecrato.
units.tr: Who, then, will think this new abuse of bishops strange, whether they obtained this power or claimed it for themselves? It is most certain that there is no crime so horrible and so detestable, not even parricide excepted, for whose impunity the Roman curia has not set a price, and a fairly cheap one at that. By this method capital punishment is commuted into repentance and redeemed by money paid, provided one comes to kiss that slipper and to see that penitentiary, that is, Penitentiopolis. I say the same of asylums of whatever kind, by which people reach pardon through various steps, and for which the ecclesiastics have contended so long. But I ask you: who thinks this pleasing and acceptable to God? Who thinks it seemly for the Church that temples and cemeteries [κοιμητήρια] become the caves and hiding-places of robbers and lost men, when God himself plainly commands that a murderer be dragged from the horns of his altar to punishment? We see this done in the case of the great commander Joab, for crimes committed many years before, and by the most just decree of David himself (1 Kings 2.6 and 31), and certainly not for that reason was the altar or holy place consecrated again.

units.la: Nec vero pugnat istud cum Domini institutione, sex vrbes refugij Israëlitis assignantis, quum fcopus eius minime fuerit sceleratorum impunitas, sed, vt diserte Lex ipsa monet. Num.35. & Deut.19. asylum aduersus cæsi hominis proximorum ac necessariorum iram, ne malum malo cumularent: & vt fortuita aut nó spontanea cædes, vt qui vim vi repellere coactus effet, à spontanea dolo malo & irremissibili distinguerétur. Nam qui ad asylum confugerat, ilico iudicio sistebatur, & neci etiam fi reum esse contigisset addicebatur. Tantùm igitur abest vt istiusmodi asyla concesserint impunitatem reis, vt contrà etiam ei qui cædem inopinatam fecerat non parua nota inureretur, in Vrbem asyli fui sub pœna mortis ad mortem vsque Maximi Pontificis relegato. Quanto igitur interuallo hæc vrbium perfugia, ab iis de quibus agimus iniustis asylis, merito plerisque locis à bonis Magistratibus sublatis absunt? At Romæ nequaquam, abominationis sedi, in qua tot asyla sunt, non tantum quot templa & κοιμητήρια, sed etiam quot Cardinalium palatia.
units.tr: Nor does this conflict with the Lord's institution, which assigned six cities of refuge to the Israelites. Its aim was by no means the impunity of the wicked. As the Law itself plainly advises (Num. 35; Deut. 19), it was an asylum against the anger of the slain man's kinsmen and relatives, so that they would not heap evil upon evil, and so that an accidental or unintended killing would be distinguished from a deliberate, malicious and unforgivable one. For whoever had fled to asylum was at once brought before judgement, and if he was found to be guilty, he was given over to death. So far were such asylums from granting impunity to the guilty that, on the contrary, even one who had committed an unexpected killing was branded with no small mark, being confined to the city of his asylum under penalty of death until the death of the High Priest. How far, then, are those cities of refuge from those unjust asylums we are speaking of, which good magistrates have rightly removed in most places! But not at Rome, the seat of abomination, where there are as many asylums not only as temples and cemeteries but even as palaces of cardinals.

units.la: Quos omnes tam magnos tamque apertos abutus si cum iis coniunxeris quæ fraude & malis artibus patratur, Deus bone, quid aliud esse dixeris orbem terrarum quàm Lacum humano sanguine stagnantem, & vindictam à Domino iam pridem, aduersus talium impunitatum auctores ac fautores flagitantem? Et ne procul excurram, annus est cum dimidio ex quo Deus bello nos afflixit, & ad miraculum vsque vi illa cœlesti & superiore nos hactenus aduersus hostium insultus texit, tu vero Geneua quàm multo sanguine humano innocentio fœdata es? annon vero Iustitia veluti consopita iacet? quàm multos in patibulum abreptos oportuit, quos elato capite in medio nostrum conspicimus? quot vero cædes incruentas quas sciuimus à raptoribus admissas negleximus, Deo licet monente & cœlitus fulminante? Vos vero templi huius quàs hoc tempore columnas intueor, mihi meisque in hoc munere collegis testes aduoco, nos ab hoc scelere immunes, qui monere, hortari, obtestari non destitimus, sed frustrà, eos qui surdiores habent aures vobis quæ tamen eltis columnæ lapilapideæ. Vtinam illis Deus aures aperiat, cor flectat, & propter seipsum, & quod sacrosanctum eius Nomen super nos invocatum est noltri miserea-tur. Nos interea cum Dauide precemur, Psal.28.3. Ne trahat nos Dominus cum impiis & cum operariis iniquitatis: & iterum, Psal.26.9. Ne colligat cum peccatoribus animam nostram, & cum viris sanguinolentis vitam nostram.
units.tr: If you join all these great and open abuses with those carried out by fraud and evil arts, good God, what else would you call the whole world than a lake stagnant with human blood, and one that has long been crying out to the Lord for vengeance against the authors and supporters of such impunity? And, not to wander far, it is a year and a half since God afflicted us with war, and has covered us, even to a miracle, with that heavenly and higher power against the assaults of enemies up to now. But you, Geneva, how often have you been defiled with innocent human blood? Does not justice lie as if asleep? How many men dragged to the gallows ought there to have been, whom we see walking about among us with head held high? How many bloodless murders, which we know robbers committed, have we neglected, though God warns and thunders from heaven? I call to witness you, whom I see at this time as the pillars of this temple, and my colleagues in this office with me, that we are free of this crime. We have not ceased to warn, exhort and beseech, but in vain, to those whose ears are deafer, though you are stone pillars. May God open their ears, bend their hearts, and have mercy on us, for his own sake and because his most holy Name has been invoked over us. Meanwhile let us pray with David: "Do not drag me away with the wicked, nor with the workers of iniquity" (Ps. 28.3); and again, "Do not gather my soul with sinners, nor my life with bloodthirsty men" (Ps. 26.9).

units.la: Pilatus igitur, vt ad historiam revertamur, hoc niueo fundamento nixus sibi & Iesu Christo puta-uit optimè consultum, si cum cum perditissimo homine collatum, mortiq; eripere, & hac se necessitate eam contra conscien-tiam condemnandi explicaret: quod consilium Dominus vt prius illud fregit. Nos enim oportuit experiri reipsa Christum sponsorem esse & exsoluere paratum quę peccatis electorum debebantur, inde initio usque ad mundi consummationem: vt hac ratione celeratissimus illi collatus, etiam iustus habeatur. Ita tamen ista cōtigerunt & per ea instrumenta sunt administrata, vt Domini nostri Iesu Christi sponsoris innocentia fiat conspectior quo magis est aduersus eum accusatorum vanitatem, ut a Pilato Christo Domino nostro ab omni crimine liberato. Contra furor Sacerdotum eo cuasit, vt populo non tantum persuaserint Barrabam magno clamore postulandum, sed etiam iudici poenam qua vellent innocentem affici præscripserint, crucem nimirum, cruentum & ignominiosum supplicij genus, de quo
units.tr: Pilate, then, to return to the history, relying on this snow-white foundation, thought it best for himself and for Jesus Christ if he set him beside the most abandoned man, to snatch him from death, and by this necessity to explain away condemning him against his conscience. But the Lord broke this counsel, as he had before. For it was necessary for us to experience in fact that Christ is the surety and ready to pay what was owed for the sins of the elect, from the beginning to the consummation of the world. By this method the most wicked man was set beside him, and so he is considered righteous. Yet these things happened, and were carried out through those instruments, in such a way that the innocence of our Lord Jesus Christ, the surety, becomes more conspicuous, the more the vanity of the accusers is set against him, so that by Pilate our Lord Christ is freed from every crime. On the contrary, the fury of the priests went so far that they persuaded the people not only to demand Barabbas with loud clamour, but also prescribed to the judge that the innocent man be punished in whatever way they wished, namely the cross, a bloody and ignominious kind of punishment, of which

units.la: Quod Barrabas Christo prælatus est, certissimum est satisfactio nis pro peccatis nostris testimonium. dicturi fumus.
units.tr: That Barabbas was preferred to Christ is a most certain testimony of the satisfaction made for our sins, as we shall say.

units.la: Hic vero duo quædam obseruanda nobis occurrunt, primum quanta sit populi leuitas & inconstantia, vt qui sedent ad gubernacula mature consiliis & monopoliis occurrant, quæ facilius impediuntur quàm franguntur: quæ vtinam Deus à nobis, hoc tempore tam calamitoso præsertim auertat.
units.tr: Two things here call for our attention. The first is how great the fickleness and inconstancy of the people is, so that those who sit at the helm of government are soon met with plots and conspiracies, which are more easily hindered than broken. May God turn this from us, especially in these so calamitous times.

units.la: Alterum, vt quoties eligendi sunt quibus munera publica vel leuissima committantur, à precibus initium fiat, cum recta conscientia & legitimo examine, præeunte tum probitatis tum capacitatis eorum qui ad hæc munera vocantur, regula illa, quam eximiam Moses socer Iethro nobis præscripsit, Exod. 18. 21. vt nimirum viri graues, Deum timentes, veraces, turpis lucri osores eligantur. Nam, vt omnium temporum historiæ tum sacræ tum prophanæ testantur, & hic Status ab hinc annis quinquaginta non sensu expertus est, & vt ait Sapiens, Euectis improbis, vbique magna dissimulatio.
units.tr: The second is that whenever men are to be chosen to whom public offices, even the slightest, are to be committed, the process should begin with prayer, and be conducted with a right conscience and a lawful scrutiny, the integrity and ability of those called to these offices being weighed beforehand. Let us observe that rule which Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, set before us as outstanding (Exod. 18. 21.): namely, that men who are grave, who fear God, who are truthful, and who hate base gain be chosen. For, as the histories of every age, both sacred and profane, bear witness, and as this State has experienced within the last fifty years, and as the Wise Man says, when the wicked are raised up, concealment is everywhere great.

units.la: Prouerb. 28. 12. & væ regioni, cuius rex puer est. Eccl. 10. 13. Denique nauis salus in nautis ipsis, post Deum, & in eo præsertim qui sedet ad gubernacula positâ est.
units.tr: Prov. 28. 12. Woe to the land whose king is a child. Eccl. 10. 13. Finally, a ship's safety lies in the sailors themselves, after God, and especially in the one who is placed at the helm.

units.la: HOMILIA VICESIMAQVINTA.
units.tr: HOMILY TWENTY-FIFTH.

units.la: LVC. 23.
units.tr: LUKE 23.

units.la: 16. Castigatum ergo eum dimittam.
units.tr: 16. I will therefore chastise him and let him go.

units.la: IOH. 19.
units.tr: JOHN 19.

units.la: 1. Tunc ergo assumpsit Iesum Pilatus, & flagellauit.
units.tr: 1. Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him.

units.la: 2. Et milites contexuerunt coronam è spinis, & imposuerunt ipsius capiti, & pallio purpureo induerunt eum.
units.tr: 2. And the soldiers plaited a crown of thorns, put it on his head, and clothed him in a purple robe.

units.la: 3. Et dicebant, Aue Rex Iudæorum. Et bacillis eum cædebant.
units.tr: 3. And they said, Hail, King of the Jews! And they struck him with rods.

units.la: 4. Egressus est ergo rursum Pilatus foras, & dixit eis, Ecce adduco vobis eum foris, vt noueritis me nullum in eo crimen invenire.
units.tr: 4. Pilate went out again and said to them, Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find no crime in him.

units.la: 5. Egressus est ergo Iesus foras, ferens spineam illam coronam, & purpureum illud pallium. Et dixit eis (Pilatus) Ecce homo.
units.tr: 5. Then Jesus came out, bearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. And Pilate said to them, Behold the man!

units.la: 6. Quum autem intuiti essent eum primarij Sacerdotes & (eorum) ministri, clamauerunt, dicentes, Crucifige, crucifige, Dixit eis Pilatus, Accipite eum vos, & crucifigite. Ego enim non invenio in eo crimen.
units.tr: 6. When the chief priests and their officers saw him, they cried out, saying, Crucify, crucify! Pilate said to them, Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no crime in him.

units.la: 7. Responderunt ei Iudæi, Nos legem habemus, & secundum legem nostram debet mori, quia Filium Dei se fecit.
units.tr: 7. The Jews answered him, We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.

units.la: 8. Quum ergo audiuisset Pilatus hunc sermonem magis timuit.
units.tr: 8. When Pilate heard this saying, he was the more afraid.

units.la: 9. Et rursus ingressus est in Prætorium, & dixit Iesu, Vnde es tu? Iesus autem responsum ei non dedit.
units.tr: 9. And he went again into the Praetorium and said to Jesus, Where are you from? But Jesus gave him no answer.

units.la: Vi semel à recta via deflexit, quò longiùs prouchitur, licet modò in hanc, modò in illam semitam excurrat, eò magis aberrat à recto tramite, donec tandem ipsum inueniendi spes omnis tollatur. Hac ratione audaces in capiendo, fures euadunt, de furibus latrones fiunt: & in genere qui semel conscientiæ vim attulit, paulatim eam peccato vendit & mancipat. Huius rei exemplum esto miser iste Pilatus, qui quum conscientiæ parere recta monenti & æquitati studere debuisset, expedire se hoc negotio cogitauit, reu ad alium se adhuc peiorem, remittédo. Qua quum non succeßisset via, in peius ruit, quum Christo ex Gratia vitam condonare tentasset, cū profligatissimo & sceleratissimo nebulone ipso collato. Iam verò tandem à recto & æquo procul aberrans, etiam publicè infamia notatum cædere non erubescit, quam pœnam vir probus, ipsa morte grauiorem ducat. Quînam verò in tantos errores incidit? Nimirum sensu suo non conscientia audita, unde factum vt sensum perdiderit: non modò sciens prudens peccans, quod nullus vnquam sanæ mentis homo fecerit, sed, quod longè peius est, sibi persuadens, se laude aliquid dignum facere, non illato quod Christo poterat supplicio, quem se hac ratione castigatum morti putabat erepturum: En, vt sæpe Satan se in Angelum falsæ Lucis ad nos excæcandos transformet.
units.tr: Once a man has turned aside by force from the straight way, the further he goes, the more he wanders from the right track, now into this path, now into that, until all hope of finding it again is lost. In the same way bold men, in seizing things, become thieves, and from thieves they become robbers; and in general, whoever has once done violence to his conscience gradually sells it to sin and makes it a slave. Let that wretched Pilate be an example of this. Though he ought to have obeyed conscience, which rightly admonished him, and to have pursued justice, he thought to extricate himself from the affair by passing the responsibility on to another, one even worse. When this way did not succeed, he fell into something worse still, when he tried to grant Christ his life as a favour, setting him beside a most abandoned and wicked scoundrel. At last, wandering far from what is right and equitable, he is not ashamed to have a man scourged in public and branded with infamy, a punishment which an upright man regards as worse than death itself. But how did he fall into such great errors? Surely because he listened to his own feeling and not to conscience, and so it came about that he lost his judgement: not only sinning knowingly and deliberately, which no man of sound mind has ever done, but, what is far worse, persuading himself that he was doing something worthy of praise, in that he would inflict on Christ a punishment which, he thought, would then rescue him from death. See how often Satan transforms himself into an angel of light to blind us.

units.la: Exempli gratia, ne Veterum historias altius repetam, cui melius Pilatum comparauero, quàm nostri seculi plerisque iudicibus, qui quum longè abessent à furiosorum illorum vaesana crudelitate: & si non arguerètur à conscientia de nostræ religionis veritate, saltem ex inimicorum animis & nostrorum fratrum simplicitate & constantia illam cognoscerent, contra conscientiam tamen hos quidem ad remos, illos ad flagra damnarunt, alios exilio perpetuo multarunt, ita etiam multum sibi deberi existimantes? vt eos omittam qui peius adhuc hac in parte se gesserunt, Satanæ suam operam præstantes in tentandis & sollicitandis nonnullis infirmis, qui de felicibus confessoribus & nominis Dei testibus, apostatæ facti sunt, & Filij Dei abnegatores, cum animarum perditione, iuxta Christi sententiam, Matt. 10 32. nisi quibus Deus ex misericordia meliorem mentem & seriam pœnitentiam dedit. Quàm verò nos hoc tempore decet ardentibus precibus Deum pro fratribus interpellare, quorum tantam multitudinem videmus hostium nostrorum furore perculsam, lapsam esse infirmitate, vt hanc illis gratiam concedat, vt lapsos erigat, nobisque vires ad perseverandum cum iis qui hactenus imperterriti ftete-
units.tr: To give an example, without going back too far into the histories of old, with whom can I better compare Pilate than with many judges of our own age? They were far removed from the mad cruelty of those furious men. Even if conscience did not convict them of the truth of our religion, they might at least have recognised it from the spirit of our enemies and from the simplicity and constancy of our brethren. Yet against conscience they condemned some of these to the galleys, others to the lash, and fined others with perpetual exile, thinking that they were thereby earning much merit for themselves. I say nothing of those who have behaved even worse in this matter, lending their labour to Satan in tempting and soliciting some weak people, who, having been apostates from happy confessors and witnesses of the name of God, became deniers of the Son of God, to the perdition of their souls, according to Christ's sentence, Matt. 10:32, except those whom God in his mercy has given a better mind and sincere repentance. How much we ought at this time to beseech God with burning prayers for our brethren, whom we see struck down by the fury of our enemies and fallen through weakness, that he may grant them this grace, to raise up the fallen, and that he may supply us with strength to persevere with those who have hitherto stood fast undaunted,

units.la: Q. iij. runt, quotidie nouas sufficiat.
units.tr: Q. iij. ...and may daily supply us with new strength to persevere.

units.la: Ad Pilatum reuertamur, quem sein hoc negotio pessime gestisse iam docuimus. At Dei prouidentia, nihil minus illo cogitante, sic eius linguam duxit, vt ore proprio tum crassam ignorantiam tum malam conscientiam testatam fecerit: & innocentia Christi iam quinto palam & aperte patefacta fuerit. Nam etsi Pilatus non satis aperte loquutus esset omni crimine Christum liberans, quem, si quod corde premebat esset eloquutus, pari cum vxore testimonio palam iustum & innocentem ac vitae integrum sceleris que purum pronuntiasset: tamen quum satis clare dixisset, vt narrat Mat. 27.23. & Marc. 15. 14. Sein Christo nullum crimen inuenire, qua tandem igitur ratione concludit, se castigatum illum esse dimissurum? An non perinde hoc est ac si dixisset, Innocentem hominem iustum pronuntio, sed tamen castigatum & infamia notatum dimittam, vt itaque vobis etiam praeter officium meum satisfaciam? En quem exitum obliqua consilia tandem, quanuis fero, sortiantur. Age igitur in omnibus negotiis sincere & integre agamus, nullosque magis amentes iis esse sciamus, qui se difficili negotio aliquo, Deo laeso vel proximo putant explicare.
units.tr: Let us return to Pilate, whom we have already shown to have behaved very badly in this affair. Yet by God's providence, though he was thinking of nothing less, his tongue was so guided that by his own mouth he bore witness both to his gross ignorance and to his bad conscience, and the innocence of Christ was now openly and plainly revealed for the fifth time. For although Pilate did not speak quite openly in freeing Christ from every charge, if he had uttered what he kept pressed in his heart, he would have declared him plainly just, innocent, of integrity of life and pure of any wrong, with the same testimony as his wife. Yet since he said clearly enough, as Matt. 27:23 and Mark 15:14 relate, that he found no crime in Christ, by what reasoning then does he conclude that he will release him after chastising him? Is this not just the same as if he had said, I pronounce this man innocent and just, but nevertheless I will release him chastised and branded with infamy, so that I may satisfy you even beyond my duty? See what end crooked counsels finally meet, however much they may prosper for a while. Come then, let us act sincerely and uprightly in all our affairs, and let us know that none are more mad than those who think they can extricate themselves from some difficult business by wronging God or their neighbour.

units.la: Interea vero Christus caeditur, & modis indignis tractatur. Sed in quem tandem poena recidit? Flagellatus quidem plagarum dolores cum summa ignominia coniunctos passus est, sed in suam gloriam hac ratione intrroiit, Luc. 24 26. 24.26.cuius respectu no pluris illa fecit, quàm sudorem agricola meilem sperans: aut fortis Imperator vulnera virtutis suae & victoriae quam exspectat spe excitatus. Nos autem e ius membra tantum abest vt eius vulnera laedant,aut ignominia dedecus adferat,vt contrà quae à carnificibus illi vices nostras implenti sunt inflicta vulnera, virgae nos illi ferreae eximant, qua qui nobis hac ratione conciliatus est hostes suos conterit Psal.2.9. Et ignominia in hominum conspectu , quam ipsi eramus promeriti non ipse, (qui quae non rapuit, reppendit.Psal.69.4.) nos decoros coram iudice reddit tantum abest vt in eo nos oporteat offendi.Matth.11.6. At quû aduenit iudicij tempus, quas poenas dedit Pilatus innocenti, quem tam scelerate ceciderat?Quàm magnis ictibus virgae illius ferreae contusi sunt tum Sacerdotes,tum qui illis ducibus tanto furore,Crucifigendum Christum erant vociferati ? Nempe narrant historiae Pilatum ab Imperatore quem magis quàm Deum metuerat Ioh.19.12. omnibus dignitatibus exautoratum', sibi ipsi manus intulisse & in alios tam horrenda Dei iudicia immissa, vt sine horrore nullus eam historiam legat.
units.tr: Meanwhile Christ is scourged and treated in shameful ways. But on whom does the punishment at last fall? He indeed suffered the pains of the blows joined with the utmost disgrace, but by this means he entered into his glory (Luke 24:26). Looking to that glory, he valued the suffering no more than the farmer values his sweat while hoping for the harvest, or than a brave general values his wounds, spurred on by hope of the virtue and victory he awaits. As for us, his members, far from his wounds harming him or his shame bringing dishonour upon him, the wounds inflicted by the executioners, who were carrying out our part, free us from that iron rod by which he, who has reconciled us to himself in this way, crushes his enemies (Ps. 2:9). And the disgrace in the sight of men, which we ourselves had deserved, he himself, who restored what he had not stolen (Ps. 69:4), makes us honourable before the judge. So far is it from being fitting that we should be offended in him (Matt. 11:6). But when the time of judgement comes, what punishments will Pilate pay to the innocent man whom he so wickedly condemned? With what great blows of that iron rod will they be bruised, both the priests and those who, led by them, shouted with such fury that Christ should be crucified? Indeed, the histories relate that Pilate, stripped of all his dignities by the Emperor, whom he feared more than God (John 19:12), laid violent hands on himself, and that such dreadful judgements of God were sent upon others that no one can read that history without horror.

units.la: Oro vos autem fratres , quibus iudiciis nos ipsi nostris oculis conspeximus, & quidem admodum recenter magna illa capita deprensa, quae vestigiis eorum de quibus hic agitur inhaeserunt?Quid vero vos adhuc reliqui,an impuné laturos tatum facinus, aut meliorem fore vestram conditionem speratis, & in primis qui caput eorum est, & veluti rota cui clauì infixi sunt, à quibus adhuc miseri Dei filij transfiguntur? Næ suo tandem loco & tempore Dei seueram vindictam experiemini.
units.tr: I beg you, brethren, consider the judgements we ourselves have seen with our own eyes, and indeed quite recently, when great heads were seized, who had followed in the footsteps of those of whom we are speaking here. And what of you who remain? Do you hope to bear so great a crime with impunity, or that your condition will be better, especially he who is their head, and as it were the wheel to which the nails were fixed, by whom poor sons of God are still being led astray? Surely in its own place and time you will experience the severe vengeance of God.

units.la: Operæpretium autem est nos ad nostram instructionem attentius hic admirādam Dei prouidentiam expendere. Carnifices quidem cum per contemptum ac contumeliam coronant: sed Pater cœlestis eorum manibus ad cum in monte Sionis coronandum vtitur. Psal. 2. 6. quandoquidem in perpessionibus triumphus eius. Purpuram illi induunt & spinis coronāt, quare carnifices isti tanquam veri Prophetæ, duo nos magna huius regis arcana docent, nempe regnū capitis nobis communicandum, non in his terris consistere, nec ex hoc mundo esse, suo veluti suffragio quod dixerat Pilato Christus. Ioh. 18 36. comprobantes: deinde quę via ducat in illud, nempe si capiti conformes siamus, primùm in spinis, deinde in veste purpurea, id est in perpessionibus ipsius, & tandem in gloria. Rom. 8. 17. 2. Tim. 2. 12. quarum spinarum tam superbi sunt aculei, vt nullam aliam gloriandi materiam quàm illam Apostolus agnoscat. Gal. 6. 17. Absit igitur carnificum istorum, aut eius à quo iussi sunt factum approbeum: sed dicam tamen ei qui verè Christianus esse volet, hanc scholam frequentandam, in qua veri Christianismi θεωρίαν & praxin ediscat. Sic perditi isti carnifices virgis & colaphis cæsum per contumeliam Regem Iudæodæorum appellarunt, & erat ipse reuera, nec vllus alius. Eadem mente, Bene esse, ipsi precati sunt: & tunc sane ad Regalem benedictionem propius accedebat, sicut ipse nos admonet Christus tunc in nobis reuera Dei benedictionem sensibiliter obsignandam, quum propter ipsum, aduersum nos quiduis mali fuerint loquuti, & nō etiam persequuti. Matt.5.11.
units.tr: It is worth while, however, for our instruction, to weigh carefully the providence of God, which is here to be admired. The executioners indeed crown him in contempt and insult, but the heavenly Father uses their hands to crown him on Mount Zion (Ps. 2:6), since his triumph lies in his sufferings. They clothe him in purple and crown him with thorns; so these executioners, like true prophets, teach us two great secrets of this King: that his kingdom is to be shared with us and does not consist in these lands, nor is it of this world, as Christ himself confirmed when he said to Pilate (John 18:36); and then what way leads to it, namely that, if we are conformed to the head, first in thorns, then in the purple robe, that is, in his sufferings, and at last in glory (Rom. 8:17; 2 Tim. 2:12). So sharp are the thorns of this crown that the Apostle acknowledges no other matter for boasting than these (Gal. 6:17). Far be it from us, then, to approve the deed of those executioners or of him by whose command they acted. But I will say to whoever wishes to be a true Christian that he must frequent this school, in which he may learn the theory [θεωρίαν] and practice of true Christianity. So these lost executioners, having scourged him with rods and blows, called him in mockery the King of the Jews, and he indeed was the King, and no other. With the same intent they cried, Long may he live! And then indeed he was drawing nearer to the royal blessing, as Christ himself admonishes us that God's blessing is then truly and perceptibly sealed upon us, when for his sake men have spoken all kinds of evil against us and have not only persecuted us (Matt. 5:11).

units.la: Prodit interea Christus habitu ignominiosissimo, spectatores omnes qui tam tristi spectaculo commoti non sunt, vsfanæ crudelitatis accusans. Quos si omnes merito condemnamus, quid nobis faciendum nos ipsos intuētibus? Nostra enim peccata & iniquitates hæc omnia in sponsorem nostrum accersiuerunt. Hic se igitur mortales tanquam in speculo contemplentur, vt quales in seipsis sint coram Deo cognoscant, & deiiciantur, non autem suas plumas admirati efferatur & insolescant.
units.tr: Meanwhile Christ appears in the most ignominious guise, accusing of raging cruelty all the spectators who are not moved by so sad a spectacle. If we rightly condemn them all, what must we do when we look at ourselves? For our sins and iniquities brought all these things upon our surety. Let mortals therefore contemplate themselves as in a mirror, so that they may know what they are in themselves before God, and be cast down, not lifted up and made proud by admiring their own feathers.

units.la: Sed contrà etiam considerandum vt Pater in Filio nostras iniquitates vltus, iterum ignominiæ scandalo occurrerit, ipsius ore Pilati Christo factam insignem iniuriam palàm prædicans: quum illi hæc verba extorsit, se Christum licet nullius criminis conuictum sic tractare: quasi palàm & clarè pronuntiasset, En eum quem vestra importunitate impulsus, contra ius & æquum omne sic tractaui. Metuamus igitur Dominum, fratres, metuamus, inquam, cum qui quum sic illi visum est nullis testibus aliis quàm nobis ipsis ad nos damnandos opus habet.
units.tr: But on the other side we must also consider that the Father, avenging our iniquities in the Son, again confronts the scandal of the ignominy, proclaiming through the mouth of Pilate the notable injury done to Christ. When Pilate extorted from him these words, he was in effect saying that he was treating Christ thus, though Christ was convicted of no crime, as if he had said plainly and clearly: "Behold the one whom I have so treated, contrary to all law and justice, because you pressed me so importunately." Let us therefore fear the Lord, brothers, fear him, I say, who, when it seemed good to him, needs no witnesses other than ourselves to condemn us.

units.la: Quoties autem sceleratos magis ac magis furere & despumare videmus, ne tantū eorum Diabolicum furorem detestemur: sed quid no stra ferat natura corrupta consideremus, non tantùm ad malum omne procliuis, sed etiam monita magis ac magis excandescens aduersus monitorem, tantùm abest vt compescatur aut mitigetur: quod ipse nos Apostolus suo ipsius exemplo docet Rom. 7.7. Tantùm abest igitur vt eorum quę Deus iubet aut vetat ad salutem cognitio sufficiat, vt Pelagiani olim docuerūt, & adhuc hodie qui non multò maiorem beneficij Christi cognitionem habent arbitrantur, vt contrà, nisi Deus ex mera gratia penitus mentem nostram immutet, mandatum rei bonæ concupiscentiam nostram, penitus ipsi reluctantem, ad malum moueat: & contrà rei malæ prohibitio, ad quā ferimur natura, tantò magis aduersus bonum & recta monentem irritet: quod in rebus minimis experimur, & in ipsis infantibus conspicimus. Quid hic igitur opus est facto? Agnoscendum nimirum nobis quàm detestabiles natura coram Deo nascamur, vt nobis ipsis displiceamus potiùs quàm oculis nostris sapiamus, qui ad nostram maledictionem accedit cumulus: Deúmque precemur assiduè vt nos immutet, & nostram suæ Lucis splendore mentem illustret, vt quod bonum est agnoscamus & eius amore ducamur: & malum eminus conspicari fugiamus: & in nobis efficiat vt velimus & efficiamus pro gratuita sua beneuolentia. Nam alioqui quò maior erit boni scientia, eò maius studium mali, nullo tam detestando facinore existente in quod non suo impetu homo feratur, & indurescat, nisi Sancto Dei Spiritu mutetur ac regatur. Immo plerumque accidit ut qui diurinarum rerum quæ mandatæ prohibitæve sunt maiorem allecuti sunt scientiam peiores evadant: testibus primariis Sacerdotibus & satellitibus, si cum Pilato conferantur, nunquam sacras literas edocto, & tamen Doctorum istorum sceleri magna contentione resistente, cru delitatemque ipsorum detestante. Quod enim dixit, Crucifigant ipsi eum si velint, minimè sanè permissurus dixit: sed perinde est ac si dixisset, nolle se ipsorum esse Carnificem, quod etiam ab illis est probè intellectum.
units.tr: Whenever we see the wicked raging and foaming more and more, we should not only detest their diabolical fury, but also consider what our corrupt nature bears. It is prone not only to every evil, but, when admonished, grows more and more inflamed against the admonisher, so far is it from being restrained or softened. The Apostle himself teaches us this by his own example, Rom. 7.7. So far, therefore, is the knowledge of what God commands or forbids from being sufficient for salvation, as the Pelagians once taught, and as those still do today who think that they have no much greater knowledge of the benefit of Christ. On the contrary, unless God, by sheer grace, utterly changes our mind, a command to do good stirs up our concupiscence, which strongly resists it, towards evil; and, conversely, the prohibition of an evil, towards which we are carried by nature, irritates it all the more against the good and right admonition. We experience this in the smallest matters and observe it even in infants. What then is needed here? We must acknowledge how detestable we are by nature when we are born before God, so that we displease ourselves rather than be wise in our own eyes, since a heap of curses comes upon us. And we must pray constantly that God change us and illuminate our mind with the splendour of his light, so that we may recognise what is good and be led by love of it, and flee from looking upon evil from afar; and that he bring it about in us that we will and do what is right, by his free goodwill. For otherwise, the greater the knowledge of good, the greater the zeal for evil, since there is no crime so detestable that man is not carried into it by his own impetus and hardened, unless he is changed and ruled by the Holy Spirit of God. Indeed it often happens that those who have attained a greater knowledge of the divine things commanded or forbidden turn out worse. The chief priests and attendants are witnesses of this, if they are compared with Pilate, who was never taught the sacred letters, and yet with great effort resisted the crime of those teachers and detested their cruelty. For when he said, "Let them crucify him themselves if they wish," he surely said it as one who would by no means permit it. It was just as if he had said that he did not wish to be their executioner, and they also understood this well.

units.la: Quid si Iudæi ut scriò dictum arripuissent? Hæsisset sanè attonitus, quòd tantundem de iure Imperatoris Romani decessisset, ac pro- inde læsæ Maiestatis reus factus esset, quibus adde & in posterum istud futurum fuisse pes- simi exempli, non fugiente Pilatum quàm ini- quo animo Iudæi Romanorum iugum fer- rent. Se tamen in hoc discrimen coniiciebat. Quod plerumque vias obliquas quærentibus quibusdam difficultatibus exiricent vsu venit. At diuina prouidentia longè aliter noltræ salutis causa prospexerat. Christum enim, pa- candis ac tranquillandis nostris conscientiis oportuit (licet quòd ad eius personam attinet iniquissimè sit condemnatus) iudicis sententia quam coram Dei tribunali eramus promèriti, tanquam vadem & sponsorem nostrum, non autem per tumultum & seditionem condemnari & crucifigi.
units.tr: What if the Jews had seized upon his words as if they had been said in earnest? He would surely have been astonished, because so much of the right of the Roman emperor would have been surrendered, and he would thereby have been made guilty of treason. Add to this that it would have been a most evil precedent for the future, and Pilate did not fail to see how unwillingly the Jews bore the Roman yoke. Yet he was thrusting himself into this danger, as often happens to those who seek crooked ways out of certain difficulties. But divine providence had provided far otherwise for the cause of our salvation. For, in order to appease and quiet our consciences, it was necessary that Christ be condemned, not through tumult and sedition, but by the sentence of a judge, as our surety and guarantor, the sentence which we had deserved before the tribunal of God. (As far as his person is concerned, he was condemned most unjustly.)

units.la: Transeamus ad Sacerdotes, qui se à Pilato notari sentientes toties repetita illa protestatione, nullius se criminis reum Christum, saltem capitalis inuenisse, saeuitiam suam ac crudelitatem nitentes in uolucro pietatis & religionis tegere, excipiunt Iesum Christum si non Romanis Legibus capitalis criminis reus sit, esse tamen Lege sua diuina, cuius esset ab Imperatore concessa ipsis obseruatio. Exempli gratia, dicunt Iesum Christum blasphemum & impium, quod se Dei Filium, ac proinde Deum esse dixerit: hac voce Filij Dei non eo sensu intellecta quo Angelis, Regibus ac Principibus & in vniuersum fidelibus omnibus,iis qui non sunt de Ecclesia oppositis, tribuitur. Iob.1.6. Psalm.82.6. Genes.6.2.
units.tr: Let us pass on to the priests. Perceiving that they were being noted by Pilate through that protestation, repeated so often, that he had found Christ guilty of no crime, at least no capital one, they strove to cover their cruelty and savagery under the cloak of piety and religion. They reply that Jesus Christ, if he is not guilty of a capital crime under Roman laws, is nevertheless so under his own divine law, the observance of which had been granted to them by the emperor. For example, they say that Jesus Christ is a blasphemer and impious because he said that he was the Son of God, and therefore God, this expression "Son of God" being understood not in the sense in which it is attributed to angels, kings and princes, and to all believers in general, and to those outside the Church who are opposed to it. Job 1.6; Ps. 82.6; Gen. 6.2.

units.la: Ac sane, primum quidem hoc axioma certissimum est & Lege Dei nititur, lata aduersus idololatras Apostatas & blasphematores. Exo. 22.20. Deut.13.2.&5.&8. &15. & Deut.17.5. & Leuit.24.16. Nam si verbis in Deum blasphemus capitis reus est, quisque Deos peregrinos & ab hominibus factos colit, quid co futurum est qui seipsum Deum esse praedicarit? Deinde non immerito Christo id imputabatur, non aliter de Deo loqui solito quam Patrem cum vocando, sibique veram & essentialem Deitatem attribuendo, quam etiam verbis & operibus testaretur. Iohan.5.17. & 8. 58.Matth.9.6.& 22.45.Qua igitur in re sita hæc est calumnia? Quòd Lex quæ de meris putis hominibus agit, de eo minimè loquatur qui quum verus Deus effet naturam nostram aflumpferat, ille ipse Legislator per Mosis ministerium loquutus. Hoc autem fuisse Iudæis certum & indubitatum principium, sic oportere Christum filium esse Dauidis & verum hominem, vt verus etiam esset Dei Filius, licet Iudæis non parum in doctrina fœderis diuini cum hoc populo caligantibus, ex ipsis Caiaphæ verbis luce clarius est, Matth.26.ver. 63.Marc.14.vers.61.Luc.22.vers.70. Quamobrem antequam hoc principiū aduersus Christum torquerent, quærendum fuerat, verúsne Deus esset Iesus Christus,nécne : ac proinde verus ille Patribus promissus Messias:quod si studio discendi inquisiuissent, vt contrà sponte aduersus Lucem oculos occludebant, non difficulter inuenirent, tum ex ipsa Iesu Christi doctrina per Prophetarum oracula confirmata : Iohan.5. vers.49. Act. 17. vers.11. tū etiam ex ipsius operibus, non aliunde quàm ab ipsa vera Deitate manantibus. Iohan.10.38. eúmque vt verum Seruatorem essent amplexati, quem vt blasphemum & Apostatam criminabantur.
units.tr: Indeed, first, this axiom is most certain and rests on the Law of God, which was laid down against idolaters, apostates and blasphemers. Exo. 22.20; Deut. 13.2, 5, 8, 15; Deut. 17.5; Lev. 24.16. For if a man who blasphemes God with words is liable to capital punishment, and so is whoever worships foreign gods made by men, what will become of him who has declared himself to be God? Next, it was not undeservedly imputed to Christ, since he was accustomed to speak of God in no other way than calling him Father, and attributing to himself true and essential Deity, which he also attested by his words and works. John 5.17; 8.58; Matt. 9.6; 22.45. What, then, is the calumny in this matter? It is that the Law, which deals with mere men, does not speak of him who, being true God, had assumed our nature, that very Lawgiver having spoken through the ministry of Moses. Now, that this was a certain and indubitable principle for the Jews, that Christ must be the son of David and a true man, and also be the true Son of God, although the Jews, in no small measure, were in the dark about the doctrine of the divine covenant with this people, is clearer than light from the very words of Caiaphas, Matt. 26.63; Mark 14.61; Luke 22.70. Therefore, before they turned this principle against Christ, they ought to have inquired whether Jesus Christ was God or not, and so whether he was that true Messiah promised to the Fathers. If they had inquired with zeal for learning (whereas, on the contrary, they willingly closed their eyes against the Light), they would not have found it difficult to discover this, both from the very doctrine of Jesus Christ, confirmed by the oracles of the prophets, John 5.49; Acts 17.11, and also from his works, which flow from nothing else than true Deity itself, John 10.38. They should then have embraced him as the true Saviour, rather than accuse him as a blasphemer and apostate.

units.la: Talis etiamnum est hodie nostri tem- poris Sacrificulorum inscitia malitiosa, & malitia inscia, eundem animum adferentium, & eandem accusandorum Christianorum formam obseruantium. Nam vt sibi ipsi Caiaphas reluctabatur, Messiam agnoscens Dei filium fore, & tamen blasphemiæ Iesum qui se Christum & Dei Filium diceret accusans: sic hodie quibuscum nobis res est Sacrificuli, Dei quidè gratiam admittunt, sed repetè suum liberum arbitrium cum meritis obtrudunt. Vnicum adorandum Deum fatentur, sed varias adorationis species illico somniantes, non modò mortuos homines, sed eorum etiam ossamenta & statuas colunt. Iesum Christum Seruatorem ac Redemptorem agnoscunt, sed simul suas satisfactiones, & indulgentias numerata pecunia redemptas venditant, quod quid aliud est dicere, quàm Deum pretium persoluentibus apothecam dimittere? Agnoscunt Christum ex quo semel homo factus est, eundem semper esse, fuisse ac futurum esse, sed tamen addunt credendum eum realiter & essentialiter præsentem adesse in tot panibus quot consecrarint: & in tot locis simul quot Missa celebratur: quod perinde est acsi dicas cum Esse simul & non Esse verum hominem, Iesum Christum spem suam dicunt, sed simul etiam Mariam Virginem cœli Reginam vitam suā, spem, misericordiæ reginam: quam, (eò impudentiæ deucnerunt) rogat Nato iure matris imperet, peccatorúmque Expiatricem nuncupant. Nam ecce illorum verba, O fœlix puerpera, Nostra pians scelera, Iure matris impera Redemptori. Mira etiam de Christi oblatione in Crucis arbore canūt: sed simul eum etiam
units.tr: Such, even today, is the malicious ignorance and ignorant malice of our sacrificers, who bring the same mind and observe the same pattern in accusing Christians. For just as Caiaphas struggled against himself, acknowledging that the Messiah would be the Son of God, and yet accused Jesus, who called himself Christ and the Son of God, of blasphemy, so today the sacrificers with whom we have to deal admit the grace of God, but repeatedly thrust their free will together with merits upon it. They confess that one God alone is to be adored, but straightway, dreaming up various kinds of adoration, they worship not only dead men but also their bones and statues. They acknowledge Jesus Christ as Saviour and Redeemer, but at the same time they peddle their satisfactions and indulgences, bought for counted money. What else is this than to say that God lets go his wares to those who pay the price, as an apothecary does? They acknowledge that Christ, since he once became man, is the same always, has been and will be, but nonetheless they add that he is to be believed really and essentially present in as many breads as they have consecrated, and in as many places at once as Mass is celebrated. This is just as if you said that he is a true man while at the same time not being one. They call Jesus Christ their hope, but at the same time they also call the Virgin Mary, queen of heaven, their life, hope and queen of mercy, whom (to such a pitch of impudence have they come) they ask to command her Son by a mother's right, and whom they name the Expiatrix of sinners. For look at their words: "O happy mother, atoning for our crimes, command the Redeemer by a mother's right." They also sing wonderful things about Christ's offering on the tree of the Cross, but at the same time him also

units.la: ad nostri seculi Sacerdotes Romanos in multis maximi momenti doctrinæ capitibus. etiam realiter iterum ad altare suum offerunt* Vitam praesentem praedicant tempus illud esse quo sibi homines Dei gratiam promereantur: sed hanc etiam falsitatem alio non minus falso dogmate satisfactionibus nimirum pro mortuis oppugnant. Christus paradisum aperuerit, cuius tamen Romanus Pontifex cum suis ministris claves habeat. En quibus artibus Satan ab omni antiquitate comiscuit veritatem veneno, quo minus attentos errorum omnium veneno potatos inficeret.
