Denique, si qui se Deum dicit, verum Deum vera sua Deitate spoliat, ac proinde laesae Maiestatis divinae crimine tenetur, quid hodierna Romana Ecclesia aliud erit quàm officina in qua generis omnis Dij excuduntur? Deū enim aliquē facere, nō est simpliciter Dei nomen alicui tribuere, quum ipsis Angelis, Regibus ac Principibus, immo veris omnibus Christianis in Sacra Scriptura nomen istud quadam ratione commune sit: sed rei alicui tribuere quod verae Deitati proprie & incommunicabiliter est proprium. En igitur tot Deos ab hominibus creatos, quot Sanctos ac Sanctas paradisi, Romana in terris Ecclesia colit: preces enim ab illis exaudiri illa invocatio praesupponit, ac ipsis proinde Deum quod sibi proprium est, ea quae in terris fiunt & dicuntur audiedi videndiqué communicasse. Excipiunt autem, (speciosa licet effugio, Sanctos in paradiso ea in Trinitate tanquam in speculo conspicere. At somnia so miniis cumulant. Interea tamen Paradifo excepti Sancti, iltorum Deos, sic fabricare peritorum facta & doctrinam impobantes, in partem iltius blasphemiæ nequaquam veniût. Quid igitur dicturi sumus de offamentis & aliis reliquiis, & statuis ac imagunculis quibus eorum altaria gemunt, adeò vt ne canes quidem,equi & porci abiis abfinr:quibúsque vim diuinam spiritualem extraordinarie quibuf-uis morbis medendi tribuunt: & thura mittunt, quod apud ipsos Ethnicos foli diuinitati debiti cultus fuit indicium?Hos igitur ad D. Petrum & D.Iohannem Act.3.12.& ad D.Paulum.Act.14.14.relego.At hæc quantula pręiis quæ sibi Pontifex Romanus œcumenicus attribuit? Ius enim ac potestatem Legem conscientiis ferendi sibi arrogare, annon est se Deum facere? Peccata pro arbitrio retinere, vel remittere, nonne Dei folium est inuadere? At Dei verbo quidquam adiicere vel detrahere, explacito illud dispensare & immutare, animarum plena plaustra in inferos deducere, vt nemo quærat cur id faciat, non quidem est Deum se facere,sed supra omne quod Deus est sese efferre.Quod Apostolus olim de isto disertè prædixit 2.Thess.2.4.Tu vero Domine quousque tales blasphemias feres? Quousque tandem miseri amentes in istarum sordium cœno volutabimini?
units.tr: ...to the Roman priests of our age on many doctrines of the greatest importance. They even offer Christ again, really, on their altar. They proclaim that this present life is the time in which men earn God's grace for themselves. But they defend this falsehood with another dogma no less false, namely satisfactions for the dead. Christ opened paradise, yet the Roman Pontiff, together with his ministers, holds the keys. See by what arts Satan, from all antiquity, has mixed truth with poison, so that he might infect those less attentive with the poison of all errors. Finally, if anyone calls himself God, he strips the true God of his true deity, and is therefore held guilty of the crime of injured divine majesty. What, then, will the present Roman Church be but a workshop in which gods of every kind are forged? To make someone God is not simply to give the name of God to someone, since in Holy Scripture that name is in a certain sense common to angels, kings and princes, indeed to all true Christians. It is to attribute to a thing what is properly and incommunicably proper to the true Deity. So behold the many gods made by men, as many as the saints and saintesses of paradise whom the Roman Church on earth worships. For that invocation presupposes that the saints hear their prayers, and so that they have been given what is proper to God, namely to hear and see the things done and said on earth. They make an exception, though a specious escape: that the saints in paradise behold these things in the Trinity as in a mirror. But they heap up dreams. Meanwhile, the saints taken up into paradise have no share in the guilt of that blasphemy, though those who fashion their gods in this way, by the deeds and doctrine of unskilled men, do. What then shall we say of the bones and other relics, and of the statues and little images with which their altars groan, so that not even dogs, horses and pigs keep away from them; to which they attribute a divine spiritual power of healing every kind of disease extraordinarily, and before which they send incense, which among the heathen themselves was the sign of worship due to divinity alone? These things I refer back to Peter and John, Acts 3:12, and to Paul, Acts 14:14. But how small are these things compared with what the Roman Pontiff, the ecumenical one, claims for himself! To arrogate to himself the right and power of making laws for consciences: is this not to make himself God? To retain or remit sins at his will: is this not to usurp the throne of God? But to add or take away anything from the word of God, to dispense with and change it at his pleasure, to drive wagons full of souls into hell so that no one asks why he does it: this is not indeed to make himself God, but to raise himself above everything that God is. This the Apostle long ago foretold plainly of him, 2 Thess. 2:4. But you, Lord, how long will you bear such blasphemies? How long, wretched madmen, will you wallow in the mire of these filths?

units.la: Eadem autem aduersum nos aduersarij via procedunt.Quærentibus enim de ipsorum potestate, sit-ne à Deo, an vero,potius tyrannis ex diametro vnius Christi proprio officio re-pu-
units.tr: The adversaries proceed in the same way against us. For when they are asked about their power, whether it is from God or is rather a tyranny in direct conflict with the proper office of Christ alone, they...

units.la: Conformitas agendi veteris Sacerdotum ad pugnans,satisfactu abunde putant, si authoritate se tueantur, quam Deus Ecclesiae suae dedit, cum Apostolo dicentes veritatis eam esse columnam : audiendam esse : a Sancto illam Spiritu regi ac gubernari. Quod libenter ipsis concedimus : at non de hoc controvertitur. Manendum igitur in quaestionis terminis, An ipsi nimirum ea Ecclesia sint, necne : an sit eorum a Spiritu Sancto doctrina, necne: an quos sibi honores & dignitates ordinum attribuunt a Deo sint, necne : an denique iure sibi vindicent quod verae Ecclesiae proprium est, an vero sit ab ipsis vsurpatum nefarie. Simili ratione ad Reges Principes & populos aduersum nos armandos non solum gladio Iustitiae, tanquam aduersus omnium hominum flagitiosissimos: sed etiam caedibus ac lanienis infandis, nulla iuris seruata forma (qua in re longe sunt Caiapha & furente populo Iudaico deteriores) mactandos, Magistratuum officium, & veri cuiusque Christiani ad veram Religionem aduersus eiusdem perturbatores zelum praetendunt. At non hoc controvertitur, est enim illud extra dubium. Sed quaeritur, simulne ipsi illi perturbatores, falsaeque doctrinae auctores & promotores, vt calumniantur, an autem ipsimet (vt olim Elias Achabo in re simili. 1. Reg. 18 17.) veram religionem Christianam profanent, sus deque vertant, & a genuino sensu detorqueant. En quibus artibus Satan ab omni tempore depraedatus sit eos & adhuc hodie depraedetur, & donec Dominus semel adferat remedium depræda turus est qui se decipi & alios decipere gaudent. Domino vero maximas agamus gratias, nobis ad veritatem sua conspiciendam & contrarium detestandum oculos largito: supplicibúsque votis ab ipso contendamus vt perseuerantiam nobis ac constantiam in huius veritatis cognitione donet, tum in iis quæ sunt eius personæ propria, vt verum Deum & hominem in vnitate personæ fateamur, tum quæ ad eius officium in æternum permansurum pertinent. Vnicus enim ac summus ipse Rex est, omnem potestatem in corpora & animas adeptus, vt solus conscientiis nostris Leges figat. Propheta est, & verus diuini consilij enarrator, de nostra salute per Prophetas olim loquutus, & qui tandem ipse in mundum assumpta carne veniens salutis doctrinam patefecit, prædicarique & literis ab Apostolis & Euangelistis fidis suis seruis, ad Ecclesiæ suæ salutem ad consummationem vsque seculorum mandari iussit. Denique solus & æternus est Sacerdos, cuius oblatione semel facta & nunquam repetenda sumus reconciliati, mediator vnicus in cœlo, inter nos & Deum patrem, vt quidquid petimus in eius Nomine sanctissima perfectissimaque intercessione ipsius impetremus.
units.tr: In the manner of acting of the old priests, they think it quite sufficient for their defence if they shelter behind the authority which God gave to his Church, saying with the Apostle that she is the pillar of the truth, that she is to be heard, and that she is ruled and governed by the Holy Spirit. This we gladly concede to them, but this is not what is in dispute. Let us therefore keep to the terms of the question: whether they themselves are that Church or not; whether their doctrine comes from the Holy Spirit or not; whether the honours and dignities of orders which they claim for themselves are from God or not; and finally whether they rightly claim for themselves what is proper to the true Church, or whether they have wickedly usurped it. In a similar way they pretend zeal for the true Christian religion to arm the magistrates, princes and peoples against us, not only with the sword of justice, as against the most wicked of all men, but also to slaughter us with unspeakable butcheries, with no form of law observed (in which matter they are far worse than Caiaphas and the raging Jewish people). But this is not in dispute, for it is beyond doubt. The question is whether those very disturbers, the authors and promoters of false doctrine, are slandering us, or whether they themselves (as Elijah once said to Ahab in a similar matter, 1 Kings 18:17) profane the true Christian religion, turn it upside down and twist it from its genuine sense. See by what arts Satan has plundered them from every age and still plunders them today, and he will go on plundering until the Lord at last brings a remedy, those who rejoice to be deceived and to deceive others. But to the Lord let us give the greatest thanks, who has granted us eyes to behold his truth and to detest its opposite, and with prayers let us ask him to grant us perseverance and constancy in the knowledge of this truth, both in those things which are proper to his person, that we confess the true God and man in the unity of one person, and in those which pertain to his office, which will remain for ever. For he is the one and supreme King, who has obtained all power over bodies and souls, so that he alone fixes laws for our consciences. He is the Prophet and the true interpreter of the divine counsel, who spoke of our salvation through the Prophets of old, and who at last, coming into the world in assumed flesh, revealed the doctrine of salvation and commanded it to be preached and committed to writing by the Apostles and his faithful Evangelists, his servants, for the salvation of his Church until the end of the ages. Finally, he alone is the eternal Priest, by whose offering, made once and never to be repeated, we have been reconciled, the one Mediator in heaven between us and God the Father, so that whatever we ask in his name we obtain through his most holy and most perfect intercession.

units.la: En quomodo quos aliis sapientiæ, bonitatis ac pietatis exéplo præire oportuerat, cæcitatis tamé ac malitiæ simul rei sint, Deũ ipsum & rationem oppugnantes sua ratione, quod quid aliud est quàm velle Deum ipsum suis armis
units.tr: Behold how those who ought to have gone before others by the example of wisdom, goodness and piety are nevertheless at the same time guilty of blindness and malice, attacking God himself and reason by their own reasoning. What else is this than to wish to conquer God himself with their own weapons?

units.la: Pilatus homo Ethnicus voce hac Filii Dei territus. armis expugnare? Audiamus iā vt se illoru re- spectu Pilatus gelserit. Dicitur maiore quàm antea metu perculsus. Ecquid igitur metuit? Tumultum fateor, aut seditionem, animad- uersis animis Sacerdotum & plebis, & eorum clamoribus:at quod iterum Christum in præ- torium introducit, & vnde sit perquirit, satis testantur eum longè maius quiddam suspica- tum. Nam si solam seditionem tantoperè me- tuisset, quid impediebat eum quominus ipsis Christum non exspectatis aliis accusarionibus plectendnm traderet? Non est igitur dubium quin hac Filij Dei voce perculsus sit, & sopita prius conscientia veluti lancinata sit,etsi quid rei esset prorsus ignoraret. Primùm enim,etsi nimium multi,teste Propheta, Psal.14. 1.& có- tumeliis illis quas,proh dolor!audimus aduer- sus Deū & eius Prophetas euomi, iampridem ex suis animis religionis sensum omnè euelle- re conati sint: nunquam tamen efficere po- tuerunt etiam omnium sceleratissimi quin contemptum illum Dei morsus quidam im- pieratis & apprehensionis iusti Dei iudicij se- queretur,& eos arroderet. Testis ipse facinoro- sorum omnium primus Cain. Gen. 4. 9. & 13. Deinde, Ethnicorum idololatria in qua Pila- tus educatus fuerat, minus nouum ei faciebat quod Caiaphæ tamen & Iudæis erat inaudi- tum, hominem esse Deum,& Deorum ipso- rum quosdam filios nuncupari. Iouem enim suum Saturni filium credebant. Et hæc causa metuendi Pilato fuit, cogitanti quibus Chriftum affecisset contumeliis, & ad quæ cogebatur à Iudæis meditanti. Ideo seorsum eum interrogauit vnde esset, non simpliciter de patria inquirens, sed vt hac ratione, quis esset, cúrue se Dei filium nuncuparet sciscitaretur. At nobis longè sanè aliter quàm Pilatus de Deo inquirendum est, ad cuius cognitionem & timorem perueniamus: verùm tamen non immeritò multos eorum qui sese Christiano nomine plurimùm venditant, ad huius Ethnici scholam, cuisunt longè inferiores, ablegamus. Nam si Ethnicus iste, vmbram tantum Diuinitatis procul inspiciens, & in superstitione educatus, ad solam Filij Dei vocem perculsus tremuit: quid futurum est scurris illis & contemptoribus de Deo tàquam de re ludicra quæretibus & loquentibus, atque adeò totam Scripturam, & nominatim huius historiæ qua de agimus locos nonnullos in salcs & dicteria, & Romanos pasquillos conuertentibus?
units.tr: Pilate, a heathen man, was terrified by this word of the Son of God. Let us now hear how Pilate conducted himself towards them. He is said to have been struck with greater fear than before. What, then, did he fear? I grant that it was a tumult or a sedition, as he saw the minds of the priests and the people and heard their shouts. But that he brings Christ into the praetorium again and asks where he is from sufficiently shows that he suspected something far greater. For if he had feared only sedition so greatly, what prevented him from simply handing Christ over to be punished, without waiting for other accusations? There is no doubt, then, that he was struck by this word of the Son of God, and that his conscience, previously dozing, was as if torn open, although he was entirely ignorant of what the matter was. For first, although very many men, as the Prophet says (Ps. 14:1), have tried to root out every sense of religion from their minds, and although we hear, alas, such insults poured out against God and his Prophets, yet even the most wicked of all have never been able to avoid a certain biting of conscience, a sense of the impiety of contempt for God and of the apprehension of the just judgment of God, which gnaws at them. The first of all criminals, Cain, is himself the witness (Gen. 4:9, 13). Next, the idolatry of the heathen, in which Pilate had been brought up, made it less strange to him that a man should be God, and that some of the sons of those gods should be called men, which was nevertheless unheard of to Caiaphas and the Jews. For they believed that Jupiter was the son of Saturn. And this was the cause of Pilate's fear, as he considered what insults he had heaped upon Christ and what the Jews were forcing him to do. Therefore he questioned him apart, asking where he was from, not simply inquiring about his country, but to find out in this way who he was and why he called himself the Son of God. But we must inquire about God in a way far different from Pilate, so that we may come to the knowledge and fear of him. Yet not without reason do we send away to the school of this heathen, to which they are far inferior, many of those who vaunt themselves very much in the Christian name. For if this heathen, looking only at a shadow of the Deity from afar, and brought up in superstition, trembled when struck only by the voice of the Son of God, what will become of those buffoons and despisers who discuss and speak of God as of a matter for jest, and who turn the whole of Scripture, and especially some of the passages of this history with which we are dealing, into jokes and witticisms and Roman lampoons?

units.la: Vos verò deieratores, blasphemos, Diabolispeiores, qui Deum & Christum proscindi-tis, quantum in vobis est, quo loco tandem habebimus? Horrent enim eum Diaboli aduersus quem ita debacchamini. Vah! quinam eò deuenêre qui Christiano nomine glorian-tur, vt tam horrendum, tam abominandum crimen, non modò inter Christianos inultum iaceat, sed etiam non minus quàm ipse cibus ac potus, immò ipse etiam sermo sit frequens, & vsitatum? Deus bone! tantam esse tuam tàmque diuturnam patientiam! Et tamé illud vitium ad nos vsque qui Reformatæ Ecclesiæ nomen profitemur penetrauit. Insignis est Achabi historia. 1. Reg. 21. in qua legimus quum miser ille Nabothus falsò blasphemiæ accusatus esset, à conciuibus Senioribus putà & Magistratibus indictū publicū ieiuniū, tanquā ad iram Dei à tota regione auertēdam. Quid vero nos? Deieratur, blasphematur, quis vero tagitur? Quòd si ieiunium illud imitaremur, ecquod obsecro cibum capiendi tempus nobis relinqueretur? Quid aliud igitur euenturum putamus, nisi maturè tum publicè tum priuatim occurratur, quàm vt in nos eius qui tanto gloriæ suæ zelo ducitur, horrendus ac stupendus furor incumbat? Nullus vero nobis excusationi locus relictus est. Veniam igitur à Domino supplices potiùs deprecemur, alij nimium huius sibi conscij criminis: alij nimium in coercendo segnes ac muti. At si vel leuiter quis offenditur, ad ius illico prouocatur, aut vi vis repellitur. Quid futurum igitur est deieratoribus & blasphemis? Nam quot modis tam sacrosanctum illud & pretiosum Dei nomen sine causa temerè profundimus? At Pilatus ad solam Filij Dei vocem totus cohorrescit. Nos ne vero adeo stupidos vt nō animaducrtamus horrendam illam Domini criminationem, Deum pro innocente non habiturum eum qui Nomen suum in vanum assumpserit? Agite igitur singuli, cuiuscunque gradus, dignitatis ac conditionis, ista sedulò pensitemus. Magistratus, cum qui tanto vos honore dignatus
units.tr: But you swearers, blasphemers, worse than devils, who tear apart God and Christ as far as you can, where shall we finally place you? For the devils shudder at the one against whom you rage in this way. Alas! To what have those come who glory in the Christian name, that so horrible, so abominable a crime lies not only unpunished among Christians, but is as frequent and common, indeed, as food and drink, or even as ordinary speech? Good God! How great and how long-lasting is your patience! And yet this vice has penetrated even to us who profess the name of the Reformed Church. The history of Ahab is notable (1 Kings 21), in which we read that when that wretched Naboth was falsely accused of blasphemy, his fellow citizens, the elders and magistrates, proclaimed a public fast, as if to turn away the wrath of God from the whole region. But what of us? We swear, we blaspheme, and who is punished? If we were to imitate that fast, what time, I ask you, would be left to us for taking food? What then do we think will happen, unless we are met in good time, both publicly and privately, before that terrible and astonishing fury of him who is driven by such zeal for his own glory falls upon us? Yet no ground for excuse has been left to us. Let us therefore rather humbly beg pardon from the Lord: some of us are too conscious of this crime; others are too slow and silent in restraining it. But if someone is even slightly offended, he is at once called to law, or else repelled by force. What then will become of swearers and blasphemers? For in how many ways do we rashly and needlessly pour out that most sacred and precious name of God? But Pilate, at the mere voice of the Son of God, wholly shudders. Are we so stupid that we do not notice that dreadful threat of the Lord, that he will not hold him innocent who takes up his name in vain? Come then, each of you, of whatever rank, dignity and condition, let us weigh these things carefully. Magistrates, revere him who has honoured you with such dignity. Parents, attend to the lessons you give your children. And you, common people, worship and venerate him from whom you have this dignity, that you may be called his people. Soldiers, fear him who is girded with a sword far different from the one you bear; and since your life is so often in danger, think about the state after this life, and remember never to let the sentence of this excellent Sage be blotted out by any old age: "A man who swears much is full of iniquity, and the scourge will not depart from his house." (Ecclus. 23.12)

units.la: R. iij. est, reueremini. Parentes, quæ liberis documenta præbeatis attendite. Tu vero plebs, eum colè ac venerare à quo hanc dignitatem habes, vt populus eius nuncuperis. Milites, eum metuite qui lôgè alio, quàm quem geritis gladio, accinctus est: & quum toties vita vestra periclitetur, sterio de statu post hanc vitam futuro cogitate: & huius eximiæ Sapientis nulla vnquam vetultate delendæ sententiæ memores estote. Vir qui multum iurat plenus est iniquitatis, & non abscedet à domo eius flagellum. Ecclesiastici. 23.12.
units.tr: To return to the history: Christ, as he had more than once before, disdained to answer Pilate, not because he was standing before Pilate to defend his innocence, which was itself plainly attested enough, but in order to bear patiently, without opening his mouth, whatever the Father had decreed concerning him (Isa. 53.7). Then, because he foresaw that whatever answer he had brought from the sacred Scriptures would be taken away from Pilate by fear and would be made ridiculous. And this is most worthy of observation: when we are called by the Lord to confess his most sacred name, we should flee the two extremes above all. For he who forbids pearls to be offered to swine also bids us confess his name openly and plainly. Only the Holy Spirit teaches what must be done in this matter and what measure is to be kept, bringing a good conscience, and not swelling with ambition or trembling with fear when we ought to speak.

units.la: Vt ad historiam reuertamur, dicitur Christus Pilatum respôso dedignatus, vt antea non semel, quòd non suæ innocentiæ, quæ satis ipsam aperte testabatur, tutandæ causa coram Pilato staret, sed quæcunque de ipso Pater decreuerat, non aperto suo ore tolerandi. Esa. 53. 7. Deinde quòd satis prouideret quodcunque ex sacris scripturis responsum attulisset, Pilato potiùs metu illud adempturum & ridiculum fore. Et hoc obseruatu dignissimum est, vt quum à Domino ad sacrosancti Nominis eius confessionem vocamur, duo potissimum extrema fugiamus. Nam qui margaritas porcis exhiberi prohibet, palam etiam & aperte nomen suum confiteri nos iubet. Solus autem Sp. S. quid hac in re facto sit opus, quæve tenenda mensura, docet, bonam conscientiam adferentes, non autem vel ambitione turgentes, vel metu quum loquendum est pauentes.
units.tr: To return to the history: Christ, we are told, disdained to answer Pilate, as he had on earlier occasions too, not because he was standing before Pilate to defend his innocence (which was already openly attested well enough), but so that he might bear without opening his mouth whatever the Father had decreed concerning him. Isa. 53. 7. Next, because he foresaw that whatever answer he gave from the sacred Scriptures would be taken away by Pilate, either through fear, or would be treated with ridicule. And this is most worthy of observation: when we are called by the Lord to confess his most holy Name, we should flee two extremes above all. For he who forbids pearls to be cast before swine also bids us confess his name openly and plainly. The Holy Spirit alone teaches what must be done in this matter and what measure is to be kept, bringing a good conscience, and being neither puffed up with ambition nor trembling with fear when we must speak.

units.la: Iesus Christus igitur de facto proprio & de intenintentata aduersus ipsum accusatione interro-gatus nihil, ob allatas à nobis superius causas respondit. At quum de potestia sua sic loquentem Pilatum audiret vt de Dei honore ageretur, Dei Patris causam egit, Pilato licet Maximi tunc in orbe Imperatoris personam repraesentante, & singulos quid hac in parte sui sit officij docuit, & eorum in primis quibus in Ecclesia docendi munus incumbit, tum consolando, tum etiam arguendo. 1. Tim. 3. 16. Sed in primis diligenter est notanda prudentia illa quam adhibuit in reprehendendo, Pilati dignitate nulla ratione laesa, seruataque rei quam coram suo Iudice sustinebat personarum circunstantiarum, vt reliquarum omnium similium, maxima est habenda ratio, vt adhortationibus, monitionibus ac reprehensionibus modus adhibeatur, vt monitor opportuna loquutus suum effectum consequatur. Pilatus contra, licet nonnihil commotus, in Christo tamen nihil nisi humile & abiectum conspiciens: sibique esse contumeliosum arbitratus se respondere dedignatum, & in hac animi perturbatione sese altius paulo extulerit: non tamen est penitus ira percitus & indignatus: Viris igitur ad aliquem dignitatis gradu euectis esse ipsum oportet exemplo, in cohibendis animi passionibus, quum tamen hodie passim conspicias vnius noctis homines tam animi esse impotentes, & multo minore de causa sic ferocire, vt sint penitus intolerandi. Faxit vero Deus Opt. Max. vt haec omnia no-
units.tr: Jesus Christ, then, when questioned about his own affairs and about the accusation brought against him, which was unproven, made no answer, for the reasons we gave above. But when he heard Pilate speaking of his power in such a way that the honour of God was at stake, he pleaded the cause of God the Father, even though Pilate then represented the person of the Emperor Maximus in the world. He taught each person what his duty is in this matter, and especially those to whom the office of teaching in the Church is entrusted, both by consoling and also by rebuking. 1. Tim. 3. 16. But above all we must carefully note the prudence he showed in rebuking, so that Pilate's dignity was in no way injured, and, while keeping the circumstances of the person and of the matter before his own judge, the greatest regard is to be had, as in all similar cases, so that the mode of exhortation, admonition and rebuke is adapted, and the one who admonishes, speaking at the right moment, obtains his effect. Pilate, on the other hand, although somewhat moved, yet seeing nothing in Christ but what was humble and abject, and thinking it an insult to himself to deign to answer, raised himself a little higher in this disturbance of mind; yet he was not wholly provoked to anger and indignation. Men raised to some degree of dignity ought therefore to be an example to others in restraining the passions of the mind, whereas today you may see everywhere men of one night's standing so lacking in self-control, and growing so fierce over a much slighter cause, that they become utterly intolerable. May God, the best and greatest, grant that all these things, fixed more deeply in our minds, bear their necessary fruit, both in the knowledge of how to rebuke and in bearing reproofs with an even mind. If this teaching found a place among men, truly the occasion of many confusions would be cut off, which we see reigning everywhere to our great sorrow.

units.la: R. iiij. stris mentibus altius infixa fructus necessarios ferant, tum in scientia reprehendendi, tum reprehensiones æquo animo ferédi, quæ doctrina si locum apud homines obtineret, næ multis confusionibus ansa præcideretur, quas passim regnare nostro summo dolore conspicimus.
units.tr: R. iiij. May these things be fixed more deeply in our minds and bear necessary fruit: both in knowing how to rebuke, and in bearing rebukes with an even temper. If this teaching held a place among men, indeed many confusions would be cut off at their source, which we see reigning everywhere to our great sorrow.

units.la: HOMILIA VICESIMASEXTA.
units.tr: HOMILY TWENTY-SIX.

units.la: MATTH. 27.
units.tr: MATTHEW 27.

units.la: 24. Videns autem Pilatus se nihil proficere, sed maiorem tumultum fieri, accepta aqua abluit manus coram turba, dicens, Innoxius sum à sanguine huius iustivos videritis.
units.tr: 24. When Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but that a greater tumult was arising, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just man; see to it yourselves.

units.la: 25. Et respondens universus populus dixit, Sanguis eius super nos & super filios nostros.
units.tr: 25. And the whole people answered and said, His blood be upon us and upon our children.

units.la: IOH. 19.
units.tr: JOHN 19.

units.la: 10. Dicit ergo ei Pilatus, Mihi non loqueris? Nescis me potestatem habere crucifigendi te, & potestatem habere te dimittendi?
units.tr: 10. Pilate therefore said to him, Do you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have power to crucify you, and power to release you?

units.la: 11. Respondit Iesus, Non haberes potestatem adversum me ullam, nisi hoc tibi datum esset superne: propterea qui me tradidit tibi, maius peccatum habet.
units.tr: 11. Jesus answered, You would have no power against me at all, unless it had been given you from above; therefore he who delivered me to you has the greater sin.

units.la: 12. Ex eo tempore studebat Pilatus eum dimittere: Iudaei vero clamabant, dicentes, Si hunc dimiseris, non es amicus Caesaris: quicunque se regem facit contradicit Caesari.
units.tr: 12. From that time Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, saying, If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend; whoever makes himself a king opposes Caesar.

units.la: 13. Pilatus ergo quum audisset hunc sermonem, eduxit foras Iesum, consedit quo in tribunali, in loco qui dicitur Lithostrotos, Hebraicè autem Gabbatha.
units.tr: 13. When Pilate therefore heard this saying, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat, in the place called the Pavement, but in Hebrew Gabbatha.

units.la: 14. Erat autem parasceue Pascha, hora vero quasi sexta: tum dicit Iudaeis, Ecce rex vester.
units.tr: 14. Now it was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour; and he said to the Jews, Behold your king.

units.la: 15. Illi vero clamauerunt, Tolle, tolle, Crucifige eum. Dicit eis Pilatus, Regem vestrum crucifigam? Responderunt primarij Sacerdotes, Non habemus regem nisi Caesarem.
units.tr: 15. But they cried out, Away with him, away with him, crucify him. Pilate said to them, Shall I crucify your king? The chief priests answered, We have no king but Caesar.

units.la: VVM ad humanae societatis coseruationem necesse sit alios parêre, alios vero imperare, quae ipse Deus ordinem constituit, si quid est in rebus humanis scitu & obseruatu dignissimum, haec ipsa certè est rite imperandi & parendi scientia. Qua de re vtraque multa sunt nobis à viris sapientibus tradita & monumentis consignata documenta pro humana prudetia: vt qui nec istud ignorarunt, Regna & alias id genus Dignitates à Summo Numine pendêre, cui vel potentissimos rationem oporteat reddere: quamobrem etiam Iustitiam appellarunt Dei filiam, & Reges Διοξμεῖς & Διοτρεφεῖς nuncuparunt: & similes alias egregias, veras & graues hac de re sententias protulerunt. Sed imperfecta illa, prae iis quae in schola diuina, puta scriptis Prophetarum & Apostolorum discuntur, e quibus etiam quicquid est vere bonum & sanctum haurire nos oportet, quod ipse Dei Filius, ore suo ipsius hoc loco testatur, paucis quidem verbis, sed quibus vt fundamento superstruendum quicquid de Magistratibus superioribus & inferioribus, eorumque officiis & auctoritate recte tradi potest.
units.tr: Since the preservation of human society necessarily requires that some obey and others command, and since God himself has established this order, if there is anything in human affairs most worthy of being known and observed, it is certainly this very science of commanding and obeying rightly. Concerning this, wise men have handed down to us many teachings on both sides, recorded in writings for the benefit of human prudence: they recognised that kingdoms and other such dignities depend on the Supreme Power, to whom even the most powerful must render an account. For this reason they also called Justice the daughter of God, and named kings [Διοξμεῖς] and [Διοτρεφεῖς], and they put forward other excellent, true and weighty sayings of the same kind. But those teachings are imperfect compared with what is learned in the divine school, that is, in the writings of the Prophets and Apostles, from which we must draw whatever is truly good and holy, as the Son of God himself testifies here with his own mouth. His words are few, but on them, as on a foundation, whatever can rightly be taught about superior and inferior magistrates, their duties and their authority, may be built.

units.la: Iesus Christus igitur hic loquens vt suae exinanitionis tempore, & habita formae ipsius servilis ratione, Phil.2.7. quatenus Pilatum in sce potestatem habere agnoscit, quamuis ipse innocens, & Pilatus Ethnicus esset, docet nos officium subditorum erga Magistratus, etiam infidelis & tyrannice agentes, modo tamen ipsis ita morem geramus, ne eius quod Deo pro nostrae vocationis ratione debemus, simus immemores. Act.4 19. & 5.29. quam ipse Christus normam praescripsit, Luc.20.25. Sed etiam Christum alio respectu, quatenus nimirum erat & est verus ab aeterno Deus cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto, licet id minime Pilatus intelligeret, de seipso loquutum esse sciamus, quasi Pilatum his verbis compellaret, Qualem me aspicis coram te nocenti similem, is tamen ego sum preter cuius arbitrium nec ipse Dominus tuus Imperator esset, nec tu hanc provinciam in Iudaea sustineres: nec habet accusatores mei quo se efferant quod me comprehensum in hunc statum redegerint: nec quo tu ipse insolescas quod quòd stem pro tribunali tuo iudicandus.Nam comprehensus ac vinctus sum libens: stóque reus coram tuo tribunali quòd ea sit & mea & Patris mei voluntas. Istud, inquam, Christus his verbis significare voluit, non ipsi tantùm Pilato, nec suis solis aduersariis, sed nobis, vt hanc in eius Ecclesia doctrinam addisca-mus.
units.tr: Jesus Christ, then, speaking here in the time of his humiliation and taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2.7), in that he acknowledges that Pilate has power over him, though he himself is innocent and Pilate is a heathen, teaches us the duty of subjects towards magistrates, even unbelieving and tyrannical ones, provided that we obey them in such a way as not to forget what we owe to God according to our calling (Acts 4.19; 5.29). This is the rule that Christ himself prescribed (Luke 20.25). But we should also know that Christ, in another respect, namely as he is and was from eternity the true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, though Pilate did not understand this, spoke of himself, as if he were addressing Pilate with these words: "You see me before you in the likeness of a guilty man, yet I am the one apart from whose will neither your Lord the Emperor would be what he is, nor would you hold this province in Judea. My accusers have no ground for boasting that they brought me to this condition, nor have you any reason to be puffed up because you stand before your tribunal as judge of me. For I am taken and bound willingly, and I stand as a defendant before your tribunal because this is both my will and the will of my Father." This, I say, is what Christ meant by these words, not only for Pilate himself or for his adversaries alone, but for us, so that we might learn this doctrine in his Church.

units.la: Horum autem ad expositionem vt acceda- mus, primùm obseruandum est, etiamsi Deus singulis pro suo ordine Magistratibus vitę ne- císque potestatem attribuerit, non absolutam tamen eam accepisse, sed commissam tantùm, atque adeò certis terminis à bonis legibus & decretis circunscriptam,quum ea vox Rege dignà sit (aiebat Imperator quidam Romanus, quamuis non Christianus) qua sese Legibus esse astrictum fateatur. Ad hæc, quū ad Deum proprie ac iure pertineant exitus mortis.Psal. 68. 21. & ne passerculus quidem in terram sine voluntate patris cadat.Matth.10.29.&Regum corda sint in manu Domini, quæ quocunque velit,flectat,Prouerb.21.1. sciant vel potentissimi suarum sententiarum executionem plane à Deo pendere,quum etiam quoties ipsi visum est accidat, vt qui ad supplicium trahebatur euadat. 1.Sam.14.vers.45. & contrà moriatur, cui vita fuerat condonata. 1. Sam. 15. vers 33.
units.tr: In order to approach the explanation of these words, we must first observe that although God has given to each magistrate, according to his rank, the power of life and death, he has not given it as an absolute power, but only as one entrusted, and therefore limited by fixed bounds of good laws and decrees. For the word is worthy of a king (as a certain Roman emperor, though not a Christian, used to say) by which he confesses that he is bound by the laws. Moreover, since the outcomes of death belong to God properly and by right (Ps. 68.21), and not even a sparrow falls to the ground without the will of the Father (Matt. 10.29), and the hearts of kings are in the hand of the Lord, which he turns wherever he wills (Prov. 21.1), even the most powerful should know that the execution of their sentences depends entirely on God, since it happens whenever it seems good to him that one who was being led to punishment escapes (1 Sam. 14.45), and, on the contrary, that one dies to whom life had been granted (1 Sam. 15.33).

units.la: Non tamen propterea non agnoscenda talis Magistratibus à Domino concelsa potestas, quibus minimè gladium quo vti nequeant dederit. Rom.13.4. Interea cauendum ne in Dei folio collocentur, quibus suppereminet, & cuius timore timor & reuerentia debita Magistratibus est dirigenda. Quæ si à subditis obseruanda regula, quanto diligentius etiam Magistratus dare operam debent ne supra suū gradum efferantur, ipsos alioquin iræ Dei horrendis iudiciis manentibus, quorum stupendæ illæ Pharaoni, Sennacheribo, Nebucadnezari, Antiocho Magno, duobus Herodibus, Patri & filio Agrippæ dicto, ac monstris illis inter Romanos Imperatores, & aliis tyrannis irrogatæ poenæ testes sunt. Quain re Pilatus grauiter lapsus est. Nam toties cognitam Christi innocentiam publicè professus, quum tantopere iactat potestatem ipsum crucifigendi, quid aliud agit quàm quod latro viatori intercepto vitā ie posse eripere minitans? Hinc illi tam magni & superbi tituli, quos in dies Principū vanitate & populorū adulationibus augeri cōspicimus, vt vix iā vllus Deo titulus proprius videatur esse futurus. Exèpli gratia, quàm multos ho die videmus detestandā Romanorū Imperatorū fuorū monstra indigetantiū imitatos idololatria nō erubescere suos Principes Diuos nūcupare, quod longè maius est quàm si Diuinos diceret? Sed quid non? Vix annus agitur vicesimus ex quo quidā ex prophanis illis nostri seculi poetis, qui totū terrarū orbē Ethnica & detestanda prophanitate complent, ausus est Regē suum Optimum Maximum appellare, quod inter Ethnicos idololatras superstitio- si sitfissimi,soli magno suo Deo Ioui reseruarunt.
units.tr: Nevertheless, this power granted to magistrates by the Lord is not on that account to be denied, since he has not given the sword to those who cannot use it (Rom. 13.4). Meanwhile, care must be taken that those over whom they stand are not placed on God's throne, and that the fear and reverence due to magistrates should be directed by the fear of God. If this rule is to be observed by subjects, how much more diligently should magistrates take pains not to rise above their own rank, lest the terrible judgments of God's wrath remain over them. Of these, the dreadful punishments inflicted on Pharaoh, Sennacherib, Nebuchadnezzar, Antiochus the Great, the two Herods, the father and the son called Agrippa, and those monsters among the Roman emperors and other tyrants, are witnesses. In this matter Pilate fell grievously. For after having so often publicly acknowledged Christ's innocence, when he so boasts of his power to crucify him, what else does he do than what a robber does when, threatening a traveller he has seized, he says he can take away his life? Hence come those grand and proud titles which we see growing day by day through the vanity of princes and the flattery of the people, so that scarcely any title proper to God seems likely to remain. For example, how many today do we see, imitating the detestable monsters of the Roman emperors, who were deified, not ashamed to call their princes divine, which is far worse than if they called them godly? But why say more? Scarcely twenty years have passed since one of those profane poets of our age, who fill the whole world with heathen and detestable profanity, dared to call his king Optimus Maximus, a title which among the heathen idolaters, the most superstitious of men, they reserved only for their great god Jupiter.

units.la: Quod si merito vituperatur in Magistrati-bus à Deo cõstitutis, quid fiet Pótifice isto Ro mano,animarū quidé in rebus spiritualibus ty ráno:in tēporalibusvcrò sibi quod suū non est vindicâte?Quid fiet etiâ omnibus iis qui rebus tēporalibus simul & Ecclesiasticis, contra ex- pressam Filij Dei prohibitionem dominantur? Matt.21.25.Non eodé igitur sunt isti loco, quo Magistratus àDeo ordinati,quos sua potestate bene vti oportet,vt eius tamen abusus nihil i- psorū dignitati deroget : quū cōtrà impuri isti homines, præter omnia diuina & humana iu- ra, quam sibi vẽdicant potestatem vsurparint, vt huius ipse vsus nihil aliud sit quàm abusus.
units.tr: If this is rightly blamed in magistrates set up by God, what will become of that Roman Pontiff, a tyrant over souls in spiritual matters, and in temporal matters claiming for himself what is not his? What will become also of all those who rule over temporal and ecclesiastical affairs at once, in direct contradiction to the express prohibition of the Son of God (Matt. 20.25)? These men, therefore, are not in the same position as magistrates ordained by God, who ought to use their power well, yet whose abuse of it does nothing to detract from their dignity. Whereas these impure men, beyond all divine and human laws, have usurped the power they claim for themselves, so that its very exercise is nothing but abuse.

units.la: Voce deinde hac DANDI, quicunque interhomines ad eos honores eueĉti sunt,successio- ne vel electione,vel alia ratione legitima mo- netur,nec fortunæ,nec syderibus,nec suæ indu striæ aut meritis vllâ eorū parte acceptâ ferre, sed illi soli per quê Reges regnât. Prou.8.15.& de quo Ps.75 8. dicitur,nec ab Oriente,nec ab Occidéte,neq; à Meridie exaltatione cõtinge- re,sed ab vno Deo qui hūc extollit,illū depri- mit.Hinc laudatissima illa Christianorū Regū çósuetudo,sese per Dei gratiâ Regēs prædicā- di,modò semper illius in regnorū suorū admi- nistratione recordetur. At Reuerédiss.Cardi- nales, magno abusu sibi hūc titulū scribētes, verè diceret, si pro,Dei gratia restitueret, Ira Dei, hominesin sensum reprobum dantis.
units.tr: Next, by this word GIVING, it is shown that whoever has been raised to those honours among men, whether by succession, election, or another lawful means, must acknowledge that in no part does he owe it to fortune, to the stars, to his own industry or merits, but only to him through whom kings reign (Prov. 8.15), and of whom Psalm 75.8 says that exaltation comes neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south, but from the one God who lifts up this man and brings down that one. Hence comes the most praiseworthy custom of Christian kings, who style themselves kings by the grace of God, provided they always keep this in mind in the government of their kingdoms. But the most reverend Cardinals, writing this title for themselves with great abuse, would speak truly if, instead of "by the grace of God," they wrote "by the wrath of God, who gives men over to a reprobate mind."

units.la: Ad hæc,dextrè intelligēda hęc vox DANDI.Hic.n.donator suę donationi tēp°& terminos ex voluntatis arbitrio ponit, & iis conditionibus vt ea ritè & honestè vtamur: addita commin atione aduersus ingratos, ea spoliandos. 1. Sam.13.14.& 1.Reg. 14.10. An enim æquum esset, huic donatori, Deo æterno & omnipotenti, minus esse iuris quàm donatoribus inter mortales reuocandæ suæ donationis propter donatarij ingratitudinem: aut minus esse authoritatis Reges & Imperatores solio deturbandi, ipsorum perfidiæ causa, quàm patronis à suis clientibus literas & instrumenta clientelaria auferendi?
units.tr: Moreover, this word DANDI ("given") must be understood correctly. For the giver sets the time and limits of his gift according to his own will, and sets conditions under which we may use it rightly and honourably, with a threat added against the ungrateful, that they will be stripped of it (1 Sam. 13:14; 1 Kings 14:10). For would it be fair that this giver, the eternal and almighty God, should have less right to revoke his gift than human givers have to revoke their gifts on account of the ingratitude of the recipient? Or that he should have less authority to cast kings and emperors from their thrones because of their treachery than patrons have to take back from their clients the letters and documents of clientage?

units.la: Cæterùm eius est qui dedit rescindere donationem: quod facit quando & quibus extraordinariis mediis ipsi libet, aut vt ferunt leges & instituta vnicuique regno vel Reipub. peculiaria. Tu verò priuate, quisquis es, tu seditiose qui sceptrum ei conaris eripere, cui Deus tibi imperaturo dedit, quid agis? Nū vis esse Deo superior suæ donationis futuro vindice? Nonne contrà æquū est vt is qui sceptrum à Deo accepit, eo tibi caput comminuat? Ac certè plerunque seditiosis talis exitus contingit: quem etiamnum à diuina bonitate imprecari debemus aduersus infelicissimam illam improborum reliquam societatem coniuratorum in regni Gallici diadema, in eum quem videmus tam miserum ac deplorandum statum redacti.
units.tr: Yet it belongs to the one who gave to annul the gift; he does so when and by whatever extraordinary means he pleases, or according to the laws and customs peculiar to each kingdom or commonwealth. But you, whoever you are, a private person, you who seditiously try to snatch the sceptre from him to whom God gave it so that he might rule over you, what are you doing? Do you wish to be superior to God, the future avenger of his own gift? Is it not rather right that he who received the sceptre from God should crush your head with it? And certainly it is often the case that seditious men meet with such an end. From the divine goodness we ought to pray that this same end befall the most wretched remnant of that wicked society of conspirators against the crown of France, and the one whom we see reduced to so miserable and deplorable a state.

units.la: Præterea notanda vox illa SVPERNE, qua monentur superiores caueant ne in suis cogitationibus ita se inferiores despiciant, vt fui gradus intentiore admiratione elati obli- uiscantur fe, praeter sceptrum quod accepe- runt ad tempus a Domino, homines esse sicut reliquos, quibus eos tandem aliquando futura mors adaequabit.Psal.82.6. & 7.Contra potius singulis momentis Regem Regum suspiciant tam excelsum vt nihil cum lateat: qui iratus vindemiat spiritum Principum & terribilis est Regibus terrae. Pfal. 76.12.quibus exemplis historiae tum sacrae tum prophanae plenefunt, praeter iam a nobis nostro tempore conspecta & Deo fauente,conspicienda: Viceuerfa boni Principes & Magistratus, quum certo sciant sibi defensorem esse supra omnes coelos, illo freti cum sancta & vere generosa magnanimi- tate officio fungi debent.
units.tr: Furthermore, note the word SUPERNE ("from above"), by which superiors are warned to take care that in their thoughts they do not so despise their inferiors, nor, lifted up by the admiration of their own rank, forget that apart from the sceptre they have received for a time from the Lord, they are men like the rest, to whom future death will at last make them equal (Ps. 82:6-7). Rather, they should look up every moment to the King of kings, so exalted that nothing is hidden from him, who in anger gathers the spirit of princes and is terrible to the kings of the earth (Ps. 76:12). Both sacred and profane histories are full of such examples, besides those which we have already seen in our own time and which, God willing, we shall yet see. Therefore good princes and magistrates, since they know with certainty that they have a defender above all the heavens, ought to discharge their duty relying on him, with a holy and truly noble magnanimity.

units.la: Etsi autem hic agitur proprie de Magistra- tuum auctoritate in suos subditos,idipsum ta- men & ad reliquos humanae societatis gradus legitimos extendi debet,quum Deus legitimae omnis supereminentis potestatis author fit at- que confcruator,Rom.13.1.Memententote igitur heri & herae vobis quidem ius esse domini in seruos vestros & ancillas,non tamen vt iis tanquam bestiis abutamini,quum sint tantum mercenarij: atque etiam Dominus Legis suae 4. praecepto vel ipsis bestiis cauerit,iubens eas lubleuari, & boui trituranti vetans os ligari Deut.25.4.nec praeter rationem Angelus alinae Balaami patrocinetur.Num.22.10.& 12.Videte ergo quid agatis, vos qui veltrorum famulo- rum & ancillarum aut aliorum operarum mercedem retinetis, & in ius vocari propterea nō erubescitis. Dicam etiam aliquid amplius, Dominum, quum hominibus bestiarum carnem vtendam fruendam dederit, voluisse tamen earum sanguinem, quasi sibi dicandum effundi,acsi diceret,Vobis quidem earum corpus permitto: animam vero qualiscunque sit seruari mihi volo. Quae Lex etsi cum cerimonialibus aliis abrogata sit, istud tamen ex ea supererst,homines moderatè & humaniter pecoribus ipsis vti debere, non in tyrannorum morem, vt qui secus illis vtuntur grauem animadvertionem mereantur.
units.tr: Although here the matter concerns properly the authority of magistrates over their subjects, the same must also be extended to the other legitimate grades of human society, since God is the author and preserver of all lawful superior power (Rom. 13:1). Remember therefore, masters and mistresses, that you indeed have the right of lords over your servants and maidservants, yet you must not abuse them as beasts, since they are only hired workers. Indeed the Lord, in the fourth commandment of his Law, provided even for beasts, commanding that they be given rest, and forbidding that the mouth of the ox treading out the grain be muzzled (Deut. 25:4); nor without reason did the angel defend the ass of Balaam (Num. 22:10, 12). See therefore what you are doing, you who withhold the wages of your servants, maids, or other workers, and are not ashamed to be summoned to court on that account. I will say something more: the Lord, although he gave men the flesh of beasts to eat and enjoy, nevertheless wished their blood to be poured out as if consecrated to himself, as if he were saying: "I grant you their bodies; but I wish their souls, whatever they may be, to be reserved for me." Although this Law has been abrogated together with the other ceremonial laws, there remains from it this principle: men ought to use the beasts themselves moderately and humanely, not in the manner of tyrants, who treat them otherwise and deserve grave punishment.

units.la: Vos etiam parentes potestatem quidem in liberos, quinetiam coercendi eosius habetis vobis Supernè datum: sed cauete diligenter ab vtroque hoc extremo, nempe ne quis nec ei le erit castigationes adhiberi, sitis in iis segniores,aut modo illis nō adhibeatis.Quibus apud nos neglectis, praesertim castigatione, haud scio an alia vlla ciuitas sit pro circunstantiis vbi plures perditi iam aut perdendi pueri reperiantur. Vicissim vero, liberi considerate, parentibus vestris Supernè istam in vos potestatem datam, cui nisi vos sponte submittatis, væ vobis tantam benedictionem in terris parentes habendi,in maledictionem conuertentibus.
units.tr: You parents also have from above the power over your children, and indeed the right to correct them; but take careful heed against both extremes: that you be neither too lax in correcting them, nor fail to apply correction at all. Among us, when these things are neglected, especially correction, I scarcely know whether any other city, given its circumstances, can be found where more boys are already lost or in danger of being lost. In turn, children, consider well that the power over you has been given from above to your parents; unless you submit to it willingly, woe to you, who turn into a curse the great blessing of having parents on earth.

units.la: Vos itidem mariti,capita quidem vestrarum vxorum estis, ex eius instituto qui in Superis est, quíque matrimonium tanto dignatur honore, vt Ecclesiam, Sponsam suam vocet. At vicisvicissim recordamini Deum non ex calcaneo sed ex latere Adami mulierem eduxisse, vt si-gnificaret, eam ita marito subiici & inferio-rem esse, vt socia sit tamen, itaque seruire o-portere, vt nihilo magis serua sit aut manci-pium.Procul igitur absint rixæ illæ contume-liosæ,colaphi,percussiones, & alia his similia, quæ non Dominationem, sed tyrannidem, & inhumanitatem in Ecclesia nullo modo fe-rendam, dico, quasi in iis locis vbi aliquis in-stitutus est ciuilis & Ecclesiasticus ordo nulla melior alia cogendi mulieres ad debitam o-bedientiam maritis præstandam esset ratio. Vos verò mulieres (eas compello quæ hanc in partem peccant, quales nimis multæ)quarum aliæ vanitati,aliæ ebrietati addictę,aliæ rerum domesticarum incuriosæ,aliæ contumaces,(su-perbæ duri oris & indomitæ, num Deum vo-bis inferiorem fore putatis?Num in vestri gra-tiam sacrosanctam matrimonij Legem abro-gare Dominus cogetur?Quid miramini vos iu-sto Dei iudicio ferre pœnas vestris periuriis debitas,quum leuissima quaque occasione ab-iiciatis,maritis à vobis coram Deo, Angelis i-psius & Ecclesia promissam reuerentiam & obsequium? Quòd si Deus tam grauem pœ-nam minatur ei,qui aliquē ex minimis offen-derit, Matth. 18. 6. quid tot tam male moratis familiis fiet, quæ vniuersam ciuitatem offen-dere non desinunt? Vtinam verò Dominus Deus noster, Deus omnis ordinis ipsi conse-crandi, eiusmodi vitiis mederi, & intra suam
units.tr: You husbands likewise are the heads of your wives, by the appointment of him who is in heaven, who has so honoured marriage that he calls the Church, his bride, by its name. Yet in turn, remember that God formed the woman not from Adam's heel but from his side, to signify that she is so subject to her husband and inferior to him, yet a companion, and so ought to serve him, that she is in no way a slave or a chattel. Far therefore be those abusive quarrels, blows, beatings, and other things like them, which I say are not lordship but tyranny and inhumanity, in no way to be tolerated in the Church, as though, in places where a civil and ecclesiastical order has been instituted, there were no better method of compelling wives to render their husbands due obedience. But you women (I address those who sin in this respect, and there are all too many of such), some of you devoted to vanity, some to drunkenness, some careless of household affairs, some contumacious, proud, hard-mouthed and unmanageable: do you think God will be inferior to you? Will the Lord be compelled to abrogate the sacred law of marriage for your sake? Why do you marvel that you bear, by the just judgment of God, the punishments due to your perjuries, since on the slightest occasion you cast off the reverence and obedience you promised your husbands before God, his angels, and the Church? But if God threatens so grave a punishment against him who offends one of the least (Matt. 18:6), what will become of so many households so badly governed, which do not cease to offend the whole city? Would that the Lord our God, God of every order, who is to be consecrated to himself, would wish to heal such vices and to keep each one within his own calling,

units.la: S. j. quemque vocationem continere velit, vt ipsi primum omnes, deinde singuli iis quibus eos subiecit Dominus, sese morigeros praebeant.
units.tr: so that first all of you, and then each one, may show yourselves obedient to those whom the Lord has set over you.

units.la: Postremo, Iesus Christus indicat Pilato, si peccauerat nimiam sibi potestatem arrogando, non leuius ab eo peccatum esse, hic se tam indignis modis tractando. Nam quum ait eos qui se illi tradiderant, maius peccatum habere, Pilatum noluit excusatum quasi vacantem culpa: sed Christus quum hac de re nollet disceptare, quod sciret horam suam aduenisse ita loquutus est, vt soli conscientię Pilati conclusionem colligendam relinqueret. Porro, duo quaedam intellectu digna ex hoc loco discenda sunt. Primum, non omnia sane peccata esse aequalia, vt fanatici quidam somniarunt. Abest tamen diabolicam illam Peccatorum in Venialia & Mortalia distinctionem admittamus vt in scholis aduersariorum male intelligitur: ita vt aquam suam lustralem, & ineptas, imo impias superstitiones substituant in locum sanguinis ipsius Agni, ad peccatorum illorum Venialium expiationem: contra testante Apostolo indistincte, stipendium peccati esse mortem, & quidem aeternam, quanquam in alia peccata asperiorem quam in alia futuram, vt docet ipse Christus Matth. 10. 15. Alterum est, maiore alterius cuiusuis peccato, non excusari minus alterius peccatum: ac proinde vehementer eos falli, & frustra excusationes captare, culpamue a se amoliri, quod dicant se ad male agendum fuisse provocatos. Itaque improbi subditi superiorum tyrannidem suae rebellioni praetexentes: iniuriam, iniuria propulsantes: famuli inobedientiae suae culpam in acerbitatem herorum, vxores in asperitatem maritorum: liberi in feucritatem parentum reiicientes non ideo tamen necapud suam ipsorum coram Deo conscientiam, nec apud fani iudicij homines excusantur.
units.tr: Lastly, Jesus Christ tells Pilate that if he had sinned by arrogating to himself too much power, his sin was no less grave in treating him in such unworthy ways. For when he says that those who delivered him up to Pilate have the greater sin, he did not wish to excuse Pilate as though he were free of blame; but Christ, since he was unwilling to dispute this matter, knowing that his hour had come, so spoke as to leave to Pilate's own conscience the drawing of the conclusion. Moreover, two things worthy of notice are to be learned from this passage. First, that not all sins are indeed equal, as certain fanatics have dreamed. Yet let us not admit that diabolical distinction of sins into venial and mortal, as it is badly understood in the schools of our opponents, so that they substitute their lustral water and foolish, indeed impious, superstitions in place of the blood of the Lamb himself for the expiation of those venial sins; the Apostle testifies without distinction that the wages of sin is death, and indeed eternal death, although it will be heavier for some sins than for others, as Christ himself teaches (Matt. 10:15). The second is that the greater sin of another does not excuse the lesser sin of anyone else; and therefore those who think they are deceived, and catch at vain excuses, or shift the blame from themselves, saying that they were provoked to do evil, are greatly mistaken. Thus wicked subjects, who pretend the tyranny of their superiors as a cover for their rebellion, repelling injury with injury; servants, who lay the blame for their disobedience on the harshness of their masters; wives, on the roughness of their husbands; children, on the severity of their parents: none of these is excused, either before their own conscience before God, or before men of sound judgment, because of this.

units.la: Quod singulos moneo & obtestor ne leui cogitatione praetereant, sibi Dei propositio, his praesertim calamitosis temporibus iudicio, quibus videmus hunc errorem plurimorum mentibus etiam qui reformatam Religionem profiteri sese iactitant, de honoris, vt vocant puncto, tam altas egisse radices, vt sibi dedecori ducant, sibique perpetuae ignominiae notam inultam fore credant, nisi acceptam iniuriam ipsimet vlciscantur: quod sane tam bene cum Euangelio quam igni cum aqua conuenit. Scio quidem, vel saltem suspicor fore vt mihi non credatur, nihilominus tamen verum id esse afferere non desistam, Dixit enim Deus, Mihi vindicta. Quisquis autem seipsum vlciscitur, iudicem, testemque & executorem, in sua ipsius causa agit praeter omne ius & aequum. Verum aducrsus malum istud remedium secundum Dei timorem fuerit Iustitia, quae rite & fortiter sine personarum acceptione in iniuriosos eiusmodi homines sola spe impunitatis talia perpetrantes vindicet. Denique, vt paucis absoluam, qui mihi non crediderit, tandem coram Domino recténe an se-cus fecerit est experturus.
units.tr: I urge and earnestly beg each of you not to pass over lightly what God has set before us, especially in these calamitous times. We see this error so deeply rooted in the minds of many, even of those who boast that they profess the reformed religion, concerning what they call the point of honour: they think it a disgrace and an everlasting stain on their name to leave an injury unavenged unless they avenge it themselves. Truly this agrees with the Gospel no better than fire agrees with water. I know, or at least suspect, that I will not be believed, yet I will not stop affirming that this is true. For God said, "Vengeance is mine." Whoever avenges himself acts as judge, witness and executioner in his own cause, contrary to all law and fairness. Against this evil the remedy, in the fear of God, is justice, which acts promptly and bravely, without respect of persons, to punish such men who commit these deeds relying only on the hope of impunity. In short, whoever does not believe me will at last find out before the Lord whether he has acted rightly or otherwise.

units.la: Cæterùm D. Iohannes fusè commemorans hunc postremum actum, ab aliis Euangelistis fere prætermissum, ostendit quemadmodum Dei prouidentia,huic offendiculo ex ignomi-nia Iesu Christi superioribus longè maiori sc-quuturo prospicere volens, remedium adhi-buerit per eundem Pilatum, qui studiosius quàm antea operam dedit, vt Iesum Christum tanquam innocentem liberaret: quod facere non poterat quin semet ipse damnaret quod eum tam duriter excepisset. Præterea testimo-nium istud Pilati ad eius iustificationem quem moxe est condemnaturus valde confirmatur i-pso aduersariorum contrario conatu: qui ma-gis ac magis rabiem suam expromunt, ne mi-nimam quidem scdati animi, qualis ad iustitiæ tribunal afferendus, præsertim quū de hominis vita agitur, specie præsc feretes. Nec enim lo-quuntur, sed rabidorum instar canum, vlulat, vt loquitur Propheta Ps. 22. qui instar cómen-tarij in hanc historiam adhiberi potest. Quò verò manifestius adhuc desperatam suam im-probitatem patefaciant, quum probationes proferre, aut saltem simulare ipsos oporteret, ipsimet ludici dictant & præscribunt suppli-cij genus, idque apud ipsos Iudæos antea vsu non receptum, qui ex ligno quidem nocentes suspendebant, sed nequaquam cruci affigebat. Nec enim censebantur in Israëlitis Gabaoni-tæ, qui septem Saulis filios tali supplicio asse-cerunt,
units.tr: Moreover, John, relating in detail this last act, which the other Evangelists nearly passed over, shows how God's providence, wishing to provide against the stumbling block of the shame of Jesus Christ, which was to follow far greater than before, supplied a remedy through that same Pilate. Pilate applied himself more eagerly than before to free Jesus Christ as innocent, though he could not do this without condemning himself for having treated him so harshly. Besides, Pilate's testimony to the justification of the man whom he was soon to condemn is strongly confirmed by the very contrary effort of his adversaries, who more and more reveal their rage, showing not even the slightest semblance of a calm mind, such as ought to be brought before the tribunal of justice, especially when a man's life is at stake. For they do not speak, but howl like mad dogs, as the Prophet says in Psalm 22, which can be used as a commentary on this history. In order to reveal their hopeless wickedness even more plainly, when they ought to have produced proofs, or at least pretended to, they themselves dictate and prescribe to the judge the kind of punishment, one not previously in use among the Jews, who hanged guilty men from a tree but never fixed them to a cross. Indeed the Gibeonites, who put seven sons of Saul to such a death among the Israelites, were not thought to have done so, but among the remnants of the Amorites, as the history clearly relates, 2 Sam. 21. Furthermore, by the law of God a blasphemer was ordered to be stoned, not crucified.

units.la: Iesum Christum idem os iterum iustificat, à quo de-inde condemnatum etiā inimicorū eius ad-uersus eū agendi ratio. cerunt, sed in Amorrhæorum reliquiis, vt dif-ferte narrat historia, 2. Sam. 21. 2. Quinimo Le-ge Dei blasphemus non crucifigi sed lapidari iubebatur. Nec sane immerito Sp. S. toties totque modis testificari nobis voluit nostri Ser-uatoris innocentiam. Nam ei siqua vel mini-ma inhæsisset macula, tantum abest vt nostep Seruator futurus fuerit, vt ipse contra Redem-ptore indiguerit.
units.tr: Jesus Christ is again justified by the same mouth, from which afterwards the manner of his enemies' treatment of him condemned him. Nor, certainly, without good reason did the Holy Spirit wish to bear witness to us so often and in so many ways to the innocence of our Saviour. For if even the least stain had clung to him, so far from being our Saviour, he would himself have needed a Redeemer.

units.la: Nihilominus tamen, vt nemo est tam scele-ratus qui non fucare suam improbitatem co-netur, Iudæi quum animadverterent non mo-ueri Pilatum læsæ diuinæ Maiestatis crimina-tione vt ipsis obsequeretur, alia via sunt ipsum aggressi, Iesum Christum læsæ Maiestatis Im-perialis accusantes, sed miranda tamen & in-audita prorsus ratione, nempe hanc accusa-tionem vt indubitatam & probatam ingeren-tes, additis etiam minis, fore vt ipsum met Iu-dicem accusarent & convincerent apud Cæ-sarem, si pergeret difficultates nectere.
units.tr: Nevertheless, as no one is so wicked that he does not try to disguise his wickedness, the Jews, when they saw that Pilate was not moved by the charge of offence against the divine majesty to comply with them, attacked him by another way, accusing Jesus Christ of treason against the imperial majesty. They did this in a manner truly wonderful and unheard of: they thrust this accusation upon him as undoubted and proven, adding threats that, if he persisted in raising difficulties, they would themselves accuse and convict the judge himself before Caesar.

units.la: Hic autem Pilatus, præterquàm quod accu-sationis falsitas perse clara erat, & nulla cri-minatio absque probatione admitti debet, ta-tis intelligere potuit ex Iesu Christi verbis de auctoritate Magistratibus supernè data, pro-cul eum ab hoc crimine abfuisse: & quod in-tus conscientia dictabat, securum eum aduer-sus istiusmodi minas facere potuit. Verùme-nimucrò, quòd malè administratæ prouinciæ (vt testatur Iosephus) apud se conuincetur, verisimile est cum inde metum contraxisse, que iustissima prauæ conscientiæ merces est.
units.tr: Now Pilate, apart from the fact that the falsity of the accusation was plain, and that no charge ought to be admitted without proof, could understand from the words of Jesus Christ about the authority given by God from above to magistrates that Jesus was far from this crime. And what his conscience told him inwardly enabled him to face such threats without fear. But indeed, since, as Josephus testifies, he was convicted before them of having governed his province badly, it is likely that he then conceived fear, which is the most just reward of a guilty conscience.

units.la: Vtcunque sit quoniam Deus oculis corporeis non cernitur, & minarū eius sonū tantum aures carneæ percipiūt, quū sint homines visibiles, & eorū minæ sensibiles imbecillitati naturæ nostræ: propterea vsuuenit (nisi speciali virtute nostros animos Deus fulciat,) vt vel mi nimæ alicuius rerū mundanarū iacturæ metus facile Dei iudiciorū apprehensione ex nostris metibus excutiat, cuius rei, quàm multa, proh dolor! & nimis multi quotidie in oculos excm pla incurrūt? Sacto igitur Dei Spiritu regi nos oportet, vt cū Dauide merito dicamus, Ps.27.2. Dominus robur vitæ meæ, à quo expauescere? Dominus lux mea & salus mea, à quo timere? Hæc sanè gratia semper fideles Dei seruos aduersus Satanæ mūdiqúe furores sustinuit, Heb. 11.33. quā à Domino dies noctésque ardentissimis precibus efflagitare debemus, tam duris præsertim rebus, quibuscū vnà cū tot miseris Dei filiis fratribus nostris hodie colluctamur.
units.tr: However that may be, since God is not seen with bodily eyes, and ears of flesh perceive only the sound of his threats, while men are visible, and their threats are perceptible to the weakness of our nature, it therefore happens (unless God supports our souls with a special power) that the fear of the slightest loss of worldly things easily drives out of our minds the apprehension of God's judgments. Of this, how many examples, alas, and how very many, meet our eyes every day! It is therefore necessary that we be ruled by the Spirit of God, so that we may rightly say with David: "The Lord is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" (Ps. 27:1). "The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?" This grace has always upheld the faithful servants of God against the furies of Satan and the world, Heb. 11:33. We ought to beg for it from the Lord day and night with the most ardent prayers, especially in such hard circumstances, in which today we struggle together with so many wretched children of God, our brothers.

units.la: Historia deinceps narrat Pilatum quum suos hactenus irritos conatus videret, populi istius furori cedere apud se costiruisse, ac dimisso Barabba, pro tribunali aduersus Christū sententiā tulisse. Premente tamen ipsum conscientia ante illis postremū exprobrat, turpe illis & ignominiosum fore Regé ipsorū crucifigi. Etsi autē ex indignatione & ira profecta Pilati vox est, minimè tamen ibi subsistendum. Singularis enim in istis elucet diuina Prouidentia ex imo pectore perditorum istorum hanc vocem educens, cens, qua, solum Cæsarë & alium nullum Regem se agnoscere professi sunt. Qua voce arrepta Deus iam tum extemplo recisos eos & abiectos in miseram illam & deplorandam conditionem quâ adhuc hodie patiuntur dedit. Itaque priusquâ Iesus Christus, instatibus iniquissimè Iudæis à Pilato dânaretur, ipsi scipsos ore proprio condemnantes ei scpœnæ tũ spirituali tũ corporeæ addixerût, qua Creator nullâ gratiore in ingratâ creaturâ statuere posset. En igitur admirandũ rerum, eos à quibus iam iam erat condemnandus, & morte afficiendus, quatenus, homo, quòd nimirũ sic factum voluit, ipsemet iudicans, immo sententiâ aduersus eos latam quatenus vnâ cum Patre Deus exequés. Quid si Dominus noster in illa sua exinanitione tam horrendam sententiam aduersus furentes suos inimicos tulit & simul est exequutus, quid iam ad Patris dextram sedentem factypum putaris, accepta in cælo & in terra omni potestate? Næ satis illud ab ascensione sua in cœlis ad hunc vsque diem ostendit, & hinc ad vltima vsque secula ostensurus est, vltimo præsertim illo die, quo ij qui ipsum per suorum latera confoderint cum in gloria sua maximo suo dispendio conspecturi sunt. En igitur horrendâ Iudæorum responsione, quam non immerito Petrus iisdem tam expressè non semel exprobrat. Act. 2. 36. & 3. 14. & 4. 11. quæ nimirũ iustam elegentis ritus reiectionem comprobauit: & nihilominus tantò admirabiliorem post modò reddidit Dominj misericordiam
units.tr: The history then relates that Pilate, seeing his attempts so far in vain, resolved to yield before the fury of that people. Having released Barabbas, he pronounced sentence against Christ from the judgment seat. Yet, troubled in conscience, he reproached them once more: it would be shameful and disgraceful for them that their King should be crucified. Although this word came from Pilate's indignation and anger, we must not stop there. For in these words the singular providence of God shines forth, drawing this word from the deepest hearts of these wretched men, in which they professed that they acknowledged only Caesar and no other king. Seizing upon this word, God at once gave them, cut off and cast away, into that miserable and deplorable condition in which they still suffer today. Thus, before Jesus Christ was condemned by Pilate at the most unjust insistence of the Jews, they, condemning themselves by their own mouth, consigned him to a punishment both spiritual and bodily, such as the Creator could not inflict on an ungrateful creature with any greater favour. Behold then the wonder: he by whom they were about to be condemned and put to death, man as he is, judging by what he himself willed, and indeed pronouncing sentence against them, is at the same time carried out by God together with the Father. What if our Lord, in that his self-emptying, pronounced and at the same time executed so terrible a sentence against his raging enemies? What, then, must we think of him now sitting at the right hand of the Father, having received all power in heaven and on earth? Surely his ascension into heaven has shown this down to this day, and will show it to the last ages, especially on that last day, when those who pierced his sides will see him in his glory to their greatest loss. Behold, then, the dreadful answer of the Jews, which Peter, not without reason, rebukes them for many times in such plain words: Acts 2:36, 3:14, 4:11. This answer indeed proved the just rejection of the elect people, and yet afterwards made the mercy of the Lord all the more wonderful.

units.la: {a} nis ipsorũ elicit, vnde magis commeda-tur Dei clementia quod exce-perit ea quos ipsi vi-sum est. immensam erga eos quibus Spiritum resipiscentiæ & cordis compunctionem per suorum Apostolorum prædicationem largitus est: pro quibus etiam in ipsa Cruce precatus erat. Luc. 23. 34.
units.tr: Whence God's clemency is the more commended, that he received those whom they themselves had cast off: he bestowed his immense mercy on those to whom, through the preaching of his Apostles, he granted the Spirit of repentance and a contrite heart, and for whom he even prayed on the Cross itself, Luke 23:34.

units.la: Præterea vero non leuiter istud notatu dignissimum prætereundum est, istos perditos non solum malitia & crudelitate in Christum impulsos, sed etiam contra mentem & sententiam suam illa protulisse, quum nihil minus quàm voluntariam Imperatori Romano exhibendam obedientiam meditarentur, illius contra quam Christo falsò imponunt rebellionis rei, ut ex historiis perspicuum est, & ipse tandem exitus ostendit, ab ipsorum rebellione profecto urbis ipsius, atque adeo gentis totius in hunc usque diem excidio. En vero peruersi nostri ingenij fructus in iis præsertim qui conscientiæ resistere assuescunt, quale in improbis istis horrendum seculis omnibus extat exemplum. Quum enim ex seipsis hypocriseos & avaritiæ pleni essent, non modo monenti Domino Iesu Christo non auscultarunt, sed etiam inde illud tam perditè atrox in eum concepe-runt odium, quo tandem ita occæcati fuerunt, (sua tamen hypocrisi quasi extremo asylo seruata) ut à Christo vindictam expetentes, tanquam ab hoste suo capitalissimo, pro gratia quam ab eo recipere ipsos oportuerat, sponte suis pedibus fœderis fundamentum proculcarint, quo à cæteris populis discernebantur: licet ipsorum oculis obuersante Pilati exemplo, plo,
units.tr: Moreover, it must not be passed over lightly that these wretches were driven against Christ not only by malice and cruelty, but also spoke these words against their own intention and judgment. They were far from planning voluntary obedience to the Roman emperor, and they were falsely charged with rebellion against him, as the histories make clear. The outcome itself shows this, since the rebellion of these same men brought about the destruction of that city, and of the whole nation, down to the present day. Here is the bitter fruit of our perverse nature, especially in those who are accustomed to resist conscience, and in these wicked men there stands before all ages a horrible example. For though they were full of their own hypocrisy and greed, they not only did not heed the Lord Jesus Christ when he warned them, but from this they conceived such a utterly wicked and savage hatred against him that at last they were blinded. Keeping their hypocrisy as a last refuge, they sought vengeance from Christ as from their chief enemy, and in return for the grace they ought to have received from him, they of their own accord trampled underfoot the foundation of the covenant by which they were set apart from other peoples, even though the example of Pilate was before their eyes.

units.la: Iudæi præter mentem dixerunt, quod Deus aduersum eos iustissime ratum fecit. plo, miseri Ethnici, eos etiam, si aures ad audiendum habuissent, sui officij admonentis. Quàm igitur horrendum est obfirmato animo Deo resistere! quàm metuenda excæcatio & obduratio quibus ipsi nostræ perniciei insanabilis efficimur instrumenta!
units.tr: The Jews said, beyond their own intention, what God most justly confirmed against them. Wretched Gentiles too, if they had had ears to hear, would have been admonished by their duty. How dreadful it is to resist God with a hardened mind! How fearful is the blindness and hardening by which we ourselves become instruments of our own incurable ruin!

units.la: Verùm altera ipsorum ad Pilatum respon-sio,(vt Matth.27.5.commemoratur) spatio interposito quo penitarent id quod iam erant vociferati,& ceremonia ipsa Pilati suas manus lauantis admonitis ipsis, quum nimirum vniuersus populus conclamauit, Sanguis eius super nos & super filios nostros, veluti sigillum fuit & obsignatio totius ipsorum improbitatis,& horrendi quod deinceps experti sunt iudicij. Dixerunt igitur sibi nullum esse Regem præter Cæsarem. Cæsarem igitur in eius veluti sedem eucxerunt cui renuntiabant: & ipse Dominus verba ipsorum arripiens Cæsari illi quem expetebant ipsos permisit, vt suo damno permutationem illam maximo sibi fuisse detrimento senserint. Immo non ita multo post experti sint eum etsi repudiatum, esse tamen etiam inuitis ipsis & repugnantibus Regem, sed ferreum illud sceptrum gestante, de quo fit mentio Psal.2.6. & 9. cuius iusti furoris etiam esset administer quem sibi Cæsarem, delegerant. Nam reste ipsa historia verissima, etiam à Iudæo prolixè conscripta, minimeque su specta, vnica vrbis Hierosolymorum obsidione, responsio illa vndecies centum millia hominum peremit, præter captiuorum nonaginta millia,& extremum totius gentis excidium, vt ab eo tempore nunquam in populi corpus coaluerit. Præterea quòd non tantùm dixissent, Sanguis eius super nos, sed etiam addidissent, & super liberos nostros, hinc factum est vt in eos iræ Dei flamma tot ab hinc seculis adhuc perduret.
