units.tr: Yet their other answer to Pilate (as is recorded in Matthew 27:25), given after an interval in which they might have repented of what they had already shouted, and when Pilate's ceremony of washing his hands was a warning to them, when the whole people cried out, "His blood be on us and on our children," was like a seal and attestation of their whole wickedness, and of the dreadful judgment they afterwards underwent. They said therefore that they had no king but Caesar. So they lifted Caesar to the place of him whom they rejected, and the Lord himself, taking up their words, allowed them the Caesar they wanted, so that they found that exchange to their great loss. Indeed, not long after, they experienced that he, though rejected, was nonetheless king over them even against their will and resistance, bearing that iron sceptre of which Psalm 2:6 and 9 speaks, and the very Caesar they had chosen became the agent of his just wrath. For the history, most true and written at length even by a Jew, and least suspect, reports that that answer destroyed eleven hundred thousand people in the siege of Jerusalem alone, besides ninety thousand captives, and the final destruction of the whole nation, so that from that time it has never grown together again into a body of people. Moreover, because they had said not only "His blood be on us," but had added "and on our children," it has come about that the flame of God's anger has lasted against them for so many centuries.

units.la: Porrò nostrum est de istis serio cogitare.Nā si Deus naturalibus ramis non pepercit, quid fiet tantùm infitiiis, vt loquitur Apostolus Rom.11.21. quorum eadem fuerit aut maior etiam infidelitas atque rebellio? Maiorem aio, nec sine causa. Lux enim, quæ per Apostolorum prædicationem,ab exciso infelici isto populo nobis illuxit, longè maior fuit superioris ætatis Lucc,ex ipsius etiam Christi testimonio, licet in propria persona ipsis apparuerit. Matth.13.13. & Iohan.14. verf.12. Nec vnquam etiam veteris populi & reiecti tot tantæque fuerunt contumaciæ quot quantæque sunt nostræ: nec Domini erga illos maior ac diuturnior patientia fuit ea quam tot ab hinc seculis erga nos continuat.
units.tr: Further, it is our duty to think seriously about these things. For if God did not spare the natural branches, what will happen to the grafted ones, as the Apostle says (Romans 11:21), whose unbelief and rebellion are the same or even greater? Greater, I say, and not without cause. For the light that shone upon us from that wretched, cut-off people through the preaching of the Apostles was far greater than the light of the former age, by Christ's own testimony, although he appeared to them in his own person (Matthew 13:13; John 14:12). Nor were the rebellions of the old, rejected people ever so many and so great as ours are, nor has the Lord's patience toward them been greater or longer than that which he has continued toward us for so many centuries.

units.la: Iudæi verò, quemadmodum historia testatur, semel Iesum Christum crucifixerunt. At quum Iesus Christus sibi factū imputet, quod vni ex minimis suorum factum est, siue bene, Matth.25 40.siue male. 1.Sam.8 7. & Act.9.4. quoties ab hinc solis annis sexaginta apud egregios illos Catholicos Romanos Christianos, imò ab iisdem est crucifixus? quot apud eos Iudæ,quot Caiaphæ? quot denique generis ris omnis tortores apud ipsos reperti sunt & adhuc hodie reperiuntur?
units.tr: The Jews, as history testifies, crucified Jesus Christ once. But since Jesus Christ counts as done to himself whatever is done to the least of his own, whether well (Matthew 25:40) or ill (1 Samuel 8:7; Acts 9:4), how often in the last sixty years has he been crucified by those distinguished Roman Catholic Christians, indeed by the very same men? How many Judases and Caiaphases are among them? Finally, how many torturers of every kind have been and still are found among them today?

units.la: Adhæc, salte aliqua fuit exterior in hoc Iudæorum facto iudicij forma, & pro tribunali iuridica lata sententia, cuius etiam executio iustitiæ speciem præ se tulit. At ecce nostri seculi iuris formulam, Occidite, cædite, submergite,cófodite,præcipites date,raptate, quicquid vesanus furor suaserit,agite:quibus egregiis facinoribus veniam & paradisum merebitis,testibus ipsis Romæ palàm ea de re conspicuis picturis, diplomatibus concessis,Regum,Reginarum ac Principum interfectoribus:ac denique indigetationibus ipsorum.
units.tr: Besides, in the deed of the Jews there was at least some outward form of judgment, and a sentence was pronounced from a tribunal, and its execution bore some appearance of justice. But behold the legal formula of our age: "Kill, slay, drown, stab, throw down headlong, seize, do whatever mad fury suggests." By these splendid crimes you will earn pardon and paradise, as the pictures publicly displayed in Rome on this very matter bear witness, and as the grants of indulgences show, to the slayers of kings, queens and princes, and finally to their invokers.

units.la: Iudæi quantumlibet rabiosæ feræ, vt Pf.22. describitur,& in hac historia fumus adhuc có spectaturi Iesum Christû in cruce mortuû cernè tesvlterius progressi nó sunt:nostri vero perse-cutores quodnam obsecro crudelitatis genus intactum reliquerunt,quo nó sævierint,& sint adhuc hodie in miserorum Dei filiorum cadaucra multis plagis confolla sævire parati?
units.tr: The Jews, however savage beasts as Psalm 22 describes them, and though they were still going to watch Jesus Christ dead on the cross and to look on the smoke of this history, did not go any further. Our persecutors, however, what kind of cruelty, I beg you, have they left untried, in which they have not raged, and which they are still ready to inflict today on the corpses of the wretched sons of God, heaping on them many blows?

units.la: Nec istud eis satis est. Qualiter enim ipsum adhuc Iesum Christû tractât,quantû in eis est, & prout opinantur?Hinc detestabiles illi blasphemi homines,à quibus discerpitur,dilaniatur, abnegatur, mille maledictis ore impuro impetitur,vt mirû sit terrâ absorbendis hominib.nó dehiscere. Quis vero Magistratus inter eos cómouetur?Boni vero illi Patres spirituales ipsimet vt plurimû magnopere rei,nõne cófes-sione auriculari apud presbyterû, nó melioré ipsis edita, vel pretio numerato ex sua æstimatione scelera illa omnia solent expiare?
units.tr: Nor is this enough for them. In what way do they still treat Jesus Christ himself, so far as lies in their power, and as they suppose? Hence those detestable blasphemers, by whom he is torn apart, mangled, denied, and assailed with a thousand curses from impure mouths, so that it is a wonder the earth does not open and swallow the men. Yet what magistrate among them is moved? And those good spiritual fathers themselves, who are for the most part deeply guilty, do they not usually expiate all those crimes by ear confession to a priest, which is no better than their own, or by money paid down according to their own valuation?

units.la: Inde vero Iesus Christus solio suo ne sit amplius Ecclesiæ suæ Monarcha spiritualis deiicitur, ab eo quem palàm conscientiis Lege ferre non pudet: vt & à munere suo Prophetico & declaratoris paternæ voluntatis, ab eodem profligato & perdito latrone spoliatur, sibi ius & potestatem amputàdi, immutandi, adiiciendi verbo Diuino ex sui arbitrij voluntate attribuente. Quòd ad Sacerdotium ipsius æternum attinet, primùm tot ei comites addūt quot fingere possunt: Intercessionem vero si (pectes, quisquc sua merita sanguini eius admiscet. Iudæi non vlterius morte in eum sæuierunt, at boni nostri Catholici, si creditur eorū doctrinæ, viuum illum detibus dilaniant, & sanguinem hauriunt exsorbéntque, realiter, actualiter & essentialiter: vt à Canibalibus Americanis hoc vno differant quod hi carnem eius invisibiliter & devotione, illi vero Canibalæ, visibiliter & bruta crudelitate comedunt.
units.tr: Thence Jesus Christ is cast from his throne, so that he may no longer be the spiritual Monarch of his Church, by one whom they are not ashamed to set up openly as law over consciences. He is stripped of his prophetic office and of the office of declaring the Father's will, by this same abandoned and lost robber, who claims for himself the right and power to cut away, change and add to the Divine Word by the will of his own judgment. As for his eternal priesthood, first they add as many companions to him as they can invent. If you look at his intercession, anyone mixes his own merits with his blood. The Jews did not rage against him further than death, but our good Catholics, if their doctrine is to be believed, tear the living one with their teeth, and drink and swallow his blood, really, actually and essentially. In this they differ from the American cannibals only in this: that the latter eat his flesh invisibly and in devotion, while these, the cannibals, eat it visibly and with brutal cruelty.

units.la: Nos vero qui Christianorum reformatorum nomine gloriamur, & per nos solos ltat quominus reipsa tales simus, quid nisi hypocritæ maxima ex parte sumus, Iesum Christum ore quidem approbantes, sed reipsa Mammonæ alij, abdomini alij, aliis alij cupiditatibus inseruientes? Annon præterea non pauci sunt inter nos, qui fœtido & abominando ore suo contaminant eius nomen & blasphemas in cum vocesiactant, vt fit apud prophanissimos & & imperitiffimos homines? annon passim e-briofi,scortatores,adulteri,fœneratores,fures, fallaces homines, coitiones & monopolia facientes,verbi quod apud nos personat cõtemptores conspiciuntur? tum viros tum mulieres eorum quæ singulis diebus proponuntur magis ignaros quàm sint asini ad molam? Denique obsecro auaritia ne an charitas apud nos regnat? Dei dilectio an verò mundi? an vix centesimus quisque Papa ciurato Iesum Christum induit? Ecquos verò pœna manet grauior quàm quos Deus maioribus beneficiis ac donis cumulauit?
units.tr: As for us, who glory in the name of reformed Christians, and who are kept from being such in reality only by our own name, are we not for the most part hypocrites, confessing Jesus Christ with our lips, but in fact serving one man's Mammon, another's belly, and others other lusts? Are there not, moreover, not a few among us who defile his name with their foul and abominable mouths, and hurl blasphemies against him, as happens among the most profane and ignorant men? Are not drunkards, fornicators, adulterers, usurers, thieves, deceitful men, those who form cartels and monopolies, in a word those who deserve the name of contemners, seen everywhere among us? Are not men and women of this sort, who are set before us every day, more ignorant than asses at the mill? Finally, I beg you, does greed or charity reign among us? The love of God, or rather of the world? Is there scarcely one in a hundred who puts on Jesus Christ, though he is sick? And what punishment remains heavier than for those whom God has loaded with greater benefits and gifts?

units.la: Ecquis verò tandem est istarum confusionum futurus finis. Næ si iam tum Apostolorum temporibus erat metuenda illa horrenda comminatio de qua nos Gentes admonet Apostolus, Rom.ii.v.25. quum ait fore vt quemadmodum insiti sumus in locum Iudæorum, qui solum Regem Cæsarem habere voluerunt, sic quum Gentium plenitudo introierit,illi vicissim restituantur, annon hodie post tot elapsa iam ex illa prædictione secula non contremiscemus, quum hodie nisi prorsus cæci sumus executionem eius non modò inchoatã, sed etiam non mediocriter promotam intueamur? non solùm tot auulsas arbores aut excisas, verùm etiam totas sylvas integras non exiguo numero deiectas, combustas & prorsus consumptas?non modò septem Ecclesiarum Asiæ candelabra,quibus erat Iohan. comminatus Apoc.i.20. sed etiam totius Asiæ & Aphricæ, maiorisque partis Europæ sic extincta lumina,vt vix vllum vel obscurissimum appareat vestigium nominis illius Ecclesiæ Græcanicæ,non minus prope corruptæ ac deformatæ quàm sit hodie Romanensis? Immanem aprum illum Mahumetum tot præclaras & eximias vineas depastum atque populatum?Psal.80.13.& 14.De Occidente verò,nonne videmus mysterium iniquitatis Apostolorum temporibus inchoatum,iam ad fastigium perductum? defectionem & excidium Imperij Romani aduentantemhominem peccati & perditionis filium sedentem & adoratum tanquam Deum in templo Dei? 2.Thessal.2.verf. 7. Imaginem bestiæ, quæ est Ecclesia Apostatica Romana, Imperij Romani effigies loquentem, cum Regibus & Principibus auscultantibus? meretricem vrbi sepcicolli insidentem, vt pluribus docet Iohan.in Apocaly. fulgur verbi diuini iterum nobis exortum, sicut Iesus Christus pollicitus erat. Matt.24.27. Solem istius Lucis iam ad occasum etiam in medio nostri vergentem? Denique quid amplius restat, nisi ipse secundi aduentus Domini dies? dies vltimi furoris Domini aduersus sceleratos, & maximè aduersus maximorum ipsius beneficiorum contemptores? Eheu igitur, fratres! agite vigilemus & præcemur, ne dormientes intercipiamur. Luc.12. verf. 37. & præparemur potius in occursum iponsi, prudentum virginum exemplo, vna cum lampadibus nostris accensis, Matth. 25. 7. Tempus enim est, aut nunquam erit.
units.tr: Who, then, will be the end of these confusions? Indeed, if already in the times of the Apostles that dreadful threat was to be feared, of which the Apostle warns us Gentiles in Rom. 11:25, when he says that, just as we have been grafted into the place of the Jews, who wanted only Caesar as king, so when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, they in turn will be restored, shall we not today, after so many centuries have passed since that prediction, tremble? Today, unless we are utterly blind, we see its execution not only begun but also considerably advanced: not only so many trees uprooted or cut down, but whole forests, not a few, felled, burned and utterly consumed. Not only the seven candlesticks of the churches of Asia, against which John threatened (Rev. 1:20), but the lights of all Asia and Africa and the greater part of Europe so extinguished that scarcely any, even the faintest, trace of the name of that Greek Church appears, a church hardly less corrupted and deformed than the Roman one is today. That huge boar, Muhammad, has devoured and laid waste so many splendid and choice vineyards (Ps. 80:13-14). And in the West, do we not see the mystery of iniquity, begun in the times of the Apostles, now brought to its height? The defection and fall of the Roman Empire; the man of sin, the son of perdition, who sits and is worshipped as God in the temple of God (2 Thess. 2:7)? The image of the beast, which is the apostate Roman Church, speaking with the image of the Roman Empire, with kings and princes listening to it? The harlot sitting on the city of seven hills, as John teaches at length in the Apocalypse? The lightning of the divine Word has risen again among us, as Jesus Christ promised (Matt. 24:27). The sun of that Light is now sinking towards its setting even in our midst. Finally, what remains except the very day of the Lord's second coming, the day of the last wrath of the Lord against the wicked, and above all against those who despise his greatest benefits? Alas, then, brothers! Come, let us watch and pray, lest we be taken while sleeping (Luke 12:37), and let us rather prepare ourselves to meet the bridegroom, after the example of the wise virgins, with our lamps lit (Matt. 25:7). For it is time, or it will never be.

units.la: Ex hoc praeterea loco est obseruandum ma-ximum & immedicabile peccatum committi solitum linguae leuitate, manante à violentis & immoderatis perturbationibus quibus nimium facile cedituׄr. Est enim verisimillimum Iudaeos si Regis vocem expendissent, & quae invita generaliter proferebant, fuisse miraturos quinam illa sibi excidisset. Et tamen Deus (paucis exceptis quibus & otium & gratiam ad se redeundi & sua dicta retractandi fecit) conditionem accepit, quum enumerari non possint animae ex hoc infelici populo perditae & quotidie pereuntes propter hanc vocem temere sic abeis effutitam. Quapropter, fratres, Dominum precemur ut nostras cogitationes & linguam regat, & saltem memoria repetamus quod a quodam ex sapientibus huius mundi scite dictum est, voces alatas esse ad euolandum non ad reuolandum. Excusetur igitur licet quod per leuitatem aut iracundiam effutitur, Deus tamen si ex verbis iporum loquaces ciusmodi homines iudicet (ut olim istos iudicauit, & quemque iudicare poterit) nullus est excusationi futurus locus, frustra sperantibus tam facilem veniam, quam in loquendo temerarij sunt. Denique abiit cum Domino iocari velimus. Serio enim loquitur & percutit. Quid fiet igitur deieratoribus, & istis Diabolo in ore toties habentibus? Vtinam in hoc speculo seipsos diligenter contemplentur, quam illis à Domino gratiam supplex oro. Et quoniam res & locus ad id me inuitant, duo quædam recentiora & verissima exempla Dei iudiciorum in istiusmodi homines subiungam. Scio quendam in Gallia fuisse patrem familias cognitione veritatis donatum & eandem amplexatum, qui quum per iracundiam vnum ex filiis Diabolo deuouisset, repente à Diabolo filium correptum, quo deinde licet ardentibus & assiduis Ecclesiæ ad Deum precibus eiecto, tamen adolescentem illum vix sanitati redditum paulò post morte sublatum esse. Alterum exemplum in hac regione contigit non procul in quendam qui quum ad fraudem peieraffet, repente in apoplexiam incidit, ex qua nunquam postea loquutus, intra paucos dies interiit. Quæ vt quotidiana exempla non sint Dei iudiciorum, illa tamen quando & in quos ipsi libet exercet: quorum nihilominus vita detestanda & sæpe miserabilis istiusmodi hominum exitus exempla sat multa nobis suppeditant.
units.tr: Furthermore, from this passage we must observe that the greatest and incurable sin is commonly committed through lightness of tongue, flowing from violent and immoderate disturbances to which we yield all too easily. For it is most likely that the Jews, had they weighed the king's words, and those things which they uttered in general without intending them, would have been amazed at who had let them slip. And yet God (except for a few whom he granted both leisure and grace to return to themselves and to retract their words) has taken the condition of that people, since the souls lost from this unhappy nation, and perishing every day, on account of this word thoughtlessly spewed out, cannot be counted. Therefore, brothers, let us pray the Lord to govern our thoughts and our tongue, and at least let us recall what was wisely said by one of the wise men of this world, that winged words are for flying away, not for flying back. Let whatever is uttered through lightness or anger be pardoned, if you like; yet if God judges such talkative men by their own words (as he once judged those men, and as he will be able to judge anyone), there will be no place for excuse, and vainly will they hope for such easy pardon, since they are so rash in speaking. Finally, let us never wish to joke with the Lord. For he speaks in earnest and strikes. What, then, will happen to swearers, and to those who have the Devil so often in their mouths? Would that they would diligently contemplate themselves in this mirror; this I humbly beg the Lord to grant them. And since the matter and the place invite me to it, I shall add two rather recent and most true examples of God's judgments upon such men. I know of a certain father of a family in Gaul, who had been given the knowledge of the truth and had embraced it, who, when in anger he devoted one of his sons to the Devil, was suddenly seized by the Devil, and the son, although the Church, with burning and constant prayers to God, drove him out, was scarcely restored to health, and a little later was taken away by death. The other example occurred in this region, not far from here, in a certain man who, having committed perjury for the sake of fraud, suddenly fell into an apoplexy, from which he never spoke again, and died within a few days. Although these are not everyday examples of God's judgments, yet he exercises them when and upon whom he pleases; nevertheless, the detestable life and often wretched end of such men supply us with quite many examples.

units.la: Vt ad propositam historiam reuertamur, ita quidem sese infelices Iudæi gesserunt. Iam vero vt se Pilatus gesserit, inspiciamus, quem merito miretur aliquis maiore ad minas Cæsareæ Maiestatis quàm ad Dei Filij nomé metu perculsum fuisse, non audita quæ intus de Christi innocentia loquebatur eius conscientia. Verùm hoc vsuuenit hominibus, vt magis homines quos intuentur, quàm Deum quem non vident metuant & reformident. Ad hæc non du-
units.tr: To return to the history proposed, the unhappy Jews conducted themselves in this way. Now let us look at how Pilate conducted himself, whom one may rightly wonder at, struck with fear more by threats to Caesar's majesty than by the name of the Son of God, although his conscience was speaking within him of the innocence of Christ. But it happens to men that they fear and dread more the men they see than God whom they do not see. Besides these things, not

units.la: Horrendum exemplum in Pilato eorum quæ homines plus quam Deum timentibus euenire solent. dubium est quin malè administratæ prouinciæ sibi malè conscius Pilatus, (quod Iudaica historia testatur & aliquid apud Lucam 13. 1. indicatur) inde metuendi causas, quibus abreptus est, habuerit, præter metum ne ingens aliqua seditio excitaretur. Quòd enim ad Iesu Christi causam attinet, sibi metuendi nullam occasionem habebat, etiamsi delatus apud Imperatorem esset, ob non sumptum de illo supplicium. Nam contrà victurum fuisse iudicio verisimile est: siquidem historiæ profanæ testantur, Tiberium tunc Imperatorem, quantumuis immanem tyrannum, cognito qualis fuisset Christus, adeò commotum fuisse, vt eum etiam in cæterorum suorum Deorum numerum referre tentarit, quam de re ad Senatum retulerit, & etiam vrserit, cui in Iudaicæ Religionis odium minimè tamen Senatus assensit, non minus ferente Domino se in Capitolio cum Romano illo Ioue, quàm passus olim fuerat in Philistæorum templo cum ipsorum numine Dagone collocari. 1. Sam 5 2. Quam verò mercedem inde Pilatus retulit? Nimirum, vt propterea quòd magis homuncionem & hunc populum quàm Deum metuisset, contrà quàm de se Dauid profitetur. 2. Sam. 24. 14. hic quidem populus, cui suæ conscientiæ dispendio gratificatus erat, non destiterit tamen cum iudicio ob alia facinora apud Imperatoris tribunal persequi: Imperator verò, de Christo quidem nihil cogitans, Dei tamen manus fuerit, qua in id ipsum quod metuerat, coniiceretur, condemnato eo propter malefi-cia & Viennam relegato, vbi miserè, sibi ipsi mortem conscivit, vt ferunt. Et talis quidem cos exitus manet, qui suae conscientiae detri-mento lucrum & commoda quaeuis conse-ctantur.
units.tr: A dreadful example in Pilate of what usually happens to those who fear men more than God. There is no doubt that Pilate, badly conscious of having governed his province badly (which Jewish history attests, and something of it is hinted at in Luke 13:1), had reasons for fear by which he was carried away, besides the fear that some great sedition might be stirred up. For as far as the cause of Jesus Christ is concerned, he had no occasion for fear, even if he had been denounced before the Emperor, since no punishment had been taken from him on account of it. For it is likely that he would have prevailed in judgment: indeed, profane histories testify that the Emperor Tiberius at that time, however savage a tyrant he was, when he learned what sort of man Christ was, was so moved that he even tried to count him among his other gods; he reported this matter to the Senate and also urged it, but the Senate by no means assented to this, out of hatred for the Jewish religion, the Lord no less bearing himself in the Capitol with that Roman Jupiter than he once suffered himself to be placed in the temple of the Philistines with their god Dagon (1 Sam. 5:2). But what reward did Pilate then obtain from this? Surely, that because he had feared a mere man and this people more than God, contrary to what David professes of himself (2 Sam. 24:14), this people, to whom he had gratified himself at the cost of his own conscience, nevertheless did not cease to pursue him before the Emperor's tribunal on account of other crimes. The Emperor, indeed, thinking nothing at all about Christ, was nevertheless the hand of God, by which he was cast into that very thing which he had feared, Pilate being condemned on account of misdeeds and banished to Vienne, where, wretchedly, as they report, he took his own life. And such is the end of those who pursue gain and advantages of any kind to the detriment of their conscience.

units.la: Caeterum protestatio & caeremonia qua v-sus est, ex peculiari quidem Dei prouidentia contigit, quo minus esset excusabilis huius populi peruersitas, praesertim ad Pharisaeos ar-guendos quibus sua lauacra tanto erant in pre-tio. Matth. 7. 3. verum quacunque de causa aut more Pilatus ita publicè manus lauerit, vana illa omnia & ridicula fuere. Non enim lauan-tur ideo manus vt illico polluantur: sed contrà lauacrum praesupponit pollutionem. Ac sanè apud prophanos authores legimus redeuntes olim ex bello milites, quantumuis iusto ac le-gitimo, tamen propter fusum humanum san-guinem (qua in re quàm fuerunt iis dissimiles qui sponte sedato animo in homines quoslibet sanguinem (?) antequam sacra diis suis facerent ab-lui solitos, quasi se antea polluissent. Quid fa-cit hic igitur Pilatus? nempe contrarium eius quod opinatur patefacit. Nam praeter iniusti-tiam qua iam Iesum Christum affecerat, hanc etiam insuper sibi foedâ maculam inurit, quòd innocentem quem poterat absoluere condem-net. Excipiet aliquis, Pilatum à quo propriè non manarit illa condemnatio, vt qui Chri-stum toties dimittere tentarit: & quidem non simpliciter sollicitatum, vt à serpente Eua: & ab
units.tr: Moreover, the protestation and ceremony which he used happened by a special providence of God, so that the perversity of this people might be less excusable, especially for refuting the Pharisees, to whom their washings were so precious (Matt. 7:3). But for whatever reason or custom Pilate so publicly washed his hands, all those things were vain and ridiculous. For hands are not washed so that they may immediately be polluted; rather, washing presupposes pollution. And indeed we read in profane authors that soldiers returning from war, however just and lawful, were nevertheless accustomed to wash themselves because of the human blood shed (in which matter how unlike they were to those who, of their own accord and with a calm mind, shed blood from any men whatever, before they performed sacred rites to their gods, as if they had previously been polluted!). What, then, does Pilate do here? Surely he reveals the opposite of what he supposes. For besides the injustice with which he had already treated Jesus Christ, he also stamps on himself this foul stain, that he condemns the innocent man whom he could have acquitted. Someone will object that Pilate, from whom that condemnation did not properly proceed, as one who had tried so often to dismiss Christ, and indeed not simply solicited, as Eve was by the serpent, and by

units.la: Protestatio & caeremonia qua Pilatus vsus est Christi innocentiam facit magis ac magis, & idaorum su-rorem, ac tandem etiam Pilatum sensum omnem amisisse. ab vxore Adamus: sed etiam vi metuque Iudaeorum impulsum esse dignum excusatione.
units.tr: The protest and ceremony that Pilate used make Christ's innocence ever more evident, along with the fury of the Jews, and show that Pilate at last had lost all sense of right. Adam, it is true, was led astray by his wife; but Pilate, it may be said, was driven by the force and fear of the Jews and so deserves some excuse.

units.la: Sed illa inanis est exceptio. Duplex enim est coactio. Vna quae consensum prorsus tollit, ac proinde excusanda: altera quae consensum trahit, & omni excusatione indigna. Exempli gratia, si quis palam omnem idololatriam damnans, vi tamen manifesta trahatur, hanc sane in partem peccasse dici non potest. Pariter, si cui in manus pugio immittatur, & vis reluctanti adferatur, vt brachium & manus eius adigantur cum pugione in alterius pectus, quis, obsecro, caedis cum ausit accusare? Quis etiam honestam puellam scorraram dicat, si vinctis pedibus ac manibus aut alia vi cui resistere nulla ratione potuerit violata sit? Verum si quis diu reluctatus metu flammarum ni adorauerit idolum perterritus, tandem cedit & illud adorat: si quis caedem patret, veritus ne ipsemet ni caedem inferat, interficiatur, si virgo metu mortis propositae, pudicitiā malit quàm viram profundere, minime sane coactio illa dicenda erit, consensui repugnans, sed coactionis species quae assensum voluntatis pertraxerit, cui nullus idcirco excusationis locus conceditur. Nihilominus tamen magis peccat qui sponte peccat & malo suo delectatur. Haec autem dico habita ratione tribunalis & iudicij Dei, quantumlibet se homines excusent, & iudices in causis ciuilibus eos subleuent qui metu adacti aliquid promiserint, qui possit aliquem alioqui constantem à sua constantia di-
units.tr: But that objection is empty. For there are two kinds of compulsion. One takes away consent altogether, and so deserves excuse; the other draws consent out of a person, and deserves no excuse at all. For example, if someone who openly condemns all idolatry is nonetheless dragged off by manifest violence, he cannot be said to have sinned in that respect. Likewise, if a dagger is put into a man's hand and force is applied to his unwilling arm and hand, so that they are driven with the dagger into another's breast, who, I ask, would dare to accuse him of murder? Or who would call an honest girl a whore if she was violated while her feet and hands were bound, or by some other force she could in no way resist? But if someone, after long resistance, terrified by the fear of flames, at last gives way and worships the idol, or if someone commits murder, fearing that he himself will be killed unless he kills, or if a virgin, faced with the threat of death, prefers to lose her chastity rather than her life, then that cannot rightly be called compulsion opposed to consent, but rather a form of compulsion that has drawn the assent of the will, and for which no room for excuse is therefore granted. Nevertheless, he who sins willingly and delights in his own wickedness sins more. I say this with regard to the tribunal and judgment of God, however much men may excuse themselves, and judges in civil cases may relieve those who, driven by fear, have promised something; for fear could move someone who was otherwise steadfast away from his steadfastness.

units.la: Insignis distinctio duplicis coactionis. mouere. Dominum igitur precemur vt vbique tum publicis tum priuatis in rebus, sacrosanctum verbum suum in nobis copiose velit habitare. Colos. 3.16. vt dilectionem quam Deo nostro debemus, eiusque erga fideles suos seruos benevolentiam & auxilium opponamus hominum comminationibus, omnium pollicitationibus & illecebris, quibus vel tantillum ab officio quod Deo & proximis debemus dimoveamur: & contra vt sanam & rectam conscientiam retinentes, cognitione Diuinae voluntatis bene instructam regulam vnicam omnium nostrarum cogitationum, dictorum factorumque sequamur.
units.tr: A remarkable distinction between the two kinds of compulsion. We should therefore pray to the Lord that, everywhere, in public and in private affairs, he will be pleased to let his most holy Word dwell abundantly in us (Col. 3.16), so that we may set against the threats of men, all their promises and enticements, by which we might be moved even slightly from the duty we owe to God and to our neighbours, the love we owe to our God and his goodwill and help toward his faithful servants; and, on the other hand, that, keeping a sound and upright conscience, well instructed by the knowledge of the divine will, we may follow the one rule of all our thoughts, words and deeds.

units.la: HOMILIA VICESIMASEPTIMA.
units.tr: HOMILY TWENTY-SEVENTH.

units.la: MATTH. 27.
units.tr: MATTHEW 27.

units.la: 26. Tunc dimisit eis Barabbam: Iesum autem quum flagellasset, tradidit vt crucifigeretur.
units.tr: 26. Then he released Barabbas to them, but when he had scourged Jesus, he delivered him up to be crucified.

units.la: 27. Tunc milites praesidis quum abduxissent Iesum in praetorium, congregerunt ad eum vniuersam cohortem.
units.tr: 27. Then the soldiers of the governor, when they had led Jesus away into the palace, gathered together the whole band before him.

units.la: 28. Et quum exuissent eum, circumposuerunt ei chlamydem coccinam.
units.tr: 28. And when they had stripped him, they put a scarlet robe about him.

units.la: 29. Et coronam e spinis contextam imposuerunt eius eius capiti, & arundinem in dextram eius: & genu ante eum summisso, illudebant ei, dicentes, Aue rex Iudæorum.
units.tr: 29. And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand; and kneeling down before him, they mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!

units.la: 30. Et quum insputissent in eum, ceperunt arundinem illam, & verberabant caput eius.
units.tr: 30. And when they had spat upon him, they took the reed and struck his head with it.

units.la: 31. Et postquam illusissent ei, exuerunt eum chlamyde, induerúntque eum vestimentis suis, & abduxerunt eum vt crucifigerent.
units.tr: 31. And after they had mocked him, they took off the robe, put his own garments on him, and led him away to crucify him.

units.la: 32. Exeuntes autem inuenerunt quendam Cyrenæum, nomine Simonem: hunc angariauerunt vt attolleret crucem eius.
units.tr: 32. As they went out, they found a certain Cyrenian named Simon; him they compelled to bear his cross.

units.la: MARC. 15.
units.tr: MARC. 15.

units.la: 15. Pilatus igitur volens turbæ satisfacere, dimisit eis Barabbam, & Iesum flagellatum tradidit vt crucifigeretur.
units.tr: 15. So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas to them, and handed Jesus over, having been scourged, to be crucified.

units.la: 16. Milites verò abduxerunt eum intra aulam, id est prætorium, & convocauerunt totā cohortē.
units.tr: 16. The soldiers then led him away inside the courtyard, that is, the praetorium, and called together the whole cohort.

units.la: 17. Et induerunt eum purpura, & circumposuerunt ei plexam coronam spineam.
units.tr: 17. They clothed him in purple and placed around him a crown woven of thorns.

units.la: 18. Et cœperunt eum salutare, (dicentes) Aue rex Iudæorum.
units.tr: 18. And they began to salute him, saying: Hail, King of the Jews.

units.la: 19. Et verberabant eius caput calamo, & inspuebát in eum, ac summissis genibus adorabát eum.
units.tr: 19. And they struck his head with a reed, spat upon him, and bowing their knees, worshipped him.

units.la: 20. Quum autem illusissent ei, exuerunt eum purpura, & induerunt eum vestimentis propriis (ipsius:) eduxerúntque vt crucifigerent eum.
units.tr: 20. When they had mocked him, they took off the purple and put his own garments back on him, and led him out that they might crucify him.

units.la: 21. Præterea angariarunt prætereuntem quēdam Simonem Cyrenæum (venientem rure, patrem Alexandri & Rufi) vt attolleret crucem eius.
units.tr: 21. Moreover, they compelled a certain Simon of Cyrene, who was passing by (coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus), to carry his cross.

units.la: LUC. 23.
units.tr: LUC. 23.

units.la: 24. Tum Pilatus secundum eos iudicauit vt fieret quod ipsi petebant.
units.tr: 24. Then Pilate gave judgment that what they asked should be done.

units.la: 25. Dimisit autem eis illum qui propter seditionem & caedem coniectus fuerat in carcerem, quem petierant: Iesum vero tradidit illi eorum libidini.
units.tr: 25. He released to them the man who had been thrown into prison for sedition and murder, the one they had asked for; but Jesus he handed over to their will.

units.la: 26. Quum igitur abducerent eum, prehenso Simone quodam Cyrenaeo qui veniebat rure, imposuerunt ei crucem ferendam post Iesum.
units.tr: 26. As they led him away, they seized a certain Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid the cross on him to carry after Jesus.

units.la: 27. Sequebatur autem eum magna multitudo populi & mulierum: quae & plangebant & lamentabantur eum.
units.tr: 27. A great crowd of the people followed him, and of women, who both beat their breasts and lamented him.

units.la: 28. Conversus autem ad eas Iesus dixit, Filiae Hierusalem, ne flete super me, verum super vos ipsis flete, & super liberis vestris:
units.tr: 28. But Jesus turned to them and said, "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.

units.la: 29. Nam ecce venient dies quibus dicent, Beatae steriles, & uteri qui non genuerunt, & ubera quae non lactaverunt.
units.tr: 29. For behold, the days will come when they will say, 'Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never gave suck.'

units.la: 30. Tum incipient dicere montibus, Cadite super nos, & collibus, Operite nos.
units.tr: 30. Then they will begin to say to the mountains, 'Fall on us,' and to the hills, 'Cover us.'

units.la: 31. Nam si in virente ligno ista faciunt, in arido quid fiet?
units.tr: 31. For if they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?"

units.la: IOH. 19.
units.tr: IOH. 19.

units.la: 13. Pilatus ergo quum audisset hunc sermonem, eduxit foras Iesum, consedit que in tribunali, in loco qui dicitur Lithostrotos, Hebraice autem Gabbatha.
units.tr: 13. When Pilate therefore heard this saying, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat, in the place called the Pavement, in Hebrew Gabbatha.

units.la: 14. Erat autem parasceue Paschae, hora vero quasi sexta: tum dicit Iudaeis, Ecce rex vester.
units.tr: 14. Now it was the Preparation of the Passover, and about the sixth hour. And he said to the Jews, "Behold your king!"

units.la: 15. Illi vero clamauerunt, Tolle, tolle, Crucifige eum. Dicit eis Pilatus, Regem vestrum crucifigam? Responderunt primarij Sacerdotes, Non habemus regem nisi Caesarem.
units.tr: 15. But they cried out, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Shall I crucify your king?" The chief priests answered, "We have no king but Caesar."

units.la: 16. Tunc ergo tradidit eum ipsis ut crucifige-tur. Assumpserunt autem Iesum, & abduxe-runt.
units.tr: 16. Then therefore he delivered him to them to be crucified. And they took Jesus and led him away.

units.la: 17. Et ipse baiulans crucem suam inde venit in eum locum qui dicitur Caluariæ, Hebraice autem Golgotha.
units.tr: 17. And he, bearing his own cross, went out to the place called the Place of a Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha.

units.la: ANNON, obsecro fratres, vel leuissimum cōuitium, vel minima contumelia, vel denique minima iniuria aduersus vnicum Dei Filium perpetrata, & tenuissima iniustitia aduersus iustorum omnium iustissimum, & bonorum omnium optimum, & clementissimorum clementissimum, vel potius iustitiā ipsam & clementiam, admissa ab ingrato populo, immo desperatè perdito, nimium erat peccatum? Heu! nimis certè! ad ipsos conuincendos, condemnan-dos, & perdendos, vt ipsis tandem & ipsorum posteris accidit. At non satis erat vt docere-mur qui & quales simus, cui pœnę essemus ob-noxij, quantum sit odium Dei aduersus peccatum, vt id detestemur: quę sit profunditas, longitudo & latitudo misericordiæ eius qui pro-prio Filio nō pepercit, sed cum nostrę redemp-tionis pretium accepit: quæ vicissim inenarrabilis Filij charitas, non modò forma serui accepta, sed etiam peccatis omnibus nostris quorum erat sponsor in se receptis. Mortem igitur oportuit interuenire. Erat enim capi-tale peccatum nostrum. Quot autem ex primo
units.tr: Pray, brethren, was any insult, however slight, any affront, however small, or finally any wrong, however trivial, committed against the only Son of God, and any injustice, however faint, against the most just of all the just, the best of all good men, the most merciful of the merciful, or rather against justice itself and mercy, committed by an ungrateful people, or rather one utterly lost, was not this an exceedingly great sin? Alas, certainly exceedingly great! It was to convict, condemn and destroy them, as in the end it befell them and their posterity. But it was not enough for us to be taught who and what we are, what punishment we deserve, how great is God's hatred against sin, so that we might detest it; what is the depth, length and breadth of the mercy of him who did not spare his own Son but gave him as the price of our redemption; and, in turn, what unspeakable love of the Son, who not only took the form of a servant but also received into himself all our sins, of which he was surety. Death therefore had to intervene, for our sin was a capital crime. And how many deaths were owed by the sins born from the first sin? That is why Paul says that he became not only obedient but obedient even unto death. What more? This death had to be marked with a special kind of curse, since our crime is a crime of treason against the divine majesty in the first degree, when man has tried to make himself equal to God, and his descendants never cease to rebel against him and to behave stubbornly. For this reason the same Apostle, in the same place, names it expressly: "the death of the cross" (Phil. 2:8). And Paul does not simply say that he bore our sins in his body, but adds at once, "upon the tree" (1 Pet. 2:24), which he also expressly charges against the Jews (Acts 2:23; 5:30; 10:39). The reason is given in Deut. 21:23: the Lord in his law, foreseeing this judgment, marked this kind of punishment with a special stigma of infamy, namely that one hanging on a tree should die, whether simply bound, according to Jewish custom, or fastened with nails, by which among the ancient nations the most worthless and detestable men were punished. In short, this is what the same Apostle says in one word, when he says that he was made a curse for us (Gal. 3:10). This very thing is what we have undertaken in this text, and it is set out for us at length; it is the conclusion of all the foregoing acts, since neither Satan himself nor his ministers rested until they had brought their purpose to its end.

units.la: T. iiij. peccato nata peccata mortes merebantur? Idcirco Paulus cum non tantùm obedientem esse factum dicit, sed vsque ad mortem. Quid amplius? Hanc mortem speciali quadam execratione oportuit insigniri, siquidem crimen nostrum crimen est læsæ Maiestatis diuinæ in primo gradu, quum se Deo exæquare homo conatus sit, & eius posteri aduersus eum rebellare & contumacitér sese gerere non desinant. Quapropter idem Apostolus eodem loco, Philipp.2.8.nominatim exprimit, morte Crucis: & D. Paulus non simpliciter ait eum pertulisse in corpore suo peccata nostra, sed addit continuò, Super lignum.1. Pet. 2. 24. quod ipsum nominatim etiam Iudæis Actor. 2. 23. 5. 30. & 10. 39. exprobrat. Ratio redditur. Deut. 21. 23. Dominum nimirum in Lege sua, præuiso hoc iudicio: speciale m ignominiæ notam inuisitatem huic supplicij generi, quo pendens aliquis è ligno morerctur, siue simpliciter alligatus ex more Iudaico, seu clauis affixus, quo apud antiquas nationes vilissimi homines & abominandi supplicij genere puniebantur. In summa hoc est quod idem Apostolus vno verbo inquit, dicens, eum pro nobis factum esse execrationem. Gal. 3. 10. Istud ipsum est quod sumus aggressi hoc textu & copiosè nobis declaratur, quæ clausula est superiorum omnium actuum, quum nec ipse Satan nec eius ministri priùs quieuerint, quàm suum propositum ad finem perduxissent.
units.tr: T. iiij. The wicked. If Satan and his ministers never tire of doing evil, what excuse shall we offer before the Lord, if, with him urging us, helping us and supplying strength, we grow weary so quickly in doing good? And here, alas, too often, indeed daily, drowsiness takes hold of us, when we ought to walk, indeed run, and even fly, with all the more eagerness as we are assailed more vehemently; and the Prophets and Apostles have so often summoned us to this. For he who has run the course has the prize and the race, and will obtain the merited crown (1 Cor. 9:24; Phil. 3:14), not he who has halted in mid-course or, like Lot's wife of old, has looked back (Luke 17:31).

units.la: Improbi Quòd si Satan & ministri sui nunquam male le agendo defatigantur, quam excusationem coram Domino prætexemus, fi nos ipso cohortante,iuuante,vires sufficiente,bene agendo tam citò defatigamur?Et hic nimium sæpe proh dolor,immo quotidie, veternus nos occupat, quos non solùm ambulare, sed etiam currere, adeóque volare, tantò alacrius oportuerat, quanto vehementiùs impetimur: nos ad id toties Prophetis & Apostolis sollicitantibus.Finis enim habet laudem & curriculum qui decurrerit meritamque córonam adipiscetur 1. Cor. 9. 24. & Philipp. 3. 14. non autè qui medio cursu substiterit, aut à tergo, vt olim illa Loti vxor,respexerit.Luc.17.31.
units.tr: But what, after all, has Satan with his tireless labour and his satellites achieved? Surely he has ruined himself and his own. For this is a most certain axiom: that the impious and wicked man who persists in crimes will at last find that he has run onto his own sword, and has been the cause of his own ruin. Holy Scripture repeats this again and again, and the very wise men of this age warn well and wisely that bad counsel is worst for the one who gives it.

units.la: Cæterùm quid indefesso isto labore Satan cum suis satellitibus tandem profecit? Nimirum séque suósque pessundedit. Certissimum enim istud est axioma, pergentem in flagitiis impium ac facinorosum hominem, tandem compcrturum sese in suum ipsius mucronem incurrisse,sibiq; ipsi exitij causam fuisse: Sacra Scriptura toties illud inculcante:& ipsis huius seculi sapientibus bene ac sapienter malum consilium, consultori pessimum esse,monentibus.
units.tr: But what did Satan, with his tireless toil and his attendant minions, finally achieve? Clearly, he ruined both himself and his followers. For this is a most certain axiom: that the impious and wicked man who persists in his crimes will at last find that he has run onto his own sword and has been the cause of his own destruction. Holy Scripture repeats this again and again, and even the wise men of this age, rightly and wisely, warn that bad counsel is worst for the one who gives it.

units.la: Intelleximus igitur vt Pilatus Iudæorum importunis clamoribus victus,tandem frustrà egregiis illis suis rectus obtestationibus eorum voluntati Iesum Christum permittere statuerit, qui sententiam quoque in eum pronun-tiandam illi præscripserant. Quæ quum alij Euangelistæ leuiter attigissent, D. Iohannes qui vltimus hanc historiam conscripsit, & qui propius singula dicta factaque obseruauit, tectis nimirum oculatus ex diuina prouidentia, copiosius & specialius haec perlequutus est, atque, sententiam hanc solenniter pronunciatam fuisse, & quidem pro tribunali ex more, loco nimirum huiusmodi negotiis destinato, quem propterea Graece λιθόστρωτον, & lingua populari, Gabbatha, id est folium magnificae alicuius & eminentis structurae, nominat.
units.tr: So we see that Pilate, overcome by the importunate clamours of the Jews, finally resolved to hand Jesus Christ over to their will, though his earnest protests had been in vain, and they had prescribed the sentence to be pronounced against him. The other Evangelists touched on these matters only lightly. But St John, who wrote this history last and who observed each saying and deed more closely, being by divine providence an eyewitness, has related these things more fully and particularly. He tells us that this sentence was solemnly pronounced, and indeed from the judgment seat according to custom, namely in the place set apart for such business, which he accordingly calls in Greek the pavement [λιθόστρωτον], and in the vernacular Gabbatha, that is, the raised platform of some magnificent and lofty structure.

units.la: Non frustrà autem id factum est: nolente nimirum Patre Filium mori nec Iudaeorum insidiis, nec per tumultum, nec clanculum: sed publicè in omnium oculis & aspectu, forma iuridica, quantumuis hominum respectu iniqua: quasi nimirum coelitus Deus ab Oriente ad Occidentem, & à Meridie ad Septentrionem, vt postea per Euangelij praedicationem contigit, coelitus haec verba detonasset, Infelices homines, intuemini in hoc vnico meo Filio, quem super hoc theatrum taquam vadem & sponsorem vestrum propono, hinc quidem quantus sit meus aduersus peccatum furor, & quid sitis ipsi promeriti: inde vero quàm immensa mea & illius misericordia erga omnes hanc gratiam amplexantes. Agite igitur, fratres, discamus hanc historiam meditari, discamus, inquam, non velut per transennam summa tantum in genere capita meditari, sed singulas eius circunstantias expendere: quandoquidem ista nobis tam accurate coposeque concinnata conscripta sunt. Ecquis enim nostrum ad tale spectaculum non commoueatur? At causæ propter quas id fiat tenendæ sunt. Durius quidem sanè quouis ferro & chalybe fuerit eius pectus, quod non indignitate & iniuria tam innocenti viro facta commoueatur, humana tantum ratione factum illud examinans. At longè aliam huius mysterij considerationem esse oportet, vt nimirum nos in hoc spectaculo tanquam præcipuos debitores ipsi contemplemur, vt cum gemitibus inenarrabilibus coram Deo nostro exclamemus, Deus bone, quid nostris oculis intuendum præbes? Nos, nos fecimus, Nos rei sumus. Vnde verò ista permutatio nisi ex immensa & incomprehensibili tua bonitate? Me miserum & infelicem! quinam ita mei tuíque sum oblitus? Fili Dei, quomodo te eò vsque exinaniisti? Hanc igitur mihi, Deus, gratiam largire, vt meipsum serió in hoc spectaculo contemplatus, istorū omnium in me causam inhærentem abominatus, vera fide & viui sica amplectar, quam mihi offers absolutionem, mihi inquam, misero peccatori in iusti Filij tui qui meas partes tulit condemnatione: & gloriam mihi partam in mei vadis ac fidei soris ignominia. Icsu Christe Mundi Seruator, oro te vt me tibi per Sanctum Spiritum tuum coniungas & vnias, vt in te tam gratus sim ei cui pro me teipsum obtulisti, quàm agnosco & fateor libens me in meipso modis omnis detestandum. Hæc sunt in tam horrendo spectaculo nobis intuend₊, & ad vsum referenda, quo cœlum ac terram etiam clfe concuílà conípicimus. Quid ergo? Nóf-ne solòs saxeos & insensibiles?
units.tr: This did not happen without purpose: the Father was unwilling that the Son should die, yet by the plotting of the Jews it was not done by tumult or in secret, but publicly, in the sight and view of all, in a judicial form, however unjust it might appear in the eyes of men. It was as if God had thundered from heaven, from east to west and from south to north, as later came to pass through the preaching of the Gospel, these words: "Wretched men, look upon this one Son of mine, whom I set forth upon this stage as surety and guarantor for you. Here you may see how great is my wrath against sin and what you yourselves have deserved; and there you may see how immense is my mercy and his toward all who embrace this grace. Come then, brethren, let us learn to meditate on this history; let us learn, I say, not to pass lightly over its main heads in general, but to weigh each of its circumstances, since these things have been recorded for us so accurately and carefully arranged. For who of us would not be moved by such a spectacle? But the causes for which it happens must be kept in mind. Surely his heart would be harder than any iron or steel that was not moved by the indignity and injury done to so innocent a man, if he judged that deed by human reason alone. But we must consider this mystery in a far different way: namely, we must regard ourselves in this spectacle as the chief debtors, so that with unspeakable groanings we may cry out before our God: 'Good God, what do you set before our eyes to behold? We, we did this; we are the guilty ones. Yet whence this exchange, unless from your immense and incomprehensible goodness? Wretched and unhappy that I am! How have I forgotten myself and you so completely? Son of God, how far did you empty yourself for this?' Grant me, O God, this grace: that, seriously contemplating myself in this spectacle, and abhorring all those evils that cleave to me, I may embrace with true faith and living trust the absolution you offer me, to me, I say, a wretched sinner, through the condemnation of your righteous Son, who bore my part, and the glory won for me through the shame of the surety of my cause and of my faith. Jesus Christ, Saviour of the world, I pray you to join and unite me to yourself through your Holy Spirit, that I may be as grateful to you, for whom you offered yourself in my place, as I acknowledge and freely confess that I am in myself deserving of every kind of detestation. These are the things to be considered in so dreadful a spectacle, and to be put to use, at which heaven and earth themselves were shaken with trembling as we behold. What then? Are we alone to be stony and insensible?"

units.la: Cæterùm non abs re notatur ab Euangelistis, nominatim à Marco & Iohanne codemnationis & executionis hora, non tantùm ad præcipuas huius historiæ partes designandas, sed aliam etiam ob causam quam suo loco sum dicturus. Interea tamen inter Marcum & Iohannem in horarum supputatione quædam videri subesse repugnantiam non inficior. Nam si, vt ait Marcus, hora tertia Christus crucifixus est, quinam, quod ait Iohannes stabit circa sextam horam fuisse condemnatum? Tenendum est igitur Iudæos diem naturalem 24. horarum ab occasu Solis ad alium vsque auspicantes, noƈti duodecim horas semper tribuisse, ab occasu Solis ad ortum vsque: & dici totidem ab ortu Solis ad occasum, vt ex Iohanne ipso patet, Ioh.11.9. Sed alia fuit etiam apud eos dici & noƈtis diuidendæ ratio, noƈti quatuor attributis vigiliis: dieíque quatuor partibus: quarum prior ternis horis constans, Mane vocabatur: alter quadrans ab hora dici quarta incipiens in sextam desinebat, qui nobis est hodie Meridies, & de nomine horæ sextæ completæ in quam desinebat dicebatur: similiter tertius continens septimam, octauam & nonam horam dici, intelligebatur hac voce Nonæ horæ: quartus denique quadrans à nona ad duodecimam, Vespera dicebatur. Quum dicit igitur Iohannes Iesum Christum circ ter horam. ram sextam fuisse condemnatum, minimè sex-tam horam diei intelligit, sed proximum ini-tium secundi quadrantis duodenarum illarum diei horarum, sic dictum quòd sexta hora fini-retur. Quòd verò Marcus ait: hora tertia fuisse crucifixu, initiu intelligit huius secundi qua-drantis, qui finita hora diei tertia incipiebat. Quū hæc igitur mense Martio, æquinoctiali & Paschati Iudæorū dicato cōtigerint, Iohannes dixit Iesum Christū fuisse condemnatū paulo ante quartam horam diei ab ortu Solis incipientis, quæ fuit ex nostra consuetudine hora circiter sesqui octaua. D. verò Marcus dicit Iesum Christum præterita nona crucifixū: quod dextrè intelligendum est, puta condemnato Christo circiter sesqui octauam executionem præterita & audita nona cœpisse. Ex quibus nobis discendum est quo animo & quàm impotente improbi isti in Christum exarserint, Christo nimirum intra trium horarum spatium ad Pilatum ducto: accusato, ad Herodem misso, reductóque ac tandem condemnato, crucifixóque: qui vbi sex horas in cruce pependisset ad nonam vsque Iudæorum, quæ nobis est tertia, reliqua pars diei ad Solis occasum vsque crucis depositioni & Sepulturæ data est. Diuina verò prouidentia speciali in horarum istarum distributione maximè conspicitur, vt veritati cum umbris & figuris conueniret: tribus illis prioribus horis quibus Christus ad Pilatum ductus est, & modis illis indignissimis exceptus, & tandem etiam condemnatus, cum ordinario sacrificio matutino conuenien tibus: tribus vero posterioribus horis, quibus Iudaei Pascha comederunt, cuius in Cruce veritas pendebat, vespertinum sacrificium respicientibus.
units.tr: Moreover, the Evangelists, especially Mark and John, note the hour of the condemnation and of the execution with good reason. They do this not only to mark the main parts of this history but also for another reason, which I shall explain in its proper place. Meanwhile, I do not deny that there seems to be some disagreement between Mark and John in their reckoning of the hours. For if, as Mark says, Christ was crucified at the third hour, how is it that John says he was condemned about the sixth hour? We must hold that the Jews, who began the natural day of twenty-four hours from sunset to sunset, always assigned twelve hours to the night, from sunset to sunrise, and the same number to the day, from sunrise to sunset, as John himself makes clear (John 11.9). But they also had another way of dividing the day and night: four watches were assigned to the night and four parts to the day. The first of these parts, consisting of three hours, was called Morning. The second quarter, beginning at the fourth hour of the day and ending at the sixth, was what we today call Midday, and it took its name from the sixth hour, the hour with which it ended, being called "completed sixth." Likewise the third quarter, which included the seventh, eighth and ninth hours, was understood under the name "Ninth hours." Finally the fourth quarter, from the ninth to the twelfth hour, was called Evening. So when John says that Jesus Christ was condemned about the sixth hour, he does not mean the sixth hour of the day, but the beginning of the second of those four quarters of the twelve hours of the day, which was so called because the sixth hour ended it. When Mark says that he was crucified at the third hour, he means the beginning of this second quarter, which began when the third hour of the day was over. Since these events took place in March, the month of the equinox and dedicated to the Jewish Passover, John meant that Jesus Christ was condemned shortly before the fourth hour of the day, counted from sunrise, which by our reckoning was about half past seven. Mark, however, says that Christ was crucified after the ninth hour had passed. This must be understood correctly: when Christ was condemned, about half past seven, the execution began after the hour of the ninth had passed and was heard of. From these facts we must learn with what spirit and how violently these wicked men raged against Christ, since within three hours he was led to Pilate, accused, sent to Herod, brought back, and at last condemned and crucified. After he had hung on the cross for six hours, until the ninth hour of the Jews, which for us is three o'clock, the rest of the day, until sunset, was given over to the taking down from the cross and the burial. But divine providence is especially seen in the distribution of these hours, so that it agreed with the truth prefigured by the shadows and figures: the first three hours, in which Christ was led to Pilate, received those most shameful indignities and was at last condemned, correspond to the ordinary morning sacrifice; the three later hours, in which the Jews ate the Passover, whose truth was hanging on the cross, correspond to the evening sacrifice.

units.la: Narrantur deinceps in hac historia quae inter Domini nostri condemnationem & executionem contigerunt, in quibus primum occurrit contumeliarum omne genus & iniuriarum quibus affectus est Christus, a Pilati (a quo ut iudicij sic executionis pendebat authoritas) militibus intra Praetorium reductus tantisper dum Crux & quae ad hanc executionem erant necessaria parabatur. Hic autem rursum quaedam occurrit repugnantia in serie historiae in iis quae a Matthaeo & Marco traduntur, quasi haec a condemnatione gesta sint, quum tamen D. Iohannes ea tanquam prius facta commemoret ex Pilati coniulio, Iesum Christum producens virgis caesum, & spineam coronam gerentem pallioque purpureo indutum, fore sperantis ut hac poena & ignominia Iudaeis satisfieret. Et sane sic est historiae series intelligenda ut a Iohanne conscripta est. At Matthaeus & Marcus posteriore loco repetunt quae prius contigerant, & quorum ante non meminerant. Minime igitur illud intelligendum ac si Iesu Christo alia fuisset corona spinea impositta, & alia iterum vestae purpurea indutus fuisset. Eodem enim habitu Christus in praetorium reductus quo fuerat populo exhibitus. Sed quod contumeliis iisdem & opprobriis quibus ante in Praeto-
units.tr: Next, this history relates what happened between the condemnation of our Lord and his execution. Here first occurs every kind of insult and injury with which Christ was assailed by the soldiers of Pilate, on whose authority the judgment and also the execution depended. They led him back inside the Praetorium while the cross and the things necessary for the execution were being prepared. Here, again, there is a certain difficulty in the order of the story, in what Matthew and Mark record, as if these things were done after the condemnation. Yet St John, recounting them as having happened earlier, follows Pilate's counsel, presenting Jesus scourged, wearing a crown of thorns and clothed in a purple robe, hoping that the Jews would be satisfied by this punishment and disgrace. And indeed the sequence of the history must be understood as John wrote it. Matthew and Mark, however, relate in a later place what had happened earlier and what they had not mentioned before. So we must not understand it as though Jesus had been crowned with thorns at one time and dressed in purple at another. Christ was led back into the Praetorium in the same clothing in which he had been shown to the people. But he was subjected there to the same insults and reproaches with which he had been treated before.

units.la: Concilian tur Euan gelist ae in narratio- ne temporis quo Iesus Christus virgis caesus, & spinis coronatus, & lu dibrio habitus est. Prætorio est à militibus impetitus, idcirco duo Euangelistę hanc narrationem continuarunt, ne suæ historiæ seriem interrumperent, etsi duabus repetitis vicibus istoru pars gesta sit. Quæ porro superius hac de re diximus nihil iuuat sigillatim repetere. At tamen quam inde doctrinam elicuimus, non possumus satis sæpe & diligenter meditari & nostris mentibus infigere, ut eo magis discamus abiici velut in ipsos inferos quæ limus commeriti perpéden-tes: & vicissim immensam illam misericordiam amplectamur, ut hac tanta obedientia partam nobis gloriam fide consequamur: omni crucis ignominiæ gloriam illa opponentes, in quam hac via caput nostrum Christus cuectus est, eandem cum suis membris communicaturus.
units.tr: The Evangelists are reconciled in their account of the time when Jesus Christ was scourged, crowned with thorns, and mocked. He was assailed by the soldiers in the Praetorium, and so two Evangelists continued this narrative, so as not to interrupt the sequence of their history, although part of these events took place at two repeated times. It is useless to repeat one by one what we said above about this matter. Yet the teaching we have drawn from it cannot be pondered and fixed in our minds often and carefully enough, so that we may learn more fully how we, who deserved to be cast down like mud into the very depths, should, on the other hand, embrace that immense mercy, and so by faith obtain for ourselves the glory won by this great obedience. We should set against every shame of the cross that glory into which Christ our head was carried by this way, so that he might share the same glory with his members.

units.la: Transeamus igitur ad iter Domini ad morte pergetis, à Prætorio ad locu supplicij Golgotha nominatu. Dicitur igitur propriis vestibus indutus exiuisse, crucé suá baiulans, vel potius trahens: cui tamen oneri feredo quū impar esset, seu non erat tam robusto & firmo per se corpore, seu propter magnos cruciatus quos à captura totam noctem & totum mane perpessus erat, sub onere tato fatiscerer, (nec enim est vero simile carnifices animo cū subleuandi & ipsi parcendi adiutorem quæsiuisse) quidam qui hic tum nomine suo tum aliis indicius notatur, eā ponè ipsum ferre coactum fuisse, nimirum vnum extremum portare præeunte Christo, qui aliud extremum ferebat. Non frustrà autem tam accurate hæc circumstantia à quatuor Euangelistis obseruatur. Nam præterquàm quòd apud prophanas gentes mos illeinualuerat vt rei furcas suas ferrent, vnde apud Romanos nomen Furciferi, extra omne dubium est, carnifices vt cœperant ita perrexisse, & nullum genus contumeliarum quod ad Crucis supplicium adderent, omisisse: militarique petulantia aduersus miserum illum ex agris redeuntem insultasse. Obseruandum præterea Iudæos quum Christum vt rem pollutam abominarentur, quibus tamen non erat Religioni supplicio vltimo innocentem afficere, etiam Crucis lignum vt rem pollutam vel leui contactu attingere refugisse. At sunt hic nobis altius attollendi mentis oculi ad illius vsque prouidentiam qui pro peccatis nostris vnico Filio non pepercit, & accuratè pensitanda ex his circumstantiis quæ nos diserte docet Apostolus, & obseruare iubet, Gal.3.13. Iesum Christum nimirum factum pro nobis execrationem, vt exeat in nobis benedictio, nobis, inquam, Gentibus, quos hic Cyrenæus adumbrat, Christum sequentibus & Crucem post ipsum ferentibus, nequaquam autem carnificibus eius persequutoribus, nec Iudæis eum abominantibus & reiicientibus.
units.tr: Let us therefore pass on to the journey of the Lord to death, from the Praetorium to the place of execution called Golgotha. It is said that he went out wearing his own garments, carrying his cross, or rather dragging it. Since he was not equal to bearing that burden, either because his body was not so strong and sturdy by itself, or because of the great torments he had suffered from his arrest throughout the night and the morning, he was weakened under so great a load (for it is not likely that the executioners, in their mind, sought a helper to relieve them and spare themselves), a certain man, noted here both by name and by other signs, was compelled to carry it behind him, that is, to carry one end of it while Christ went before, carrying the other end. Nor without reason do the four Evangelists observe this circumstance so carefully. For apart from the fact that among the profane nations the custom had prevailed that condemned men carried their own gallows, whence the Romans had the name furciferi (gallows-bearers), beyond all doubt the executioners, having begun in this way, went on and omitted no kind of insult that they could add to the punishment of the cross, and with soldierly wantonness they mocked that wretched man as he came back from the fields. It must further be observed that the Jews, though they abominated Christ as a polluted thing, and yet did not scruple to inflict the final punishment on an innocent man, shrank from touching the wood of the cross, as a polluted thing, even by a slight contact. But here the eyes of our mind must be lifted higher, to the providence of him who did not spare his only Son for our sins, and we must weigh carefully from these circumstances what the Apostle clearly teaches us and bids us observe (Gal. 3.13): that Jesus Christ was made a curse for us, so that the blessing might come upon us. Upon us, I say, Gentiles, whom this Cyrenian here foreshadows, who follow Christ and carry the cross after him, and not at all upon his executioners and persecutors, nor upon the Jews who abominated and rejected him.

units.la: Hic igitur nobis vera effigies proponitur ob oculos veræ Ecclesiæ, quæ coetus est eorum de quibus Matth.10.38. dicitur, Qui non accipit crucem suam ac sequitur me, non est me dignus. Etsi verò hic de Cruce lignea agitur, abest tamen vt in ipsa materia hæreamus, quum potiùs potius Crucis nomine & Christi sequendivo-cibus intelligatur,quæcunque hominum cru-delitas in persequendis & vexandis Dei filiis tormenta excogitat,eădem ob causam & eandem ratione qua hic Christus passus est ab inimicis suis omnis generis contumelias,quicquid tandem persecutores suæ causæ præte-xant. Nam si quæcunque Crux, idest poena quam quis patitur, non est Crux Iesu Christi, quod iis plerúque contingit qui ob delicta aut ob falsam doctrinam puniuntur, & quibus sanadis nullum aliud superest remedium, non omnes sane Christi Crucem, ut Cyrenæus iste ferunt, qui aliquid patiuntur, sed suam quam ipsi sibimet effinxerunt tandem ab eadem opprimendi, quum verissimè dixerint quidam è veteribus,non pœnam sed causam veros martyres facere.
units.tr: Here, then, a true image is set before our eyes, the image of the true Church, which is the assembly of those of whom it is said (Matt. 10.38): "He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me." Although here we are speaking of a wooden cross, we must not cling to the material itself, since the name of the cross and the expression "following Christ" are rather to be understood of whatever torments human cruelty devises for persecuting and harassing the sons of God, for the same reason and in the same way as Christ here suffered every kind of insult from his enemies, whatever pretext his persecutors put forward for their cause. For if every cross, that is, every punishment that someone suffers, is not the cross of Jesus Christ, as happens for the most part to those who are punished for their crimes or for a false doctrine, and for whom there is no other remedy to be applied, then surely not all who suffer something bear the cross of Christ, as this Cyrenian did, but rather the cross which they have fashioned for themselves, by which they are at last overwhelmed. Some of the ancients spoke most truly when they said that it is not the punishment but the cause that makes true martyrs.

units.la: Obseruandum præterea aduersus eos qui-bus martyrum passiones sunt meritoriæ, non tantum oportuisse, si id ita se haberet, hunc Cyrenęum Christo in Cruce cum ipso ferenda comitem adiungi,sed in ea cum Christo etiam crucifigi. Nec enim nostræ redemptionis pretium fuisset sola illa Christi lignea Crucis gestatio. Vnicus igitur Iesus Christus suo corpore crucifixus noster est Seruator longe aliud maius Crucis onus anima sua perpessus,nimirum iram Dei aduersus nostra peccata, cui ferendæ vel ipse Christus futurus impar fuisset, nisi Deitate sua sustinente ipsum: tantum abest vt hac in parte potuerit vlla re creata iuuari.
units.tr: It must also be noted, against those for whom the sufferings of the martyrs are meritorious, that if this were so, it would not have been enough for this Cyrenian to be added as Christ's companion in carrying the cross. Christ would also have had to be crucified with him on it. The price of our redemption would not have been the mere carrying of Christ's wooden cross. Jesus Christ alone, crucified in his body, is therefore our Saviour, and he suffered in his soul a far greater burden of the cross: namely, the wrath of God against our sins. Christ himself would have been unequal to bearing that wrath unless his Deity sustained him. So far is it from being possible for any created thing to help in this part.

units.la: V. j. Vnicus, inquam, ille Iesus Christus nobis suis perpeffionibus vitam acquisiuit & est meritus. At fiquis excipiat salte Christum in ferenda lignea illa cruce fociun habuisse aliquem, aio corpore quidem aliquo modo subleuatum Iesum Christum, fine blasphemia autem aduersus officium Christi dici non posse opus illum socio habuisse in ira Dei aduersum peccata nostra ferenda. Ac sane Christus ipse prior incedens totum pondus istius crucis & intus & foris solus pertulit: sibi tamen conformes faciens in cruce ferenda quotquot eum a tergo sequuntur, pro mensura ponderis quam cuiq; distribuit: vt per patientiam & robur quod ipsemet suis largitur sese mutuo aedificent:non autem aliquid ad id quod in fe perfectissimum est, nostrae puta redemptionis meritum adiiciant.Coloff.1.24.
units.tr: I say that this one Jesus Christ alone acquired life for us by his sufferings and merited it. But if anyone excepts that Christ had some companion in carrying that wooden cross, I reply that Jesus Christ was indeed relieved in body in some way. Yet it cannot be said, without blasphemy against the office of Christ, that he had a partner in bearing the wrath of God against our sins. Christ himself went on ahead and alone bore the whole weight of that cross, both inwardly and outwardly. Still, he makes conformed to himself all who follow him from behind in carrying the cross, each according to the measure of weight he assigns to them, so that through the patience and strength which he himself gives they may build one another up. They do not, however, add anything to what is most perfect in itself, namely the merit of our redemption. Col. 1.24.

units.la: Quanta vero est eorum impudentia,qui pro Cruce Christi, non illa sane lignea ponderofissima, quae Christi crucifixum corpus sustinuit,sed poena quam Iesus Christus crucifixus in ea pro nobis pertulit, Cruces aureas & argenteas, gemmis non sanguine splendentes lubstituunt? Quos si tamen ex sermone iudices,dixeris perfectissimos IefuChrifti discipulos, & pro Sancta matre nostra Ecclesia mira patientes: monstra hominum infanda & impudentissima, vel ipsis eorum, maioris saltem partis, testibus & facie & abdomine. Crucem praeterea ferre post Christum non est signum aliquod Crucis aut coloratum aut aliqua materia teria constans gestare. Et tamen in Christia-nismum commentum illud plus quàm ridicu-lum paulatim peruasit. Ecquid autem amplius? Nimirum eò vsque deuentum est insaniæ, vt quod Crucifixi proprium est & ἀκινδύνωσιν, nò tantum materiali illi ligneæ cruci tributum sit, quam verâ Crucem vocant, illâ ipsam nem pe de qua hic agitur, repertam, vt aiunt, circi-ter trecentis à morte & passione Domini annis ab Helena Constantini Magni matre (fabulosa prorsus vt narratur historia) sed aliis omnibus etiam Crucibus quibuslibet, immo solo Cru-cis signo digitis designato. Tam nimirum ridi-culam, tam ineptam simul & abominandam idololatriam, vt cam ipse Satan delusis interea & dementatis hominibus rideat. Ac sanè fa-teor veteres illos Christianos fidei professio-nem coram tyrannis edentes crucifixum non tantum ore confessos fuisse, sed etiam signo Crucis, sed quid huic rei cum ea de qua loquor idololatria commune est? Frustra autem excipiant, minimè suam adorationem in Crucem ferri, sed in crucifixum. Id enim si verum est, quorsum obsecro, hanc Crucem, vel hunc Crucifixum illi anteponunt & pluris faciunt? Cur procul remotas Cruces summa veneratione quaerunt, tot aliis apud se posthabitis, si Crucifixo quem hæ non minùs quàm illæ repræsentant, penitus adhærent? Et tamen religiosæ adorationis speciem excogitarunt aliam distinctam qua se Deum & Sanctos venerari dicunt. Cruci suæ & Mariæ Virgini propriam, quam Hyperduliam vocant, id est, plus quàm seruitutem. Adde quòd proprio sermone indice mendacij apud Deum & homines coarguuntur, familiari nimirum ipsis hymno illo, quem his verbis blasphemis cantant, O crux aue Spes vnica, Hoc paßionis tempore, Quo carne, carnis conditor, Suspensus est patibulo.
units.tr: How great is the impudence of those who, instead of the Cross of Christ, substitute golden and silver crosses that glitter with gems rather than blood. I do not mean that most heavy wooden cross which bore the crucified body of Christ, nor the punishment Jesus Christ suffered on it for us. If you judged these people by their speech, you would call them the most perfect disciples of Jesus Christ, patient in suffering for our holy mother the Church. Yet they are unspeakable and most shameless monsters of men, as their faces and bellies show, at least to the testimony of the greater part of them. Moreover, to bear the cross after Christ does not mean carrying some sign of the cross, whether painted or made of some material. Yet that more than ridiculous invention has gradually crept into Christianity. And what more? Things have reached such madness that what belongs to the Crucified alone, and his power of keeping from harm [ἀκινδύνωσιν], is attributed not only to that material wooden cross, which they call the true Cross, found (as they say) about three hundred years after the death and passion of the Lord by Helena, mother of Constantine the Great (a story wholly fabulous as it is told). It is attributed also to all other crosses whatever, indeed to the mere sign of the cross traced with the fingers. This idolatry is so ridiculous, so inept and at the same time so abominable that Satan himself laughs at it while men are deluded and driven mad. I do grant that those ancient Christians, professing their faith before tyrants, confessed the Crucified not only with their mouths but also with the sign of the cross. But what does that have in common with the idolatry I am speaking of? They vainly object that their adoration is directed not to the cross but to the Crucified. For if that is true, why, I ask, do they prefer this cross, or this crucified one, and value it more? Why do they seek out crosses from far away with the highest veneration, setting aside so many others, if they cling wholly to the Crucified whom these represent no less than those do? Yet they have devised another, distinct kind of religious adoration by which they say they venerate God and the saints: a special one for their cross and for the Virgin Mary, which they call hyperdulia, that is, more than servitude. Add that they are convicted by their own language as liars before God and men, namely in that hymn familiar to them, which they sing with these blasphemous words: Hail, O Cross, our only hope, in this time of the passion, when the Creator of flesh was hung upon the gibbet.

units.la: Quam igitur, obsecro, sunt isti superstitiosi excusationem allaturi? Saltem enim fraudes eorum qui talibus reliquiis viuunt animaduertrent, quum certissimum sit & luce clarius, singulæ lignææ Crucis iustius particulæ, quæ istorum opera mercatorum toto passim orbe Christiano dispersæ sunt, in vnum colligerentur, vix illis vehendis nauem oneriariam sufficituram esse. Nec omissi sunt ab illis clauì, non spinea corona, non lancea, de qua suo loco dicturi sumus, non denique reliqua omnia quæ ad istud Domini supplicium concurrerunt, quasi sit illis omnibus quædam infula vis, quam vel ipsis Angelis, nemo sine idololatria tribuerit. Omitto manifestissimas impostauras, Saracenorum in primis, qui Christianos ludibrio habentes in terram sanctam commeantes, & deinceps in ea bellum gerentes, maximam istarum reliquiarum partem efflinxerunt, & magno pretio vendiderunt, merito stultam eorum superstitionem irridentes.
units.tr: What excuse, I ask, will these superstitious people bring forward? Surely they would notice the frauds of those who live by such relics. It is most certain, and clearer than light, that if all the scattered pieces of the wooden cross, which these merchants have dispersed throughout the whole Christian world, were gathered into one place, they would scarcely fill a cargo ship. Nor have the nails been left out by them, nor the crown of thorns, nor the spear (of which we shall speak in its place), nor finally all the other things that came together for that punishment of the Lord. It is as if all of them had some power, which no one without idolatry would attribute even to the angels. I pass over the most manifest impostures, especially those of the Saracens, who mocked the Christians visiting the holy land and afterwards waged war there. They fashioned the greater part of these relics and sold them at great price, rightly mocking the foolish superstition of Christians.

units.la: Atque adeo vt rata illa essent, Spiritus etiam er-
units.tr: And so that these fabrications might be believed, the spirit of error also
