It was voluntary, for salvation: not indeed for unbelievers, scorners and revilers, but for those who, converted from the filth of sins, would flee to his acknowledged mercy. Since they objected to him his trust and his inability to save himself, he refutes them by the same reasoning: far from his trust being vain, he could, if he wished, withdraw himself from all his sufferings. He truly called himself the Son of God, in whom alone trust ought to be placed, and who saves others too, his death being turned into the entrance to eternal life. Although he is still fixed to the Cross, and about to suffer the greatest of all torments, the very end of life, yet here he speaks as a victor, triumphing over all his enemies, visible and invisible. He uses the Cross no longer as a gibbet but as the throne of divine majesty, and asserts the truth of the title placed on his head: that he, though crucified, is nonetheless the Saviour, truly the Nazarene, the true King of the Jews promised, and displayed to all believers to the ends of the earth, against the power of the Devil, sin and death. In short, it was as if he had thundered that sentence from heaven itself upon the heads of his enemies. "You have fixed me to this Cross among thieves, as the most wicked of all wicked men; but in fact I will show you that you yourselves have erected for me a throne from which I shall pronounce a dreadful sentence against you. And because, through you, I did not, as I descended from the Cross, prevent those whom the Father gave me from perishing along with you, I, fixed on the Cross and in spite of your gnashing teeth, will save my own, and you will receive the most severe punishments from me."

units.la: *Vt vero fructum ex tam excellenti historia referamus, tenendum est, Spiritui Sancto minime fuisse propositum nos in duabus istis personis, quarum hic fit mentio retinere: sed hic primum ante oculos nobis repræsentari statum & conditionem in qua Seruator ille nolter nos atque omnes homines reperit, nimirum omnes detestandos & vtraque prima & secunda morte dignos. Deinde unde fit differentia illa inter mundum & Ecclesiam. Tertio nobis Ecclesiæ in his terris, & regni spiritualis nostri capitis in ea conditio ad viuum expressa proponitur: vno ex iistis latronibus representante in duratos & reprobos cum Dei filiis indiltincte.
units.tr: But if we are to draw fruit from so excellent a history, we must hold that the Holy Spirit did not intend merely that we keep in view the two persons mentioned here. Rather, he first sets before our eyes the state and condition in which that Saviour found us and all men: all deserving to be detested and liable to both the first and the second death. Then he shows whence the difference arises between the world and the Church. Third, the condition of the Church on earth, and of our spiritual Head's kingdom within it, is set forth to the life: one of the thieves represents the hardened and reprobate, mixed indistinguishably with the sons of God for the time being, until they are revealed in word and deed at their proper time; the other represents the elect and those who repent, together with their origin, the course of their life and their end. In the midst of them stands Christ, exercising his power: toward the one group in mercy, toward the other in eternal judgment.

units.la: B b. iiij. permixtos, tantisper dum suo tempore verbis & re ipsa patefiant: altero vero electos & poenitentiam ageres, quaeque ipsorum origo vitae decursus & exitus: in quorum medio statuefus Christus, potentiam suam exerens in hosquidem ad misericordiam, in illos autem ad iudicium aeternum. Et hoc ipsum quotidie veluti datis interlocutoriis sententiis exequi consipicimus, & tamen ex parte definitiuis, tantisper dum victima illa universalis pronuntiatio & executio aducnit, qua fideles tum animatum corpore mittendi sunt in integram sptatae gloriae possessionem: quicunque autem eum irriserunt, & transfixerunt omnes ad vnum cum ad aeternam condemnationem damnati conspecturi sunt, non sane pendetem in Cruce, sed in folio suo & gloria coelesti sedentem, vt Caiaphae mature praedixit: tantum abest vt ad potentiam teltandam oportuerit eum de Cruce descendere, vt illi conuitiantes potulauerant. Non abs re igitur dixi dignam hanc esse historiam quam attente considerēmus: quam fauit Deus vt in omni vita nostra diligenter meditemur, & nominatim in ipso mortis articulo.
units.tr: We see this carried out daily, as if interlocutory sentences were being given, yet in part definitive, until that universal pronouncement and execution arrives, by which the faithful, with their bodies made alive, are sent into the full possession of the hoped-for glory. But all who mocked him and pierced him will, every one of them, be condemned to eternal damnation, and they will see him, not hanging on the Cross, but seated on his throne in heavenly glory, as he foretold to Caiaphas. So far was it from being necessary, to display his power, that he come down from the Cross, as the reviling men had demanded. I was not wrong, then, to say that this history is worthy of our careful consideration: may God grant that we meditate on it diligently throughout our whole life, and especially at the moment of death.

units.la: Quod Matthaeus igitur & Marcus de hac historia obiter recensuerunt nempe, latrones etiam cum eo crucifixos, conuitia ipsi fecisse, Lucas deinde distinctius expressit. Nec tamen propterea putandum est (vt Iulianus Apostata calumniatus est hanc historiam) in iis aliquam esse repugnantiam, quum sit omnibus vsitatum & è vulgo petitum istud dicendi genus quo indefinitè & in genere dicitur, quod tamen singulis minimè conuenit. Sic quum dicitur Ioh. 7. 5 fratres id est cognati Iesu Christi non crediderunt in eum, saltem excipitur ex iis Iacobus vnus ex discipulis. Et quum dicuntur Iudæi à fœdere excisi, de vniuersa natione illud intelligitur non de singulis.
units.tr: Matthew and Mark, then, touched on this history only in passing, namely that the thieves crucified with him also reviled him; Luke later expressed it more distinctly. Nor, however, is it to be thought (as Julian the Apostate slandered this history) that there is any contradiction among them. This manner of speaking is common and taken from ordinary usage: it speaks in general and indefinitely, which nonetheless does not fit every individual. Thus when it is said at John 7. 5 that his brothers, that is, his kinsmen, did not believe in him, James, one of the disciples, is at least excepted. And when the Jews are said to be cut off from the covenant, that is understood of the whole nation, not of each individual.

units.la: Sed pluribus est hæc materia nobis explicanda, quandoquidem id locus iste postulat, & à multis pessimè intelligitur, qui sua culpa pro consolatione & ædificatione ex ea male intellecta, plurimum offenduntur. Quicquid autem obloquantur quibus hæc doctrina videtur tam noua & peregrina, quandoquidem Sacræ Scripturæ non tantum testantur esse aliquem Paradisum & aliquos inferos: seruandos quosdam, alios autem damnandos: esse in Deo misericordiam & iudicium: esse electos & reprobos: esse vasa ad dedecus & ad decus: esse vasa iræ præparata ad perditionem, & vasa misericordiæ præparata ad gloriam, in hac doctrina perseuerandum est vt pura Dei veritate, & sua ratio captiua ducenda. At diligenter excutienda est & ex Scripturis ipsis confirmanda.
units.tr: But this matter must be explained to us at greater length, since the passage demands it and many understand it very badly. Through their own fault they take offence at what, rightly understood, should be a source of consolation and edification. Whatever those may object to whom this doctrine seems so new and strange, the Holy Scriptures testify not only that there is some Paradise and some hell, that some are to be saved and others damned, and that there is mercy and judgment in God; they also testify that there are elect and reprobate, vessels for dishonour and for honour, vessels of wrath prepared for destruction and vessels of mercy prepared for glory. In this doctrine we must persevere, and lead our reason captive to the pure truth of God. Yet it must be carefully examined and confirmed from the Scriptures themselves.

units.la: Primum igitur docemur in Scripturis, Deum qui summè bonus est initiò primum hominem & primam mulierem ad suam imaginem condidisse, ac proinde ornasse ipsos summa Luce in Intelligentia, & rectitudine in voluntate, quibus hæc inferiora omnia regerent, suúmque Creatorem agnoscerent & venerarentur, mortem nunquam experturi.
units.tr: First, then, we are taught in the Scriptures that God, who is supremely good, at the beginning created the first man and the first woman in his own image. He therefore adorned them with the highest light in understanding and uprightness in will, by which they would govern these lower things, and would acknowledge and worship their Creator, never to experience death.

units.la: Deinde utrosque, sine ulla coactione, nulla naturali vitiosa inclinatione primum impulsos, sed sponte adhærentes exterius illos tentanti, adeo ut reipsa prohibitionem Creatoris violarent, tum Lucem illam tum etiam Rectitudinem perdidisse: iustoque Dei iudicio tum morti primæ cum posteris fuisse mancipatos, quæ est animæ & corporis separatio, unde sequitur corporis ipsius corruptio: tum morti secundæ, quæ est perpetua privatio felicitatis omnis, & ingressus in omnem æternam miseriam tum corpore tum anima: reliqua in hominis Intelligentia ea tantum Lucis particula, & in voluntate Discretionis inter vitium & virtutem, quantum requirebatur ad generis humani conservationem, & ad hominem coram Deo suæ ipsius conscientiæ testimonio reddendum ἀναπολόγητον.
units.tr: Then both, without any coercion and with no natural vicious inclination impelling them first, but freely cleaving to the outward tempter, actually violated the Creator's prohibition, and so lost both that light and that uprightness. By God's just judgment they were then given over to the first death, which is the separation of soul and body, whence follows the corruption of the body itself; and to the second death, which is the perpetual privation of all happiness and entry into all eternal misery, in body and soul alike. There remained in man's understanding only that small particle of light, and in his will the discernment between vice and virtue, as much as was required for the preservation of the human race, and for rendering man without excuse [ἀναπολόγητον] before God by the testimony of his own conscience.

units.la: Tertio, quandoquidem Dei providentia fertur etiam in res minimas, necessario fatendum est tantam corruptionem tam insignis Dei operis non accidisse quin eam Deus præviderit & ad suam gloriam decreverit: ut tamen sint primi illi nostri parentes prorsus inexcusabiles, sponte a Creatore deficientes, a quo tamen præmoniti & minis etiam coërciti satis superque fuerant.
units.tr: Thirdly, since God's providence extends even to the smallest things, we must necessarily confess that so great a corruption of so remarkable a work of God did not happen without God foreseeing it and decreeing it for his own glory. Yet the first parents themselves remain wholly inexcusable, since they fell away from their Creator of their own accord, though they had been forewarned and even restrained by threats, more than enough.

units.la: Quarto consideranda est Creatoris nostri sapientia & consilium, ventis hoc lapsu ut se duabus rebus quibus maxime commendatur cognosccognoscendum præberet: nempe misericor- dia, cui nullus fuisset locus nisi homo in hanc miseriam incidisset:& Iudicio suo, quod nul- lum fuisset nisi peccatum in mundum ve- nisset.
units.tr: Fourthly, we must consider the wisdom and counsel of our Creator, which by this fall offered itself to be known in the two qualities by which it is chiefly commended: namely, mercy, for which there would have been no place had man not fallen into this misery; and his judgment, which would have had no object had sin not come into the world.

units.la: Quinto igitur loco Scriptura docet omnes Adami posteros, id est omnes sine exceptione homines à prima conceptione naturaliter na- sci filios iræ & maledictionis Dei, omnis vitij ac corruptionis hostis & vindicis.Sed Creator seipsum bonitate & clementia quodammodo superans, & seinterim iustum Iudicem agno- sci volens, & decretum suum æternum nixum suo beneplacito, quod semper iustum est exe- qui, quùmq; nemini sit debitor, miseretur eo- rum quos ex hac generis humani massa tam fœda & corrupta secundum suum beneplaci- tum eximit, eos eligens in Iesu Christo Filio suo deinde vocandos,quo tempore & qua ra- tione ipsi placuerit, vt gratis ipsos iustificatos tandem etiam in eodem glorificet. Reliquos autem reprobat & merito pœnis æternis sti- pendio merito peccati addicit.
units.tr: Fifthly, therefore, Scripture teaches that all the posterity of Adam, that is, all human beings without exception, are born naturally from their first conception as children of wrath and of the curse of God, enemies and avengers of every vice and corruption. But the Creator, surpassing himself in goodness and clemency, and wishing meanwhile to be acknowledged as a just judge, has mercy, according to his good pleasure, on those whom he takes out of this mass of the human race, so foul and corrupt, and whose eternal decree rests on his good pleasure, which is always just to carry out, and since he is no one's debtor. He chooses them in Jesus Christ his Son, to be called afterwards at the time and in the manner that pleases him, so that he may freely justify them and finally glorify them in the same Christ. But the rest he reprobates, and rightly consigns them to eternal punishments as the wages of sin.

units.la: Quis hic autem de Deo merito speciose a- liquo prætextu conqueratur? Nam electi qui- dem tantùm abest vt de Deo conquerantur,vt semper illi pro infinita eius misericordia gra- tias agant, quæ infinitis partibus longè maior est quàm iiAdam nunquam lapsus esset,& hac ratione seque suo fque posteros in statu vitæ a-nimalis & tunc immortalis integrum conser-uasset. Quòd ad reprobos autem & damnandos, quum non condemnentur nisi obcaufas infeipfis inhærentes, quid obiiciant non habent, siquidem fi Deus neminem ex misericordia seruaret, sua tamen illi semper cöltaret Iustitia, quum nemo nascatur non reus æternæ damnationis. Habetis huius doctrinæ summam, cui tota Scriptura fert testimonium, ex qua electi & fideles aduersus quaslibet enarationes confirmantur, reprobos vero, incredulos & perditos penitus obstupescere & confundi necesse est.
units.tr: Who here could justly complain against God on any specious pretext? The elect are so far from complaining about God that they always give thanks to him for his infinite mercy, which surpasses by infinite degrees what they would have had had Adam never fallen, and had he in this way preserved himself and his posterity whole in the state of animal life, and afterwards immortal. As for the reprobate and those to be damned, since they are condemned only on account of causes inhering in themselves, they have nothing to object. For even if God saved no one out of mercy, his justice would still be owed to them, since no one is born free from liability to eternal damnation. You have the sum of this doctrine, to which all Scripture bears witness, and by which the elect and faithful are confirmed against any objections, while the reprobate, unbelievers and lost must necessarily be struck dumb and confounded.

units.la: Hic vero quæri solet quibus igitur indiciis hæc electio vel reprobatio, cognoscatur, ac proinde qui seruandi, qui vero damnandi sint. Nec sane curiosa quæstio est, modo bene explicetur, immo potius maxime omnium quæ in mentem hominis veniant necessaria. Aio igitur in primis, quum quæritur de aliquo an sit electus an reprobus, nobis illud occultum esse, nec etiam quæri oportere, nisi quatenus salutis alij aliorum studiosi, metuere debemus, & procurare, quisque secundum suam vocationem, & quantum in nobis est, ut non pereat qui perditorum viam ingreditur: ut contra iuuare omni studio & ædificare eos quos salutis viam sequi conspicimus: sed quum vlterius progredi nequeamus, & sæpe multorum hypocrisis & lethalis exitus patefiat etiam eorum qui sanctitatem præse ferebant: & contra, cuiusmodi hæc historia nobis exemplum suppeditat, multos ante deuios conspiciamus, subito mirum in modum ex mera Dei miseri-cordia Cordis in melius mutatos, licet quidem de horum salute bene sperare, aut illorum perditionem timere, prout eos hanc aut illam ingressos viam animadvertimus. Sed in iis tamen intra Charitatis & misericordiae caecellos subsistendum, quibus vocationis nostrae terminis contineamur, sedulo cavendes ne absolute iudicium feramus & sine ulla conditione, de iis qui adhuc in stadio decurrut. Immo & aliquid amplius dicam, cavendum esse summopere ne absolutum feramus iudicium etiam de iis quorum ex hoc mundo fuerit infaustus exitus, quum possit Deus summe misericors sic eorum cor interius afficere, ut in ipso extremo halitu ipsorum misereatur. Et ita quidem ad praecedentem quaestionem respondisse esto.
units.tr: Here it is usually asked by what signs this election or reprobation may be known, and therefore who are to be saved and who damned. Nor is this an idle question, provided it is properly explained; indeed it is perhaps the most necessary of all the questions that come into a person's mind. I say therefore, first, that when we ask whether someone is elect or reprobate, this is hidden from us, nor ought it to be asked, except insofar as, being concerned for one another's salvation, we ought to fear and to take care, each according to his calling and as far as in us lies, that whoever enters the way of the lost should not perish; and conversely to help with all zeal and to build up those whom we see following the way of salvation. But since we cannot go further, and often the hypocrisy and deadly end of many is revealed, even of those who used to display holiness; and conversely, as this history supplies us with an example, we see many who previously wandered suddenly changed for the better in a marvellous way, by the pure mercy of God working in their hearts. Although indeed we may hope well for the salvation of some, or fear the perdition of others, according as we observe them entering this or that way, nevertheless in such matters we must keep within the bounds of charity and mercy, by which we are restrained within the limits of our calling, and take care not to pass an absolute judgment, without any condition, on those who are still running the race. Indeed I will say something more: we must take great care not to pass an absolute judgment even on those whose exit from this world was unhappy, since God, being supremely merciful, can so affect their hearts inwardly that he has mercy on them even in their last breath. Let this be the answer to the preceding question.

units.la: At non sic respondero de sua electione & salute quaerentibus, quum nulla res nos propius tangat. Quid enim obsecro magis est miserandum ea conscientia, quae de Deo aut nunquam cogitat, aut haeret dubia sitne Deus eius misericors necne? De Dei autem misericordia persuasum esse ex certa cognitione, non est suverbum esse, ut nonnulli volunt, qui tamen sua merita magnopere iactare solent, quae vera est superbia illa Pharisaica, quae nobis Luc.18.11. depingitur: nam contra nemo se magis coram Deo poterit abiicere, quam qui se in morte esse fatetur, in sola Dei gratia vitam quaerens: Decque hunc honorem exhibet, ut in seipso per veram fidem obsignet Deum in promissis suis esse veracem. Ioh.3.33. Vt autem haec fiducia firma sit & minimè dubia quam omnibus tentationibus opponamus, ex iis quae pluribus persequitur Apostolus Rom.8.30.&34. & alibi, non est nobis expectanda peculiaris Dei in aurem revelatio, sed confugiendum ad ea quae docet in Verbo scripto & in Ecclesia praedicato, nēpe te (quicunque cupis de electione & salute tua certior fieri) si ore confessus fueris Dominum Iesum, & credideris in corde tuo quòd Deus excitauit eum à mortuis, seruatum iri: quae nobis issima verba Dominus dictat per Apostolum. Rom.10. 8. Est autem hac in re nobis hic ordo seruandus.
units.tr: But I will not answer in this way for those who ask about their own election and salvation, since no matter touches us more nearly. For what, I ask you, is more to be pitied than that conscience which either never thinks of God, or hangs in doubt whether God is merciful to it or not? To be persuaded from certain knowledge of God's mercy is not presumption, as some maintain, who nevertheless are accustomed to boast greatly of their merits; this is that true Pharisaic pride depicted for us in Luke 18:11. On the contrary, no one can abase himself more before God than he who confesses that he is in death and seeks life in God's grace alone, and he thereby gives God this honour, that he sets his seal within himself, through true faith, that God is true in his promises. John 3:33. So that this confidence may be firm and by no means doubtful, which we oppose to all temptations, we should not expect a special revelation of God into the ear, as the Apostle explains at length in Rom. 8:30 and 34, and elsewhere. Rather we must flee to what he teaches in the written Word and in the Church where it is preached, namely that you (whoever you are who desire to be made certain of your election and salvation), if you confess the Lord Jesus with your mouth, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, will be saved. These most sure words the Lord dictates through the Apostle, Rom. 10:8. In this matter we must observe the following order.

units.la: Qui se videt electum à Deo vt vocetur ad cognitionem Iesu Christi, in quo solo omnes electi sunt electi, & per quem solum ad suae electionis effectum perueniunt, ex eo colligat se à Deo in aliorum numero non haberi, quos hac gratia minimè dignatur.
units.tr: He who sees himself elected by God to be called to the knowledge of Jesus Christ, in whom alone all the elect are elect, and through whom alone they attain the effect of their election, let him conclude from this that he is not counted by God among the number of those whom he does not deign to honour with this grace.

units.la: Quoniam autem plures vocati sunt quàm electi, quod ex hac historia tota satis est perspicuum, Matth.20.16. idcirco progrediendum est vlterius. Igitur si animaduertas Dominum non tantùm tuas aures sono Euangelij fui feriisse, sed cor etiam aperuisse vt intelligas & credas eius sacrosancto Euangelio, tunc sane maius confidendi de tua electione argumentum habes.
units.tr: But since many are called and few chosen, as this whole history makes plain enough, Matt. 20:16, we must therefore proceed further. So if you perceive that the Lord has not only struck your ears with the sound of the Gospel, but has also opened your heart so that you understand and believe his most holy Gospel, then indeed you have a greater ground for confidence about your election.

units.la: Verùm, quoniam quaedam est fides, verae fidei electorum tantùm vmbra & simulachrum, quae sola veros fructus profert, & in aeteræternum manet, vt parabola quæ apud Matt. habetur. cap.13. declarat: idcirco nequis seipsum decipiat, scrutandum est cor nostrum an simus in illa fide 2. Cor. 13. 5. quod in iis reperietur quorum Spiritui Dei Spiritus reddit testimonium illos esse Dei filios. Rom.8.16. consentientibus nimirum (etsi non sine ingenti carnis lucta) Dei spiritu, nostróque spiritu regenito & illi pro viribus morigero, docente nos nempe Dei Spiritu vitia nostra detegstari, & formante in nobis velle & facere, cum ægritudine impotentiæ non melius volendi aut faciendi: sicut Apostolus ipse exemplo suo nos docet Rom.7.15.&24. Tunc igitur verè certa & non fallax hæc conclusio elicietur, longè vel ipso cœlo vel ipsa terra firmior, te ex electorum esse numero, nunquam periturum: & hanc etiam gratiam consequuturum vt huius Spiritus virtute bonum certamen decertes donec tandem partæ victoriæ triumpho perfruaris. Nam, inquit Apostolus Rom.14. Quot quot Spiritu Dei ducuntur, ij sunt filij Dei, qui Spiritus est adoptionis, per quem clamare dicunt, Abba Pater.
units.tr: But since there is a certain faith which is only the shadow and image of the true faith of the elect, and which alone bears true fruits and remains for ever (as the parable in Matt. ch. 13 declares), therefore, lest anyone deceive himself, our heart must be searched to see whether we are in that faith, 2 Cor. 13:5. It will be found in those to whose spirit God's Spirit bears witness that they are God's sons, Rom. 8:16: namely, when God's Spirit and our regenerate spirit agree (though not without a great struggle of the flesh), and our spirit obeys it as far as it can. God's Spirit indeed teaches us to detect our sins and forms in us the will and the deed, together with the grief of being unable to will or do better, as the Apostle himself teaches us by his own example, Rom. 7:15, 24. Then indeed this conclusion will be drawn, truly certain and not deceptive, far firmer than heaven or earth: that you are of the number of the elect and will never perish; and that you will also obtain this grace, that by the power of this Spirit you contend the good contest until at last you enjoy the triumph of the victory won. For, says the Apostle, Rom.14. As many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God, for it is the Spirit of adoption, by whom they cry, Abba, Father.

units.la: Deus igitur ex sola misericordia suos ab æterno prædestinatos vocat & Filio suo dat iustificandos, & tandem etiam in ipso glorificandos, non autem propter vlla opera fidem & pœnitentiam præcedentia aut subsequentia. Verumtamen fidei fructus quæ vera est, conuersio, & vitæ in melius mutatio, veram fidem à ficta & simulata discernunt, vnde fiamus. mum electionis nostræ testimonium sequitur non frustra monentes nos Apostolo vt cum timore ac tremore nostram ipsorum sautem consiciamus. Philipp. 2. 12. & iubente Petro, vt bonis operibus studeamus vocationem & electionem nostram firmam facere, testimonio nimirum effectuum Spiritus adoptionis in nobis: quum tamen electio nostra proprio suo nitatur fundamento non fide nostra aut pœnitentia, sed Dei nostri decreto & beneplacito, iam ante mundi constitutionem. Ephes. 1. 4. & 9.
units.tr: God therefore calls those whom he has predestined from eternity, out of sheer mercy alone, and gives them to his Son to be justified and at last glorified in him. He does not do so on account of any works, whether preceding or following faith and repentance. Nevertheless, the fruits of faith, which is true faith, namely conversion and a change of life for the better, distinguish true faith from feigned and pretended faith, and from these fruits the testimony of our election follows. We are not vainly warned by the Apostle to work out our own salvation with fear and trembling (Phil. 2.12), and, at Peter's bidding, to make our calling and election sure by good works, that is, by the evident effects of the Spirit of adoption in us. Yet our election rests on its own foundation, not on our faith or repentance, but on the decree and good pleasure of our God, made before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1.4 & 9).

units.la: En igitur fundamentum & vsus huius tam pretiosæ doctrinæ, ex qua facile colligitur qui & quales sint reprobi & damnati, nempe, minimè quidem, inquam, qui non sunt in Iesu Christo (quum hodie sint extra Christum multi cras in illo futuri, alij citius, alij serius, vt in hoc misero latrone conspicuum est in vitæ suæ extremo velut agone conuerso) sed qui extra Christum & Ecclesiam moriuntur, extra quam non est salus. Act. 4. 12. Ioh. 14. 16. & 17. 3. Necessariò igitur illi omnes pereunt, & iustè condemnantur, quùm in ipsis iusta semper condemnationis causa & non in Deo reperiatur: quorum alij quidem ob solam corruptionem & peccatum originale condemnantur, in quo nati sunt & moriuntur etiam extra Iesum Christum & eius Ecclesiam, antequam ad ætatem scientiæ alicuius & cognitionis peruenerint. Cuiusmodi sunt hodie Iudæorum liberi ex fœdere excisi, Turcarúmque & similium perditaditarum nationum iustæ damnationi destina-tarum,paucis exceptis quos Deus in Ecclesiam suamcx beneplacito suo trahit: Alij sunt tam Turcæ & Iudæi cum similibus,quàm qui se Christianos dicunt, sed excedunt ex hac vita tam parum Religionis periti quàm ipsi Athei vel Epicuri:quorum conditio quàm præcedentium est futura deterior: quû rei nimirum sint nō tātum naturalis corruptionis,sed etiā propter fructus, quos ipsa edidit in ipsis merito condemnati, quòd nimirum vixerint & mortui sint in transgressione tum eorumquæ natura ipsa de Deo docebat eos,Rom. 1. 21. tum de quibus conscientia aduersus proximum arguebat.Rom.2.15. Reliqui sunt cæteris omnibus peiores & infelicicores,docti in Dei veritate,quam modis omnibus polluerint,seu flagitiosam & derelictandam vitam ad extremum vsque vitæ suæ halitum sine pœnitentia ducentes: seu generali apostasia,odio ipsius Dei, contra Sanctum Spiritum peccantes, quibus nunquam datur donum pœnitentiæ, nec remissio peccatorum,Heb.6.4. 1.Ioh.5.16.
units.tr: Here, then, is the foundation and use of this very precious doctrine, from which it is easily gathered who and what sort of people the reprobate and damned are. They are certainly not, I say, those who are not in Jesus Christ, since many who are outside Christ today will be in him tomorrow, some sooner and some later, as is plain in this wretched thief, who was converted at the very end of his life, as if in a death struggle. Rather, they are those who die outside Christ and the Church, outside which there is no salvation (Acts 4.12; John 14.6 and 17.3). All of these necessarily perish and are justly condemned, since the just cause of condemnation is always found in them and never in God. Of these, some are condemned on account of original corruption and sin alone, in which they were born and die, outside Jesus Christ and his Church, before they reach an age of any knowledge or understanding. Such today are the children of the Jews, cut off from the covenant, and of the Turks and other nations of the same ruined kind, destined for just damnation, with a few exceptions whom God, by his good pleasure, draws into his Church. Others are Turks and Jews along with their like, and also those who call themselves Christians but depart this life as ignorant of religion as the atheists or Epicureans themselves. Their condition will be worse than that of the former, since they are guilty not only of natural corruption but also, for the fruits that corruption itself produced in them, they are rightly condemned: they lived and died in transgression both of what nature itself taught them about God (Rom. 1.21), and of what their conscience accused them of against their neighbour (Rom. 2.15). The rest are worse than all the others and more wretched: they were taught the truth of God, which they have polluted in every way, either leading a shameful and abandoned life to their last breath without repentance, or sinning against the Holy Spirit by a general apostasy, out of hatred of God himself, to whom the gift of repentance and forgiveness of sins is never given (Heb. 6.4; 1 John 5.16).

units.la: Verùm quò melius adhuc expendamus tum horrendam, sed iustissimam tamen Domini seueritatem aduersus reprobos (vt discamus minas ipsius non flocci facere,& flagitare precibus ardentibus vt malum hoc a nobis auferat) quàm infinitam & immensam eius miseri-cordiam & clementiam erga electos, quam sedulò meditemur, agnoscamus & tanto diligentius conseruemus, non erit alienum à pro-
units.tr: But so that we may better weigh both the dreadful, yet most just, severity of the Lord against the reprobate (that we may learn not to make light of his threats, and to beg with burning prayers that he take this evil from us), and his infinite and immense mercy and clemency towards the elect (which we should diligently meditate on, acknowledge, and all the more carefully preserve), it will not be out of place to pursue this purpose further. Let us discuss these two very striking examples more fully and carefully, one by one: the one a dreadful mirror of reprobation, the other, if there is any other in the holy Scriptures, an example of infinite and sudden mercy.

units.la: Cc. j. posito fi pluribus & accuratius sigillatim hæc duo exempla tam insignia discutiamus alterû quidem horrendum reprobationis speculum, alterum autem infinitæ & subitæ misericordiæ, si quod aliud extat in sacris Scripturis, exemplum: quum nominatim hic latro sierit in eorum numero quos cæteris infeliciores diximus, siquidem verisimile est illum ex Dei populo fuisse, & circumcisum. D. igitur Lucas narrat horum latronum alterum Iesu Christo conuitia fecisse, his verbis, Si tu es Christus, ille, serva teipsum & nos tecum: quæ sane verba non sunt accipienda quasi essent precatio sub conditione, sed ut indignissimum conuitium, ac si dixisset, Egregium vero te Christum, qui nec teipsum nec tuos socios seruas: adeo ut se socium ijs adiungat qui ante ipsum loquuti fuerant. Ecquis autem eum ad tantum facinus impellebat nisi sola malitia & merus furor? Sed præterea circumstantia blasphemiam auget, & hunc aliis omnibus tetriorem facit, qui vix passum à morte distans, ex quo debuit de præterita vita cogitare & de mox secuturo apud Dei tribunal iudicio, cogitationem suam auersam à corporis & animi cruciatibus ad Iesum Christum blasphemandum transferr, quibus adde Sacerdotes, ex quibus hæc didicerat, sic contra Christum furore percitos, etsi præter rationem quidem omnem exarsisse, tamen irritatos & exacerbatos, quod totics eorum errores & hypocrisin acerbius arguisset. At perditus ille, nulla occasione se ipsis locium sola peruerfitate impulsus adiungit. Quid igi-tur est, obsecro, blasphemare,fi non est hic huius criminis reus,qui veritati ipsi mendaciū impingere non veretur? Et ob hoc ipsum etiā àfocio latrone reprehenditur, officio functo prædicatoris vt paulò post dicturi fumus.Quid amplius?Etsi demus istius detcftandi hominis vocem esse supplices cum conditione preces (quod tamen non est)prophanæ tamen & non ferendæ preces illæ fuerint. Quis enim homi-nem ab alio nullis sibi officiis deuincto beneficiúpoftulante, & his eum vocibus compel-lantem ferat,Si vir bonus es hoc mihi largire? En igitur verè hominis reprobi exemplum, fine conscientia, ex iis quæ superius diximus, & præsertim quod eo tempori momeío monitus à socio spreuerit admonitionem: vnde fatis patet eum ex indignatione fræna mor-dentem ad mortem vsque arrosisse. Sed quo melius ex huius perditi exemplo discamus per quos anfractus in hanc abyssum præcipites plerique cadant, audiamus quando & qua de re fuerit à socio prius in latrocinio reprehen-sus. Em igitur de quibus cum arguit initio fa-cto vnde oportuit, Saltem non times Deum? quasi vocibus istis eum compellasset, Ego & tu hactenus nec homines, nec Magistratus, nec bonas leges in latrociniis nostris exercen-dis metuebamus. At quî fieri potest vt ne Deū quidem timeas hoc tempore talia verba effu-tiens ore tam impuro? Circunstantias etiam ad augendum peccatum adiicit, quasi diceret,
units.tr: Since this thief is clearly among those whom we called more wretched than the others, it is probable that he was of God's people and circumcised. St Luke relates that one of these two thieves reviled Jesus Christ, with these words: "If you are the Christ, save yourself and us" (Luke 23.39). These words are certainly not to be taken as a conditional prayer, but as a most unworthy insult, as if he had said: "A fine Christ you are, who saves neither yourself nor your companions!" In this way he joins himself to those who had spoken before him. Yet who impelled him to such a crime, if not sheer malice and mere fury? Moreover, the circumstances increase the blasphemy and make him more foul than all the others. He was scarcely a step from death, when he ought to have been thinking about his past life and the judgment soon to come before God's tribunal, yet he turned his mind away from the torments of body and soul to blaspheming Jesus Christ. Add to this that the priests, from whom he had learned these things, were so inflamed with fury against Christ that, though they blazed beyond all reason, they were nonetheless irritated and exasperated, because Christ had so often exposed their errors and hypocrisy more bitingly. But that lost man, with no occasion offered him, is driven by sheer perversity to join them. What then, I ask, is blasphemy, if he is not guilty of this crime, who does not hesitate to lay a lie on the truth itself? And for this very reason he is rebuked by his fellow thief, who performed the office of a preacher, as we shall say shortly. What more? Even if we grant that the voice of that detestable man was a suppliant prayer with a condition (which, however, it is not), those prayers were still profane and not to be borne. For who would endure a man, bound to him by no duties and receiving no benefits from him, begging for a favour and compelling him with these words: "If you are a good man, grant me this"? Behold, then, the true example of a reprobate man, without conscience, arising from those things we said above, and especially because at that very moment, when warned by his companion, he scorned the admonition. From this it is quite plain that he, gnawing at the bridle in indignation, went on gnawing until death. But that we may better learn from the example of this lost man by what twisting paths most people fall headlong into this abyss, let us hear when, and about what, he was first rebuked by his companion in robbery. Look at what he rebukes him for at the outset, where it was needed: Do you not even fear God? It is as if by these words he had addressed him: "You and I have hitherto feared neither men, nor magistrates, nor good laws in carrying out our robberies. But how can it be that you do not even fear God, uttering such words at this time with so impure a mouth?" He also adds circumstances to increase the sin, as if he said:

units.la: Cc. ij. Quorsum vero tam es in eum petulans, quum tua conditio non sit melior illius conditione? An non tibi insolens videretur si a circumstantibus & nostrum supplicium intuentibus conuitiis afficereris, vt tu huic conuitia facis? At longe alia est facti tui quàm illius ratio. Ego enim & tu meritis ob flagitia nostra poenis afficimur: hic autem innocentissimus vel omnium iudicio, atque adeo ipsius Iudicis à quo sumus ad mortem damnati testimonio: non te igitur pudet etiam hoc ad reliqua flagitium adiicere, quum praesertim tam prope abs à iusto Dei tribunali rationem totius vitae redditurus?
units.tr: "Why are you so insolent towards him, when your condition is no better than his? Would it not seem insolent to you if the bystanders, who look upon our punishment, insulted you as you insult him? But the reason for your deed is very different from his. For you and I are punished with penalties deservedly for our crimes, but this man is most innocent, by everyone's judgment, and indeed by the testimony of the Judge himself, by whom we have been condemned to death. Are you not ashamed to add this crime to the rest, especially since you are so near to rendering an account of your whole life before the just tribunal of God?"

units.la: Habetis eximiâ viri istius reprehensionem, tam subitò per immensam Dei misericordiam in admirandum concionatore immutati, immo in Apostolum & Euangelistam ad hunc actum inter omnes excellentissimum, vt paulo post visuri sumus. Absit igitur pudeat nos in hac schola discere quantum & quàm periculosum peccatum sit reprehensiones aequo animo non admittere, sed abiicere quas ambabus vlnis potius amplecti oportuerat: seu Deus à conscientia ipsa nostra nos excitatos admoneat, seu per quemcunque alium cuiuscunque conditionis aut aetatis alloquatur. Nam si nobis ipsis nec bene consulere possumus, nec bonum ab aliis consilium accipere, quid aliud possumus quàm immedicabilem perditionem, aut plerumque nimis seram poenitentiam expectare? Nam se quidem homo poterit indurare, Dei autem solius est cum mollire, quam sanè gratiam minimè concedit omnibus,sed cui vult, per quem & quando ipsi visum est. Agite igitur, fratres, hoc exemplum considerantes in eo proficiamus, & æternum Iehouam, cui eheu! sæpissime nos restitiße debemus ingenuè profiteri, supplices oremus vt gratiam hanc nobis largiatur, vt in iis quæ iustissima & tamen clementissima iudicia in nos hodie exercet, proficiamus, & contrà quàm huic perdito contigit eius castigationes veræ conuersionis fiant nobis initium, vt reliquum vitæ nostræ curriculum ad eius honorem & gloriam transfigamus: ne nobis in eorum esse numero cōtingat quorū conditio peior quàm Sodomorum ac Gomorrhæ futura est,
units.tr: You have here the excellent rebuke of this man, who was so suddenly changed by the immense mercy of God into an admirable preacher, indeed into an Apostle and Evangelist for this act, the most excellent of all, as we shall see shortly. Far be it from us to be ashamed to learn in this school how great and how dangerous a sin it is not to receive rebukes with an even mind, but to cast away those which we ought rather to embrace with both arms, whether God, stirring us up from our own conscience, admonishes us, or speaks to us through anyone else, of whatever condition or age. For if we can neither counsel ourselves well nor receive good counsel from others, what else can we expect but incurable ruin, or repentance that is for the most part far too late? A man can indeed harden himself, but to soften belongs to God alone. He does not grant this grace to all, but to whom he wills, through whom and when it seems good to him. Come then, brethren, let us consider this example and profit from it, and let us humbly pray to the eternal Jehovah, against whom, alas! we have very often had to resist, that he would grant us this grace: that we may profit from those judgments which he exercises upon us today, most just and yet most merciful, and that, contrary to what happened to this lost man, his chastisements may become for us the beginning of true conversion, so that we may spend the rest of our life's course to his honour and glory. Let it not befall us to be among those whose condition will be worse than that of Sodom and Gomorrah,

units.la: Matth.10.11. Quod malum à nobis pro immensa sua miseri-cordia Dominus vtinâ auertat.
units.tr: (Matt. 10.11). May the Lord, in his immense mercy, turn this evil away from us; would that he would do so.

units.tr: Cc. iij.

units.tr: HOMILY THIRTY-FIRST.

units.tr: MATTHEW 27.

units.la: A sexta autem hora tenebrae factae sunt super universam regionem usque ad horam nonam.
units.tr: Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour.

units.tr: MARK 15.

units.la: Quum vero aduenisset hora sexta, tenebrae factae sunt super totam regionem usque ad horam nonam.
units.tr: And when the sixth hour was come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour.

units.tr: LUKE 23.

units.la: Dixitque Iesu, Domine, memento mei quum veneris in regnum tuum.
units.tr: And Jesus said, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.

units.la: Tum dixit ei Iesus, Amen dico tibi, hodie mecum eris in paradiso.
units.tr: Then Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, Today shalt thou be with me in paradise.

units.la: Erat autem quasi hora sexta, & tenebrae factae sunt super totam regionem usque ad horam nonam.
units.tr: And it was about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour.

units.la: Et obtenebratus est Sol.
units.tr: And the sun was darkened.

units.la: Vivus historiae tam excellentis explicationem aggressi, dixi-mus in ea nobis mundi statum, ex peccatoribus compositi, re-praesentari: in medio quarum tenebrarum Iesus Christus adest ex ingenti sua misericordia illuminans & seruans eos quos Patri visum est eligere & illi donare: a- lios contrà merito condemnans, & nominatim eos qui veritatem in seipsis contemnunt & suffocant: quod manifestè conspicitur in hoc perdito latrone de quo satis copiosè supe-rius egimus.Superest igitur vt superiori exem-plo opponamus alterum inter omnia exempla Sacrae Scripturae certissimum & euidentissi-mum testimonium immensae Dei gratiae & misericordiae, non magis inter se contrariis Luce ac tenebris, quàm illud de quo dicturi sumus est praecedenti & repugnans atque co-trarium.Et tamen paulò ante nihil erat magis alterum alteri simile quàm isti inter se erant simillimi, non tantum in genere quod vtr-que filius Adam, sed latro vterque, & vterque in manus Iudicum traditus, & fortasse ob ea-dem latrocinia, vterque ad idem supplicium damnatus,& vterque Cruci simul affixus. Vn-de igitur tanta tamque repentina ista nunquam exspectata mutatio? Proculdubio quum ne-mo possit Iesum dicere Dominum nisi per Spi-ritum Sanctum 1.Cor. 12. 3.& non noucrimus quid precemur vt oportet nisi per eundem Spiritum Rom.8. 25. per quem etiam vera da-tur resipiscentia.2. Tim.2. 25. necessario fatendum est illud contigisse quod prior Dominus esset hunc latronem interius alloquutus, cum admiranda vi & efficacia: ac proinde hanc gratiam esse no tantum testimonium immen-siae & ineffabilis bonitatis, vt est omnium elecctorum vocatio, sed etiam prorsus extraordinariæ. Nec enim legimus misero isti latroni antea fuisse cognitum aut auditum Iesum Christum: quod li fama aliquid de ipso perceperat, non tamen Christi auditor fuerat, nec eius miracula consp exerat, dum in sylvis viatoribus insidiaretur. Immo licet Christi auditor fuisset, & eius miracula conspexisset, nisi fuisset interius ad viuum affectus & prorsus immutatus, quid humanitus poterat de illo cogitare, quem videret à Sacerdotibus & primariis suæ nationis accusatum, à Pilato condemnatum, & in medio ipsorum tanquam omnium hominum flagitiosissimū crucifixum, & præterea irrisum & ab omnibus cuiuslibet ætatis ac conditionis conuitiis affectum, ita tamen vt ad illa sine responsatione obduruerit?
units.tr: Having begun to explain so excellent a history, we said that in it the state of the world, made up of sinners, is set before us; and in the midst of this darkness Jesus Christ is present, in his great mercy illuminating and saving those whom it has pleased the Father to choose and give to him, while condemning others justly, and especially those who in themselves despise and suppress the truth. This is plainly seen in the lost thief, of whom we have already treated at sufficient length above. It remains, therefore, that we set against the previous example another testimony, the most certain and evident of all the examples of Holy Scripture, of the immense grace and mercy of God. Light and darkness are not more opposed to each other than this one, of which we are about to speak, is to the preceding and contrary to it. Yet a little before, nothing was more alike than these two men, who were most similar to each other: not only in being sons of Adam, but both were thieves, both were handed over into the hands of judges, perhaps condemned to the same punishment for the same robberies, and both were crucified together. Whence, then, came so great and so sudden a change, never expected? Surely, since no one can say that Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:3), and we do not know how we ought to pray except through the same Spirit (Rom. 8:25), through whom true repentance is also given (2 Tim. 2:25), it must necessarily be confessed that this happened because the Lord had inwardly addressed this thief, with a wonderful power and efficacy. Accordingly, this grace is a testimony not only of the immense and ineffable goodness shown in the calling of all the elect, but also of something entirely extraordinary. For we do not read that Jesus Christ had been known or heard of by that wretched thief before. Even if he had heard something of him by report, he had not been a hearer of Christ, nor had he seen his miracles, since he was lying in wait for travellers in the woods. Indeed, even if he had been a hearer of Christ and had seen his miracles, unless he had been inwardly moved to the quick and utterly changed, what could he humanly think of him, whom he saw accused by the priests and the leading men of his nation, condemned by Pilate, and crucified in the midst of them as the most wicked of all men; and besides, mocked and assailed with insults by everyone of every age and condition, yet hardened against all of it without answering?

units.la: Quid ad hæc dicturi sunt quos tanto pere merita præparatoria iactitare non pudet, si nos oportet à Deo immutari? Annon illis tandem necesse est os occludi, & confiteri salutem nō esse, neque eius qui velit, neque eius qui currat, sed solius Dei miserentis cuius vult? Rom. 9. 16. & 18.
units.tr: What will those say to this, who are not ashamed to boast so much of their preparatory merits, if we must be changed by God? Must they not at last have their mouths stopped, and confess that salvation is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Rom. 9:16, 18)?

units.la: Adde etiam quando ipsi libet: quum hic miser etiam serius quàm post vndecimam horam diei, vt ij de quibus mentio fit, Matth. 20. 6. vtpote iam vmbra mortis eum inuadente, vocatus sit. Hinc etiam præter illa superiora discimus, quemadmodum diligenter cauendum est ne peccatoribus adulemur, sic etiam sobrie de ipsis iudicandum, nec temere pro desperatis habendos, ne maximos quidem peccatores, & in quibus minima immutationis coram hominibus spes est.
units.tr: Add also that he was called when it pleased God: this wretched man was called even later than the eleventh hour of the day, such as those mentioned in Matthew 20:6, since the shadow of death was already coming upon him. From this, besides what was said above, we learn that, just as we must take great care not to flatter sinners, so we must also judge them soberly, and not rashly count them as desperate, not even the greatest sinners, in whom there is the least hope of change in the eyes of men.

units.la: At contrà vicissim qui in scelere induratur, & emendationem semper procrastinant, caveant ne hoc exemplo abutantur ad malam consequentiâ sese regendi causa, exspectantes dum eos Deus interius alloquatur. Nam contrà Vocationi ordinariæ & quæ fit per Verbi prædicationem est attendendum. Et sane miseros istos oporteret diligentius hæc intueri, animadvertentes ex duobus istis alterum tantum hanc esse gratiam à Domino consequutum: & licet Domini misericordiæ sint immensæ, non esse tamen eas contemptorum propterias, qui dicunt, Peccemus, ut gratia fiat auctior.
units.tr: On the other hand, conversely, let those who harden themselves in sin and always put off amendment take care not to abuse this example as a bad excuse for living as they please, waiting until God addresses them inwardly. For we must attend to the ordinary calling, which comes through the preaching of the Word. Indeed, these wretched men ought to consider these two cases more carefully, noticing that of the two only one obtained this grace from the Lord; and although the mercies of the Lord are immense, they are not for the sake of those who despise them and say, Let us sin, that grace may abound.

units.la: Sola igitur extraordinaria Dei gratia tantam differentiam effecit, quæ illustrior est ex collatione pœnitentiæ unius, & alterius indurationis, quæ sane digna sunt diligenti & speciali consideratione, ut in illo quidem vere electionis notas ad salutem agnoscamus, quas ad vsum nostrum referamus, ita miserete Domino: & in hoc horrendum exemplum reprobationis quod pro virili nostra fugiamus. Satis igitur copiose docuimus in historia Iudæ proditoris, veram Respiscentiam per quam Deus suos electos ad remissionem peccatorum & vitam æternam adducit, primùm esse positam in vero peccati odio, deinde in peccatorum sincera tum apud Deum tum apud proximos agnitione : ac tandem etiam in bene intellecta satisfactione. Age igitur, expendamus an haec in virum iltum omnia conueniant.
units.tr: Therefore extraordinary grace alone made so great a difference, and this is more clearly seen by comparing the repentance of the one with the hardening of the other. These things certainly deserve careful and special consideration: in the one we recognise the true marks of election unto salvation, which we should apply to our own use, and so we should have mercy on the Lord; and in the other we should flee, as far as we can, the dreadful example of reprobation. We have therefore taught sufficiently at length in the history of Judas the traitor that true repentance, through which God brings his elect to the forgiveness of sins and eternal life, is founded first in a true hatred of sin, then in a sincere acknowledgment of sins both before God and before our neighbours, and finally also in a rightly understood satisfaction. Come, then, let us weigh whether all these things agree with this man.

units.la: Ac primum quidem quinam melius eum potuisse dixerimus sua latrocinia odisse & detestari quàm iis tam expressè, tam in fe quam in socio condemnatis? Quinam vero melius illa sibi displicere testaretur non quidem metu poenae quam iam patiebatur, sed quòd in iis esset Deus offensus, quàm dum socium reprehendit tam parum cum timere Deum quàm homines antea metuissset : & quidem quum in maximo supplicii cruciatu, quod se merito pati fatetur, tam patiens est, vt eo respectu nullum solamen magis postulet quàm si nullum dolorem pateretur? Quam vero magis expressam publicam confessionem edidisset, quàm apud eum quem coram populo inuocabat tam expressis verbis editam? Nec enim habebat potestatem vitam iis quos iugulauerat,aut facultates quibus alios spoliarat restituendi. Quod potuit igitur, fecit, à Deo veniam & ab hominibus petens, apertè & palàm se iuste puniri professus. Quòd ad satisfactionem autem attinet pro peccatis apud Deum, verè ex hoc misero latrone conuerso discere nos oportet sine pudore, nec in nobis, nec in Angelis, nec in rebus vllis creatis eam reperiri: sed in eo vnico cuius se memoriae supplex commendauit, & qui supra
units.tr: And first, who could we say had better hated and detested his robberies than he, who condemned them so plainly, both in himself and in his companion? And who could more truly show that he was displeased with them, not indeed from fear of the punishment he was already suffering, but because God was offended by them, than he who rebuked his companion, having himself so little fear of God as he had before of men? And indeed, though in the greatest torment of punishment, which he confesses he suffers justly, he is so patient that in that respect he asks for no comfort more than if he suffered no pain at all. And what more open public confession could he have made than this one, uttered in such express words before him whom he invoked in the sight of the people? For he had no power to restore life to those he had slain, or the goods with which he had plundered others. So he did what he could, seeking pardon from God and from men, and openly and publicly professing that he was justly punished. As for satisfaction for sins before God, we ought to learn without shame from this wretched thief, now converted, that it is found neither in us, nor in angels, nor in any created things, but in that one alone, to whose memory he commended himself as a suppliant, and who [bore our sins upon the tree].

units.la: Hom. XXXI. Th. Bezae.
units.tr: Homily XXXI. Th. Beza.

units.la: supra lignum peccata nostra tulit.Porrò, quî-nam, obsecro, cœlestem beatitudinem à Christo postulauisset, quem suis oculis tam miserum intuebatur, nisi verum Deum Ho-minem esse sibi persuasisset? Quis verò tan-tum mysterium illum docuit, de quo disci-puli adhuc dubitabant? Addamus ad supe-riora, zelum gloriæ Dei, quem miser hic tam breui tempore & modo ineffabili conuersus pené incredibilem ostendit, non solùm in socio reprehendendo susceptam Iesu Christi innocentiæ defensione: sed etiam in tam aperte & liberè accusatoribus ipsius, Iudicibus, Gubernatoribus, Sacerdotibus, Scribis & Pharisæis & vniuerso populo dam-nandis in omnibus quæ aduersus eum fe-cerant, dixerant & tunc adhuc exequeban-tur. Quis verò tantus hic prædicator coram omnibus,eorum quæ de regno spirituali & æterno discipuli nondum à suo præceptore discere potuerât? Quantus hic animarum im-mortalitatis concionator, de qua tam multæ sunt Philosophorû disputationes: & corporû resurrectionis aduersus Sadducæos,contrariû in ipso Dei populo docentes? Act. 23. 8. Nisi enim animæ immortalitatem & corporis Ie-su Christi resurrectionè sperasset, qua ratione sese illi cómendasset quem iam iam animâ ef-flaturû aspiceret? Et de quo,quæso, regno lo-quutus esset? Huc igitur accedite nō repugnâ-tes Apostoli,& hunc miserum latroné aguo-scite lōgè fuisse diligentioré & magis docilem auditorem in schola communis vestri Magistri, tam exiguo temporis momento, & in medio densissimarum exinanitionis ipsius tenebrarum, quàm vos fueritis spatio trium annorum, eum tum publice tum priuatim audientes, dum se aduersus suos inimicos tueretur, suaeque diuinae Maiestatis radios tot editis miraculis iacularetur. Quot igitur hic res mirandae aliae aliis cumulatae? Quòd si Dominus noster Iesus Christus in spontaneae suae exinanitionis summis angustiis tam potenter operatus est, quid non facturus est ad suorum electorum salutem, & suorum hostium confusionem, iam quum ad dextram Patris sedet, omnem potestatem in coelo & terra ad suae Ecclesiae salutem habens? Et quidem modò huius viri conuersionem imitemur.
units.tr: Bore our sins upon the tree. Moreover, I beg you, how could he have asked heavenly blessedness from Christ, whom he saw with his own eyes in such misery, unless he had been persuaded that he was the true God and Man? And who had taught him that mystery, about which the disciples were still doubting? Let us add to what has been said the zeal for the glory of God, which this man, converted in so short a time and in an ineffable manner, showed almost incredibly: not only in rebuking his companion, undertaking the defence of the innocence of Jesus Christ, but also in condemning, so openly and freely, his accusers, the judges, governors, priests, scribes and Pharisees, and the whole people, for all the things they had done, said, and were still carrying out against him. And who was so great a preacher before all of them, teaching about the spiritual and eternal kingdom, which the disciples had not yet been able to learn from their teacher? How great a preacher of the immortality of souls was he, about which there are so many disputations of the philosophers, and of the resurrection of bodies, against the Sadducees, who teach the contrary in the very people of God (Acts 23:8)? For unless he had hoped for the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the body of Jesus Christ, by what reasoning would he have commended himself to him whom he saw about to breathe out his soul? And of what kingdom, I ask, would he have spoken? Come here, then, you Apostles, not resisting, and acknowledge that this wretched thief, in the brief moment of time and in the midst of the very dense darkness of his emptying, was a far more diligent and more teachable hearer in the school of your common Master, than you were in the space of three years, hearing him both publicly and privately, while he defended himself against his enemies and hurled the rays of his divine majesty through so many miracles. What wonderful things, then, are heaped one upon another here? And if our Lord Jesus Christ worked so powerfully in the greatest straits of his voluntary emptying, what will he not do for the salvation of his elect and the confusion of his enemies, now that he sits at the right hand of the Father, having all power in heaven and on earth for the salvation of his Church? And indeed, let us now imitate the conversion of this man.

units.la: Agite igitur omnes ad huius tanti doctoris scholam frequentes accedamus, immo accuramus, ex quo tot insignia mysteria Euangelij tam paucis verbis comprehensa discamus. Regem illum aeternum, iam in regnum suum, in illud nos secum tracturum per Crucem ingressum confiteamur, adoremus, & ore & corde supplices invocemus. Pudeat nos nostri, considerantes quantum tam exiguo tempore, & contra omnia sensuum suorum obiecta hic vir profecerit, quum tot iam anni labantur, ex quibus, non quidem in Cruce pendens Christus, sed in gloriam suam receptus, non desistit nec desinit adhuc nos docere, hortari, orare ut sibi reconciliemur, nec tamen adhuc ei satis attentas aures præbuerimus? Discamus etiam ab illo quanto zelo flagrarit ad Dei gloriam, & Domini nostri Iesu Christi honorem tuendum aduersus primariæ dignitatis qui præfentes aderant viros, ipsorum quos tunc patiebatur, cruciatuum sensum etiam amittens: quum tamen glacie frigidiores fimus, quando de Dei gloria agitur: & igne feruétiores quum aut de nostro honore aut de rebus istis caducis agitur. Obseruemus præterea in hoc viro tam ingenuam & apertam ac sincera-ram peccatorum confessionem ab ipso coram Deo & hominibus editam, quum tamen vix ad aliquam femioris confessionem, certissimis etiam indiciis adducamur. Dominũ, inquam, supplices oremus vt quam in Iesu Christo tantam fidé hic habuit contra omne humanũ indicium, imitemur, quum in nobis tam exigua fit & pene nulla, quibus fe tamen in cœlis regnans ostendit, cum omni potestate in cœlo & terra. Eum etiam insequamur in tanta tamque firma ipsius spe, in eo quem iam iam animam efflaturum in Cruce videbat: quum tam segnes ac remissi fimus in spe in eum figenda qui à mortuis suscitatus in cœlos ascendit: denique precemur vt eius charitatem tam liberalem palàm testatam in socio reprehenden-do, sectemur, pro eo quod alij alius ad perditionem adulamur, & mutuò scabimus.
units.tr: Come then, all of you, let us approach in crowds to the school of this great teacher, or rather let us hasten to it, so that from it we may learn the remarkable mysteries of the Gospel, comprehended in so few words. Let us confess, adore, and with mouth and heart humbly call upon that eternal King, who has now entered into his kingdom through the Cross and will draw us with him into it. Let us be ashamed of ourselves, considering how much this man has advanced in so short a time, and against all the objections of his senses. So many years have now slipped away, during which Christ, no longer hanging on the Cross but received into his glory, has not ceased and does not cease to teach, exhort and beseech us to be reconciled to him, and yet we have not yet given him attentive ears. Let us also learn from him with what zeal he burned to defend the glory of God and the honour of our Lord Jesus Christ against the men of the highest rank who were present, even while he lost all feeling of the torments he was then suffering. Yet we are colder than ice when the glory of God is at stake, and hotter than fire when our own honour or these fleeting things are in question. Furthermore, let us observe in this man so frank, open and sincere a confession of sins, made by him before God and men, when we are scarcely brought to any confession of our own, even with the most certain indications. I say, let us humbly pray the Lord that we may imitate the great faith he had in Jesus Christ against all human judgement, when in us it is so small and almost nothing, although he shows himself reigning in heaven with all power in heaven and on earth. Let us also follow him in so great and so firm a hope in him, whom he saw about to breathe out his soul on the Cross, when we are so slack and careless in fixing our hope on him who, raised from the dead, ascended into the heavens. Finally, let us pray that we may follow his charity, so generously displayed, in rebuking a companion, whereas we flatter one another to destruction and bite and devour one another in turn.

units.la: Transeamus ad Domini nostri Iesu Christi tam gratiosum & benignum, tamque simul magnificum responsum, in quo primum con-
units.tr: Let us pass on to the Lord Jesus Christ's response, so gracious and kind and at the same time so magnificent, in which first ...

units.la: fideranda est immensa nostri Seruatoris mansuetudo & ineffabilis promptitudo in audiendis iis qui ipsum vera fide & non ficto corde inuocant, adeo vt vix verus iste Resipiscens inuocare coeperit hunc Regem gloriae, licet in Cruce cum maximis corporis & animae doloribus colluctantem, quin sit exauditus ab ipso, quod Dauidi contigit. 2. Sam. 12. 13. cuius semorem & gratum testatur Psal. 32. 5. Non tamen propterea quaecunque quicunque petunt a Domino statim accipiunt, & quidem multis de causis. Nam saepe Deus preces non exaudit, aut quia nescimus quid petamus, Matth. 20. 22. aut quia male petimus. Iac. 4. 3. aut quia nobis ipsis imponentes nocitura petimus, etsi ad bonum finem nostra feretur intentio, quod etiam ipsi Apostolo contigisse videmus. 2. Cor. 12. 7. adeo vt non exauditae preces sint potius testimonium bonitatis Dei quam furoris ipsius. Nonnunquam etiam licet a Deo petenda petamus, & Deus illa nobis concedere petentibus decreuerit, tamen ea differt, & quidem aliquado tam diu vt nullas aures quibus nos audiat habere videatur, cuius sane rei permulta passim exempla in Psalmis occurrunt, adeo quidem vt aliquando sanctos in eiusmodi probationibus videamus verbis vsos modum excedentibus. Verum eiusmodi voces minime nec ab incredulitate nec a profana impatientia profectae sunt. Et ita quidem nobiscum agere Dominum oportet, primum quod apud se non tantum quod daturus est, sed etiam tempora & momcta quibus est daturus definiuit.Deinde quòd ita nostram negligentiam excitare,& fidem & spem vult acuere. Tertiò quòd quæ tam facilè obtinentur & sine difficultate, non tanti æstimantur quanti par est. Idcirco plerumque oportet vt illa nobis charius, vt ita dicam,vendat, vt ipsius dona sint nobis instar pluuiæ quæ mitis & densa guttatim in terras demissa magis eas liquefacit & fœcundat quàm in eas decidentes imbres ac nimbi vehementiores. Deniq;,vt acceptis ab ipso quæ benigna manu concesserit, memores eorum simus & quandiu vita supererit vnde prouenerint agnoscamus,ab eius nimirum gratia & mera liberalitate.In summa, licet Dominus velit aliquando nos velut importunos esse in precando,ob causas quas superius diximus, & vt ipse Christus docet,Luc. 18.5. tamen quum ipsemet in cor & os nostrum preces immittat quibus eum sumus interpellaturi , fatendum est illius esse partes semper priores, & longè illum esse ad nos exaudiendos quàm nos ad cū inuocandum promptiorem: & pastorem ab oue aberrante non quæri, sed à pastore contrà aberrantem quæri & inueniri,Matth.18.12.
units.tr: Here must be considered the immense gentleness of our Saviour and his unspeakable readiness to hear those who call upon him in true faith and with an unfeigned heart. So it is that this true penitent had scarcely begun to call upon this King of glory, although he was struggling on the Cross with the greatest pains of body and soul, before he was heard by him, just as happened to David (2 Sam. 12:13), whose joy and gratitude he bears witness to in Psalm 32:5. Yet for many reasons the Lord does not at once grant whatever anyone asks of him. For God often does not hear prayers, either because we do not know what we ask (Matt. 20:22), or because we ask amiss (James 4:3), or because we ask for things that would harm us, even though our intention is directed to a good end, as we see happened to the Apostle himself (2 Cor. 12:7). So unanswered prayers are rather a testimony of God's goodness than of his wrath. Sometimes too, although we ask for things that ought to be asked of God, and God has decided to grant them to us when we ask, nevertheless he delays them, and sometimes so long that he seems to have no ears with which to hear us. Indeed, many examples of this are found everywhere in the Psalms, so much so that at times we see the saints, in such trials, using words that exceed due measure. Yet such cries did not arise from unbelief or from profane impatience. And indeed the Lord ought to deal with us in this way: first, because he has settled within himself not only what he will give, but also the times and moments at which he will give it. Second, because he wills in this way to rouse our negligence and to sharpen our faith and hope. Third, because things that are obtained so easily and without difficulty are not valued as highly as they should be. Therefore it is often necessary for him to sell them, as it were, more dearly to us, so that his gifts may be to us like rain, which, falling gently and thickly drop by drop, softens and fertilises the earth more than heavier showers and storms falling upon it. Finally, having received from him what he has granted with a kindly hand, we should remember them and acknowledge, as long as life remains, whence they came, namely from his grace and pure liberality. In sum, although the Lord sometimes wishes us to be, as it were, importunate in praying, for the reasons we have mentioned above, and as Christ himself teaches (Luke 18:5), nevertheless, since he himself puts into our heart and mouth the prayers by which we are to entreat him, it must be confessed that the initiative always belongs to him, and that he is far readier to hear us than we are to call upon him. And the shepherd does not seek the sheep that has strayed; rather, the sheep that has strayed is sought and found by the shepherd (Matt. 18:12).

units.la: Et hoc ipsum sanè quotidie experimur, quandoquidem ipse nobis prior aures ad audiendum largitur, os nostrum ad loquendum aperit,manus dat quibus fores pulsemus, & pedes quibus in eius semitis incedamus.At si Dominus noster Iesus Christus dum adhuc aduersus mortis & iræ Dei terrores luctaretur petenti latroni tam promptu praestitit auxilium, quid non facturum eum pro suis in genere & singulis priuatim putamus, nisi per nos ipsos steterit, nunc quum in gloriae suae plenam pos-sessionem victor ingressus est, nomen adeptus quod est supra omne nomen? Agite igitur, fra-tres, calamitosis iitis, si alias vnquam, tempo-ribus, cum supplicibus & ardentibus votis in-terpellemus, vt sedatis tempestatibus tran-quillitatem nobis reuehat, non vt nostris com-modis studeamus, sed vt sanctum eius Nomen agnoscatur, & miseri ipsius filij, sub alarum e-ius tecti praesidio, ea quam expedire nouit pa-ce & quiete fruentes, debitum illi honorem & gloriam exhibeant: Harum omnium autem tempestatum ac procellarum diuturnitatem, horum quidem rebellioni, aliorum autem tar-ditati ascribamus.
units.tr: Indeed we experience this every day, since he first grants us ears to hear, opens our mouth to speak, gives us hands with which to knock at his doors, and feet with which to walk in his paths. But if our Lord Jesus Christ, while he was still struggling against the terrors of death and the wrath of God, so promptly gave help to the robber who asked it, what do we think he will not do for his people, both in general and individually, unless we ourselves stand in the way, now that he has entered, as victor, into the full possession of his glory and has obtained the name which is above every name? Come then, brothers, in these calamitous times, if ever, let us entreat him with suppliant and fervent prayers to calm the storms and restore tranquillity to us. Let us not seek our own advantage, but that his holy name may be acknowledged, and that his wretched sons, under the protection of his wings, enjoying the peace and quiet he knows to be expedient, may render him the honour and glory due. But the long duration of all these tempests and storms let us ascribe to the rebellion of some and the slowness of others.

units.la: Iam vero quae tam prompte Rex noster iste Crucifixus Poenitenti concesserit age perpen-damus. Vno verbo dico dedisse ipsi quae po-stulauit, & quidem adhuc expressius quam po-stulauerit, beneficium, inquam, Dei filiorum proprium, vitam aeternam per gratuitam pec-catorum remissionem, qui post Dei gloriam verus precum nostrarum est scopus. Nam be-neficia quidem Dei terrena haec & caduca, Deus, qui Solem suum super bonos & malos oriri facit, copiose & abundanter impiis largitur: licet ipsis in maiorem condemnatio-nem ac iudicium cedant. Sed quae hic conuer-sus latro consequitur, filiorum est portio hæreditas vt Dauid loquitur Psal. 16. 5. & 17. 14. & 15. & alibi. Quid igitur ab ipso postula-uerat?Non vt saluus & incolumis Crucis sup-plicio eximeretur, vt per conuitium socius eius flagitarat: non vt dolores leniret aut bre-uiores faceret: sed vt eius memor esset, non quidem in hoc mundo, non in hac vita,cuius imminentem exitum & futũ & eius quem o-rabat intuebatur, sed in alia vita:in qua mini-mè se ei facit æquale qui Rex eius est, sed tan-tùm sein subditorum eius numerum admitti supplex orat.Non igitur frustrà dixi nobis hic excellentissimum exemplar proponi ad quod preces nostras componamus. Minimè tamen propterea concludendum à nobis quandiu in his terris degimus non orandum esse Deum vt quæ ad caducæ huius vitæ transigendum curriculum necessaria sunt, etiam vsque ad frustulum panis benigna manu nobis largia-tur,quod sedulò nos facere quotidiana Domi-nica precatio docet. At quum hic satis cogni-tum haberet hanc vitam iamiam finiendam, velut extra mundum vno saltu, præteritis e-tiam doloribus exiliit, ad Regem hunc æter-num solum considerandum, & cũ eius gratia & fauore ex terris excedendum. Et reuera pre-ces quibus res nobis necessarias à Domino fla-gitamus quandiu in his terris degimus, sic o-portet à nobis componi, vt vltimus earum fi-nis sit Regni Dei propagatio, quum non pro-prie vitam hic nobis concedi postulemus quò viuamus, sed quò viuentes ei seruiamus, cum
units.tr: Now let us weigh carefully what our crucified King granted so readily to the penitent. In one word, I say, he gave him what he asked, and indeed more fully than he had asked: the benefit proper to the sons of God, eternal life, through the free forgiveness of sins, which, after the glory of God, is the true aim of our prayers. For God, who makes his sun rise on the good and the bad, indeed bestows earthly and perishable blessings abundantly and lavishly on the impious, although these turn to their greater condemnation and judgement. But the inheritance which this converted robber obtains is the portion of the sons, as David says (Ps. 16:5; 17:14–15) and elsewhere. What then had he asked of him? Not that he should be saved and kept safe from the punishment of the Cross, as his companion had demanded with insults; not that he should soften or shorten his pains; but that he should remember him, not indeed in this world, not in this life, whose imminent end, both his own and that of the one he was praying to, he was looking upon, but in another life, in which he does not make himself equal to him who is his King, but only humbly begs to be numbered among his subjects. Therefore I have not said in vain that here an most excellent pattern is set before us, to which we should shape our prayers. Yet we must by no means conclude from this that, as long as we dwell on this earth, we ought not to pray God to grant us, with a kindly hand, even as far as a morsel of bread, whatever is necessary for finishing the course of this fleeting life, which the daily prayer of the Lord's Prayer teaches us to do diligently. But since this man had sufficiently recognised that this life was about to end at any moment, he leapt out of the world, as it were in one bound, passing over even his pains, to consider this eternal King alone, and to depart from the earth with his grace and favour. And indeed, the prayers by which we ask the Lord for the things we need as long as we dwell on this earth ought to be so framed that their final aim is the extension of the kingdom of God, since we ask that life be granted to us here not properly so that we may live, but so that, living, we may serve him ...

units.la: Dd. j. deinceps ex hac vita excedentes in perpetuum adoraturi.
units.tr: Dd. j. Henceforth, departing from this life, they will worship forever.

units.la: Cæterùm hic etiam locus nos admonet, liceat peculiares liberationes ex variis huius vitæ periculis & calamitatibus, electos oportear totidé habere certissima testimonia paternæ Dei curæ in suis aduersus pericula protegendis, vt Psalm.34.8. & 11.copiosè docemur,non tamen his notis reprobos ab electis distingui, quia de re nos etiam Sapiens admonet Eccles. 9.1.Exempli gratia: Filij Dei exterior conditio cadé est immo longè deteriôr duorum illorum latronum conditione: & tamen is est in quo solo vera omnis benedictio posita est. Sic Dei Filij,vt loquitur Apostolus.1. Cor.4.13.mundi purgamenta & sordes facti sunt:& tamen beatissimi sunt, quibus datum est non solùm in Deum credere, sed etiam pro eo affligi. Phil.1. 29. adeò vt Apostolus vnica Christi cruce velit gloriari.Gal.6.14. Dicamus de iis qui debitas peccatis pœnas luunt.An vt de perditis hominibus sentiendū arbitrabimur?Næ si fecerimus, mendacium nobis impinget,qui eadem cum socio pœnas merito luebat, & in iisdem extrinsecus cum socio mortuus est, & tamen tanto felicior quantò eius socius detestabilior.Peccata igitur semper & in aliis & in nobis condemnabimus. At qui in Dei castigationibus proficit non ideò tamen infelix dicendus est,sed potiùs felix,quem Deus castigatum se amare docuit.Cauendum igitur summopere ne alij de aliis ex rebus externis iudicium fera-
units.tr: Moreover, this passage also reminds us that although the elect ought to have, in the special deliverances from the various perils and calamities of this life, as many most certain testimonies of God's fatherly care in protecting them from danger (as we are taught at length in Ps. 34:8 and 11), these signs do not distinguish the reprobate from the elect, as the Wise Man also warns us on this very matter, Eccles. 9:1. For example: the outward condition of the Son of God was common, indeed far worse than the condition of those two thieves, and yet he is the one in whom alone all true blessing lies. So too, as the Apostle says, the sons of God have been made the filth and off-scouring of the world (1 Cor. 4:13), and yet they are most blessed, to whom it has been given not only to believe in God but also to suffer for him (Phil. 1:29), so much so that the Apostle wishes to glory in the cross of Christ alone (Gal. 6:14). Let us speak of those who pay the penalties due for their sins. Shall we think of them as lost men? If we do, we will be lying, for the one who was rightly paying the same penalty as his companion, and who died outwardly in the same way as his companion, was so much happier as his companion was more detestable. We shall therefore always condemn sins, both in others and in ourselves. But one who makes progress under God's chastisements should not therefore be called unhappy; rather he is happy, since God has taught that he loves those whom he chastises. Therefore we must take the greatest care that no one passes judgement on another from external circumstances.

units.la: Differentia electionis & reprobationis non est positâ in statu exteriore nec vitæ istius nec mortis. mus: cuius rei testis esto inter Iobum & amicos hac de re coorta contentio, & quod Propheta Psal.39.11.& 73.de seipso testatur.
units.tr: The difference between election and reprobation does not lie in the outward state, either of this life or of death. Let the contest that arose between Job and his friends on this very matter be witness to this, and also what the Prophet testifies of himself in Ps. 39:11 and 73.

units.la: Iam vero singulas Domini voces sigillatim expendamus. Eris, inquit, vbi? In Paradiso. Quando? Hodie. Quo statu? Mecum.
