Si vero derelictus non est, qua conscientia non modo sic loquutus erit, sed etiam magnavoce vociferatus vt ab omnibus eum circumstantibus exaudiretur? Magnae profecto, fratres sunt hae difficultates, quas ipse sacro suo verbo euoluat & nos doceat oportet, vt iis non modo non offendamur, sed contrà potius aedificemur, quum non sine magnis & grauibus causis Dominus vocem istam ab omnibus exaudiri voluerit: & magnopere metuendum fit ne in sententiam illam incurramus quam aduersus eos qui offendiculum ab eo patientur pronuntiat, Luc.7.23.
units.tr: Given these things, the explanation becomes easier of that pitiable and astonishing complaint of our Lord Jesus Christ shortly before he sent forth the Spirit. It is astonishing, I say, because at first sight it seems directly and diametrically to contradict all that we must believe about Christ and seek in him. For someone might say, if these things are not well understood, that this complaint proceeded from nothing but an indignant mind. But if he was indignant, whose obedience would be called voluntary? And if it was not voluntary, how would it have atoned for our rebellion? Moreover, how could he have been forsaken by the Father, and indeed forsaken even by himself and by the Holy Spirit, since God is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit? If that is so, who will be our Saviour, since our salvation truly and properly proceeds from the one God, who effects for us the life-giving death of our Redeemer? But if he was not forsaken, with what conscience would he not only have spoken thus, but also cried out with a loud voice so that he might be heard by all standing around? Brethren, these difficulties are indeed great, and he must unfold them by his holy Word and teach us, so that we are not offended by them but rather built up, since the Lord willed this voice to be heard by all not without great and weighty causes. We must greatly fear lest we fall under that sentence which he pronounces against those who take offence at him, Luke 7:23.

units.la: In primis igitur hoc positum esto, vocibus istis non exprobrationem, non indignati animi auersationem contineri, quasi Iesus Christus cum Patre contenderet, & rationem huius tra-ctationis exposceret (nec enim ad eum vt Deū suum, & quidē iterata voce Dei sui, se conuer-teret) sed lamentabilem esse vocem animi in summis angustiis positi, & quidem Filij ad Pa-tris omnia iussa obsequentissimi, sed qui sci-psum in hoc agone dum intuetur, putat nisi aliunde auxilium sibi feratur, fore prorsus imparem tanto ferendo oneri, & quæ sibi es-sent imposita perficiendi & ad optatum finem deducendi, quasi Patrem his vocibus compel-laret, Euge Pater, adsum & quidem volens in eo statu in quo esse me voluisti, sed furoris tui sensus hos gemitus extorquet, dum miror qui fieri possit, vt nullam sentiam tui fauoris & vir tutis præsentiam, sine qua tamen quod tu in me vis efficere, & ego volens ac sponte in o-mnibus tibi parere cupio, nunquam suum for-tiri possit exitum.
units.tr: First of all, let this be laid down: these words contain no reproach and no indignant turning away of mind, as if Jesus Christ were contending with the Father and demanding an account of this treatment. He did not turn to him as his God, and indeed not with a repeated cry of "my God." Rather, these are the lamentable words of a mind placed in the greatest distress, and indeed of a Son most obedient to all the Father's commands. Yet while he looks at himself in this contest, he thinks that unless help is brought to him from elsewhere, he will be utterly unequal to bearing so great a burden and to accomplishing what has been laid upon him and bringing it to the desired end. It is as if he were addressing the Father with these words: "Well done, Father, I am here, and indeed willingly, in the state in which you wished me to be. But the sense of your wrath wrings out these groans, while I wonder how it can be that I feel no presence of your favour and power. Without that, what you wish to effect in me, and what I, willingly and spontaneously, desire to obey you in all things, can never reach its outcome."

units.la: Ab hoc igitur puro & integro fonte querela ista manauit, iam olim à Dauide totidē verbis dictata, de seipso etiam in maximis suis angu-stiis verba faciente Psal. 22. 1.sed tanquam Iesu Christifigura, quod ex psalmi reliqua parte fit conspicuum. Obiter autem magna inæqualitas hac in parte inter figuram & veritatem est obseruanda. Nam Dauidis huc Psalmum scribentis afflictissimus & calamitosissimus status, infinitis partibus erat inferior passionibus quas in Cruce Christus patiebatur, siue causam, siue mensuram, siue etiam effecta consideremus. Praeterea, licet Dauid non sine fide & spe preces illas fuderit, tamen, quod in perfectissimorum etiam Dei filiorum optimis operibus cotingit, humanum aliquid passus est, ac proinde reliquiae superfuerunt vitiositatis, quum fides nostra semper incredulitate mixta sit, & spes aliquo diffidentiae gradu. At in Christo, qui sine vitio passiones nostras omnes animales induerat, sine vitio & imperfectione, ista sicut & reliqua ipsius tum dicta tum facta fuerunt. Sic aute ad primam difficultate respondum elto.
units.tr: From this pure and unmixed fountain this complaint flowed. David had spoken it long ago in the same words, speaking of himself in his greatest distress, Psalm 22:1, but as a figure of Jesus Christ, as is evident from the rest of the psalm. Incidentally, a great inequality between figure and truth is to be observed in this part. For the most afflicted and calamitous state of David in writing this psalm was infinitely inferior to the sufferings which Christ endured on the cross, whether we consider their cause, their measure, or their effects. Moreover, although David poured out those prayers not without faith and hope, yet, as happens even in the best works of the most perfect sons of God, he suffered something human, and so remnants of imperfection remained, since our faith is always mixed with unbelief and our hope with some degree of distrust. But in Christ, who had taken on all our natural passions without sin, these things, like his other words and deeds, occurred without fault or imperfection. Thus, let the first difficulty be answered.

units.la: Ad secundam, in qua videri possit Christus a semetipso & Spiritu Sancto non minus quam Pater derelictus, quandoquidem singulae Trinitatis personae sunt vnus & idem Deus, non magis est necessaria consecutio, quam si quis dixerit Patrem & Sp.S. assumpsisse naturam nostram, sicut Filius, quod etiam veteres quidam haeretici docuerunt, quod tamen est salsissimum. Sola enim Filij persona se nobis vniuit, non tamen a Patre nec Sp.S. propterea diuisa sed tantum distincta: quod mylterium a nobis potius adorandum quam penitius extra verbi Dei cancellos scrutandum, & cauendum summopere ne Altissimum faciaciamus rebus creatis similem, quod graui oratione Dominus populo suo per Esaiam exprobrat, Esai. 46. 5.
units.tr: As to the second, in which it might seem that Christ was forsaken by himself and by the Holy Spirit no less than by the Father, since the individual persons of the Trinity are one and the same God, the inference is no more necessary than if someone said that the Father and the Holy Spirit assumed our nature just as the Son did. Some ancient heretics also taught this, yet it is most false. For the person of the Son alone united himself to us, not, however, separated from the Father or the Holy Spirit, but only distinguished from them. This is a mystery which we ought rather to adore than to probe too curiously beyond the bounds of God's Word. We must take great care not to make the Most High like created things, which the Lord rebukes his people for in a grave saying through Isaiah, Isaiah 46:5.

units.la: Harum autem tantarum difficultatum solutio in primis posita est in huius vocis DERELINQVERE consideratione, quam quum expresserit Iesus Christus suae humanitatis dignitate consideratae respectu, cauendum est ut putemus sic accipiendam quasi Pater aut Spiritus, in hoc Filij sacrificio, fuissent ab eius Deitate separati: quod profecto nunquam potuisset contingere, quum personae tres sint unus idemque essentiae infinitae Deus: nec quasi Pater aut Spiritus Sanctus, aut Filij Deitas separati fuisset ab humanitate, quam sibi Filius personaliter vniuit. Nam si morte dissoluta fuisset vnio personalis, humanitas morte obruta permansisset, tantum abest vt hac morte vindicati & in libertatem asserti vitam agere queremur. Intelligendam igitur vocem illam dicimus, quo modo saepe dicitur Deus ad nos vel accedere vel recedere, nouisse nos aut non nouisse, fauoris nimirum ipsius & specialis praesentiae respectu. Dicemus igitur intrepide in hac lucta naturam nostram in Iesu Christi persona manisse & manuram in perpetuum inseparabilem a Patre & Spiritu Sancto: sed quod ad fauorem & specialem praesentiam Deitatis, qua eximeretur sensui horrendo & obstupendo indignationis Dei aduersus peccata nostra, quae voluit in nostro sponsore poenis acerbissimis vindicare, oportuit eam ad tempus
units.tr: The solution of these great difficulties is set out first in a consideration of the word FORSAKE. Although Jesus Christ expressed it with respect to his humanity considered in its dignity, we must take care not to think it is to be understood as if the Father or the Spirit had been separated from his Deity in this sacrifice of the Son. That could never have happened, since the three persons are one and the same infinite God. Nor is it to be understood as if the Father, or the Holy Spirit, or the Deity of the Son, had been separated from the humanity which the Son personally united to himself. For if the personal union had been dissolved by death, the humanity, overwhelmed by death, would have remained, so far from our being freed by this death and set at liberty to live. We say, therefore, that the word is to be understood as it is often said that God draws near to us or withdraws, that he knows us or does not know us, namely with respect to his favour and special presence. We will say boldly, then, that in this struggle our nature remained in the person of Jesus Christ and will remain forever inseparable from the Father and the Holy Spirit. But as to the favour and special presence of the Deity, by which he would have been exempted from the dreadful and stunning sense of God's indignation against our sins, which God willed to punish in our surety with the most bitter penalties, it was necessary for it to be withdrawn for a time.

units.la: FFj. omni fauore & præsenti auxilio Deitatis destitu- tuj,nisi quantum opus erat nein hoc certamine succumberet. Et hoc ipsum veteres optimè & admodum proprie dixerunt,in hac pro peccatis satisfactione, Deitatem veluti quiescentem, idest suam operationem ob causas superius allatas non exeruisse: quod etiam in nobis experimur, quodammodo sopito corpore non tamen essentialiter animam separari,sed nihilominus suas actiones vt vigilante corpore non exercere, hoc excepto quòd intus vitam animalem fouet: qua in re posita est differentia inter viuum corpus somno sopitum, & cadauer.
units.tr: Deprived of all favour and present help of the Deity, except as much as was needed so that he would not succumb in this struggle. The ancients said this very thing most excellently and quite properly: in this satisfaction for sins the Deity lay, as it were, at rest, that is, for the reasons given above it did not put forth its operation. We experience something similar in ourselves: when the body is in some measure lulled to sleep, the soul is not essentially separated from it, yet it does not exercise its actions as it does when the body is awake, except that it still sustains animal life within. In this lies the difference between a living body sunk in sleep and a corpse.

units.la: At si,ad nostram salutem,qui nullum in se peccatū habebat,nec ipse debitor erat, in tantas pro nobis angustias redactus est, vt hac vocem tam stupendam emiserit qua cœlum & terra concussa sunt: annon fatendum est de istis seriò nocte diéque non cogitantes, sed in flagitiis inhærentes, & suscitari non ferentes, saxeos esse & ipsis saxis duriores,quæ ante Domini cöspectum liquefiunt?Psalm. 68 9.& hodie propter hominum flagitia suspirant & vnà parturiunt tantisper dum vltimus ille dies adueniat:Rom.8.21.& 22.Ecquis autem tanti stuporis & indomitæ duritiei reus est? Non tantùm sanè qui aduersus Dei cognitionem quam ipsa mundi machina docet, sine alio documento speciali obdurescunt,Rom.1.18. & 1. Cor.1. 21.. Non etiam soli Iudæi quibus in laqueum vertitur cibus cœlestis,ipsis oblatus,quod olim
units.tr: But if he, who had no sin in himself and was not himself a debtor, was for our salvation reduced to such anguish on our behalf that he uttered that astonishing cry by which heaven and earth were shaken, must we not confess that those who do not think seriously of these things night and day, but cling to their wickedness and cannot bear to be stirred up, are stony, and harder than the very stones, which melt before the presence of the Lord? (Ps. 68:9.) Even today, on account of men's wickedness, creation groans and labours together until that last day comes (Rom. 8:21–22). Yet who is guilty of such stupor and untamed hardness? Not only, indeed, are those hardened who, against the knowledge of God which the very frame of the world teaches, harden themselves without any other special instruction (Rom. 1:18; 1 Cor. 1:21). Nor are the Jews alone, to whom the heavenly food, offered to them, is turned into a snare, as the prophet once threatened (Ps. 69:23).

units.la: Propheta comminatus erat, Psal. 69.23. Non etiam soli miseri illi in pseudoecclelia superstitiosi, non tantum ad Lucem Euangelicam oculos claudentes, sed etiā ne aliis Lux luceat pro sua virili impedientes, & ita quod Matth.23.13. dicitur ratum facientes. Verùm ij præcipuè sunt qui Spiritum Sanctum cōtristant, & conscientiæ suæ obduratione in dies in seipsis abolent salutis scientiam ad condemnationem ipsis à Deo patefactam, & aduersus sapientem incantatorem aures obturant, de quibus agitur Psal.58. Atque vtinam tam procul essent illi homines à nobis quærendi, quàm inter nos nimium multi sunt. Quando verò tandem de istis seriò cogitabitis? Quando tandem ferrea illa & adamantina corda mollientur? Quando nostris cordibus insculpta Dei mandata videbimus? Tu verò, Vanitas, quando tandem exulabis, ꝛebus melioribus ac sanctioribus intus & foris locū cedens? Auari, fœneratores, & quotquot ex aliorum incommodis lucrum captatis, quando tandem charitatem induetis? Gulosi & ebriosi, quando tandem erit vobis alius quam venter, Deus? Scortatores & adulteri quando castitatem sectabimini? Eheu! quàm vereor ne nunquā id aspiciam. Quum præsertim autem videam sacrosanctum istud verbum in tam steriles terras immitti, quid possum aliud quàm breui futuram exustionem metuere Heb. 6.8. Ecquis verò non animaduertit iam ante portas cœptum incendium, immo etiam intra ipsa vrbis pomœria? Quis verò hactenus Ff. ij. illud nisi mera Dei patientia cohibuit? Quid vero? En adhuc auribus nostris inclamantem Dei Filium, Meme adsum, qui in Cruce suum vociferatus me derelictum, ut vos Patri reci-piendos conciliarem: & quidem iam ante annos quinquaginta subinde nobis idipsum inculcantem: Me me qui clementissime vos missa fame & pestilentia castigaui: qui tam multas tempestates à vestris cervicibus ut ne grandinis ictu tangeremini depuli: qui tam multas iaculatas in vos sagittas fregi: qui gladium prius quàm admouerem ostentaui: qui aprum adhuc frænatum & capistratum teneo, vosne vero tadiu exspectare velle dum tandem vltimò vos ut Ierusalem olim meam abiiciam, & iisdem vocibus compellem, Abeo, non me amplius videbitis? Ne putate vero, fratres, hos sermones nugas esse: nam ipsa nos hac in parte satis sua quemque conscientia redarguit: Itaque oro vos & obsecro serio in posterum de iis cogitate. Iam enim, si vnquam, tempus est: Ne exspectate dum qui maior est corde nostro, immo qui omnem potestatem habet in cœlo & terra decretum suum ratum & immotum proferat & exequatur.
units.tr: Nor are those wretched men alone who are superstitious in the pseudo-church, not only closing their eyes to the Gospel light but also, as far as in them lies, hindering others from being illumined by it, and so making good what is said in Matt. 23:13. Rather, the chief offenders are those who grieve the Holy Spirit and, by hardening their conscience day by day, destroy in themselves the knowledge of salvation, which was revealed to them by God for their condemnation, and stop their ears against the wise charmer, of whom Ps. 58 speaks. And would that those men were as far from us as they are, alas, too numerous among us! But when will you at last think seriously about these things? When will those iron and adamantine hearts at last be softened? When shall we see the commandments of God engraved on our hearts? And you, Vanity, when at last will you be banished, giving place within and without to better and holier things? Misers, usurers, and all of you who seek gain from the troubles of others, when at last will you put on charity? Gluttons and drunkards, when at last will your god be something other than your belly? Whoremongers and adulterers, when at last will you pursue chastity? Alas! I fear greatly that I shall never see this. Especially since I see this most holy word sown in such barren lands, what can I fear except that burning will soon follow (Heb. 6:8)? And who does not notice that the fire has already begun before the gates, indeed even within the very walls of the city? And who has hitherto restrained it, except the mere patience of God? What more? Behold, the Son of God still cries out to our ears, "Here I am," he who on the cross cried out that he had been forsaken, so that he might reconcile you to the Father to be received; and indeed for fifty years now he has repeatedly pressed this same thing upon us: "I, I, who most mercifully chastised you by sending famine and pestilence; who drove away so many storms from your necks, so that you would not be touched by the blow of hail; who broke so many arrows shot against you; who displayed the sword before I brought it near; who still hold the boar restrained and muzzled. Will you then wish to wait so long, until at last I cast you off as once I cast off Jerusalem, and address you with these words: 'Depart; you will see me no more'?" Do not think, brothers, that these words are trifles; for each person's own conscience in this matter refutes him well enough. Therefore I pray and beseech you earnestly to think about these things from now on. For now, if ever, is the time. Do not wait until he who is greater than our heart, indeed he who has all power in heaven and on earth, brings forth and carries out his decree, fixed and unchangeable.

units.la: Et ne procul abeamus, huc nos quę sequuntur in hac historia ducunt, nempe, pro eo quod circumstantes ad hunc clamore & ipsum terræ motu oportuerat comoveri, ea si non omnes, saltem plerosque aliis quos decebat bono exemplo præire, in rixam conuertisse, occasionem captantes ex vocum Eliæ, & Eli seu Eloi allusione.
units.tr: And, not to go far afield, the things that follow in this history lead us here: namely, that although those standing around at this cry, and at the earthquake itself, ought to have been moved, they turned it, if not all, at least most of them, into a quarrel, rather than setting a good example to others whom it became to lead the way. They seized the occasion from the play on the words Elijah and Eli or Eloi.

units.la: Sacrosanctum Dei verbum in sales & risum conuersum. ne tum soni tum literarum, quorum nominum illud Prophetæ est, hoc autem idem est ac Deus Meus: flagitium sane quod sine horrore legi non poterit, quum non tantum in eum feratur ad cuius in Cruce conspectum saltem oportuerat durissimos quosque commoueri, sed etiamin Deū ipsum, cuius sacrosanctum verbum in risus & sales conuertebatur.
units.tr: The most holy word of God was turned into jokes and laughter, because of the sound and letters of the names: the name of the prophet is Elijah, while the other word means "my God." This is truly a wickedness that cannot be read without horror, since it is directed not only against him, at whose sight on the cross even the hardest hearts should have been moved, but also against God himself, whose most holy word was being turned into mockery and jests.

units.la: Atque ô vtinam perditorum istorum fobo-les cum istis interiisset. Sed, obsecro, quos hodie magis contemni, irrideri, salibus & dicteriis peti conspicimus? Nonne Dei filij sunt, tum vivi tum mortui? Dicam aliquid amplius, eò deuenisse homines impudentiæ vt siquis inter cæcos illos Deum eminus cognoscentes bonæ conscientiæ & probitatis speciem retineat, statim aliorum salibus & dicteriis notari. Verbum autem Dei, præterquam quod miserè contemnitur & proculcatur accedentibus nonnullis quidem pedibus ad illud audiendum, sed corde procul recedentibus, annon prorsus abominandum & detestandum est tam multos Scripturæ locos, ex hac præsertim historia Dominicæ passionis depromptos, abire in vulgata prouerbia & risus, & quidem plerunque inter scyphos & pocula? At non hæc proculdubio leuia peccata, sed totidem blasphemiæ & impietatis coram Deo voces, etiamsi quicunque hac in re labuntur, de istis non ita serio cogitent. Nam etsi nec chartis, nec atramento, nec syllabis aut verbis hæremus affixi, quasi subinde in illis aliqua Diuinitas, vt superstitiosi & venefici docent, tamen verbum hoc, verbum, inquam, à Dei Spiritu dictatum, & à Prophetis, Apostolis & Euangelistis eius mandato monumentis ad nos tramissum, nunquam intuendum, legendum aut auscultandum, sine timore & reuerentia illi vni debita qui in illo & per illud nos alloquitur: quo tanquam sceptro ad nos regendos vtitur, & ore ad loquendum, & brachio ad feriendum, nunquam frustrà se exerente, quin vel misericordiæ vel iusti iudicij effectus producat. Ac proculdubio nunquam isti reprobi tam flagitiosè sese gessissent, nisi prius hoc ipso, cui illudebant, Verbo excæcati. Nec enim decebat Iesum Christū, Eliam, aut alium ex Prophetis quemlibet, inuocare, licet mortuos inuocare fas esset (quod nunquam tamen in Ecclesia sua Deus permisit) quum contrà per huius Crucifixi Spiritum 1. Pet. 1. 11. & 2. Pet. 1. 21. & de eo, Prophetæ loquuti sint. Ioh. 5. 30. & is sit in quo omnes promissiones firmæ & ratæ sunt 2. Cor. 1. 20. denique in quo vnico perfecti sumus. Col. 2. 10. Nihilominus tamen perget mundus in ingenio, dū Deus vltricè manu admoueat: & Dei filiorū similis etiā erit conditio: sed forti & præsenti animo simus, quum æquum non sit maiorem haberi serui quàm Domini rationem: & nos pigere non oporteat per eandem viam in regnū cœlorum ingredi perquam ingressus Dux ille noster, cuius facti sumus coheredes, in gloriam Patris receptus est, Luc. 24. 26. quum præsertim impurissimorum istorum hominum sputaDei thronum non attingant,sed in ipsorum o-ra semper recidant.
units.tr: Oh, that the offspring of those lost men had perished along with them! But, I beg you, whom do we see today more despised, mocked, and assailed with witticisms and jeers? Are they not the children of God, both living and dead? I will say something more: men have reached such shamelessness that if anyone among those blind people, who know God from afar, keeps an appearance of a good conscience and uprightness, he is at once marked out by others' jests and taunts. As for the word of God, besides being wretchedly despised and trampled underfoot, with some indeed coming with their feet to hear it but with their hearts far away, is it not utterly abominable and detestable that so many passages of Scripture, drawn especially from this history of the Lord's passion, pass into common proverbs and laughter, and that too for the most part over cups and drinking bowls? Yet without doubt these are not light sins but as many blasphemies and words of impiety before God, even though those who fall into this do not think seriously about such things. For although we do not cling to paper, ink, syllables, or words, as if some divinity dwelt in them from time to time, as superstitious people and sorcerers teach, nevertheless this word, I say, this word dictated by the Spirit of God and sent down to us in writings by his command through the Prophets, Apostles, and Evangelists, must never be looked upon, read, or heard without fear and reverence due to him alone who speaks to us in it and through it. By it, as by a sceptre, he rules us, and by his mouth he speaks, and by his arm he strikes, never exerting himself in vain, but always producing the effect either of mercy or of just judgment. And without doubt those reprobates would never have conducted themselves so shamefully, unless they had first been blinded by this very Word which they mocked. For it was not fitting to call upon Jesus Christ, Elijah, or any other of the prophets, although it would be lawful to call upon the dead (which God, however, never permitted in his Church), since rather through the Spirit of this Crucified One, the prophets spoke, and of him they spoke (1 Peter 1:11; 2 Peter 1:21; John 5:30), and he is the one in whom all the promises are sure and fulfilled (2 Corinthians 1:20), and finally the one in whom alone we are made perfect (Colossians 2:10). Nevertheless the world will continue in its wit, while God moves his avenging hand; and the condition of the children of God will be the same. But let us be strong and of present mind, since it is not right that the servant should be held in higher regard than the Lord, and we ought not to be ashamed to enter the kingdom of heaven by the same way by which our Leader, whose heirs we have become, entered into the glory of the Father (Luke 24:26), especially since those most impure men do not reach God's throne with their spittle, but it always falls back into their own faces.

units.la: Sequuntur apud historiam quæ de potione aceti in spongia Christo exhibita narrátur,quæ D.Iohannes suppleuit,aiens,horum quippe omnium testis oculatus,Christo ad eius postulationem exhibitum acetum, quum se sitire dixisset, ut nihil eorum quæ de ipso Prophetæ prædixerant omitteretur. Ad quæ duo præterea adiicit,Iesum de exhibita illa potione bibisse, qui prius tamen, quum ad supplicium duceretur exhibitam potionem recusarit,Mat. 27.34. & Marc.15.23. Hæc omnia diligenter expendenda, primum ut sciamus Prophetas non esse temerè loquutos, sed ventura sine fraude & sigillatim prædixisse, ut non abs re dixerit Dominus ne minimū Iota, aut Legis apicem, idest doctrinæ Propheticæ,cuius complementum est Euangelium,præteriturum, quin effectum suum sortiatur. Matth. 5.18. Sed præter superiora, velim illud ab iis diligenter considerari, quos quum à Sacris omnino pendere & stare oportuerit, ita tamen fuerunt audaces & perfrictæ frontis ut ad illud addere,detrahere, immutare pro arbitrio suo non vereantur, sine articulos doctrinæ & quæ fidem spectant, seu Ecclesiæ administrationem, seu vitæ morum regulam aspicias:quæ si diligenter ponderaretur, Ecclesiæ,quæ tam multis dissensionibus proscinditur,breui suam pacem redditam videremus. Hinc præterea ex Iesu Christo discamus,nefas esse mortalibus Dei filiis obedien-
units.tr: There follows in the history the account of the vinegar offered to Christ on a sponge, which St John supplements, saying (as an eyewitness of all these things) that vinegar was offered to Christ at his request, when he said that he thirsted, so that nothing of what the prophets had foretold about him should be left out. He adds two further points: that Jesus drank of the offered drink, though earlier, when he was led to execution, he had refused the drink that was offered (Matt. 27.34; Mark 15.23). All these things must be weighed carefully, first so that we may know that the prophets did not speak at random, but foretold future things faithfully and in detail. Hence the Lord did not say without reason that not one iota or tittle of the Law, that is, of prophetic teaching, of which the Gospel is the fulfilment, would pass away without achieving its effect (Matt. 5.18). Beyond what has been said, I would like those people to consider this carefully: though they ought to depend entirely on the Holy Scriptures and stand by them, they are so bold and brazen that they do not hesitate to add to them, take from them, or change them as they please. This applies whether you look at the articles of doctrine and matters of faith, the government of the Church, or the rule of moral life. If these things were weighed carefully, we would soon see the Church, which is torn apart by so many dissensions, restored to peace. Furthermore, from Jesus Christ we should learn that it is wrong for mortal sons of God to measure the obedience which each owes to God and to his neighbour according to his own judgement, as if they were to prescribe to God what they think should be done by themselves at this or that time. Yet it is hardly believable to anyone that a master could be so prescribed to by a servant of equal standing. It is therefore for the one God to command, and ours to leave aside what lies behind us and obey God when he commands (Phil. 3.14), keeping before our eyes always, first in general, what is the duty of Christians, and then what befits our particular calling. We must not think at all that any mortal, however faithful and diligent a servant, has attained the degree of perfect obedience; for we have our Lord Jesus Christ as the most perfect and most blameless pattern of all obedience from beginning to end. Rather, that is the goal at which, having overcome all difficulties, we must aim, to will and to do, according to the power and measure of the Spirit created in us (Phil. 2.13).

units.la: Ff. iiij. tiam quā quisque Deo & proximo secundùm vocationem debet metiri ex suo arbitrio, quasi Deo praescribant quid hoc vel illo tempore sibi faciendum ducant, quod tamen herum à seruo pari posse vix fit cuiquam verisimile. Dei vnius igitur est imperare, nostrum verò quae pone sunt relinquentes Deo iubenti obedire. Phil.3.14. obuersante semper nobis ante oculos primùm in genere quod Christianorum officium est, deinde quod priuatam vocationem nostram decet: minimè quidem cogitantes vllum mortalem quantumuis fidum ac diligentem seruum ad perfectae obedientiae gradum peruenisse, vt Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum itarim ab initio ad finem vsque perfectissimum & integerrimum omnis obedientiae exemplar habemus, sed quòd scopus ille sit ad quem superatis omnibus difficultatibus nobis collineandum est secundùm vim & mensuram Spiritus creatis in nobis velle & facere. Phil.2.13.
units.tr: Ff. iiij. Thirdly, let us learn that Jesus Christ, though wearied by so many pains, labours and tortures from his last supper with his disciples, did not begin to suffer thirst, but was pressed by a thirst as great as any mortal has ever endured. Experience itself teaches us how hard it is to overcome bodily suffering more than all other kinds. Truly, then, Christ put on our nature, and not only its essence but all its infirmities, not only those which arise from nature itself but those which sin has brought into man. Yet he did so without sin, and excluding those infirmities that are vicious in themselves; far from putting these on, he rather, by his Holy Spirit, governs and moderates the natural ones in us, and gradually abolishes those which are vicious in themselves.

units.la: Tertiò discamus Iesum Christum tot dolo-ribus laboribus & cruciatibus ab vltima cum suis discipulis coena fatigatum non coepisse, immo tanta quanta vllus vnquam mortalium siti pressum fuisse quam corpoream passionem quàm sit prae reliquis difficile superare experientia nos ipsa docet. Verè igitur Christus nostram naturam induit, ac non solā eius essentiam sed eius omnes infirmitates, non tantùm quae sunt ab ipsa natura, sed quas peccatum inuexit in hominem: ita tamen vt sine pecpeccato, & exceptis per fe vitiosis, quas tan- tùm abest vt induerit, vt ipse contrà Sancto suo Spiritu naturalesin nobis regat & moderetur,& per fe vitiosas paulatim aboleat.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us learn that Jesus Christ suffered a truly bodily thirst, and indeed one so great that scarcely anyone can grasp it in mind; yet he burned with a much greater zeal to fulfil that to which he had been sent by the Father, though the work was difficult and very grievous, by which he would obtain for us salvation and eternal life. Far be it from us to think that he lacked feeling of body or soul, since Scripture calls him expressly the Man of Sorrows (Isa. 53.3), and indeed of sorrows that no one can express. But he was almost forgetful of himself for our sake, so that in all his sufferings and torments not even a little word escaped him by which he complained of the pains of body or soul. Moreover, when he had first refused the myrrhed and sweetened drink that was offered, at the very moment when he was about to yield up his spirit he deferred asking for a drink, although he knew that the drink offered to him would not be welcome, nor suitable for quenching his thirst. He himself had foretold this thirst and this drink through his prophet many centuries before (Ps. 69.22), and he was not unaware of the custom of evildoers.

units.la: Præterea discamus Iesum Christum vt verè corpoream sitim,& quidem quantam vix vllus mente possit aflequi,passus est,ficmulto maiore studio eius implendi ad quod erat à Patre missus, licet arduum & grauissimum erat opus exarsisse, quo nobis salutem & vitam æternam acquireret. Absit autem putemus eum sensu corporis vel animæ caruisse, quum eum contrà Virum Dolorum Prophetam nominatim dicat, Esa.53.3 & quidem quos nemo possit exprimemere: ted quòd fui penè fit immemor pro nobis, adeò vt in omnibus suis perpeffionibus & cruciatibus ne vocula quidem exciderit qua de corporis vel animæ passionibus conquereretur. Insuper quum oblatum potum myrrhatum & deliciosum initiò recufaffet,in momentum etiam quo spiritu erat redditurus petitionem potus distulit, etsi sciebat non oblatum iri sibi gratam potionem, nec sedandæ siti idoneam, quum ipsemet hanc sitim & potionem per Propheram suum ante multa secula prædixisset,Pfal.69.22. nec ignarus etiam ipse maleficorum consuetudinis.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us learn that Jesus Christ truly suffered in a body that was thirsty, and in a degree of thirst that scarcely anyone can grasp in his mind. He did so with a much greater zeal for fulfilling what he had been sent by the Father to do, although the work was arduous and very grievous, by which he would win for us salvation and eternal life. Yet we must not think that he lacked bodily or mental feeling, since Scripture calls him by name a Man of Sorrows, Isa. 53.3, and a man who no one could express. Rather, he was almost forgetful of himself for our sake, so that in all his sufferings and torments not even a little word escaped him by which he complained of the pains of body or soul. Moreover, when he had at first refused the offered myrrhed and sweetened drink, he also put off, even at the moment when he was about to give up his spirit, the request for a drink. He knew that the offered draught would not be pleasing to him, nor suitable for quenching his thirst, since he himself had foretold this thirst and this drink through his Prophet many centuries before, Ps. 69.22. Nor was he unaware of the custom of evildoers.

units.la: Quænam,igitur obsecro,nostræ partes sunt, fi verè membra fumus ipsius? Quæ voluptas, quæ vita,quis dolor, quis languor,quod periculum, qui denique cruciatus nos auocabunt quominus omnia fine discrimine tum gloriæ Dei tum proximorum officiis alacriter postponamus? Hoc sane postulat a nobis officium nostrum: & ita veri Dei serui hactenus ambulârunt & ambulant vera illa prædicti charitate quæ sua non quærit.1.Cor.13.5.Eheu vero! quis è multis millibus vel talem vnum reperiat? Quàm multi contrà vel ob lucellum, immo vero ob rem ludicram, atque adeò, quod longè peius est, malam, conciones & preces publicas floccifaciunt, facile ia&uram arbitrates, (sed subductis, vt aiunt, sine hospite rationibus) quæ facile recuperetur: & horum etiam, maximæ saltem partis illorum, miserabilem hunc exitum intuemur, vt paulatim recedente Spiritu Sancto vltima ipsorum conditio sit priore deterior. Atque vtinam non extarent apud nos nimium frequentia exempla multorum, quibus nisi immutentur fuissent vtilius nunquam aut in Ecclesia natos esse, aut in eam aliunde nunquam ingressos: rem sane deplorandam, sed in medio nostrûm nimis frequentem, & in ipsis αὐτοζωοἱ & in multis accolis, qui tamen reipsa de se possunt prædicare se à Deo hanc gratiam accepisse vt facultates & alia commoda Christum propius sequuturi abiecerint. Sed quid iuuat à Spiritu cœpisse, & in carnem desinere? Quid prodest stomachum grauantia vomuisse ad vomitum reditur? ex mundi luto semel emersisse in illud iterum immergendos; vt solent canes & porci. 2.Pet. 2.22. Quid conducit ad salutem, quasdam facultates abiicere, sibi ipsi vero non renuntiare quæ sunt Christia-
units.tr: What, then, I beg you, are our parts, if we are truly his members? What pleasure, what life, what pain, what weakness, what danger, what torment at last, will call us away from readily setting aside everything, without exception, both for the glory of God and for the duties we owe our neighbours? This our duty certainly demands of us, and thus the true servants of God have walked until now and still walk, endowed with that true charity which does not seek its own, 1 Cor. 13.5. Alas! Who among many thousands will find even one such person? How many, on the other hand, for the sake of a little gain, or rather for a trifling and (what is far worse) wicked pleasure, make light of sermons and public prayers, readily reckoning the loss easy to recover, provided the accounts are settled, as they say, without a guest. And we see this miserable end among them, or at least among the greater part of them, so that, as the Holy Spirit gradually withdraws, their last condition becomes worse than the first. Would that there were not among us too many frequent examples of many who, unless they had been changed, would never have been better born in the Church, or never have entered it from elsewhere. This is certainly a deplorable matter, yet it is all too common in our midst, both among those who are, as it were, self-living [αὐτοζωοί] and among many residents, who nevertheless can truly declare of themselves that they have received this grace from God, namely to cast away their wealth and other advantages in order to follow Christ more closely. But what good is it to have begun in the Spirit and to end in the flesh? What profit is there in having vomited what burdened the stomach, only to return to the vomit? To have emerged once from the mire of the world, only to plunge into it again, as dogs and pigs do, 2 Pet. 2.22. What good does it do for salvation to cast away some possessions, yet not to renounce oneself, which are the first rudiments of Christian-

units.la: nae. ftianifmi prima rudimenta?
units.tr: ity?

units.la: Non solo igitur naturali bibendi appetitu Dominus impulsus fe sitire dixit,etsi verum illud erat, sed maxime desiderio implendi quae ad nostram reconciliationem requirebantur: adeo vt nostro respectu, bene intellectis illis vocibus, abeo tempore non desierit,nec ad hunc vsque diem desinat testari perpetua siti se{a}nostræ salutis laborare, vociferante ipso cum Propheta, Esa. 55 1. Vos omnes sitibundi ad aquas venire:& per Apostolum, Qui sitit,veniat, & qui vult accipiat aquam vitæ gratis. Apoc. 22.17. quod sane non ita prædicaret nisi maiore studio duceretur nobis potum illum præbendi, quàm nos ab illo postulandi.
units.tr: Therefore the Lord was not moved merely by natural desire for drink when he said that he thirsted, although that was true enough. He was moved chiefly by the desire to fulfil what was required for our reconciliation. So, with respect to us, if those words are rightly understood, he has never ceased from that time, nor does he cease to this day, to bear witness that he labours with a perpetual thirst for our salvation, crying out with the Prophet, "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters," Isa. 55.1, and through the Apostle, "Let him who thirsts come, and let him who wishes take the water of life freely," Rev. 22.17. Certainly he would not proclaim this so, were he not led by a greater zeal to offer us that drink than we are to ask it from him.

units.la: Interea tamen quotidie potum à nobis flagitat, non quidem nostris egens, Psal. 50. 12. sed quòd tanto vineam suam honore dignatur, vt ab ipsa productos fructus accipiat & gratos habeat, licet ad ipsum qui vinitor est nullum inde commodum redeat. Ioh. 15. 1. Quoniam autem antiquam vineam suam tam bene cultam visitans, nihil nisi labruscas reperit, Esa. 5. 2. ideo sepem eius eruit & peruiam apris fecit à quibus est depasta & devastata, Psal. 80. 15. ac tandem à Iudaismo ad Christianismum transplantauit, idest à Iudæis ad Gentes transtulit, à quibus non modo fructus prorsus agrestes sed etiam nullo modo potabiles producuntur: acerum illi plerumque tetterrimi odoris offerentibus, in os ipsius, dum osculantur eum vt Iudas olim, proditorie, tum doctrinæ falsitate,
units.tr: Meanwhile, nonetheless, he asks for drink from us every day. He does not need what is ours, Ps. 50.12, but he deigns to honour his vineyard so highly that he receives and welcomes the fruits produced by it, although no advantage returns to him who is the vinedresser, John 15.1. But since, visiting his former vineyard, which had been so well tended, he found nothing but wild grapes, Isa. 5.2, therefore he tore up its hedge and made it open to the boars by whom it was eaten and laid waste, Ps. 80.15. And at last he transplanted it from Judaism to Christianity, that is, he carried it from the Jews to the Gentiles. Yet from these there come forth fruits that are altogether wild, and in no way drinkable. And these, for the most part, offer him, in his mouth, while they kiss him as Judas once did, a most foul-smelling treachery, both by falsehood of doctrine

units.la: {a} aterna, sed contemnitur. tum generis omnis vitiis & facinoribus. Quis vero tantam ingrati animi significationem merito non condemnet? A qua tamen, quisquam nostrum, obsecro, dicat penitus immunem? Sufficiat nobis Dei filium in cruce semel poenę peccatis nostris debitæ accetum exhaustæ, patiamurque nos emundari & excoli ab eius Spiritu, deinceps gratum illi potum per eius misericordiam oblaturi, nihil nisi quod ipse prior dederit illi exhibituri. Est alius præterea modus hanc Iesu Christi vocem expendendi, quia etiam num vitatur hodie licet in suam gloriam receptus ex qua omnibus alimenta subministrat, tantum abest ut fame vel siti premantur, aut villis hominum donis indigeat. Sed in miserorum fratrum persona vociferatur hodie ad ostia nostra, Eusebio, Gitio, Algeo. Sed sæpissime surdis auribus occinit, quas etiam indignas iudicaturus est tam excellenti illo gloriæ & dignitatis gradu, cuius mentio fit, Matth. 25.40. quum ad eius dextram collocatis dicturus est, Quod fecistis uni ex istis fratribus meis minimis, mihi fecistis.
units.tr: eternal, but is despised. Both by every kind of vice and crime. Who, indeed, would not justly condemn such a sign of ungrateful mind? Yet which of us, I ask, would say he is wholly free of it? Let it suffice for us that the Son of God, on the cross, drained once the cup of punishment owed to our sins. Let us allow ourselves to be cleansed and cultivated by his Spirit, and henceforth, by his mercy, offer him a pleasing drink, bringing him nothing but what he has first given. There is also another way of weighing this voice of Jesus Christ: even now he is despised today, although received into glory, from which he supplies sustenance to all. He is so far from being pressed by hunger or thirst, or needing gifts from men, that today he cries out at our doors in the persons of our wretched brothers, Eusebius, Gitius, Algeus. But very often he sings to deaf ears, and he will judge them unworthy of that most excellent degree of glory and dignity which is mentioned in Matt. 25.40, when he is about to say to those placed at his right hand, "Inasmuch as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."

units.la: Cæterum non tantum dicitur Iesus Christus vociferatus esse se sitire, ut etiam expresse potum diceret: sed etiam oblatum accetum degustasse, licet non aptum ad sedandam sitim: sed etiam non porrigebatur maleficis potus, ad alimoniam, sed ad virium sustentationem. Verum illa minime respexit Iesus Christus, sed quæ de se olim erant prædicta studuit adimplere, ut de se non alio ullo Prophetas esse locuti. quutos teltaretur:qua in re Dauid sicut in aliis multis, figura fuit veri nostri Dauidis & Regis æterni veri Israëlis, ita tamen vt de fe Dauid prouerbialiter illa dixerit, de iis coqueftus qui misero & afflicto nouas afflictiones addebant: quæ deinde Dominus Christus reipfa tandem & ad literam adimpleuit.
units.tr: Moreover, it is not only said that Jesus Christ cried out that he thirsted, so that he even expressly said so, but also that he tasted the vinegar offered him, though it was not suitable for quenching thirst. The drink was not offered to the wicked to nourish him, but to sustain his strength. Yet Jesus Christ paid no regard to these things. Rather, he sought to fulfil what the Prophets had foretold of him, since they spoke of no one else. In this David, as in many other things, was a figure of our true David, the eternal King of the true Israel. Yet David spoke these words proverbially of himself, complaining of those who added new afflictions to a wretched and afflicted man. The Lord Christ afterwards really and literally fulfilled them.

units.la: Verùm in nostri Redemptoris exemplo, eximia & excellens doctrina præter superiora cõsideranda proponitur, vt nimirum non tantùm quæ nobis sunt necessaria postulemus, sed iis etiam contenti fimus quæ Deus immiserit, fiue à fe ipso, pro arbitrij fui mensura nos subleuans, fiue hominum hac in re vtatur opera, & quidem nonnunquam minimè fublcuaturus, sed contrà magis etiam per eos ipsos probaturus à quibus auxilium nos sperare & implorare potiùs decuerat. En, quæ nostræ sint hac in re partes: quum tamen plerumque fi vel à Deo vel ab hominibus præter desiderium tractemur, indignabundi murmuremus: qua in re sanè lapsi homines merito sunt reprehendendi: verùm quicunque casus ingruat, Deo primùm expositus rebus nostris angustis, &ad proximos confugiêtes, exitum Deo committamus, æquo animo quæcunque Dominus immiserit, fiue citiùs, fiue tardiùs, multum aut parum, consolationem vel nouam afflictionem ferentes, egregiam illam & insignem lobi sententiam memoria subinde repetentes, Scilicet bonum à Deo excipiemus, & malum non excipiemus? Iob.2.10.& quod Apostolus docet, Rom. 8.27. Deum amantibus omnia in bonum cedere, qui non finit vnquam nos supra vires tentari. 1. Cor. 10. 13.
units.tr: In the example of our Redeemer, a remarkable and excellent teaching is set before us, beyond what has been considered above: namely, that we should not only ask for what is necessary for us, but also be content with what God has sent, whether he relieves us from himself, according to the measure of his good pleasure, or uses the work of men in this matter. And sometimes he does not relieve us at all, but rather proves us even more through those very people from whom we ought rather to hope for and seek help. See what our part is in this matter. Yet when we are treated otherwise than we desire, whether by God or by men, we commonly murmur in indignation. In this matter fallen men are rightly to be rebuked. Rather, whatever misfortune befalls us, we should first lay our straitened circumstances open to God, and flee to our neighbours, and commit the outcome to God. Whatever the Lord has sent, whether sooner or later, much or little, bringing comfort or new affliction, we should accept with an even mind, repeating from time to time that remarkable and notable saying of Job. Surely we will receive good from God, and will we not receive evil? Job 2:10. And we should remember what the Apostle teaches, Rom. 8:28, that all things work together for good for those who love God, who never allows us to be tempted beyond our strength, 1 Cor. 10:13.

units.la: Sequitur deinceps Iesum Christum, Spiritum emisisse rursum clara voce clamantem, duos sermones protulisse, quorum alterum D. Lucas, alterum D. Iohannes enarrauit. Nec vero fine magna de causa Iesus Christus illos in agonis sui finem distulit, quo tanto accuratius considerentur, vt vltima ante suum e viuis excessum verba. Ac sane Christus in Cruce nihil maioris momenti dixit, vt fumus in eorum expositione paulo post audituri.
units.tr: Next, we come to Jesus Christ sending forth the Spirit, crying out again with a loud voice, and uttering two sayings, one of which St Luke and the other St John related. Nor did Jesus Christ defer these words to the end of his agony without a great reason, so that they might be considered all the more carefully, as his last words before his departure from this life. Indeed, Christ said nothing of greater weight on the cross, as we shall hear in their explanation shortly.

units.la: Tria sunt igitur nobis hic expendenda, primum, Cur Euangelistae nominatim hunc clamorem expresserint. Multis vero illud & magnis de causis. Prima & praecipua, vt neminem lateret hunc clamorem audientem, hunc Iesum Crucifixum breui sic ex causa naturali effaturum animam, nimirum ex violentia & cruciatibus quos in tam crudeli supplicio passus erat, vt tamen separatio animae a suo corpore procederet a pura ipsius voluntate, minime quidem quasi vitae quantum vellet producendae potestatem non haberet, aut etiam cruciatus illos quos patiebatur momento vt vellet sedandi, immo suos inimicos si voluisset praecipites in abyssum dandi, quandoquidem morientibus sensim loquendi vires deficiunt (quod in iis conspicitur qui ad vltimum vsque halitum loquuntur) ipse vero nunquam altius nec vehementius loquutus videbatur, quaquasi circumstantes sic alloqueretur, Vultis me mori, & sponte iam morior, nimirum quòd mea voluntas est vt moriar, & nulla alia de causa. Hoc vidit ille Centurio, & obseruauit, obstupefactus, vt ait Marc. 13.39. nō quòd esset Iesus Christus mortuus, sed quòd tam altè vociferatus & tāta vi Spiritum emisisset, cuius clamoris tanta vis etiam fuit vt ipsa saxa perfregerit, & velum templi, sicut paulò post visuri sumus.
units.tr: There are three things, then, to be weighed here. First, why the Evangelists expressly recorded this cry. There are many reasons, and great ones. The first and chief is that no one should be unaware that, hearing this cry, Jesus was crucified and would soon yield up his soul by a natural cause, namely from the violence and torments he suffered in so cruel a punishment. Yet the separation of his soul from his body came from his own pure will, not as if he lacked the power to prolong his life as long as he wished, or to end at once the torments he was suffering, or even to cast his enemies into the abyss if he wished. For the dying gradually lose the strength to speak (as is seen in those who speak to the last breath), but he himself seemed never to have spoken more loudly or vehemently. As if speaking to those standing around, he said, "You wish me to die, and now I die of my own accord, namely because it is my will to die, and for no other reason." The centurion saw this and observed it, astonished, as Mark 15:39 says, not because Jesus was dead, but because he had cried out so loudly and had sent forth his Spirit with such force. The force of this cry was so great that it even broke the rocks and the veil of the temple, as we shall see shortly.

units.la: Hanc ob causam etiam Iesus Christus Spiritum citius emittere voluit quàm plerique in hoc supplicio tolerent: quod Pilatus ipse miratus est. Marc. 15.44. Minimè quidem pro nobis diutius pati recusans, sed vt vel inimicis suis ostenderet ipsum suæ mortis articulum in sua esse potestate, vt moreretur quum ipse vellet, non autem ad eorum libidinem.
units.tr: For this reason also Jesus Christ willed to give up the Spirit sooner than most people endure in this punishment, which Pilate himself marvelled at, Mark 15:44. Certainly he was not refusing to suffer longer for us, but to show even to his enemies that the very moment of his death was in his own power, so that he might die when he himself willed, and not at their pleasure.

units.la: Obseruandum præterea vocem istam fuisse veluti vadimonij constitutionem suis hostibus, in propria persona, quæ breui aduersum eos & posteros effectum suum consecuta sit, secundum ea quam coram Pilato sibi ipsis acceperant imprecationem, Sanguis eius super nos & liberos nostros. Et hoc quidem tam horrendum iudicium quotidie in miseram istam nationem effunditur. Verùm non ad solos Iudæos ista pertinent, quum sit certissimum eos qui hodie Christiani vocantur, & tamen quàtum in ipsis est, tam apostata à doctrina tam perditis ac deploratis moribus, Iesum Christum connuitiis iterum exponunt, aut in misc-
units.tr: It must further be observed that this voice was, as it were, the entering of a bond upon his enemies in his own person, which would soon take effect against them and their posterity, according to the curse they had themselves accepted before Pilate: "His blood be upon us and upon our children" (Matt. 27:25). Indeed, this dreadful judgment is poured out daily upon that wretched nation. But these things do not pertain only to the Jews, since it is most certain that those who today are called Christians, and yet, as far as in them lies, have apostatised from the doctrine and live such lost and deplorable lives, expose Jesus Christ again to reproach, or in his members crucify him again...

units.la: Ibid. Marc. 13. ris membris iterū crucifigunt, Heb.6. 6. longè grauioribus adhuc esse suppliciis afficiendos.
units.tr: ...Mark 13 and Heb. 6:6. They are to be punished with far heavier punishments still.

units.la: Caeundum igitur summopere, fratres, ne in horum numero censeamur, & voxista nobis ad vsum suum nominatim est referenda, voce sua, nos etiam contrario prorsus à superiore modo Dei Filio compellante. Nam adeò clara voce vociferatus est, ne hac eius exinanitione, quam sponte ac volens subiit offendamur, Luc.7.23. sed contrà potius aedificemur, agnoscentes per hanc vocis firmitatem, non vi Satanæ, non mortis, non inimicorum in hanc mortem ipsum impulsum, sed sponte subiisse quam nobis in vitam aeternam commutaret.
units.tr: We must therefore take great care, brothers, that we are not counted among their number. This voice is to be referred by name to our use, and we are to be addressed by it in the opposite way to that in which the Son of God addressed us above. For he cried out with so clear a voice, lest we should be offended by this emptying of himself, which he undertook willingly and of his own accord, Luke 7:23, but should rather be built up, acknowledging through this firmness of voice that he was not driven to this death by the power of Satan, by death, or by his enemies, but voluntarily underwent that death which he would exchange for eternal life for us.

units.la: Discamus etiam ex hac inimicorum διάνοια sperare eos qui vocem ipsius minuere non potuerunt, (tantum abest ut suffulerint) non etiam impedituros, quicquid Satan ipse cum suis satellitibus moliatur & conetur, quominus hæc Iesu Christi vox, qua iterum ut prædixerat Aggeus Propheta, Agg. 2. 21. cœlum ac terra concussa sunt, Euangelij nimirum Sacramenti prædicatio, quæ Dei potentia est ad salutem, cuius credenti, Rom.1.16. & odor contra mortis contemptoribus iporum culpa. 2. Cor.2.16. personet quocunque & quandocunque visum fuerit illi Seruatori nostro: siquidè non est tanta visipsorum, quæ vnius Dei propria est, ut ventum illum quo huius prædicationis vis in Apostolorum vocatione est adu-brata, Act.2.2. cohibeat. Et quidem harum rerum nostra tempora, Dei summo beneficio, lucalenculentum nobis exhibent testimonium. At, dolor! vix millesima pars hominum aures ad audiendum habet, multique etiam aduersus huius sapientis incantatoris suauem cantum voces obturant, Psal. 58 5. Sed heu! heu! inquam, quàm saepe contigit, quod adhuc miseranda Iudaeorum natio suo exitio experitur, & ipse Christianismus tristè oculis nostris experimentum eius rei praebet, vt hominum rebellione Deus silentio vocem premat, non quidem sanè loquendi amissa potestate, sed hominum indignitate commotus?
units.tr: Let us also learn from this διάνοια [intention] of his enemies to hope that those who could not diminish his voice (far from it, they could not even stifle it) will not hinder, however much Satan himself with his henchmen may plot and attempt, this voice of Jesus Christ from sounding everywhere and always, as the Prophet Haggai had foretold: "I will shake heaven and earth" (Hag. 2:21). This is the preaching of the Gospel and of the Sacrament, which is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes (Rom. 1:16), and the odour of death unto death to those who despise it, through their own fault (2 Cor. 2:16), whenever and wherever it pleases our Saviour. For the wind by which the power of this preaching was foreshadowed at the calling of the Apostles (Acts 2:2) is not under their control, since it belongs to God alone, to hold back. Indeed, our own times, by the great goodness of God, give us a clear testimony of these things. But alas! Scarcely a thousandth part of men have ears to hear, and many even stop their ears against the sweet song of this wise enchanter (Ps. 58:5). But alas, alas, I say, how often does it happen, as the still pitiable nation of the Jews experiences to its ruin, and Christianity itself gives us a sad experience of this thing before our eyes, that God, moved by human rebellion, silences and suppresses the voice, not indeed having lost the power of speaking, but moved by human unworthiness?

units.la: Accedamus ad Christi verba, ex Psal. 31. 6. deprompta, Pater in manus tuas spiritum meum commendo: quae primùm propter quasdam rationes Dauidis respecțu, deinde ipsius etiam Christi qui ilidem vsus est cum Dauide communi derabimus. Dauidi enim vt homini & mille aerumnis obruto necesse fuit, vt veris omnibus Dei filiis in Deum vnicu recumbere, & in eum sèque suaque omnia reiicere. At qui hic loquitur verè Dei filius, & qui tot miraculis quod habebat in mortem imperium vere testatus erat, adeò vt alios etiam suscitatos morti eripe-ret, sibíque quod à Patre postulabat dare poterat, quomodo tali prece dicetur vsus fuisse? Ad haec tam facilis responsio quàm prima fronte videatur difficilis. Primùm igitur attendamus, quod etiam ab huius historiae principio docuimus, Iesum Christum esse quidem in vnitate personae Hominem Deum: sed non propterea tamen eius Humanitatem factam Deitatem, vt etiam Deitas facta non est Humanitas, sed talem mansisse qualis est humana natura cum anima tum corpore cum omnibus eius proprietatibus naturalibus & essentialibus, absque vitio tamen, & praeterea excellentissima praeeminentia dotatam. Iesus igitur Christus hic suae Humanitatis respectu loquitur: vt quû alias etiam dicitur, iuisse & venisse, bibisse, comedisse, & dormiuisse, & ligatus, virgis caesus, condemnatus, crucifixus, mortuus, sepultus, suscitatus, & his similia huius Hominis Dei propria, sed fuę tantùm Humanitatis respectu. Hanc ob causam toties & tam expresse, nocte & interdiu Patre orauit, suúmque ac nostrum Deum appellauit, non tantum nos exemplo suo docturus ad Deum nostrum Creatorem confugere: sed etiam ostensurus se licet verè Hominem Deum, tamen Humanitatis suae respectu verè factum fratrem nostrum, & hoc respectu tanquam rem Creatam virtute & potentia suae Deitatis sustineri & conseruari, quâ ad Deum Patrem referre consueuit: minimè quòd alia sit eius quàm Patris Deitas (nó sunt enim duae Deitates) nec duo Dij, sed respiciens Mediatoris inter Patrem & nos officium, ad quem veluti manu nos deducit, sic eum tum pro se (quatenus nimirum homo est nobis per omnia, excepto peccato, simillimus) tum pro nobis, quatenus Mediator nolter est, precibus interpellans.
units.tr: Let us come to the words of Christ, taken from Ps. 31:5, "Father, into your hands I commend my spirit." We shall first deal with these words in relation to David, and then with Christ himself, who used the same words with David. For David, being a man overwhelmed by a thousand troubles, had to lean upon God alone, as all true sons of God do, and to cast himself and all his affairs upon him. But he who speaks here is truly the Son of God, and who by so many miracles truly testified that he had power over death, so that he even snatched others back from death after raising them, and could give himself what he asked of the Father. How then can it be said that he used such a prayer? To this the answer is as easy as at first sight it seems difficult. First, then, let us attend to what we also taught from the beginning of this history: that Jesus Christ is indeed God and Man in the unity of person, yet his humanity has not thereby been made deity, just as the deity has not been made humanity; rather, the humanity has remained such as human nature is, with both soul and body and all its natural and essential properties, yet without fault, and moreover endowed with the most excellent pre-eminence. Jesus Christ therefore speaks here with respect to his humanity, just as elsewhere he is said to have gone and come, drunk, eaten, slept, and to have been bound, scourged, condemned, crucified, dead, buried, raised, and other things like these, which belong to this Man who is God, yet only with respect to his humanity. For this reason he prayed to the Father so often and so expressly, by night and by day, and called him his God and ours, not only to teach us by his example to flee to God our Creator, but also to show that although he is truly Man and God, yet with respect to his humanity he was truly made our brother, and in this respect, as a created thing, was sustained and preserved by the power and might of his deity, which he is accustomed to refer to God the Father. Not that his deity is other than the Father's (for there are not two deities, nor two Gods), but looking to the office of the Mediator between the Father and us, by which he leads us as it were by the hand to God. So he pleads with the Father both for himself (inasmuch as he is in all things like us, except sin) and for us, inasmuch as he is our Mediator.

units.la: Ac fortasse regerat aliquis, potuisse illum sibi quaecunque voluisset dare: ac proinde non
units.tr: Someone may perhaps reply that he could have given himself whatever he wished, and therefore that there was no need for him to ask anything of another.

units.la: Quomodo Christus nō fuisse necesse vt ab alio postularet. Cōcedo equidē, id, modō probè intellectum:at hīc nobis est Humanitas Christi consideranda, primum infirmitatis suæ tempore quam sponte ipsum subiisse diximus accepta serui forma, vt debitas peccatis nostris pœnas lueret, cuius respectu decuit ipsum ad Deitatem, sustentandum ab ipsa, confugere: quæ sanè fuit sponta- nea necessitas, quandoquidem volens illi sese submiserat, ad quam nos, velimus, nolimus, naturæ nostræ misera & afflicta conditione obligamur.
units.tr: How Christ was not under the necessity of asking another. I grant this, if it is rightly understood. But here we must consider the humanity of Christ: first, in the time of his weakness, which we have said he voluntarily undertook by taking the form of a servant, so that he might pay the penalties owed for our sins. In view of this, it was fitting that he should flee to his Deity for support. This was indeed a voluntary necessity, since he had willingly submitted himself to it; and to this we are bound, whether we wish it or not, by the wretched and afflicted condition of our nature.

units.la: Deinde hæc infirmitas secundùm varios i- psius gradus est consideranda, & memoria re- petenda quæ pluribus in precationis illius in horto habitæ explicatione, & tristis illius in Cruce querimoniæ sumus persequuti. Tenea- mus igitur Iesu Christo precationem hanc vl- timam fundente, duarum naturarum vnionem nullo modo fuisse dissolutam: sed Deitatem eius non se magis exeruisse & vires in ipso suas ostendisse quàm anima in deliquium patiente aut lethargico soleat. Patris verò, faciem in tantis angustiis & angoribus hæc humanitas nonnihil vt iusto furore ardentem, & terrificam intuebatur, quę pœnas nostris peccatis debitas ab ipsa, tanquam vadē & sponsore nostro reposcebat.
units.tr: Next, this weakness is to be considered according to its various degrees, and we must recall what we discussed at length in the explanation of that prayer in the garden and of his sorrowful complaint on the cross. Let us therefore hold that when Jesus Christ poured out this last prayer, the union of the two natures was in no way dissolved. Rather, his Deity did not reveal itself more openly or show its powers in him any more than a soul in a swoon or a lethargic person usually does. But this humanity, in such straits and agonies, looked upon the face of the Father as somewhat burning with just wrath and terrifying, and the Father demanded from it, as our surety and guarantor, the penalties owed for our sins.

units.la: Denique postquam quod in passionibus eius adhuc supererat, vt acerrum illi ad sirim sedan- dam in potum porrigeretur fortissimè imple- uit, & à Spiritu, veluti nouas vires sufficientes, recreatus esset. Et palam testatus non vanam fuisse quam ipsi fiduciam obiecerant, actandem victoriam suam persequens, & mortem ipse potius corripiens quàm ab ipsa correptus, hæc verba protulit, quibus inuictam constantiam prodidit, quasperabat mortem in se licet anima à corpore separata nullam esse imperium habituram. Dauid igitur tanquam verus Dei Filius est quidem iisdem verbis vsus, sed quia non accedunt Dauidis sic loquentis dolores & angustiæ, ad Iesu Christi angore quos in hæc verba prorumpens sustinebat, tantò etiâ modis omnibus ineffabiliter Iesu Christi confidentia, Dauidis fiducia & spe perfectior est.
units.tr: Finally, after he had fully fulfilled what remained of his sufferings, when vinegar was offered him to drink to quench his thirst, and after he had been refreshed by the Spirit as if given new and sufficient strength, he openly testified that the confidence they had charged him with was not vain. Pursuing his victory to the end, seizing death rather than being seized by it, he uttered these words, by which he showed unconquered constancy, since he hoped that death would have no power over him, even though his soul was separated from the body. David, then, as the true Son of God, indeed used the same words. But since the pains and anguish of David speaking thus do not match the agony Jesus Christ endured while bursting out into these words, Jesus Christ's confidence is in every way ineffably more perfect than David's trust and hope.

units.la: Obseruandum præterea Iesum Christum sic iisdem cum Dauide verbis vsum vt aliquid in illis immutarit, adiecerit & detraxerit. Nec enim Dauid vtitur hac voce Patris, sed Deum vocat, Æternum Deum veritatis à quo redemptus est: deinde Dauid sic precatus Deo commendat animam ne in mortem incidat, sed ab ea liberetur: Iesus verò Christus iam iam Spiritum emissurus, rogauit Patrem vt à corpore separatum Spiritum in custodiam ac tutelam suam depositum reciperet. Hæc igitur inter se diuersa sunt, vt in his personis etiam & temporibus est quædam differentia, sed non tamen repugnantia, quod maiorem adhuc considerationem requirit. Dauid igitur sibi vitam in his terris prorogari poltulat, vt ferebat temporis circumstantia, testatus se in tantis ærumnis calamitatibus animum minime despondere. Verum enim vero Dauidis hæc fiducia etiam vltra vitæ præsentis terminos longe ferebatur: atque adeo verbis istis aperte significabat sese paratum vitam præsentem abiicere, si talem esse Dei voluntatem animaduerteret.
units.tr: We should also observe that Jesus Christ used the same words as David, yet changed some of them, added some and left others out. David does not use the word Father but calls God the eternal God of truth by whom he has been redeemed. Then David, praying thus to God, commends his soul so that it may not fall into death but be delivered from it. Jesus Christ, on the other hand, about to send forth his Spirit at once, asked the Father to receive the Spirit, now separated from the body, into his own keeping and protection. These words therefore differ from one another, and there is a certain difference in the persons and times, but not a contradiction, which requires further consideration. David, then, asked that his life in this world be prolonged, as the circumstances of the time suggested, testifying that in such great distress and calamities he did not lose heart. Yet David's trust was also carried well beyond the limits of the present life, and so by these words he plainly signified that he was ready to lay down the present life, if he perceived that this was God's will.

units.la: Quòd autem ad verba illa attinet quibus Dauid erat vsus, pro quibus Christus nomen patris substituit, non sine causa factum est. Decebat enim Dauidem vt omnes Dei filios Æternum vocare suum Redemptorem ex sanctis promissionibus: verum licet hic sese Iesus Christus velut in ipsos inferos abiecerit, tamen non fuit necesse ipsum, nimirum Ecclesiæ caput, ab alio nec à seipso redimi, vt debitores iræ Dei, tanquam præcipuos debitores oportet: sed alios ipse suo sanguine redemit, quod etiam præ se ferebat impositum Iesu nomen. Matt.1.21. ratam Esaiæ Prophetiam faciens, Es. 61.1. quam ipse in Nazarethæ Synagoga prius exposuerat, Luc.4.18. Substituit igitur Christus Patris vocem, tanquam sibi conuenientem & speciali ratione propriam, nempe quatenus est verus Dei Filius coëssentialis & coæternus cum Deo Patre suo: deinde etiam quatenus Homo-Deus per vnionem personalem factus est. Factus vero frater noster, fecit commune fratribus suis, per eximium illud adoptionis beneficium, & vnionem illam spiritualem qua fit nobiscum omnibus suis bonis, tam eximium, tam suaue, tam gratum Patris reconciliati nomen, quod ipsi tamen proprium & speciale manet ob duas superiùs allatas rationes, quæ quum ampliorem tractatum requirant, in aliud tempus reiiciemus. Interim danda nobis opera ut tot tamque insignia documenta quæ ex hac historia collegimus ad usum nostrum referamus, & ad sequentium perceptionem ad gloriam Dei Opt. Max. & Patris nostri in Christo Iesu, & ad nostram ædificationem præpa remur. Amen.
units.tr: As for the words David used, for which Christ substituted the name of Father, this was not done without reason. It was fitting that David, from the holy promises, should call the eternal God his Redeemer, as all the sons of God do. But although Jesus Christ here cast himself, as it were, into the very depths of hell, it was not necessary that he, the head of the Church, be redeemed by another or by himself, as debtors of God's wrath must be, as chief debtors. Rather, he redeemed others with his own blood, which the name Jesus he bore also signified (Matt. 1.21), fulfilling the prophecy of Isaiah (Is. 61.1) that he had earlier expounded in the synagogue of Nazareth (Luke 4.18). Christ therefore substituted the Father's name as fitting for himself and proper to him by a special reason, namely insofar as he is the true Son of God, of one essence and coeternal with God his Father; and also insofar as he was made God-man through the personal union. But having been made our brother, he made what is his own common to his brethren, through that outstanding benefit of adoption and that spiritual union by which all his goods become ours. Such an outstanding, sweet and welcome name, the name of a reconciled Father, nevertheless remains proper and special to him, for the two reasons set out above. Since these require a fuller treatment, we will defer them to another time. Meanwhile, let us take care to apply to our own use the many and distinguished lessons we have gathered from this history, and to prepare ourselves for understanding what follows, to the glory of God the best and greatest, and of our Father in Christ Jesus, and to our edification. Amen.

units.tr: HOMILY THIRTY-THIRD.

units.tr: 50. Jesus, however, when he had cried out again with a loud voice, gave up the Spirit.

units.tr: 51. And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom; and the earth quaked, and the rocks were split.

units.tr: 30. When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished, and bowing his head he gave up the Spirit.

units.la: AGGRESSI expositionem duorum sermonum Christi sub ipsum exitus ipsius è vita momentum, hæsimus in voce Patris quam propriam vnius esse Iesu Christi diximus, primum diuinæ ipsius naturæ respectu, in qua solus & vnicus est Filius: deinde ratione etiam humanitatis non per se consideratę, sed quatenus in hoc æterno Dei Filio subsistit vnione personali, adeò vt hæc persona non sint duo Filij Dei, vt itatim ab initio huius historiæ pluribus docuimus.
units.tr: Having undertaken the explanation of the two sayings of Christ at the very moment of his departure from life, we stopped at the word Father, which we said belongs to Jesus Christ alone: first with respect to his divine nature, in which he alone is the only Son; then also with respect to his humanity, not considered in itself but insofar as it subsists in this eternal Son of God by personal union, so that these are not two Sons of God, as we taught at length at the beginning of this history.

units.la: At nulla ex tam excellenti consideratione rediret ad nos vtilitas nisi alias etiam ex iis fructum percepturi adiiceremus. Prima est Christum suo exemplo nos hic docere ad quæ in maximis nostris afflictionibus & calamitatibus, & quidem quæ vitari non possunt, qualis est vitæ exitus, nobis sit confugiendū, ad Deum putà, Patris nomine insignem, & quidem potiore iure quàm in his terris Patres ac Matres vocare consueuimus. Infinitis enim partibus nostræ redemptionis & adoptionis beneficium est generatione paterna maternáque maius. Sed præterea, quod longè maius est, nulla est
units.tr: But no benefit would come back to us from so excellent a consideration unless we also added the other fruits we are to gain from it. The first is that Christ teaches us here by his own example to what refuge we must flee in our greatest afflictions and calamities, and indeed in those that cannot be avoided, such as the end of life: namely to God, marked with the name of Father, and with a better right than we usually call fathers and mothers on this earth. For the benefit of our redemption and adoption exceeds paternal and maternal begetting in infinite respects. But moreover, what is far greater, there is no

units.la: Gg. iiij. dilectionis, quo Pater cœlestis nos complectitur, cum amore parentum in hac caduca & misera vita comparatio, quod ipsemet iam olim difertissimis verbis testatus est, Esa. 49. 15. Matth. 7. 11. & ab omni ævo immensis & inefabilibus effectis conspicuum fecit.
units.tr: Gg. iiij. comparison between the love with which the heavenly Father embraces us and the love of parents in this frail and wretched life. He himself long ago testified to this in the most eloquent words, Isa. 49.15; Matt. 7.11, and has made it visible from all eternity by immense and inexpressible effects.

units.la: At secunda consideratione longius adhuc deducimur. Nam certò nos persuasum hoc oportet habere Iesum Christum ore & corde verba hæc pronunciasse, minimè seorsim & diuisim, sed coniunctim cum membris, quorum est caput: quod etiam in vltima sua Cœna distinctis & expressis verbis dixerat. Ioh. 17. 11. & 12. Quò etiam tam pretiosa hæc ipsius à resurrectione verba, Ascendo ad patrem meum & patrem vestrum, ad Deum meum & Deum vestrum sunt referenda. Quis autem in dubium vocet quin hæc commendatio sit à Patre tam in capitis quàm in cæterorum membrorum gratiam exaudita?
units.tr: But by the second consideration we are led even further. For we must be certain that Jesus Christ uttered these words with mouth and heart, not separately and apart, but together with the members of which he is the head; as he had also said in his final Supper in distinct and express words, John 17.11 and 12. To these same very precious words of his after the resurrection, I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God, these also are to be referred. Who then could doubt that this commendation was heard by the Father, in favour of the head as much as of the other members?

units.la: Quinam igitur nobis ex hoc mundo excedentibus metus, aut quænam ægritudo superet, quum anima ex hoc corpore migrans tam feliciter domicilium mutet? quod satis fuisse perequuti sumus in historia latronis conuersi. Ne amplius igitur dicamus nullum esse aduersus mortis terrores remedium: sed contrà potius mortem ipsam præsens adferre aduersus suum ipsius aculeum, veluti solet Scorpio, remedium. Mors enim sic animum à corpore separans, simul etiam à peccati seruitute, vindicat & victorem ad eum à quo missus erat remittit, vt reipsa perfruafruatur felicitate quam dum in terris ageret spe tantum possidebat. Corporis vero, licet in terram putrefaciendum reuertatur, nihilominus tamen praeterquam quod non patietur eam putrefactionem in aeternum perituram, sed excoquendum & suo tempore conformandum corpori gloriosò sui capitis, Phil.3.21. longe melior est conditio, quanquam ad tempus putredine obruti, quàm dum in terris viueret: quatenus nimirum insensibile factum, & in puluerem redactum, tot tantisque huius vitae miseriis eximitur: & maximè propterea quod amplius non est instrumentum agens nec patiens, in hac miserâda peccati seruitute, in carnis aduersus Spiritum lucta. En cur tantopere Simeon ille propter hunc exitum, Luc. 2.29. Dominum nostrum adhuc infantem vlnis suis complexus, laetetur. Quid faciendum igitur nobis, eum iam victorem ad dexteram Dei Patris sedentem oculis fidei conspicientibus & inuocantibus? Tale fuit Apostoli desiderium, Philipp.1.23. & Rom. 7.24. Et hoc tamen ad id ipsum, quod idem docet Apostolus, Philipp.3. 12.24. est exigendum.
units.tr: What fear, then, or what sorrow could overcome us when we depart from this world, since the soul, leaving this body, so happily changes its dwelling? We have discussed this sufficiently in the history of the converted thief. Let us therefore say no more that there is no remedy against the terrors of death; rather, let death itself, as the scorpion does, supply a remedy against its own sting. For death, separating the soul from the body, at the same time frees it from the bondage of sin and sends the victor back to him by whom he was sent, so that it may actually enjoy the happiness which, while it lived on earth, it possessed only in hope. As for the body, although it returns to the earth to be decayed, nevertheless, apart from the fact that it will not suffer that decay forever, but will be refined and in due time conformed to the glorious body of its Head, Phil. 3.21, its condition is far better, although for a time overwhelmed by putrefaction, than while it lived on earth: namely, because it has become insensible and reduced to dust, and is freed from so many and so great miseries of this life, and above all because it is no longer an instrument acting or suffering in this wretched bondage of sin, in the struggle of the flesh against the Spirit. See why that Simeon, Luke 2.29, rejoiced so greatly at this departure, embracing our Lord while still an infant in his arms.
