At tales sunt superstitiosorum mores, quibus etiam optime cum hypocritis conuenit, quod hodie maxime si alias vnquam experimur. Absit autem vt in eorum numero censeamur: contra vero faciamus initium ab interiori, nempe conscientiae rectitudine quam ex Dei verbo informatam perpetuo retineamus.
units.tr: (The scruple of the Jews, resting in part on a firm foundation but called more to use,) they shrank from entering the praetorium lest they be defiled (John 18.28), yet they did not fear to defile themselves with so many and such unspeakable crimes, and to drive the judge to condemn an innocent man to the cross; which the Lord once rebuked them for, namely straining out the gnat but swallowing the camel (Matt. 23.24). Such are the manners of superstitious people, and they agree very well with hypocrites, which we experience today more than at any other time. May we be far from being counted among their number. On the contrary, let us begin from within, namely with rectitude of conscience, which, formed by the Word of God, we should keep constantly.

units.la: Externas autem actiones, quod attinet, quidem nos a Legis ceremonialis Iudaeorum iugo Dominus liberauit, vt cauendum ne aliud ab illo iugum accersamus (qua in re Catholici Romani hodierni graviter peccant vt diximus alias) sic non est cum quibusdam sentiendum Deum interiora tantum inspicere. Nam contra vt animam & corpus & interius & exterius hominis ipse condidit, sic etiam ab utroque se coli postulat. Verum externas actiones, tam quae religionem spectant quam alias, ad ordinem in Ecclesia pie & religiose cum bona sanctaque discretione constitutum, oportet exigi.
units.tr: As for external actions, although the Lord has freed us from the yoke of the ceremonial Law of the Jews, we must take care not to bring upon ourselves another yoke in its place (in which matter the Roman Catholics of today sin grievously, as we have said elsewhere). Yet it is not right, as some think, that God looks only at the inward parts. For just as he created the soul and body of man, both inward and outward, so he also asks to be worshipped by both. Indeed, external actions, both those that concern religion and others, must be required to conform to the order established in the Church, piously and religiously, with good and holy discretion.

units.la: De crurum fractione, seu Iudaei prius illud a Romanis in quibusdam factitari viderant, ne in tam graui supplicio poena diuturniorem fieret, seu nullum crudelitatis genus in torquendo Do-
units.tr: As to the breaking of the legs: either the Jews had seen the Romans practise this beforehand in some cases, so that the punishment in so grievous a torment would not be prolonged, or they wished that no kind of cruelty in torturing should be left untried against our Lord Jesus Christ, since no torment, however harsh, satisfied the raging fury of their hatred.

units.la: Domino nostro Iesu Christo voluerunt inta-ctum, nullo Cruciatu quantumuis aspero rabiem efferatam eorum explente, iterum hic admiranda Dei prouidentia apparet, primùm in eo quòd à Pilato istiusmodi fractionem crurum impetrarunt. Nam alioquin Prophetiæ veritas prædicentis hoc in Christo non factum iri, nequaquam esset conspicua. Deinde, quòd Deus mente & consilio suorum hostium in contrariam partem vsus sit vt nempe voluntas eorum Dei consilio penitus repugnans, ad ea quæ Deus statuerat implenda viam aperiret.
units.tr: Here again the wonderful providence of God appears: first, in that they obtained from Pilate this breaking of the legs. For otherwise the truth of the prophecy foretelling that this would not be done to Christ would not have been evident. Second, in that God, using the mind and counsel of his enemies, turned them to the opposite side, so that their will, which was wholly opposed to the counsel of God, opened a way for the fulfilment of what God had decreed.

units.la: Hinc duo summè necessaria doctrinæ capita nobis colligenda: prius de Dei nostri Prouidentia, quam considerare debemus non tantùm circa res huius mundi magis insignes verissimam, vt quidam olim prophani Philosophi docuerunt, sed etiam ad minima quæque se extendentem, à quibus ne excipienda quidè vllo modo sunt hominum dicta, facta vel cogitationes, nec ipsa rerum momenta aut casus, quicunque tandem ferantur. Fortuitò igitur nihil fit, & Fortunę nomine, quod Epicuris & Atheis relinquimus, nihil magis prophanum.
units.tr: From this two most necessary heads of doctrine are to be gathered. The first is concerning the providence of our God, which we must consider as most true not only with regard to the more notable things of this world, as some profane philosophers taught long ago, but as extending even to the smallest things, from which by no means are excluded the words, deeds or thoughts of men, nor the very moments or chances of things, whatever they may be. Therefore nothing happens by chance, and that name of Fortune, which we leave to the Epicureans and atheists, is nothing more profane.

units.la: Alterum est, quum ij ipsi qui Deo resistunt, quantum in ipsis est, in hac ipsa tamen eorum contumacia subditi sint eius prouidentiæ & potentiæ à quo aguntur, quandoquidè omnia ad suam gloriam & salutem suorum disposuit, vt etiam sceleratorum hominum rebellione ad id ipsum implendum quod maximè velint infectum abatatur: sequi necessariò nihil esse.
units.tr: The second is that, although those who resist God, so far as lies in them, are nevertheless subject, even in this very obstinacy of theirs, to his providence and power by whom they are moved, since he has disposed all things for his own glory and the salvation of his people, so that even by the rebellion of wicked men what they most wish is hindered from being accomplished: it must follow that nothing is done in vain.

units.la: Ll. j. quo terreantur DeiFilij,licet cœlo & terra in-uicem aduersus ipsos conspirantibus,& rui-nam minantibus.Quod vtinam omni tempore diligenter consideremus, sed nominatim in hac bellica probatione, cum qua adhuc hodie tantopere luctamur.
units.tr: Let the sons of God be terrified by nothing, though heaven and earth conspire against them and threaten ruin. Would that we always considered this diligently, and especially in this warlike trial with which we still struggle so hard today.

units.la: Porrò Legis huius diuinæ fundamentum propius est considerandum, qua iubentur ca-dauera pendentium ex ligno intra vesperam deponi, quoniam (inquit texrus Deut. 21.23. Qui pendet, est Dei maledictio. Quod quum Apostolus disertè obseruarit,Gal.3.13.leuiter à nobis prætereundum non est. Agnosco igitur omnes legitimè factas executiones lata à iudi-ce sententia non tantùm notam quandam in-samiæ coràm hominibus inurere,sed etiam ef-se testimonium speciale & visibile furoris Di-uini aduersus peccatum, etsi Deus vitam sic fi-nientes & pœnitentiam agentes misericordia sua complectatur,nonnunquam maiore quàm quos pacifica in lectis suis morte contingit e viuis excedere, quod superius in historia con-uersi latronis obseruauimus.Sed prætereà Deus hoc supplicij genus speciali quadam infamia notauit,vt hodie magis ignominiosam suspe-sionem videmus quàm capitis truncationem. Idcirco nos Apostolus tam suprà dicto loco, quàm Philip.2.8. monet vt consideremus non tantùm Iesum Christum pro nobis esse mor-tuum, sed nominatim hocmortis genere, in quo Deus specialem iram aduersus peccatum demonstrabat, quemadmodum idem etiam Apostolus. Gal. 3. 13. non tantùm dicit Iesum Christum pro nobis mortuum, sed etiam pro nobis factum maledictionem, vt erat ab Esaia Propheta prædictum, Esa. 53. 4. ne dubitemus nos ab illo plane in libertatem à Legis maledictione esse assertos. Hæc sunt igitur in hac historia cognitione dignissima, de quibus si natio illa deplorata serio cogitasset, eum adorasset & hodie adoraret quem non tantùm ex ligno pendere, vt ferebat mos Iudæorum, sed etiam, quò suam explerent libidinem, Cruci affigi voluerùt, vt erat apud Romanos & gentes alias prophanas vsitatum.
units.tr: Further, the foundation of this divine Law is to be considered more closely, by which it is commanded that the bodies of those hanging on a tree be taken down before evening, since (the text says) "he who hangs is cursed by God" (Deut. 21.23). Since the Apostle has expressly noted this (Gal. 3.13), it is not to be passed over lightly by us. I acknowledge, therefore, that all executions lawfully carried out under a sentence pronounced by a judge not only impress a certain mark of infamy before men, but are also a special and visible testimony of the divine wrath against sin, even though God embraces with his mercy those who end their life in this way and repent, and sometimes they depart from life with greater (suffering) than those whom a peaceful death in their own beds overtakes, as we observed above in the history of the converted thief. But moreover God marked this kind of punishment with a special infamy, so that today we see hanging on a gibbet to be more ignominious than beheading. Therefore the Apostle, both in the passage cited above and in Philippians 2.8, admonishes us to consider not only that Jesus Christ died for us, but especially by this kind of death, in which God displayed his special wrath against sin. In the same way the Apostle, in Galatians 3.13, says not only that Jesus Christ died for us but also that he was made a curse for us, as the prophet Isaiah had foretold (Isa. 53.4). Let us not doubt that by him we have been plainly set free from the curse of the Law. These, then, are the things most worthy of knowledge in this history; if that unhappy nation had seriously considered them, they would have adored, and would today adore, him whom they made hang not only on a tree, as the custom of the Jews was, but also, to satisfy their lust, wished to be fastened to a cross, as was usual among the Romans and other profane nations.

units.la: Cæterùm abolita Iudaica politia vnà cum ipsa natione in eo quod habuit peculiare, cauendum nobis à quorundam fanaticorum ingeniis de ea re conquerentium, quasi nostris adhuc temporibus Lex illa vigeret de depo-nendis ex patibulis istiusmodi sententia iudi cum damnatorum cadaueribus, quæ nefas sit in publico pendere. Nam contrà tanta est hominum hodie malitia, vt expediat nonnun-quam eiusmodi homines in exemplum aliorum etiam post mortem statui. Fateor tamen nisi magnis de causis ad id cogantur Magistratus, laudandos eos qui in clementiorem partem inclinant, & hac in parte modum adhibent, quod Dei beneficio clementer in hac vrbe fieri conspicimus.
units.tr: Yet although the Jewish polity has been abolished, together with the nation itself in what was peculiar to it, we must beware of the wits of certain fanatics who complain about this matter, as if that law still held in our own times, requiring that the bodies of men condemned by judicial sentence be taken down from the gallows, since it would be wrong for such bodies to hang in public. For on the contrary, human malice today is so great that it is sometimes expedient for such men to be exposed, even after death, as an example to others. I admit, however, that unless the magistrates are compelled to do so for weighty reasons, we should praise those who incline to the more merciful course and observe moderation in this matter, as by God's blessing we see being done mercifully in this city.

units.la: Sequitur in historia, ex Pilati concessione, sracta latronibus esse crura nondum mortuis: qua in re conspicimus licet tantum distaret latro vnus ab alio quantum atrum ab albo, Deum tamen voluisse quod ad mortem primam attinet aequalia omnia ipsis contingere. Absit tamen inde colligamus ex hodiernorum Romanensium doctrina, Deum peccata condonantem solam Culpam remittere, poenam autem & satisfactionem retinere: Diabolicam vere doctrinam, vt superius pluribus explicauimus.Nec vero longius testimonium quo secus hoc esse probemus quam in hoc misero latrone conuerso quaerendum, cui dictum est ipsum fore (spiritu ipsius puta ex corpore migrante) non in inferis, non in Limbo, non denique in Purgatorio,sed in Paradiso, cu eo quem Regem suum agnouerat:quod commune omnibus in Christo morientibus esse docuimus.Certissimum igitur istud est,Iesum Christi vnicum nostrum verum esse Seruatorem, prorsus delevit peccatis nostris per suum sanguinem,& obedientiam sua nobis in plena & perfectam iustitiam imputatam quae in ipso est,& non in nobis.
units.tr: The history goes on to say that, by Pilate's permission, the legs of the robbers were broken while they were not yet dead. In this we see that, although one robber differed from another as much as black from white, God nonetheless willed that all of them should share equally in the first death. Let us not, however, conclude from this, as the doctrine of the Papists today does, that God, when he forgives sins, removes only the guilt and retains the punishment and satisfaction. This is indeed a diabolical doctrine, as we explained at length above. Nor need we seek any clearer testimony to prove the contrary than in this wretched robber who was converted, to whom it was said that he would be (that is, when his spirit departed from the body) not in hell, not in Limbo, and not finally in Purgatory, but in Paradise, with him whom he had acknowledged as his King; which we have shown to be common to all who die in Christ. It is therefore most certain that Jesus Christ, our only true Saviour, has utterly blotted out our sins through his blood, and has imputed to us his obedience, which is full and perfect righteousness, which is in him and not in us.

units.la: At plena haec a morte secunda liberatio, non impedit quominus Deus plane peccatori conuerso reconciliatus suos explorer, atque adeo corporaliter & temporaliter,quando, & quos voluerit, etiam vsque ad mortis primae inclusiue poenas castiger. Nequaquam vero(sicuti mentiuntur adueisarij) quo poenae illae pro peccatis satisfaciant, aut sint ipsis, vt loquuntur,meritoriae:sed in iis quidem quos explorat, aut quibus etiam sic vtitur, vt velit eos omne genus crudelitatis pro iustitia pati,non sunt illa in la in poenis reponenda, sed contra in maximo pretio habenda, summoque decori ducenda, quum eos suis insignibus vestiat, vt in eorum constantia, quam deinceps coronat gloria inenarrabili, glorificetur, Rom. 8. 17. in iis vero quos castigat (siue ad mortem id faciat siue secus) ad documentum ipsorum facit, vt sub Domini ferula, non tanquam indignantis iudicis aduersus improbos, sed tanquam Patris, medicinam quae suis conueniat cognoscentis, proficiant: & ad aliorum etiam exemplum: quae sic omnia moderatur, vt nonnunquam etiam peccatores, quos ipsi visum est, poenis capitalibus, quas erat meriti, eximantur: Testis esto de qua apud Iohan. 8. 11. mentio fit adultera: & quae quotidie in oculos exempla incurrunt: quum tamen secus agi cū hocmisero latrone conuerso voluerit. Qua re docemur nō temerè de Dei odio vel amore ex rebus prosperis vel aduersis iudicandum: teste Iob historia, & Sapientis admonitione, Ecclef. 9. 1.
units.tr: But this full deliverance from the second death does not prevent God, who has been reconciled to the sinner who is converted, from testing his own people and chastising them bodily and temporally, when and whom he wills, even to the point of the penalties of the first death. Yet in no way (as our adversaries falsely claim) are those penalties imposed so that they satisfy for sins, or are, as they put it, meritorious for the sufferers. Rather, in those whom he tests, or whom he so uses that he wills them to suffer every kind of cruelty for righteousness' sake, these sufferings are not to be counted as punishments but are to be held in the highest esteem and reckoned a great honour, since he clothes them with his own badges, so that he may be glorified in their constancy, which he afterwards crowns with inexpressible glory (Rom. 8. 17). In those whom he chastises, whether unto death or otherwise, he does it for their instruction, so that under the rod of the Lord, not as a judge angry with the wicked but as a Father who knows what medicine suits his children, they may profit; and also as an example to others. He so governs all these things that sometimes he even releases from the capital punishments that they deserved those sinners whom he chose; witness the adulteress mentioned in John 8. 11, and the examples that daily come before our eyes. Yet he willed it otherwise in the case of this wretched robber who was converted. From this we are taught not to judge rashly about God's hatred or love from prosperous or adverse circumstances, as the history of Job and the warning of the Wise Man bear witness (Eccl. 9. 1).

units.la: Sed vt ad textum reuertamur, narrat historia, Iesu Christo crura non fracta fuisse, cuius rei duae causae adferuntur: prior militum respectu, quos non opus fuit mortem maturare iam ante mortui, quod ex eorum testimonio firmum erat & indubitatum, quipropius illud inquisierant. Altera Dei prouidentiae respectu qui longè aliter decreuerat, vt testatur Euangelista ex iis quae Exod. 12. 42. scripta sunt. Hic verò quaedam occurrunt difficultates ordine a nobis explicandae. Ll. iij.
units.tr: But to return to the text: the history relates that the legs of Jesus Christ were not broken, and two reasons are given for this. The first has regard to the soldiers, who had no need to hasten death, since he was already dead, as their testimony made certain and beyond doubt, for they had examined the matter closely. The second has regard to God's providence, which had decreed quite otherwise, as the Evangelist testifies from what was written in Exod. 12. 42. Here, however, certain difficulties arise, which we must explain in order.

units.la: Prima, non de Christo scripta videri quae in illo Moßis loco scripta sunt, sed de agno Paschatis: nec de re semel tantum in aliquo perficienda: sed quoties Festum Paschatis celebrabatur observanda. Facilis responsio: Iohannem vel potius Sp. Sanctum haec Euangelistae dictatem optime adaptasse veritati quae de figura prius dicta fuerant. Nam extra omne dubium in Ecclesia Dei fuit hunc agnum tam in ipsa quàm ceremoniarum respectu, quibus illum sacrificari oportebat & comedi, fuisse instar figurae & speciali pictura Iesu Christi, suam Ecclesiam a tyrannide Diaboli, peccati & mortis, in libertatem asserentis, introducendam tandem in veram ipsius quietem & tranquillitatem, cuius erat terra Canaan figura, teste ipso Ioanne Baptista, vocante Iesum Christum, Agnum qui tollit mundi peccata, & ipso Apostolo adhuc expressius, 1.Cor.5.7.
units.tr: The first is that what is written in that passage of Moses seems not to be written about Christ but about the Passover lamb, and not about a thing to be accomplished only once, but about something to be observed whenever the Feast of the Passover was celebrated. The answer is easy: John, or rather the Holy Spirit, has most aptly adapted these words of the Evangelist to the truth that had been previously spoken of in figure. For beyond all doubt there was in the Church of God the understanding that this lamb, both in itself and in respect of the ceremonies by which it was to be sacrificed and eaten, was a figure and a special picture of Jesus Christ, who asserts his Church in liberty from the tyranny of the Devil, sin and death, and who will at length bring her into the true rest and tranquillity of which the land of Canaan was a figure. So testifies John the Baptist himself, when he calls Jesus Christ the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, and the Apostle himself even more expressly (1 Cor. 5. 7).

units.la: Altera quaestio est, cur in Paschatis ceremonia Deus illius agni ossa frangi prohibuerit: ac proinde cur Deus noluerit ossa Iesu Christi confringi, ut esset quaedam inter figuram & veritatem analogia. Aio itaque quod ad ceremoniam Agni Paschalis, qua Deus populo suo praesentabat non tantum in genere liberationem ex Aegypto, verum etiam illius liberationis admirandam rationem, quantaque cum festinatione, relictis quae a tergo erant, (quo etiam panes Azymi cum festinatione coacti rapiebant) Aegypto egredi ipsos oporteret, hanc etiam festinationem repraesentatam fuisse.
units.tr: The second question is why, in the ceremony of the Passover, God forbade the bones of that lamb to be broken; and therefore why God did not will the bones of Jesus Christ to be broken, so that there might be a certain analogy between figure and truth. I say, then, that in the ceremony of the Paschal Lamb, by which God presented to his people not only in general their deliverance from Egypt, but also the wonderful manner of that deliverance, and how great the haste with which they had to leave Egypt, leaving behind what was at their back (for which reason they also snatched up unleavened bread, being driven by haste), this haste was also represented.

units.la: fc fe quum festinanter edere iussi sunt, vt dicitur expressè, Exod.12.11. ac proinde non immorari in frangendis aut arrodendis ossibus, quod plerumque fit quum per otium cibus sumitur.
units.tr: For they were ordered to eat it in haste, as is expressly stated in Exod. 12. 11, and therefore not to linger in breaking or gnawing the bones, which usually happens when food is taken at leisure.

units.la: Quod si quis ad liberationem nostram spiritualem referat, non absurdum erit dicere Dominum ea re docere voluisse cupientes eum sequi, & in veram quò nos deducit quietem ingredi, nullam satis magnam adhibere posse diligentiâ in deserenda & fugienda Ægypto nostra, quæ hic mundus est & nos ipsi, contentos cum festinatione frui rebus ad hoc iter peragendum necessariis, nec ossibus nec medullis inhærentes, quod solent qui in rebus caducis & corruptioni obnoxiis animum collocant, de quibus Pas.17.14.agit.
units.tr: But if anyone refers this to our spiritual deliverance, it will not be absurd to say that the Lord wished by this to teach those who desire to follow him, and to enter into the true rest to which he leads us, that no diligence can be great enough in forsaking and fleeing from our Egypt, which is this world and ourselves; and that they should enjoy with haste the things necessary for accomplishing this journey, not clinging to the bones or marrow, as those do who set their minds on fleeting things subject to corruption, of whom Ps. 17. 14 speaks.

units.la: Quocunque vero tandem hæc ceremonia spectauerit, hic scire nobis sufficiat quod docet Sp.Sanctus, iam tunc Dominum voluisse quæ olim erant in corpore veri illius Agni Redemptoris nostri perficienda prædicere, sicut & multas alias circumstantias in Dauidis persona præfiguratas, quorum expressa testimonia Euangelistæ diligenter annotarunt, vt Iesum Christum verum illum esse Messiam Patribus promissum & præfiguratum sigillatim cognoscamus.
units.tr: Yet whatever purpose this ceremony was intended to serve, it is enough for us to know here what the Holy Spirit teaches: that already then the Lord willed to foretell what was to be fulfilled in the body of that true Lamb, our Redeemer, just as he also prefigured many other circumstances in the person of David, whose explicit testimonies the Evangelists carefully noted, so that we may know individually that Jesus Christ is that true Messiah promised to the Fathers and prefigured by them.

units.la: Sin vlterius progressi quidam adhuc penitius inquirant in mysterium quod hic latere putant, cur non permiserit Iesus Christus vlum ex suis ossibus confringi, aio nobis ea re duo representari. Prius, licet mortuum corpus, Ll. iiij.
units.tr: But if some, going further, inquire more deeply into the mystery which they think lies hidden here, why Jesus Christ did not permit any of his bones to be broken, I say that two things are represented to us by this. The first is that, although his body was dead,

units.la: nonmagis tamen in hostium fuisse potestate, & eorum libidini permissum, quàm dum in viuis vitam ageret: à quibus nihil passus est quàm quod ipsemet pati voluit.
units.tr: it was nonetheless no more in the power of his enemies, and no more subject to their lust, than while he lived among the living; from them he suffered nothing except what he himself willed to suffer.

units.la: Deinde quòd per ossa corporis soliditas & firmitudo intelligitur, ideo Iesus Christus ossa sua ab omni fractione eximens, docuit nos a- nimae à corpore solutione viuificam eius po- tentiam nullo modo imminutam esse, nec Dei- tatis respectu, nec etiam humanitatis, necsibi nec suis. Nam ipse quidem per hanc ipsam mortem noltram infirmitatem exuit, in glo- riam Dei Patris ingressurus, Act.17.3.Membra verò sua tantùm abest vt sit ad tuendum imbe- cilliot, vt contrà ex eius morte vitam hauriant.
units.tr: The second is that by the bones of a body the solidity and firmness of the body is understood. Therefore Jesus Christ, by keeping his bones free from every breaking, taught us that the life-giving power of his soul was in no way diminished by its separation from the body, neither in respect of his Deity nor of his humanity, neither for himself nor for his own. For he indeed, by this very death of ours, put off weakness, to enter into the glory of God the Father (Acts 17. 3). His members, far from being weaker in order to be preserved, rather draw life from his death.

units.la: Et hoc ipsum paulò post ipse Dominus con- spicuum fecit, emissa aqua & cruore ex corpo- re suo lanceae ictu saucio, sicuti paulò post di- cturi lumus. Idcirco Propheta psalm.34.21.pa- lam profitetur Dominum ossa omnia iusto- rum tueri, idest singulorum ipsius filiorum vt nullum ex ipsis conteratur. Minimè quidem profecto quòd omnium illorum ossa à fractio- ne licut ossa Iesu Christi conseruentur. Nam e- tiam feris obiectos quosdam ex Dei fidelissi- mis seruis videmus, & ab iis corporibus suis di- laniatos, eo ipso teste qui quum Romam be- stiis obiiciendus duceretur, aiebat se abire vt moleretur ac pura coram Deo farina fieret. sed quod eădem vi & potestate qua caput ossa sua ne confringerentur prohibuit, vltimo die me- brorum suorum ossa confracta vel in pulueram etiam etiā redacta sint restituturus, sicut eius incorruptione à qua corpus suum exemit in sepulchro, abolenda est nostra corruptio, & in gloriam spiritualem æternam commutanda, quatenus cum ipso vestiantur.
units.tr: The Lord himself made this plain a little later, when water and blood flowed from his body through the wound of the spear, as we shall say shortly. Therefore the Prophet plainly declares in Psalm 34:21 that the Lord keeps all the bones of the righteous, that is, that none of his individual sons is crushed. Certainly this does not mean that the bones of all of them are preserved from breaking as the bones of Jesus Christ were. For we see that some of God's most faithful servants were thrown to wild beasts and torn apart in their bodies. That same witness, when he was being led to Rome to be thrown to the beasts, said that he was going so that he might be ground and become pure flour before God. But the same power and authority by which he kept his own bones from being broken will, on the last day, restore the broken bones of his members, even those reduced to dust. Just as by the incorruption in which he freed his body in the sepulchre, our corruption is to be abolished and changed into eternal spiritual glory, so that we may be clothed with him.

units.la: Tertia quæstio nascitur ex verbis Apostoli, 1.Cor.11.24. qui Sacrosanctæ Cœnæ formulam explicans, hac vtitur loquendi phrasi, Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis frangitur, quum legamus apud Lucam, Hoc est corpus meum quod pro vobis datur,Luc.22.19. Aio vero Apostolum nihil minus quàm de emendando Euangelista, vel huic historiæ contradicendo cogitasse: sed ea docentem quæ in Sacramentalibus ritibus per fractionem panis repræsentatur, hac vsu voce, quò melius modū quo pro nobis Christus seipsum dedit exprimeret, eius humanitate nimirum velut in partes dissecta, spiritu quidem ipsius in cœlos abeunte, corpore vero iis terris manente: ac corpore quidem eius mirn modis lacero & aperto tot virgarum ictibus, & perforatis manibus ac pedibus, & doloribus infinitis fracto, quibus etiam eius ad mortem vsque anima est afflicta. Quæ mysteria quum Sacramentaliter nobis in Sacrosanctæ Cœnæ panis fractione repræsententur, aio non sine magno errore in Ecclesia Christiana ceremoniam illam paulatim abolitam, quam ipse Dei Filius præscripserat, & tota vetus Ecclesia retinuerat: & pro fractione panis substitutos singulos paruos panes sigillatim distribuendos: quasi verò non expresse dicamur omnes eundem panem edere ad denotandam vnionem Ecclesiæ cum vnico suo capite, vt nominatim Apostolus, de sacrosancta Cœna loquens, 1. Cor.10.17.nos docet.
units.tr: A third question arises from the words of the Apostle in 1 Cor. 11:24, who, explaining the form of the most holy Supper, uses this phrase: "This is my body, which is broken for you." Yet we read in Luke: "This is my body which is given for you" (Luke 22:19). I say that the Apostle did not think at all of correcting the Evangelist or of contradicting this history. Rather, in teaching what is represented in the sacramental rite by the breaking of bread, he used this word so that he might better express the manner in which Christ gave himself for us: namely, his humanity as if cut into parts, his Spirit indeed going into heaven, but his body remaining on earth. That body was torn and opened in marvellous ways by so many blows of rods, its hands and feet pierced, broken by infinite pains, by which his soul also was afflicted even to death. Since these mysteries are represented to us sacramentally in the breaking of the bread of the most holy Supper, I say that it is no small error that in the Christian Church that ceremony, which the Son of God himself prescribed and the whole ancient Church retained, has gradually been abolished. In place of the breaking of bread, single small loaves are distributed one by one, as if we were not plainly told that we all eat the same bread, to signify the union of the Church with its one head. The Apostle teaches us this by name, speaking of the most holy Supper (1 Cor. 10:17).

units.la: Sequitur apud historiam alterius Prophetiæ impletio, qua quum prædictum sit vltimo die visuros Iesum Christum qui ipsum perfoderint, Zach.12.10. necessario & illa sicut superiores oportuit impleri speciali Dei prouidentia, nihil minus tamen cogitantibus quorum vsus est opera in iis implendis quæ tot ante seculis prædixerat & decreuerat. Dicitur igitur quidam ex militibus, Pilati nimirum, lancea Iesu Christi latus perfodisse, seu Iudæis gratificaturus, vt quidam existimarunt, seu periculum facturus an revera Iesus Christus mortuus esset, nec-ne: quod verisimilius est: quo militis facto Dominus visus est vt obuiam iretur eorum calumniæ qui alioquin aduersus Domini resurrectionem obloqui potuissent, viuum adhuc e Cruce depositum, deinde medicatis vulneribus sanatum, & in alias regiones ablegatum.
units.tr: The history goes on to the fulfilment of another prophecy, in which it was foretold that on the last day they would look on Jesus Christ whom they had pierced (Zech. 12:10). Necessarily this too, like the earlier ones, had to be fulfilled by the special providence of God, although those whose work was used in fulfilling it were thinking of nothing less, since God had foretold and decreed these things many centuries before. It is said, then, that one of the soldiers, namely one of Pilate's, pierced the side of Jesus Christ with a lance. Some have thought he did it to please the Jews; others, which is more likely, to test whether Jesus Christ was truly dead or not. By the soldier's deed the Lord appears to have met the calumny of those who might otherwise have spoken against his resurrection, since he was taken down from the Cross still alive, and then, his wounds having been treated with medicines, he was healed and sent away to other regions.

units.la: Nam etiam licet tot tantaque sint, tam clara & aperta mortis ipsius testimonia, nihilominus extiterunt iam pridem hæretici adeo perfrictæ frontis qui affirmarent, alij quidem specie tenus ista cotigisse: alij miraculose à Iesu Christo suppositum Simonem Cyrenæum, vt ait Mahumetus in Alcorano. Quod si esset, quid noltra, quæso, salute fieret? Tam igitur illustria hæc testimonia (& nominatim Euangelistæ testis oculati tam sancte hæc affirmantis fidem) omni-
units.tr: For although the testimonies of his death are so many, so great, so clear and open, there have nonetheless long since arisen heretics of such brazen effrontery who asserted that some things happened only in appearance, and others that, by a miracle, Simon of Cyrene was put in Jesus' place, as Muhammad says in the Alcoran. But if that were so, what, I ask, would become of our salvation? These illustrious testimonies, then, and especially the faith of the eyewitness Evangelist who affirms these things so solemnly, must be set against

units.la: omnibus illis mendaciis & sceleratis somniis opponamus.
units.tr: all those lies and wicked dreams.

units.la: Accedit autem etiam ad superiora crassissima: & pudenda maximè impostura, etiamnum hodie nostris ab aduersariis recepta, qua primùm vocem illam Graecam λόγχην volunt esse nomen istius militis: deinde ad historiam sua adiicientes somnia, doctorum contemplatiuorum more, militem illum fuisse Centurionem aiunt, & quidem cæcum, qui quum oculos abluisset sanguine & aqua quæ ex Domini latere profluxerat, confestim sanatus & Christianum factum tandemque Domini Martyrio insignem fuisse. Et is est Diuus eorum Longinus, satis repente indigetatus, cuius adorentur reliquiæ. Nam harum impostururarum hic est finis.
units.tr: Moreover, there is also added to the above a very gross and shameful imposture, still received today by our adversaries. First, they want the Greek word lonchē (λόγχην) to be the name of that soldier. Then, adding their own dreams to the history, in the manner of learned contemplatives, they say that the soldier was a centurion, and indeed a blind one, who, when he had washed his eyes with the blood and water that flowed from the side of the Lord, was at once healed, became a Christian, and was finally distinguished by martyrdom for the Lord. And this is their divine Longinus, quite suddenly given a name, whose relics are worshipped. For this is the end of these impostures.

units.la: Porrò fabulis istis & aliis similibus valere iussis, quæ hic adduntur attenta consideratione digna sunt, quod ea etiam Euangelista, tanquam maximi momenti rem tam expressè notarit, nempe, ex latere perfoslo statim aquam & sanguinem profluxisse. Nec verò fuit tantopere laborandum in quærendis causis vnde sanguis hic aqua permixtus ex corpore mortuo promanaret: multòque minus in miraculum transformandū, licet hoc facto ad verè admirandi effecti considerationem deducamur: Nam qui humani corporis anatomes non sunt penitus ignari, norunt membrana quadam cortegi, in qua semper aliquid sit liquoris, quo veluti rore quodam calor cordis irrigatur, quo velut officinam esse scimus in quo sanguis vitalis purior & arterialis formatur, quæ in Iesu Christi corpore paulò ante quàm hæc contingerent mortuo, tam repente non potuerunt alterari. Fuerunt igitur ista primum visibile & sensibile testimonium quo Iesu Christi mortis in Cruce veritas probata est, vulnerato ipso corde, & quidem eo vulnere, quo licet antea non mortuum tamen oportu erit confestim saucium expirare. Naturalis igitur ille sanguinis & aquæ fluxus ex hastæ vulnere fuit. At longè altius nos Deus hoc facto docet ascendere, in quo mysterium continetur longè supra cœlos omnes supereminens, ut ipse alibi Diuus Iohannes admonet. 1. Iohan. 5. 6. nempe Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum venisse non tantùm per aquam, sed etiam per aquam & sanguinem: At ista consideratione ampliorem requirunt, semel facto visibili & conspicuo quod hodie nobis spiritualiter contemplandum & recipiendum est, tam in verbi prædicatione quàm in Ecclesiæ Christianæ Sacramentis: idem arcanum quod Veteres Patres viderunt & sperarunt in figuris veteris fœderis: ut non sine magnis de causis hanc historiam Euangelista nobis nominatim commendarit.
units.tr: Moreover, having bidden farewell to these fables and others like them that are added here, what deserves careful consideration is that the Evangelist noted this so expressly, as a matter of the greatest importance: namely, that water and blood flowed out at once from the pierced side. Nor was there any need to labour so much in seeking the causes from which this blood, mixed with water, flowed out of a dead body, much less to turn it into a miracle, although by this deed we are led to consider a truly wonderful effect. For those who are not wholly ignorant of human anatomy know that there is a certain membrane around the heart, in which there is always some liquid, by which the heat of the heart is watered as with a kind of dew. We know that this is the workshop in which the purer vital and arterial blood is formed, and in the body of Jesus Christ, which was dead shortly before these things happened, such things could not so suddenly have been altered. These things were therefore the first visible and sensible testimony by which the truth of the death of Jesus Christ on the Cross was proved: his heart was wounded, and with a wound such that, although he was not yet dead, he would necessarily have expired at once. That natural flow of blood and water, then, came from the wound of the spear. But God teaches us through this deed to ascend far higher, for in it a mystery is contained that surpasses all the heavens, as the Apostle John elsewhere reminds us (1 John 5:6): that Jesus Christ our Lord came not only by water, but by water and blood. But such a matter requires a fuller consideration, since a visible and conspicuous thing has once been done, which today is to be contemplated and received spiritually, both in the preaching of the Word and in the Sacraments of the Christian Church. It is the same mystery that the Fathers of old saw and hoped for in the figures of the Old Covenant. For this reason the Evangelist has commended this history to us by name, not without great causes.

units.la: Quandoquidem igitur duo sunt ad salutem nostram necessaria, quorum alterum (peccatum scilicet in nobis ipsis quo rei fimus condemnationis) tolli oportet: alterum verò, quod in nobis non est, ad salutem, tamen omni-
units.tr: Since, therefore, there are two things necessary for our salvation, of which one (namely the sin in us by which we are liable to condemnation) must be taken away, and the other, which is not in us, is nonetheless

units.la: Totum no fira salutis mysterium visibiliter exhibitum omnino necessarium, (rectitudo nimirum cum Dei voluntate in Lege patefacta con- ueniens) in alio quæri & reperiri oportet: aio hac historia nobis visibiliter & palpa- biliter ante oculos poni cum in quo & per quem peccatum, quod in nobis est, de- leatur: & contrà, in quo & per quem, re- periatur id quo ius ad vitam æternam adi- piscimur: Iesum Christum, inquam, cru- cifixum, ex cuius corpore sanguis & aqua hæc manarunt, in quibus sic pro nobis su- sis & in nos manantibus inest tota vis pec- cata nostra purgandi, tam propter abso- lutam pro nobis factam solutionem, gratis nobis imputatam cum perfecta rectitudine & plena erga Legem obedientia quàm per re- nouationem in nobis ipsis inchoatam ad vi- tam spiritualè & æternam. Denique id ipsum est quod sub vetere Fœdere expectabatur inde ab ipsa promissione Adamo facta, Genef. 3.15. & primùm per vetera sacrificia, deinde per Circuncifionem, ac tandem per aquam expia- tionis, & alias istiusmodi figuras adumbraba- tur, quarum erat corpus & substantia Iesus Christus venturus, in quibus figuris veteres Patres eum spiritualiter viderent & amplecterentur, Col. 2.17. Id ipsum etiā est quod suo tempore nobis est exhibitum, & quotidie prædicatur in Nouo Euangelico Fœdere, ad quā prædicatione ante factu hoc cuius hic me minimus duo Sacramenta Dominus adiecerat, quibus non tantùm significatur nobis, sed etiam exhibetur idem Iesus Christus, qui venit in iustificationem & sanctificationem, spiritualiter etiam in ipsis à nobis, putà in Baptismo & Sacrosancta Cœna videndus & amplectendus. Non igitur abs re quidam ex Veteribus dixit,duo Ecclesię Sacramenta èIesu Christi latere manasse, quòd nimirum corpus illud in Cruce mortuum, & hæc aqua & sanguis sic ex hoc vulnerato corpore profluens, visibiliter & sensibiliter omnibus illa intueri volentibus exhibita, sint id ipsum quod non potuit olim à patribus in veteribus Sacramentis, nec à nobis hodie in nouis nisi fidei oculis conspici.
units.tr: wholly necessary for salvation (namely the righteousness that agrees with the will of God revealed in the Law), this whole mystery of our salvation, visibly set forth, must be sought and found in another. I say that this history places before our eyes, visibly and tangibly, the one in whom and through whom the sin that is in us is removed, and conversely, the one in whom and through whom we obtain the right to eternal life: Jesus Christ, I say, crucified, from whose body this blood and water flowed. In these, flowing out for us and into us, lies the whole power of cleansing our sins, both through the complete satisfaction made for us, reckoned to us freely, with perfect righteousness and full obedience to the Law, and through the renewal begun in ourselves unto spiritual and eternal life. Finally, this is what was expected under the Old Covenant from the very promise made to Adam (Gen. 3:15). It was shadowed first by the old sacrifices, then by circumcision, and at last by the water of purification and other such figures, of which Jesus Christ, who was to come, was the body and substance. In these figures the Fathers of old saw him spiritually and embraced him (Col. 2:17). This is also what has been set forth in its time to us, and is preached daily in the New Evangelical Covenant. Before this deed, of which we are now speaking, the Lord had added two Sacraments to that preaching, by which not only is Jesus Christ signified to us, but the same Jesus Christ, who came for justification and sanctification, is also exhibited, and is to be seen and embraced spiritually in these same Sacraments, namely in Baptism and in the most holy Supper. It is therefore not without reason that one of the ancients said that the two Sacraments of the Church flowed from the side of Jesus Christ. For that body dead on the Cross, and this water and blood flowing thus from the wounded body, are presented visibly and sensibly to all who wish to look upon them. They are the very thing that the Fathers could not in the old Sacraments, nor we today in the new, behold except with the eyes of faith.

units.la: At hic primùm discamus, Quis Sacramentorum auctor sit, vnus nempe Deus Pater per Filium suum, quem omnes hæ promissiones tam Veteris quàm Noui Fœderis respexerunt. Is enim est per cuius Spiritum Moses & Prophetę veterem populum sunt alloquuti,1.Cor. 10.& 1.Pet.1.11.
units.tr: But here let us first learn who the author of the sacraments is: one God, the Father, through his Son, whom all these promises of both the Old and the New Covenant looked to. For it is he through whose Spirit Moses and the prophets spoke to the old people: 1 Cor. 10 and 1 Pet. 1.11.

units.la: Is est,qui quum ipsemet in terras venisset,& figuras impleuisset, in ipsorum locum substituit in perpetuum ad finem vsque seculorum Baptismum, primum per Iohannis Baptistæ ministerium, Luc. 1.76. deinde ore proprio, Matth.28. 19.& Marc. 16. 16.ac tandem Sacrosanctam Cœnam, Matt. 26.26. Marc.14.22. Luc.22.19.& 1.Cor. 11.23. & 24.Ore igitur ipso Iesu Christi duo illa vera Ecclesiæ Christianæ Sacramenta, nempe Baptismus & sacrosancta Cœna,
units.tr: He is the one who, when he himself had come into the world and fulfilled the figures, put in their place, for ever until the end of the ages, Baptism: first through the ministry of John the Baptist, Luke 1.76; then by his own mouth, Matt. 28.19 and Mark 16.16; and finally the most holy Supper, Matt. 26.26, Mark 14.22, Luke 22.19 and 1 Cor. 11.23-24. Therefore, by the very mouth of Jesus Christ, those two true sacraments of the Christian Church, namely Baptism and the most holy Supper,

units.la: Dei folium est vitam æternam polliceri, & eiusdē sigilla imprimere. Coena, nec alia vlla præter hæc duo sunt instita, quemadmodum ex eiusdem interioribus & non aliunde vis eorum omnis & efficacia manat.
units.tr: are the covenant of God, promising eternal life, and impress its seals. No other sacraments besides these two have been instituted, since all their power and efficacy flows from his inward working and from nowhere else.

units.la: Quapropter quicquid prætexatur, aut quæcunque tandem vetustas adferatur, non licuit vllı mortali,ac ne ipsis quidem Angelis in Ecclesiam Dei vllum ritum Sacramentalem inuehere.Nam si inter homines nefas est priuato, vel Principis ministro, quicunque tandem ille sit vel monetam cudere, vel in publico sigillo quicquam immutare, addere vel detrahere, quinam illud licere dixerimus mortali,quicunque tandem ille sit, in iis quæ conscientiam & diuini cultus essentiam spectant? Ac si inutile est sigillum sine instrumento cui apponatur, quid Sacramentum sine Dei promissione, nisi mera illusio & fallacia futurum est? Quum verò Sacramenta & eorū administratio pars sint Apostolicæ prædicationis, annon mirum est Christianos, pro tot nouis Sacramentis & hominum inuentionibus recipiendis,non potius mentem ad tam horrendam Apostoli vocem, & quidem bis repetitam, Gal. 1. aduertisse, Etiamsi Angelus e cœlo euangelizet vobis præter id quod vobis euangelizauimus, anathema esto. Et tamen harum inuentionum quæ partim à Iudaismo abolito, partim ab Ethnicismo, quod ipsi fateri coguntur, sunt haustæ, & quicquid prætexatur in hominum cerebro natæ, patroni, non erubescunt eas Traditionum Apostolicarum nomine designare. Sed quum facilè certis & indubitatis testimoniis doceri possit, quo auctore, quo tempore, quibus ra-tionibus in Ecclesiam istiusmodi ritus inuecti sint, tam impudens est eorum ratiocinatio vt respònso sit indigna.
units.tr: Therefore, whatever is pretended, and whatever antiquity is brought forward, no mortal, nor even the angels themselves, has been permitted to introduce any sacramental rite into the Church of God. For if it is wrong among men for a private person, or a servant of the prince, whoever he may be, to strike coin or to alter anything in the public seal, adding or removing, by what right shall we say that a mortal, whoever he may be, may do so in matters that concern conscience and the essence of divine worship? And if a seal is useless without the instrument to which it is applied, what will a sacrament without God's promise be but mere illusion and deceit? Since the sacraments and their administration are part of apostolic preaching, is it not remarkable that Christians, in receiving so many new sacraments and human inventions, have not rather turned their minds to that dreadful voice of the Apostle, repeated twice indeed, Gal. 1: "Even if an angel from heaven preach to you beyond what we have preached to you, let him be anathema"? Yet these inventions, which are partly drawn from abolished Judaism and partly from heathenism (as they themselves are forced to confess), and whatever is pretended, born in the brains of men, their defenders are not ashamed to designate by the name of Apostolic Traditions. But since it can easily be shown, by certain and indubitable testimonies, by whose authority, at what time and on what grounds such rites were introduced into the Church, their reasoning is so shameless that it is not worth an answer.

units.la: Eâdem ratione tam eorum audacia condemnatur qui vsum alterius signorum Sacramentalium à sacrosancta Cœna sustulerunt, quàm eorū qui propterea quòd ex Christi latere sanguis & aqua sic defluxerūt, etiā miscendam aquam vino in sacrosanctæ Cœnæ celebratione docent. Nam vt superius diximus, nec corpus naturale & essentiale Iesu Christi, nec vitalis hæc aqua fluens ex eius corde, nec sanguis hic ex ipsius venis manans, tanquam Sacramenta nobis proponuntur, sed sunt illud ipsum quod tam veterum Sacramenta sub vetere Fœdere, quàm Noua sub Nouo nobis repræsentant.
units.tr: By the same reasoning, the audacity is condemned of those who removed the use of one of the sacramental signs from the most holy Supper, and equally of those who, because blood and water flowed thus from Christ's side, also teach that water is to be mixed with the wine in the celebration of the most holy Supper. For, as we said above, neither the natural and essential body of Jesus Christ, nor this living water flowing from his heart, nor this blood issuing from his veins, are set before us as sacraments; rather, they are that very thing which the sacraments of the old covenant under the Old, and the new under the New, represent to us.

units.la: Non igitur quorundam verborum pronuntiationi, nec hominibus ipsis pronuntiantibus, & quæ Deus in Sacramentorum administratione fieri iussit facientibus, tribuenda est mutatio vel consecratio Sacramentalis, quarum aqua in Baptismo, & panis ac vinum in Sacrosancta Cœna, res prius communes & ad vsum huius vitæ spectantes fiunt Sacramenta, sacra nempe signa & sigilla noui Fœderis & communicationis nostræ cum Iesu Christo & omnibus eius beneficiis in vitam æternam. Nam ea profecto non aliunde pendere quàm à Dei voluntate & institutione possunt, quam ipse Deus nobis per hæc verba sic pronuntiata & expressa per fideles suos seruos patefacit. Sed hoc longè peius est, quòd hodierni Romani, quũ de Cœnæ pane & vino agitur, quæ in Missam transformarunt, hac voce Mutationis aut Consecrationis Sacramentalis non intelligunt hanc mutationem rerum communium in Sacramenta, sed contrà suam Transsubstantiationem hoc nomine designent, id est substantiæ signorum huius panis & huius vini annulationem & exinanitionē. Denique hic etiam accedit cumulus ad hūc errorē quo manifeste signa Sacramentalia abolentur, vt dicant etiam Sacrificulorum suorum intentionem vt perfecta sit consecratio requiri: quod si verum est, sequitur neminem ad eorum Missam accedere posse cum fide, aut orare, sed semper dubitantem de eo quod in Missa sua attollitur, &Sacrificulorum manibus accipitur, siquidem nihil de intentione consecrantis panem hunc & hoc vinum, certum habere quisquam poterit: quum magnam contrà dubitandi occasionem tum ignorantia tum depravati & corrupti mores suorum sacrificulorum præbeant.
units.tr: Therefore the change or sacramental consecration, by which water in Baptism, and bread and wine in the most holy Supper, things previously common and belonging to the use of this life, become sacraments (holy signs and seals of the new covenant and of our communion with Jesus Christ and all his benefits unto eternal life), is not to be attributed to the pronouncing of certain words, nor to the men who pronounce them and do what God has commanded in the administration of the sacraments. For these things can depend on nothing other than the will and institution of God, which he reveals to us through these words, so pronounced and expressed by his faithful servants. But this is far worse: that the present-day Romanists, when they speak of the bread and wine of the Supper, which they have transformed into the Mass, do not understand by this word "change" or "sacramental consecration" this change of common things into sacraments, but on the contrary designate by this name their transubstantiation, that is, the annihilation and emptying of the substance of these signs, this bread and this wine. Finally, to this error there is also added a heap by which the sacramental signs are plainly abolished, namely that they say the intention of their sacrificers must also be required for the consecration to be complete. If this is true, it follows that no one can approach their Mass with faith or pray, but must always doubt what is lifted up in their Mass and taken into the hands of the sacrificers, since no one can be certain of the intention of the one consecrating this bread and this wine; whereas both the ignorance and the depraved and corrupt morals of their sacrificers provide a great occasion for doubt.

units.la: Idem est o de verorum & legitimè administratorum Sacramentorum vi & effectis iudicium, quũ nemini possint hæc effecta nisi Deo vni, sine insigni blasphemia & idololatria tribui: Patri nimirum, quatenus in hunc ipsum filium suum nobis dedit: Filio, quatenus in ipso Dei promissiones ratæ sunt & firmæ. 2. Cor. 1. 20. Sancto Spiritui quatenus ipse nos in-
units.tr: The same judgment holds concerning the power and effects of true and lawfully administered sacraments, since these effects can be attributed to no one but the one God without a notable blasphemy and idolatry: to the Father, insofar as he gave us this very Son; to the Son, insofar as in him the promises of God are ratified and confirmed, 2 Cor. 1.20; to the Holy Spirit, insofar as he himself

units.la: Mm. j. tus illuminat ad hanc veritatem intelligendam, & approbandam, & credentium cordibus applicat & obsignat, quorum etiam Spiritui testimonium adoptionis ipsorum reddit, Rom. 8. 14. & 16. quo respectu nostr etiam Euangelista, 1. Ioh. 5. 8. cum hoc sanguine & cum hac aqua Spiritus Sancti testimonium coniungit. Quis vero miretur hac idololatriam & impietatem, qua vis delendi peccata & spiritualiter in nostris conscientiis operandi, aquae Baptismi tribuitur, quae ne Angelis quidem ipsis competit: quum non minorem vim aquae suae lustrali, Signo Crucis, Cereis, offamentis mortuorum certis verbis ex collo pendentibus ad uersus quoslibet morbos, & suo Agnus Dei, ac denique quibuscunque rebus somniauerint tribuant?
units.tr: illuminates us to understand and approve this truth, and applies and seals it to the hearts of believers, to whose spirit he also gives the testimony of their adoption, Rom. 8.14 and 16. In this respect too our Evangelist, 1 John 5.8, joins the testimony of the Holy Spirit with this blood and this water. Who then would be surprised at this idolatry and impiety, by which the power of blotting out sins and of working spiritually in our consciences is attributed to the water of Baptism, a power which does not belong even to the angels, since they attribute no less power to their lustral water, to the sign of the cross, to candles, to the amulets of the dead hung from the neck with certain words against any diseases, to their Agnus Dei, and finally to whatever things they have dreamed up?

units.la: Siquis igitur quaerat, quis sit horum sacrorum signorum vlus & effectum, aio exipsius opere Pauli Apostoli, Rom. 4. 11. de Circumcisione loquentis, & Diui Petri, 1. Pet. 3. 21. illa esse posita primum in eo quod sunt ex Dei mandato signa & testimonia visibilia Iesu Christi, & omnium eius beneficiorum in vitam aeternam. Deinde non tantum in memoriam reuocare & significare ingentem illum thesaurum, veluti pictura nihil aliud efficit nisi quod refricat memoriam eorum quae oculis nostris subiicit, sed esse praeterea sacra sigilla, quae tum verbo tum promissione Sacramentali testentur, & faciant nos certiores, ca quae exterius significantur, etiam offerri, exhiberi & dari fidei hominis interio terioris: quam ob causam Apostolus non tantùm ea signa vocat, sed etiam σφραγίδας : adeò vt huius excellentis visus respectu, & vt sciamus Deum nunquam alterum sine altero præbere (puta signum exterius, sensibus exterioribus, & rem significatam, animæ & fidei credentis) sæpe nomen rei significatæ tribuatur signo, veluti quum Panis Cœnæ dicitur Corpus Domini, & Vinum, Sanguis Domini, Sacramentaliter: & effectum rei significatæ datur signis: veluti quum huius panis & huius vini communicatio vocatur corporis & sanguinis Domini communicatio, 1.Cor.10.16. veluti quum etiam dicimur Baptismo (quo proprie significatur exterior huius Sacramenti actio) mori, sepeliri & resurgere in Christo, Rom.6.4. & Colos.2.12.
units.tr: If anyone therefore asks what the use and effect of these sacred signs is, I answer, from the very work of the Apostle Paul, Rom. 4.11, speaking of circumcision, and of the divine Peter, 1 Pet. 3.21, that they were first instituted in this: that by God's command they are visible signs and testimonies of Jesus Christ and of all his benefits unto eternal life. Then, they do not only recall these things to memory and signify that vast treasure, as a picture does nothing else than refresh the memory of the things it sets before our eyes, but they are also sacred seals which, by the word and sacramental promise, attest and make us more certain that the things outwardly signified are also offered, presented and given to the inward faith of the man. For this reason the Apostle calls them not only signs but also seals [σφραγίδας]. So much so that, with respect to this excellent use, and so that we may know that God never gives the one without the other (that is, the outward sign to the outward senses, and the thing signified to the soul and the faith of the believer), the name of the thing signified is often given to the sign, as when the bread of the Supper is called the body of the Lord, and the wine the blood of the Lord, sacramentally; and the effect of the thing signified is given to the signs, as when the communion of this bread and this wine is called the communion of the body and blood of the Lord, 1 Cor. 10.16; and as when we are said in Baptism (by which the outward action of this sacrament is properly signified) to die, be buried and rise again in Christ, Rom. 6.4 and Col. 2.12.

units.la: Verùm ad hanc confusionem coniunctam cum manifesta idololatria & impietate fugiendam, aliis locis nobis exponuntur quæ sint tribuenda signis, & quæ Deo proprie conueniant, vnico agenti intus in nobis spiritualiter, quod ex eius præscripto exterius nostris sensibus per signa visibilia repræsentatur.
units.tr: But to avoid this confusion, joined with manifest idolatry and impiety, other passages set out for us what is to be attributed to the signs and what properly belongs to God, the one agent working inwardly in us spiritually, which is represented outwardly to our senses through visible signs in accordance with his appointment.

units.la: Nihilominus falsa est expositio illa quam adferunt coniunctionis Sacramentalis rei significatæ cum signis: qua volunt necessariò vbicunque signum est, ibi rem esse significatam: ex quo errore manauit opinio quæ tantopere Christianum orbem hodie exercet, tam eorum puta qui volunt signorum substantiam euanescere, vt substantiæ veri corporis & veri sanguinis Domini nostri Iesu Christi locus fiat: Mm. ij. quam eorum qui signorum quidem fubftan- tiam non abolent, sed volunt tamé cum signis veram substantiam etiam corporis & fangui- nis Iesu Christi realiter coniungi: adeò vt vtri- que doceant veri corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi substantiam non minus ore & manibus quàm panem & vinum recipi. Qua profecto doctrina prorsus euertitur tam veritas corpo- ris Iesu Christi ante & post Filij Dei incarna- tionem: quàm articulus Ascensionis ipsius su- pra cœlos omnes, & Reditus ipsius ex illis, vl- timo tandem die tantùm futuri, præter alia nō pauca absurda & ridicula commenta, quibus, istorum hominum vere mõftrofum ingenium patefit. Et tamen Spiritus erroris tantam habet efficaciam in Occidentali Christianismo, vt hæc pro totius religionis Christianæ fundamentis habeantur : sicuti contrà Orientalis & Meridionalis Christianismus Alcorano Mahumeti ceflit. Nos verò contrà sciamus veritatem Sacramentalis coniunctionis in eo positam quod Deus (à quo vno Sacramentorum auctoritas & efficacia pendet) nunquam offert credentibus signa sine re significata, sed diuersè tamen & diuersis obiectis, vt duę res longè diuersæ sunt. Signa igitur, puta aqua Baptismi & panis ac vinum Sacrosanctæ Cœnæ, quum natura sua corporea sint & sensibilia, sensibus & instrumentis corporeis singulorum offeruntur: quoniam autem id fit in Ecclesia, extra vsum eorum naturalem, ad accedentium animis res ad vitam spiritualem spectantes exhibenhibendas (Iesum Christum nimirū & eius beneficia Iustificationem & Sanctificationem) quod mysterium in eo solo consistit quod vera fides sola potest videre & apprehendere, idcirco res hæc cœlestis per terrena signa repræsentata, semper quidem omnibus accedentibus offertur à Domino, sed ore & manibus spiritualibus percipienda, fide nimirum, instrumento non corporeo, sed Spiritui regeneranti proprio. Inde fit vt quibus hanc gratiam Deus largitus est, vt ad Domini mensam (aut etiam ad Baptismum si fuerint adulti) accedant tam manus & os spirituale adferentes, fidei nimirum, quàm corporeum, tum signorum tum rei per illa significatæ fiant participes, ad maius fidei & salutis ipsorum incrementum. At qui manus tantum & os corporeum adferunt, res tantùm corporeas, aquam in Baptismo, & panem & vinum in sacrosancta Cœna percipiût, & quidem ad condemnationem, quòd cum tanto contemptu receperint non simpliciter aquam, panem aut vinum, sed res sacras ipsis oblatas tanquam signa, pignora & sigilla tam immensi tamque pretiosi instrumenti, putà communicationis Iesu Christi & omnium ipsius beneficiorum ad vitam æternam. Ex quibus apparet quantopere hallucinentur qui concludunt impericissimè, propterea quòd Dominus signa nunquam offert sine re significata, nunquam etiam alterum sine altero posse recipi. Et propterea (quod adhuc est magis absurdum) tam res terrenas, nempe signa, quàm res spirituales, res significatas, vno & eodem instrumento corporeo manibus & ore percipi.
units.tr: Nevertheless, that explanation is false which they offer of the sacramental connection between the thing signified and the signs. They hold that wherever there is a sign, the thing signified is necessarily present there. From this error has sprung the opinion that so greatly troubles the Christian world today: on the one hand, of those who want the substance of the signs to vanish so that room is made for the substance of the true body and true blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and on the other, of those who do not abolish the substance of the signs, but want the true substance of the body and blood of Jesus Christ really joined to the signs, so that both teach that the substance of the true body and blood of Jesus Christ is received no less with mouth and hands than bread and wine. Indeed, this doctrine utterly overturns the truth of the body of Jesus Christ both before and after the incarnation of the Son of God, as well as the article of his Ascension above all the heavens and his return from them, to come only on the last day, besides many other absurd and ridiculous inventions by which the truly monstrous character of these men is revealed. And yet the spirit of error has such power in Western Christianity that these things are held to be foundations of the whole Christian religion, whereas, on the contrary, Eastern and Southern Christianity has yielded to the Koran of Mahomet. We, however, know on the contrary that the truth of the sacramental connection lies in this: that God, from whom alone the authority and efficacy of the sacraments depends, never offers signs to believers without the thing signified, yet he does so in a different way and with different objects, since these are two very different things. Therefore the signs, namely the water of Baptism and the bread and wine of the most holy Supper, since by their nature they are bodily and sensible, are offered to the senses and bodily instruments of individuals. But since this happens in the Church, outside their natural use, in order to exhibit to the minds of those who come the things pertaining to spiritual life (namely Jesus Christ and his benefits, justification and sanctification), a mystery which consists solely in this, that true faith alone can see and apprehend, this heavenly thing, represented through earthly signs, is always offered by the Lord to all who come, but it is to be received with spiritual mouth and hands, that is, by faith, an instrument not bodily but proper to the regenerating Spirit. Hence it comes about that those to whom God has granted this grace, who come to the Lord's table (or to Baptism, if they are adults) bringing both spiritual hands and mouth, namely of faith, as well as bodily ones, become partakers both of the signs and of the thing signified by them, to the greater increase of their faith and salvation. But those who bring only bodily hands and mouth receive only bodily things, water in Baptism and bread and wine in the holy Supper, and indeed to their condemnation, because they have received with such contempt not simply water, bread or wine, but the sacred things offered to them as signs, pledges and seals of so immense and so precious an instrument, namely the communication of Jesus Christ and of all his benefits to eternal life. From these things it appears how greatly those are deceived who conclude most foolishly, because the Lord never offers signs without the thing signified, that the one can never be received without the other. And therefore (which is even more absurd) both earthly things, namely the signs, and spiritual things, the things signified, are received by hands and mouth through one and the same bodily instrument.

units.la: Denique discimus ex hac tam insigni & eximia historia adversus omnes istos errores solli Iesu Christo datam potestatem & auctoritatem Sacramenta suae Ecclesiae tam veteri quàm Novae constituendi. Praeterea illum duo tantùm, Baptisimum & sanctam Coenam, in locum omnium illorum veterum institui- sc. Tertio rem significatam in utroque Sacramento, esse ipsum Iesum Christum, corpus nimirum ipsius Cruci pro nobis affixum, & vim illam spiritualem peccatorum nostrorum expiatricem, & nostrae corruptionis expurgatricem, quae se visibiliter conspiciendam praebuit ex ipsius latere profluens in hac aqua & hoc sanguine receptaculis spirituum vitalium humanitatis ipsius. Denique ab ipso solo & unico pendere omnino vim & salutarem & vivificam gratiae ipsius, quatum inpraedicatione verbis ipsius tam simplicis ac nudi quàm coniuncti cum administratione sacrorum eius Sacramentorum, ex ipsius instituto, percipimus.
units.tr: Finally, from this so remarkable and excellent history we learn, against all those errors, that the power and authority to institute the sacraments of his Church, both of the Old and of the New, was given to Jesus Christ alone. Moreover, we learn that only two, Baptism and the holy Supper, were instituted in place of all those old ones. Thirdly, the thing signified in each sacrament is Jesus Christ himself, namely his body fixed to the Cross for us, and that spiritual power which expiates our sins and cleanses our corruption, which, flowing from his side, showed itself visibly to be seen in this water and this blood, the receptacles of the vital spirits of his humanity. Finally, all the saving and life-giving power of his grace depends wholly on him alone, which we receive in the preaching of his Word, as simple and bare as it is, and joined with the administration of his sacraments, by his own appointment.

units.la: Ex quibus probè intellectis discimus non sine magnis de causis Diuum Euangelistam, nostrae incredulitatis non ignarum tot verbis & repetitis phrasibus usum, ut nos de harum rerum veritate, quarum ipse testis esset oculatus certiores faceret. Dominum igitur supplices oremus nobis hanc gratiam concedat, ut non minus dubitemus de iis quae oculis nostris non conspicimus, nec in simplici verbi praeprædicatione, nec in Sacrorū Sacramentorum administratione, quàm si reipsa in oculos nostros incurrerent, quandoquidem ad Dei verbum, tantus támque fidelis testis accedit, vt apud Deum nostrum in eorum albo censeamur quos ipsemet Dominus Thomam alloquens beatos prædicat. Ioh. 20. 29. eorum puta, qui non viderunt & crediderunt, vt ipsemet Petrus expresse loquitur, 1. Pet. 1. 8. idipsum omnibus veræ charitatis officiis tam apud Deum quàm apud homines testatum facientes
units.tr: From these things, rightly understood, we learn that the divine Evangelist, aware of our unbelief, used so many words and repeated phrases not without great reasons, so that he might make us more certain of the truth of these things, of which he himself was an eyewitness. Let us therefore humbly pray the Lord to grant us this grace, that we doubt no less about those things which we do not see with our eyes, both in the simple preaching of the Word and in the administration of the holy Sacraments, than if they were actually to fall under our eyes. For such a great and so faithful witness comes to the Word of God that before our God we may be counted among those whom the Lord himself, addressing Thomas, calls blessed (John 20:29), namely those who have not seen and yet have believed, as Peter himself expressly says (1 Pet. 1:8), all of us bearing witness to this by every office of true charity, both before God and before men.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: Mm. iiij.
units.tr: Mm. iiij.

units.la: HOMILIA TRICESIMA SEXTA.
units.tr: HOMILY THIRTY-SIXTH.

units.la: MATTH. 27.
units.tr: MATTHEW 27.

units.la: 57. Quum autem serum diei esset, venit homo dives Arimathaeensis nomine Ioseph, qui & ipse fuerat discipulus Iesu.
units.tr: 57. When evening had come, a rich man of Arimathea named Joseph, who had himself also been a disciple of Jesus, arrived.

units.la: 58. Is adiit Pilatum, & petiit corpus Iesu. Tunc Pilatus iussit reddi corpus.
units.tr: 58. He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered that the body be given to him.

units.la: 59. Et Ioseph quum accepisset corpus, involuit illud syndone pura.
units.tr: 59. Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen cloth.

units.la: 60. Posuitque in monumento suo novo quod exciderat in petra: & advoluto saxo magno ad ostium monumenti, abiit.
units.tr: 60. He laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out of the rock, and after rolling a great stone to the door of the tomb, he went away.

units.la: 61. Erat autem illic Maria Magdalene & altera Maria sedentes contra sepulchrum.
units.tr: 61. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the sepulchre.

units.la: 62. Postero autem die, quae est post Parasceuen, coacti sunt primarii Sacerdotes & Pharisaei ad Pilatum,
units.tr: 62. On the next day, which was after the Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate

units.la: 63. Dicentes, Domine, meminimus planum illum dixisse quum adhuc viveret, Tertio post die suscitabor.
units.tr: 63. and said, "Sir, we remember that this deceiver said, while he was still alive, 'After three days I will rise again.'

units.la: 64. Iube ergo muniri sepulchrum usque in diem tertium: nequando veniant discipuli eius nocte, & furentur eum, dicántque populo, Suscitatus est è mortuis, & erit vltimus error peior priore.
units.tr: 64. Give orders therefore that the sepulchre be guarded until the third day, lest his disciples come by night, steal him away, and tell the people, 'He has risen from the dead,' and the last error be worse than the first."

units.la: 65. Dixitque eis Pilatus, Habetis custodiam, abite, munite sicut scitis.
units.tr: 65. Pilate said to them, "You have a guard. Go, make it as secure as you know how."

units.la: 66. Ipsi autem profecti munierunt sepulchrum, obsignato lapide cum custodia.
units.tr: 66. So they went and made the sepulchre secure, sealing the stone and setting the guard.

units.la: MARC. 15.
units.tr: MARK 15.

units.la: 42. Quum autem serum diei iam esset, (quoniam erat parasceue, hoc est ante sabbathum.)
units.tr: 42. When evening had already come (because it was the Preparation, that is, the day before the sabbath),

units.la: 43. Veniens Ioseph ortus Arimathaea, honoratus Senator, qui & ipse expectabat regnum Dei, fidenti animo introiit ad Pilatum, & petiit corpus Iesu.
units.tr: 43. Joseph of Arimathea, an honourable senator, who himself also waited for the kingdom of God, came boldly in to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.

units.la: 44. Pilatus autem miratus est si iam mortuus esset, & aduocato Centurione interrogauit eum, an iamdudum mortuus fuisset.
units.tr: 44. Pilate wondered whether he was already dead. Summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he had been dead for some time.

units.la: 45. Et re cognita ex Centurione, donauit corpus Iosepho.
units.tr: 45. When he had learned this from the centurion, he gave the body to Joseph.

units.la: 46. Is autem emit sindonem, & detractum eum inuoluit sindone: depositque in monumento quod erat excisum e petra, & aduoluit saxum ad ostium monumenti.
units.tr: 46. Joseph bought a linen cloth, took him down, wrapped him in the cloth, laid him in a tomb that had been hewn out of rock, and rolled a stone to the door of the tomb.

units.la: 47. Maria Magdalene vero & Maria mater Iose spectabant vbi poneretur.
units.tr: 47. But Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses watched where he was laid.

units.la: LVC. 23.
units.tr: LUKE 23.

units.la: 50. Tum ecce vir nomine Ioseph, senator, vir bonus ac iustus.
units.tr: 50. And behold, a man named Joseph, a councillor, a good and just man,

units.la: 51. Qui non assensu fuerat consilio ac facto eorum, ortus Arimathaea ciuitate Iudaeorum: qui & ipse expectabat regnum Dei.
units.tr: 51. who had not consented to their counsel and deed, from Arimathea, a city of the Jews, who himself also waited for the kingdom of God.

units.la: 52. Hic, inquam, adiens Pilatum, petiit corpus Iesu.
units.tr: 52. This man, I say, went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.

units.la: 53. Et detractum inuoluit sindone, posuitque illud in monumento quod erat in saxo incisum, in quo nondum quisquam positus fuerat.
units.tr: 53. He took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and laid it in a tomb cut into the rock, in which no one had yet been laid.

units.la: 54. Porrò dies erat Parasceues, & Sabbathum succedebat.
units.tr: 54. Now it was the day of Preparation, and the sabbath was about to begin.

units.la: 55. Subsequutæ etiam mulieres quæ cum eo venerant ex Galilæa, spectarunt monumentum, & quomodo positum esset corpus eius.
units.tr: 55. The women also who had come with him from Galilee followed after, looked at the tomb, and saw how his body was laid.

units.la: IOH. 19.
units.tr: JOHN 19.

units.la: 38. Post hæc autem rogavit Pilatum Ioseph Arimathæensis (ut qui esset discipulus Iesu, sed occultus propter metum Iudæorum) ut tolleret corpus Iesu: quod permisit Pilatus, Venit ergo & sustulit corpus Iesu.
units.tr: 38. After this, Joseph of Arimathea (who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews) asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate permitted it. He came therefore and took away the body of Jesus.

units.la: 39. Venit autem & Nicodemus (is qui venerat ad Iesum nocte primum) ferens mistu-ram myrrhæ & aloës libras quasi centum.
units.tr: 39. Nicodemus also came (he who had first come to Jesus by night), bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.

units.la: 40. Acceperunt ergo corpus Iesu, & obuinxerunt illud linteis cum aromatibus, sicut mos est Iudæis funerare.
units.tr: 40. They took therefore the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the Jewish custom of burial.

units.la: 41. In eo autem loco ubi fuerat crucifixus, erat hortus, & in horto monumentum nouum, in quo nondum quisquam positus fuerat.
units.tr: 41. In the place where he had been crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb, in which no one had yet been laid.

units.la: 42. Ibi ergo propter Parasceuen Iudæorum, quòd monumentum illud prope esset, posuerunt Iesum.
units.tr: 42. There therefore, because of the Preparation of the Jews, since the tomb was near, they laid Jesus.

units.la: MATERIA quam nuper auspi-cati sumus tam est diues & abundans vt nunquam exhauriri posse videatur. Idcirco priùs quàm de sepultura disseramus, aliqua præterea superioribus de eadem re supersunt adiicienda. Igitur Euangelista magis ac magis dodocturus summam cõucnientiam eorum quæ Christo in Cruce contigerunt, cum iis quæ per Prophetas Spiritus prædixerat, locum adfert ex Zacharia Propheta, Zachar. 12. 10. in quo dicuntur qui Messiam, de quo loqui- tur, perfoderint, eundem conspecturi. Qui locus vulgò quasi per exprobrationem & comminationem exponitur, veluti siquis ante rei ad supplicium damnati oculos cæsum ab eo poneret, quò tanto magis detestandum ipsius facinus appareat. Immo collegerunt quidam Christum vltimo die in iudicio apparituram, cum manibus & pedibus perforatis, & latere perfossō, qua de re, Deo iuuante, fumus aliquid in historiæ resurrectionis tractatione dicturi.
units.tr: This subject, which we have recently taken up, is so rich and abundant that it seems it can never be exhausted. Therefore, before we discuss the burial, some further points on the same matter remain to be added to what has been said above. The Evangelist, now coming more and more to the close agreement between what happened to Christ on the Cross and what the Spirit had foretold through the Prophets, cites a passage from the prophet Zechariah (Zech. 12:10), in which those who pierced the Messiah, of whom he speaks, are said to look upon him. This passage is commonly explained as a rebuke and a threat, as if someone were to set before a man condemned to execution the eyes he had put out, so that the crime may appear all the more detestable. Indeed, some have gathered that Christ will appear on the last day in judgment with his hands and feet pierced and his side wounded; and on this matter, God helping, we shall say something in our treatment of the history of the resurrection.

units.la: Equidem admitto Deum nunquam pœnitentiam agentibus suam misericordiam pollicéri, quin contrarium vel tacitè vel expresse scelleratam vitam agentibus comminetur. At quæ apud Zachariam eodem versu præcedunt, satis ostendunt his verbis nullas Dei minas contineri, sed potius promitti tam miserando populo pro tam horrendi & detestandi facinoris quas erat meritus pœnis, ingens beneficium, conuersio nimirum huius miseri populi ad pœnitentiam, à quo tamen tantopere Deus sit offensus, vt declarat Apostol. Rom. 11. 25. Præterea certum est apud Prophetam illā Transfodiendi vocem de populi istius rebellione, & nominatim de omnibus aduersus Iesum Christum blasphemiis dici. Nam eo respectu se dicit Dominus vulnerari & veluti transfodi, sicuti Saulem alloquutus dicebat, Cur me perse-queris? Act. 9. 4. facti nimirum atrociratem, & blasphemorum ac perditorum Dei hostium intentionem considerans, licet illa Dei Maiestatem non feriant, cui nihil addi nec detrahi potest. Sed hoc tantum sibi proposuit Euangelista, nempe ostendere quę Propheta in genere de efferata illa & plus quam barbara rebellione continua istius populi dixerat, aduersus Christum implerum iri, in propria verbi istius significatione quo vsus est Propheta, sicut & alio idem significante, Pfal. 22. 17. & item alio eiusdem significationis, quum de blasphemia loquitur, Leuit. 24. 10. Et haec quidem de huius Prophetiae applicatione dicta funto. Nostrum vero est inspicere, num Iudaeos merito propter tam atrocia facinora nostro calculo notantes, incauti nos ipsos feriamus: hoc excepto, Iesum Christum non amplius in hominum esse potestate iterum iudicandum. Sedet enim ille contra Victor & triumphans ad Dei Patris fui dextram, omnem potestatem habens in coelo & terra.
