At non apud Turcas, apud quos blasphemi palo induuntur, quique non ferunt Iesum Christum impune blasphemis vocibus peti, quem pro insigni viro & magno Dei Propheta habent: verum apud eos qui nomine Christiano (sed heu!heu inquam! quam immerito) gloriantur, Iesum Christum abnegari videmus, blasphemis vocibus & deieratiombus horrendis peti, immo tam horrendis modis transfodi & proscindi vt mirum fit non corruisse iam pripridem cœlorum machinam in homines, aut illis absorbendis imam terram non dehiscere, quum sit eorum tanta tamque perfricta rabies vt maxima pars istiusmodi hominum ne os quidem aperiat quin tam execrandas istiusmodi abominationes vomant. O tempora! ô hominum mores! vidimus ea tempora quibus siquid procul etiam ad ista accederet hoc loco, tota vrbs commoueretur: & aduersus istiusmodi homines statutæ pœnæ vigerent. At iam nonne totus aër impuris iltis vocibus fœtet? Annon terra sub nostris pedibus gemit? annon etiam mota est? Quis vero ad hæc commouetur? Quis arguit? Quis inquirit? Quis pœnas repetit? O immensam & admirandam Dei bonitatem! Sed vicissim quàm horrenda iudicia! Tu vero saltem Domine Deus & Pater clementissime largire nobis, hæc vitia damnantibus, ac gementibus, quibus mederi datum non est, vt aduenient e iusto tuo furore cum improbis non censeamur. Nam quicquid hominesin vtramque autem securi dormiant, Deus tamen se cuncta hominum facta & sermones audire, videre & annotare tandem est patefacturus. Nec ita diu est ex quo Deus ratum fecit in quodam inter Christiani orbis Reges nō minimo quod iamprídem de deieratoribus dixerat Propheta, Psal. 55. 24. Eccles. 23. 12. & 27. 15. Cæterum vti diximus, illa Deum non feriunt, nec etiam gloriosam nostri Redemptoris humanitatem: sed contra quæ detestandi isti homines in cælum sputa euomunt in eorum ora impura recidunt. Nihilominus tamen quum factum sibi ducat Dominus quod fit vni ex minimis ipsius filiis quid vobis Ecclesiae Dei persecutoribus futurum est, adueniente eo in iudicium irrevocabile, quem iam a vestris Patribus non definitis lapidibus obruere, contundere, gladiorum & cruciatuum omni genere transfodere, cremare, submergere, ad nihilum redigere, nulli tam immani, tam efferae, tam nefariae crudelitati quae in mente veniat parcentes? Qui, quum tame isti carnifices mortuu animaduertetes eius ossibus abstinuerint, ea tamen in viuentium eius membrorum persona etiam ad imas vsque medullas confringitis? An vos speratis expleta rabie aduersus innocentes impune laturos?
units.tr: I readily admit that God never promises his mercy to those who repent without either silently or expressly threatening those who lead a wicked life. But the words that precede this verse in Zechariah sufficiently show that no threats of God are contained in these words; rather, a great benefit is promised to this most wretched people, in place of the punishments it deserved for so horrible and detestable a crime, namely the conversion of this wretched people to repentance. Yet God is so greatly offended by this people, as the Apostle declares (Rom. 11:25). Moreover, it is certain that in the Prophet that word "pierce" is spoken of the rebellion of this people, and specifically of all the blasphemies against Jesus Christ. For in that respect the Lord says that he is wounded and, as it were, pierced, just as he spoke to Saul, "Why do you persecute me?" (Acts 9:4), considering, of course, the atrocity of the deed and the intention of the blasphemers and destroyers, the enemies of God; although these things do not strike the majesty of God, to which nothing can be added or taken away. But the Evangelist intended only this: to show that what the Prophet had said in general about the savage and more than barbarous, continuing rebellion of this people would be fulfilled against Christ, in the proper meaning of the word the Prophet used, just as in another passage with the same meaning (Ps. 22:17), and likewise in another with the same meaning, when he speaks of blasphemy (Lev. 24:10). And let these things be said about the application of this prophecy. It is our task, however, to consider whether, while we rightly mark the Jews with our judgment for such atrocious crimes, we ourselves, being careless, strike the same blow. Except that Jesus Christ is no longer in the power of men to be judged again. For he sits victorious and triumphant at the right hand of the Father, having all power in heaven and on earth. But it is not so among the Turks, among whom blasphemers are impaled, and who do not suffer Jesus Christ to be assailed with blasphemous words with impunity, whom they regard as an eminent man and a great prophet of God. Rather, among those who glory in the Christian name (but alas, alas, I say, how undeservedly!), we see Jesus Christ denied, assailed with blasphemous words and horrible oaths, and indeed pierced and torn in such horrible ways that it is a wonder the machinery of the heavens has not long since fallen on men, or the deep earth has not opened to swallow them. Their rage is so great and so hardened that the greater part of such men does not open its mouth without vomiting forth these execrable abominations. O times! O manners of men! We have seen times when, if anything even remotely approaching such things had been said here, the whole city would have been stirred, and the penalties established against such men were in force. But now is not the whole air stinking with those impure voices? Does not the earth groan beneath our feet? Has it not even been shaken? Yet who is moved by these things? Who makes accusation? Who inquires? Who demands punishment? O immense and admirable goodness of God! But in turn, how terrible are his judgments! Do you, at least, Lord God and most merciful Father, grant to us, who condemn these vices and lament them, which we are not permitted to cure, that we may not be counted among the wicked when they come from your righteous wrath. For whatever men may sleep securely in the meantime, God will at last make known that he hears, sees and records all the deeds and words of men. Nor is it long since God made good, in a certain one of the kings of the Christian world, not a small part of what the Prophet had long ago said about swearers (Ps. 55:24; Eccles. 23:12; 27:15). Yet, as we have said, those things do not strike God, nor the glorious humanity of our Redeemer; rather, the spittle these detestable men spew up into heaven falls back into their own impure mouths. Nevertheless, since the Lord counts as done to himself whatever is done to one of his least children, what will become of you, persecutors of the Church of God, when he comes to irrevocable judgment? You whom your fathers have not ceased to stone, crush, pierce with swords and tortures of every kind, burn, drown, and reduce to nothing: will you spare none of such cruelty, so monstrous, so savage, so wicked, that it may come into the mind? Although those executioners, when they saw him dead, refrained from breaking his bones, you break even to the innermost marrow in the person of his living members. Do you hope that, once your rage against the innocent is satisfied, you will go unpunished?

units.la: Haeretici, qui quantum in vobis est Iesum Christum discerpitis, alij Deitatem illi suam tollétes: vt Arriani, alij Humanitatem, vt Marcionitae: alij in duo diuidentes vt Nestoriani: alij vix illi partem aliquam relinquentes nec Regni spiritualis in noltras conscientias: nec dignitatis in voluntate Patris de nostra salute nobis reuelanda: nec etiam aeterni Sacerdotij, siue ad peccatorum nostrorum satisfactionem, oblatione ipsius semel facta, siue adeius pro nobis intercessionem in coelo: qui denique monstrosa devotione gloriamini de carnium eius esu & dentibus ipsis laceratione, & substantiae sanguinis ipsius hausţu, licet vt dicitis, inuisibiliter: an inquam, putatis fieri posse quocunque specioso praetextu vtamini, vt, quum grauiora in Iesu Christi personam designesignetis quàm sint vnquam vel à Iudæis, vel Romanis patrata, Deus qui ipsis non pepercit, vobis parcat? Næ longè aliter se res habet, nisi meliorem mentem induatis, præsertim ad tubæ cantum quo nostro seculo cœpimus excitari. Nam adhuc hodie vociferatur Dominus se paratum eos à quibus perfossus est ad se conuertere. Agite igitur, fratres, qui huc conuenimus, & quibus hoc Deus ex immensa sua gratia concedit vt tubæ sonum audiamus, tanti beneficij memores & grati simus, ab eius abusu nobis cauentes, ne olim centuplas pœnas luamus. Et præterea Dominum ex animo & continuò precemur, vt omnes istos ossium fractores & lateris eius perfossores ad meliorem mentem reuocet, vt simul omnes seriam eximo pectore pœnitentiam de præteritis peccatis agentes, & intus & foris immensam illi debitam gloriam reddamus.
units.tr: You heretics, who as far as you can tear Jesus Christ apart: some of you take away his Deity, as the Arians did; others take away his humanity, as the Marcionites did; others divide him into two, as the Nestorians did; and others leave him hardly any part at all, neither a spiritual kingdom over our consciences, nor the dignity, in the Father's will, of revealing our salvation to us, nor even his eternal priesthood, whether in the satisfaction for our sins by the one offering made once, or in his intercession for us in heaven. Finally, you who boast of a monstrous devotion in eating his flesh, tearing it with your teeth, and drinking the substance of his blood, though invisibly, as you say: do you think, I ask, that whatever specious pretext you use, God, who did not spare him, will spare you, when you inflict on the person of Jesus Christ harsher things than were ever inflicted on him by Jews or Romans? Indeed the matter stands quite otherwise, unless you put on a better mind, especially at the sound of the trumpet by which we have begun in our age to be roused. For even today the Lord cries out that he is ready to turn to himself those by whom he was pierced. Come then, brothers, who have gathered here, and to whom God in his immense grace grants that we hear the sound of the trumpet: let us be mindful of so great a benefit and be grateful, taking care to guard against its abuse, lest we someday pay penalties a hundredfold. Moreover, let us pray to the Lord from the heart and without ceasing, that he call all those breakers of bones and pierers of his side back to a better mind, so that all of us together, with sincere heart, may do serious repentance for past sins, and render to him, inwardly and outwardly, the immense glory that is his due.

units.la: Reliqua est nobis historia sepulturæ Dominí exponenda, in qua primo loco sunt causæ discutiendæ propter quas Dominus qui statim ab emisso Spiritu poterat resurgere, voluerit tamen suum corpus sepulchro condi: & quidem saltem triginta sex horarum spatio in eo contineri, totum puta Sabbathum, (cuius initium à Solis occasu diei Veneris erat) & integram tertij diei noctem, qui cœperat ab occasu Solis dici Sabbati: vt sub aurorae primi diei hebdomadis resurgeret, Seruatorem igitur nostrum oportet à nobis confide- rari, primùm in statu suæ exinanitionis, & in ferui forma, quemadmodum loquitur Apo- ftolus,Phil. 2. 7. & 8.qui fuit inde ab eius con- ceptione, vsque ad mortem Crucis inclusiuè. Deinde in statu gloriç,ad quam veluti per gra- dus eue&us est, putà, resurrectionem eius, de- inde sessionem ad Dei Patris gloriâ, post rea- lem & visibilem eius supra omnes cœlos A- scensionem: vt media fit inter vtrumque statum eius sepultura, plus tamen ad gloriam quàm ad exinanitionem vergens: maximè fi, quomodo, & à quibus sepulti volucrit attendamus, non autem simpliciter in terram abiici, quod Crucifixorum cum ipso cadaueribus factum est.
units.tr: The remaining task is to set out the history of the Lord's burial. In this, the first thing to be discussed is the causes for which the Lord, who could have risen immediately after giving up the Spirit, nevertheless willed his body to be shut up in the tomb: and indeed to be contained in it for at least a span of thirty-six hours, namely the whole Sabbath (whose beginning was at sunset on Friday) and the entire night of the third day, which began at sunset on the Sabbath day, so that he would rise at dawn on the first day of the week. We must therefore consider our Saviour first in the state of his humiliation and in the form of a servant, as the Apostle speaks, Phil. 2.7 and 8, which lasted from his conception up to and including the death of the cross. Then in the state of glory, to which he was raised as if by steps: namely his resurrection, then his sitting at the glory of God the Father, after his real and visible ascension above all the heavens. So the burial lies midway between the two states, yet inclines more toward glory than toward humiliation, especially if we consider how and by whom he willed to be buried, and not simply cast into the earth, which is what happened to the bodies of the crucified along with him.

units.la: Primum igitur Iesus Christus voluit hac se- pultura magis ac magis suæ mortis veritatem, testatam facere, facta nimirum eius à Pilato diligenti inquisitione: & corporis eius in omniu qui spectare voluerunt conspectu depositione à Cruce: ac tandem corpore obuoluto findone, & in sepulchro recondito, & quidem in loco propinquo, & ipsis eius hostibus non incognito, quibus omnibus ad eius resurrectionem fidem faciendam via pateficeret.
units.tr: First, then, Jesus Christ willed by this burial to make the truth of his death more and more attested: namely by the diligent inquiry made of him by Pilate, by the taking down of his body from the cross in the sight of all who wished to look on, and finally by wrapping the body in a linen cloth and hiding it in a tomb, and indeed in a nearby place, not unknown to his very enemies. By all of these means a way would be opened to producing faith in his resurrection.

units.la: Deinde Principem victorem imitatus est, qui hostibus superior eos intra vallum vsque penitus perdendos insequitur. Hic ille Christi hostis, Mors est, cuius stimulu Christus in ipso fregit, corpore suo corruptioni exemplo, morteműque ipsam cum ea collatus in terram prostrauit, idem vltimo die magna sua virtute facturus, suorum corporibus eius vn- guibus ereptis, licet ea longo temporis inter- uallo captiua suis faucibus continuerit.
units.tr: Then he imitated a victorious prince, who, superior to his enemies, pursues them within their rampart until he has utterly destroyed them. Here is that enemy of Christ, Death, whose sting Christ broke in himself, offering his body as an example to corruption; having grappled with death itself, he cast it to the ground, and on the last day he will do the same with great power, snatching the bodies of his own from its claws, though for a long interval of time it has held them captive in its jaws.

units.la: Tertiò, Dominus magna illa sua virtute na- turæ nostræ spiritualem corruptionem oppu- gnauit & expugnauit: quam ipse quidem in seipso non sensit, sed quatenus est illi, sicut o- mnia nostra peccata, imputata & imposita. Præterea tétationes omnes cum quibus exte- rius est conflictatus, superauit, nihil enim in i- pfo mundi huius Princeps inuenit, Ioh.12 31.& 16. 11. & 14. 30. Quibus viribus suos etiam in- struens, dicitur in nobis veterem hominem suo Spiritu conficere. Quemadmodum autem sepultura corporea mortem ipsam consequi- tur, formam corporis eius putrefactione de- struens: sic Vetus noster homo paulatim mori- tur & in nihilum redigitur hac ipsa virtute quæ Dominum nostrum in sepulchro, licet mortuum, est comitata: ac tandem, cadem vi quam Iesus Christus in fe ostendit, Morte ve- lut vltimo ictu profligata, quum corpus suum illi ereptum in vitam spiritualem & æternam suscitauit, nobis etiam per Sanctum eius Spiri-tum communicata, pro morientis in nobis ve-teris hominis modo nouum hominem format, nec cessat vnquam ab hoc opere nō tantum dum in anima nostra viuimus: sed in hoc etiam mi-fero corpore sepulto, donec post corruptio-nem induat æternam incorruptionem, vt fe-cundùmmenfuram nostram corpori ipsi gloriosò nostri Seruatoris conformes fiamus, Phil.3.21.quod mysterium in Baptismo potissimùm nobis repræsentatur, per quem vt dixi baptisamur in eius mortem, & vnà cum ipso sepelimur,resurgentes à mortuis in vitæ nouitatem.Rom.6.3.&4.
units.tr: Thirdly, the Lord by that great power of his assailed and overcame the spiritual corruption of our nature. He did not feel it in himself, but it was imputed to him and laid upon him, like all our sins. Moreover, he overcame all the temptations with which he was assailed from outside; for the prince of this world found nothing in him, John 12:31, 16:11, 14:30. By these same powers, instructing his own, he is said to destroy the old man in us by his Spirit. Just as bodily burial follows death, destroying the form of the body by putrefaction, so our old man gradually dies and is reduced to nothing by that very power which accompanied our Lord in the tomb, though dead. Finally, by the same force which Jesus Christ showed in himself, death having been struck down as if by a last blow, when he raised his body, snatched from death, to spiritual and eternal life, which is communicated to us also through his Holy Spirit, he forms a new man in place of the dying old man in us. He never ceases this work, not only while we live in soul, but also while this wretched body lies buried, until after corruption it puts on eternal incorruption, so that, according to our measure, we may be conformed to the glorious body of our Saviour, Phil. 3.21. This mystery is chiefly represented to us in Baptism, through which, as I have said, we are baptized into his death and buried together with him, rising from the dead to newness of life, Rom. 6.3 and 4.

units.la: His itaque rebus sic probè intellectis pergamus historiam expendere, quæ narrat Dominum se iam tum ex manibus & hostium suorum potestate asserentem, cui se priùs ad mortem vsque submiserat, duos insignes viros elegisse, quorum manibus è Cruce deponi & sepulchro voluit condi.Quod ex consensu Pilati factum etiam dicitur, nequis hæc gesta dolo vel vi maiore calumniaretur, quum ipsi hostes Iesu Christi à Pilato impetraussent vt crucifixorum corpora de cruce deponerentur.
units.tr: With these things rightly understood, let us go on to examine the history, which relates that the Lord, already then asserting himself free from the hands and power of his enemies, to whom he had previously submitted himself even unto death, chose two distinguished men by whose hands he willed to be taken down from the cross and buried in a tomb. It is also said that this was done with the consent of Pilate, lest these deeds be slandered as done by fraud or greater force, since the very enemies of Jesus Christ had obtained from Pilate that the bodies of the crucified be taken down from the cross.

units.la: Deus igitur admiranda quadam occulta prouidentia hæc omnia sic administrauit: quod maximè conspicuum est ex virorum istorum elogiis,quæ nominatim quatuor Euangelistæ annotarunt. Alter enim eorum, Iosephus quòd ad exteriores qualitates diues erat & magni nominis Senator.Nicodemus verò dicitur alibi,Iohan. 3. 1. & 10. vnus ex præcipuis inter Iudæos & doctor in Israële.Non igitur immeritò quis miretur,quî fiat vt Dominus qui dum viueret pauperibus se potiùs adiunxerat,voluerit tamen ab istius notæ hominibus sepeliri. Aio verò Dominum licet à pauperibus meliùs quàm à diuitibus agnitus sit, nullum tamen à se pauperem vel diuitem suam doctrinam se-ctastatum repulille: quum nec diuitiæ diuitibus ad vitam æternam viam faciant, nec pauperes ab eadem propter inopiam repellantur: sed bonos diuites & bonos pauperes Deus ex æquo per misericordiam beatos faciat: vel ipso teste Lazaro paupere in sinum Abrahami diuitis asportato, Luc.16.22. Tales erant hi duo de quibus agimus, quos fuisse Christi discipulos, sed occultos Euangelistæ testantur, exspectantes tamen regnum Dei, & nominatim Iosephum consilio & facto aduersus Iesum Christum non fuisse suffragatum. Nicodemus autem is est qui se alias fortiter opposuerat Sacerdotum & Pharisæorum consilio, Ioh. 6.50. missis ab iis ministris à quibus prehenderetur.
units.tr: God, therefore, by a certain wondrous hidden providence, ordered all these things thus; which is especially evident from the accounts of these men, which the four Evangelists recorded by name. For one of them, Joseph, was rich in external circumstances and a senator of great name. Nicodemus, however, is elsewhere said, John 3.1 and 10, to be one of the principal men among the Jews and a teacher in Israel. Hence someone might not unreasonably wonder how it happens that the Lord, who while living had rather joined himself to the poor, nevertheless willed to be buried by men of such standing. But I say that the Lord, although he was better recognized by the poor than by the rich, nevertheless did not reject any poor or rich man who followed his teaching; for riches do not make a way to eternal life for the rich, nor are the poor shut out from it on account of their poverty, but God makes good rich men and good poor men alike blessed through mercy, as the poor man Lazarus, carried into Abraham's bosom while the rich man looked on, bears witness, Luke 16.22. Such were these two of whom we speak, whom the Evangelists testify to have been Christ's disciples, but secret ones, nonetheless awaiting the kingdom of God; and in particular, that Joseph did not support Jesus Christ by counsel or deed against him. Nicodemus, moreover, is the one who had otherwise strongly opposed the counsel of the priests and Pharisees, Ioh. 6.50, when the ministers sent by them to arrest him were present.

units.la: Multæ præterea speciales rationes fuerunt propter quas viros elegit alicuius nominis & dignitatis: ac primum quidem quod quum per sepulturā sibi via faceret ad suam gloriā, voluit eam honestare, vt de hostibus suis triumphum inchoaret adhuc mortuus corpore, quod ex præsse prædictum ab Esaia fuerat his verbis, Esa.53 9. Dedit cum impiis sepulturam eius, & cum diuite inter mortuos suos, eo quod iniquitatem non fecerit, neque dolus fuerit in ore eius. Deinde aio Dominum, etsi potuit alia via si voluisset sepulturæ suæ prouidere, tamen hunc modum disposuisse tam obtinendi à Pilato veniam, adhibito ad hanc rem alicuius dignitatis viro, quàm cohibendi, propter horum vtrorum auctoritatem, audaciam & rabiem Caiapharum & Sacerdotum, qui hæc spectare, non sine magna indignatione potuerunt. Denique haec ita gesta aperta Luce, & a tantis viris, plurimum faciunt ad veritatem mortis Domini aduersus quasuis calumnias allerendam: qua in re se maxime Dei prouidentia, sicut in reliquis omnibus quae hactenus vidimus, & deinceps vi suri sumus admirandam praebet.
units.tr: There were also several particular reasons why God chose men of some name and standing. First, since by his burial he was making his way to his glory, he wished to honour that burial, so that he might begin his triumph over his enemies even while his body was dead. This had been foretold by Isaiah in these words (Isa. 53.9): "And they made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death, because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth." Next, I say, although the Lord could have provided for his burial by another way had he wished, he nevertheless arranged it in this manner: first, to obtain pardon from Pilate by bringing in a man of some dignity for this business; and second, to restrain, by the authority of these two men, the audacity and rage of Caiaphas and the priests, who could not look on these things without great indignation. Finally, these things were done in the open light and by such great men, and they contribute greatly to establishing the truth of the Lord's death against any calumnies whatever. In this matter, God's providence shows itself most admirable, as it does in all the other things we have seen so far and shall see hereafter.

units.la: At fructum aliquem ex hoc loco perceptu-ris, diligenter examinandae sunt hae qualitates, quod longe differant aliae ab aliis: qua in re homines sponte sua falli plerumque videmus. Et quidem omnes illae Dei dona sunt, ac proinde magnopere commendandae, at non aequales inter se: quapropter praecipuae in illis sunt diligenter quaerendae, & semel inventae retinendae. Quas qui cupit consequi, petat oportet, licuti & in quem finem petendae sunt ab eo qui solus habet, & nullus alius, Pater nimirum luminum, Iac. 1. 17. Ut vero semel partem retineantur, immo & augeantur, ut talentorum similitudo docet, Matth. 25. ad cum vsum referendae sunt ad quem nobis concedantur, nempe ad datoris gloriam & proximi utilitatem. His ita positis, quibus nemo cum ratione contradixerit, facile dignosci potest quot modis ea in re peccetur, & unde tot in orbe terrarum confusiones nascantur, futuro alioquin mundo veluti Paradisi suburbio, si rectam singuli viam insistererent. pro eo quod est instar inferorum. At caecis nostris affectibus abripimur, ut alij potiora dona postponant longe minoribus, seu iam adeptis, seu quibus adhuc inhiant: alij vero logè pcius adhuc fe gerât, eoufq; excæcati vt obliti benedictionum quas erant consecuti, maledictiones pro viribus prosequantur. Alter abusus in eo consistit, quòd quærentes quę per fe sunt exoptanda, alij quidem ea nec ab eo postulant à quo sunt exspectanda, nec eo quo par est animo, nec ad eum finem ad quem illa referri oportuit: alij verò fraudibus aut aperta vi rapiant. En verò quis fit tandem exitus: Nepe rebus partis abusi, idest, obliti gloriam datori debitam reddere, & proximos ex officio iuuare, Dei, benedictiones vertunt in causas & instrumenta horrendorum ipsius iudiciorum. Exempla tam frequentia sunt, vt singulis momentis passim in toto terrarum orbe in oculos & aures omnium incurrant: & pauci tamen ad sanam mentem conuertantur, vt tristi querela docet illud ipsum Propheta Pfal. 49. & sapiens in Ecclefiaftc. Quid ergo? Nimirum in verbi Dei schola meliora discuntur. Nam ibi firmissime & fuiffime docemur, quæ in breuissimo sed vere diuino compendio, putâ precatione ordinaria paucis continentur, primùm quid possimus ac debeamus tanquàm nobis necessarium & vtile flagitare: deinde à quo fit petendum, quoue affectu: ac tandem in quem finem illa omnia referenda sint. Quorum omnium verissimos ac certissimos commentarios habemus exempla tor insignium & illustrium virorum, qui nobis ad viuum in sacris historiis depinguntur, in quibus hi viri de quibus agimus non vltimum locum obtinent & sunt nobis propius considerandi.
units.tr: If we are to gain any fruit from this passage, these qualities must be carefully weighed, since they differ greatly from one another; and in this matter we see that men are commonly deceived of their own accord. Indeed, all of them are gifts of God and so are to be greatly commended, but they are not equal among themselves. Therefore the chief ones among them must be diligently sought, and once found, retained. Whoever desires to obtain them must ask for them, both from the one who alone has them and no one else, namely the Father of lights (Jas. 1.17), and for the purpose for which they are to be asked. Moreover, so that they may be kept in part, indeed even increased, as the parable of the talents teaches (Matt. 25), they must be directed to the use for which they are given to us, namely the glory of the giver and the benefit of our neighbour. With these things laid down, which no one could reasonably contradict, it is easy to see in how many ways people go wrong in this matter, and whence so much confusion arises in the world. Otherwise the world to come would be like a suburb of Paradise, if each person walked the straight path; instead, it becomes what is like hell. But our blind affections carry us away, so that some put far lesser gifts, either already obtained or still craved, before the greater ones; and others, behaving far worse, are so blinded that, forgetting the blessings they have received, they pursue curses with all their strength. The other abuse consists in this: when they seek things that are in themselves to be desired, some do not ask for them from the one from whom they are to be expected, nor with the right attitude, nor for the end to which they ought to be referred; others snatch them by fraud or open force. And see what finally comes of it: having abused the things they have obtained, that is, having forgotten to render the glory due to the giver and to help their neighbours as duty requires, they turn God's blessings into causes and instruments of his own dreadful judgments. Examples are so frequent that they meet our eyes and ears everywhere in the whole world, every moment; yet few are converted to a sound mind, as the Prophet in Psalm 49 and the wise man in Ecclesiastes teach with a sorrowful complaint. What then? Surely in the school of God's Word better things are learned. For there we are most firmly and surely taught what we can and ought to ask for, as something necessary and useful to us, in the briefest yet truly divine summary, namely the ordinary prayer; then from whom it is to be asked, and with what disposition; and finally, to what end all these things are to be referred. We have the most true and certain commentaries on all of these in the examples of the outstanding and illustrious men who are painted for us to the life in the sacred histories, and among these men, those of whom we are speaking hold no lowest place, and are to be considered by us more closely.

units.la: Iosephus igitur his titulis ornatur,ut dines, Senator honestus,rectus & integer coram Deo & hominibus dicatur.Idem etiam de Nicodemo statuendum, ut superius docuimus. Porrò si de iliis qualitatibus vtra vtri præponderet, ferendum est iudicium, non alio iudice quàm ipso naturali sensu licet corruptissimo nobis opus est.Sed tamen illud ipsum ex sancto consilio quod viri isti sunt hac in re secuti agnoscendum:Nam oblecro suscipere facinus quod ipsi suscepérunt,& quod fecerunt,facere,annon est diuitias & honores abiicere, immo vitam ipsam profundere,furorique nationis illius exponere? At quinam hoc consilium inter se inierunt? Nempe sincerus erga Deum amor & & zelus, charitasque in proximum ipsos in hanc conclusionem duxit, silentio suo nolentes tantam aduersus Deum offensam,& hominum respectu iniustitiam prodere. Et sane quiddam huic non absimile laudatum est a miseris & ignaris quibusdam Ethnicis, quod isti edocti in schola divina melius didicerant, ut sumus paulo post dicturi.
units.tr: Joseph, then, is adorned with these titles: he is called rich, an honourable councillor, upright and blameless before God and men. The same must be said of Nicodemus, as we showed above. Moreover, if it is to be judged which of these qualities outweighs the other, we need no other judge than natural reason, though it is very corrupt. Yet this very judgment must be recognised from the holy counsel which these men followed in this matter. For I ask you: to undertake the deed these men undertook, and to do what they did, is it not to cast away riches and honours, and even to pour out life itself, and to expose oneself to the fury of that nation? But what resolution did they make between themselves? Namely, a sincere love and zeal for God, and charity towards their neighbour, led them to this conclusion: they were unwilling, by their silence, to betray so great an offence against God and such injustice in respect of men. And indeed something not unlike this has been praised by some wretched and ignorant heathens, which these men, taught in the divine school, had learned better, as we shall say a little later.

units.la: Et hæc quidem est de hac re certissima veritas. Sed quis fidem adhibet? aut, quis credens serio de iliis cogitat? Nam si forte seponantur ab Oriente ad Occidentem & a Meridie ad Septentrionem qui vitam degunt nihil nisi de caducis opibus & honoribus cumulandis cogitantes, aut ea saltem in præcipuis bonis habentes, quæso quantula pars hominum superiorum erit? Et tamen an non rerum istarum natura & quotidiana nostra seu aliorum experientia satis testantur quàm illæ sint labiles, quantóque labore, curis & molestiis vel quæratur vel retineatur? Omitto ipsorum fruitionem esse brevissimam & momentaneam, etiam iis quibus illis ad exitum vsque vitæ suæ frui contingit. Sed quis ignorat hunc potum quò plus est potus plus etiam sitiri? Quis nescit quousque rerum illarum sitis cupidos abripiat & transfuersos agat? quos equidem non modò imprudentes, sed prorsus amentes esse merito dixero.
units.tr: This is indeed the most certain truth about the matter. But who gives it credence? Or who, believing it in earnest, thinks about it? For if, from the East to the West and from the South to the North, one were to sift out those who live their lives thinking only of piling up perishable wealth and honours, or at least holding these as their chief goods, I ask you, how small a part of mankind would be left above? And yet do not the nature of these things, and our daily experience and that of others, sufficiently testify how unstable they are, and with how much toil, cares and troubles they are either sought or kept? I pass over the fact that their enjoyment is very brief and momentary, even for those to whom it falls to enjoy them until the end of their life. But who does not know that the more one drinks of this drink, the thirstier one becomes? Who does not know how far the thirst for such things carries away and drives askew those who crave them? I would rightly call such people not only imprudent but utterly mad.

units.la: Nam, vt omittam cætera, sensus ipse communis dictat, & ipse Christus idipsum nobis in memoriam revocat, neminem viuere exsuperabundanti, testibus ipsis ebriosis & gulosis hominibus, qui sanè se non nutriunt sed suffarcinant & ventrem onerant: deinde quærentem aliquid, non alibi quærere, quàm in eius cuius est manibus oportere. Ecquis autem opes, honores, & vitam ipsam habet in manibus nisi Deus vnicus? At non ab eo eadem exspectant, opum aut honorum terrenorum cupidi. Sed ad eius potius inimicum confugiunt quicunque rationibus obliquis aut etiam malis artibus ditescere, aut ad summos honores euehi cogitant: quem tamen nullo vnquam hominum amore duci nec etiam fore vt eis bene velit certum est: & præterea nullam à se potestatem habere quicquam efficiendi, montes licet aureos polliceatur. Nec enim huius mundi Princeps appellatur, nisi quòd eo Dominus vtitur suorum iudiciorum aduersus de- uios ministro, quibus chare versipellis iste mercator suas merces vendit vt tandem ipsi- met experiantur: sed fero nimis quod Dominus moner, & ipsos etiam oportuerat a fe ipsis didi- cisse, Nihil prodesse homini faceiti iactura ani- mae fi totum mundum lucretur. Sed quid agas? Surdo mundo frustra canitur. Et inde putidum illud & blasphemum prouerbium natum est, Omnia pecunia donat: quod quid aliud est, vt paucis absoluam, quam rem istam creatam insensibilem, in ipsius aeterni Dei viuentis folio collocare, quae tamen ipsa per fe directe nec vestiendi nec alendi vim habet? Quid igitur magis impium ac blasphemum? Non ita Salomon ille Sapiens sensit, sed contra Sapientiam a Domino flagitauit: quam tamen quum acceperet & multas insuper a Domino diuitias & opes, non ira fapuit vt illaesus eas spinas manibus contrectaret. Et reuera tam periculosa est opum abundantia, vt omnium temporum experientia plus fatis quotidie confirmet illud Christi, difficilius esse diuitem intrare in regnum coelorum, quam camelum per foramen acus, Matth. 19 24.
units.tr: For, to pass over other things, common sense itself dictates, and Christ himself recalls this to us, that a man's life does not consist in the abundance of what he possesses (Luke 12.15). The drunkards and gluttons themselves are witnesses: they do not nourish themselves, but cram and burden their belly. Again, one who seeks something ought to seek it nowhere but from the one in whose hands it lies. But who holds riches, honours and life itself in his hands except the one God? Yet those who desire earthly wealth or honours do not expect these things from him. Rather, whoever thinks to grow rich by crooked means, or even by evil arts, or to be raised to the highest honours, flees to his enemy. Yet it is certain that this enemy is moved by no love of any man, and will not even wish them well; and besides, he has no power of his own to bring anything about, even though he promises mountains of gold. For he is not called the prince of this world except in that the Lord uses him as a minister of his own judgments against the disobedient, by which this crafty merchant sells his wares, so that at last they themselves may experience them. But it is too much to bear that the Lord warns, and that they ought to have learned from themselves: "What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses his soul?" (Matt. 16.26). But what can you do? The world is sung to in vain, for it is deaf. And from this came that foul and blasphemous proverb, "Money answers all things." What else is this, to put it in a few words, than to set that created, insensible thing on the throne of the eternal living God itself, when in itself it has no power, directly, either to clothe or to feed? What, then, could be more impious and blasphemous? Solomon, that wise man, did not think so; rather he asked the Lord for wisdom, and when he had received it, and many riches and wealth besides from the Lord, he was not so foolish as to handle those thorns with his hands unhurt. And indeed the abundance of riches is so perilous that the experience of all ages confirms, more than enough every day, that saying of Christ: it is harder for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven than for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle (Matt. 19.24).

units.la: Nihilominus tamen extra dubium est, vitae praefentis commoda merito in Dei benedictionibus haberi: sed quum adeo sint tractatu difficilia nae admodum sapit qui sibi thesauros in coelo recondit, & magnus esse cupit in regno coelorum ad Dei gloriam, contentus ea mensura quam Dominus ei pro bona volun- tate tatc sua distribuit, potius de administrando ex donatoris arbitrio quod accepit, quàm de ma- iore & graviore administratione quærenda solicitus. Sin veremur ne nos talibus egenos aliquando fieri contingat, tam certam illam támque opulentam ipsius ore Domini prola- tam promissionem memoria repetamus, secu- lis etiam omnibus comprobatam, Quærite primùm regnum Dei, & hæc omnia vobis adiicientur, Matth. 6.33. Ecquid amplius? Accedite, tam qui præ reliquis diuites dici potestis, quàm vos ipsi egeni, scientiam à me accepturi, ex qua siquidem Deus mentiri nonpoteft, discatis tutissimè & sine novarū tabularum metu, belli, pestis ac famis tempore centuplum, si non eodem æré, in rebus tamen longè magis pretiosis lucrari.
units.tr: Nevertheless, it is beyond doubt that the goods of this present life are rightly counted among God's blessings. But since they are so difficult to handle, he is truly wise who lays up treasures for himself in heaven and who, desiring to be great in the kingdom of heaven to God's glory, is content with the measure that the Lord distributes to him by his good pleasure. Such a person is more concerned about administering at the giver's disposal what he has received than about seeking a greater and weightier administration. But if we fear that we may at some time become needy of such things, let us call to mind that sure and rich promise, spoken by the Lord's own mouth and confirmed in every age: "Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you" (Matt. 6:33). What more? Come, you who may be called richer than the rest, and you who are poor in yourselves, to receive knowledge from me. By it, since God cannot lie, you may learn most surely, and without fear of any cancellation of debts, that in a time of war, plague and famine you will gain a hundredfold, if not in the same coin, then in things far more precious.

units.la: Vt nimirum in egenorū omnis ætatis ac sexus, virorū ac mulierum, iuuenū & senum, viduarum & orphanorum tanta multitudine quos passim per vicos palantes conspicimus, & ad portas nostras lamentabiles gemitus ac ploratus edentes ipsius Iesu Christi miserea- mur, per eorum ora, se fame, siti, frigore necari vociferantem. Eia, fratres, ne ad hoc spectaculum cæcutiamus. Aures benignas istis gemitibus præbeamus. Agite fugiamus horrendum illud iudicium vltimo die instar tonitru iaculandum in immisericordes & ἀνελεήμονας, Abite maledicti in ignem æternum qui praeparatus est Diabolo & Angelis eius: Deum vero supplices oremus vt in eorum numero cen-
units.tr: So that, of course, we may have compassion on Jesus Christ himself, who in the mouths of the needy, of every age and sex, of men and women, of the young and the old, of widows and orphans, whom we see wandering everywhere through the streets in such great numbers, and who raise piteous groans and cries at our gates, cries out that he is being killed by hunger, thirst and cold. Come, brothers, let us not be blinded to this spectacle. Let us lend kindly ears to these groans. Come, let us flee that dreadful judgment which on the last day will be hurled like a thunderbolt against the merciless [ἀνελεήμονας]: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." Rather, let us pray humbly to God that we may be counted among their number

units.la: seamur quibus dicetur cum effectu, Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis à iactis mundi fundamentis, Matth. 25. 34. & 41. Fratres, iam dicta est sententia, perscripta, & proculdubio sine prouocatione sigillatim implenda. Non sum tamen nescius in quas angustias plerique ante bellum mediocris conditionis homines redacti sint, nec adhuc belli aut laborum finem apparere: at vnica emergendi est quam dico ratio. Omni itaque diffidentiae tam certam promissionem opponamus, & nullo tempore Christianam Charitatem frigere perpendamus. Itaque pro importuna parsimonia & tenacitate, consideremus potius nos in terra sterili sementem non facere, nec in loco perituro: nihilque Deum à nobis in miserorum fratrum persona reposcere, quod non suum potiore iure quàm nostrum sit, quod tamen tanquam gratis oblatum accipit, honore quaestorum & dispensatorum suorum nos afficiens. Vos igitur, fratres, oro & obtestor per Dei misericordiam ut praesenti animo sitis: ac cum spero qui quum voluit panes & piscículos multiplicauit, quíque ab hinc paucis annis istud ipsû apud nos miraculû toties iterauit, huic collectę extraordinarię futurae sic benedicturû, & eius administris hac gratiam daturum, vt, licet id obtineri non posse videatur, cessante apud nos mendicitate, nobis magnum Domino gratias agendi praebeatur argumentum, & magnam animis nostris consolationem recipiendi.
units.tr: be counted among those to whom it will be said with effect, "Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world" (Matt. 25:34 and 41). Brothers, the sentence has already been pronounced, written down, and will undoubtedly be carried out one by one, without appeal. I am not unaware into what straits many people of modest means have been driven since before the war, and that no end to the war or to their labours is yet in sight. Yet there is only one way out, which I am speaking of. Let us therefore set against all distrust so sure a promise, and let us never think that Christian charity grows cold. Thus, instead of unseasonable thrift and stinginess, let us consider that we are not sowing in barren ground or in a place that will perish, and that God asks nothing from us in the person of our poor brothers which is not rightfully his rather than ours. Yet he receives it as if freely offered, honouring us by making us his almoners and stewards. So I beg and entreat you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to be of good courage. I hope that he who, when he willed, multiplied the loaves and little fishes, and who a few years ago repeated that same miracle among us so many times, will bless this extraordinary collection as it is to be made, and will grant grace to his ministers, so that, though it may seem impossible to obtain, the begging among us may cease, and that we may be given a great reason to give thanks to the Lord and to receive great consolation in our hearts.

units.la: Et hæc quidem nobis digna visa sunt quæ notaremus ex elogiis quæ Iosepho & Nicodemo tributa sunt, quorum zelum & sinceram charitatem erga eum quem mortuum putabat instar aliorum hominum faxit Deus vt imitemur, quum nobis tam multos viuentes quibus opem feramus ob oculos ponat. Magnam igitur eius curam gesserunt quem hominis mortui loco tantum habebant, ac proinde nec ab eo sibi præstitum beneficium rependi, nec etiam ab ipsius cognatis exspectabant: qua in re pulcherrimum habemus sincerae amicitiae exemplum, vt bene monuerunt huius mundi sapientes, & longe melius ipse Dominus docuit, Luc. 6. 34. Heus igitur adeste, fœneratores, mundi pestis, monopoliorum institutores, coitionem facientes vt ex egenorum necessitate rem augeatis, & qui subuentionis prætextu miseros ad imas vsque medullas exugitis: Vos, inquam, qui sæpe vno ictu patres ac matres, viduas & orphanos conficitis, An nunquam fore diuino iudicio locum speratis? Cærum obseruandum huic veræ charitati non tantum esse locum oportere erga proximos, sed etiam & quidem maximè erga Deum. Nam etsi Dominus eximmensa sua bonitate debito rem se omnibus cum colentibus constituat, & eò vsque se demittat vt ad nostrum officium omnis generis pollicitationibus nos alliciat (etsi Deo nihil dare possumus sed tantum clientelarem fidem & obsequium de acceptis bonis exhibere, quum à nobis nihil proficisci possit quod ipsi commodet,Psa.16.2.) tamen si Deum amamus propter bona quæ ab eius manu expectamus, non est istud sane Deum amare, sed seipsum: quum sit amandus tantum propter ipsius amorem, ad quem ut unicum verum & ultimum scopum, cogitationes, sermones & opera nostra oportet collineare.
units.tr: What I said, that the charity of these men regarded the man whom they simply held as a dead man, also warns us in what respect our charity ought to extend even to the dead: namely, that we ought to take care of their reputation against injustice, and, if we were truly their friends, to extend the love with which we embraced them while they lived to their posterity or their kinsmen as well. We see a singular example of this friendship in the story of Ruth (Ruth 1:8). Yet it usually happens that if guardianships, which are burdensome, are at issue, friendship with the dead is extinguished. On this matter more has been said above in this history (John 19:23). But in this respect, as in all others, the good sacrificers of our time have easily found a way by which, even after the true heirs of the dead have been repulsed, they install themselves without a proxy, and so swallow whole houses from fathers to children, under the specious pretext, of course, of leading the dead into Paradise, adding to the avarice of the priests under the Law that famous fable of the bellowing of souls in Purgatory (cf. Matt. 15:6 and Luke 20:47). There remains a final quality of these men, most distinguished and worthy of commendation: that they were disciples of Jesus Christ and were waiting for the kingdom of God. I admit that they were secret disciples because of fear of the Jews. I called this quality more distinguished than all the others because, if this deed had been done by them from hatred of injustice alone, or from the impulse of natural friendship only (for God does not allow all to be [ἀγορᾷ]), it would have been merely the image of virtues, lacking the chief and essential form, namely the knowledge and love of the true God, of whose glory fear and zeal are as it were the soul of all true virtues and good works that God creates in each of the faithful. Therefore the Holy Spirit himself moved and impelled those two men to this work.

units.la: Quod vero dixi charitatem horum virorum cum respexisse hominem quem non alio quàm mortui simpliciter loco haberent, nos etiam admonet quo respectu nostram charitatem etiam in mortuos oporteat ferri: quatenus nimirum eorum famæ adversus iniustitiam nos oportet consulere, & , si vere amici fuimus, charitatem qua vivos complexi sumus in eorum posteros aut necessarios etiam extendere, cuius amicitiæ exemplum singulare in Ruthæ historia conspicimus, Ruth.1.8. quum plerumque tamen usu veniat ut si de tutelis agatur, quæ onerosæ sint, amicitia cum mortuo extinguatur, qua de re plura superius in hac historia, Ioh.19.23. Verum hac in parte, sicut in reliquis omnibus, boni Sacrifici nostri temporis facile viam invenerunt, qua se mortuis veris eorum hæredibus etiam repulsis, sine procuratore substituerent, ut ita domos integras à Patribus ad liberos deglutiant, speciose prætextu scilicet mortuos in Paradisum intromittendi, fabulam illam insignem vitulationis animarum in Purgatorio ad Sacerdotum sub Lege auaritiam adiicientes: de quibus fit mentio, Matth.15.6, & Luc.20.47. Superest vltima & maximè insignis ac commendatione digna horum virorum qualitas, fuisse ipsos Iesu Christi discipulos & Dei regnum expectasse. Addi fateor fuisse occultos discipulos propter metum Iudaeorum. Hanc qualitatem reliquis omnibus insigniorem dixi, propterea quòd si solo iniustitiae odio hoc facinus gestum ab ipsis esset, aut amicitiae naturalis tantum impulsu (nec enim Deus permittit omnes ἀγορᾷ esse) virtutum tantum illa simulachrum fuisse futura, deficiente praecipua & essentiali forma, nempe cognitione & amore veri Dei, cuius gloriae timor ac zelus est velut anima verarum omnium virtutum bonorumque operum quae Deus in singulis fidelibus creat. Itaque viros illos duos hoc in opere Spiritus Sanctus egit & impulit.
units.tr: When I said that these men showed love toward a man whom they regarded simply as dead, this also reminds us in what respect our charity ought to extend even to the dead. We must, of course, defend their good name against injustice and, if we were truly their friends, extend the love with which we embraced them while they lived to their children or relatives as well. We see a singular example of such friendship in the story of Ruth (Ruth 1:8). Yet it usually happens that if guardianships, which are burdensome, are in question, friendship with the dead comes to an end. I have said more about this earlier in this history (John 19:23). In this matter, as in all others, our pious sacrificing priests of today have easily found a way, so that, even when the true heirs are rejected, they install themselves without a proxy, and so swallow whole houses from fathers to children. They do this under the specious pretext, of course, of bringing the dead into Paradise, adding to it that notorious fable of the fleecing of souls in Purgatory, a greed worthy of the priests under the Law. Of this greed mention is made in Matthew 15:6 and Luke 20:47. There remains one last quality of these men, the most striking and most worthy of commendation: that they were disciples of Jesus Christ and were waiting for the kingdom of God. I admit that they were secret disciples because of fear of the Jews. I have called this quality more remarkable than all the others because, if this deed had been done by them from hatred of injustice alone, or from natural friendship alone (for God does not suffer all men to be good [ἀγαθοί]), it would have been only a likeness of virtue, lacking the chief and essential form, namely the knowledge and love of the true God. The fear and zeal for his glory is, as it were, the soul of all true virtues and good works that God creates in each of the faithful. Therefore the Holy Spirit moved and impelled those two men in this work.

units.la: Quod dicuntur occulti fuisse Iesu Christi discipuli propter metum Iudaeorum non ad laudem eorum praeteriti temporis respectu dicitur: qua in re multa sunt nobis ediscenda quae partim imitemur, partim incusemus, vt nec minorem eorum culpam faciamus nec etiam maiorem quàm oporteat. Aio igitur duo quedam esse praecipua capita quibus spes omnis officiorum quae alij ab aliis exspectare possumus, nititur: egregiam eius ad quem nos conferimus voluntatem & potestatem. Addo tertium longe illis duobus adhuc certius, immutabilitatem. Haec praeterquàm quòd in vnico Deo est, nulla res etiam est creata cum Deo in potentia & bona voluntate erga suos comparanda:cuius voluntatis in nostræ salutis mysterio multa excellentissima & expressissima reftimonia habemus, in verbo ipsius expressa & perscripta:tum immensæ potentiæ in naturalibus testimoniis tam in cœlis quàm in terra passim conspicuis. Quibus concessis, sequitur neminem, quicunque casus aut periculum eum vrgeat, aut immineat, posse vel tantillum ab officio quod Deo & proximo debet recedere, quin prorsus amens fit. At hominum natura corrupta sic apprehendit quæ in sensus externos incurrunt, vt pro eo quod altius mentem ipsos oporteret attollere ad Dei prouidentiam vsque & promissiones eius factas rectam viam tenentibus, maxima pars Dei prorsus obliuiscatur, cum eius hoste fe posse transigere sibi persuadentes : sed hic est lapsus turpissimus ex quo plerique nunquam surrexerunt : alij vero in horrenda præcipitia feruntur, alij aliis magis minúfuc periculose, vt grauiter ruár, quod in ipso Petro conspeximus : & nostro fec} culo nimis frequentes sunt in religione apostasiæ: & nimis horrendi in mutua conuersatione defectus. At hic lapsus ex infirmitate manat, in qua necesse est etiam fortissimos quosque à Domino sustineri, &c, ex Apostoli plerisque locis repetita doctrina, eos qui firmi sunt imbecillitates infirmorum portare, Rom. 15. 1. non autem nutantem parietem pede pulsare. Tales hi viri fuerunt, ad tempus sic ab ampleftenda palàm Iesu Christi doctrina deterriti, vt nihilominus eius discipuli fuerint, quaslibet occasiones nes aucu pantes quibus cum minimo discrimine id facerét, quam ob causam Nicodemus noctu ad eum venit, Ioh.3. Ac sanè Dominus dum admonet ne metuamus homines, sed eum qui est in cœlis, Matth.18.28. non ideò condemnat, ut quidam fanatici docuerunt, sanctam prudentiam quam cum simplicitate nostra vult esse coniunctam, Matth. 10. 6. sed metum tantùm ac diffidentiam quibus ab officio nostro vel latum vnguem auocamur. Quæ nequis in dubium vocet, intuenda sunt pleraque certissima & manifestissima exempla tum in ipso Domino nostro Iesu Christo manus suorum dum eius hora veniret fugientis: tum in fidelissimis eius Apostolis, Act. 9. 25. & Ecclesia Hierosolymitana, Act. 12. 12. & 17. & 19. 31. & 20. 3. præter veteris Ecclesiæ, Heb. 11. 38. & veræ Ecclesiæ Christianæ primitiuæ testimonia. Igitur quod de viris istis narratur ostendit factum id esse potiùs ex infirmitate, quam sola Dei gratia excusat, quàm ex prudentia & consilio bene compositio. Quæ tamen omnia sic moderatus est Dominus, ut viros istos nec hypocrisis, nec diffidentiæ cum infidelitate coniunctæ possimus accusare. Nam expressè dicitur Iosephus non consensisse in Caiaphæ & sociorum eius conspirationem: quod ipsum de Nicodemo verisimile fit etiam ex iis quæ de ipso, Ioh. 7 51. narrantur.
units.tr: That they are said to have been secret disciples of Jesus Christ because of fear of the Jews is not said in praise of them with respect to past time. In this matter there is much for us to learn, some of which we should imitate and some of which we should censure, so that we make their fault neither smaller nor greater than it should be. I say, then, that there are two principal heads on which all hope of the duties that we may expect from one another rests: the excellent goodwill and the power of the one to whom we turn. I add a third, far more certain than those two: immutability. Apart from the fact that this belongs to God alone, no created thing can be compared with God in power and good will toward his own. Of this will we have many most excellent and most express testimonies in the mystery of our salvation, expressed and written down in his Word; and of immense power, in natural testimonies visible everywhere in heaven and on earth. Granting these things, it follows that no one, whatever chance or danger presses upon him or threatens him, can withdraw even a little from the duty he owes to God and neighbour without becoming utterly mad. But the corrupt nature of man so grasps what strikes the external senses that, instead of lifting the mind up to God's providence and his promises, which keep the right way, the greater part forget God altogether, persuading themselves that they can come to terms with his enemy. Yet this is a most shameful fall, from which many have never risen. Others are carried into dreadful precipices, and others into lesser but still dangerous slips, so that they fall heavily, as we saw in Peter himself. In our own age apostasies from religion are far too frequent, and defections in mutual dealings are all too dreadful. But this fall springs from weakness, in which it is necessary that even the strongest be upheld by the Lord. Drawing on the doctrine the Apostle repeats in many places, the strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak (Rom. 15:1), and not to push with the foot at a leaning wall. Such were these men: for a time they were so frightened from openly embracing the teaching of Jesus Christ that nevertheless they remained his disciples, seeking whatever occasions they could by which they might do so with the least danger. For this reason Nicodemus came to him by night (John 3). Indeed, when the Lord warns us not to fear men but him who is in heaven (Matt. 18:28), he does not, as some fanatics have taught, condemn holy prudence, which he wills to be joined with our simplicity (Matt. 10:16). He condemns only fear and distrust, by which we are drawn away from our duty even by a hair's breadth. Lest anyone call this into doubt, we must consider the very certain and manifest examples: first in our Lord Jesus Christ himself, whose own disciples fled when his hour came; then in his most faithful Apostles (Acts 9:25); and in the Church of Jerusalem (Acts 12:12, 17; 19:31; 20:3); besides the testimonies of the old Church (Heb. 11:38) and of the true primitive Christian Church. Therefore what is related of these men shows that the deed came more from weakness than from prudent and well-ordered counsel, which the grace of God alone excuses. Yet the Lord has so tempered all these things that we cannot accuse these men of hypocrisy, nor of distrust joined with unbelief. For it is expressly said that Joseph did not consent to the conspiracy of Caiaphas and his associates. This is likely to be true of Nicodemus too, from what is related of him in John 7:51.

units.la: At verò licet multò grauius lapsi fuissent, annon tamen adeò excellens illa fides, & tam admiranda constantia, quam hoc egregio facinore, ieo tepore quo sola desperatio & diffi-dentia quòd ad homines locu habitura videbatur, praeteritos lapsus operit, & exemplum admirandum praebet, tum infirmis ne infirmitati suae ditius indulgeant, tum constantibus & magnanimis, vt in melius proficiant?
units.tr: But even if they had fallen far more gravely, does not that outstanding faith and admirable constancy, shown in this remarkable deed at a time when only despair and distrust seemed to have any place among men, cover their earlier lapses? Does it not also offer an admirable example, both to the weak, so that they may not indulge their weakness more freely, and to the steadfast and magnanimous, so that they may advance toward something better?

units.la: Apage igitur, quosdam nostri temporis male feriatos homines, sibi & aliis persuadentes se excusandos etiam dum polluuntur idololatriis & impietatibus Romanis, abutentes Iosephi & Nicodemi exemplis: quasi verò Deus tantum interiore cultu delectetur, detestandos potius quàm refutatione dignos, donec Deus hanc ipsis gratiam largiatur vt falsam doctrinam & corruptos mores eiurent.
units.tr: Away, then, with certain men of our own time, badly idle, who persuade themselves and others that they may be excused even while they are polluted by Roman idolatries and impieties, abusing the examples of Joseph and Nicodemus. As if God took delight only in inward worship! Such men are to be detested rather than refuted, until God grants them the grace to abjure false doctrine and corrupt morals.

units.la: Caeterum functionem publicam exercentes, atque adeò singulos Christianos, pro facultate quàm habent malum impediendi, cauere oportere temerè quod hic de Iosepho dicitur in exemplum trahant, quòd videlicet non consensiLet in ea quae in Christum erat verbis & reipsa decreta. Nam saepe nimis contingere videmus vt plerique rem magnam praestitisse sibi videantur, si cuius litis aut causae diiudicationi non interfuerint, aut alicuius alterius controuersiae in qua sententiae videantur in aliquam iniustitiae speciem inclinare. Ac concedo equidem minus id malum esse quàm in iniquorum consilio sedere: sed aio vehementer ad liberandas conscientias requiri vt quisque secundum vocationem suam, malo resistat fortiter, & conuenientibus omnibus ratiorationibus illud impediat: qua in re si nihil promoucat, saltem, quod est maximi momenti conscientiam suam apud Deum & homines liberauerit.
units.tr: Moreover, those who exercise public office, and indeed every Christian according to the power he has to hinder evil, should take care not to rashly draw into example what is said here about Joseph, namely that he did not consent to the decrees made against Christ, either in words or in deeds. For we often see that many people think they have done a great thing if they were not present at the judgement of some lawsuit or cause, or of some other controversy in which the sentences seem to lean toward some kind of injustice. I grant indeed that this is a lesser evil than sitting in the council of the wicked. But I say that, to free consciences, it is strongly required that each person, according to his calling, resist evil boldly and hinder it by every suitable argument. If he achieves nothing in this, at least he will have freed his conscience before God and men, which is of the greatest importance.

units.la: Denique quod hic dicitur etiam Iosephus expectasse regnum Dei, mirum fortasse cuiam videatur, quum haec beatitudo Domini resurrectione nitatur, de qua tamen hos viros minime cogitasse nobis, tum ipsa ratio sepeliendi, tum nominatim illud Aloes & Myrrhae pondo praeparatum a Nicodemo, fidem faciut: non minus quam mulieres aut discipulos ipsos, de quibus in sequentibus acturi sumus: tam parum attenti fuerant in iis considerandis & memoriae infigendis quae de sua resurrectione tertio die futura Dominus toties praedixerat, ut ne hostibus quidem ipsius essent incognita. Respondeo, factum crassissima Legis Doctorum culpa, iusto Dei iudicio excaecatorum (quod ipsis Dominus toties exprobrat, & nominatim Matth. 15. 14. & in ipsius Nicodemi persona, Ioh. 3. 10.) ut Legis doctrina & Prophetiae ad Novum foedus pertinentes, ignorarentur, & in ipsis Synagogis adulterarentur; praeterquam quod etiam plenior & dilucidior arcani nostrae salutis declaratio in adventum Domini & Apostolorum eius reseruabatur. Quibus autem voluit Dominus maiorem sui cognitionem largiebatur, ut videmus Zachariam, Elizabetham, Sanctam Virginem, Simeonem, Annam prophetissam, & alios ipsis similes tantorum mysteriorum speciali cognitione fuisse præditos: & Dominum, excitato per Ioannis Baptistæ prædicationem populo, pedetentim tenebras illas difcuffiffe, tum in propria persona docendo, tum deinde per Apostolos in iis qui prædicationem illorum attentis animis exceperunt. Hi igitur viri Fœderis fundamentum retinentes, tempus illud nimirum adesse quo Deus populum suum ad veram felicitatem ac beatitudinem adduceret, quam verus Meffias erat allaturus, Iesu Christi doctrinam vt verissimam retinebant, quantum quidem aliquid ex ea perceperant. Quapropter falsos Pastores ista nihil iuuant, miserum vulgus fidem illam suam implicitam, quam vocant, docentes, quòd hac ratione non tantùm in Christianæ Religionis bruta ignorantia, sed etiam in omni superstitione & idololatria, fouent. Obseruanda deinde phrasis illa loquendi, ex qua Ecclesiam & eius conditionem, quæ REGNI DEI, & Regni cœlorum nomine designatur, omnibus contumeliarum ac Crucis generibus opponendam esse discamus, vt omnibus huius mundi coronis ac sceptris nostram conditionem licet in mundo odio habiti, & mille modis indignißimis cruciati, longè tamen anteponamus. Nos enim ij sumus quibus datum est Filios Dei fieri & eius cohæredes qui omnem in cœlo & terra potestatem est adeptus.
units.tr: Finally, the statement here that Joseph also expected the kingdom of God may perhaps seem strange, since this blessedness rests on the Lord's resurrection, which these men by no means had in mind. The very manner of burial makes this evident, and especially the mention of the hundred pounds of aloes and myrrh prepared by Nicodemus. So too with the women and the disciples themselves, of whom we shall speak below: they had been so inattentive in considering and fixing in memory what the Lord had so often foretold about his resurrection on the third day that the thing was not even unknown to his enemies. I answer that this came about through the very gross fault of the doctors of the Law, blinded by the just judgement of God. The Lord often reproaches them for this, particularly at Matt. 15:14, and in the person of Nicodemus himself at John 3:10. As a result the teaching of the Law and the prophecies pertaining to the New Covenant were unknown and were corrupted even in the synagogues. Besides this, a fuller and clearer declaration of the hidden mystery of our salvation was reserved for the coming of the Lord and his Apostles. But to those whom the Lord willed, he gave a greater knowledge of himself. Thus we see that Zachariah, Elizabeth, the Holy Virgin, Simeon, Anna the prophetess, and others like them were endowed with a special knowledge of such great mysteries. And the Lord, after the people had been stirred up by the preaching of John the Baptist, gradually dispelled those shadows, both by teaching in his own person and afterwards through the Apostles, among those who received their preaching with attentive minds. These men, therefore, holding to the foundation of the Covenant, that the time had surely come in which God would lead his people to the true happiness and blessedness which the true Messiah was going to bring, held the teaching of Jesus Christ as most true, so far as they had perceived something of it. Hence false ministers gain no help from these things. They teach the wretched common people that implicit faith, as they call it, and in this way they foster not only the brutish ignorance of the Christian religion but also every superstition and idolatry. Next, we must observe the manner of speaking by which we learn that the Church and its condition, which is designated by the name KINGDOM OF GOD and kingdom of heaven, is to be set against every kind of reproach and cross. Thus we value our condition far above all the crowns and sceptres of this world, even though we are hated in the world and tortured in a thousand most unworthy ways. For we are those to whom it has been given to become sons of God and his co-heirs, he who has obtained all power in heaven and on earth.

units.la: Sequitur deinceps apud historiam sepelien-di modus, qui fuit honestissimus, quali ab omni vetustate viros insignes sepultos fuisse legimus. gimus,cuius rei supra rationem reddidimus,& de qua deinceps adhuc aliquid dicturi sumus: dum interim hic specialem Dei prouidentiam obseruamus,quod voluit,in conspectu suorum hostium, Domini corpus ab vrbe non procul asportari, sed in horto vicino satis omnibus noto collocari,quo sic multis aduersus eius resurrectionem calumniis obuiam iretur.Et proterea in nouo sepulchro in quo norant omnes nullum adhuc sepultum condi: ne ipsius inimici quempiam alium resurrexisse calumniarentur.Quibus adde voluisse etiam Dominum suum sepulchrum ingenti saxo tegi, non nisi magna vi & strepitu mouendo abiis qui fortasse corpus Domini furari tentassent. Quid amplius? Nempe vt a se ipsis hostes ipsius pudore afficeretur, voluit Deus a Iudaeis Pilatum de custodia sepulchro apponenda rogari,& ab eodem suos milites illis denegari,sed tamen ipsis concedi, vt per eos milites quos ipsi de suis eligerent custodiri sepulchrum iuberent. Et haec quidem omnia sic ex eorum arbitrio & voluntate gesta, vt etiam sigillo sepulchrum obsignaretur. Quorsum vero haec omnia tandem? Adeo mirabiliter eorum omnis conatus inuersus est, vt ipsum sigillum, quo se facile prohibituros sperabat id quod non erat nescij fuisse praedictum, non sane ab homine plano, sicut illum postea calumniati sunt, sed a Dei Filio, Dei resurrectionem longe clarius quam reliquae omnes circumstantiae obsignarit.
units.tr: Next in the history comes the manner of burial, which was most honourable, as we read that distinguished men were buried from all antiquity. We have given the reason for this above, and we shall say something more about it below. Meanwhile here we observe God's special providence. He willed that, in the sight of his enemies, the Lord's body be carried away from the city, not far off, and placed in a nearby garden known to all. In this way many calumnies against his resurrection might be met. And for this reason it was placed in a new sepulchre, in which everyone knew that no one had yet been buried, lest his enemies should slander that someone else had risen. To these add that the Lord willed his sepulchre to be covered with a huge stone, which could not be moved except with great force and noise, against those who might perhaps try to steal the Lord's body. What more? So that his enemies might be shamed by their own doing, God willed that the Jews should ask Pilate to set a guard at the sepulchre, and that Pilate should deny them his own soldiers but nevertheless allow them to order the sepulchre to be guarded by those soldiers whom they themselves chose from their own men. And all these things were done so entirely by their decision and will that the sepulchre was even sealed with a seal. But why all these things in the end? So wonderfully was all their effort turned upside down that the very seal, by which they hoped to prevent easily what they knew had been foretold, was set on by no ordinary man, as they later slandered him, but by the Son of God, and it attested the resurrection of God far more clearly than all the other circumstances.

units.la: Idem profecto cunctis aduersus Dei veritas
units.tr: Doubtless the same must happen to all who rise up today against the truth of God,

units.la: ipsi veri tem hodie insurgentibus contingat oportet, cuius, adeò sunt amentes, vt cursum vel apertam vi, vel per fraudes & cuniculos, quibus hodie maximè locus est, impedire se posse sibi persuadent. Sed frustra, Dei beneficio, quum omnium istorum Euangelij persecutorum artes & lanienæ, totidem sint aduersus eos furoris ipsorum testimonia, contráque inuictę illius potentiæ τεκμήεια, quem iterum tot annos iam sepelierunt, ac veluti repagulis & sigillis clausum continuerunt, donec iterum, vt ita dicam, in Ecclesiæ suæ instauratione resurgeret. Idem fit falsis illis doctoribus, quorum scripta lucem iis quæ conantur obscura facere maiorem adferunt.
units.tr: and against the truth itself. They are so foolish that they persuade themselves they can stop its course, whether by open force or by frauds and underground mines, which are especially at home today. But in vain, by God's favour. For the arts and butcheries of all these persecutors of the Gospel are so many proofs of their own madness, and against them stand the evidences [τεκμήρια] of that invincible power, whom they have buried for so many years and, as if shut in with bars and seals, have kept enclosed, until he rose again, so to speak, in the restoration of his Church. The same happens to those false teachers, whose writings bring a greater light to the very things they try to make obscure.

units.la: Cæterum, corporum humanorum sepulturam ipsa natura veluti suo digito in omnium hominum animis insculpsit, qua fiat manifestum, differentiam quæ est inter hominem dum viuit & cæteras animantes morte non interire: ac proinde mortuorum cadauera non proculcul, vt bestiarum abiicienda, sed cum honore & respectu quodam efferenda, & hominum oculis subducenda. Natura igitur id docuit, ad quam accedunt præterea consanguinitas, cognatio & affinitas, aliáque inter se hominum veræ amicitiæ vincula quæ ipsa mors nequit dissolucre. Quapropter merito populos qui sepulturam neglexerunt tanquam barbaros & inhumanos habitos fuisse videmus. Sed præter superiora illa omnia minimè dubitandum quin primi Patres tam istam Creatoris sensententiam, Puluis es & in pulverem reuerteris meditati, quàm probè Resurrectionis doctrinam edocti (quæ semper vnica fuit fidelium aduersus mortem consolatio, testte ipso Iuda in iis quæ de libro Enoci adfert, Iud.15.) mortuos suos sepulchris tàquam in quietis suæ cubilibus vsque ad suscitationè eorum códiderint. cuius esto rei testis vox illa Dormiendi, qua Iosephus vtitur. Genef.46.30. inter veteres patres merito censendus. En etiam cur ab omni vetustate lauari solerét cadauera, deinde prout ferebant facultates, condiri: minimè quidem sanè tanquam sperarent patres se corruptionem expugnaturos, sed suæ resurrectionis fiduciam testaturi: cuius rei curam speciale Dei populum præsertim ex eo exemplo quod Act. 9.37. legitur gessisse videmus.
units.tr: Moreover, nature itself has engraved the burial of human bodies, as with its own finger, in the minds of all men. By this it is made plain that man, while he lives, differs from the other animals, and that he does not perish at death. Therefore the corpses of the dead are not to be cast out like those of beasts, but are to be carried out with honour and a certain respect, and withdrawn from human eyes. Nature therefore taught this, and to it are added kinship, blood-relation and affinity, and the other bonds of true friendship between men, which death itself cannot dissolve. Hence we see that peoples who neglected burial were rightly regarded as barbarous and inhuman. But beyond all these things, there is no doubt that the first Fathers, meditating on that sentence of the Creator, "You are dust and you will return to dust", and well taught the doctrine of the resurrection (which has always been the only consolation of the faithful against death, as Jude himself attests in what he cites from the book of Enoch, Jude 15), laid their dead in sepulchres as in the couches of their rest, until they should be raised up. Of this the word "sleeping", which Joseph uses (Gen. 46:30), is a witness, and he is rightly counted among the ancient fathers. Here too is the reason why from all antiquity bodies were customarily washed and then, as means allowed, anointed. This was surely not because the fathers hoped to conquer corruption, but to testify to their confidence in the resurrection. We see that the special people of God took this care, especially from the example read in Acts 9:37.

units.la: Et huius quidem ablutionis & similis circa sepulturam studij hunc fuisse finem ipse Apostolus testatur, 1.Cor.15.29. argumentum ex hoc more lauandorum mortuorum ducens. Sic enim Baptisandi vocem eo loco sicut & Marc. 7.4. & Heb.9.10. intelligendam reor.
units.tr: The Apostle himself shows that the purpose of this washing, and of similar care in burial, was this, when he draws an argument from the custom of washing the dead in 1 Cor. 15:29. For I think the word "baptizing" is to be understood in that place as it is in Mark 7:4 and Heb. 9:10.

units.la: Hic fuit igitur Patrum temporibus mortuos sepeliendi & terra condendi mos, etiam à caeteris nationibus obseruatus, sed qui paulatim degenerauit, præter immensas impensas & luxum magnorum virorum, hac ratione sibi quærentium immortalitatem, vt pulchrè monet, Psal.49.15. Atque adeò mirum est tã multas nationes prophanas, pro sepeliendis mortuis eos ad flammas condemnasse: quæ fuit barbara & merito damnanda consuetudo: fi- cut etiam sponte sua tandem obsoleuit. Huic vero lauandi mortuos consuetudini,sua fuerunt tempora, vt aliis multis istiusmodi sub Lege ritibus. At quum hoc tempore tam pretiosum pignus futurae resurrectionis habeamus,istiusmodi mortuorum ablutio,quam obseruant adhuc diligenter Monachi, magis illius quàm animarum studiosi, reliquiae sunt adhuc Iudaismi.
units.tr: So in the times of the Fathers it was the custom to bury the dead and lay them in the earth, and other nations also observed it. But it gradually degenerated, along with the huge expenses and display of great men who in this way sought immortality for themselves, as Psalm 49:15 aptly warns. It is remarkable that so many profane nations condemned their dead to the flames instead of burying them. That was a barbarous custom and rightly to be condemned, and it too fell out of use of its own accord in the end. This custom of washing the dead had its own time, as did many other such rites under the Law. But since we now have so precious a pledge of the future resurrection, this washing of the dead, which the Monks still observe diligently, being more concerned with the body than with souls, is a remnant of Judaism.

units.la: Sin aliquis quaerat, quis in mortuorum sepulturis fit modus obseruandus, aio in genere bene obseruata regula quam Apostolus 1. Theff. 4. 13. praescribit duo extrema fugienda. Vnum,omnia superflua vitanda. Alterum,obseruandum quod facit ad aedificationem,habita ratione circunftantiarum,temporum,locorum & personarum, cum honesta simplicitate à qua omnis absit ambitio,& superstitio: quarum illa ex diametro pugnat cum iis quae spectaculum illud sepulturae nos de naturae nostrae tam momentanea & caduca conditione docet:haec vero à malè compositis viuorum in mortuos affectibus manauit.
units.tr: If anyone asks what measure is to be observed in the burial of the dead, I answer that in general the rule which the Apostle prescribes in 1 Thess. 4:13 is well observed, and two extremes must be avoided. The first: all superfluous things are to be avoided. The second: whatever contributes to edification is to be observed, with regard to circumstances, times, places and persons, and with honest simplicity, free of all ambition and superstition. The former fights directly against what that spectacle of burial teaches us about the momentary and frail condition of our nature. The latter springs from the ill-ordered affections of the living towards the dead.

units.la: Caeterum nouus & insolens forsitan alicui istius sepulturae sumptus & expensa videbitur in eum qui dū viueret fatis erat testatus quàm ab istis rebus alienus effet, vsitatis alioquin eis temporibus & ἀδιαφόροις,pro personarum dignitate ob eas quas superius audiuimus causas. Primùm igitur praeter duas illas superius à nobis allatas rationes sciendum in primis nullum istos Domini hac de re mandatum accepisse, sed à sola tum duorum illorum virorum simplici charitate & egregia in Christum voluntate, tum mulierum etiam de quibus historia sequens est aliquid dictura. Deinde notandum Dominum sua prouidentia sic omnia gubernasse, vt non passus sit hunc apparatum suum effectum sortiri, vnctione in crastinum dilata, & ipso resurgente priusquàm mulieres ad sepulchrum aduenirent. Immo contrà Dominus per Angelos suos illas arguēs quòd viuentem inter mortuos quaererent, non tantùm id de visitatione ipsius ad sepulchrū, sed de apparatu mortuis potius quàm viuis conuenienti intellexit.
